001-243363:
The case of *Selimi and Krasnići v. Serbia* concerns two Serbian nationals, Mr. Abdurahim Selimi and Ms. Bahrije Krasnići, whose pensions from the Serbian Pensions and Disability Insurance Fund (SPDIF) were suspended. Both had been granted pensions by an SPDIF branch office in Kosovo and received regular payments until early 1999. Following the establishment of international administration in Kosovo in June 1999, their pension payments stopped.

The applicants repeatedly complained to the SPDIF and later initiated formal requests for the resumption of payments, which led to protracted administrative and judicial review proceedings. The core of their complaint before the European Court of Human Rights was the length of these proceedings and the continued non-payment of their pensions since 1999, invoking Article 6 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

The first applicant, Mr. Selimi, had his old-age pension suspended on 1 March 1999. He requested resumption in 2013. The SPDIF dismissed his request, arguing that he was already receiving a basic Kosovan pension and could not receive two pensions simultaneously. His case underwent numerous remittals between administrative bodies and the Administrative Court. A key issue was the SPDIF’s failure to properly justify its decisions, including its assumption that he had not opted for the Serbian pension. In 2024, it was discovered that Mr. Selimi had died. His wife sought to continue the proceedings. The second applicant, Ms. Krasnići, had her survivor’s pension suspended on 15 February 1999. Her request for resumption in 2017 was also rejected by the SPDIF on the grounds that she was receiving Kosovan pensions and could not receive both. Her case similarly involved multiple remittals and procedural delays. A significant complication arose after her death in 2021, as her son, wishing to pursue the case, faced obstacles in providing a power of attorney certified by Serbian authorities, as he lacked a Serbian identity card.

Both applicants also appealed to the Serbian Constitutional Court. It found a violation of their right to a trial within a reasonable time and awarded them compensation for non-pecuniary damage, but dismissed their property rights claims as premature while the administrative proceedings were ongoing. The case highlights the applicants' struggle to navigate a complex legal process to restore their pension rights, which had been suspended due to the geopolitical changes in Kosovo.
001-245690:
In *Minasyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 54620/16), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 6 November 2025. The applicant, Zhorzh Minasyan, an Iranian national born in 1941 who lives in Yerevan, was represented by lawyer L. Manaseryan. The Armenian Government was represented by Y. Kirakosyan. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 1 September 2016. The Court gave notice only of the complaint concerning the right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The case concerns the applicant’s allegation that he was denied access to the Court of Cassation in breach of Article 6 § 1.

The underlying dispute arose in 2014, when the applicant lodged civil claims with the Armavir Regional Court against a private company. He sought certain payments and annulment of a contract. On 29 April 2015, the Armavir Regional Court dismissed his claims. The applicant appealed. On 25 December 2015, the Civil Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the lower court’s judgment. The applicant received the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision on 8 January 2016.

On 28 January 2016, the applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. In his appeal, he mentioned the date on which the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision had been served on him and provided evidence of that service. The key procedural dispute concerned the one-month time-limit for lodging an appeal on points of law.

On 9 March 2016, the Court of Cassation declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible. It found that the appeal had been lodged outside the one-month time-limit, which it counted from the date of the Civil Court of Appeal’s decision rather than from the date of service. It further noted that no request to restore the time-limit had been submitted. In doing so, it relied on Article 233.1 § 1 (1) of the Armenian Code of Civil Procedure, under which an out-of-time appeal lodged without a request to restore the time-limit must be declared inadmissible.

The applicant complained before the European Court that this decision denied him access to the Court of Cassation, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore narrow: the applicant filed his cassation appeal on 28 January 2016, within one month of receiving the appellate decision on 8 January 2016; he expressly referred to and evidenced the service date; nevertheless, the Court of Cassation treated the deadline as running from the date of the appellate decision, 25 December 2015, and refused to examine the appeal because it was out of time and no restoration request had been made. The case thus focuses on whether that procedural approach improperly restricted his right of access to the highest Armenian civil court. The Court adopted the judgment on 9 October 2025, and it was delivered on 6 November 2025.
001-244000:
In *Gullotti v. Italy* (Application no. 64753/14), the European Court of Human Rights considered complaints concerning the limitation of a prisoner’s correspondence and the effectiveness of remedies against decisions renewing that limitation. The applicant, Giuseppe Gullotti, an Italian national born in 1960 and detained in Parma Prison, had been convicted of mafia-type offences, including participation in a mafia-type organisation, murder, extortion, unlawful possession of weapons, and breach of preventive measures. Arrested in 1998, he was imprisoned under the special regime in section 41 bis of the Prison Administration Act. That regime imposed severe restrictions, including limits on visits, a telephone ban, limits on receiving money and parcels, and monitoring of incoming and outgoing correspondence subject to a judicial order under section 18 ter.

The applicant’s correspondence was monitored at least between 5 July 2012 and 27 May 2013. From at least 4 December 2012, the Reggio Emilia sentence supervision judge limited his correspondence to relatives admitted for family visits. On 7 January 2013 the prison governor requested a renewal. On 8 January 2013 the Reggio Emilia sentence supervision judge renewed the limitation for three months, until 7 April 2013. The judge relied on the applicant’s alleged continuing prominent role in Cosa Nostra despite detention since 1998, citing investigative sources, statements by cooperating prisoners, and a favourable opinion from the District Anti-Mafia Prosecution Office.

The applicant appealed. On 12 March 2013 the Bologna sentence supervision court upheld the order, reiterating that he remained a member of the criminal organisation and had not distanced himself from it. On 21 March 2014 the Court of Cassation declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible, finding the limitation justified.

While those appeal proceedings were pending, the Reggio Emilia sentence supervision judge renewed the limitation three more times, on 8 April, 9 July, and 7 October 2013, each for three months. The 8 April and 7 October orders were based on the same reasoning as the 8 January order. Separately, on 30 October 2013, the Minister of Justice renewed the section 41 bis regime for two years, relying on anti-mafia information that the applicant was a mafia-clan leader in the Barcellona Pozzo di Gotto area with strong criminal connections, and citing 2003 wiretapped conversations referring to the impossibility of communicating with him in person or by mail.

On 21 November 2013, the Bologna sentence supervision court granted an appeal against the 8 April 2013 order, finding its reasoning inadequate. It noted that the order vaguely referred to investigative sources without detailing their content, and failed to consider relevant contrary information, including a 2009 Turin decision granting early release and positive prison reports from Parma and Cuneo in 2013. The applicant then asked that the 9 July and 7 October 2013 orders be declared unlawful as based on the same grounds, but on 22 January 2014 the Bologna court declared that request inadmissible as not provided for by law. Meanwhile, on 31 December 2013, after the Bologna decision, the Reggio Emilia judge rejected a further request to renew the correspondence limitation.

The legal framework allowed correspondence restrictions or monitoring under section 18 ter by reasoned order for up to six months, renewable for periods of up to three months, to prevent crimes, maintain prison security, and protect investigations. Appeals lay under section 14 ter, with subsequent review by the Court of Cassation.

The applicant lodged his application on 20 September 2014. The Court gave notice to the Italian Government of complaints under Article 8 (right to respect for correspondence) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) concerning the judicial order of 8 January 2013; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The case thus concerns the limitation of the applicant’s correspondence during detention and whether the appeal against decisions renewing that limitation was effective.
001-247556:
In *Editorial Board of the Newspaper and Internet Portal Magyar Hang and Alhambra Press Bt v. Hungary* (Application no. 52586/22), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) examined a complaint under Article 10 of the Convention. The first applicant was the editorial board of the newspaper and internet portal *Magyar Hang*; the second applicant, Alhambra Press Bt, was its publisher.

On 17 August 2020, *Magyar Hang* published an online article entitled “Párbeszéd lodges criminal complaint in the Visegrád luxury hotel affair.” The article reported on a press conference held that day by B.T., a member of the opposition party Párbeszéd Magyarországért, concerning the allegedly fraudulent sale of a hotel in Visegrád. I.T., a businessperson and the Prime Minister’s son-in-law, was one of the shareholders of the company that sold the property.

According to the article, B.T. filed a criminal complaint suspecting misappropriation of funds causing particularly significant financial disadvantage. B.T. relied on press reports, stating that I.T.’s company, Hotel VSGRD Kft, had bought a hotel for around 1.6 billion Hungarian forints, planned to turn it into a luxury hotel, but left it half-finished. It was then allegedly sold to the business circle of X for 3.65 billion forints. B.T. claimed that I.T.’s business circle did not make value-increasing investments justifying the difference between purchase and sale prices, which exceeded two billion forints. The article also stated that Hotel VSGRD Kft had achieved a net profit of 1.21 billion forints, of which 1.075 billion was taken out as dividends.

I.T. asked the first applicant to publish a retraction, denying that he had acquired the hotel for around 1.6 billion forints through Hotel VSGRD Kft or sold it to the business circle of X for 3.65 billion. He said he had personally nothing to do with the price difference and briefly described investments on the property. When *Magyar Hang* refused, I.T. brought a civil action before the Budapest High Court, alleging dissemination of false statements.

On 13 November 2020, the High Court dismissed the action. It held that the article was based on B.T.’s press release and criminal complaint, that I.T. was a “special public figure” due to his real-estate, property-development and tourism activities and media appearances, and that he could rebut the statements himself. The court found that the article had faithfully reported statements by public figures, clearly indicated their source, and contained no further journalist discussion.

On 18 March 2021, the Budapest Court of Appeal upheld the decision for different reasons. It found the purchase-price statement true, held that I.T. lacked standing regarding the resale statement, and treated the statements about investments and value increase as value judgments.

On 13 October 2021, the Kúria reversed. It held that although the article recapitulated statements by a public figure, B.T., partly on a matter of public interest, the lower courts wrongly compared the case to public-funds cases. The hotel transactions did not involve public expenditure. I.T. could be a “public figure” only in relation to his economic role, wealth, and interest in public funds or procurement, but not here. The Kúria stated that the article factually reported the press conference, but regarding the estimated sales price, the applicants should have given I.T. an opportunity to refute the statements before publication, relying on Constitutional Court decision no. 34/2017. Public balance sheets did not prove the purchase and resale amounts. It ordered the first applicant to publish a retraction concerning the purchase and resale and the second applicant to pay I.T.’s legal costs and court fees of 322,200 forints.

On 28 June 2022, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional complaint. It held that I.T. was not a public figure, as he did not discuss politics or matters of general interest publicly and could not be considered a public figure solely because of his business interests or family ties. He could not be expected to respond by his own means, and the failure to give him an opportunity to publish a refutation was unacceptable. The applicants complained that the retraction order and costs award violated their Article 10 right to freedom of expression.
001-245686:
Besik Zakaidze, a Georgian national, alleged that criminal proceedings against three private individuals who attacked him were ineffective, and complained under Articles 2, 6 and 8 of the Convention.

On 9 February 2021, an altercation arose after the applicant asked a neighbour to repay borrowed money. Three neighbours verbally and physically assaulted him. Emergency services reported difficulty speaking and swallowing, jaw pain/deformation and nausea. Hospital diagnosis included fractures to his lower jaw, nose excoriations, intracranial trauma and concussion. After two jaw surgeries, he was discharged on 16 February 2021 in stable condition.

A criminal investigation was opened the same day under Article 126 § 11 (b) of the Criminal Code (violence committed by a group). The applicant was interviewed in hospital; the three suspects were questioned and all admitted verbally and physically assaulting him. None was remanded in custody. Investigators conducted an on-site inspection, photographed the scene, and questioned witnesses.

On 9 March 2021 the applicant complained to prosecutors about delay and asked for information about charges. He was told the investigation was ongoing and that charges depended on further investigative measures. A forensic examination of his medical file was ordered on 10 March. On 19 April he complained to the Chief Prosecutor and the Ministry of the Interior that the offence had been classified too leniently, that the assault continued until third parties intervened, that his ability to work was reduced, and that he had suffered medical expenses and psychological damage. He requested reclassification and victim status. No response followed.

On 21 April 2021 he was granted victim status. The next day he received a decision listing his rights as a victim, but it contained a pre-typed statement that he did not wish to review the case file or receive information about the progress of the case. He signed it. On 24 May he complained that the investigator had misled him into signing this waiver and had pressured him to give a less severe account of the assault. This complaint was not answered.

On 1 July 2021 a forensic report classified his jaw fractures and concussion as less severe bodily injuries causing long-term harm to health, consistent with 9 February 2021. On 8 July charges were reclassified from group violence to intentionally causing less serious harm to health under Article 118 § 3. The applicant was again granted victim status.

On 22 July 2021 the Mtskheta District Court held a hearing without informing the applicant. The prosecutor and three defendants participated online; all pleaded guilty. Using simplified proceedings, the court examined no evidence and convicted all three. Each received a suspended three-year sentence and an order not to approach or communicate with the applicant.

The applicant complained on 2 August that his position had not been heard and that the sentence was disproportionate. He requested access to the case file and a copy of the decision. The prosecutor did not reply, and the court later refused access, saying he should have requested it pre-trial. The prosecution appealed for a stricter penalty. On 6 September the applicant wrote to the Court of Appeal, complaining that the first-instance hearing had taken place in his absence and that neither he nor his lawyer had been informed. He asked for an oral hearing and to give evidence.

On 3 November 2021 the Tbilisi Court of Appeal increased the suspended sentences to four years and added 200 hours of community service. The applicant attended, but no evidence was examined because the appeal was limited to sentencing. The judge read his written submissions. The court upheld suspended sentences, citing guilty pleas, lack of criminal record, cooperation, no reoffending, family/financial circumstances, and the non-approach order. It stated that a victim’s request for strict punishment could not automatically determine sentencing.

On 30 May 2022 the Supreme Court rejected the prosecution’s cassation appeal. It noted the applicant could bring a separate compensation claim and that lack of compensation did not affect sanction. Later, on 21 February 2023, the Mtskheta District Court dismissed the applicant’s civil compensation claim for failure to pay court fees; this was upheld on appeal on 26 June 2023. The applicant lodged his Convention application on 24 August 2022, alleging ineffective criminal proceedings and violations of his rights as a victim.
001-241743:
In *Macharik v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 51409/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention concerning the applicant’s criminal conviction, based mainly on the content of her email communications obtained by the police under a judicial order.

On 14 November 2011, a judge of the Prague 3 District Court issued an order under Article 88a of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“CCP”) at the request of a prosecutor, following a police proposal. The order concerned a suspected tax-evasion case involving M.P., the authorised representative of the P. company, and representatives of roughly forty other companies. It required a communications service provider to disclose all data on past telecommunications traffic passing through the P. company’s mailbox up to that date, including registration data, IP addresses, and the contents of all messages. The order stated that the Constitutional Court’s judgment repealing section 97(3) of the Electronic Communications Act was not an obstacle, because the necessary guarantees were met and the suspected offence was serious, punishable by five to ten years’ imprisonment.

On 30 November 2011, the service provider gave the police registration data and the contents of the mailbox, including messages written by the applicant that had been forwarded to M.P. by another suspect. The provider noted that, in line with the Constitutional Court’s case-law, it did not store operational and location data. After inspecting the applicant’s messages, the police opened a criminal investigation into her activities. On 16 August 2012, she was charged with tax evasion for entering invoices for fictitious leases of advertising space into accounting records and filing a tax return based on those invoices. She unsuccessfully sought to have the email messages removed from the case file, arguing that their content could not be considered communications data within the meaning of Article 88a CCP, and that service providers were not authorised to store message content.

The applicant was indicted on 24 June 2013. On 18 March 2015, the Prague Municipal Court convicted her as an accomplice to tax evasion, imposing a suspended two-year sentence and a fine of 50,000 Czech crowns. The court found that the emails proved the leasing agreements and invoices had been backdated. On the lawfulness of the evidence, it held that the order should have been based on Article 88 CCP, concerning the content of communications, rather than Article 88a, concerning communications data. However, it considered this a merely formal shortcoming because the conditions under Article 88 had been met.

On 23 September 2016, the Prague High Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, holding that Article 88 regulated interception of future communications, while Article 88a covered past traffic data; the district judge had therefore correctly relied on Article 88a. On 28 March 2018, the Supreme Court dismissed her appeal on points of law. It held that Article 88 could not cover past email content, while Article 88a concerned only communications data, such as operational and location data. It noted that data stored on tracked computers should be obtained under Article 158d CCP, but because Article 88a imposed stricter requirements than Article 158d and practice had been inconsistent at the relevant time, the evidence was not inadmissible. On 27 March 2019, the Constitutional Court dismissed her constitutional appeal, reasoning that both Articles 88a and 158d had been used for email content at the time, and Article 88a provided stricter proportionality guarantees.

The applicant alleged that the obtaining and use of her email content violated Article 8 (privacy of correspondence) and Article 6 § 1 (fair trial), because Article 88a did not legally authorise interference with the content of past communications.
001-244020:
**Case: Yıldırım v. Türkiye (Application no. 24775/19)**

The case concerns an application lodged against Türkiye with the European Court of Human Rights on 26 April 2019 under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant, Ramazan Yıldırım, born in 1978, was represented by Mr M. Çam, a lawyer practising in Çorum. The Turkish Government were given notice of the application. A Committee of the Second Section, composed of Judges Gediminas Sagatys (President), Stéphane Pisani, and Juha Lavapuro, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 19 June 2025 and delivered the judgment on 10 July 2025.

The facts, as set out in the appended table, relate to domestic administrative proceedings brought by the applicant. The subject matter was an annulment action before the administrative courts in respect of the termination of the applicant’s secondment contract of 3 March 2012. That termination was based on suspicion of his affiliation with FETÖ/PDY. In essence, the authorities ended the applicant’s secondment arrangement on grounds connected to an alleged affiliation with that organisation or movement. The applicant challenged the termination by seeking annulment before the administrative courts.

The domestic proceedings produced decisions at three levels. First, the Kastamonu Administrative Court gave a decision on 8 November 2017. Second, the Ankara Court of Administrative Appeals gave a decision on 20 June 2018. Third, the Turkish Constitutional Court gave a decision on 2 November 2018. These decisions are the domestic judicial decisions relevant to the applicant’s complaints before the Strasbourg Court.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained of the lack of reasoning or inadequate reasoning in court decisions. He also raised another complaint under the provisions of the Convention, although the provided excerpt does not specify the content of that further complaint. The central alleged violation, as summarised in the facts and appended table, is therefore that the domestic courts did not adequately or properly reason their decisions in the administrative proceedings concerning the termination of his secondment contract. The complaint is directed at the quality of judicial reasoning rather than solely at the substantive termination decision, although the termination on suspicion of FETÖ/PDY affiliation forms the essential factual background. The applicant’s inability to obtain a sufficiently reasoned judicial response to his annulment action is the key factual link to the alleged violation.

The case was determined by a Committee of the Second Section. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. Overall, the key facts relevant to the alleged violation(s) are: the applicant’s secondment contract was terminated on 3 March 2012 on suspicion of FETÖ/PDY affiliation; he brought an annulment action in the administrative courts; those proceedings ended with decisions of the Kastamonu Administrative Court, the Ankara Court of Administrative Appeals, and the Turkish Constitutional Court on the dates listed; and he then applied to the ECtHR on 26 April 2019, alleging lack of or inadequate reasoning in the court decisions, along with one further Convention complaint not detailed in the provided excerpt.
001-238788:
**Ibrahimi and Others v. Albania** (Applications nos. 81057/17 and 4 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered on 14 January 2025. The five applications concerned proceedings before Albanian courts in which the applicants’ constitutional complaints against Supreme Court decisions were rejected by the Constitutional Court as lodged out of time. The central alleged violation was that the Constitutional Court calculated the four-month time-limit from the date the Supreme Court adopted its decision, rather than from the date the applicants were actually served with or effectively learned of that decision. This, the applicants argued, restricted their right of access to the Constitutional Court and, in one case, other fair-trial rights.

The common pattern was that the Supreme Court decided each case, but the decision was served on the applicants much later. The applicants then filed constitutional complaints within four months of service or notification. Nonetheless, the Constitutional Court declared the complaints inadmissible because more than four months had passed since the Supreme Court’s adoption of the decision. In four applications, the Constitutional Court also held that a stamp showing that a party had requested service was not decisive proof of the date of first service, and that the burden was on the party to prove it had not been served earlier.

In **Ibrahimi v. Albania** (no. 81057/17), the applicant had been convicted of murder and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court adopted its decision on 25 June 2015. A letter notifying him of the decision was served by prison authorities on 12 May 2017. He lodged a constitutional complaint on 5 June 2017, complaining that he had not been informed of the Supreme Court hearing and had been denied legal assistance. The Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible on 16 June 2017 as out of time. His case also raised alleged violations of his right to participate in person in the criminal proceedings and to defend himself through legal assistance of his own choosing before the Supreme Court.

In **Selimi v. Albania** (no. 57542/18), a property dispute, the Supreme Court adopted its decision on 25 June 2015; it was served on the applicants on 18 October 2017. They lodged a constitutional complaint on 13 February 2018, which was rejected as out of time on 30 May 2018.

In **Nika v. Albania** (no. 32939/21), the applicant challenged her dismissal as a forestry inspector. The Supreme Court decided on 27 May 2020, and the decision was served on 14 January 2021. She filed a constitutional complaint on 18 January 2021, but it was rejected on 26 February 2021 as out of time.

In **Dedaj v. Albania** (no. 54121/21), the applicant challenged his dismissal from work. The Supreme Court decided on 27 July 2020, and service occurred on 1 April 2021. He lodged a constitutional complaint on 9 June 2021; it was declared inadmissible on 26 July 2021.

In **Industri Ndërtim (IN) SH.P.K. v. Albania** (no. 7386/22), a company involved in civil contractual proceedings, the Supreme Court adopted its decision on 17 February 2021. It was served on the company on 4 June 2021. The company filed a constitutional complaint on 29 September 2021, which the Constitutional Court rejected as out of time on 29 October 2021. The application also concerned the company’s right to participate in proceedings before the Tirana District Court.

The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning access to the Constitutional Court and the additional fair-trial complaints in the Ibrahimi and Industri Ndërtim cases, while declaring the remainder inadmissible. The third party Res Publica was granted leave to intervene.
001-241978:
In *Ezeoke v. the United Kingdom*, the applicant, Obina Christopher Ezeoke, a British national, was arrested on 18 September 2016 for the murders of a woman (“BE”) and her 21-year-old nephew. The killings were believed to be a gang-related revenge attack, although the victims were not involved in gang violence and were not the intended targets. Ezeoke denied responsibility and later, in February 2017, raised an alibi: that he had been at CG’s flat in London with CG, her two children, her sister RM, and friend AMC.

He was charged on 20 September 2016, but the case led to five trials. The first began in March 2017. After four weeks, the trial judge fell ill; the jury was discharged and the case had to restart. The second trial began in April 2018. Ezeoke gave evidence and called CG, but not RM or AMC, and disclosed JC as another key witness. After about 42 hours of deliberation, the jury could not reach a majority verdict. A retrial was granted. The third trial began in January 2019; the jury again failed to agree, and a further retrial was granted in April 2019. The judge found the case exceptionally grave, with a cogent circumstantial prosecution case and a strong public interest in obtaining a verdict.

The fourth trial began in February 2020. The jury retired on 18 March 2020, but by 24 March the Covid-19 public-health emergency had reduced it to eight members, insufficient for a valid verdict. The jury was discharged. The prosecution sought a fifth trial. Ezeoke opposed it as oppressive and unfair due to delay: four juries had been empanelled, he had given evidence three times, and he had been held in Category A custody since arrest. The trial judge nevertheless ordered a fifth trial on 20 April 2020. He noted the fourth trial ended because of the pandemic, not jury disagreement; had it been a third retrial following disagreement, he would not have allowed it. He found the prosecution evidence largely documentary, CCTV, telephone and scientific, and that Ezeoke had been a confident witness. Although delay affected CG, her recollection had already been affected before her first police account. He concluded a fair trial was possible and a further trial would not be an abuse of process.

The fifth trial ran from 7 July to 9 September 2020. Ezeoke was convicted of both murders by an 11-1 majority and sentenced to life imprisonment with a 40-year minimum term.

Ezeoke appealed, arguing that the fifth trial breached Article 6 § 1 of the Convention because it was unfair and held after an unreasonable delay. He claimed the repeated trials and delay degraded defence evidence, especially CG’s, creating an imbalance and rendering the conviction unsafe. The Court of Appeal refused leave in October 2021, finding the trial judge’s discretion was not perverse, that he was best placed to assess fairness, that exceptional pandemic arrangements ensured the fifth trial proceeded quickly, and that delay did not make the outcome unsafe. Ezeoke then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 15 December 2021, complaining under Article 6 § 1 about the length and fairness of the criminal proceedings. The Government were given notice of those complaints; the remainder was declared inadmissible.
001-240184:
The case concerns criminal convictions arising from transactions between Glitnir bank hf. and the company BK-44 before Iceland’s 2008 financial crisis. The first applicant, Jóhannes Baldursson, was a Glitnir executive. The second applicant, Birkir Kristinsson, worked in Glitnir’s Private Banking department and owned BK-44.

In 2007, Glitnir granted BK-44 a loan of approximately ISK 3.79 billion to buy 150 million Glitnir shares owned by Glitnir itself. The loan was allegedly approved without the required loan or risk committee consent and without sufficient security. It was also alleged that the first applicant and co-accused E.S. verbally agreed to give BK-44 a put option guaranteeing that Glitnir bore the entire market risk on the shares. The option was not registered in Glitnir’s systems and was settled in July 2008, with Glitnir bearing the loss. The prosecution alleged fraud by abuse of position, market manipulation, aiding and abetting, and accounting violations. In 2014, the Reykjavik District Court convicted both applicants and two co-accused. The applicants received five-year sentences. In 2015, the Supreme Court upheld the convictions but reduced the first applicant’s sentence to three years and the second applicant’s to four years.

Two sets of facts are particularly relevant to the alleged violations. First, the second applicant’s changing procedural status: he was interviewed as a suspect in December 2011, then as a witness later that month without counsel, and again as a suspect in June 2012. He argued that once he had been treated as a witness, the investigation against him had been terminated, and there was no “new evidence” justifying its reopening. He relied on section 57(3) of the Criminal Procedures Act and the ne bis in idem guarantee. The prosecution relied on recorded phone calls from late 2007 received after his witness interview. The District Court rejected his dismissal request. The Supreme Court held that the investigation had not formally been terminated, so section 57(3) was not engaged, but it excluded the second witness interview from evidence. One judge dissented.

Second, after the criminal proceedings ended, information emerged about the financial interests of Supreme Court justices who had decided the applicants’ case. Justice M.S. had inherited Glitnir shares in 2002, sold them in 2003 and 2007, and from January 2007 had an asset-management contract with Glitnir; in early 2008 he placed ISK 61,450,000 in asset management, partly in equity funds, and later suffered losses. Justice Ó.B.Þ. had acquired Glitnir shares in July 2007 by inheritance and sold them in December 2007. Justice G.B. had held shares in Kaupthing and Landsbanki, but not Glitnir. The Committee on Judicial Functions considered equity funds and similar assets not subject to reporting under the applicable rules. When the applicants requested information, the Supreme Court provided declarations but refused details on equity-fund holdings.

The first applicant also challenged the reliability of testimonies and the District Court’s findings, especially regarding his role in granting the loan and settling the put option. The prosecutor accepted that the District Court had overstated the evidence concerning the loan decision. Before the Supreme Court, the applicants and witnesses were not reheard; the court relied on transcripts and documentary evidence. These facts underlie the complaints about fair trial, impartiality of the Supreme Court, and the second applicant’s rights concerning renewed suspect status and self-incrimination.
001-247564:
**Summary of *Černý and Others v. The Czech Republic* (Applications nos. 37514/20 and 4 others)**

The case concerns five Czech criminal defence lawyers whose privileged communications with their client, Z., were seized, extracted, and placed on a criminal case file, then disseminated to prosecutors and co-defendants. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private life and correspondence), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention.

The facts centre on two parallel criminal proceedings against Z. – one concerning membership of a criminal group, false accusations, and bribery; the other concerning tax evasion. The applicants represented Z. in these proceedings. On 2 December 2016, during a search of Z.'s home, police seized his smartphone and tablet, both containing correspondence between Z. and his defence lawyers, draft court submissions, notes on legal strategy, and witness questioning preparation – material protected by legal professional privilege.

On 23 November 2017, the Brno Municipal Court ordered an expert examination of the devices' contents, requesting extraction of all data including deleted communications. Z. objected formally on 1 December 2017, emphasising the privileged nature of the material and warning that disclosure would expose his defence strategy to co-defendants and prosecutors. The court did not respond and dismissed his objections without reasons during a hearing on 10 January 2018.

By 18 February 2018, over 20,000 pages of material had been extracted and placed on the case file. On 28 February 2018, the presiding judge, K., distributed the contents and expert report to the prosecutor and all co-defendants on Blu-ray discs. On 27 March 2018, K. stated that none of the data had been found relevant as evidence, yet refused to remove it from the file. On 1 June 2018, K. told a journalist that the content constituted evidence, that all parties had the right to see it, and that privileged communications "did not matter" as there had been no electronic interception.

Subsequent attempts to remove the material failed. The Ministry of Justice declined to initiate disciplinary proceedings against K., acknowledging a lacuna in the law regarding lawyer-client communications on seized devices, but noting that Articles 88(1) and 158d(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (prohibiting use of intercepted privileged communications) could not be applied by analogy. The Brno Regional Court rejected applications under Section 174a of the Courts and Judges Act, and the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants' constitutional appeal on 20 November 2019, holding that privilege belonged to the client, not the lawyer, and that the lawyers' fundamental rights were therefore not affected.

In parallel compensation proceedings, the Prague 2 District Court initially found official misconduct and awarded each applicant CZK 25,000. However, the Prague Municipal Court reversed this, awarding only written apologies to three applicants, finding the first applicant had not demonstrated damage and the fifth (a trainee lawyer) lacked an independent relationship with the client giving rise to privilege. The Supreme Court subsequently held in related proceedings that the Municipal Court's failure to store privileged material separately before assessing relevance constituted official misconduct.

The key violation alleged is the State's failure to protect lawyer-client privileged communications from seizure, extraction, and disclosure to third parties, and the absence of effective domestic remedies to prevent or redress this interference.
001-238800:
**Tverdokhlebova v. Ukraine (no. 15830/16)** concerns an application lodged on 12 March 2016 by Ms Roza Borisovna Tverdokhlebova, a Ukrainian national born in 1965 who lives in Kyiv. She complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that she had been deprived of her title to a plot of land through proceedings of which she had not been informed.

In 2011 the Brovary District State Administration allocated a 1.8-hectare plot for individual farming to a person identified as D. D. later divided the land into two plots of 1.62 hectares and 0.18 hectares and changed its purpose to “gardening.” In November 2013 the applicant bought the smaller 0.18-hectare plot from D. The sales contract stated the land’s value as UAH 147,600, equal to USD 18,000 on the day of signing, and recorded that D. had received that amount in US dollars.

In June 2014 a local prosecutor applied to the local court seeking invalidation of the decision allocating the disputed land to D., D.’s title, the contract between D. and the applicant, and the applicant’s title. The prosecutor argued that the land was located within Bohdanivka village and therefore could not have been disposed of by the Brovary District State Administration. The local court rejected the claims, but on 14 May 2015 the Kyiv Region Court of Appeal granted them. The appellate court relied on another set of proceedings concerning the original larger plot, between different parties, in which a forensic technical expert assessment had concluded that the land lay within Bohdanivka village. The appellate court invalidated the applicant’s title and restored the land to the village’s ownership.

The applicant alleged that she had not been informed of the proceedings by either the local court or the court of appeal. She submitted that all relevant summonses had been sent to an allegedly non-existent address at 6 Krasovskyy Street in Brovary, while she actually resided in Kyiv. She noted that the 2013 sales contract, which was available to and relied on by the prosecutor, indicated her Kyiv address. Letters and summonses in the case file had been sent to the wrong address, and registered letters had been returned as undelivered. She stated that she learned of the proceedings only in May 2015, after the appellate judgment, when her representative examined the case file. She then filed a cassation appeal alleging a gross procedural violation due to lack of notification, erroneous application of land legislation, and disregard of evidence. D. also appealed. On 16 September 2015 the Higher Specialized Court for Civil and Criminal Cases upheld the appellate findings, stating that the facts had been comprehensively established, domestic law duly applied, and other cassation arguments not borne out by the file.

The Government later informed the Court that the applicant had sued D. to recover the money paid for the land. On 10 December 2019 the Brovary Local Court upheld her claims under Article 216 of the Civil Code, awarding UAH 426,393.20 (USD 18,000 at the then exchange rate) plus UAH 4,037 (about EUR 154) for notary fees and land tax. This judgment was upheld on appeal on 4 June 2020 and became final. Enforcement proceedings began in July 2022, but the applicant alleged non-enforcement without providing details or showing she had challenged the bailiffs. In 2021 she obtained permission to prepare technical documentation for a 0.18-hectare plot in Bohdanivka for individual farming, but did not say whether that process was completed or whether she obtained title.

These facts underpin the alleged violations: under Article 6, the unfairness of proceedings because the applicant allegedly was not properly notified and could not participate in the case that annulled her title; under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the deprivation of her land title through the prosecutor’s action and the resulting court decisions.
001-245447:
The case *Urusbiev and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (ECHR, Fifth Section, 23 October 2025) joined five applications concerning detention in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”). The applicants alleged that MRT de facto authorities unlawfully deprived them of liberty and held them in inadequate material conditions, often without proper medical assistance. Their complaints mainly arose under Articles 3 and 5 of the Convention; some also relied on Articles 8, 10, 6, 13 and 14, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

**Application no. 33519/15 (Urusbiev):** The applicant, stateless and resident in Dubăsari, allegedly fired a weapon in an MRT bar on 2 January 2001. Criminal proceedings were initiated, but he absconded. On 17 September 2014 he was apprehended in MRT-controlled Dubăsari. On 19 November 2014 the “MRT Tiraspol City Court” convicted him and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment; the “MRT Supreme Court” upheld this on 23 December 2014. He complained under Article 5 § 1 that his detention from 17 September 2014 was unlawful because it was ordered by an unlawful de facto court.

**Application no. 40836/15 (Ilcenco and Ilcenco):** A father and son, both journalists in Tiraspol. On 18 March 2015 their home was searched on charges of instigating extremism and subverting the “MRT Government.” The father was arrested and held in Tiraspol police station, then transferred on 24 March 2015 to Tiraspol prison no. 3 until 17 July 2015. Professional belongings were seized. While detained, he continued publishing articles with his lawyer’s help; after publication, authorities searched his cell and removed his pens and paper. He alleged Article 3 violations (inhuman detention conditions and lack of medical assistance), Article 5 § 1 (unlawful four-month detention by an unlawful de facto court), and Article 34 hindrance of his right to apply to the Court. The son had no separate main complaints.

**Application no. 558/16 (Vardiaşvili):** Arrested on 9 June 2015 for alleged expiry of a short-term “MRT” residence permit and held three days in Dubăsari police station. On 11 June 2015 he was released, taken to the “Dubăsari border post,” expelled from the MRT, and banned from returning for six months. He complained of inhuman detention conditions under Article 3 and unlawful three-day detention under Article 5 § 1.

**Application no. 862/16 (Ahmetşin):** On 13 March 2015 convicted by a de facto MRT first-instance court of embezzlement and taken into custody. He was held in Tiraspol police station, then Tiraspol prison no. 3. On 28 April 2015 the “MRT Supreme Court” upheld the conviction and reduced his sentence to three and a half years. On 18 May 2015 he was transferred to Hlinaia prison no. 1. On 1 December 2015 Moldova’s Supreme Court declared the MRT judgments null and void. He complained of Article 3 conditions and lack of medical assistance, and Article 5 § 1 unlawful detention for three and a half years.

**Application no. 83954/17 (Mustea):** On 23 March 2017 the “Tiraspol City Court” ordered his detention for an undetermined period on theft charges; on 18 May 2017 it was extended three months. He was held in Tiraspol police station and then Tiraspol prison no. 3. He was released on 2 June 2017 after the “MRT Supreme Court” found pre-trial detention unnecessary. He complained under Articles 3 and 5 § 1.

The common thread is that all applicants were detained under orders or judgments of the unrecognised MRT authorities, in MRT detention facilities, and alleged unlawful detention, poor conditions, and inadequate medical care.
001-246024:
In *Zvonar v. Ukraine* (Application no. 20532/16), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1959, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the deprivation of land he had purchased from local authorities after a prosecutor successfully challenged the sale.

In February 2009, the applicant began renting a 0.42-hectare plot near the Drahobrat ski resort by Yasinia. He apparently built a cable transportation system there and used the land for tourism. On 17 November 2010 and 11 January 2011, the Rakhiv District State Administration (“the Rakhiv DSA”) adopted decisions allowing him to buy the land. Those decisions stated that the land was outside urban settlements and was for non-agricultural use. On 14 January 2011, the applicant signed a sale and purchase contract with the Rakhiv DSA and paid UAH 460,056—approximately EUR 43,850 at the time. He later obtained ownership certificates for plots into which the land had been divided, designated for the “construction and maintenance of recreational facilities.”

In July 2012, at the request of the local prosecutor, the State Agricultural Inspectorate of the Zakarpattia Region inspected the allocation. It concluded, citing Article 122 § 3 of the Land Code, that the Rakhiv DSA had lacked authority to dispose of the land. According to the Inspectorate, local State administrations could dispose of land outside urban settlements only if it was designated for agricultural use or water management, or for local community infrastructure such as schools or hospitals. Because the land was for recreational purposes, the prosecutor sued the applicant, seeking to set aside the 2010 and 2011 decisions and to invalidate the sale contract and the applicant’s title. The prosecutor acted in the interests of the Zakarpattia Region State Administration (“the Zakarpattia RSA”), which was allegedly empowered to dispose of the land, and the Yasinia village council, which was supposedly entitled to receive the profit. Both authorities objected to the prosecutor’s claims, arguing that the Rakhiv DSA had acted within its powers and that the sale had been lawful.

On 18 December 2013, the Rakhiv Local Court allowed the prosecutor’s claims in full. It found that the Rakhiv DSA had acted ultra vires and ordered the land reclaimed under Article 387 of the Civil Code, which permits recovery of property that left an owner’s possession without a proper legal basis, even from a bona fide owner. On 20 May 2014, the Zakarpattia Region Court of Appeal quashed that judgment. It reasoned that the Zakarpattia RSA’s objection effectively approved the sale, and that under Article 241 of the Civil Code an ultra vires act later approved by the represented person could be deemed valid. The Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court (“the HSCCC”) quashed that judgment and remitted the case, holding that recreational land could be disposed of only by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine.

On 17 March 2015, the Court of Appeal upheld the Local Court’s conclusion but amended its reasoning: because the land was recreational, only the Cabinet could dispose of it, not the Rakhiv DSA or Zakarpattia RSA, so the transfer had been unlawful. On 7 October 2015, the HSCCC dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal and upheld that judgment.

The applicant argued that invalidating the contract would not benefit the State but would damage it, because the State would have to reimburse the price he had paid. However, he did not expressly raise during the domestic proceedings the issue of restitution rules for invalid contracts—under which the parties must be restored to their prior positions, meaning that if the land was reclaimed from him, he should have been reimbursed. These facts form the basis of his complaint that the invalidation and reclamation of his land amounted to an unjustified and disproportionate deprivation of possessions.
001-243885:
In *N.T. v. Cyprus* (Application no. 28150/22), the applicant, a Cypriot national born in 1992, complained that the Cypriot authorities failed to effectively investigate and prosecute her rape allegation, in breach of positive obligations under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, and that she suffered gender-based discrimination contrary to Article 14 read with Articles 3 and 8.

The alleged rape occurred on 1 January 2011, when the applicant was 18 and A.T. was 20. She reported it to police on 10 April 2021. She stated that after a night out with her friend C.S., A.T. and his friend G.H., A.T. insisted they enter his father’s warehouse. She initially resisted but went inside to use the bathroom. A.T. took her upstairs, grabbed and tried to undress her, forced her onto boxes, and raped her orally and vaginally despite her resistance. She said she froze, later scratched and bit him, and asked him to stop; he continued and bit her neck. Afterwards she had bruises and bite marks, which C.S. later saw. She told a male friend, D.N., and two psychologists about the rape. She decided to report after a Facebook conversation with S.N., who said A.T. had also raped another classmate.

Police opened an investigation immediately. They took statements from the applicant, C.S., D.N., S.N., G.H., and a psychologist. C.S. corroborated seeing the applicant’s bruised neck and strange behaviour, and described a separate 2010 incident in which A.T. tried to force her to perform oral sex. G.H. claimed he heard nothing unusual and that the applicant did not seem upset. A.T. refused to answer police questions. The police recommended prosecution, and in May 2021 an indictment for rape was filed; the case was referred to the Assize Court, where A.T. pleaded not guilty and was released on bail.

The applicant later gave two supplementary statements. In the first, she disclosed affectionate Facebook messages to A.T., including a 2011 message saying she loved him, and said she initially blamed herself, believed she had given him the wrong message, and wanted to protect him. In the second, she revealed that on 1 January 2010 she had had consensual sex with A.T. in the same warehouse, with C.S. and G.H. downstairs, and had orally told police but asked that it not be recorded. Prosecutors then reassessed her credibility, citing inconsistencies, ongoing texts until 2013, affectionate language, and her statements that she may have implied consent. On 1 December 2021 the Deputy Attorney General discontinued the prosecution by *nolle prosequi*, citing doubts about credibility, possible subjective belief in consent, and low prospects of conviction. The applicant sought reasons and the case file; her request for the file was refused. A.T. publicly announced the withdrawal. The applicant complained to the ECtHR that the authorities’ failure to continue the prosecution and their reliance on victim-blaming assumptions violated Articles 3 and 8, and discriminated against her as a woman under Article 14.
001-245460:
In Sakellaris and Others v. Greece (Application no. 43594/16), four Greek nationals—Konstantinos Sakellaris (born 1962), Dimitrios Diskos (born 1967), Stefanos Lazaridis (born 1977), and Vasilios Tzouvaras (born 1974)—lodged an application against Greece with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The application was introduced on 20 July 2016. The applicants were represented by Mr G. Papastergiou, a lawyer practising in Veroia. The Greek Government was given notice of the application. The case was examined by the Third Section sitting as a Committee, composed of Judges Diana Kovatcheva, Canòlic Mingorance Cairat, and Vasilka Sancin, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 2 October 2025 and adopted its judgment on 23 October 2025. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The key facts relate to the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment obtained by the applicants. According to the appended table, the judgment was delivered by the Supreme Administrative Court, Judgment no. 4917/2012, and became final on 18 December 2012. That domestic judgment was in the applicants’ favour. However, the Greek authorities did not enforce it. The table records the start date of the non-enforcement period as 18 December 2012, the date on which the judgment became final. The end date is stated as “pending,” meaning that the judgment remained unenforced at the time the table was prepared. The total length of non-enforcement is recorded as more than 12 years, 6 months, and 23 days. The provided excerpt does not describe the underlying subject matter of the domestic judgment, the nature of the applicants’ original claims before the Supreme Administrative Court, or the specific reasons why the judgment was not executed.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights about two matters. First, they alleged the non-enforcement of the domestic judgment in their favour. Second, they alleged the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law by which they could secure enforcement of that judgment or obtain redress for the continuing failure to execute it. In substance, the case is not about the original administrative dispute, but about the Greek State’s failure to comply with a final and binding judicial decision and the absence of an adequate domestic mechanism to challenge that failure.

The essential facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the Supreme Administrative Court’s final judgment of 18 December 2012 in the applicants’ favour; the authorities’ failure to enforce it; the continuing and pending nature of that non-enforcement; the lengthy period of non-enforcement, recorded as more than 12 years, 6 months, and 23 days; and the applicants’ claim that no effective domestic remedy was available. The procedural details identify the applicants, their representative, the respondent Government, the application date, and the Court’s composition. The provided judgment excerpt records the facts and complaints but does not set out the Court’s legal analysis, the specific Convention Articles invoked, or the final outcome on the merits.
001-243081:
In *Radelić v. Croatia*, the applicant, Dražen Radelić, was the sole shareholder and director of Radelić d.o.o. The company went bankrupt in November 2010, the bankruptcy was concluded in December 2010, and in March 2011 the company was struck off the register and ceased to exist.

In March 2011 the Croatian State Attorney’s Office indicted the applicant for business fraud and forgery of documents. It alleged that between August 2003 and February 2004 he presented thirty-six foreign bank cheques for cashing, falsely claiming they were payment for services rendered abroad, intending to obtain significant pecuniary gain for the company.

In 2014 the Split Municipal Court convicted him of forgery and imposed a suspended sentence, while acquitting him of business fraud. On appeal, the acquittal was quashed and a retrial was ordered. In 2017 the Municipal Court convicted him of business fraud and imposed a one-year suspended sentence. Critically, it also ordered confiscation of HRK 854,743.39—about EUR 113,440—as proceeds of crime from the applicant personally. He was ordered to pay that amount into the State budget within six months; failure could result in revocation of the suspended sentence. The court reasoned that the company had been struck off and had no legal successor, and that the applicant, as sole founder, shareholder, and authorized representative, should therefore pay the confiscated amount under Article 77 of the Penal Code.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the money had been paid into the company’s account, not to him personally; that the company had paid taxes and used the funds for its operations; and that he had not personally benefited. The Split County Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the confiscation. It held that the illegal gain had been acquired for the company through the applicant’s criminal acts, but because the company no longer existed and had no successor, confiscation from the applicant was justified by analogy with section 252(5) of the Commercial Companies Act, concerning a management board member’s liability to creditors for gross breach of duty.

The Split County State Attorney’s Office later proposed that a request for protection of legality be lodged, arguing that confiscation from the applicant personally was unlawful: the indictment alleged gain for the company, no evidence showed the gain was transferred to the applicant, and if the company had been liquidated the court should have ordered compensation to victims, though no injured party or civil claim existed. The Principal State Attorney did not lodge the request.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint was dismissed in 2021; the Constitutional Court found no breach of his right of ownership. Enforcement efforts later failed because his bank accounts lacked sufficient funds.

The European Court of Human Rights gave notice only of the complaint concerning the confiscation of proceeds of crime. The key issue was whether confiscating proceeds from the applicant personally—even though the proceeds were allegedly acquired by and for the company, which had ceased to exist—was compatible with the Convention, particularly his property rights and the lawfulness of the measure. Relevant facts included that he was not found to have personally acquired or retained the proceeds, that domestic Supreme Court case-law suggested proceeds could not be confiscated from a perpetrator when acquired for a company, and that the State Attorney’s Office itself considered the confiscation unlawful.
001-241871:
In **Marzouki and Others v. Bulgaria** (Application no. 48636/19), judgment of 27 February 2025, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by three applicants: Mohamed Nabil Marzouki, a Tunisian national born in 1981; Mariam Mohamed Nabil Marzouki, his daughter, born in 2010 and a Bulgarian national; and Yana Dimitrova Yankova, the child’s mother, born in 1976 and also Bulgarian. The first applicant had permanent residence in Bulgaria. The case concerns his removal from Bulgaria and his separation from the second and third applicants, allegedly disrupting their family life.

In early 2018, the first applicant travelled to Serbia. On 1 February 2018, when he returned, Bulgarian border authorities refused him entry and gave him a standard refusal form. Two grounds were checked: that an alert had been issued for the purpose of refusing entry, and that he was considered a threat to public order, internal security, public health or international relations.

Through a legal representative, the first applicant sought judicial review of the refusal. In those proceedings, the border police explained that they had acted on a decision of the State Agency for National Security (SANS) dated 1 February 2018. That SANS decision imposed a five-year entry ban on the ground that the applicant posed a national security threat. The Sofia Region Administrative Court upheld the refusal of entry on 29 October 2018, finding that the border police had been bound to act after the SANS decision.

The SANS decision was served on the applicant’s representative only on 31 July 2018, after the representative requested a copy upon learning of it during the refusal proceedings. The decision contained no specific reasoning to justify the conclusion that the applicant threatened national security. Instead, it referred to a classified document called a “Proposal.” That Proposal was later declassified and submitted by the Government in the Strasbourg proceedings.

After receiving a copy of the SANS decision, the representative applied for judicial review of it. However, the Supreme Administrative Court declared the application time-barred in a final decision of 6 March 2019. It held that the fourteen-day time-limit had started to run on 1 February 2018, when the applicant had allegedly been “orally informed” of the decision. That finding apparently referred to the standard refusal form given to him at the border. According to the Supreme Administrative Court, the applicant had been validly informed of the SANS decision in that manner under Article 61 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, as worded at the time, which allowed oral notification of administrative decisions to interested parties.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained that the first applicant’s removal from Bulgaria was unjustified and had disrupted their family life together. They further complained under Article 13, read in conjunction with Article 8, that there were no effective domestic remedies for those alleged violations. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore include the first applicant’s permanent residence and family ties in Bulgaria, the five-year entry ban based on an unreasoned national-security decision, the reliance on classified material, the delayed service of the SANS decision, and the domestic courts’ treatment of the judicial-review application as time-barred because of the alleged oral notification at the border. These facts are central to the alleged breaches of Article 8 and Article 13.
001-243781:
In *Karović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Applications nos. 43201/22, 555/23, 5241/23 and 23976/23), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined four applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants—Zlatan Karović, Tarik Kršlak, Vanja Bradarić and Osman Šabanović—are nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina residing in Sarajevo or Ilidža. Their applications were lodged between 11 August 2022 and 2 June 2023. The Court gave notice to the Government only of complaints concerning non-enforcement of domestic decisions under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The underlying facts concern final domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour against Sarajevo Canton, one of the ten cantons of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Between 2015 and 2018, the Sarajevo Municipal Court delivered judgments on 5 and 19 February 2015, 24 February 2017, and 23 April 2018, ordering Sarajevo Canton to pay the applicants various sums for unpaid work-related benefits, together with default interest at the statutory rate and legal costs. The corresponding writs of execution were issued by the same court on 19 February 2021, 5 May 2016, 5 July 2017 and 13 June 2018.

Despite these final and enforceable decisions, enforcement was not carried out. One applicant, Mr Šabanović, obtained a Constitutional Court decision on 12 January 2022 finding violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Constitutional Court ordered Sarajevo Canton to take the necessary steps to secure enforcement of the decision in his favour and awarded him 300 convertible marks (BAM) in compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

On 13 January 2022, Sarajevo Canton adopted an enforcement plan covering all domestic decisions against it, published in the Official Gazette of Sarajevo Canton no. 4/22. The plan provided that creditors who renounced their claims for default interest and legal costs would receive their principal claims without delay. For creditors who did not accept that arrangement—including the present applicants—the plan stated that decisions would be enforced in chronological order within five years, by the end of 2026, with up to 0.8% of the total budget allocated for that purpose. It also stated that Sarajevo Canton reserved the right not to adhere to the plan if it received fewer funds in future.

On 6 April 2022, the Constitutional Court rejected Mr Karović’s case, considering the Sarajevo Canton enforcement plan acceptable. However, according to the available information, the decisions in favour of all four applicants remained unenforced. As of 31 December 2024, their positions in the chronological queue of pending decisions against Sarajevo Canton were: Mr Šabanović, 1,017; Ms Bradarić, 2,299; Mr Karović, 3,092; and Mr Kršlak, 5,797.

The alleged violations therefore arise from the continued failure of the respondent State to enforce final domestic decisions awarding the applicants unpaid work-related benefits, interest and costs. The applicants complain that this non-enforcement breached their right to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 and their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key factual issue is whether the Sarajevo Canton enforcement plan, its chronological payment schedule extending to 2026, and the applicants’ high queue positions sufficiently justify the prolonged non-enforcement of binding judgments in their favour.
001-245279:
In *Mendieta Borrego v. Spain* (Application no. 3958/24), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 16 October 2025. The applicant, Eva Mendieta Borrego, a Spanish national born in 1977 and living in Gelida, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that Spain’s refusal to grant her a survivor’s pension after her partner’s death breached her property rights. The application was lodged on 25 January 2024 and belongs to a group of cases following *Valverde Digon v. Spain* and related judgments.

The key facts concern the applicant’s cohabitation with her partner since 2003. In June 2008, her partner divorced his wife. The couple had three children together: one born in January 2008 and two born in 2009. Under the legal regime in force in Catalonia until March 2014, civil partnerships were not required to fulfil any formal registration requirement for surviving partners to be entitled to a survivor’s pension, provided other conditions were met. That changed after the Spanish Constitutional Court’s judgment no. STC 40/2014 of 11 March 2014, published on 10 April 2014. From that date, access to survivor’s pensions for civil partnerships throughout Spain, including Catalonia, required the partnership to have been formally registered at least two years before one partner’s death.

The applicant and her partner were never married and never registered as “de facto” or civil partners. On 7 June 2015, the applicant’s partner died. She then applied to the National Institute of Social Security (INSS) for a survivor’s pension. On 2 July 2015, the INSS rejected her application because she did not meet the legal requirements, specifically because she had not formalised a civil partnership at least two years before her partner’s death. Her administrative appeal was dismissed on 24 August 2015.

The refusal was upheld by the domestic courts. On 29 December 2017, Labour Court no. 4 of Barcelona dismissed her claim. The court suggested that the two-year registration requirement might be impossible to comply with for de facto partners who registered after the Constitutional Court’s judgment if one partner died before the two-year period expired. It also did not rule out modifying the two-year criterion in exceptional circumstances, such as illness or disability, where compliance was impossible or very difficult. However, it found no such circumstances in the applicant’s case, so the requirement applied fully. On 11 March 2019, the High Court of Justice of Catalonia upheld the refusal on appeal, again citing the lack of registration two years before the partner’s death. Her cassation appeal was rejected. On 27 October 2023, the Constitutional Court declared her amparo appeal inadmissible.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the domestic authorities’ refusal to grant her a survivor’s pension breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In essence, she complained that the new eligibility requirement—formal registration at least two years before death—was applied retrospectively and unforeseeably to her existing unregistered partnership, making it impossible for her to qualify despite her long cohabitation and the couple’s three children. The Government’s objection to examination by the Committee was rejected, and the Court considered the parties’ observations before deliberating in private on 18 September 2025.
001-244592:
**Rutkauskas v. Lithuania (Application no. 15816/20)** is an Article 9 case before the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section). The applicant, Mr Erikas Rutkauskas, a Lithuanian national born in 1992, lives in Pakriauniai and is a Jehovah’s Witness and religious minister. He lodged the application on 25 March 2020, represented by S.H. Brady Heath. The Lithuanian Government was represented by its Agent. The Court gave notice to the Government and received the parties’ observations. A Committee composed of Judges Eicke, Ilievski and Sagatys, with Deputy Section Registrar von Arnim, deliberated on 1 July 2025 and delivered judgment on 26 August 2025.

The key facts concern the applicant’s refusal to perform military service on grounds of religious belief and conscience. Having been called up under Lithuania’s Law on Conscription to perform military service, he refused. He requested instead to perform civilian service. The military authorities did not answer that request. On 7 September 2015 they also decided not to exempt him from initial mandatory military service. Those decisions—the refusal to exempt him and the failure to address his request for alternative civilian service—formed the factual basis of his later complaints.

The applicant challenged the military authorities’ decisions before the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court. On 31 October 2017 that court dismissed his appeal. He then appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court. In that appeal, he asked the court to suspend the case and refer a question to the Constitutional Court: whether the State’s failure to include in the Law on Conscription an exemption from both mandatory military service and alternative national defence service for conscientious objectors breached the right to freedom of religion. He also argued that the military authorities had not assessed his request to perform alternative civilian service and that the first-instance court had overlooked this omission.

By a final ruling of 16 October 2019, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the impugned decisions. It relied on the Constitutional Court’s ruling of 4 July 2017 and the Supreme Administrative Court’s earlier ruling of 10 April 2019 in *Teliatnikov v. Lithuania*. It held that the constitutional duty of a citizen to perform mandatory military service or alternative national defence service applied to ministers of both traditional and non-traditional churches and religious organisations. Accordingly, there was a legal basis for the military authorities’ decision not to release the applicant from mandatory military service. The Supreme Administrative Court further held that questions related to the applicant’s status as subject to conscription—such as whether he was medically fit, which type of service should apply, or what the conditions of service should be—were not the subject matter of the case.

The applicant complains under Article 9 of the Convention that, despite his genuinely held religious beliefs and conscience, he was denied the right to refuse military service. He states that he never denied his civic obligations, but that Lithuanian law did not provide for alternative civilian service. The alleged violation is therefore that he was required to perform military service or alternative national defence service, while his conscientious objection and request for civilian service were not accommodated or properly assessed by the domestic authorities.
001-242059:
In *Stojević v. Croatia* (Application no. 39852/20), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the confiscation of undeclared cash. The applicant, Mr Zvonko Stojević, a Croatian national born in 1952 and living in Vienna, complained that Croatia had violated his property rights by confiscating EUR 100,000.

The relevant events occurred on 7 December 2011, when the applicant attempted to leave Croatia carrying EUR 100,000 in cash. He failed to declare the money to Croatian customs authorities. Since failure to declare cash exceeding EUR 10,000 was an administrative offence under domestic rules on foreign currency operations and money-laundering prevention, the money was temporarily seized and administrative-offence proceedings were initiated.

In his defence, the applicant stated that he had borrowed the money from a certain Mr A.P. in order to travel to the United Kingdom, where he intended to obtain a loan. He submitted a certificate co-signed by A.P. confirming that A.P. had lent him the money and that the applicant was to repay it with unspecified interest. A.P. also testified and confirmed that he had lent the money to the applicant.

By decision of 21 February 2014, the Ministry of Finance found the applicant guilty of the administrative offence. It fined him 5,000 Croatian kunas, approximately EUR 665. More significantly for the Convention complaint, it also confiscated the entire EUR 100,000 in cash. The Ministry rejected the applicant’s defence as unconvincing, finding that he had failed to demonstrate the legitimate origin of the money—namely, that it had been lent to him by A.P.—and had also failed to demonstrate its purpose.

The applicant appealed, specifically challenging the confiscation measure. On 16 December 2015, the High Court for Administrative Offences dismissed his appeal and upheld the Ministry’s decision. He then lodged a constitutional complaint alleging, among other things, a violation of his right to property. The Constitutional Court dismissed that complaint by decision of 15 April 2020, notified to his representative on 20 April 2020.

On 31 August 2020, the applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights. The Court gave notice to the Croatian Government only of the complaint concerning the right to property and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Before the Court, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the confiscation of the entire EUR 100,000 was disproportionate and imposed an excessive burden on him, thereby violating his property rights.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore that the applicant was stopped while exiting Croatia with undeclared cash; the full amount was seized; he was fined a relatively modest amount but also permanently deprived of the entire EUR 100,000; he attempted to prove that the money had a lawful origin as a loan from A.P.; and the domestic authorities rejected that explanation as insufficiently substantiated. The ECtHR’s examination was limited to whether that complete confiscation amounted to a disproportionate interference with his right to property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-242762:
The case *Fortuzi v. Albania* (Application no. 29237/18) concerns complaints before the European Court of Human Rights about the length of domestic proceedings relating to property restitution and the applicant’s lack of access to Albania’s Constitutional Court. The applicant, Gazmend Fortuzi, an Albanian national born in 1937, was represented by lawyer S. Mëneri. The Court’s Third Section gave notice to the Albanian Government of the complaints concerning the length of proceedings and access to the Constitutional Court, and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

In 1995 the applicant asked the Durrës Regional Office for Restitution and Compensation of Property to restitute property that his father had sold to third parties. The Durrës Office rejected the request on 28 June 2007. In July 2007 the applicant appealed to the Tirana Agency for Restitution and Compensation of Property, which also rejected his request on 13 September 2007.

On 10 May 2010 the applicant brought a civil action before the Tirana District Court, seeking annulment of those administrative decisions and recognition of his ownership of the property.
