The District Court dismissed his claim on 21 October 2011. He appealed on 4 November 2011. In the Tirana Court of Appeal, hearings were adjourned on 17 May, 7 and 20 June, and 17 July 2012 because his lawyer was absent. On 20 November 2012 the Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance decision. On 20 September 2014 the applicant lodged a further appeal with the Supreme Court, which dismissed it on 8 December 2015. The Supreme Court’s decision was not served on the applicant.

The access-to-court complaint arose from subsequent events. On 8 November 2016, Law no. 99/2016 was published. It shortened the time-limit for lodging a constitutional complaint from two years to four months from “obtaining knowledge of the interference” with a constitutional right or freedom, and entered into force on 1 March 2017. The applicant learned of the Supreme Court’s decision on 22 June 2017, when he obtained it from the Registry of the Tirana District Court. On 21 October 2017 he lodged a constitutional complaint. The Constitutional Court dismissed it on 7 December 2017 as being out of time, counting the four-month period from the date the Supreme Court’s decision had been adopted rather than from the date the applicant learned of it. The Government claimed the applicant received the Constitutional Court’s decision on 7 December 2017; the applicant claimed he received it on 12 December 2017 and submitted a notification showing that the decision was sent to him on 12 December 2017.

The applicant died on 28 March 2023. His wife, Ildika Fortuzi, and his children, Gledion Fortuzi, Eldira Fortuzi, and Adhurin Fortuzi, expressed a wish to pursue the application. The key alleged violations are therefore the excessive length of the property-related administrative and civil proceedings and the denial of effective access to the Constitutional Court, particularly because of the time-limit calculation and the alleged lack of service of the Supreme Court’s decision.
001-243553:
The applicant, K.V. Mediterranean Tours Limited, is a Cypriot company that owns a building complex in the fenced-up area of Famagusta, in northern Cyprus. Its shareholders and directors are of Greek Cypriot origin. The company abandoned the property after the 1974 Turkish military operation in Cyprus.

On 23 July 2010 the company applied to the Immovable Property Commission (“IPC”) seeking compensation for loss of use of its property, statutory interest, restitution, compensation for non-pecuniary damage, and legal costs. When the authorities of the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”) did not reply, the company applied for a default judgment on 1 November 2010. Between 7 December 2010 and 25 June 2012, ten hearings on the default application were adjourned at the request of the “TRNC” Office of the Attorney General, which said a necessary property report had not been prepared. On 23 October 2012 the applicant complained about delays.

At a hearing, the Attorney General’s office indicated that the property appeared to be registered in the name of a religious organisation, the Abdullah Paşa Foundation, managed by the Evkaf Administration. On 23 November 2012 the IPC admitted the Evkaf Administration as a third party because it might be affected by the claim. The applicant challenged that decision and the delays before the “TRNC” Administrative Court. On 6 November 2015 the Administrative Court held that the Evkaf Administration could not be admitted as a third party because this would make restitution impossible. It also held that it lacked jurisdiction to rule on complaints about adjournments and delays before the IPC.

On appeal, the “TRNC” High Administrative Court ruled on 29 November 2016 that it had exclusive jurisdiction over all matters relating to IPC proceedings, but that adjournments and delays were not subject to judicial review. Relying on a 27 December 2005 judgment of the “TRNC” Famagusta District Court, it found that the Evkaf Administration was the current registered owner of the property and should therefore be admitted as a party.

On 11 December 2019 the “TRNC” authorities filed submissions with the IPC. From 9 January 2020 the applicant company and its representative refused to attend IPC hearings. Further hearings were scheduled in 2020, but they did not attend. On 22 February 2024 the applicant’s representative attended a hearing and agreed to consider compensation proposals, but later stated that settlement could be reached during the proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights. The IPC proceedings remain pending.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights on 25 May 2017. It alleged a lack of effectiveness of the IPC proceedings, a violation of its right to a fair and impartial tribunal, and discrimination under Articles 6, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key alleged violations concerned: (1) the excessive length of proceedings before the IPC; (2) the practice applied to the Famagusta fenced-up area, particularly the intervention of the Islamic Foundation/Evkaf Administration in the proceedings; and (3) the alleged lack of impartiality of the High Administrative Court as the higher judicial authority for IPC cases.

Under Law no. 67/2005, the IPC may decide on restitution, exchange, or compensation. The applicant bears the burden of proving ownership as of 20 July 1974. The defendant is the Ministry and/or the “TRNC” Attorney-General. Persons holding property rights may be invited to participate as interested parties. The case arises from the broader property issues following the 1974 Turkish military operation in northern Cyprus.
001-242534:
In *Heinz and Haiderer v. Austria*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 3 April 2025 after deliberating in private on 13 March 2025. The case originated in two applications against Austria lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants, Robert Carsten Heinz (born 1965) and Wilhelm Haiderer (born 1969), both complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings. The Austrian Government were given notice of the applications.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are set out in the appended table. In application no. 33010/22, Robert Carsten Heinz, represented by Karl Schelling of Dornbirn, introduced his application on 4 July 2022. The domestic civil proceedings began on 21 September 2012 and ended on 4 January 2022. The total length was 9 years, 3 months and 15 days, spanning four levels of jurisdiction.

In application no. 31668/23, Wilhelm Haiderer, represented by Stefan Gloß of St. Pölten, introduced his application on 31 July 2023. The domestic civil proceedings began on 8 July 2014. According to the appended table, those proceedings were still pending at the relevant time. The total length was therefore more than 10 years, 6 months and 21 days, spanning three levels of jurisdiction.

The central alleged violation is the excessive length of civil proceedings, engaging the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicants’ complaints focus on delay in the domestic civil litigation rather than on the substantive outcome of their cases. The durations are substantial: Heinz’s proceedings lasted nearly a decade and passed through four judicial levels, while Haiderer’s had already exceeded ten and a half years and remained unresolved, having passed through three levels. These facts are directly relevant to assessing whether the Austrian authorities failed to comply with the reasonable-time requirement.

The application in Heinz’s case was lodged after the domestic proceedings had ended in January 2022, whereas Haiderer’s application was lodged while the domestic proceedings were still pending. Both applicants were legally represented before the Court. The Court’s task was to examine whether the total length of the proceedings was unreasonable and whether any effective domestic remedy or justification for the delay existed.

However, the excerpt provided does not disclose the subject matter of the underlying civil disputes, the reasons for the delay, any domestic decisions concerning length complaints, or the Court’s final findings on the merits. It primarily records the procedural history, applicant details, and overall durations. The Committee was composed of Anne Louise Bormann (President), Sebastian Răduleţu, and András Jakab, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. In essence, the case concerns two Austrian civil litigants alleging that their proceedings, lasting approximately 9 years and more than 10 years respectively, violated the reasonable-time guarantee.
001-245810:
Constantinou and Others v. Cyprus concerns five applications (nos. 77396/14, 45039/20, 45089/20, 45101/20 and 45899/20) lodged by 450 Cypriot nationals against Cyprus. The applicants complain about State deductions from public-sector salaries and pensions during Cyprus’s economic crisis. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of complaints under Article 6 § 1 (applications nos. 45039/20, 45089/20, 45101/20 and 45899/20), Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (all applications), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 (application no. 77396/14); the remaining complaints were declared inadmissible.

The first set of facts concerns Law no. 112(I)/2011. Enacted on 31 August 2011 and effective from 1 September 2011, it imposed a tiered “extraordinary contribution” deducted monthly from the gross salaries and pensions of officials, employees and pensioners in the civil service and wider public sector. Deductions began at salaries over €1,500 and ranged from 1.5% to 3.5%. Initially valid for 24 months, the law was extended to 31 December 2016. A similar contribution was later imposed on private-sector workers from January 2012. The applicants challenged the law before the Supreme Court, arguing that their salaries were property protected by Article 23 of the Constitution and that the deductions violated Articles 23, 24 and 28 of the Constitution and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In Charalambous and Others (11 June 2014), the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges 9–3. The majority held that the law was not a tax, that salary was a proprietary right but did not guarantee a particular amount, and that the relatively small deductions did not affect the core of the right. It found the measure justified by the severe financial crisis and public interest. Dissenting judges considered the deductions an unconstitutional deprivation or restriction because fiscal consolidation was not among the permissible grounds in Article 23 § 3.

The second set of facts concerns Law no. 168(I)/2012. Enacted on 6 December 2012 and effective from 1 December 2012, it reduced the emoluments and pensions of public and wider public-sector officials, employees and pensioners. Deductions initially ranged from 0% to 12.5%, later rising to as much as 17.5%, with no expiry date; they were discontinued on 1 January 2023. The applicants challenged the reductions in the Administrative Court. In 2018 and 2019, the first-instance court found the reductions unconstitutional under Article 23, because the public-interest justification relied on by the State was not among the exceptions in Article 23 § 3. On appeal, the Supreme Court in Avgousti and Others (10 April 2020) reversed 9–4. The majority held that salaries and pensions were property rights but did not guarantee a specific amount; the reductions were temporary, income-related, effective and did not affect the core or living standards, and were justified by the economic crisis. Dissenting judges argued that Article 23 afforded stricter protection than Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, that public interest was not a permissible ground, and that the reductions amounted to unconstitutional restrictions without compensation.

Before the ECtHR, the key alleged violations are that the deductions interfered with the applicants’ property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; that the domestic proceedings failed to comply with Article 6 § 1; and that the measures were discriminatory under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. The central factual backdrop is Cyprus’s severe economic crisis, the State’s fiscal consolidation measures, and the conflicting domestic court decisions on whether public-interest salary and pension cuts were constitutional.
001-242058:
The case of **Pápics and Others v. Hungary** (Applications nos. 13727/20 and 15 others) concerns 16 Hungarian applicants serving life imprisonment without release on parole. The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 4 March 2025. The central alleged violation is Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman and degrading punishment. The applicants complain that their whole-life sentences, combined with the fact that mandatory pardon proceedings can take place only after they have served forty years, constitute inhuman and degrading punishment.

The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The Hungarian Government was represented by Z. Tallódi. The Court gave notice of the Article 3 complaint in application no. 49294/20 and of all remaining applications to the Government, and declared the remainder of application no. 49249/20 inadmissible. Judge P. Paczolay, the judge elected in respect of Hungary, withdrew from sitting in the case.

The applicants are Hungarian nationals born between 1966 and 1990, residing in Szeged, Budapest, Tiszalök, and Szekszárd. Most were represented by Evelyn Frank; Róbert Magyar was represented by Csilla Csugányné Lakatos.

The key facts are that each applicant was convicted by final judgment in Hungary and sentenced to life imprisonment without release on parole. The final convictions occurred between 2007 and 2023. The offences included aggravated murder, murder, robbery, incitement to murder, abuse of firearms, causing bodily harm, and other crimes. Several applicants were sentenced as recidivists or multiple recidivists. The sentences were imposed by various Hungarian courts of appeal or high courts.

Specific examples from the appended table include: Ferenc Pápics (b. 1968), sentenced by the Pécs Court of Appeal on 10 February 2009 for aggravated murder; József Ottlakán (b. 1973), sentenced as a recidivist by the Szeged Court of Appeal on 10 May 2023 for murder, robbery, and other crimes; Zoltán Sipőcz (b. 1978), sentenced by the Győr Court of Appeal on 17 February 2009 for aggravated murder; János Navratil (b. 1980), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Szeged Court of Appeal on 27 February 2014 for murder and robbery; József Áldott (b. 1977), sentenced by the Győr Court of Appeal on 2 October 2007 for aggravated murder and abuse of firearms; Róbert Magyar (b. 1970), sentenced by the Debrecen Court of Appeal on 13 March 2012 for incitement to murder and other crimes; Tibor János Mészáros (b. 1975), sentenced by the Szeged Court of Appeal on 29 April 2015 for murder, robbery, and other crimes; Lajos Tétényi (b. 1990), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Győr Court of Appeal on 10 October 2019 for murder; Zoltán Maczák (b. 1976), sentenced by the Szeged Court of Appeal on 29 June 2015 for aggravated murder; Krisztián Kovács (b. 1984), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Pécs Court of Appeal on 30 May 2018 for murder and other crimes; Attila Rézműves (b. 1967), sentenced by the Budapest High Court on 18 March 2016 for aggravated murder, upheld on appeal on 14 September 2016; Mihály Balog (b. 1966), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Budapest Court of Appeal on 10 December 2020 for robbery and other crimes; János Dániel Nagy (b. 1974), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Győr Court of Appeal on 24 May 2017 for murder; István Szűcs (b. 1980), sentenced by the Szeged High Court on 22 September 2011 for multiple aggravated murders; József Sándor (b. 1973), sentenced as a recidivist by the Budapest Court of Appeal on 4 July 2017 for aggravated multiple murder; and Gábor Horváth (b. 1982), sentenced as a multiple recidivist by the Győr Court of Appeal on 1 February 2022 for aggravated murder, robbery, and causing bodily harm.

The common fact relevant to the alleged Article 3 violation is that none of the applicants has access to ordinary parole. Instead, mandatory pardon proceedings can occur only after forty years of imprisonment. The applicants argue that this regime leaves them without a realistic prospect of release and therefore amounts to inhuman and degrading punishment.
001-244594:
**Vervele v. Greece** (Application no. 34012/20, Third Section, judgment 26 August 2025) concerns the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings in Greece and the effectiveness of the domestic remedy for that delay. The applicant, Ms Nikoletta Vervele, a Greek national born in 1945, worked as a cleaner at Ippokrateio General Hospital of Athens from 1984. On 22 June 2001 she brought a civil action against the hospital, claiming EUR 75,739.72 in salary supplements and allowances allegedly owed for the period 1 June 1994 to 31 December 2000 under an indefinite employment contract.

A prior related action was already pending. On 23 June 1994, the applicant had sued the same hospital for salary supplements and allowances for 1 January 1986 to 31 May 1994. In judgment no. 882/2000, the Athens Court of First Instance partly allowed that claim and awarded her EUR 15,298. The hospital appealed, and the appeal was heard on 15 January 2002. In the meantime, in the 2001 action, the Athens Court of First Instance by decision no. 871/2002 of 15 April 2002 adjourned the case under Article 249 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It considered it necessary to wait for a final judgment in the earlier action in order to avoid conflicting judgments. That earlier action was only concluded on 24 February 2011, when the Athens Court of Appeal delivered judgment no. 826/2011 dismissing the hospital’s appeal and confirming the first-instance award.

The applicant made repeated requests for a hearing in the 2001 action—on 5 April 2004, 7 June 2007, 19 May 2009 and 23 August 2010. The action was eventually heard on 24 May 2012. On 7 June 2012, by decision no. 1091/2012, the Athens Court of First Instance adjourned again because decision no. 871/2002 and the hospital’s observations were missing from the case file. On 14 December 2012 the applicant requested a new hearing date. The next hearing took place on 18 February 2015. By judgment no. 942/2015, delivered on 20 April 2015, the first-instance court partly upheld her action. It ordered the hospital to pay EUR 21,250.66 plus statutory interest for 1999–2000, but found that claims concerning 1994–1998 had become time-barred under the two-year limitation period in Article 48 § 3 of Legislative Decree no. 496/1974.

The applicant appealed on 18 May 2015. The appeal was presented on 25 September 2015, and a hearing was scheduled for 19 April 2016, but it was adjourned because of a lawyers’ strike and rescheduled for 5 December 2017. By decision no. 5366/2018, delivered on 1 November 2018 and finalised at the applicant’s expense on 6 December 2018, the Athens Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and partly upheld the action, ordering the hospital to pay EUR 55,757 plus statutory interest.

The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law on 28 November 2018, presented it on 14 December 2018, and the case was heard on 21 May 2019. By judgment no. 246/2020, delivered on 27 February 2020, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. The judgment became final on 10 March 2020, and an official copy became available on 9 April 2020.

The civil proceedings therefore lasted from 22 June 2001 until final cassation in 2020—approximately 18 years and 8 months. The key alleged violations were: (i) unreasonable length of proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, given the prolonged adjournment pending the earlier action, repeated delays in fixing hearings, further adjournments, the lawyers’ strike, and delays at appeal and cassation; and (ii) lack of an effective domestic remedy under Article 13, notwithstanding Greece’s Law no. 4239/2014 on just satisfaction for excessive length. The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 August 2020. The Court gave notice only of the Article 6 § 1 length complaint and the Article 13 complaint; the remainder was declared inadmissible.
001-245684:
Case of Vainik and Others v. Estonia (Applications nos. 3184/21, 17982/21, 43852/21 and 44600/21) concerns a total ban on smoking in Estonian prisons. The applicants—Denis Lvov, Rene Vainik, Nikolai Šmeljov and Dmitri Tsajun—were prisoners in Viru Prison when the ban entered into force on 1 October 2017. They alleged that the ban violated their rights under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice only of the complaint concerning the total smoking ban and declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible.

The ban had two main sources. On 6 October 2016, the Minister of Justice amended the Internal Prison Rules by adding section 641(31), which prohibited detainees from possessing smokable tobacco products and items used to assemble or smoke them. On 24 April 2017, the governor of Viru Prison amended the prison’s house rules to completely ban smoking on its premises. Both measures took effect on 1 October 2017.

Before the total ban, indoor smoking in prisons had already been prohibited since 2010, and tobacco was kept in lockers. Smoking was only allowed in designated outdoor areas. The number of cigarettes prisoners could take with them during outdoor walks was gradually reduced: from five until May 2016, to three, then two, and finally one cigarette per day shortly before the total ban.

All applicants were smokers. The first applicant, Lvov, had smoked for over thirty years and alleged that the ban caused depression, sleeping problems and loss of appetite. The second applicant, Vainik, was serving a life sentence and had been diagnosed with nicotine addiction in 2015; he argued that smokers could suffer withdrawal symptoms of varying intensity. The third applicant, Šmeljov, stated he had smoked for thirty years and suffered fatigue, headaches, weakness, sleeplessness and loss of appetite. The fourth applicant, Tsajun, claimed heavy nicotine addiction and severe withdrawal symptoms.

The applicants challenged the ban through prison complaints, complaints to the Ministry of Justice, and actions before the Tartu Administrative Court. The first applicant’s claim was ultimately refused because he did not pay the State fee after the administrative court, while accepting he lacked funds, found his claim lacked prospects of success. The second applicant’s complaint was dismissed after constitutional review proceedings. The third and fourth applicants initially succeeded: on 12 June 2019, the Tartu Administrative Court declared section 641(31) unconstitutional, set it aside, annulled the Viru Prison smoking ban and ordered reconsideration.

However, in judgment no. 5-19-40 of 17 December 2019, the Supreme Court of Estonia declared section 641(31) constitutional. It accepted that the ban interfered with property rights and the right to free self-realisation, but found legitimate aims: protecting non-smokers’ health, preventing fire risk, stopping cigarettes from being used as illegal currency, maintaining prison security and order, and ensuring efficient use of resources. It stated that protecting smokers’ own health or forcing them to quit was not a legitimate aim. Less restrictive measures were considered less effective. The Supreme Court also found withdrawal symptoms unlikely to be severe because of the gradual reduction and the availability of counselling and treatment, and held that the ban was not degrading treatment.

After that judgment, the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld the Viru Prison house-rule ban on 18 March 2021, and the Supreme Court refused further appeals. The applicants’ Convention complaints therefore centre on whether the total smoking ban, including the prohibition on possessing tobacco, subjected them to degrading treatment and an unjustified interference with private life.
001-243997:
In *Mediakompaniya Slovo, TOV and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 22347/14), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered a judgment on 10 July 2025. The applicants were Mediakompaniya Slovo, a publishing company; Mr Vasylenko, its director and editor-in-chief of the newspaper *Subbota Plus*; and Ms Vasylenko, the newspaper’s editorial director. The application, lodged on 7 March 2014, concerns their complaint under Article 10 of the Convention that Ukrainian courts ordered them to retract statements published in *Subbota Plus*.

The case centres on an article written by Mr Vasylenko and published on 21 March 2013, titled “Drained profitability of [V.]”. V. was a large municipal water-supply company. The article alleged serious corruption and mismanagement at V. It stated, among other things, that there had been embezzlement and squandering of tens of millions of hryvnias of State money; that funds were withdrawn through contracts with intermediary companies and inflated purchases; that private enterprises “pocketed” State money; that V. gave a 16 million hryvnia interest-free loan to a private person; that fraud occurred during renovation works; that pipes were unlawfully sold rather than installed; that employees who raised problems were fired or demoted; and that oversight officials failed to check anything. The article also referred to “right” suppliers, “watchmen”, and the likelihood that equipment would be bought from favoured suppliers “not without a sweetener”. It concluded that V. was on the verge of bankruptcy because of corruption, irresponsibility, lack of professionalism, and moral bankruptcy of its management.

In April 2013, V. sued all three applicants, seeking retraction of the statements and compensation for non-pecuniary damage. The applicants argued that the statements were value judgments not susceptible of proof, that the information was not negative, and that it was not clear from the article that the information referred to V.

On 17 June 2013, the Zhovtnevyi District Court of Zaporizhzhya found against the applicants. It examined each disputed statement and held that they were statements of fact, not value judgments. It further found that the applicants had not proved that the statements were true. The court ordered them to retract the information and to publish the operative part of the judgment in the next issue of *Subbota Plus*. It also prohibited them from disseminating the information contained in those statements “by any possible means (on the television or in printed media, on the radio, on the internet, in interviews, in conversations with any person, or by any other means).” The applicants were ordered to pay V. 1 Ukrainian hryvnia in non-pecuniary damages and UAH 458 in court fees. The court relied in particular on Article 278 of the Civil Code as in force at the material time. The applicants’ appeals were rejected, with a final decision by the Higher Specialized Court on 9 September 2013.

According to the Government, the writs of execution were never submitted to the Bailiffs Service. Ms Vasylenko died on 28 June 2020. On 29 March 2023, Mr Vasylenko informed the Court that Mediakompaniya Slovo did not wish to pursue the application.

The key Article 10 issue is whether the domestic orders—requiring retraction, publication of the judgment, and a sweeping ban on further dissemination—amounted to a disproportionate interference with the applicants’ freedom of expression, particularly in the context of public-interest allegations of corruption at a municipal utility.
001-245104:
**Summary of *Georgios Papadopoulos v. Cyprus* (Application no. 21454/21)**

The case concerns the repeated annulment of the applicant’s declaration as an elected Member of Parliament (MP) in Cyprus following the 2016 parliamentary elections.

**Background and Initial Election**

In the May 2016 elections, the applicant was a candidate for the Solidarity Movement in the Limassol constituency. Ms E.T., then president of Solidarity and a Member of the European Parliament (MEP), was declared elected as the party’s representative for Limassol. However, on 27 May 2016, Ms E.T. informed the Chief Returning Officer (CRO) that she would not take the seat in order to retain her MEP position. Cypriot law at the time only provided for filling seats vacated *after* the parliamentary term began, not seats not taken *before* the term commenced.

**First Declaration and Annulment**

On 31 May 2016, the CRO applied section 35(1) of the Elections Law by analogy and declared the applicant, the runner-up, elected. After the applicant affirmed his duties in Parliament, two individuals filed an electoral petition. On 31 May 2017, the Electoral Court annulled the applicant’s election, unanimously holding that section 35(1) only regulated seats vacated during the parliamentary term. Since Ms E.T. had never been affirmed and her seat was “not taken” rather than “vacated,” the CRO’s analogical application was impermissible in the absence of clear legislation.

**Second Declaration and Annulment**

Parliament amended section 35(1) in June 2017 to cover “not taken” seats, and on 5 July 2017 the CRO declared the applicant elected once more. The applicant took up his duties. A new electoral petition followed. On 30 April 2018, the Electoral Court, by a 6-5 majority, annulled the election for the second time and declared the 2017 amendment unconstitutional. It held that Article 66 of the Constitution addressed only “vacated” seats, not “not taken” ones. The seat had never lawfully belonged to Solidarity, and the retroactive amendment violated the principle of non-retroactivity by conferring rights retrospectively on the applicant.

**Third Declaration and Annulment**

In October 2019, Parliament amended Articles 66 and 71 of the Constitution and section 35 of the Elections Law to expressly include “renounced” and “not taken” seats. On 29 October 2019, the Returning Officer declared the applicant elected a third time. Another petition followed.

On 29 October 2020, the Electoral Court, by a 10-1 majority, annulled the election again. The court invoked the “basic structure doctrine,” holding that while constitutional amendments were generally permissible, they could not undermine the Constitution’s fundamental principles. The court found that the Twelfth Amendment and the 2019 Law violated the principle of non-retroactivity, the finality of prior Electoral Court decisions, and popular sovereignty by targeting a specific individual and applying to a seat already adjudicated as never lawfully held by Solidarity. The court concluded that had the amendments applied only to future cases, they would have been acceptable, but their retroactive effect unlawfully appointed a particular person as MP.

**Core Alleged Violation**

The applicant, a Cypriot national, lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 April 2021, complaining about the Electoral Court’s repeated decisions to annul his declaration as an elected MP, raising issues under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections).
001-243878:
A.R., a British national born in 1978 and a qualified teacher working as a taxi driver, was charged in March 2010 with raping a 17-year-old female passenger. The allegation was that he drove her to a secluded location and forcibly had sex with her without consent. He denied any sexual contact, and there was no forensic evidence linking him to the complainant. On 21 January 2011 he was acquitted at trial.

The alleged violations arise from two enhanced criminal record certificates (“ECRCs”) issued in 2011 and 2012. In March 2011, an ECRC was issued for his application for a college lecturer post. Although A.R. had no convictions or cautions, the ECRC disclosed, under police “other relevant information,” that he had been charged with rape, acquitted, and included a summary of the complainant’s account and his denial. In March 2012, a second ECRC for a private hire driver licence contained the same information.

A.R. objected, arguing that disclosure was highly prejudicial because there was no conviction, that the jury had rejected the complainant’s evidence, and that he would have to defend himself in every future job application. His internal appeals failed. The police reviewing officer considered the information relevant and sufficient, relying on the fact that the CPS had authorised a rape charge, the medical evidence, the complainant’s distress, and the absence of an apparent motive to lie. She reasoned that the allegation was more likely true than false and that the acquittal did not prove innocence. Disclosure was justified as necessary to protect vulnerable persons, especially given his proposed roles as a lecturer and taxi driver.

A.R. sought judicial review under Articles 6 § 2 and 8 of the Convention. The High Court accepted that Article 8 was engaged but found the disclosure reasonable, proportionate, and necessary to protect young and vulnerable persons. It found no breach of Article 6 § 2. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, holding that the ECRC did not undermine the acquittal and that there was no procedural link to the criminal trial; the Article 8 balance had been correctly struck. The Supreme Court granted permission only on Article 8 and dismissed the appeal in July 2018. It held that disclosure interfered with private life but was proportionate. The police were not required to conduct a “mini-trial” or reassess the trial evidence. Although the reviewing officer’s “more likely than not” approach was flawed, the chief officer could rely on the information as “not lacking substance” and possibly true, given its seriousness, relevance, and recency. The Supreme Court nevertheless raised concerns about how employers use ECRCs and the risk of unfair stigmatisation of acquitted persons.

The ECtHR application concerns whether the 2011 and 2012 disclosures violated A.R.’s rights under Article 8, by interfering with private life, and Article 6 § 2, by undermining the presumption of innocence following acquittal.
001-245390:
In *A.J. and L.E. v. Spain* (Applications nos. 40312/23 and 40388/23), two Spanish nationals lodged complaints against Spain under Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They alleged that the Spanish authorities failed to conduct an effective criminal investigation into their complaints of sexual assault by chemical submission, and that crucial evidence in police custody was lost or manipulated.

The alleged facts concerned the night of 7–8 December 2016, when the applicants went to a bar in Pamplona and met two men, D.C.M. and R.G.S. The applicants claimed that after drinking alcohol with the men they had no recollection of events until waking the next morning in one man’s residence, undressed and with the physical sensation of having had sexual intercourse. They alleged they had been drugged and rendered unable to consent. On 11 December 2016 A.J. attended a health centre. The medical report noted no genital lesions but activated the protocol for suspected sexual assault involving chemical submission and notified the police. L.E. did not seek immediate medical attention.

The National Police UFAM unit investigated. On 27 December 2016 police arrested the two men, and on 29 December the court questioned them. Both admitted sexual intercourse but claimed it was consensual. Restraining orders were imposed. Formal proceedings opened in January 2017. During the investigation, it emerged that R.G.S. was the brother-in-law of a UFAM police officer assigned to the case. Several pieces of potentially crucial evidence also disappeared or were compromised while in police custody: the full forensic report on R.G.S.’s mobile phone vanished after being sent from Madrid to Pamplona in April 2017; bar video surveillance footage was partially lost or altered; and a hard drive containing forensic data from both suspects’ phones, including backups, was wiped and overwritten.

In November 2018 the investigating court declined to prosecute. It found the applicants’ accounts credible but held that there was insufficient evidence of non-consensual acts. No timely toxicological evidence supported chemical submission, physical discomfort could not be definitively linked to the alleged events, and forensic examination showed no injuries typically associated with violent sexual assault. In October 2021 the court concluded the proceedings without charges. It noted that hair analysis found no chemical submission substances but that both applicants had prescription medication that could have increased alcohol’s effects. Taxi drivers, bar staff, and a friend had observed nothing clearly unusual. The court acknowledged the investigation had been “notably affected” by irregularities and missing digital evidence, but still found insufficient substantive evidence. The Audiencia Provincial upheld the closure in June 2022 and provisional dismissal in September 2022. The Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal inadmissible in July 2023 on procedural grounds.

Separate investigations were opened into the alleged police misconduct, including digital evidence deletion, video manipulation, and hard-drive erasure. These were discontinued or closed for lack of evidence of intentional wrongdoing, and an internal disciplinary file remained suspended. The ECtHR’s key focus was therefore whether Spain breached its procedural obligations under Articles 3 and 8 by failing to effectively investigate the alleged chemically facilitated sexual assault and by losing or mishandling critical evidence.
001-240242:
**Case: A.R.E. v. Greece (App. No. 15783/21)** concerns the alleged “pushback” of a Turkish national from Greece to Türkiye in May 2019, raising issues under Articles 2, 3, 5, and 13 ECHR.

The applicant, a Turkish national born in 1992, had been accused of membership in FETÖ/PDY. She was detained for 28 months, then sentenced in March 2019 to six years and three months’ imprisonment, but released pending appeal with a ban on leaving Türkiye. On 4 May 2019, she crossed the Evros River into Greece with two other Turkish nationals seeking international protection. Near Nea Vyssa, she contacted her brother, an asylum seeker in Greece, using WhatsApp live location. She sent photos and videos stating she feared unlawful removal. She and her brother also emailed UNHCR, explaining their fear of pushback and danger if returned to Türkiye.

A lawyer, N.O., traveled to Nea Vyssa. Shortly afterward, police arrived and arrested the three Turkish nationals. The applicant alleged that police refused to let the lawyer enter the vehicle but allowed him to follow in his car. At the police station, she requested asylum for the first time; she repeated the request at the Orestiada border guard station in Neo Cheimonio. She claimed she was then held unofficially until 7 p.m., when the alleged pushback began.

She described being transferred in a green van and later in a larger lorry with 31 migrants. Their belongings—bags, shoes, mobile phones, and money—were confiscated. She had injured her leg and was forced to walk barefoot, worsening her injury. Near the Evros River, masked men in camouflage, probably police officers, made them disembark. Those who resisted, including Syrians, were allegedly beaten. When she shouted “asylum,” an officer allegedly replied in Turkish, “you will see where we will take you.” Around 11 p.m., they were placed in a small inflatable boat and returned to Türkiye in several crossings. Turkish gendarmerie arrested them. She was taken to Edirne Prison and later Gebze Prison. Her brother lost her WhatsApp location at 6:52 p.m. on 4 May 2019.

Domestically, the Greek Council for Refugees filed a complaint in June 2019 alleging abuse of power, unlawful detention, life-endangerment, bodily harm, torture, and other offences. In December 2019, the Orestiada prosecutor dismissed the complaint for lack of evidence. On appeal, further investigation heard lawyer N.O. and journalist Z.K. N.O. stated he had seen the applicant in Nea Vyssa, witnessed her arrest, and later saw the van at the Orestiada border guard station. Z.K. described communications with the applicant and her brother and the location tracking. In September 2020, the prosecutor again dismissed the case, finding no substantiating evidence, noting no arrest of a person with the same name, stating police had orders and did not conduct pushbacks, and concluding asylum would have been possible if she had been detected.

The Greek Government denied all allegations. It argued that the evidence was unverified, that photos and videos lacked metadata, that the applicant’s brother never testified, and that N.O.’s account was unreliable. The applicant maintained that she had submitted evidence, including a Turkish court decision referring to her pushback, and that she had indeed been arrested and imprisoned in Türkiye. The case therefore turned on whether the alleged pushback, detention, and risk of ill-treatment in Türkiye were established and whether Greece violated the Convention.
001-242857:
The case of *Lubarda and Milanov v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 6570/19 and 43604/19) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights, Third Section. The judgment was delivered on 29 April 2025. The applicants are two Serbian nationals, Zoran Lubarda and Slađan Milanov. Their applications alleged violations of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically the right to a fair trial, in minor-offence proceedings concerning road-traffic offences.

The first applicant, Lubarda, was convicted in 2017 of failing to comply with a traffic light signal. He was fined EUR 120, banned from driving for three months, and received penalty points. The second applicant, Milanov, was convicted in 2015 of driving while intoxicated, described as being in a state of complete intoxication. He was fined EUR 850, banned from driving for eight months, and also received penalty points. Although the cases were dealt with as minor offences, both offences were potentially punishable by imprisonment. Under Serbia’s Minor Offences Act, if the fines were not paid, they could be converted into effective prison sentences — up to 15 days for Lubarda and up to 60 days for Milanov. This factor was relevant to whether Article 6’s criminal-fair-trial guarantees applied.

In both cases, police officers drew up reports at the scene of the incidents. The applicants signed those reports but later disputed their contents in court. Their convictions were based on the police reports and on evidence given by the police officers. However, the police officers’ evidence was taken in court but not during the main hearings in the applicants’ cases. Neither applicant nor their lawyers were summoned to the examination of those witnesses, even though both had explicitly requested to be present and to cross-examine them. In Lubarda’s case, the request was refused on grounds of efficiency and economy of proceedings. In Milanov’s case, the court held that cross-examination would not have led to a different determination of facts because the officer’s witness evidence was consistent with the report Milanov had signed.

Both applicants appealed against their convictions. The Appeals Court upheld the convictions, and the Constitutional Court subsequently also upheld them. The final domestic decisions were notified to Lubarda on 1 August 2018 and to Milanov on 26 February 2019. They then lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights, relying on Article 6 of the Convention. They complained that the minor-offence proceedings against them had not been fair because they were not given an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses whose statements formed the basis of their convictions. The Government was given notice of the applications and submitted observations, and the Court rejected the Government’s objection to examination by a Committee. The central alleged violation was therefore the lack of cross-examination of police witnesses in proceedings that carried potential imprisonment, contrary to the applicants’ fair-trial rights under Article 6.
001-244728:
**Case: Radchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 21217/17), European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), judgment 11 September 2025.** The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1977, alleged violations of Articles 10 and 13 of the Convention. The case concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a domestic court judgment ordering the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Ukraine to provide him with public environmental information.

The applicant’s request was prompted by several environmental incidents in the Kyiv Region in June 2015: massive fires at a petroleum storage depot on 8 June, a plastic goods warehouse on 12 June, and peat burning from 9 June. On 17 June 2015, relying on the Law on Access to Public Information and the Law on Protection of Environment, he asked the Ministry for: (i) air pollution levels by district and dangerous gases; (ii) measures to combat pollution and improve air quality; (iii) the Ministry’s own measures against technogenic catastrophes; and (iv) the names and addresses of the owners of the depot and warehouse, their responsibility, and compensation for damage.

The Ministry, acting through the State Ecologic Inspectorate, replied but, as later court judgments established, provided none of the requested information. The reply referred to a general ban on inspections, a special request to inspect the P. company, and soil and water tests. The applicant sued. On 17 September 2015, the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court granted his claim. It found the Ministry’s reply contained none of the requested information and gave no explanation for the refusal. It held that the Ministry had broad environmental duties, that the requested information was public, and that environmental danger information had to be communicated within 48 hours. It ordered a full reply within that time-limit.

On 26 October 2015, the Ministry sent another letter, providing information about air-quality monitoring bodies, links to data on the Kyiv Regional Sanitary and Epidemic Service website, and a 2015–16 plan concerning the petroleum depot fire. The applicant considered this incomplete and sought enforcement and judicial control. On 25 November 2015, the Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court acknowledged the Ministry’s omissions. It found that air-quality measurements were scattered and irregular, and that ecological information was not systematically gathered or publicized, causing a “systemic violation of the citizens’ right to information about the environment,” partly due to legislative inconsistencies. The court stated that those systemic problems could not be resolved through an individual court judgment and issued a separate ruling addressed to the Ministry, the Cabinet of Ministers, the National Security and Defence Council, and a parliamentary committee.

The applicant then initiated enforcement proceedings in respect of the 17 September 2015 judgment. The Ministry sent further replies. A letter of 21 September 2018 stated that a governmental commission created on 9 June 2015 had conducted laboratory air monitoring, disseminated daily information, taken measures, and found no excess pollution, but that the Ministry did not possess part of the requested information concerning air pollution levels. The enforcement proceedings were terminated and reopened multiple times. Courts essentially held that the Ministry could not be exempted from fully enforcing the judgment, despite claiming unavailability of certain information. In October 2019, the enforcement proceedings were definitively terminated for impossibility of enforcement “without the debtor’s participation.” A bailiff complained to the police about possible wilful non-enforcement, but no criminal proceedings were instituted for lack of elements of an offence. The applicant’s challenge failed.

In October 2016, the applicant also complained to the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights. The Commissioner found that the Ministry did not possess comparative air pollution data, that only “existing” information is public, and requested the Cabinet to ensure the Ministry complied with its environmental obligations.

The alleged violations therefore concern the failure to enforce a final judgment ordering the provision of public environmental information and the alleged absence of an effective remedy, under Articles 10 and 13.
001-242788:
In *Andersen v. Poland* (Application no. 53662/20), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) examined an application lodged on 18 November 2020 by Mr Bartholomew Kyle Andersen, a Polish national born in 1988 who lives in Colwyn Bay, United Kingdom. The applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. His complaint concerned Poland’s refusal to recognise his same-sex marriage contracted abroad and the absence of any other form of legal recognition or protection for his relationship.

The key facts are these. On 7 May 2016, the applicant married his same-sex partner in Conwy, United Kingdom. In February 2017, he requested the Goszczyn Civil Status Office to register his marriage contracted abroad in the Polish civil registry. The Civil Status Office refused. It reasoned that entering a same-sex marriage in the Polish Registry would be contrary to the “basic principles of the Polish law.” The applicant appealed. The Mazowiecki Governor upheld the refusal. The Warsaw Regional Administrative Court also upheld the decision. The applicant then brought a cassation appeal. On 25 February 2020, the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his cassation appeal. The judgment was notified to the applicant on 21 May 2020.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that there was a total lack of recognition of his relationship in Poland. He complained that his marriage contracted abroad was not recognised by the Polish authorities in any way. He further complained that it was impossible for him to enter into any type of legally recognised union with his same-sex partner in Poland. According to the application, there was no other form of legal recognition and protection available for his relationship. The alleged violation under Article 8 therefore concerned the combined effect of the refusal to register his foreign same-sex marriage and the absence of any alternative legal framework recognising or protecting same-sex relationships in Poland. The case thus raised issues about the legal recognition of same-sex couples, the effect of such non-recognition on private and family life, and the State’s positive obligations under Article 8.

The Polish Government was given notice of the application and was represented by its Agent, Mr J. Sobczak of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The parties submitted observations. The Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture was granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section and submitted third-party comments. The case was decided by a Committee of the First Section composed of Judges Erik Wennerström (President), Raffaele Sabato, and Artūrs Kučs, with Liv Tigerstedt as Deputy Section Registrar.

The judgment was delivered on 24 April 2025. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are that the applicant had a validly contracted same-sex marriage abroad, sought its registration in Poland, was refused at every domestic level on the ground that same-sex marriage conflicts with basic principles of Polish law, and had no alternative form of legally recognised union or protection available to him in Poland. The applicant’s Article 8 complaint therefore focused on the total non-recognition of his same-sex relationship and its consequences for his private and family life.
001-244593:
In *B.A. v. Iceland* (Application no. 17006/20, judgment 26 August 2025), the applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1975, complained under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14, that the Icelandic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into her allegations of domestic violence and sexual assault and discriminated against her on gender grounds in handling such cases.

In December 2017, B.A. lodged a police complaint against her former cohabitant, F.Þ., alleging physical, psychological, and sexual violence during their relationship between 2011 and 2014. She claimed F.Þ. humiliated and criticised her, isolated her from family, and controlled her life. The abuse allegedly intensified during her pregnancy and escalated into physical and sexual violence. She described four sexual-violence incidents: being coerced into sexually stimulating F.Þ. while hospitalised during pregnancy; being raped at a rehabilitation clinic; being raped in the hallway of their home; and being raped while sleeping, which left bruising. She also alleged two physical incidents—a brief chokehold and a headbutt. She stated she never sought immediate medical attention after any incident.

During the police investigation, F.Þ. was questioned in September 2018. He denied all wrongdoing and attributed relationship difficulties to the applicant’s excessive alcohol consumption. He admitted sexual intercourse at the rehabilitation clinic but denied rape. While denying psychological violence, he admitted controlling behaviour when urging her to stop drinking or avoid work while intoxicated. Eleven witnesses were questioned. Several observed changes in the applicant after cohabitation began, including reduced contact with others. Some described F.Þ. humiliating her or displaying anger. One witness heard the applicant scream and found her trembling and scared after an alleged chokehold. No one directly witnessed the physical or sexual violence; most accounts were based on disclosures after the relationship ended. The file contained a Stígamót certificate from December 2017 stating she had attended since April 2015 and reported severe mental, physical, and sexual violence by F.Þ.; psychiatric records from 2012 and 2017 documenting depression and anxiety; and a psychologist’s February 2019 statement diagnosing PTSD following an alleged sexual offence.

In June 2019, police discontinued the investigation. As to sexual violence, they found insufficient evidence given F.Þ.’s denial and concluded further investigation would not improve the evidentiary position. As to physical violence, Article 218b of the General Penal Code—the domestic-violence provision—had not been enacted until 2016, so the conduct could only be considered under Article 217; the two-year limitation period had expired. In September 2019, the State Prosecutor upheld this decision, finding Article 218b could not apply retroactively, the Article 217 offence was time-barred, and the sexual-violence evidence—including witness testimony and expert documentation of distress—was not sufficiently strong to overcome F.Þ.’s denial or likely to secure a conviction. Further investigative measures were deemed unlikely to change the position. The applicant’s lawyer later raised whether the conduct could constitute gross defamation of a closely related person under Article 233b; the State Prosecutor replied that its review had not been limited to the police’s classification.

The alleged violations therefore centred on the authorities’ alleged failure to effectively investigate domestic violence and sexual assault and on gender-based discrimination in the handling of such cases, contrary to Articles 3, 8, and 14.
001-238661:
This case concerns seven San Marino nationals who served as officers in the Uniformed Unit of the Fortress Guard, originally on temporary contracts between 2006 and 2008. They claimed their enrolment should have become permanent after a successful one-year probationary period under Law no. 132/1987, as amended by Law no. 99/1997, which also governed career advancement. Their employment was repeatedly extended until 18 January 2016, when Parliament acknowledged their permanent recruitment under Article 63(1) of Law no. 189/2015 and assigned them a “Scale 5” career category.

Between late January and early February 2016, the applicants asked the Public Administration Personnel Management Office (“PAPMO”) to reconstruct their careers, which would affect salary and entitlements. The acknowledgments of receipt indicated that those dates started the deadline for concluding the proceedings and that remedies lay under Law no. 68/1989. No immediate reply followed. On 25 July 2016, while their requests were pending, the legislature adopted Delegated Decree no. 88/2016. Its Article 1 provided that, for persons recruited under Article 63 of Law no. 189/2015, the economic effects of retrospective career reconstruction could only run from 1 February 2016, without payment of arrears and without payment of the statutory withholding taxes normally due under Article 54 of Law no. 41/1972.

PAPMO then carried out the applicants’ career reconstruction in line with Law no. 88/2016. Each applicant allegedly suffered losses of around EUR 25,000 or more. In 2018, they asked the Minister of Foreign and Political Affairs and the Director General of Civil Service to intervene so that arrears could be paid under ordinary provisions. On 7 November 2018, the authorities confirmed that the reconstruction complied with Law no. 88/2016 and noted that the applicants had not been employed under the ordinary procedure in Law no. 132/1987, as amended by Law no. 99/1997.

On 20 March 2019, the applicants applied to the Judge of First Instance, exercising administrative jurisdiction, seeking annulment of the 7 November 2018 decision. They argued that Law no. 88/2016 was unconstitutional because it conflicted with Articles 4 (equality) and 9 (equitable remuneration) of the Declaration of the Citizens’ Rights, and asked for referral to the Constitutional Court. On 9 December 2019, the Judge of First Instance refused the referral as manifestly ill-founded, finding it legitimate to apply different conditions to persons employed through extraordinary procedures.

The applicants then challenged the judge’s continued involvement. On 17 July 2020, the Judge for Extraordinary Remedies dismissed that challenge but noted, in an obiter dictum, that the impugned provision had to be examined in light of Convention principles. He observed that the applicants had suffered a legislative interference in pending proceedings begun in January/February 2016, before the July 2016 decree. The case was returned to the Judge of First Instance.

On 4 November 2020, the Judge of First Instance dismissed the claim. He found that Law no. 88/2016 clarified Article 63(1) of Law no. 189/2015, was a lex specialis, and prevailed over ordinary rules. The applicants had benefited from permanent recruitment without any public competition, unlike officers recruited through public selection, so their different remuneration was not unreasonable, and no violation of Article 9 of the Declaration was established. On appeal, the applicants reiterated their constitutional challenge and added Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, though they later withdrew the constitutional request. On 30 March 2022, the Judge of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment, emphasising that the applicants had been recruited through an ad hoc process rather than a public competition, and ordered them to pay costs.

The Strasbourg Court gave notice of the complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and declared the remainder inadmissible. The central alleged violations concern the legislative intervention in pending career-reconstruction proceedings and the resulting loss of salary arrears and entitlements.
001-245463:
The case of *Panopoulou and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 28983/20) concerns an application lodged against Greece with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The application was introduced on 6 July 2020 by thirteen applicants, represented by Mr A. Papakonstantinou, a lawyer practising in Athens. The Greek Government were given notice of the application. Following communication of the case, the parties attempted but failed to reach a friendly settlement. The Third Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 23 October 2025.

The applicants’ details are set out in the appended table. They appear to be members of the Panopoulou and Antypas families, born between 1935 and 1991. The listed applicants include Nikoleta Panopoulou, Alexandra Gkioka, Dimitrios Gkiokas, Kalliopi Panopoulou, Magdalini Panopoulou, Alexandra Panopoulou, Kalliopi Panopoulou, Gavriela Panopoulou, Ioanna Panopoulou, Vasilios Antypas, Ioannis Antypas, and Gerasimos Antypas. The application is brought by thirteen applicants in total.

The key domestic proceeding was a judgment of the Athens Administrative Court of First Instance, Judgment no. 14300/2005, dated 30 November 2005. That judgment became final. According to the appended table, the period of non-enforcement began on 22 August 2006. The end date of the non-enforcement period is recorded as “pending.” The total length of non-enforcement is therefore stated as more than 18 years, 5 months, and 21 days.

The applicants complained before the European Court of Human Rights about the non-enforcement of that domestic judgment. They also complained of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law in that regard. In substance, the alleged violations concern the continued failure of the Greek authorities to give effect to a final domestic court decision and the absence of an adequate domestic mechanism to challenge or remedy that non-enforcement. The case therefore centres on a prolonged period during which a final administrative judgment remained unexecuted, with no effective domestic redress available to the applicants.

The available judgment excerpt records the procedural steps and factual details relevant to those complaints. It does not, in the extract provided, set out the Court’s legal reasoning or final conclusion on the merits. The essential facts relevant to the alleged violations are the existence of a final domestic judgment dated 30 November 2005, the commencement of non-enforcement on 22 August 2006, the continuation of that non-enforcement for over eighteen years and five months at the time recorded, and the applicants’ related complaint that Greek law provided no effective remedy for that situation. The case thus focuses on the prolonged non-execution of a final administrative judgment and the alleged lack of effective domestic remedies for that non-enforcement.
001-244894:
In *Chonin and Others v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 30116/23), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 30 September 2025. The application was lodged on 20 July 2023 by ten Bulgarian nationals, two of whom also hold Belgian or German nationality. The applicants were represented by Bulgarian lawyers. The Government was represented by the Ministry of Justice. The Governments of Belgium and Germany did not intervene.

The case concerns the alleged excessive length of restitution proceedings under Bulgaria’s Restitution of Title to Forests and Forestry Land Act (“the Forests Restitution Act”). The Court gave notice to the Bulgarian Government only of the complaints concerning the lengthy duration of the restitution procedure; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The applicants are heirs of Ms F. and collectively inherited about four-fifths of her estate. Ms F. had owned an afforested island in the Danube and mainland forests, all of which were nationalised in 1948. After the Forests Restitution Act was adopted in 1997, the applicants initiated restitution proceedings concerning those properties. The earlier stages of the proceedings were described in *Popov and Chonin v. Bulgaria* (no. 36094/08, 17 February 2015), brought by one of the current applicants.

In a decision dated 12 December 2000, the competent land commission, later renamed the Agriculture Department, recognised the heirs’ right to compensation in lieu of restitution for 93.38 hectares of forestry land. Restitution in kind was not possible because the land originally owned by Ms F. was located in a frontier zone and was classified as exclusive State property. Under the Forests Restitution Act, compensation could only be provided through equivalent State-owned land. As a result, the authorities spent years trying to identify suitable substitute plots. Although a 2007 court judgment identified one such plot and ordered its transfer to the applicants, that judgment was ultimately deemed unenforceable because the land formed part of a national park.

The parties informed the Court of later developments. In a series of decisions issued in 2013 and 2018, the Agriculture Departments in Montana and Berkovitsa allocated forestry land totalling about 59 hectares to the applicants. These decisions were served on Mr Chonin, who acted as representative for all applicants, in 2018. He challenged the decisions, arguing that the quality of the allocated forests was inferior to that of Ms F.’s original forests. The decisions were nevertheless upheld in final court judgments given in 2023 and 2024.

An additional plot of about 5.3 hectares has been identified, but the process of officially allocating it to the applicants remains ongoing. The competent authorities are still working to locate further plots to compensate the applicants for the remaining approximately 29 hectares of forestry land. Thus, more than two decades after the initial compensation decision, the restitution process remains incomplete. The central alleged violation concerns the prolonged duration of those restitution proceedings.
001-246017:
Lasku and Others v. Albania (Application no. 6045/14) is a case brought by 13 Albanian nationals against Albania, lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 31 December 2013. The Court gave notice of complaints concerning legal certainty, property rights, and length of proceedings; the remainder was declared inadmissible. The principal complaint is under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention: that domestic authorities annulled three final property commission decisions, breaching legal certainty. Related property and length issues arise from intertwined civil and administrative proceedings over the same land.

In 1996–97, the Tirana Commission on Property Restitution and Compensation recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over three plots totaling 1,070 sq. m and ordered their restitution. The Immovable Property Registration Office (IPRO) registered their title. In 1996, the Tirana Municipality issued a building permit for a gas station on 700 sq. m of that land. The applicants built it with M. company; in 1998 the IPRO registered their title to the gas station. The applicants then transferred administration and possession to M. company under a cooperation agreement to share profits equally.

In 2000, M. company sued the applicants for ownership of the building and land; the applicants counterclaimed for possession. In 2004, both claims were dismissed because the cooperation agreement prevented awarding possession to either party. In 2003, the applicants sued M. company for their profit share. The Tirana Court of Appeal allowed the claim in 2013, and the Supreme Court upheld that judgment in 2022. In 2021 the applicants complained about the length of these proceedings; in 2023 the Supreme Court dismissed the complaint, saying the case had already been adjudicated and the delay was attributable to Albania’s judicial reform.

The central alleged violation concerns a 2007 amendment to the Property Act that empowered the director of the Agency for the Restitution and Compensation of Property—successor to the Commission—to review and annul former commission decisions ex officio, with no time limit. On 27 November 2007, the Agency annulled the three Commission decisions restoring the 1,070 sq. m plots. It reasoned that the original commission lacked jurisdiction: the 1993 Property Act allowed it to recognise property rights and decide on restitution, but not to order actual restitution. It also said the land could not be restituted despite being registered as state property. The decision recognising the applicants’ inherited rights remained in force.

The applicants challenged that annulment. The District Court allowed their claim, but the Court of Appeal quashed that judgment in 2010 and the Supreme Court upheld it in 2012. In 2013 the Constitutional Court found violations of the applicants’ fair-trial rights by the Supreme Court and remitted the case. On retrial, in 2014 the Supreme Court again dismissed the applicants’ appeal. In 2015 the Constitutional Court dismissed their constitutional complaint, finding that the Agency’s review power was still in force when the Court of Appeal adjudicated and that its own judgments did not have retroactive effect. However, in 2010 and 2011, the Constitutional Court had annulled such amendments as unconstitutional, finding violations of legal certainty and property rights.

Separately, in 2008 the applicants brought another claim against M. company. The District Court terminated their agreement but dismissed their restitution claim; the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld that outcome in 2011 and 2022. In 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed their complaint, although it found the second set of proceedings before the Supreme Court excessively lengthy, holding it lacked jurisdiction to award compensation. In legalisation proceedings, M. company built an unauthorised construction, legalised in 2013; in 2014 the State sold M. company a 595.8 sq. m plot that formed part of the applicants’ claimed land. The applicants did not challenge the legalisation or sale. In 2016 the IPRO removed their names from the building’s owners and registered it to M. company; an administrative appeal was submitted, but no court proceedings were instituted.

The key alleged violations are therefore: annulment of final decisions undermining legal certainty; interference with property rights; and excessive length of proceedings without effective compensation.
001-238658:
In *Petrosyan v. Armenia*, the applicant, Heghine Petrosyan, is the mother of H. Movsisyan, who died in custody on 28 November 2012 while detained in Shushi Detention Centre in the unrecognised “Nagorno-Karabakh Republic” (“NKR”). The case concerns his death and the ensuing investigation, raising issues under Articles 2 and 13 of the Convention.

In June 2011, H. Movsisyan, aged 18, was conscripted into the Armenian army and assigned to a military unit of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces. Although he reportedly had health problems, he was found fit for combatant service. From the outset he had difficulty adapting, refused duties, and on 27 June 2011 left his unit; after being returned, he cut his left forearm with a razor blade during a conversation with the battalion commander. He was diagnosed with an “organic psychopathic-like disorder [and] non-adaptive decompensation with attempted suicide.” In August 2011 the Central Military Commission found him unfit for peacetime military service, fit only for non-combatant wartime service, and he was discharged in September 2011.

Meanwhile, criminal proceedings had been brought against him for evasion of military service, later changed to self-mutilation to evade service. In January 2012 the court authorised his detention, and in July 2012 he was arrested. In September 2012 he was transferred to Shushi Detention Centre. On 20 November 2012 he was convicted and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment.

Seven days later, during the night of 27-28 November 2012, he was found hanged by a bedsheet from the window bars of his cell. The official version was suicide. An autopsy concluded mechanical asphyxiation by hanging, with no alcohol detected. A later forensic report noted a scratch on his right forearm inflicted before death. Guards claimed they checked cells every ten to fifteen minutes; cellmates said they were asleep and woke only when the guard shouted. The “NKR” prosecutor’s office opened a case concerning alleged incitement to suicide. In March 2013 it terminated the proceedings, finding no threats, ill-treatment, psychological pressure or violence by detention staff or inmates. It attributed the suicide to his psychiatric disorder and recent conviction.

Separately, Armenia’s Special Investigative Service opened a case concerning official negligence, later combined with the NKR case. In December 2013 that investigation was also terminated for absence of crime, finding no negligence by investigators, prosecutors, the judge, or medical experts. In parallel, the General Prosecutor appealed H. Movsisyan’s conviction; the Court of Appeal acquitted him in April 2013, finding he had been unfit for service and unlawfully prosecuted. The Court of Cassation later terminated proceedings because of his death.

The applicant’s alleged violations focus on the state’s failure to protect her son’s life and to conduct an effective investigation. Key facts are that he died in state custody while known to have a psychiatric disorder and a prior suicide attempt. The authorities allegedly failed to monitor suicide risk or provide adequate psychological or medical care. The investigation relied heavily on detention staff and cellmates, and the applicant argued it failed to clarify crucial issues: how the hanging occurred within minutes, whether adequate first aid was given, the origin of the forearm injury, the link to his earlier suicide attempt, and possible liability of officials and experts. She was denied victim status and access to the case file, and courts refused to compel production of the full evidence, limiting her ability to challenge the termination. The case thus concerns whether Armenia complied with its positive obligation to protect a detainee’s life and conducted an effective, accessible investigation, and whether the applicant had an effective remedy.
001-242757:
In *Sadigov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 48665/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined an application by Ildirim Sadigov, an Azerbaijani national born in 1949. The case concerns the alleged unlawful demolition of his property and the domestic courts’ alleged failure to award adequate compensation, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

The building was constructed in 1955 and used as a State-owned canteen. In 2004, the applicant’s mother, who managed the canteen, purchased it under preferential privatisation conditions. The privatisation documents stated that the building had an area of 120 square metres and that she paid 3,300,000 old Azerbaijani manats (AZN 600). A technical passport was issued the same year. After the mother’s death in 2005, the applicant inherited the building. In November 2007, the Barda District Territorial Department of the State Agency on Registration of Immovable Property Rights issued a title deed confirming his ownership. The title deed and accompanying technical passport stated that the building’s area was actually 210.1 square metres and that its depreciation rate was 30%. The building housed a State-run college until January 2008.

On 3 March 2008, the Tartar District Executive Authority (“TDEA”) ordered demolition. It stated that the building, located within a public park, had been unused for several years, had deteriorated, was unusable, and did not meet modern architectural standards. The TDEA ordered demolition in the public interest without compensation. The applicant was offered five nearby plots of land as in-kind compensation but declined. The building was demolished on 13 March 2008.

The applicant sued the TDEA for AZN 117,000 in pecuniary damage for the building, AZN 60,000 in non-pecuniary damage, and AZN 25,000 for medical expenses. He claimed that although the building had been unusable at the time of privatisation, he had later fully renovated it. In August 2008, the Tartar District Court awarded him AZN 660 in pecuniary damage. On appeal, the Ganja Court of Appeal quashed that judgment and directed that the claim be examined in commercial proceedings.

In December 2008, the Ganja Local Economic Court ordered an expert valuation based on the 2004 and 2007 technical passports. The expert found the parameters essentially identical, set the price at AZN 520 per square metre, and valued the building at AZN 109,200 (about EUR 104,600 at the time). In January 2010, however, the Ganja Local Economic Court found the demolition unlawful but awarded only AZN 660 in pecuniary damages and AZN 200 in non-pecuniary damages. It rejected the expert valuation as unrealistic, found the 1955 building dilapidated and unfit for use, and dismissed the repair documents as unsigned or unapproved. It treated the AZN 660 privatisation price as adequate compensation and noted that the five-plot offer remained valid.

The Supreme Court intervened twice. In October 2010, it quashed an appellate judgment because market value could not be determined on the basis of privatisation documents and because the lower courts had not compared the expert data with the real estate register. In May 2011, the Ganja Court of Appeal awarded AZN 109,200 based on the expert report. In September 2011, the Supreme Court quashed that award because depreciation had not been considered for the old, long-used building. On re-examination, a fresh BDTD valuation in May 2012 estimated the building at AZN 16,808 (about EUR 16,253). The Ganja Court of Appeal awarded that sum, finding the building completely unusable, as the applicant himself had stated. The Supreme Court upheld this on 11 February 2013. The applicant complained to the ECtHR that the domestic courts had failed to afford him adequate redress for the unlawful demolition of his property.
001-245701:
The applicant, David Kyrian, a Czech national born in 1982, is the biological father of a child born in December 2013 from an extramarital relationship with the mother that began in 2012. Because the mother was married, her husband became the child’s legal father by presumption; the child lived with the legal parents. The applicant’s biological paternity was confirmed by a DNA test he arranged in 2015. Until February 2016 he saw the child two to four times a month when the mother visited him.

In April 2016 the applicant applied to the Příbram District Court under Article 927 of the Civil Code for contact rights. On 18 May 2016 the court granted provisional contact every Wednesday afternoon and every second Sunday in summer holidays. The Prague Regional Court upheld that decision on 9 November 2016, noting an emotional bond and the child’s right to know his biological father.
