Conflicts during visits led to supervised visits in July and August 2016. From September 2016 to November 2017 contact mostly followed the judgment, but the child’s psychological condition worsened.

In September 2017 the applicant sought more contact; the mother sought prohibition, alleging verbal abuse and that the child refused visits, was anxious and seeing a psychologist. The legal father alleged the applicant had physically assaulted him. A judgment of 3 October 2017 dismissing both requests was quashed by the Regional Court for insufficient fact-finding; it noted a weakening bond and recommended counselling. After mediation in April 2018, contact continued until mid-July 2018. On 17 July 2018 the District Court approved a mediated agreement granting contact every Wednesday afternoon and every second Sunday in summer. Later visits were missed because the child refused; an incident with the legal parents led to police being called. Two supervised visits in October 2018 ended in conflict. A psychologist report of 10 October 2018 described the child as strongly attached to his mother and legal father and stressed by imposed contact.

In December 2018 the legal parents requested prohibition. In 2020 the Český Krumlov District Court and České Budějovice Regional Court ruled that no contact regime should be set, finding no positive emotional bond or harm from lack of contact. An expert opinion cited the child’s developmental delay, attachment to his legal father, the applicant’s pressure and conflicts, and considered no contact in the child’s best interests at that time. A constitutional appeal was dismissed on 13 October 2022.

On 23 April 2021 the applicant lodged a new application seeking contact every Wednesday afternoon. At a hearing on 24 August 2021, the legal parents described the child’s anxiety; the guardian ad litem advised dismissal. An expert report of 18 March 2022 found previous conflicted visits traumatic and did not recommend contact, though future contact was not excluded. A psychologist report of 20 March 2022 noted anxiety attacks. At a hearing on 24 March 2022, the applicant alternatively sought written communication via the guardian and regular information about the child’s development. The legal parents refused, citing distress and alleging he lingered near the child’s kindergarten or their home, bordering on stalking. The guardian opposed all requests.

On 24 March 2022 the Příbram District Court dismissed the claim but warned the legal parents about non-cooperation and ordered respect for the applicant’s biological parenthood. It found contact contrary to the child’s best interests and no basis for information rights. On 12 September 2022 the Prague Regional Court upheld that judgment. On 24 January 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional appeal.

Subsequently, the legal parents divorced in April 2022 but shared custody and continued living together. The mother later moved out and resumed a relationship with the applicant, who had occasional contact through her. In 2024 shared-custody proceedings, the child said he did not want to see the mother mainly because he feared the applicant; the court placed the child with the legal father, and the mother’s contact application was dismissed because she would not meet without the applicant.
001-241986:
In *I.C. v. the Republic of Moldova*, the applicant is a Moldovan woman born in 1974 with a moderate intellectual disability. Abandoned at birth, she had no known relatives and had lived in State care her entire life. In 2011 the Soroca District Court deprived her of legal capacity owing to her intellectual disability, and no subsequent guardian appears to have been appointed. At the relevant time, she had spent twenty-four years in a State neuropsychiatric asylum.

In 2013 a couple, L.P. and I.P., approached the asylum asking for a person who could be a “bride” for G.B., an employee on their farm. They first requested that the applicant stay with them for a month, then sought her permanent placement. In March 2013 the Ministry supported termination of her asylum placement for integration into the P. family, and the asylum director issued an order releasing her. The applicant lived on the farm from 15 January 2013 to 23 October 2018.

The applicant alleged that she worked every day from about 4 a.m. until dark, feeding livestock, cleaning stalls, carrying milk, and disposing of rubbish. She was paid only occasionally and in small amounts. She alleged that I.P. began raping and sexually abusing her, using psychological control and exploiting her intellectual disability, lack of family, and lack of any alternative place to live. She said she could not refuse. I.P. allegedly threatened to kill her dogs and told her the police would not intervene because his son was in the police. L.P. allegedly beat, insulted, and threatened her, and sometimes chased her away; the applicant occasionally stayed in abandoned train cars before being found and returned.

On 23 October 2018 the applicant fled and called a disability hotline, reporting forced labour, sexual abuse by I.P., and abuse and threats by L.P. An NGO contacted the police, and on 25 October 2018 the applicant lodged a formal criminal complaint. She described sexual acts by I.P., said she had refused but was persuaded, feared L.P. finding out, and had nowhere to go. A multidisciplinary meeting assessed her situation as high risk and removed her temporarily from the family.

A criminal investigation for rape and sexual violence began on 29 October 2018. The applicant was granted victim status and repeated her allegations, adding that I.P. had threatened to kill her dog. Medical examinations found a sexually transmitted disease but no signs of violence. The Labour Inspectorate found no formal labour relations. Psychiatric and psychological reports described moderate intellectual disability, high suggestibility, limited ability to understand or resist, and dependency on caregivers. A later independent forensic psychological report found trauma and PTSD symptoms.

In February 2019 I.P. was charged with rape and sexual abuse. In March 2019 the applicant requested additional investigation of human trafficking and sexual harassment. In September 2019 I.P. and L.P. were charged with human trafficking involving two or more perpetrators, based on forcing the applicant to work without pay through threats and violence. In December 2019 the prosecutor charged I.P. with human trafficking, treating the sexual relations as non-commercial sexual exploitation and essentially dropping separate rape and sexual abuse charges. The applicant’s objections and appeals were rejected, and the case was sent for trial.

The applicant complains under Articles 3, 4, and 8, alone and with Article 14, and under Articles 6 and 13, that Moldova failed to protect her from ill-treatment and human trafficking and failed to effectively investigate her allegations. Key facts include her known disability and institutional background, State-approved deinstitutionalisation into an unmonitored farm placement, alleged unpaid labour and sexual abuse, threats and dependency, and the later investigation’s reclassification or dropping of core abuse charges.
001-244851:
**Case summary: Hora v. the United Kingdom (App. no. 1048/20)**

In *Hora v. the United Kingdom*, the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) considered an application by Michael Christopher Hora, a British national detained at HMP Bure, Norwich. The case concerns his ineligibility to vote in the United Kingdom general election of 12 December 2019 while serving a prison sentence. He complained under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (right to free elections). The Court gave notice only of the complaint concerning his ineligibility to vote in that election; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The key facts are that Hora was convicted on 10 October 2007 of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault committed in the victim’s home. His defence that the sexual relations were consensual was rejected by the jury. He had a previous conviction for rape in similar circumstances in 2000, for which he had been sentenced in 2001 to seven years’ imprisonment, reduced on appeal. Following the 2007 conviction, he received an indeterminate sentence of imprisonment for public protection with a minimum term of four years, less 296 days spent on remand. The minimum term expired in 2011, but he remained in detention because the Parole Board had not recommended his release. At the time of the 2019 general election, he was therefore still a convicted prisoner in custody.

Under section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1983, a convicted person detained in a penal institution pursuant to sentence is legally incapable of voting at any parliamentary or local election. Limited exceptions exist, such as imprisonment for contempt, default, or being on remand. Hora did not fall within any exception and was thus ineligible to vote in the 2019 election.

Hora brought no domestic proceedings. Although UK courts may consider the Convention compatibility of primary legislation, they cannot disapply statutory provisions. A domestic court had already declared section 3 incompatible with a Convention right in *Smith v. Scott* (2007). Hora considered that seeking another declaration of incompatibility would be futile. In *R (Chester) v. Secretary of State for Justice* (2013), the UK Supreme Court had also declined to make a further declaration, noting that the matter was for Parliament and that a lifelong ban for serious offenders might be compatible with the Convention under *Scoppola v. Italy (no. 3)*.

The broader factual context is the long-running political dispute over prisoner voting following *Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2)* (2005). The Committee of Ministers repeatedly urged the UK to implement that judgment. The UK government consulted and proposed limited enfranchisement, including for prisoners sentenced to less than four years, and a draft bill was published. A Joint Committee later recommended allowing prisoners serving 12 months or less to vote and permitting pre-release registration. However, Parliament repeatedly opposed relaxing the ban. The government eventually introduced administrative changes, including clarifying at sentencing that prisoners lose the right to vote and allowing certain prisoners on temporary licence or home detention curfew to vote. These did not remove the blanket ban on detained prisoners. Scotland later allowed prisoners sentenced to 12 months or less to vote in Scottish Parliament and local elections; a proposed Welsh change was abandoned during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The alleged violation is therefore that section 3 imposed an automatic blanket ban on voting for all convicted prisoners in custody, regardless of the nature or gravity of the offence, sentence length, or individual circumstances. Hora, still detained after his minimum term, was unable to vote in the 2019 general election, and he claimed this breached Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.
001-245246:
The applicant, Georgia Tsatani, born in 1952, was a prosecutor at the Athens Court of Appeal. On 23 March 2016 V.T., President of the Court of Cassation, informed her that she had opened a preliminary disciplinary investigation against her. This followed letters dated 24 February 2016 from the Cypriot Minister of Justice and Attorney-General expressing concern about the applicant’s decision to close criminal investigations into a media-covered fraud case involving Greek and Cypriot individuals. V.T. sent the applicant evidence and reports and invited written defence within ten days.

On 30 March 2016 the applicant wrote to the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation, arguing that he had exclusive competence and asking him to launch a preliminary investigation. She also complained that D.P., Deputy Minister of Justice, had referred in Parliament on 29 March 2016 to the confidential disciplinary proceedings. On 1 April she replied to V.T., complaining that she had not been offered an oral defence and that the alleged disciplinary acts were unclear. On 4 April V.T. provided a detailed statement and invited written and oral defence within a fresh ten-day period. The applicant submitted written defence and a recusal request against V.T., alleging bias: V.T. had served as interim prime minister in September 2015 and allegedly had special relations with D.P. and the Cypriot officials; V.T. had allegedly leaked confidential information, asked prejudicial questions and supplied an incomplete file.

On 12 April 2016 V.T. referred the case to a Vice-President of the Court of Cassation to continue the preliminary investigation. She stated that the recusal request was an abuse of process and unfounded, that her relations with the Cypriot officials and D.P. were official, that she had not acted under Cypriot pressure, and that she had conducted the investigation herself because of high socioeconomic interest. On 21 April the applicant complained to the Vice-President that V.T. had issued a press release about the recusal request and asked that no further action be taken pending a decision on recusal. On 5 May the Vice-President concluded the investigation and proposed disciplinary action; she declared the applicant’s reiterated recusal request inadmissible for lack of standing.

On 24 June 2016 V.T. brought disciplinary proceedings against the applicant before the seven-member disciplinary council of the Court of Cassation. She maintained that the recusal request was inadmissible because it had not been lodged with the Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation and was, at most, an invitation to withdraw; she had not dismissed it but had delegated the investigation. On 10 October 2016 the seven-member council found the applicant guilty of serious negligence damaging the prestige of the judiciary: she had terminated investigations within the Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s exclusive competence and breached a Greece–Cyprus EUROJUST agreement. It imposed sixty days’ salary deprivation. It found the recusal request inadmissible and the delegation lawful. The applicant appealed. On 16 March 2017 the nine-member disciplinary council dismissed her appeal. It held that the recusal request had not been validly submitted and was in any event unfounded; V.T. had not dismissed it but had lawfully referred the investigation. On 22 March 2021 the nine-member council rejected a request to reopen.

The record also notes V.T.’s press release of 18 April 2016, reported in the press on 18–19 April, in which she called the recusal request unfounded and an abuse of process, and D.P.’s parliamentary statements of 29 March 2016 mentioning the pending disciplinary investigation. The applicant complained that she had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because V.T., who had opened the investigation and dealt with the recusal request, subsequently brought the disciplinary action against her.
001-245444:
**Case: Ayala Flores v. Italy (Application no. 16803/21)** concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights arising from the enforcement of a demolition order against the applicant’s home. The applicant, a Peruvian national born in 1957, lived in Procida, Italy.

In the early 1990s, the applicant and her husband built a small 30 sq. m dwelling on land owned by him in Procida and made it their home. The construction was erected without a building permit in an area subject to seismic risk, landscape constraints, and an absolute ban on building because it was classified as of specific environmental interest.

In August 1996, the municipality found that the premises had been built without authorisation. In September 1996, it ordered restoration of the site within sixty days, and in 1998 it issued a demolition order. In 1999, the applicant and her husband were prosecuted for unauthorised construction under Law no. 47 of 1985 and for breaking police seals placed on the site after further modifications. In 2002, the Naples District Court convicted them, imposed a suspended five-month prison sentence and a €300 fine, and ordered demolition of the construction. In 2003, the Naples Court of Appeal partly declared the offences time-barred but upheld convictions for unauthorised construction and violation of seals, reduced the sentence, and lifted seizure solely to allow demolition. The judgment became final in October 2003.

In December 2004, the applicant applied for a building amnesty under Decree-Law no. 269 of 2003 and paid the required fees, but the application went unanswered. Under the relevant law, building work in areas subject to landscape and environmental constraints could not benefit from amnesty. Her husband died in 2009, and she continued living in the dwelling.

In 2016, the public prosecutor began enforcing the demolition order. The municipality served an eviction notice in February 2016, and in March 2016 the prosecutor ordered the applicant to demolish the dwelling within ninety days or have it demolished at her expense. The applicant asked the municipality to recognise an overriding public interest in keeping the structure.

She then lodged an application for review of the enforcement order (*incidente di esecuzione*) before the Naples Court of Appeal, seeking annulment, revocation, or suspension of the demolition order. Her original grounds did not invoke Article 8. She later submitted additional written submissions claiming that the construction was her only home, that she had lived there for over fifteen years after conviction, and that she had financial difficulties. Citing *Ivanova and Cherkezov v. Bulgaria*, she argued that enforcement would disproportionately affect her Article 8 rights. The Government disputed that these submissions had actually been filed.

In 2018–2019, the Court of Appeal dismissed her application, treating the demolition order as a mainly restorative and mandatory measure under Cassation case-law. It did not address her Article 8 submissions. In 2020, the Court of Cassation rejected her further appeal as inadmissible, finding the Article 8 complaint lacked self-sufficiency because the additional submissions had not been attached or proven filed. It nonetheless reasoned that although loss of a home should permit proportionality review, her complaint was generic and did not show individual circumstances outweighing the public interest. It found no legitimate expectation after fifteen years because she knew the construction was unauthorised, that demolition was necessary to restore the site, and that no state of necessity was proven.

After the case was communicated, the Government submitted inspections from 2020, 2022, and 2024 indicating the construction was not inhabited and was unfit for use or suitable only as storage; later reports noted unauthorised fencing and shutters. The applicant submitted statements that she lived there and had nowhere else, a residence certificate since 2001, proof of a monthly pension of €551.59, annual household income of €4,943, and a surveyor’s report on her limited means and age. By April 2025, the dwelling had not been demolished.

The key Article 8 issue was whether enforcing the demolition order, and the domestic review of its proportionality, adequately protected the applicant’s right to respect for her home.
001-245821:
**Case: Aslan and Others v. Türkiye (Applications nos. 12531/21 and 8 others)**

This case is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 13 November 2025. It originated in nine applications lodged against Türkiye under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates between 12 February 2021 and 7 April 2023. The Turkish Government was given notice of the applications.

The central complaint was that each applicant had been held in pre-trial detention for an excessive length without relevant and sufficient reasons. In applications nos. 18927/21 and 16303/23, the applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The applicants and key detention facts were as follows. Dilan Aslan (b. 1991) was detained from 16 March 2020 to 27 October 2020, a period of 7 months and 12 days, by the Denizli 2nd and 3rd Assize Courts. Mehmet Bozkurt (b. 1975) was detained from 5 July 2015 to 5 June 2020, lasting 4 years, 11 months and 1 day, by the Ağrı Assize Court. Ayşegül Çağatay Gökçe (b. 1991) was detained from 25 June 2011 to 31 March 2020, a period of 8 years, 9 months and 7 days, by Istanbul magistrate and assize courts. Sadun Kaya (b. 1968) was detained from 2 July 2018 to 16 September 2022, lasting 4 years, 2 months and 15 days, by the Kocaeli 1st and 2nd Assize Courts. Şeyhmus Çeri (b. 1997) was detained from 17 August 2016 to 10 October 2018, a period of 2 years, 1 month and 24 days, by the Şanlıurfa Assize Court. Mensur Akar (b. 1995) was detained from 18 April 2016 to 3 January 2019 and again from 20 December 2019 to 27 October 2022, totaling 6 years, 6 months and 23 days, by the Hakkari Assize Court. Helin Yapıcı (b. 1994) was detained from 23 March 2016 to 6 April 2021, a period of 5 years and 15 days, by the Diyarbakır Assize Court. İrfan Yıldız (b. 1980) was detained from 16 February 2017 to 27 March 2019 and from 25 December 2019 to 25 June 2020, periods of 2 years, 1 month and 12 days and 6 months and 1 day, by Istanbul magistrate and assize courts. Mücahit Doğan (b. 1983) was detained from 31 December 2021 to 27 December 2022, a period of 11 months and 28 days, by Küçükçekmece magistrates’ courts and the Küçükçekmece Criminal Court of First Instance.

The detention decisions relied on recurring grounds. These included strong suspicion that the applicant had committed an offence, the nature of the offence, the severity of the potential sentence, and, in most cases, the fact that the offence was among “catalogue offences” listed in Article 100 § 3 of the Turkish Code of Criminal Procedure. Authorities also cited risks of absconding and tampering with evidence. Some decisions referred to the scope of the case, outstanding evidence such as expert reports, the applicant’s contacts, the insufficiency of alternative judicial supervision measures, and—in İrfan Yıldız’s case—the alleged risk of ISIS terror acts on special days. The applicants’ essential complaint was that these reasons were not relevant and sufficient to justify detention of such length, making their continued pre-trial detention excessive. The appended table set out the specific periods, competent courts, lengths of detention and stated grounds for each applicant.
001-242073:
**Case:** *Monteiro and Trinta Santos v. Portugal*  
**Applications nos.:** 40620/22 and 44221/22  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section  
**Judgment:** 6 March 2025 (Committee)

The case originated in two applications against Portugal lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The first applicant, António Augusto Monteiro (born 1986), introduced application no. 40620/22 on 12 August 2022. The second applicant, Hugo David Trinta Santos (born 1984), introduced application no. 44221/22 on 6 September 2022. Monteiro was represented by Mr R. Mendes Martins, a lawyer practising in Lisbon, and Trinta Santos by Mr V. Carreto, a lawyer practising in Torres Vedras. The Portuguese Government were given notice of the applications.

Both applicants complained under Article 3 of the Convention about the inadequate conditions of their detention in Coimbra Prison. In application no. 44221/22, Trinta Santos also complained under Article 13 of the lack of an effective domestic remedy in respect of the alleged Article 3 violation.

As regards Monteiro, the appended table shows that he was detained in Coimbra Prison from 27 December 2021 to 3 December 2022, a duration of 11 months and 7 days. He was again detained in the same prison from 30 June 2023 and remained there pending at the time of the application, a period of more than 1 year and 6 months. The table records that he shared a cell with two inmates, with 3.10 m² per inmate and one toilet. His specific grievances for both periods were overcrowding, lack of privacy for the toilet, lack of fresh air, inadequate temperature, passive smoking, poor quality of food, infestation of the cell with insects or rodents, and a mouldy or dirty cell.

As regards Trinta Santos, he was detained in Coimbra Prison from 15 July 2022 and remained there pending, a period of more than 1 year and 6 months. The table records that he shared a cell with two inmates, with 2.25 m² per inmate and one toilet. His specific grievances were overcrowding, inadequate temperature, lack of requisite medical assistance, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of fresh air, and lack of or insufficient quantity of food.

The applicants’ complaints therefore centre on severe overcrowding and associated physical conditions in Coimbra Prison. Monteiro’s cell space was recorded as 3.10 m² per inmate, while Trinta Santos’s was 2.25 m² per inmate. Both cells held two inmates and had one toilet, which is directly relevant to the complaints of overcrowding and lack of privacy. Additional alleged deficiencies included poor ventilation, inadequate temperature, passive smoking, poor food, hygiene problems, pests, and, for Trinta Santos, lack of requisite medical assistance. Trinta Santos further alleged that domestic remedies were ineffective or unavailable, giving rise to his Article 13 complaint.

The Court’s judgment concerns whether these detention conditions reached the threshold of inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3 and, in Trinta Santos’s case, whether Portugal provided an effective domestic remedy under Article 13. The appended table provides the core factual basis for the alleged violations.
001-242768:
**Federici v. France (Application no. 52302/19)** concerns an applicant’s complaint that his appearance in a glass dock during criminal proceedings before an assize court of appeal, and the court’s refusal to let him answer questions from the witness stand, violated Article 6 §§ 1, 2 and 3(b) of the Convention (fair trial, presumption of innocence, and rights of the defence).

The applicant, Jean-François Federici, a French national born in 1957, was indicted for murder committed as a member of an organised group and for conspiracy to commit a crime. In 2011, while under court supervision, he absconded. In December 2014, the Assize Court tried him in absentia and sentenced him to thirty years’ imprisonment. He was arrested in 2016, placed in pre-trial detention, and retried. In January 2017, the Assize Court again sentenced him to thirty years’ imprisonment and ordered confiscation. He appealed.

The appeal hearings took place in April 2018 in the Aix-en-Provence Law Courts, in its standard courtroom. The applicant was assisted by two lawyers. He appeared in a glass dock pursuant to Article 318 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure. The dock was an open-roofed glass enclosure measuring 3.68 metres by 2.47 metres. It had two perforations (hygiaphones) at human height for communication with defence counsel, two slots for passing documents, fixed microphones for hearing the accused, and a loudspeaker allowing him to hear courtroom microphones. It also had a glass door to the courtroom and a solid security door to a secure waiting area.

On 6 April 2018, the applicant was heard regarding his personality. He did not complain of hearing difficulties and did not ask to be questioned outside the dock. On 10 April, his lawyer requested that he appear outside the glass dock, relying on Article 6 of the Convention, the preliminary article of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and recital 20 of Directive (EU) 2016/343. The lawyer argued that members of the public had undergone security checks and that the applicant had a hearing impairment which sometimes made it difficult for him to hear questions. On 11 April, the applicant was questioned while remaining in the dock.

In an interlocutory judgment of 13 April 2018, the Assize Court dismissed the request. It held that Articles 318 and D.294 of the Code of Criminal Procedure required courts to take security measures necessary for the accused’s appearance, considering the danger he posed and the need to protect him. It noted that Article 5 of Directive 2016/343 did not prevent physical restraints where necessary for security or to prevent absconding or contact with third parties. The court emphasised that the applicant faced life imprisonment, was in pre-trial detention, and had absconded for more than four years. It observed that, despite his hearing problems, he had been able to answer questions and communicate confidentially with his lawyers and was free to move within the dock. It concluded that the measure was lawful, proportionate, and necessary, and did not breach the presumption of innocence, human dignity, or defence rights. The same day, he was convicted of double murder as a member of an organised group and sentenced to thirty years’ imprisonment.

The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing insufficient reasoning and citing Belousov v. Russia. On 10 April 2019, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, finding that the Assize Court’s reasoning did not show he had been prevented from communicating with his lawyers. The case also referenced criticism of glass docks by the Public Defender’s Office and the Inspector-General of Custodial Premises, and French case-law permitting docks where free movement and confidential communication are ensured.
001-242521:
Six Dutch limited-liability companies in two groups complained that intercept data lawfully obtained in criminal investigations had been transmitted to competition authorities and used against them, violating Article 8, and that they lacked an effective domestic remedy under Articles 8 and 13. The first group (Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V., Burando Holding B.V., Port Invest B.V.) collected waste liquids in Rotterdam. The second (Janssen de Jong Groep B.V., Janssen de Jong Infrastructuur Nederland B.V., Janssen de Jong Infra B.V.) operated in construction.

First group: In late 2006 the VROM-IOD began criminal investigation “Toto” into the I. company for suspected forgery and environmental offences. An investigating judge authorised interception of telephone calls by I. employees, including calls with Ships Waste Oil Collector employees; some suggested price-fixing. On 21 October 2008 the public prosecutor approved transmission to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) of a 21 April 2008 official record and transcripts; transmission occurred on 29 June 2009. Further transcripts and recordings were authorised on 23 October 2009. NMA inspectors visited premises on 29–30 June 2010 and questioned managers, playing an intercepted recording. More data were sent in 2010 after approvals in June, July and August; the last transmission was 8–9 September 2010. In the criminal case, the I. company and an employee settled on 11 March 2010 for EUR 50,000 and EUR 4,000; on 5 July 2010 the Rotterdam Regional Court declared the prosecution inadmissible. The NMA’s 28 December 2010 report found collusion from 30 August 2005 to 31 July 2007 contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act. On 16 November 2011 it fined Ships Waste Oil Collector EUR 834,000 and the other three jointly and severally EUR 1,861,000, with Burando’s liability capped at EUR 621,000.

The companies objected that the intercepts were not transmissible “criminal data,” that there was no prior judicial review, that Ships Waste Oil Collector was never suspected, that the settlement prevented ex post facto judicial review, that the NMA lacked intercept powers, and that prior contacts lacked a legal basis. On 11 July 2013 the Rotterdam Regional Court held the data were criminal data but excluded them because the prosecutor’s approvals lacked an identifiable weighing of interests; it quashed the NMA decisions. On 9 July 2015 the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment, finding the data qualified as criminal data, a compelling general interest existed, written reasoning was not required, and the transmissions did not breach Article 8. It held the criminal case ended when the 5 July 2010 ruling became final on 19 July 2010. On 20 October 2016 the Regional Court found infringement from 1 January 2006 to 31 July 2007 and reduced fines; on 30 October 2018 the Supreme Administrative Court restored the original fines.

Second group: Around 2007 the “Cleveland” investigation by the Public Prosecution Service and Rijksrecherche examined suspected bribery of local officials; the Janssen companies were suspects. Interceptions were authorised for bribery, fraud and forgery. In July 2008 police gave NMA officials confidential access to transcripts; on 19 August 2008 the prosecutor provided a CD of about thirty recordings for information only. On 9 December 2008 the NMA opened a Competition Act investigation; on 16 December 2008 the prosecutor permitted use of the Cleveland information. Transcripts were transmitted on 24 December 2008. In civil proceedings, the provisional-measures judge on 26 June 2009 dismissed the Janssen companies’ claims, finding the data were criminal data and the transmission compatible with Article 8. NMA reports of 17 December 2009 and 25 February 2010 found infringement; on 29 October 2010 it imposed a EUR 3,000,000 joint fine. The objection was dismissed on 8 March 2012. On 13 June 2013 the Rotterdam Regional Court quashed the decision because no identifiable weighing of interests by the prosecutor existed, although the data were criminal data.
001-244588:
In *Ftiti v. Greece* (Application no. 37957/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Cherif Ftiti, a Tunisian national, concerning the effectiveness of his right of appeal under Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention. The applicant had lived in Greece since 1996 and held a residence permit; he also had two children born in Greece.

On 29 December 2009, the applicant was arrested in Rethymno on suspicion of aggravated livestock theft committed jointly and was detained pending trial. On 17 February 2010, the Chania Mixed Jury Court convicted him and sentenced him to seventeen years’ imprisonment and a €1,000 fine. The first-instance court ruled that any appeal would not have suspensive effect and ordered his deportation after completion of his sentence. It did not give reasons for refusing to suspend execution of the sentence.

The applicant lodged an appeal. On 30 January 2014, he attended a hearing before the Crete Criminal Court of Appeal, but the case was adjourned to 13 November 2014 because key prosecution witnesses were absent. On 27 October 2014, the prison director informed the prosecutor that the applicant did not wish to be transferred to court for the 13 November hearing, as his lawyer would represent him. On the day of that hearing, the applicant requested an adjournment, saying he could not contact his lawyer. On 20 January 2015, while still detained, he was notified that the appeal hearing had been rescheduled for 1 November 2015.

On 25 February 2015, the Chalkidiki Criminal Court of First Instance granted the applicant conditional release under Article 105 of the Criminal Code, finding that he had served three-fifths of his sentence after deductions for work and had demonstrated good behaviour. He was formally released on 6 March 2015, but was transferred to the Department of Illegal Migration in Triglia and placed in a detention facility for migrants. On 22 April 2015, he was deported to Tunisia and banned from entering the Schengen area. He was therefore removed from Greece before his appeal was heard.

On 26 October 2015, the Crete Mixed Jury Court of Appeal requested the prosecutor at the Chania Court of First Instance to secure the applicant’s attendance at the forthcoming hearing. That request could not be forwarded to him because he had not appointed a new representative and had provided an incomplete residential address in Tunisia. On 1 November 2015, the appeal court rejected the appeal because the applicant failed to appear. The appeal was thus dismissed as unfounded or unsupported (*ανυποστήρικτη*) on account of his absence, without a substantive examination.

The relevant domestic framework included Article 497 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which governs the suspensive effect of appeals. An appeal may lack suspensive effect where the accused has no known stable residence, may abscond, or where restrictive measures are insufficient. Under Article 497 § 9, a detained accused who is far from the court need not appear. The Court referred to its case-law in *Fırat v. Greece* and *Martzaklis and Others v. Greece*.

The alleged violation under Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 was that the applicant’s right of appeal was rendered ineffective: he was conditionally released and expelled before the appeal hearing, yet the appeal was later dismissed solely because he did not appear. The key issue was whether the Greek authorities’ conduct and the domestic procedure deprived him of a practical opportunity to have his criminal appeal examined.
001-238839:
**Case Summary: Malgazhdarov and Others v. Russia**  
*European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Committee Judgment, 16 January 2025*  
*Applications nos. 4562/23 and 7 others*

The case concerns eight applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained primarily of disproportionate measures taken against solo demonstrators. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The Court, sitting as a Committee, deliberated in private on 5 December 2024 and adopted the judgment on 16 January 2025.

The applicants were individuals who held or participated in solo demonstrations in Moscow in early 2022. Their details are set out in the appended table. Anton Aleksandrovich Malgazhdarov (born 1990), application no. 4562/23, demonstrated on 5 January 2022 in support of protests in Kazakhstan. The other applicants took part in anti-war protests: Taisiya Yevgenyevna Yazrikova (born 1987) on 26 February 2022; Varvara Vladimirovna Obrosova (born 1986) on 27 February 2022; Natalya Viktorovna Ladygina (born 1964) on 26 February 2022; Olga Gennadyevna Nikitina (born 1983) on 2 March 2022; Mikhail Aleksandrovich Salomatin (born 1981) on 5 March 2022; Polina Valeryevna Kuzavleva (born 1986) on 5 March 2022; and Anna Vladimirovna Danilina (born 1988) on 6 March 2022. All demonstrations took place in Moscow.

In each case, the applicants were subjected to administrative charges under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Russian Code of Administrative Offences (CAO). The penalties imposed were fines ranging from RUB 10,000 to RUB 20,000. For example, Malgazhdarov received a RUB 10,000 fine; Yazrikova, Obrosova, Nikitina, and Kuzavleva received RUB 20,000 fines; Salomatin received RUB 15,000; and Danilina and Ladygina received RUB 10,000. The first applicant’s case also included a “distance requirement” and the event was classified as an assembly post facto, though no equivalent detail is provided for the other applicants.

The final domestic decisions were issued by the Moscow City Court between 15 September 2022 and 25 October 2022. This indicates that the applicants exhausted domestic remedies before applying to the European Court. Their applications were lodged with the Court at various dates in January and February 2023.

The key alleged violation is that the Russian authorities imposed disproportionate administrative penalties on individuals engaged in solo demonstrations. The applicants complained specifically of “disproportionate measures against solo demonstrators.” While some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention, the appended table and the provided facts focus on the administrative fines imposed for solo protests. The central issue before the Court was therefore whether these fines constituted an unjustified interference with the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, primarily under Article 11 of the Convention. The facts relevant to that alleged violation include the peaceful nature of the solo demonstrations, the absence of any indicated violence or disruption in the table, the administrative classification of the events, the imposition of financial penalties, and the final review by the Moscow City Court. The Court’s task was to assess whether these measures complied with Convention standards. The provided text does not include the Court’s full reasoning or final disposition, but it identifies the case as concerning Russia’s treatment of solo demonstrators and the fines imposed under CAO Article 20.2 § 5.
001-243782:
In *M.L. v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 30206/23), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 8 of the Convention concerning a barring order that prohibited the applicant from approaching his daughter within 100 metres and from visiting her home and school. The applicant also alleged that the domestic court failed to reassess the need for that order every two months, as required by domestic law.

The applicant married D.B.L. in July 2013, and their daughter D. was born in December 2013. In December 2021 he filed for divorce and sought custody. In March 2022 the Social Care Centre recommended that he be granted custody. After moving out in June 2022, he initially stayed with D. every other week, but he later stated that he had not seen her since 2 October 2022. In January 2023 the Centre established contact rights allowing him to see D. every other weekend and on Wednesdays. He repeatedly complained that the mother did not comply and that D. refused contact due to the mother’s and her family’s influence. His appeal against the contact-rights decision was dismissed in April 2023.

Separately, criminal proceedings arose. In October 2022 the mother reported that the applicant had sent threatening messages. In March 2023 she reported that he had physically and psychologically abused D. between October 2022 and March 2023, including hitting, kicking, insulting and threatening her. On 1 March 2023, police interviewed D., who said she had not seen the applicant since October 2022 because she did not want to, and alleged that he had hit her in the face and body and had threatened and insulted her when they previously spent time together. Police also interviewed her teacher, school psychologist, pedagogical expert and maternal grandmother. The teacher described D. becoming withdrawn and upset and refusing to leave school with the applicant.

On 6 March 2023 the police temporarily detained and interviewed the applicant. He denied the accusations and maintained that he had not seen D. since 2 October 2022. The police filed a criminal complaint against him for bodily injury through domestic violence and violence against a child. The public prosecutor requested protective measures under the Criminal Proceedings Act. The same day, a pre-trial judge issued the barring order, prohibiting the applicant from approaching D. and the mother within 100 metres and from visiting D.’s school or their apartment. The order was to last until a final criminal judgment, with reassessment every two months. The judge cited the seriousness of the offences, the possible sentence, the need to prevent influence over the victims, and D.’s psychological and physical health.

The applicant appealed on 9 March 2023, arguing that he could not have abused D. during the alleged period because he had barely seen her. He submitted evidence of the contact-rights decision and his complaints about non-enforcement, and an expert report disputing the threatening messages. On 15 March 2023 a three-judge panel dismissed the appeal, finding a reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences and confirming the barring order.

In parallel civil proceedings, protective measures were ordered against both parents in November 2022 and again in June 2023, including prohibitions on arguing or threatening in D.’s presence and a requirement to attend counselling. The case therefore concerned whether the barring order and its prolonged validity interfered disproportionately with the applicant’s family life under Article 8, particularly given the alleged failure to reassess it every two months.
001-245886:
**Case: Kashbullina and Others v. Russia**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, sitting as a Committee  
**Judgment date:** 13 November 2025  
**Applications nos.:** 1964/22 and four others  

This case originated in five applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants complained of disproportionate measures taken against them as organisers or participants of public assemblies in St Petersburg, in connection with various public events held in breach of regional COVID-19-related restrictions. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Court deliberated privately on 23 October 2025 and delivered judgment on 13 November 2025; the judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applicants and relevant facts, as set out in the appended table, are as follows:

1. **Alena Valeriyevna Kashbullina**, born 1998, application no. 1964/22, lodged on 3 December 2021. She was represented by Natalya Andreyevna Baranova of Moscow. The event was a rally titled “Free Navalnyy” in St Petersburg on 2 February 2021. She was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) and fined RUB 10,000. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 3 June 2021.

2. **Aleksandra Vadimovna Eller**, born 1990, application no. 37658/22, lodged on 19 July 2022. She was represented by Baranova. The event was an anti-war protest in St Petersburg on 24 February 2022. She was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 CAO and sentenced to detention for five days. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 22 March 2022.

3. **Sergey Aleksandrovich Fedorov**, born 1997, application no. 37671/22, lodged on 16 July 2022. He was represented by Baranova. The event was an anti-war protest in St Petersburg on 27 February 2022. He was charged under Article 20.2.2 § 1 CAO and fined RUB 15,000. The final domestic decision was given by the St Petersburg City Court on 22 March 2022.

4. **Oksana Nikolayevna Shurukhina**, born 1977, application no. 39709/22, lodged on 2 August 2022. She was represented by Baranova. The domestic authorities treated the assemblies as breaches of regional COVID-19-related restrictions.
