001-243562:
Á.F.L. v. Iceland (Application no. 35789/22) concerns the deprivation of the applicant’s custody of his daughter and the alleged discriminatory failure to provide him with reasonable accommodation for his disability. The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1990, was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and a mild intellectual disability. He had a history of alcohol and drug abuse but had been sober since 2012 and was employed. His daughter, V.F., was born in February 2019. Child Protection Services (“CPS”) became involved amid parental conflict, the mother’s mental-health problems, the applicant’s diagnoses and reported domestic violence. In September 2019 the applicant assumed care of V.F.

With parental consent, V.F. was placed at Mánaberg, a CPS residential diagnostic and guidance facility. The applicant joined her there in October 2019 after the mother left. Staff knew of his impairment and gave extensive guidance, later moving him to a supported “apartment” within the facility. A December 2019 psychologist’s report found that although the applicant did not test at the level of intellectual disability, his cognitive difficulties and autism affected his parenting. He needed extensive assistance and could not care for V.F. alone. A January 2020 Mánaberg report noted progress but concluded he still required targeted support, guidance, a support family and counselling.

A discharge plan placed the applicant and V.F. with the paternal grandmother, with Mánaberg follow-up visits four times a week, a YLFA counsellor twice a week, a support family and continued counselling. Reports from March to June 2020 found the applicant affectionate but lacking insight into V.F.’s physical, social and emotional needs, stimulation and initiative. Concerns grew about V.F.’s motor skills, emotional control and possible attachment disorder. YLFA recommended more extensive support and eventually foster care. CPS increased support, but COVID-19 disrupted services. In June 2020 reports warned V.F. urgently needed a primary caregiver who could provide security.

In July 2020 the Child Protection Committee ruled that V.F. be removed for two months pending reassessment; she was placed with a foster family. An August 2020 parenting-capacity report found the applicant attached and cooperative but that autism and intellectual challenges restricted his ability to recognise and meet V.F.’s needs. V.F. improved significantly in foster care. The District Court upheld the removal. In September 2020 the CPC decided to seek deprivation of custody after the applicant refused to relinquish it.

A court-appointed expert report in April 2021 considered the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and Icelandic disability-support legislation. It validated earlier findings, concluding the applicant lacked basic parenting skills, was slow to acquire them and could not benefit sufficiently from further support. Returning V.F. to the previous situation was not justified. At trial, the applicant argued he had not received enough support, that his ADHD had improved with medication and that additional services under Act no. 38/2018 on Services for Disabled People with Long-Term Support Needs should have been tried. His witnesses, including disability experts, said earlier measures had not fully accounted for his needs. A YLFA counsellor testified that extra services could not compensate for the lack of bonding and care.

In September 2021 the District Court deprived the applicant of custody under the Child Protection Act, finding extensive measures had been tried, the child’s best interests were paramount and no realistic additional measures existed. The Court of Appeal upheld the decision in February 2022, noting disability alone cannot justify deprivation but that the statutory conditions were met and the support experience had been considered. The Supreme Court refused leave in March 2022. The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 8 and 14 that the authorities failed to provide reasonable accommodation—necessary support measures for his disability—before depriving him of custody, thereby discriminating against him.
001-238843:
**Case: Abbate and Others v. Italy**  
**Applications nos. 27814/23, 27974/23, 33199/23, 33278/23 and 35651/23**  
**European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Judgment of 16 January 2025**

The case originated in five applications against Italy lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained primarily of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions given in their favour. They also raised other Convention complaints. The Italian Government was given notice of the applications.

The applicants were Ferdinando Emilio Abbate, Daniela Jossa, Lucio Benigni (in two applications), and Maria Stella Saveriano. The domestic decisions at issue generally ordered the Ministry of Economy and Finance or the Ministry of Justice to pay lawyers’ legal fees, in the context of the lawyer acting as *avvocato antistatario*—that is, a lawyer entitled to collect fees directly from the opposing party.

In application no. 27814/23, introduced on 26 June 2023, Ferdinando Emilio Abbate relied on numerous judgments of the Latium Administrative Court dated 5 June 2017 and 20 July 2017, as well as Rome District Court orders of July 2019 enforcing several of those judgments. These decisions ordered the Ministry of Economy and Finance to pay legal fees. The non-enforcement periods ended between 2 and 24 March 2023. The delays ranged from approximately 3 years and 8 months to 5 years and 9 months, depending on the decision. Thus, by the time enforcement occurred, the applicant had faced lengthy delays of several years.

In application no. 27974/23, introduced on 5 July 2023, Daniela Jossa relied on three decisions: Rome Court of Appeal, 25 September 2017; Naples Court of Appeal, 4 July 2018; and Naples Court of Appeal, 6 August 2020. These ordered the Ministry of Justice to pay legal fees. Enforcement remained pending. The periods of non-enforcement had lasted more than 7 years, 1 month and 11 days; more than 6 years, 4 months and 1 day; and more than 4 years, 2 months and 30 days respectively.

In application no. 33199/23, introduced on 23 August 2023, Lucio Benigni relied on four Naples Court of Appeal decisions dated 20 January 2017, 3 December 2018, 20 December 2018, and 22 September 2020. They ordered the Ministry of Justice to pay legal fees. Enforcement was still pending, with delays exceeding 7 years, 9 months and 16 days; 5 years, 11 months and 2 days; 5 years, 10 months and 16 days; and 4 years, 1 month and 14 days.

In application no. 33278/23, introduced on 23 August 2023, Maria Stella Saveriano relied on four Naples Court of Appeal decisions dated 22 November 2018, 21 February 2019, 15 March 2019, and 22 May 2019. These also ordered the Ministry of Justice to pay legal fees. Enforcement remained pending. The delays exceeded 5 years and 11 months, 5 years and 8 months, 5 years and 7 months, and 5 years and 5 months respectively.

In application no. 35651/23, introduced on 11 September 2023, Lucio Benigni relied on five Naples Court of Appeal decisions dated 16 June 2017, 30 January 2019, 18 September 2019, 10 December 2020, and 15 April 2021. These ordered the Ministry of Justice to pay legal fees. Enforcement was still pending, with delays ranging from more than 3 years and 6 months to more than 7 years and 4 months.

The key alleged violation therefore concerns the failure or delay by Italian authorities in enforcing binding domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour. In Abbate’s case, enforcement eventually occurred in March 2023 after delays of several years. In the other applications, enforcement remained pending at the time of introduction, with delays exceeding several years. The applicants alleged that this prolonged non-enforcement breached their Convention rights, particularly fair-trial and property-protection guarantees.
001-243887:
**Arvanitis and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited v. Cyprus** (Application no. 49917/22) is a European Court of Human Rights case, Fifth Section, judgment of 3 July 2025, concerning an alleged violation of Article 10 (freedom of expression). The applicants are Christos Arvanitis, a journalist and columnist, and Phileleftheros Public Company Limited, publisher of the Cypriot daily *Phileleftheros*. They complained that a civil defamation judgment against them in Cyprus breached their right to freedom of expression.

The dispute arose from an article written by Arvanitis and published by the second applicant on 1 July 2007, entitled “Property-Dignity, One-Nil.” It responded to a June 2007 article by C.K., a lawyer, in the Greek newspaper *To Vima*. C.K. had described recovering two family paintings left in occupied Cyprus after the 1974 Turkish invasion: he recovered one after paying money and the second by replacing it with a forgery, inspired by the film *The Thomas Crown Affair*. Arvanitis’s article criticised C.K.’s conduct, questioned whether he advised clients similarly, and suggested that paying a ransom, bargaining with thieves, and prioritising property over dignity harmed Greek-Cypriot property claims. The issue sold 24,482 copies.

In November 2008, C.K. sued the applicants for civil defamation. He claimed the article damaged his personal and professional reputation, falsely portraying him as prioritising material goods over national interests, harming compatriots, and negotiating with thieves. The applicants defended the article as true and as fair comment on a matter of public interest, arguing it was based on C.K.’s own published account and expressed honest opinion in a public debate about Greek-Cypriot property in the occupied areas.

On 18 September 2014, the Nicosia District Court found for C.K. and awarded EUR 12,000 plus interest. It held that the article was defamatory and went beyond opinion, directly attacking C.K.’s personality and professional standing by depicting him as someone who gave up his dignity, sold out his compatriots, and bargained with thieves. The court noted the article was published when C.K. was representing clients before the England and Wales Court of Appeal on occupied-property matters, thereby calling his reputation into question. It found the article lacked factual basis: C.K. had never said he bought a painting, only that he recovered it; paying money did not necessarily mean a purchase; and C.K. had not said he negotiated with the Turkish tavern owner or new owner. Arvanitis had failed to contact C.K. or verify the amount paid (1,000 CYP) against the painting’s value (over 50,000 CYP), or whether it amounted to a ransom. The court rejected fair comment because, although property issues were of public interest, the article contained vulgar, bad-faith personal attacks. It also found that other individuals and State bodies had paid to recover cultural goods, which was not reprehensible, and that failure to seek C.K.’s views showed lack of good faith. C.K. was not a public figure.

On appeal, the Supreme Court upheld the judgment on 24 June 2022. It agreed that C.K. was a private individual, that the article was not true, that “recovered” did not mean “bought,” and that the accusation of bargaining with thieves or buying from a new owner was unsupported. It also agreed that fair comment did not apply.

The applicants applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 20 October 2022. The Court gave notice solely of the Article 10 complaint. The key issue is whether the domestic civil defamation judgment and damages award unjustifiably interfered with the applicants’ freedom of expression.
001-242855:
In *Umid-T LLC v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 7949/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined complaints brought by Umid-T LLC, a company registered in Baku, concerning the expropriation of its commercial property. The applicant was represented by M. Mustafayev; the Azerbaijani Government was represented by Ç. Əsgərov. The application was lodged on 4 February 2013. The Court gave notice of complaints under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The case concerned the allegedly unlawful expropriation of an LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) filling station owned by the applicant company. A 2005 ownership certificate showed Umid-T LLC as owner of the station, located adjacent to the Heydar Aliyev Airport–Mardakan–Bilgah motorway. The station stood on an 800 sq. m plot allocated to the company for that purpose, although the land itself remained State-owned.

On 28 August 2009, the Cabinet of Ministers issued a decision to expropriate land and any immovable property on it for State needs in connection with reconstructing the motorway. AzerYolServis OJSC, a State-owned company operated by the Ministry of Transport, was designated as the authorised State body responsible for expropriation. On 25 September 2009, AzerYolServis sent the applicant written notification of the impending expropriation. On the same day, the applicant’s property was demolished.

On 19 March 2010, the applicant received AZN 400,000 (approximately EUR 365,600 at the material time). This consisted of AZN 333,333 for the market value of the property and an additional 20% compensation under Presidential Decree no. 689 of 26 December 2007. The amount was based on a valuation report commissioned by AzerYolServis from a private company; a copy of that report was not provided to the Court.

The applicant lodged a complaint before Baku Administrative-Economic Court No. 1 against AzerYolServis and the Baku City Executive Authority (“the BCEA”). It asked the court either to order the BCEA to allocate it an 800 sq. m plot and AzerYolServis to restore the demolished property to its original condition, or to award AZN 667,088 for the value of its commercial property, plus AZN 100,000 for pecuniary damage, AZN 100,000 for damage to business reputation, and AZN 31,123 for delayed payment. In support, the applicant produced a private valuation estimating the market value at AZN 889,240. It contended that it had only been partly compensated, that payment had been made six months after demolition, and that the expropriation had violated the procedure prescribed by domestic law.

On 20 December 2011, the first-instance court dismissed the claim. It found that the expropriation had been carried out in accordance with the law and that the compensation was sufficient. It rejected the applicant’s valuation report, observing that the market value of expropriated property under the expropriation procedure had to be established by a competent State authority. By judgments of 16 May 2012 and 24 October 2012, respectively, the Baku Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeals.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that it had been unlawfully deprived of its commercial property and that the compensation awarded was inadequate. It further complained under Articles 6 and 13 that the domestic courts had failed to give reasons for their judgments and that it had not had an effective domestic remedy for protecting its Convention rights.
001-118647:
**Case: Hagyó v. Hungary (Application no. 52624/10, ECtHR, 23 April 2013)**

The applicant, Miklós Hagyó, a Hungarian national, former Vice-Mayor of Budapest and former Member of Parliament, was arrested on 14 May 2010, shortly after losing parliamentary immunity following the 2010 general elections. He was charged with aggravated fraudulent breach of trust involving the misuse of funds at the Budapest Transport Company. Criminal proceedings had previously been opened against senior transport officials and a close colleague in the same context.

On 17 May 2010, the Buda Central District Court ordered his pre-trial detention. The prosecution alleged risks of absconding and collusion. The court relied on the seriousness of the charges, the fact that the applicant had sold properties, and an unspecified “element” suggesting he might leave the country. It also found a real risk of collusion because his immunity had only recently been removed and further investigative steps remained. The applicant’s appeal was rejected on 26 May 2010.

The defence repeatedly sought release or less coercive measures, including house arrest. It argued that the applicant had known for months that indictment was likely but had not fled; that the case had attracted intense publicity; that he had denied rumours of leaving and had offered cooperation; that he had paid off a 16 million HUF debt; and that he had not concealed evidence or influenced witnesses. The courts nonetheless prolonged detention at statutory intervals, often using stereotyped reasoning, mainly citing the prospect of a severe sentence, without an individualised assessment of his personal circumstances.

A key Article 5 complaint concerned equality of arms. The defence’s requests to consult the case file and evidence underlying the absconding allegation were disregarded. The prosecutor’s office refused access, and a complaint to the Chief Public Prosecutor remained unanswered. The evidence of his alleged intention to abscond was never disclosed, making it difficult effectively to challenge the detention.

As to Article 3, the applicant suffered from asthma, chronic sinusitis, gluten and dairy allergies, and chronic left-ear inflammation. On admission he weighed 130 kg. He was held at Budapest Penitentiary for over four months in cells of 3.52 m² per person, and another four months in cells of 4.7 m² including fixtures. From November 2010 he was permanently placed in a 4.7 m² cell. He was allowed only one hour outside per day. He received medication, a special diet, baths, and medical examinations; an expert confirmed serious health problems but considered them treatable in prison. He lost 37 kg, suffered an asthma attack, and refused some medication and one hospital transfer because it coincided with a family visit. Requests for larger cell space, less humidity, more fresh air, and better nutrition were largely unsuccessful. An extra daily outdoor hour was refused in November 2010 but granted in December.

Under Articles 8 and 13, the applicant complained about restricted family contact. From 9 November 2010, all meetings and phone calls with his common-law wife were banned due to an alleged collusion risk, the authorities claiming the couple intended to circumvent controlled family visits. His complaint to the Chief Prosecutor was unanswered. Related criminal proceedings against him for giving his wife a false retainer ended in acquittal, and wardens stated all visits had been supervised. His 11-year-old daughter never visited because of her own health, though extra phone time was granted in September 2010 and January 2011 in addition to regular calls.

Pre-trial detention lasted until 23 February 2011, when it was replaced by house arrest because his serious health problems reduced the absconding risk. House arrest continued until 10 June 2011. The applicant alleged violations of Article 5, Article 3, and Article 8 alone and with Article 13.
001-128040:
**Summary of *Pyrantienė v. Lithuania* (Application no. 45092/07)**

The case of *Pyrantienė v. Lithuania* concerns an application brought by Ms. Kotrina Pyrantienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1942, against the Republic of Lithuania. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to property, after domestic court decisions deprived her of land she had owned for nine years without adequate compensation.

The facts of the case begin in 1994, when a local authority assigned a 0.5-hectare plot of land to the applicant. On 6 August 1996, the Kaunas Region Administration confirmed the sale of this land to her. Subsequently, on 24 September 1996, the applicant acquired the plot from the State for 61 "single-use investment vouchers" and duly registered the property in her name with the Land Registry. She then used the land for agricultural purposes, growing and selling vegetables. This situation persisted for several years.

The applicant's ownership was challenged in December 2001 when third parties filed a civil claim seeking the restoration of their ownership rights to the same plot. On 2 October 2003, the Kaunas Regional Court, acting as an appellate court, ruled in favour of the third parties. It quashed the 1996 administrative decision as unlawful and cancelled the sale of the land to the applicant, ordering its return to the State. The court's reasoning was that the State authorities had no right to sell the plot because the former owners had already lodged a request for its restitution under the post-Soviet restitution laws in 1991. The land-sale agreement with the applicant was thus declared null and void. The case was remitted to a first-instance court to determine the issues of restitution and compensation. The applicant's subsequent appeal to the Supreme Court was rejected as out of time on 6 February 2004.

Following this, the land was officially transferred to the former owners in September 2005. In the proceedings to determine the compensation owed to the applicant, an independent expert valuer assessed the property. The valuation established that the plot's market value in September 2005 was 112,500 Lithuanian litai (LTL), whereas its value in August 1996 had been LTL 18,000. Despite this expert evidence, the Kaunas Regional Court on 5 October 2006 awarded the applicant only LTL 1,466. The court justified this minimal sum by stating it corresponded to the price the applicant had originally paid in investment vouchers in 1996, rather than reflecting the property's current or even its 1996 monetary value.

The applicant's appeals were unsuccessful. On 26 February 2007, the Court of Appeal upheld the lower court's decision, rejecting her argument that the Civil Code required awarding her the highest value of the property since she had been deprived of it due to an error by State authorities. On 8 May 2007, the Supreme Court refused to accept her cassation appeal for examination, finding no important legal issues.

The core of the applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights was that the compensation she received was manifestly inadequate. She had been deprived of property she had lawfully acquired and possessed for nine years, a deprivation caused by the State's own unlawful actions, yet was compensated with a sum far below its established market value, thereby violating her right to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions.
001-120073:
**Summary of Mohammed v. Austria (Application no. 2283/12)**

The case of *Mohammed v. Austria* concerns a Sudanese national, Mr. Salaheldin Mohammed, who lodged an application against the Republic of Austria with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 January 2012. The applicant alleged that his forced transfer to Hungary under the Dublin Regulation would breach Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13 concerning his second asylum application.

The applicant arrived in Austria on 9 October 2010, having travelled through Greece and Hungary. He lodged an asylum application, but on 5 January 2011, the Federal Asylum Office determined that Hungary had jurisdiction under the Dublin II Regulation and ordered his transfer. The applicant did not appeal this decision. He subsequently went into hiding, thwarting a planned transfer attempt in May 2011.

On 21 December 2011, the applicant was detained in Vienna, and the following day, the Federal Police Authority ordered his detention pending forced transfer to Hungary. On 30 December 2011, he lodged a second asylum application, which had no suspensive effect on the transfer order. He argued that the Asylum Court’s own practice at the time acknowledged a real risk of Article 3 violations for asylum-seekers transferred to Hungary. This practice was based on a UNHCR letter of 17 October 2011, which detailed serious concerns about detention conditions in Hungary, including routine detention of asylum-seekers, ill-treatment by police, and inadequate judicial review of detention. The UNHCR also highlighted that Hungary treated Dublin returnees as second-time applicants, limiting their access to asylum proceedings and increasing the risk of refoulement to Serbia.

The applicant’s detention was upheld by the Vienna Independent Administrative Panel on 5 January 2012. On 10 January 2012, the Administrative Court dismissed his motion for suspensive effect but noted that immigration police would still need to refrain from transferring him if the situation in Hungary breached Article 3. The applicant also applied to the Federal Police Directorate to establish that his transfer would constitute a risk under the Immigration Police Act, but this was rejected on procedural grounds as no relevant proceedings were pending.

The applicant’s transfer was scheduled for 12 January 2012. However, on 11 January 2012, the European Court of Human Rights applied an interim measure under Rule 39, requesting the Austrian Government to stay the transfer until further notice.

The case raised significant issues regarding the protection of asylum-seekers under the Dublin Regulation, particularly in light of documented deficiencies in Hungary’s asylum system. The applicant argued that his transfer would expose him to a real risk of inhuman or degrading treatment and that he had no effective domestic remedy to prevent it.
001-126636:
**Beltram and Beltram Cerovšek v. Slovenia (Application no. 10017/10)** concerned two Slovenian nationals, Marijan Beltram and Anuška Beltram Cerovšek, who alleged that the length of civil proceedings in Slovenia violated their right to a trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The case arose from a civil action instituted on 2 October 2007 before the Ljubljana District Court against O.J. concerning defects in an apartment the applicants had purchased. On 2 April 2008 the applicants requested a hearing. Two days later, the District Court replied that their case could not be granted priority and that no hearing could be scheduled until the end of 2008.

On 6 February 2009, after the case had been pending for about fourteen months, the applicants lodged a supervisory appeal. They relied on the Court Rules, under which a first-instance decision should be issued within eighteen months in civil proceedings. On 26 February 2009 the President of the Ljubljana District Court dismissed the supervisory appeal, stating that the case was not a priority case and that, under the order of precedence for non-priority cases, a hearing would likely be scheduled in the second half of 2009.

On 5 March 2009 the applicants lodged a motion for a deadline with the Ljubljana Higher Court. That motion was dismissed on 27 March 2009, again by reference to the order of precedence and the fact that the case was not considered priority. On 25 May 2009 the applicants lodged a constitutional appeal against the dismissal of both the supervisory appeal and the motion for a deadline, alleging a violation of their right to a trial within a reasonable time. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 3 November 2009.

After the domestic remedies were exhausted, the applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 February 2010.

The domestic proceedings continued slowly. On 22 January 2010 the Ljubljana District Court held a main hearing and appointed a construction expert. On 2 March 2010 it dismissed that expert and appointed another. Two hearings were postponed between April and June 2010. On 27 September 2010 the court held a hearing, heard the expert, issued an order requiring the construction company K.Z. to provide documentation concerning the construction of the apartment, and adjourned the hearing until 8 December 2010.

On 15 October 2010 K.Z. appealed against the order, arguing that it was insufficiently precise. The hearing of 8 December 2010 was therefore postponed. On 17 February 2011 the Ljubljana Higher Court granted K.Z.’s appeal and remitted the case to the first-instance court. On 9 March 2011 the District Court indicated that a new order would be issued and adjourned the hearing. A new order was issued on 24 March 2011. After K.Z. informed the court on 14 April 2011 that the documents would be available at its office, the court on 19 April 2011 asked the expert to inspect them and supplement his opinion. The supplementary opinion was submitted on 7 October 2011.

At a hearing on 11 January 2012 the court granted the applicants’ motion to appoint a noise-exposure expert. That expert was appointed on 4 April 2012, and the opinion was received on 25 May 2012. On 24 August 2012 the court held a main hearing and allowed the construction expert’s opinion to be amended in light of the noise-pollution opinion. The supplemented construction opinion was submitted on 15 October 2012. On 15 March 2013 the District Court held a main hearing, heard the construction expert, and issued a decision largely granting the applicants’ claim. The decision was served on 17 April 2013. Both parties appealed, and the proceedings were still pending before the Ljubljana Higher Court at the time of the European Court’s judgment.

Relevant domestic law provided that civil proceedings before a first-instance court lasting more than eighteen months were considered to involve judicial delay. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were therefore the repeated inability to obtain a timely hearing, the rejection of the applicants’ supervisory appeal, motion for a deadline and constitutional appeal, and the continuing delays caused by court scheduling, expert replacements, and K.Z.’s appeal.
001-126352:
In *Brzuszczyński v. Poland*, the applicant, Piotr Brzuszczyński, a Polish national, complained under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights that his criminal trial was unfair. The central issue was the domestic courts’ reliance on out-of-court statements by R.N., the actual killer, who died before trial and was never available for questioning by the defence.

The underlying facts concerned the murder of E.U. in May 2001. R.N. killed E.U. after pretending to sell him a car. The applicant and R.N. were arrested on 6 June 2001; R.N. had a loaded gun. R.N. was interrogated four times: twice on 7 June, again on 8 June, and on 25 July 2001. In his first statements, he confessed to the murder, claimed that Brzuszczyński had supplied the gun, and said they had planned to split the victim’s money. He repeated those allegations on 8 June and 25 July. On 25 July he changed some details, mentioned an unnamed man present at the killing, said he himself had been kidnapped and ordered to dig his own grave, then stopped and said he would write to the prosecutor. On 31 August 2001 R.N. committed suicide in his prison cell. Because of his death, he was never heard in court, and the applicant could not cross-examine him.

In May 2002 the applicant was indicted for aiding and abetting murder by providing the gun, illegal possession of a firearm with a silencer, and attempted extortion of ransom from the victim’s family. He denied all involvement, stating that he had never possessed or supplied any gun. In May 2003 the Warsaw Regional Court convicted him of aiding and abetting armed robbery, illegal possession of the gun, and aiding and abetting extortion, sentencing him to eight years’ imprisonment. The court relied heavily on R.N.’s investigation statements, found them credible, and noted that hearing R.N. in court would have been useful but was impossible because of his death.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the trial court had selectively used parts of R.N.’s testimony and ignored contradictory evidence. R.N.’s friends and ex-wife testified that R.N. had possessed a gun long before the murder; other witnesses said R.N. never told the truth, and one said he used drugs. The prosecutor also appealed, arguing that the evidence supported a murder conviction.

In December 2003 the Warsaw Court of Appeal quashed the judgment. It found that the first-instance court had failed to examine all evidence and that its assessment lacked consistency. Because R.N. could not be heard in court, the trial court was required to assess his statements with particular thoroughness. It had failed to address numerous witnesses. The appellate court instructed the lower court to determine whether the gun had been provided by the applicant or had already been in R.N.’s possession, consider fingerprint evidence, and establish whether the applicant had a gun permit.

On retrial, after 19 hearings, the Regional Court convicted the applicant in November 2007 of aiding and abetting murder, illegal possession of a gun, and aiding and abetting extortion, sentencing him to 15 years’ imprisonment. It again relied on R.N.’s statements, supported by about 40 witnesses and documentary evidence. It found that the applicant and R.N. were close, financially troubled friends; that R.N. planned to kill a buyer; and that the applicant knew of the plan, provided the gun, and expected half the proceeds. It found R.N.’s early statements spontaneous, detailed, and corroborated, and rejected defence evidence suggesting R.N. had possessed the gun earlier.

The alleged Article 6 violation therefore arises from the conviction being based significantly on the untested statements of a deceased witness, R.N., whom the applicant never had an opportunity to examine.
001-117132:
In *Insanov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 16133/08), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Ali Binnat oglu Insanov, an Azerbaijani national and former Minister of Health Care from 1993 to 2005. The applicant complained about detention conditions, inadequate medical treatment in detention, unfairness of civil proceedings concerning his detention conditions, unfairness of the criminal proceedings against him, and other Convention violations. The Court communicated complaints under Article 3 (conditions of detention and lack of adequate medical treatment), Article 6 (fairness of civil and criminal proceedings), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), while declaring other parts inadmissible.

The criminal case began in October 2005. After being questioned at the Ministry of National Security, Insanov was detained on suspicion of abuse of official authority, embezzlement of public funds, and complicity in an attempted coup allegedly planned after the November 2005 parliamentary elections. He was formally charged with offences including preparation to organise public disorder, actions aimed at usurping State power, high-level embezzlement, abuse of official authority, and repeated and high-level bribe-taking. His pre-trial detention was extended several times by the Nasimi District Court until April 2007; his appeals were dismissed. A search of his home found large amounts of cash in various currencies, gold and jewellery, and property deeds. In January 2007, a new indictment was issued and a separate criminal case was severed and sent to the Assize Court. The charges concerned, among other matters, unlawfully creating conditions for privatisation of State health-care property worth about €23.5 million, receiving bribes, embezzling public funds to publish a book, taking bribes for pharmacy licences, failing to comply with final domestic judgments, and forgery in public office.

Key fair-trial complaints arose before and during the trial. The defence alleged it could not properly familiarise itself with the case file or photocopy materials. The Prosecutor General rejected this, saying the defence had access to all 43 volumes and signed a record of familiarisation. The Assize Court refused to suspend proceedings on this ground. During hearings from February to April 2007, the applicant complained that he could not confer confidentially with his lawyers, that he was not allowed meetings at the detention facility at weekends, and that he was forced to discuss defence strategy in the presence of prosecutors and judges. He also alleged that the court repeatedly refused short adjournments for confidential consultations. The Government maintained that the court had adjourned once on 30 March 2007 and had reminded the MNS Detention Facility of his right to meet his lawyers.

A further central issue was the refusal to summon defence witnesses. Insanov repeatedly asked the Assize Court to hear experts and officials to challenge three audit reports of June, August, and December 2006, which concluded that he had abused his powers to unlawfully privatise State health-care assets. These reports were decisive evidence for his conviction. He argued that the reports were contradictory, that some experts had refused to sign or had reservations, and that privatisation authority lay with the State Committee for Management of State Property and the Ministry of Economic Development. He claimed his role was limited to submitting proposals and confirming non-objection, so those agencies’ officials were responsible for any unlawful privatisation. The handling of these witness requests formed a key part of his Article 6 complaint.

Overall, the case concerns whether the applicant’s detention and medical treatment violated Article 3, whether the criminal and civil proceedings were fair under Article 6, and whether his property rights were breached under Protocol No. 1.
001-121569:
The applicant, N.M.B., is an Iraqi national born in 1973 and originally from Baghdad. He arrived in Sweden on 12 December 2007 and applied for asylum the following day. In his application against Sweden, lodged on 15 November 2010, he alleged that his deportation to Iraq would involve a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. He was represented by Mr T. Stilus; the Swedish Government were represented by Ms C. Hellner and Ms H. Lindquist.

In support of his asylum claim, the applicant stated that he was a Christian academic employed at a university in Baghdad. In April 2006 he began working for a committee established to develop research methods at the university. The committee was soon accused of cooperating with Americans. On 20 June 2006 the applicant wrote to the Minister of Education, accusing a university colleague, a member of the Iraqi Islamic Party (IIP), of corruption and of counteracting the committee’s work. The colleague learned of the accusation and threatened the applicant.

On 27 June 2006 armed men attempted to kidnap the applicant’s daughter. Her mother called the police; after some shooting, the daughter was released. On 30 June 2006 the applicant received a letter calling him and his family Christian traitors and stating that they would be killed if he did not quit his job. On 8 July 2006 he reported the incidents to the police, and the family moved in with relatives. On 16 July 2006 the head of the committee was kidnapped and killed, after committee members had received threatening letters; the committee’s work then ended. On 3 October 2006 the applicant fled with his family to Syria.

On 15 January 2008 the applicant’s parents, who lived in Baghdad, were shot at; his father was kidnapped and tortured until he told the kidnappers the applicant’s whereabouts. In October and December 2008 the applicant received threatening messages on a website. In one, the Islamic Brigade, a militia within the IIP, warned him against returning to Iraq.

On 17 March 2009 the Migration Board rejected the asylum application. It did not question that the applicant was a Christian and had worked for the university committee, but did not find it likely that his work had made him a suspect of cooperating with Americans. It noted that he had quit the job three years earlier and that there was nothing to indicate a remaining work-related threat. It also found that he had not made plausible that his accusation against a former colleague had harmed that person or the IIP, and it questioned the credibility of the alleged attack on his parents. The Board further noted that the security situation in Baghdad and Iraq as a whole had improved.

The applicant appealed, claiming a risk of persecution as a Christian and an academic. He added that members of the IIP had asked for him and had written threatening messages on the wall of his old house in December 2009. He also stated that he had reported to the police his suspicion that high-profile members of the Ministry of Education were responsible for the kidnapping attempt against his daughter.

On 9 June 2010 the Migration Court upheld the Board’s decision. It held that the incidents did not constitute persecution on religious grounds. It found that the applicant had exaggerated his story by adding the police report about his suspicions, that his work for the committee was limited in scope and had ended long ago, and that, absent political activity, his letter to the Ministry was unlikely to cause the alleged threat. It concluded that there was no individual threat against him.

On 3 November 2010 the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal. The applicant subsequently claimed impediments to enforcement, invoking the general situation for Christians in Baghdad and attacks in November 2010 in the residential area where he had lived. On 26 January 2011 the Migration Board declined to reconsider the case, finding no new circumstances justifying reconsideration. The record also referred to the earlier case M.Y.H. and Others v. Sweden for relevant domestic law and information about Iraq.
001-115883:
**Summary of Sizarev v. Ukraine (Application no. 17116/04)**

The case of *Sizarev v. Ukraine* originated from an application lodged against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 May 2004 by Mr. Konstantin Konstantinovich Sizarev, a Ukrainian national born in 1958. The applicant, a former court assistant with no prior criminal record, raised multiple complaints under the Convention, including the lawfulness and length of his pre-trial detention, the conditions of his detention, the authorities’ failure to ensure his physical safety and to investigate an assault against him, and being handcuffed while in hospital.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations began on 3 October 2003, when a certain Mr. K. complained to the police that the applicant had beaten him. Initially, no prosecution was initiated. However, on 24 February 2004, the Yevpatoriya City Prosecutor’s Office opened a criminal case against the applicant on suspicion of deliberately inflicting bodily harm of medium severity on Mr. K. — an offence punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment.

On 18 March 2004, the applicant was ordered not to leave town, and on 25 March 2004 he appointed his wife, Ms. D., as his representative. From 8 to 29 April 2004, the applicant was on sick leave due to a leg injury and consequently failed to appear before the investigator when summoned.

On 19 April 2004, the investigator applied to the Saky City Court requesting the applicant’s pre-trial detention as a more appropriate preventive measure, citing the applicant’s failure to comply with the summons and the fact that his actual place of residence was unknown. On 22 April 2004, the court ordered the police to ensure the applicant’s appearance.

On the morning of 27 April 2004, the applicant was arrested. On the same date, the Saky City Court held a hearing, attended by the applicant and the prosecutor, to consider the investigator’s detention request. The applicant’s request for his wife to be present was rejected.

In ordering the applicant’s pre-trial detention, the Saky Court acknowledged that detention was normally ordered where the likely penalty exceeded three years’ imprisonment, but found it possible to make an exception in this case. It noted that the applicant had failed to appear in response to several summonses, did not actually live at the address he had given to the authorities, and had left Yevpatoriya on many occasions without informing the investigator, in breach of the obligation not to leave town. Additionally, the victim, Mr. K., complained that the applicant had threatened him. The court concluded that these factors sufficed to consider the case exceptional within the meaning of Article 155 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and ordered pre-trial detention pending trial.

Also on 27 April 2004, Ms. D. lodged an appeal on the applicant’s behalf. She argued that pre-trial detention was contrary to criminal procedural legislation given the minor nature of the crime. She contended that the Saky Court had failed to consider medical records confirming the applicant had been undergoing treatment since 8 April 2004, providing a valid reason for his failure to attend the investigation. She further pointed out that the court had disregarded the fact that the applicant had two minor children and that she, his wife, was disabled. Finally, she complained that the hearing had taken place in her absence.

These facts form the basis of the applicant’s complaints before the European Court regarding the lawfulness of his detention and the fairness of the proceedings leading to it.
001-122434:
**Case: Moskalenko and Others v. Ukraine (Application no. 1270/12 and 249 other applications)**

The case originated in 250 applications lodged against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants were Ukrainian nationals whose details were set out in appended tables. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government on 11 December 2012. The Government was represented by its Agent, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy. A Fifth Section Committee delivered judgment on 18 July 2013.

Several procedural issues arose because some applicants had died. Mr Vasiliy Spiridonovich Grunskiy and Mr Petro Andriyovych Plyaka died, and their spouses, Ms Valentina Petrovna Grunskaya and Ms Valentyna Oleksandrivana Kuzmina, expressed the wish to pursue the applications on their behalf. The Government also informed the Court that Mr Viktor Mykolayovych Motuzkov and Ms Olga Mykhaylivna Moroz had died. No replies were received from their addresses after the Court warned that, absent response, it would assume that no one was entitled or wished to pursue those applications.

The central factual basis of the case concerned the non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions. On the dates listed in the appended tables, Ukrainian domestic courts delivered decisions according to which the applicants were entitled to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain their enforcement in due time. The table shows a large number of decisions from local and administrative courts across Ukraine, including Chernihiv, Nizhyn, Zhytomyr, Korosten, Feodosiya, Druzhkivka, Kharkiv, Lviv, Zaporizhzhya, Poltava, Kyiv and other locations. The relevant domestic decisions dated from 1997 to 2011, and many applicants held more than one final decision in their favour. For example, Mr Oleksandr Petrovych Moskalenko had a decision of the Desnyanskyy District Court of Chernihiv dated 29 January 2010; Mr Oleksandr Vasylovych Neshcheret and Mr Viktor Vasylyovych Neshcheret had a decision of the Nizhyn Court dated 28 April 2010; and Ms Oksana Ruslanivna Dmytrenko had a decision of the Zhytomyr Circuit Administrative Court dated 26 January 2009. Other applicants had decisions concerning various district, city, circuit and administrative courts.

The applicants complained primarily about the failure of the Ukrainian authorities to enforce those final and binding judgments. In Convention terms, this alleged non-enforcement engaged the right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, particularly the right of access to court and the requirement that civil rights and obligations be determined within a reasonable time. It also engaged Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, protecting the peaceful enjoyment of possessions, because the final judgments gave rise to enforceable pecuniary entitlements or required specific actions in the applicants’ favour. The applicants essentially alleged that although domestic courts had recognised their rights, the State failed to ensure that those rights were realised in practice, resulting in prolonged delay and uncertainty. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues, but the main case concerned the systemic or repeated failure to enforce final domestic decisions.

The case therefore belonged to a group of repetitive applications concerning Ukraine’s longstanding problem of non-enforcement of domestic judgments. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that final and enforceable decisions existed in the applicants’ favour, that the authorities did not enforce them in due time, and that the applicants consequently suffered delay and loss of the benefit of those judgments. The Court was called upon to determine whether that situation amounted to a violation of the Convention.
001-120968:
The applicant, Ms Marija Jeznik, is a Slovenian national born in 1940 who lives in Vuzenica. The respondent is the Republic of Slovenia. The case originated in an application against Slovenia lodged on 1 July 2008. The applicant was represented by Odvetniška Družba Marčič in Ostali, O.P., D.N.O., a law firm from Slovenj Gradec. The Slovenian Government were represented by their Agent. On 27 April 2012 the application was communicated to the Government and, under Protocol No. 14, assigned to a committee of three judges.

In 1994 the applicant began investing in commercial papers of the company Kompas Consulting d.d. through the company Kompas Maribor D.O.O. At the end of 1994 such trading was prohibited by the Securities Market Act, but the applicant continued the activity until 1996. In 1996 she instituted enforcement proceedings against Kompas Maribor D.O.O. before the Maribor District Court. She sought payment of lost investments from Kompas Maribor for not informing her of the legislative amendments and for continuing with the trading of commercial papers. She further complained before the domestic courts that, because Kompas Consulting d.d. was bankrupt, she could receive back only a small proportion of her investments in bankruptcy proceedings.

On 14 October 1996 the Maribor District Court issued a writ of execution. On 12 November 1996, following an objection, the case was referred to contentious proceedings. On 4 February 1998 the Maribor District Court rendered a judgment rejecting the applicant’s request. She appealed. On 24 November 1998 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the appeal and remitted the case for re-examination. The second-instance court found that, because the applicant had clarified during the appeal phase that she was seeking compensation for damages only, this constituted a new fact that the first-instance court would have to deliberate upon.

On 24 October 2001 the Maribor District Court rendered a judgment. The court found that, given the contractual arrangements, the company Kompas Maribor D.O.O. could not be held responsible for the damages sustained. The applicant appealed. On 15 September 2004 the Maribor Higher Court upheld the first-instance judgment and rejected the appeal. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. On 25 January 2007 the Supreme Court rejected her appeal. She lodged a constitutional appeal. On 10 December 2007 the Constitutional Court rejected her appeal.

The record also states that relevant domestic law is set out in Tomažič v. Slovenia (no. 38350/02, 13 December 2007). The domestic proceedings therefore comprised two first-instance decisions, two decisions of the Maribor Higher Court, one Supreme Court decision, and one Constitutional Court decision. The applicant pursued her claim through the ordinary courts and then through constitutional review, and her domestic appeals were ultimately rejected at the final stages of those proceedings.
001-115854:
Case Qama v. Albania and Italy (Application no. 4604/09) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fourth Section on 8 January 2013, final on 8 April 2013. The applicant, Flamur Qama, an Albanian national born in 1960 and living in Durrës, lodged the application on 23 December 2008 against Albania and Italy. He alleged breaches of Articles 6 § 1 and 8 of the Convention because the Albanian and Italian authorities allegedly failed to secure his right of contact with his child, who was in Italy. The application was communicated to the respondent governments on 21 September 2009, and the Court decided to examine admissibility and merits together.

The applicant had a son born on 25 August 1994. In September 1999, the applicant’s late spouse, who was suffering from a serious disease, entered Italy irregularly with the son in order to obtain medical treatment. The applicant later joined them in Italy. In August or September 2002, after disagreements with his in-laws, the applicant was expelled from Italy because he did not have a residence permit. His wife and son remained in Italy, as their status had not yet been regularised. The wife died on 7 October 2002.

Following the mother’s death, custody proceedings began in Italy. On 17 October 2002, the applicant’s sister-in-law, Z., applied to the Ancona Youth Court seeking custody of the child. On 30 December 2002, a report from the local social health centre stated that the child feared returning to live with his father because of the father’s alleged ill-treatment of the deceased mother. The report also said the father had abandoned the child and spouse without notice when they most needed him.

On 4 June 2003, the Italian court granted Z.’s request. It entrusted Z. with custody of the child under the supervision of the Social Service of Senigallia and appointed the Mayor of Senigallia as temporary guardian. The court suspended the parents’ parental rights, reasoning that they had allowed the child to leave Albania without addressing the serious difficulties he would face. It prohibited the child’s removal from Italian territory and assigned the International Social Service (ISS), an NGO, to investigate the applicant’s family situation. Crucially, the court made no provision for the applicant’s visiting or contact rights with his child.

On 25 September 2003, the ISS, after attempting to contact the applicant, informed the Italian court that he refused to speak to them and simply requested that the child be returned to him. From contacts with neighbours, the ISS reported that the applicant had remarried, his new wife was pregnant, he was unemployed, and he was living on his spouse’s income. On 22 March 2004, the Italian social services updated the court: the child’s status in Italy had been regularised and his situation appeared balanced.

The applicant’s central complaint was that, despite being the father, he was left without effective contact with his son in Italy. He argued that both Albania and Italy failed to protect his family life and his right of access to the child, raising issues under Article 8, and that the proceedings did not satisfy Article 6 § 1. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the father’s expulsion, the mother’s death, the Italian custody order suspending parental rights without contact arrangements, the child’s placement with the aunt, the ISS investigation, and the applicant’s limited ability to maintain or restore contact from Albania.
001-127399:
The applicant, Mr Aleksey Gennadyevich Tarasov, a Ukrainian national born in 1965 and living in Makiyivka, alleged that police had ill-treated him and that his right to mount a defence had been violated.

On 13 January 2000 Makiyivka police arrested him and held him in police custody until 25 January 2000. He alleged that he had no access to a lawyer and was forced to confess. He claimed repeated severe beatings during interrogation, suffocation with a plastic bag and gas mask, and electric shocks applied to his genitals. The Government stated that his rights to legal representation and freedom from self-incrimination were explained and that he signed waivers; he was questioned about a car theft and confessed, and also confessed to involvement in a robbery. On 14 January 2000 an ambulance took him to hospital; medical reports recorded abdominal trauma and a bruise in the lumbar region. On 15 January 2000 criminal proceedings were instituted against him for garage theft, theft of non-ferrous metals and attempted robbery. On 16 January 2000 he was charged with car theft; he denied guilt and said his earlier confession had been made under duress. Further charges followed on 18 January 2000. On 25 January 2000 he was transferred to the SIZO. On 29 February 2000, at a confrontation with co-accused D., he denied guilt and refused to sign the report. On 2 March 2000, with lawyer M. present, he denied guilt and alleged duress. On 13 March 2000 his mother appointed lawyer I.

The trial began on 17 March 2000. During hearings the applicant claimed his confession had been extracted by beatings and ill-treatment and sought witnesses. On 2 June 2000 witnesses U.G. and U.A. testified that they had heard him screaming and had seen him after beatings. On 8 June 2000 the court refused to summon the ambulance doctor but ordered a forensic medical examination. Health issues affected proceedings: in August 2000 he was not brought to court due to renal colic; in September 2000 the SIZO said he was fit; in October 2000 it said his health was very poor; in August 2001 it said he could participate and recommended a stretcher. On 21 December 2001 he was transferred to court by ambulance and brought in on a stretcher, with a doctor present and lawyer N. representing him. He said he felt unwell and lost consciousness; the Government said his health was satisfactory and that he took part in final pleadings.

On 25 December 2001 the Gornyatskiy Local Court of Makiyivka convicted the applicant and others of theft and robbery and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. It relied on his prior confessions plus co-defendants’ testimony, victims, witnesses, material evidence and stolen goods. It rejected his ill-treatment complaint and did not accept U.G. and U.A.’s testimony, citing lack of support and their relationship with him. Appeals in January and February 2002 were left without examination for procedural defects, with extensions granted. On 13 May 2002 he lodged a cassation appeal complaining of torture, lack of access to a lawyer, falsification of case-file documents, failure to question cellmates, and pronouncement of judgment in his absence because his lawyer had convinced him to waive his right to be present at the last hearing, depriving him of arguments and closing submissions. On 29 October 2002 a Supreme Court panel found the first-instance judgment well-founded, no procedural violations, and his ill-treatment allegations duly checked and rejected.

Separately, on 14 March 2000 he wrote to a human rights NGO. On 25 May 2000 the prosecutor refused criminal proceedings over the alleged ill-treatment. On 2 August 2000 the regional prosecutor quashed that refusal and ordered further investigation. On 7 September 2000 the Makiyivka prosecutor again refused for lack of proof. In November 2000 the court ordered another forensic examination; from November 2000 to May 2001 experts noted scars and pigmentations and found no link between the January 2000 injuries and later health problems. In August 2003 he challenged the 7 September 2000 decision; on 6 November 2003 the district court quashed it and remitted the case. On 20 May 2005 cellmates were re-questioned. On 15 June 2005 the prosecutor refused proceedings for lack of corpus delicti, citing police denials, conflicting cellmate statements, destroyed SIZO records and no evidence; the applicant did not challenge that decision. A CPT report on its September 2000 visit described similar allegations and visible marks; the applicant said the passage concerned him.

001-115850:
Davit Jashi, a Georgian national born in 1973, was arrested on 28 September 2005 for drug possession and detained in Tbilisi No. 5 Prison. Prior to these proceedings, he had suffered serious cranial traumas that deteriorated his mental health. On 28 December 2005, a psychiatric report concluded that a definitive diagnosis required a comprehensive examination in an appropriate medical setting. Acting on this, the Zugdidi District Court ordered on 20 January 2006 that Jashi be admitted to Poti Psychiatric Hospital for a forensic psychiatric examination, specifying that his trial could only resume after obtaining results. Despite this final ruling, authorities refused to enforce it.

On 9 March 2006, Jashi was transferred to Zugdidi Prison under a strict regime. His representatives requested interim measures from the European Court of Human Rights on 7 April 2006, seeking enforcement of the psychiatric examination order. The Court declined to indicate interim measures but gave urgent notice to the Government on 26 April 2006, requesting explanations for non-enforcement and documentation of medical treatment provided.

A subsequent court order on 23 May 2006 directed Jashi's admission to the National Forensic Bureau's psychiatric ward, where he was transferred on 31 May 2006. A panel of State psychiatric experts issued a report on 14 June 2006 finding that Jashi had an organic personality disorder but retained criminal responsibility and did not require compulsory psychiatric treatment. He was returned to Zugdidi Prison the following day.

After his return, Jashi attempted suicide on 15 June 2006 by slashing his wrists and exhibited aggressive behaviour. Neither he nor his lawyers had been informed of the medical report's contents. On 4 July 2006, the Court applied Rule 39, indicating that Jashi's mental health should be examined by a parity-based panel of psychiatric experts in an appropriate medical establishment, with adequate medical treatment to follow.

Jashi made further suicide attempts on 12 July 2006 (drug overdose) and 22 July 2006 (slashing wrists with electrical wiring). He was transferred to the NFB psychiatric ward from 27 July to 18 August 2006, where a parity-based panel issued a report largely reiterating the previous findings but noting depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation. The prison authority then admitted him to the prison hospital's psychiatric ward, where he remained until 31 August 2008.

While in the prison hospital, medical examinations conducted between August 2007 and June 2008 revealed serious cardiac conditions including cardiac ischemia, class III-IV angina, arterial hypertension, and grade II-III heart failure. Medical reports recommended treatment in a specialised cardiology hospital and a coronary angiogram. In July 2008, Jashi was diagnosed with viral hepatitis C. Although offered an angiogram in a private hospital on 15 July 2008, he declined.

The applicant's representatives repeatedly requested transfer to a cardiology hospital. On 9 December 2008, the Court indicated that Jashi should be placed in a cardiology hospital for treatment consistent with the second medical report's recommendations. Prison authorities offered transfers on multiple occasions in December 2008 and January 2009, which Jashi refused without explanation. He was finally transferred to Guli Hospital, a private cardiology facility, on 3 April 2009, where he remained until 15 May 2009. Due to his iodine allergy, a coronary angiogram was deemed imprudent, but supervised cardiology drug treatment significantly improved his condition. Subsequent hepatitis C treatment with antiviral drugs from July to December 2009 proved successful.
001-118335:
The applicant, Mustafa Abdi, a Somali national, arrived in the United Kingdom on 7 May 1995 and claimed asylum. His claim was refused, but he was granted exceptional leave to remain until February 2000. On 23 July 1998 he was convicted of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. On 20 May 2002 the Secretary of State decided to make a deportation order; on 27 May 2002 detention was authorised. He appealed and made a fresh asylum claim; appeal rights were exhausted on 4 December 2003. He was assessed as high risk of sexual offending and medium risk of general offending. His release became automatic on 3 September 2003, but he remained detained. On 5 April 2004 a deportation order including detention authority was issued and served on 19 April 2004.

He claimed Isaaq clan membership from Somaliland, with parents born in Hargeisa, although he was born in Mogadishu. Authorities initially sought removal to Somaliland but required clan-history bio-data; he did not cooperate. In August 2004 the last carrier willing to take enforced returns to Somalia withdrew; only voluntary returns with a disclaimer were possible. In November 2004 he refused to sign a disclaimer. Bail was refused in December 2004; further asylum representations in March 2005 were refused as a fresh claim in September 2005; bail was again refused on 11 October 2005, when an immigration judge was wrongly told enforced removal would soon be possible. In July 2006 an agreement with African Express Airlines made enforced removals possible; the first took place on 30 November 2006. In September 2006 he obtained permission to seek judicial review of his detention, but interim release was refused. Removal directions for 29 November 2006 were cancelled pending judicial review.

In domestic proceedings, the Administrative Court on 7 December 2006 applied the Hardial Singh principles. It held detention lawful up to August 2004; unlawful from 3 December 2004 to 30 June 2006 because of length, impossibility of removal, and misleading statements; and lawful after 30 June 2006 because immediate removal was again possible. Both sides appealed. On 30 July 2007 the Court of Appeal allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal and dismissed the applicant’s, holding the disputed period lawful because he could have returned voluntarily and posed a high reoffending risk. Permission to appeal to the House of Lords was refused on 13 December 2007.

In the separate deportation-order challenge, revocation was refused on 1 February 2007. An Immigration Judge allowed his appeal; the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal ordered reconsideration on 10 May 2007. After a reconsideration hearing on 26 February 2008, a rehearing was ordered. On 18 December 2008 the Tribunal reheard the case and dismissed the appeal by determination of 1 July 2009. The Court of Appeal allowed his appeal on 23 April 2010, but the Supreme Court allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal on 24 November 2010. Removal directions were issued on 6 December 2010 for 8 December 2010; on 7 December 2010 an interim measure prevented removal. He remained in immigration detention. He had been released on bail after 13 April 2007 but was re-detained on 3 April 2008 after breaching bail. The application concerns only the first period of detention, ending shortly after 13 April 2007.

Monthly reviews occurred during 3 September 2003–13 April 2007. In April 2006 the Home Office introduced an unpublished policy presuming detention of Foreign National Prisoners pending deportation; it was not disclosed until mid-2008 or published until September 2008, while published policy stated a presumption of release.
001-115876:
**Case Summary: Tomić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 14284/08)**

The case of *Tomić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* concerned the non-enforcement of final and enforceable domestic judgments awarding war damages. The applicants were five citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Ruža Tomić, Ljeposava Kovačević, Dobrinka Jovanović, Marko Tomić and Janko Tomić. They lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 February 2008, alleging violations arising from the failure of the authorities to enforce final domestic judgments in their favour. The case was similar to earlier cases such as *Čolić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* and *Runić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*.

The key facts began on 13 March 2001, when the Srebrenica First Instance Court ordered the Republika Srpska, an Entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to pay the applicants 31,500 convertible marks (BAM), within 15 days, in respect of war damage, together with default interest at the statutory rate. That judgment became final on 20 April 2001. On 1 April 2002, the Banja Luka District Court issued a writ of execution. Despite the final judgment and the execution order, the awarded sums were not paid.

The applicants then complained to the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the non-enforcement. On 26 June 2007, the Constitutional Court found a breach of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. However, the applicants did not claim compensation, and the Constitutional Court’s practice at the time indicated that such a claim would most likely have been refused.

Afterward, the authorities carried out an extensive information campaign explaining the options for settling the Republika Srpska’s public debt, including debt arising from domestic judgments. On 18 January 2010, three applicants—Ms Ljeposava Kovačević, Mr Marko Tomić and Mr Janko Tomić—informed the authorities that they agreed to receive legal costs in cash and the principal debt and default interest in government bonds. On 15 June 2010, government bonds were issued to them, and they subsequently sold some or all of those bonds on the Stock Exchange. The remaining applicant, Ms Dobrinka Jovanović, was not issued government bonds. The summary of the facts states that she did not accept the issuance of bonds in lieu of cash as a means of enforcement.

The relevant domestic law included the Domestic Debt Act 2012, which entered into force on 13 January 2012 and repealed the Domestic Debt Act 2004. As regards war damage, the 2012 Act envisaged the same solution as the old Act, but changed the maturity of government bonds from 14 years to 13 years. However, the new Act was not relevant to the bonded applicants because the applicable provisions were those of the 2004 Act, which had been in force when the bonds were issued. For Ms Jovanović, the key point was that she had not accepted bonds in lieu of cash as enforcement.

The alleged violations therefore centred on the failure to enforce final domestic judgments awarding war damages, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 30 August 2010, the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government and to rule on admissibility and merits at the same time under Article 29 § 1 of the Convention.
001-122429:
**Summary**

The case of *Schädler-Eberle v. Liechtenstein* (Application no. 56422/09) concerns an application lodged by Karolina Schädler-Eberle, a Liechtenstein national born in 1925, against the Principality of Liechtenstein under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant owned two plots of land in the Municipality of Triesenberg.

**Background:** On 25 and 27 February 2000, Triesenberg adopted its first-ever land development plan (*Zonenplan*) by referendum. Under this plan, the applicant's two plots were designated as falling within a zone where building construction was not authorised. On 28 March 2000, the applicant, represented by counsel, objected, contesting the plan's lawfulness as breaching her right to equality and protection of property, and requested that her plots be designated building land.

The Municipality dismissed her objection (decision issued 22 January 2001), finding the plots were not fully developed for lack of complete water installations. It held that the non-building designation was justified by environmental and landscape protection, since the plots lay outside the year-round inhabited area, and distinguished them from three fully developed areas where buildings had already been erected. On 27–28 April 2004, the Government dismissed her complaint, endorsing the Municipality's reasoning and finding that even if the plots might have been building land under provisional building rules of 1983, she had no claim to such designation in the first land development plan. It found no need to hear the parties in person or inspect the property.

**Administrative Court proceedings:** On 14 May 2004, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court, requesting it to obtain documents, hold a public oral hearing, designate her plots as building land or grant compensation for factual expropriation, and declare the referendum void. She also asked to question witnesses who would allegedly show the referendum had been manipulated. On 30 June 2004, the Administrative Court dismissed her complaint without a public oral hearing. It found nothing indicated the plan breached her legitimate expectations, and that even if officials had raised hopes about future building designation, the adopted plan did not so designate the land. It concluded that taking evidence or holding a hearing was unnecessary, and found no proof the referendum was unlawfully manipulated.

**Constitutional Court proceedings:** On 26 August 2004, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. She alleged under Article 6 that the Administrative Court had refused to take evidence in an adversarial manner in a public oral hearing, despite her express request and despite no prior authority having held an oral hearing—contrary to the court's practice in comparable cases. She further complained under Article 6 about the referendum's adoption procedure, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the plan disproportionately interfered with her property rights.

On 4 November 2008 (served 14 April 2009), the Constitutional Court dismissed the referendum complaint as inadmissible for failure to exhaust domestic remedies, rejected the remainder as ill-founded, but *ex officio* found a violation of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time. On the oral hearing issue, it held that Liechtenstein's reservation to Article 6 § 1 concerning publicity of hearings was valid and applied to the National Administrative Justice Act, so the public/oral hearing requirement did not apply to the Administrative Court. However, the right to a fair trial was not covered by the reservation; the court found the Administrative Court could determine all factual and legal questions from written observations and documents, and the legal question was not complex, so the refusal did not violate the right to a fair trial.
001-122187:
In *Rudnichenko v. Ukraine* (no. 2775/07, ECtHR, 11 July 2013), the applicant, a Ukrainian national, complained that his pre-trial detention was unlawful and unreasonably long. He later added complaints that the trial judge had not been impartial and that he had been unable to secure the attendance of a key witness at trial.

The detention facts arose from two incidents. On 6 January 2006, at about 6 p.m., the applicant was caught breaking into N.’s car and trying to dismantle equipment. N. handed him over to the police. A police report referred to the car theft, N.’s complaint, the applicant’s apprehension, and his drunkenness; it noted he had to be handcuffed. On 7 January 2006, the Leninskyy District Court ordered three days’ administrative detention for being drunk in public. On 9 January 2006, an investigator arrested him on suspicion of robbery. On 12 January 2006, the same court remanded him in custody for two months, relying on the fact that he had been caught in flagrante delicto, had been drunk, was unemployed, and had committed the offence within a year of release from prison. He was represented by a lawyer from 13 January 2006.

The applicant repeatedly sought release, without success. His lawyer complained that his detention from 6 to 12 January 2006 had been unlawful and asked the court to summon N. and the arresting police officers, because they could show that he had in reality been detained as a criminal suspect, not merely as an administrative offender. On 29 March 2006, the court found that the investigation authority had violated criminal procedure by arresting him only on 9 January 2006, but it rejected the complaint as disclosing no significant violation. On appeal, the Sevastopol Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 6 June 2006, holding that the administrative detention from 6 to 9 January was outside the scope of review and that the later detention was lawful. The witness request was said to have no basis in the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The impartiality and witness-attendance complaints arose from an earlier incident on 22 October 2005 involving an attempted break-in of K.’s car. K. caught one thief, B., while the applicant allegedly escaped. B. was tried separately and, on 7 February 2006, convicted by Judge R. of robbery. The judgment relied on B.’s statements implicating the applicant as his accomplice and instigator. The applicant was not a party to those proceedings. Later, K. and B. identified the applicant. On 7 March 2006, the applicant was indicted for robberies involving K. and N., and the case was sent to trial.

On 25 April 2007, the case was assigned to Judge R., the same judge who had tried B. On 12 October 2007, Judge R. sought recusal, stating that she had already expressed an opinion about the incident involving both the applicant and B. The President of the Leninskyy Court rejected the recusal request. On 14 November 2007, Judge R. convicted the applicant of robbery following conspiracy with B. and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment, relying on B.’s prior trial statements, which were read out at the hearing. The applicant had unsuccessfully requested B.’s attendance and questioning; the Government later said the request was made at an inappropriate stage. The applicant was acquitted regarding the N. incident, which was reclassified as attempted petty theft.

On appeal, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) that B. had not been summoned and that statements from a trial in which he had not participated were used against him. He also argued that Judge R. had admitted having a preconceived opinion. On 28 July 2009, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction without its own judicial investigation, finding B.’s statements concordant with other evidence. Cassation was rejected on 14 January 2010. The alleged violations therefore concerned Article 5, regarding unlawful and lengthy detention, and Article 6, regarding an impartial tribunal and the right to examine a key witness.
001-116827:
This case originated in an application (no. 50254/07) lodged by Mr Lampros Papadakis, a Greek national, against the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.
