The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 of the Convention concerning his defence rights, particularly because evidence was given by an undisclosed undercover witness, and of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning a court order that he reimburse storage costs for his seized car.

The criminal proceedings arose from an investigation into suspected drug trafficking involving Greek and Macedonian nationals. On 10 November 2005 the public prosecutor authorised special investigative measures, including secret surveillance, audio-visual recording, and undercover agents. The order permitted DEA undercover agents from Athens to take part. According to the investigation, the applicant allegedly met undercover agents and co-accused persons in Skopje and Thessaloniki. On 10 November 2005, a meeting took place in a Skopje café bar where the sale of about 10 kg of cocaine was allegedly discussed. On 14 November 2005, a cocaine sample was allegedly handed to an undercover agent in Thessaloniki. On 18 November 2005, the applicant was arrested in Skopje, while other suspects were arrested elsewhere and cocaine was found in a car at the border.

On 19 November 2005, an investigating judge opened an investigation. The applicant remained silent when questioned. An undercover agent, whose identity was not disclosed, gave evidence in Greek with Macedonian interpretation. He implicated the applicant and described meetings and negotiations concerning the drug deal. In December 2005, the public prosecutor indicted the applicant and others for drug trafficking.

At trial, the applicant sought a direct confrontation with the undercover agent who had testified during the investigation. The prosecution said the agent’s identity was unknown to it, and the court attempted to secure the witness’s attendance through the Ministries of Justice of the respondent State and Greece. On 21 June 2006, a different undercover agent appeared in a specially secured room. The applicant and his lawyers were not present during the examination. The witness, a DEA agent, testified in English with Macedonian translation and described the operation, the applicant’s alleged role, and the alleged drug negotiations.

After the testimony, the court provided a transcript and gave the accused and their lawyers one hour to prepare written questions. Defence counsel requested at least 24 or 48 hours, arguing that the evidence was new and that they had not been given prior notice. The court refused, noting that the witness had only a 24-hour leave to remain. When the time expired, the applicant and his lawyers stated that they could not formulate questions. The applicant later submitted five written questions, but on 11 July 2006 the trial court refused to admit them, stating that the defence had already been given an opportunity to question the witness. The defence insisted that direct questioning of both undercover agents was necessary, especially because their statements allegedly contained inconsistencies.

These facts formed the basis of the Article 6 complaint: the use of an unidentified undercover witness, the inability to confront or effectively cross-examine him, the lack of adequate time to prepare questions, and the rejection of later questions. The applicant also complained that he had been ordered to pay storage costs for his seized car, which he alleged amounted to an unjustified interference with his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-119465:
**Gavula v. Ukraine (Application no. 52652/07)**

**Summary of Key Facts**

The case of *Gavula v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Vitaliy Vasilyevich Gavula, a Ukrainian national, on 19 November 2007. The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 5 § 3 (right to trial within a reasonable time) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, he complained that his arrest was unlawful, that the conditions of his detention were inhuman and degrading, and that his pre-trial detention was excessively lengthy.

The applicant was arrested on 6 February 2003 at approximately 3 p.m. in an apartment rented by an acquaintance, D., and taken to a police station. He alleged that at the police station he was handcuffed, beaten, and had his nose broken. He was questioned that same evening and admitted to robbing an apartment. The Government disputed the arrest date, claiming it occurred on 7 February 2003.

On 10 February 2003, the Dniprovskiy District Court ordered the applicant’s placement in pre-trial detention on the grounds that he was accused of a serious crime and could abscond or hinder the investigation. This detention was subsequently extended on multiple occasions, beginning with an extension until 7 June 2003.

Between May 2003 and September 2007, the criminal case against the applicant was presented to the court but referred back for further investigation on five separate occasions. Each time, the court also ordered that the applicant remain in pre-trial detention. On 11 December 2006 and 15 January 2007, the Dniprovskiy Court denied the applicant’s requests for release, citing without elaboration that he could “continue his criminal activity,” abscond, or hinder the investigation.

The applicant’s complaints of ill-treatment were repeatedly examined by prosecutors. Between 2006 and 2008, the Dniprovskiy District Prosecutor’s Office refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers on multiple occasions. These refusals were sometimes overturned by courts or senior prosecutors and referred back for further examination, but ultimately the complaints were rejected. The prosecutor’s decision of 27 March 2008 was upheld by the Dniprovskiy Court on 3 June 2009, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal on 2 September 2009, and the Supreme Court of Ukraine on 17 January 2010.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant was held in the Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Centre (SIZO) no. 13 from 26 February 2003 until August 2010—a period of over seven years. He described his cell as cold, damp, and infested with cockroaches, with dirty bedding and filthy sanitary facilities. Official correspondence indicated severe overcrowding: at one point, the applicant was held in a cell measuring 52.06 square metres with eighteen other detainees. A 2009 report by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) following an inspection of the Kyiv SIZO described serious overcrowding, appalling material conditions, and levels of hygiene that could “easily be described as inhuman and degrading treatment.”

On 1 March 2010, the Dniprovskiy Court sentenced the applicant to eight and a half years’ imprisonment for robbery. This sentence was upheld on appeal. The applicant was released on probation on 26 March 2011.
001-127617:
**Summary of the Case of Majs Eksport-Import v. Serbia**

The case of *Majs Eksport-Import v. Serbia* (Application no. 35327/09) concerns an application lodged against the Republic of Serbia with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 June 2009. The applicant is Majs Eksport-Import, a company registered in Serbia. The core of the case revolves around the applicant's inability to enforce final domestic court judgments against a debtor company that was undergoing insolvency proceedings and was predominantly socially owned.

The facts are as follows: On 7 March 2000, the applicant entered into a contract with Beogradski Pamučni Kombat (the debtor), which subsequently failed to meet its contractual obligations. On 11 December 2001, the Commercial Court in Belgrade initiated insolvency proceedings against the debtor. The applicant timely lodged its pecuniary claim within these proceedings on 12 March 2002. However, because the claim was disputed, the applicant was compelled to initiate a separate civil suit on 11 October 2002 to have its claim formally determined.

The Commercial Court in Belgrade ruled in favor of the applicant in two separate judgments. On 2 September 2004, it ordered the debtor to pay the applicant EUR 6,686.15. This judgment became final. Subsequently, on 4 April 2005, the court determined the remainder of the claim, ordering the debtor to pay an additional EUR 11,409 and 80,500 Serbian dinars for the costs of the civil proceedings. This second judgment became final on 9 June 2005.

A critical fact is the status of the debtor company. Throughout the insolvency proceedings, it remained registered as a predominantly socially owned company. On 18 December 2009, the Commercial Court terminated the insolvency proceedings against the debtor. This decision became final on 11 January 2011, and the debtor was erased from the Companies’ Register on 1 June 2011. This meant that the debtor company effectively ceased to exist, making the enforcement of judgments against it impossible.

The alleged violation stems from the events of 30 September 2009. On that day, the applicant lodged an application for the enforcement of the judgment of 4 April 2005, specifically in respect of the awarded costs. The Commercial Court in Belgrade allowed the application and issued an enforcement order on the same day. However, this order proved ineffective because the debtor's assets were tied up in the ongoing insolvency proceedings, which were terminated shortly thereafter, leading to the company's erasure. The parts of the judgments concerning the principal amounts were to be enforced within the insolvency proceedings, which ultimately concluded without the applicant being paid.

The applicant's complaint before the European Court of Human Rights is that the Serbian authorities failed to enforce the final judgments rendered in its favor, thereby violating its right to a fair trial and the protection of property under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key issue, consistent with the Court's established case law on socially owned companies in Serbia, is the respondent State's liability for the debts of a company it effectively controlled during insolvency, which was unable to settle its obligations. The applicant exhausted all domestic remedies available, including initiating enforcement proceedings before the domestic courts, before lodging the application with the European Court. The case was communicated to the Serbian Government on 11 October 2011.
001-126349:
**Mijanović v. Montenegro** concerned an application lodged on 4 May 2006 by Mr Borislav Mijanović, a Montenegrin national, alleging that a final domestic judgment in his favour had not been enforced, thereby violating his property rights. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows.

The applicant had brought compensation proceedings against “Radoje Dakić,” a joint-stock company predominantly owned by State capital. On 24 September 2003 the Court of First Instance in Podgorica ruled in his favour, ordering the debtor to pay EUR 159,879.33 plus statutory interest, together with EUR 6,216.26 for legal costs. On 6 July 2004 the High Court in Podgorica upheld that judgment, and on 27 December 2005 the Supreme Court dismissed the debtor’s appeal on points of law. The judgment thus became final and enforceable.

On 24 September 2004, at the applicant’s request, the Court of First Instance issued an enforcement order by means of a bank account transfer. On 31 October 2005 the Central Bank informed the court that the judgment had not been enforced because the debtor’s bank account lacked funds. In February 2006 the Minister of Justice also told the applicant that enforcement was impossible due to insufficient funds and invited him to identify other accounts. On 9 March 2006 the applicant supplied details of several accounts. On 16 March 2006 the court ordered the Central Bank to block all the debtor’s accounts and provide data on available funds, with payment to be made primarily from the designated account and, if insufficient, from other accounts.

On 24 March 2006 the Central Bank reported that the debt had been attached to one of the debtor’s accounts. The applicant complained on 3 and 13 April 2006 about delays, arguing that the Central Bank had attached the debt to an account with no funds, making enforcement impossible. The court reaffirmed its earlier decision on 26 April 2006. By 28 April 2006 the Central Bank stated that the relevant account had been attached and other accounts blocked. On 13 September 2006 it informed the court that enforcement was awaiting an inflow of funds, but noted that fifteen other claims against the debtor had priority over the applicant’s claim.

In March 2007 the applicant sought a change in the means of enforcement. On 29 March 2007 the Court of First Instance asked him to specify his request within eight days or it would be considered withdrawn. His representative received the request on 2 April 2007. On 24 April 2007 the bailiff requested that the case file be archived because the applicant’s representative had failed to amend the request, which was therefore treated as withdrawn. The enforcement order remained registered and awaiting funds. On 4 May 2009 the applicant filed a new enforcement request, proposing sale of the debtor’s immovable assets. On 15 July 2009 an enforcement order to that effect was issued, but there is no evidence that the domestic authorities made any attempt to enforce it. The enforcement proceedings remained ongoing.

A central fact was the State’s ownership of the debtor. Between 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force for Montenegro, and the end of 2005, the State and its bodies directly or indirectly owned 52.196% of the debtor’s stock; from 2006 onwards they owned 50.579%. The applicant also alleged that the debtor had substantial assets and income: land sales by the Privatisation Council for EUR 7,618,000 and EUR 1,400,000, a State grant of EUR 1,200,000, and profits of about EUR 2,000,000, totalling EUR 12,218,000. He claimed the debtor avoided using the official bank account and opened accounts elsewhere. Since December 2005 he complained to numerous officials. He died on 21 April 2010; his daughter was later declared his sole heir in respect of the judgment debt.

The alleged violations therefore concern Montenegro’s prolonged failure to enforce a final judgment against a majority State-owned company despite available assets, interfering with the applicant’s right to court enforcement and property.
001-119968:
**Case summary: *Eremia v. the Republic of Moldova* (ECtHR, 28 May 2013)**

The applicants were Lilia Eremia and her daughters, Doina and Mariana. They alleged that Moldova failed to fulfil its positive obligations under Articles 3, 14 and 17 of the European Convention on Human Rights to protect them from domestic violence by a private individual and to punish the aggressor. The first applicant’s husband, “A,” was a police officer. According to the applicants, A. frequently came home drunk and assaulted Lilia, often in the presence of their daughters. After the birth of their second daughter, the violence worsened.

On 2 July 2010, Lilia petitioned for divorce after A. assaulted her and verbally abused their teenage daughters. A. then became more violent, regularly assaulting and insulting Lilia and the daughters. On 30 August 2010, Lilia reported being punched in the head. A. was fined only 200 Moldovan lei by an administrative court on 18 September 2010 and received a formal warning from the Ministry of Internal Affairs on 30 September 2010. On 5 November 2010, A. assaulted Lilia again. On 11 and 12 November 2010, he assaulted her in front of the daughters and nearly suffocated her, causing her to lose her voice for a day and a half. A forensic examination on 23 November 2010 found no injuries.

On 9 December 2010, the Călăraşi District Court issued a protection order. It found that A. had beaten, insulted, threatened and psychologically abused Lilia, mistreated the family pet, and that his violence in front of the daughters harmed their psychological well-being. A. was ordered to stay away from the home for 90 days, with a 500-metre exclusion zone and a prohibition on contacting the applicants or committing violence. The order was served on 12 December 2010.

Despite the order, A. harassed Lilia on 16 December 2010 and entered the family home on 19 December 2010. The Government claimed the applicants permitted this; the applicants denied it and said A. assaulted Lilia, destroyed possessions and verbally abused the third applicant. On 10 January 2011, police allegedly pressured Lilia to withdraw her criminal complaint because a criminal record could harm A.’s job and their daughters’ prospects. On 11 January 2011, a meeting with the prosecutor took place with A. present. The next day, the prosecutor refused to initiate a criminal investigation.

On 13 January 2011, A. returned home, assaulted Lilia, simulated strangling her, and threatened to kill her and her aunt if she did not withdraw the complaint. A medical expert found haematomas on her neck and clavicle consistent with her account. A criminal investigation was finally opened on 17 January 2011, but social workers later advised Lilia to reconcile, saying she was “neither the first nor the last woman to be beaten up by her husband.”

On 1 April 2011, the prosecutor found that A. had admitted physically and psychologically abusing three family members and that there was evidence of guilt. Nevertheless, because the offence was considered “less serious,” A. did not represent a danger to society, supported three minors and was respected at work, the investigation was suspended for one year and A. was conditionally released from criminal liability. The applicants’ appeal was rejected. The original protection order was later partly revoked on appeal, removing the 500-metre exclusion zone and explicit prohibitions on harassment and violence.

These facts underpinned the applicants’ complaints that the authorities failed to protect them from repeated domestic violence, discouraged prosecution, failed to enforce protection measures, and treated the violence leniently and discriminatorily.
001-126133:
The case of **Tuncer Güneş v. Turkey** (Application no. 26268/08) originated in an application against Turkey lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 16 May 2008 by Gülizar Tuncer Güneş, a Turkish national born in 1966 and living in Istanbul. The applicant, a lawyer, married on 30 March 2005. Under Article 187 of the Turkish Civil Code, a married woman must bear her husband’s surname. The same provision allows her to retain her maiden name in front of her husband’s surname, and the applicant did so. However, she wanted to use only her maiden name, “Tuncer”.

On 9 May 2007 she applied to the Şişli Court of First Instance for permission to use only her maiden name. On 18 July 2007 that court dismissed her request. It held that Article 187 required married women to bear their husband’s name throughout the marriage and did not entitle them to use their maiden name alone. The applicant appealed, but on 22 November 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance judgment. The domestic courts therefore definitively refused her request to bear only her maiden name.

The domestic legal framework was central to the alleged violations. Article 187 of the Civil Code provided that married women shall bear their husband’s name but may, by written declaration, keep their maiden name before that surname. By contrast, married men were not subject to the same obligation and could bear their own surname after marriage. The Turkish Constitution guaranteed equality before the law and equal rights for women and men under Article 10. Article 90, as amended in 2004, gave international human rights agreements precedence over domestic law in cases of conflict. Despite this, in a decision of 10 March 2011, the Constitutional Court dismissed an objection brought by three family courts challenging Article 187’s constitutionality. The Court also referred to relevant international law as set out in **Ünal Tekeli v. Turkey**, a similar case concerning surname rules for married women.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that the domestic courts’ refusal to allow her to bear only her maiden name unjustifiably interfered with her right to respect for her private life under Article 8 of the Convention. She further claimed that Turkish law permitted married men, but not married women, to bear their own surname after marriage. According to her, this distinction constituted discrimination on grounds of sex and was incompatible with Article 14 of the Convention. The essence of her complaint was therefore twofold: first, that the compulsory use of her husband’s surname affected her private and professional identity; and second, that the sex-based legal rule imposed a heavier burden on married women than on married men.

The application was communicated to the Turkish Government on 22 October 2010. The Court decided to examine the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time under Article 29 § 1. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant was legally required to take her husband’s surname, was permitted only to add her maiden name before it, and was refused by the domestic courts the right to use her maiden name alone, even though married men could retain and use their own surname.
001-115864:
In *Röman v. Finland* (Application no. 13072/05, judgment 29 January 2013), the applicant, Mirja Anneli Röman, was born in Finland in 1954 out of wedlock and initially bore her mother’s maiden name. In 1954 her mother and biological father concluded a child-support agreement verified by social services. In 1956 her mother married another man, and in 1961 the applicant’s surname was changed to that of her mother’s husband. The spouses agreed that the biological father would never be mentioned. Although the church register—which served as the official population register until 1993—listed the mother’s husband as the applicant’s stepfather, the later State population register recorded him as her father.

The applicant eventually began to question her biological origins. In 2001 she discovered the church-register discrepancy and located a copy of the child-support agreement in social-services archives, which enabled her to identify her biological father. On 25 September 2002 the State population-register information was corrected. On 6 February 2003 she initiated paternity proceedings against her biological father in the Vantaa District Court, claiming she had only learned in December 2001 that her mother’s husband was not her biological father.

The domestic courts dismissed her claim as time-barred. Under the Implementing Act of the Paternity Act, which entered into force on 1 October 1976, paternity proceedings for children born before that date had to be initiated within five years—by 1 October 1981. The law also barred proceedings after the putative father’s death. The District Court found that the applicant had been an adult during the five-year period and could have questioned her mother or checked the church register. It held that applying the time-limit did not violate the Constitution or the Convention. The Helsinki Court of Appeal upheld that decision on the same grounds. On 12 October 2004 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. In 2005 the Deputy Parliamentary Ombudsman considered that the national courts had acted within their margin of appreciation. In 2007 a private DNA test showed 99.99% certainty that the identified man was her biological father; he died in 2008.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Under Article 8, she complained that the absolute five-year time-limit prevented her from having her biological father’s paternity legally established, interfering with her private life and her right to know her origins and identity. She argued that she had no real opportunity to bring proceedings within the limitation period because her family had concealed the truth and official records were inconsistent; she only discovered the relevant facts in 2001. Under Article 14, she alleged discrimination because children born after the Paternity Act entered into force could seek establishment of paternity without the same five-year time-limit or the bar following the father’s death. She was thus treated differently on grounds of birth status, date of birth, and origin. The Government relied on legal certainty and protection of putative fathers, but the case raised whether the rigid transitional rule struck a fair balance, particularly given modern DNA evidence.
001-118737:
The applicant, Grupa Zastava Vozila, A.D., is a Serbian company. In 1996 it concluded a contract with PS ZA AVTO p.o. before a notary concerning joint investments. On 1 December 1997, PS ZA AVTO instituted proceedings before the Ljubljana District Court seeking annulment of that contract and the notarial protocol. The applicant company was the defendant in those domestic proceedings.

On 14 July 1998, the District Court ordered the claim to be served on the applicant company in the Republic of Serbia with the assistance of the Ministry of Justice through diplomatic channels. On 29 October 1998 the court made an inquiry with the Ministry about service. On 12 November 1998 the Ministry informed the court that it was still waiting for a reply from the Serbian authorities. On 30 May 2000, ZASTAVA AVTO d.o.o. requested third-party intervention. On 6 June 2000 the court made another inquiry with the Ministry concerning service. On 29 June 2000 the applicant company’s representative sent an authority form and a request for joinder with another case. On 17 May 2001 the applicant company requested that a hearing be set. The first hearing, scheduled for 11 October 2001, was postponed. On 12 October 2001 the State Attorney’s Office submitted a request for third-party intervention. On 10 June 2002 the court allowed both third parties to participate in the proceedings.

On 12 September 2002 the applicant company lodged a counterclaim. Because of the counterclaim, the court postponed the hearing set for 19 September 2002. On 3 February 2003 the court held a settlement hearing, but the parties did not reach a settlement. On 14 April 2003 the court held the first hearing. On 23 April 2003 the applicant company requested an extension of the deadline for submitting documents; the deadline was extended by one month. On 10 November 2003 the court appointed a financial expert. On 23 February 2004 the court granted the expert’s request for an extension of the deadline for submitting the report. On 3 May 2004 the expert submitted the report. On 6 October 2004 the court held a hearing.

On 13 December 2004 the District Court rendered judgment in favour of the applicant company; the notarial protocol and the contract remained in force. The plaintiff appealed. On 7 November 2006 the Ljubljana Higher Court delivered judgment amending the first-instance judgment and ruling against the applicant company. The applicant company lodged an appeal on points of law. On 12 May 2008 the Supreme Court delivered judgment upholding the appeal court’s decision. The applicant company lodged a constitutional appeal. On 13 May 2010 the Constitutional Court rejected the appeal as unfounded.

The applicant company lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 11 November 2010. It was represented by Ms M. Kranjčevič, a lawyer practising in Ljubljana. The Slovenian Government were represented by their Agent. The Serbian Government indicated that they did not intend to take part in the proceedings.
001-121573:
In *N.M.Y. and Others v. Sweden* (Application no. 72686/10), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined the case of three Iraqi nationals—two women and one man, born in 1963, 1966 and 1971—who originated from Baghdad. Their names were not disclosed. They arrived in Sweden on 17 September 2008 and applied for asylum two days later. They alleged that their deportation to Iraq would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

The applicants are Christians and had lived together in Baghdad. They claimed they had been regularly harassed and insulted because of their faith. The two female applicants had been forced to wear a veil to avoid trouble. In 2006, armed men stopped a car carrying the two female applicants and their mother. When the men saw a hanging cross in the car, they forced the passengers out and took the vehicle. On 17 August 2008, armed men came to the applicants’ house and told another brother that the applicants should convert to Islam before 1 September 2008, the start of Ramadan, or be killed. The men also wrote a message with the same content on the wall of the house. The applicants left Iraq on 20 August 2008.

On 30 December 2008, the Migration Board rejected their asylum applications. It accepted that there was a threat against the applicants based on their religious beliefs and the difficult situation in Baghdad at the time. However, it found the threat limited to Baghdad because the applicants had not held prominent professional or religious positions; nothing suggested they would be of particular interest outside Baghdad. They could relocate to central or northern Iraq. This applied regardless of whether they had a social network there. As they had shared a household in Iraq, the female applicants would not lack a male relative upon return.

On appeal, the applicants maintained that Iraqi authorities would not protect them. They emphasized that their case did not rest only on the general situation for Christians; they had experienced several specific incidents because of their Christian beliefs. They further argued that the risk was not geographically limited to Baghdad: as Christians, they risked persecution throughout Iraq, so no internal flight alternative existed. The Migration Board replied that they could relocate to the Kurdistan Region and noted direct flights from Sweden to Erbil.

On 16 September 2009, the Migration Court upheld the Board’s decision. It considered the incidents to be criminal acts related to the general security situation in Baghdad at the time. It noted that two years had passed since the incidents and that the security situation in Baghdad had improved. Thus, the circumstances did not show a concrete and individual threat against the applicants upon return. On 9 November 2009, the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal.

On 21 November 2010, the applicants lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that deportation to Iraq would violate Articles 2 and 3. On 22 December 2010, the President of the Section applied Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Swedish Government that the applicants should not be deported to Iraq during the proceedings. The application was communicated to the Government on 12 September 2011. The Court’s judgment became final on 27 September 2013. Relevant domestic law and country information about Iraq were cross-referenced to *M.Y.H. and Others v. Sweden* (no. 50859/10, 27 June 2013).
001-127813:
**Belousov v. Ukraine (Application no. 4494/07)**

The case originated from an application against Ukraine by Mr. Vyacheslav Belousov, a Ukrainian national. The alleged violations stem from events beginning on 18 July 2005, when several police officers in civilian clothes came to the hostel where the applicant lived and invited him to accompany them to the Kominternivskyy District police station in Kharkiv.

According to the applicant, upon arrival at the police station around noon, he was questioned regarding complaints from two mothers implicating him in the sexual abuse of their minor daughters. The applicant alleged that three police officers—S.B., A.O., and V.M.—urged him to confess under threat of torture. When he insisted on his innocence, the officers allegedly cleared a desk, covered it with a blanket, and placed him on it with his hands handcuffed behind his back. They then painfully twisted his arms, punched him in various parts of his body, and squeezed his genitals. Subsequently, three additional officers joined and took turns applying various techniques to cause him pain, beat him, and strangle him. Unable to withstand the torture, by 5 p.m. the applicant confessed to a crime he maintained he never committed.

At approximately 6 p.m., seven or eight police officers took the applicant back to his hostel, where they examined his room, seized several items including a bed cover, a rug, and personal belongings, and returned him to the police station. Critically, no documentary record of his arrest was drawn up at that stage. The applicant was not permitted to contact his family, and it was only at approximately 7 p.m. on 19 July 2005 that he first met with a lawyer hired by his relatives.

Witnesses at the hostel provided accounts corroborating the applicant's version of events. The concierge and three neighbours had seen the applicant leaving with police officers at about 11 a.m. on 18 July; at that time, he appeared sober, neatly dressed, and in good health. When they saw him approximately seven hours later, he was limping, stooping, had bruises and swellings on his face, and his clothes were dirty and wrinkled. Some neighbours noted he arrived handcuffed and that police prevented him from explaining what was happening. That evening, an unidentified person telephoned the police hotline demanding an investigation into the applicant's arrest and detention. Following this complaint, M.K., the Deputy Chief Officer, arrived to conduct an inquiry.

On 19 July 2005 at approximately 8:40 p.m., more than 33 hours after the applicant had been taken into police custody, an investigator finally drew up an arrest report. The applicant was brought before a judge only on 22 July 2005—four days after his detention—who remanded him in custody for ten days. He was released on 29 July 2005 subject to an undertaking not to abscond. In September 2005, one of the mothers who had complained of sexual abuse against the applicant withdrew her complaint, stating it had been lodged under pressure from the police.

Regarding the investigation of the applicant's complaints, a forensic expert examined the applicant on 19 July 2005 and certified that he was suffering from minor bodily injuries, including soft tissue swelling, numerous bruises, and scratches on various parts of his body, particularly the face and groin area, inflicted by blunt objects within the past one to three days. The applicant lodged a formal complaint on 20 July 2005 alleging unrecorded detention and ill-treatment, and criminal proceedings were instituted on 1 August 2005.

The investigation that followed was marked by repeated suspensions and renewals. On 28 December 2009, the prosecutor's office discontinued the proceedings, acknowledging that the applicant had been de facto arrested on 18 July 2005, but had only been documented on 19 July 2005—a delay that could give rise to disciplinary proceedings but did not qualify as a criminal offence. The office also found insufficient evidence of torture and characterised the visit to the applicant's home as a lawful crime scene inspection conducted with the applicant's consent. This decision was subsequently quashed by courts on multiple occasions, with the investigation repeatedly remitted for further investigation before being stayed again when the perpetrator could not be identified.

The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 6, and 13 of the Convention, complaining of torture, unlawful detention, unlawful search, failure to be brought promptly before a judge, and the ineffectiveness of the investigation into his complaints.
001-122892:
Lay Lay Company Limited v. Malta (Application no. 30633/11) concerned a Maltese-registered company’s complaint that it was denied access to court under Article 6 § 1 to contest the refusal of its building permit, and that this also violated its property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 1984, A., for the applicant company, and C. purchased about 4,500 sq. m of land in Ghaxaq. The company claimed it was a building site under the Building Development Areas Act 1983. In August 1984 an application to build garages with upper floors was lodged in C.’s name before the Planning Area Permits Board (PAPB). In September 1985 the applicant company acquired C.’s share and became sole owner, but did not inform the PAPB.

On 10 July 1986 the PAPB approved the application as per plans, subject to payment of road contribution costs. The company began building. However, the contribution bill was sent to C. and remained unpaid. A 1987 minute noted that no permit had been issued because the applicant had failed to pay and works were in hand. C. was warned that construction was not covered by a permit. In 1992 a fresh bill (about EUR 7,962) was sent to C., passed to A., and paid by the applicant on 14 December 1992. Clearance was issued.

After the PAPB was replaced by the Planning Authority (later MEPA) in 1993, the file was moved, lost, and not acted upon. On 7 October 1996, a Development Control Unit manager wrote that the permit could not be issued because the 1986 bill had “fallen through” and the 1992 payment came after a decision not to accept payment six years after billing. The applicant did not appeal within thirty days or seek judicial review then, later claiming it did not understand this as a formal refusal.

In 1999, after more delays, the company filed a judicial protest. MEPA issued a stop notice. In 2003 the Development Appeals Board rejected the company’s appeal, finding that the PAPB had never issued a permit, its recommendation was not a permit, and payment of the contribution did not automatically lead to approval. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal in 2004. It emerged that MEPA treated the 1996 letter as the refusal, which had become final because the thirty-day appeal period had lapsed.

In constitutional redress proceedings begun in 2004, the company complained under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the failure to issue the permit, the stop notice, and the absence of a contestable decision. The First Hall rejected the claims: the company had no permit and no possession of development rights; it had built without a permit; enforcement was proportionate. On Article 6, it found the company could have challenged the authority’s conduct or the 1996 letter but failed to do so. In 2011 the Constitutional Court upheld this, finding no permit and no legitimate expectation, and that the 1996 letter sufficiently conveyed a refusal. The company remained passive and did not appeal. Meanwhile, a 2006 local plan placed the property outside the development zone, and the contribution payment was not refunded.
001-115981:
In *Claes v. Belgium*, the applicant, André Claes, a Belgian national with severe mental disabilities, alleged that his prolonged detention in prison psychiatric facilities unsuitable for his condition violated Article 3 and Article 5 §§ 1(e) and 4 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The case concerned his detention, principally in the psychiatric wing of Merksplas Prison, and the Belgian authorities’ failure to transfer him to an appropriate psychiatric or disability-care institution.

In 1978, Claes was found not criminally responsible for the repeated rape of his under-age sisters between 1973 and 1977 because of severe mental disabilities. He was committed to psychiatric detention. Over the following years, he was released and detained again after further sexual offences and aggressive incidents. In 1983, the Mental Health Board ordered his transfer to a private psychiatric clinic, but he was returned to a prison psychiatric wing in 1984 after aggressive behaviour and another sexual assault. In 1987, he was arrested for indecent assault on a young girl and placed in Turnhout Prison’s psychiatric wing. In 1994, following incidents involving young girls and female staff, and reports describing him as manipulative and potentially dangerous, the Mental Health Board ordered his return to Merksplas Prison.

Psychological assessments in 1998 recorded an IQ of 72 and classified him as mentally disabled. From 1998 onwards, Belgian authorities repeatedly tried, without success, to find a non-prison psychiatric or residential institution willing to accept him. Reports between 2002 and 2008 documented the ongoing failure to secure a suitable placement. A 2004 report noted that a structured establishment was needed to reduce reoffending risk, but no place was available; he was placed on a waiting list for a private care home. Later reports described growing suffering, frustration, and the need for intensive, specific care, while noting that his behavioural problems made institutions reluctant to take him.

The Mental Health Board repeatedly extended his detention in Merksplas until he could be placed in the Flemish system for social integration of people with disabilities. In 2007 and 2008, Claes sought urgent court injunctions ordering the Belgian State to find him a suitable institution. These applications were dismissed because the urgent applications judge and Court of Appeal held that the ordinary courts lacked jurisdiction; the Mental Health Boards had exclusive power to decide the place of detention. Appeals to the Higher Mental Health Board and Court of Cassation also failed.

A 2008 visit report noted unsatisfactory conditions: Claes spent days in communal areas and at night shared a dormitory with twenty-four other people, with unsatisfactory sanitation. In 2009, the Mental Health Board acknowledged his right to treatment but said it had no power to order the authorities to provide a suitable place. It considered his detention lawful and not intended to be inhuman or degrading, though it accepted that detention without adequate treatment might raise an Article 3 issue in conjunction with Article 5. It refused release because of the danger he posed, particularly to children.

In September 2009, Claes was released on a trial basis to the Martine van Camp Centre. However, in June 2011, after aggressive behaviour, he was returned to Louvain Prison’s psychiatric wing. The key alleged violations therefore concerned his long detention in a prison environment unsuitable for his mental disability, inadequate treatment and care, the State’s failure to provide an appropriate placement, and the lack of effective judicial review of the place and conditions of his detention.
001-126918:
**Budrevich v. the Czech Republic** (Application no. 65303/10) concerned a Belarusian national, Mr Andrei Budrevich, who alleged that he had no effective remedy under Article 13 of the Convention against his expulsion to Belarus. He entered the Czech Republic in October 2006 using an assumed name and applied for asylum, claiming persecution in Belarus for distributing advertisements supporting opposition candidate Aliaxandr Milinkevich. His first asylum request was rejected in 2007 as not credible; the Hradec Králové Regional Court upheld that decision in 2008, and the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his cassation appeal in 2009 because he failed to provide grounds.

His true identity was revealed in December 2009 after Czech police sent his fingerprints to Belarus. Shortly afterward, Belarus requested his extradition for drug-related offences. In April 2010, the Plzeň Regional Court found the extradition request inadmissible because there were reasonable fears that criminal proceedings in Belarus would violate Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention. It relied on reports describing political persecution, lack of judicial independence, inhuman detention conditions, ill-treatment by police, and unfair trials in Belarus.

Meanwhile, the applicant had been convicted of several thefts in Czech criminal proceedings. In November 2008, the Prague 10 District Court imposed a thirty-month expulsion order. In March 2009, the Prague 8 District Court imposed a one-year prison sentence and a five-year expulsion order. Execution of expulsion was repeatedly stayed because of his asylum proceedings.

The applicant lodged four asylum requests. His second request in January 2010 and third request in September 2010 were rejected as repeated requests containing no new circumstances. A key issue was that, when deciding the second request, the Ministry of the Interior already knew of Belarus’s extradition request but merely asked the applicant whether he knew of any prosecution against him. He said he did not. The Supreme Administrative Court later quashed that decision, holding that the Ministry should have informed him of the extradition request and examined whether the new prosecution and extradition request constituted new circumstances. The third request was also affected by invalid service, as later confirmed by the Supreme Administrative Court. His fourth request in November 2010 eventually led to subsidiary protection in October 2011, later extended, although asylum itself was refused.

Expulsion became imminent after the third asylum request was rejected on 30 September 2010. The District Court cancelled the suspension on 25 October 2010. On 4 October 2010, before boarding a plane, the applicant attempted suicide by cutting his neck. He appealed on 9 November 2010, but the Prague Municipal Court rejected the appeal as belated, finding that service on 5 November 2010 made the deadline 8 November. On 9 November 2010, the European Court of Human Rights applied Rule 39, indicating that the applicant should not be removed to Belarus. The District Court then again stayed the expulsion on 10 November 2010.

Domestic law was central to the alleged Article 13 violation. Under the Asylum Act, judicial review of asylum decisions did not have suspensive effect where a repeated request was inadmissible under Section 10a(e). The Criminal Code made expulsion inadmissible if asylum or subsidiary protection had been granted, or if there was a risk of persecution, torture, or inhuman or degrading treatment. The Code of Criminal Procedure required suspension of expulsion where an asylum request was not manifestly unfounded and barred execution during subsidiary protection. The applicant argued that these mechanisms failed to provide an effective remedy against expulsion, especially given non-suspensive review, the authorities’ failure to inform him about the extradition request, and the risk he faced in Belarus.
001-118045:
In *Julius Kloiber Schlachthof GmbH and Others v. Austria* (Applications nos. 21565/07, 21572/07, 21575/07 and 21580/07), four Austrian-registered companies that slaughter cattle and pigs complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Under the Agricultural Market Act (*Agrarmarktgesetz*), they were liable to pay agricultural marketing charges to Agrarmarkt Austria (“AMA”), the national agricultural marketing board, calculated by the number of animals slaughtered.

In 2006 AMA issued payment orders against each applicant for unpaid contributions. On 5 July 2006 it ordered the first company to pay EUR 56,573.62 for 2003 and 2004 plus a 10% surcharge. On 30 May 2006 it ordered the second company to pay EUR 12,556.43 for 2004 and 2005 plus 10%; the third to pay EUR 5,936.01 for 2005 and 2006 plus 10%; and the fourth to pay EUR 96,050.48 for 2005 and 2006 plus a 60% surcharge. These surcharges formed the core of the later complaints.

The companies appealed, arguing that the AMA contribution system breached EU State-aid rules, and requested oral hearings. The Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water, acting as appeal authority, dismissed the appeals on 17 July 2006 without a hearing. The Minister relied on a European Commission decision of 30 June 2004, which had raised no objection to AMA’s quality assurance scheme and quality mark as compatible State aid, and on Administrative Court decision no. 2005/17/230 of 20 March 2006. The Minister said a hearing was unnecessary because it was only required when a panel decided an appeal against a tax office or regional finance directorate, not in this procedure.

The applicants then lodged complaints with the Constitutional Court and the Administrative Court. Before the Constitutional Court, they alleged that the surcharges violated their constitutional right to property. Before the Administrative Court, they argued that the appeal authority was not a “court” under Court of Justice case-law, preventing review of the Commission’s decision through Article 234 EC proceedings. They also said the authorities’ findings on the surcharges were insufficient, particularly whether objective and subjective elements of the offence were met. Relying on Article 6, they complained that there had been no public hearing and that the “criminal charge” against them had not been decided by an impartial tribunal established by law. They asked the Administrative Court for a public hearing.

On 25 September 2006 the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the complaints for lack of prospects of success. On 30 January 2007 the Administrative Court dismissed the complaints in separate decisions, referring to its earlier decision no. 2005/17/230 and dismissing the cases without further proceedings in camera. It held that Article 6 of the Convention was not relevant.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained in particular that proceedings concerning the imposition of surcharges on unpaid AMA contributions had not been decided by a tribunal within the meaning of Article 6 § 1. The applications were communicated to the Austrian Government on 23 October 2008, and the Court decided to rule on admissibility and merits together. The key alleged violation therefore concerned the absence of a tribunal/public hearing in proceedings that imposed financial surcharges for non-payment of AMA contributions.
001-119972:
In *Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 31848/07, judgment of 30 May 2013), the applicant, Ahmadshah Mammadshah oglu Zeynalov, an Azerbaijani farmer born in 1935, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 April 2007. He alleged in particular that the Supreme Court’s examination of the criminal case against him had not complied with the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention.

The case arose from a dispute over ownership rights to a plot of land between the applicant and the Sadan Municipality in the former Davachi district. On 29 December 2004, the Davachi District Court convicted the applicant under Article 188 of the Criminal Code for violating a lawful owner’s right to a plot of land by unauthorised occupation or cultivation. He was fined 100 conventional financial units—550,000 old Azerbaijani manats, equivalent to 110 new Azerbaijani manats (AZN), or approximately EUR 84 at the time. The court found that he had unlawfully occupied and cultivated 0.8 hectares of land owned by the Municipality, relying on witness statements and information from the State Committee of Land and Cartography (“the SCLC”).

The applicant appealed, arguing that the disputed plot formed part of a larger 50-hectare parcel belonging to his family farming business. On 18 March 2005, the Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law, alleging that the lower courts had erred in assessing the facts. On 9 August 2005, the Supreme Court, sitting as a panel of three judges including judge N.H., quashed the Court of Appeal’s judgment and remitted the case for fresh examination. It noted that the conviction had been based on insufficient evidence.

On remittal, the Court of Appeal sought detailed information from the SCLC and the Municipality about the exact location, measurements and ownership of the plot. The Municipality stated that official records showed the land belonged to it, and the SCLC conducted an on-site inspection and concluded that the plot was part of the Municipality’s estate. On 12 July 2006, the Court of Appeal again upheld the applicant’s conviction. The applicant appealed once more. On 10 October 2006, the Supreme Court, again composed of a panel of three judges including judge N.H., dismissed his appeal and upheld the Court of Appeal’s judgment. It found that all relevant evidence had been examined and that there had been no substantive or procedural breaches.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 6 violation concern judge N.H.’s repeated participation in the Supreme Court’s examination of the same criminal case. Under Article 109.1.6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a judge cannot participate if he has already participated as a judge in the examination of the same criminal case in a court of first instance, appeal or Supreme Court. Article 109.2 requires such a judge to disqualify himself or herself. Furthermore, in decision no. 3 of 24 November 2005, the Plenum of the Supreme Court stated that a judge must withdraw when legal grounds for disqualification exist, even if the parties have not raised an objection, and that a judge who has already heard a criminal case at first instance, appeal or cassation cannot take part in its re-examination. The applicant’s complaint therefore focused on the alleged lack of an impartial tribunal because the same Supreme Court judge first quashed and remitted the case and later sat on the final cassation panel, contrary to domestic disqualification rules. The application was communicated to the Government on 10 November 2010, and the Court decided to rule on admissibility and merits together.
001-138597:
The case of *Vilnes and Others v. Norway* (Applications nos. 52806/09 and 22703/10) concerned seven former North Sea divers—Dag Vilnes, Magn Håkon Muledal, Anders Lindahl, Sigurdur P. Hafsteinsson, Knut Arvid Nygård, Bjørn Anders Nesdal, and Per Arne Jakobsen—who worked in Norwegian oil-related diving during the “pioneer era” (1965–1990). They alleged that Norway violated Articles 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the first four also Article 3, because they suffered serious health damage from dangerous diving operations and inadequate state protection, supervision, and information.

The applicants worked at depths up to 150–180 metres, and in test dives to 300, 400, 450 and 504 metres. They used bounce and saturation diving with heliox, diving bells, and decompression chambers. Many experienced decompression sickness, neurological injuries, encephalopathy, PTSD, hearing loss, chronic obstructive lung disease, and other disabilities. Health studies at the University of Bergen, NUTEC, and Haukeland Hospital later suggested possible links between diving and central nervous system damage.

Key regulatory facts were central to the alleged violations. Until 1978, the Labour Inspection Authority supervised diving; thereafter the Petroleum Directorate took over. Safety rules set limits, such as a sixteen-day saturation period and a twenty-nine-metre umbilical, but the Directorate granted liberal, almost automatic dispensations, extending saturation periods to twenty-four or thirty-two days and permitting longer umbilicals. Decompression tables used by diving companies were kept confidential and not disclosed to Norwegian authorities, despite warnings, including a 1969 letter from Newcastle University, that standard tables were inadequate and that long-term effects such as bone necrosis were a serious hazard.

The individual applicants described repeated life-threatening incidents. Vilnes suffered spinal decompression sickness in 1977 due to rapid decompression, gas cut-off, umbilical entrapment, and a 1983 saturation dive at 180 metres with equipment, communication, and decompression failures; he developed PTSD and neurological damage. Muledal completed about 500 days of saturation diving, suffered bends and gas cuts, participated in a 360-metre test dive, and developed HPNS, COPD, and encephalopathy. Lindahl suffered decompression sickness roughly twenty times, including sudden decompression causing unconsciousness and convulsions, and later had PTSD and lung disability. Hafsteinsson suffered bends in deep dives, a near explosive decompression, hearing damage, COPD, and PTSD. Nygård narrowly escaped a crane ball and an oxy-arc explosion, and suffered COPD, PTSD, and encephalopathy. Nesdal had bends, dizziness, was trapped in a shaft and hooked by an ROV umbilical, and witnessed fatal accidents. Jakobsen had fifteen to twenty bends, was dragged by his umbilical, experienced diving-bell seal failure and wire break, and recovered bodies after the Alexander Kielland disaster; he was diagnosed with PTSD.

The applicants became disabled and received disability pensions and ex gratia compensation under state schemes. A state commission, the Lossius Commission, reported in 2002/2003 that many pioneer divers had serious medical problems, high disability and suicide rates, and recommended a compensation scheme. The Government denied legal liability but established compensation arrangements and a Special Compensation Board. Nevertheless, the applicants alleged that Norway had failed to provide adequate regulation, supervision, information about health risks, and protection, thereby causing or failing to prevent their injuries. These facts formed the basis for their complaints under Articles 2, 8, and 3.
001-126807:
In *De Luca v. Italy* (Application no. 43870/04), the European Court of Human Rights considered an application lodged by Mr Giovanni De Luca, an Italian national living in Benevento, against Italy on 10 December 2004. The applicant alleged that the insolvency declared by his debtor, the municipality of Benevento, prevented him from collecting money owed to him.

The key facts began in December 1993, when Benevento declared itself insolvent (*stato di dissesto*) under Legislative Decree no. 66 of 1989, later amended and replaced by Legislative Decree no. 267 of 2000. In January 1994, the municipality’s financial management was entrusted to an extraordinary liquidation committee (OSL), responsible for drawing up a list of admissible claims for the debt repayment procedure. Under Article 248 § 2 of Legislative Decree no. 267/2000, from the declaration of insolvency until approval of the statement of accounts, no enforcement procedure could be initiated or pursued concerning claims registered with the OSL. Paragraph 4 also suspended statutory interest and inflation compensation on those debts during that period. Domestic case-law initially held that these restrictions did not apply to claims considered certain and payable by a judicial decision issued after the declaration of insolvency, regardless of when the claim arose. Such claims could therefore be enforced.

However, Law no. 140 of 28 May 2004, in force from 13 June 2004, changed this. Section 5(2) provided that insolvency rules applied to claims arising before 31 December of the year preceding the rebalancing of the budget, even if those claims had been established by a judicial decision after that date. The Consiglio di Stato later applied this provision in 2004 and 2005.

The applicant had filed a damages claim against Benevento on 28 October 1992, seeking unpaid rent and compensation for damage to his property. By judgment of 18 November 2003, deposited on 10 February 2004, the Benevento District Court allowed his claim and ordered the municipality to pay him EUR 17,604.46 in damages, plus statutory interest and inflation compensation. The judgment was served on the municipality on 9 April 2004 and became final on 9 May 2004. In resolution no. 4088 of 21 June 2005, the OSL acknowledged a debt of EUR 42,028.58 owed to the applicant. On 7 February 2006, the OSL offered a friendly settlement of 80% of the sum claimed. The applicant refused.

The domestic insolvency scheme aimed to satisfy creditors proportionately (*par condicio creditorum*) and to rebalance the municipality’s accounts. The municipality continued to exist and perform public functions. The OSL’s competence was limited to debts predating the insolvency, and enforcement was barred for registered past debts, with interest and inflation compensation suspended. Creditors could lodge appeals against OSL decisions, and the Constitutional Court had upheld the system in 1994, citing public interests and the need to prevent further financial deterioration.

The applicant’s complaint was that the insolvency of Benevento prevented him from collecting the sum owed. The central facts relevant to the alleged violation were that he held a final judicial judgment against the municipality, but the 2004 law subjected his judicially certified claim to the insolvency procedure, blocking enforcement and suspending interest and inflation compensation. Although the OSL acknowledged the debt and offered a reduced settlement, the applicant declined it, and the debt remained unpaid through ordinary enforcement. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 August 2006, with the Chamber deciding to rule on admissibility and merits together under Article 29 § 1 of the Convention.
001-127809:
**Summary of Gerashchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 20602/05)**

The case of *Gerashchenko v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Anatoliy Sergeyevich Gerashchenko, a Ukrainian national, on 19 July 2006. The applicant alleged multiple violations of the Convention, including ill-treatment by police, an unlawful home search, unlawful and prolonged pre-trial detention lacking judicial review, and self-incrimination under duress without legal assistance. The Court also examined possible monitoring of his correspondence with the Court under Articles 8 and 34.

The key facts centre on events beginning 2 July 2004. Following a prior drug conviction in December 2003, the applicant became a suspect when another individual, Mr B., claimed to have purchased drugs from him. On 19 May 2004, the Suvorivskyy Court authorised a search of the applicant's home based on this statement.

On 2 July 2004, an undercover police operation allegedly involved the purchase of liquid opium from the applicant. According to the authorities, police then conducted a search, seizing marked banknotes, drug production equipment, and liquid opium found in the applicant's pocket. However, the applicant provided a starkly different account. He alleged that plain-clothed officers broke into his property without identifying themselves, beat him, dragged him into the house by his hair, and handcuffed him. He claimed the police then planted the drugs and banknotes on him. His family and an acquaintance, Mr Zh., witnessed the search. The search report stated it lasted from 4 to 7:30 p.m., but the undercover agent's report claimed the drug purchase occurred at approximately 6 p.m.—two hours after the search began. The applicant was arrested and taken to a police station.

The pre-trial investigation raised significant concerns. On 3 July 2004, a neurosurgeon found no acute injuries, but on 7 July, the applicant was hospitalised with a diagnosed contusion of the right kidney after complaining of pain and stating he had been beaten during arrest. This information was recorded by police. The applicant was not provided formal legal representation until 15 July 2004. Detention was repeatedly extended by the Suvorivskyy Court, initially for ten days, then for two months on 15 July, and again for three months on 3 September, based on the seriousness of charges and his criminal record. The applicant's request for a forensic medical examination to document his injuries was rejected by the investigator on 30 September 2004, on grounds that he was slandering police to evade liability.

During the trial, key discrepancies emerged. On 20 December 2005, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal quashed the initial conviction, citing factual discrepancies regarding the search timing and conflicting witness statements about where the body search occurred. Critically, the appellate court noted the search warrant of 19 May 2004 was issued for a different criminal case, and the applicant's allegations of beating and evidence fabrication had not been thoroughly investigated. Despite this, the applicant was re-convicted on 6 June 2007, and this conviction was upheld on appeal on 4 December 2007. His subsequent cassation appeals to the Supreme Court were returned for procedural failures and ultimately dismissed without a merits examination in August 2008.

Additionally, during his detention, the applicant's correspondence with the Court faced obstacles. Letters from the pre-trial detention centre (SIZO) bore stamps, but a letter sent on 21 October 2008 never reached the Court. The Government claimed it was dispatched by the prison, but the applicant noted the administration charged for postage to the Court, which he could not afford. Furthermore, the SIZO's logbook of detainees' complaints for 2004–2005 was destroyed in January 2009, and investigation materials into his ill-treatment allegation were destroyed in January 2010. The applicant was released on parole on 4 August 2009 while serving a later, unrelated sentence.
001-126360:
In **Velinov v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia** (Application no. 16880/08, judgment of 19 September 2013), the applicant, Pančo Velinov, a Macedonian national, complained that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 §§ 1, 2 and 5 of the Convention because his detention was unlawful, he was not promptly informed of the reasons for his arrest, and he received no compensation. He also alleged under Article 6 that the compensation proceedings concerning his detention were unreasonably lengthy, and under Article 13 that he lacked an effective remedy for that delay.

The underlying facts concerned a minor-offence conviction. In 2000, misdemeanour proceedings were brought against Velinov, a bus driver, for driving an unroadworthy bus. On 22 September 2000, the Štip Court of First Instance convicted him and fined him 2,000 Macedonian denars (about EUR 33), payable within fifteen days after the judgment became final. The judgment became final on 27 September 2001. On 14 November 2001, because the fine apparently remained unpaid, the court ordered him to pay and to appear on 26 November 2001 with proof of payment. The notice was served on his son.

On 7 February 2002, a judge converted the unpaid fine into a two-day prison sentence. On 12 February 2002, the detention order was served on Velinov personally, and he was told to begin serving the sentence on 15 March 2002 at Štip Prison. The prison was also informed. On 13 February 2002, Velinov paid the fine, indicating the case file number on the payment slip, but he did not submit proof of payment to the trial court. Consequently, the court remained unaware that the fine had been paid.

On 28 October 2002, police arrested Velinov at his home. According to the Government, he was not informed of the reasons for his arrest; the applicant said he learned the reasons in the afternoon of 29 October 2002. The domestic court later found that the police had the arrest order in their hands but did not hand it over and did not inform him of the reasons. He was held in Štip Prison. On 29 October 2002, after he submitted a copy of the payment slip, the prison released him on the basis of a notification from the trial court that the fine had been paid. He had been detained for approximately one day.

Velinov sought compensation. On 22 November 2002, he asked the Ministry of Justice for an out-of-court settlement of 310,000 MKD (about EUR 5,060) for non-pecuniary damage. The Ministry rejected the request on 10 December 2002, stating that he had not shown any wrongful conviction or detention. On 17 January 2003, he brought a civil action against the State. The proceedings were slow: the claim was forwarded to the Solicitor General only in March 2007, a preparatory hearing was held in May 2007, and hearings took place in June 2007. On 19 June 2007, the trial court dismissed his claim. It found that the notices had been properly served, that Velinov knew about the conversion and the need to submit proof but paid without notifying the court, and that the police had an arrest order. The court concluded that the State was not responsible and that his own conduct had caused the detention. The Štip Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 10 September 2007.

The applicant argued that he had discharged his obligation by paying the fine, that the State should have registered the payment, and that the detention order had not instructed him to submit proof. He also contested the finding that the earlier notice had been served on his son, noting that no handwriting expert examination had been conducted. These facts formed the basis of his complaints about unlawful detention, lack of information, absence of compensation, and the length of the compensation proceedings.
001-115885:
The case originated in 119 applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants included Ukrainian nationals and companies based in Ukraine, and one Russian national. The appended tables list each application number, date of introduction, applicant’s name and date of birth where known, and the enforceable domestic decisions. The applications were introduced between 17 March 2006 (no. 12405/06) and 5 January 2011 (e.g. nos. 4347/11, 4443/11, 4676/11 and 4710/11). The lead application was brought by Nina Grygorivna Varava and eight other applicants. Other applicants included, among many others, Viktor Kyrylovych Kyryk (no. 42557/06), Oleksandr Ivanovych Polezhay (no. 48587/06), Tetyana Fedorivna Dudina (no. 55854/07), Viktor Yeliseyevich Khapun (no. 6761/08), Antonina Mykhaylivna Golubnycha and Alla Mykolayivna Shevchuk (no. 24392/08), and Dagir Magomedovych Kogermanov (no. 12172/08). Mr Borovskyy (no. 39477/07) died during the proceedings; his wife, Ms Borovska, expressed the wish to pursue the application. The Russian Government, informed of its right to intervene in application no. 12172/08, declined to do so. The Ukrainian Government were represented by their Agent, Mr N. Kultchytskyy.

On the dates set out in the appended table, domestic courts and commissions on labour disputes delivered decisions according to which the applicants were entitled to various pecuniary amounts and/or to have certain actions taken in their favour. Those decisions became final and thus enforceable. Examples include the Oktyabyrskyy District Court of Poltava decision of 5 August 2004 in the lead application; Labour Disputes Commission decisions of 21 January and 14 August 1998 in no. 48587/06; Slovyansk Town Court decisions of 20 October 1997 and 8 February 2002 in no. 26361/09; the Vinnytsya Regional Administrative Court decision of 14 September 2007 in no. 55854/07; Torez Court decisions of 6 May 2003 and 6 November 2006 and a Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal decision of 11 February 2008 in no. 6761/08; a Dnipropetrovsk Administrative Court of Appeal decision of 25 September 2008 in no. 1300/10; and an Avtozavodskyy District Court of Kremenchuk decision of 15 June 2009 in no. 4710/11. Many applications introduced in April 2010 relied on Krasnyy Liman Court decisions of 2003–2004. The enforceable decisions listed in the table ranged in date from 1997 to 2009 and were issued by town and district courts, labour dispute commissions, administrative courts and courts of appeal.

The applicants alleged that they were unable to secure enforcement of these decisions in full or in due time because the national authorities failed to take action. The applications mainly concerned non-enforcement of domestic decisions given in the applicants’ favour and excessive delays in the enforcement of those decisions. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues. The applications were communicated to the Government on various dates.
001-120067:
The case *Kononova and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 11770/03 and 89 other applications) was a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 6 June 2013. It originated in 90 applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were Ukrainian nationals, one Russian national, and companies based in Ukraine. The Russian Government declined to intervene in the application by the Russian national. In nine applications, the original applicants died during the proceedings, and their next-of-kin expressed a wish to continue. In two applications, a brother and sister pursued their deceased father’s complaint concerning the same unenforced judgment.

The factual core of the case was the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions. On various dates, Ukrainian courts and labour disputes commissions issued decisions in the applicants’ favour. These decisions entitled them to specified pecuniary amounts or required certain actions to be taken for them. The decisions became final and enforceable. Despite this, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. The responsible State authorities—bailiffs, the State Treasury, or other bodies—failed to execute the decisions, sometimes for many years. In several cases, domestic courts themselves acknowledged bailiffs’ misconduct, but enforcement still remained delayed. Some underlying decisions dated back to 1996, 1998, 1999, and 2000. For example, Kononova obtained a judgment from the Suvorovsky District Court of Kherson on 6 June 2003, amended by the Kherson Regional Court of Appeal on 11 February 2004. Other applicants had final awards concerning pensions, labour payments, social benefits, and commercial claims. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government between 2003 and 2011. Some applicants also raised unrelated factual and legal matters, but the central issue remained the failure to enforce final decisions.

The pattern was repetitive. Pikush’s 1996 decision remained unenforced even though the same court acknowledged bailiffs’ misconduct in 2005. Lyovochkina’s 2001 judgment was accompanied by a 2006 finding of bailiffs’ misconduct. Ternovik’s 1999 judgment, Kolosov’s 1998 judgment, and Prudkyy’s 1999 military court judgment also remained unexecuted for lengthy periods. Some domestic decisions were later amended or quashed on appeal, but the non-enforcement complaint concerned the period when they were final and binding. The amounts and required actions varied, yet the common feature was finality and enforceability followed by State inaction.

Relevant to the alleged violations, the applicants complained that the lengthy non-enforcement violated Article 6 §1 of the Convention, because the right to a fair trial includes the right to execution of final judgments. They also alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, arguing that the State’s failure to pay or execute the awards interfered with their peaceful enjoyment of possessions. In addition, they complained under Article 13 that Ukraine lacked an effective domestic remedy for non-enforcement. The Court examined whether the State was responsible for the delays and whether effective remedies existed. The key facts for the alleged violations were therefore the existence of final, enforceable domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour, the State’s failure to enforce them within a reasonable time, and the resulting uncertainty and financial loss.
001-127812:
In *Matrakas and Others v. Poland and Greece* (Application no. 47268/06, judgment of 7 November 2013), three Polish applicants—two sons and their mother—complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that Poland and Greece had failed to provide adequate assistance in proceedings to recover maintenance from the children’s Greek fathers. The case concerned cross-border recovery under the 1956 New York Convention, under which the Kraków Regional Court acted as the Transmitting Agency and the Greek Ministry of Justice as the Receiving Agency.

The first applicant, represented by his mother, applied in 1988 to recover maintenance from his father, P.M., a Greek national. The request was transmitted to Greece. Although the Greek authorities initially reported that P.M. had been summoned but had not appeared, progress soon stalled. There were repeated Polish requests for information, diplomatic interventions, a 1990 agreement, and a 1992 notarial acknowledgment by P.M. that he would pay monthly maintenance. Payments remained sporadic. Polish courts issued default maintenance judgments in 1994, 1995, 1997, 2001 and 2004. Greece refused recognition or enforcement: first under the 1979 bilateral agreement, relying on the alleged sole jurisdiction of Greek courts; later under the New York Convention, arguing that Greek private international law applied because the debtor lived in Greece. Polish authorities considered that position incorrect and pointed to the Lugano Convention. New requests and documents were exchanged. Only in 2007 did the Greek authorities seek enforcement before the Thessaloniki Court, but hearings were repeatedly adjourned. In 2008 the mother settled with P.M.; he paid €9,700 for maintenance up to 2005, and the case was closed in 2009.

The second applicant obtained a 2004 Polish judgment declaring Y.M. his father and ordering maintenance. In 2005 his mother filed a New York Convention request, which was transmitted to Greece. Greek authorities were slow and often failed to confirm receipt or respond to inquiries. In 2009 the Greek Ministry filed an enforcement claim in Thessaloniki, but the court dismissed it, finding the Ministry lacked standing because EU Regulation 44/2001 applied and the second applicant himself had to seek enforcement. A separate recognition claim by the mother was dismissed because Y.M. had not been properly served in the Polish proceedings—he received the summons after the hearing—so recognition would violate public order. The appeal was dismissed in 2011.

The third applicant obtained a 2002 Polish divorce judgment against Y.M. awarding her maintenance. Her 2003 New York Convention request was transmitted to Greece. In 2007 the Thessaloniki Court recognised the Polish divorce judgment as enforceable. Enforcement against Y.M. began, but auctions of his apartments failed for lack of bidders, and a later request for open sale was dismissed in 2012. A new maintenance application was filed in 2010.

The applicants’ Polish complaints under the 2004 Act on excessive length were rejected. Polish courts held that they had acted only as a Transmitting Agency, with no influence over Greek authorities, though they had sent reminders and sought diplomatic assistance. The applicants alleged that both Poland and Greece failed to provide adequate assistance in the maintenance-recovery proceedings, causing excessive delay and undermining effective access to court under Article 6 § 1.
001-121574:
D.N.M. v. Sweden (ECtHR, App. No. 28379/11, judgment 27 June 2013) concerned an Iraqi Kurd and Sunni Muslim born in 1988 who sought asylum in Sweden and alleged that deportation to Iraq would expose him to honour-related killing or ill-treatment. His claim rested on a secret relationship in Kirkuk with a Sunni woman whose brothers disapproved. In June 2007, the brothers allegedly caught them hugging and attacked him with scissors. He was hospitalised for a week. The brothers reportedly said their honour could only be restored by killing him.
