While he was in hospital, they burned down his shop, assaulted his father, and threatened to cut him to pieces. His father allegedly gave them permission to kill him if they found him. Police initially protected him in hospital but later said they could not help because the matter was honour-related. He hid with relatives in another part of Kirkuk and left Iraq in September 2007.

He applied for asylum on 16 October 2007. On 13 November 2008, the Migration Board rejected the application. It found his story partly contradictory and vague: he claimed police protected him yet also failed to protect him; the brothers could have killed him during the first attack; he remained in Iraq from June to September without harm; and he did not explain why the woman was not attacked. The Board concluded that the alleged threat from the brothers was not credible. On appeal, he added that neighbours had intervened, police protection was temporary, police later lacked resources, he had hidden at his cousin’s home, and he had learned second-hand that the woman had been killed and his father assaulted again. He said internal relocation was impossible because he lacked a network outside his home province and the family could find him. The Migration Board maintained credibility concerns, but accepted that, if his account were credible, he could not rely on state protection. It argued that internal flight alternatives existed in central Iraq or the Kurdistan Region.

On 4 September 2009, the Migration Court upheld the rejection but accepted much of his story as probable: the relationship, the hugging, the scissors attack, the shop burning, and the beating of his father. It gave little weight to second-hand information about the woman’s death and renewed assault on his father. Although two years had passed and the family’s interest may have diminished, the court held that the risk in Kirkuk could not be disregarded and that the Board had accepted he could not count on state protection. It found the threat local to Kirkuk and surrounding areas, and that internal relocation—for example to the Kurdistan Region—was reasonable and relevant even without a social network. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal on 28 October 2009, and a later request for reconsideration was refused on 18 August 2010.

Country information before the Court described honour crimes as a serious, often unpunished problem in Iraq. UNHCR guidelines noted that honour violence affected men as well as women, that penal provisions could be lenient, and that impunity was frequent. For men at risk of honour crimes in the Kurdistan Region, there were reportedly no protection facilities other than detention or prison. UK guidance indicated police were often tribally based and society tolerant of honour concepts, though Kurdistan had amended its law to punish honour killings more severely. UNHCR also warned that persons fleeing non-state actors, including honour-killing threats, might still be within reach of persecutors; internal relocation in southern and central Iraq was often not viable, and protection in Kurdistan was not automatic in honour cases. These facts framed the applicant’s alleged Article 3 risk and the disputed availability of state protection and internal relocation.
001-126635:
**Delfi AS v. Estonia** (Application no. 64569/09) concerned an Estonian internet news portal, Delfi AS, one of Estonia’s largest news portals. The applicant company alleged that its freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights was violated when Estonian courts held it liable for offensive comments posted by readers on its website.

Delfi publishes up to 330 news articles daily. At the relevant time, readers could post comments automatically beneath articles; comments were not pre-moderated or edited by Delfi. Articles attracted about 10,000 comments daily, mostly under pseudonyms. Delfi operated a notice-and-take-down system: readers could mark a comment as *leim* (an insulting, mocking, or hate-inciting message), and such comments were removed expeditiously. Delfi also automatically deleted comments containing certain obscene word stems, and victims could notify Delfi directly, after which comments were removed immediately. Delfi posted rules stating that comments were not its opinion, that authors were responsible, and that threats, insults, incitement, and obscenity were prohibited.

On 24 January 2006, Delfi published an article titled “SLK Destroyed Planned Ice Road.” SLK was Saaremaa Laevakompanii, a ferry company; L. was a supervisory board member and sole or majority shareholder. The article attracted 185 comments on 24–25 January 2006. About twenty contained personal threats and offensive language against L., including calls to lynch, drown, burn, or otherwise harm him, and insults. On 9 March 2006, L.’s lawyers asked Delfi to remove the offensive comments and claimed EEK 500,000 (about EUR 32,000) in non-pecuniary damages. Delfi removed the comments that same day and refused damages, relying on its notice-and-take-down system.

L. then brought a civil suit against Delfi. The Harju County Court initially dismissed the claim, finding Delfi’s liability excluded under the Information Society Services Act because the comment environment was separate and Delfi’s role was mechanical and passive. The Tallinn Court of Appeal reversed, and the Supreme Court declined Delfi’s appeal. On remand, the County Court found for L. under the Obligations Act, holding the Information Society Services Act inapplicable. It treated Delfi as the publisher of the comments, found the disclaimer insufficient, and held the comments vulgar, humiliating, and defamatory, impairing L.’s honour, dignity, and reputation. It awarded EEK 5,000 (EUR 320). The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, reasoning that although Delfi was not required to pre-moderate comments, it should have created an effective system for rapid removal and could not place the monitoring burden on victims. It found Delfi was a content service provider, not a technical intermediary, because it invited comments.

The Supreme Court dismissed Delfi’s appeal. It held Delfi was a provider of content services, not a mere technical intermediary: it integrated the comment environment into its portal, invited users to comment, had an economic interest through visits and advertising revenue, set comment rules, and could remove comments while users could not edit or delete them. Delfi and comment authors were considered publishers. Delfi should have prevented clearly unlawful comments or removed them on its own initiative once aware; its failure to act was unlawful.

Delfi complained to the European Court of Human Rights that being held liable for third-party comments breached Article 10. The key issue was whether domestic courts’ imposition of liability for anonymous offensive comments, despite Delfi’s notice-and-take-down measures, violated freedom of expression. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 16 June 2015.
001-138919:
**Summary of Donohoe v. Ireland (Application no. 19165/08)**

The case of *Donohoe v. Ireland* concerns an application brought by Mr. Kenneth Donohoe, an Irish national, against Ireland under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his trial was unfair, in violation of Article 6 of the Convention, due to the non-disclosure of the sources of evidence provided by a Chief Superintendent without adequate counterbalancing measures.

The facts stem from events on 10 October 2002, when an off-duty Garda detective observed suspicious, coordinated activity involving three cars in a housing estate near Dublin. Police subsequently stopped a van and arrested five men, discovering items including a sledgehammer, pickaxe handles, balaclavas, fake Garda uniforms, and cable ties. A related Nissan Almera was found to contain false registration plates, a stun gun, and a blue flashing light. The applicant was linked to the events through a Nissan Micra owned by his partner, which was allegedly used in the operation. He was arrested on 24 October and 30 October 2002. During police interviews regarding his suspected membership of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), an unlawful organisation, the applicant answered no questions.

The applicant was tried before the Special Criminal Court (SCC) and charged with IRA membership. The prosecution's case rested on four strands: (i) the belief evidence of Chief Superintendent PK, who testified that he believed the applicant was an IRA member based on confidential sources; (ii) evidence associating the applicant with the activities at Corke Abbey; (iii) documents found at his home; and (iv) inferences drawn from his failure to answer material questions during police interviews, pursuant to section 2 of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act 1998.

The central issue arose when the applicant sought an inquiry into the basis of Chief Superintendent PK's belief. The prosecution opposed this, citing informer privilege to protect lives and State security. The SCC directed PK to produce relevant files for its private review, but not for disclosure to the defence. After reviewing the files, the SCC was satisfied that PK had adequate and reliable information and that the files contained nothing to assist the defence. The SCC convicted the applicant, but only after finding corroborating evidence—including his association with the Corke Abbey events and his silence during interviews—to support PK's belief evidence.

The applicant's appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal was refused. It held that the trial court's procedure—reviewing the secret files and requiring corroboration—provided sufficient counterbalancing measures to the non-disclosure, ensuring a fair trial. The Supreme Court's prior jurisprudence in *DPP v. Kelly* also supported the necessity of such limitations on cross-examination in cases involving threats to life or State security.

In his application to the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that the non-disclosure of PK's sources, combined with the lack of adequate counterbalancing measures, rendered his trial unfair. The key facts relevant to this alleged violation are the use of secret belief evidence, the trial court's private review of undisclosed material, and the reliance on corroborating evidence and adverse inferences from silence to secure the conviction.
001-119055:
Saint-Paul Luxembourg S.A. v. Luxembourg (Application no. 26419/10) concerned a search and seizure carried out at a newspaper publisher’s premises. The applicant company, Saint-Paul Luxembourg S.A., had its registered office in Luxembourg and published the Portuguese-language weekly *Contacto Semanário*. On 17 December 2008, *Contacto* published an article about families who had lost custody of their children. The article alleged that the Central Social Welfare Department (SCAS) had instigated the custody withdrawals. It named two teenagers and the social worker handling their case, and described sensitive allegations: the girl had reportedly suffered attempted rape, while the boy had allegedly burnt a friend with a cigarette. The article was signed “Domingos Martins,” but no journalist with that exact name appeared on the Press Council’s official list; a similar name, “De Araujo Martins Domingos Alberto,” did appear.

The social worker complained to the SCAS Director, who complained to the Attorney General, alleging defamation of the social worker and of Luxembourg’s judicial and social system. The social worker also lodged a complaint on 5 January 2009. On 30 January 2009, the public prosecutor opened a judicial investigation for breach of section 38 of the Youth Welfare Act—which prohibited publishing facts liable to disclose the identity or personality of minors under prosecution or subject to youth measures—as well as defamation or calumny.

On 30 March 2009, an investigating judge issued a search and seizure warrant for the applicant’s registered office in its capacity as publisher of *Contacto*. The warrant authorised seizure of any documents or items connected with the alleged offences, including material to identify the article’s author or the *Contacto* employee who wrote it. On 7 May 2009, police executed the warrant at the newspaper’s premises. The Government later stated that the sole aim was to identify the author. According to the police report, the journalist gave officers a copy of the newspaper, a notebook, various documents, and a computer file and CD containing the article. He was assisted by the publishing house’s lawyer and *Contacto*’s editor-in-chief and signed the search report without adding comments.

The applicant claimed that cooperation had been forced, saying police conveyed that the journalist had no option but to comply. However, an internal company report of 8 May 2009 indicated that the journalist said he had no objection to giving a copy of his notes, the editor-in-chief suggested handing over an electronic version, and a USB stick was inserted into the journalist’s computer in the presence of the company’s lawyer, who did not object. The police report of 11 May 2009 stated that the journalist, with the editor-in-chief’s agreement, was willing to cooperate; police nevertheless handed over the warrant and explained that refusal could lead to pressure. The report said the journalist voluntarily handed over items, including documents that served to exonerate him; no journalistic sources were mentioned; and the operation lasted twelve to fifteen minutes without pressure and politely. The accuracy of the police report and seizure record was not challenged in the domestic courts.

On 10 May 2009, the applicant and the journalist sought annulment of the warrant and its execution. The next day the investigating judge discontinued the seizure and ordered return of all items. The *chambre du conseil* dismissed the nullity application on 20 May 2009, and the Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 27 October 2009. Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of its right to freedom of expression and its right to respect for its “home” or “domicile” under the Convention.
001-119049:
The applicants are Arne Kristiansen (born 1931), a Norwegian national, and Tyvik A/S, a Norwegian limited liability company. On 30 November 1990 Kristiansen filed patent application no. 19905214 with NIPO, the Norwegian Industrial Property Office, for a method of propulsion of aircraft and sea vessels.

On 21 March 1991 NIPO preliminarily found the application not patentable because it lacked a concrete solution and questioned whether the invention had any effect. It required practical tests at an independent research institute. Kristiansen disputed the need, citing costs, but said prototypes were under construction. Between 1992 and 1994 there was correspondence about confidentiality; in 1993 the Military Supreme Command said secrecy was not needed. On 9 May 1994 Kristiansen supplied further information. On 24 February 1995 NIPO repeated its test request. On 23 May 1995 he submitted theoretical views and a 1965 report, arguing tests were superfluous. On 27 November 1996 he complained of delay; NIPO apologised on 9 December 1996 and prioritised the case. On 16 December 1996 NIPO maintained the test requirement; exchanges followed, including protests about NIPO’s technical competence and two academic statements in 1997. On 5 May 1999 NIPO maintained its position and set a 5 November 1999 deadline. Kristiansen’s registered letter of 26 October 1999, received 11 November 1999, complained again but made no new arguments. NIPO discontinued examination under section 15(2) of the Patents Act. On 18 February 2000 it maintained shelving because the substantive requirements had not been met.

On 8 March 2001 Kristiansen petitioned the Parliamentary Ombudsman. Following an inquiry, on 30 August 2001 NIPO annulled the discontinuation and allowed until 28 February 2002 to respond to its 5 May 1999 letter. He replied on 24 September 2001 without new arguments. On 2 October 2001 NIPO refused the application because the alleged technical effect was not made probable. On 23 January 2002 the Ombudsman found no grounds to continue.

On 27 November 2001 Kristiansen appealed to the Board of Appeals. Its first meeting was on 13 September 2004; the Board indicated a new claim formulation might lead to a patent, but only for sea vessels, communicated on 29 September 2004. A meeting followed on 2 February 2005. On 14 February 2005 NIPO learned that 50% ownership had been transferred to Tyvik AS. On 14 November 2005 the Board concluded the invention had technical effect but did not decide other patent requirements; the applicants had been advised how to amend the claims but were unwilling. The Board set aside NIPO’s decision and remitted the case.

On 29 November 2005 NIPO found the subject-matter not novel. On 13 March 2006 the applicants complained to the Ombudsman, alleging prejudice by a NIPO officer; the Ombudsman said it could not decide until processing ended but assumed due diligence. Exchanges continued between 31 May and 11 June 2006; NIPO suggested changes and the applicants disagreed. On 20 June 2007 NIPO formally refused the application for lack of novelty. On 20 August 2007 the applicants appealed. On 29 November 2007 the Board, having examined the case on 12 November 2007, found conditions unmet for aircraft but possible for limited sea vessels; it warned refusal might be confirmed if claims were not redefined, and discussed splitting the aircraft and sea-vessel parts, with the aircraft part likely rejected. The applicants commented on 28 January 2008 and altered the claims. On 22 September 2008 the Board confirmed refusal on different reasoning: it found the results industrially achievable and no novelty for aviation, but unlike NIPO found the application could have succeeded for limited sea transport; applicants had been advised to exclude aviation but were unwilling. They apparently did not challenge that decision before the Norwegian courts.

The applicants later said 2003 applications based on no. 19905214 were granted in the United States, Russia, China, Singapore and through the EPO. The Government said Espacenet showed no priority claimed from no. 19905214; the EPO patent claimed priority from separate no. 20015844, based on knowledge from no. 19905214, with additional features. Under the Patents Act 1967, section 1 requires industrial application and technical effect; section 2 requires novelty; section 15 allows shelving; section 27 sets appeal and court time limits; section 40 sets a twenty-year term, so a granted patent would have expired on 30 November 2010.
001-118590:
In *Trunk v. Slovenia* (Application no. 41391/06), the applicant, a Slovenian national born in 1957, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the length of two sets of domestic proceedings was excessive. He also alleged under Article 13 that no effective domestic remedy existed for that complaint. He had been a public servant at the Centre for Educational and Extracurricular Activities and was laid off after disciplinary proceedings.

In the first set of proceedings (*III Pd 489/96*), on 11 October 1996 the applicant sued the Ministry of Education and Sport and the Centre before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court. He sought annulment of the termination of his employment contract and related rights and benefits. The first hearing was not held until 23 February 1998. After the applicant withdrew his claim against the Ministry, a decision was issued on 22 September 1998. Hearings took place between October 1998 and November 1999, and on 22 December 1999 the first-instance court rejected his claim. He appealed. On 5 April 2002 the Ljubljana Higher Labour and Social Court allowed the appeal in part and remitted the case because a preliminary submission by the defendant had not been sent to the applicant. On 18 June 2002 the first-instance court gave judgment, followed by a corrigendum on 25 September 2002. The applicant appealed. On 27 August 2004 the Higher Labour and Social Court gave judgment, treating one later request concerning benefits as a request for a supplementary judgment and rejecting the remainder. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law, which was initially rejected on procedural grounds in November 2004; after a successful appeal, the Supreme Court rejected it on 25 October 2005. A constitutional appeal followed. On 7 June 2006 the first-instance court issued another judgment, and the appeal was rejected on 5 October 2006. On 12 February 2007 the Constitutional Court rejected the constitutional appeal.

In the second set of proceedings (*VP 371/96*), on 20 December 1996 the applicant’s former employer sued him before the Ljubljana District Court for restitution of work-related material. In May 1997 the court ordered him to return the material, but that decision was annulled in July 1997; an appeal was rejected in October 1997. In December 1997 the case was transferred to the Piran District Court for lack of jurisdiction. In November 1998 the applicant lodged a counterclaim for payment for computer updates and car expenses. The proceedings were stayed in January 2001 and resumed in April 2001. In October 2001 the proceedings were terminated after the plaintiff withdrew its claim, but the applicant pursued his counterclaim. In February 2002 the Piran District Court declined jurisdiction, and the case was transferred to the Ljubljana Labour Court. Four hearings were held between April 2002 and March 2003, after which judgment partly upheld the applicant’s request. Both parties appealed. In November 2004 the Higher Labour and Social Court upheld the appeals and remitted the case. On 23 March 2007 the Labour Court again partly upheld the applicant’s request. An appeal led to a Higher Labour and Social Court judgment on 10 September 2008.

The first set therefore lasted from 11 October 1996 to 12 February 2007, over ten years, while the second lasted from 20 December 1996 to 10 September 2008, over eleven years. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were the lengthy intervals between procedural steps, repeated remittals, jurisdictional transfers, a stay of proceedings, successive appeals, and the applicant’s own later requests and counterclaim.
001-128204:
Mr Vladlen Mikhaylovich Putistin, born in 1934, lives in Kyiv. He is the son of Mr Mikhail Putistin, a former Dynamo Kyiv footballer who played in the 1936 USSR championship, when Dynamo took second place. On 9 August 1942 his father took part in the “Death Match” between FC Start—mostly Dynamo Kyiv professionals then working in a Kyiv bakery—and Flakelf, a team of German Luftwaffe pilots, air-defence soldiers and airport technicians. FC Start won 5–3. The match allegedly involved Flakelf’s lack of sportsmanship, physical challenges, threats and unfair refereeing by an SS officer. The victory allegedly led to the players’ arrest and transfer to a local concentration camp, where four were eventually executed. In 2002 Kyiv authorities commemorated the 60th anniversary, with wide media coverage.

On 3 April 2001 Komsomolska Pravda published “The Truth about the Death Match,” by journalist O.M. It discussed a planned film about the 1942 events and included an interview with future director/producer A.S. and D.K., plus a picture of the 1942 match poster with the footballers’ names. The article named four executed Dynamo Kyiv players—Kuzmenko, Klimenko, Korotkikh and Trusevych—but did not name the applicant’s father; his name was not legible on the poster. D.K. stated that only four Dynamo players were in the Start team created by the local bread factory, that those four were executed, and that other players worked in the police and collaborated with the Gestapo.

In July 2001 the applicant sued Komsomolska Pravda and the journalist, alleging the article suggested his father had collaborated with the occupying police and Gestapo. He sought rectification of the untrue information and non-pecuniary damages. He supplied State Security Service documents showing no archive information about his father’s alleged collaboration and no criminal proceedings against him; the archives and Kyiv Regional State Archives confirmed his father had participated in the Death Match and had been detained at Syrets concentration camp. On 25 December 2001 the Obolonskyy District Court of Kyiv rejected the claim. It found that the applicant was not directly affected, that the article concerned a film script, that it did not name his father or the applicant, and that it made no allegation that his father had collaborated with the Gestapo. On 13 March 2002 the Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, and on 15 November 2002 the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s points-of-law appeal.

In other domestic proceedings, on 27 April 2000 the Moskovskyy District Court ordered Dzerkalo Tyzhnia to rectify information about the applicant’s father; on 29 April 2000 it published a correction that he played for Dynamo, was arrested in summer 1942 with other players and sent to Syrets, and escaped in October 1942. In May 2002 Argumenty i Fakty stated that only four Death Match players were arrested and sent to Syrets, without naming the applicant’s father. After his request, issue no. 27 named all eight arrested players, including his father. His subsequent suit ended on 28 December 2004 with a final Supreme Court ruling against him. On 12 May 2003 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court ordered Fakty i Komentari to publish a rectification concerning the applicant’s father; the order was upheld on appeal on 21 October 2003 and in cassation on 31 August 2005, while his damages claim was rejected.
001-127401:
The case of *Bandaletov v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Gennadiy Vitalyevich Bandaletov, a Ukrainian national, on 18 May 2006. The applicant alleged a violation of his right to a fair trial, specifically complaining that he had not been legally represented during the initial stage of the pre-trial investigation.

The underlying events began on the evening of 20 April 2005, when an elderly couple, Mr. and Ms. L., were murdered in their apartment. The applicant lived in the flat below them. On 21 April 2005, a criminal investigation was launched, and police questioned several individuals, including the applicant's stepson and wife, as well as the son of one of the victims. On that same day, the applicant himself was questioned by police and confessed to the double murder. He claimed a longstanding conflict with Ms. L. over noise from his flat refurbishment had culminated in a violent confrontation, during which he stabbed both victims. He also admitted to disposing of the knife, a broken stool, and his blood-stained T-shirt.

A critical fact relevant to the alleged violation is that this initial confession on 21 April 2005 was made without a lawyer present. The applicant was not formally arrested as a suspect until the following day, 22 April 2005, at 11:30 a.m. It is not recorded where the applicant was or whether he was in custody between the questioning on the 21st and his formal arrest on the 22nd; the applicant did not claim he was detained during this period.

Following his arrest on 22 April, a lawyer, Mr. T., was appointed for him. Approximately thirty minutes after the arrest, the applicant signed a report acknowledging that he had been informed of his defence rights. From noon to 1 p.m. that day, he was questioned again in the presence of his lawyer and confirmed his earlier confession. Later that afternoon, a videotaped crime reconstruction was conducted, again with his lawyer present, where he repeated his testimony and stated he was acting of his own free will. The applicant was subsequently formally charged on 29 April and continued to cooperate with the investigation, repeating his confession with his lawyer present.

At his trial, which began in August 2005, the applicant was represented by a new lawyer and maintained his confession, expressing sincere remorse. He was ultimately convicted and was serving a life sentence at the time of the European Court's judgment.

The central factual issue before the Court was therefore the lack of legal assistance during the applicant's first interrogation on 21 April 2005, a time when he was a suspect but had not yet been formally arrested or charged. The applicant's subsequent confessions were all made with a lawyer present, but his initial, unassisted confession formed a key part of the prosecution's case. The case hinges on whether this initial questioning, which yielded a confession later used at trial, violated his right to legal assistance under Article 6 of the Convention.
001-118592:
In *Orožim v. Slovenia* (Application no. 49323/06), the applicant, Štefanija Orožim, a Slovenian national born in 1939 and living in Lesce, lodged an application against Slovenia on 13 November 2006. She alleged that the length of the domestic proceedings to which she was a party was excessive, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and that there was no effective domestic remedy for that complaint, contrary to Article 13. The application was communicated to the Slovenian Government on 14 January 2011.

The underlying proceedings began in 1993, when the company DOMPLAN Kranj instituted enforcement proceedings against the applicant before the Kranj Basic Court. An enforcement order was issued on 20 April 1993. The Convention entered into force in respect of Slovenia on 28 June 1994. On 28 July 1994 the case was reassigned to the Radovljica District Court. The enforcement order was served on the applicant on 23 December 1994, and she lodged an objection. On 13 September 1995 the enforcement order was annulled, and the case was to be adjudicated in contentious proceedings. On 3 October 1995 the creditor lodged another request for enforcement, and an enforcement order was issued on 23 October 1995. On 26 January 1999 the Radovljica District Court joined the two cases. A first-instance hearing was held on 23 April 2001, and on 9 July 2001 the first-instance court rendered judgment upholding the creditor’s requests. The applicant appealed, but on 24 April 2002 the Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal.

On 7 October 2002 the creditor lodged a request for enforcement based on the 9 July 2001 judgment. On 14 October 2002 the Radovljica District Court issued an enforcement order. On 30 October 2002 the applicant lodged an objection to the order and simultaneously requested postponement of enforcement, expressing willingness to reach a settlement. Her objection was not sent to the creditor until 12 September 2003. The creditor responded on 5 March 2004. Only on 25 May 2006 did the first-instance court hold a hearing and issue a decision concerning the objection against the enforcement order. The creditor appealed. On 8 March 2007 the creditor requested that the proceedings be terminated following an out-of-court settlement between the parties. The decision terminating the proceedings was issued on 16 March 2007.

The domestic proceedings therefore extended from 1993 until 2007, continuing long after the Convention entered into force in Slovenia. The facts most relevant to the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation include the overall duration of the enforcement and contentious proceedings, the joining of the cases, the first-instance judgment and appeal, and especially the lengthy intervals after the applicant’s October 2002 objection: her objection was transmitted to the creditor only in September 2003, the creditor replied in March 2004, and the court did not decide the objection until May 2006. The applicant filed her Convention application in November 2006, while the domestic proceedings were still pending. As to Article 13, she complained that Slovenian law provided no effective domestic remedy for the excessive length of the proceedings. The relevant domestic law was referred to by citing *Nezirović v. Slovenia* (dec.), no. 16400/06, 25 November 2008.
001-123422:
In *Rousk v. Sweden*, the applicant, Mr Jim Rousk, owned a close company and was required to file a special income tax return for the 2002 tax assessment year. He failed to do so. After an order and a proposed discretionary assessment, the Tax Authority in November 2002 imposed taxes, tax surcharges and a delay charge totaling SEK 232,572 (approximately EUR 27,000), payable by 26 February 2003. The applicant neither appealed nor requested respite from payment. Because tax debts to the State are immediately enforceable, the claim was transferred to the Enforcement Authority in April 2003.

On 28 May 2003 the Enforcement Authority issued a writ of execution attaching the applicant’s site-leasehold right and the house where he and his wife lived. His total enforceable debts were SEK 255,329; the property’s tax value was SEK 1,372,000, with a mortgage of SEK 960,200. The applicant said he only became aware of the writ in July/August 2003. He appealed on 10 August 2003, arguing that the tax debt was not final, that he had not been properly served, that he would submit his tax return and had requested respite, and that selling his home would have serious economic, social and medical consequences. He submitted a medical certificate showing depression, psychiatric care since February 2003, and antidepressant treatment.

Meanwhile, the Enforcement Authority scheduled a public auction for 3 September 2003. The applicant requested a stay on 28 July 2003, citing illness and payment of another debt. The Enforcement Authority refused on 30 July, and the District Court rejected his appeal on 28 August. An independent valuation on 28 July estimated the property at SEK 1,850,000–2,150,000. On 3 September at 1:45 p.m., the auction proceeded and the highest bid of SEK 1,600,000 was accepted. On the same day, the Tax Authority granted the applicant respite from payment of the taxes and surcharges; the decision was registered at 2:02 p.m. The applicant later argued that the Enforcement Authority could have verified the respite during the pause between bidding rounds, especially since he had informed it of his request. The Enforcement Authority maintained that the respite was not shown before the auction and that other State debts of SEK 23,775 justified the sale. The enforceable tax debt was later reduced to SEK 6,721, and the distribution protocol was corrected.

After the applicant refused to vacate by 1 October 2003, the Enforcement Authority ordered his eviction. He requested respite, citing his and his wife’s poor health, lack of alternative housing, and the pending appeal against the sale. The Enforcement Authority and courts refused to postpone. On 22 October 2003 the eviction was enforced with police and movers present. Some belongings were stored, but other items were discarded or destroyed, including food, flowers and a bed that could not be removed intact. The auction cost SEK 45,660 and the eviction SEK 71,115. In January 2004 the applicant received SEK 524,343 remaining from the sale after debts and costs.

The applicant alleged that the Enforcement Authority’s measures violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of property) and Article 8 (private and family life and home). The key alleged violations concerned the attachment and sale of his home for a relatively small tax debt, the refusal to stay the sale and eviction despite illness and lack of alternative housing, and the timing of the Tax Authority’s respite order relative to the auction. He exhausted domestic remedies through the District Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court.
001-119676:
**Summary of Komarova v. Ukraine (Application no. 13371/06)**

The applicant, Mrs Svetlana Ivanovna Komarova, a Ukrainian lawyer born in 1960, lodged an application against Ukraine on 22 March 2006. She alleged that her pre-trial detention had been excessively lengthy, that she had been detained in inhuman conditions, and that she had not received adequate medical care, in violation of the Convention.

On 1 April 2004, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant for alleged attempted bribery of a judge and fraud. She was arrested the same day. On 3 April 2004, the Dnipropetrovsk Prosecutor's Office sought her pre-trial detention, arguing she posed a flight risk due to her financial means, foreign travel passport, prior criminal record (a 2000 fraud charge for which she was pardoned), lack of a permanent residence or office, and the possibility she might hinder the investigation, pressure witnesses, or destroy evidence.

On 3 April 2004, the Babushkinskiy District Court ordered her to remain in custody pending further investigation. The applicant stated in court that she had been subjected to psychological pressure by arresting officers, that she might be pregnant, and that she had a dependent student son. On 9 April 2004, the court formally ordered her continued detention, citing the seriousness of the charges, multiple addresses given, and the risk of absconding or continuing criminal activity. Subsequent extensions followed on 21 May 2004 (to 1 August 2004), with the Regional Court of Appeal adjusting the end date to 1 July 2004 on 27 May 2004, and further extensions on 25 June 2004.

The investigation concluded, and the case was sent to the Samarskiy District Court, which accepted it on 9 August 2004. On 18 July 2006, the court found her guilty on thirteen counts of fraud and attempted bribery, sentencing her to seven years' imprisonment. However, on 28 December 2006, the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction on appeal by both parties and remanded the case for fresh investigation, extending her detention based on her personality, the seriousness and number of charges, and the circumstances of the offences.

Between 2007 and 2009, the case was repeatedly sent back for further investigation or to rectify procedural errors, with the courts continuing to extend her detention on grounds that there were "no grounds" to believe detention was no longer necessary. Importantly, her lawyer's submissions regarding her numerous illnesses and need for release were consistently not addressed. On 18 January 2008, the court acknowledged she was bedridden per her medical report but still found this insufficient for release. On 20 June, 7 August, 30 October, and 3 November 2008, and in January 2009, requests for release were rejected, with the court accepting she suffered from multiple diseases but not finding this a sound reason for release.

On 28 April 2009, the Samarskiy Court sentenced her to five years and twenty-seven days' imprisonment for fraud, and she was released the same day. The Supreme Court rejected her leave to appeal on 11 February 2010.

Regarding medical care, the applicant was held in the Dnipropetrovsk Pre-Trial Detention Centre (SIZO) from 14 April 2004. Between April 2004 and February 2008, she received treatment for hypertension, eye problems (myopic astigmatism, angiosclerosis, hypertensive angiopathy, amblyopia, retinopathy, optic nerve atrophy), a skin disease, neurological conditions (hypertensive encephalopathy), pneumonia, and other ailments. She was examined by various specialists, given electrocardiograms, ultrasound scans, X-rays, and blood and urine tests. However, on 16 August 2007, SIZO authorities noted she needed diagnosis and treatment in cardiology and ophthalmology departments, and on 11 December 2008, SIZO informed the court she needed supervision by a doctor, cardiologist, and ophthalmologist. The applicant refused certain treatments, including gastric endoscopy and admission to the medical ward for pneumonia.
001-122664:
The case concerns three British nationals, Douglas Gary Vinter, Jeremy Neville Bamber and Peter Howard Moore, each serving mandatory life imprisonment for murder in England and Wales and subject to whole life orders. They lodged applications against the United Kingdom on 11 December 2009, 17 December 2009 and 6 January 2010, alleging that the whole life orders amounted to ill-treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

Under the domestic regime, murder carries a mandatory life sentence. The trial judge sets a minimum term; exceptionally, a whole life order may be made where the offence’s seriousness is exceptionally high. A whole life prisoner cannot be released except at the Secretary of State’s discretion on compassionate grounds, generally where terminally ill or seriously incapacitated. For pre-2003 Act cases, tariffs or whole life tariffs were set by the Secretary of State; transitional provisions allowed the High Court to review and either set a minimum term or make a whole life order.

Vinter, born in 1969, received life imprisonment on 20 May 1996 for murdering a work colleague, with a ten-year minimum. He was released on licence on 4 August 2005. In February 2008 he killed his wife; he pleaded guilty to murder on 21 April 2008. The trial judge imposed a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 25 June 2009, finding that a whole life order was appropriate because he was already a convicted murderer.

Bamber, born in 1961, was convicted on 28 October 1986 of murdering his parents, adoptive sister and her two children, who were shot and killed on 7 August 1985. The prosecution alleged premeditation, financial gain and staging of the scene. The trial judge recommended a minimum of twenty-five years; the Lord Chief Justice commented that he would never release him. In 1988 the Secretary of State imposed a whole life tariff; Bamber was informed on 15 December 1994. In 2008 the High Court reviewed the tariff and imposed a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 14 May 2009. His application to certify a point of law for the House of Lords was refused on 23 June 2009.

Moore, born in 1946, was convicted on 29 November 1996 of four murders of homosexual men, each stabbed repeatedly with a combat knife. The attacks occurred on 23 September 1995, around 7 October 1995, 30 November 1995 and shortly before Christmas 1995. The trial judge recommended that he never be released; the Lord Chief Justice suggested thirty years. On 27 September 2002 the Secretary of State set a whole life tariff. In 2008 the High Court rejected the thirty-year recommendation and made a whole life order. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 26 February 2009. He was told on 14 August 2009 that he could not apply to certify a point of law for the House of Lords because permission to appeal had been refused.
001-119688:
In **Maksymenko and Gerasymenko v. Ukraine** (Application no. 49317/07), the applicants alleged that Ukraine violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention by invalidating the 1995 privatisation of a hostel they had bought in 2004, together with all subsequent transfers of ownership, thereby depriving them of possessions. The first applicant lived in Malyn; the second applicant died in 2009, and his widow pursued the application on his behalf.

In 1995, decision no. 492 transformed State enterprise M. into a joint-stock company, effectively privatising it. An audit showed that M.’s immovable property included several hostels. In 2000, M. was reorganised into four companies, including S., which acquired ownership of the hostels. In 2003, S. was declared insolvent. The liquidator informed local authorities that selling the hostels could create social tensions and suggested the town take them over. In January 2004, the mayor replied that the hostels were not State-owned and that the creditors should decide. In July 2004, the board of creditors agreed to sell one hostel to the applicants. On 21 August 2004, a sale contract was signed; the applicants paid UAH 41,160 (about EUR 6,127) and became equal owners.

After the purchase, the applicants discovered that electricity cables and meters needed replacement and that occupants had not paid rent. In January 2005, they asked the electricity company to cut off supply until a new contract was signed. A cut-off was scheduled, but on 21 January 2005 a prosecutor ordered that electricity not be cut off because he was preparing legal proceedings on behalf of the hostel occupants. The applicants told authorities they had bought the hostel to live there, that occupants had refused to participate in the sale and had not paid rent or communal charges for six months. They asked S. to rehouse the occupants and requested them to vacate by 30 March 2005.

On 26 January 2005, G., a nineteen-year-old occupant with a young child, sought help from the prosecutor after being asked to leave. On 18 February 2005, the prosecutor sued on G.’s behalf in the Malynsky District Court, seeking invalidation of the 16 November 1995 decision and all later ownership transfers. The prosecutor argued that privatisation was unlawful under section 2(2) of the State Housing Stock Privatisation Act, which prohibited privatising rooms in hostels. He also claimed the transfer breached law and “moral principles,” violated occupants’ constitutional housing rights, harmed State interests, and affected G., a vulnerable single mother. He requested that ownership be transferred to Malyn Town Council.

The applicants counterclaimed for compensation, arguing that occupants had refused to participate in the sale, had not paid, and had caused S.’s insolvency. The court returned the counterclaim for lacking logical consistency and causation, and the applicants did not re-lodge it. In January 2006, the first-instance court rejected the prosecutor’s claim. On 8 June 2006, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal quashed that decision and invalidated the 1995 privatisation and all subsequent transfers. It held that State housing stock, including hostels, could not be privatised under section 3 of the State Property Privatisation Act. It awarded the applicants UAH 41,160 to be paid by S. and transferred ownership to the Council. The applicants appealed, citing a contradictory appellate decision, missed time-limits, and S.’s insolvency. On 21 May 2007, the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal rejected the cassation appeal without explanation. The Council took over ownership in July 2007. S. failed to pay compensation, and by late 2008 occupants had privatised twelve of the fourteen apartments under amended legislation.

The alleged violation therefore arises from the retroactive invalidation of the 1995 privatisation and all later transfers after the applicants had bought the hostel as bona fide purchasers. The key facts include their 2004 purchase, the prosecutor’s action prompted by an occupant’s complaint, the 2006 invalidation based on domestic law prohibiting State housing stock privatisation, the transfer of ownership to the municipality, and the ineffective or unpaid compensation.
001-139175:
The case *T.A. v. Sweden* concerned an Iraqi Sunni Muslim from Baghdad, born in 1979, who arrived in Sweden in November 2007 and applied for asylum. He alleged that deportation to Iraq would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, exposing him to a real risk of death or inhuman and degrading treatment.

The key facts related to his work for US-linked security companies and claimed targeting by Shi’a militias. From 2003 he worked for security companies; from January 2007 he worked for Iraq’s largest security company, which had US military connections. He had access to Baghdad’s Green Zone, could bear arms, and search suspects. In May 2007 his clan disowned him over this affiliation. In October 2007, Badr militia members visited his home and told his wife he must report; al-Mahdi militia made the same demand. On 20 October 2007 a threatening letter was placed on his car, telling him to stop working for US troops or be killed. His employer offered no help. On 1 November 2007 his house in Karrada was completely destroyed by shell fire—only that house was hit—and he suspected the militias; police took no action. He left Iraq days later, leaving his wife and son. In October 2008 men assaulted his wife and son at his in-laws’ home while asking his whereabouts. A further threatening letter was allegedly found at his destroyed house later in 2008. He feared persecution or ill-treatment from the militias and his clan, and possible US military retaliation because he had brought service identification cards.

Swedish authorities rejected his asylum claim. On 3 March 2009, the Migration Board ordered deportation. It found identity unproven but Iraqi origin plausible. General violence in Iraq did not itself justify asylum. It found no religious or political persecution, noted he had lived in Shi’a-dominated Karrada without incident until October 2007, and classified the threats as local militia-related rather than persecution, with no future risk. It viewed the delayed threats as peculiar, his accounts as vague and speculative, and found that threats linked to US work had ended when he stopped that job. It saw no connection between incidents, noted long gaps, found the clan threat unexplained, and concluded the incidents were local to Karrada, so as a Sunni he could relocate to a Sunni area. On 16 April 2010 the Migration Court upheld the decision, agreeing there was no remaining threat: perpetrators were unknown, a year had passed before the family assault, his wife and child had remained in Baghdad, over two years had passed since his security work, and the incidents reflected the 2007 security situation. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave on 4 June 2010.

Before the ECtHR, he submitted additional evidence: ID cards, certificates, recommendation letters, photos of training with US military, photos of his injured wife and child, and Arabic documents including a police report, witness statements and police account from October 2008 describing four men searching his home, destroying property and leaving a threatening note.

The alleged violation was that removal to Iraq would expose him to a real risk of death or ill-treatment. Country information noted continuing armed violence and particular risks for persons perceived as affiliated with US forces. UNHCR guidelines stated former MNF-I/USF-I employees, contractors and families could be targeted by armed groups as collaborators; Shi’ite groups such as Badr and Jaysh al-Mahdi had targeted those considered collaborators. UK guidance, however, indicated that violence, though serious, did not place all civilians in central Iraq at risk solely by presence, and Shi’a militia intent had declined after US withdrawal.
001-126451:
In *Sardón Alvira v. Spain*, the applicant, a Spanish national, was prosecuted in connection with the collapse of GESCARTERA, a registered investment agency. In June 2001, Spain’s CNMV took control of GESCARTERA after difficulties in determining its financial situation and the destination of clients’ funds. Criminal proceedings followed before the Audiencia Nacional against executives and others for continuous fraud, misappropriation, and false commercial statements. The applicant was investigated as an agent for one of GESCARTERA’s offices, *Asesoría y Gestión de Patrimonios, S.A.* (“AGP”), and was ultimately charged with continuous misappropriation and continuous making of false statements in commercial documents.

In March 2008, the Audiencia Nacional convicted the applicant and others. It found that GESCARTERA had been systematically stripped of assets by some of the accused, including the applicant, to the prejudice of investors. The court found that the applicant was not merely an agent but the *de facto* administrator of AGP; that he had knowingly misappropriated invested funds in cooperation with GESCARTERA’s main shareholder; and that he had prepared and supplied false documents to attract and retain clients. He was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment for misappropriation and two years for false statements, plus fines. Under Article 116 of the Criminal Code, he was made jointly civilly liable for compensation of EUR 87,995,626.91. Separately, the Audiencia Nacional found that, as an investor, the applicant had withdrawn EUR 88,671.78 more than he had invested. Other persons, including relatives, had been summoned under Article 122 of the Criminal Code as potential gratuitous beneficiaries of crime proceeds and were ordered to reimburse their gains.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. In October 2009, the Supreme Court partly allowed his appeal. It found insufficient evidence that he had managed invested funds or participated in preparing false documents, held that his presumption of innocence had been violated, quashed the findings implying active criminal participation, and acquitted him of both offences. However, the Supreme Court upheld the Audiencia Nacional’s finding that, as an investor, he owed EUR 88,671.78 and ordered him to reimburse it under Article 122, which applies to anyone who has gratuitously participated to economic advantage in the proceeds of an offence. It relied on its reasoning in a co-appellant’s case: because the applicant had argued that his gain as an investor was lawful, his defence had also addressed the possibility of Article 122 civil liability, even though the prosecution had sought liability under Article 116 as a principal offender.

The applicant lodged an *amparo* appeal with the Constitutional Court, alleging a violation of his right to a fair trial. He argued that the Supreme Court had recharacterised the facts and found him liable in a different capacity—as an economic beneficiary of crime proceeds—without any prior accusation or hearing on that issue. The legal requirements for Article 122 beneficiary liability differed from principal liability under Article 116; as a beneficiary he might have been unaware of the crime but still obliged to restore gains. He claimed his defence would have been different had he been promptly informed of this new civil-liability basis. The Constitutional Court declared the *amparo* inadmissible in February 2010 for failure to justify its special constitutional significance.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained that he had not had a fair hearing before the Supreme Court, that the Supreme Court had wrongly interpreted domestic civil-liability law, that the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court had failed to give sufficient reasons, and that he had suffered discriminatory treatment compared with other GESCARTERA investors treated as victims. These facts formed the basis of his alleged violations of fair-trial and equality guarantees under the Convention.
001-138558:
Three Romanian nationals—Mihai Vlad, Flaviu Plaţa and Vasilica Bratu—lodged applications against Romania on 5 October 2006, 14 September 2007 and 9 November 2007. The applications concerned the length of domestic proceedings and the alleged absence of remedies in that respect; they were communicated to the Government and later joined.

Mr Vlad (born 1945, Bucharest) was detained on 30 January 1994 on suspicion of first-degree murder; the prosecutor opened an investigation and authorised his detention the next day. He was indicted on 18 November 1994 for murder and aggravated theft. Hearings before the Timiş County Court ran from February to December 1995. The case was remitted to the prosecution on 13 December 1995, but that was reversed on appeal on 22 April 1996. On 22 November 1996 he was convicted and sentenced to 18 years. On 14 April 1997 the appeal court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. On 15 September 1997 he was again convicted and sentenced to 18 years; his appeal was dismissed on 12 March 1998. On 28 October 1998 the ICCJ allowed a further appeal and returned the case to the prosecution because the investigation was incomplete. A new indictment followed on 8 July 1999. His requests for a counter forensic report and removal of the panel were rejected. On 5 May 2000 he was convicted and sentenced to 15 years; the ICCJ allowed an appeal on 9 November 2000 and returned the case to the prosecution. A new indictment was issued on 15 October 2001. On 12 April 2002 the ICCJ transferred the case to Dolj County Court. On 9 September 2003 that court convicted him and sentenced him to 15 years. Five appeal hearings were adjourned for failure to properly summon him. On 16 May 2005 the Craiova Court of Appeal rejected leave to appeal as time-barred; the ICCJ quashed that and ordered retrial. On 2 November 2005 the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and on 6 April 2006 the ICCJ dismissed his appeal on points of law.

Mr Plaţa (born 1969, Bucharest) learned on 6 March 1997 of a civil estate-division suit brought by his aunt before Bucharest District Court no. 2. On 19 May 1998 the ICCJ transferred it to District Court no. 6. Hearings were adjourned because authorities failed to submit documents. On 21 January 1999 the proceedings were stayed at his request and resumed on 22 November 1999. After a dispute about service in China, the court on 6 September 2001 annulled procedural acts from 16 December 1999 to 22 February 2001. On 13 December 2001 the action was allowed in part. An appeal led to a constitutional review; on 11 February 2003 the Constitutional Court upheld the relevant provision. On 18 November 2003 the Bucharest County Court dismissed the appeal. On 27 January 2005 the Court of Appeal allowed an appeal on points of law and sent the case back for retrial. On 28 October 2005 the County Court again quashed and remitted. On 21 June 2006 the District Court ruled in part, upheld on 15 November 2006 and 29 March 2007. Enforcement later stalled: on 7 September 2011 a bailiff declared he could not enforce the judgment, and a complaint remained pending before District Court no. 6.

Mrs Bratu (born 1964, Bucharest) was questioned by police on 4 May 1998 on suspicion of misconduct in public office and indicted on 30 June 1998 before Bucharest District Court no. 1. A new forensic accounting report was ordered on 26 May 1999 and submitted in November 1999. On 24 May 2000 the State’s civil claim was dismissed as time-barred; on 20 July 2000 she was convicted and given a suspended one-year sentence. On 29 June 2001 the county court upheld the criminal part but ordered retrial on the civil part; on 13 December 2001 the Court of Appeal rejected her appeal on points of law on the conviction. On 31 May 2002 the District Court allowed the civil action in part. After an appeal in June 2002, the Bucharest County Court scheduled 22 hearings pending documents from public authorities; on 8 November 2004 it increased compensation. On 28 January 2005 the Court of Appeal set aside the appeal decision and ordered a new appeal trial. The retrial was adjourned 17 times for improper service and missing documents. On 9 September 2005 the court fined the chief prosecutor; the documents arrived 19 months later. On 23 March 2007 the County Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the 31 May 2002 decision. On 11 May 2007 the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal on points of law.

The record also contains domestic law on reasonable time, tort liability and disciplinary liability, Law no. 202/2010, and a civil complaint about protraction of proceedings from 15 February 2013. The Government argued that existing remedies and case-law could expedite proceedings or compensate delays; Council of Europe materials noted structural delay problems and reforms.
001-115770:
In *Zarochentsev v. Ukraine* (Application no. 39327/06), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Mr Aleksey Gennadyevich Zarochentsev, a Ukrainian national born in 1974, living in Bakhchysaray. The application was lodged on 8 December 2006 and concerned the alleged excessive length of criminal proceedings brought against him, primarily under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant was represented by Mr A. V. Lesovoy, and the Ukrainian Government was represented initially by Mr Y. Zaytsev and later by Ms V. Lutkovska.

The relevant facts began on 7 March 2001, when the Kyivskyy District Prosecutor of Simferopol opened a criminal case against the applicant on suspicion of embezzlement while he was employed as a shop manager. Similar criminal proceedings were also instituted against the shop director, Mr Z. Between 30 May and 9 August 2001, the investigation was stayed because the authorities could not establish the applicant’s whereabouts, and he was placed on a wanted list. He was apprehended on 13 August 2001.

On 23 August 2001, the Kyivskyy District Court of Sevastopol remanded the applicant in custody pending trial. However, on 29 August 2001, the Court of Appeal of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea quashed that ruling and released him under an obligation not to leave the town. On 13 November 2001, the applicant and Mr Z were indicted, and the case was referred to the Kyivskyy Court for trial.

The trial began on 3 December 2001. The court held nine hearings in total. Five adjournments, amounting to about five months, occurred at the applicant’s request or because of his absence. A further adjournment of about five months was caused by the judge’s absence. The examination of the case was also delayed by about a year after the court ordered a repeated forensic accounting evaluation at the prosecutor’s request.

On 14 February 2005, the Kyivskyy Court, again at the prosecutor’s request, remitted the case for additional investigation. On 5 April 2005, the Court of Appeal upheld that ruling. After April 2005, the investigation was stayed on three occasions: for eight months, for one year and three months, and for about one year, respectively. Each stay was based on the authorities’ inability to establish the whereabouts of the applicant and Mr Z. However, all those rulings by the investigator were later quashed by the Prosecutor’s Office of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea as unfounded, and new investigators were assigned to the case.

Meanwhile, according to the applicant, he repeatedly enquired about the progress of the investigation and requested disciplinary action against the prosecutors and investigators involved. By a letter dated 18 February 2011, the Crimea Prosecutor’s Office informed the applicant, in reply to his enquiry of 18 January 2011, that the criminal proceedings against him and Mr Z had been terminated on 27 December 2010 for lack of corpus delicti in their actions.

Overall, the criminal proceedings against the applicant lasted from 7 March 2001 until 27 December 2010, nearly ten years. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation include the prolonged investigation, repeated stays due to unestablished whereabouts, the remittal for additional investigation, the forensic accounting delay, multiple adjournments, and the eventual termination of the case without conviction. The central complaint was that the domestic authorities failed to conduct the proceedings within a reasonable time.
001-117134:
In *Salakhov and Islyamova v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 2 and 3 concerning the detention and death of Linar Salakhov, an HIV-positive Ukrainian national, and related complaints by his mother, Aliya Islyamova.

Salakhov tested HIV-positive in September 2005 and was informed in February 2006, but did not register for medical monitoring. On 20 November 2007 he was arrested on suspicion of robbery and detained in the Bakhchysaray police temporary detention facility (ITT) and later Simferopol Pre-Trial Detention Centre (SIZO). The applicants alleged he told authorities about his HIV status and feared for his health; the Government claimed he did not disclose it. Initial medical examinations found no complaints.

In late May 2008 he complained of fever, rhinitis, and sore throat, and was diagnosed with an acute respiratory viral infection. On 31 May an infectious disease specialist noted two months of fever and weight loss and recommended an HIV test. It was scheduled for 2 June but not carried out because he was transferred. On 3 June hospital examinations led to diagnoses including ulcer, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, chronic bronchitis, and suspected HIV. On 5 June an infectious disease specialist diagnosed pneumocystis pneumonia, oropharyngeal-esophageal candidiasis, and HIV at the fourth clinical stage. Although his condition was “moderately severe” and required treatment, the doctor concluded there was no urgent need for hospitalisation. His mother bought medication, which was administered in the ITT. A lawyer’s request for release on health grounds was rejected on 6 June. On 13 June another specialist preliminarily assessed HIV at stage II and again found no urgent need for hospitalisation.

On 16 June the applicants asked the European Court to indicate an interim measure. On 17 June the Court, under Rule 39, indicated that Salakhov “should be transferred immediately to a hospital or other medical institution” for appropriate treatment. The next day, despite this, another doctor stated he did not require urgent hospitalisation, and the court rejected his release. On 20 June the Aids Centre diagnosed HIV stage IV, systemic candidosis, continuous fever, and significant weight loss, and concluded he required inpatient treatment. He was transferred to Central Hospital under police guard and allegedly handcuffed to his bed. On 26 June he was moved to Hospital No. 7, where diagnoses included pneumocystis pneumonia, anaemia, severe immunosuppression (CD4 count 48), and encephalitis. He remained handcuffed during treatment from 26 June to 18 July. Antiretroviral therapy began on 10 July. On 18 July security measures were lifted; he was taken home but readmitted the next day and died on 2 August 2008.

After his death, the mother complained of inadequate medical care and ineffective investigation. A Ministry of Health commission blamed the delayed application for monitoring and the severity of the disease, not the doctors. Prosecutors repeatedly refused criminal proceedings; those decisions were quashed and remitted. A November 2010 forensic report found that the 5 June conclusion that urgent hospitalisation was unnecessary did not correspond to the diagnoses, and that pneumocystis pneumonia alone warranted urgent inpatient treatment. By 18 June he required urgent hospitalisation. The experts could not determine a causal link to death because no autopsy was performed. In December 2010 criminal proceedings were opened concerning alleged negligence by Central Hospital doctors; later investigation into ITT/SIZO staff was repeatedly refused and remitted, with courts noting failures to investigate SIZO staff and medical complaint records.

These facts formed the basis for alleged violations concerning inadequate medical care in detention, failure to comply with the Rule 39 interim measure, handcuffing in hospital, an ineffective domestic investigation, and the mother’s own suffering under Article 3.
001-126800:
**Summary of *Klinovská v. Slovakia* (Application no. 61436/09)**

The case of *Klinovská v. Slovakia* originated from an application lodged against the Slovak Republic with the European Court of Human Rights on 10 November 2009. The applicant, Ms. Margita Klinovská, a Slovak national born in 1969, alleged a violation of her right to a hearing within a reasonable time, as guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The core of her complaint concerned the excessive length of civil proceedings she had initiated in Slovakia.

The relevant facts began on 15 November 2004, when the applicant filed an action for damages with the Bratislava I District Court. She sued the Ministry of Finance and three other public authorities, a number that later expanded to eight defendants. Her claim was based on the State Liability Act, arguing that the defendants had failed in their supervisory duties, thereby allowing two private non-banking investment institutions to operate illicitly. These institutions had collapsed in the 1990s after soliciting large-scale public investments with promises of high returns. The applicant sought compensation for the financial loss she suffered due to this failed investment.

The domestic proceedings were protracted and procedurally complex. The applicant repeatedly submitted new evidence, was asked to provide further particulars of her claim, and requested that additional defendants be joined to the case. The District Court had to obtain observations from all defendants and, in 2011, even had to request fresh observations on a procedural point due to an error in its previous summonses. The first hearing on the merits did not take place until 15 March 2012, over seven years after the action was filed. Two more hearings followed, and on 9 November 2012, the District Court discontinued proceedings against three defendants and dismissed the action against the others. The applicant subsequently appealed, and this appeal was still pending at the time of the European Court’s judgment.

Prior to applying to the European Court, the applicant pursued two domestic remedies regarding the delays. First, on 16 March 2009, she complained to the President of the District Court. In a response dated 16 April 2009, the President acknowledged that there had been undue delays caused mainly by objective factors, apologised to the applicant, and informed her that the presiding judge had been instructed to prevent further delays. Second, on 25 May 2009, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court under Article 127 of the Constitution, alleging a violation of her right to a hearing within a reasonable time. However, on 11 June 2009, the Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. It reasoned that the complaint to the District Court President had been an effective remedy, as the President had reacted adequately and taken necessary measures. The Constitutional Court concluded that, at that time, the District Court was proceeding with the case properly, and advised the applicant that she could raise a new constitutional complaint if further delays occurred, without needing to first address the District Court President again.

The applicant’s subsequent application to the European Court of Human Rights centred on the allegation that the length of the proceedings before the Bratislava I District Court was excessive, violating her right to a timely hearing under the Convention.
001-115884:
In *Slyusar v. Ukraine* (Application no. 39797/05, judgment 17 January 2013), the applicant, Yuriy Slyusar, alleged that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation into the disappearance and presumed death of his twin brother, Se. The case centred on the procedural obligation under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights to investigate suspicious deaths effectively.

The key facts began in April 2003. Se. made a will in the applicant’s favour, leaving him an apartment and other property. Between 16 and 17 April 2003, Se. disappeared. He had been living with his former wife, G., and their son, S., despite a sham divorce. Neighbours later reported hearing the water heater, running water, and sounds resembling cleaning in the early hours of 17 April. The applicant’s friends who visited the apartment that evening noticed the carpet was missing, that S. had a wound on his hand, and that G. and S. appeared very nervous.

On 18 April 2003, the applicant and G. reported Se.’s disappearance. Police examined the apartment and seized stained wallpaper, traces of a brown substance, a bathroom pipe, a stool, clothing, deeds, cash, and Se.’s passport. On 26 April, police refused to open criminal proceedings for lack of evidence. That decision was quashed on 20 May, and a kidnapping investigation began. It was later reclassified as murder in October 2003, and the applicant was recognised as a victim in December 2003.

The investigation was marked by serious deficiencies. Forensic examinations produced inconclusive and inconsistent results: some blood traces might have belonged to S. or G., while another examination excluded them. S. and G. were arrested in July 2003 but released soon after, and proceedings against them were terminated. In 2006, M., an acquaintance of G., stated that G. had told him S. killed Se. during an inheritance quarrel, hitting him with a dumbbell, cutting up the body, and hiding it. Confrontations followed, but S. denied involvement. S. was briefly arrested again in February 2006 and released. Lie-detector records were later lost. In 2008, S. left for Australia. Se.’s body has never been found, and the proceedings remained pending.

In January 2006, the General Prosecutor’s Office itself acknowledged major shortcomings. It found that the investigation had been chaotic, that unsubstantiated decisions to drop proceedings had been taken, that the case had been repeatedly transferred, and that the applicant’s allegations about G., S., and M. had not been properly checked. It also noted initial delays, tactical mistakes, perfunctory witness questioning, failure to conduct a reconstruction concerning whether neighbours could hear cleaning, and failure to investigate a possible financial motive. By 2011, sixteen different investigators had handled the case. Disciplinary measures were occasionally taken against officers, but the investigation remained unresolved.

The applicant also faced defamation proceedings brought by S. and G. over a TV programme, though the claims were ultimately rejected. He eventually obtained a declaration that his brother was dead, but property disputes and complaints against officials largely failed.

The central alleged violation was that the authorities failed to conduct an effective, thorough, prompt, and independent investigation into Se.’s suspicious disappearance and presumed death. The key facts relevant to that complaint are the delayed opening of a murder case, repeated investigative failures, lost or insecure evidence, failure to pursue obvious leads and suspects, numerous transfers of the case, and the continued impunity and unresolved nature of the investigation. These facts underpinned the applicant’s claim that Ukraine breached its procedural obligations under Article 2 of the Convention.
001-127410:
In *Rooney v. Ireland* (Application no. 32614/10, 31 October 2013), the European Court of Human Rights considered complaints under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention concerning the excessive length of two Irish civil actions and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. The applicant, an Irish farmer and barrister, challenged measures taken under the State’s bovine tuberculosis (“TB”) eradication scheme.

The first action began in November 1987, after some of the applicant’s cattle were destroyed under the scheme. He brought High Court proceedings challenging the scheme’s constitutionality. The case generated lengthy interlocutory litigation, with numerous hearings in 1988–1990 concerning discovery, amendment of pleadings, joinder of defendants, judgment in default of defence, striking out claims, and the refusal to appoint a shorthand writer. In February 1990 the High Court refused his motions for judgment in default, struck out claims against some defendants, and refused other relief. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 111/1990). In October 1990 the Supreme Court directed a special case in the High Court and adjourned the appeal. The High Court rejected the special case in May 1991; the Supreme Court rejected the related appeal (no. 224/1991) and appeal no. 111/1990 in December 1991. However, the Supreme Court failed to deal with the High Court’s refusal of judgment in default of defence—an omission later described by the Supreme Court as a clear oversight.

The applicant made repeated attempts to reopen the appeal and clarify whether the case had been fully determined. In December 2000 and July 2001 the Supreme Court refused motions to set aside earlier judgments. In October 2001 it made a vexatious litigant order against him, which impeded further progress. In July 2007 he appealed against a High Court refusal to hear a motion to amend his statement of claim (appeal no. 217/2007). In March 2010 the Supreme Court found that claims outside the special case could still be pursued and that the default-judgment appeal had not been determined due to oversight. A later High Court refusal in November 2010 was appealed (no. 430/2010) and remained pending.

The second action began in November 1995, after the applicant’s herd was restricted from April 1993 to July 1996 under the same scheme. He claimed the restriction was unlawful and that the scheme breached statute, the Constitution, the Convention, and EU law. Discovery was obtained in December 1997. A Notice to Admit Facts was refused in November 2002, and a Notice of Trial was served in December 2002. The High Court heard the case over ten days in May and June 2004 and dismissed it in July 2004. The applicant appealed in August 2004 (no. 387/2004), filed written submissions in July 2006, and a Certificate of Readiness in January 2007. In November 2007 he failed to have the appeal prioritised. In May 2009 the Registrar stated that the waiting time after certification was 31 months and no hearing date had been allocated. The appeal was eventually heard with appeal no. 217/2007 in October 2009, but the Supreme Court’s March 2010 judgment did not expressly determine the 2004 appeal. The State Solicitor later agreed the appeal had been omitted. After further listings, the Supreme Court dismissed the 2004 appeal in November 2010.

These facts underpinned the applicant’s complaints that the civil proceedings were unreasonably long and that Ireland provided no effective remedy for that delay.
001-120969:
This case originated in an application lodged on 18 November 2008 by Mr Evgueni Lavrechov, a Russian national, against the Czech Republic. He alleged that his property rights had been violated by the forfeiture of bail security of CZK 10,000,000 (approximately EUR 400,000) that he had paid in criminal proceedings against him.

The applicant represented a Russian company that had bought a share in a Czech company, S., and he served on the board of directors and later as chairman. In June 2001 he was charged with insider trading and fraud, including allegedly concluding contracts disadvantageous to company S. and causing damage of CZK 88,000,000. He was placed in pre-trial detention on 20 June 2001.

In January 2002 the applicant sought release on bail. His request stated that he was aware of the statutory conditions under which bail could be forfeited. On 17 January 2002 the Ostrava Regional Court granted bail in the amount of CZK 10,000,000, citing the gravity of the charges and the risk that he would abscond. He was released on 22 February 2002. The bail conditions required him to stay at his address in the Czech Republic, receive mail there, attend hearings, and comply with the court’s conditions; he acknowledged that the security could be forfeited if he did not comply.

In June 2002 the court allowed him to travel to Russia until 18 June 2002, on condition that he attend a hearing scheduled for 19–21 June 2002. He had made three previous trips to Russia and had always returned.
