On 17 June 2002 his lawyer informed the court that the applicant’s passport and Czech visa had been stolen in Moscow on 14 June 2002 and that he was seeking a new passport. The hearing was adjourned. A summons sent to his Czech address was returned undelivered, and his lawyer said he had no direct contact details for him in Russia. The August 2002 hearing was cancelled because the applicant still had no passport and objected to being tried in absentia.

The date on which he obtained a new passport is disputed, but he did not inform the Regional Court. In March 2004 the court attempted to summon him to an address in Podolsk, Russia, warning that his conduct could lead to forfeiture of bail. Russian authorities replied that he was not registered or living there and that his whereabouts were unknown. The applicant learned of a September 2004 hearing and obtained a short-term visa, but then faxed the court seeking adjournment based on health problems and new lawyers, without giving his address. In December 2005 the Regional Court decided to try him in absentia, finding that he had avoided proceedings by remaining outside the Czech Republic since June 2002 and had violated bail conditions.

In October 2006 the Regional Court acquitted the applicant, holding that he had merely engaged in standard business activities. This was upheld in June 2007. In November 2007 the Regional Court ordered return of the bail because he had not been duly informed of the consequences of non-compliance and no statutory ground for forfeiture applied. In December 2007 the High Court reversed that decision and ordered forfeiture. It reasoned that he must have known of the possibility of forfeiture from his earlier declarations; although his lost passport initially prevented return, he later failed to collect correspondence at the Podolsk address, did not keep in contact with the court, and appeared to have avoided prosecution. The Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal on 3 June 2008. The alleged violation therefore concerns whether forfeiture of the bail was compatible with his property rights, given the acquittal, the initial passport difficulties, notification problems, and the domestic courts’ differing conclusions on whether he had breached bail conditions or been properly warned.
001-118591:
In *Mežnarič v. Slovenia* (Application no. 41416/06), the European Court of Human Rights considered a Slovenian national’s complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention. The applicant, Marijan Mežnarič, born in 1950 and living in Šmarje pri Jelšah, lodged his application on 21 September 2006. He alleged that domestic proceedings involving him had lasted excessively and that no effective domestic remedy existed for that delay. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 March 2012.

The underlying proceedings began on 13 June 1995, when the Žiri Municipality brought enforcement proceedings against the company KODA SPAAR d.o.o. before the Kranj Basic Court. A writ of execution was issued on 28 June 1995, but the company objected. On 5 September 1995 the first-instance court annulled the writ. On 6 November 1995 the case was referred to the Kranj District Court to be decided in contentious proceedings.

A lengthy jurisdictional phase followed. On 21 November 1999 the court declared it lacked jurisdiction and referred the case to the Škofja Loka Local Court. That court initiated a jurisdictional dispute on 25 November 1999. Only on 30 August 2000 did the Ljubljana Higher Court assign the case back to the Kranj District Court.

On 17 October 2000 the first-instance court received an extract from the Register of Companies showing that KODA SPAAR d.o.o. had been struck out under Article 580 §§ 5–6 of the Companies Act. On 8 January 2001 the creditor requested continuation of the proceedings against the applicant, since he had been the company’s founder and owner. On 27 August 2001 the first-instance court granted continuation against the applicant. The applicant appealed and requested exemption from court fees on 10 September 2001. The Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal on 24 October 2001, and his subsequent request for protection of legality was also rejected.

On 27 August 2002 the Kranj District Court stayed the proceedings pending a Constitutional Court decision concerning suspension of a chapter of the Financial Operations of Companies Act. Proceedings resumed on 17 January 2003. On 17 December 2003 a settlement hearing was held; the applicant requested legal aid, exemption from fees, and filed a counterclaim for damages. On 11 February 2004 the first-instance court annulled the 1995 writ. The Ljubljana Higher Court remitted the case on 16 February 2005. On 31 August 2005 the first-instance court upheld the writ; the applicant appealed. On 21 June 2006 the Higher Court upheld the appeal and annulled the writ. On 4 September 2006 the applicant sought reimbursement of legal costs, but his request was rejected on 10 October 2006.

The domestic-law background included the 2006 Act on Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay, which became operational on 1 January 2007, after the applicant’s ECtHR application. Its transitional Section 25 allowed settlement offers and court actions for cases already filed with the international court. The Companies Act and Constitutional Court decision U-I-135/00 § 61 made former shareholders potentially liable as universal successors of struck-off companies, explaining why the applicant was drawn into the proceedings. The key alleged violations were therefore the excessive length of proceedings from 1995 to 2006 and the lack of an effective remedy at the relevant time.

001-108680:
**Case Summary: Varapnickaitė-Mažylienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 20376/05)**

The applicant, Jolanta Varapnickaitė-Mažylienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1960, was engaged in protracted custody proceedings concerning her son with her former husband. The case before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the alleged violation of her right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention, and her claim that she lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

The facts centre on a series of media publications in 2001. On 31 March 2001, the daily newspaper *Respublika* published, at the applicant’s own expense, an open letter she had written to the Children’s Rights Ombudsman complaining about the Children’s Welfare Service (CWS). In this letter she disclosed her and her son’s full names, her son’s date of birth, her former husband’s name, and detailed the chronology of the custody litigation, including psychiatric treatment and doctors’ reports. On 3 April 2001, *Lietuvos Aidas* published an interview in which she again divulged names of her son, former husband, and CWS employees, and quoted medical and social-care reports. The Government also submitted that she disclosed similar information on a television programme in May 2001.

The alleged violation, however, arose from an article published by *Lietuvos Aidas* on 15 June 2001, titled “The overworked employees of the CWS are convinced that you cannot buy a child’s love.” In that article, the CWS director and employees commented publicly on the case, describing the mother’s divorce, her new relationship, and her alleged conduct. More significantly, the article cited the child’s medical records obtained from the Vilnius Child Development Centre Psychiatric Unit, revealing psychiatric conclusions that the boy was hostile towards his mother, that conflicts had arisen with her new husband, that the mother had suspected sexual abuse (which was not confirmed), and that on one occasion the mother had pulled the boy’s hair and bitten him. Although the article did not name the applicant or her family or disclose their residence, it contained detailed private and health information.

The applicant complained to the Children’s Rights Ombudsman, who partly criticised the CWS but also admonished the applicant for breaching her son’s privacy by publicising family matters. The director of the Child Development Centre informed her that the CWS had acted unethically in disclosing the medical records. On 11 October 2001, the Inspector of Journalistic Ethics warned the editors that the article breached the applicant’s honour and dignity and that, despite apparent anonymity, she was recognisable and portrayed negatively.

The applicant sued the CWS for damages, claiming 50,000 Lithuanian litai. On 15 December 2003, the Vilnius City Second District Court dismissed her action, finding that the article contained no data permitting her identification and that she had failed to prove deliberate disclosure of private information. This was upheld by the Vilnius Regional Court on 18 June 2004 and by the Supreme Court on 29 November 2004. The Supreme Court held that the Inspector’s and medical institution’s findings were not binding and that the applicant had not been clearly identifiable.

Notably, however, on the same day the Supreme Court issued a separate ruling expressing disapproval of the CWS employees’ conduct. It observed that publicly commenting in detail on a particular child’s circumstances and health was incompatible with the child’s interests, that no legitimate public interest warranted publication, and that such disclosure could only cause distress.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that Lithuania had failed to protect her private life and had not provided an effective remedy. The key factual dispute concerned whether the 15 June 2001 article, despite not naming her, allowed her identification and whether the domestic courts adequately protected her privacy against the CWS’s disclosure of confidential medical and family information.
001-113328:
This case, *Rrapo v. Albania*, concerned the extradition of Almir Rrapo, an Albanian and United States national, from Albania to the United States despite an interim measure issued by the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39. Before the Court, the applicant alleged breaches of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention because his extradition exposed him to the risk of the death penalty and related treatment, and a breach of Article 34 because the Albanian authorities failed to comply with the Court’s interim measure.

The applicant was arrested in Tirana on 2 July 2010 at the request of the United States Embassy, after applying to renew his American passport. The Embassy requested his provisional arrest for extradition under the 1933 Extradition Treaty. Albanian courts authorised and repeatedly extended his detention. On 30 August 2010, the United States formally requested his extradition. The diplomatic note listed nine counts, including membership in an organised racketeering enterprise, conspiracy to distribute large quantities of marijuana and controlled substances, robbery, firearms offences, kidnapping in aid of racketeering, and the murder of E.S. in aid of racketeering. Five charges carried a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, two carried forty years, one carried twenty years, and the murder charge carried either death or life imprisonment.

Albanian courts granted extradition. The applicant objected that the United States had not provided assurances against the death penalty. The District Court and Court of Appeal rejected that objection, holding that no legal obligation required such assurances. On 1 November 2010, the Court of Appeal ruled in favour of extradition. The Minister of Justice then ordered extradition by 16 November 2010 and asked the United States whether the applicant would face capital punishment. On 8 November 2010, the United States Embassy sent diplomatic note no. 91, assuring Albania that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed on Rrapo for the charges for which extradition was granted.

Meanwhile, the European Court had intervened. On 12 October 2010, the President of the Fourth Section indicated under Rule 39 that the applicant should not be extradited until ten days after notification of the Court of Appeal’s decision. On 2 November 2010, after the Court of Appeal’s decision, the measure was prolonged until fifteen days after notification of the Supreme Court’s decision. On 15 November 2010, the President decided that the Rule 39 measure remained in force despite the United States’ assurances. The Albanian authorities were explicitly reminded that failure to comply with a Rule 39 measure could breach Article 34.

On 24 November 2010, Albania extradited the applicant to the United States without prior notice to him or his lawyer. The Government later claimed the extradition was prompted by the United States’ assurances and by the imminent expiry of his detention on 1 December 2010, which would have required his release and created a risk of absconding. On 26 November 2010, the Supreme Court quashed the lower extradition decisions, finding that the courts had failed to obtain death penalty assurances and had not properly assessed evidence of guilt. By then, however, the applicant had already been extradited. In the United States, he later pleaded guilty and, in July 2012, was sentenced to 80 months’ imprisonment.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the capital nature of one charge, the timing and content of the United States’ death penalty assurances, the Albanian courts’ initial failure to obtain such assurances, and Albania’s decision to extradite while a binding Rule 39 interim measure remained in force.
001-111044:
The case of *Scoppola v. Italy (No. 3)* (Application no. 126/05) concerns an application lodged by Franco Scoppola, an Italian national, alleging that his disenfranchisement following a criminal conviction violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights (right to free elections).

In September 1999, following a violent family dispute, the applicant killed his wife and injured one of his sons. He was arrested the next day. In November 2000, under the summary procedure he had elected, the Rome preliminary hearings judge found him guilty of murder, attempted murder, ill-treatment of his family, and unauthorised possession of a firearm. Although the judge noted that life imprisonment was warranted, the summary procedure reduced the sentence to thirty years' imprisonment and a lifetime ban from public office under Article 29 of the Italian Criminal Code. The judge found aggravating circumstances, including that the crimes were committed against his own family and triggered by a trivial incident, and no remorse. Both the prosecution and the applicant appealed. In January 2002, the Rome Assize Court of Appeal sentenced him to life imprisonment, and in January 2003 the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal.

Under Italian law, a life sentence entails a lifetime ban from public office, which in turn results in permanent forfeiture of the right to vote under section 2 of Presidential Decree no. 223/1967. The applicant's disenfranchisement was not mentioned in the judgments against him. In April 2003, the electoral committee deleted his name from the electoral roll.

In June 2004, the applicant lodged a complaint with the electoral committee, citing *Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2)*, alleging that his disenfranchisement was incompatible with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The complaint was rejected, and his appeal to the Rome Court of Appeal was dismissed in November 2004. The Court of Appeal distinguished *Hirst*, noting that unlike the UK's blanket ban, Italian law applied the voting ban only where the offence was punishable by a particularly heavy sentence, including life imprisonment; the automatic application to any custodial sentence was lacking. The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing that the disenfranchisement was an automatic consequence of the ancillary penalty, had nothing to do with the offence committed, and the courts had no power to decide whether to apply it. In January 2006, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, referring to the Grand Chamber's *Hirst* judgment and noting that in Italian law only offenders sentenced to at least three years' imprisonment were deprived of the right to vote, with temporary bans for sentences of three to five years and lifelong bans for sentences of five years to life.

Separately, in *Scoppola v. Italy (no. 2)*, the Grand Chamber found violations of Articles 6 and 7 regarding his life sentence, and in April 2010 the Court of Cassation reduced his sentence to thirty years' imprisonment. However, the disenfranchisement remained the subject of the present application.
001-112576:
M. and Others v. Italy and Bulgaria (App. no. 40020/03, ECtHR, 31 July 2012) concerned four Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin: L.M., who was a minor at the time; her parents S.M. and I.I.; and her sister-in-law K.L. They alleged violations of Articles 3, 4, 13 and 14 of the Convention arising from events in Italy in May–June 2003.

The applicants claimed they travelled to Italy after X, a Serbian Roma man, promised work and accommodated them in a villa in Ghislarengo. After several days, X allegedly said his nephew Y wanted to marry L.M. When her parents refused, X threatened them with a gun; they were beaten, threatened with death, and forced to return to Bulgaria on 18 May 2003, leaving L.M. behind. L.M. alleged that she was then kept under constant surveillance, forced to steal, beaten, threatened with death, and repeatedly raped by Y while tied to a bed. During one forced robbery she was injured and taken to hospital, but the family removed her before treatment. On 24 May 2003 the mother returned to Italy and complained to Turin police that she and her husband had been beaten and threatened and that L.M. had been kidnapped and might be forced into prostitution.

On 11 June 2003, eighteen days after the complaint, Italian police raided the villa, found L.M., and made arrests. At the police station, L.M. and her mother alleged they were treated roughly, threatened with perjury and libel charges, denied proper interpretation or legal assistance, and forced to sign documents they did not understand. L.M. was later placed in a shelter and then returned to Bulgaria. The applicants claimed that no effective investigation followed against the alleged kidnappers and that Italian authorities failed to cooperate with Bulgaria to question the father.

The Italian Government disputed this account. It stated that the complaint was promptly transmitted to Vercelli police and prosecutors; police identified and surveilled the villa and raided it on 11 June. After questioning L.M., her mother, and X, Y and Z, and after photographs appeared to show a wedding and payment of a bride price, the prosecutor concluded that the events involved a consensual marriage agreement, not kidnapping. Proceedings were therefore opened against L.M. and her mother for perjury and false accusations. The juvenile case against L.M. was later dropped as socially irrelevant; the mother was acquitted in 2006 because the evidence did not establish guilt. The Bulgarian Government largely relied on the Italian account and said Bulgarian authorities forwarded the father’s complaint to the embassy and helped contact Italian authorities.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants principally alleged that Italy failed to take adequate steps to prevent L.M.’s ill-treatment by the Serbian family, especially by securing her swift release, and failed to conduct an effective investigation into that ill-treatment. They also alleged ill-treatment by Italian police during questioning, lack of lawyer and interpreter safeguards, discriminatory treatment as Roma and Bulgarian nationals, and inadequate assistance from Bulgarian consular authorities. The case thus centred on whether the States complied with positive obligations to protect a minor from serious abuse, investigate credible allegations of ill-treatment, and ensure fair treatment during police questioning.
001-110949:
**Julin v. Estonia** concerned four applications brought by Vyacheslav Julin, an Estonian national serving a prison sentence. He alleged ill-treatment by prison officers and the absence of an effective investigation; denial of access to court regarding prison conditions and officers’ actions; a humiliating strip-search violating private life; and ill-treatment through restraint measures.

**Application no. 16563/08:** In 2007, while in Murru Prison, the applicant was placed in punishment cells nos. 140 and 122. He complained of degrading conditions: dirty, unopenable windows, poor ventilation, cold, dim or no lighting, high noise, inadequate plumbing and toilet facilities, bad smells, and dirty bedding. On 11 July 2007 he was assaulted by fellow prisoners and sustained thirteen stab wounds. After hospital treatment, he returned to Murru Prison and was held for ten days in cell no. 147 in the closed disciplinary section, where he again complained of poor conditions. On 7 August 2007 he was transferred to Tartu Prison on the day of a planned family visit, so the visit did not occur. In Tartu’s reception section, he later sewed his mouth shut and began a hunger strike, mainly due to fears about a cellmate; he was then placed in a locked isolation cell and subjected to additional restrictions. His administrative complaints about prison conditions and the family visit were blocked because courts refused to exempt him from the State fee, finding his claims not sufficiently important or likely to succeed. His complaints were returned for non-payment.

**Application no. 40841/08:** In 2007 the applicant was punished for a prohibited transaction and placed in cell no. 155 in Murru Prison. He complained of similar degrading conditions and challenged the lawfulness of the punishment. Again, his request for exemption from the State fee was refused, and his complaint was returned for non-payment.

**Application no. 8192/10:** On 26 May 2009, after returning from a court hearing to Tartu Prison, the applicant was strip-searched. He alleged that, although seven prisoners were escorted together, only he was searched that way; five officers were present. He said he was ordered to undress, lift his sexual organ and squat, and was laughed at. Officer O. wanted to perform a digital rectal examination, but the applicant refused, insisting a doctor should do it. He was taken to the medical unit, where a female doctor performed the rectal examination in the presence of two officers. His request for a male doctor was rejected, and he was warned force could be used. The Government disputed his account. His compensation claim was refused by the prison, and the administrative court declined to examine it for failure to comply with the mandatory pre-litigation procedure.

**Application no. 18656/10:** On 22 October 2009, a conflict arose over tobacco. Prison reports stated the applicant became aggressive, threatened officers, used foul language, banged on the door, and struck an officer’s hand. He was placed in a restraint bed from 10:40 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., monitored hourly. The applicant alleged he was provoked, did not resist, was subdued by masked officers, handcuffed and restrained, and was denied food, drink and toilet access for nine hours. Further handcuff restrictions were imposed. On 23 October 2009, officers reported that he refused to be handcuffed and used offensive language; force was used. A nurse recorded an abrasion near his left eye and bluish marks on his neck. The applicant alleged officers hit him with a shield, pushed his face against bars, grabbed his neck, put fingers in his nostrils, and forced him down. Disciplinary proceedings led to two twenty-day punishment-cell sanctions. Prosecutors refused to open a criminal investigation, relying on prison reports and finding the force lawful; the applicant was not interviewed and was refused legal aid.

These facts formed the basis of his complaints under the Convention concerning ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, humiliating search, and lack of access to court.
001-109581:
In *Austin and Others v. the United Kingdom* (Applications nos. 39692/09, 40713/09 and 41008/09), four applicants complained under Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that their confinement inside a police cordon—known as “kettling”—during a demonstration in central London amounted to a deprivation of liberty.

The events occurred on 1 May 2001 at Oxford Circus. The applicants were among those contained within a police cordon for several hours. The first applicant, Ms Austin, was a demonstrator who needed to leave at about 3.45 p.m. to collect her 11-month-old daughter from a crèche. She told police officers on the cordon, but was refused permission to leave and eventually left at about 9.30 p.m. The second applicant, Mr Black, was a passer-by trying to cross Oxford Circus to reach a bookshop. He was advised to take another route, but was met by riot police and forced into the cordon. He asked to leave and was told there was an exit for non-protesters at Bond Street, but when he went there no exit existed. He was released at about 9.20 p.m. The third applicant, Ms Lowenthal, worked in the Oxford Circus area and was on her lunch break when police blocked her return to work. She was caught inside the cordon and held until about 9.35 p.m. The fourth applicant, Mr O’Shea, also worked locally and was caught while walking through Oxford Circus on his lunch break; he was able to leave at approximately 8 p.m.

The police imposed the cordon at about 2 p.m. to contain a crowd gathered for a “May Day Monopoly” protest against capitalism and globalisation. The police relied on intelligence indicating that 500 to 1,000 hard-core demonstrators intended confrontation and violence. Previous similar protests in London and abroad had involved serious disorder. The police had nearly 6,000 officers deployed. The cordon became fully effective by about 2.20–2.25 p.m. No announcement was made until 4 p.m., although the commander accepted it could have been made earlier. Conditions inside became uncomfortable: cold and wet weather, no food or water, no toilets or shelter. There was sufficient space and no crushing.

The police repeatedly planned controlled release, but delayed it because of missile throwing, attempts to break through the cordon, violence outside, and insufficient resources to escort released people safely. Individual releases numbered perhaps 400, mostly before 4 p.m.; 12 occurred between 4 and 5 p.m., 89 between 5 and 6 p.m., 59 between 6 and 7 p.m., and 12 after 7 p.m. Collective release began around 7 p.m., was halted, resumed at 7.30 p.m., halted again, resumed at 8 p.m., and was almost complete by 9.45 p.m. Over 100 people were arrested.

In domestic proceedings, the High Court found that the containment amounted to a deprivation of liberty under Article 5, but dismissed claims for false imprisonment on necessity grounds and found no breach of Articles 10 or 11. The Court of Appeal reversed the Article 5 finding, holding that the confinement was not a deprivation of liberty, comparing it to crowd control at football matches or motorway closures. The applicants then brought their complaints to Strasbourg, where the Grand Chamber ultimately considered whether the cordon engaged Article 5 § 1.
001-114244:
**Summary of *Hode and Abdi v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 22341/09)**

The case of *Hode and Abdi v. the United Kingdom* concerns a challenge to United Kingdom immigration rules that prevented a refugee from being joined by a spouse whom he married after fleeing his country of origin. The application was brought by Mr. Ilyas Elmi Hode, a Somali national and recognised refugee in the UK, and his wife, Ms. Hawa Aden Abdi, a Djibouti national.

The key facts are as follows. The first applicant, Mr. Hode, arrived in the UK in February 2004 and was granted asylum in March 2006. Due to a change in the Immigration Rules on 30 August 2005, he was granted five years’ limited leave to remain, rather than indefinite leave. In 2006, he was introduced to the second applicant, and they married in Djibouti in April 2007. This marriage was a "post-flight" marriage, as it occurred after Mr. Hode had left Somalia. The couple lived together in Djibouti until Mr. Hode returned to the UK in May 2007.

In November 2007, Mrs. Abdi applied for a visa to join her husband in the UK. Her application was refused. The central legal obstacle was the UK’s Immigration Rules at the time. Paragraph 352A, which governed family reunion for refugees, only permitted a refugee to be joined by a spouse if the marriage had taken place *before* the refugee fled their country of habitual residence. As a post-flight spouse, Mrs. Abdi did not qualify. She also could not qualify under the general rule for spouses (paragraph 281), which required the sponsor to be a person "present and settled" in the UK. Because Mr. Hode only had limited leave to remain, he did not meet the definition of being "settled."

Mrs. Abdi appealed the refusal. An Immigration Judge accepted that the couple had a genuine marriage and that the refusal engaged their right to family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, the appeal was dismissed. The judge found that the refusal was not disproportionate, noting that the couple had never enjoyed family life together in the UK and that Mr. Hode could potentially live with his wife in Djibouti, despite practical difficulties. Subsequent applications for reconsideration were also refused.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the UK’s immigration rules, which prevented them from cohabiting as a family in the UK, constituted a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for family life) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention. They argued that they were discriminated against as post-flight spouses of a refugee, a category treated less favourably than other groups, such as students or workers, whose spouses were permitted to join them in the UK without a similar restriction.

The factual background is further defined by subsequent events. In April 2011, the UK government amended the Immigration Rules (introducing paragraph 319L) to allow post-flight spouses of refugees to join them during their initial period of limited leave. However, Mrs. Abdi did not re-apply. By this time, Mr. Hode’s five-year leave had expired, and he had been granted Indefinite Leave to Remain, technically making him "settled" and thereby eligible to apply under the standard spouse rules. The case before the Court, however, concerned the situation as it stood when the original application was refused.
001-109062:
Dimitar Ivanov v. Bulgaria (Application no. 19418/07) concerned a Bulgarian national born in 1974, living in Dinkata. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 April 2007. He alleged that the criminal charges against him had not been determined within a reasonable time, that he lacked effective remedies for that delay, and that the prohibition on his leaving Bulgaria was unlawful and unjustified.

The criminal proceedings began after an incident on 6 October 1994, when the applicant confessed before the police to committing robbery earlier that day together with two other individuals. The stolen goods were confiscated by the police the same day. However, criminal proceedings against him were not formally instituted until 4 October 1995. The case then appears to have remained dormant for approximately nine years, until 5 October 2004, when witnesses were questioned.

During 2001–2004, before being charged, the applicant left Bulgaria on several occasions and returned each time. On 6 October 2004, while he was abroad, an ex officio lawyer was appointed for him and he was charged in absentia with robbery. The first hearing in the case was held on 14 January 2005, with the applicant present. On 12 April 2006, the Pazardzhik District Court found him guilty and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment, suspended for three years. Following an appeal by his co-defendant, the Pazardzhik Regional Court, in a final judgment of 12 October 2006, upheld the lower court’s judgment, including the applicant’s conviction and sentence.

Separately, on 9 March 2007, the Pazardzhik Regional Police Directorate ordered a ban on the applicant leaving Bulgaria. The order was based on his conviction and pending his rehabilitation, relying on section 76(2) of the 1998 Bulgarian Identity Papers Act. The applicant challenged the order, arguing that he was unable to provide for his family in Bulgaria and that he had employment opportunities in Serbia. On 25 May 2007, while attempting to leave Bulgaria, he was refused passage by a border police official because of the prohibition.

By a final judgment of 10 October 2007, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the travel ban. It reasoned that it fell within the administrative authority’s discretion to impose such a ban and that the authority’s assessment was not subject to judicial control. The court also held that domestic law had been complied with, since such a restriction could be imposed where a conviction was in place and before the convicted person’s rehabilitation. It further considered other factors, such as the applicant’s inability to find employment in Bulgaria, irrelevant.

The relevant domestic law and practice concerning travel bans on convicted individuals pending rehabilitation were set out in Nalbantski v. Bulgaria (no. 30943/04, §§ 25–29, 10 February 2011). The provisions concerning rehabilitation of persons convicted with a suspended sentence were also summarised in that judgment at § 30.

The key facts for the alleged violations were therefore the lengthy criminal proceedings—from formal institution in October 1995 to final conviction in October 2006, including a long inactive period—the alleged absence of effective remedies for that delay, and the post-conviction travel ban imposed in March 2007 and upheld in October 2007 without judicial control over the administrative discretion.
001-112465:
In *Wenerski v. Poland (No. 2)*, the European Court of Human Rights considered a Polish national’s Article 3 complaint about inadequate detention conditions, especially overcrowding. Ernest Wenerski, born 1970, had a long criminal record and had been detained since 1997. The application concerned five periods in Łódź Remand Centre: 1 September 2004–10 March 2005; 20 May–30 November 2005; 14 December 2005–19 January 2007; 5 February–22 July 2007; and 8 January 2009–June 2010.

Wenerski suffered from epilepsy with regular seizures and had a personality disorder. Medical experts concluded that his epilepsy did not itself require special detention conditions, but recommended a bottom bunk in a non-overcrowded cell. Psychiatric and psychological experts found his personality disorder developed early and was not caused by overcrowding.

During the first four Łódź periods, Wenerski had numerous epileptic fits, often causing minor injuries such as cut lips, bruises, abrasions, bumps, a bitten tongue, and a head cut. He usually received first aid from cellmates; a doctor was called during the day, and an ambulance at night or on holidays. Yet on at least two occasions he received no medical help after a fit. Once the warden told cellmates to turn him on his side and put something in his mouth; in another cell no assistance was given because the warden thought he was simulating. He also self-mutilated and received adequate treatment after self-injury.

The core complaint concerned conditions. Domestic courts found that from 2002–2006 the statutory minimum space in Łódź Remand Centre was reduced because of nationwide overcrowding and renovations. During Wenerski’s first four terms, he occupied 14 different cells measuring 10.5–12 sq m, shared by four to six prisoners, giving only 2–2.4 sq m per person. The courts found this overcrowding was not temporary, as he spent years with about 2 sq m. Examples included a cell designed for two being used by six, and a 12 sq m cell for four being occupied by six. Overcrowding harmed prisoners’ health and sanitary conditions, increased stress and aggression, and Wenerski had quarrels, fights, and disciplinary punishments. On one occasion, despite medical advice, he was assigned a top bunk without a ladder or safety rail. He alleged cells were dirty, unventilated, infested with bugs and mould; toilet annexes had only partial fabric screening, no privacy, and constant odour.

In his civil action begun 18 February 2005, Wenerski sought PLN 70,000 for overcrowded, unsuitable conditions that allegedly worsened his health and caused distress and pain from epileptic injuries. The Łódź Regional Court on 26 May 2009 found his rights to dignity and humane treatment violated by severe, long-term overcrowding and awarded PLN 2,000. It noted epilepsy was independent of detention conditions, but overcrowding may have affected his personality disorder and increased injury risk. On appeal, the Łódź Court of Appeal increased compensation to PLN 5,000 on 30 October 2009. No cassation appeal was available. His complaints to penitentiary authorities were dismissed as manifestly ill-founded. He lodged the Strasbourg application on 16 June 2009, complaining mainly under Article 3 of inadequate conditions, particularly overcrowding.
001-114486:
The case concerns Ms H., a Finnish national born in 1963 who was registered male at birth. Although she had long felt she was female, she married a woman in 1996 and they had a child in 2002. In 2006 she was diagnosed as transgender, began living as a woman, and later underwent gender reassignment surgery in September 2009. She changed her first names, passport, and driver’s licence, but her identity number remained male. According to the applicant, this continued to disclose her transgender status in everyday situations.

In June 2007 the applicant asked the local Register Office to confirm her as female and to change her identity number. The Register Office refused. Under the Finnish Act on Confirmation of the Gender of a Transsexual, confirmation of a new gender required that the person was not married or in a civil partnership, unless the spouse consented to the marriage being transformed into a civil partnership. The applicant’s wife did not consent. The applicant and her wife wished to remain married; divorce would have conflicted with their religious convictions. The applicant also argued that transforming their marriage into a civil partnership would reduce legal security and adversely affect their child, partly because a child could not have two mothers and the applicant could no longer be a legal father or mother.

The Helsinki Administrative Court rejected her appeal in May 2008, relying on the same marital-status requirement. It found that same-sex partners could obtain partial family-law protection through registered partnership and that the law did not violate the applicant’s constitutional rights or those of her child. In February 2009 the Supreme Administrative Court rejected her further appeal. It held that Finnish law allowed marriage only between a man and a woman, that civil partnership was essentially comparable to marriage in juridical and economic terms, and that changing marriage into a gender-neutral institution was a matter for Parliament. The court considered the existing law to fall within the State’s margin of appreciation under the Convention. A later extraordinary appeal, filed after the applicant’s surgery, was refused in August 2010.

Separately, the applicant sought reimbursement for hormonal medicine. In October 2007 the Social Insurance Institution refused reimbursement because she had not yet received a new identity number. The Social Security Appeal Board later allowed her appeal in January 2010. The Ombudsman for Equality also found in 2008 that conditioning reimbursement on the identity number placed transgender persons in a different position from others receiving the same treatment and recommended a change in practice.

The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention that her right to private and family life had been violated, and that she had been discriminated against, because full legal recognition of her new gender was made conditional on transforming her marriage into a civil partnership. The Court also decided ex officio to examine the case under Article 12. The central alleged violation was therefore that Finnish law forced her to choose between legal recognition of her gender identity and preserving her existing marriage and family status, while the male identity number continued to reveal her transgender status.
001-112588:
**Summary of Drakšas v. Lithuania (Application no. 36662/04)**

The case of *Drakšas v. Lithuania* concerns the interception of the applicant’s telephone conversations and the subsequent public disclosure of their contents, raising issues under Article 8 (right to respect for private life) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Mr Algirdas Drakšas, was a founding member of the Liberal Democrats political party and a member of the Vilnius City Municipal Council. On 16 March 2003, the State Security Department (SSD) intercepted a telephone conversation between the applicant and Jurij Borisov (J.B.), a major contributor to the electoral campaign of State President Rolandas Paksas. This interception was conducted under a court order authorising the tapping of J.B.’s telephone.

On 17 September 2003, the SSD requested authorisation to tap the applicant’s telephone, based on operational information linking him to J.B. and A.Z., and to a Russian citizen, V.F., who was suspected of spying. The Attorney General submitted a request to the Vilnius Regional Court, which authorised the tapping for three months. The court order was classified as secret and not disclosed to the applicant. The authorisation was based on suspicions that the applicant was involved in smuggling strategic goods, other serious crimes, and attempts to unlawfully take over shares of a road-building company, “Žemaitijos keliai.”

Between 18 September and 11 November 2003, the SSD intercepted the applicant’s conversations, including five calls with the State President and his advisers. Notably, one call was from the President to the applicant. On 1 November 2003, the SSD declassified the recording of the 16 March 2003 conversation between the applicant and J.B. and sent it to the Attorney General’s Office. The following day, this conversation was broadcast on national television (LTV and LNK). The SSD denied leaking the material.

On 11 November 2003, the Attorney General wrote to the SSD, noting that the media had revealed the existence of recordings of the applicant’s conversations with the President. The Attorney General stated that such recordings, if they existed, were unlawful under Article 6 § 3 of the Law on Operational Activities, which prohibits operational activities targeting the head of State. The SSD was ordered to destroy any such recordings and prevent their disclosure. The operational investigation against the applicant was terminated the same day.

The applicant lodged a complaint with the Attorney General on 12 November 2003, alleging unlawful tapping and a breach of privacy. He was informed that his conversations had been monitored lawfully and that his conversations with the President were recorded while tapping his phone, not the President’s. He was advised to seek a civil remedy for the media disclosure.

The applicant attempted to challenge the lawfulness of the court order authorising the tapping before the Vilnius Regional Court and later the Court of Appeal. Both attempts were rejected. The Court of Appeal President stated that granting access to such secret orders would undermine the effectiveness of covert investigations.

On 15 March 2004, the recordings and transcripts of the applicant’s conversations with V.F., J.B., and the State President were deposited with the Constitutional Court for the President’s impeachment proceedings. Prosecutors did not restrict their disclosure. At a public hearing on 19 March 2004, some recordings were played and broadcast on national television. The applicant’s request to open a criminal investigation into this disclosure was refused by prosecutors and upheld by the Vilnius City Second District Court.

The applicant also sought access to the recordings of his conversations held by the SSD but was refused by the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court and the Supreme Administrative Court, which held that the information had wider implications and was protected as evidence in criminal proceedings.

Relying on Article 8, the applicant complained that his telephone conversations had been intercepted and disclosed to the public. He also complained under Article 13 that he lacked an effective domestic remedy for these violations.
001-109575:
**Summary of Levin v. Sweden (Application no. 35141/06)**

The case of *Levin v. Sweden* concerns an application brought by Ms. Eleonor Levin, a Swedish national, against the Kingdom of Sweden under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) concerning the severe contact restrictions imposed following the state’s taking of her three children into public care.

The applicant is the mother of three children: T. (born 1999), S. (born 2001), and D. (born 2002). Following her separation from the children's father in 2003, the applicant was granted sole custody. She later married J. in 2004. The family had been known to social services since 2002. In spring 2005, concerns arose from daycare staff regarding the children's hygiene, hunger, and hyperactive behavior, as well as the applicant's apparent stress. The applicant herself sought help from a psychiatric clinic (BUP) in March 2005. On 3 May 2005, in a state of despair, the applicant contacted BUP again. A social emergency unit, accompanied by police and a physician, visited her home and found it destitute—lacking furniture, electricity, and running water. The applicant was in a confused state and blamed the conditions on her son, S. The children were immediately placed in a temporary family home, and the applicant was committed to compulsory psychiatric care the following day.

After her release, the applicant had frequent but contentious contact with social services. She withdrew consent for the voluntary placement of her daughters, T. and D., leading the Social Council to take them into public care on a provisional basis in summer 2005. On 19 September 2005, the Council applied for a permanent care order for all three children. A comprehensive investigation cited the applicant’s serious lack of parenting ability, noting the children were dirty, had endless appetites, and exhibited developmental delays and trauma. The applicant initially believed her son caused the home’s destruction but later realized her husband, J., was responsible; they subsequently divorced. Despite this, the County Administrative Court granted a permanent care order on 19 October 2005, finding the applicant lacked the ability to care for the children and that there was a serious risk of harm to their health and development. This decision was upheld on appeal in January 2006, and leave to appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court was refused in February 2006.

The central issue arose from the contact restrictions. Following the care order, the applicant had limited, supervised visits with each child. In December 2006, the Social Council, based on an investigation in consultation with BUP, drastically restricted her contact to once every six months (balancing the father's contact rights). The investigation found the children—particularly T. and S.—suffered severe negative reactions (anxiety, bedwetting, stomach pains, fear) before and after contact with the applicant, jeopardizing their positive development in their foster homes. The applicant appealed, arguing for more frequent contact, but the restrictions were upheld by the County Administrative Court in April 2007 and the Administrative Court of Appeal in October 2007.

The restrictions were reviewed every three months. In November 2008, a court slightly increased contact to four times per year, four hours each time. However, upon the Administrative Court of Appeal's request, the children were consulted in early 2009. T. stated she did not want to meet her mother more than twice a year and found meetings exhausting, causing headaches and concentration issues. S. did not want to talk about his mother, showed signs of fear, and wanted to see her only once a year. D. was more positive but did not want to meet alone. A neuropsychological exam in February 2009 revealed the applicant met the criteria for ADHD (mainly inattentive type), though it noted this "could hardly be sufficient to 'disqualify her as a parent'." In May 2009, the Administrative Court of Appeal upheld the lower court's decision, finding increased contact was not in the children's best interests due to the negative reactions of T. and S. The applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights focused on these contact restrictions as a breach of her right to family life under Article 8.
001-111369:
**Summary of the Case of G v. Germany (Application no. 65210/09)**

The case of *G v. Germany* concerns an application lodged against the Federal Republic of Germany with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 December 2009. The applicant, a German national born in 1968, alleged that the order for his retrospective preventive detention and its execution violated Article 7 § 1 of the Convention, which prohibits punishment without law. The applicant's identity was granted anonymity by the Court.

The key facts revolve around the applicant's criminal history. In February 1992, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court convicted the applicant, a first-time offender, of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder, committed between 1988 and 1990. The victims were four young women he did not know, and the crimes were committed treacherously to satisfy his sexual desires. Psychiatric and psychological experts diagnosed him with a sadistic sexual deviation, lack of empathy, and brain damage, concluding he suffered from a serious mental abnormality and acted with diminished criminal responsibility. He was deemed liable to reoffend and dangerous to the public. Consequently, he was sentenced to fifteen years' imprisonment and ordered to be placed in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code, as this was considered a more suitable measure than preventive detention at the time.

In March 1994, after therapy failed, the court ordered him to serve his prison sentence first. He served his full sentence by March 2005 and was transferred back to a psychiatric hospital in April 2006. However, in April 2007, the Kassel Regional Court terminated his psychiatric placement under Article 67d § 6, finding that he had never actually suffered from the condition that diminished his criminal responsibility. On the same day, the court ordered his provisional detention pending a decision on retrospective preventive detention. The applicant had been detained since August 2007.

In March 2008, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court ordered his retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b § 3 of the Criminal Code. The court found that the requirements were met: he had been placed in a psychiatric hospital after committing several murders, and a comprehensive assessment showed it was very likely he would again commit serious offences, causing considerable harm. Experts considered him highly dangerous due to his lack of empathy and refusal to undergo treatment. The applicant appealed, but the Federal Court of Justice dismissed his appeal in September 2008. He then lodged a constitutional complaint, arguing that the retrospective preventive detention breached the prohibition on retrospective punishment and the protection of legitimate expectations.

In August 2009, the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his complaint as ill-founded. It held that preventive detention was not a penalty but a purely preventive measure for public protection, and thus Article 66b § 3 did not violate the ban on retrospective criminal laws or double punishment. It further found that the public interest in protecting society from dangerous offenders outweighed the applicant's legitimate expectations, even though the sentencing court in 1992 had deliberately declined to order preventive detention. The Constitutional Court deemed the measure compatible with the right to liberty, emphasizing the limited disadvantages compared to his prior psychiatric detention.

The applicant remained in preventive detention, with reviews in 2009 and 2011 refusing suspension or termination, as he was still considered dangerous. He also unsuccessfully sought reopening of his proceedings based on the European Court's judgment in *M. v. Germany*. The case before the Court centered on whether this retrospective preventive detention, ordered after his original sentence and psychiatric placement had ended, constituted a violation of Article 7 § 1 of the Convention.
001-114087:
**Case of Andreşan v. Romania (Application no. 25783/03)** concerns allegations that the applicant, Mr Ilie Andreşan, was ill-treated by police while in custody and that the subsequent investigation into his complaint was ineffective.

The applicant, a Romanian national born in 1982, lived in Luduş. On 30 April 2001, his employer, I.N., informally told two police officers, N.D. and C.B., that money had been stolen from his house and that he suspected the applicant. The officers arrested the applicant in the street, handcuffed him in front of other people, and took him to the police station. There, he was allegedly kept handcuffed and beaten continuously to force him to confess to the theft. He signed a confession.

He was then taken, still handcuffed, to his parents’ house, where police searched the premises. They found 1,000,000 Romanian lei, seized it, and handed it directly to I.N. The applicant alleged that during the search the officers continued to beat him in front of his parents and tried to make him reveal where the rest of the money was hidden. When he refused, he was taken back to the police station and beaten again until I.N. took pity on him and asked the officers to release him. I.N. then drove the applicant home and reportedly said that the applicant had been so severely beaten by police that he felt pity for him.

On 2 May 2001, after I.N. lodged an official theft complaint, the applicant was again taken to the police station, where he alleged the abuse continued.

On 8 October 2001, while giving a statement about the theft accusations, the applicant retracted his earlier confessions and accused officers N.D. and C.B. of beating and threatening him on 30 April and 2 May to make him confess. He lodged a complaint for abuse of position and wrongful arrest without legal basis. The complaint was sent to the military prosecutor.

During the investigation, witnesses gave conflicting accounts. Two witnesses knew nothing; one said he saw the applicant being hit and arrested; a neighbour said an officer hit the applicant and pushed him into the car like a “bag of potatoes.” The accused officers and I.N. denied the allegations.

On 12 June 2002, the military prosecutor dismissed the complaint. He noted that the applicant had produced no medical evidence and found it hard to believe that a victim with injuries would not have gone to a forensic doctor. He also noted that the applicant had not complained against the police and that witness statements were contradictory, so it could not be established with certainty whether the officers had done what was alleged.

The applicant challenged the decision. He complained that only four witnesses had been heard, while his parents—key witnesses in front of whom he said he was beaten—were not questioned. He also said he and his lawyer had not been allowed to participate in interviews or question witnesses, and that local authorities had pressured witnesses. His complaint was dismissed by letter on 7 July 2003. A judicial complaint was later heard by the Târgu-Mureş Court of Appeal, which on 10 September 2004 found it ill-founded. The court relied exclusively on statements from the criminal investigation, refused the applicant’s request to re-examine witnesses, and upheld the prosecutor’s decision despite contradictory evidence and lack of medical evidence. On 24 November 2004, the High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed his appeal, reasoning that while the criminal proceedings against the applicant were pending, parallel criminal investigations against the investigators were not possible.

Separately, the applicant was indicted for theft on 5 November 2002 but was acquitted on 1 March 2005. The district court found that the house search and seizure had been unlawful, struck the evidence from the record, and held that on 30 April 2001 the applicant had been subjected to violence and that his confession had been made under duress from the police and I.N. This judgment was upheld on appeal and became final on 18 January 2006.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s alleged violations: ill-treatment in police custody and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation into his credible complaint.
001-111666:
In *Toniolo v. San Marino and Italy*, the applicant, Giuseppe Toniolo, was an Italian national resident in San Marino. In 2009 Italian authorities were prosecuting him, inter alia, for money laundering. On 3 July 2009 the Rome Tribunal ordered his preventive detention. On 10 August 2009 the Rome Prosecutor asked the San Marino authorities to extradite Toniolo and place him in preventive detention, relying on the 1939 Italy–San Marino Convention on Friendship and Good Neighbourhood. The Italian Ministry of Justice was also asked to authorize the extradition request.

On 12 August 2009 the Commissario della Legge (CL) accepted the request and ordered Toniolo’s arrest and preventive detention pending extradition under the 1939 Convention, noting that San Marino had also ratified the 1957 European Convention on Extradition. Toniolo was arrested and notified that day. On 14 August the CL asked the Captains Regent to authorize extradition pending the official Italian request. On 20 August Toniolo and his lawyer were heard, and a request for house arrest was refused. On 26 August Italy’s embassy informed San Marino that San Marino had become party to the 1957 Convention on 16 June 2009 and that Italy would submit its formal extradition request within the Convention’s 40-day period, requesting an extension if necessary.

Toniolo challenged the detention on 24 August, arguing that there were no urgent grounds under the 1939 Convention. On 7 September the appeal judge dismissed this, holding that preventive detention facilitated extradition and that urgency arose from the risk of absconding and San Marino’s geographical situation. The judge nevertheless stated that the applicable law was now the 1957 Convention. He noted that San Marino had made a reservation when ratifying the 1957 Convention that its bilateral agreement would prevail, but Italy had neither made nor acknowledged such a reservation. The same day Toniolo sought release after 30 days under the 1939 Convention. On 11 September the CL rejected this, saying the 1957 Convention prevailed and allowed up to 40 days.

On 18 September Italy submitted the formal extradition request and documents. The CL found the 1957 conditions fulfilled, the Captains Regent authorized extradition under the 1957 Convention, and the CL ordered Toniolo’s extradition. He was extradited on 19 September. He was picked up at 12:50 a.m. and notified of the extradition order ten minutes later, but refused to sign, claiming it should be given to his lawyer. He was transferred to Italian police at 2:45 p.m.; the order was notified to one of his lawyers at 4:15 p.m.

Toniolo brought domestic proceedings challenging both the preventive detention and the extradition. He argued that there was no danger, flight risk or need to protect the community; that the charges were unfounded; that the extradition request had been improperly submitted; and that the authorities had wrongly mixed the 1939 and 1957 Conventions. Because San Marino’s reservation made the 1939 Convention prevail for it while Italy applied the 1957 Convention, he claimed the legal basis was conflicting and unworkable. He also alleged defence-rights breaches: he was not heard before extradition, his lawyers were not notified of or allowed access to him during the extradition, and he was not notified of the relevant authorizations except the 18 September order.

The domestic courts rejected his complaints. The Terza Istanza Penale held that the 1957 Convention governed, that any reliance on the 1939 Convention did not prejudice his liberty, that Toniolo and his lawyers had been properly notified and had access, and that the extradition request was sufficiently justified. It confirmed the detention and extradition orders. Toniolo was released by the Italian courts on 12 February 2010 after statutory detention time-limits expired. Before the European Court of Human Rights, he alleged that his preventive detention and subsequent extradition breached Article 5 § 1 of the Convention.
001-115166:
Tarbuk v. Croatia (Application no. 31360/10) concerned the retroactive removal of a compensation claim for pre-trial detention following a general amnesty. The applicant, Dušan Tarbuk, a Croatian national born in 1956 and living in Zagreb, was arrested on 23 October 1995 and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of espionage connected to Croatia’s Homeland War. He was arrested as part of a group of eighteen persons suspected of the same offence.

On 24 September 1996, Croatia enacted the General Amnesty Act, granting amnesty for criminal offences committed in connection with the war between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996, except for the gravest breaches of humanitarian law, including war crimes and genocide. Pursuant to that Act, criminal proceedings against Tarbuk were discontinued on 7 October 1996, and he was immediately released.

On 9 June 1998, Tarbuk brought a civil action against the State in the Zagreb Municipal Court, seeking damages for his detention. He relied on Article 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provided that anyone who had been in pre-trial detention but against whom criminal proceedings had not been instituted or had been discontinued by a final decision was entitled to compensation.

However, after Tarbuk had lodged his civil claim, the Code of Criminal Procedure was amended. On 2 June 1999, a new Article 484(a) was introduced, providing that no compensation was to be granted in connection with detention where proceedings had been discontinued pursuant to a pardon or amnesty under special laws or decisions. On 27 October 1999, another amendment specified that Article 484(a) applied to criminal offences committed between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996. That amendment therefore directly covered Tarbuk’s situation.

The domestic courts rejected Tarbuk’s compensation claim. On 28 May 2004, the Zagreb Municipal Court dismissed the claim on the ground that it had no legal basis. On 31 January 2006, the Zagreb County Court dismissed his appeal, holding that Article 484(a) had extinguished his compensation claim and that the provision had retroactive effect. On 28 August 2007, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, expressly confirming that Article 484(a) applied retroactively and excluded the application of Article 480.

On 19 November 2007, Tarbuk lodged a constitutional complaint, arguing that the retroactive application of Article 484(a) to his civil action—filed about a year before the provision came into force—had extinguished his right to compensation. On 5 November 2009, the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, endorsing the lower courts’ reasoning.

The alleged violation concerned the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Tarbuk complained that the retroactive application of Article 484(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to his pending civil claim deprived him of a fair hearing and effectively extinguished a claim he had already brought under the law in force at the time. The European Court of Human Rights communicated this fair-trial complaint to the Croatian Government on 5 September 2011 and decided to examine admissibility and merits simultaneously.

Relevant domestic law included Article 25 of the Croatian Constitution, providing a right to compensation for unlawful deprivation of liberty, and Article 29, guaranteeing a fair hearing. The Code of Criminal Procedure contained Article 480, which originally founded Tarbuk’s claim, and Article 484(a), which later barred it. The General Amnesty Act provided the underlying amnesty. In Constitutional Court decision no. U-I-2023/2002 of 7 December 2005, the Constitutional Court had upheld Article 484(a), reasoning that compensation depended on the unlawfulness of detention; amnesty or pardon did not affect the lawfulness of detention, and the legislature could exclude compensation for persons amnestied. The case thus centred on whether the retroactive application of Article 484(a) violated Tarbuk’s fair-trial rights by removing his compensation claim after he had already initiated civil proceedings.
001-115165:
In **Ball v. Andorra** (Application no. 40628/10), the applicant, Mr Toby Nigel Ball, a British national living in Andorra, complained about the Andorran courts’ failure to enforce a final contact schedule allowing him to see his two children. He relied on Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the Convention.

The applicant married in February 2003 and had two children, a son born in 1992 and a daughter born in 2003. He left the family home in March 2004, and the children remained with their mother. In the ensuing legal separation proceedings, the separation judge on 13 June 2005 granted custody to the mother and set up a contact schedule for the applicant. In July 2006, following criminal complaints by the mother, psychological reports and a public prosecutor’s submission, the judge provisionally suspended the contact schedule, allowing only telephone contact.

In December 2006 the mother petitioned for divorce. The applicant sought restoration of contact. On 2 April 2007 the separation judge restored the contact schedule for the daughter and appointed a psychologist to examine the family with a view to restoring contact with the son. The mother appealed. On 19 June 2008 the High Court of Justice partially reversed that decision, striking down the psychologist’s appointment but upholding the restoration of the contact schedule established by the separation judgment. The applicant then applied for enforcement.

However, on 24 July 2008 the separation judge again provisionally suspended the contact schedule, relying on a psychologist’s report that said contact was not desirable pending treatment. On 21 October 2008 the divorce judgment was delivered. It granted custody to the mother and established a contact schedule that remained suspended pending a psychologist’s assessment and possible treatment; the judge relied on reports and the son’s testimony that he did not want contact with his father. The applicant appealed.

On 12 February 2009 the High Court, hearing the appeal against the July 2008 suspension, held that because a divorce judgment had now been delivered, the separation judgment should be set aside and the divorce judgment enforced. It deprived the July 2008 decision of effect. The applicant asked for clarification, specifically whether the 19 June 2008 decision in the separation proceedings should be enforced while the divorce judgment was not yet final or enforceable. On 23 April 2009 the High Court refused clarification, stating that during a suspensive appeal against the divorce judgment, neither that judgment nor previous decisions adopted in separation proceedings were enforceable. Thus, despite the earlier final contact decision, no contact schedule could be enforced during the pending divorce appeal.

The applicant’s subsequent appeal for annulment was dismissed on 28 May 2009. He then lodged a constitutional appeal, arguing that the impossibility of enforcing the final 19 June 2008 decision while the divorce appeal was pending denied him a fair hearing and violated his right to meaningful contact with his children. On 12 October 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible as devoid of constitutional content, finding the High Court’s decisions neither arbitrary nor illogical. A final appeal was dismissed on 21 December 2009.

The key alleged violation was therefore that the domestic courts’ procedural handling created a prolonged deadlock: the applicant had a final contact decision in his favour, but it became unenforceable due to the pending divorce proceedings and suspensive appeal, preventing him from maintaining meaningful contact with his children. The case was communicated to the Andorran Government in April 2011, and the United Kingdom waived its right to intervene.
001-108599:
**Summary of Harkins and Edwards v. the United Kingdom (Applications nos. 9146/07 and 32650/07)**

The case of Harkins and Edwards v. the United Kingdom concerns two separate applications brought against the United Kingdom before the European Court of Human Rights. Both applicants faced extradition to the United States and alleged that, if extradited, they would be at risk of sentences incompatible with Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Specifically, they argued that the death penalty or life imprisonment without parole (LWOP) would violate this provision.

The first applicant, Phillip Harkins, a British national born in 1978, was sought by the United States for a murder committed in Jacksonville, Florida, in August 1999. Harkins was indicted for first-degree murder and attempted robbery with a firearm. The prosecution initially filed a notice to seek the death penalty, but this was later withdrawn. The case against him relied heavily on the testimony of a co-accused, Terry Glover, who claimed Harkins shot the victim during a robbery. Harkins maintained that the shooting was accidental and denied being present. Under Florida’s felony murder rule, a defendant can be convicted of murder without premeditation if a death occurs during a serious felony such as armed robbery. The maximum penalty for first-degree murder in Florida is life imprisonment without parole.

Harkins was arrested in the United Kingdom in 2003. The United States requested his extradition, and in 2005, the US Embassy provided a diplomatic note assuring that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed. The Secretary of State ordered his surrender in 2006. Harkins challenged this decision, arguing that the assurance was inadequate and that he could still face the death penalty or an irreducible life sentence. The High Court rejected his claim in 2007, finding no real risk of the death penalty and that any life sentence would not be grossly disproportionate given the seriousness of the alleged offence. Further representations were refused in 2010, and judicial review was dismissed in 2011.

The second applicant, Joshua Daniel Edwards, a United States national born in 1987, was sought by the United States for charges arising from a 2006 incident in Maryland. He was indicted on eleven counts, including first-degree murder, attempted murder, and assault. The allegations were that Edwards, after being mocked, left an apartment and returned with others, producing a handgun and firing shots that killed one man and wounded another. The prosecution indicated it would not seek the death penalty but might seek life imprisonment without parole. Diplomatic notes assured that the death penalty would not be sought or carried out.

Edwards was arrested in the UK in 2007, and the Secretary of State ordered his extradition. He appealed, arguing that a sentence of life imprisonment without parole would violate Article 3. The High Court dismissed his appeal, relying on existing domestic precedent. Both applicants lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights, which applied interim measures under Rule 39 to prevent their extradition pending the Court’s decision.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations centre on whether the potential sentences—death penalty or life imprisonment without parole—would breach Article 3. For Harkins, the risk of an irreducible life sentence under Florida’s felony murder rule was central, along with the adequacy of diplomatic assurances. For Edwards, the possibility of a discretionary life without parole sentence in Maryland was the focus. Both cases raised questions about the compatibility of harsh sentencing regimes with the Convention’s prohibition on inhuman or degrading treatment in the context of extradition.
001-114658:
In *Sýkora v. the Czech Republic*, Milan Sýkora, a Czech national with a psycho-social disability, alleged that his rights to liberty and private life were violated by the removal of his legal capacity and his subsequent involuntary detention in a psychiatric hospital. He had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and had received psychiatric treatment in the past, but had not taken medication for years because he believed it damaged his eyesight.

The legal-capacity proceedings began in 2000, when the Brno Municipal Court deprived him of legal capacity at the request of the City of Brno. The court relied on a 1998 expert report by Dr H., which stated that the applicant suffered from paranoid schizophrenia. Although the applicant was aware of the proceedings, he was not summoned to appear, the judgment was not served on him, and he was formally represented by a court employee who had never met him and did not participate substantively. That decision became final in December 2000. After the applicant appealed, the Regional Court quashed it in August 2001 and remitted the case. In 2004, the Municipal Court again deprived him of legal capacity, relying on a new report by Dr H. prepared without examining him because he refused medical examinations. The court again did not hear him, did not serve the judgment on him, and appointed the City of Brno as guardian. The judgment became final in January 2005. The applicant learned of it only in June 2006 and appealed. The Regional Court quashed the decision in October 2006. In 2007, the Municipal Court finally decided not to deprive him of legal capacity. In total, he was deprived of legal capacity for about two and a half years.

In separate proceedings, the applicant sought damages from the State for procedural violations. The Ministry of Justice awarded him compensation for the unreasonable length of proceedings and accepted that the judgments had not been served on him, but said that a finding of violation was sufficient satisfaction. His damages action was rejected by the ordinary courts and, in 2012, the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal.

The involuntary detention occurred in November 2005. Following a verbal argument with his partner, the police and an ambulance were called. Although the police found no violence and his partner said he had not been aggressive, an ambulance doctor took him to the Brno-Černovice Psychiatric Hospital. The applicant disagreed but did not resist. On admission, two examinations concluded that he suffered from schizophrenia. He insisted there was no reason for detention. Despite warning that neuroleptic medication harmed his eyesight, he was ordered to take it and, when he refused, it was administered by injection; his eyesight allegedly deteriorated.

The hospital notified the Municipal Court of his involuntary admission, but also contacted his guardian, the City of Brno, which consented to the detention on 14 November 2005. The employee who signed the consent had never met the applicant and did not inform him. A lawyer from the Mental Disability Advocacy Center challenged the detention and requested release. The applicant was released on 29 November 2005. However, no court ever reviewed the lawfulness of his detention. After release, he was told that no review proceedings had been instituted because his guardian had consented. Later complaints and constitutional appeals were dismissed, partly because he was no longer detained and partly because the guardian’s consent was considered sufficient.

The alleged violations therefore concerned Article 5 (unlawful detention and lack of judicial review), Article 8 (private life and autonomy, including forced medication and incapacitation), and related fair-hearing and effective-remedy issues.
001-113819:
**Harroudj v. France (Application no. 43631/09)**

The applicant, Ms Katya Harroudj, is a French national born in 1962 who lives in Villeurbanne, France. The case concerns her inability to adopt a child placed in her legal care under the Algerian institution of *kafala*.

Zina Hind was born in Algeria on 3 November 2003 and was abandoned at birth by her anonymous mother. As her father was also unknown, she became a ward of the Algerian State, with the director of social services in Boumerdès appointed as her guardian.

On 13 January 2004, the President of the court of Boumerdès granted the applicant—then aged 42 and unmarried—the right to take the child into her legal care (*kafala*), and authorised the child to leave Algeria and settle in France. A subsequent Algerian court decision authorised the child's name change to Hind Harroudj. The child arrived in France on 1 February 2004 and has since lived with the applicant and the applicant's mother.

On 8 November 2006, the applicant applied for full adoption of Hind. She argued that adoption was the solution most consistent with the child's best interests under Article 3 § 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child and Article 1 of the Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption.

On 21 March 2007, the Lyons *tribunal de grande instance* dismissed her application. It noted that *kafala* already gave her parental authority and that, under Article 370-3 of the French Civil Code, a child could not be adopted where the law of his or her country prohibited adoption—which Algerian law did, as Article 46 of the Algerian Family Code states that "adoption is prohibited by the Sharia and by legislation."

The Lyons Court of Appeal upheld this judgment on 23 October 2007. It reasoned that the choice-of-law rule referring to the child's personal law was non-discriminatory and compliant with Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and with international law. It noted that Article 4(a) of the Hague Convention requires the State of origin to establish that the child is adoptable, which was not the case since Algeria prohibits adoption.
