The court distinguished *kafala* from adoption, observing that *kafala* preserves the child's interests by conferring legal status on the care provided by guardians and is expressly recognised by Article 20 § 3 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. It also noted that Islamic law makes other provision for inheritance.

The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. She submitted that it was in the child's interest for a legal parent-child relationship to be established between them, and that her inability to adopt entailed a disproportionate interference with her family life. She further argued that denying her the right to adopt established a difference in treatment regarding the child's family life on account of the child's nationality and country of origin, as children born in countries that do not prohibit adoption could be adopted in France.

On 25 February 2009, the Court of Cassation dismissed her appeal. It found that the Court of Appeal had not established any difference in treatment or disregarded the right to respect for family life, holding that *kafala*—expressly recognised by Article 20 § 3 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child—preserves the child's best interests on a par with adoption.
001-115210:
In the European Court of Human Rights case *Milić v. Montenegro and Serbia* (Application no. 28359/05, judgment 11 December 2012), the applicant, Ivan Milić, a Serbian national born in 1966 and living in Belgrade, complained that a final domestic judgment ordering his reinstatement was not enforced and that no effective domestic remedy existed for this non-enforcement. He lodged the application on 19 July 2005 against Montenegro and Serbia. The case was communicated to both Governments on 15 March 2010, and the Court decided to examine admissibility and merits together.

The central facts concerned his employment with the Clinical Centre of Montenegro, a State-run medical institution. On 20 June 2002 the Court of First Instance in Podgorica ordered the Clinical Centre to reinstate him. That judgment became final on 4 February 2003 and was confirmed by the Supreme Court at third instance on 16 December 2003. Despite this, on 23 April 2003 the Clinical Centre informed the applicant that it could not comply and would seek an alternative solution. On 22 May 2003 the Court of First Instance issued an enforcement order, confirmed on 26 June 2003, but reinstatement at the Clinical Centre did not occur.

Instead, on 19 August 2003 the Clinical Centre concluded an agreement with the Special Hospital in Risan, another State-run medical institution, under which the latter accepted the applicant as its employee. On 30 September 2003 the applicant told the State Prosecutor that he did not approve of this arrangement. On 17 October 2003 the Special Hospital in Risan issued a decision making him its employee as of 30 October 2003, which he received on 20 October 2003. This effectively transferred him to a different employer without his consent, although domestic labour law required an employee’s consent for transfer to another employer.

Separately, on 6 May 2004, on the applicant’s claim, the Court of First Instance ordered the Clinical Centre to pay him EUR 4,456 in salary arrears for September 2001 to 3 February 2003. This judgment was upheld on 5 October 2004 and apparently later enforced. The applicant also began working at the Clinical Centre of Serbia on 3 February 2003, initially for nine months, later on a permanent basis.

In 2009, the Montenegrin Government stated that on 21 October 2009 the applicant concluded an Agreement on Termination of Employment with the Clinical Centre of Montenegro, terminating his employment as from 3 February 2003 and waiving all further claims. On 26 October 2009 he withdrew his enforcement request. On 5 November 2009 the Court of First Instance terminated the enforcement proceedings and all related enforcement activities; that decision became final on 17 November 2009.

Relevant domestic law included the 2007 Montenegrin Constitution and 2008 Constitutional Court Act, which permitted a constitutional appeal after exhaustion of effective remedies; the 2007 Right to a Trial within a Reasonable Time Act, providing a request for review and fair-redress compensation; the Enforcement Procedure Acts of 2000 and 2004; and Labour Acts of 2003 and 2008 requiring consent for transfer. The alleged violations therefore focused on the State’s failure to enforce the final reinstatement judgment, the forced transfer to another State institution, and the absence of an effective remedy for the prolonged non-enforcement.
001-114273:
**Summary of PETA Deutschland v. Germany (Application no. 43481/09)**

The case of *PETA Deutschland v. Germany* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by PETA Deutschland, the German branch of the animal rights organisation People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals. The applicant association complained that German court injunctions prohibiting its planned advertising campaign violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The facts concerned a campaign planned by PETA in March 2004 under the heading "The Holocaust on your plate." The campaign, which had already been conducted in the United States, consisted of a series of posters. Each poster juxtaposed a photograph of Holocaust victims with a photograph of animals kept in mass livestock farming conditions, accompanied by short captions. One poster showed emaciated, naked concentration camp inmates alongside starving cattle under the heading "walking skeletons." Another displayed piled-up human corpses next to a pile of slaughtered pigs under the heading "final humiliation." A further poster showed rows of inmates lying on wooden bunks alongside rows of chickens in laying batteries, with the heading "if animals are concerned, everybody becomes a Nazi." A final poster depicted a starving, naked male inmate alongside starving cattle, bearing the title "The Holocaust on your plate" and the text stating that twelve million humans were killed in the Holocaust between 1938 and 1945, while as many animals are killed every hour in Europe for human consumption.

In March 2004, three individuals—P.S., C.K., and S. Korn—filed a request with the Berlin Regional Court for an injunction to prevent PETA from publishing seven specified posters via the internet, in public exhibitions, or in any other form. The plaintiffs were, at the time, the president and two vice-presidents of the Central Jewish Council in Germany. All had survived the Holocaust as children, and C.K. had lost her family in the Holocaust. They argued that the campaign was offensive, violated their human dignity, and infringed the personality rights of C.K.'s deceased family members.

The Berlin Regional Court granted the injunction on 18 March 2004, a decision confirmed on 22 April 2004. The court held that the plaintiffs had a valid claim under sections 823 and 1004 of the German Civil Code, in conjunction with section 185 of the Criminal Code and Articles 1 and 2 of the German Basic Law. It found that while the posters constituted protected expressions of opinion, they placed the fate of Holocaust victims on the same level as that of animals. Although the campaign's primary aim appeared to be criticism of animal farming conditions rather than debasement of Holocaust victims, this comparison was considered arbitrary given the Basic Law's central emphasis on human dignity. The court concluded that the expression violated the plaintiffs' human dignity as Holocaust victims, particularly by depicting them in a most vulnerable state.

The Berlin Court of Appeal rejected PETA's appeals on 27 August 2004 and 25 November 2005. In the main proceedings on 2 December 2004, the Regional Court confirmed its injunction. On 20 February 2009, the Federal Constitutional Court rejected PETA's constitutional complaint. While expressing doubts about whether the campaign actually violated human dignity, it found the injunction justified without relying on such a violation. The court accepted that the Basic Law distinguishes human life and dignity from animal protection interests, and that the campaign trivialised the fate of Holocaust victims, thereby affecting the plaintiffs' personality rights. It noted that the self-image of Jews in Germany includes belonging to a group singled out by fate, owing a special moral obligation from others, forming part of their dignity.

Consequently, PETA Deutschland brought its case to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging a violation of its freedom of expression.
001-113137:
**Falter Zeitschriften GmbH v. Austria (No. 2)** concerned an Article 10 complaint by the publisher of the Vienna weekly *Falter* after Austrian courts ordered it to pay damages under the Media Act for defamation of a judge.

The case arose from criminal proceedings against H.P., a security officer at the Traiskirchen Reception Centre, who was accused of raping K., a Cameroonian asylum seeker. In May 2005 the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court acquitted H.P. on the principle of *in dubio pro reo*. The written judgment included a passage noting K.’s alleged prior prostitution in her country of origin, which the court said allowed an inference that she might have become involved with the accused to gain some advantage.

In issue 19/05, *Falter* published an article titled “‘Sex with a nigger woman’” about the case. The article described K.’s background, her asylum claim, her rape complaint, and the investigation and trial. It strongly criticised the proceedings, reporting that police had called K. “the nigger woman,” that she was repeatedly linked to prostitution, and that the accused gave shifting accounts. It also referred to the Court of Appeal’s earlier finding that rape and coercion appeared made out and its order that H.P. be prosecuted. The article criticised Judge I.K., who presided over the acquittal, claiming that she had alleged K. had immoral motives, attributed “the basest intentions” to her without proof, ignored relevant evidence, and delivered a scandalous judgment. It contrasted the acquittal reasoning with the Court of Appeal’s assessment and accused the trial court of failing to address evidence such as the torn red underpants and the fact that the accused admitted locking the room and removing the key.

Judge I.K. brought defamation proceedings under section 6 of the Media Act and Article 111 of the Criminal Code. She claimed the article stated that she had grossly misused her office and sought compensation and retraction. The applicant argued that the statements were true and that the article was protected criticism, focused not on the acquittal itself but on the treatment of the victim and the judgment’s reasoning. It sought to prove truth through witnesses and case files, and unsuccessfully sought the assigned judge’s disqualification because the claimant’s lawyer had previously represented that judge.

The Vienna Regional Court found for Judge I.K. It held that the article gave a biased account, sided with K., and treated contrary evidence as incredible. The applicant had not proved the truth of the impugned statements. The court found that the criminal judgment had assessed the evidence extensively, that the prostitution reference had some basis in the file, and that it could not be established that the judge made base insinuations or disregarded evidence. The accusation that a judge had acted without factual basis and from racist motives deliberately to acquit an accused was a severe defamation. The “scandal” value judgment was based on factual assertions that had been disproved. Applying *Prager and Oberschlick v. Austria*, the court accepted that the press could criticise the justice system but held that this attack exceeded permissible limits and endangered public confidence in the judiciary. It ordered EUR 7,000 compensation plus publication of a summary. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

The applicant company complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Media Act judgment ordering it to pay damages infringed its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.
001-114473:
The applicants, Mr and Mrs Van Colle, are British nationals. Their son, Giles Van Colle, an optometrist born in 1975, was murdered on 22 November 2000 by Daniel Brougham. Brougham had worked for Giles under the alias Lee Jordan, concealing a criminal record. After a dispute over equipment and unpaid repairs, Brougham left in December 1999.

In February 2000 police arrested Brougham on suspicion of theft from “Southern Counties” and found optical equipment; Giles later identified some as his. On 23 April 2000 Brougham was charged with theft and obtaining property by deception concerning Giles, Southern Counties and Alpha Optical, and was bailed unconditionally.

During 2000 Brougham attempted to deter witnesses. In summer he offered Mr H £1,000 not to give evidence; this was not reported until after the murder. On 10 August he offered Mr P £650 for Alpha Optical material. On 13 October he telephoned Mr P and offered a bribe, which Mr P reported to DC Ridley. On the same day Brougham telephoned Giles and threatened that he knew where Giles lived, where his businesses were and where his parents lived, and that if Giles did not drop the charges he would be in danger. Giles reported this to DC Ridley between 16 and 18 October. On 19 October DC Ridley took statements from Giles and Mr P and sent them to the CPS.

On 28 and 29 October fires occurred at Mr P’s wife’s car and at Mr P’s business premises. They were initially considered possibly accidental; later, during the murder investigation, experts found they had been started deliberately. On 5 November DC Ridley was seconded to an unconnected murder investigation. On 9 November the CPS served additional evidence including the 19 October statements. That day Brougham telephoned Giles again, using aggressive language and telling him to get Alpha Optical to drop the charges. Giles left a message for DC Ridley and later provided a written account sent on 20 November. On 22 November DC Ridley arranged to take a statement the next day and intended to arrest Brougham for witness intimidation. That evening Brougham shot Giles dead. Brougham was convicted of murder in March 2002.

In domestic disciplinary proceedings, on 12 June 2003 a Police Disciplinary Panel found DC Ridley guilty of failing to perform his duties conscientiously and diligently regarding the intimidation of Giles and Mr P. It found an escalating situation of intimidation and that DC Ridley failed thoroughly to investigate, analyse links between events, or consider arrest. He was fined five days’ pay.

The applicants, the first as administrator of Giles’s estate, brought a claim against the Chief Constable of Hertfordshire under the Human Rights Act 1998, seeking damages for breaches of Articles 2 and 8. The Chief Constable accepted the Panel’s findings and that DC Ridley gave inadequate consideration to responses to the threats, but argued that the criticisms were made with hindsight, that Brougham’s drastic act could not reasonably have been predicted, and that the errors were not sufficiently exceptional to be unlawful.

On 10 March 2006 the High Court found violations of Articles 2 and 8 and awarded damages. On 24 April 2007 the Court of Appeal dismissed the Chief Constable’s appeal, upholding findings that DC Ridley should have recognised a real and immediate risk and taken protective steps. On 30 July 2008 the House of Lords allowed the Chief Constable’s appeal, holding that the domestic courts had misdirected themselves and that the relevant risk test had not been met.

The applicants lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 28 January 2009, complaining under Articles 2 and 8 that the police failed to protect their son’s life from Brougham, a criminal accused in proceedings in which Giles was a witness.
001-111628:
In *Malkhasyan v. Armenia*, the applicant, an Armenian national, was prosecuted under Article 301 of the Criminal Code for public calls aimed at violently overthrowing the government. On 2 December 2006 he spoke at an assembly organised by the NGO “Unity of Armenian Volunteers” before about 150 people. He allegedly called the authorities “bandits” and “internal enemies” and called for armed struggle and rebellion. On 8 December the National Security Service opened criminal proceedings. After a search of his flat on 9 December, he was questioned as a suspect on 10 December and allegedly admitted making the statements. An arrest record was drawn up at 2:30 p.m. that day, and his passport was seized. On 12 December he was formally charged. He claimed the remarks were made while intoxicated and irritated and that he had not intended to incite rebellion.

On 12 December the investigator sought a two-month detention order, arguing that the applicant might abscond or unlawfully pressure persons involved in the case. The District Court granted detention, finding a risk that he would obstruct the investigation. Appeals and bail applications were dismissed, with courts relying on the seriousness of the charge and on the fact that a co-accused was also suspected of illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Detention was later extended on 7 February and 5 April 2007, each time for two months. The applicant objected that there was no evidence for the alleged risks, that his passport had been seized, that he had family and property in Armenia, and that the authorities already possessed a recording of his speech. At the 7 February extension hearing, his lawyer asked that the applicant be present; the court refused, saying no prior request had been made and that detainee presence was not required by law. On appeal, the Court of Appeal admitted that the time limits under Article 139 § 1 of the Criminal Procedure Code had not been observed by the investigator and District Court, but held this was not serious enough to affect the outcome. The applicant also argued that detention should run from 9 December, when he was actually deprived of liberty, not from the 10 December arrest record.

On 3 April 2007 the applicant was registered as a parliamentary candidate. He argued that continuing detention without the Central Election Committee’s consent violated Article 111 § 6 of the Electoral Code and prevented him from campaigning equally. The Court of Appeal rejected this, distinguishing imposition of detention from its extension and finding the grounds valid.

The key alleged violation concerns 10–22 June 2007. The detention period authorised on 5 April expired on 10 June. On 13 June the applicant asked the detention facility to release him because the order had expired. On 19 June the facility refused, stating that the case had been transmitted to the District Court. On 22 June the trial judge set the case down for trial and stated that the preventive measure would remain unchanged. Thus, the applicant remained detained for twelve days after the expiry of the last court-authorised detention period before any new reasoned detention decision. He complained to the European Court that this detention was unlawful and that the domestic courts failed to provide adequate reasons for his continued detention. He was later convicted and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment.
001-110812:
**Case: Madah and Others v. Bulgaria** (Application no. 45237/08), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 10 May 2012.

The applicants were Mohammad Rasoul Madah, an Iranian national, his Bulgarian partner Maria Kerkenezova, and their son Daniel Mohammad Rasoul Madah, a Bulgarian national born in 2006. The first applicant had visited Bulgaria since the 1990s, obtained a temporary residence permit in 1992 based on business activity, and was granted permanent residence in 2001. In 2004 he met the second applicant, and from early 2005 they lived together. Their son was born in April 2006 after a complicated pregnancy and suffered from fragile health, with frequent pulmonary disease.

On 27 December 2005, the head of the National Security Service ordered the first applicant’s expulsion, finding that he posed a threat to national security. The order deprived him of his residence right and banned him from entering Bulgaria for ten years. It gave no factual grounds and relied on a classified internal document dated 15 December 2005, which was not served on him, although he was later able to consult it during court proceedings. That document alleged that he was involved in drug trafficking to finance the militant Kurdish separatist group Kongra-Gel, the former PKK. The expulsion order stated that he should be detained pending expulsion, was immediately enforceable, and could be appealed to the Minister of Internal Affairs but was not subject to judicial review.

On 21 February 2006 the first applicant was served with the expulsion order. On the same day, the Migration Directorate ordered his detention pending expulsion. He was arrested and held in Sofia, then transferred in July 2006 to a special detention facility outside the city. He was released on 28 October 2006. After release, he was reportedly interviewed at the Iranian embassy about alleged connections with a Kurdish separatist organisation.

The first applicant challenged the expulsion order before the Sofia City Court on 9 March 2006, arguing that it was unlawful and referring to his difficult family situation, including the second applicant’s complicated pregnancy. He also appealed to the Minister of Internal Affairs, but that appeal was returned as out of time and because court proceedings were pending. In court, he submitted a certificate from the National Investigation Service stating that no criminal proceedings were pending against him. He denied involvement in the alleged activities and invoked his family situation, the Convention, and the case of *Al-Nashif v. Bulgaria*. The National Security Service submitted a copy of the internal document. The court did not order the head of the National Security Service to produce further information or evidence about the reasons for expulsion. On 26 July 2007, the Sofia City Court dismissed his appeal, treating the internal document as an official certification that he was a threat to national security and as binding on the court. On appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that judgment by a final decision of 28 May 2008. It found the deportation lawful and justified by the internal document, held that it did not violate the Convention because the applicant could challenge it before a court, and accepted that the executive had rightly found him to be a threat based on information about drug trafficking and terrorist financing. It did not examine the evidence allegedly supporting that assessment.

The first applicant also challenged his detention. On 16 October 2006, the Sofia City Court suspended execution of the detention order, finding that the authorities had failed to prove the measure’s necessity and noting the eight-month duration and his family situation. He was released on 28 October 2006. In a final judgment of 23 February 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court discontinued the proceedings without ruling on the merits, holding that the detention order was subordinate to the expulsion order and was not independently subject to judicial review.

The applicants alleged that the first applicant’s proposed expulsion to Iran would expose him to a risk of ill-treatment, contrary to Article 3; that it would unlawfully and disproportionately interfere with their family life, contrary to Article 8; and that they lacked effective remedies, contrary to Article 13. The key facts relevant to those allegations included the reliance on secret national-security evidence, lack of meaningful disclosure, inability to effectively challenge the threat assessment, lengthy detention pending expulsion, and the first applicant’s family ties in Bulgaria, including a Bulgarian partner and a young child with health problems.
001-111394:
**Summary of the Case of Genderdoc-M v. Moldova**

The case of *Genderdoc-M v. Moldova* (Application no. 9106/06) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 March 2006 by Genderdoc-M, a Moldovan non-governmental organisation advocating for the LGBT community. The applicant alleged a violation of their rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically concerning the freedom of peaceful assembly.

The key facts revolve around the applicant’s attempt to hold a peaceful demonstration. On 7 April 2005, Genderdoc-M applied to the Chişinău Municipal Council for authorisation to hold a demonstration in front of the Parliament on 27 May 2005. The stated purpose was to encourage the adoption of laws protecting sexual minorities from discrimination.

The application was rejected. On 27 April 2005, the Municipal Council refused it, claiming the demonstration was baseless since a law on the protection of national minorities was already in place. On 6 May 2005, the Mayor’s Office also refused permission, reiterating the previous reason and adding that legal provisions dictated who had the power of legislative initiative.

Genderdoc-M contested the Mayor’s Office decision, arguing it was illegal and discriminatory. On 2 June 2005, the Chişinău Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicant, declaring the Mayor’s Office decision void. The court found the refusal’s justification legally ungrounded, stating that the law did not permit such reasons for banning an assembly. The court held that authorisation should not be conditional on the nature of the problems the assembly intended to address. The Mayor’s Office subsequently appealed this decision.

On 7 September 2005, the Supreme Court of Justice allowed the appeal, quashed the Court of Appeal’s decision, and remitted the case for re-examination. In the new proceedings, the Mayor’s Office shifted its justification, arguing that the assembly for promoting sexual minority rights would endanger public order and social morality. They also claimed the organisers had not assumed responsibility for the demonstration's management. Genderdoc-M again argued the ban was illegal and discriminatory.

On 14 June 2006, the Court of Appeal found against the applicant. This decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of Justice on 18 October 2006. The Supreme Court justified its ruling on two main grounds. First, it found that Genderdoc-M had failed to provide undertakings for various obligations required by domestic law on assemblies, such as designating responsible persons, creating a group with police to maintain order, and establishing a route. Second, the court considered there was a risk that the demonstration would breach public order.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that the refusal to authorise the demonstration violated Article 11 (freedom of assembly and association) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention. The central issue was whether the domestic authorities' interference with the right to peaceful assembly was justified. The case file highlights the shifting official justifications for the ban—from legally flawed reasoning about existing legislation to concerns over public order and alleged procedural shortcomings by the organisers—which formed the basis of the alleged violation of the right to peaceful protest.
001-113806:
In *Hartman v. Slovenia* (Application no. 42236/05), the applicant, Andrej Hartman, a Slovenian national, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 November 2005. He complained under Article 6 § 1 that the criminal proceedings against him were excessively long, and in substance under Article 13 that no effective domestic remedy existed for that delay. The application was communicated to the Government on 8 September 2009.

The criminal proceedings began on 14 November 1997, when the Ministry of the Interior’s Kranj Criminal Police Unit issued a detention decision and the applicant was arrested. On 16 November 1997 he was brought before an investigating judge and remanded in custody. The prosecutor requested a criminal investigation against him and six others on 17 November 1997; the investigation opened on 27 November 1997. On 11 May 1998 an indictment was lodged. The applicant was charged with six offences involving unlawful manufacture of and trade in heroin. The case concerned an organised drug-trafficking network, with six co-accused facing about twenty related offences.

The first hearing before the Kranj District Court took place on 6 October 1998. Between then and 15 March 2000, the court held sixty-nine hearings, heard forty-eight witnesses, inspected video cassettes, secret surveillance reports, wiretaps, and documents from Spain, the United Kingdom, Hungary, Austria, Bulgaria, and Romania. The applicant was placed under house arrest on 30 December 1999. On 15 March 2000 the District Court convicted him and sentenced him to fifteen years’ imprisonment; the judgment was served on 11 April 2000.

The applicant appealed on 21 April 2000. On 30 November 2000 the Ljubljana Higher Court mainly upheld the conviction, remitted part of the case for re-examination, and reduced the sentence to fourteen years. After the applicant fled while under house arrest, an arrest warrant was issued on 3 December 2000. The second-instance judgment was served on his attorney on 3 January 2001. On 31 March 2001, counsel filed a request for protection of legality with the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court received the file on 25 May 2001 but rejected the request only on 21 December 2004, served on 7 January 2005.

Meanwhile, on 5 June 2002 the District Court terminated the remitted part of the proceedings after the indictment was withdrawn. The applicant also sought reopening; that request was rejected on procedural grounds on 5 August 2004, and the appeal was rejected on 3 August 2005. Having returned to Slovenia, he was taken to Dob pri Mirni Prison on 10 December 2002 to serve his sentence.

On 1 March 2005 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. The Constitutional Court rejected it as unfounded on 5 May 2006, served on 11 May 2006. On 17 November 2006 he requested extraordinary mitigation of sentence; on 21 June 2007 the Supreme Court reduced the sentence to thirteen years and eight months. Further reopening requests followed: counsel filed one on 13 December 2007, and the applicant’s own request was received on 26 February 2008. These were rejected on 16 September 2008; on appeal, the Higher Court remitted the case on 12 March 2009, but the District Court rejected the request again on procedural grounds on 16 July 2009. An appeal remained pending before the appeal court as of 13 October 2009.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern proceedings running from November 1997 through at least October 2009, including lengthy periods before the Supreme Court and Constitutional Court, and the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy for the excessive length.
001-110810:
**Case:** *Kotsev and Ermenkova v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 33864/03), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 10 May 2012.

The applicants were two Bulgarian nationals, Mr Valentin Konstantinov Kotsev and Ms Yarmila Anguelova Ermenkova. They lodged their application on 13 October 2003. Mr Kotsev died on 20 November 2005; his widow and minor son later expressed a wish to continue the proceedings on his behalf.

The applicants and the parents of a Mr B.I. were co-owners of a building and plot of land in Sofia. In 1992 B.I.’s parents sold him one quarter of the property. In 1993 B.I. began constructing an adjoining building. Between 1996 and 2005 the authorities five times ordered that the construction be halted or the building demolished. B.I. challenged all these orders by way of judicial review. Two sets of judicial-review proceedings, in which the applicants joined as interested parties, formed the background to the alleged violations.

**The 1996 proceedings:** On 21 March 1996 the mayor ordered demolition of the building erected by B.I., finding it could not be legalised. In April 1996 B.I. sought judicial review before the Sofia City Court. In March 1999 the court allowed the applicants, as well as B.I.’s wife and brother, to join the proceedings. At least fifteen hearings were held between 8 June 1999 and 26 October 2007, at intervals of four to eight months. Five hearings failed because various parties had not been duly summoned. At least six hearings between January 2005 and October 2007 were adjourned because a newly added party living in Toronto, Canada, had to be summoned by letter rogatory. The Sofia City Court rendered judgment in 2010; according to the applicants’ latest correspondence in October 2010, the case was then pending before the second-instance court.

**The 1999 proceedings:** On 16 June 1999, after being alerted by the applicants, the building control authorities ordered B.I. to pull down the building. On 13 July 1999 B.I. and his wife sought judicial review. At the first hearing on 26 November 1999 the applicants intervened as interested parties. Some twenty hearings were held until February 2006, scheduled at intervals of two to nine months. At least four hearings were adjourned because parties had not been properly summoned, including B.I.’s brother in Canada. After the brother’s death in 2002, at least six hearings were adjourned because his widow, also in Canada, could not be summoned by letter rogatory. As of October 2010 the proceedings were still pending before the Sofia City Court.

**Domestic complaints about delay:** On 23 November 2000, 18 December 2002, and again in 2007, the applicants complained to the Sofia City Court and the Supreme Judicial Council about the slow progress of the proceedings. In 2007 the Ministry of Justice replied that there were no delays attributable to the authorities. However, in 2002 the Ministry of Justice informed the local authorities that an inspection by a representative of the Supreme Judicial Council’s Inspectorate had established that a delay had occurred, caused by B.I.’s abuse of process and the high case-load of the Sofia City Court. The Inspectorate had written to the Chairman of the Sofia City Court about the delays.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore concern the prolonged duration of two sets of judicial-review proceedings, repeated adjournments due to summoning problems—especially of parties or relatives abroad—and the applicants’ unsuccessful domestic complaints about delay. The relevant domestic law on “complaints about delays” was summarised in *Finger v. Bulgaria* (no. 37346/05, § 43, 10 May 2011).
001-110249:
# Summary of Jirsák v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 8968/08)

**Parties and Allegation**

Mr Zdeněk Jirsák, a Czech national born in 1953, lodged an application against the Czech Republic on 13 February 2008, alleging that the conditions of his detention in Valdice Prison were inhuman and degrading, in violation of Article 3 of the Convention. He was represented by Mr W. Firla; the Government by Mr Vít A. Schorm.

**Detention Conditions**

The applicant served his sentence in Sections C and D of Valdice Prison between 2000 and 2005. Between 10 November 2000 and 29 January 2001, he shared cell no. 223—measuring 35.816 sq. m. including a separate toilet—with nine other prisoners, yielding roughly 3.58 sq. m. of living space per inmate. The cell had bunk beds along both long walls, two windows (each 1.44 sq. m., partially openable) covered externally with yellow translucent fibreglass, ten lockers, two tables, and ten chairs. The applicant worked nine hours each working day in the prison laundry, had one hour of daily outdoor exercise, could shower twice weekly, received one warm meal daily (plus two hot meals four times weekly), and had access to cultural activities, sports, books, and newspapers.

**The Injury and Medical Treatment**

On 28 January 2001 at 7:30 p.m., the applicant broke his ankle while climbing down from his bunk bed, which he attributed to dizziness caused by stuffy air. He did not immediately seek help, taking Ibuprofen instead. The next morning, unable to walk, he was taken to the infirmary. The prison doctor visually examined him, deemed him heavily intoxicated with medicaments without testing, declined an x-ray because the operator was on holiday, and sent him to solitary confinement rather than a hospital. On 30 January he was finally x-rayed, his fracture confirmed, and he was transferred to Prague Prison Hospital, where he was operated on 31 January 2001. Treatment lasted seven months, and he later developed arthritis.

**Disciplinary and Employment Consequences**

On 26 March 2001 the applicant was found guilty of self-intoxication, receiving five days under the closed regime (he did not appeal), and was dismissed from his prison job for absence due to intoxication. He also was not paid sickness benefit.

**Domestic Remedies**

In November 2001 the applicant filed a criminal complaint against the prison director. The Regional Prosecutor's Office found it unjustified (1 February 2002). The High Prosecutor's Office later expressed doubts about the authorities' conduct and forwarded the matter to the Ministry of Justice, noting concerns that the applicant had not been x-rayed despite a medical report showing he was no longer intoxicated, and that he had been punished without consideration of his painkiller use. In February 2004, responding to an overcrowding complaint, the High Prosecutor's Office acknowledged that some Valdice sections were overcrowded. An October 2005 complaint to the Prison Directorate General was found unsubstantiated.

In civil proceedings for damages, the Jičín District Court (7 April 2005) rejected his claim, finding the cell dimensions complied with Order no. 20/1977 (7 cubic metres per prisoner), relying on a prison report rather than measuring the cell. The Hradec Králové Regional Court upheld this (19 October 2005), the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal (10 May 2007), and the Constitutional Court rejected his constitutional appeal as manifestly ill-founded (24 October 2007), without forwarding the lower courts' observations to him. A separate 2007 personality-rights claim against the prison doctor was dismissed in 2010, and a 2010 State-liability claim remained pending.

**Relevant Standards**

The CPT (2002) criticized insufficient living space and the abolition of the 3.5 sq. m. standard, recommending 4 sq. m. per prisoner; Valdice operated at 108% capacity. The 2004 amendment introduced a 4 sq. m. minimum but permitted exceptions during nationwide overcrowding. The UN Human Rights Committee (2001) also expressed concern about prison overcrowding.
001-110950:
**Summary of Shuvalov v. Estonia**

The case of *Shuvalov v. Estonia* (Applications nos. 39820/08 and 14942/09) originated from two applications lodged by Mr. Ardi Shuvalov, an Estonian national and a former judge at Harju County Court, against the Republic of Estonia. The applicant alleged a violation of his right to the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, stemming from public statements made by the prosecution during criminal proceedings against him.

The underlying facts concern a criminal case presided over by the applicant since 2003, involving a businessman, D., charged with multiple offences. In January 2006, the security police received a statement from D. alleging that his business partner, N., had claimed he could arrange a favourable judgment through the applicant in exchange for a bribe. N. allegedly demanded 200,000 Estonian kroons (EEK) as a "good-will gesture" and a further 900,000 EEK for D.'s acquittal. Based on this information, the police initiated a criminal investigation into bribery offences in January 2006.

Authorities authorized covert surveillance, interception of communications, and undercover audio recording of both N. and the applicant. Crucially, they also authorized a simulation of the offence of giving a bribe to entrap the applicant and N. On 27 February and 6 April 2006, D. provided N. with funds totaling 600,000 EEK, with the second transfer leading to N.'s immediate arrest. N. then claimed the applicant had demanded the money. Later on 6 April, under police instruction, N. met with the applicant and gave him 200,000 EEK while equipped with recording devices. The applicant was subsequently arrested and detained as a suspect; he surrendered the money and was released the next day.

The core of the alleged violation relates to actions following the arrest. On 9 April 2006, the Public Prosecutor’s Office published a press release titled "A judge suspected of accepting a bribe," detailing the suspicion, the simulated offence, and the arrest. While not initially naming the applicant, his identity quickly became public. Prosecutor V., who led the investigation, made numerous public statements to television, newspapers, and news agencies over the following months. These statements asserted that the criminal proceedings were initiated based on specific information, that a successful simulation had occurred, that the main evidence was gathered, and that it was the applicant who had demanded the bribe. A second press release on 6 October 2006 announced the case had been sent to court, reiterating the charges that the applicant demanded a large bribe and promised a favourable judgment.

The applicant argued that these public statements by the prosecutor, an authoritative source, violated his presumption of innocence. He contended the prosecutor presented the allegations as established fact, gave legal assessments that he had committed the crime, and disclosed details from the preliminary investigation. The applicant also filed a separate claim for non-pecuniary damage against the Public Prosecutor’s Office in administrative courts, arguing the statements infringed his presumption of innocence and right to private life. Both the Tallinn Administrative Court and the Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed his claim, finding that the Public Prosecutor’s Office had acted lawfully, that there was elevated public interest given the suspect was a judge, and that the information released did not exceed the objective need to inform the public or amount to an opinion on his guilt. The Supreme Court declined to examine his further appeals. The case thus reached the European Court of Human Rights regarding the alleged infringement of the presumption of innocence due to these pre-trial and trial-phase public communications.
001-110702:
Application no. 30287/09 was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 April 2009 by Mr Selim Seta, a Kosovar national born in 1942 who lives in Besian. The application was lodged against the Hellenic Republic. The Greek Government were represented by their Agent, Mr F. P. Georgakopoulos, President of the Legal Council of the State. On 5 July 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. Although the case is named Seta v. Greece and Germany, the supplied factual record describes the application as having been brought against the Hellenic Republic; apart from the applicant’s allegation involving a German national and his prior residence in Germany, no factual events concerning Germany are set out.

The facts concern events beginning on 14 June 2002, when the applicant was arrested by the Greek authorities at the Greek-Albanian borders. He was charged with drug trafficking after 25 kg of heroin was found in the car he was driving. On the same day, the Ioannina First Instance Prosecutor prosecuted him for illegal drug trafficking and ordered his detention on remand by order no. 25/2002. The applicant alleges that his arrest was a set-up by a German national with whom he had had disagreements in Germany, where the applicant had allegedly lived for an unspecified period, and that the drugs were placed in the car without his knowledge.

In the domestic criminal proceedings, on 20 May 2003 the Ioannina First Instance Criminal Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twenty years’ imprisonment by judgment no. 81/2003. On an unspecified date the applicant lodged an appeal. On 5 June 2007 the Ioannina Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment by judgment no. 58/2007. On 8 September 2007 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation challenging that decision. According to the record, in the grounds of appeal the applicant did not raise any complaint regarding interpretation service at the moment he was arrested or afterwards during the proceedings. The hearing before the Court of Cassation was originally set for 12 March 2008 but was adjourned to 19 November 2008. As it appears from the case file, those proceedings were still pending before the Court of Cassation.

The supplied record contains no further concrete events, dates, domestic decisions, or allegations. It does not describe any other domestic proceedings, evidence, or steps taken by the applicant beyond those set out above. The factual account is therefore limited to the applicant’s arrest, prosecution, conviction, appeal, cassation proceedings, and his allegation about how the drugs came to be in the car.
001-108607:
The applicants, Pavel and Vitalie Levinţa, Moldovan nationals, were arrested in Russia in October 2000 and extradited to Moldova. They were allegedly ill-treated to compel self-incriminatory statements and convicted by Moldovan courts relying in part on those confessions. In an earlier case (Levinţa v. Moldova, no. 17332/03, 16 December 2008), the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3 and 6. On 3 April 2009 the applicants lodged an extraordinary appeal seeking annulment of their convictions. On 8 September 2009 they applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging in particular detention without legal basis and without reasons, inability to present their case fully, and failure to decide on detention pending trial within a reasonable time.

On 8 February 2010 the Plenary Supreme Court of Justice accepted the extraordinary appeal, quashed all previous judgments, ordered re-hearing and verification of the ill-treatment complaint, and stated that the applicants were to continue to be detained, with the trial court to decide the preventive measure. On 10 February their lawyer complained to the Minister of Justice and Prosecutor General, seeking immediate release because no valid detention order existed. The Prosecutor General’s Office referred to the 8 February judgment; the Ministry of Justice said it had not been informed of any judgment concerning the applicants after 16 April 2002.

On 15 March 2010 the Supreme Court sent the case to the Chişinău Court of Appeal. On 13 April the applicants’ lawyer asked that court for immediate release, while the prosecution requested 30 days’ detention pending trial; the applicants said no supporting evidence was submitted. After hearings were postponed on 14 and 16 April, on 19 April the Court of Appeal found continued detention necessary to ensure proper conduct, citing reasonable grounds to suspect exceptionally serious crimes and risks of absconding or obstruction. It rejected release and ordered 30 days’ detention from 2 p.m. on 14 April, then relinquished jurisdiction to the Supreme Court.

On 22 April the lawyer appealed, arguing absence of a valid court decision or warrant, breach of presumption of innocence, detention beyond the statutory 12-month maximum, lack of evidence of risk, and procedural delay. On 13 May the Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded.

Later on 13 May, the lawyer was allegedly called at short notice about a 4 p.m. Court of Appeal hearing on a prosecution request, submitted 7 May, to extend detention by 60 days. He was in Anenii Noi on another case. The applicants were absent; a State-appointed lawyer represented them and objected. The court granted the extension for reasons similar to 19 April. A dissenting judge noted the request reached the Supreme Court on 11 May, criticised the lack of specific risk evidence and absence of the chosen lawyer, and concluded defence rights were breached.

On appeal, the lawyer repeated his arguments and added that the applicants had been held two hours after the previous order expired and had not agreed to the State-appointed lawyer. On 3 June 2010 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal, finding no breach because the applicants refused to appear and the lawyer had been informed; it also found the earlier order ran until 14 May. It held post-quashing detention could be exceptional and based on a prosecution request, citing risks of obstruction or absconding, prior absconding, international wanted status, extradition, and lack of social ties, income or employment. Later, release requests were made monthly and rejected; on 28 December 2010 detention was replaced by house arrest, and on 4 February 2011 by an undertaking not to leave the country during investigation.
001-108859:
The case *Yavuzdoğan v. Turkey* originated in application no. 8472/07, lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 February 2007 by Mr Duran Yavuzdoğan, a Turkish national born in 1943 and living in Eskişehir. He invoked Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant died on 20 May 2009. On 25 May 2010 the Court was informed that his successors—Döndü Yavuzdoğan, Ayşe Yavuzdoğan, Tülay Arslan (Yavuzdoğan), Erkan Yavuzdoğan, Şenay Yavuzdoğan, and Seyit Yavuzdoğan—wished to pursue the application. For practical reasons, the Court continued to refer to Mr Duran Yavuzdoğan as “the applicant,” although his successors were now to be regarded as such. The Turkish Government was represented by its Agent. On 4 September 2009, the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government.

The underlying facts concern a property dispute between the applicant and the Turkish State Railways. On 13 October 2000, the Turkish State Railways brought compensation proceedings against the applicant before the Eskişehir Civil Court of First Instance. The administration alleged that the applicant was unlawfully occupying its property. In the same proceedings, it also requested that the unlawful occupation of the building on the property be stopped and that the building be demolished. The domestic proceedings therefore concerned both financial compensation and the applicant’s continued occupation and use of the property.

On 21 June 2005, the Eskişehir Civil Court of First Instance partially granted the administration’s request. It ordered the applicant to pay the plaintiff the principal amount of TRL 1,374,000,000, plus TRL 787,205,000 as interest. It also decided that the building on the property should be demolished. The applicant challenged the judgment. On 22 February 2006, the Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance judgment of 21 June 2005. The applicant then sought rectification of the Court of Cassation’s judgment. On 5 October 2006, the Court of Cassation dismissed that request.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation(s) center on the domestic civil proceedings and the resulting interference with the applicant’s occupancy of the property. The proceedings began on 13 October 2000 and ended at the latest on 5 October 2006, when the rectification request was dismissed—a period of approximately six years. The first-instance judgment was delivered only on 21 June 2005, and the Court of Cassation upheld it on 22 February 2006. The applicant lodged his Convention application on 12 February 2007. He died in May 2009, and his successors pursued the case. The Government was notified in September 2009. However, the supplied excerpt does not expressly set out the applicant’s specific complaints or the Court’s findings on violations. The key facts presented are therefore the chronology of the State Railways’ compensation and demolition action, the domestic courts’ orders requiring payment and demolition, the appellate stages, and the procedural continuation by the applicant’s successors. These facts would be relevant to any complaint concerning the length or fairness of the civil proceedings and any alleged interference with property rights.
001-115377:
**Case: Michaud v. France (Application no. 12323/11), ECtHR, 6 December 2012**

The applicant, Patrick Michaud, was a French national born in 1947 and a member of the Paris Bar and Bar Council. The case concerned France’s anti-money-laundering framework and its application to lawyers.

The background involved three EU anti-money-laundering Directives: 91/308/EEC, amended by 2001/97/EC, and replaced by 2005/60/EC. These measures extended obligations beyond banks to “independent legal professionals.” France transposed them through Law no. 2004-130 and Decree no. 2006-736 into the Monetary and Financial Code. The Code imposed duties of customer due diligence, reporting suspicions to the financial intelligence unit, internal procedures, staff training, and monitoring. Failure could lead to disciplinary sanctions or being struck off.

On 12 July 2007 the National Bar Council adopted regulations implementing these obligations for lawyers. Lawyers were bound when participating in financial or real-estate transactions, managing client funds or securities, opening accounts, forming or administering companies, or creating or managing trusts. They were not bound when acting as legal counsel or in judicial proceedings. The regulations also stated that lawyers must always ensure professional confidentiality.

On 10 October 2007 Michaud appealed to the Conseil d’Etat to set aside the National Bar Council’s decision. He alleged that the Council lacked regulatory power in this area. More importantly for the alleged Convention violations, he argued that the “obligation to report suspicions” was incompatible with Article 7 ECHR because the term “suspicions” was undefined and lacked legal certainty. He also claimed that the reporting obligation breached Article 8 ECHR, as it jeopardised legal professional privilege and the confidentiality of lawyer-client exchanges, relying on *André and Another v. France*. He further requested a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union on compatibility with Article 6 TEU and Article 8 ECHR.

By judgment of 23 July 2010, the Conseil d’Etat rejected the main submissions. On Article 7, it found that the reporting obligation was not unclear because it referred to Article L. 562-2 of the Monetary and Financial Code. On Article 8, it held that any interference was justified by the general interest in combating money laundering. It noted the safeguard excluding information received or obtained by lawyers in the course of judicial proceedings or as legal counsel, except where the lawyer was involved in money laundering or the advice was provided for that purpose. The Conseil d’Etat found no excessive interference with professional confidentiality and declined to refer the matter to the CJEU.

The wider context included FATF Recommendations 12 and 16 and the Council of Europe’s 2005 Convention, which required suspicious-transaction reporting for lawyers but preserved professional secrecy or legal professional privilege. EU Directive 2005/60/EC applied to independent legal professionals in financial or corporate transactions, allowed a self-regulatory body to receive reports first, and exempted information obtained when ascertaining a client’s legal position or defending them in proceedings. Recital 48 required ECHR-consistent implementation. In *Ordre des barreaux francophones et germanophone* (2007), the CJEU upheld the Directive, finding no fair-trial breach because the obligations mainly concerned financial or corporate activities, not judicial proceedings, and were justified by the need to combat money laundering.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the compulsory reporting and internal-procedure duties imposed on French lawyers, the claimed threat to lawyer-client confidentiality, the alleged lack of legal certainty surrounding “suspicions,” and the domestic court’s finding that the safeguards and public interest made the measures compatible with Articles 7 and 8 ECHR.
001-111518:
**Summary of *Murtić and Ćerimović v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (App. No. 6495/09)**

The case originated in an application by Mr. Fikret Murtić and Ms. Raska Ćerimović, two citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, against the State for the non-enforcement of a domestic human rights decision. The core of their complaint concerned the violation of their property rights, specifically their inability to exercise rights attached to shares they held in a company, Agrokomerc.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation began in 1991 when the applicants, employees of Agrokomerc, acquired "internal shares" as part of the company's reorganisation from a socially-owned to a joint-stock company. Their shares were paid for through permanent deposits and deductions from their salaries between 1991 and 1994. This process created a significant internal share capital held by employees.

However, in August 1994, amidst armed conflict, the State took control of Agrokomerc's management. Following this takeover, the applicants were effectively prevented from exercising any shareholder rights, despite the company's balance sheets continuing to list their privately-held capital until 1999. Their employment was also suspended in 1995, and they were never re-hired.

In 2000, the applicants appealed to the Human Rights Chamber for Bosnia and Herzegovina. In its decision of 8 March 2002, the Chamber found that the applicants had acquired protected "possessions" in the form of their paid-up internal shares under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights. It ruled that the subsequent transfer of ownership to the State, based on an audit that invalidated the internal shares without the applicants' effective participation, violated their property rights and their right to a fair hearing under Article 6 of the Convention.

The Chamber ordered the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina to take specific remedial steps, including employing international auditors to determine the company's complete and accurate ownership structure, establishing the value of the applicants' shares, and formally registering them so the applicants could exercise their shareholder rights.

The enforcement of this decision was fraught with delay. An initial audit by Deloitte & Touche in 2003 still failed to assign the value of the applicants' shares, preventing them from attending the 2004 shareholders' meeting. It was not until 2007—more than five years after the Chamber's binding decision—that the applicants were finally issued individual share certificates and their shares were formally registered. By this time, their shares were assigned a market value (BAM 4,510 for the first applicant and BAM 10,000 for the second).

Finally, in 2009, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina concluded that the Human Rights Chamber's decision had been fully implemented. This was despite the significant and prolonged delay.

The key violation alleged by the applicants was not the original State takeover of their shares, but the State's failure to promptly and effectively enforce the 2002 decision that was meant to remedy that initial violation. The applicants complained that the non-enforcement of the domestic decision in their favour violated their rights under the Convention. The central issue for the European Court of Human Rights was whether this belated implementation, taking over six years, constituted a failure by the State to comply with its positive obligation to enforce a final and binding domestic decision, thereby perpetuating the initial violation of their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-110936:
**Summary of *Hatice Duman v. Turkey* (Application no. 43918/08)**

The case of *Hatice Duman v. Turkey* originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 September 2008 by Ms Hatice Duman, a Turkish national born in 1974. She was represented by lawyer F. Ertekin. The Turkish Government was represented by its Agent. The application was communicated to the Government on 8 February 2010. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the applicant’s arrest, pre-trial detention, and the judicial review of that detention. On 9 April 2003, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership in the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party), an illegal organisation. On 13 April 2003, she was brought before the public prosecutor and an investigating judge, who ordered her pre-trial detention.

On 23 July 2003, the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment against the applicant and eight other persons. The charges included attempting to undermine the constitutional order of the State, membership of an illegal organisation, and aiding and abetting such an organisation. Following the abolition of the State Security Courts by Law no. 5190, the criminal proceedings were resumed by the Istanbul Assize Court.

During the proceedings before the Istanbul Assize Court, the court repeatedly extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention and rejected her requests for release pending trial. It relied on reasonable grounds to suspect that she had committed the offence, the severity of the criminal charge against her, and the state of the evidence in the case file. At a hearing on 1 April 2009, the Istanbul Assize Court again rejected the applicant’s claim that her detention had been unreasonably lengthy and her request to be released pending trial.

The applicant challenged that decision by lodging an objection with the higher division of the Assize Court. In the course of the proceedings for review of her detention, the applicant alleged that neither she nor her lawyer was given an opportunity to make oral submissions against the lawfulness of her continued detention in a hearing. She also alleged that they were not notified of the observations submitted by the public prosecutor. On 17 April 2009, the 13th Chamber of the Istanbul Assize Court rejected the applicant’s objection against the prolongation of her detention, taking into account the nature of the criminal charge and the establishment of reasonable suspicion that she had committed the alleged crime.

On 4 May 2011, based on the evidence before it, the Istanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant of attempting to undermine the constitutional order, pursuant to Article 146 § 1 of the former Criminal Code, and sentenced her to life imprisonment. According to the latest information in the case file, the applicant lodged an appeal against the judgment with the Court of Cassation, and those proceedings were still pending. The applicant was serving her sentence in Gebze Prison.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the lengthy period of pre-trial detention from April 2003 until conviction in May 2011, the repeated judicial extensions of detention and rejections of release requests, and the alleged procedural shortcomings in the detention-review proceedings. In particular, the applicant complained that the review of her continued detention was not adversarial: she and her lawyer were allegedly denied an oral hearing and were not informed of the public prosecutor’s observations. These circumstances formed the basis of her complaints before the European Court of Human Rights, principally concerning the length of pre-trial detention and the effectiveness of judicial review of detention under Article 5 of the Convention.
001-114514:
**I.G. and Others v. Slovakia** concerned three Slovak nationals of Roma origin—I.G., M.K., and R.H.—who alleged that they were sterilised in Krompachy Hospital without their informed consent and that Slovak authorities failed to provide effective redress. They complained under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 8 (private and family life), 12 (right to marry and found a family), 13 (effective remedy), and 14 (non-discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The alleged violations arose from tubal ligations performed during Caesarean deliveries. The first applicant, born in 1983, was sterilised on 23 January 2000 during her second Caesarean section, when she was 16 years old. She claimed she was not told about the sterilisation; the next morning she was asked to sign a document because “all women who had Caesarean sections had to sign it.” She only learned of the sterilisation in 2003 while reviewing her medical file. A typewritten “Request for authorisation of sterilisation,” dated the day of delivery and bearing her signature, was in the file, together with a sterilisation committee decision citing medical reasons. She later suffered serious infection and underwent a hysterectomy. Her civil claim was dismissed because the later hysterectomy was found to have broken the causal link between the unlawful sterilisation and her infertility.

The second applicant, born in 1981, was sterilised on 10 January 1999 during her second Caesarean section, when she was 17 and unmarried. She alleged that neither she nor her parents were advised beforehand or consented. She learned four years later, during a criminal investigation, that her file contained a “Request for sterilisation” with her signature dated 9 January 1999 and a committee approval. She suffered medical side-effects, her partner left her, and her social status in her Roma community declined. In civil proceedings, a court eventually found that hospital staff had acted unlawfully by not obtaining her guardians’ approval, but awarded only EUR 1,593.3, refusing a higher award for alleged social exclusion.

The third applicant, born in 1972, was sterilised on 11 April 2002 during her fourth delivery, a Caesarean section for twins. She claimed she was given pre-medication, felt dizzy, and was asked to sign a paper she could not read. She was allegedly told only after discharge that she had been sterilised. She learned details during police questioning in 2003. She died in 2010, and her children sought to continue the application; the domestic court discontinued her civil action because the right claimed had extinguished on death.

The applicants also alleged inferior, segregated treatment at Krompachy Hospital, including “Gypsy rooms,” separate bathrooms and dining facilities, and verbal abuse. They linked this to racial prejudice and cited the *Body and Soul* Report on coercive sterilisation of Roma women in Slovakia. The Government disputed the allegations and relied on a Ministry of Health expert report and hospital statistics denying forced sterilisation.

Their attempts to obtain redress included criminal complaints from 2003. The investigation was repeatedly discontinued, including findings that no criminal offence had been committed and that the sterilisations complied with the 1972 Sterilisation Regulation. Constitutional complaints led to partial findings: in 2005 the Constitutional Court found a breach of Articles 3 and 13 concerning rejection of their complaint, and in 2006 it found procedural violations of Articles 3 and 8 and ordered reinvestigation. Nevertheless, later prosecutorial decisions again found no offence. Civil claims largely failed or produced minimal compensation, and constitutional complaints were mostly rejected as manifestly ill-founded.

The key alleged violations were therefore the non-consensual sterilisation of Roma women in a public hospital, particularly minors without guardian consent, and the State’s failure to investigate effectively and provide adequate compensation.
001-111419:
**Summary**

*Dadiani and Machabeli v. Georgia* (Application no. 8252/08) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) on 12 June 2012 and became final on 12 September 2012. The applicants, Elene Dadiani and David Machabeli, are Georgian nationals living in Tbilisi; the second applicant is the first applicant’s nephew. The first applicant’s mother had been deprived of her land and other assets by the Soviet authorities in the 1920s. In 2004, the applicants brought an action against the relevant local authority seeking restitution of their ancestral lands. They relied on archival documents confirming their ancestor’s title and on general rules of property protection and inheritance under Georgian and international law.

On 31 January 2005, the Gurjaani District Court established the applicants’ joint ownership of land in the village of Bakurtsikhe, identified as “plot no. 604.” The defendant local authority did not appeal, and the judgment became binding. On 15 February 2005, the applicants’ lawyer obtained an enforcement writ stating that Dadiani and Machabeli were recognised as co-owners of plot no. 604.

On 26 October 2005, the applicants submitted the final judgment and enforcement writ to the Gurjaani Public Registry for enforcement. By letter of 2 November 2005, the registrar refused to register the land in their names, saying the documentation was incomplete. The registrar noted that the final judgment neither indicated the size of plot no. 604 nor specified whether it was agricultural or non-agricultural. The lawyer was asked to submit his identity document, proof of authority to represent the applicants, the original enforcement writ, and a cadastral plan. The applicants claimed that their lawyers visited the registry several times and raised concerns about non-enforcement, but that they could not produce an amended final court decision. The registry continued to refuse registration for various reasons. The judgment of 31 January 2005 remains unenforced.

In a separate set of proceedings, on 25 May 2005 the applicants lodged another action claiming ownership of plot no. 646, adjacent to plot no. 604, on the same legal basis. The action was registered by the Gurjaani District Court on the same day. According to the applicants, examination of this second action had not yet started.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the authorities’ failure to enforce the domestic judgment in their favour. They also alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 on account of the inexplicable delay in the second set of proceedings. Finally, they complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the expropriation of their ancestral lands by the Soviet authorities.

Relevant domestic law included the National Public Registry Agency’s registration functions; the Land Registration Act, which allowed the registrar to request any document necessary for registration and required immediate compliance; Article 1005 of the Civil Code, providing for State liability for damage caused by a public servant; Article 381 of the Criminal Code, criminalising non-execution or obstruction of binding judicial decisions by officials; and the General Administrative Code, which excluded enforcement of final court judgments from its scope. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government on 28 April 2008 and decided to rule on admissibility and merits simultaneously. The central factual issues concerned the refusal to register plot no. 604, the continued non-enforcement of the final judgment, and the prolonged inactivity in the second restitution proceedings.
001-110942:
The applicant, a Latvian national, lodged application no. 37862/02 against Latvia on 2 October 2002. He alleged that he had not received appropriate dental treatment and had not been able to receive long-term family visits in detention.

In the domestic criminal proceedings, the applicant was arrested on 1 October 1999 on suspicion of aggravated robbery. On 11 April 2002 the Kurzeme Regional Court convicted him of aggravated robbery and sentenced him to six years and one month’s imprisonment. On 5 June 2002 the Criminal Chamber of the Supreme Court upheld the first-instance judgment on appeal. On 20 September 2002 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law at a preparatory meeting. On 23 August 2004 the Jelgava Court applied a pre-release scheme and ordered his release before the end of his sentence.

As to family visits, the applicant’s wife gave birth to their son on 18 May 2000. During pre-trial detention he received two short-term visits from his wife, on 16 November 2000 and 20 November 2001, and four short-term visits from his aunt. He was able to receive long-term visits while serving his sentence from 5 October 2002. Until his release on 23 August 2004 he received six long-term visits from his wife, each lasting about sixteen hours. Under the domestic rules in force until 14 May 2001, a Minister of the Interior instruction required approval for short-term visits and allowed one short-term visit of up to one hour per month with written permission. From 14 May 2001 a transitional instruction of the Minister of Justice allowed one short-term visit per month with written permission. Later rules included Cabinet Regulation no. 211 (2003), Cabinet Regulation no. 288 (2006) and the Law on Custody Procedure of 18 July 2006. In a domestic judgment of 19 December 2001, the Constitutional Court found that the transitional instruction and internal remand-prison regulations had not been made public and were internal normative acts; some rules were unconstitutional, but not those concerning short-term visits. In a domestic judgment of 23 April 2009, the Constitutional Court found no State obligation to ensure long-term visits and considered the restriction of such visits compatible with the Constitution, but held that the blanket one-hour monthly restriction on short-term visits was disproportionate. That restriction was abrogated from 1 December 2009, and since 11 August 2011 detainees have been entitled to visits of at least one hour from relatives or other persons at least once a month.

As to dental treatment, according to the Government the applicant first complained on 29 June 2000; a prison doctor prescribed Ibuprofen and advised him to consult a dentist. On 16 August 2000 he complained of toothache; the doctor prescribed Analgin and advised a dentist. On 18 August 2000 a dentist found caries in one tooth and noted two missing teeth and remains of twenty-one damaged teeth, with eight healthy teeth; the applicant refused the recommended treatment. On 10 August 2001 he again complained of toothache and was prescribed Analgin. On 19 September 2001 a psychiatrist considered his headaches related to dental cavity problems and advised a dentist. On 25 October 2001 a dentist diagnosed periodontal disease and four teeth were extracted. On 26 November 2001 the applicant complained to the General Inspectorate that he had not received appropriate dental care and needed prosthetics; the complaint was transferred to the Prisons Administration. On 11 December 2001 the Prisons Administration replied that several extractions had been made free, eight teeth remained, and it was presumed he had not taken appropriate care before detention; prosthetics could be provided only at his own expense and no funds were allocated. On 27 December 2001 he complained to the President’s Chancery; the complaint was transferred via the Ministry of Justice and General Inspectorate to the Prisons Administration. On 12 February 2002 the Prisons Administration stated it had already answered on 11 December 2001 and reiterated that prosthetics could not be provided free in prisons. Cabinet Regulation no. 358 (1999), in force until 28 March 2007, provided that convicted persons receive minimum free health care and that the Prisons Administration provide emergency dental care within its budget; detained persons received care excluding planned in-patient treatment, with in-patient treatment only in acute circumstances.
001-114085:
Paweł Pawlak, a Polish national born in 1965 and owner of a pawnshop, was arrested on 11 June 2001. He was suspected of large-scale fraud while leading an organised criminal group, extortion and threatening witnesses. The Lublin District Court remanded him in detention, relying on strong suspicion, the likelihood of a severe sentence and the risk that he would obstruct proceedings. More charges followed: aggravated fraud, attempted fraud, illegal possession of a gas gun, amphetamine possession, document forgery and corrupting a police officer. In December 2002 the prosecution filed an indictment containing twelve charges against him and eleven co-defendants. His pre-trial detention was repeatedly extended until 14 March 2006—about four years and nine months—on grounds including the severity of the charges, the complexity of the case, the organised nature of the alleged crimes and the risk of interference with witnesses. Some periods overlapped with a sentence in another case. Ultimately, several charges ended in acquittals, discontinuance or reclassification/time-barring; appellate courts criticised the investigation as relying on unreliable witnesses.

The Article 3 complaint concerned the “dangerous detainee” regime. On 1 February 2002, at the prosecutor’s request, the Radom Remand Centre classified the applicant as a dangerous detainee, citing alleged organised crime, illegal gun possession, risk of corruption and escape. He was placed in a high-security ward. He alleged he was held in a solitary cell, had only solitary walks, was subjected to body searches—including anal inspection—each time he left or entered his cell, and was shackled when escorted outside, later preventively shackled for walks, baths, visits and court. The regime was repeatedly extended. Domestic courts quashed some decisions: on 3 December 2002 and 11 December 2003, the Lublin Regional Court found the reasons inadequate or unlawful, noting that fraud/gun charges did not justify dangerous status and fears of corruption were hypothetical. Despite this, the applicant said he remained in a dangerous cell until 24 December 2003. Prison authorities later admitted that after the 11 December 2003 ruling he should have been transferred immediately to an ordinary cell. The Government disputed some claims, saying it could not establish whether he was always solitary and that CCTV was not installed in all cells or sanitary facilities.

As to Article 5 § 3, the applicant complained that his pre-trial detention was excessively long. The extensions relied on the likely severe sentence, complexity, risk of obstructing proceedings and the organised nature of the alleged group. He appealed unsuccessfully, citing the lengthy detention and deterioration of family ties.

The Article 8 complaint concerned restrictions on family contact during the dangerous-detainee regime. The applicant claimed his mother was refused visits between December 2002 and September 2003 because she was to testify, and that he received only closed visits from his wife, daughter and mother. The Government maintained that from February 2002 to December 2003 he received numerous visits, but all were conducted without direct contact and lasted 60–90 minutes.
