The President of the Lublin District Court justified temporary visit bans by the need to secure the proceedings, the risk of pressure on co-accused witness R.P., and the applicant’s aggressive behaviour towards R.P.; the mother’s visit was refused because she was a witness. Thus the key facts concern prolonged pre-trial detention, the harsh and repeatedly reviewed “dangerous detainee” regime (isolation, searches, shackles), and severe no-contact restrictions on family visits.
001-108433:
Standard Verlags GmbH, a Vienna-based limited liability company and owner of the daily newspaper Der Standard, lodged application no. 34702/07 against Austria on 3 August 2007, alleging a violation of the right to freedom of expression. In its issue of 4 April 2006, in the economics section, Der Standard published an article entitled “Haider’s Hypo now also facing criminal investigation”. The article concerned losses at Hypo Alpe-Adria Bank. It reported that the Klagenfurt public prosecutor’s office had initiated an investigation into suspected embezzlement by Hypo senior managers, partly in light of a Financial Market Authority audit. It mentioned criticisms by Jörg Haider and Martin Strutz. It also named Christian Rauscher, described as the son of a former SPÖ regional government member responsible for finance, as the person whom Wolfgang Kulterer and Jörg Haider had blamed for speculative losses of 328 million euros. The article stated that Rauscher had headed the bank’s treasury department in 2004 together with Andreas Zois, that he had not been dismissed but demoted and transferred, and that he had been relieved of his duties only after the losses became known.

On 16 June 2006 Rauscher brought proceedings against the applicant company under section 7a of the Media Act, seeking disclosure of his identity in breach of that provision. He submitted that he was not a public figure and that his position at the bank had not justified naming him. He asserted that he had acted in accordance with instructions and under supervision when authorising the transactions, and that publication of his name had harmed his professional advancement and had not been justified by public interest. The applicant company replied that the article had not portrayed Rauscher as responsible but rather as a “scapegoat”. It argued that the public interest in disclosing his name outweighed his private interests because he had held a leading position at the bank and because of his father’s political role. It also said the reporting had been neutral.

By judgment of 18 July 2006, the Vienna Regional Criminal Court dismissed Rauscher’s action. It found that the article contained information that Rauscher was suspected of a criminal offence and that naming him could damage his professional advancement. It found that he had been head of the treasury department from 1996 to 2006, that he had been responsible for authorising or refusing foreign currency transactions, and that he had been answerable only to the bank’s executive board. It found that 45% of the bank was owned by the Land of Carinthia, that losses of 288 to 328 million euros had been incurred in 2004, and that Rauscher’s father had been a regional government member responsible for finance until 1996 and had sat on the bank’s supervisory board while Rauscher headed the treasury. The Regional Court accepted that Rauscher was not a public figure and that his father’s position did not justify naming him. However, it found a connection between his professional activity and public life because the Land, and thus taxpayers, bore a considerable share of the losses, and because Rauscher had led the department that caused them. It held that the public had an overriding interest in identifying those responsible, so Der Standard had been entitled to name him.

On 14 February 2007, the Vienna Court of Appeal granted Rauscher’s appeal and ordered the applicant company to pay EUR 5,000 compensation and reimburse his procedural costs. It agreed that Rauscher had been presented as suspected of embezzling a large sum. It held that the Regional Court had wrongly weighed the interests. It reasoned that the public interest had to be assessed objectively and with reference to the person’s identity; mere interest in reporting a crime was insufficient. It applied a strict standard, noting that the public generally has no legal right to know the identity of persons concerned. At the time of publication, the investigation was at an early stage; no proceedings had been brought against Rauscher, and the article concerned rumours of accusations by two senior bank officials. The Court of Appeal found no independent value in disclosing his name that outweighed his interest in anonymity, and considered the name had been used to link him to his father and create a sensational story. It found that the public interest in responsibility did not justify identifying him while suspicions were vague and uncertain. Given the negative consequences for Rauscher, the gravity of the accusation, and Der Standard’s wide circulation, it considered EUR 5,000 appropriate.
001-114096:
**CASE OF TONOV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA** (Application no. 48704/07) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), delivered on 30 October 2012. The applicants were three Bulgarian nationals: Mr Iliya Atanasov Tonov (b. 1975), Ms Vatka Markova Udvareva (b. 1930), and Ms Pena Marinova Karalakova (b. 1927). Tonov and Udvareva lived in Sofia; Karalakova lived in Tryavna. The case concerned the annulment of their title to a flat and their subsequent inability to obtain compensation bonds.

In 1968, the second applicant, Ms Udvareva, and her husband purchased a 97-square-metre flat from the Sofia municipality. The flat had become State property through the nationalisations carried out by the communist regime in Bulgaria after 1947. In 1998, after the time-limit to bring an action under section 7 of the Restitution Law was renewed, the pre-nationalisation owner of the flat sued Ms Udvareva and her husband. The former owner sought a declaration that their title was null and void. During the pendency of the proceedings, Ms Udvareva’s husband died. His grandson, Mr Tonov, inherited his share of the flat. As a result, Mr Tonov and Ms Udvareva each owned one half of the flat, and Mr Tonov joined the civil proceedings.

The domestic proceedings ended with a final judgment of the Supreme Court of Cassation on 23 April 2007. The domestic courts found that Ms Udvareva’s and Mr Tonov’s title was null and void ab initio. The reason was that the 1968 sale had been flawed: a document related to the sale had not been signed by the municipality official who had the relevant power. On an unspecified date, Ms Udvareva, who had been living alone in the flat, vacated it.

On 20 September 2007, Ms Udvareva and Mr Tonov requested compensation bonds. Under domestic law, such a request had to be made within two months following the final judgment of the Supreme Court of Cassation. Their request was dismissed because it had not been submitted within that two-month period, which had begun on 23 April 2007. Consequently, they did not receive compensation bonds for the loss of their property.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 October 2007, invoking Article 34 of the Convention. They were represented by Mr N. Runevski, a lawyer practising in Sofia. The Bulgarian Government were represented by Ms R. Nikolova of the Ministry of Justice. On 6 December 2010, the application was communicated to the Government. The relevant background facts, domestic law, and practice had been summarised in the Court’s earlier judgments in *Velikovi and Others v. Bulgaria* and *Tsonkovi v. Bulgaria*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation(s) are that the applicants lost their property by a final domestic judgment that annulled their title due to a formal defect in the original municipal sale, a defect not attributable to them. They were then refused compensation bonds solely because they missed a strict two-month deadline following that final judgment. The applicants complained before the Court that this annulment and the refusal of compensation amounted to a violation of their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The Court was therefore called upon to assess whether the deprivation of property and the denial of compensation imposed a disproportionate burden on the applicants.
001-113432:
**Summary of Vikulov and Others v. Latvia**

The case of *Vikulov and Others v. Latvia* (Application no. 16870/03) originated from an application lodged by three Russian nationals—Mr Sergey Vikulov, his wife Mrs Galina Vikulova, and their son Mr Anton Vikulov—against the Republic of Latvia on 9 May 2003. The applicants alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 5 § 1(f) (right to liberty regarding expulsion), and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights, concerning their detention and deportation.

The first applicant was a Soviet army officer stationed in the Latvian SSR from 1985, supervising a radar station in Skrunda. Following Latvia's independence in 1991 and the Russian Federation's assumption of jurisdiction over former Soviet armed forces, the applicants acquired Russian citizenship. Bilateral treaties in 1994 required the complete withdrawal of Russian armed forces and the radar station's dismantling by 2000. The first applicant was demobilised effective 11 November 1998, and the family's service visas expired on 30 November 1998.

In October 1998, the applicants sought residence permits, citing family ties (the second applicant's parents and daughter in Latvia) and the third applicant's enrolment in a State school. This request was dismissed on 8 April 1999, as they had entered Latvia due to military service and lacked a legal basis for permanent residence. Appeals were unsuccessful. Subsequent requests for temporary permits in March 2000 led to an order on 23 May 2000 requiring them to leave by 12 June 2000, with a five-year re-entry ban. Appeals through three court levels were dismissed, with the Supreme Court's final decision on 19 February 2003.

On 3 September 2003, during the execution of these orders, the applicants were arrested by the State Border Guard Service and placed in the Rīga detention unit for illegal immigrants. On 8 September 2003, a non-appealable deportation decision was issued. Their detention was extended by a court on 12 September 2003, which noted they lacked lawful residence and identity documents. They were transferred to the Olaine accommodation centre from 12 to 15 September 2003, then returned to Rīga, and deported to Russia on 17 September 2003.

The applicants described harsh detention conditions. In Rīga, they were held together in a small (3m x 3m), dirty cell with two steel bunk beds, a lavatory pan, and a washbasin. They alleged foul air, constant light, ants in food, and poor-quality meals. They were allowed only two 15-minute outdoor walks in fourteen days. They had limited family visits (twice) and were denied return to their home for belongings before deportation. On 9 September 2003, following an incident with an aggressive detainee, a woman was placed in their cell for up to two days despite protests. On 16 September 2003, a man was placed in their cell, forcing the first applicant to sleep on the floor. At Olaine, conditions were similarly poor: a dirty cell with dilapidated walls, a high fence with barbed wire, and a watchtower. They had to cook their own food in a shared kitchen.

The second applicant suffered heart problems during detention, including a heart attack on the deportation day, and received some medical treatment. The Government contested many claims, providing documentation on cell sizes, pest control, food regulations, and authorised visits. The case involved third-party intervention by the Russian Government and referenced CPT reports. The core alleged violations concerned the conditions of detention and the lawfulness and necessity of the measures leading to deportation.
001-114439:
The case arose after the Netherlands daily newspaper *De Telegraaf* published articles on 21–22 January 2006 by journalists Joost de Haas and Bart Mos. The articles revealed alleged State secrets from the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) concerning criminal Mink K., suspected corruption, and AIVD informants. The newspaper claimed the documents had circulated in criminal circles and said it had returned them to the AIVD. The AIVD then lodged a criminal complaint concerning unlawful disclosure of State secrets.

On 26 January 2006, the National Police Internal Investigations Department ordered the publisher to surrender documents and/or copies containing State secrets about operational activities of the BVD/AIVD. To protect the journalistic source, the originals were sealed and placed with an investigating judge pending objection proceedings. The publisher objected under Article 10 of the Convention, arguing that surrender would breach journalistic source protection. The Regional Court dismissed the objection, reasoning that the documents existed independently of the journalists’ will and were themselves the object of a criminal act. The Supreme Court upheld that decision in 2008. It found that the documents contained State secret information and that source protection, though important, was not absolute and could yield to weighty State interests, including protection of national security.

In parallel, the applicants alleged that the AIVD used special surveillance powers—telephone tapping and observation—against De Haas and Mos from late January 2006 onwards in order to identify their journalistic source. The State refused to confirm or deny such use. The applicants brought civil injunction proceedings under Articles 10 and 8 of the Convention, seeking cessation of the measures, destruction of data, and an order preventing transfer of information to the Public Prosecution Service. The Provisional Measures Judge assumed surveillance had occurred and found it contrary to Article 10, ordering provisional measures. The Court of Appeal held that surveillance against journalists was not per se unlawful, but became unlawful insofar as it continued after another target had been identified; it also ordered that data not be handed to the prosecution until the Supervisory Board for Intelligence and Security Services found it lawfully obtained. The Supreme Court upheld that approach, stressing that national security and prevention of dissemination of confidential information could justify interference, but only with extreme reticence and an overriding public-interest need.

The Supervisory Board later found the AIVD investigation broadly lawful but identified lapses: tapping a non-target breached subsidiarity; unrelated conversations were transcribed and retained; some tapping occurred before ministerial consent; and some numbers were wrongly attributed. The Minister declared the complaint partly well-founded regarding excessive transcription and retention, but unfounded on the main points, maintaining that special powers against the journalists were lawful, though they indirectly interfered with source protection.

The journalists were later questioned as witnesses in criminal proceedings against suspected leakers. They refused to answer questions capable of revealing their source and were initially ordered detained for non-compliance, but the Regional Court released them, recognising source protection and noting that the State-security issue was diminished because the leak had already become public. In the criminal case against one suspect, forensic examination of the seized documents found no traces.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 10 due to measures, including special surveillance powers, used to identify journalistic sources. The second and third applicants additionally alleged a violation of Article 8 resulting from surveillance.
001-110164:
The applicant, Thomas Boulois, a French national born in 1972, was detained at Schrassig Prison in Luxembourg. On 15 December 1998 he was remanded in custody. By judgment of 22 October 2001, the Criminal Division of the Court of Appeal sentenced him to fifteen years’ imprisonment, three years suspended, for assault occasioning actual bodily harm, rape and false imprisonment accompanied by acts of torture committed on 10 December 1998. His divorce became final on 19 October 2000, and between 14 June 2001 and 13 April 2005 domestic court decisions concerned visiting rights in respect of his three minor children. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair hearing and access to a court in connection with decisions refusing his prison-leave requests.

While imprisoned, he made requests for conditional release, transfer to Givenich semi-open prison and prison leave. In October 2003 he submitted his first prison-leave request to the Attorney-General, seeking one day’s leave to complete administrative tasks, meet friends and deal with personal matters. He said he had not yet paid civil damages because of debts. Two psychologists certified in October and November 2003 that he had undertaken psychotherapy and wished to understand his offences and avoid reoffending. On 5 November 2003 the Prison Board refused the request through the Attorney-General’s representative, citing a risk of deportation because an application to the Ministry of Justice of 25 June 2003 remained undecided, a risk of absconding, lack of reflection on his crime, and the need to begin paying the civil party. On 17 January 2004 he made a second request on the same grounds; his lawyer argued it would aid rehabilitation and repayment. On 17 March 2004 the Attorney-General’s representative confirmed that the 5 November refusal remained valid.

On 25 May 2004 the applicant applied to the Administrative Court for judicial review of the 5 November 2003 and 17 March 2004 decisions. On 6 December 2004 the Administrative Court raised jurisdiction of its own motion; the Government left the issue to the court, while the applicant argued the court had jurisdiction. On 23 December 2004 the Administrative Court declined jurisdiction, distinguishing prison-treatment measures from decisions altering the nature or scope of a sentence; it held that granting or refusing prison leave altered the scope of the sentence and was judicial, not administrative. On 14 April 2005 the Higher Administrative Court upheld that ruling, finding that the request concerned execution of the sentence and was judicial in nature; the “scope” meant the manner of execution. It rejected the applicant’s arguments that no other remedy existed and that he had suffered a denial of justice.

Further prison-leave requests followed. On 11 August 2004 he requested leave to attend courses; on 21 September 2004 this was refused because he could attend courses in prison and had made no substantial compensation efforts. On 14 October 2004 he sought leave for St Nicholas with his children; on 14 December 2004 this was refused because visiting rights were not clearly established. On 24 February 2005 he requested leave for courses, identity papers, driving licence and debt repayment; on 23 March 2005 it was refused for failure to give reasons. On 12 July 2005 a sixth request was refused for risk of not returning. On 4 May 2006 a seventh was refused for lack of effort, especially regarding compensation, and refusal to abide by conditions.

After May 2006, the applicant wrote five times to the Attorney-General’s Department about repayment and reintegration conditions; on 6 November 2006 he was told no reply was intended. The Attorney-General later agreed to an interview on 20 November 2006, but the applicant says it never took place. Later, on 31 October 2008 he received one day’s leave; between 12 December 2008 and 19 June 2009 he received five two-day leaves; on 20 March 2009 he was transferred to Givenich semi-open prison and granted ten days’ leave for work and administrative tasks; on 24 June 2009 he signed a vocational rehabilitation contract as a cook; on 25 September 2009 conditional release was granted. Requests to suspend his sentence were refused on 25 September and 11 December 2009 and 26 February 2010. On 15 July 2010 his sentence was suspended and he left Givenich.

Under domestic law, the 1986 Law included prison leave among sentence-execution measures; leave could be granted for family, rehabilitation or reintegration reasons or as a trial for conditional release. Consideration was given to personality, progress and risk of reoffending. For sentences over two years, such measures were taken by the Attorney-General or representative in accordance with a majority decision of a board including a judge and a public prosecutor.
001-110486:
In *Sarkizov and Others v. Bulgaria* (ECtHR, 17 April 2012), four Bulgarian nationals complained principally that their criminal conviction was based to a decisive extent on anonymous witness testimony and that their defence rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) were unacceptably restricted. The second and fourth applicants also alleged that post-release travel bans were unjustified and lacked effective domestic remedies, contrary to Articles 8 and 13 and Article 2 §§ 2–3 of Protocol No. 4.

The criminal proceedings began on 12 October 2004 for sexual procurement. The prosecution alleged that the applicants induced, procured or transported women into prostitution. Several witnesses, including Mr Zh.M., Mr N.P., Ms R.M. and Ms D.M., were questioned before a judge at the pre-trial stage, but neither the applicants nor their lawyers attended those interviews. Three other witnesses were granted anonymity. Anonymous witnesses nos. 15 and 16 were questioned before a judge in October 2004. The applicants and their lawyers were then given the records and invited to put questions, but they stated in writing that they had none. Witness no. 17 was questioned before a judge on 27 October 2004; some applicants and lawyers attended, while others were absent. Those present also stated that they had no questions. The anonymous witnesses described prostitution arrangements, travel abroad, recruitment and money transfers.

At trial, the anonymous witnesses repeatedly failed to appear. The prosecution said that some were abroad or could not be found. The applicants’ lawyers repeatedly asked that they be found and questioned and challenged the need for anonymity. The District Court ordered efforts to secure their attendance but eventually, on 28 March 2006, read out and admitted their pre-trial statements when they were absent. It convicted the applicants of inducing or attempting to induce women into prostitution, procuring or transporting the anonymous witnesses and other women. Sentences ranged from three years’ imprisonment plus fines to five years’ imprisonment plus a fine. The court found that the victims’ statements, including the anonymous ones, were corroborated by other evidence: other witness statements, international money-transfer reports, border-control reports and secret surveillance material. On appeal, the Regional Court upheld the conviction on 17 July 2006 and refused to question the anonymous witnesses again. The Supreme Court of Cassation later dismissed a reopening request, holding that there had been no procedural breach, that the anonymous testimony had not been the sole or decisive evidence, and that the applicants had had the opportunity to question those witnesses but had declined.

As to the travel bans, the second applicant was conditionally released in April 2007. In June 2007 the police prohibited him from leaving Bulgaria pending rehabilitation. His appeal was dismissed in January 2008; the Supreme Administrative Court said the ban complied with law and aimed to prevent criminally active persons from travelling until reformed. The fourth applicant was released and in April 2008 received a similar ban pending rehabilitation. His appeal was dismissed in December 2008; the court held that the administrative assessment was not subject to judicial control and that police need not state reasons. The bans were tied to judicial rehabilitation and would have lasted until at least October 2010 or 2011, but after a 2009 amendment they ceased in July 2010.

Domestic law required protected-witness decisions to state reasons, judicial verification of identity, immediate access by the accused and lawyer to records, and a right to put questions. Conviction could not be based exclusively on anonymous testimony. The key fair-trial issue was therefore whether reliance on anonymous pre-trial statements, coupled with the later inability to question those witnesses at trial, breached Article 6. The travel-ban complaints concerned whether the restrictions and limited judicial review breached private life, liberty of movement and the right to an effective remedy.
001-112529:
**Case: Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania**  
**ECtHR, Fourth Section, judgment of 31 July 2012 (revised 4 November 2014)**

The case originated in four applications brought by twenty Albanian nationals against Albania. The applicants complained that the Albanian authorities failed to enforce final administrative decisions recognising their inherited property rights and awarding them compensation in lieu of restitution. They alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (fair hearing/access to court), Article 13 (effective remedy), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicants’ claims arose from Albania’s post-communist property restitution and compensation scheme. Under the relevant legislation, local property commissions could recognise former owners’ rights and, where the original property could not be restored because it was occupied or otherwise unavailable, award compensation through various statutory forms. Although the commissions issued decisions in the applicants’ favour, those decisions were not enforced.

In application no. 604/07, the Vlora Commission in 1995 recognised the applicants’ inherited title to a 5,000 sq. m plot and decided they would be compensated. The applicants wrote to the Commission in 1995, 1996 and 2002 but received no official response. In 2007 the Agency stated that it was still preparing property valuation maps and allocating funds. In 2008 the Agency’s director decided ex officio to verify the lawfulness of the 1995 decision. No further decision followed, and the 1995 decision remains unenforced.

In application no. 43628/07, the Lezhë Commission recognised the applicants’ title to 3,434 sq. m in 1994, restoring 713 sq. m and awarding compensation for the remaining 2,721 sq. m. The applicants challenged the decision, and in 1996 the Lezhë District Court ordered an additional 1,187 sq. m to be restored, bringing the restored total to 1,900 sq. m. However, the remaining 1,534 sq. m remained uncompensated.

In application no. 46684/07, the Korçë Commission recognised title to 4,000 sq. m in 1996 and, because the land was occupied, decided compensation was due. In 1999 the same Commission recognised title to 59,546 sq. m of agricultural land and awarded compensation in State bonds of 1,018,236 Albanian leks. No bonds or other compensation were provided. The Government claimed that in 2009 the applicants received ALL 2,000,000 from the Financial Compensation Fund for 200 sq. m, but submitted no supporting document.

In application no. 34770/09, the Tirana Commission in 1995 recognised the applicant’s title to two plots of 63 sq. m and 597 sq. m, deciding that because they were occupied he would be compensated and had a right of first refusal over two buildings. Another 1995 decision recognised 800 sq. m, of which 178 sq. m were restored, leaving 622 sq. m to be compensated. In 2009 the Agency rejected his compensation claim because he had already benefited from the 178 sq. m restitution. He did not appeal within the statutory 30-day period.

Domestically, the 1993 and 2004 Property Acts created complex restitution and compensation mechanisms, later administered by the Agency. Constitutional Court case-law held that commission decisions were final, enforceable, and capable of creating legal expectations similar to court decisions, and that the Agency director could not annul them ex officio. Nevertheless, compensation remained largely unimplemented due to incomplete valuation maps, insufficient funds, fragmented legislation, and repeated delays. The alleged violations therefore centred on the prolonged non-enforcement of final administrative compensation decisions, the absence of effective remedies, and unjustified interference with the applicants’ property rights.
001-114082:
*Catan and Others v. Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 43370/04, 8252/05 and 18454/06) was a Grand Chamber case brought by Moldovan nationals living in Transdniestria. The applicants were children attending three Moldovan/Romanian-language schools in the separatist “Moldavian Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”) and their parents. They alleged violations of Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), Article 8 (private and family life), alone and read with Article 14 (discrimination), arising from the closure and harassment of their schools by the MRT authorities. The applications were lodged in 2004, joined, declared partly admissible in 2010, and heard by the Grand Chamber in 2012.

Transdniestria is an unrecognised separatist region of Moldova. After the 1991–92 conflict, the MRT exercised de facto control there. Russian military forces—formerly the Soviet 14th Army, later the Russian Operational Group—remained, and Russian peacekeepers operated under the 1992 ceasefire. The applicants alleged that Russia also gave political, economic and military support to the MRT, including arms, energy, pensions/aid and Russian citizenship. The MRT imposed a language policy requiring “Moldavian” to be written in Cyrillic. Latin-script schools were banned, and from 1999 schools linked to foreign states had to register with the MRT or lose recognition. In July 2004 the MRT began closing Latin-script schools.

The individual facts concerned three schools.

**Evrica School, Rîbniţa (Catan and Others):** It used premises on Gagarin Street built with Moldovan public funds and followed Moldova’s curriculum in Latin script. It refused MRT registration because that would require Cyrillic and an MRT curriculum. In February 2004 the building was transferred to the MRT education department. In July 2004 MRT police stormed the school and evicted women and children; parents were allegedly pressured to withdraw children, with threats to jobs and parental rights. After OSCE intervention, the school registered as a foreign private school and reopened in a rented former kindergarten, which was inadequate. Requests to return to Gagarin Street were refused. It suffered vandalism and intimidation, and enrolment fell from 683 (2002–03) to 345 (2008–09).

**Alexandru cel Bun School, Tighina/Bender (Caldare and Others):** The school was warned it would close if it did not register. In July 2004 its water and electricity were cut and it was told to leave its premises. Teachers, pupils and parents occupied the building; MRT police failed to retake it. Utilities were restored after international negotiations. The school reopened in three separate rented buildings lacking proper facilities. Enrolment fell from 1,751 to 901.

**Ştefan cel Mare School, Grigoriopol (Cercavschi and Others):** Originally Cyrillic, it sought to switch to Latin script in 1996. The MRT responded with hostile media, intimidation and threats. In August 2002 police stormed the school and evicted teachers, pupils and parents. A pupil committee president was arrested and given 15 days’ administrative imprisonment. About 300 pupils left. The school was relocated to Doroţcaia, under Moldovan control, with pupils bused daily; they faced searches, identity checks and harassment. Enrolment fell from 709 to 169.

The applicants complained to both respondent Governments. Russia generally urged negotiations between Moldova and the MRT; Moldova said it could do no more. The key factual dispute for the alleged violations was whether these interferences with education and private life were attributable to Moldova and/or Russia and whether they amounted to discrimination.
001-113648:
Mitkus v. Latvia concerned Andris Mitkus, a Latvian national, who alleged violations arising from criminal proceedings, two civil cases, his HIV/hepatitis C infection in prison, and press publication of his identity and health information.

Criminal proceedings: On 20 July 1999 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of extortion. While detained, on 26 November 1999 he was charged with robbery committed on 18 July 1999. He protested his innocence, saying neighbours could confirm he had been working in his yard. In July 2000 a confrontation took place with witness M.B., who implicated him; the applicant denied involvement. After the pre-trial investigation ended in August 2000, he requested an identity parade, but a prosecutor refused in September 2000 because the victim had said he could not recognise his attackers. At trial in June–July 2002, the victim and M.B. did not appear. The victim’s pre-trial statements were read because he claimed disability prevented attendance. M.B., though ordered to be brought by police, could not be found, so his pre-trial statements were also read despite the applicant’s objection; M.B.’s evidence directly implicated him. The applicant also claimed M.B. had a motive to lie. The court convicted him of robbery on 2 July 2002 and sentenced him to eight years, relying on co-accused, the victim, M.B., and other witnesses, and rejecting alibi witnesses because they were called by him and recalled events after a long delay. His appeals complained about absent witnesses, including S.K-a and S.K-s, but the Supreme Court rejected them; the Senate noted he had not repeated some requests at the appeal hearing. He also complained of delay, and the Ministry of Justice referred to the court’s heavy workload.

Infection and civil claim against Central Prison: In March 2003 the applicant learned he was HIV positive from 2002 tests and later that he had hepatitis C. He denied drug use or homosexual activity and believed he was infected in Central Prison. Prison records showed a negative HIV test on arrival in July 1999 and a positive test in September 2002. The prison suggested a possible “window” period, pre-arrest infection, or infection in prison through hygiene/sex; it said single-use syringes had been used. The applicant alleged a multiple-use glass syringe was used for his 1999 blood sample. His damages claim was rejected in February 2004; the nurse testified that single-use syringes were used. On appeal, he requested to attend, but the Supreme Court heard the case on 30 September 2004 in his absence because he was detained. His cassation appeal was dismissed without addressing that absence. He also complained to prosecutors, but no criminal investigation into the infection was opened.

Newspaper civil claim: In November 2003 the newspaper Rīgas Balss published an article, “Prison Doctors Accused of Injecting AIDS,” naming “prisoner Andris M.,” describing his alleged infection claim, convictions and sentence, and printing a recognisable photo of him behind bars. The applicant had asked that his identity not be disclosed; the court later prohibited media from revealing it. He sued for non-pecuniary damages. The first-instance court found the publication contravened data-protection law but dismissed for lack of proved damage. The appeal court heard the case in his absence on 2 February 2006 and dismissed it, holding media not subject to data-protection legislation; cassation was refused.

He therefore alleged breaches of Articles 6 and 8 concerning unfairness, length, exclusion from hearings, failure to investigate/protect against infection, and disclosure of sensitive private information.
001-114243:
The application was lodged on 30 July 2005 by three citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Emina Ališić, Aziz Sadžak and Sakib Šahdanović, against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Serbia, Slovenia and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. The first applicant is also a German citizen; all live in Germany. Before the dissolution of the SFRY, Ališić and Sadžak deposited foreign currency with Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo, and Šahdanović with the Tuzla branch of Investbanka. Their balances were approximately DEM 4,715.56, DEM 129,874.30 and DEM 63,880.44; Šahdanović also had USD 73 and 4 Austrian schillings. They alleged that they could not withdraw their “old” foreign-currency savings from those accounts.

In the SFRY, banks were organised as basic and associated banks. Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was a basic bank; in 1978 it and others founded Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana. Foreign-currency deposits were State-guaranteed and largely “redeposited” with the National Bank of Yugoslavia. Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo shipped foreign currency to the National Bank of Slovenia; between 1984 and 1991 DEM 244,665,082 was shipped to Ljubljana and DEM 41,469,528 returned. In 1990, Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo became a branch without legal personality of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana, which took over its rights, assets and liabilities. Investbanka became independent with headquarters in Serbia and branches in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Tuzla. From 1990/91, SFRY measures restricted withdrawals of foreign-currency savings, at times to DEM 500 at a time and DEM 1,000 per month.

After the SFRY dissolved in 1991/92, each successor State adopted measures. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the State and Entities addressed “old” savings. The FBH assumed liability in 1997, but later legislation expressly excluded savings in branches of Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana and Investbanka. A 2006 State law excluded those branches but required the State to help clients recover from Slovenia and Serbia. Domestic Constitutional Court decisions, including AP 164/04 of 1 April 2006, AP 423/07 of 14 October 2008 and AP 14/08 of 21 December 2010, found neither Bosnia and Herzegovina nor its Entities liable and ordered help in recovering from Slovenia and Serbia. The Sarajevo branch had about DEM 250 million in savings at 31 December 1991. A domestic Ljubljanska Banka Sarajevo was set up in 1993 and purported to assume liability; in November 2004 the Sarajevo Municipal Court held it was not the successor and deleted the 1993 register entry. Bankruptcy proceedings against it began in 2010 and remained pending. The Tuzla branch of Investbanka closed on 1 June 1992. A Serbian court made a bankruptcy order against Investbanka in 2002; bankruptcy remained pending, and in 2011 Serbia began a criminal investigation into transfer of the Tuzla archives in 2008.

Other States took measures. Croatia stated it repaid old savings in domestic banks and foreign branches, and repaid citizens’ savings transferred from Ljubljanska Banka Ljubljana’s Zagreb branch; some remaining clients obtained payment from forced sale of branch assets in Croatia, while others sued in Croatian or Slovenian courts. Serbia in 1998 and 2002 agreed to repay certain domestic-bank savings, but left successor-State citizens’ and branch savings frozen pending succession; after Investbanka’s 2002 bankruptcy, 322 clients of Bosnian branches unsuccessfully sought payment, and 20 sued without success. Slovenia assumed the SFRY guarantee in 1991; after restructuring, old Ljubljanska Banka retained liability for branches in other successor States. In 1997 proceedings concerning those branches were stayed pending succession negotiations; in December 2009 the Constitutional Court declared the stay unconstitutional. Thereafter Ljubljana District Court judgments ordered the old bank to pay savings in the Sarajevo and Zagreb branches; one Sarajevo-branch judgment became final on 16 November 2010. Claims against Slovenia were rejected in three final cases. The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia repaid old savings in domestic banks and local branches of foreign banks regardless of citizenship. The 2001 Agreement on Succession Issues, in force from 2 June 2004, provided for negotiations under BIS auspices on SFRY guarantees of hard-currency savings; after failed rounds, the BIS ended its role in 2002.
001-115396:
**F.N. and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 28774/09)**

**Summary of Key Facts**

The applicants are a family of four Uzbek nationals—a husband (F.N.), his wife, and their two minor children—who arrived in Sweden in December 2005 and applied for asylum. They alleged that deportation to Uzbekistan would expose them to a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment).

The first applicant claimed a history of persecution dating back to 1995, when he was allegedly arrested during a mosque raid, held in solitary confinement, and later convicted in 1998 as a "Muslim separatist" before receiving clemency. He asserted that he was placed on an authorities' blacklist of suspected Islamists.

The central event concerns his alleged participation in the Andijan demonstrations of 13 May 2005, during which Uzbek security forces opened fire on protesters. The first applicant claimed he fled the scene, but police subsequently arrested him at home, detained him for four days, and tortured him to extract a confession. He alleged release was secured through bribery, after which he went into hiding for six months before the family fled Uzbekistan illegally.

The second applicant claimed she was interrogated and subjected to degrading treatment regarding her husband's activities. The third applicant, a minor with pre-existing health issues, reportedly developed anxiety and learning difficulties. The family submitted documentary evidence including a medical certificate, a summons naming the first applicant as a witness, and posters of wanted persons purportedly listing him among Andijan suspects.

Swedish authorities rejected the asylum claims. The Migration Board and Migration Court found the applicants' accounts lacking credibility, citing vague testimony, inconsistent statements, and an "escalation" of their story over time. The courts noted that the first applicant traveled freely after the demonstration despite claimed road closures, questioned whether police would arrest someone not identified as a demonstrator, and found the wanted posters had "very low evidentiary value" due to formatting inconsistencies. The summons appeared to call him as a witness, not a suspect.

The applicants later introduced additional claims, including the first applicant's membership in the opposition party Birdamlik while in Sweden (sur place activities) and his alleged criminal charges related to the Andijan events. They argued that failed asylum seekers face particular risk upon return, referencing international reports documenting endemic torture in Uzbekistan and the vulnerability of those connected to Andijan.

Swedish courts rejected these claims, finding the Birdamlik activities limited and unproven to be known by Uzbek authorities. The authorities suggested the family could return without detection, possibly via neighboring countries. The applicants alleged that Migration Board contact with the Uzbek Embassy regarding travel documents would identify them as failed asylum seekers, increasing their risk. The courts found this speculative, noting other legitimate reasons for such contact existed.

The applicants lodged their case with the European Court of Human Rights in May 2009, which applied Rule 39 (interim measure) preventing deportation pending consideration.
001-108580:
**Ustyantsev v. Ukraine** (Application no. 3299/05) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Sergey Vladimirovich Ustyantsev, who complained under the Convention about the conditions of his detention, the length of his pre-trial detention and trial, and the lack of compensation for his lengthy detention.

In September 2001, the applicant was implicated in two criminal matters. On 7 September 2001, a group allegedly including him burgled a house. On 12 September 2001, he stole a car and was involved in a collision; he was caught the same day. He was charged with car theft on 13 September 2001, and on 14 September the Leninskyy District Court of Odessa authorised his detention on remand. By 7 November 2001, the car theft investigation was completed and the case sent to court.

On 11 January 2002, the court learned that burglary proceedings were also pending against the applicant. It remitted the car theft case for further investigation and joinder with the burglary case, while confirming his detention. On 17 January 2002, after the cases were joined, the applicant attempted suicide in protest. He made further suicide attempts and went on hunger strikes later. On 2 February 2002, he was formally charged with burglary. The joined case was transferred to the District Court by 14 March 2002.

The trial was delayed repeatedly because victims and witnesses failed to appear. The court complained to the prosecutor and police about failures to secure attendance, noting that delays lengthened detention in the overcrowded SIZO with poor sanitary conditions. On 3 March 2003, the District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to nine years’ imprisonment, continuing his detention pending appeal. The applicant alleged the judgment was given in his and his lawyer’s absence and that he learned of it only on 11 March 2003. On 31 July 2003, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal quashed the burglary conviction and remitted it for retrial, reducing the car theft sentence to five years and six months. The Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on 22 March 2005.

On retrial of the burglary charge, hearings were delayed by defence lawyers’ and witnesses’ non-appearance. In April 2005, a handwriting examination found that the applicant’s signatures had been forged on crucial procedural documents. On 1 June 2005, the court remitted the case for additional investigation and issued a special ruling against the investigator. On 4 October 2005, the proceedings were discontinued for lack of proof.

As to detention, the Government stated the applicant was held in the SIZO during several periods from 15 September 2001 to 10 February 2006, and in various correctional colonies. He was released on parole on 22 January 2007, then rearrested in August 2007 on suspicion of a new crime. The applicant alleged that in the temporary detention centre detainees were fed once daily and lights remained on at night. In the SIZO, he alleged overcrowding—about one square metre per person, with a cell of 7.5–10 square metres holding four detainees, including a toilet and washstand—constant lighting, a concrete floor, no facilities to prepare his defence, and lack of basic necessities, medical assistance, press, gym access, and private correspondence. He also complained of overcrowded prison vans and lack of food in court holding rooms. His health allegedly deteriorated, including chronic prostatitis, thrombophlebitis, and a venereal disease.

The Government disputed these claims, stating cells provided at least 2.5 square metres per person, basic furniture, separated toilets, sufficient light and ventilation, adequate food, daily walks, eight hours’ sleep, weekly baths, a library, and medical care. Medical records showed pre-existing conditions and later treatment.

The applicant unsuccessfully sought civil compensation for detention conditions; his claim was dismissed in April 2006 and his appeal in September 2006. He lodged his Convention application on 1 November 2004, alleging violations of Article 3 regarding conditions in the Odessa Remand Centre, excessively long pre-trial detention and trial, and inability to obtain compensation. On 16 March 2009, the Court communicated the complaints to the Government.
001-114492:
Case Hristozov and Others v. Bulgaria (Applications nos. 47039/11 and 358/12) concerned ten Bulgarian nationals, most of whom suffered from terminal cancer. They had exhausted conventional treatments—surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and hormone therapy—or had been advised that such treatments would not work or were unavailable in Bulgaria. They approached a private Sofia clinic, the Medical Centre for Integrative Medicine OOD, which told them about MBVax Coley Fluid, an experimental anti-cancer product developed by the Canadian company MBVax Bioscience Inc. The product had not been authorised in any country, but had been allowed for “compassionate use” in several countries. The company offered to supply it free of charge to the clinic for patients who could no longer benefit from conventional treatment, in exchange for data on its effects.

Each applicant applied to the Bulgarian authorities for permission to use the product. In letters dated June, July and August 2011, the Director of the Medicines Executive Agency refused. He stated that MBVax Coley Fluid was an experimental product not authorised or undergoing clinical trials in any country. Under Bulgarian Regulations no. 2 of 2001, unauthorised medicines could not be authorised for use in Bulgaria. Bulgarian law made no provision for compassionate use outside clinical trials, unlike some other European countries. The Minister of Health agreed with that position, as did the Ombudsman in relation to some applicants. The applicants did not seek judicial review.

One applicant, Mr Petrov, travelled to Germany, obtained the product free of charge and received it seven times, but returned to Bulgaria because he could not afford living expenses or clinic fees. Four applicants—Mr Hristozov, Mr Petrov, Mr Behar and Ms Pencheva—died after lodging their applications, and their heirs continued the proceedings. The Government disputed whether MBVax Coley Fluid was a medicinal product and whether it was undergoing clinical trials. The applicants argued that it was undergoing a phase one clinical trial in Germany, relying on United States National Cancer Institute and National Library of Medicine websites, and therefore complied with Article 83 § 2 of Regulation (EC) no. 726/2004 on compassionate use. The Government rejected that assertion.

The applicants alleged that the authorities’ refusal to allow them to use the experimental medicinal product for compassionate use breached their right to life, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, and violated their right to respect for private and family life. They also alleged that they had no effective remedy in that respect. The Court joined the applications, declared them partly inadmissible, and gave the Government notice of the complaints concerning the refusal to permit use of the product and the alleged lack of effective remedies. It decided to examine the merits together with admissibility. The central factual issue was whether Bulgaria’s refusal to permit compassionate use of an unauthorised but potentially life-saving experimental medicine, when conventional treatment had failed and the applicants were terminally ill, unjustifiably interfered with their Convention rights.
001-111429:
**Summary of *Bajsultanov v. Austria* (ECtHR, 2012)**

The applicant, Ruslan Bajsultanov, is a Russian national of Chechen origin. He arrived in Austria with his wife on 25 July 2003 and applied for asylum the same day. He claimed that he had supported Chechen fighters during the first Chechen war (1994–96), but did not participate in the second war. In summer 2003, mercenaries allegedly came looking for him during a “cleaning operation,” relying on an old file about him. When they could not find him, they beat his father and later the family home was burned down. His father advised him and his wife to leave Chechnya and Russia.

In 2005, Austria granted the applicant asylum, accepting that he faced a real risk of ill-treatment if returned to Russia. His wife was granted asylum in 2007, partly because she would share the risk as his spouse; their daughter and son were also granted asylum. The family settled in Graz.

However, between 2005 and 2008 the applicant was convicted of several criminal offences: attempted theft (2005); attempted resistance to public authority, aggravated damage to property, and aggravated bodily harm (2006); and aggravated bodily harm (2008), after he hit a prostitute with an empty bottle. He received suspended and custodial sentences, served his sentences, and was released in August 2009.

In October 2008, the Federal Asylum Office lifted his asylum status and declared his expulsion to the Russian Federation permissible. Referring to section 7 of the 2005 Asylum Act and Article 33(2) of the 1951 Refugee Convention, it found that he had been convicted of particularly serious offences, that the convictions were final, that he posed a danger to society, and that the public interest in expulsion outweighed his interest in asylum protection. It also concluded that the security situation in Chechnya had improved and that he would not face a real risk of ill-treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. As to Article 8, the office found he had not integrated well in Austria, had only begun learning German in 2007, and still had strong family ties to Chechnya, including parents and six siblings with whom he maintained regular telephone contact. The Asylum Court upheld that decision in August 2009, and the Constitutional Court declined to deal with his complaint in March 2010.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that lifting his asylum status and his planned expulsion to Russia would expose him to a real risk of ill-treatment under Article 3 and would separate him from his wife and two children, who had independent asylum status in Austria, contrary to Article 8. He maintained that he could not return to Chechnya because of his past and that many returnees had disappeared or been killed. His father had allegedly told him that he remained at risk. Austrian authorities noted that his family in Chechnya had no problems with the security services and that the FSB had told his father they were only looking for the applicant. His wife confirmed she visited him in detention and intended to continue living with him as a family after release.

Country information before the Court described continuing serious human rights problems in the North Caucasus, including abductions, disappearances, torture, impunity, and risks for returnees, former rebels, their relatives, and people complaining to authorities. Some reports noted reduced violence in Chechnya but stated the situation remained far from normal. The Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 on 23 September 2010, indicating that Austria should not expel the applicant until further notice.
001-109572:
Gas and Dubois v. France (Application no. 25951/07) concerned access to second-parent adoption for a same-sex couple in France. The applicants, Ms Valérie Gas and Ms Nathalie Dubois, are French nationals who had lived together since 1989 and entered a civil partnership (PACS) in 2002. In 2000, Ms Dubois gave birth in France to a daughter, A., conceived in Belgium through anonymous donor insemination. Because the donor was anonymous under Belgian law, A. had no established legal tie to her father and was legally recognised only by her mother. The child lived continuously in the applicants’ shared home, and both women jointly raised her.

In March 2006, Ms Gas applied to the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance for a simple-adoption order in respect of A., after Ms Dubois gave her express consent before a notary. The public prosecutor objected under Article 365 of the French Civil Code. On 4 July 2006, the first-instance court found that the statutory conditions for adoption were satisfied and that the applicants were actively and jointly involved in A.’s upbringing, providing her with care and affection. Nevertheless, it refused the application. It reasoned that the requested adoption would transfer parental responsibility to the adoptive parent and thereby deprive the birth mother, Ms Dubois, of her parental rights, which would run counter to the child’s interests and to the applicants’ own intentions.

The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld that refusal on 21 December 2006. It also accepted that Ms Gas ensured A.’s emotional and material well-being and that the formal adoption conditions were met. However, it held that the legal consequences of adoption would not be in the child’s interests. Under Article 365, the only exception allowing parental responsibility to be shared is where a person adopts the child of his or her spouse. Since the applicants were not married—and could not marry under French law—Ms Dubois would lose all parental responsibility, and a later delegation of parental responsibility would not sufficiently eliminate the risks to the child. The Court of Appeal regarded the application as seeking legal recognition and legitimisation of the couple’s joint parenting. The applicants appealed on points of law but did not pursue the proceedings; in September 2007 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal forfeited.

The case therefore concerned the absence of any legal means in France for a same-sex couple to obtain second-parent adoption. Under French law, marriage was not available to same-sex couples. A civil partnership did not create kinship, inheritance, or adoptive ties and had no effect on parental responsibility. Simple adoption preserved the child’s original family ties but vested parental responsibility solely in the adoptive parent, unless the adoptive parent was married to the child’s mother or father. Same-sex couples could not benefit from that exception. Full adoption would sever the legal tie with the birth mother and was therefore not a realistic option. Assisted reproduction was also reserved for opposite-sex couples.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that they had been discriminated against compared with heterosexual couples. Relying on Article 14 of the Convention taken together with Article 8, they claimed discriminatory treatment based on sexual orientation and a breach of their right to respect for private and family life, because French law provided no legal route for same-sex couples to access second-parent adoption. The Court declared the application admissible on 31 August 2010.
001-111521:
The case of *Khoniakina v. Georgia* concerned a Georgian national and former Supreme Court judge, Mrs Adelina Khoniakina, born in 1926. She had served as a Supreme Court judge from 1956 and retired in May 2000. Under the original version of section 36 of the Supreme Court Act, she received a life-long pension equal to her final salary, adjustable in line with changes in the salaries of serving Supreme Court judges. In 2001, section 36 was amended to remove that adjustment clause. Later amendments reintroduced adjustment, but a December 2005 amendment, effective 1 January 2006, rephrased section 36 to provide retired Supreme Court judges with State compensation fixed at GEL 1,200 (EUR 551). The 2005 amendment was given retroactive effect. From February 2006, the State Social Insurance Fund applied it to the applicant, reducing her pension from the previously adjustable level.

The applicant brought two pension disputes. In the first, begun in 2004, she challenged the removal of the adjustment clause. On 21 February 2006, a majority of the Supreme Court’s Administrative Division ruled in her favour, holding that the 2001 amendment could not retroactively deprive already-retired judges of their adjustment right and ordering arrears up to December 2005. Judge S. dissented, arguing that the amendment did not necessarily worsen her position and that her pension should be adjusted only between March 2005 and January 2006.

In the second dispute, the applicant challenged the application of the December 2005 amendment to her pension from February 2006. On 31 May 2006, she sued the Fund, arguing that the retroactive reduction of her pension was unlawful. The Tbilisi City Court dismissed her claim on 19 September 2006, and the Tbilisi Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 6 March 2007, stating that Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 did not guarantee a pension of a particular amount. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal on 9 July 2007, relying on the Convention case-law against retroactive interference with civil rights and arguing that the domestic courts had resolved an analogous issue inconsistently with the Supreme Court’s 21 February 2006 judgment.

On 10 October 2007, a Supreme Court bench composed of Judge S. and two other judges declared her cassation appeal inadmissible without a hearing and without addressing her arguments. The applicant requested that the decision be set aside, complaining that Judge S. should not have participated because he had already expressed a clear opinion on the same legal issue in the earlier pension dispute. She relied on domestic provisions allowing a judge’s exclusion where impartiality could be doubted. On 26 December 2007, the Supreme Court rejected that request, finding that Judge S.’s earlier dissenting opinion was not evidence of actual or implied bias.

The applicant complained before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, alleging bias because Judge S. participated in the cassation decision after having already expressed an opinion on the same issue, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, alleging that the retroactive December 2005 amendment and fixed GEL 1,200 pension unlawfully interfered with her retirement pension rights and legal certainty. The Court gave notice of these complaints to the Georgian Government on 8 April 2009.
001-111175:
**Summary: Keskinen and Veljekset Keskinen Oy v. Finland**

This case originated in application no. 34721/09 against Finland, lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 30 June 2009 by Mr Vesa Petteri Keskinen, a Finnish national, and Veljekset Keskinen Oy, a Finnish limited liability company. The applicants alleged in particular that their right to a fair trial had been violated because the Vaasa Appeal Court convicted the first applicant and ordered forfeiture of the profit gained by the applicant company without holding an oral hearing.

The facts concerned an ice fishing competition organised by the applicants in February 2005. It was the seventh such event they had organised. The entrance fee was 20 euros. The applicants rented a lake and stocked it with 5,551 marked salmon: one weighing five kilos, 50 weighing about three kilos, 500 weighing about two kilos, and 5,000 weighing about one kilo. Winners were those who caught the most fish, and anyone catching a marked salmon won a prize according to its weight. The fisherman of the five-kilo salmon would win one million euros; the three-kilo fish carried a 20,000-euro gift certificate; the two-kilo fish a 2,000-euro certificate; and the one-kilo fish a 200-euro certificate. Each participant could buy only one entrance ticket and use only one rod and hook. The event attracted 27,731 participants. Of the 5,551 marked salmon, 2,188 were caught. Prizes awarded included three 20,000-euro certificates, 48 2,000-euro certificates and 2,137 200-euro certificates.

Regulatory authorities had previously examined the competition. When the 2003 event was organised, the Ministry of the Interior asked the applicant company to clarify its nature and concluded in March 2003 that it was partly a lottery under the Lotteries Act because fishers of marked salmon received separate prizes. This interpretation was sent to the county administrative board and local police, but the 2003 competition had no legal consequences. Preparations for the 2005 event began in 2004 and involved many local persons, including police. The Ministry again asked the applicant company to clarify the event. On 17 and 21 January 2005 it concluded that the event might constitute a lottery. This view was communicated to local police and leading county police officials. The applicants informed the police well in advance, and the police did not prohibit the event, although they had the right to do so if organising it was illegal.

Criminal proceedings were brought in 2006. The public prosecutor charged the first applicant, inter alia, with organising a lottery without a permit in connection with the ice fishing competition, because the outcome was partly based on luck. The prosecutor also asked that the profit gained from the offence by the applicant company be forfeited to the State.

On 5 June 2006 the Seinäjoki District Court, after an oral hearing, dismissed all charges against the first applicant and the forfeiture request against the applicant company. The court found that the lottery had been illegal, but that the first applicant’s misinterpretation of the law was excusable because the provisions were unclear, similar events had been organised before, and the authorities had not prevented the event.

The public prosecutor appealed to the Vaasa Appeal Court, reiterating the charges and requesting an oral hearing. He wanted two Ministry of the Interior civil servants heard about the Ministry’s role, the question of intent, and the applicants’ reactions to the Ministry’s queries and guidelines. As to forfeiture, he argued that an oral hearing was needed to assess evidence and the amount of profit. The applicants also appealed regarding costs and expenses and requested an oral hearing. They wanted two witnesses heard about the nature, content and organisation of the competition, and the company’s financial manager heard about the financial outcome. If no oral hearing was held, they asked to be allowed to submit further comments. Both parties had an opportunity to comment on the other’s appeal.

On 8 August 2007 the Vaasa Appeal Court rejected the request for an oral hearing. It sentenced the first applicant to 50 day-fines, amounting to 13,300 euros, for breach of the lottery provisions. It found that the facts and background were undisputed, that the written correspondence between the Ministry and the applicants had already been included in the District Court’s judgment, and that the Ministry’s role as supervisory and expert organ was apparent from the Lotteries Act. It therefore considered an oral hearing clearly unnecessary. It also found that the forfeiture did not require an oral hearing and that no further comments were needed. The alleged violation thus concerned the Appeal Court’s decision to convict the first applicant and order forfeiture of the applicant company’s profit without an oral hearing.
001-111938:
In *X v. Finland* (Application no. 34806/04), the applicant was a Finnish paediatrician, X, who continued in private practice after retirement. In 1995, V’s mother brought V to X, suspecting that V had been sexually abused by her father; X examined the child and took photographs. In 2000, V was taken into public care. In December 2000, V’s mother failed to return her to the support centre, and V stayed with her mother until found in April 2001. X examined V on 26 December 2000.

In April 2001, X was arrested as a suspect in depriving V of liberty from 16 December 2000. Her home and practice were searched; she was remanded in custody on 20 April and released on 25 April. A restraining order was issued in May 2001 but quashed in June 2001. In April 2002, X was charged with aggravated deprivation of liberty or, alternatively, aiding and abetting it. The prosecution alleged that her opinions, advice and actions contributed to the mother’s abduction of V and that X unlawfully isolated V. The trial was held in camera in October 2002. X rejected her appointed public defender and defended herself. The District Court rejected her requests to hear several witnesses relevant to the background of the charge.

In October 2002, the District Court ordered a psychiatric assessment of X and V’s mother. X went into hiding and failed to attend hospital, leading to detention orders in absentia. In October 2004, she was arrested and taken to Vanha Vaasa Hospital for assessment. Dr A.K. concluded that X suffered from delusional disorder, had not been criminally responsible at the time of the alleged offence, and needed a guardian for the criminal proceedings. In February 2005, the Forensic Psychiatry Board ordered involuntary treatment under the Mental Health Act. The District Court released X from detention, but she remained hospitalised.

X refused medication. From March 2005, she was forcibly injected with antipsychotics—first Zyprexa, then Risperdal Consta every two weeks—with dosage changes. She alleged an assault during forced medication in July 2005. She was moved to an open ward in November 2005, discharged in January 2006, and involuntary care officially ended in June 2006.

For Article 6, the key facts are that the Board found X’s capacity reduced and that she needed a guardian. On 2 March 2005, the District Court appointed her public defender, M.S., as guardian without an oral hearing, relying on the psychiatric assessment. X opposed this. Her appeals were rejected without an oral hearing, and the Supreme Court refused leave. She also complained that she could not examine witnesses appearing on her behalf.

For Articles 5 and 8, X alleged that her involuntary admission and forced medication were unlawful and unnecessary. She appealed the February 2005 confinement to the Supreme Administrative Court, which held an oral hearing in October 2005 but dismissed her appeal, finding reliable medical evidence that she was mentally ill, needed treatment, and that other services were inadequate. Later continuation decisions were upheld, some without oral hearings. X relied on contrary opinions from Drs K.A., E.P. and M-P.H., but they were not accepted.

For Article 13, X alleged no effective remedy against forced medication. She complained to the National Forensic Medical Authority, the Chancellor of Justice/Parliamentary Ombudsman, the police, and the State Provincial Office. The Authority found no deviation from accepted practice; the police closed the investigation; the Ombudsman declined because matters were pending elsewhere; and the State Provincial Office found no further measures necessary. Some decisions were not appealable.
001-109072:
**Summary of Hardy and Maile v. the United Kingdom**

**Case Background:**
The case concerned the construction and operation of two liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals at Milford Haven harbour in Wales. The applicants, Alison Hardy and Rodney Maile, were members of "Safe Haven," a local residents' group opposed to the terminals. They alleged that the United Kingdom failed in its duties under Articles 2 (right to life) and 8 (right to private life) of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the regulation of hazardous activities and dissemination of relevant information.

**Key Facts:**
The applications involved two sites: the Dragon terminal (proposed by Petroplus) and the South Hook terminal (proposed by Qatar Petroleum and ExxonMobil). Both required planning permission from local authorities and hazardous substances consent. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) served as a statutory consultee but had no legal competence to assess risks from ships at sea. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) had general responsibility for vessel safety, while the Milford Haven Port Authority (MHPA) managed shipping movements under the Port Marine Safety Code.

Planning permissions for the Dragon site were granted in March 2003, with extensions approved in September 2004. South Hook permissions were granted in November and December 2003. Hazardous substances consents followed in 2004. Throughout these processes, environmental statements were prepared, public consultations occurred, and MHPA expressed confidence in safely handling LNG vessels based on risk assessments and simulator exercises.

However, significant gaps existed in risk assessment. The HSE examined shore-side operations but stopped work on marine spill scenarios because marine risks fell outside its legal remit. A September 2003 HSE report noted that potential vapour clouds could engulf populated areas but lacked data to complete ignition probability analysis. Objectors raised concerns about ship collisions at jetties and the absence of comprehensive quantified risk assessment for tankers. The applicants argued there was no single overriding authority addressing all safety issues.

MHPA conducted numerous risk assessments but refused to disclose reports citing commercial confidentiality. The applicants contended that relevant safety information was not made publicly available for debate before consents were granted.

**Judicial Review Proceedings:**
In March 2005, the applicants sought judicial review of the planning permissions and hazardous substances consents. The High Court refused leave in July 2005 on grounds of delay—the claims were filed outside the three-month limit—and because quashing decisions would cause substantial hardship to operators and detriment to good administration. The applicants had known of the relevant decisions by August to October 2004.

**Alleged Violations:**
The applicants alleged that the respondent State failed to: (1) properly regulate hazardous activities by ensuring comprehensive risk assessment covering marine risks; (2) disseminate information about risks to those affected; and (3) provide adequate access to safety information. They argued these failures breached the State's positive obligations under Articles 2 and 8, particularly regarding the regulation of dangerous industrial activities near populated areas.
001-110171:
In *Kaperzyński v. Poland* (Application no. 43206/07), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined the applicant’s complaint under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant, Przemysław Kaperzyński, a Polish national born in 1964, was at the material time editor-in-chief of the local weekly newspaper *Iławski Tydzień*.

On 17 October 2005, the newspaper published an article co-authored by the applicant, entitled “Municipality in danger; authorities fail to see problem.” The article concerned the sewage system in the Iława municipality. It alleged that the sanitary situation posed significant public health risks; that extensive investment was needed but funds were lacking; that municipal authorities were acting slowly and incompetently; that they prioritized saving money over preventing health risks; that water quality was unsatisfactory; and that the mayor, despite two terms in office, had failed to address the problems properly.

On the same day, the mayor of Iława sent a letter complaining about the article. Its first paragraph was ironic and questioned the applicant’s intentions, suggesting he had acted in his own personal interest. The mayor also criticized the article’s tone, doubted whether the newspaper had readers, and then requested publication of a rectification under section 31 § 1 read with section 32 of the Press Act 1984. He asserted that developing the sewage network was a municipal priority, listed completed projects from the previous five years and planned projects for 2007–2013, stated that water quality was monitored by appropriate services, and referred to modernization and overhaul projects.

The applicant neither replied to nor published the mayor’s letter. The municipality later brought a private bill of indictment against him before the Elbląg District Court for failure to publish a rectification or reply, an offence under section 46 § 1 of the Press Act. The applicant argued that the mayor’s letter could not reasonably be treated as a rectification: it was not factual or objective, contained personal criticism and innuendo, resembled a “reply,” exceeded the permitted length, and infringed his and other journalists’ personal rights. He also relied on section 33 of the Press Act, which required refusal of publication if the content was incompatible with principles of social coexistence.

On 13 December 2006, the District Court found the applicant guilty. It held that he was clearly obliged to publish the letter as a rectification or reply, knew of that obligation, and had no objective grounds for refusing. It emphasized that he neither published the letter nor explained his refusal. He was sentenced to four months’ restriction of liberty, in the form of twenty hours’ community service per month, suspended for two years; deprived of the right to practise journalism for two years; and the judgment was ordered to be displayed at the Iława Municipal Office. The court reasoned that his failure prevented a fair public debate and undermined confidence in the democratically elected municipal executive. On 29 March 2007, the Elbląg Regional Court upheld the judgment.

Relevant domestic law under the Press Act obliged an editor-in-chief to publish, free of charge, a factually based rectification of untrue or inaccurate statements, or a factually based reply to material infringing personal rights. Section 46 criminalized refusal. Constitutional Court judgments in 2004 and 2010 found related provisions imprecise; in 2010, sections 46 § 1, 31, and 32 § 1 were declared incompatible with Article 46 of the Polish Constitution, though they remained applicable for up to eighteen months. The applicant alleged that his criminal conviction for refusing to publish the mayor’s letter breached his right to freedom of expression under Article 10.
001-110271:
In *Balogun v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 60286/09), the applicant, Mr Moshood Abiola Balogun, a Nigerian national born in 1986, alleged that his deportation to Nigeria would breach Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Article 3 was engaged by his claimed risk of suicide and mental health deterioration upon removal; Article 8 concerned his alleged family and private life in the United Kingdom.

The applicant claimed to have arrived in the UK aged three, but official records began in 1994, when he was eight, after a family court sought clarification of his immigration status in his aunt’s residence-order application. In 2003 his aunt applied for indefinite leave to remain, listing him as a dependant. Southwark Social Services also applied, stating that the aunt had thrown him out in January 2002 and that he had entered foster care; he alleged beatings by his aunt and her boyfriend from age three. Indefinite leave was granted in December 2003 outside the immigration rules. He lived in foster care from 2002 until age eighteen, then in council accommodation alone.

In February 2007, aged twenty, he was convicted of two counts of possessing Class A drugs with intent to supply and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He pleaded guilty on the basis that he had been coerced by a group he feared after being shot in 2005. In October 2007 the Secretary of State notified him of the intention to deport him. The Secretary of State found no evidence he had been in the UK since age three; his aunt said he was left with her at age five; the first official record was at age eight. Even accepting a long stay, only four years had been with valid leave.
