It held that the relevant value was the original HRK 5,000 stated in the civil action, as the claimant had not formally amended the claim itself. This value fell below the statutory threshold for Supreme Court appeals. The applicant alleged this arbitrary re-evaluation by the Supreme Court deprived her of access to the highest court.
001-174424:
The applicant, M.O., is an Eritrean national born in 1990. He grew up in Eritrea, entered Switzerland illegally on 23 June 2014 and applied for asylum the next day. He was heard by the Swiss asylum authorities on 1 July 2014, 11 March 2015 and 29 January 2016, with an interpreter and translated records; NGO witnesses attended the later hearings. He claimed he left school after eighth grade, was called up for military service, tried to avoid it, reported for duty, attempted to escape, was caught, beaten and imprisoned in Wi’a. In the first hearing he said he was detained from June 2012 to September 2013; in the second he said March to October 2013. He described limited military training, no weapon use, and no superior, unit or military number. He said he escaped from prison, stayed briefly in Eritrea, left illegally via Mereb on 3 October 2013, was picked up by Ethiopian soldiers and later registered in the Hitsas refugee camp. In the third hearing he said a smuggler, not a neighbour, had helped him; he left A. at about 6 p.m., lost his way and was apprehended around 3–4 a.m. He submitted a student card, church deacon card, Italian food-distribution card, marriage certificate from 2010, his son’s baptism certificate from 2012, a deacon attestation and a UNHCR letter confirming registration in Hitsas on 8 November 2013. He stated he was married and had a son born in October 2012.

On 8 March 2016 the State Secretariat for Migration rejected the asylum request and ordered his departure. It found his account not credible because of contradictions about the detention period, military training, schooling, departure and illegal exit. On 14 April 2016 the applicant appealed to the Federal Administrative Court. He argued that his deacon status had delayed conscription until the 2010 change in practice, that poor students were sent to Wi’a, that he tried to escape and was detained from March to September 2013, and that his family arranged a smuggler. He attributed date errors to poor education, stressed consistent elements, scars and fear, and relied on the UNHCR registration and the impossibility of legal exit. He claimed refugee status for fear of ill-treatment for desertion, alternatively temporary admission based on post-flight grounds and Article 3.

On 9 May 2016 the Federal Administrative Court rejected the appeal. It found the asylum claim not credibly demonstrated, citing irreconcilable school dates, a substance-poor military account, and fundamental contradictions on detention duration and dates. It found his departure account insufficient and said the UNHCR camp letter did not establish individual persecution risk. It held removal possible, permitted and reasonable under the Aliens Act, noting he was young, healthy and had a support network. The State Secretariat set a voluntary departure deadline that expired on 17 July 2016.

The record also contains country information describing Eritrea’s open-ended national service, forced labour, punishment of deserters and draft evaders, strict exit controls and risks for illegal exit and returnees, including detention and ill-treatment. The applicant alleged before the Court that expulsion to Eritrea would violate Articles 3 and 4 of the Convention.
001-174386:
The case *Svorcan v. Montenegro* (Application no. 1253/08) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 December 2007 by Olga Svorcan, a Serbian national born in 1950 and living in Belgrade. The Montenegrin Government was represented by V. Pavličić. On 3 December 2014, the Court communicated to the Government only the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the proceedings in question; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The underlying facts concerned civil property litigation. In the first set of proceedings, on 18 September 1995, the applicant and her family members instituted proceedings before the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi, seeking division of their joint property. On 5 May 1997, that court discontinued the proceedings and instructed the parties to initiate a separate civil case because a number of contentious issues remained.

The second set of proceedings began on 8 September 1997, when the applicant’s cousins brought a claim against the applicant and her parents before the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi. On 30 December 1997, the cousins lodged an additional claim concerning the same matter. The two claims were joined and examined in the same civil proceedings. On 1 October 2002, the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi ruled against the applicant and her parents. On 25 June 2004, the High Court in Podgorica upheld that judgment on appeal. The judgment thereby became final and was served on the applicant on 15 July 2004.

On 17 August 2004, the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law (*revizija*) with the Supreme Court of Montenegro. This appeal was misplaced until 20 January 2006, when the applicant’s lawyers intervened and urged the authorities to find it. On 12 January 2007, the applicant amended her appeal on points of law. On 14 February 2008, the Supreme Court of Montenegro rejected the appeal as unfounded. That decision was served on the applicant on 6 March 2008.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the prolonged duration of the civil proceedings. The second set of proceedings ran from September 1997 until the Supreme Court’s decision was served in March 2008—approximately ten years and six months. The first-instance phase lasted from 1997 until October 2002, about five years; the High Court appeal phase lasted from 2002 until June 2004, about two years; and the Supreme Court phase lasted from August 2004 until March 2008, about three years and seven months. A notable delay was the period during which the appeal on points of law was misplaced: from 17 August 2004 until 20 January 2006, roughly seventeen months, before it was located following the applicant’s lawyers’ intervention. After it was found, the applicant amended it in January 2007, and the Supreme Court decided it in February 2008.

The only complaint that survived for examination was that the length of these civil proceedings violated the applicant’s rights. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-171489:
**Case: Babak Hasanov v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 43137/13 and 43153/13), ECtHR, 16 February 2017.**

The applicant, Babak Hasanov, was an Azerbaijani national and a member of the opposition Popular Front Party of Azerbaijan. The case concerned two administrative arrests and convictions following opposition demonstrations in Baku on 17 November 2012 and 10 March 2013.

For the first demonstration, organisers gave notice to the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA), which refused authorisation in general terms, saying the assembly would not comply with the Law on Freedom of Assembly and that the proposed square was a public leisure area. Organisers nevertheless proceeded. The applicant attended; he claimed the demonstration was intended to be and remained peaceful. Participants demanded democratic reforms and protested against restrictions on freedom of assembly. Police dispersed the demonstration shortly after it began. The applicant was arrested, allegedly by plain-clothes officers, taken to a police station, and charged under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) for deliberately failing to comply with a lawful police order. He refused to sign the administrative-offence report and claimed he was never served copies of case documents and had no access to a lawyer after arrest or in custody.

For the second demonstration, no proper prior notice was given to the BCEA; information was spread through Facebook and the press. The protest concerned the deaths of soldiers. The applicant attended and was again arrested when police dispersed the assembly. He was charged under Article 298.2 of the CAO for participating in a public assembly not organised in accordance with the law. A State-funded lawyer was instructed to assist him.

In both cases, the applicant was brought before the Sabail District Court soon after arrest—on 17 November 2012 in the first case and on 11 March 2013 in the second, after an overnight police custody. He alleged the hearings were very brief, that the public was excluded without a formal closure decision, and that he was not allowed to hire a lawyer of his choice. State-funded lawyers were appointed. In the first case, no submissions by that lawyer were recorded; in the second, the lawyer merely said in general terms that the applicant was not guilty. The first court heard no witnesses. The second questioned three police officers, who said the applicant was arrested for staging an unauthorised demonstration, and a defence witness, who said he and the applicant were arrested before entering the assembly area.

On 17 November 2012, the applicant was convicted under Article 310.1 and sentenced to seven days’ administrative detention. On 11 March 2013, he was convicted under Article 298.2 and sentenced to six days’ administrative detention. His appeals argued that the demonstrations were peaceful, his arrests unlawful, and the hearings unfair. He also complained that the courts ignored his second-degree disability, which under domestic law should have prevented administrative detention. In the first appeal he had a lawyer of choice; in the second he was unrepresented. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals on 26 November 2012 and 27 March 2013.

At the relevant time, Article 5 IV of the Law on Freedom of Assembly did not require prior written notification for spontaneous assemblies. Article 298 of the CAO originally punished assembly-rule breaches by reprimand or a small fine, while Article 310.1 allowed a fine or administrative detention up to fifteen days if a fine was inadequate. Law no. 462-IVQD, effective 1 January 2013, amended Article 298 to expressly punish participation in assemblies organised in breach of the rules and introduced detention up to fifteen days. Law no. 457-IVQD increased the Article 310.1 fine. International documents, including PACE Resolution 1917 (2013) and a Council of Europe Commissioner report, criticised the restrictive climate for assembly in Azerbaijan, the blanket ban on protests in central Baku, and the chilling effect of increased penalties.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s communicated complaints under Articles 3, 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11 of the Convention, particularly concerning freedom of assembly, liberty, fair trial, and legality of penalties.
001-178701:
The case concerns two applications lodged by Austrian media companies Standard Verlagsgesellschaft mbH and derstandard.at GmbH, later merged. The applicant company publishes the daily newspaper *Der Standard* and the online news portal *derstandard.at*. It alleged a violation of its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The dispute arose from articles published on 25 and 26 November 2011 concerning the Carinthian Regional Hospital Operating Company (KABEG), a public-law institution operating five hospitals. The articles reported a “spying accusation” against KABEG’s board of management. According to disclosed minutes, I.M., the board member responsible for human resources, had allegedly ordered the spying on a confidential employees’ meeting of doctors at Klagenfurt Regional Hospital by sending an informant who prepared a transcript. The medical director, who had criticised KABEG management and accused it of using “Stasi methods,” was dismissed without notice shortly after the meeting. The article further stated that K.S.—chairperson of KABEG’s supervisory board, leader of the Freedom Party of Carinthia in the regional parliament, and brother of the Deputy Governor—was “supposed to be the spiritus rector” of the spying operation. It noted that K.S. had also pressured journalists over critical KABEG reports.

K.S. brought two sets of proceedings. First, he initiated private prosecution for defamation under the Media Act, claiming compensation and publication of the judgment. The applicant argued that the “spiritus rector” statement was a permissible value judgment with a factual basis: K.S. was close to I.M., supported her in the public debate, had been linked to other spying allegations, and had publicly announced practices of investigating and spying on politically unpopular individuals. The Vienna Regional Criminal Court initially rejected the claim, finding the term neither defamatory nor an allegation of specific conduct. The Vienna Court of Appeal reversed, holding that, in context, the statement suggested K.S. was the “spin doctor” or initiator of the spying operation and thus amounted to a defamatory statement of fact. The applicant expressly declined to prove the truth of that allegation. The Regional Criminal Court therefore ordered the applicant to pay €3,000 compensation—€1,500 for each publication—and to publish the judgment under Section 6 of the Media Act. The Court of Appeal upheld this, and the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s renewal application, finding the interference justified and the compensation low.

Second, K.S. obtained a civil injunction under Article 1330 of the Civil Code prohibiting the applicant from repeating that he had been or was supposed to have been the “spiritus rector” of the spying operation. After the Media Act proceedings ended, the Commercial Court granted the injunction, treating the criminal conviction as binding. The Court of Appeal confirmed that the final conviction under the Media Act bound the civil courts as to both the facts and the legal assessment, including the defamatory meaning of the statement, and refused leave for an ordinary appeal. The applicant did not lodge an extraordinary appeal.

The key alleged violation was that these domestic decisions interfered with the applicant’s freedom of expression by treating the “spiritus rector” statement as a defamatory fact, imposing media-law compensation and a civil injunction, and giving the criminal conviction binding effect in later civil proceedings.
001-178352:
**Summary of *Leuska and Others v. Estonia* (Application no. 64734/11)**

The case concerned four applicants: Ms K. Leuska, Mr A. Leuska, Ms P. Esop, and Ms K.-B. Esop. On 17 July 2010, the first and second applicants’ son was killed in a traffic accident, and the fourth applicant sustained serious injuries. The third applicant is the fourth applicant’s mother. The applicants joined the criminal proceedings against the suspect, J., as victims.

On 9 and 10 December 2010, the applicants lodged a civil action within the criminal proceedings against J., seeking compensation for non-pecuniary damage and reimbursement of legal costs incurred in the criminal proceedings. On 28 January 2011, they concluded an out-of-court settlement with J. and informed the prosecutor that they agreed to the settlement procedure. On 4 February 2011, their consent was recorded in a report signed by the prosecutor and their representatives. The report noted that the applicants had given up their non-pecuniary damage claims but had not given up their claim for reimbursement of legal costs. At that time, they had not submitted an itemised list of costs or supporting documents.

On 11 February 2011, J. consented to the settlement procedure. The prosecutor, J., and J.’s counsel signed a settlement agreement stating, inter alia, that the victims had withdrawn the civil claims lodged in the criminal proceedings. On 14 February 2011, the Harju County Court committed J. for trial and scheduled a hearing for 7 March 2011. Only J., his counsel, and the prosecutor were summoned; the applicants were not summoned.

On 4 March 2011, the applicants lodged a claim for legal costs of EUR 6,483.66 and submitted supporting documents, which the County Court received on 7 March 2011. At the hearing, J., his counsel, and the prosecutor attended. According to the court record, the judge disclosed the applicants’ costs claim. J. asked the court not to examine it, arguing that it had been absorbed by the out-of-court settlement agreement. The applicants alleged that they had not been allowed to address the court despite being present in the court building.

In its judgment of the same date, the Harju County Court convicted J. of traffic and driving offences, imposed a suspended prison sentence, withdrew his driving licence, and ordered him to pay certain State expenses. It held that the victims had given up their civil claims. The judgment made no reference to the applicants’ claim for reimbursement of legal costs.

The applicants appealed, complaining that they had not been allowed to attend the hearing and that their costs claim had been left undecided. On 23 March 2011, the County Court refused to examine the appeal, finding that the applicants were not parties to the court proceedings and had no right to appeal under Articles 246 and 318 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed their appeal on 13 April 2011, relying on the rules that a victim cannot revoke consent to the settlement procedure and need not be summoned to a settlement hearing. The Supreme Court refused to examine the appeal on 3 October 2011, but noted that in settlement proceedings courts should still verify unresolved questions, including costs, and should not overlook such matters.

The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the Harju County Court had failed to decide their claim for compensation for legal costs incurred as victims and had failed to hear oral evidence from them. These complaints were communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-170456:
Mr Boštjan Koprivnikar, born in 1979 and detained in Dob pri Mirni, lodged application no. 67503/13 against Slovenia. He alleged that the overall thirty-year prison sentence imposed on him breached Article 7 of the Convention. He was represented by M. Petek; the Government by A. Vran.

On 23 April 1999 the 1999 Amendment to the 1994 Criminal Code entered into force. It introduced a maximum thirty-year prison sentence for the most serious intentional offences. The then applicable rules on combining multiple sentences provided that if any offence carried a thirty-year sentence, only that sentence was to be imposed; otherwise, the overall sentence had to exceed each individual sentence but could not exceed their total or twenty years’ imprisonment.

On 17 September 2004 the Ljubljana District Court convicted the applicant of robbery and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. He served that sentence from 7 December 2007 to 7 December 2011.

On 1 November 2008 the 2008 Criminal Code entered into force. It set the general maximum term at thirty years and introduced life imprisonment for certain serious crimes. Its Article 53 provided that if two or more thirty-year sentences were imposed, an overall life sentence was to be imposed; if prison sentences were imposed for all multiple offences, the overall sentence had to exceed each individual sentence but could not exceed their total or twenty years. It contained no separate rule for the situation where only one of the combined sentences was thirty years.

On 16 June 2009 the Ljubljana District Court convicted the applicant of paying with a bad cheque and fraudulent use of a bank card between 19 January and 19 August 2005, sentencing him to five months’ imprisonment. That judgment became final on 7 October 2009, and he began serving the sentence on 7 December 2011.

In the meantime, on 9 April 2009 the Ljubljana District Court found the applicant guilty, with another person, of murder committed on 15 September 2002. It sentenced him to thirty years’ imprisonment, the maximum under the 1994 Criminal Code applicable at the time of the offence. The Ljubljana Higher Court upheld the conviction on 9 December 2009, and it became final that day.

On 28 November 2011 the applicant applied to the Ljubljana District Court to join the three prison terms into an overall sentence. On 13 January 2012 the District Court joined the three sentences—including the completed robbery sentence—and imposed an overall thirty-year sentence. Applying the 2008 Criminal Code before the 2011 Amendment, it noted that Article 53 conditions had been met but not previously applied. It acknowledged that Article 53 § 2(2) provided a maximum of twenty years, but held that the legislature had made an obvious error, later rectified by the 2011 Amendment, because the 1994 Code had provided that a thirty-year sentence combined with others would consist only of that term.

The applicant appealed, arguing lack of legal basis, breach of the rule of law and nullum crimen et nulla poena sine lege, and that semantic interpretation should prevail and ambiguities should not be construed to his detriment. On 29 May 2012 the Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal and upheld the judgment, reiterating the lower court’s reasoning. On 6 December 2012 the Supreme Court rejected his application for protection of legality, disagreeing that semantic interpretation had priority and relying on historical and systematic interpretation. On 24 April 2013 the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint.

On 24 March 2015 the applicant was convicted of another murder committed between 30 June and 15 September 2002 and sentenced to thirty years; a new overall thirty-year sentence covered the prior overall sentence, another four-month sentence, and the new thirty-year sentence. His appeal and protection-of-legality application were dismissed, the latter by the Supreme Court on 2 June 2016.
001-176765:
In *Vučinić v. Montenegro* (App. no. 44533/10, ECtHR, 5 September 2017), the applicant, Petar Vučinić, a Montenegrin national born in 1949, lodged an application under Article 34 of the Convention. The only complaint communicated to the Government concerned the length of civil proceedings; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Government objected to the case being examined by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The factual background was that the applicant had worked for an export trading company based in Ljubljana, Slovenia. After the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, his employer closed its Podgorica office on 15 October 1991. Under the domestic law then in force, the applicant was entitled to compensation amounting to 24 monthly salaries. In October 1991 he founded a new trading company in his former employer’s offices. On 25 March 1992 he requested a certificate allowing his new company to continue providing services from the Secretariat of Commerce and Development in Podgorica. He received that certificate on 3 October 1997 from the Ministry of Commerce.

The alleged length violation arose from two sets of civil proceedings. In the first set, on 29 December 1998 the applicant sued the Court of First Instance in Podgorica for pecuniary loss suffered while awaiting the certificate. On 10 March 1999 the Court of First Instance found it lacked competence and rejected the claim. The High Court quashed that decision on 17 September 1999 and remitted the case. On 30 April 2004 the Court of First Instance ruled partly in the applicant’s favour. The High Court overturned that judgment on 24 January 2008 and rejected his claim. The Supreme Court quashed the High Court’s judgment on 7 May 2008 and remitted the case. On 11 June 2009 the High Court again rejected the claim, and on 4 March 2010 the Supreme Court upheld that decision. It was served on the applicant on 1 April 2010.

In the second set, on 23 April 2002 the applicant lodged a claim for payment of the 24 monthly salaries against the Municipality of Podgorica and the Republic of Montenegro. On 5 February 2004 the Court of First Instance rejected the claim. The High Court quashed that decision on 9 November 2004 and remitted the case. On 16 May 2006 the Court of First Instance again rejected the claim. On 27 May 2008 the High Court partly quashed that judgment and remitted the quashed part. The applicant appealed on points of law concerning the upheld part; the Supreme Court rejected that appeal on 3 March 2009. On 16 January 2010 the Court of First Instance rejected the claim in the remitted part, and the High Court upheld that decision on 4 June 2010. On 18 January 2011 the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s appeal on points of law, served on him on 7 February 2011. In 2011 he lodged a constitutional appeal; on 19 April 2013 the Constitutional Court rejected it, and that decision was served on 28 May 2013.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the civil proceedings exceeded a reasonable time. The first set lasted from December 1998 to April 2010, over eleven years. The second lasted from April 2002 to February 2011, nearly nine years, with a further constitutional appeal until May 2013. Multiple remittals, repeated re-hearings, and successive appellate cycles were central to the alleged violation under Article 6 §1 of the Convention, namely the right to a hearing within a reasonable time.
001-174404:
In *Arnarson v. Iceland* (App. No. 58781/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined an Icelandic journalist’s complaint that a domestic defamation judgment violated his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant, Ólafur Arnarson, was a journalist and freelance writer for the web-based media site *Pressan*. The dispute arose from public debate about the Federation of Icelandic Fishing Vessel Owners (“LIU”), an organisation representing fishing vessel owners and safeguarding their economic, legal and social interests. “A” was the LIU’s chief executive officer.

Arnarson claimed that a private website, “B,” published anonymous blogs that constantly lobbied for the LIU and discredited persons who spoke against it. On 21 July 2010, the newspaper *DV* published an article about rumours that the LIU was providing financial support to website B, allegedly ISK 1,500,000 per month. The article did not mention A. The same day, Arnarson published an article on *Pressan* under the headline “LIU pays 20 million for offensive material,” referring to the *DV* article. A sent a statement to *Pressan* denying that the LIU had supported website B; this was published on 23 July 2010.

On 24 July 2010, Arnarson published a response. He stated that A had to do better than merely denying direct payments and that the LIU, directed by A, was accountable for the offensive anonymous material on website B. He also questioned whether respectable representatives of the LIU’s member companies had agreed to the organisation’s funds being paid through intermediaries to “gossips” such as the owners of website B.

In a later article, Arnarson stated that the LIU supposedly supported website B with almost ISK 20 million annually through companies owned by Mr Y, who also owned website B. He added that he knew some LIU board members were unaware of the support because the payments were well disguised in the organisation’s financial records. He further wrote that he had been told it was possible that no LIU board members knew that the organisation’s millions were being used to support anonymous slander on website B, and that A alone had decided to use the funds that way. He noted that he had not received confirmation of that last statement. A photograph of A appeared beside the article.

On 28 December 2011, A lodged defamation proceedings before the Reykjaness District Court, requesting that four statements be declared null and void. On 29 November 2012, the District Court found that only one statement was defamatory: the statement that some LIU board members were unaware of the support because payments were well disguised, and that A alone may have decided to use the funds for anonymous slander. The court held that readers could understand this as implying accounting deception or fraud by abuse of position and negligence, namely that A had allocated LIU funds against the board’s will and without authorisation. Since Arnarson could not prove the statement true, the court declared it null and void and ordered him to pay A ISK 300,000 in non-pecuniary damages plus interest and ISK 450,000 in costs.

The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 25 February 2013. Arnarson complained under Article 10 that the District Court judgment—final after the refusal of leave—interfered with his right to freedom of expression and was not necessary in a democratic society. The key facts therefore concerned a journalist’s public-interest reporting on alleged lobbying, anonymous online attacks, and misuse of LIU funds by its CEO, balanced against the CEO’s reputation rights. The case raised whether the domestic courts properly considered the public debate, A’s public role, and whether the statements were factual accusations or value judgments/insinuations.
001-172855:
The application was lodged on 28 January 2014 by six Albanian and Greek nationals against Greece. They were represented by K. Tsitselikis and A. Spathis. The Greek Government was represented by State Legal Council delegates; the Albanian Government did not intervene. At the time of lodging, the applicants were detained in Korydallos Prison, Athens.

The first applicant was held in Korydallos from 7 March 2013 and remained there when observations were submitted, except for temporary transfers to Ioannina Prison (3–11 July 2013) and Komotini Prison (2–17 December 2013). The second applicant was detained in Korydallos from 22 March 2013 and the third from 21 August 2013; both remained detained when they submitted observations. The fourth applicant was in Korydallos from 26 June 2013 to 1 May 2014, except for periods in Chania Prison from 17 July to 3 September 2013, 27 November to 10 December 2013, and 6–17 February 2014. The fifth applicant was in Korydallos from 22 May 2013 to 19 June 2014, except 20–28 March 2013. The sixth was in Korydallos from 30 January 2013 to 15 August 2014.

The applicants alleged overcrowding: the prison held about 2,400 prisoners though designed for 700. They were detained in wings A and D in 9 sq m cells, including sanitary facilities, shared by three or four prisoners, leaving under 3 sq m each. Toilets were only partially separated; heating and hot water were insufficient; inmates used a washbasin to wash themselves, dishes and clothes. Cells were dirty and infested with cockroaches and pests, with no extermination. Rubbish was not properly collected and food remains stayed in cells and corridors for days. Prisoners were not adequately separated by health condition or drug use. Medical care was inadequate, especially psychological care. Inmates were confined to cells 16 hours daily, with no recreational or educational activities, and ate poor-quality meals in cells. The prison was understaffed and unsafe.

The Government submitted that the first to fifth applicants were held in wings A and D. Cells measured 9.60 sq m and held three, rarely four, detainees. The first applicant was also held in wing E: one cell of 10.44 sq m and another of 42.78 sq m holding 10–22 detainees, though 22 only briefly. All cells had windows with sufficient light and were furnished with washbasin, toilet, beds, table, chairs and usually shelves. Wings A–D had twelve communal showers each and wing E nine; each wing provided 2,000 litres of hot water daily. Sheets and blankets were provided unless detainees used their own. There was central heating and summer fans. Cells were disinfected and cleaned twice daily by detainee crews; rubbish bins existed. The infirmary was open 24 hours with eighteen doctors and three nurses; transfers to Korydallos Prison Hospital, Psychiatric Hospital or external hospitals were possible. Medical records showed treatment, and social services assisted. Menus were varied. Prisoners had four to five hours daily in the yard, sport, television, a lending library and book club, jobs, and “second chance” school. The Government made no observations on the sixth applicant.

The CPT’s report on its April 2013 visit, published 16 October 2014, stated that Korydallos Men’s Prison held more than 2,300 prisoners for an official capacity of 840. Cells designed for single occupancy, measuring 9.5 sq m, routinely held three or four inmates; some slept on mattresses on the floor or in toilet areas. Cell A-3 in wing E measured 36 sq m, had 16 beds but held 27 inmates, leaving under 1.5 sq m per person; nine slept on the concrete floor on filthy mattresses, two in the toilet area, and the cell was infested with cockroaches and bed bugs. Cell B-3 had 14 beds and held 19 prisoners, five on mattresses on the floor; there was no artificial light at night and the toilet was filthy. Garbage containers were full of food waste. Health-care resources had deteriorated: four GP posts were abolished, no full-time doctor worked there, visiting GPs provided only 15 hours weekly and sometimes failed to attend, and two-monthly rotations hindered continuity; the CPT considered at least four full-time GPs necessary. A wing of about 400 inmates usually had one or two officers by day; at night eight officers covered the entire prison.

The relevant domestic law and practice were described in the earlier judgment Kanakis v. Greece (no. 2).
001-176964:
**Goldnagl v. Austria** (Application no. 6822/12) concerned an Austrian national, Ingrid Goldnagl, born in 1939. She married T.G. in 1965; they separated in 1990 and divorced in 1996 due to T.G.’s sole fault. The case before the European Court of Human Rights arose from the extraordinary length of civil proceedings concerning spousal maintenance.

On 2 August 1991 the applicant lodged a maintenance claim with the Döbling District Court and sought interim provisional maintenance. An interim order was issued in February 1992 and confirmed in June 1992. After T.G. failed to comply, enforcement proceedings were granted in July 1992. The main maintenance case then generated numerous hearings, expert reports on T.G.’s income, and appeals. In March 1997 the District Court partly granted and partly dismissed the claim; both parties appealed, and the Regional Court quashed that judgment in October 1997. Further hearings and a second expert report followed.

In 1998–1999 T.G. obtained a stop to enforcement, and the applicant’s appeal was dismissed in April 1999. In May 1999 she sought fresh interim maintenance and a freeze on T.G.’s pension fund and redundancy money. In June 1999 the District Court ordered monthly payments of 20,000 Austrian Schillings and barred payouts from those funds. T.G.’s objections and appeals were dismissed by January 2000. T.G. then sought a reduction because of retirement; the decision rejecting that request was quashed, and further hearings followed. The main proceedings continued with hearings in 1999, 2001, and 2002; an expert supplement was requested in February 2002 and submitted in April 2003.

In July 2003 private insolvency proceedings were opened against T.G. The liquidator sought lifting of the interim maintenance order, and the maintenance proceedings were suspended. The applicant sought acknowledgment of a maintenance claim of EUR 632,253.65 in the insolvency proceedings, but the liquidator refused. In October 2003 the District Court lifted the freeze on T.G.’s pension and redundancy money but maintained provisional maintenance; the liquidator appealed. The applicant requested continuation in November 2003. In 2004 the Regional Court rejected the liquidator’s appeal, but the Supreme Court partly granted an extraordinary appeal. T.G. then sought a reduction because of insolvency; that request was dismissed in June 2005 and confirmed in September 2005.

In September 2005 the applicant filed a request to accelerate the proceedings under the Court Act. The Regional Court partly granted it in November 2005 and ordered a hearing within four weeks. A January 2006 hearing did not proceed because the applicant was hospitalized; an April 2006 hearing was then adjourned for letters of request to Zurich. In September 2006 the applicant sought further letters of request, and in March 2007 she filed a second acceleration request. The Zurich court submitted T.G.’s bank data in September 2007; further witnesses were heard in February 2009. In May 2009 the applicant asked to suspend maintenance payments from the insolvency opening, which was granted in August 2009.

In March 2010 the District Court issued a partial judgment on maintenance until July 2003. The applicant appealed; the Regional Court confirmed in January 2011, and the Supreme Court rejected her extraordinary appeal in June 2011, making the partial judgment final. In October 2011 she requested continuation for the period after July 2003. Further hearings took place in 2014 and 2015, and the proceedings apparently remained pending.

Separately, T.G.’s insolvency proceedings continued. In December 2011 the applicant filed a fresh maintenance claim in the Salzburg District Court against the liquidator. It was initially rejected as res judicata in February 2012, but that decision was quashed in April 2012. Hearings occurred between 2013 and 2014; in August 2015 the Salzburg District Court partly granted her claim, but she appealed, and those proceedings also remained pending.

The applicant lodged her ECtHR application on 26 January 2012. On 12 May 2015 the Court communicated only the complaint concerning the length of proceedings; the remainder was declared inadmissible. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the maintenance proceedings’ duration from 1991 onward, repeated appeals and expert delays, insolvency-related suspension, two acceleration requests, and the fact that the main proceedings were still apparently pending years later.
001-175667:
**M v. the Netherlands** (Application no. 2156/10), a 2017 European Court of Human Rights case, concerned a Netherlands national employed by the AIVD, the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service, as an audio editor and interpreter. Because of his role, the applicant had access to classified information and was bound by a duty of secrecy. He was suspected of forwarding copies of classified documents to unauthorized persons, including individuals then under covert AIVD investigation for possible terrorist activity. On 30 September 2004 he was arrested, charged with divulging State secret information, and detained on remand.

The alleged Article 6 violations arose from the way national-security secrecy shaped the criminal proceedings. The AIVD informed the applicant that he remained bound by secrecy and that discussing covered matters with anyone, including his defence counsel, could constitute a further offence. His lawyers were also warned they could be prosecuted if they disclosed State secrets to third parties. At trial before the Rotterdam Regional Court, defence counsel protested that these restrictions undermined effective communication and defence preparation. They requested the internal AIVD report forming the basis of the prosecution, which was absent from the case file, and unredacted copies of the allegedly leaked documents, which were included only in redacted form. They also sought an unconditional release from the secrecy duty. The prosecutor added some documents but refused unconditional release.

The AIVD head granted only a conditional exemption: the applicant could discuss covered matters solely with two named counsel; he could not reveal AIVD staff or source identities; he could discuss only material contained in the case file; the information had to be strictly necessary for the defence; and counsel’s use of such information required consultation with the investigating judge. The AIVD would then determine whether State secrets were at stake. Witnesses were also affected. Some AIVD witnesses refused to answer based on secrecy. Unnamed AIVD staff were heard at a secret location, heavily disguised, with voice distortion, and an AIVD official present could prevent answers. Requests to hear numerous other witnesses were refused, partly for lack of time.

On appeal, the Court of Appeal accepted that the secrecy duty restricted confidential lawyer-client consultation and could, if unmitigated, prevent a fair trial. It nonetheless found the conditional release not unreasonable and said that if the defence believed it necessary to breach secrecy to secure a fair trial, it could invoke Article 6 as a justification; the Advocate General initially assured no prosecution would follow. Yet during the appeal hearing, when the applicant began naming AIVD staff, the Advocate General objected and threatened prosecution. The court excluded the public. Defence counsel later submitted questions naming AIVD members and sources and addressing working methods, but the Advocate General again threatened prosecution if those questions were answered. The Court of Appeal convicted the applicant and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment.

The Supreme Court later reduced the sentence by two months for excessive length but upheld the conviction. It stated that if disclosure were necessary for a fair trial and the defence handicap was not sufficiently compensated, the prosecution should be declared inadmissible. The applicant alleged that the AIVD had exercised decisive control over the evidence, restricting his and the courts’ access to information, controlling its use, making it impossible to instruct counsel effectively, and preventing him from offering witness evidence, in violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b), (c), and (d) of the Convention.
001-173624:
In *Krunoslava Zovko v. Croatia* (Application no. 56935/13, 23 May 2017), the applicant, a Croatian national born in 1965, alleged that the administrative proceedings concerning her sick-leave entitlement were unfair under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The central issue was whether her sick leave from 27 October 2011 should have been based on a work-related injury sustained on 20 April 2009, which would have entitled her to compensation for lost salary.

On 20 April 2009, the applicant was injured in a car accident while returning home from work. On 8 May 2009, the Croatian Health Insurance Fund recognised the injury as work-related, and she received sick leave from 21 April to 3 July 2009. In October 2011, she visited an emergency centre due to neck and back pain and was found to have a severely sore spine with deformity. The next day, her general practitioner found her unable to work and granted sick leave from 27 October 2011, but classified it as based on illness rather than the 2009 work-related injury.

On 3 November 2011, the applicant complained, arguing that the 2011 sick leave should be linked to her 2009 work injury, and submitted medical documentation. Her GP referred her for expert medical evaluation. On 6 December 2011, an authorised doctor at the Zagreb Office of the Fund, specialising in physical medicine and rehabilitation, examined her medical documentation and found no direct causal link between the 2009 work injury and the 2011 sick leave. After the applicant requested a written decision, the Zagreb Office, by decision of 23 January 2012, refused to grant the sick leave on the basis of the work-related injury and dismissed her compensation claim.

The applicant appealed to the Central Office, submitting further medical documentation. An in-house medical commission of three doctors examined her overall medical file and, on 16 March 2012, reported that the 2011 sick leave could not be granted on the basis of the 2009 work injury. On 5 April 2012, the Central Office dismissed her appeal, relying on that report.

The applicant then brought an administrative action in the Zagreb Administrative Court. She contested the Fund’s expert findings, relied on her own medical documentation, alleged a causal link, and requested that she be heard and that an independent expert medical report be obtained. On 27 August 2012, the Administrative Court held a public hearing. The applicant did not attend but was represented by counsel, who reiterated her arguments and evidence proposals. The court dismissed her request to hear her and to obtain a further expert report, then closed the hearing. On 31 August 2012, it dismissed her action, holding that two expert medical bodies and her GP had established no causal link and that she had failed to cast doubt on those findings.

Her constitutional complaint alleged unfairness because she had been excluded from commissioning and obtaining the administrative authorities’ expert reports, while the Administrative Court refused to hear her or order an independent expert report. The Constitutional Court dismissed it as manifestly ill-founded on 6 February 2013. Before the European Court, the communicated complaint concerned the fairness of these administrative proceedings, particularly the reliance on expert medical findings and the refusal of an independent expert examination and hearing.
001-172463:
**Case: Ković and Others v. Serbia**  
**Applications nos. 39611/08, 50121/13 and 2490/14**  
**Judgment: 4 April 2017 (Third Section, Committee)**

The case concerned three Serbian nationals—Nikola Ković, Zoran Ranković and Ivan Bojanić—who complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that various administrative and civil proceedings involving them had exceeded a reasonable time. Their applications were lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 July 2008, 5 June 2013 and 16 December 2013, respectively.

On 18 December 2014, the Court communicated to the Serbian Government the applicants’ complaints concerning the length of administrative and civil proceedings. The remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The Government objected to the case being examined by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are set out in the appended table.

**Nikola Ković** (born 21 July 1941) had proceedings that began in October 2001 and on 9 November 2001. Those proceedings were still pending at the time of the table. Since 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force in respect of Serbia, the total length was 10 years and 8 months before one level of jurisdiction. Ković obtained a decision of the Constitutional Court of Serbia finding a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. Under the regulations then applicable, the Constitutional Court established his right to seek compensation for non-pecuniary damage before the Commission for Damage Compensation. He submitted his compensation request to the Commission on 26 December 2010, but had received no response by the time of the case. This unresolved compensation procedure is a significant fact concerning the effectiveness of the domestic remedy after the Constitutional Court’s finding.

**Zoran Ranković** (born 3 September 1954), represented by Mile Petković, had proceedings that started on 25 July 2002 and ended on 18 May 2012. Since 3 March 2004, the total length was 8 years and 2 months across two levels of jurisdiction. The Constitutional Court found a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time and awarded him a certain sum in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

**Ivan Bojanić** (born 22 April 1978), represented by Dragan Radin, had proceedings that began on 11 March 2004 and ended on 25 May 2011. Since 3 March 2004, the total length was 7 years and 2 months across two levels of jurisdiction. The Constitutional Court also found a violation and awarded him compensation for non-pecuniary damage.

In essence, the applicants’ alleged violation was the excessive length of administrative and civil proceedings contrary to the reasonable-time requirement of Article 6 § 1. The central factual elements are the long durations after 3 March 2004, the number of judicial levels involved, and the prior Constitutional Court decisions. For Ković, the key additional fact is that his subsequent compensation request remained unanswered; for Ranković and Bojanić, the key facts are that the Constitutional Court found violations and awarded them non-pecuniary damages. The Court was therefore called upon to assess whether the length of the proceedings breached Article 6 § 1 in light of those domestic findings and remedies.
001-173802:
**Vardanean v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia** (Application no. 22200/10) concerned two Moldovan nationals, Ernest Vardanean and Irina Vardanean, husband and wife and both journalists. At the time of the events, they lived in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The first applicant worked for a Russian news agency and a Moldovan newspaper. The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 April 2010 against both Moldova and Russia.

The key facts underlying the alleged violations began on 7 April 2010, when agents of the MRT secret service arrested the first applicant on charges of treason and/or espionage for the Republic of Moldova. On the same occasion, the applicants’ apartment was searched and many belongings were seized, including pictures, computers and a bank card. Both applicants later complained about that search.

The first applicant alleged that he had been arrested and detained unlawfully. He further alleged that he had been convicted after unfair criminal proceedings and that the lawyers representing him in the Strasbourg proceedings had not been able to gain access to him. During his detention in the MRT, he met several times with representatives of the MRT secret services, including the chief of the secret services. He was led to believe that his family might suffer if he refused to cooperate. He was asked to record a video in which he admitted having worked for the Moldovan secret services; that video was aired on Transdniestrian television. On another occasion, he was asked to write a letter to foreign ambassadors to Moldova “disclosing” that Moldovan secret services were spying on foreign embassies in Chisinau. He was later given to understand by MRT secret service representatives that the letter had served to create tensions between Chisinau and Western countries and that the whole matter, including his arrest, was being coordinated from Moscow. This allegation was relevant to Russia’s role and responsibility in the case.

On 16 December 2010, a tribunal from the “MRT” convicted the first applicant and sentenced him to fifteen years’ imprisonment. Following international pressure, on 5 May 2011 the president of the “MRT” pardoned him. After that date, the applicant and his family moved to Chisinau. During his detention, the second applicant could visit him only on a limited number of occasions. Lawyers representing the first applicant in the Court proceedings were denied access to him on the ground that they were not members of the “Transdniestrian Bar Association.” This fact was relevant to the complaint about fairness of proceedings and effective access to legal representation.

The Moldovan authorities made numerous attempts to secure the first applicant’s release. They raised the issue with the European Union and the United States in Brussels in April 2010, distributed a circular letter during the April 2010 session of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, and raised it during Committee of Ministers meetings in January and February 2011. The situation was also raised with OSCE representatives in Chisinau, and the Moldovan Prosecutor’s Office opened a criminal investigation into the detention in the “MRT,” although it was later discontinued. Moldova also awarded financial assistance to the first applicant’s family during his detention and transferred to them ownership of a flat in Chisinau worth EUR 53,000 after his release.

The complaints communicated to both respondent Governments were: the first applicant’s unlawful arrest and detention, his unfair criminal conviction, and the inability of his lawyers to access him; and both applicants’ complaint about the search of their home. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-170648:
In *Fortunskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 14729/06), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 2 February 2017. The applicant, Viktor Georgiyevich Fortunskiy, a Ukrainian national born in 1955, lodged his application on 27 March 2006. He was granted legal aid and represented by A. Kristenko.

The case arose from the applicant’s criminal conviction. On 20 December 2005, the Odesa Regional Court of Appeal, sitting as a first-instance court, convicted the applicant and eighteen others of gang-related crimes committed in the Odesa Region between 1995 and 1999, including banditry, illegal possession of firearms, theft, robbery, burglary, infliction of bodily injuries and murder. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment with confiscation of property. The conviction relied mainly on incriminating statements by co-defendants and on stolen objects found during a search of the applicant’s wife’s home on 2 October 1999.

At trial, the applicant denied the charges or refused to give statements. He alleged that he had been ill-treated by police before trial, but the trial court rejected this complaint, relying mainly on the prosecutor’s office’s earlier finding that the complaint was unsubstantiated and on detention-centre authorities’ statements that he had no injuries. During trial, he claimed an alibi and asked the court to summon a witness to confirm that in June 1998 he had lived in another region of Ukraine and could not have committed a crime in Odesa. That request was refused, as were two other requests by the applicant and his lawyer to summon witnesses, partly because they did not specify the relevant charges or explain the importance of the testimony. The applicant also alleged that the presiding judge was not impartial because the judge had allegedly studied with the investigator and one witness was a relative, but he provided no supporting documents. On 20 May 2005, allegedly to protest the trial’s unfairness, he stitched his lips and went on hunger strike; a medical examination found no mental illness.

For his appeal, the applicant requested time to study a 171-volume case file. He was given access between March 2006 and February 2007, but claimed the time was too short and he sometimes had to study the file with other convicts in one cell, so he did not review everything. He lodged an initial appeal on 17 March 2006 and amended it on 23 July 2007, arguing that his conviction was based on false evidence, that the first-instance court was biased, and that it unlawfully refused to summon witnesses. In July 2006, he asked the Court of Appeal to appoint a free lawyer for his appeal and Supreme Court proceedings. A judge told him to request the local bar association; the bar association replied that the Court of Appeal could appoint counsel. He resubmitted the request, but it remained unanswered. On 30 October 2007, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction while excluding the theft charges.

The applicant also complained about detention and access to the Court. He alleged that on 22 November 2007 SIZO guards beat him, causing a head injury; he received no medical assistance and was placed in isolation until 21 December 2007, during which he could not send letters to the Court. After transfer to Dnipropetrovsk Correctional Colony, copies of case documents were taken, his letters to the Court were allegedly blocked or delayed, and he was not allowed phone calls to relatives. The Government denied these claims, relying on SIZO reports describing him as inclined to self-mutilation, incidents where he insulted guards and hit his head, and disciplinary isolation. They maintained that his letters were duly dispatched, requested documents were attached, and he had full access to his case file.

The key alleged violations therefore concerned fair-trial rights, especially refusal to summon an alibi witness, lack of effective legal assistance on appeal, impartiality and access to the case file; ill-treatment and lack of medical assistance in detention; and interference with correspondence/access to the Court.
001-174814:
Case No. 30721/15, *Petrović v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia*, European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 22 June 2017 (final on 22 September 2017). The applicant, Mr Dušan Petrović, a Macedonian and Serbian national, lodged the application on 18 June 2015. He died on 29 March 2016, and his sons, Žika and Aleksandar Petrović, continued the application. The complaints concerning the length of proceedings and the lack of an effective remedy in that regard were communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Serbian Government did not intervene.

The underlying facts concerned restitution proceedings. On 11 December 2002 the applicant instituted proceedings for restitution of a hotel in Skopje that had been confiscated from his predecessor in 1948. On 7 June 2004 a commission within the Ministry of Finance dismissed his claim. His appeal was dismissed by a second-instance commission within the Government on 16 November 2004. Thereafter, the case went back and forth several times between administrative bodies and courts at two levels of jurisdiction. At the time relevant to the application, the restitution proceedings were still pending before the Higher Administrative Court, awaiting a decision on the applicant’s appeal of 26 January 2016 against a judgment of the Administrative Court. The restitution claim had therefore remained unresolved for many years.

Because of the delay, on 3 July 2014 the applicant applied to the Supreme Court for a length-of-proceedings remedy. He sought a ruling that the restitution proceedings had been excessively long, compensation, and a three-month time-limit for the court dealing with his restitution claim to decide. The Supreme Court requested the case file from the Administrative Court between 8 July 2014 and 20 January 2015; the file was forwarded on 13 February 2015. On 28 April 2015 the first-instance panel of the Supreme Court found that the relevant period began on 16 November 2004, that the case was not complex, and that there had been no delays attributable to the applicant. It found a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time and awarded him the equivalent of EUR 810 in compensation. Service of that decision on the applicant, who lived in Serbia, involved further delays and requests between the Ministries of Justice of the two States from June 2015 to March 2016.

The applicant appealed, complaining that the Supreme Court itself had taken too long to decide his length complaint. He relied on section 36(4) of the Courts Act, which required the Supreme Court to decide such complaints within six months. He also argued that the compensation awarded was too low. On 21 March 2016 the second-instance panel of the Supreme Court ruled partly in his favour. It found that the proceedings had lasted ten years, five months and twelve days, and increased compensation to the equivalent of EUR 1,050.

Under domestic law, section 35(6) of the Courts Act made the Supreme Court competent to decide length complaints in accordance with the Convention and the Court’s case-law. Section 36(4) required it to decide within six months of the complaint being lodged, while section 36(5) allowed it to set a time-limit for the pending proceedings and award compensation.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the prolonged restitution proceedings, the repeated remittals, the Supreme Court’s own delay in deciding the length complaint beyond the statutory six-month period, and the modest compensation awarded. These facts underpinned the complaints that the restitution proceedings exceeded a reasonable time and that the domestic length remedy was not effective.
001-174413:
In *Toleski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia*, the applicant, Gorgi Toleski, a Macedonian national, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the extraordinary quashing of a final restitution order in his favour violated legal certainty and unlawfully interfered with his property rights.

In 1966, the Municipality of Ohrid appropriated the right of use of nationalised building land, including a 764 sq. m plot, from the applicant’s predecessor. In 2001, the applicant was declared heir of the right to seek restitution, and in 2002 he requested the land’s return. On 1 September 2003, the Ohrid Restitution Commission granted restitution. It found that no public-interest structures were planned, but rather “beach service facilities and a leisure centre”; the plot was undeveloped building land within the Ohrid lakeshore strip. Authorities had no information that compensation had been paid, and the Municipality confirmed no compensation had been sought. The decision was served on the Solicitor General but was not appealed, becoming final on 29 October 2003. In April 2004, possession was restored to the applicant.

In 2004, a campsite association provided the Solicitor General with documents allegedly showing the plot was developed building land used by the campsite and that compensation had been paid to the applicant’s predecessor. The Solicitor General asked the Appeal Commission to annul, declare null and void, or quash the final restitution decision. The applicant denied compensation and argued factual errors could not justify supervisory review. In 2005, a Ministry of Finance inspection found the land vacant, not servicing surrounding structures, intended for beach facilities and a leisure centre, and therefore not of public interest; possession could be restored.

On 11 June 2007, the Appeal Commission accepted the Solicitor General’s request and declared the restitution order null and void under section 267(1)(3) of the Administrative Procedure Act, finding enforcement impossible. Relying on section 8 of the Restitution Act, it concluded compensation had been paid and the land was developed building land forming part of the campsite. It stated the final restitution order had been based on a wrong application of law and erroneous, incomplete facts.

The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s challenge on 4 September 2009, upholding the annulment. It found the land was part of the Ohrid lakeshore and of general/public interest under the Protection of Lakes Act and Waters Act, making enforcement legally impossible. The Supreme Court declared his appeal inadmissible in 2010. Requests to reopen proceedings and for protection of legality also failed.

After the final nullity, restitution proceedings resumed. In 2011, the Restitution Commission dismissed the request; the Administrative Court quashed that decision; in 2012, the Commission again upheld restitution. The Solicitor General challenged this, and in 2013 the Administrative Court dismissed the challenge, but in 2014 the Higher Administrative Court quashed the judgment, finding the land part of the Ohrid lakeshore strip and of public interest. The proceedings were stayed pending inheritance and civil disputes. The applicant died in 2013, and his children continued the case.

Separately, in 2009, the Bitola Court of Appeal upheld the applicant’s action against the campsite association for disturbance of possession of the same plot. Land Registry records in 2010 showed the association had use since 1966, while the State remained owner.

The alleged violations therefore concerned the 2007 nullification of a final, executed restitution decision years after it became final and after possession had been restored, based on later evidence and alleged public interest/compensation. The applicant claimed this breached legal certainty and his property rights.
001-174997:
**Summary of the Case of Albertina Carvalho e Filhos Lda v. Portugal**

The case of *Albertina Carvalho e Filhos Lda v. Portugal* (Application no. 23603/14) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 March 2014. The applicant, a Portuguese company headquartered in Valongo, alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically concerning the excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy to address this delay.

The underlying facts pertain to enforcement proceedings initiated by the applicant company on 18 July 2005 against a debtor identified as M.C. The company sought to recover a debt of EUR 32,992.99 plus EUR 18,413.35 in accrued interest, totaling EUR 51,406, along with continuing interest until full repayment.

A judicial enforcement officer was appointed by the Valongo Court on 12 October 2005, accepting the role the following day. The debtor was summoned on 20 November 2005 and subsequently lodged an opposition to enforcement on 14 December 2005, which was joined to the main enforcement proceedings. The applicant replied to this opposition on 30 May 2006.

A significant period of procedural activity, marked by delays, followed. Between February 2007 and August 2008, steps were taken regarding the potential freezing of the debtor's bank accounts. Meanwhile, in the opposition proceedings, a preparatory decision was issued on 22 February 2008. A notable disruption occurred when the applicant's lawyer withdrew on 29 November 2010, and by January 2011, the court could not contact the applicant at its provided address.

In December 2011, a hearing in the opposition proceedings was scheduled for May 2012, but was postponed multiple times—first to November 2012 due to the illness of the debtor's lawyer, and finally held on 6 March 2013. Concurrently, the enforcement proceedings faced administrative hurdles. For reasons not specified, a new judicial enforcement officer was appointed on 3 January 2012. The transition between officers proved inefficient, with discussions regarding the transmission of case documents lasting from September to December 2012. Further correspondence between the new officer and the court about the applicant's legal representation occurred between April and October 2013.

A first-instance decision against the applicant in the opposition proceedings was rendered on 29 April 2013. The applicant appealed to the Oporto Court of Appeal, which upheld the decision on 20 May 2014. A subsequent appeal to the Supreme Court of Justice was rejected on 11 September 2014 by the Oporto Court of Appeal due to a failure to submit grounds of appeal. This final decision terminated the enforcement proceedings, concluding a process that had lasted over nine years.

The applicant company complained that the duration of these civil proceedings was excessive, violating the "reasonable time" requirement. It further argued that Portuguese law did not provide an effective remedy to challenge this delay. The case was communicated to the Portuguese Government on 18 November 2015, focusing on these two complaints, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-175658:
**Case: Magát v. Slovakia (Application no. 44646/15)**

The case originated in an application against the Slovak Republic lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 3 September 2015 by Anton Magát, a Slovak national born in 1957 who lives in Zákopčie. The Government of the Slovak Republic was represented by its Agent, Ms M. Pirošíková. On 8 March 2016, the Court communicated to the Government only the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The judgment was delivered by the Third Section on 25 July 2017 and rectified on 5 September 2017.

The relevant facts began on 28 February 2011, when the applicant’s son sued him in child-maintenance proceedings before the Čadca District Court (file no. 10 C 38/2011). During those proceedings, the applicant made an incomplete submission on 21 April 2011, which he supplemented the following month, saying that he had been waiting for a response from the Centre for Legal Aid regarding his request for a legal-aid lawyer. He also lodged two complaints with the president of the District Court about the excessive length of the proceedings, on 9 February 2012 and 29 February 2012. Both complaints were unsuccessful, and his further appeals to the appellate court for review were likewise unsuccessful.

The District Court took various steps in the case. It asked several public authorities, including the Social Security Authority and the Job Centre, to provide information relevant to the proceedings. Between May 2012 and April 2014, the court dealt with the appointment of a guardian for the applicant, who at that time was undergoing ambulatory psychiatric treatment. The guardian appointment was eventually revoked in September 2014 because the Centre for Legal Aid had appointed a lawyer for the applicant in June 2014. The District Court also joined the case file to another set of proceedings for several months. In January 2014, the judge responsible for the case changed. The court further scheduled several hearings, but these were either adjourned or cancelled.

On 13 May 2015, the Constitutional Court rejected the applicant’s complaint alleging a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time in the District Court proceedings. It found the complaint manifestly ill-founded. It concluded that the District Court had proceeded with the matter actively and properly, apart from a few minor exceptions, such as the joining of the case file to another set of proceedings, the change of judge, and a procedural error made during one hearing. In particular, the Constitutional Court took into account that the applicant had complained about excessive delays to the president of the District Court and had challenged the outcomes further on appeal on each occasion.

After the Constitutional Court’s decision, the District Court took several additional steps. It requested further information from, among others, the applicant’s employer. It scheduled a hearing for 12 August 2015, which was adjourned to 31 August 2015. That latter hearing was then postponed to an unspecified date because the court had to deal with a procedural request from the plaintiff, which was also challenged on appeal. In the absence of any further information from the parties, it appears that the proceedings remained pending and that no judgment on the merits had been delivered by the District Court.

The alleged violation before the European Court of Human Rights therefore concerned the excessive length of the child-maintenance proceedings. The key issue was whether the proceedings before the Čadca District Court complied with the applicant’s right to a hearing within a reasonable time, given the delays arising from the guardian appointment, the joinder of the case file, the change of judge, adjourned or cancelled hearings, and procedural requests and appeals. The other aspects of the application were declared inadmissible, leaving only the length-of-proceedings complaint for the Court’s consideration.
001-172100:
In *Porowski v. Poland* (Application no. 34458/03, judgment of 21 March 2017), the applicant, Dariusz Porowski, a Polish national, complained that his detention on remand had been unlawful and excessively long, that his correspondence with his lawyer was censored, and that criminal proceedings involving him and third persons were unfair and unreasonably lengthy.

The key facts concerned two overlapping criminal cases. In the first case, the applicant was arrested on 11 July 2000 and remanded in custody by the Jarosław District Court on suspicion of attempted extortion, false imprisonment and threats to kill. His detention was repeatedly extended. He was convicted on 13 December 2001 and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, but that conviction was quashed on 23 April 2002. During the retrial, his detention continued and was extended through 2003. On 7 November 2003 he was again convicted and sentenced to five years; the judgment was upheld in March 2004, and his cassation appeal was dismissed in December 2004. He did not use the 2004 Act remedy for complaints about excessive length.

In the second case, on 10 November 2000—while already detained in the first case—the applicant was remanded in custody by the Mińsk Mazowiecki District Court on suspicion of armed robbery and false imprisonment. His detention was extended many times. A central issue was that the Polish courts treated the statutory two-year maximum for detention on remand as applying only to “effective” detention in a given case. Because the applicant was already deprived of liberty in the first case, the courts considered that his detention in the second case had not yet begun to run for the purposes of that limit. They therefore extended the measure beyond the ordinary two-year period, including while proceedings were stayed for psychiatric observation. In February 2003 his release was ordered in the second case, but he remained in custody because of the first case. From July 2005, after he had finished serving the first sentence, the authorities began counting the second-case remand period anew. He was convicted in September 2005, but that judgment was quashed in February 2006. He was ultimately released on 10 April 2008 after the appellate court quashed another conviction and lifted the preventive measure. He was later convicted again in October 2009.

The applicant also filed a constitutional complaint against Article 263 §§ 3 and 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He argued that the “effective detention” interpretation denied protection to detainees concurrently held in another case, and that the two-year limit did not protect detainees after a first judgment was quashed. The Constitutional Court discontinued part of the complaint after a related provision was declared unconstitutional in case SK 17/07; the remaining part was rejected for lack of standing.

As to correspondence, letters sent by the applicant to his defence lawyer in 2001 and 2003, and to the Strasbourg Court in 2001 and 2002, bore Jarosław District Court stamps and handwritten notes stating “censored.” Criminal proceedings against judges were discontinued; the domestic court found that no one had opened or read the correspondence and that the stamps had been applied automatically.

Finally, the applicant complained about proceedings concerning prison staff. He had reported alleged offences by Przemyśl Prison staff in June 2001, but the investigation was discontinued in November 2002, a decision upheld in February 2003. The case thus centred on overlapping remand detention, the calculation of statutory detention limits, censorship of privileged correspondence, and the length and fairness of criminal proceedings.
001-177228:
Vilenchik v. Ukraine (Application no. 21267/14) concerned an application by Andrew Vilenchik, a US national living in Minneapolis, Minnesota. He married S., a Ukrainian national, in Minneapolis in July 2009. Their son, M., was born there in August 2009 and lived with them in Minneapolis; M. held a US passport. In June 2011 the family travelled to Ukraine for a holiday and to visit S.’s relatives. On 13 July 2011 the applicant returned alone to the USA, while M. remained in Ukraine with S. The applicant claimed he expected S. and M. to return by 16 August 2011, but S. changed her plans and stayed in Ukraine. S. disputed this, saying the applicant had asked her to remain, had sent all her and M.’s belongings and M.’s vaccination certificate in August 2011, and had later holidayed with them in Ukraine in July 2012.

In June 2012 the applicant began divorce and custody proceedings in Minnesota. S. argued that the Minnesota court lacked jurisdiction over custody because M. had been in Ukraine for more than six consecutive months. In September 2012 the Minnesota court dissolved the marriage but reserved custody, finding it had no jurisdiction. On 14 August 2012 the applicant asked Ukraine’s Ministry of Justice to secure M.’s return under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. In April 2013 the Ministry, acting for the applicant, brought proceedings in the Desnyansky District Court alleging wrongful retention. On 19 June 2013 that court found M. had initially arrived in Ukraine with both parents’ agreement, but was later retained without the father’s consent. It ordered M.’s return to Minneapolis, accompanied by both parents. A supplementary decision of 2 July 2013 provided for transfer to the applicant if return was not voluntary.

S. appealed, relying on Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention, alleging a grave risk of psychological harm or an intolerable situation. On 14 August 2013 the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal quashed the return orders. It found M. was settled in Ukraine, closely bonded to his mother, and that returning him without her—she allegedly could not remain in the USA—would harm him. It also noted the applicant had not provided details of his US residence, living conditions, or income. On 20 November 2013 the Higher Specialised Court quashed that decision and reinstated the return orders.

The case then underwent extraordinary review. On 18 June 2014 the Supreme Court found divergent application of the Hague Convention and remitted the case. On 30 July 2014 the Cassation Court quashed the Court of Appeal decision for procedural breaches and failure to establish relevant facts. On 5 September 2014 the Court of Appeal again dismissed the applicant’s claim. It found no wrongful retention, because the applicant had allegedly consented or acquiesced: his divorce claim did not expressly object to M.’s stay in Ukraine; he holidayed with S. and M. in July 2012; and he sent M.’s vaccination certificate in August 2012. Alternatively, it held that even if retention was wrongful, return could be refused under Articles 12, 13, and 20 because M. was settled in Ukraine and returning without his mother was not in his best interests. The Cassation Court upheld that decision on 4 December 2014.

The applicant’s alleged violation was that the Ukrainian authorities failed to ensure his son’s return to the USA under the Hague Convention, despite earlier domestic return orders. The key facts are therefore the child’s habitual residence in the USA, the disputed timing and nature of the retention, the contested consent or acquiescence, the conflicting domestic rulings, and the ultimate refusal to enforce return.
001-178904:
