Relevant to the alleged violation, the old regime left defamation damages to the jury, gave trial judges little power to provide meaningful guidance, and limited appellate intervention. Retrials before a new jury would not be told the prior award, the Supreme Court’s reasoning, or the original amount. The later Defamation Act 2009 introduced judicial directions, party submissions on damages, and express power for the Supreme Court to substitute damages, but it did not apply retroactively. The applicant’s Convention complaint therefore focused on the alleged inadequacy and ineffectiveness of domestic safeguards against disproportionately high defamation awards.
001-175121:
In *Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy and Satamedia Oy v. Finland* (Application no. 931/13), two Finnish companies alleged that Finland violated Article 10 (freedom of expression) and Article 6 § 1 (excessive length) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The first applicant, Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy, had since 1994 collected tax data from Finnish authorities and published individuals’ taxable income and assets in the *Veropörssi* newspaper. Under Finnish law, certain tax information—such as name, year of birth, municipality, earned and capital income, taxable net assets, and total taxes—was public and accessible to anyone.

In 2002, *Veropörssi* published 17 issues covering different geographical areas. Each issue listed alphabetically, by municipality and income bracket, the names of about 1.2 million people whose annual taxable income exceeded certain thresholds, mainly FIM 60,000–80,000 (approximately EUR 10,000–13,500), together with their income and taxable net assets rounded to the nearest EUR 100. In 2003, the first applicant transferred the published data on CD-ROMs to the second applicant, Satamedia Oy. With a mobile operator, Satamedia started an SMS service: by sending a person’s name to a service number, a user could receive that person’s tax information if it was in the database. From 2006, Satamedia also published *Veropörssi*.

The Data Protection Ombudsman advised the companies to stop publishing tax data in the manner and to the extent done in 2002, and to stop passing the data to the SMS service. He asked the Data Protection Board to prohibit the processing, arguing that the Personal Data Act applied and that the journalism derogation did not cover collecting and passing on tax data. The Board refused in 2004, finding that the journalism exception applied and that the SMS service used already published data. The Ombudsman appealed. The Helsinki Administrative Court rejected the appeal in 2005, interpreting the journalism derogation broadly and noting that the data were already public. The Ombudsman further appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, which in 2007 requested a preliminary ruling from the CJEU.

In 2008, the CJEU held that the activities involved processing personal data. The journalistic-purpose exception had to be interpreted broadly, but privacy derogations could apply only so far as strictly necessary; whether the activities were journalistic was for the national court to decide. In 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the earlier decisions and referred the case back to the Data Protection Board, requesting a prohibition. It reasoned that the case concerned personal data processing, not public access to tax data or the right to publish as such. Collecting data in a background file for journalistic use could be protected if properly secured. However, publishing the background file almost verbatim on a large scale as municipality/income catalogues was not processing solely for journalistic purposes and was unnecessary for public debate. Passing the data to Satamedia for the SMS service was also not journalistic: it was not disclosure to the general public but an individual query about another person’s data.

The Board then prohibited the first applicant from processing tax data as in 2002 and from forwarding it to an SMS service, and prohibited the second applicant from collecting, storing or forwarding such data. Appeals were rejected by the Turku Administrative Court in 2010 and the Supreme Administrative Court in 2012, which reiterated that the measures did not amount to prior censorship or a ban on publishing tax information as such. The SMS service shut down and the newspaper later ceased or was heavily reduced. The companies alleged that these prohibitions breached Article 10 and that the domestic proceedings were excessively long under Article 6.
001-177349:
In *Becker v. Norway* (Application no. 21272/12), the applicant, Ms C. Langum Becker, was a Norwegian journalist for DN.no, the online edition of *Dagens Næringsliv*. She alleged that Norwegian courts compelled her to give evidence capable of identifying one or more journalistic sources, violating her right under Article 10 of the Convention to receive and impart information.

The underlying facts concerned criminal proceedings against Mr X for market manipulation and insider trading under the 1997 Act on the Trade of Financial Assets. Mr X was accused of asking attorney Mr Y to draft a letter about the Norwegian Oil Company (DNO), addressed to a bond trustee company, suggesting that several bondholders were seriously concerned about DNO’s finances. In reality, the letter was written only on Mr X’s behalf; he owned just one bond, acquired the same day he requested the letter. On Friday 24 August 2007, Mr X faxed the letter to the applicant and spoke with her by telephone. The next day, she published an article entitled “Fears of DNO collapse,” which prominently relied on the letter. DNO stock fell by 4.1% on the next trading day. Other media reported on the matter, and the Oslo Stock Exchange suspected market manipulation. The Financial Supervisory Authority investigated; Mr X confirmed that he had initiated the letter and was the source of the DN article.

Police questioned the applicant in June 2008. She confirmed receiving the letter by fax at 5:35 p.m. on 24 August 2007 and the article’s publication time. She accepted the information was price-sensitive but refused further details, invoking journalistic source protection.

During Mr X’s trial in February 2011, the applicant was summoned as a witness. She refused to answer questions about contacts with Mr X or other possible sources, relying on Article 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 10. The prosecutor requested an order to testify, arguing that the press could be abused by investors to influence share prices, that source consent was irrelevant, and that the case was already sufficiently disclosed. On 15 February 2011, Oslo City Court ordered her to testify about her contacts with Mr X as source, expressly limiting the order so as not to cover other unknown sources. The prosecutor said no postponement was needed because the case was sufficiently disclosed without her statement. Mr X was convicted on 3 March 2011.

The applicant appealed. Borgarting High Court rejected the appeal on 28 April 2011, and the Supreme Court rejected it by three votes to two on 30 September 2011. The majority held that Article 125’s source protection did not apply where the source had come forward or was otherwise identified, because there was no source left to protect; the order was limited and the crime serious. The minority argued that source protection protects the public interest in free information flow, not the source, and should not disappear because a person claimed or was believed to be the source, especially since that could expose other sources.

In Mr X’s appeal, the High Court again heard the applicant on 13 January 2012. She refused questions about her contacts with Mr X; the judge warned of a fine. On 25 January 2012, the High Court fined her NOK 30,000 (about EUR 3,700), with ten days’ imprisonment in default, for contempt. She did not appeal that fine. Mr X was convicted the same day.

The applicant lodged her ECtHR application on 13 March 2012. She alleged that being compelled to give evidence that could enable one or more journalistic sources to be identified violated her Article 10 right to receive and impart information. The central issue was whether an order to testify about contact with a known or self-identified source, while formally excluding other sources, breached journalistic source protection.
001-177080:
**M.L. v. Norway** (Application no. 43701/14) concerned a Norwegian mother’s complaint under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the domestic authorities had violated her right to respect for family life by placing her younger son, X, in a non-relative foster home rather than with the maternal grandmother and stepfather.

The applicant, born in 1987, had two sons, who were half-brothers. Her older son, born in 2008, was taken into permanent public care in 2010 and placed with the applicant’s mother and stepfather. Her younger son, X, was born in February 2012. The applicant had been diagnosed with a hyperkinetic disorder and had a history of psychiatric treatment.

In June 2012, after receiving notifications from authorities and a private individual about the applicant’s inability to care for X, the municipal child welfare authorities placed him in emergency foster care. The County Social Welfare Board upheld that emergency placement. The child welfare authorities then petitioned the Board for a public care order, requesting that X be placed in a foster home and that the applicant be granted supervised access.

Although the maternal grandmother and stepfather had previously been approved as foster parents for the older son, the authorities opposed placing X with them. They cited difficulties in cooperating with the grandmother, the couple’s relatively advanced age—born in 1962 and 1955 respectively—the grandmother’s recent illness, and her failure to prioritise visiting X. The applicant objected. She argued that the grandparents were suitable, that the alleged cooperation problems were merely disagreements, that age was not decisive, and that a family placement would keep the brothers together and be more stable and less stigmatising.

In October 2012, after hearing the parties and ten witnesses, the Board granted the public care order and decided that X should remain in the home where he had already been placed as an emergency measure. The Board accepted that family placement had many positives and that the grandparents were in many respects well suited. However, it found serious doubts: X might be inherently vulnerable and possibly have attention-related difficulties, given the applicant’s diagnosis and her brother’s ADHD; there had been some cooperation difficulties; the grandmother seemed uncertain about the applicant’s ability to care for X and had not attended contact sessions; and the grandparents were relatively old for long-term foster care of a small child while already caring for the older brother. The Board concluded that the disadvantages outweighed the advantages. X was transferred to a non-relative foster home in January 2013.

The applicant appealed. In July 2013, the City Court upheld the Board’s decision. It found serious deficiencies in the applicant’s care and agreed that public care was necessary. On the foster placement question, the City Court acknowledged the advantages of placing X with relatives and keeping the brothers together. However, the court-appointed psychologist did not recommend the grandparents. Key concerns included the applicant’s very different emotional ties to her two sons: she had largely renounced her role as mother to the older son but was expected to maintain contact with X. If X lived with the grandparents, the mother’s contact might increase and hinder his attachment to the foster home. The grandmother had also said she primarily wanted to be a mother to the applicant. The City Court further noted that X had already experienced two broken relationships, had formed an attachment to his new foster mother, was thriving, and would risk “contact injury” if moved again. It also cited the challenges of older foster parents caring for two preschool boys with different needs.

The High Court refused leave to appeal in October 2013, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee rejected the appeal in December 2013. The applicant therefore alleged before the European Court that the refusal to place X with her mother and stepfather breached Article 8.
001-170361:
**Case Stamova v. Bulgaria (Application no. 8725/07)**

The applicant, Ms Elka Dimitrova Stamova, was a Bulgarian national and sole trader who rented a municipally-owned shop in Primorsko from 28 April 1993. The shop was a metal structure on a concrete foundation on municipal land. In September 1995 she asked Tsarevo Municipal Council to sell her the shop under the preferential privatisation procedure for tenants of State and municipal property, also expressing interest in buying the land. When the council did not reply, she sought judicial review of its tacit refusal.

In a final judgment of 4 November 2003, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the lower court’s rejection and found that the applicant had a valid lease and that all statutory conditions for privatising the shop were met. It remitted the case with instructions that the municipal council open a privatisation procedure and offer to sell the shop to her. After administrative boundary changes, a second final judgment of 28 November 2005 again confirmed that she met the conditions and referred the matter to Primorsko Municipal Council. The council explicitly refused to sell in November 2005 and October 2006. In a third final judgment of 31 March 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court annulled those refusals as null and void, holding that the council was obliged to sell the shop to the applicant and noting that no evidence supported the council’s claim that the shop no longer existed.

Despite these judgments, the sale was never completed. Meanwhile, the authorities took steps against the applicant’s possession. In 1996 the municipal company managing the shop told her she had no lease for 1996 and asked her to vacate; its later rei vindicatio claim was dismissed in 2002, with the Supreme Court of Cassation holding that her lease could not be terminated pending privatisation. In 1999 the mayor ordered the shop demolished, but the regional governor revoked the order in 2000 because the mayor lacked competence absent a municipal council decision and because the lease could not be terminated pending privatisation. Also in 1999, the municipal company sold the shop to a private company. The buyer, assisted by municipal employees, prevented the applicant from entering. After she complained, the prosecutor found the buyer’s conduct abusive and police helped her regain possession. Electricity was cut off until 2001. The buyer’s rei vindicatio claim was dismissed in a final judgment of 14 October 2003, which found that the buyer had not acquired ownership and that the applicant was protected from eviction pending examination of her privatisation proposal.

Later, Primorsko Municipal Council deemed the shop dilapidated and unsafe due to corrosion and ordered its sale for demolition. In 2005 it sold the shop to an individual, and on 14 February 2006 the mayor ordered that buyer to demolish it. Although the mayor revoked his order the next day, the buyer dismantled the shop on 18 February 2006 with police assistance. The applicant learned of the demolition only from an acquaintance and had not known about the sale. The parties disputed what happened to her belongings: the Government said they were listed and taken for safekeeping; the applicant said they were destroyed.

In 2006 the applicant sought criminal proceedings against the mayor and council chairperson for breach of duties and obstruction of a final judgment. In February 2007 the prosecutor refused, reasoning that the refusals came from a collective body while criminal responsibility was personal. Further privatisation requests in 2006 and 2008 led the municipality to cite complexity and form a commission; the Privatisation Agency stated that the municipality remained obliged to comply with court judgments.

In 2011 the applicant claimed damages under the State and Municipalities Responsibility for Damage Act. Against the municipality concerning the demolition order, courts found she lacked standing because she was not its addressee. Against the municipal council, she sought pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages for failure to implement the final judgments, including rent paid from January 1998 to February 2006, destroyed belongings, lost income, lost investment opportunity, and stress and depression supported by medical records. The first-instance court declared the claims admissible in January 2014.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the municipal authorities’ failure to sell the shop as ordered by three final judgments breached her right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and that she lacked an effective remedy.
001-173091:
The applicant, Mr Ulrich Sommer, is a German criminal defence lawyer practising in Cologne. In 2009 he represented a client in criminal proceedings. After those proceedings ended and the client was imprisoned, the client’s fiancée transferred €1,500 from her private bank account to the applicant’s professional bank account. The transfer reference stated “Prof Dr Sommer fees” followed by the client’s surname.

In 2010–2011, the Bochum public prosecution office investigated several individuals suspected of commercial gang fraud. One suspect was the applicant’s former client, who again retained him as defence counsel. During the investigation, authorities inspected bank accounts of several persons, including the client and his fiancée. They found that the fiancée had received €7,400 suspected to come from illegal activities and had transferred €1,500 to the applicant’s account as legal fees.

On that basis, the prosecution contacted the applicant’s bank. On 1 March 2011, the prosecutor requested a list of all transactions concerning the applicant’s bank account from 1 January 2009 onward and asked the bank not to inform him. The request relied on Articles 161a, 51, 70 and 95 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 1 April 2011, the prosecutor sent further questions, asking for information on other accounts, rights of disposal, balances, closed accounts, addresses, foreign transfers, all transactions since January 2009, and connected credit cards. The bank complied with both requests. The prosecutor did not formally order the bank to produce the information but pointed to witness obligations and possible coercive consequences for non-compliance.

The information was analysed by police and prosecutors, and a list of 53 transactions considered relevant was placed in the investigation file as evidence. Consequently, anyone with access to the case file—including lawyers for co-accused—could see the applicant’s banking information and the names of clients who had transferred fees.

The applicant only learned of the measures on 31 January 2012, when he was granted access to the investigation file as defence counsel. On 24 April 2012, he asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to return all bank data and destroy related records. He stressed that his role as a criminal defence lawyer was known to the prosecutor and that disclosure of the banking information affected his clients’ interests. He argued that the investigative measures lacked a legal basis.

On 2 May 2012, the Chief Public Prosecutor refused. He said there was suspicion that the money transferred by the fiancée came from illegal activity, so it was legitimate to investigate whether further transfers had occurred between the applicant and his client or the client’s fiancée. He added that the information had to remain in the investigation file and that there was no legal basis for returning or removing it. He cited Article 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure because the bank was a public-law bank and therefore considered an authority.

The file was later transferred to the Bochum Regional Court for trial against the client. The applicant asked the court to return the data. On 19 July 2012, the Regional Court refused. It found the investigation lawful, that the bank had provided information voluntarily, and that the documents could only be returned to the bank, not to the applicant. It also held that the seizure prohibition under Article 97 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not apply because the information had not been in the applicant’s possession. However, to protect lawyer-client privilege, it separated the documents from the general file and restricted access.

The Hamm Court of Appeal confirmed that decision on 13 September 2012, finding the measure proportionate and the safeguards inapplicable, particularly because the bank was not a person assisting the applicant or involved in his professional activities under Article 53a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 19 September 2013, the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint without reasons.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged under Article 8 that the public prosecution office had collected and stored information about his professional bank account in a disproportionate manner, circumventing safeguards protecting lawyer-client confidentiality.
001-170349:
**Tsartsidze and Others v. Georgia** (Application no. 18766/04) concerned thirteen Georgian nationals, all Jehovah’s Witnesses, who alleged that they had been subjected to religiously motivated violence and that the Georgian authorities and courts failed to protect them or provide redress. They invoked Articles 6, 8, 9, 11, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application covered five separate incidents.

In **Case no. 1**, on 16 September 2000, Jehovah’s Witnesses travelling to a convention in Marneuli were stopped by police checkpoints and prevented from reaching the site. At the same time, police allowed a coach carrying Orthodox extremists led by Father Basil Mkalavishvili to proceed. The attackers destroyed religious objects and seized property at Mr Tsartsidze’s premises, including 1.5 tonnes of religious literature, which was burned. Police present refused to intervene. The applicants’ administrative complaint was dismissed; the domestic courts accepted that the police had not known about the convention and had been engaged in an anti-drug operation, and found no intentional or negligent breach by officers.

In **Case no. 2**, on 26 October 2000, plainclothes police entered Mr Aliev’s home in Marneuli as about thirty Jehovah’s Witnesses prepared to meet. They ordered the meeting stopped, insulted participants and confiscated religious books and Bibles. Mr Aliev and Mr Mikirtumov were taken to a police station, where they were threatened: Mikirtumov was told to leave Marneuli, and Aliev was told not to host further religious gatherings. Their complaint was dismissed. The court rejected eyewitness statements because the witnesses were Jehovah’s Witnesses and therefore allegedly interested, while accepting police denials.

In **Case no. 3**, on 2 September 2000 in Kutaisi, Mr Dzamukov was stopped by police while carrying religious tracts. His literature was confiscated, he was taken to a police station, struck by officers and briefly strangled with his tie. The next day, Mr Gabunia was punched by a police officer, had his bag seized, and his religious literature was torn up; two Bibles were kept by officers. He was threatened with being dumped in the Rioni River. The domestic courts dismissed the complaint, emphasising that there was no medical evidence, questioning the credibility of Jehovah’s Witness witnesses, and stating that criminal proceedings, not administrative proceedings, were required to establish police guilt.

In **Case no. 4**, on 1 April 2001, Jehovah’s Witnesses returning from a meeting in Dviri, Borjomi region, were attacked by local residents. Mr Gogoladze was wounded and his bag torn away; Ms Tvaradze and Ms Kapanadze were struck. The deputy governor and local governor allegedly watched, insulted the victims and left with the assailant. The courts dismissed the claim because the governors had no legal duty to maintain public order and had not personally organised or carried out the attack.

In **Case no. 5**, on 27 March 2001, Orthodox extremists led by Mr Bluashvili burst into Mr Gogelashvili’s flat in Rustavi during a Jehovah’s Witness meeting. They insulted the participants, confiscated religious literature, threw benches and literature from windows, and Mr Kurua was briefly strangled by his tie. A video allegedly showed a plainclothes police officer observing without intervening. The next day the literature was burned at Rustavi market, again without police reaction. The domestic courts found that an attack had occurred but held that police passivity or breach of duty had not been proven, and the Supreme Court ultimately found no intentional or negligent breach.

Overall, the facts centred on alleged police passivity or complicity, failure to prevent or investigate religiously motivated attacks, dismissive treatment of Jehovah’s Witness evidence by domestic courts, and the absence of effective compensation or redress under Georgian law.
001-229927:
Ms Karina Volodymyrivna Tsyoge fon Manteyfel, a Russian national born in 1978 living in Elektrostal, lodged application no. 29804/16 against Ukraine on 19 May 2016. She was represented by lawyers V. Lebid and M. Tarakhkalo, practising in Kyiv. The application concerns her compulsory psychiatric treatment. She suffers from paranoid schizophrenia and was subject to a court-ordered compulsory medical measure in criminal proceedings in which she had been charged with murder.

From 23 August 2010 to 14 November 2017 the applicant was detained in various psychiatric hospitals under different supervision regimes. During that period the domestic courts periodically reviewed her detention on the basis of submissions from the hospitals and extended her compulsory inpatient treatment. The most recent order for continued compulsory inpatient treatment was issued by the Samarskyy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk on 19 August 2016. According to the applicant, that order expired on 19 February 2017 because the Psychiatric Assistance Act required reviews of such orders at least every six months.

The Dnipro Psychiatric Hospital submitted requests on 13 January and 19 May 2017 for the applicant to continue compulsory inpatient treatment. Those requests were dismissed by the court on 13 May and 2 November 2017 respectively, and the court ordered that she be treated as an outpatient. The applicant was discharged from hospital on 14 November 2017.

The domestic courts did not examine the applicant’s subsequent appeals against the courts’ orders or her requests for release. Under the relevant law at the time, she did not have locus standi to lodge an appeal or initiate a review of the lawfulness of her continued detention. After 19 February 2017, requests for her immediate release lodged by her mother and her lawyer were dismissed by the hospital on the ground that there had been no court decision ordering her release.

In August 2017 the applicant brought a civil claim against the hospital. By a final domestic judgment of 19 June 2019, the Supreme Court partly allowed that claim. It declared that her continued detention after 19 February 2017—after expiry of the six-month period from the 19 August 2016 court decision and in the absence of any further decision extending her detention—had no basis in law. The Supreme Court noted in particular that the Psychiatric Assistance Act’s provision that extension of a compulsory medical measure was to be carried out each time for a period not exceeding six months was a guarantee against unlawful detention. The Supreme Court ordered the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal to rule on the amount of compensation to be awarded to the applicant.

In January 2021 the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal awarded the applicant 30,000 Ukrainian hryvnias for non-pecuniary damage. That judgment was not appealed by the parties and became final. The award remains unpaid to the applicant.
001-235896:
**Case summary: Melandri v. San Marino (Application no. 25189/21)**

The applicant, Vincenzo Secondo Melandri, an Italian national, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(a) and (b) of the Convention—fair trial, prompt information of the nature and cause of the accusation, and adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence—and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1—protection of property. The case arose from criminal proceedings in San Marino for money laundering and the subsequent confiscation of his assets.

In November 2012, San Marino’s Financial Intelligence Agency reported to the Investigating Judge several banking transactions by the applicant and L.C. at a San Marino bank as possible money laundering. Between September 2009 and March 2010, the applicant deposited large sums into an account in his name—approximately EUR 4,865,830 in cash and about EUR 500,000 in cheques. L.C., introduced by the applicant, opened an account for company O., and EUR 310,000 was later credited to company O. by company A.G., which was traceable to the applicant.

The FIA learned from press reports that the applicant and L.C. had been involved in Italy’s “Operation Baccus,” promoted by the Bari Anti-Mafia District Directorate. Italian proceedings concerned money laundering, extortion, usury, fraud against the State and fictitious wine-sector operations intended to defraud Italian tax authorities and the EU. Italian courts found the applicant guilty of issuing false invoices and criminal association. San Marino authorities obtained Italian documentation by letters rogatory, which allegedly showed that the deposited funds were not compatible with the applicant’s lawful savings but were proceeds of criminal activity.

San Marino opened criminal proceedings no. 865/2012. In November 2013, the Investigating Judge charged the applicant with money laundering under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code and ordered preventive seizure of a life insurance policy worth roughly EUR 6.8 million, a bank account and other assets. In April 2015, the applicant was indicted on two charges: first, transferring and concealing money derived from crimes through apparent commercial operations with company A.G., including deposits, investments, transfers and the opening of a life insurance policy, with conduct continuing until the policy was seized on 5 December 2013; second, together with L.C., transferring EUR 310,000 through company O. The applicant was represented by counsel throughout.

At trial, the applicant argued that there was no proof of the illicit origin of the funds and that self-laundering had only been introduced by Law no. 100/2013, after the alleged conduct. In January 2019, the first-instance court convicted him of money laundering, but only for acts after 29 July 2013, when Law no. 100/2013 entered into force. He was sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment, and the seized property was confiscated under Article 147 of the Criminal Code.

On appeal, in November 2020, the Judge of Appeal upheld the first charge but changed its legal basis. It found that the applicant had committed self-laundering, which was prosecutable because Law no. 99/2010 already excluded the exception for false-invoice predicate offences. The offence was found to run from 10 March 2011 to 27 December 2011. The applicant was acquitted of the second charge, his sentence reduced to four years and three months, and the confiscation confirmed. In December 2020, the Enforcement Judge ordered confiscation of the previously seized assets, including the life insurance policy, to the San Marino State treasury. The Article 6 complaints therefore appear to concern the fairness of proceedings and the applicant’s ability to know and respond to the case against him, particularly after the appellate court recharacterized the offence and applied a different legal basis. The Protocol No. 1 complaint concerns the mandatory confiscation of his property.
001-235692:
In *L.B. v. Slovakia* (Application no. 5541/22), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) examined a Slovak father’s complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention concerning his right to contact with his minor son, the enforcement of interim orders, and the length of custody proceedings.

The applicant’s son was born in 2013. In February 2019, the child’s mother started proceedings in the Nové Mesto nad Váhom District Court seeking arrangements for parental rights and obligations. Interim orders in March and July 2019 allowed the applicant regular contact with his son, and that contact reportedly went smoothly until the end of September 2019.

On 6 March 2020, the District Court ordered regular contact between March and June 2020 at the Centre for Children and Family in Nové Mesto nad Váhom. Because the Centre was closed until late May 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the first meeting did not occur until 4 June 2020. On 3 June 2020, the Trenčín Regional Court varied the order so that contact would take place on Thursdays from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. at the Centre. On 6 October 2020, after establishing on 25 August 2020 that scheduled contact had not taken place, the District Court ordered enforcement of the March 2020 interim order. On 20 October 2020, the Constitutional Court dismissed as manifestly ill-founded the applicant’s complaint about the protracted conduct of the District Court.

On 12 January 2021, the court ordered the parents, grandparents and child to attend regular social counselling sessions at the Centre and required the Centre to inform the court of each session. Contact scheduled for June, July and August 2021 did not take place. In its final report of 31 August 2021, the Centre stated that it had not been possible to re-establish contact and recommended further variation so it could work with the child individually, without the mother present. On 22 August 2021, the District Court discontinued enforcement of the March 2020 interim order because it had become unenforceable following the January 2021 interim order. On 22 September 2021, the court invited the mother to comply voluntarily. On 26 October 2021, the District Court again ordered counselling sessions, with the child to attend without his mother. On 11 November 2021, the Constitutional Court declared inadmissible the applicant’s second complaint, in which he alleged that his right to family life was violated because court inaction prevented contact with his son. The Centre later reported that scheduled contact in December 2021 and January and February 2022 had not occurred because the mother and child failed to attend.

On 10 February 2022, the District Court ordered that the child reside with the mother and that the applicant pay monthly maintenance of EUR 50. It also ordered both parents and the child to undergo three months of psychological counselling; after therapy, the applicant would be allowed contact every other weekend from Friday 3.30 p.m. to Sunday 6 p.m. On 16 February 2022, the court ordered the mother, under penalty of a fine, to ensure the child attended counselling under the October 2021 interim order. On 13 April 2022, the mother was fined EUR 100 for non-compliance. On 24 March 2022, the applicant was convicted of dangerous stalking of the child’s mother and obstructing execution of a court order, receiving a six-month suspended sentence. The Centre reported that the mother missed most counselling sessions between June and October 2022. On 2 August 2022, the mother was charged with obstructing execution of a decision by a public authority.

On 20 October 2022, the Regional Court upheld the October 2021 interim order. On 9 November 2022, it upheld the District Court judgment on counselling and ruled that, after therapy, the applicant would have contact every second Saturday from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. for two months, then every second week from Saturday 9 a.m. to Sunday 5 p.m. On 5 February 2023, the mother appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court, which apparently remains pending. The applicant complained under Article 8 that slow and inefficient court decision-making prevented him from obtaining regular contact with his son, and under Article 6 that the custody proceedings exceeded a reasonable time.
001-230271:
A.I. and Others v. Greece (App. no. 13958/16), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment 18 January 2024, concerned an Afghan father and his two minor children. They alleged violations of Article 3 regarding living conditions in Idomeni camp and Article 3 read with Article 13 regarding deficient access to the asylum procedure.

On 25 February 2016 the applicants were registered at Fylakio Reception and Identification Centre (RIC), Evros. The father suffered from a hip cyst and underwent surgery. On 2 March 2016 they left the RIC for Idomeni, intending to reach northern Europe; they considered Greece unsafe. They stayed in Idomeni until May 2016. They alleged severe overcrowding—over 10,000 people—exceeding the camp’s capacity. They lived in a tent without adequate weather protection and complained of poor hygiene and sanitation, infection risk, and inadequate food. They suffered bronchitis, fever and lung problems; the father’s cyst became infected and bled; they could not obtain medical assistance; the children were hungry. They claimed the authorities knew of their vulnerability—the father’s medical condition and the children’s ages (4 and 7)—and that conditions cumulatively breached Article 3.

As to asylum access, they alleged they were not informed about asylum procedures during police registration. The Greek Asylum Service made Skype the only way to express an intention to apply and schedule registration at the Regional Asylum Office (RAO). They had no internet or device, the Skype lines were overloaded, and in-person applications were no longer available. Even using Skype would not confer asylum-seeker status. On 3 March 2016 an administrative expulsion order was issued; enforcement was suspended for one month for the father and six months for the children. They claimed the suspension could be lifted before they could apply, exposing them to refoulement. An interim measure request to the ECtHR on 11 March 2016 was refused on 1 April 2016.

In May 2016 they moved to Diavata camp, living in a tent without electricity and with inadequate food. They received a pre-registration asylum-seeker card but kept no copy. The father was referred to hospital but no interpreter was available; the children could not attend school, became ill, and no pediatrician was available. They alleged authorities knew they were present, but they still could not submit an asylum request despite recorded interest. After Idomeni’s evacuation, pre-registration did not ensure access to asylum. These conditions, without safeguards for vulnerable persons, allegedly exceeded the Article 3 threshold and risked refoulement. In December 2016 they left for other countries; they returned to Greece in September 2018 and were homeless in Athens until December 2019. They applied for international protection on 12 October 2018 and were recognised as refugees on 22 April 2020.

The Government argued Greece faced an extraordinary humanitarian emergency caused by unprecedented migrant flows and the Western Balkan route closure. Idomeni was an unofficial camp built by NGOs, municipalities, IOM and UNHCR, with tents, toilets, showers, water, healthcare from hospitals/NGOs, and food from NGOs/shops. Police informed residents about border closure and transfers; the camp was evacuated on 24–26 May 2016 and residents moved to state facilities. Idomeni was never official accommodation; the applicants were not detained and went there voluntarily; no record of their presence existed. On asylum, pre-registration in June/July 2016 provided cards and health/education access; vulnerability was assessed; there was no indication authorities refused registration. During the RIC, applicants were informed they could apply before the RAO but did not express a wish. Their first application was on 12 October 2018, with no evidence earlier attempts were impossible. Skype appointments operated alongside personal appearance and did not preclude attendance at the RAO.
001-233215:
In *Sacharuk v. Lithuania*, Aleksandr Sacharuk, a Lithuanian national and former member of the Seimas (Parliament) from 2008 to 2012, complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 that the Supreme Court panel which upheld his conviction was not impartial, and under Article 7 that his conviction was not foreseeable.

The key facts concern his conduct as an MP in January 2010. Between 14 and 19 January 2010, he used another Seimas member L.K.’s parliamentary identity card to register and vote electronically in L.K.’s place during L.K.’s absence. L.K. was abroad in Southeast Asia without parliamentary authorisation. The Seimas Ethics and Procedures Commission concluded that Sacharuk had deliberately voted for another member, breached Article 111 § 4 of the Seimas Statute—which required MPs to vote in person—and breached the Code of Conduct for State Politicians. It proposed a warning as a disciplinary sanction.

The Seimas Special Investigation Commission later found the accusation well-founded and referred the matter to the Prosecutor General’s Office, suggesting possible criminal offences under Articles 300 and 302 of the Criminal Code. Because Sacharuk had parliamentary immunity, the prosecutor sought the Seimas’ consent to prosecute. On 17 June 2010, the Seimas did not lift his immunity: 46 voted in favour, 12 against, and 28 abstained. The prosecutor therefore refused to start a pre-trial investigation, but noted possible elements of offences under Articles 228, 300 and 302.

Impeachment proceedings followed. On 27 October 2010, the Constitutional Court concluded that Sacharuk had breached his parliamentary oath and grossly violated the Constitution by deliberately voting for L.K. eight times. However, on 11 November 2010, the Seimas failed to annul Sacharuk’s mandate: 80 votes were in favour, short of the required 85. He therefore remained an MP; L.K.’s mandate was annulled.

In June 2011, the Code of Criminal Procedure was amended to allow prosecution of persons who had lost immunity. Sacharuk’s term ended in November 2012. On 20 November 2012, the prosecutor annulled the earlier refusal and opened a pre-trial investigation because immunity no longer barred prosecution. Sacharuk was charged under Article 228 § 1 (abuse of office), Article 300 § 3 (forgery), and Article 302 § 2 (unlawful use of a document).

The Vilnius Regional Court acquitted him in July 2015, and the Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal in May 2016. Those courts relied on an established practice in the Seimas of MPs voting for absent colleagues from the same political group, the availability of disciplinary warning under the Seimas Statute, the absence of major damage, and the applicant’s alleged lack of awareness of criminal liability. The Supreme Court quashed the acquittal in December 2016 and remitted the case, holding that such practice did not eliminate criminality and that the lower courts had assessed the evidence one-sidedly.

On retrial, the Court of Appeal convicted Sacharuk in June 2017 under Article 228 § 1 and Article 302 § 1, imposing a fine of €1,882; the Article 300 charge was discontinued as time-barred. The court found direct intent, major non-pecuniary damage to the State, and noted his legal education and parliamentary experience. The Supreme Court dismissed his final appeal on 13 February 2018.

Regarding Article 6 impartiality, Judge D.B. had participated in the earlier Supreme Court panel that quashed the acquittal and made adverse comments on the merits. She later sat as reporting judge on the final panel. Sacharuk requested her removal, but the court refused, finding prior participation insufficient to raise doubts about impartiality.

Regarding Article 7 foreseeability, Sacharuk argued that only disciplinary liability—a warning—was foreseeable, that similar conduct by other MPs had not been prosecuted, and that criminal prosecution became possible only after the 2011 procedural amendment. The domestic courts ultimately held that criminal liability was foreseeable and that unlawful practice did not excuse him.
001-238269:
**Summary of *Kasım Özdemir and Mehmet Özdemir v. Türkiye* (Application no. 18980/20)**

The case of *Kasım Özdemir and Mehmet Özdemir v. Türkiye* concerns a father and son who were shot and injured by a gendarmerie officer during a confrontation in their village. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life) and 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights, primarily focusing on the use of force against them and the subsequent ineffectiveness of the domestic investigation.

The incident occurred on the morning of 10 November 2014 in Deliosman village. Three gendarmerie officers were pursuing a suspect vehicle that had ignored their order to stop. The vehicle entered the applicants' village, and a confrontation ensued. According to the applicants, upon arriving in the village, one of the officers, C.Ç., began firing shots into the air. The first applicant (the son) warned him not to shoot, as it would frighten the children. In response, Officer C.Ç. shot him in the leg. When the second applicant (the father) arrived at the scene and saw his injured son, the officer shot and wounded him as well. Both sustained serious fractures to their tibia and fibula.

The official gendarmerie account starkly differs. The officers claimed they were ambushed by a hostile crowd of villagers who threw stones, damaged their vehicle, and attempted to seize their rifles. Officer C.Ç. stated that after firing multiple warning shots that were ignored by a violent mob intent on lynching them, he was forced to shoot two individuals who were actively attacking him and attempting to take his weapon. He maintained he fired in self-defence, aiming only at their legs to neutralize the threat.

The domestic investigation heavily favoured the officers' version of events. The Kilis public prosecutor decided not to prosecute Officer C.Ç., concluding that his actions were justified under self-defence and the legal framework for police use of force. Conversely, the prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings against the applicants and other villagers for resisting public officers. The Kilis Criminal Court convicted the applicants, finding that the first applicant had grabbed the officer's rifle and the second had attempted to draw a weapon, leading the officer to shoot them. Their sentence was suspended.

The applicants' appeals to the Constitutional Court were unsuccessful. The Constitutional Court found no violation, accepting that the use of force was necessary and proportionate given the crowd's attack on the officers. It also determined the investigation was adequate.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained about the disproportionate use of force and the failure of the national authorities to conduct an effective and impartial investigation. The key factual disputes at the heart of the case were the nature of the confrontation and whether the applicants posed a direct threat to Officer C.Ç. when they were shot. The applicants contended they were unarmed victims, while the official records, supported by the testimony of the officers and others, portrayed them as active participants in a violent riot aimed at preventing law enforcement from performing their duties. The Court was therefore tasked with assessing the evidence to determine if the force used was absolutely necessary and if the investigation was sufficiently thorough to establish the true facts.
001-231088:
**Vlahović v. Montenegro** (Application no. 62444/10), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 22 February 2024, final on 24 June 2024. The applicant, Zoran Vlahović, a Croatian national born in 1964 and living in Split, complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the non-enforcement of domestic judgments and decisions delivered in his favour in 2010.

The applicant was co-owner of two plots of land, nos. 1084/4 and 1084/10, in Herceg Novi. He owned one third and one half of the plots respectively; a certain M.D. owned smaller fractions. The land was registered as an uncategorised road. In June 2005, M.D. constructed a sewage collection system and paved the road in concrete without the approval of the other co-owners or authorisation from the Municipality of Herceg Novi. The applicant and another co-owner sued M.D.

Expert evidence showed that the concrete paving altered rainwater drainage, accelerating water flow and likely causing flooding, soil deposits and erosion to adjacent land. The sewage system had been built without prior administrative authorisation and might not have complied with construction standards.

On 26 February 2010, the Herceg Novi Court of First Instance found that M.D. had violated the applicant’s rights by unlawfully paving the entirety of the plots and constructing a sewage system on plot no. 1084/10. It ordered M.D. to remove the objects within fifteen days. On 8 February 2011, the Podgorica High Court upheld that judgment, making it final. Separately, on 29 and 30 March 2010, the municipal police ordered M.D. to remove the sewage system and concrete paving; those decisions were upheld in April 2010.

Enforcement became complicated after M.D. transferred his ownership rights to the municipality free of charge on 18 May 2010, and the municipality sought to expropriate the plots in December 2010. Between December 2010 and May 2019, the municipal police repeatedly postponed enforcement; all postponements were quashed. On 15 April 2011, an enforcement order was issued, but it was quashed in October 2011 because M.D. was no longer a co-owner and expropriation proceedings were pending. In 2012, the courts dismissed the applicant’s request to enforce against the municipality because the judgment had been against M.D., not the municipality, and advised him to bring separate civil proceedings.

In April 2015, the Court of First Instance imposed an interim measure prohibiting removal of the concrete and sewage system until the expropriation proceedings ended. It found that enforcement would cause nearly irreparable damage to occupants, as the road was the only access to their homes and was needed for water and sewage infrastructure. In 2017, the Supreme Court held that expropriation proceedings could not obstruct enforcement of decisions ordering removal. Nevertheless, in April 2021, enforcement was terminated because circumstances entirely prevented it, notably that the respondent was no longer a co-owner. The applicant was again advised to pursue separate civil proceedings against the municipality.

The applicant repeatedly sought enforcement against M.D. and the municipality, relying on section 28 of the Enforcement Act. In June 2023, the Constitutional Court quashed a 2019 decision rejecting that reliance and found a violation of Article 6 due to insufficient reasoning. By 12 December 2023, the expropriation proceedings were still pending, the 2015 interim measure remained in force, and the 2010 judgment and two administrative decisions in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced. The key alleged violations therefore concern the prolonged failure to enforce final domestic decisions in the applicant’s favour, engaging Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-233206:
The case originated in application no. 53600/20 against Switzerland, brought by Verein KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz, a Swiss non-profit association, and four of its members. The association promotes effective climate protection on behalf of its members, mainly women over 70. It has over 2,000 members with an average age of 73; nearly 650 are aged 75 or older. The four individual applicants were older women who described serious health effects from heatwaves. Ms Schaub (born 1931) collapsed during hot weather, had a pacemaker, suffered severe gout and was once hospitalised; she died during the proceedings. Ms Volkoff Peschon (born 1937) had cardiovascular problems, had to stay indoors, adjust medication and measure blood pressure, and suffered breathing difficulties. Ms Molinari (born 1941) had asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease worsened by heat. Ms Budry (born 1942) had asthma and said heatwaves drained her energy and restricted her activities.

The applicants alleged that Swiss authorities’ omissions in climate-change mitigation violated their rights under Articles 2, 6, 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed that climate change, especially more frequent and intense heatwaves, disproportionately threatened older women’s life, health and physical integrity. They argued that Switzerland had a positive obligation to protect them by adopting and implementing sufficient measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

In November 2016, relying on section 25a of the Federal Administrative Procedure Act and Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention, the applicants requested the Federal Council, the Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications, the Federal Office for the Environment and the Federal Office for Energy to issue a formal decision on alleged omissions in climate protection. They sought measures to reduce Swiss greenhouse gas emissions in line with the Paris Agreement target of holding global warming well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, or at least not exceeding 2°C. Their requests included at least a 25% domestic reduction below 1990 levels by 2020, a 50% reduction by 2030, initiation of preliminary legislative proceedings, information to Parliament and the public, a higher CO2 tax, and building and transport measures. Alternatively, they sought a declaration that the omissions were unlawful. They contended that current targets and measures were insufficient, unconstitutional and incompatible with the Convention and international law.

The DETEC rejected the request for lack of standing. It found that no individual rights or obligations were affected because the request concerned general, abstract regulation and political choices, not a “real act” affecting individual legal positions, and amounted to an actio popularis. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal, finding no close proximity or interest worthy of protection. It considered climate-change impacts to be general, held that older women were not sufficiently differentiated from the public, and found no genuine, serious dispute directly decisive for civil rights under Article 6, with Article 13 absorbed by Article 6. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed the final appeal. It held that the alleged omissions did not affect the applicants’ rights with sufficient intensity at present; their rights under Articles 2 and 8 were not threatened enough; they had no subjective right or arguable claim; and the action was an inadmissible actio popularis better pursued through political means.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ alleged violations before the Grand Chamber: that Switzerland’s inadequate climate mitigation breached positive obligations to protect life and private/family life, and that domestic authorities denied them access to court and an effective remedy.
001-231331:
**Case: Wa Baile v. Switzerland (ECtHR, Third Section, judgment of 20 February 2024, final 20 May 2024)**  

The case concerns an alleged racial profiling identity check and the subsequent failure of Swiss authorities to determine whether the applicant had been discriminated against because of his skin colour.

The applicant, a Swiss national born in 1974 living in Bern, was stopped for an identity check on the morning of 5 February 2015 at Zürich railway station while on his way to work. Three municipal police officers approached him at about 7 a.m. The officer in charge later reported that his attention had been drawn by a “dark-skinned” male who seemed suspicious because he allegedly averted his gaze upon seeing the police and tried to avoid them. The officer suspected a breach of the Federal Aliens Act and decided to check his identity. The applicant refused to comply. The officers then took him aside, asked him to raise his hands and spread his legs, and searched his pockets and backpack until they found a document confirming his identity. He was then allowed to leave.

The applicant claimed that he was the only person checked in a crowd of people going to work, whom he described as almost all white, and that he received no explanation for why he had been stopped. He alleged that the check amounted to racial profiling and discrimination based on his skin colour.

In the criminal proceedings, the applicant was fined CHF 100 for refusing to comply with police orders, plus CHF 150 in procedural costs. The District Court found both the applicant’s and the officer’s accounts credible, but concluded that there was nothing to show that the applicant’s skin colour had been a decisive factor. It also held that even if the identity check had been unlawful, the police order had not been null and void, so the applicant was still obliged to comply; any unlawfulness could be established later by administrative courts. The Cantonal Court upheld the conviction, finding no indication of manifestly discriminatory grounds and emphasising the busy railway station context and the officer’s credible explanation. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, holding that his discrimination complaint relied on a different version of the facts from that established below and was therefore inadmissible.

In parallel administrative proceedings, the applicant sought a declaration that the identity check had been unlawful. After several lower bodies dismissed his request, the Administrative Court of the Canton of Zürich held on 1 October 2020 that the check had been unlawful: even accepting the officer’s account that it was prompted by the applicant looking away, that was not a sufficient justification. However, the Administrative Court expressly left open whether the check had also been discriminatory on the ground of skin colour. The applicant appealed to the Federal Supreme Court, seeking a ruling on discrimination under Article 14 read with Article 8 of the Convention. In December 2020, the Federal Supreme Court declared his appeal inadmissible, finding that he had already obtained full satisfaction and merely sought additional reasoning, which did not give him a legitimate interest.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 14 of the Convention read in conjunction with Articles 6 and 8, and under Article 13. The central alleged violations were that the identity check had been based on racial profiling, that the domestic authorities had failed to decide whether he had been subjected to such discrimination, and that he lacked an effective remedy in that respect.
001-237290:
**Case: H.T. v. Germany and Greece (Application no. 13337/19, judgment 15 October 2024)**

The case concerns H.T., a Syrian national, who alleged that Germany violated Article 3 of the Convention by removing him to Greece on the same day he expressed an intention to seek asylum there, and that Greece violated Articles 3 and 5 §§ 1 and 4 in respect of his subsequent detention and its judicial review.

H.T. first arrived in Greece on 30 June 2018, on Megisti island, where he was detained. On 4 July 2018 Greece ordered his removal to Türkiye under the EU-Türkiye Statement. On 18 July 2018 he applied for asylum in Leros, but a geographical limitation confined him to Leros. He alleged that conditions in the Leros Reception and Identification Centre were overcrowded and inadequate, and he left the island. His asylum application was discontinued on 13 August 2018 after he failed to attend an interview. He then left Greece.

On 4 September 2018, H.T. was stopped entering Germany from Austria by bus. He used a stolen Bulgarian identity card but also possessed a Syrian identity card and a Greek arrival certificate. He told German police that he wished to apply for asylum in Germany and to join his brother in Dortmund. He was provisionally arrested, informed of his rights in Arabic, and questioned with an interpreter. Germany refused him entry and returned him to Athens by plane the same day under the 2018 administrative arrangement between Germany and Greece concerning refusal of entry to protection seekers at the German-Austrian border. The arrangement applied where a Eurodac hit showed that the person had already requested protection in Greece after 1 July 2017. A Eurodac hit confirmed his earlier Leros asylum application. Germany notified Greece of the refusal.

H.T. alleged that he never agreed to return to Greece, that his asylum application was not registered in Germany, that he had no lawyer or reliable legal information, and that he received contradictory information: an initial written refusal said he would be returned to Austria, while the later refusal-of-entry decision for asylum-seekers, issued shortly before departure, was allegedly explained only orally in English, without an Arabic interpreter.

On arrival in Athens, Greek authorities arrested and detained him with a view to executing the earlier removal decision. He was initially held in the Attica Directorate for Foreigners for up to six months, then transferred to Leros police station and the Leros Reception and Identification Centre. The detention grounds included risk of absconding, lack of documents, danger to public order, and the pending removal to Türkiye. H.T. sought continuation of his asylum proceedings and challenged his detention before the Rhodes Administrative Tribunal. He alleged that his detention was unlawful because he was an asylum-seeker and that conditions violated Article 3: he claimed he was held 24 hours a day in a cell, had no outdoor exercise, endured dampness, poor ventilation, lack of hygiene items, delayed medication, and no recreation or outside contact. EASO later identified him as vulnerable, suffering from an anxiety-depressive disorder, and exempt from the border procedure. He was released on 27 November 2018. Greece recognised him as a refugee on 7 April 2020.

The key alleged violations therefore arose from Germany’s immediate removal of an asylum-seeking individual to Greece despite claimed risks of inhuman or degrading treatment and without individual assurances or a Dublin III procedure, and from Greece’s detention of him allegedly in unlawful and inadequate conditions, with ineffective judicial review.
001-237960:
In *Votta Ronza v. Italy* (Application no. 38083/10), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, examined an application brought by Anna Votta Ronza, born in 1957, against Italy. The applicant was represented by Mr G. Romano, a lawyer practising in Rome. The Italian Government were given notice of the application. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 7 July 2010.

The central alleged violation concerned the non-enforcement of a domestic decision. According to the appended table, the relevant domestic decision was given by the Campania Regional Administrative Court (R.G. 5620/2012) on 28 December 2013. That decision concerned Consorzio AS.CO.S.A. – Associazione Costruttori S. Antimo, and it ordered payment of compensation to the applicant for the unlawful occupation of her land in view of its expropriation. In substance, a domestic administrative court had recognised the applicant’s right to compensation for the occupation of her property in connection with expropriation, but that compensation order allegedly remained unenforced.

The non-enforcement period began on 28 December 2013, the date of the domestic decision. By the time the Court dealt with the case, enforcement was still pending. The length of the enforcement proceedings was recorded as more than ten years, seven months and sixteen days. This prolonged failure to execute the domestic decision formed the factual core of the applicant’s complaint. She complained of the non-enforcement of a domestic decision and also raised other complaints under the Convention. The excerpt does not set out the full merits reasoning, but the principal alleged violation is clearly the continued failure to secure compliance with the administrative court’s compensation order.

The underlying facts therefore involve a land dispute: the applicant’s land was allegedly occupied unlawfully with a view to expropriation, and a domestic court ordered compensation. The subsequent non-enforcement meant that the applicant did not receive the compensation awarded to her for more than a decade. The delay and continuing failure to enforce the decision were the key facts relevant to her application before the European Court. Such non-enforcement complaints ordinarily engage fair-trial and property-protection concerns under the Convention, although the provided extract does not detail the Court’s final findings on those points.

Procedurally, the First Section Committee comprised Krzysztof Wojtyczek (President), Lətif Hüseynov and Erik Wennerström, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 17 October 2024 and delivered its judgment on 14 November 2024. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are thus the existence of the domestic administrative decision ordering compensation for unlawful occupation/expropriation of the applicant’s land; the identity of the debtor, Consorzio AS.CO.S.A.; the start of non-enforcement on 28 December 2013; the fact that enforcement remained pending; and the resulting period of non-enforcement exceeding ten years, seven months and sixteen days.
001-237435:
Zdjelar v. Croatia (Application no. 58566/19) concerns an application brought by Cena and Robert Zdjelar, Croatian nationals living in Germany. In 1984 they bought a flat in Karlovac, Croatia, which they used during holidays. In autumn 1991, during the war in Croatia, I.B. and his family, internally displaced persons, occupied the flat. On 14 April 1992, the Karlovac Township authority allocated the flat to that family for temporary use; that decision was set aside on 5 July 1996.

On 27 September 1995, the Temporary Takeover and Administration of Certain Property Act (“the Sequestration Act”) entered into force. It provided that property in previously occupied territories belonging to persons who had left Croatia after 17 October 1990 could be sequestered by the State. Local authorities took possession of such property, and their sequestration commissions could temporarily accommodate others there. On 27 September 1996, Karlovac Township’s Sequestration Commission allocated the applicants’ flat for temporary use to Ms Đ.V.

The applicants applied for repossession on 1 March 1999. On 16 October 2000, the Karlovac Township Housing Commission set aside the 1996 allocation and ordered Đ.V. to vacate. After eviction proceedings, the flat was handed back to the applicants on 30 July 2001.

On 25 April 2002, the applicants sued Karlovac Township in the Karlovac Municipal Court for compensation for damage caused by the unlawful disposals of their flat. They claimed both the 1992 and 1996 decisions were unlawful and that the Township was liable for physical damage and lost rent. The Township denied liability. During the proceedings, the Municipal Court, at the applicants’ initiative, invited the State to intervene; the State declined on 11 May 2009.

After a remittal, the Municipal Court dismissed the action on 27 May 2013. On appeal, the Karlovac County Court on 8 January 2014 partly reversed. It allowed the claim for the period between 5 July 1996 and 30 July 2001. It found the 1996 allocation unlawful because Karlovac had never been occupied, the applicants had not left Croatia after 17 October 1990, and Đ.V. was not eligible for accommodation in sequestered property. It held the Township and the State jointly and severally liable. It upheld dismissal for the earlier period, finding the 1992 decision lawful. On 17 February 2014, the Township paid the applicants HRK 240,163.89 (EUR 31,875.26) as the judgment debt.

The Township, but not the applicants, appealed on points of law. The applicants replied, but the Municipal Court did not forward their reply to the Supreme Court. On 24 June 2014, the Supreme Court reversed the County Court and dismissed the claim for 5 July 1996 to 30 July 2001. It held that under section 13 of the State Administration System Act, the State was solely liable for damage caused not only by its own bodies but also by local authorities in administrative matters conferred on them. Since the State had conferred powers under the Sequestration Act on local authorities, and the applicants had sued only the Township, their claim had to be dismissed. On 18 April 2019, the Constitutional Court dismissed their constitutional complaint.

Meanwhile, the Township brought an unjust-enrichment action. By a judgment of 12 April 2017, final on 30 January 2020, the applicants were ordered to repay the amount received under the County Court’s judgment.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained that the Supreme Court’s dismissal of their civil action because they had sued the Township rather than the State violated Article 6 § 1 (right of access to a court) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (right to property). Complaints concerning the length of the civil proceedings and discrimination were declared inadmissible.
001-234129:
In *T.V. v. Croatia* (ECHR, Second Section, 11 June 2024), the applicant, a Slovenian national, complained under Articles 2, 3 and 13 about the death of her partner, V.D., during a Croatian police intervention and the alleged ineffectiveness of the ensuing criminal investigation.

V.D. suffered from schizophrenia. On 16 November 2017 he left a Slovenian psychiatric institution and entered Croatia. Croatian border police were informed by Slovenian police that he had travelled to Opuzen and posed a danger to himself and others. The same day, after a fight at a hotel, hotel staff called the Metković police. The responding officers allegedly knew V.D. might be a mentally disabled person in distress.

At the hotel car park, four officers found V.D. sitting on his car, visibly mentally distressed and mumbling. He emptied his pockets but refused orders to turn around and spread his legs. He took out his phone, shouted that he would press a button and “blow up” everyone, then sat on the ground. After repeated warnings, Officer G. used pepper spray. V.D. lay on his side, bleeding from biting his lips and tongue. Three officers then forced him onto his stomach and put his hands behind his back. He resisted, banged his head on the pavement, and bit off part of his little finger. Police called an ambulance at about 2:35 p.m.; officers, joined by a fifth, continued holding him face down until the ambulance arrived around 2:47 p.m. A doctor gave him a sedative and noted he was bleeding, blue in the face, and had swallowed part of his finger. He was transported face down, restrained with three straps, on a roughly 1.5-hour journey to Dubrovnik General Hospital. After a second sedative, he was found dead. The coroner recorded natural death from cardiac arrest.

The scene was washed before inspection. The official autopsy found no violent death, only scratches, a finger fragment in the oesophagus, and five broken ribs likely from a fall; it deemed the injuries grave but not causally linked to death. A police report found the force lawful and proportionate. The applicant arranged a second autopsy in Ljubljana, which found additional inflammation, lung and brain swelling, myocardial fibrosis, acute cardiac arrest, and two front teeth recently knocked out.

In November 2018 the applicant filed criminal complaints against the police for serious bodily injury resulting in death and against the ambulance doctor and nurse for medical negligence. The complaints were rejected in February 2019 based on natural causes. After higher-level review, interviews took place in 2020 and a formal investigation opened in October 2020. A May 2021 forensic report concluded V.D. suffered a violent death from mental trauma: grave injury resulted from his resisting police while prone, self-harming, and officers pressing hard on his back. Those factors, combined with police and medical actions, aggravated his agitated mental state and led to shock and cardiac arrest as the mechanism of dying. It found no medical negligence but stated medical staff should have sat next to him during transport.

In August 2021 the complaint was again rejected: force was proportionate, no fatal injuries were caused, and medical staff were not negligent. This was upheld. In July 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint, finding the investigation independent and thorough despite delays, and that V.D. died from serious mental trauma caused by extreme agitation and resistance, with police measures lawful and proportionate. Civil damages proceedings remained pending.

The alleged violations concern whether the police use of force and prone restraint against a mentally ill person, delayed medical assistance, and conflicting medical evidence breached substantive Articles 2 and 3, and whether the investigation was effective and adequate under Articles 2, 3 and 13.
001-231871:
Tretyakov and Others v. Russia (Applications nos. 33610/18 and 21 others) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section Committee on 4 April 2024. The applicants were 22 individuals who lodged applications against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates between 2018 and 2021. The Russian Government was given notice of the applications. The central complaint was the excessive length of their pre-trial detention; some applicants also raised other Convention complaints, but the appended table focused on detention facts.

According to the table, each applicant was detained in Russia under orders issued or reviewed by district, town, city, regional, or supreme courts. The detention periods varied widely. Dmitriy Tretyakov was detained from 14 March 2018 to 28 March 2019, lasting 1 year and 15 days, with orders from the Frunzenskiy District Court of Vladivostok and the Primorskiy Regional Court. Igor Dontsov was detained from 6 September 2017, still pending when he applied and possibly as of 16 September 2022, totalling 5 years and 11 days; Moscow City Court handled his orders. Dmitriy Martynov was detained from 1 February 2017 to 6 February 2019, lasting 2 years and 6 days, under Moscow courts.

Reyal Rasulov had one of the longest periods: from 15 August 2015, pending at application and possibly as of 16 September 2022, amounting to 7 years, 1 month and 2 days; Karelia courts issued the orders. Oleg Krasnov was detained from 28 February 2017, pending as of 16 September 2022, for 5 years, 6 months and 20 days. Dmitriy Gusakov was held from 18 July 2017 to 29 August 2022, for 5 years, 1 month and 12 days. Ilya Vyguzov was detained from 27 July 2018, pending, for more than 4 years, 7 months and 19 days. Sergey Zakharov was detained from 25 May 2018, pending, for 4 years, 3 months and 23 days, while Mikhail Fomin was held from 20 June 2018, pending, for 4 years, 2 months and 28 days.

Other examples include Vyacheslav Kruglov, detained from 5 March to 19 July 2019 (4 months and 15 days); Nikita Kolesnikov, from 17 May 2018 to 12 August 2019 (1 year, 2 months and 27 days); Vasiliy Sukhorukov, from 30 January 2019 to 27 January 2020 (11 months and 29 days); and Aleksandr Petrov, from 25 September 2019 to 16 January 2020 (3 months and 23 days), the shortest listed period. Aleksandr Pisarev had two detention periods: 21 April 2018 to 18 June 2019 and 20 June to 16 September 2019, together about 1 year, 4 months and 27 days.

Several applicants remained in detention pending the application and possibly until 16 September 2022, including Safonov, Tran, Mezin, Belov, Podrezova and Kachayev. The courts involved included district and regional courts across Moscow, St Petersburg, Vladivostok, Karelia, Samara, Perm, Tula, Chita, Astrakhan, Tver, Novosibirsk, Izhevsk, Krasnoyarsk and other regions.

The key factual issue was whether these pre-trial detention periods, many lasting years and several still pending, were excessively long. The applicants complained that Russia violated their Convention rights, principally the right to liberty and security requiring trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial. The Court deliberated on 14 March 2024 and adopted its judgment on 4 April 2024.
001-231078:
**Case: Lypovchenko and Halabudenco v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia**  
**Applications nos. 40926/16 and 73942/17 – ECtHR judgment of 20 February 2024**

The case concerns alleged human-rights violations in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”), a separatist administration on Moldova’s territory. The applicants were Oleksandr Lypovchenko, a Ukrainian national, and Oleg Halabudenco, a Moldovan national. Both complained against Moldova and Russia.

**Mr Lypovchenko’s case (no. 40926/16)**  
On 7 July 2015, the de facto “MRT authorities” arrested Lypovchenko and charged him with extremism for allegedly critical social-media posts and an old diary note stating that “Transnistria can be ruled only if the UN forces are introduced”. He was detained from 9 July 2015 to 28 March 2016. During proceedings, the “MRT court” refused to let him choose his own lawyer or represent himself, relying on an alleged schizophrenia diagnosis. In January 2016 he was removed from the courtroom until sentencing. On 28 March 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to three years and six months’ imprisonment in a semi-open prison; the sentence was upheld on 10 May 2016.

He alleged overcrowded detention, passive smoking, limited outdoor access, unfit food and water, and only weekly showers. In August 2016 he was transferred to a closed-regime prison for alleged disciplinary breaches. He went on hunger strike several times and was forcibly hospitalised and subjected to psychiatric assessment and psychotropic medication without consent in 2015 and 2016. He alleged inadequate medical care for hepatitis C, thrombophlebitis, dermatitis, varicose veins and other conditions, and was refused external consultations. He also alleged ill-treatment in April 2016 after hunger strikes and refusal to hand over a copy of his sentence to his mother. The “MRT militia” refused to investigate and confirmed that prisoners could not give documents to visitors. Requests for his medical file were refused. Moldova opened a criminal investigation into his kidnapping and the usurpation of official powers by “MRT officials”; the Moldovan Supreme Court later quashed the “MRT” judgments.
