Therefore, the prosecution’s appellate submissions were disclosed, in effect, only after the appellate court had already ruled.

The applicants challenged this before the Serbian Constitutional Court. On 26 November 2015, the Constitutional Court dismissed their complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It noted that the Code of Criminal Procedure did not require second-instance courts to provide an accused person with a copy of the prosecutor’s observations filed in reply to the accused’s appeal. In other words, domestic law did not oblige the Court of Appeal to disclose the prosecution’s written response to the defence.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 about their inability to comment on the Higher Public Prosecutor’s written observations submitted in reply to their defence statements of appeal in the proceedings before the Court of Appeal. The central factual basis of the alleged violation was that the prosecution’s appellate submissions were not communicated to the defence, depriving the applicants of an opportunity to respond before the Court of Appeal reached its final decision.

The case was communicated to the Serbian Government, represented by Agent Zorana Jadrijević Mladar. The parties submitted observations. The Fourth Section Committee, composed of Judges Tim Eicke, Ana Maria Guerra Martins, and Mateja Đurović, deliberated in private on 22 October 2024 and delivered judgment on 19 November 2024. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are thus the non-communication of the Higher Public Prosecutor’s written observations, the applicants’ lack of any chance to comment on them, and the domestic Constitutional Court’s rejection of the complaint on the basis that such communication was not required by the Code of Criminal Procedure.
001-233761:
**Case: Saakashvili v. Georgia (Apps nos. 6232/20 and 22394/20), ECtHR, 23 May 2024**

The case concerns two criminal prosecutions of Mikheil Saakashvili, former President of Georgia (2004–2013) and later a Ukrainian national. The applications alleged violations of Articles 6, 7 and 18 of the Convention—fair trial, legality of conviction, and improper political motive. The prosecutions formed part of the post-2012 Georgian Dream government’s “restoration of justice,” following thousands of complaints against former officials of the United National Movement. Saakashvili left Georgia in 2013, became a Ukrainian citizen, and was tried and convicted in absentia while represented by his chosen lawyers.

**First application (no. 6232/20): battery and misuse of authority.** On 14 July 2005, V.G., a member of parliament, was attacked in Tbilisi by armed men in riot-police uniforms. He was severely beaten, permanently disfigured, and his belongings were seized. V.G. linked the attack to an interview he had published shortly before, in which he insulted the President and his wife. An initial investigation was discontinued in 2005 but reopened in November 2012. Evidence included testimony from V.G., his bodyguard and driver; former Defence Minister I.O., who said Saakashvili personally ordered him to arrange the attack before it was reassigned to Interior Minister Merabishvili; former Parliament President N.B., who said Saakashvili implied V.G. deserved the beating; secret-surveillance officers who testified they monitored V.G. and tampered with his car brakes; riot-police participants who described the assault; and phone data showing contacts between Saakashvili and officials before and after the incident. In November 2014 he was charged with complicity in battery and misuse of authority. In June 2018 the Tbilisi City Court convicted him in absentia; the Supreme Court upheld the conviction in July 2019, imposing six years’ imprisonment plus a two-year ban on public service. He complained that the conviction relied on hearsay and politically hostile witnesses, but domestic courts found their testimony corroborated by other evidence.

**Second application (no. 22394/20): abuse of official authority.** In January 2006, Sandro Girgvliani and L.B. were abducted and beaten by Interior Ministry officers; Girgvliani was killed. Four officers were convicted in 2006. In November 2008, Saakashvili granted them presidential clemency, halving their sentences; they were released on licence in September 2009 after serving about three years. The ECtHR in *Enukidze and Girgvliani v. Georgia* (2011) found a procedural Article 2 violation and criticised the investigation and lenient treatment. After a 2012 repeat investigation, the four officers said they had acted on orders of CSD Director D.A., who allegedly promised them pardons, better prison conditions and compensation if they confessed and stayed silent about others, including the Interior Minister’s wife. Former officials I.O. and N.B. testified that Saakashvili knew the details and promised pardons to protect his political team. Clemency Commission members said the pardon bypassed normal procedure and no applications were considered. In November 2014 he was charged with abuse of power for granting the pardon to pervert justice. In January 2018 he was convicted in absentia. On appeal he argued judicial bias, reliance on hearsay, and that exercising presidential clemency could not constitute a crime. The alleged violations therefore concern whether the proceedings were fair, whether convicting him for the pardon breached the principle of legality, and whether the prosecutions pursued an improper political purpose.
001-234516:
In *B.A. v. Cyprus*, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 concerning the detention of a Syrian asylum-seeker on national-security grounds.

The applicant entered Cyprus from Türkiye via the occupied areas on 28 January 2019. On 8 February 2019 he and two relatives presented themselves at the Ledras crossing point and sought international protection. They were taken to the Aliens and Immigration Service, where fingerprints and photographs were taken. The Counter Terrorism Office and Cyprus Intelligence Service were informed. Initial background checks reportedly found no relevant information, but the AIS suspected possible irregular immigration activity.

On 11 February 2019 the applicant formally applied for asylum and received confirmation designating his residence in Nicosia. That same day, AIS interviewed him and his relatives with an interpreter, together with police, CIS and CTO officers. The authorities noted old injuries allegedly caused by shrapnel and bullets. They concluded that the applicant matched a “foreign fighter” profile: he was 23, had come from a war zone, and had moved from Damascus to Al-Harra in Daraa Province, an area mainly controlled by ISIS. After initial resistance, he consented to a phone inspection. Police found a password-encrypted application containing photographs of him and his relatives holding Kalashnikov rifles and wearing military uniforms. A judge issued a search warrant for their premises at Pournara. Further checks allegedly revealed family links and earlier police information about a relative hosting and trafficking Muslim preachers. On the same day, the Director of the Civil Registry and Migration Department issued detention orders under section 9ΣΤ(2)(e) of the Refugee Law on national-security grounds. On 12 February 2019 the applicant was notified, told he could challenge the order by recourse within 75 days, and detained. He was later held at Menoyia until release on 30 November 2021.

Domestically, the applicant challenged the detention order in the Administrative Court. At the hearing, the State submitted classified security documentation. The court added it to the file but refused to disclose it to the applicant. It also admitted a FRONTEX handbook over the applicant’s objection. On 25 April 2019 the Administrative Court dismissed the recourse, finding the detention lawful and based on specific national-security reasons, with alternatives ineffective. On 20 July 2021 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, holding that it could not question the executive’s national-security assessment and that the detention was compatible with EU law and Article 5 § 1(f). Separately, the Asylum Service rejected his asylum claim on 28 May 2019, excluding him for war crimes; that recourse remained pending with suspensive effect.

The applicant also filed habeas corpus petitions. The first, in July 2019, was dismissed in August 2019 on the basis that the State had acted with reasonable diligence and that lawfulness had already been determined. Internal reviews in late 2019 and early 2020 concluded the risk still existed. A second habeas corpus petition in January 2020 led to refusals of disclosure and release; the court found 12 months not excessive and noted the pending asylum proceedings. In June 2021 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal, stating that no specific executive steps were required to demonstrate dangerousness while proceedings were pending and that continued detention was justified because he remained an asylum-seeker and could not be removed. Further reviews in 2021 relied on suspected terrorist membership, phone photographs, and lack of alternatives to detention.

These facts grounded the alleged violations: under Article 5 § 1, that the detention was unlawful, particularly where Cyprus had authorised his stay as an asylum-seeker and allegedly relied on secret or insufficient national-security evidence; and under Article 5 § 4, that he lacked a speedy and effective procedure to challenge the lawfulness of his detention because courts refused disclosure, deferred to the executive, and delayed habeas/appeal proceedings.
001-235470:
In *Bielau v. Austria*, the applicant, Dr Klaus Bielau, was an Austrian general practitioner with a “holistic medicine” website on which he described himself as an expert on vaccinations and vaccine damage. The case concerned disciplinary proceedings brought against him over an article on vaccination posted on that website, dated 27 June 2016.

In the article, Bielau suggested that a tick bite could not cause death, that viruses were not proven pathogenic agents, and that conditions such as meningitis were healing reactions rather than the result of viral infection. He also claimed that chemical vaccinations could never protect against disease because people do not become ill through bacteria and viruses; that nature knew no diseases; and that vaccination had not eradicated or made a single disease disappear. The article used provocative language and referred ironically to “only vaccination protects.”

On 27 June 2017, after a hearing, the Disciplinary Commission for Styria and Carinthia of the Austrian Medical Association found Bielau guilty of disciplinary offences under section 136(1)(1) and (2) of the Medical Practitioners Act. Relying on an expert report by a prominent immunologist, the Commission found that he had denied the existence of pathogenic viruses, claimed vaccinations never protected against disease, claimed nature knew no diseases, and claimed that no disease had disappeared through vaccination. It considered these statements one-sided, negative, contrary to the state of science and medical experience, and therefore unobjective. They violated section 53 of the Medical Practitioners Act and the Regulation on Medical Practitioners and the Public, damaged the reputation of the medical profession, and breached professional duties. He was fined EUR 2,000, suspended for a one-year probationary period, and ordered to pay EUR 1,500 in costs.

Bielau challenged the decision before the Styria Regional Administrative Court, relying on his right to freedom of expression. He argued that the statements had to be read in context, were provocative rather than literal, were not directly related to his professional practice, and were not untrue or unobjective. The Regional Administrative Court held an oral hearing with a second expert, who also concluded that the statements contradicted current medical science. The court dismissed his complaint, finding that the statements were one-sided and scientifically unsupported. It stressed that doctors must provide objective information, especially about vaccination, and that the restriction served the protection of health and public trust in the medical profession. The Constitutional Court declined to consider the case, and the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his extraordinary appeal. The Supreme Administrative Court found that the website had an advertising purpose connected to his medical practice, that the statements were unobjective and potentially damaging to the profession’s reputation, and that the relatively low, suspended fine was proportionate under Article 10 § 2 of the Convention.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Bielau complained under Article 10 that the disciplinary sanction violated his right to freedom of expression. The key issue was whether the domestic authorities’ interference—punishing him for public statements about vaccination—was justified as necessary in a democratic society for the protection of health and the rights of others, or whether it disproportionately restricted his freedom to impart information and ideas.
001-231227:
In *Executief van de Moslims van België and Others v. Belgium* (ECtHR, 13 February 2024), the applicants were thirteen Belgian nationals and seven NGOs, including Muslim representative bodies, Turkish and Moroccan religious authorities, and Belgian nationals of Muslim and Jewish faith. They challenged regional bans on ritual slaughter without prior stunning in Flanders and Wallonia, alleging violations of Articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Previously, Belgian federal law required stunning before slaughter but exempted slaughter prescribed by religious rites. After animal welfare became a regional competence in 2014, Flanders and Wallonia ended that exemption. The Flemish Decree of 7 July 2017 amended the 1986 animal welfare law so that vertebrates may not be killed without prior stunning, except in cases of force majeure, hunting or fishing, and pest control. For religious slaughter, stunning had to be reversible and could not cause the animal’s death; for cattle, a transitional rule allowed stunning immediately after the throat was cut until reversible stunning became practicable. The Walloon Decree of 4 October 2018, in force from 1 September 2019, contained an equivalent rule: animals must be stunned or anaesthetised before killing, with limited exceptions, and religious slaughter required reversible, non-lethal stunning. Breaches were punishable by imprisonment and substantial fines. The Brussels-Capital Region retained the earlier exemption.

The applicants argued that Jewish and Islamic religious precepts, at least as understood by parts of those communities, require the animal to be fully conscious at the time of slaughter and to die solely from bleeding. They claimed that mandatory stunning—even reversible, non-lethal stunning—was incompatible with those precepts, making it difficult or impossible to obtain ritually slaughtered meat in the two regions. They alleged that this breached their freedom to manifest religion under Article 9 and discriminated against them under Article 14, particularly because hunting and fishing were exempted and because non-religious slaughter was treated differently.

Some applicants brought annulment proceedings before the Belgian Constitutional Court. That court referred preliminary questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union. In *Centraal Israëlitisch Consistorie van België* (2020), the CJEU held that EU law did not preclude a member State from requiring reversible, non-lethal stunning in ritual slaughter. It found an interference with religious manifestation but considered it limited, justified by animal welfare, and proportionate, with a wide margin of appreciation. The CJEU also rejected the discrimination complaint concerning hunting and fishing.

In 2021, the Belgian Constitutional Court dismissed the annulment actions. It held that the restriction was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of animal welfare and public morals, and was necessary and proportionate. It noted that reversible stunning was permitted, that import of non-stunned meat remained possible, and that there was no unjustified inequality. The applicants then brought the case to the ECtHR, which gave notice to Belgium of the complaints under Articles 9 and 14 and declared the remaining parts inadmissible. The key issue was whether the regional bans on unstunned ritual slaughter unjustifiably interfered with religious freedom and discriminated against Jewish and Muslim believers.
001-236140:
**Case: S.F. v. Finland (Application no. 35276/20), judgment of 8 October 2024**

The applicant, S.F., is an Eritrean national born in 1982 and living in Vantaa, Finland. She and her three minor children were granted asylum in Finland by the Finnish Immigration Service on 27 October 2016, and she was notified of that decision on 8 November 2016. She received refugee status because she was found to face persecution in Eritrea on account of her political opinions. The asylum decision included information, in Finnish, about family reunification procedures, including where and how to apply and the relevant time-limit. In particular, it explained that where the sponsor in Finland had refugee status and the family had been established before the sponsor arrived in Finland, a family member could apply for a residence permit without satisfying the maintenance requirement if the application was submitted within three months of notification of the positive asylum decision.

The Government submitted that immigration records showed the applicant had discussed family reunification with a social worker in November 2016 and January 2017, assisted by a Tigrinya interpreter. On the latter occasion she was allegedly specifically informed about the three-month deadline and the consequences of exceeding it, and was given application forms, the contact details of the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi, and information about applying online.

The applicant’s husband, also Eritrean, had refugee status in Uganda and lived in Kampala. On 30 January 2018—about fifteen months after the applicant was notified of her asylum decision—he applied for a residence permit on family reunification grounds at the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi. He presented an Eritrean passport issued on 18 May 2017. In his February 2019 interview, he said he had fled Eritrea in 2014 after being penalised for leaving military service without permission to visit his family.

By decision of 20 February 2019, the Immigration Service refused the husband’s application. It accepted that he was a member of the applicant’s family but found that the applicant did not meet the maintenance requirement under section 39 of the Aliens Act. The three-month exception in section 114(4) did not apply because the applicant had been notified on 8 November 2016, while the husband applied only on 30 January 2018. The required monthly income was EUR 2,900, or EUR 34,800 annually; the applicant’s income consisted only of social security benefits, and she had not shown continuous income sufficient to support her husband. It was assumed he would need social assistance.

The Immigration Service found no exceptionally serious grounds for derogating from the maintenance requirement. The couple had been partly imprecise about the delay. The husband claimed he had tried to contact Finnish consular authorities in Kampala in spring 2017, but the honorary consulate did not handle residence permits; he was advised to apply in Nairobi but did not do so before January 2018. The Immigration Service found this insufficient, noting that passport stamps indicated he had visited Kenya and Eritrea before then, that he was in good health, had refugee status and a support network in Uganda, and was settled there. It also considered the children’s best interests but found they did not warrant a permit for a father who had spent little time with them; the oldest child said he had never had a relationship with him, and the youngest was born after the father left Eritrea.

The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 6 September 2019, holding that the late application meant the maintenance requirement applied. It found the applicant depended on social welfare, the delay reasons were financial or passport-related, and the alleged health problems were unsubstantiated. It concluded that the children’s best interests did not require derogation merely because family ties might be interrupted. A minority of judges would have derogated because the required income was unrealistic in the applicant’s circumstances. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 26 February 2020. The case therefore concerns the refusal of family reunification and its compatibility with the applicant’s right to respect for family life.
001-233213:
M.B. v. the Netherlands (Application no. 71008/16) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the alleged unlawfulness of an asylum-seeker’s immigration detention under Article 5 of the Convention. The applicant, M.B., is a Syrian national born in 1997. He left Syria in December 2013, stayed in Türkiye, and entered the Netherlands in October 2015. On 26 October 2015 he applied for asylum and was accommodated in a reception centre.

The key facts leading to the detention arose after two other asylum-seekers told police that M.B. had claimed he was involved in a terrorist organisation in Syria and had detonated car bombs. A criminal investigation followed. On 30 November 2015 he was arrested on suspicion of participating in an organisation with the purpose of committing terrorist offences and placed in pre-trial detention. He was later charged with participating in a terrorist organisation between March 2013 and October 2015.

At trial, the public prosecutor argued that although there was lawful evidence for a conviction, he was not convinced beyond reasonable doubt and sought acquittal. Nevertheless, on 29 August 2016 the Rotterdam Regional Court convicted M.B. and sentenced him to ten months’ imprisonment. It relied on his statements, a witness statement, a 2013 tweet in which he said he belonged to Al Qaida, WhatsApp conversations from 2015, and photos and videos on his phone. His criminal detention ended on 23 September 2016.

On the same day, the Deputy Minister of Security and Justice ordered his placement in immigration detention under section 59b(1)(b) and (d) of the Aliens Act 2000. The order was based on two grounds: first, that detention was necessary to obtain information for assessing his asylum application and because of a risk of absconding; second, that he posed a threat to national security or public order because of his criminal conviction for a terrorist offence. The Deputy Minister stated that M.B. posed a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat, that less restrictive measures were unsuitable, and that a prospect of deportation was not required for detention under section 59b.

M.B. appealed, arguing that his detention breached Article 5 § 1(f) of the Convention because there was no prospect of deportation to Syria and no return decision had been taken while his asylum application remained pending. He relied on the CJEU’s judgment in N. but sought to distinguish it because no return decision had been issued in his case.

On 10 October 2016, the Regional Court of The Hague dismissed his appeal. It held that section 59b transposed Article 8(3) of the EU Reception Conditions Directive into Dutch law, and that the CJEU in N. had upheld the validity of detention based on protection of national security or public order. It further found that the absence of an expulsion procedure did not automatically violate Article 5, and that under Saadi v. the United Kingdom, detention of an unauthorised entrant was permissible if not arbitrary. The court found the risk of absconding insufficient to justify detention under section 59b(1)(b), but held that section 59b(1)(d) alone provided a sufficient basis because of the criminal conviction. The Council of State dismissed a further appeal on 8 November 2016.

Later, M.B.’s continued detention was found to breach a procedural time-limit, and the detention order was lifted on 13 December 2016 with compensation. In his criminal appeal, he was acquitted on 12 December 2017 for lack of sufficient evidence, confirmed by the Supreme Court. The freedom-restricting measure imposed after detention was lifted on 18 January 2018, and on 29 March 2018 he was granted an asylum-based residence permit retroactive to 26 October 2015.

The alleged violation therefore concerned Article 5 § 1(f): whether immigration detention pending an asylum assessment, based on a threat to public order or national security following a criminal conviction, was lawful when no deportation or extradition proceedings were in progress and no return decision had been issued.
001-230729:
**Case name:** *Kowalik v. Poland* (Application no. 37910/21), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Committee judgment of 8 February 2024.

The applicant, Paweł Kowalik, born in 1980, lodged an application against Poland on 15 July 2021 under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Polish Government were given notice of the application. The applicant complained of two principal matters: the excessive length of criminal proceedings concerning him, and the lack of any effective remedy in Polish domestic law for that excessive length. These complaints correspond to the reasonable-time guarantee under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

The key facts are set out in the appended table. The criminal proceedings began on 7 May 2017. At the time relevant to the application, they were still pending. The total length of the proceedings was recorded as more than 6 years, 6 months and 4 days. The proceedings had reached only one level of jurisdiction. This chronology is central to the alleged violation: the applicant did not complain principally about the substantive outcome of the criminal case, but about the State’s failure to conclude it within a reasonable time and its failure to provide effective domestic redress for the delay.

The table also records that the applicant made use of the domestic remedy under the Polish 2004 Act concerning complaints about breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The Warsaw-Praga Regional Court issued decisions on those complaints: on 6 December 2019 in case no. VI S 133/19, with a domestic award of PLN 2,000; and on 10 February 2021 in case no. VI S 12/21. The provided text does not set out the reasoning of those decisions or the later procedural history of the criminal case. Nevertheless, the fact that the applicant had already pursued the 2004 Act remedy and then applied to Strasbourg is significant, because it underpinned his allegation that the domestic remedy had not been effective in his case and that the criminal proceedings remained excessively long.

The Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Péter Paczolay, Gilberto Felici and Raffaele Sabato, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 18 January 2024 and adopted the judgment on 8 February 2024. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the criminal proceedings started on 7 May 2017; they remained pending; their total duration exceeded six and a half years; they had reached only one level of jurisdiction; and the applicant had obtained a domestic award of PLN 2,000 under the 2004 Act, plus a further decision in February 2021, yet still complained that the length was excessive and that no effective domestic remedy existed. No details concerning the nature of the criminal charge, the evidence, or the merits of the criminal case are included in the provided text. The case accordingly forms part of the Court’s recurring examination of Polish length-of-proceedings complaints under Article 6 § 1 and the effectiveness of domestic remedies under Article 13.
001-238270:
CASE OF GIANNAKOPOULOS v. GREECE (Application no. 20503/20) concerns an Article 8 complaint by Mr Georgios Giannakopoulos, a Greek national, that the Greek courts refused to examine his custody application after his children were taken to Germany by their mother. The applicant married E.B., a German national, in 2009; they lived in Rhodes and had two children, born in 2010 and 2012. After separating, E.B. applied for interim custody in Greece. In decision no. 590/2013 of 18 October 2013, the Rhodes One-Member Court of First Instance granted her custody, set the applicant’s contact schedule, and noted there was no evidence she would leave for Germany. E.B. had assured the court that she would remain in Rhodes with the children.

In December 2013, E.B. travelled with the children to Germany for a Christmas visit, saying she would return by 13 January 2014. She did not return and settled permanently in Germany. The applicant served the Greek decision on the German authorities in July 2014. In January 2015, the Greek court granted him interim custody in decision no. 26/2015, finding a substantive change of circumstances: E.B. had misled the court, moved to Germany, and obstructed his contact rights. The applicant also obtained enforceability certificates for that decision.

On 29 January 2015, the applicant sought sole custody of the children in Greece. The Greek courts declined jurisdiction. They found that, by the time he applied, the children were habitually resident in Germany. They had lived there for over a year, attended nursery or school, adapted well, spoke German, and had family and social ties there. The mother, who had sole custody, could determine their place of residence. The Dodecanese Court of Appeal (decision no. 302/2017) and the Court of Cassation (decision no. 927/2019) upheld that conclusion. They held that Article 10 of the Brussels II bis Regulation on child abduction did not apply because the mother had sole custody and there had been no wrongful removal. Article 12 on prorogation did not apply because E.B. had not accepted Greek jurisdiction.

The applicant argued that the Greek courts had wrongly ignored several key matters: that the children’s removal breached his contact rights under decision no. 590/2013; that E.B. had misled the Greek court to obtain custody; that decision no. 26/2015 had later granted him interim custody; that German courts had rejected the mother’s request to disregard that decision and had initially suspended proceedings pending the Greek courts’ clarification of jurisdiction; and that the children’s stay in Germany had not been long enough to establish habitual residence.

In parallel German proceedings, the Düsseldorf District Court ordered the children’s return to Greece in June 2015, but the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal reversed that decision in November 2015. It found that the Hague Convention return application had been lodged after the one-year period and that the children were settled in Germany. A constitutional complaint was dismissed. German custody proceedings were initially suspended pending the Greek courts’ jurisdiction decision; after the Court of Cassation ruling, a German court granted parental responsibility to E.B. in October 2021. Separately, a Greek misdemeanour court convicted E.B. in 2018 for breaching decisions nos. 590/2013 and 26/2015 between December 2013 and March 2015.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8 that the Greek courts’ rejection of his custody application for lack of jurisdiction violated his right to respect for family life. He alleged misinterpretation of the Brussels II bis Regulation, an erroneous finding that the children were habitually resident in Germany, and disregard of the wrongful removal, his contact and custody rights, and the related German proceedings.
001-233236:
**Case of Levanov and Others v. Russia** (Application no. 40953/21 and 18 others) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights’ Third Section, sitting as a Committee, in a judgment dated 25 April 2024. The case concerns 19 applicants who lodged applications under Article 34 of the Convention at various dates. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications.

The applicants complained of disproportionate measures taken against them as organisers or participants of public assemblies. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The appended table sets out the relevant facts for each applicant.

The public events at issue were two main groups: the “Free Navalnyy” rallies in January–April 2021 and anti-war protests in February–March 2022. The events took place in several Russian cities, including Chelyabinsk, Moscow, Petrozavodsk, Belgorod, Krasnoyarsk, Voronezh, St Petersburg and Volgograd.

In each case, the applicants were subjected to administrative or criminal offences under the Russian Code of Administrative Offences (CAO). The provisions included Article 19.3 § 1 (failure to comply with a lawful police order), Article 20.2 §§ 2, 5, 6.1 and 8 (violations of rules on public assemblies), and Article 20.2.2 § 1 (violations of rules for public events). The penalties imposed included administrative detention, fines and community work. Detention ranged from 7 to 13 days. Fines ranged from RUB 5,000 to RUB 20,000. One applicant received 80 hours of community work.

Specific examples from the table include: Aleksandr Levanov, for the “Free Navalnyy” rally in Chelyabinsk on 23 January 2021, was convicted under Article 19.3 § 1 and detained for 13 days; the final domestic decision was by the Chelyabinsk Regional Court on 27 January 2021. Kristina Ramires, for the Moscow rally on 31 January 2021, was convicted under Article 20.2 § 6.1 and detained for 7 days. Sergey Tolmachev, for the Chelyabinsk rally on 23 January 2021, was convicted under Article 20.2 § 8 and detained for 11 days. Sergey Filenko was fined RUB 5,000 twice in respect of Petrozavodsk rallies on 23 January and 21 April 2021 under Article 20.2 § 5.

Several applicants received RUB 10,000 fines under Article 20.2 § 5, including Kristina Isayeva, Aleksey Bavkin, Nikita Kabakov, Daniel Cherkashin, Aleksey Merkulov, Artem Shchelokov, Aleksandr Abramov, Svetlana Semenyuk and Mikhail Militsin. Mariya Antyusheva was fined RUB 5,000. Kseniya Mayorova was fined RUB 20,000 under Article 20.2 § 2, and Nadezhda Stepanenko was fined RUB 20,000 under Article 20.2 § 5.

Regarding anti-war protests, Olga Korobitsina and Marek Pasierb were each fined RUB 10,000 under Article 20.2.2 § 1 in St Petersburg. Vladimir Toborovets received 80 hours of community work under Article 20.2 § 8 in Voronezh. The final domestic decisions were issued by various regional and city courts, including the Chelyabinsk Regional Court, Moscow City Court, Supreme Court of the Republic of Karelia, Belgorod Regional Court, Krasnoyarsk Regional Court, Voronezh Regional Court, St Petersburg City Court and Volgograd Regional Court, between January 2021 and May 2022.

The applicants alleged that these measures were disproportionate and violated their Convention rights in connection with public assemblies. The provided excerpt sets out the procedural history and factual basis of those complaints but does not include the Court’s merits analysis.
001-233111:
Mr Guðmundur Gunnarsson (born 1976, Kópavogur) and Mr Magnús Davíð Norðdahl (born 1982, Reykjavík) lodged applications against Iceland on 6 and 20 May 2022. The case arose from the 25 September 2021 elections to Althingi. In the Northwest constituency, the smallest in Iceland, Gunnarsson stood as the top candidate for the Liberal Reform Party (Viðreisn), and Norðdahl as the top candidate for the Pirate Party (Píratar).

According to the Northwest constituency’s senior electoral commission, the initial vote count was finalised in the early morning of 26 September 2021. The reported result was that Liberal Reform received 1,072 of 17,666 votes, meaning Gunnarsson qualified for a levelling seat, while the Pirate Party received 1,082 votes, leaving Norðdahl a few votes short of a constituency seat.

At around noon that day, the National Electoral Commission telephoned the Northwest senior electoral commission, noting a very narrow margin of two votes in the Northwest and South constituencies that could affect levelling-seat allocation, and suggested a recount. A recount of Liberal Reform’s votes in the Northwest reduced its tally to 1,063, nine votes fewer. A full recount followed in the early afternoon: six parties lost between one and nine votes and four gained between one and ten; Liberal Reform ended with 1,063 votes and the Pirate Party with 1,081, one vote less than initially. A recount in the South constituency produced no changes. The Northwest recount led to a national reallocation of levelling seats. Gunnarsson lost his levelling seat, and the Northwest levelling seat went from Liberal Reform to the Centre Party.

The applicants lodged separate complaints on 1 and 5 October 2021, along with fifteen other complaints. Gunnarsson alleged that the recount lacked a legal basis; that ballots had been improperly stored and handled between counts; that party agents were not informed of the recount and could not observe it; and that changes in votes, blank ballots and invalid ballots were inconsistent and unexplained. He also disputed Althingi’s role in deciding electoral disputes and argued the defects could have influenced the outcome. Norðdahl alleged improper storage and handling of ballots and failure to inform him, as his party’s list agent, about the recount, depriving him of the chance to observe it. He argued it was sufficient that the defects could have influenced the result.

The Preparatory Credentials Committee, composed of nine members none elected in the Northwest, adopted procedural rules on 8 October 2021. It conducted an extensive inquiry over less than two months, obtaining documents, comments and information, questioning witnesses and experts, holding thirty-four meetings and making field visits to the count facility. The applicants appeared before it on 22 October 2021 and were invited to comment on draft descriptions in November. Most material was published on Althingi’s website, except confidential material and closed-hearing material. Gunnarsson’s lawyer requested access to various items, including material from a pending criminal investigation; Althingi provided some materials but refused others as confidential, and later refused a repeated request.

On 23 November 2021 the Preparatory Credentials Committee issued a ninety-page report identifying irregularities in the Northwest recount. It found that ballots had not been sealed and were left unattended in open boxes in a closed but unsupervised hotel room; one entrance could not be locked, hotel staff had keys, cameras did not cover the area, and the commission chairman had been alone there for about half an hour. It also found defects concerning the absence or insufficient notification of agents, changed numbers of valid ballots, and failure to secure agents’ participation in validity rulings. Other deviations concerned verification, mixing and counting procedures, and incomplete minutes.

On 25 November 2021 the Credentials Committee issued recommendations. Its majority found no indication of tampering and no effect on results, recommending confirmation of all sixty-three newly elected members. Minority members recommended annulling the Northwest or nationwide results and holding re-elections. Althingi debated the recommendations for over five hours and rejected the minority proposals. By forty-two votes to five, with sixteen abstentions, it confirmed the credentials. Under domestic law, Article 46 of the Constitution leaves Althingi to decide whether members are legally elected; the Act on Parliamentary Elections and Standing Orders govern complaints and credentials scrutiny.
001-234008:
In *Maļinovskis v. Latvia* (Application no. 46084/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) examined complaints under Article 3 of the Convention concerning alleged ill-treatment in prison and the State’s alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation. The applicant, Jānis Maļinovskis, a Latvian national born in 1969 and detained in Riga, was represented by lawyer J. Dadukina; the Latvian Government was represented by K. Līce.

The key incident occurred on 30 January 2013 at Riga Central Prison. Three prison guards used physical force to subdue the applicant in the prison yard when he attempted to collect a packet thrown to him from a prison cell window by another prisoner. The parties disputed the nature and degree of force used. The applicant alleged that he was forced to the ground, that his face was smashed into the concrete floor approximately twenty times, and that he received approximately twenty kicks. He alleged that his nose was broken as a result.

Medical evidence shortly after the incident showed bruising to the applicant’s forehead, head, left ear and nose, along with superficial scratches. The next day, after transfer to Daugavgrīva Prison, a doctor recorded scratches, a bruised face and chest, and a broken nose.

On 4 February 2013 criminal proceedings were instituted. The investigation went through six rounds, each ending with an investigator’s decision to terminate proceedings for lack of *corpus delicti*. All termination decisions except the last were quashed by a superior prosecutor. In the first four rounds, prosecutors found that the investigation had not been thorough. The first round included a forensic examination and interrogations of the applicant and several Riga Central Prison officials. In December 2013, a superior prosecutor instructed the investigator to identify potential prisoner witnesses. The second round involved additional witnesses, another forensic examination, and information gathering; in March 2015, further instructions were given to interrogate witnesses more thoroughly and identify additional witnesses. The third round included interrogation of a prison guard, but no new witnesses were identified. In the fourth round, a confrontation was held between the applicant and a witness, and a senior Prisons Administration official and other witnesses were interrogated. In November 2017, a prosecutor again instructed further investigative measures, found this round excessively lengthy, and requested an internal audit; the Prisons Administration and investigator admitted deficiencies.

In the fifth round, the investigator obtained information on the applicant and several guards, interrogated the applicant and witnesses, and terminated proceedings both for lack of *corpus delicti* and because the offence had become time-barred. That decision was quashed in February 2019 because the two grounds contradicted each other. In the sixth round, no investigative measures were taken. By final decision of 8 May 2019, a superior prosecutor upheld termination of the criminal proceedings.

Separately, on 8 March 2013 the applicant complained to the Prisons Administration about the use of force as an “action of a public authority.” After dismissal, he applied to the Administrative District Court, but those proceedings ended on 16 January 2015 after he withdrew his application.

The applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 14 August 2019, complaining under Article 3 that prison guards had used excessive force against him and that the ensuing investigation had been ineffective and excessively lengthy. The Court gave notice of the ill-treatment and investigation complaints to the Government and declared the remainder inadmissible. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected. The judgment was delivered on 6 June 2024.
001-233412:
The case *Tsaava and Others v. Georgia* concerns five applications brought by twenty-six Georgian nationals against Georgia under the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants include journalists, photographers, camera operators and demonstrators. They complain about the excessive use of force by police during the dispersal of a large demonstration in Tbilisi on 20–21 June 2019 and about the alleged failure to conduct an effective criminal investigation. Most invoke Articles 3 and 13; some also invoke Articles 10 and 11.

The protest began after a Russian State Duma member and IAO president, S.G., sat in the Georgian Parliament Speaker’s chair and addressed the assembly in Russian. Public anger led to a demonstration outside Parliament. Initially peaceful, it gathered around 12,000 people. Police formed a cordon blocking access to Parliament. As opposition politicians demanded resignations, snap elections and proportional representation, tensions grew. Some protesters tried to break through the cordon and enter the Parliament yard. Scuffles continued for hours, with demonstrators throwing bottles and other objects, seizing police shields and batons, and some officers being assaulted. Police responded with batons, shields, tear gas, rubber bullets and later a water cannon. Shooting began around 11:55 p.m. without warning. Tear gas and rubber bullets were fired repeatedly, sometimes simultaneously, as demonstrators returned to the area. Dispersal continued until about 6:45 a.m. In total, 342 people were arrested and over 200 injured, including about eighty police officers and forty journalists.

The applicants’ individual circumstances are central to the alleged violations. Many were injured by rubber bullets, tear gas or physical beatings. Several journalists were filming, photographing or livestreaming, wearing press badges, and allegedly posed no threat when hit. For example, Merab Tsaava was photographing when his hand was hit; Beslan Kmuzov was moving calmly and gesturing when hit in the head; Zaza Svanadze had his hands raised when hit in the thigh; other journalists were hit in the back, shoulder, hand or eye. Some demonstrators suffered grave injuries: one lost an eye, another lost most sight in an eye, others sustained a broken jaw, fractures, chest wounds or wounds from which rubber bullets were retrieved. Some applicants alleged they were beaten during arrest or detention. Medical reports classified several injuries as minor, serious or grave; some applicants were denied victim status in the domestic investigation.

On 22 June 2019 the General Prosecutor’s Office opened an ex officio investigation under Article 333 of the Criminal Code into alleged abuse of authority by MIA officers through violence or weapons during the dispersal. It was later extended to alleged unlawful interference with journalists’ work. All applicants were questioned, but some were refused victim status because the investigation had not established an offence against them. The Public Defender monitored the investigation and recommended examining the role of mid- and high-level MIA officials and the supervision of rubber-bullet use. The GPO later stated that decisions to use non-lethal projectiles had been taken by individual officers independently and that not all use was necessarily excessive. The case therefore concerns whether the police force was excessive and whether Georgia carried out an effective investigation.
001-237959:
**Case: Al-Habeeb v. Denmark (Application no. 14171/23)**

The case concerns an Iraqi national, Mr Hamza Azeem Thamer Al-Habeeb, who complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that his expulsion from Denmark with a twelve-year re-entry ban disproportionately interfered with his private and family life.

The applicant entered Denmark in 1998 at the age of seven. In 1999 he was granted residence under section 7(2) of the Danish Aliens Act (subsidiary protection), and in 2002 he received permanent residence. He grew up in Denmark, attended Danish primary, secondary and commercial/technical schools, speaks fluent Danish, and worked for four years as an assistant social educator. His parents and siblings live in Denmark. In 2020 he married a Danish national in a Muslim ceremony, and in March 2021 their daughter, also a Danish national, was born. He has no relatives in Iraq, speaks broken Arabic, and does not read or write Arabic.

The applicant had previous convictions: in 2010, attempted robbery at age 17, sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment; in 2011, attempted aggravated violence, sentenced to three months’ imprisonment; and in 2019, repeated violence, sentenced to three months’ imprisonment, when he was warned of the risk of expulsion.

The index offence occurred on 26 July 2020. By judgment of the District Court of Roskilde on 28 September 2021, the applicant was convicted under Article 245 § 1, read with Article 247 § 1, of the Danish Penal Code of assault of a particularly offensive, brutal or dangerous nature. The court found that he, together with three masked co-offenders, had stabbed the victim five times in the back, groin and lung; one stab hit the victim’s right lung and could have been fatal without medical treatment. He was sentenced to two years and three months’ imprisonment. The court also ordered his expulsion from Denmark with a twelve-year re-entry ban.

In deciding on expulsion, the District Court considered his long lawful residence, permanent residence status, Danish family and social ties, and his possible EU-law derived right of residence through his Danish daughter. It found no relationship of dependency that would compel his daughter to leave the European Union if he were expelled. It accepted that his ties with Denmark were stronger than those with Iraq but found that the gravity of the stabbing, his prior violent offences, and the risk of future serious offences outweighed the considerations against expulsion. It also noted that his family could maintain contact through visits, telephone or online communication. The High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment on 19 May 2022, and the Appeals Permission Board refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court on 20 December 2022. The applicant was expelled to Iraq on 5 July 2022 and later moved to Sweden to live with his family; his wife became pregnant with their second child in August 2023.

Relevant to the alleged Article 8 violation was the twelve-year re-entry ban. Under Danish law, courts may reduce a normally permanent ban if a longer ban would certainly breach Denmark’s international obligations. Re-entry after a time-limited ban depends on obtaining a residence permit or visa. Iraq is in visa group 5, meaning high immigration risk, and visas are generally granted only in extraordinary circumstances. Statistics showed very few expelled persons obtained residence permits or visas. Danish courts generally do not consider future readmission prospects when imposing time-limited bans. The applicant’s complaint therefore concerns whether expulsion and the lengthy ban disproportionately interfered with his private and family life given his settled status, Danish family ties, and practical barriers to returning.
001-230725:
In *Kowalski v. Poland* (Application no. 4771/20), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 8 February 2024. The applicant, Piotr Kowalski, born in 1979, was represented by Dawid Cupiał, a lawyer practising in Warsaw. He lodged his application with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention on 2 January 2020. The Polish Government was given notice of the application.

The applicant’s central complaints were that the criminal proceedings in his case had been excessively long and that Polish domestic law did not provide him with an effective remedy for that delay. These allegations correspond to the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

According to the appended table, the criminal proceedings began on 30 June 2014 and ended on 10 June 2020. They therefore lasted 5 years, 11 months and 12 days, and were examined at two levels of jurisdiction. The table does not set out the nature of the charges, the complexity of the case, the number or length of hearings, or the specific reasons for the delay. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are thus the start and end dates, the total duration, and the fact that the case went through two judicial instances.

A significant domestic-remedy fact is that the applicant made a complaint under the Polish 2004 Act concerning the breach of the right to have a case heard within a reasonable time. The Warsaw Regional Court decided that complaint on 14 November 2019 in case no. X S 146/19. The appended table labels this as a “Domestic award (in Polish zlotys),” but the excerpt provided does not specify the amount awarded. The timing is important: the domestic complaint was decided more than five years after the criminal proceedings started, and the criminal case continued for approximately another seven months after that decision. The applicant nevertheless maintained that this mechanism did not amount to an effective remedy for the length of the proceedings.

The Court, composed of President Péter Paczolay and Judges Gilberto Felici and Raffaele Sabato, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 18 January 2024 and adopted the judgment on 8 February 2024. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In summary, the facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant was involved in criminal proceedings lasting almost six years across two levels of jurisdiction; that he attempted to use the domestic length complaint under the 2004 Act, obtaining a decision from the Warsaw Regional Court in November 2019; and that he then applied to Strasbourg, complaining that the overall length was excessive and that domestic law lacked an effective remedy. The excerpt does not include the Court’s detailed reasoning or final holding, but it identifies the case as one concerning prolonged criminal proceedings and the adequacy of Poland’s domestic remedial response.
001-238072:
In *Souroullas Kay and Zannettos v. Cyprus* (Application no. 1618/18, judgment of 26 November 2024), the European Court of Human Rights examined two main complaints under Article 6: whether the applicants’ criminal trial was fair because their conviction rested to a decisive extent on the testimony of an accomplice granted immunity from prosecution, and whether the refusal to give them access to the prosecution’s forensic disk image breached Article 6 § 3(b) taken together with Article 6 § 1.

The case arose from a 2013 commission of inquiry into a suspicious land deal in Dromolaxia, near Larnaca airport. The land, originally owned by a Turkish Cypriot, had been sold to a private company and then resold to CYTA’s pension fund for an office complex. The authorities suspected bribery, money laundering, and an inflated price. During police searches, computer hard drives were seized and copied for forensic examination. Searches were conducted using terms including a misspelling of “Poleson.”

N.L., a property entrepreneur and chairman of the financially troubled ALKI Larnaca football club, was arrested in August 2013 with two police officers on suspicion of bribing officers to produce a false report about the landowner’s residency. He initially refused to answer questions. After being released, he promised to cooperate. An investigator told him to reveal everything, without making promises, but said that if his statements proved true, he might suggest using him as a prosecution witness. Between September and November 2013, N.L. made four written statements admitting complicity in a conspiracy and implicating several people, including the applicants Gregoris Souroullas and Venizelos Zannettos, and Polleson Holdings Ltd. He alleged that Souroullas was involved in laundering bribe money paid to a CYTA trade-union representative, and that Zannettos, AKEL’s financial director, threatened to block the deal unless N.L. repaid personal loans of former ALKI executives. The Attorney-General decided not to prosecute N.L. on 5 November 2013. The applicants were charged and tried with six co-accused before the Larnaca Assize Court.

At trial, the prosecution relied mainly on N.L. Five defence lawyers cross-examined him over five days, attacking his credibility and alleging collusion with politically motivated investigators. After N.L. testified, proceedings against him were discontinued. During the trial, the prosecution asked its forensic examiner to search the disk image again. She extracted two unsigned draft contracts between N.L.’s company and Polleson, which the prosecution used to support the claim that Souroullas knew of the illicit origin of funds. The defence argued that those documents must have been seen earlier and concealed. Investigators said they had overlooked them due to the volume of material and a misspelling.

The defence then sought access to the prosecution’s disk image. Although the defence had a copy, it claimed the hash value differed and the copy was inexact. It wanted its expert to inspect the prosecution’s image to determine when the documents had been opened, potentially proving collusion or that N.L.’s testimony had been dictated. The Assize Court refused the request.

In December 2014, the Assize Court convicted Souroullas of money laundering and Zannettos of extortion, sentencing them to six and a half and three and a half years respectively. It cautioned itself about accomplice evidence but found N.L. credible, describing his testimony as “indestructible and sincere,” and relied on it to a “most decisive” extent, with no corroboration. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions, calling N.L.’s testimony the “foundation” and finding no improper dealings. It also held that denial of access to the disk image did not disadvantage the defence because it had a copy containing all trial documents. The ECtHR thus considered whether these facts violated the applicants’ fair-trial rights.
001-235346:
**Summary of W.R. v. The Netherlands**

The case of *W.R. v. The Netherlands* concerns the alleged unfairness of criminal proceedings due to the lack of legal assistance during initial police interviews, violating Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, a Dutch national, was arrested on 12 January 2014 on suspicion of manslaughter following the disappearance of his ex-wife. Police had discovered blood spatters and a pungent odour of a combustible substance at his home. Upon arrest, the applicant was informed of his right to consult a lawyer prior to questioning. He did not respond when asked if he wished to consult an assigned lawyer, so the Legal Aid Duty Roster Service was notified. He consulted with his lawyer later that morning.

That evening, police questioned the applicant without his lawyer present. After being informed of his right to remain silent, he gave a detailed confession, admitting to killing the victim and offering to show police relevant locations. This led to an on-site visit where the victim's body was discovered. In a subsequent interview on 13 January, again without counsel, he provided further details, including his admission that he had conceived a plan to kill the victim, laid out a knife and tarpaulins in his garage beforehand, and later executed this plan.

The core of the applicant's complaint stems from the use of these statements, made without a lawyer present, in his subsequent trial. In the first-instance proceedings, the Regional Court admitted the evidence, finding the police had acted in accordance with the case-law of the Supreme Court, which at the time only guaranteed the right to *consult* a lawyer, not to have one present during questioning.

However, the legal landscape evolved. The Supreme Court later accepted, in December 2015, that suspects had a right to have a lawyer present during police interviews, effective from March 2016. This change followed the European Court of Human Rights' *Salduz* judgment and EU Directive 2013/48/EU.

Despite this shift, the applicant's conviction for murder was upheld on appeal in December 2015. The Court of Appeal relied heavily on the detailed confession from 12 and 13 January 2014 to establish premeditation. The applicant's defence argued for the exclusion of these statements, but this was rejected. The Supreme Court later acknowledged the Court of Appeal had erred in its legal reasoning on the exclusion issue but ultimately dismissed the appeal, noting that the applicant had consulted a lawyer between his arrest and the first substantive interview.

The applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights centered on the unfairness of using evidence obtained during police interviews where he was not assisted by a lawyer, as this violated his right to a fair trial. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are the police interviews conducted on 12 and 13 January 2014, during which the applicant made incriminating statements without his lawyer being present, and the subsequent reliance on this evidence to convict him of murder.
001-230281:
The case of *Rizzo Striano v. Italy* (Application no. 54800/16) concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a domestic court decision awarding the applicant damages and compensation in connection with land occupied for an aqueduct. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 September 2016 under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant, Maurizio Rizzo Striano, born in 1957, was represented by Mr I. Toscano, a lawyer practising in Rome. The Italian Government were given notice of the application.

The key domestic decision was issued by the Regional Public Water Court (Naples District Court), R.G. 2475/96, on 21 January 2002. It ordered the Reclamation Consortium of the Plain of Sybaris and the Middle Crati Valley (*Consorzio di Bonifica della Piana di Sibari e della Media Valle del Crati*, “the Consortium”) to pay the applicant damages for the occupation of his plot of land for the construction of an aqueduct and compensation for the establishment of an aqueduct easement over that land. The domestic judgment therefore established a clear monetary entitlement in the applicant’s favour against the Consortium.

According to the appended table, the non-enforcement period began on 27 September 2005. The end date of non-enforcement was recorded as pending, and the length of non-enforcement was stated as more than 18 years and 9 days. This means that for over eighteen years, the applicant had a domestic court order in his favour but did not receive the payments due from the Consortium. The applicant’s complaint before the European Court was therefore that the domestic decision awarding him damages and compensation had not been enforced.

The essence of the alleged violation is that the Italian State failed to ensure compliance with a final domestic judgment against a public or semi-public entity. The applicant had successfully obtained a ruling ordering payment for the occupation of his land and for the aqueduct easement, but the sums remained unpaid for an exceptionally long period. This prolonged failure to enforce the domestic decision deprived the applicant of the practical benefit of his successful litigation and formed the factual basis of his complaint to the Court.

Procedurally, the case was examined by the First Section sitting as a Committee, composed of Judges Wojtyczek, Hüseynov and Jelić, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court rejected the Government’s objection to the examination of the application by a Committee. The Committee deliberated in private on 14 December 2023 and adopted the judgment on that date; the judgment was delivered on 18 January 2024. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore relatively narrow: a final domestic decision of 21 January 2002 awarding damages and compensation; a debtor identified as the Consortium; a non-enforcement period beginning on 27 September 2005 and still pending; and a delay exceeding eighteen years and nine days. The applicant’s central complaint was that this continued non-enforcement breached his Convention rights, principally by denying him the effective enjoyment of a final judicial award and by leaving him without timely redress against a public debtor. The Court was thus called upon to assess whether Italy had failed to secure enforcement of the domestic decision within a reasonable time.
001-230260:
**Rizzo and Others v. Malta** (Application no. 36318/21, judgment 16 January 2024) concerns three Maltese nationals and the compatibility of Malta’s old rent laws with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The applicants held the perpetual utile dominium of a property at No. 17, Triq Gort, Paceville, St Julian’s, inherited following their aunt’s death on 26 February 1994. In January 1972, their predecessor in title had leased the property under a temporary sub-emphyteusis for twenty-one years. When that expired on 18 January 1993, the tenant—a Maltese citizen using the property as his ordinary residence—relied on Act XXIII of 1979, amending Chapter 158, the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, to retain possession under a lease at the statutory annual rent of approximately €303. The rent later increased to about €454 in 2008, €502 in 2013, and €519 in 2016.

In April 2019, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings before the First Hall, Civil Court, in its constitutional competence. They alleged that the Ordinance, as amended, granted the tenant the right to retain possession under a unilateral lease for an indeterminate time without a fair and adequate rent, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They limited their claims to 31 December 2018, sought compensation, and did not demand the tenant’s eviction. A court-appointed expert valued the property in 2019 at €850,000 with development potential, or €320,000 in its existing state. Annual market rental values were estimated at €1,980 in 1993, €3,120 in 1998, €4,080 in 2003, €6,360 in 2008, €6,240 in 2013, and €10,560 in 2018.

By judgment of 25 January 2021, the First Hall found a violation of the applicants’ property rights, holding that they had suffered a disproportionate burden. It awarded €30,000 in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage for the violation until 10 April 2018, when new Article 12B of the Ordinance provided a further remedy. The applicants were not ordered to bear costs, despite not succeeding on all claims. No party appealed.

In parallel, Act XXVII of 2018, published on 10 July 2018 and in force from 1 August 2018, amended the Ordinance and introduced Article 12B. In April 2019, the applicants also instituted ordinary proceedings before the Rent Regulation Board. They sought recognition of the occupants as tenants, a means test, an increase in rent to no more than 2% of the open market value on 1 January 2019, or eviction within five years if the tenant failed the means test. On 2 December 2020, the RRB found that the tenants satisfied the means test and increased annual rent to €5,000 for the first two years and €7,500 for the following four. The tenants appealed and the applicants cross-appealed; the Court of Appeal confirmed the decision on 17 December 2021.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 July 2021. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13, declaring the remainder inadmissible. The case therefore concerns, in particular, the effectiveness of an appeal to the Constitutional Court for Article 13 purposes following developments in domestic case-law on old rent laws raising Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 issues.
001-237294:
In *Daugaard Sorensen v. Denmark* (App no. 25650/22), the applicant, a Danish national born in 2000, alleged that she was raped by A during the night of 6–7 June 2021. She reported the incident to the police on 7 June and was interviewed in the presence of a lawyer.

On 8 June 2021, the District Court remanded A in custody on suspicion of rape under Article 216 § 1 of the Penal Code and non-consensual sexual activity under Article 225. The court cited reasonable suspicion, outstanding witness interviews, and a risk that A might interfere with the investigation. Police investigated the case, interviewed the applicant and others, examined the crime scene and the applicant’s clothing, and searched A’s home. A was released on 18 June 2021.

On 30 July 2021, the first-instance prosecutor dropped the charges under section 721(1)(ii) of the Administration of Justice Act, finding insufficient evidence because there were two opposing statements and no conclusive corroboration. The applicant appealed on 18 August 2021. On 16 September 2021, the Regional State Prosecutor reversed the decision and decided to proceed with the prosecution.

Under section 724(2), notice of that decision had to be served on A by 30 September 2021—within two months of the initial drop decision—via Digital Post or registered letter. Due to a database typing error, the prosecutor wrongly assumed A could not receive Digital Post and sent a registered letter. Another database error omitted A’s c/o address, so the letter was returned on 23 September 2021 marked “addressee unknown at this address.” Internal guidelines required checking the address, whether A had moved, whether the deadline had expired, and whether to reattempt service. Because of a further error, the office did not recheck, and A was not notified before the deadline.

On 13 October 2021, the first-instance prosecutor filed an indictment. In November, A’s defence lawyer sought dismissal because the two-month time-limit had not been met. The prosecutor agreed, and on 16 November 2021 the District Court dismissed the case against A. It was therefore no longer possible to prosecute him for the alleged rape. On 30 November 2021, the prosecutor apologised to the applicant’s lawyer for the procedural error.

The applicant sought compensation. On 21 December 2021, she applied to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board for injury to feelings under the State Compensation to Victims of Crime Act. On 15 November 2022, the Board rejected her claim, finding she had not sufficiently established that she had been the victim of a crime. She did not bring civil proceedings against the Board.

In December 2022, the Director of Public Prosecutions informed her lawyer that she could claim compensation against the police and prosecutor for administrative errors and discussed the Chapter 93a summary procedure. On 31 January 2023, the applicant claimed pecuniary and non-pecuniary compensation from the prosecutor under Chapter 93a, including pain and suffering, medical and rehabilitation expenses, ruined clothes, and injury to feelings. Items relating to pain, medical costs, and clothes concerned the reported rape; injury to feelings concerned both the rape and the administrative errors. On 24 April 2023, the prosecutor rejected the claims as outside the scope of Chapter 93a. The Director of Public Prosecutions upheld that decision on 30 June 2023, noting she could ask a court to decide or bring civil proceedings. The applicant did not bring civil proceedings.

The applicant complained under Articles 3, 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the collapse of the rape prosecution due to the Regional State Prosecutor’s failure to comply with the statutory notification deadline, caused by multiple administrative errors, and the alleged lack of an effective remedy or compensation for that failure.
001-237797:
In *Zahariev v. North Macedonia*, the European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Borislav Zahariev Zahariev, a Bulgarian national, concerning domestic criminal proceedings and his claim of diplomatic immunity. The applicant worked as financial director of a telecommunications company in North Macedonia between 2004 and 2009. In January 2007 his wife began working as an official at the Bulgarian Cultural and Information Centre attached to the Bulgarian embassy. On 24 January 2012 an investigating judge opened an investigation against the applicant and another person for abuse of office and tax evasion allegedly committed in 2008 relating to his telecom employment. An indictment followed on 11 February 2013.

In June 2013 the applicant informed the Skopje Court of First Instance that he held a special identity card issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs granting him absolute immunity from prosecution. The card stated that he enjoyed immunity from criminal jurisdiction, arrest or police custody in North Macedonia. The applicant relied on his status as a family member of embassy administrative/technical staff under Article 37(2) of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. He argued that the exception in Article 37(2) applied only to civil and administrative jurisdiction, not criminal jurisdiction. He later relied on the ICJ *Arrest Warrant* case, arguing that immunity from criminal jurisdiction did not distinguish official and private acts and could only cease in limited circumstances, including express waiver by Bulgaria, which had not occurred.

The domestic courts did not accept his immunity claim. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed prosecutors and courts that the applicant had held special identity cards from 2007, extended through 30 May 2014, but that his immunity derived from his wife’s status. The Ministry noted that in February 2010 the embassy had asked to cancel his registration because Article 42 of the Vienna Convention prohibited diplomatic agents from engaging in professional or commercial activity for personal profit; that the applicant had been employed; and that after 2014, given pending criminal proceedings, only his wife’s card was extended. A Ministry representative stated that the applicant could not both be employed and enjoy immunities, and that he could not invoke immunity given Article 31(1)(c) and Article 42.

The applicant was convicted in absentia in 2015, but the appellate court remitted the case for reconsideration of immunity. On 24 December 2019 the trial court again convicted him in absentia of abuse of office and sentenced him to five years. It held that his immunity had ceased when he took private employment contrary to Article 42; that he had not invoked immunity during the investigation; and that the embassy had never waived or requested extension of his card after 2014. The appellate court confirmed the conviction on 9 March 2021, also relying on Article 31(1)(c). The Supreme Court confirmed on 3 November 2021, reasoning that the applicant had lost immunity due to breach of Article 42 and had not invoked it.

The ECtHR complaint, lodged on 27 May 2022, was communicated to the Government only under Article 6 of the Convention concerning the lack of a fair hearing. The central alleged violation was therefore that the domestic courts’ judgments dismissing the immunity argument lacked adequate reasoning and fair consideration, particularly regarding whether the applicant enjoyed criminal immunity at the time of indictment and the correct interpretation of the Vienna Convention. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-237504:
The case of *Agayev & Zulfugarzadeh Company v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 31222/14) concerns alleged unlawful expropriation by the Baku City Executive Authority (“BCEA”) and the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment. The applicant company, based in Baku, owned two rooms (34.83 sq. m in total) in a house that was shared with two individual co-owners, according to an ownership certificate issued by the Technical Inventory and Ownership Rights Registration Department of the BCEA.

The background is similar to *Khalikova v. Azerbaijan*. On 16 February 2011, the Head of the BCEA issued order no. 76, stating that buildings and houses on certain streets were to be demolished to construct a new garden-park complex known as the Winter Park, and that residents were to be relocated. On 23 September 2012, the BCEA began demolishing the house. The next day, the applicant company asked the State Land and Cartography Committee (“SLCC”) to issue a plan and measurements of the land underlying and attached to the house.

On the same date, the company brought proceedings against the BCEA and several other State authorities (“the first claim”). It sought invalidation of the BCEA order and compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. It claimed that its share in the house was actually 55.73 sq. m, rather than the 34.83 sq. m stated in the ownership certificate, and that 69.48 sq. m of the underlying and attached land belonged to it under domestic law. After the SLCC refused its request, on 22 November 2012 the company lodged a separate claim against the SLCC, asking the courts to order it to issue the relevant plan and measurements (“the second claim”). In November 2012, the house was completely demolished.

By final judgment of 17 October 2013, the Supreme Court dismissed the second claim. It found that the plot of land did not constitute the applicant company’s possessions because there were no legal grounds. Article 9 of the Law on Land Reform, which transferred land underneath private residential houses lawfully used by citizens from State ownership into the occupants’ private ownership, did not apply to the applicant company because it was a legal person. The court also found no evidence of an agreement with the co-owners concerning use of the land or their consent to the company’s privatisation of 69.48 sq. m.

By final judgment of 29 January 2014, the Supreme Court upheld the lower court’s judgment partly granting the first claim. It awarded the applicant company AZN 62,694 in compensation, calculated at AZN 1,500 per square metre for its share in the house plus an additional 20% under Presidential Decree no. 689. It dismissed the company’s claims concerning the additional surface area and the plot of land, holding that it had no rights over them. As of the latest communication with the parties in 2022, the Supreme Court’s judgment of 29 January 2014 remained unenforced.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant company complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the interference with its property rights was unlawful and unjustified. It further complained under Article 6 that the final judgment of 29 January 2014 had not been enforced. It also alleged violations of its right to a reasoned decision under Article 6 and its right under Article 13. The Court gave notice of the complaints under Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, declaring the remainder inadmissible. The key factual issues concern the demolition and expropriation of the house, the scope of the company’s property rights in the land, the compensation awarded, and the failure to enforce the final compensation judgment.
001-237438:
**J.B. and Others v.
