Malta** (Application no. 1766/23) concerns six Bangladeshi nationals who claimed to be unaccompanied minors aged 16–17 when they arrived in Malta on 18 November 2022 after being rescued at sea. They were initially held at the Ħal Far Initial Reception Centre (“China House”). The applicants alleged that they were detained without any document or explanation in a language they understood and in inadequate conditions. They claimed they were held with adults in small rooms, with insufficient and poorly maintained washrooms, no meaningful access to outdoor or common areas, no prayer room, limited access to telephones—including for contacting lawyers—no leisure or educational activities, no heating, inadequate winter clothing, limited drinkable water, and insufficient medical and psychosocial support. The Government disputed these accounts.

On 30 November 2022, the Principal Immigration Officer issued detention orders to determine or verify the applicants’ identity or nationality and to obtain elements supporting their possible international protection claims, citing a risk of absconding. On 6 December 2022, the Immigration Appeals Tribunal (“IAB”) confirmed the legality of the detention in a single mass hearing concerning the whole group that had arrived by boat. The IAB noted that all applicants except the first were minors and that a legal guardian should be appointed, but still found the detention of the entire group lawful.

The applicants’ lawyers accessed them in January 2023. The applicants confirmed they were minors and said they had informed the authorities, including at the IAB hearing. Their representatives referred them to the Agency for the Welfare of Asylum Seekers and filed an urgent review request for some applicants, which remained unanswered. On 11 January 2023, the European Court of Human Rights indicated interim measures under Rule 39, asking Malta to ensure conditions compatible with Article 3 and with the applicants’ status as unaccompanied minors. The applicants were later transferred to Safi Detention Centre, where they were held with other minors; they alleged conditions were similar apart from room size and one hour of daily outdoor access.

Age-assessment proceedings concluded in January 2023 that the applicants were adults. The applicants alleged the process was hasty, not holistic or multidisciplinary, and that in one case a bone test was conducted without knowing consent. They appealed. Procedural problems followed: only the first applicant’s appeal was initially scheduled; detention officers told the IAB that the others wished to withdraw, and the IAB accepted this without consulting their lawyers; declarations of adulthood were later signed without representatives or an interpreter. Vulnerability reports later showed elevated anxiety, depression, PTSD, and in some cases suicidal thoughts. Release requests based on vulnerability were not answered in writing. In May 2023, the IAB rejected the first applicant’s appeal, finding him adult due to a genuine passport showing birth in 2002, but upheld the others’ minority claims. Most were released to an open centre for minors; the first was moved with adults and later left Malta.

The Court gave notice to the Government of complaints under **Article 3** (conditions of detention), **Article 5 §§ 1 and 4** (lawfulness and judicial review of detention), and **Article 13 in conjunction with Article 3** (effective remedy regarding conditions). The key alleged violations concern the detention of presumed minors, inadequate reception and detention conditions, failure to treat them as minors or conduct proper individual assessments, and ineffective remedies.
001-234604:
**Maçi v. Albania** (Application no. 21051/10) is a European Court of Human Rights case, Third Section, judgment of 4 July 2024. The applicants, Altin Maçi and Skënder Maçi, are heirs of Mr Sh. M. They complain about Albania’s failure to enforce domestic decisions given in favour of their predecessor.

The relevant facts begin with a 1996 decision by the Tirana Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties. On 5 November 1996, the Commission found that Mr Sh. M. had been the former owner of a plot of land confiscated during the communist era. Relying on a field report, the Commission noted that a two-storey building and a road had been built on the plot. Under the operative part of the decision, the Commission returned to Mr Sh. M. title to one-third of the land on which the building stood and granted him the right to erect an additional third floor. It also ordered that his ownership be registered with the Immovable Property Registration Office (“IPRO”). As regards the remainder of the plot, the Commission ruled that he should receive compensation in one of the ways provided by law. No appeal was filed, and the 1996 decision became final on 5 December 1996. Its enforcement has remained pending for more than 27 years.

In 2004, Mr Sh. M. brought a claim before the Tirana District Court against the Ministry of Economy, the Municipality of Tirana and the IPRO, seeking delimitation of the exact boundaries of the plot. The court ordered an expert report which identified and described the plot and its boundaries. The property bordered public property, initially described by the Government as a “public square” and later as a “public road.” Mr Sh. M.’s title was confirmed by a 1994 ownership certificate. According to the expert report, the total surface area was 720 sq. m. The Municipality and the IPRO accepted the claim, while the Ministry of Economy did not express a position.

On 27 April 2004, the District Court upheld Mr Sh. M.’s claim and ordered the IPRO to register his title as defined in the expert report. Mr Sh. M. died on 17 May 2004, and the applicants were recognised as his heirs. The 2004 judgment became final on 3 June 2004. About two weeks later, the same court issued an enforcement writ. The non-enforcement period for this judgment began on 3 July 2004 and has continued for approximately 20 years.

The enforcement difficulties centred on the remaining 129 sq. m of the 720 sq. m plot. The IPRO informed the applicants that it had registered only 591 sq. m in their name. It claimed that the remaining 129 sq. m formed part of a public square owned by the Municipality of Tirana and therefore did not belong to the applicants. According to the IPRO, the court-appointed expert had made a mistake in measuring the plot. The IPRO asked the State Attorney’s Office to begin proceedings to invalidate the applicants’ title over those 129 sq. m. The State Attorney forwarded the request to the Municipality, asking it to start proceedings; the Municipality responded that it was for the State Attorney to initiate them. In 2023, the State Attorney stated that it was still examining the possibility of challenging the 2004 judgment.

These facts are relevant to the alleged violations because final and binding domestic decisions in favour of the applicants’ predecessor were not fully enforced. The authorities’ contradictory positions and prolonged inaction left the applicants unable to secure full registration and enjoyment of the property. The case therefore concerns alleged breaches of the right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, particularly the execution of final judgments, and the right to protection of property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-233409:
In *Maisaia v. Georgia* (Application no. 75969/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 3 of the Convention concerning the applicant’s alleged ill-treatment in prison and the domestic authorities’ alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation. The applicant, Vakhtang Maisaia, a Georgian national born in 1972, lodged the application on 26 November 2014. The Court gave notice only of the Article 3 complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected.

The key facts concern events in Georgian detention. On 5 May 2009, the applicant was arrested and placed in police custody on suspicion of espionage, an offence for which he was later convicted. On 8 May 2009, he was transferred from police custody to Tbilisi Prison No. 8, known as Gldani Prison. During admission, a doctor examined him and recorded that he had no injuries, was in good health, and suffered from no medical condition.

On 25 August 2010, the applicant complained that prison guards had ill-treated him the previous day, 24 August 2010, in Gldani Prison. The Investigation Unit of the Ministry of Prisons opened a criminal investigation the same day. A medical examination was immediately commissioned and found marks of ill-treatment—multiple bruises and lesions on his face and body. Investigators questioned witnesses, including cellmates and prison guards. One cellmate confirmed that the applicant had been beaten by prison guards. Other witnesses claimed the applicant had inflicted the injuries himself by hitting his head and body against the wall and window bar in his cell.

When questioned on 25 August 2010, the applicant stated that, beyond the 24 August incident, he had been subjected to ill-treatment in Gldani Prison on a regular basis. He alleged systematic physical and psychological abuse between 8 May and 23 June 2009. He named the alleged abusers and provided further details about the circumstances of the 24 August ill-treatment. On 13 September 2010, the World Organisation Against Torture, an international human rights observer based in Geneva, issued a statement expressing concern about the applicant’s safety. Based on information from his family, the statement said that after reporting ill-treatment in Gldani Prison, he began receiving death threats from prison guards.

Between 22 September 2010 and May 2012, the applicant repeatedly enquired—at least four times—about the investigation’s progress with the Ministry of Prisons and the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office. Relying on the medical opinion confirming injuries, he repeatedly requested aggrieved-party status. His letters were either unanswered or the authorities advised that the investigation was ongoing. In September 2012, footage of repeated ill-treatment of inmates in various prisons, including and in particular Gldani Prison, was disseminated in the Georgian media, a matter known as the “prison scandal.” On 13 January 2013, the applicant was released under an amnesty.

Between February 2013 and October 2014, the applicant made at least six further enquiries to the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office about progress, if any, and again requested aggrieved-party status. These enquiries were either left unanswered or he was told to wait for certain investigative measures to be completed. According to the case file, the criminal investigation into his ill-treatment in Gldani Prison remained ongoing, but no other details about its progress were known.

The central Article 3 issues were whether the applicant suffered ill-treatment by prison guards, allegedly as part of large-scale and systematic prisoner abuse, and whether the State conducted an effective investigation. Key facts include the medical evidence of injuries after his complaint, conflicting witness accounts, his broader allegations of systematic abuse, threats after reporting, the wider prison scandal, and repeated delays and failures to grant him victim status or inform him of meaningful progress.
001-201139:

Jerko Livančić (application no. 15313/15, introduced 20 March 2015), represented by Kapetan Hatidža of Travnik, relied on a Novi Travnik Cantonal Court decision of 7 June 2012. The non-enforcement period began on 28 September 2012 and ended on 13 June 2016, lasting 3 years, 8 months and 17 days.

001-205797:
In *Kornilova v. Ukraine* (Application no. 47283/14), the applicant, Ms Tetyana Kornilova, a Jehovah’s Witness, complained under Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention that the Ukrainian authorities had failed to adequately take into account the alleged religious-prejudice motive behind an assault against her.

On 7 March 2013, the applicant and another Jehovah’s Witness, Ms N.S., were conducting door-to-door visits in Nosivka, distributing invitations to a religious service. The invitations showed an image of Jesus Christ and the words “One Died for All,” with smaller text identifying the event as a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting. At about 1 p.m., they called at the house of V.S., a fifty-year-old man they did not know. According to the applicant, when V.S. saw the invitations and Bible in their hands, he immediately punched her in the head, began cursing at them, called them “shtundas”—a colloquial term for evangelical Protestants—and threatened to set his dog on them.

On 9 March 2013, the applicant sought medical care and was diagnosed with concussion and a facial bruise. She was hospitalised until 19 March. The same day, she complained to the police. The case was preliminarily classified under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code, covering intentional infliction of minor injury.

In her police statement, the applicant said she was a Jehovah’s Witness and that V.S. had cursed, called them “shtundas,” and hit her without reason. N.S. largely corroborated this, stating that V.S. hit the applicant immediately after seeing her and repeatedly cursed and called them “shtundas.” V.S. claimed the women had come onto his property, refused to leave, and tried to recruit him; he became angry and slapped one of them. He later said he acted due to the “sudden emergence of hostility,” alleging the applicant had insulted him about his “man’s health.” He denied religious intolerance, said he did not know she was a Jehovah’s Witness, and claimed “shtundas” had no religious meaning for him. A forensic expert found minor injuries with short-term health effects, possibly caused by a slap or a punch.

On 15 May 2013, the applicant asked the investigator to reclassify the offence as discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2, arguing V.S. knew she was a Jehovah’s Witness and hit her for that reason. On 17 May, the investigator refused, finding that “sudden hostility” had been established and that no religious hatred motive was shown. At trial, the applicant again sought reclassification as discriminatory acts or hooliganism under Article 296, invoking Articles 3, 9 and 14 and arguing that the State had a duty to uncover any religious motive behind violence.

On 16 July 2013, the Nosivka District Court convicted V.S. under Article 125 § 2, fined him about EUR 78, awarded the applicant about EUR 278 in non-pecuniary damages, and found the injury was inflicted due to “sudden emergence of hostility.” No aggravating circumstances were found. The applicant appealed, arguing that the authorities had failed to examine religious hatred and that religious enmity should have been treated as an aggravating factor under Article 67. The prosecutor maintained that no religious motive had been identified. On 26 September 2013, the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding no religious motive established. On 8 January 2014, the High Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters upheld the lower decisions.

The key alleged violation was therefore that the authorities treated the attack as an ordinary minor assault motivated by personal hostility, despite evidence of the applicant’s religious activity, the use of a religious slur, and the immediate violent reaction to her religious materials. They refused to reclassify the offence as religiously motivated discrimination and did not consider religious enmity as an aggravating circumstance, thereby allegedly failing to protect her rights under Articles 3, 9 and 14.
001-200434:
The case originated in an application (no. 52682/07) against Azerbaijan lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by the Religious Community of Jehovah’s Witnesses in Baku and Mr Oddvar Hansen, a Norwegian national. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6 (fair trial), 9 (freedom of religion), and 14 (non-discrimination) of the Convention. The Court communicated those complaints to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The applicant community is a local Jehovah’s Witnesses community registered in Baku. Hansen owned a private building and leased it, without payment, to the community for religious meetings. On 24 December 2006, about 200 Jehovah’s Witnesses met for worship at their meeting hall on the second floor of that building. According to the applicants, a raid involved more than forty officials, including officers from the Khatai District Police Department, a representative of the State Committee for Work with Religious Associations, officials from the Khatai district prosecutor’s office, and the Ministry of National Security. The authorities conducted search and seizure procedures to prevent an unauthorised religious meeting. An investigator’s record stated that eighteen items were seized in the presence of attesting witnesses, including computers, computing equipment, and religious literature.

On 7 February 2007, the applicants lodged a complaint in court supervisory proceedings before the Khatai District Court, relying on the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They asked the court to find the search unlawful and order the return of the seized property. Affidavits dated 2 and 30 March 2007 showed the property was returned to the community chairman. On 7 May 2007, the Khatai District Court partly allowed the complaint. It held that the search and seizure were unlawful because they had been carried out without a court order, contrary to the CCrP. It noted that the property had already been returned.

On 10 May 2007, the Khatai district prosecutor appealed, seeking to quash the favourable part of the decision. He argued that the authorities had not broken into the building because the doors were open and the owner had permitted entry. On 21 May 2007, the Baku Court of Appeal examined the case in the applicants’ absence but in the presence of the prosecutor and a police representative. It stated that the applicants had been notified but failed to appear or explain their absence. The appellate court allowed the prosecutor’s appeal and found the search and seizure lawful, relying on Article 177.6 of the CCrP, which provided that no court order was required when the owner permitted entry. That decision was not amenable to further appeal.

The applicants alleged that they had not received notice of the hearing or a copy of the prosecutor’s appeal. They said their lawyer learned only on 22 May 2007 that the first-instance decision had been appealed and quashed. Under domestic law, such court supervisory appeals are examined by a three-judge appellate chamber within three days in camera. A complainant has the right to participate, but non-attendance by notified parties does not prevent examination. The appellate decision is sent to the parties within three days and cannot be appealed.

The alleged violations therefore concerned whether the raid and seizure unlawfully interfered with freedom of religion under Article 9; whether the appellate proceedings were unfair under Article 6 because the applicants lacked notice and an effective opportunity to respond; and whether the measures or proceedings involved discrimination under Article 14. The applicants also relied on property rights under Protocol No. 1 in seeking return of the seized items.
001-200213:
In Aleksandrov v. Ukraine (Application no. 56483/09, judgment of 9 January 2020), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, examined a Ukrainian applicant’s complaint that domestic authorities hindered his right of individual petition under Article 34 of the Convention by refusing to provide him with copies of documents from his criminal case file for use in his application to the Court.

The applicant, Ruslan Alekseyevich Aleksandrov, born in 1978 and detained in Berdychiv, had been convicted by the Crimea Court of Appeal on 25 December 2008 of two counts of rape and one count of murder. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 21 May 2009 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that conviction. He was serving his sentence at Berdychiv correctional colony no. 70 in Zhytomyr Region.

On 5 October 2009 the applicant informed the European Court of Human Rights of his intention to file an application. By letter of 10 May 2010, the Court acknowledged receipt of his application form and attachments and asked him to submit copies of domestic courts’ decisions and other documents relevant to his case by 10 August 2010. This request made the criminal case-file documents important for his Strasbourg application.

Between 2009 and 2013, the applicant repeatedly asked the Crimea Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Ukraine for access to his case file or for copies of procedural documents. He stated that those documents had been requested by the European Court. The domestic authorities, however, largely refused or obstructed these requests. On numerous dates—including 2 February, 11 June, and 7 and 9 July 2009; 10 March, 28 April, 1 and 21 July, 4 August, and 5 November 2010; 16 March and 5 October 2011; and 10 May 2012—the Crimea Court of Appeal rejected his applications for access to the file. It explained that there was no legal basis for providing copies of documents from a criminal case file after the conviction had become final.

On 17 February 2012 the applicant again asked the Crimea Court of Appeal to provide documents from his file so that he could send them to the European Court. On 29 February 2012 Judge G. replied that he had already received all copies permitted by law. For additional procedural documents intended for the European Court, he would need to present confirmation that the Court had requested them and a list of those documents, both drafted by an authorised person. On 22 March 2012 the Crimea Court of Appeal rejected a further application because the proceedings concerning the applicant had ended. On 19 November 2012 the applicant asked the court to authorise his mother to study his criminal case file. On 4 December 2012 the Deputy President of the Crimea Court of Appeal refused, stating that only participants in criminal proceedings had a right of access to the file.

On 24 June 2013 the applicant again requested copies, indicating that the European Court had asked for them. On 11 July 2013 Judge T. told him that he had to pay a fee of UAH 46 and send confirmation of payment, after which the requested copies would be sent. The applicant did not pay. According to him, he had insufficient funds because he had no income and no legal counsel.

On 30 May 2018 the Government were given notice of the complaint under Article 34 concerning the authorities’ failure to provide copies of documents from the applicant’s case file; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The key alleged violation was therefore that the Ukrainian authorities, despite knowing the documents were needed for the applicant’s ECtHR application, failed to facilitate his access to them, thereby hindering his effective exercise of the right of individual petition.
001-204995:
**Case: Starishko v. Ukraine (Application no. 61839/12), ECtHR, 15 October 2020**

The case concerned Mr Anatoliy Petrovych Starishko, a Ukrainian national born in 1980 who is serving a life sentence in Vinnytsya Prison No. 1. He lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 July 2012. The Court gave notice to the Ukrainian Government of two main complaints: first, that his life sentence lacked any genuine prospect of release, i.e. was irreducible; and second, that restrictions on his right to receive visits during his post-conviction detention from 2000 to 2014 violated the Convention. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The applicant was represented by Ms Ganna Ovdiyenko, a lawyer practising in Kharkiv. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna.

The key facts were as follows. On 14 December 1999 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court found the applicant guilty of several counts of aggravated murder and theft and sentenced him to the death penalty. On 30 May 2000 the Supreme Court replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment and upheld the verdict in the remaining part. Thus, from 2000 onwards, the applicant was detained under a life sentence.

During the period from 2000 to 2014, the applicant received only ten short-term visits, each lasting between one and four hours, from his mother, his sister and, on three occasions, a friend. During these meetings, the applicant communicated with the visitors through a glass partition, and their conversations were listened to by a prison officer.

The relevant legal framework concerned both life imprisonment and visiting rights. Legal provisions on life imprisonment and presidential clemency were summarised in *Petukhov v. Ukraine (no. 2)* (no. 41216/13, §§ 75-90, 12 March 2019). Under the Correctional Labour Code of 1970, repealed with effect from 1 January 2004, life prisoners had the right to one short-term visit every six months, conducted in the presence of a staff member of the prison (Article 39). The Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences of 11 July 2003, in force from 1 January 2004, kept that rule unchanged until 16 February 2010, when life prisoners became entitled to one short-term visit every three months (Article 151). Further details on visiting entitlement and its evolution are found in *Trosin v. Ukraine* (no. 39758/05, §§ 26 and 29, 23 February 2012) and *Bigun v. Ukraine* (no. 30315/10, §§ 15-19, 21 March 2019).

Relevant Council of Europe documents and CPT reports on life imprisonment are cited in *Petukhov*. Material on family visits to prisoners is quoted in *Khoroshenko v. Russia* (no. 41418/04, §§ 58-67, ECHR 2015), while excerpts from relevant CPT reports are quoted in *Bigun* (no. 30315/10, § 22).

The alleged violations therefore centred on whether the life sentence regime—where release depended on presidential clemency rather than an ordinary parole mechanism—made the sentence de facto irreducible, and whether the severe restrictions on visits, including the limited number of visits, the glass partition and the monitoring of conversations, breached the applicant’s rights under the Convention, particularly regarding private and family life. The Court adopted its judgment on 22 September 2020 and delivered it on 15 October 2020.
001-202411:
Keaney v. Ireland concerned an Irish national, Vincent Keaney, who complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the delay of eleven years between commencing his civil proceedings and the final judgment violated the “reasonable time” requirement. The case was also communicated together with others raising similar delay complaints, with a specific question whether Ireland provided an effective domestic remedy under Article 13 for such Article 6 delay.

Factually, in 1996 Keaney used lottery winnings to buy the Scotts Building in Cobh, intending to run it as the Titanic Bar and Restaurant. He bought an intoxicating liquor licence and began renovations. Structural defects exhausted his funds, and further borrowing proved insufficient. He sought advice from J.S., a financial consultant, who introduced M.N., a publican. Around 2000, Keaney and M.N. entered a series of agreements: the premises were assigned to them as tenants in common in equal shares; TQTC was incorporated with Keaney holding 49% and M.N. 51%; the premises were leased to TQTC and the liquor licence transferred. Relations deteriorated, TQTC traded until December 2002 and failed, and a July 2003 attempt to separate their interests through “heads of agreement” and further transactions also failed. M.N. ultimately took possession of the premises.

On 8 February 2006, Keaney issued High Court plenary proceedings against eighteen defendants, alleging deceit, fraud, misrepresentation and undue influence arising from the 2000–2003 transactions, and seeking to set those transactions aside. The case was admitted to the Commercial List on 3 April 2006. From the outset, the pleadings were poorly particularised. The High Court repeatedly ordered amended statements of claim. Defendants brought motions to strike out all or part of the claims. On 16 January 2007, the High Court struck out claims against numerous defendants and limited claims against others; further strike-outs followed in March 2007. By early 2007, claims against fourteen of the eighteen defendants had been struck out. Keaney delivered several further amended statements, some of which the High Court found non-compliant or nonsensical, while allowing final opportunities to amend. A final statement of claim was delivered on 1 July 2008. On 19 December 2008, the High Court dismissed all remaining claims, finding Keaney had failed and that aspects of his case bordered on abuse of process.

Keaney issued notices of appeal between February 2007 and February 2009. Appellate progress was then extremely slow. In February 2014, the Supreme Court directed books of appeal within four weeks; they were filed in March 2014. In March 2015, the respondents said the books were incomplete, and the Supreme Court made a peremptory order. Submissions were eventually filed in June 2015. The first appeal was heard on 24 June 2015 and judgment delivered on 23 July 2015, upholding the strike-out and criticising unsubstantiated allegations as an abuse of process. In the second appeal, the Supreme Court in September 2014 required books or dismissal; later, in March 2016, it directed submissions within six to eight weeks, but Keaney filed only in February 2017. That appeal was heard on 28 February 2017 and judgment delivered on 5 April 2017, finding no basis to overturn the High Court. A third appeal was not pursued.

The alleged Article 6 § 1 violation was therefore the cumulative delay from institution on 8 February 2006 to final judgment on 5 April 2017. As to Article 13, Irish law recognised a constitutional right to reasonable expedition and possible damages, and the ECHR Act allowed damages where no other remedy existed. However, following McFarlane v. Ireland, the Committee of Ministers found that Ireland still lacked an effective remedy for excessive length, despite proposed legislation. These facts framed Keaney’s complaint that the lengthy proceedings lacked an effective domestic remedy.
001-206516:
In *Tretiak v. Ukraine* (Application no. 16215/15), a Fifth Section Committee judgment delivered on 17 December 2020, the applicant was Oleksandr Anatoliyovych Tretiak, a Ukrainian national born in 1972 and living in Kamenolomnia, Autonomous Republic of Crimea. At the relevant time he was temporarily living in Strizhavka, a village in the Vinnytsya District, and was working there for the Jehovah’s Witnesses organisation. He complained under Articles 3, 9, 14 and 18 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the Ukrainian authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation into an attack on him, which he believed had been motivated by animosity towards him as a Jehovah’s Witness.

The key facts concerned an attack on the evening of 26 November 2013. The applicant was returning home after making visits around the village on behalf of the Jehovah’s Witnesses when he was attacked in the street where he lived. According to the applicant, three individuals took part. From the assailants’ conversation, he gathered that the ringleader was called Ruslan and the second individual was called Yevgen. Other Jehovah’s Witnesses who knew local residents identified them as Ruslan I. and Yevgen I., both of whom lived in houses near the site of the attack. The third person present at or nearby the incident was later identified as A.D., Yevgen I.’s father-in-law.

The identity and background of the alleged attackers were particularly relevant to the alleged violations. Yevgen I. was at the time an inspector at the Vinnytsa city traffic police office. According to the applicant, Yevgen I. had previously served as a neighbourhood police officer in the village where the attack occurred. The applicant also stated that A.D. had previously served in correctional institutions. These alleged ties to law-enforcement or correctional bodies were relevant to his complaint that the authorities had not properly investigated the attack or pursued those responsible, particularly given his belief that the attack was religiously motivated.

The applicant believed the attack was caused by religious hatred. He described the sequence of events as follows: Ruslan I. and A.D. stopped him; they smelled of alcohol. Ruslan I. hit him on the head, while A.D. urged him on. The applicant thought he had been mistaken for someone else. Nevertheless, in his submissions before the Court, he maintained that the attack was linked to animosity towards him as a Jehovah’s Witness.

Before the Court, the applicant invoked Articles 3, 9, 14 and 18. Article 3 concerns the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment; Article 9 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion; Article 14 prohibits discrimination; and Article 18 limits restrictions on Convention rights to their stated purposes. The central alleged violation was that the authorities failed to carry out an effective investigation into a violent attack that the applicant believed was religiously motivated. The application was lodged on 9 March 2015. The applicant was represented by Mr K. Chernychenko and Mr A. Carbonneau. The Ukrainian Government was represented by its Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government and considered the parties’ observations. The Fifth Section Committee comprised Arnfinn Bårdsen (President), Ganna Yudkivska and Mattias Guyomar, with Martina Keller as Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 26 November 2020 and delivered the judgment on 17 December 2020.
001-204602:
**Case Summary: Aggerholm v. Denmark (Application no. 45439/18)**

The case concerns an Article 3 complaint by Mr Niels Lund Aggerholm, a Danish national suffering from paranoid schizophrenia. In 2005 he was convicted of five incidents of violence and threats against a civil servant and was sentenced to committal to a psychiatric hospital. From 2007 to 2011 he was held in a high-security psychiatric unit under a “dangerousness decree.” He was later treated in an open ward but was moved to a closed ward, P4, in September 2012 due to irritability and threatening behaviour. On 3 January 2013 he was restrained, but that measure is not the subject of the Court’s case.

The alleged violation concerns an incident on 8 February 2013. At 1:15 p.m. the applicant was strapped to a restraint bed with a belt and wrist and ankle straps—a five-point restraint—and remained restrained until 9 February 2013 at 12:05 p.m., approximately 22 hours and 50 minutes. He complained that this breached Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant appealed both restraint incidents to the Psychiatric Patients’ Complaints Board. The chief physician who ordered the measures, H.H., submitted a brief written statement but could not attend due to illness. On 21 March 2013 the Board found both measures unlawful. As to 8 February, it noted that the applicant did not want to participate in a medical consultation and was described as very angry, but concluded that it had not been documented that he exposed himself or others to an immediate risk of harm to body or health.

H.H. later told the Health Authority that she decided to restrain the applicant because he had a lot of pent-up anger after she revoked his day release, and she wanted to act before anyone was hurt. She acknowledged that the Board had declared the decision unlawful. The Health Authority found no lack of care or conscientiousness.

Daily records showed that on 7 February the applicant was frustrated and angry, and made remarks about H.H. that staff interpreted as threats, including “We have to do something about her.” After speaking with a doctor, he appeared calm. On 8 February, H.H. recorded that his day release was revoked, that he refused to sit or talk, was white-faced and showed pent-up anger, and after about 1.5 hours remained extremely angry and was considered dangerous. He came to the belt room voluntarily and was restrained. During the restraint, a social and healthcare assistant was constantly present, and doctors checked on him four times. One foot strap was released at 6:55 p.m., toilet visits were allowed, and at 10:46 p.m. he was still considered potentially dangerous. The next morning he was cooperative and was released at 12:05 p.m.

The applicant sought compensation and acknowledgment of an Article 3 violation. The City Court consulted the Medico-Legal Council, which found that the conditions for restraint were present, that it was necessary to avoid an immediate risk to others, that medical assessments were sufficiently frequent, and that the chief physician’s assessment was justified. The City Court dismissed the claim, finding the restraint and its duration necessary and less intrusive measures impossible. The High Court affirmed as regards the 8 February measure, finding no reason to overrule the chief physician and that sufficient evaluations had been made. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

Under the Mental Health Act, compulsory restraint may be used only when necessary to prevent an imminent risk of harm to body or health; it must be proportionate and least intrusive; a doctor must decide, the chief physician must approve straps, constant watch is required, and medical review must occur at least four times every 24 hours. The key factual tension is that the Complaints Board found no documented immediate danger, while later medical and court reviews found the restraint justified. The Court must assess whether the 22-hour-50-minute restraint and its review complied with Article 3.
001-203976:
Case Glavinić and Marković v. Croatia (ECtHR, 30 July 2020) concerned two Croatian nationals’ complaints that the length of judicial proceedings in their cases was excessive and that domestic authorities had failed to remedy the situation.

The first applicant, Jela Glavinić, was defendant in a civil action filed on 8 January 2003 in the Zadar Municipal Court seeking annulment of a gift contract. She responded in February 2003. The first-instance judgment was not delivered until 10 July 2014, dismissing the claim; it was served on 9 September 2014 and became final on 20 April 2015. The proceedings thus lasted about 11.5 years. She used domestic length remedies. In October 2013 she lodged a request for protection of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time with the President of the Zadar Municipal Court. In December 2013 the president found the request well-founded and ordered the judge to decide within six months. The time-limit was not met. In July 2014 she sought compensation from the Zadar County Court. In October 2014 the County Court awarded her HRK 1,000, finding the length excessive but also holding that she had contributed to the delay “to a certain extent” by failing to attend hearings on 9 April and 13 June 2014. She appealed, arguing that the April hearing was adjourned because another defendant had not been properly summoned and that the June hearing was held despite her absence. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in December 2014, served in January 2015. Her complaint was that the length was excessive and the compensation inadequate.

The second applicant, Aleksander Marković, applied on 20 July 2012 to the Karlovac Municipal Court for enforcement of a 27 January 2010 judgment ordering company T. to perform construction repairs. A writ of execution was issued on 14 February 2013, but company T. appealed on 27 February 2013. The appeal remained pending until 10 February 2017, when the Karlovac County Court quashed the writ and remitted the case. In fresh proceedings, on 5 July 2017 the Municipal Court issued a new writ ordering compliance within thirty days or payment of HRK 1,000 per day. However, on 10 April 2017 the Zagreb Commercial Court had opened “emergency administration proceedings” against company T.’s parent company A. and its subsidiaries under emergency legislation. As a result, all civil and enforcement proceedings were stayed, non-financial claims were transformed into financial claims, and creditors had to register claims. The applicant registered a claim of HRK 1,400,000; the administrator did not contest it. In July 2017 the company informed the Municipal Court, and on 17 October 2017 enforcement was stayed. In July 2018 a settlement was concluded and approved, entitling the applicant to 14.4% of his claim in financial instruments if implemented, or 2.6% in liquidation. Implementation was ongoing.

As to domestic remedies, in September 2014 the second applicant lodged an acceleratory request with the Karlovac County Court president, which was dismissed in November 2014 on the basis that three years had not elapsed and no breach was found. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in December 2014. In February 2015 he lodged a constitutional complaint under section 63 of the Constitutional Court Act, arguing that enforcement proceedings were urgent and statutory time-limits had been breached. The Constitutional Court treated it as a complaint under section 62 against the Supreme Court’s decision and declared it inadmissible, because such decisions were not subject to constitutional review. He alleged excessive length of the enforcement proceedings and failure of the domestic authorities to remedy the violation.

The legal context involved the 2013 Courts Act, which made a purely acceleratory remedy primary and a combined compensatory and acceleratory remedy available only if the set time-limit was ignored. Constitutional Court practice required exhaustion of those remedies before a length complaint. The ECtHR examined whether these remedies were effective and whether the applicants’ rights under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention were violated.
001-206266:
In *Berkman v. Russia* (Application no. 46712/15), the applicant, Yelena Vladimirovna Berkman, complained about the Russian authorities’ response to an LGBTI public event and about her arrest and detention. On 27 September 2013, LGBTI rights activists notified the St Petersburg authorities of their intention to hold a meeting marking Coming Out Day on 12 October 2013 at the Field of Mars. The event was planned from 2 p.m. to 3.30 p.m., with about 150 people expected and some participants arriving at 1.30 p.m. to prepare. The authorities forwarded the notice to the police and reminded the organisers that they could be liable under domestic law for inciting hatred or for promoting “non-traditional” sexual relationships to minors. The police deployed around 540 officers, including special-purpose units, apparently because clashes with counter-demonstrators were anticipated. No crowd barriers or perimeter fence were installed at the site.

At about 1 p.m. the applicant arrived to help prepare the meeting. According to her, the participants—about twenty or thirty people—were unable to gather because the area was blocked by more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators. Many counter-demonstrators wore national costumes and some were armed with whips. They insulted, pushed and punched the LGBTI participants, surrounded them and followed them. The participants asked police officers for help, but the police did not react until counter-demonstrators insulted the police themselves. The police then arrested several counter-demonstrators, took them to a police bus and released them. The released counter-demonstrators continued their verbal and physical attacks.

At 1.55 p.m. police officers surrounded a group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, and said they had breached public order by using foul language. The officers ordered them to a police bus and took them to central police station no. 28 under Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The Government later stated that ninety-three people in total had been arrested for disorderly conduct and taken to three police stations before release. The applicant argued that only Coming Out Day participants were taken to police stations.

The applicant was detained under Article 27.3 of the Code from 2.30 p.m. to about 6.30 p.m. Administrative records stated that she had been detained at 1.55 p.m. for disorderly conduct under Article 20.1, namely using foul language and ignoring police warnings, and that she was taken to the station to ensure prompt examination of her case. She signed the records but noted her disagreement. On 8 November 2013, the Dzerzhinskiy District Court terminated the administrative proceedings against her for lack of evidence. Similar charges against other participants were mostly terminated; one conviction was later quashed on appeal.

The applicant brought civil proceedings challenging the lawfulness of her arrest and detention and later alleging that the authorities had failed to ensure the safety of the meeting participants. In October 2014 the district court dismissed her claim, relying on a video recording and finding that she had been an active participant in the conflict, that her arrest was lawful and that her detention had not exceeded forty-eight hours. The appellate court upheld that decision in March 2015, finding the arrest a lawful interim measure taken to facilitate administrative proceedings because the tension at the scene prevented police from identifying offenders. Cassation appeals were unsuccessful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 11 and 14 of the Convention because the authorities failed to ensure the peaceful conduct of the public meeting and allegedly discriminated against her because of her support for LGBTI people. She also alleged under Article 5 that her arrest, removal from the event and subsequent detention were arbitrary and unlawful.
001-206371:
In *Parinov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 48398/17), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 10 December 2020. The applicant, Mr Borys Parinov, a Ukrainian national born in 1953 and living in Lugansk, died in September 2018; his wife and son continued the application. He alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining that proceedings concerning his share in a limited liability company were excessively long and that, as a result, he could not recover that share. The Court communicated the duration-related complaints and declared inadmissible his complaint about the alleged lack of impartiality of the liquidation manager.

In April 2000 the applicant became a shareholder in a limited liability company. On 30 May 2005 he withdrew from the company, but the other shareholder failed to return his share. In December 2007 domestic proceedings began; by April 2008 a final ruling acknowledged his withdrawal. Meanwhile, the company sold two commercial buildings in December 2007 and January 2008 to company B., which resold them to company K. in January and February 2008.

In June 2008 the applicant sued for reimbursement of the value of his share. The Commercial Court opened proceedings and ordered seizure of the company’s assets. After learning of the property sales, in December 2009 he amended his claim to seek reimbursement and invalidation of the sale contracts. In February 2010 the court allowed part of his claim, but the appellate court amended that decision in April 2010. In November 2010 the Higher Commercial Court quashed the lower decisions and remitted the case. On 29 December 2011, on fresh consideration, the Higher Commercial Court terminated the reimbursement claim because the issue had been examined in insolvency proceedings; the invalidity claim was rejected for lack of standing.

Separately, in October 2010 insolvency proceedings began against the company at the request of company P., imposing a moratorium on debt payments. The applicant filed a creditor’s claim in December 2010. In April 2011 the Commercial Court recognized him as a creditor for UAH 4,100,439 (about EUR 356,560), corresponding to his share. The insolvency proceedings were repeatedly suspended and resumed from 2011 to 2013. In February 2014 the company was declared insolvent, liquidation began, and D. was appointed liquidator. The court found the company had only two vehicles, whose location was unknown.

From July 2014 to April 2015 the Commercial Court did not operate because of armed conflict in eastern Ukraine; it resumed in Kharkiv. In July 2015 the insolvency case was reopened. In August 2015 the liquidator asked to be dismissed. Between October 2015 and September 2019, the creditors’ committee repeatedly failed to decide on his withdrawal, despite court orders to convene meetings and appoint a new liquidator. Attempts to find a new liquidator via the automatic system failed because candidates did not consent or did not reply. The liquidator reported that liquidation was suspended because of the conflict and his relocation. Hearings in October 2019 and April 2020 were adjourned due to non-attendance, with no resolution on the liquidator. In July 2019 the applicant’s wife was admitted as a creditor/heir.

The applicant also filed a criminal complaint in September 2011 against company officials. A fraud case was opened, closed in February 2014 for lack of corpus delicti, quashed in September 2016, and the investigation remained ongoing. These facts underpinned the complaints that the proceedings were excessively long, lacked an effective remedy, and prevented him from recovering his company share, thereby interfering with his possessions.
001-203048:
**Case Summary: Albul and Others v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 18899/19 and 49871/19)**

This case is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 18 June 2020. The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention about the excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of any effective remedy in domestic law for that complaint. The Court deliberated in private on 28 May 2020 and adopted its judgment on 18 June 2020.

The factual details are set out in the appended table. Application no. 18899/19 was introduced on 29 March 2019 by Tamara Afanasiyivna Albul, born 26 May 1957, who was represented by Anatoliy Borysovych Bogachev of Odesa. The table records civil proceedings with start dates of 25 June 2012 and 2 March 2015, and end dates of 13 November 2014 and 3 October 2018. The total length was 5 years, 11 months and 22 days, across three levels of jurisdiction. Thus, by the time the application was lodged, the proceedings involving the applicant had lasted nearly six years cumulatively, passing through first-instance, appellate and cassation review.

Application no. 49871/19 was introduced on 13 September 2019 by Dmitriy Georgiyevich Lapin, born 19 December 1964, and Valentina Pavlovna Lapina, born 30 April 1939. Their civil proceedings began on 29 July 2009 and were still pending at the time the case was before the Court. The total length was more than 10 years, 9 months and 8 days, across three levels of jurisdiction. This application therefore alleged an ongoing and exceptionally long delay, far exceeding the duration in the first application.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the duration and procedural history of the domestic civil proceedings. In both applications, the proceedings passed through three levels of jurisdiction. In the first, the total length was just under six years. In the second, the proceedings had already exceeded ten years and nine months and had not concluded. These periods formed the basis for the applicants’ complaint under Article 6 § 1 that their civil cases were not heard within a reasonable time.

The applicants also complained under Article 13 that Ukrainian law did not provide any effective remedy through which they could challenge the excessive length of the civil proceedings. The Court’s review, as framed by the applications, concerned whether the length of the proceedings was compatible with the “reasonable time” requirement and whether the applicants had an effective domestic remedy for that length complaint.

The provided text does not set out the Court’s substantive findings or any award, but it identifies the factual matrix: two sets of civil proceedings against Ukraine, one lasting almost six years and another pending for over a decade, both involving three levels of jurisdiction. Those facts were the basis for the alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention.
001-202750:
The applicant, an Afghan national, alleged that Slovak authorities failed to inform him of the reasons for his arrest, returned him to Ukraine, where he was detained in inadequate conditions despite his alleged minor status and could not participate effectively in detention proceedings, and that he was later returned to Afghanistan without an adequate risk assessment. He also alleged that an NGO representative was denied access to him in Ukraine, preventing an interim-measure application to the Court. He claimed birth in 1993 or 1994; Slovak and Ukrainian authorities recorded 14 January 1992.

He came from Kunduz. His father, who worked for Afghanistan’s National Security Department, was killed around 2005, possibly by Taliban-linked persons. In 2010 his maternal uncle received a threatening letter and arranged for him to leave. In May 2010 smugglers took him through Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia. He stayed in Moscow for a month and entered Ukraine in early July 2010, remaining in Kyiv for three months. His brother-in-law later crossed into Slovakia, travelled to Spain and sought asylum.

On 23 September 2010 at 4.10 p.m. Slovak border police arrested him crossing illegally with three other Afghans; he had no identity papers. At 7.25 p.m. he was interviewed with Slovak-English and English-Pashto interpretation. His birth date was recorded as 14 January 1992. He said he wished to reach western Europe and did not request asylum in Slovakia. The record was signed by police and the Slovak-English interpreter, not by him or the Afghan interpreter. Slovakia said he refused to sign; two others signed similar records.

On 24 September 2010 an expulsion decision and five-year entry ban were issued. He received Pashto guidelines, though some case-specific details were in Slovak. At 2 p.m. he was handed to Ukrainian authorities. He alleged that in Slovakia he had no interpretation, asylum information or lawyer; tried to request asylum and said he was a minor; and received no written return decision or appeal information.

In Ukraine he was held at the Chop Border Guard facility, where he alleged overcrowding and lack of guaranteed daily exercise. He said he told a guard via other detainees and a Caritas representative that he was 14 and wished to apply for asylum, but no action was taken. The SBCS ordered voluntary departure and sought forcible expulsion and detention. On 1 October 2010, according to the court, the SBCS and applicant asked for written proceedings in their absence. On 13 October 2010 the Zakarpattya Circuit Administrative Court ordered expulsion and detention pending expulsion, relying on his recorded 1992 birth date, illegal entry, lack of means or relatives in Ukraine, and a UNHCR publication indicating no risk in Afghanistan. The applicant alleged he was unaware of the proceedings, had no lawyer, did not understand his rights, signed a waiver without understanding, was not served the decision and missed the ten-day appeal deadline.

On 14 October 2010 he was moved to temporary accommodation in Volyn; he alleged he again said he was 14. On 20/22 February 2011 the Afghan Embassy interviewed him and issued a travel document recording his birth date as 14 January 1992. On 23 February 2011 he applied for asylum, saying he would be killed if returned. On 2 March 2011 he was interviewed. On 9 March 2011 the Regional Migration Service rejected the application as inadmissible, citing manifestly unfounded facts, failure to meet the refugee definition, his Afghan travel document, failure to seek asylum earlier and lack of identity documents. On 11 March 2011 he was transferred to Mukacheve and notified. On 12 March 2011 an NGO partner of UNHCR was allegedly denied access to provide legal advice, preventing an interim-measure application. On 14 March 2011 he was expelled to Kabul. He alleged that about three weeks later unknown people sought him at home and left a threatening letter, causing him to relocate frequently.
001-203931:
Levchuk v. Ukraine (Application no. 17496/19), judgment of 3 September 2020, concerns Ms Iryna Levchuk, a disabled Ukrainian woman living in Rivne. She alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention arising from the dismissal of her civil eviction claim against her ex-husband, O.L., who had repeatedly subjected her and their minor children to psychological and physical violence.

In 2006 the applicant married O.L.; they lived in a flat co-owned by O.L. and his mother. They had triplets in 2007, and in 2008 Rivne City Council provided the family with social housing as protected tenants. According to the applicant, O.L. abused alcohol, harassed, threatened and physically assaulted her, often in the children’s presence. In 2009 a forensic report certified a broken nose and eye haemorrhages; in 2011 police refused criminal proceedings for an assault. In 2015 she reported O.L. kicking her; criminal proceedings under Article 125 were opened but later closed after she withdrew her complaint. She also reported child-support arrears and repeated harassment. In 2016 police issued warnings, and O.L. was charged with administrative domestic violence under Article 173-2 for insulting and threatening her and piercing a blanket with a knife. A family welfare assessment found the children were distressed by their father’s drunken arguments and neglect; school staff described psychological ill-treatment. In April 2016 she reported another violent outburst, and medical evidence showed haemorrhages and a foot sprain. In July 2016 a court found O.L. administratively guilty of domestic violence but relieved him of liability with an oral reprimand because the applicant requested this and the parties allegedly resolved their differences.

In June 2016 the applicant sued to evict O.L. under Article 116 of the Housing Code, arguing that living with him was impossible because he systematically abused alcohol, mistreated, threatened and harassed her and the children, creating constant risk of psychological and physical violence. She submitted medical certificates, police complaints, administrative and criminal proceedings, and evidence of child-support arrears. In April 2017 the Rivne Town Court allowed eviction, finding O.L. abused alcohol, caused scenes, intimidated the applicant in front of the children, threatened violence, and that earlier corrective measures had failed. The Rivne Regional Court of Appeal reversed in June 2017 and dismissed the claim. It found hostile relations between the former spouses but no proof that O.L. systematically breached living rules or that authorities had applied corrective measures; complaints alone, it said, did not justify the “extreme” measure of eviction. It merely warned O.L. to change his attitude. The Supreme Court upheld that decision in August 2018. The applicant and O.L. later became co-owners of the flat and still share it. In December 2019 she filed a fresh criminal complaint, and in November 2019 she began proceedings to deprive O.L. of parental rights.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged that the dismissal of her eviction claim breached Article 8 by failing to protect her private and family life from domestic violence, Article 6 by denying a fair hearing, and Article 13 by leaving her without an effective remedy. The key facts centre on the documented pattern of domestic violence, the authorities’ repeated inadequate responses, and the domestic courts’ refusal to remove the abusive ex-husband from the shared home despite prior findings against him.
001-206511:
**Yukhymovych v. Ukraine** (Application no. 11464/12) concerned the fatal shooting by police of the applicant’s son, Ruslan Yukhymovych, during an attempted arrest in March 1999 and the subsequent investigation. The applicant, a Ukrainian national, alleged violations of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights—both the substantive right to life and the procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation—after his son was shot twice by police.

The events began when B. complained to the Lviv Regional Department for Combatting Organised Crime that unknown persons had threatened her and extorted USD 25,000. Police identified the applicant’s son and his friend Z. as suspects, allegedly members of an organised criminal group. On 1 March 1999, the DCOC approved an operation to arrest them using the “Sokil” special police unit. On 4 March 1999, the applicant’s son and Z. arrived by taxi at B.’s house. Z. entered first, followed by the applicant’s son. Police officer M. shouted “Freeze, police!” and Z. was arrested. The applicant’s son fled. Officers M. and O. chased him. During the operation, O. shot the applicant’s son twice. He died from his injuries.

The key disputed fact was whether the applicant’s son had a gun and posed a threat when shot. Police claimed he disobeyed orders, fled, and pointed a “Valtro” gas gun at officers. A “Valtro” gun was allegedly found near his body and later placed in a plastic bag inside the house. His fingerprints were found on the gun. However, witnesses to the on-site inspection did not clearly see a gun. The taxi driver initially said he saw a gun, then withdrew that statement. The alleged accomplice Z. initially said the applicant’s son had left his gun in the car and that the gun in the house was not his; he later changed his testimony. Forensic reports were also contradictory regarding the location, order, and distance of the shots. Initial examinations suggested death was caused by a chest wound, while later reports described two back wounds, with the fatal wound inflicted near the gate. Experts could not conclusively determine the order of shots. Additional injuries—a bruise on the forehead and wounds to the head and lip—were noted but never adequately explained.

The investigation was marked by repeated terminations and reopenings. An internal police inquiry quickly found the shooting lawful. The prosecutor initially refused to open a criminal case, then reopened it. Between 1999 and 2018, proceedings were terminated and set aside many times. Domestic courts repeatedly criticised the investigation for failing to resolve contradictions about whether the applicant’s son had a gun, failing to secure the scene, allowing the car to be towed without permission, losing evidence, and taking a formalistic approach. The applicant’s son’s clothes were returned to the applicant and later destroyed, preventing further forensic examination. As of 2018, the proceedings were still pending.

The applicant complained that the police used lethal force without justification and that the State failed to conduct an effective, independent, and prompt investigation into his son’s death. The case therefore centred on whether the shooting complied with Article 2’s strict requirements on the use of force and whether the prolonged, contradictory, and repeatedly defective investigation violated the procedural limb of Article 2.
001-203492:
Damian Walczak, a Polish national born in 1971 living in Plewiska, was arrested on 16 December 2014 and charged with organised-crime and robbery-related offences. The Poznań-Nowe Miasto District Court ordered his detention on remand until 16 March 2015; the Poznań Regional Court later extended it until 16 June and then 16 September 2015. He was released on 4 February 2016. He alleged that during detention he was deprived of personal contact with his wife, M.W., for a significant period.

On 30 December 2014 M.W. applied to visit him. On 5 January 2015 the Poznań-Nowe Miasto District Prosecutor refused because she was a witness in the proceedings; no appeal was lodged. Applications of 26 February and 17 March 2015 were dismissed on 27 February and 24 March 2015 because evidence still needed to be heard from M.W.; again no appeals were lodged. On 3 April 2015 M.W. refused to testify at the investigation stage and applied again. On 7 April 2015 the prosecutor refused, saying she could still be asked to testify while the investigation was ongoing; no appeal was lodged. A 27 May application was dismissed on 5 June 2015, without interlocutory appeal. On 10 June 2015 M.W. applied again; on 15 June 2015 the prosecutor dismissed it, saying a visit could impede proceedings because she knew other witnesses and had access to the applicant’s computer. On 28 August 2015 the Poznań Regional Prosecutor dismissed the applicant’s interlocutory appeal against that decision. Applications of 15 June and 15 July 2015 were dismissed on 25 June and 24 July 2015; the applicant’s own request of 29 June 2015 was dismissed on 6 July 2015.

On 27 August 2015 the prosecutor allowed M.W. to visit; the visit took place on 30 August 2015. On 3 September 2015 the prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment. On 10 September 2015 the Poznań Regional Court dismissed M.W.’s application to visit because she was a witness, served on her on 14 September 2015. On 24 September 2015 the Regional Court dismissed her interlocutory appeal. It held that her statement that she would not testify against her husband was irrelevant because court proceedings had not begun and she could change her mind when summoned. It also held that investigation-stage visits allowed by the prosecutor were irrelevant because those decisions could not be assessed by the court. A further request of 15 September 2015 was marked “examined” on 17 September 2015. On 1 October 2015 M.W. requested a visit and stated she would rely on her right to refuse to testify. On 2 October 2015 the Regional Court allowed the visit, which took place on 11 October 2015. Her later requests were granted. There were no significant subsequent developments, and M.W. was not asked to testify at later hearings.

Under Article 217 of the 1997 Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences, visits required permission from the investigating prosecutor or, once trial had begun, the trial court; interlocutory appeals were available under Article 217 § 1c, but § 1d restricted further appeals if a refusal was upheld within three months.
001-203885:
**Summary of Mugemangango v. Belgium (Application no. 310/15)**

The case concerned a post-election dispute in Belgium. The applicant, Germain Mugemangango, was the top candidate on the PTB-GO! list for the Charleroi constituency in the 25 May 2014 elections to the Walloon Parliament. His list received 16,554 votes—fourteen votes short of the 16,567.83 threshold required to qualify for the "related lists" (apparentement) system, which could have won him a seat. Separately, 21,385 ballot papers in Charleroi were declared blank, spoiled, or disputed.

The day after the elections, the applicant requested a recount from the main electoral board and the Hainaut central electoral board. Both refused, stating they lacked jurisdiction and referring him to the Walloon Parliament.

On 6 June 2014, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Walloon Parliament under section 31 of the Special Law of 8 August 1980, seeking re-examination of the 21,385 ballot papers and a recount of any valid votes wrongly declared void. He alleged numerous irregularities: counting station fatigue (some counts lasted over twelve hours without breaks); poor physical conditions; hurriedly set-up stations and insufficiently trained officers; ballot papers discovered days after the election with no record of whether they were counted; ballot design problems (boxes too small, red pencils not marking pink ballots clearly); and witnesses reporting that ballot papers with non-identifying marks were wrongly declared spoiled despite validly cast votes. He submitted witness accounts and press articles.

The Credentials Committee, chosen by drawing lots, heard the applicant and his lawyer publicly on 10 June 2014, then deliberated privately. Notably, two committee members who had stood in the same constituency as the applicant chose not to vote on his complaint, though they remained present during deliberations and the vote. One member was absent for part of the proceedings. The committee initially rejected a proposal to declare the complaint admissible but ill-founded (2-2), then after further deliberations found it admissible and well-founded (3-1), proposing that blank and spoiled ballots be checked and all Charleroi ballots recounted. The committee's accompanying note concluded that the distribution of seats could change if the 21,385 ballots were recounted and deemed valid, potentially affecting other Hainaut constituencies through the related lists system.

On 13 June 2014, the committee presented its findings at the plenary session. The Walloon Parliament rejected them by 43 votes to 32. All members voted, including those elected in the applicant's constituency. A motion to approve all credentials then passed 43-28 with four abstentions. The Parliament's reasoned decision stated that most grievances concerned inherent features of the electoral system; press articles were inadmissible evidence; witness statements should have been recorded officially at the time; the number of spoiled ballots was lower than in 2009; and handwritten annotations spoiled ballots under Article 157 of the Electoral Code. Some members were alarmed that ballots marked with non-red pencils were inconsistently declared spoiled, but no official record existed.

Belgian courts consistently declined jurisdiction over election disputes, vesting final authority in Parliament. The applicant complained of a lack of safeguards against arbitrariness and the absence of a remedy before an independent and impartial authority, relying on Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.
001-206159:
The applicant, Project-Trade d.o.o., is a Croatian limited liability company registered in Zagreb. It was a shareholder in Croatia Bank d.d. (the bank), holding 1,251 shares with a nominal value of HRK 200 each. On 23 February 1999 the Croatian National Bank (CNB) appointed a temporary administrator at the bank; the term was extended on 23 August 1999. On 18 June 1999, based on an expert report that the bank’s debts largely exceeded its share capital and threatened financial-market stability, the CNB proposed recovery and restructuring of the bank.

On 23 September 1999 the Croatian Government adopted the Decision on the recovery and restructuring of Croatia Bank, published on 27 September 1999. From publication, all existing shares of the bank were revoked and cancelled. New shares in the amount of HRK 204.6 million were to be issued to the State Agency for Deposit Insurance and Bank Resolution (DAB). The powers of the bank’s governing bodies and the rights of shareholders were extinguished. The recovery process was completed on 13 September 2000. The Decision was slightly amended on 25 May 2000, and the Constitutional Court later held that it was subordinate legislation rather than an individual legal act.

In 1999 and 2000, five shareholders of the bank, but not the applicant company, filed four petitions with the Constitutional Court challenging the Government Decision. They alleged violations of Croatian constitutional rights, argued that the bank had been in good standing and that the Decision was unnecessary. After obtaining expert opinions, on 30 January 2003 the Constitutional Court discontinued the proceedings because the 1994 Recovery and Restructuring of Banks Act had been repealed on 31 May 2000. It stated that the Decision’s effects interfered with individual rights of founders and former shareholders, but that judicial protection was available in civil proceedings under the Obligations Act and section 19(2) of the Courts Act, and ultimately by constitutional complaint. Two dissenting judges argued that the review could have continued, that the Decision was unconstitutional, and that no effective remedy, especially a judicial one, existed. One dissent contested that civil proceedings could succeed without a finding that the Government Decision was unconstitutional.

On 12 September 2003 the applicant company brought a civil action in the Zagreb Commercial Court against the bank and DAB. It sought a declaration that it still held 1,251 shares, an order that DAB transfer corresponding shares to it, and an order that the bank register it as holder. The applicant argued that the Government Decision revoking and cancelling its shares was economically unjustified because the bank had been in good standing, that statutory requirements had not been met, and that the Decision violated Articles 48 § 1, 49 § 4 and 50 of the Croatian Constitution, as allegedly acknowledged by the High Commercial Court in a judgment of 21 December 2004 in another case.

On 21 February 2006 the Zagreb Commercial Court dismissed the action. On 18 June 2008 the High Commercial Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal and upheld the first-instance judgment, served on 16 September 2008. It reasoned that under point 7 of the Government Decision all existing shares had been extinguished and new shares issued to DAB, so the applicant’s shares no longer existed and could not be returned. The applicant had argued on appeal that the first-instance court misapplied substantive law, that the Government Decision was unconstitutional, and that the Government had to compensate the market value of the revoked shares under Article 50 § 1 of the Constitution. The applicant company lodged its application with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 December 2013.
001-203165:
In *Stavropoulos and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 52484/18), three Greek nationals—Nikolaos Stavropoulos, Ioanna Kravari, and Stavroula-Dorothea Stavropoulou—complained about an entry in a birth register. The first and second applicants were the parents of the third applicant, born in 2007. The family lived in Oxford, United Kingdom.

On 17 August 2007, the first applicant, authorised by the second, went to the Amarousio registry office to register their daughter’s birth. When the registrar entered the child’s forename, he added in parentheses an abbreviation of the Greek word for “naming” (*ονοματοδοσία*). The applicants objected to this notation. They argued that Greek law did not require registry offices to specify whether a child had been named by a civil or Christian act. In their view, the note implied that the child had not been christened, thereby revealing their religious beliefs and the child’s religious status. They alleged violations of their right to freedom of religion and of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, because the register allegedly disclosed sensitive personal data.

On 19 October 2007, the applicants applied to the Supreme Administrative Court for annulment of the birth registration insofar as it contained the note “naming.” They claimed the entry referred to the fact that their child had not been christened and exposed their religious beliefs. On 6 March 2018, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the application as inadmissible, finding that the applicants lacked legal interest. It relied on Articles 25 and 26 of Law no. 344/1976. The court held that a child’s first name could be registered only through “naming”—a declaration by the parents or guardians before the competent registry office—regardless of whether the child was later christened. The note “naming” merely repeated the title of Article 25 and was the only legal way of acquiring a name. It therefore could not be said to discriminate against the applicants or cause the alleged harm.

The relevant legal framework reinforced the distinction between civil naming and religious christening. Article 25 of Law no. 344/1976 provided that a newborn’s name is recorded in the birth registration act following a declaration by the parents exercising parental responsibility, or by a guardian. Article 26 provided that a christening is recorded separately in the side section of the birth act within ninety days, upon declaration by the officiating priest, and includes the date of christening and any name given to the child. State Legal Council opinion no. 431/2006 stated that if parents did not declare a name simultaneously with or before a christening declaration, they had to make a special naming declaration; merely noting the name during christening registration did not suffice for the child to acquire a first name. A Ministry of Interior circular similarly stated that a christening declaration could not be treated as a naming declaration unless it met Law no. 344/1976’s conditions.

The Greek Ombudsman, intervening, observed that the view that only non-christened children are “named,” or that christened children need not be named, was inconsistent with the law and effectively forced citizens to register a religion inadvertently. The Ombudsman’s 2006 report noted wider problems concerning religious freedom and the administration’s reluctance to embrace the State’s religious neutrality.

The applicants’ core complaint was that the registry notation “naming” amounted to an official record distinguishing civil naming from religious christening, disclosing that the child had not been christened and thereby revealing their religious beliefs in breach of Articles 9 and 8 ECHR. The domestic court’s rejection on standing grounds was the final domestic act before the Strasbourg application.
001-200815:
**Case:** *Klopcovs v. Latvia* (Application no. 26902/13)  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section  
**Judgment date:** 13 February 2020

The applicant, Mr Boriss Klopcovs, a Latvian national born in 1951 and living in Riga, lodged his application on 11 April 2013. On 18 December 2013 the Latvian Government were given notice only of the complaint concerning the **length of proceedings**; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. Therefore, the key facts relevant to the admissible alleged violation concern the duration of the administrative proceedings he brought after prison authorities interfered with his correspondence.

In 2005 the applicant was detained in Riga Central Prison pending trial. During June, July and August 2005, the prison administration controlled and stopped his correspondence addressed to private persons and institutions. On 14 and 25 September 2005 he complained to the Prisons Administration about those actions and the reasons given. The Prisons Administration rejected his complaints on 11 and 24 October 2005.
