On 4 October and 16 December 2005, the Ministry of Justice found the prison administration’s actions and the Prisons Administration’s replies lawful.

On 22 September 2006 the applicant brought administrative proceedings against the Ministry of Justice. The Prisons Administration later joined the proceedings. On 21 October 2008 the Administrative District Court found the prison administration’s actions unlawful, but rejected the applicant’s claim for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages of 5,406 Latvian lats (approximately EUR 7,692). On 3 December 2009 the Administrative Regional Court quashed that decision and remitted the case to the first-instance court. On 27 April 2010 the first-instance court again found the actions unlawful and rejected the damages claim. The applicant appealed only as regards damages, but his appeal was not accepted because it was late. The opposing parties’ appeals were accepted, and appellate proceedings began.

On 15 February 2012 the Administrative Regional Court found that the prison administration had acted unlawfully only insofar as the applicant had not been informed of the reasons for stopping his letters and insofar as one letter had been stopped unlawfully. The remainder of his claims were dismissed. On 26 October 2012 the Senate of the Supreme Court gave a final decision upholding the appellate judgment and dismissing the cassation complaints of both the Prisons Administration and the applicant.

The administrative proceedings thus ran from 22 September 2006 to 26 October 2012, lasting over six years and passing through first instance, appeal, remittal, a second first-instance judgment, a second appeal, and cassation. There were ten hearings. None were postponed because of the applicant’s unjustified absence. However, after the hearing of 22 February 2008, the applicant failed to return 77 pages of case documents. On 23 May 2008 he explained that he believed the documents were for his personal use and did not know they had to be returned. The first-instance court reobtained them from another case file in September 2008, and at least one hearing was apparently adjourned because of this. The applicant also initiated several ancillary proceedings challenging various procedural decisions of the first-instance and appellate courts.

These facts were relevant to assessing whether the length of the administrative proceedings exceeded a reasonable time and whether any delays were attributable to the authorities or to the applicant. The only admissible Convention complaint was the length-of-proceedings complaint; the other complaints, including those concerning the stopping of his correspondence, were declared inadmissible.
001-204584:
In *Mirgadirov v. Azerbaijan and Turkey* (App. no. 62775/14, judgment 17 September 2020), the applicant, Rauf Mirgadirov, is an Azerbaijani national and well-known journalist/political analyst. In July 2010 he moved to Turkey, where he lived in Ankara and worked as a correspondent for the newspaper *Zerkalo*. Turkish authorities had granted him a press card and residence permit valid until 31 December 2014. On 8 April 2014, however, the Turkish Directorate General of Press and Information annulled his press card; he was informed orally the next day, without written reasons. On 11 April he requested written confirmation, but received none. On 18 April the Migration Management authorities decided to deport him under Law no. 6458. That night, while travelling by bus to Georgia with his family, police stopped the bus, found his residence permit had been revoked, and took him to the Ankara Security Directorate. He was allegedly told he was arrested because he was no longer legally resident. Police documents stated he was notified of the deportation procedure, his illegal presence, administrative detention and his rights, including access to a lawyer, but he refused to sign them; he claimed he was never properly notified. His requests for a lawyer and to contact his wife were allegedly ignored. On 19 April he was taken to Esenboğa Airport, signed a twelve-month entry ban, and was placed on a flight to Baku under police control. The official deportation and administrative detention decision was issued on 21 April.

Upon arrival in Baku on 19 April 2014, Azerbaijani Ministry of National Security agents arrested him. At 5:15 p.m. he was recorded as a suspect for high treason under Article 274 of the Criminal Code. At 5:20 p.m. he was questioned in the presence of a State-appointed lawyer. He admitted meeting L.B., head of an Armenian NGO, and D.S., former head of Armenian intelligence, in Turkey, Armenia and Georgia to discuss the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and regional affairs, but denied providing any State secrets, military, socio-political or economic information, or the location of military units. On 21 April he was charged with high treason: the authorities alleged he had been recruited by Armenian intelligence and had collected and supplied State secrets, photographs and technical drawings for use against Azerbaijan. The same day, the Nasimi District Court ordered his pre-trial detention for three months, citing the serious nature of the charge and risks of absconding or obstructing the investigation.

The applicant complained that his Convention rights were violated by his arrest, detention and de facto deportation from Turkey and his subsequent detention in Azerbaijan. Against Turkey, he invoked Article 5 §§ 1 and 2 (unlawful detention on 19 April and lack of reasons), Article 5 § 3 (failure to bring him before a judge), Article 5 § 4 (inability to challenge detention), and Article 10 (freedom of expression as a journalist). Against Azerbaijan, he invoked Article 5 § 1(c) (no reasonable suspicion), Article 5 § 1 (unlawful detention from 19 to 20 November 2014), Article 5 § 3 (lack of justification for pre-trial detention), Article 5 § 4 (courts’ failure to assess release arguments and his lawyers’ absence from the 20 November 2014 Nasimi District Court hearing), Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), Article 8 (unlawful restrictions during the investigation), and Article 18 in conjunction with Article 5.
001-202619:
The case of **Łabudek v. Poland** (Application no. 37245/13), a First Section Committee judgment of 4 June 2020, concerned an alleged violation of **Article 5 § 3** of the European Convention on Human Rights—the right to trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial—based on the excessive length of the applicant’s detention on remand after **23 July 2011**. The applicant, Zdzisław Łabudek, a Polish national born in 1961, was held in Wojkowice Detention Centre.

On 18 January 1999 the applicant was arrested and remanded in custody on charges of participating in an organised armed criminal group and committing numerous violent offences, including two murders. His trial before the Katowice Regional Court began on 20 February 2001. On 13 February 2008 the Katowice Regional Court convicted him, together with thirty-five other accused, of membership in an organised armed criminal group, arms trafficking, two murders, three robberies, three attempted robberies, illegal possession of firearms and other offences. He was sentenced to life imprisonment with eligibility for conditional release after thirty years. On 18 February 2010 the Katowice Court of Appeal partly quashed the judgment and remitted the case, particularly regarding the applicant. On 11 February 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed cassation appeals.

Meanwhile, on 25 May 2010, the applicant’s detention on remand in the present case was lifted, but he was then serving a prison sentence in another set of criminal proceedings until 22 July 2011. On 27 June 2011 the Katowice Regional Court again ordered his detention on remand in the same proceedings. It relied on the high probability that he had committed the offences and the severity of the possible penalty. It also cited a risk of obstruction because he had already been sentenced to life imprisonment and had close ties with co-accused and witnesses from the same organised criminal group. The court noted that the applicant had previously maintained discipline and punished disobedience within the group, had attempted to contact and influence one witness, had threatened another, and had planned to murder a witness in another case. It concluded that no other preventive measure could sufficiently secure the proceedings.

The detention was extended repeatedly: on 17 January, 21 June and 18 December 2012; 13 June and 10 December 2013; 9 June and 17 December 2014; 11 June and 3 December 2015; and 10 May and 12 October 2016. The courts relied on the same grounds: reasonable suspicion, the maximum possible penalty, risk of collusion, absconding or further serious offences, and witness interference. Some decisions noted that the crown witness evidence had not yet been obtained and that proceedings were interrupted because a co-accused was detained in another case. The applicant’s appeals against several extensions were dismissed, with the Katowice Court of Appeal agreeing that continued detention was necessary. Between 11 June 2015 and 6 April 2016 he served a prison sentence imposed in another case. On 12 October 2016 the Katowice Regional Court convicted him as charged and imposed life imprisonment with conditional release after thirty years. His appeal was pending.

The proceedings after remittal were extensive. From 26 May 2011 to 12 October 2016, 174 hearings were held: 28 in 2011, 44 in 2012, 34 in 2013, 26 in 2014, 24 in 2015 and 18 in 2016. Of 276 scheduled hearings, 102 were adjourned, mainly due to illness of witnesses, accused or judges, or justified absence of experts. The court heard numerous witnesses, including a crown witness, obtained forensic reports, and the case file reached 75,000 pages.

The applicant lodged his application on 15 April 2013. The Court gave notice only of the complaint under Article 5 § 3 concerning the length of detention on remand after 23 July 2011, declaring the remainder inadmissible. It rejected the Government’s objection to Committee examination. The key issue was therefore whether the detention on remand after 23 July 2011 was excessively long.
001-201329:
In *Sigríður Elín Sigfúsdóttir v. Iceland*, the applicant, a former director of corporate banking at Landsbanki, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that her criminal proceedings were heard by a tribunal that was not independent and impartial and that her right to be presumed innocent was violated. The case arose from Iceland’s 2008 financial crisis. On 30 September 2008, the company Imon ehf., owned by investor M.A., purchased 250,000,000 Landsbanki shares using a loan from Landsbanki, secured by the shares and Imon’s capital certificates in Byr Savings Bank. The applicant, as a member of Landsbanki’s credit committee, approved the loan on 3 October 2008, four days before Landsbanki collapsed on 7 October 2008.

A Special Prosecutor later investigated. In March 2013, the applicant was indicted for fraud by abuse of position and market manipulation, along with two co-defendants. In June 2014, the District Court of Reykjavik acquitted her. In October 2015, the Supreme Court overturned the acquittal, convicted her of abuse of position and aiding and abetting market manipulation, and sentenced her to 18 months’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court panel consisted of Justices M.S., V.M.M., E.T., H.I.J. and Þ.Ö.

In December 2016, media reports revealed that several Supreme Court justices had owned shares in Icelandic banks before the 2008 crash, raising concerns about undisclosed conflicts of interest. The applicant stated that this was the first time she learned of these holdings. She requested information from the Committee on Judicial Functions. The Committee explained that Justice M.S. had inherited Glitnir shares but sold them in 2003 and 2007; Justices V.M.M. and E.T. were appointed only in 2010 and 2011 and had previously held shares lost in the bank collapse; the other judges had reported no shareholdings. The Supreme Court later published information and provided details to affected parties. Justice E.T. reported Landsbanki shares with a nominal value of ISK 87,383, purchased for ISK 374,112 and valued at ISK 1,738,922 on 3 October 2008, as well as Glitnir shares with a nominal value of ISK 287,124. Justice V.M.M. reported Landsbanki shares acquired between March and September 2007 with a nominal value of ISK 428,075, purchased for ISK 14,753,256 and valued at ISK 8,518,692 on 3 October 2008; they became worthless after the State takeover.

In December 2016, the applicant applied to reopen her case. She argued that the financial interests of Justices E.T., M.S. and V.M.M. meant the Supreme Court panel lacked impartiality under Article 70 of the Icelandic Constitution and Article 6 of the Convention. On 12 May 2019, the Committee on Reopening of Judicial Proceedings accepted the request under section 228(1)(d) of the Criminal Procedures Act. It found that Justice V.M.M.’s substantial Landsbanki shareholding and resulting financial loss could reasonably justify fears that the panel lacked impartiality. The Committee noted that the Supreme Court had stated that the applicant’s “imprudent decisions” on loans could have caused financial loss to Landsbanki shareholders, and that the information about V.M.M.’s holdings had not been known to the applicant at trial. The Committee did not decide the impartiality of the other justices. The reopening proceedings remained pending before the Supreme Court. The applicant’s ECtHR application, lodged on 2 June 2017, centred on these undisclosed shareholdings and the alleged resulting lack of objective impartiality.
001-202991:
In *Shebaldina v. Ukraine* (Application no. 75792/11), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Ms Alla Petrivna Shebaldina, a Ukrainian national born in 1959 and living in Bilgorod-Dnistrovskyy, Odessa Region. The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the domestic courts refused to award her a social allowance to which she was entitled under domestic law. She also raised a related complaint under Article 13 of the Convention. The Court gave notice of those complaints to the Ukrainian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

From 1988 until 2006 the applicant worked as a teacher in a State specialised child-care centre. Under Article 57 of the 1991 Education Act, as in force at the material time, she was entitled to seniority and recreation allowances. However, between 1997 and 2002 she did not receive those allowances. On 3 December 2007 she lodged a claim with the domestic courts against the centre and the regional department of the State Treasury. She sought arrears of UAH 2,244.30, an index-linked adjustment of UAH 4,336.17, compensation for non-pecuniary damage of UAH 10,000, and costs and expenses of UAH 1,484.

On 28 October 2010 the Bilgorod-Dnistrovskyy Town Court partly allowed the claim. It found that the applicant was entitled to the seniority and recreation allowances and that the centre was in arrears. It ordered the centre to pay her UAH 2,244.30 in arrears, UAH 4,336.17 as an index-linked adjustment, and UAH 1,400 in legal costs. The court dismissed her claim for non-pecuniary damage. It reasoned that the centre’s failure to pay had resulted from a lack of State budget funding, and that the centre could therefore claim reimbursement from the State budget.

On 29 April 2011 the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal quashed that judgment and dismissed the applicant’s claim. It found that the applicant had worked in the centre, which had dual status as a healthcare and educational institution, and that in 1997–2002 she had not received allowances due under Article 57, with arrears of UAH 2,244.30. However, under the 2004 Act on the Restructuring of Indebtedness under Article 57 of the Education Act, payments for that period were recognised as a debt to be paid by the State from the State budget. The arrears therefore constituted a State budget debt, not a debt of the centre, which had not received the relevant funds. The regional department of the State Treasury was not a proper defendant. The court also dismissed the index-linking and non-pecuniary damage claims because the 2004 Act did not provide for them. On 21 July 2011 the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court declined to examine the merits of the applicant’s cassation appeal.

The applicant submitted domestic case-law showing that the Court of Appeal had previously upheld claims by two other employees of the same centre for recovery of Article 57 allowances for 1997–2003, holding that payment was not conditional on the availability of State budget funds. The key alleged violation was therefore that, despite recognising her statutory entitlement, the domestic courts ultimately denied her the allowance and left her without payment. The Article 13 complaint concerned the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy for that breach.
001-205539:
The case *Baz v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40962/13) is a European Court of Human Rights Fifth Section Committee judgment delivered on 5 November 2020. The applicant, Mekhmet Takhır Dıno Baz, a Turkish national born in 1976 and living in Mykolayiv, complained under Article 5 § 1 (f) of the Convention that his detention in Ukraine in the context of extradition proceedings was unlawful. The Court communicated only that complaint; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The key facts concern the applicant’s immigration status, criminal proceedings in Ukraine, and Turkey’s extradition request. In 2004 the applicant arrived in Ukraine and on 23 March 2011 was granted refugee status. On 18 October 2012, however, the State Migration Service revoked that status, finding that he had provided false information: he had claimed political persecution in Turkey while concealing that he was wanted by Turkish law-enforcement authorities on suspicion of a criminal offence. Ukrainian courts upheld the revocation at three levels, with the final decision on 3 April 2013. Meanwhile, on 14 March 2013, the applicant applied for subsidiary protection. On 13 August 2013 that application was rejected as inadmissible because his refugee status had been revoked, but on 27 February 2014 the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court quashed that refusal and ordered the authorities to examine the application on the merits. Subsequent developments were not in the case file.

Separately, on 25 September 2012 the applicant was detained in Ukraine on suspicion of using forged documents. He was later released subject to an undertaking not to abscond, and on 14 March 2013 the Kharkiv Leninsky District Court convicted him and sentenced him to two months’ imprisonment. His appeal outcome is unknown.

The extradition context is central. On 20 June 2011 the Istanbul 13th Higher Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for the applicant on suspicion of participation in terrorist and separatist activities on 5 August 1998. On 3 October 2012 that court sent an extradition request to the Ukrainian judicial authorities, specifying that the charge would become time-barred on 15 August 2013 and assuring respect for Convention rights. On 14 November 2012 the State Security Service detained the applicant with a view to extradition. The next day the migration service confirmed he was not a Ukrainian national. On 16 November 2012 the Mykolaiv Tsentralny District Court ordered his detention pending extradition. On 17 June 2013 the Istanbul court issued a second arrest warrant on the same charge.

After being transferred to Kharkiv in connection with the domestic criminal case, the Kharkiv Zhovtnevy District Court on 17 July 2013 held that continued detention was justified, relying on the two Turkish warrants, the extradition request, and a prosecutor’s extradition inquiry finding no impediments. The court noted the applicant’s conviction but observed it was not final. On 30 August 2013 the Zhovtnevy Court released him because the limitation period for the offence had expired on 15 August 2013 and Article 10 of the European Convention on Extradition barred extradition in such circumstances. On 23 September 2013 the Ministry of Justice rejected Turkey’s extradition request.

Relevant Ukrainian law prohibited extradition of refugees or persons under subsidiary protection (Article 589 § 2 of the 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure) and barred extradition decisions while protection applications remained pending (Article 590 § 4). Detention pending extradition was permitted under Article 584, but for no more than twelve months and subject to judicial review. The applicant’s complaint therefore focused on whether his detention with a view to extradition remained lawful given the lapse of time, the extradition bar, and his protection-related proceedings.
001-204812:
Smbat Ayvazyan v. Armenia (no. 49021/08), an ECtHR judgment dated 8 October 2020, arose from Armenia’s disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election and the ensuing opposition protests. The applicant, a former MP, government minister and opposition party council member, supported Levon Ter-Petrosyan and actively participated in daily rallies and sit-ins at Freedom Square in Yerevan. He stayed overnight at Freedom Square on 23–24 February 2008.

On 24 February 2008, while driving home, the applicant was stopped, taken to the police anti-organised-crime unit, and allegedly searched. Police claimed an anonymous tip had reported armed passengers. A spring baton was allegedly found in his coat, and a Makarov-type pistol was later found in his car. The pistol was subsequently found by an expert to be ineffective and not a firearm. The applicant claimed the baton was planted and that he was coerced into admitting ownership by threats to prosecute his friends instead. He denied any illegal possession.

That evening he was taken for a drug test, which was negative. On returning to Kentron Police Station, three officers alleged that he disobeyed orders, pushed officer K.H., and punched him in the chest. The applicant denied any such incident, saying he merely stated that his arrest was unlawful. Relatives, friends, a lawyer and a journalist had gathered outside expecting his release. A forensic medical examination found no injuries on K.H.

On 25 February 2008, a criminal case was opened under Article 316 §1 of the Criminal Code for non-life-threatening assault on a public official. An arrest record was drawn up at 1:35 a.m. On 27 February the applicant was charged, and the District Court ordered his detention for two months, finding risks that he might reoffend, abscond or obstruct the investigation. The applicant argued that the detention was unsubstantiated and politically motivated.

After the violent clearance of Freedom Square on 1–2 March 2008 and the declaration of a state of emergency, criminal proceedings no. 62202608 were opened concerning mass disorder. On 11 March the applicant’s case was joined to that investigation. On 12 March he was prohibited from contact with the outside world. His detention was extended on 21 April and 20 June 2008, with the courts citing generic risks and the investigation into case no. 62202608. The investigator later admitted that no sufficient evidence implicated the applicant in that case. On 18 June his case was disjoined, and on 26 June he was additionally charged under Article 235 §4 for illegally carrying a cold weapon—the baton. The investigation ended on 7 July and the case went to trial.

At trial, police officers testified against him. The applicant denied guilt and sought to call defence witnesses, including relatives, supporters, a journalist and two detained friends, who could confirm that no incident occurred outside the police station. The court refused, finding their evidence unnecessary or the persons unidentified. He also sought to question police officers S.H. and A.H., but that request was postponed and never revisited. On 19 November 2008 he was convicted of assaulting officer K.H. and illegally carrying the baton, sentenced to two years’ imprisonment and a fine. Appeals were dismissed and the Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible. He was later amnestied.

The case concerned alleged violations of Article 5 §§1, 3 and 4 (unlawful initial detention, insufficient reasons for detention, and refusal to examine his detention appeal), Article 6 §§1 and 3(d) (unfair trial and inability to call and question witnesses), and Articles 10, 11 and 14 (prosecution and conviction allegedly targeting his political activism and participation in peaceful opposition demonstrations, and discrimination on political grounds).
001-201351:
M.A. and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 5115/18, ECtHR, 20 February 2020) concerned five Chinese Uighur Muslims from the Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region (“XUAR”). They alleged that their intended expulsion from Bulgaria to China would expose them to death or ill-treatment, in violation of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. The Court had issued an interim measure under Rule 39 indicating that they should not be removed to China.

The applicants fled China at different times, claiming persecution by Chinese authorities. The second applicant alleged that security agents demanded he collect data on clients; when he refused, charges were brought against him, his mother and sister were arrested, and he fled via Malaysia and Turkey. The third applicant alleged police monitoring of his family, childhood arrests for praying, detention and torture after discussing the 2009 Urumqi riots, later arrest for wearing a beard, and targeting after secretly teaching Uighur. He fled through Southeast Asia and Turkey. The fourth applicant alleged repeated detention and fines for breaching China’s family-planning rules after his children were born, then fled with his wife through Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand and Turkey. The first and fifth applicants similarly claimed persecution in the XUAR and arrived in Turkey.

In 2017, believing Turkey had agreed to deport Uighurs to China amid improving Turkey-China relations, the applicants left Turkey and entered Bulgaria unlawfully on 26 July 2017. Bulgarian border police apprehended them and issued repatriation orders. They were placed in an alien detention centre. On 1 December 2017 they applied for asylum. The State Refugees Agency rejected their applications on 18 December 2017, and the Haskovo Administrative Court upheld those decisions on 29 January 2018. It found that they had not shown individual persecution, accepted that Chinese counterterrorism measures in Xinjiang were justified, and said their past problems were not proven to be based on ethnicity or religion. It also found no indication that Turkey intended to repatriate Uighurs.

In parallel, in January 2018 the State Agency for National Security ordered their expulsion on national security grounds. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed judicial reviews for the second, third and fourth applicants in May 2019. It relied on confidential information alleging that after leaving China they had stayed in Syria, received training from the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (“ETIM”), a terrorist organisation, and had contacts with ETIM, Islamic State-linked persons, and human traffickers. It concluded that they could threaten Bulgaria’s national security. It further stated that any risk they would face on return to China concerned the implementation, not the lawfulness, of the expulsion.

International bodies and NGOs, including Amnesty International, the World Uighur Congress and members of the European Parliament, urged Bulgaria not to return the applicants to China. They cited documented cases of Uighurs forcibly returned to China who were detained, tortured, or sentenced to death. Country information described mass detentions, re-education camps, torture, severe restrictions on Uighurs in Xinjiang, and particular suspicion of Uighurs with foreign ties. The applicants’ central complaint was therefore that expulsion to China would expose them to a real risk of arbitrary detention, ill-treatment or death.
001-204194:
**Summary of Ivashchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 41303/11)**

The case of *Ivashchenko v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Valeriy Volodymyrovych Ivashchenko, a Ukrainian national, on 27 June 2011. The applicant, a former Deputy and acting Minister of Defence of Ukraine, complained under Article 3 of the Convention that he had not received adequate medical treatment while in detention and was confined in a metal cage during court hearings. He further complained under Article 5 that his pre-trial detention was unlawful, lengthy, and lacked justification, and that no effective procedure existed to challenge its lawfulness.

The relevant facts began in August 2010. Following an operational inquiry by the Security Service of Ukraine into alleged unlawful activity at a State-owned enterprise managed by the Ministry of Defence, the General Prosecutor’s Office instituted criminal proceedings against the applicant on 20 August 2010. He was suspected of abuse of power for signing a financial rehabilitation plan that allegedly caused State property losses. On 21 August 2010, after appearing before an investigator, he was arrested on grounds that eyewitnesses had identified him and to prevent him from evading investigation or obstructing the truth.

On 24 August 2010, the Pechersk District Court of Kyiv ordered his pre-trial detention, citing risks of absconding and hindering the investigation, without further detail. This order was upheld on appeal, and subsequently extended multiple times on the same grounds. On 4 March 2011, the District Court decided he would remain in detention for an unspecified period without providing particular reasons. During trial, on 1 and 19 August 2011, the applicant requested removal from the metal cage used during hearings; the court refused, stating it was in accordance with domestic legislation and not for the court to decide.

Regarding medical treatment, the applicant had suffered since 1995 from chronic conditions including spinal osteochondritis, arthritis, and cerebral atherosclerosis, requiring inpatient treatment at least twice yearly. After his placement in the Kyiv Pre-trial Detention Centre (SIZO) on 25 August 2010, his health deteriorated. He was diagnosed with additional conditions in May 2011. Various medical examinations from June 2011 to January 2012 consistently noted his chronic diseases had worsened. Medical professionals, including the head of the Main Military Clinical Hospital (MMCH) and chief doctors, repeatedly stated that adequate treatment could not be provided at the SIZO, that he required inpatient neurological care and physiotherapy unavailable there, and that without timely treatment, his condition, including spinal dysfunction and muscle atrophy, could further deteriorate, potentially risking paralysis. Despite these recommendations and a court statement of no objection to his inpatient treatment at the MMCH, transportation was refused by the prison escort service in January 2012. Treatment recommendations were only partially implemented. The applicant was found guilty by the District Court on 12 April 2012 and sentenced to five years, but was released on 14 August 2012 after the Court of Appeal imposed a suspended sentence.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 due to inadequate medical care and the cage confinement, and of Article 5 due to unjustified, lengthy detention and lack of effective review.
001-205166:
In **Pasquini v. San Marino (No. 2)** (Application no. 23349/17), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention concerning the presumption of innocence. The applicant, Enrico Maria Pasquini, an Italian national living in San Marino, was at the relevant time chairman and sole shareholder of S.M.I., a fiduciary company operating in San Marino.

Following a Central Bank inspection of S.M.I.’s headquarters, a report was submitted to the investigating judge alleging suspicious financial operations by the applicant and another person, B., the company’s director. Criminal proceedings were instituted. The applicant was charged with exercising fiduciary activity without a licence, three counts of obstruction of surveillance, misreporting to shareholders and supervisory boards, and continuing aggravated embezzlement. The prosecution alleged that between April 2009 and March 2010 the applicant had personally withdrawn EUR 2,633,055.77 from a fiduciary account opened by company S. and administered by S.M.I. It claimed he was the beneficial owner of company S. and had used fictitious invoices for non-existent services provided by foreign companies, thereby embezzling funds to the detriment of S.M.I. Company S.M.I., then in compulsory liquidation, joined the criminal proceedings as a civil party.

On 8 April 2014 the first-instance judge convicted the applicant and B. of all charges. The applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and a fine, and was ordered to compensate S.M.I. in an amount to be quantified in separate civil proceedings. An interim compensation order of EUR 2,633,055.77 was made in favour of the civil party. The judge found a complex system of foreign broker companies, simulated brokerage operations, tax-haven entities, and bank accounts formally registered to brokers but actually traceable to the applicant and B.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the limitation period for embezzlement had expired. On 1 December 2015 the Judge of Criminal Appeals acknowledged the limitation issue but referred a constitutional question concerning Article 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, because it allegedly prevented the appeal judge from deciding civil claims once an offence was time-barred. Law No. 189 of 2015 subsequently introduced Article 196 bis, allowing the appeal judge, when declaring an offence time-barred, to decide civil obligations arising from it. The Constitutional Court returned the file for reconsideration.

By judgment of 19 September 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted the applicant and B. of exercising fiduciary activity without a licence; acquitted the applicant of one obstruction count; and declared the remaining obstruction counts, misreporting, and aggravated embezzlement time-barred, discontinuing those charges. It upheld the compensation order. The appeal judge stated that the first-instance reasoning had not indicated that the alleged facts never occurred or that the accused had not committed them, so there was no room for any finding other than discontinuance. Nevertheless, he examined the evidence underlying the aggravated embezzlement conviction exclusively to decide civil compensation.

The applicant complained to the Court that his presumption of innocence had been violated: although there had been no finding of guilt, the appeal judgment reflected the judge’s conviction that he was guilty, and he was ordered to pay damages precisely on the basis of a declaration of criminal responsibility not ascertained in the criminal proceedings. On 4 September 2017, notice of the Article 6 § 2 complaint was given to the Government; the remainder was declared inadmissible. The Italian Government did not intervene.
001-201531:
Application no. 53044/13 originated in an application against Montenegro lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention on 12 July 2013. The applicant was Draga Piletić, born on 4 January 1928. She was represented by Ana Đukanović, a lawyer practising in Podgorica. The Montenegrin Government were given notice of the application. Draga Piletić died on 22 December 2015. The application was thereafter pursued by her heirs, Nina Đikanović, born on 4 December 1959, and Jelka Tomašević, born on 2 June 1954.

The applicant complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings. The appended factual table identifies the relevant starting date for the domestic civil proceedings as 3 March 2004. That date is described in the table as either the start of the proceedings or the date of entry into force of the Convention in respect of Montenegro. The domestic proceedings ended on 18 October 2011. The total length of the proceedings was recorded as 7 years, 7 months and 15 days. The proceedings took place before three levels of jurisdiction. The relevant domestic decision is identified as a decision of the Supreme Court of Montenegro, Rev.U.no. 18/10/2011.

Beyond those entries, the supplied record does not describe the subject matter of the civil dispute, the parties to the domestic civil case, the claims or relief sought, the procedural steps taken before the domestic courts, or the content of the domestic decision. It also does not set out any arguments made by the applicant or the Government before the European Court of Human Rights on the substance of the complaint, except that the applicant alleged that the civil proceedings had been excessively long and that the Government had been given notice of the application.

001-206345:
In *D. v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 25397/09, judgment 8 December 2020), the applicant, a Moldovan woman born in 1990, complained of unlawful arrest and ill-treatment by police during mass arrests following Moldova’s 5 April 2009 parliamentary elections. The election results triggered protests in Chișinău over alleged electoral fraud. On 7 April 2009, protests turned violent, and after 1 a.m. on 8 April police and special forces launched a massive operation to restore order. A later parliamentary inquiry found that excessive force was used and that all people still present in the main square were arrested regardless of whether they had been violent.

On the evening of 7 April 2009, the applicant went with her roommate R. to the Great National Assembly Square, where they met her relative V. Boboc. She claimed they were part of a group of about fifty young people standing peacefully and discussing the day’s events. Around 1 a.m. on 8 April, their group was surrounded by police, masked special forces, and plain-clothed officers armed with automatic rifles and rubber sticks. The young people were ordered to lie down and were kicked and severely beaten with rubber sticks and rifles. The applicant’s head was hit against the pavement, and she received several blows. While being taken to a police car, she and R. saw police kicking Boboc, who was unconscious and no longer reacting. He died several days later.

At Buiucani police station, approximately twenty young men and three young women, including the applicant and R., were allegedly ordered to stand with their hands against the wall and were beaten whenever they tried to speak or move. The young men were taken one by one into an office and ordered to lower their trousers; sounds of beating and screams followed. The men returned with clear signs of ill-treatment, and one was released completely naked. The three women were insulted and shouted at but not physically assaulted. No explanation was given for the arrest. Around 5 a.m. on 8 April 2009, the women were released and advised to leave the city. The applicant alleged unlawful detention for over five hours without being informed of the reasons, without access to relatives, and without prompt judicial review.

On 13 April 2009, she gave a concealed-identity television interview. Authorities later sought to uncover her identity. On 14 April, a doctor found a 16 by 15 centimetre injury to her right foot; fearing for her life, she falsely attributed it to an unknown street attacker. On 4 May 2009, she complained to the Prosecutor General about ill-treatment and unlawful detention. Medical examinations at the Memoria Rehabilitation Centre between 4 and 15 May 2009 documented headaches, vertigo, insomnia, nightmares, heartache, anxiety, flashbacks, post-traumatic stress disorder, and consequences of cranial trauma.

On 1 June 2009, she was interviewed by an investigating judge and a prosecutor. Witness protection was refused, with authorities saying concealed identity was sufficient. On 22 July 2009, the military prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation into her allegations. It was joined to a broader investigation into police beatings, but was suspended on 15 January 2013 because, despite questioning about 200 special forces members and reviewing videos, investigators could not identify which officer used force against which victim or whether force was necessary. Separately, officer G. was convicted of negligence for failing to act while at Buiucani station when young people, including the applicant and R., were ill-treated; the Supreme Court upheld that conviction in 2016. In November 2012, the Government paid the applicant MDL 7,000 (about €447) under a compensation scheme. The parliamentary commission found that arrests continued until 12 April 2009. These facts underpinned her complaints under Articles 3 and 5 of the Convention and the alleged lack of an effective investigation.
001-206342:
**Summary of *Stafeyev v. Russia* (Application no. 32984/06)**

**Background and Investigation**
The case concerns the applicant, Mr. Vyacheslav Vladimirovich Stafeyev, a Russian national born in 1978. On 19 February 2001, the bodies of the Sh. family (a man, his wife, and their thirteen-year-old son) were discovered in their flat, having apparently been killed the previous day. In November 2004, while detained for another crime, the applicant's fingerprints were entered into a police database. On 8 December 2004, investigating officers were informed that fingerprints found in the victims' flat matched the applicant's. A subsequent search of the applicant's home uncovered items stolen from the victims' flat.

Police officers visited the applicant in detention on 8, 9, and 10 December 2004, questioning him informally. The applicant alleged that he confessed on 10 December 2004 under duress; the Government maintained he spontaneously confessed on 8 December 2004. On 10 December 2004, the applicant was informed of his rights, waived his right to a lawyer, and reiterated his confession during an interview. He confessed again on 16 December 2004, again without a lawyer. On 20 January 2005, assisted by counsel, he retracted his confession.

**Trial Proceedings**
The Sverdlovsk Regional Court conducted the trial. On 15 September 2005, it excluded the applicant's statements of 10 and 16 December 2004 as inadmissible because they were made without a lawyer and later retracted. However, the court admitted the 8 December 2004 confession. The applicant denied guilt, claiming he had visited the family on 16 February 2001 (not 18 February) and that his confession was coerced.

On 14 December 2005, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of three counts of murder, robbery, and destruction of property, sentencing him to life imprisonment. The judgment relied on fingerprint evidence, the search results, police testimony that the applicant voluntarily confessed after being informed of the fingerprint match, and the 8 December 2004 confession.

**Appeal Proceedings and Alleged Violations**
The applicant's trial lawyer appealed on 14 November 2005, raising numerous factual and legal issues. The appeal hearing was scheduled for 15 May 2006. However, the lawyer failed to appear. The applicant, participating via video link, requested new counsel. The Supreme Court assigned lawyer R. and adjourned to 29 May 2006.

On 23 May 2006, R. visited the applicant, but detention facility authorities allegedly limited their meeting to fifteen minutes, with guards repeatedly interrupting. On 25 May 2006, the applicant requested additional time with R. via a letter to the Supreme Court, but the request apparently arrived after the hearing.

On 29 May 2006, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction. R. was present, and the applicant participated via video link. The applicant alleged poor video quality and that the court refused to admit his 25 May request. The Government claimed the applicant complained about video quality on 30–31 May 2006, but a 2013 certificate stated no transmission failures were recorded.

**The Complaint**
The European Court of Human Rights granted notice solely on complaints regarding the lack of effective legal assistance on appeal and the poor quality of the video link before the Supreme Court. The core alleged violation centers on whether the applicant had adequate time and facilities to consult his assigned appellate lawyer, R., given the fifteen-minute meeting constraint, and whether procedural fairness was compromised during the appeal hearing.
001-205140:
Talalikhina v. Ukraine (Application no. 13919/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case, Fifth Section, judgment of 22 October 2020, concerning the lawfulness and length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention, the length of the criminal proceedings against her, and the lack of effective remedies in that regard.

The applicant, Olga Vasilyevna Talalikhina, a Ukrainian national born in 1954 living in Sevastopol, was initially involved in criminal proceedings instituted on 5 September 2007 on charges of theft. She was questioned as a suspect and signed an undertaking not to abscond. On 30 October 2007 the theft case was referred to court for trial. While those proceedings were pending, on 13 April 2009, the applicant was involved in a drunken brawl with her cohabitant at home. She allegedly hit the man with a hammer. He was taken to hospital and died a few days later. On 17 April 2009 the applicant was arrested and questioned in relation to that incident.

On 20 April 2009 the Leninskyy District Court of Sevastopol ordered her pre-trial detention. On 15 June 2009 the Sevastopol City Prosecutor approved a bill of indictment charging her with aggravated infliction of serious bodily harm resulting in the victim’s death and referred the case to the District Court. The applicant remained in custody. On 6 July 2009 the Nakhimovskiy District Court of Sevastopol committed her for trial and ruled that the preventive measure should remain in place.

Her detention continued for over three years. On 5 August 2011 and 10 May 2012 the District Court dismissed her applications for release as unfounded, considering that there were no grounds to change the preventive measure. Only on 20 June 2012 did the District Court change the custodial preventive measure, accepting her relatives as guarantors, and the applicant was released. In the meantime, on 19 September 2012, the prosecutor dropped the theft charge against her for lack of constituent elements of the crime. On 6 February 2013 the District Court convicted her of unintentional homicide of her cohabitant and sentenced her to two years’ imprisonment.

The relevant legal framework included Article 156 of the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, then in force, which provided that detention during the pre-trial investigation should not exceed two months. A judge was, however, empowered to extend pre-trial detention following a request to that effect. The applicant’s complaints therefore focused on whether her detention from April 2009 to June 2012 was lawful and justified, whether the criminal proceedings—especially the homicide case, but also the earlier theft case—were excessively long, and whether Ukrainian law provided effective domestic remedies for those alleged violations. The Court gave notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government on 2 May 2019 and adopted its judgment on 22 October 2020.

001-206360:
In *Chernov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 16432/10), the applicant, Mr Oleksandr Gennadiyovych Chernov, a Ukrainian national born in 1965 and living in Sumy, complained under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention that he had been tried and punished twice for the same offence. The case concerned events on 20 June 2007, when, at about 10 p.m., the applicant was drunk outdoors on Prokofyeva Street in Sumy. He uttered obscenities, reacted aggressively to remarks by police officers, cursed them, attempted to start a fight, and thereby breached public order and offended human dignity and morals.

On 21 June 2007 the Zarichnyy District Court of Sumy found the applicant guilty of “minor disorderly acts” under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced him to three days’ administrative detention. That decision became final and could not be appealed. The applicant served the sentence from 21 to 23 June 2007.

On 28 January 2008, however, the prosecutor lodged an objection against the administrative decision. The prosecutor argued that the same facts gave rise to criminal liability under Article 296 of the Criminal Code, because Article 9 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that administrative liability applied only where the underlying facts did not lead to criminal liability. On 6 February 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court annulled its earlier decision, and on 25 February 2008 the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal upheld that annulment.

In parallel, criminal proceedings had been initiated. On 16 July 2007 a prosecutor opened a criminal case against the applicant under Article 296 of the Criminal Code concerning the same events of 20 June 2007, alleging disorderly acts and physical injuries to two victims, Mu. and P. Forensic examinations in June and September 2007 found minor physical injuries that may have been inflicted on 20 June 2007. The applicant was placed on a wanted list on 4 August 2007, arrested on 23 December 2007, and indicted on 29 January 2008 under Article 296 § 3.

On 14 July 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court convicted the applicant under Article 296 § 3 and sentenced him to two years’ imprisonment. The court did not mention the earlier administrative proceedings or the three-day detention. On 7 October 2008 the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction because of inconsistencies—particularly as to the time of the offence—and because the sentence was too lenient, and remitted the case for fresh examination. Judge Ma., who had decided the administrative case, withdrew from the criminal case on 29 October 2008, noting that she had annulled the administrative decision after criminal elements became apparent.

On 29 December 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court again convicted the applicant. It found that on 20 June 2007 he had pulled Mu.’s gold neck chain, damaged it, beaten Mu., and later damaged P.’s t-shirt, punched her in the face, caused minor injuries, and damaged her glasses. He was sentenced to two years and one month’s imprisonment. On 10 March 2009 the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years. On 24 September 2009 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that decision. It rejected the applicant’s double-jeopardy complaint, reasoning that the administrative decision had been annulled and the administrative case closed, so he had not been tried twice.

The applicant’s central complaint was therefore that, despite serving an administrative detention for the same conduct, he was later criminally convicted and punished for the same facts. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the complaint under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The applicant, Ms Lina Alekseyevna Filozofenko, is a Ukrainian national born in 1938 who lives in the Odessa Region. She holds the special status of a “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act in force as of 1 January 2006 (“the 2006 Act”). A “child of war” is defined there as a person who on 2 September 1945 was no more than 18 years of age. Under section 6 of the 2006 Act, the applicant was entitled to a special supplement to her pension amounting to 30% of the minimum pension. She complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the State’s failure to pay that supplement. The application (no. 72954/11) against Ukraine was lodged on 18 November 2011.

On 11 December 2008 the applicant lodged a claim with the domestic courts against the State Pension Fund. She asked the courts to recalculate her pension in accordance with section 6 of the 2006 Act for 2006–2008 and to pay her the outstanding debt.

On 10 June 2009 the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court partly allowed the claim. It found that, in 2006, section 6 of the 2006 Act had been suspended by the State Budget Act 2006. Amendments to the latter Act, which entered into force on 1 April 2006, had empowered the Cabinet of Ministers to set up a mechanism for a pension increase. However, no such mechanism had been set up in 2006, so the applicant’s claims relating to 2006 were rejected. As to 2007 and 2008, the court noted that section 6 had been suspended and modified, respectively, by the 2007 and 2008 State Budget Acts. On 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008, however, the Constitutional Court had found that suspension and modification unconstitutional. The court therefore held that the State Pension Fund should recalculate the applicant’s pension only for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008.

On 1 November 2010 the Odessa Regional Administrative Court of Appeal partly amended that judgment. It upheld the lower court’s findings as regards the applicant’s 2006 claims. It also upheld her right to a pension increase for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008. However, it held that because she had missed a one-year statutory period for lodging a claim, the 2007 claim could be allowed only for the period from 11 to 31 December 2007. On 18 May 2011 the Higher Administrative Court upheld the appellate judgment.
001-202524:
**Summary**

The case of Makuchyan and Minasyan v. Azerbaijan and Hungary (Application no. 17247/13) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by two Armenian nationals: Mr Hayk Makuchyan, a member of the Armenian military, and Mr Samvel Minasyan, uncle of the deceased G.M., a lieutenant in the Armenian army. The case concerned the brutal murder of G.M. and the attempted murder of the first applicant by an Azerbaijani military officer, R.S., and the subsequent pardon and glorification of the perpetrator.

In January 2004, the first applicant and G.M. arrived in Budapest, Hungary, to participate in a three-month English language course under NATO's "Partnership for Peace" programme. Participants included two officers from the Azerbaijani army, one of whom was R.S. On 19 February 2004, at around 5 a.m., R.S. murdered G.M. while he slept by decapitating him with at least twelve blows of an axe. R.S. then attempted to break down the first applicant's door, allegedly yelling "Open the door, you Armenian! We will cut the throats of all of you!" He was stopped by police.

During questioning, R.S. admitted he strongly disliked Armenians due to losing relatives in the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and that he had decided to kill the Armenian participants on the anniversary of the conflict's beginning. He bought an axe and sharpening stone two days prior. He admitted murdering G.M. on account of his Armenian origin and showed no remorse.

On 13 April 2006, the Budapest High Court found R.S. guilty of exceptionally cruel and premeditated murder of G.M. and preparation of the murder of the first applicant. The court concluded the crimes were committed with vile motives and exclusively because of the Armenian nationality of the victims. R.S. was sentenced to life imprisonment with possibility of conditional release after thirty years. This was upheld on appeal in February 2007.

In 2012, Azerbaijan requested R.S.'s transfer under the Council of Europe Convention on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons. Azerbaijan's Ministry of Justice assured Hungary that enforcement would continue without conversion of the sentence and that a life sentence could only be released on parole after at least twenty-five years. On 17 August 2012, Hungary agreed to the transfer. On 31 August 2012, R.S. was transferred to Azerbaijan and immediately released on a presidential pardon issued the same day.

Following his release, R.S. was promoted to major, provided with a state-owned flat, and awarded salary arrears. Numerous Azerbaijani officials and public figures made statements glorifying R.S. and his actions, with some describing him as a patriotic role model for Azerbaijani youth.

The applicants alleged that Azerbaijan violated Article 2 of the Convention by granting the presidential pardon, and Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 2 because the Armenian ethnic origin of the victims was the main reason for the murder and subsequent actions, including the pardon and glorification of the perpetrator. They also complained that Hungary violated Article 2 by granting the transfer request without obtaining adequate binding assurances that R.S. would be required to complete his prison sentence in Azerbaijan.

**Dykusarenko v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 7218/19 and 17854/19) is a European Court of Human Rights case against Ukraine. The applicant, Oleksiy Mykolayovych Dykusarenko, born 9 February 1985, was represented by Mr S.M. Rybiy, a lawyer practising in Dnipro. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 21 January 2019 and 11 March 2019 respectively. The Ukrainian Government were given notice. A Fifth Section Committee, composed of Judges Kucsko-Stadlmayer, Mits and Hüseynov, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 19 March 2020 and adopted its judgment on 9 April 2020.

The key facts concern the applicant’s detention in Dnipro detention facility no. 4. According to the appended table, he was held there from 27 October 2014 to 6 July 2019, a total period of 4 years, 8 months and 10 days. The available living space was reported as 3.65 to 3.95 square metres per inmate. The applicant alleged that the conditions of this detention were inadequate.

The specific grievances recorded for the detention period include: lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; lack of toiletries; lack or insufficient quantity of food; lack of or insufficient electric light; no or restricted access to a shower; lack of privacy for using the toilet; poor quality of potable water; and a mouldy or dirty cell. These conditions form the factual basis of his complaints.

As to the alleged violations, in application no. 17854/19 the applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that the conditions of his detention were inadequate, amounting to inhuman or degrading treatment. He also complained under Article 13 that there was no effective remedy in domestic law in respect of those conditions. In application no. 7218/19 he also raised complaints under Article 5 §§ 3 and 5 and Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Article 5 §§ 3 and 5 concern the right to liberty and security, particularly the right to be brought promptly before a judge and the right to compensation for unlawful detention, while Article 6 § 1 concerns the right to a fair trial. The appended table records the same detention facility, period, space per inmate and specific grievances for both applications, indicating that the conditions of detention were central to both applications.

The case therefore centres on the applicant’s lengthy detention in Dnipro detention facility no. 4, the very limited personal space, and the multiple alleged deficiencies in material conditions—bedding, hygiene, food, lighting, shower access, toilet privacy, water quality and cell cleanliness. These facts underpinned his claims that Ukraine violated Article 3 and Article 13, and, in application no. 7218/19, also Article 5 §§ 3 and 5 and Article 6 § 1. The provided excerpt sets out the procedure and factual allegations but does not include the Court’s full merits analysis or final conclusions on the violations.
001-203559:
**Case: Romanov v. Ukraine (Application no. 63782/11)**

The applicant, Ilya Romanov, a Russian national, was a communist revolutionary involved with a group that printed and distributed newspapers in Ukraine during anti-Kuchma protests. The publications, including *Soviet of Workers’ Deputies* and *Rada of Workers’ Deputies*, contained articles calling for armed revolt, civil war, overthrow of the constitutional order, and Soviet rule. In October 2002, an explosive device was detonated near the SBU headquarters in Kyiv.

In December 2002, Romanov was arrested in Kakhovka after police reportedly found a gun, bullets, a homemade explosive device, and a detonator. He alleged unrecorded detention and said he requested a lawyer, Chet. On 21 December 2002, at SBU premises in Mykolayiv, he made a handwritten “explanation” confessing to the SBU explosion, manufacturing explosives, and distributing the newspapers. He claimed the investigator dictated the statement after psychological ill-treatment. He later confirmed confessions during a crime reconstruction with lawyer Sk., but alleged Sk. was investigator-chosen, not effective, and that his self-incriminating statements were coerced and obtained in breach of defence rights. A co-defendant, Sm., also confessed and implicated him.

Charges were changed in May 2003 to include dissemination of material calling for violent overthrow of the constitutional order, banditry, terrorism, illegal drug production/possession, and unlawful possession of firearms and explosives. In July 2004, the Odessa Regional Court convicted Romanov of terrorism, dissemination, banditry, and weapons offences; he was acquitted of drug offences and sentenced to ten years. In July 2005, the Supreme Court quashed the banditry conviction but upheld the rest.

Romanov complained that his trial was unfair: he lacked adequate time and facilities to prepare his defence, was denied chosen counsel during key investigative steps, was represented ineffectively, could not participate effectively, and was convicted for his political beliefs. He also alleged a lack of effective remedies for these complaints.

As to detention, he was held in Odessa SIZO from March 2003 to November 2005. He alleged overcrowding, a cold cell with an unglazed window, sleeping on the floor, poor sanitation, lack of hot water and bedding, and a flooded disciplinary cell. The Government denied this, describing ordinary cells with toilet, heating, light, weekly showers, and daily walks. Romanov also alleged superficial medical care and untreated spine problems later recognised as a disability. During court transfers, he claimed early-morning departures, long waits in unheated windowless assembly cells, missed meals, and exhaustion preventing proper preparation. The Government described shorter hearings and arranged meals.

In 2006, his transfer from Yenakieve to Polytska Prison took nearly two months via several SIZOs. He alleged overcrowded, unventilated train compartments, no food, water, or sanitary access for long periods, poor transit cells, beatings, disrespect, and correspondence problems. The Government said relevant travel documents were destroyed but claimed conditions were adequate.

The Court gave notice of complaints concerning Odessa SIZO conditions and transfer to Polytska; adequate defence facilities; effective participation and legal representation; conviction for political beliefs; and lack of effective remedies. These implicated Articles 3, 6, 9/10/11, and 13 of the Convention.
001-202529:
In *Avto Atom Doo Kochani v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 21954/16), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 28 May 2020. The applicant, Avto Atom Doo Kochani, was a limited-liability passenger transport company registered in Kochani, North Macedonia. It was registered for VAT and regularly declared VAT on outgoing invoices. It also declared VAT on incoming invoices, allowing it to deduct input VAT from its periodic VAT obligations.

The dispute arose from the applicant’s VAT deductions for 2004 and 2005. One of its suppliers, a petrol station, issued invoices that showed a tax number and expressly charged VAT. The applicant paid those invoices in full and claimed the corresponding input VAT deductions. In March–April 2007, the Internal Revenue Office audited the applicant’s VAT obligations for 2004–2005. The audit found that the petrol station supplier had not been registered for VAT. On 2 May 2007, relying on that finding, the IRO issued a payment order imposing additional VAT of MKD 3,266,792. The IRO considered that the VAT deducted on the basis of the supplier’s invoices had been unlawful.

The applicant contested the payment order but paid the amount in several instalments during 2007 and 2008. Its administrative claim was ultimately dismissed by the Administrative Court on 28 January 2015, after two remittals. The Administrative Court held that the applicant was not entitled to the deduction because the supplier had not been VAT-registered, and it treated as irrelevant the fact that VAT had been declared on the supplier’s invoices. The Higher Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 20 October 2015, endorsing the same reasoning.

Additional facts were relevant. The supplier had been founded on 19 August 2003 and was struck off the companies list on 30 June 2006. Its founder and sole owner was convicted on 25 December 2009 of failing to register for VAT (tax evasion) and received a suspended prison sentence. He paid a tax debt of MKD 595,470 (about EUR 9,650). The supplier itself was not prosecuted because it had been liquidated.

Under the applicable domestic VAT Act, sections 33 and 34 governed deductions, and section 55 provided that an entity which declared VAT on an invoice despite not being registered for VAT owed the declared amount. The Court had previously summarised the relevant law in *Euromak Metal Doo v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (no. 68039/14, 14 June 2018).

The applicant company complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property). It alleged that the State’s additional VAT demand and the domestic courts’ refusal to allow the input VAT deduction amounted to an unjustified interference with its possessions. The key factual issue was that the applicant had relied on invoices that appeared VAT-compliant, had paid the supplier in full, and had otherwise complied with its VAT obligations, yet was required to bear the VAT burden after the supplier was found to be unregistered. On 21 February 2018, the Court gave notice of the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected. The case thus focused on whether the refusal of the VAT deduction imposed a disproportionate burden on the applicant.
001-203645:
In *N.H. and Others v. France* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, judgment of 2 July 2020), five single adult asylum-seekers in France alleged that the authorities failed to provide the in-kind and financial support required by national law, forcing them to sleep rough in inhuman and degrading conditions for months. They relied on Article 3 of the Convention. Two applicants also complained under Article 13 read with Article 3, and N.H. additionally invoked Article 8, alone and with Article 13.

N.H., an Afghan national, arrived in France in March 2013. He obtained a mailing address and tried to lodge an asylum claim on 4 April 2013, but was given an appointment for 9 July 2013 because of administrative delays. His urgent application for interim relief was rejected; the Conseil d’État found that a three-month wait did not amount to a serious and manifestly unlawful interference with the right of asylum. At the July appointment, a Dublin II procedure began because his fingerprints had been registered in Denmark under another identity. His claim was eventually registered, but in October 2013 the prefect refused him permission to stay, treating the asylum claim as abusive. Until then he had no material support, lived rough near the Canal Saint-Martin, had only occasional emergency accommodation, limited meals and showers, and no State medical aid until late October. OFPRA later granted him subsidiary protection.

S.G., K.T. and G.I. arrived in France in 2013 and claimed asylum in the Languedoc-Roussillon region. They were offered Asylum Reception Centre accommodation subject to availability and accepted it because doing so was necessary to qualify for the Temporary Waiting Allowance. OFII then told them no places were available and placed them on the National Reception Scheme waiting list, advising them to call the 115 emergency accommodation helpline. Because emergency facilities were at capacity, they lived in tents on the banks of the Aude river. S.G. also suffered from leg injuries and chronic hepatitis C. Their urgent applications for accommodation were rejected in October 2013 on the grounds that facilities were full, priority had to be given to families and vulnerable persons, and the State’s conduct did not amount to a serious and manifestly unlawful interference with the right of asylum. Legal aid for appeals to the Conseil d’État was refused or considered futile. G.I. later withdrew his asylum claim and sought voluntary return.

A.J., an Iranian journalist, arrived in France in September 2014. On 23 October 2014 he tried to lodge an asylum claim, but it was not registered; he received an appointment for 7 January 2015. Without asylum-seeker status, he could not obtain material support. The prefect said the national reception scheme was full and told him to call 115. He spent only a few nights in an overcrowded emergency centre. His urgent applications were dismissed by the Paris Administrative Court and the Conseil d’État. On 22 January 2015 he finally received a provisional stay, an asylum form and an accommodation offer. Pôle emploi refused the Temporary Waiting Allowance until OFPRA registered his claim in February 2015; he was later housed and recognised as a refugee.

The legal context was that French law at the time required asylum-seekers to obtain permission to stay before lodging an asylum claim, and access to reception support depended on status. Reception Directive 2003/9/EC required minimum material reception conditions throughout the asylum process. The applicants alleged that delays in obtaining appointments, registration and status created gaps in which they were left without lawful status, accommodation or financial aid, and were forced to live rough. The Government disputed some facts, arguing that notices allowed them to remain, that emergency accommodation was available through 115, and that some applicants did not make sufficient use of it or voluntarily left facilities.
001-203294:
**Dmytrenko and Bezdorozhniy v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 59552/11 and 7096/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning Ukraine’s alleged failure to pay a pension supplement to two Ukrainian nationals. The applicants, Mykola Dmytrenko and Mykhaylo Bezdorozhniy, both held the special status of “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act in force as of 1 January 2006. Under Article 6 of that Act, they were entitled to a special pension supplement amounting to 30% of the minimum pension.

The first applicant, born in 1943, lives in Donetsk. The second applicant, born in 1936, died in 2015. His son and heir later informed the Court of his death and expressed a wish to pursue the application. The applications were lodged with the Court on 12 September 2011 and 29 January 2012.

The applicants brought domestic court proceedings against the Pension Fund of Ukraine, claiming the pension supplement for the period between 2 April and 31 December 2006. Their claims were rejected by final decisions in 2011. The Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine, on 13 May 2011, and the Donetsk Administrative Court of Appeal, on 18 August 2011, found that amendments to the State Budget Act 2006 had, with effect from 2 April 2006, required the supplement to be introduced gradually during 2006 according to a procedure to be established by the Cabinet of Ministers. Because no such procedure had been adopted in 2006, the domestic courts concluded that there was no legal basis for allowing the claims.

Separately, the second applicant had obtained a judgment from the Kuybyshevskyy District Court of Donetsk on 31 December 2010. That court ordered the Pension Fund to calculate and pay him the pension supplement for the periods between 9 July and 31 December 2007 and between 22 May 2008 and 31 December 2010. The judgment became final on 18 August 2011 but remained unenforced.

Before the European Court, the Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna. The Court decided to give notice to the Ukrainian Government only of the applicants’ complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the State’s failure to pay the pension supplement for the period between 2 April and 31 December 2006. The remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

The core alleged violation is therefore that, despite the applicants’ statutory entitlement as “children of war” to a 30% pension supplement, they did not receive that supplement for the relevant 2006 period because the domestic authorities had not adopted the required implementing procedure, and the domestic courts refused their claims. This, the applicants argued, amounted to an unjustified interference with their possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case was heard by the Fifth Section Committee, composed of Judges Mits, Yudkivska and Hüseynov, with Anne-Marie Dougin as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. Judgment was delivered on 2 July 2020. The relevant domestic law and practice were summarized by reference to *Sukhanov and Ilchenko v. Ukraine*.
001-204660:
In *Minyaylo and Others v. Ukraine*, three Ukrainian nationals complained to the European Court of Human Rights that police had ill-treated them and that domestic authorities had failed to investigate their complaints effectively. They also raised other complaints under Articles 5 §§ 1 and 5 and 6 § 1 of the Convention.

**Mr Minyaylo** alleged ill-treatment between 13 and 15 February 2005 at Mukacheve and Lviv railway police stations. He claimed officers hit him on the head and torso with water-filled plastic bottles, punched and kicked him, made him lie undressed on the floor, handcuffed his left foot to his right hand, and twisted his arms behind his back to force him to confess to stealing from train passengers. At Lviv, he was allegedly handcuffed to a radiator for hours without food or drink. Medical evidence included ambulance reports for hypertensive crises, a detention-facility certificate recording no injuries on arrival, and a later SIZO certificate noting abrasions on his left calf, right knee, and chin. A forensic report described the injuries as minor but could not establish their timing. He had been arrested on 12 February 2005 on suspicion of robbery, questioned without a lawyer, transferred to Lviv SIZO on 15 February, and gave self-incriminating statements before being remanded. He complained on 18 February 2005. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings; several decisions were quashed, and the courts ultimately found his ill-treatment complaint without merit. The authorities concluded he had not been ill-treated and that any minor injuries could have occurred during arrest.

**Mr Kindra** alleged that on 23 August 2008 plain-clothes police officers asked him into their car, handcuffed him, and took him to Krasnoarmiysk city police station. There, officers allegedly demanded that he confess to arson together with his son, repeatedly punched and kicked him for over an hour—including in his son’s presence—and denied him access to a lawyer. He was released after his son confessed. Hospital records the next day showed a displaced left cheekbone fracture, hematomas around the left eye, and haemorrhage; he underwent surgery and inpatient treatment until 15 September 2008. A forensic report classified the injuries as intermediately serious, with timing possibly consistent with his account. He complained on 24 August 2008. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open proceedings, but those decisions were quashed. Criminal proceedings began in January 2011 and were suspended in December 2011 because no perpetrator was identified. The investigation was marked by limited notification to the applicant.

**Mr Kharchenko** alleged that on 5 January 2010 Kremenchuk district police officers forced him to confess to theft, punched and kicked him, handcuffed him to a chair, and electrocuted his thighs with a black device containing two electrodes. A forensic report found multiple small burn marks on both thighs, classified as minor and possibly dating to 5 January. Later reports considered electric current a probable cause and cigarette or match contact improbable, though a stun-gun model stocked by Kremenchuk police was not considered probable. He was questioned without a lawyer and gave self-incriminating statements later retracted. He complained on 6 January 2010. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to institute proceedings; those decisions were quashed. An internal review found irregularities, including that his presence at the police station was undocumented. Criminal proceedings for police misconduct were opened in March 2013, closed and reopened several times, and finally closed in December 2013 for lack of evidence. The authorities concluded the origin of his injuries could not be established and that they could possibly have been self-inflicted.

The case thus centres on alleged police ill-treatment and allegedly ineffective domestic investigations under Article 3, along with additional Article 5 and Article 6 complaints.
001-202622:
In *Potoroc v. Romania* (Application no. 37772/17, judgment 2 June 2020), the European Court of Human Rights examined the applicant’s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention concerning his continued detention and prison conditions despite serious illness. The applicant, born in 1953, suffered from brain damage following strokes, hemiparesis, prostate adenoma, impaired hearing, and severe psycho-organic syndrome comparable to pre-senile dementia. He used a wheelchair, required permanent assistance, and needed continuous medical care.

In 2009, he received a final 15-year prison sentence for international drug trafficking. He was imprisoned at Rahova Prison from February 2011. Although he spent 350 of 529 days in prison hospitals until August 2012, he refused placement in Rahova’s medical wing because it was on the first floor, had no ramps, and made outdoor access difficult; he was therefore placed in a regular cell. Disability commissions concluded he did not need a personal assistant and had no functional deficiency.

In May 2012, the applicant applied for interruption of his sentence on health grounds, relying on Article 3. A July 2012 forensic report recommended Colibaşi Prison Hospital and found prison healthcare adequate, but could not guarantee treatment would actually be provided. In August 2012, the Argeş County Court allowed his release due to his “deplorable” health and humanitarian considerations.
