001-191721:
**Bigović v. Montenegro** (Application no. 48343/16) concerned Ljubo Bigović, a Montenegrin national born in 1976. He was arrested on 16 February 2006 on suspicion of criminal enterprise, attempted extortion, and aiding and abetting the aggravated murder of a high-ranking police officer, S.Š., who had been killed in August 2005. On 19 February 2006 an investigating judge ordered his detention, initially for one month, under Article 148 § 1(1) of the then Code of Criminal Procedure, mainly because the gravity of the offences created a risk that he would abscond.

The applicant’s detention became the core of his later complaints. It was extended repeatedly—on 16 March, 15 April, 16 May, 15 June, and 12 July 2006, and again on 15 August 2006, 21 October 2008, and 11 March 2009. Many extensions relied on the same grounds: the gravity and number of offences, possible sentence, risk of absconding, and, later, risk to public order. Several decisions were issued collectively for multiple defendants, sometimes without specifying the duration of the extension, and often with brief or boilerplate reasoning.

An indictment was filed on 14 August 2006. The applicant was convicted at first instance on 7 August 2009 and sentenced to 30 years’ imprisonment, but that judgment was quashed on 17 February 2010. A second conviction on 9 May 2011 was also quashed on 30 December 2011. A third first-instance conviction on 9 October 2012 was upheld in 2013, then quashed by the Supreme Court on 2 April 2014. Throughout, his detention continued.

Relevant to the alleged Article 5 violations, the applicant argued that his detention was unlawful because it was not regularly reviewed and because decisions extending it were insufficiently reasoned. In particular, from 2012 the High Court extended detention “until further notice” under Article 179 § 2 of the 2009 Code, relying on risk of absconding and public-order grounds. On 1 August 2014 he applied for release, complaining about the length of detention, lack of regular review, insufficient reasoning, poor conditions, and lack of medical care. He repeatedly urged the courts to decide, but no timely ruling followed. The Court of Appeal eventually dismissed the request on 13 February 2015 after hearing a medical expert. On 20 February 2015 the Court of Appeal extended detention under Article 175 § 4, but the Supreme Court quashed that extension on 12 March 2015 because that provision did not exist and the decision lacked reasoning on his health. A new extension followed on 16 March 2015. His constitutional appeal was dismissed on 28 December 2015, served on 25 March 2016.

Relevant to the Article 3 complaints, the applicant suffered from serious ulcerative colitis, diagnosed in 2013, requiring a special diet and Vedolizumab (VDZ), which was not registered in Montenegro. Treatment was delayed, he was hospitalised repeatedly, and his family sometimes purchased doses abroad. Medical experts warned that stress, inadequate diet, and detention conditions could worsen his illness and even threaten his life. He also had eye surgery, knee problems, and psychiatric issues. He alleged overcrowding, lack of running water, limited outdoor exercise, lack of special diet and disinfectant, and inadequate medical care. The Government disputed this, describing improved cells and available care. The ECtHR later communicated his complaints concerning conditions of detention, medical care, unlawfulness and length of detention, irregular review, insufficient reasoning, and lack of a speedy decision on release.
001-198884:
The case *Pikhun v. Ukraine* concerned a Ukrainian national and former police officer. A criminal investigation for illegal arms possession began in September 2006. He was arrested and detained several times, then released. Later, charges of murder, threats, and abuse of power were brought against him. On 30 November 2009 he was arrested on new charges of firearms theft.

The applicant’s main Article 3 complaint concerned alleged police ill-treatment on 30 November 2009. He claimed that, after refusing to answer questions about the new charges, three police officers physically assaulted him at the prosecutor’s office: they throttled him, handcuffed him, and hit his head against a parked car. The alleged ill-treatment continued at the police station, where officers allegedly stubbed a cigarette out on his left hand and demanded that he not assert his rights during the investigation. A temporary detention centre report of 22 December 2009 recorded a head wound, scratches on his head and neck, and bruises on his wrists; he complained of headache and stomach sickness and received ambulance care. He repeatedly requested medical-examination documents, but these requests were refused. From 1 December 2009 he submitted numerous complaints to the prosecution authorities and gave a detailed account on 3 December 2009. The Government stated that on 29 January 2010 an investigator refused to open criminal proceedings, finding no offence: the police had forcibly stopped and handcuffed him after he attempted to flee, no cigarette burns were found, and wrist bruises resulted from handcuffs. The applicant reportedly did not challenge that decision. Prosecutors later said his ill-treatment complaints had not been forwarded because the criminal case was before the trial court. In February 2010 his challenge to that reply was discontinued because no procedural decision had been taken. In November 2013 the trial court noted that the events could indicate ill-treatment and notified the regional prosecutor; in February 2014 the Regional Court quashed that ruling and instructed the trial court to examine the complaints. It was not clear whether that instruction was implemented.

Regarding Article 5, on 3 December 2009 the District Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. On 28 January 2010 the same court, in the absence of the applicant and his defence lawyer, extended his detention until 30 March 2010. His appeal was returned unexamined on 4 February 2010 because the case was already before the trial court. On 26 February 2010 the District Court remitted the case for additional investigation and ordered continued detention without giving reasons or time-limits.

As to Article 6, the criminal proceedings were lengthy. On 4 October 2011 the District Court convicted the applicant of threats, theft, and unlawful use of firearms, sentencing him to four years’ imprisonment. On 13 December 2011 the Regional Court quashed the sentence, remitted the case, and released him with an undertaking not to abscond. The prosecution later limited the charges to firearms theft. On 22 November 2013 he was convicted but exempted from liability due to expiry of time-limits. On 20 February 2014 that decision was quashed and remitted. According to the applicant, on 11 December 2018 the trial court terminated the proceedings after charges were dropped. The trial held 86 merits hearings; 66 were adjourned because the prosecution, victim, expert, or witnesses failed to appear; 21 due to the applicant’s or defender’s absence; and 18 due to the judge’s inability to sit. The latter adjournments extended the proceedings by about one year and six months.
001-192424:
In *Ifandiev v. Bulgaria*, the applicant, a Bulgarian journalist and writer, complained under Article 10 of the Convention about domestic defamation proceedings brought by K.T., a prominent politician and trade-union leader. In 2003 the applicant published a book, *The Shadow of Zion*, discussing Judaism, Zionism, Freemasonry and their alleged impact on world history. On pages 69–70, after comparing communists and Nazis to Freemasons, the text stated that after the “democratic changes” many communists and people connected with their secret services had become Freemasons. A list of names followed, including K.T., described as a “pseudo trade unionist.” A footnote cited a 2002 article by another author.

In September 2005 K.T. brought a tort action, alleging that the book falsely defamed him by presenting him as a Freemason, a communist connected with the former secret services, and a pseudo trade unionist. K.T. said he was a fervent Orthodox Christian, had never been a member of the Communist Party or its youth organisation, had no secret-service links, and had fought for human rights and democracy. He claimed the allegations humiliated him, harmed his national and international prestige, and caused non-pecuniary damage.

The applicant defended his statements, arguing that he had relied on earlier publications, including the one cited in the footnote. He also claimed K.T. had said he was a member of the Maltese Order, intended to prove secret-service connections through witnesses, and asserted that K.T. had bragged about links to leading communist figures. The applicant argued the expressions were not offensive or defamatory and that no damage had been shown. He was legally represented throughout.

In July 2008 the Sofia City Court allowed K.T.’s action and ordered the applicant to pay BGN 15,000 (about EUR 7,670) in moral damages plus default interest. Although it referred to Article 10, it found the applicant had exceeded acceptable criticism. It held the allegations untrue: Freemasonry contradicted K.T.’s Orthodox faith; secret-service links were disproved by official archive attestations and unconvincing witnesses; and “pseudo trade unionist” was a gratuitous offence aimed at discrediting him. The court treated insult as subjective, so K.T.’s feeling offended sufficed. It found serious harm to his honour and dignity within the trade-union community and internationally, aggravated by health problems and hospitalisation.

The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in October 2009. It added that even if K.T. had mentioned the Maltese Order, the applicant had not shown this was equivalent to Freemasonry; earlier publications did not make the allegations less defamatory or truer; and K.T.’s status as a public figure justified higher damages. In August 2010 the Supreme Court of Cassation refused to accept the applicant’s appeal on points of law, confirming that whether an allegation is offensive depends on how the addressee and his social circle perceive it, even if that perception does not conform to common understanding of the facts.

K.T. later instituted enforcement proceedings. In October 2011 a bailiff calculated the total due at BGN 31,549 (about EUR 16,100), including principal, interest and costs. Enforcement was discontinued in 2016 after K.T. abandoned payment attempts; only BGN 4.55 (EUR 2.32) had been seized.

After the application was communicated, the applicant published blog comments in June 2018 accusing the Government Agent of lies and offensive language and making insulting remarks about Bulgarian judges and the Court. Notice of the freedom-of-expression complaint was given to the Government on 22 January 2018; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-191717:
In *M.T. v. Ukraine* (Application no. 950/17), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 19 March 2019. The applicant, M.T., is a United States national born in 1946 who currently lives in Berlin, Germany. His identity was anonymized under Rule 47 § 4 of the Rules of Court. He was represented by Mr L. Drozdovskyy, a lawyer practising in Kyiv, while the Ukrainian Government was represented by its Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna. The application was lodged on 20 December 2016, and notice was given to the Government on 20 March 2017. The applicant complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention that the domestic courts had failed to establish his paternity, thereby restricting his right of access to a court.

The key facts concern the applicant’s relationship with a child born in Ukraine. In 2005, while working as an English teacher in Kyiv, the applicant began a private relationship with a married woman living in Kyiv. In 2006, the woman gave birth to a child. Her husband was named as the father on the child’s birth certificate. In 2007, a DNA test established that the applicant was in fact the child’s biological father. Despite the birth certificate, the child’s mother did not prevent the applicant from having access to the child. She accepted monthly financial support from him, and the applicant also bought a car for the mother. In 2011, the applicant wrote a will bequeathing all his property to the child in question. He maintained regular contact with the child until 2015.

The situation changed in 2015 when the child’s mother informed the applicant that she had divorced her husband and had decided to marry a German national and move with the child to Germany. The applicant opposed the decision to emigrate. In response, the mother denied him access to the child and prevented him from communicating with her. This denial of access appears to have been the trigger for the applicant’s attempts to establish legal paternity through the Ukrainian courts, because without a formal paternity declaration, his legal standing to seek contact, custody, or other protective measures concerning the child was limited or non-existent. The applicant alleged that the domestic courts failed to establish his paternity, which in turn restricted his right of access to a court and interfered with his private and family life.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the applicant’s biological paternity, confirmed by DNA testing in 2007; the legal presumption that the mother’s husband was the child’s father on the birth certificate; the applicant’s established de facto family life with the child, demonstrated by regular contact, monthly financial support, the purchase of a car for the mother, and a will naming the child as sole beneficiary; and the mother’s later refusal of access and communication after her decision to relocate to Germany. These facts underpin the applicant’s complaints under Article 6, concerning access to court to obtain a paternity determination, and Article 8, concerning respect for his private and family life. The provided text does not include the Court’s subsequent reasoning or final conclusion on those complaints.
001-193251:
In *Liblik and Others v. Estonia*, six applications were brought by four Estonian nationals and two companies. They alleged violations under Article 6 of the Convention (excessive length of criminal proceedings) and Article 8 (retrospective justification of secret surveillance authorisations violating private life and correspondence). The Article 8 complaints were raised by the second and third applicants and the applicant companies.

The underlying criminal case concerned suspected high-level corruption involving exchanges of land in conservation areas for land that could be developed. Criminal proceedings were instituted on 18 August 2005 without informing the applicants. Between 23 August 2005 and 11 October 2006, the Internal Security Service carried out secret surveillance on the first, second and third applicants, with surveillance of the third applicant starting on 16 December 2005. Communications between the fourth applicant and the surveilled persons were also intercepted. Separately, the third applicant had been under secret surveillance from 2 September 2004 to 2 January 2005 in earlier proceedings that were later terminated without prosecution; material from that surveillance was transferred to the present case’s surveillance file in December 2006.

Surveillance was authorised by 44 prosecutor decisions concerning covert observation and communication data, and by 21 preliminary investigation judge decisions concerning covert listening and interception. The prosecutors’ decisions contained no reasoning. The judges’ authorisations used general, boilerplate reasoning: they stated that the prosecutor’s application was justified, the offence serious, and other investigative means impossible or especially complicated, sometimes adding references to public officials or offences relating to office. The reasoning was not tied to specific evidence.

Other relevant facts included the second applicant finding a surveillance device in his office on 25 September 2005; searches on 3 October 2006 at offices connected with the first, second and third applicants and the second applicant company; a search on 20 September 2007 of the first applicant company’s premises; and the fourth applicant being questioned as a suspect on 16 October 2007. Two accused, including the fourth applicant, were members of Parliament when pre-trial proceedings ended, so parliamentary consent was needed to lift immunity and charge them. Consent was given on 24 March 2009. Pre-trial proceedings lasted about three and a half years and ended on 31 March 2009 when charges were submitted to the trial court.

The first-instance court heard the case over 92 hearing days and acquitted the applicants on 19 June 2012. It found the surveillance unlawful and excluded the resulting evidence, but did not decide whether the authorisations had been sufficiently reasoned. On appeal, the Court of Appeal convicted the applicants on 19 June 2013, finding the surveillance lawful and the evidence admissible after reviewing the surveillance files. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions on 30 June 2014. It accepted that the proceedings were long and “close to being excessively lengthy,” but found them not excessive given the complexity, volume of evidence, many witnesses, and absence of significant State delays. It also held that insufficient reasoning in the authorisation decisions did not automatically make surveillance unlawful or the evidence inadmissible, because domestic courts could conduct an ex post facto review of whether the substantive conditions—probable cause and the ultima ratio principle—had been met. The Supreme Court reviewed the files and concluded those conditions had been satisfied.

The applicants’ Strasbourg complaints thus focused on the overall length of the proceedings—roughly six years eight months to eight years nine months depending on the applicant—and on the domestic courts’ retrospective validation of secret surveillance authorisations that had been unreasoned or boilerplate, allegedly breaching their privacy and correspondence rights. The remaining complaints were declared inadmissible.
001-189589:
In *Fil LLC v. Armenia* (Application no. 18526/13), the applicant, a private construction company registered in Yerevan, complained to the European Court of Human Rights that civil proceedings it began in 2008 were excessively long and that no effective domestic remedy existed for that delay. The key facts concern a payment dispute and repeated, ultimately prolonged efforts to obtain a forensic technical examination.

On 7 May 2007 Fil LLC contracted with company S. to perform construction work on premises belonging to company H. After completing the work, Fil LLC claimed S. had not paid in full. On 18 January 2008 it brought compensation proceedings against S. in the Yerevan Civil Court, which admitted the claim on 21 January 2008.

On 20 February 2008 the Civil Court ordered a forensic technical examination of the construction work and stayed the proceedings. The expert soon reported that he needed access to company H’s premises, but H was not a party. The court resumed proceedings and joined H as a third party on 4 April 2008. On 15 May 2008 it ordered another forensic examination and again stayed the case. On 28 October 2008 the expert stated that the examination could not be performed because he had not been able to access H’s premises. Proceedings resumed on 19 November 2008.

On 19 February 2009 the Civil Court granted Fil LLC’s claim. However, S. appealed. On 23 April 2009 the Civil Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and remitted the case, reasoning that without an expert opinion on the disputed construction work the judgment was unfounded. The case was eventually taken over by the Shengavit District Court of Yerevan on 29 July 2009.

The pattern then repeated. On 26 August 2009 the District Court ordered a forensic examination and stayed proceedings; on 31 May 2010 the expert again reported lack of access to H’s premises. Proceedings resumed on 7 June 2010. On 16 July 2010 the court ordered another examination, this time with assistance from the Department for the Enforcement of Judicial Acts, but the outcome was unclear. On 21 June 2012 the expert again said the examination could not be carried out because of lack of access. Proceedings resumed on 27 June 2012. On 3 October 2012 Fil LLC filed additional submissions, and the same day the District Court ordered yet another forensic examination and stayed the proceedings.

That stay lasted until 2015. In late 2014 and early 2015 Fil LLC enquired with the Bureau of Forensic Examinations and complained to the Ministry of Justice. The Bureau said in December 2014 that no expert in the relevant field was available, but expected the examination in January 2015. In May 2015 the Minister of Justice replied that although the examination would take one day and the report about five days, it had not been done because of the lack of an expert, access difficulties, and excessive workload; it could proceed if access were granted. On 30 June 2015 the Bureau sent the expert opinion, and the District Court resumed proceedings on 9 July 2015.

Further hearings were held in 2015 and 2016, and new examinations were ordered in June and August 2016. On 10 October 2016 the District Court granted Fil LLC’s claim in part. S. appealed, but on 23 March 2017 the Civil Court of Appeal rejected the appeal and upheld the judgment. No cassation appeal was lodged, and the decision became final. The proceedings had thus lasted from January 2008 to March 2017—about nine years and two months. These facts formed the basis of Fil LLC’s complaints of excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.
001-189795:
Case Mashinyan and Ramazyan v. Armenia (Application no. 65124/09, ECtHR, 14 February 2019) originated in an application by five Armenian nationals from Shnogh village. The applicants jointly owned a 1.622-hectare plot of arable land used to grow crops and feed livestock. In the 1970s, the Teghout copper-molybdenum deposit was discovered nearby. In 2001, Armenian Copper Programme CJSC received a 25-year mining licence. On 1 November 2007, Government Decree no. 1279-N designated parts of Shnogh and Teghout as expropriation zones for State needs, changing the land-use category for the Teghout mining project. Teghout CJSC, founded by Armenian Copper Programme, was to acquire the listed plots, including the applicants’ land.

Teghout CJSC offered to buy the applicants’ plot for AMD 818,000 plus the statutory 15%, totaling AMD 940,700 (about EUR 2,045). The applicants did not reply because they considered the amount too low. On 12 May 2008, Teghout CJSC sued to compel them to sign an expropriation agreement. It relied on a valuation report by Oliver Group LLC, which estimated the land’s market value at AMD 818,000 (about EUR 1,780). In the Lori Regional Court, the fourth applicant represented the family, argued that the valuation was too low, and asked for time to obtain an alternative valuation. The applicants claimed no other valuation company was willing to assess their land independently. During the proceedings, Teghout CJSC submitted a corrected Oliver Group report raising the market value to AMD 900,000; with the 15% addition, total compensation became AMD 1,035,000 (about EUR 2,250).

On 26 September 2008, the Regional Court granted Teghout CJSC’s claim and awarded the applicants AMD 1,035,000. The applicants appealed, arguing that the market value had been seriously underestimated, that compensation was inadequate, and that two different valuations from Oliver Group cast doubt on the report’s credibility. They also argued that the court should have ordered an independent valuation. On 29 January 2009, the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment, finding that the market value had been correctly estimated based on the report in the case file. The applicants then appealed on points of law, claiming the Regional Court had failed to order an independent valuation despite having the power to do so, and that the valuation report was not an expert opinion and should not have been admitted as evidence. On 24 June 2009, the Court of Cassation declared the cassation appeal inadmissible for lack of merit.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial). The key facts relevant to those allegations were the compulsory expropriation of their land for the Teghout mining project, the disputed and relatively low compensation, the domestic courts’ reliance on valuations commissioned by the expropriating company, the corrected valuation submitted mid-proceedings, the applicants’ inability to obtain an independent valuation, and the courts’ refusal to order an independent expert valuation. Domestic law required expropriation only for prevailing public interest, with prior adequate compensation equal to market value plus 15%, and fair adversarial proceedings with equality of arms. The Government justified the expropriation by the public interest in economic and infrastructure development and increased production and exports under Decree no. 1279-N. The case therefore concerned whether the property interference was lawful and proportionate and whether the valuation and compensation process satisfied fair-trial safeguards.
001-196879:
The case *Kožul and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 38695/13) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 April 2013 by five Bosnian nationals: Ivan, Dinko, Dražen, Petar and Ruža Kožul. They live in the vicinity of Široki Brijeg. The applicants complained about the authorities’ prolonged failure to enforce a final demolition order concerning industrial buildings erected illegally next to their homes. On 10 July 2017, the Government were given notice of the complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The relevant domestic facts began on 4 February 2002, when the local authorities ordered a private company, Paškić d.o.o. Široki Brijeg, to demolish its industrial buildings. The buildings had been erected illegally next to the applicants’ homes. The decision became enforceable on 18 April 2002. However, it was not enforced.

On 13 October 2005, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found a violation of the applicants’ right to a fair trial. It ordered the local authorities concerned to enforce the 4 February 2002 decision without further delay. In that decision, the Constitutional Court considered it unnecessary to examine the applicants’ separate complaints under Article 8 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 27 May 2006, the Constitutional Court further found that its earlier decision of 13 October 2005 had still not been enforced.

Despite these rulings, enforcement remained ineffective. The local authorities reportedly issued more than thirty calls for tenders in order to find a company able and willing to demolish the illegal buildings. None succeeded. The authorities also imposed more than thirty fines on Paškić for its failure to comply with the demolition order. Those fines ranged between 50 and 300 convertible marks (BAM), but they did not secure compliance.

Criminal enforcement also proved unsuccessful. On two occasions, the competent public prosecutor investigated the matter, because non-enforcement of a Constitutional Court decision may constitute a criminal offence. The prosecutor decided not to prosecute, first on 15 May 2007 and again on 30 January 2017. The reason given was a lack of evidence that the officials concerned had acted with criminal intent.

As of 18 March 2019, the latest information available to the Court, the Constitutional Court’s decision remained unenforced. Thus, for many years after the final demolition order and despite repeated domestic judicial findings, the illegal industrial buildings continued to stand next to the applicants’ homes.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the existence of a final enforceable demolition order in the applicants’ favour; repeated domestic findings that it had not been enforced; the Constitutional Court’s orders requiring urgent enforcement; the authorities’ numerous but ineffective tenders and fines; the prosecutor’s decisions not to prosecute; and the continuing non-enforcement as of 2019. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention, concerning the right to fair trial and enforcement of final judgments, respect for home and private life, and the availability of an effective remedy.
001-196836:
In *Denis and Irvine v. Belgium*, the applicants were both subject to compulsory confinement imposed under Belgium’s old Social Protection Act of 9 April 1930. They complained that their continued detention after a change in legislation violated Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that they lacked effective remedies under Articles 5 § 4 and 13. The key legal issue arose because Belgium’s new Compulsory Confinement Act of 5 May 2014 entered into force on 1 October 2016, narrowing the criteria for compulsory confinement and introducing discharge rules, including final discharge after a three-year probationary period.

The first applicant, Jimmy Denis, a Belgian national, was placed in compulsory confinement by the Turnhout Criminal Court in 2007 for theft. A psychiatrist had described him as having a psychotic personality, alcohol and drug dependence, and a severe mental disturbance making him incapable of controlling his actions and dangerous to society and himself. He received conditional discharges but these were repeatedly revoked for non-compliance. After the new Act entered into force, he sought final discharge, arguing that theft could no longer justify compulsory confinement and that his detention was therefore no longer lawful under Article 5 § 1. On 25 January 2017, the Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court refused final discharge and maintained his placement in the social protection unit of Merksplas Prison. It found that the new Act did not apply retrospectively to old confinement orders and that final discharge required a sufficiently stable mental condition and completion of a minimum three-year conditional discharge period. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, holding that Article 7 did not apply to preventive measures, that Article 5 § 1 did not invalidate a final confinement order merely because the law changed during execution, and that current dangerousness had to be assessed in light of the applicant’s present mental condition and risk factors, not only the original offence. On 18 July 2017, he was again conditionally discharged to a psychiatric hospital in Zoersel.

The second applicant, Derek Irvine, a British national, was placed in compulsory confinement in 2002 for attempted aggravated burglary under the 1930 Act. A psychiatrist found him to suffer from a serious personality disorder and psychotic disorder, making him incapable of controlling his actions. He was conditionally discharged in 2003 to a Scottish psychiatric hospital, but escaped and was found in Belgium in 2010. He was returned to the psychiatric wing of Turnhout Prison. Efforts to place him in Scotland failed, and although the Antwerp Social Protection Committee ordered his placement in a forensic psychiatry centre in Ghent or Antwerp, no bed was available, so he remained in prison. In December 2016, he sought final discharge, raising the same arguments as Denis. A psychosocial report and psychiatrist noted ongoing schizophrenic symptoms treated with injections, and recommended continued confinement in a forensic centre. On 25 January 2017, the Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court maintained his confinement in Turnhout Prison pending a bed and dismissed his final discharge request on the same grounds as in Denis’s case. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 21 February 2017. He was later placed in the Antwerp forensic psychiatry centre in 2018.

Both applicants alleged that their detention was no longer lawful under Article 5 § 1 because their original offences could no longer lead to confinement under the new Act, and that the three-year probation requirement denied them access to a court capable of ordering immediate release, contrary to Articles 5 § 4 and 13. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 June 2021.
001-196152:
In *Savran v. Denmark*, the applicant, Arıf Savran, is a Turkish national born in 1985 who moved to Denmark in 1991 at age six to join his father. He lived lawfully in Denmark for about 14 years and eight months by the time of the relevant criminal proceedings. His mother and four siblings lived in Denmark. He had no close family in Turkey, had not visited since 2001, spoke Kurdish but only a little Turkish, and claimed no social network there.

In 2001 he was convicted of robbery. In 2007–2008 he was convicted of assault under highly aggravating circumstances for a May 2006 attack in which he and others beat a man with cudgels or blunt objects, causing traumatic brain injury and death. He was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment and expelled from Denmark with a permanent re-entry ban. The Supreme Court upheld the expulsion in 2009, also ordering committal to forensic psychiatric care.

Psychiatric evidence was central to the case. Earlier reports found no mental disorder at the time of the offence but noted mild mental retardation and personality disorder. Later he was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, mild intellectual disability, and cannabis dependence. He received antipsychotic treatment, including Risperdal Consta injections and clozapine/Leponex tablets, requiring regular monitoring. Treating psychiatrists considered him motivated and stable in a structured setting, but warned that interrupting treatment created a high risk of pharmaceutical failure, resumed drug abuse, worsening psychotic symptoms, and aggressive behaviour. One psychiatrist believed equivalent intensive follow-up and support would not be available if the applicant settled in a small village in Turkey. The applicant stated he had no home or social network in Turkey, that his mother’s property there had been demolished, and that he feared being unable to obtain or adhere to treatment.

In 2012, review proceedings began under the Penal Code. In 2014, the City Court changed his sanction from forensic psychiatric care to psychiatric treatment and revoked the expulsion under section 50a of the Aliens Act, finding that his health made enforcement conclusively inappropriate. It relied on the high risk of relapse without intensive outpatient follow-up and uncertainty about real access to relevant treatment in Turkey. On appeal, in January 2015 the High Court reversed and upheld expulsion. Based on MedCOI and Danish Foreign Ministry information, it found that the same medication was available in the Konya area, that psychiatric treatment was available at public and private facilities, that he could apply for free or subsidised coverage, and that Kurdish-speaking hospital staff existed. It also emphasised the gravity of the killing and that he had no spouse or children in Denmark. Leave to appeal was refused in May 2015.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Savran alleged that deportation to Turkey would violate Article 3, because his mental illness and lack of adequate treatment created a risk of inhuman or degrading treatment, and Article 8, because expulsion disproportionately interfered with his private and family life given his long residence and family ties in Denmark and weak ties to Turkey. The key factual dispute was whether his serious psychiatric condition and need for continuous, structured treatment made expulsion incompatible with those Convention rights.
001-192787:
In *Pasquini v. San Marino*, the applicant, an Italian national living in San Marino, was the owner and director of S.M.I., a fiduciary company. His complaints under Article 6 § 1 concerned the composition of the Court for Trusts, the legal costs required to bring proceedings there, the refusal of leave to appeal, and the impartiality of the Judge of Civil Appeals.

The underlying dispute began when B. entrusted Z. to open a fiduciary account with S.M.I. B. later alleged that S.M.I. had failed to return part of the proceeds—LIT 9,035,264,332—from the purchase and later sale of shares in company A.N. In civil proceedings no. 300/2001, the first-instance judge found that S.M.I.’s financial statement was incomplete and unreliable. Relying only on credit entries, the judge concluded that S.M.I. owed B. approximately EUR 4,662,778.93. Because the evidence was not complete, the judge required B. to take a “supplementary oath.” B. did so on 30 June 2008. The appeal was dismissed on 9 June 2011, confirming the debt. A further appeal to the Third-Instance Judge was declared inadmissible in 2012.

The applicant then challenged B.’s oath. He filed a criminal complaint accusing B. of false oath. On 31 July 2015, Judge L.F., a Judge of Civil Appeals acting as Judge of Criminal Appeals, dismissed the applicant’s complaint and upheld the closure of the investigation. Judge L.F. found no evidence that B. had committed perjury and noted that the parties had deliberately decided not to record all operations under the fiduciary mandate. This earlier involvement became relevant to the applicant’s later complaint that the same judge was not impartial when refusing him leave to appeal in the connected civil proceedings.

In 2014, the applicant sought to reopen the civil case and brought a *jactitation suit* asking the court to declare that B.’s supplementary oath had been false. He claimed new evidence showed that B. had not provided the funds for the A.N. share purchase and that S.M.I. had instead paid off a LIT 9,900,000,000 debt owed to an Italian bank. The Chief Justice referred the case to the Court for Trusts, established by Constitutional Law no. 1 of 2012.

On 3 December 2014, the President of the Court for Trusts assigned the case to a panel of two judges, including himself. He also calculated the fees under “Rules on Court Fees and Judicial Remunerations” that he had issued the previous day. Although the claim had an undetermined value, the President used EUR 4,662,778.93 as its value. He set court fees at EUR 6,000 and the variable judge remuneration at EUR 23,000, plus EUR 500 expenses. The applicant was ordered to pay all court fees and half of the total amount—EUR 17,750—at least seven days before the first hearing, failing which his claim would be barred. These facts formed the basis of his complaint that the Court for Trusts’ composition was irregular and not prescribed by law, and that the costs criteria were not specified by law, hindering his access to court.

On 18 September 2015, the Court for Trusts partly accepted the applicant’s claim. It found that he had standing and accepted the *jactitation suit* as admissible despite finding no new evidence, because the parties before it differed from those in the original civil proceedings. The applicant ultimately alleged that the Court for Trusts was irregularly composed, that substantial legal costs based on unspecified criteria and the refusal of leave to appeal violated his right of access to a court, and that the Judge of Civil Appeals who refused leave was not impartial, having previously expressed an opinion on the same facts in a connected case.
001-193469:
**Garumov v. Ukraine (Application no. 70043/17)**

The case of *Garumov v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged by Mr Magomedganipa Gadzhiyevych Garumov, a Russian national born in 1967, against Ukraine. The applicant was arrested on 1 June 2017 on suspicion of kidnapping and subsequently placed in pre-trial detention at the Kyiv SIZO (pre-trial detention centre). His application to the European Court of Human Rights raised two principal complaints: (1) the lack of adequate medical treatment while in detention, and (2) the authorities' failure to provide relevant and sufficient reasons justifying his continued pre-trial detention.

Regarding the first complaint, the applicant suffered from serious medical conditions, including ischemic heart disease and second-stage hypertension, for which he received treatment in the SIZO medical unit from July 2017. On 3 September 2017, he suffered a haemorrhagic stroke and was diagnosed with third-stage hypertension; he was hospitalised until 8 September 2017. Subsequent medical consultations with a neurologist and cardiologist recommended further in-patient treatment at a neurology-specialised facility, along with an MRT scan, massages, and rehabilitation exercises. A neurologist warned that without adequate treatment, another intracerebral haemorrhage and disability could result. On 21 September 2017, during a court hearing, the applicant fell unwell and was taken to hospital by ambulance. The District Court ordered the SIZO administration to ensure an urgent forensic examination. A forensic examination completed on 2 February 2018 concluded that the applicant suffered from cerebrovascular disease, acute stroke, discirculatory encephalopathy, and third-degree hypertension, and that further examination and in-patient treatment at a neurology-specialised facility were imperative. Despite a court order on 8 May 2018 allowing his transfer to a medical facility at his or his relatives' expense, the SIZO authorities required documentation confirming the facility's readiness to admit him. He was eventually transferred to Kyiv City Hospital No. 4 on 4 June 2018, discharged on 22 June 2018 with only insignificant improvement, and recognised as a category 2 disabled person on 5 July 2018.

Regarding the second complaint, the applicant's pre-trial detention was repeatedly extended by courts at both pre-trial and trial stages, including on 27 July, 22 and 28 September, and 15 and 29 November 2017, and later on 9 February, 28 March, 24 April, 13 June, 11 September, 7 November 2018, and 11 February 2019. The courts consistently cited the severity of the possible sanction, the need for additional investigative steps, and the persistence of risks of absconding or obstructing proceedings, but provided no further details or individualised reasoning. Some decisions also referenced the applicant's Russian nationality, lack of a permanent residence, social ties, and employment in Ukraine, and the fact that he had not surrendered his passport. Notably, on 29 November 2017, the court maintained non-custodial preventive measures for two co-accused. The applicant objected to the extensions, citing his poor health following a stroke, stable family relationships in Ukraine (a civil partner and two children born there), a permanent residence permit, and the fact that he had not attempted to abscond. He also applied for house arrest on several occasions. The courts did not address these arguments in their decisions.
001-190020:
**Medyanikov v. Ukraine** (Application no. 31694/06) is a European Court of Human Rights case lodged by Ukrainian national Eduard Valeryevich Medyanikov on 19 September 2006. The applicant was convicted by the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal on 25 November 2004 of several crimes and sentenced to life imprisonment with confiscation of property; the Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 23 February 2006 with certain changes. He had been detained since 26 August 2003 in various facilities, initially pending investigation and trial, and later after sentencing. At the relevant time he was serving his life sentence in Ladyzhynska colony no. 39. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government in 2011 and, in 2017, specifically notified the complaints under Articles 3 and 34 concerning alleged lack of adequate medical treatment in detention and alleged hindrance of the right of individual petition. The remainder of the application, including complaints about the fairness of the criminal proceedings, was declared inadmissible.

The admissible Article 3 complaint concerned the applicant’s medical treatment, particularly for tuberculosis and hepatitis C. On 25 January 2007, while detained in SIZO No. 5 in Donetsk, he was diagnosed with tuberculosis; other evidence indicated the diagnosis may have been made on 1 February 2007. After the criminal proceedings ended, he was transferred to Ladyzhynska colony on 16 March 2007. A preliminary examination on 20 March 2007, including laboratory tests and an X-ray, placed him under medical supervision for residual tuberculosis. According to the Government, he was regularly examined and treated by colony doctors between 20 March 2007 and 26 February 2018, and his health improved after each treatment course. However, the Government did not specify the frequency of examinations or the nature of treatment.

In December 2011 a blood test revealed hepatitis C. The applicant claimed he was denied copies of the test results. The Government stated that on 28 February 2012 a colony doctor diagnosed chronic persistent hepatitis in remission and prescribed treatment. On 16 May 2012, doctors from the Vinnytsya Regional Centre for HIV/AIDS Control and Prevention diagnosed hepatitis C in remission without hepatic impairment; symptomatic treatment was allegedly prescribed, but its nature was not specified. The Government also claimed the applicant received necessary medicine and a special diet, again without specifying frequency or content. From 23 February to 20 March 2015 he received treatment in a multi-disciplinary hospital in Stryzhavska colony no. 81, after which his health reportedly improved, though the treatment type was not described. As of 26 February 2018, he remained under colony doctors’ supervision and his health was described as satisfactory. The applicant therefore alleged that his detention lacked adequate medical care for tuberculosis and hepatitis C.

The Article 34 complaint concerned alleged interference with his right to submit an application to the Court. The applicant stated that he made numerous requests to domestic authorities, especially the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, for copies of documents needed to substantiate his Strasbourg application. Between August and November 2006 he requested a copy of his indictment; this was refused on 8 August and 6 September 2006, partly because he had already received it and because no legal requirement obliged the court to provide it. A copy was eventually sent on 21 July 2008. Between April and August 2009 he requested court records from his criminal case and his accomplice’s case; these were initially refused as lacking legal basis. On 10 September 2009 he made another request. On 2 October 2009 the Court of Appeal sent some copies but excluded court hearing records, saying their transmission was not covered by then-applicable legislation. On 21 April 2011 the Government Agent’s Office sent the hearing records. In January 2017 the Court of Appeal refused his requests for a copy of his request to extend the cassation appeal time-limit and a copy of the 26 October 2016 ruling dismissing that request, stating the case file had been sent to the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters. The applicant never received those documents. These facts formed the basis of his alleged hindrance of the right of individual petition.
001-194303:
**Case Summary: Petrov and Korostylyov v. Ukraine**

**Case Name:** *Petrov and Korostylyov v. Ukraine*  
**Applications nos.:** 19591/18 and 19596/18  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee  
**Judgment date:** Strasbourg, 11 July 2019  
**Final:** Yes, subject to editorial revision.

The case originated in two applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Both applications were introduced on 18 April 2018. The applicants were represented by Mr O.A. Ignatov, a lawyer practising in Dnipro, Ukraine. Notice of the applications was given to the Ukrainian Government. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of their detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. These complaints relate to the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment and the right to an effective remedy.

The first applicant, **Oleg Pavlovych Petrov**, born 14 March 1975, was detained at Dnipropetrovsk law enforcement agency no. 4 (former SIZO no. 3) from 20 March 2014 to 26 September 2018. The total duration of detention was 4 years, 6 months and 7 days. The space per inmate was between 2.6 and 3.3 square metres. Petrov alleged numerous specific grievances: lack of fresh air; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; infestation of the cell with insects and rodents; lack of privacy for the toilet; lack of toiletries; lack or insufficient quantity of food; no or insufficient disinfection of barbering and haircutting tools; no or restricted access to a shower; overcrowding; and poor quality of food.

The second applicant, **Vitaliy Volodymyrovych Korostylyov**, born 25 January 1954, was held at Dnipro Penitentiary Facility no. 4 from 30 October 2013, pending, for more than 5 years, 6 months and 11 days. The space per inmate was 3.3 square metres. Korostylyov alleged: infestation of the cell with insects and rodents; lack of fresh air; lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; lack of privacy for the toilet; lack of toiletries; lack or insufficient quantity of food; a mouldy or dirty cell; no or restricted access to a shower; overcrowding; passive smoking; and no or restricted access to warm water.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the lengthy periods of detention, the very limited cell space per inmate, and the cumulative material conditions of confinement. Both applicants alleged overcrowding and severe deficiencies in hygiene, sanitation, ventilation, food, bedding, privacy and access to showers. Korostylyov also alleged passive smoking and a mouldy or dirty cell, while Petrov alleged inadequate disinfection of barbering and haircutting tools. The applicants further claimed that no effective domestic remedy existed in Ukrainian law to address these detention conditions.

The Court’s task was to assess whether these conditions, individually or cumulatively, amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment and whether the absence of an effective domestic remedy violated the Convention. The main body of the judgment refers to the appended table for the list of applicants and the relevant details of the applications. The judgment was adopted on 20 June 2019 and delivered on 11 July 2019.
001-194106:
**Case Name:** *Haddad v. Spain* (Application no. 16572/17), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 18 June 2019.

The applicant, Mr Wael Haddad, a Syrian national living in Madrid, fled Syria in January 2012 with his Spanish wife and their three minor children because of the armed conflict. One month after arriving in Spain, his wife lodged a criminal complaint of domestic violence. On 2 February 2012, the Coslada judge no. 1 issued a protection order barring the applicant from approaching or communicating with his wife and children, requiring him to wear a tracking bracelet, and temporarily withdrawing his parental responsibility and contact rights. His wife nevertheless twice left an emergency shelter and returned to live with him despite the barring order; the applicant was arrested for violating it but released.

In June 2012, after the mother said she could no longer care for the children, the Madrid regional government declared the three children abandoned and assumed guardianship under the urgent procedure. The applicant was not informed. The children were placed in residential care in Murcia, and in July 2012 Murcia took over guardianship; the mother was allowed visits. In February 2013, the applicant, through the Spanish Muslim Association, sought information and contact, but the child protection department said there were no plans to return the children and that visits by outsiders were undesirable. A guardianship hearing notice was published in the official gazette, and child protection staff telephoned him twice. He did not attend, saying he would appeal if necessary. In April 2013 the children were placed in the care of the child protection department; a notification was sent but left at the post office and not collected.

Reports in June and July 2013 referred to alleged physical and emotional abuse by the applicant and criticised the mother’s vulnerable personality, instability, lack of resources and parenting capacity. They recommended placing the daughter in foster care with a view to adoption and suspending birth-family contact. In September 2013, the regional child protection board decided on temporary foster care with a view to adoption. The daughter was placed with a foster family, and the pre-adoption proposal made no provision for visits by her birth parents.

A key development was the applicant’s acquittal. On 27 September 2013, the criminal court acquitted him of all domestic-violence charges and set aside the earlier criminal and civil measures. The acquittal became final in November 2013. The applicant then contacted child protection, reported stable work and income, and requested contact with his children. In February/March 2014, the department refused contact with his daughter and provisionally refused contact with his sons, noting the daughter’s good adjustment to pre-adoption fostering and the sons’ fear of their father.

In May 2014 the applicant appealed the daughter’s foster placement. In February 2015 the Murcia first-instance judge authorised her placement in foster care with a view to adoption, finding it served her development and best interests. The applicant appealed, arguing that he had been acquitted, had never been assessed as a possible carer, and that abandonment had resulted from the mother’s conduct and their flight from war. The regional government replied that he had shown no interest after June 2012 and had not appealed the administrative care decision. In April 2016 the Audiencia Provincial dismissed his appeal, relying on the child’s best interests, her strong bonds with the foster family, and the serious harm removal would cause. His two sons were returned to him in February 2016. His constitutional amparo appeal was declared inadmissible in October 2016 for lack of constitutional significance.

The case concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention arising from the declaration of abandonment, the daughter’s foster-care/adoption-oriented placement, the denial of contact, and the alleged failure to consider the father’s rights and his subsequent acquittal.
001-198472:
In P.R. v. Austria (Application no. 200/15), the applicant was an Austrian national, born in 1968 and living in Vienna. After completing legal studies at Karl-Franzens-University Graz, he was awarded the academic degree Magister iuris in February 1997 and received a diploma certificate (Sponsionsurkunde) bearing his then surname, S.

In 2010 the applicant applied to the Vienna Municipality to change his surname from S. to R. He relied on section 2(1)(10) of the Name Amendment Act 1988, which permits a surname change where the applicant credibly shows it is necessary to avoid unacceptable economic or social disadvantages that cannot otherwise be avoided. He claimed he had suffered discrimination because of the “oriental origin” of his surname and submitted empirical studies. On 12 February 2010 the Vienna Municipality granted the change. The decision was constitutive and had ex nunc effect, but it contained no detailed reasoning.

The applicant then asked the University of Graz on 6 May 2010 to issue either a rectified diploma certificate or a notice of award (Verleihungsbescheid) bearing his new surname. On 19 August 2010 the university’s Director of Studies rejected the request. He found no legal basis to issue a new document: the degree had been awarded under the old law; the name change had no retroactive effect; and since August 1997 degrees had been awarded by formal written decision, so issuing a new notice would amount to a second award of the same degree. On 11 November 2011 the University Senate dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It held that the right to hold an academic degree was linked to the person awarded it, not to a subsequently changed name. Although the name-change ground under section 2(1)(10) applied to the applicant, the Municipality’s decision did not oblige the university to amend diploma certificates.

The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court that the refusal violated, among other rights, Article 8 of the Convention. He argued that he had lawfully changed his name to avoid discrimination, but without an amended diploma he would have to submit the old certificate to potential employers. That would force him to reveal his former surname and produce the Municipality’s name-change decision, requiring explanations and causing social stigmatisation. On 11 June 2012 the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the complaint as unlikely to succeed. It found no sufficient indication of a rights violation, noting that laws such as the Non-Discrimination Act could address discriminatory treatment by employers. The case was remitted to the Administrative Court, which dismissed the complaint on 26 June 2014. It held that there was no subjective right to have all previously issued documents changed after a name change, and no provision requiring university authorities to act after a degree had been awarded. It saw no reason to seek constitutional review of the applicable law.

Relevant domestic law provided that a name change under the Name Amendment Act is constitutive and ex nunc. Personal-status law treats a person’s name and academic degree as personal-status data; authorities issue personal-status documents reflecting the current register, and identity documents can be renewed to include the academic degree. Under the old university law, degrees were certified in a ceremony with a certificate containing the recipient’s name; under the 1997 and 2002 laws, degrees are awarded by formal written decision. Unjustified use of an academic degree is punishable by a fine of up to EUR 15,000.

The alleged violation was therefore that Austria’s refusal to issue a new diploma certificate after a lawful surname change breached the applicant’s right to respect for private life under Article 8 ECHR.
001-199381:
**Case A.S. v. Norway** (Application no. 60371/15) concerned a Polish national, A.S., living in Norway, and her son X, born in December 2009 after artificial insemination. X had no registered father, and A.S. had sole parental responsibility. From April 2010, when X was under four months old, child welfare services received numerous notifications from health visitors and family members alleging a lack of interaction between A.S. and X. After attempts at assistance and guidance failed, X was placed in an emergency foster home on 27 March 2012, aged two years and three months.

On 18 September 2012, the County Social Welfare Board ordered that X be placed in long-term foster care, finding pervasive and extensive deficiencies in A.S.’s caregiving and serious neglect of X’s physical and emotional needs. Contact rights were set at two hours twice a year under supervision, later reduced to one hour twice a year. The Board indicated that the placement was intended to be long-term, so contact was meant only to let X know his origins, not to maintain an attachment or prepare for reunification. The City Court confirmed the care order on 25 February 2013.

In spring 2014, A.S. sought termination of the foster placement or, alternatively, extended contact. On 5 November 2014, the County Social Welfare Board rejected her request after a two-day hearing with eleven witnesses. It denied her contact rights and also decided she should not be informed of X’s whereabouts. A.S. brought the case to the City Court, which heard fourteen witnesses, including her GP, psychiatrist, a counsellor, and two privately engaged psychologists. The court refused to appoint its own expert or to allow the private experts to observe A.S. and X together.

In its judgment of 27 March 2015, the City Court found that A.S. would not be able to provide X with proper care at that time or in the future. It relied heavily on X’s vulnerability and special needs. Before entering care, X had shown low cognitive, motor and linguistic functioning, emotional flatness, eating problems, compulsive behaviour, and excessive sleep needs, with possible autism-spectrum symptoms. After placement, he improved significantly and formed a secure attachment to his foster parents, whom he called mum and dad. An expert testified that X had suffered relational and developmental trauma while in his mother’s care, leaving him highly vulnerable to change and stress. Returning him to A.S. would seriously jeopardise his mental health. The court also found A.S.’s basic intuitive parenting skills remained inadequate and that courses and work experience had not changed this. Contact sessions showed she still could not see X’s perspective, and X had severe reactions after contact, especially in November 2014, including regression, bed-wetting, and retching, lasting two months. The court therefore denied contact, finding exceptional and strong reasons because the risk of harm to X outweighed A.S.’s interests. It also withheld the foster parents’ address, concluding that although kidnapping risk was not substantiated, A.S. would likely make unannounced contact, causing disproportionate harm to X.

The High Court refused leave to appeal on 22 May 2015, and the Supreme Court’s Committee on Leave to Appeal rejected her appeal on 3 July 2015. A.S. alleged that the refusal to terminate foster care, the denial of contact, and the withholding of information about X’s whereabouts violated her and X’s right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention.
