001-196893:
**Summary**

*Samoylenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 45050/10) concerned an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 2 August 2010 by Oleg Nikolayevich Samoylenko, a Ukrainian national born in 1962. The Fifth Section Committee judgment was delivered on 24 October 2019. The applicant complained that the Ukrainian authorities failed to give relevant and sufficient reasons to justify his pre-trial detention, that court decisions extending his detention in April and June 2010 were taken in his and his lawyer’s absence, and that no effective procedure existed for him to challenge the lawfulness of his detention. These complaints implicated, in substance, the right to reasoned pre-trial detention and the right to judicial review of detention. The applicant died on 6 October 2017; his wife, Tatyana Samoylenko, later expressed the wish to pursue the proceedings. Notice had been given to the Government on 9 December 2015.

The key facts began on 8 February 2010, when the Dnipropetrovsk regional prosecutor’s office arrested the applicant on suspicion of fraudulent business activities. On 11 February 2010, the Zhovtneviy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk extended his custody to ten days for a personality assessment. On 18 February 2010, the District Court ordered his detention on remand. It relied on findings that he was unemployed, had poor character references from his place of residence, and could potentially influence witnesses or abscond. The applicant, represented by counsel, appealed, stressing that he had no prior criminal record, a permanent residence, a family to support, including a pregnant wife and ailing elderly parents, and health conditions that might worsen in detention. On 24 February 2010, the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the detention order. It found no evidence that his health was incompatible with detention and noted that the offence was quite serious, punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment.

The alleged violations mainly arose from subsequent extensions. On 6 April 2010, the District Court extended detention until 8 June 2010, citing the need for further investigation and the absence of grounds for release. That hearing took place with the prosecutor but without the applicant or his lawyer; the applicant claimed they were not summoned. He appealed, but according to him the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on an unspecified date, again with only the prosecutor present and without summoning him or his lawyer. He did not submit a copy of that appellate decision. On 7 June 2010, the Court of Appeal, acting as a first-instance court, extended detention until 8 July 2010. It stated there were no grounds for release. The hearing was held with the prosecutor; the applicant said he and his lawyer were not summoned. That decision was not subject to appeal.

Later, the criminal case was transferred to a trial court and the applicant’s detention was maintained. On 6 September and 28 October 2010, he applied for release pending trial. On 2 November 2010, the trial court dismissed the applications as unfounded. It found the imputed crimes serious enough to potentially warrant ten years or more imprisonment, noted that he pleaded not guilty and refused to testify, and ruled—without details—that he might influence witnesses and obstruct proceedings if released.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that his detention was extended without sufficient reasoning, that he was excluded from key hearings, and that he lacked an effective avenue to challenge the lawfulness of his detention.
001-194188:
In *Korban v. Ukraine* (ECtHR, 4 July 2019), the applicant was a Ukrainian politician, former deputy head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional State Administration, and leader of the UKROP party, which sharply criticised President Poroshenko. He complained under Article 3 about ill-treatment during transport, forced participation in court hearings after heart surgery, and confinement in a metal cage; under Article 5 §§ 1, 3, 4 and 5 about unlawful detention; under Article 18 read with Article 5 about politically motivated detention; and under Article 6 § 2 about public statements breaching the presumption of innocence.

From August 2014, criminal proceedings were opened against him concerning alleged kidnapping of officials, car theft, embezzlement of charity funds, creation of a criminal organisation, and interference with an electoral officer. On 31 October 2015, a Prosecutor General’s Office investigator, accompanied by special forces, forced entry into his home in Dnipropetrovsk and arrested him. The arrest report relied on a template ground that eyewitnesses had identified him as the offender, but left the space for “specific facts and data” blank. He was taken to Kyiv. On 2 November 2015, he was transported 150 km to Chernigiv in an ordinary minibus; he alleged he was held from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. without food, water or toilet access, while the Government denied this.

On 3 November, when the 72-hour arrest period expired, he was released in the courtroom but immediately re-arrested at 8:42 a.m. on a new charge of aggravated interference with an electoral officer, again using the same template arrest ground. He complained that both arrests were unlawful and arbitrary, but domestic courts rejected or failed to properly examine the complaints. On 6 November he was placed under 24-hour house arrest with an electronic tag; on 28 December this was replaced by pre-trial detention.

On 25 December 2015 he was admitted to the Amosov Institute with ischemic heart disease, hypertensive crisis, acute coronary syndrome and unstable angina, and underwent urgent coronary angioplasty with two stents. Despite his postoperative condition, hearings were held from 26 to 28 December 2015 on changing his preventive measure. He was brought to court in a wheelchair with a medication infusion device; the hearings ran through the weekend and night, lasting about thirty hours. The judge ordered his detention to secure attendance. He alleged that being forced to participate while so weak amounted to Article 3 ill-treatment. During hearings on 13, 22 and 25 January 2016, he was held in a metal cage, later replaced by a transparent box.

Under Article 5, he alleged unlawful arrest and re-arrest without judicial warrant, ineffective judicial review, and lack of compensation. Under Article 18 read with Article 5, he argued his detention was politically motivated: he led an opposition party, ran in elections, and was arrested after criticising the President; officials publicly described him as a criminal-group leader. Under Article 6 § 2, he cited statements by the President, the Head of the Security Service, the Prosecutor General’s assistant, and an investigator calling him the leader of a criminal group involved in kidnappings, embezzlement and illegal arms, before any conviction. Several charges were later discontinued for lack of evidence; he had earlier entered a friendly settlement and received a suspended sentence for one kidnapping charge.
001-199168:
**Kardava v. Ukraine (Application no. 19886/09)** concerned a Georgian national, Tamaz Kardava, who was arrested in Kyiv on 7 August 2008 on suspicion of robbery; narcotic drugs were found on him. He was taken to the Shevchenkivskyy District police station and initially detained under the Code of Administrative Offences. On 10 August 2008 an investigator ordered his custody on suspicion of robbery and drug possession, and on 12 August 2008 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court remanded him. His pre-trial detention was later extended, and in July 2009 his case was referred to trial. Requests for release in October 2009 and March 2010, based largely on his health, were refused because the court found no evidence that he would not evade investigation or obstruct the truth, and considered his poor health insufficient to alter the preventive measure.

The applicant complained under Article 3 that police officers ill-treated him and that authorities failed to investigate. He alleged he was beaten during his arrest on 7 August 2008 and again on police premises; on 11 August 2008 officers allegedly beat and abused him to obtain a confession. Medical records noted haematomas on his right shoulder and left thigh and a closed chest injury on 11 August. On 15 August his health deteriorated and he was hospitalised with a closed head injury, multiple blunt internal injuries including kidney contusion, and a broken rib; he also had chronic hepatitis C and other conditions. From 14 August 2008, the applicant, his family and his lawyer complained to prosecutors, courts and the Ombudsman. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open criminal proceedings—on 8 September and 9 December 2008 and 9 April, 8 October and 10 December 2009—finding his allegations unfounded. Higher prosecutors or courts quashed those refusals because inquiries were not full or objective. On 30 March 2010 a court noted that the December 2008 forensic report had not analysed his August–October 2008 medical records and that his injuries, the applicant and the doctors should be verified. On 24 June 2010 the prosecutor again refused to investigate, relying on the December 2008 report.

The applicant also complained under Articles 2 and 3 that detention authorities failed to provide adequate medical assistance. He was held mainly in Kyiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO). Between 15 August and 2 October 2008 he was treated in hospital for injuries and illnesses; doctors reported improvement but recommended continued neurological inpatient treatment. Later examinations noted after-effects of head injury, chronic hepatitis C, gastroduodenitis, heart disease, hypertension and other conditions. In November 2009, after deterioration with cirrhosis and portal hypertension, he was placed in the SIZO medical unit; doctors found no grounds for urgent external hospitalisation, though it was “advisable.” In February 2010 he was taken to hospital with severe liver failure, hepatorenal syndrome and other conditions. He returned to the SIZO in March 2010, where doctors suggested transfer to a hospital in Bucha Correctional Colony; he refused, citing solitary confinement and lack of facilities. On 1 April 2010 he was taken to Kyiv Emergency Hospital, where he died on 7 April 2010. An autopsy found pulmonary heart disease, pneumonia with abscess, splenomegaly and cirrhosis. Investigations into his death were refused in October 2010, quashed in March 2011, and again refused in April 2011. These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations.
001-196423:
In *Milovanović v. Serbia*, the applicant, Ms Mirjana Milovanović, a Serbian national, complained that Serbian authorities failed to enforce domestic child-custody decisions and to facilitate her reunion with her children. The case concerns a prolonged custody dispute.

The applicant had twins, D. and K., in May 1996 with M.M. She left the matrimonial home in March 2001. In January 2002, while returning from a medical check-up, M.M. intercepted her, took the children, and until 2010 systematically prevented contact, threatening violence. He moved with the children into a house he had begun building.

In 2002 the applicant sought divorce, sole custody and maintenance. In June 2002 the Belgrade Second Municipal Court divorced the parties and awarded custody to her; in September 2002 the District Court upheld the divorce but quashed the custody decision. In November 2002 she sought interim custody. On 27 February 2003 the Municipal Court issued an interim custody order requiring M.M. to hand over the children within 24 hours. It became enforceable on 14 June 2003 but was never enforced.

On 6 October 2005 the Municipal Court granted the applicant sole custody, set M.M.’s contact rights and maintenance, and barred his contact for three months. It noted his destructive behaviour and the children’s appalling living conditions—lack of hygiene, windows and water—requiring immediate removal. The judgment became final on 16 November 2006 and enforceable on 9 January 2007, but remained unenforced.

Enforcement efforts included fines of RSD 5,000, 20,000 and 25,000, but bailiffs found no assets. Attempts in 2003–2004 to reunite the family failed because M.M.’s house was empty or he was absent. A June 2005 transfer at the children’s school failed: the children were terrified and rejected their mother, and the social care centre sent only a lawyer, not its expert team. A September 2005 social report found the applicant had good parental capacity but considered disrupting the children’s current living arrangement not to be in their best interests; enforcement was terminated, then that decision was quashed in April 2006. In 2007 social services advised that enforcement was in the children’s best interests, but in February 2008 the enforcement court terminated enforcement of the interim order because it was no longer valid and told the applicant to file a new request under the final judgment.

In March 2008 enforcement was ordered for the final judgment. M.M.’s appeal was rejected in April 2009. Hearings followed in 2009–2010. In October 2009 the children said they wished to meet their mother and suggested weekend visits; the court ordered counselling and weekend stays, but M.M. obstructed contact. Social services advised against forcible enforcement; in April 2010 contact was reduced to Tuesdays and Sundays. The file was later transferred to criminal and constitutional courts, causing further delay. The final custody judgment remained unenforced, and contact was sporadic.

M.M. was convicted in 2006 of child abduction for failing to hand over the children, receiving a suspended sentence; he was acquitted in December 2012, with appeal pending. Deprivation of parental rights proceedings were later withdrawn.

In February 2009 the applicant filed a constitutional appeal. In May 2012 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a fair trial due to protracted enforcement of the final custody judgment, ordered expedited enforcement, dismissed the interim-order complaint as out of time, and awarded no damages.

The applicant alleged that, despite enforceable interim and final custody orders, Serbian authorities failed to take effective measures—fines, bailiff action, social-service and police support, and forcible transfer where necessary—to enforce custody and facilitate her reunion with her children.
001-192983:
**Kamenova v. Bulgaria** (Application no. 61731/11) is a European Court of Human Rights case lodged on 9 September 2011 by Ms Hristina Georgieva Kamenova, a Bulgarian national born in 1947 and living in Vratsa. The case concerns the prolonged failure of the Bulgarian authorities to complete the restitution of land formerly owned by her father.

In 1991, following adoption of the Agricultural Land Act, which provided for restitution of formerly collectivised land, the applicant applied for restitution. On 20 May 1996, the Oryahovo land commission decided that the heirs of the applicant’s father—the applicant and her sister—were entitled to restitution of, among other property, an 11,800-square-metre plot classified as “forest.” The decision stated that the heirs had established the father’s title by notarial deed and that the plot was “situated in an area under section 4” of the transitional provisions of the Agricultural Land Act. Section 4 concerned plots formerly offered by the Communist authorities for private use; those use rights were to be discontinued, and restitution to pre-collectivisation owners could occur only after preparation of a detailed cadastral plan and a plan of newly created plots.

After 1996, the applicant repeatedly contacted authorities seeking completion of the restitution and was told to await those plans. The relevant plans for Oryahovo municipality were approved in 2010. In 2012, the Ministry of Agriculture and Forests told her that completion of restitution for section 4 plots was within the municipality’s competence. However, on 23 April 2013, the municipality informed her that her plot was not within the section 4 area, was not covered by the newly created plots plan, and was considered State property managed by the Ministry. The Ministry then directed her to its local branch, the Oryahovo Agriculture Department.

On 21 August 2013, the Department confirmed that the municipality lacked competence but told the applicant she had either to have the exact borders of her plot identified in a different procedure concerning land not covered by section 4, or to apply for restitution under the Forests Restitution Act, for which the relevant time-limits had already expired. On 11 April 2017, the Department stated that the 1996 decision was final and that the time-limit for seeking its revocation or rectification had expired. The Ministry then instructed the applicant to submit a written request under section 45d of the Regulations on the Application of the Agricultural Land Act. That instruction was repeated by the Vratsa Regional Directorate and the Ministry in June and August 2017.

On 8 September 2017, the Department listed the documents needed to complete restitution: a section 45d written request; an inheritance certificate; notarial deeds, court decisions and other title documents; municipality documents concerning the section 4 procedure; and a geodesist’s plan showing the plot’s exact borders. On 19 September 2017, the applicant submitted only the section 45d request, without the remaining documents. The Department reiterated the need for those documents in October and November 2017 and requested relevant documents ex officio from the municipality. No further developments were reported.

Under domestic law, section 45d requires a written request to the Agriculture Department after a restitution-right decision becomes final, but a decision ordering restitution can only be taken after the exact borders of the plot have been traced. The Forests Restitution Act, enacted in 1997, had set a 30 June 1999 application deadline; a later alternative action to establish entitlement was revoked in 2007. The alleged violation therefore concerned the authorities’ prolonged and unresolved failure to finalise the restitution and give effect to the applicant’s recognised property right.
001-190025:
In *Beketov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 44436/09, judgment of 19 February 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by a Ukrainian national under Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention. The applicant, born in 1970, had undergone surgery for an umbilical hernia in April 2007.

On 9 or 10 February 2008 he was arrested in connection with suspicion of abduction and murder and placed in a cell at the Shevchenkivskyy district police station in Kyiv. He alleged that between 10 and 16 February 2008 police officers beat him to force a confession. In particular, Officer G., the first deputy head of the police station, allegedly kicked him in the face and abdomen, injuring the area of his prior hernia operation. On 16 February 2008 he confessed and signed undated documents. That same day he was transferred to the Kyiv Temporary Detention Facility (ITT), where a medical examination noted a bruise under his right eye, classified as a minor physical injury.

According to the applicant, the Kyiv Pre-trial Detention Centre (SIZO) refused to admit him because of his poor health. He was returned to the ITT, and an ambulance took him to the Kyiv Medical Emergency Hospital, where he stayed from 20 to 25 February 2008 and was treated for “contusion to the abdomen and facial tissue.” On 26 February 2008 he was placed in the SIZO, where a doctor diagnosed a post-operative condition following his 2007 hernia operation.

His defence lawyer complained to the prosecutor’s office about ill-treatment in May and August 2008, naming Officer G. Between September 2008 and 2013, the prosecutor’s office repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings, finding no constituent elements of an offence. Domestic courts quashed those decisions multiple times because investigators failed to question the applicant, Officer G., cellmates, ITT and SIZO staff, emergency medical personnel, and arresting officers; failed to establish the origin of the applicant’s injuries; and failed to follow court instructions. In 2013 the matter was entered into the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations, but proceedings were again terminated and decisions quashed. No final information about further developments was provided.

The applicant also alleged inadequate medical treatment in detention. He suffered constant abdominal pain, navel fistula, suture sinus, omphalitis, a urachal cyst, and cardiac and other conditions. SIZO doctors provided outpatient treatment and antiseptics, and surgeons recommended elective surgery. In September 2009, during a court hearing, an ambulance team suspected peritonitis and recommended urgent hospitalisation, but the prison escort allegedly refused. In October 2009 the Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 requiring appropriate medical treatment; it was lifted in December 2009. In January 2010 the applicant was hospitalised at Buchanska Prison Hospital and underwent surgery to remove the navel fistula. The Government later said medical documentation after February 2010 had been lost.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant alleged that SIZO cells lacked natural light, had dim electric light constantly on, beds without mattresses or linen, and poor-quality and insufficient food. He also alleged that on court hearing days he received no food or water because Ukrainian law made no provision and court buildings had no facilities. Under Article 13, he complained that no effective domestic remedies existed for these violations. These facts formed the basis of his Article 3 complaints concerning ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, inadequate medical care, poor detention conditions, and lack of food and water on hearing days, as well as his Article 13 complaint.
001-191359:
The case concerns eight applications against Ukraine: application no. 54503/08 and seven others. The applicants are Viktor Viktorovych Korol and seven other individuals. The applications were lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention on the various dates set out in the appended table. Notice of the applications was given to the Ukrainian Government.

The applicants complained that they did not receive adequate medical care in detention. Some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention. The supplied record does not identify the specific Convention provisions or the substance of those additional complaints.

The appended table gives the following details:

- Eduard Lvovich Soloveychik, born 20 October 1981, application no. 25725/09, lodged on 30 March 2009, represented by Olga Viktorovna Belyayeva of Dnipro, principal medical conditions: HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis and hepatitis.
- Andrey Vladimirovich Dubrova, born 15 August 1975, application no. 51967/09, lodged on 5 July 2009, represented by Taras Oleksandrovych Kalmykov of Kharkiv, principal medical condition: HIV/AIDS.
- Oleksiy Ivanovych Kravchenko, born 20 January 1956, application no. 65987/09, lodged on 16 November 2009, no representative listed, principal medical condition: peptic ulcer.
- Yevgeniy Anatolyevich Levchenko, born 11 March 1974, application no. 29273/10, lodged on 28 May 2010, represented by Oleg Igorovych Veremiyenko of Kyiv, principal medical conditions: HIV/AIDS and tuberculosis.
- Ruslan Petrovych Drygin, born 27 December 1981, application no. 38721/10, lodged on 2 July 2010, represented by Andriy Anatoliyovych Kristenko of Kharkiv, principal medical condition: consolidated ankle fracture.
- Ivan Sergiyovych Zhukov, born 11 July 1984, application no. 54570/16, lodged on 19 September 2016, represented by Vasyl Ivanovych Melnychuk of Kyiv, principal medical condition: kidney disease.

001-188991:
In *Ēcis v. Latvia*, the applicant, Mr Mārtiņš Ēcis, a Latvian national born in 1981, was convicted in December 2001 of kidnapping, aggravated murder and aggravated extortion and sentenced to twenty years’ imprisonment. The conviction became final in 2002. Under section 504(1) of the Sentence Enforcement Code, he was initially placed at the maximum-security level of a closed prison and was later transferred to the medium-security level of that closed prison. He alleged that this prison regime discriminated against him on the ground of sex, contrary to Article 14 of the Convention read in conjunction with Article 8. He argued that male prisoners convicted of serious or especially serious crimes began serving their sentences in closed prisons, while women convicted of the same crimes began serving their sentences in partly-closed prisons. This difference affected restrictions on visits, telephone calls, progression between security levels, and eligibility for prison leave.

The key event arose in 2008. On 30 September 2008 the applicant was informed that his father had died. On 2 October 2008 he requested permission to leave prison to attend the funeral. The prison director refused, stating that he had no authority to grant leave because the applicant was serving his sentence at the medium-security level of a closed prison. Under the Sentence Enforcement Code, only prisoners serving at the medium- or minimum-security level of partly-closed prisons were eligible for such leave. The applicant claimed that a woman convicted of comparable offences would have been placed in a partly-closed prison and would therefore have been able to attend the funeral. The alleged discrimination was thus directly connected to the refusal of compassionate leave.

He pursued domestic remedies. The Ministry of Justice rejected his complaint, reasoning that the legislature had chosen different sentence-execution frameworks for men and women and that there was no discrimination because both sexes were imprisoned and subject to restrictions. The Ombudsperson found the restriction proportionate and necessary, noting that closed prisons housed particularly dangerous convicts under tightened security and maximum surveillance. The Constitutional Court declined to institute proceedings on three complaints in 2008. It held that the applicant’s legal reasoning was evidently insufficient, mainly because he had not demonstrated that men and women convicted of serious crimes were in comparable situations, and because he had not specified the human right in conjunction with which he alleged discrimination. In his third complaint, he added the funeral refusal and referred to private life, family life and freedom of expression.

The relevant domestic law provided that both closed and partly-closed prisons had maximum, medium and minimum security levels. All prisoners began at the maximum level under a progressive sentence-execution system. Section 504(1) placed men sentenced for serious or especially serious crimes in closed prisons, while section 505(1) placed women serving sentences for intentionally committed crimes in partly-closed prisons. Prisoners in closed prisons, regardless of security level, and those at the maximum level in partly-closed prisons, could not receive prison leave. Only prisoners at the medium or minimum level in partly-closed prisons could leave for up to seven days annually, or up to five days following the death or life-threatening illness of a close relative. International materials cited included the Nelson Mandela Rules, the Bangkok Rules, the European Prison Rules and CPT reports, which emphasised non-discrimination, individualised security and allowing prisoners to attend funerals when circumstances permit. The applicant lodged his application on 12 December 2008; the discrimination complaint was communicated to the Government on 25 March 2015, while the remainder was declared inadmissible.
001-193994:
In *Svit Rozvag, TOV and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 13290/11 and 2 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 27 June 2019, final on 27 September 2019. The applicants were two Ukrainian companies and one Ukrainian national. They held prepaid multi-year gambling licences, each having paid the equivalent of EUR 150,000, and generally operated gambling businesses. The first applicant operated at least fifteen gambling establishments in Kharkiv.

The case arose from Ukraine’s 2009 gambling ban. In late 2008 the Cabinet proposed a new regulatory system that would allow existing licensees time to comply and preserve licences for their issued terms. In March 2009 two MPs introduced a competing bill for total prohibition of gambling from 1 January 2010, citing crime and youth gambling. On 7 May 2009 a fire at a gambling establishment in Dnipro killed nine people and injured eleven, drawing public attention. That same day the Cabinet instructed the Ministry of Finance to suspend all gambling licences for one month. On 8 May the Ministry suspended all licences until 7 June 2009. On 15 May Parliament adopted the Prohibition Law, banning gambling except limited activities such as lotteries, with no compensation provision. The President vetoed it, citing property protections, lack of grounds for collective licence revocation, and committed business expenses; Parliament overrode the veto on 11 June. The law entered into force on 25 June 2009, and the applicants’ licences were deemed revoked by operation of law.

The applicants sought compensation in domestic courts but failed. The first applicant claimed damages initially about UAH 11,461,690 (about EUR 905,426), later increased to about EUR 3,219,900, for unused licence fees, gambling equipment, tax-control software, premises refurbishment, and lost profit. It argued that the five-year licence was a guaranteed property right, that the Licensing Law allowed only individual revocation on specified grounds, and relied on Civil Code provisions including the “Legislative Takings Clause” requiring compensation for lawful termination of property rights. The commercial courts dismissed the claim, finding no unlawful State action, noting the Prohibition Law had not been declared unconstitutional and provided no compensation; appeal courts also did not address Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 or ECtHR case-law. The second applicant separately claimed reimbursement of unused licence fees (about UAH 360,349.59, roughly EUR 30,160), also rejected. She also challenged the Cabinet and Ministry’s one-month licence suspension; the first-instance administrative court found it unlawful, but the appellate court quashed that ruling, citing the Cabinet’s constitutional power to instruct ministries.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that the prohibition and revocation of their previously acquired multi-year licences violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The second applicant additionally alleged a breach based on the Ministry’s 8 May 2009 suspension shortly before total prohibition. The first and second applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 that domestic courts failed to give sufficient reasons, particularly by not addressing their arguments under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and the Court’s case-law. The first and third applicants alleged under Article 13 that they lacked an effective remedy for the alleged property-rights infringement. On 3 November 2017 notice was given to the Government; remaining complaints were declared inadmissible.
001-189621:
**Summary of *Andreyeva v. Ukraine* (Application no. 24385/10)**

The applicant, Ms Yevdokiya Ivanovna Andreyeva, a Ukrainian national born in 1935 and living in Snizhne, Donetsk region, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights concerning the death of her son and the alleged failure of the Ukrainian authorities to conduct an effective investigation.

On 14 January 2004, the applicant's son, born in 1967, was found dead in her barn. The same day, police officers inspected the scene and reported that he had committed suicide by hanging. On 24 January 2004, the investigator of the Snizhne Prosecutor's Office refused to initiate criminal proceedings after pre-investigation inquiries, finding no elements of a crime. On 11 February 2004, a forensic medical examination concluded that death was caused by strangulation by a rope loop, possibly resulting from the body's weight pulling against the rope, with no other injuries found.

On 5 April 2005, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office quashed the 24 January 2004 decision as premature and unfounded, finding that possible reasons for suicide had not been examined and that relatives and acquaintances had not been questioned. Numerous investigating instructions were issued. Between 2005 and 2012, investigators questioned various persons and ordered additional medical examinations. Medical experts eventually noted numerous fractures on the son's body, opining they were inflicted after death, possibly during exhumation. The applicant's husband informed authorities that when he saw the corpse, it was in a sitting position and the rope loop was not tightened. The applicant argued it was a violent murder, suspecting several individuals: police security guards who allegedly took her son from a local bar before he was found dead; a local police officer who had a dispute with him; a woman employed by him and her husband; his brothers-in-law; a business partner; and people from a local gambling club, as her son transported money from the club.

Investigators refused to initiate criminal proceedings on 25 April 2005, 26 March 2006, 20 August 2008, 17 February and 12 December 2011, 15 February 2012, and 17 September 2012, each time on the ground that no elements of a crime were established. These decisions were repeatedly quashed by supervising authorities as unsubstantiated, with further investigative measures ordered and numerous instructions given.

On 7 December 2012, relying on the new Code of Criminal Procedure, the applicant requested an investigation into the alleged murder. Criminal proceedings were instituted that day. However, they were terminated on 24 December 2012, 22 July and 30 September 2013 because no elements of a crime could be established. Those decisions were quashed by supervising authorities. Notably, on 5 December 2013, the Snizhne Town Court quashed the 30 September 2013 decision, finding the investigation had not been thorough or comprehensive. The court noted that the possible involvement of local police had not been properly examined, the role of the applicant's son's brother-in-law had not been clarified though he might have been the first to find the body, the applicant had not been questioned on all relevant issues, and evidence of her son's suicidal tendencies had not been assessed. On 1 April 2014, the criminal proceedings were closed once more on the ground that no elements of a crime could be established.

The case thus concerns the adequacy and effectiveness of the domestic investigation into the applicant's son's death between 2004 and 2014, including repeated refusals to initiate or continue proceedings and the failure to properly examine alternative theories of violent death.
001-192202:
**Summary of the Case of Bjarni Ármannsson v. Iceland**

The case of *Bjarni Ármannsson v. Iceland* (Application no. 72098/14) concerns an Icelandic national, Mr. Bjarni Ármannsson, who was the CEO of Glitnir, one of Iceland's largest banks, from 1997 to 2007. The case centers on his complaint that he was subjected to double punishment—both administrative tax penalties and criminal sanctions—for the same tax offences, violating the principle of *ne bis in idem* under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The events began in July 2009 when Iceland’s Directorate of Tax Investigation initiated an audit of the applicant’s tax returns, focusing on whether he had declared profits from selling shares received upon stepping down as CEO. After questioning the applicant and concluding its investigation in October 2010, the Directorate referred the matter to the Directorate of Internal Revenue for possible tax reassessment and informed the applicant of potential criminal proceedings. In May 2011, the Internal Revenue notified the applicant of reassessed taxes for 2007–2009, but this was later amended in January 2012, cancelling the reassessment related to the share sale profits.

On 15 May 2012, the Directorate of Internal Revenue issued a final ruling, finding that the applicant had failed to declare significant capital income from 2006 to 2008. It revised his tax returns upward, re-assessed his taxes, and imposed a 25% surcharge. The applicant paid both the taxes and the surcharge and did not appeal, so the decision became final in August 2012.

Meanwhile, in March 2012, the Directorate of Tax Investigation had referred the matter to the Special Prosecutor for criminal investigation. Despite objections from the applicant’s lawyer, the Special Prosecutor proceeded, and on 17 December 2012, indicted the applicant for aggravated tax offences for failing to declare income in his 2007–2009 tax returns, including capital income from property sales, dividends, interest, and foreign exchange gains from 2006 to 2008.

The applicant sought dismissal of the criminal case, arguing it violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, but the District Court rejected this on 23 April 2013. On 28 June 2013, the District Court convicted him, finding gross negligence sufficient for criminal liability under tax law. He was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years, and fined ISK 38,850,000 (approximately EUR 241,000). The fine accounted for the tax surcharges already imposed, though no calculation was detailed.

The applicant appealed, and on 15 May 2014, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction and fine but increased the suspended prison sentence to eight months. The Supreme Court also rejected his *ne bis in idem* claim.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that the applicant was first subjected to a final administrative tax penalty (re-assessment and 25% surcharge) for failing to declare income, and subsequently prosecuted and criminally punished for the same conduct. This dual process—administrative and criminal—for identical tax offences forms the basis of his complaint under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, which prohibits being tried or punished twice for the same offence. The domestic courts rejected this argument, leading to his application to the European Court of Human Rights.
001-195861:
**Case Summary: Živanović and Others v. Serbia (Application nos. 29171/16 and 8 others)**

The case of *Živanović and Others v. Serbia* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) by nine Serbian nationals. The applications, lodged between May 2016 and January 2017, all shared a common complaint: the excessive length of civil proceedings in violation of their right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were represented by a single lawyer, Ms. R. Dugošija.

The key facts of the case revolve around the prolonged duration of civil litigation for each applicant, which occurred across two or three levels of jurisdiction. The proceedings for the majority of the applicants began in 2005 or 2006 and concluded in 2013, with total lengths ranging from approximately six years and eight months to nearly eight years.

The specific details for each applicant are as follows:

- **Bogoljub Živanović:** Proceedings lasted from 20 September 2005 to 22 May 2013, a total of 7 years, 8 months, and 3 days. The case went through two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Zoran Stojković:** Proceedings lasted from 11 January 2006 to 5 June 2013, a total of 7 years, 4 months, and 26 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Mileta Joksimović and Dragan Tabaković:** Both applicants' proceedings lasted from 8 September 2005 to 21 August 2013, a total of 7 years, 11 months, and 14 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Goran Jolić:** Proceedings lasted from 28 August 2006 to 8 May 2013, a total of 6 years, 8 months, and 11 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Siniša Savković:** Proceedings lasted from 3 October 2005 to 20 February 2013, a total of 7 years, 4 months, and 18 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Dragan Savić and Ljubiša Đorđević:** These applicants had the longest proceedings, lasting from 8 September 2005 to 3 June 2016. This amounted to a total of 10 years, 8 months, and 27 days, spanning three levels of jurisdiction.
- **Vene Aleksov:** Proceedings lasted from 8 September 2005 to 23 October 2013, a total of 8 years, 1 month, and 16 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.

In all nine cases, the applicants sought redress at the national level by lodging a constitutional appeal with the Serbian Constitutional Court. However, in every instance, between November 2015 and September 2016, the Constitutional Court declared their appeals inadmissible.

The applicants subsequently turned to the ECtHR, alleging that the Serbian judicial system had failed to ensure their cases were heard within a "reasonable time," as required by Article 6 of the Convention. The ECtHR's judgment, delivered on 19 September 2019, addressed these common grievances regarding the systemic issue of judicial delays in Serbia.
001-198882:
**Radzevil v. Ukraine** (Application no. 36600/09) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Boris Radzevil, who lodged his application on 27 June 2009. He died on 12 January 2016, and his wife wished to pursue the proceedings. The European Court of Human Rights communicated the complaints concerning the applicant’s right not to incriminate himself, his right to defend himself through the legal representative of his choosing, and the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The facts arose from a road incident on 12 September 2002. The applicant was driving to work in a white Toyota when, near a pedestrian crossing, a pedestrian, G., began to cross the street. According to the applicant, an oncoming red vehicle passed at very high speed, after which G. suddenly fell into the applicant’s lane, possibly after being hit by that vehicle, slipping, or falling for another reason. The investigation and domestic courts nevertheless concluded that G. had been hit by the applicant’s car. The applicant stopped, placed G. in the rear seat, and an ambulance took G. to hospital; the applicant left before police arrived. G. died the same day from cerebral, chest and upper-limb injuries.

Later that day, the applicant went to the hospital to enquire about G. A police officer, T., asked why he was there. According to T., the applicant said he had accidentally hit G. with his car and agreed to show the accident site. Police then took him to the site and drew up a scene inspection report, although no traces of the accident were found. The applicant later denied showing the site or participating in that measure and noted that he had not signed the report.

Also on 12 September 2002, the applicant signed an “explanation” addressed to the Illichivsk police. It stated that G. had unexpectedly emerged from behind a moving vehicle as the applicant slowly drove through the pedestrian crossing and had fallen onto the bonnet of his car; when the applicant braked, G. fell onto the road. The document contained a note that the applicant had been familiarised with Article 63 of the Constitution, which protects the right not to incriminate oneself. The applicant later claimed that he had not had his glasses, had signed without reading, had not made the stated admission, and had not been properly informed of his right not to incriminate himself. He also alleged that the note about Article 63 was written in different ink and had been added later.

On 20 September 2002, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant for breaching traffic regulations causing a fatal accident. At some point, K., a licensed advocate, was admitted as his defence lawyer. On 11 December 2002, formal charges were brought, his status changed from suspect to accused, and he was placed under an obligation not to leave the town. According to the applicant, during questioning that day in the presence of his lawyer, he retracted the 12 September explanation, saying it had been given under psychological pressure.

The length complaint arose from delays after the case was sent to the Illichivsk Court. On 31 July 2003, the court remitted the case for additional pre-trial investigation. It returned to court on 15 October 2003. Hearings were adjourned several times due to absent witnesses. On 19 April 2004, the court ordered forensic medical, technical and reconstruction examinations; only some were carried out by 24 February 2005. The trial judge’s term expired on 30 March 2005, and a new judge took over on 29 November 2005. On 4 July 2006, the new judge ordered a fresh reconstruction because the 2004 order had apparently not been implemented; it was carried out on 10 July 2006. At trial, the applicant denied breaching traffic rules or hitting G. and argued that no expert evidence proved contact between his car and G.’s body. On 13 December 2006, the Illichivsk Court convicted him, sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment, deprived him of his driver’s licence for two years, and granted amnesty.
001-193590:
In *Clasens v. Belgium*, the applicant, John Clasens, a Belgian national born in 1983, was serving a final criminal sentence in Ittre Prison when a prison staff strike affected Brussels and Wallonia from 25 April to 22 June 2016. Because Belgian law at the time did not guarantee minimum prison services during strikes, ordinary detention regimes were suspended to varying degrees. Ittre Prison had 386 prisoners and 420 places; most cells were single-occupancy, about 9 m², with a wash basin and partitioned toilet.

From 26 April 2016, the regime at Ittre deteriorated sharply. According to a 3 May 2016 urgent order by the President of the Walloon Brabant Court of First Instance, prisoners had telephone calls only on 26, 29 and 30 April and 1 May; showers on 27 and 29 April and 1 May; exercise on 28 and 30 April; healthcare and medicines continued normally; but there were no family visits. Pickets blocked food-delivery lorries, raising the prospect that food supplies would stop by 5 May. The applicant and other prisoners brought an urgent application under Article 584 of the Judicial Code, alleging that these conditions violated Article 3 of the Convention. The judge partly granted relief, ordering the State to provide three meals per day, one hot; showers every other day; phone access every other day; two family visits per week; and access for lawyers and the Supervisory Board, subject to a €10,000 fine per infringement.

The State sought further court orders prohibiting blockades at prison entrances and mobilised police, prison directorates, civil protection, the Red Cross and the army. The CPT visited Ittre from 7 to 9 May 2016. It reported limited access to showers, medicines for anxiety and stress, collective exercise once a week, 24-hour cell confinement, interrupted canteen supplies, no cleaning or hygiene products, no visits, and insufficient staff to top up telephone accounts. After the strike ended, the Ittre Prison Supervisory Board found on 23 June 2016 that prisoners had had no lawyer visits before 16 June, almost no family visits, only one meal per day, telephone contact about every three days, and until 16 June left their cells only once every three days for exercise or a shower. No other activities were provided. A 25 May 2016 unannounced visit noted staff presence varying from 4 to 20, with police reinforcements and a night regime.

On appeal, the Brussels Court of Appeal largely upheld the 3 May 2016 order by judgment of 26 April 2017, though it reduced the fines to a maximum of €250 per day. Applying *Vasilescu v. Belgium* and *Muršić v. Croatia*, it found a prima facie breach of Article 3: prisoners were treated as objects at the mercy of striking staff, uncertain when the strike would end, confined to cells without activities, deprived of family and lawyer contact, and exposed to distress exceeding the suffering inherent in imprisonment.

Enforcement difficulties continued, and the applicant forwarded an order to pay outstanding fines; the State appealed. No minimum-service legislation existed during the strike, although a new Act of 23 March 2019 was adopted to guarantee minimum services from 1 July 2019. The CPT later issued a public statement describing the 2016 strikes as crossing a “red line” and creating conditions that could amount to inhuman or degrading treatment. The applicant alleged that his detention conditions violated Article 3 and that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.
001-197215:
The case *Baralija v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 30100/18) was brought by Irma Baralija, a Bosnian national born in 1984 and resident of Mostar. She is president of the local branch of the political party *Naša stranka*. She complained of her inability to vote and stand in local elections. Mostar, with a population of 105,797, is the cultural and economic capital of Herzegovina and one of the largest cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its last local elections were held in 2008.

The electoral deadlock stemmed from the legal regime for the Mostar City Council. Under the Election Act 2001 and the Statute of the City of Mostar, the 35-member Council was elected in a city-wide constituency and in six city-area constituencies, each electing three councillors. Residents of the Central Zone could vote only for the 17 city-wide councillors; they could not vote for area councillors and had no committee representation. In 2010, following a request from the Croat caucus, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared sections 19.2(1)-(3) and 19.4(2)-(8) of the Election Act 2001 and section 17(1) of the Mostar Statute unconstitutional. It found that the arrangement failed to secure equal suffrage, was incompatible with Article 25(b) of the ICCPR, and violated the constitutional prohibition of discrimination. The Court gave the Parliamentary Assembly six months to amend the provisions.

The Parliamentary Assembly did not do so. On 18 January 2012, the Constitutional Court adopted a ruling on non-enforcement, and the invalid provisions ceased to have effect on 28 February 2012. No new provisions regulating Mostar city council elections were adopted. As a result, local elections could not be held in Mostar in the 2012 or 2016 election cycles. By September 2019, the relevant legal framework still had not been adopted. The mayor, elected by the city council in 2009, continued in a “technical mandate.” Because the council could not be constituted, from 2013/2014 special entity legislation allowed the mayor to adopt the city budget in its place, renewed each fiscal year.

The applicant alleged that she was unable to exercise her right to vote and to stand for election in Mostar, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the Convention. The Court gave notice of that complaint to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The key alleged violation was therefore the State’s prolonged failure to provide a legal framework for local elections in Mostar, leaving the applicant and other residents unable to participate in municipal elections. International bodies repeatedly highlighted the situation: the High Representative reported that political parties had failed to agree on amendments to the Election Law; the Council of Europe Congress and Parliamentary Assembly urged a solution; and the European Commission noted that Mostar citizens had not been able to elect a municipal council since 2008. These facts formed the background to the applicant’s discrimination complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.
001-196600:
**Case of Kopytets and Shtopko v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 9706/19 and 9709/19) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee. It was delivered in Strasbourg on 17 October 2019, after private deliberations on 26 September 2019. The Committee comprised André Potocki (President), Ganna Yudkivska, and Yonko Grozev, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applications were brought against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The case concerns complaints by two applicants about the excessive length of criminal proceedings and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. In application no. 9709/19, the second applicant also raised a complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention.

The key facts are set out in the appended table. The first applicant, Valeriy Vasylyovych Kopytets, born 26 October 1967, lodged application no. 9706/19 on 6 February 2019. He was represented by Karyna Valeriyivna Kopytets of Slobozhanske. The criminal proceedings involving him began on 10 August 2011 and, as of the information before the Court, remained pending. The total length of the proceedings was therefore more than 8 years and 27 days. Those proceedings involved one level of jurisdiction.

The second applicant, Valentyn Vasylyovych Shtopko, born 23 March 1975, lodged application no. 9709/19 on 7 February 2019. No representative is indicated in the appended table. The criminal proceedings involving him commenced earlier, on 22 September 2009, and were also still pending at the relevant time. Their total duration exceeded 9 years, 11 months and 15 days. Those proceedings had passed through two levels of jurisdiction. This longer duration and the involvement of two jurisdictional levels are central to his excessive-length complaint.

The applicants’ principal alleged violation was that the criminal proceedings against them had not been completed within a reasonable time, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They further alleged that Ukrainian law did not provide an effective remedy for that delay, contrary to Article 13 of the Convention. In the second application, Mr Shtopko additionally alleged a violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, which guarantees freedom of movement; however, the appended table does not set out the specific factual basis for that complaint.

The judgment therefore originated from two separate but related Ukrainian criminal cases, both of which had been pending for many years by the time the applicants applied to the Strasbourg Court. The essential facts relevant to the alleged violations are the dates on which the criminal proceedings began, their unresolved status, their total duration, the levels of jurisdiction involved, and the dates on which the applicants introduced their applications. The Court’s task was to assess whether these delays breached the Convention’s reasonable-time requirement and whether the applicants had an effective domestic remedy for the length of the proceedings.
001-189740:
In *Yakuba v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national with prior drug-related convictions, complained under Article 3 that police ill-treated him during arrest; under Article 6 that he could not examine the video recording of an undercover drug purchase or examine the undercover agent; and under Article 34 that the authorities refused to provide copies of documents needed for his application to the European Court.

The case arose from an undercover test-purchase operation. P., apparently a private individual recruited by police as an undercover agent, was given cash before attesting witnesses and, out of their sight, allegedly made three drug purchases from the applicant on 26 February and 6 and 9 March 2007. The first purchase was video-recorded by hidden camera. On 9 March 2007 the applicant was arrested. Police pushed him to the ground and handcuffed him. The applicant alleged that after he was immobilised they continued to drag him around, causing pain and humiliation. He initially admitted having a drug-filled syringe in his sleeve and trying to destroy the drug during arrest, later denying possession of the syringe but still admitting buying drugs for personal use that day. The arresting officers reported that force was used because he tried to destroy evidence.

On 15 March 2007 his lawyer requested a medical examination, alleging beatings during arrest and later at a police station. A medical expert found abrasions on his right hand, shin and both knees, possibly sustained on 9 March; leg abrasions could have resulted from a fall. On 8 May 2007 prosecutors refused to open criminal proceedings against the police. The applicant did not appeal that refusal but continued to raise ill-treatment before the criminal courts, which rejected his complaints as unsubstantiated and held that force during arrest was lawful and the prosecutors had properly examined the matter.

As to the fair-trial complaint, on 20 April 2007 an investigator viewed the video with witnesses and recorded that it showed the applicant selling drugs to P. The applicant’s lawyer asked to watch it, but on 27 April 2007 the investigator refused, citing protection of P.’s identity. P. was questioned pre-trial. The indictment listed P. as a trial witness and the video report as evidence. During trial the applicant asked for the video to be disclosed and for P., a possible defence witness B., and a forensic expert to be examined. Those requests were refused for unknown reasons. On 26 June 2007 he was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to eight years, based largely on police and attesting-witness testimony, P.’s pre-trial statements, a banknote found on him, and forensic traces. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 25 March 2008, also relying on the investigator’s video report, and the Supreme Court refused cassation review on 4 September 2008.

Finally, while preparing his European Court application, the applicant asked the trial court for copies of procedural documents. On 10 October 2008 the trial court refused, saying domestic law provided no procedure for a convict to examine a case file after criminal proceedings ended. Similar refusals followed in 2009 and 2013, and the Court of Appeal gave a similar response in October 2008. These facts formed the basis of his Article 34 complaint that Ukraine obstructed his right to individual application.
001-194240:
**Case: Antonov and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia**  
(Applications nos. 315/10, 1153/10, 1158/10)  
European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, Judgment of 2 July 2019.

The case concerned six Moldovan, Russian and Ukrainian nationals detained in the Transdniestrian region of Moldova under the de facto authority of the “MRT”. The applicants alleged serious violations arising from their arrest, detention conditions, ill-treatment and denial of contact with relatives in facilities controlled by the “MRT” authorities, including IVS Tiraspol and Hlinaia prison in Grigoriopol. The Russian Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

In Application no. 315/10, Evghenii Antonov, a Russian national, was arrested in Tiraspol in August 2009 and accused of possessing a hunter’s knife and marijuana. He was held initially at IVS Tiraspol and later moved to Hlinaia prison. Shortly after arrest, he told Iryna Antonova that he was in a dark, damp cell lacking basic hygiene. She was refused permission to see him. On 19 October 2009, the OSCE was refused access to IVS Tiraspol, where about 90 detainees, including Antonov, were on hunger strike protesting ill-treatment and inhuman detention conditions. Complaints to Moldovan, Russian and “MRT” authorities were unsuccessful. Antonova saw him briefly at a court hearing in December 2009 and said he appeared tired and weak. He was convicted in November 2010, with proceedings pending before the “MRT” Supreme Court.

In Application no. 1153/10, Alexandru Băluţă, a Moldovan national, was arrested in Tiraspol in December 2004 and accused of murder and arson. He alleged he was severely beaten. Released in 2007, he left to work abroad and was rearrested in September 2009. He was held at IVS Tiraspol and then Hlinaia prison. He allegedly endured a dark, damp cell without basic hygiene or daily walks. His mother, Tamara Băluţă, claimed food and items she sent, except bread, did not reach him, and all requests to visit were refused. She learned in October 2009 that many detainees were on hunger strike against abuse and inhuman conditions. She alleged that on 16 October 2009 riot police entered the prison and beat prisoners. The OSCE was again refused access on 19 October 2009. Complaints to Moldovan, Russian and “MRT” authorities were unsuccessful. The “MRT” prosecutor’s office replied that investigators were not obliged to authorise detainee meetings with relatives and that visits had been refused, without further reasons.

In Application no. 1158/10, Oleksandr Bezrodnii, a Ukrainian national and NGO leader, was arrested in Tiraspol on 23 July 2009, accused of stealing roses and endangering militia officers and security agents. He was held at IVS Tiraspol and later Hlinaia. On 29 July 2009, Liudmila Bezrodnyaya saw him at court with blood on his face, a green substance on his head and bruises; he said he was being ill-treated to obtain self-incriminating statements. A court ordered his detention for an undetermined period. In September 2009 he described a basement cell with no daylight, shared with persons having HIV and tuberculosis, insufficient beds, one shower a month, a rarely cleaned toilet in the cell, dampness, no ventilation, parasitic insects, almost no hygiene products, inedible mouldy food and no medical assistance despite injuries. Food and items sent by Bezrodnyaya were rejected or destroyed. In October 2009, prison staff warned that riot police would be called if the hunger strike continued. A Moldovan anti-torture committee member reported ill-treatment and hunger strike, and the “MRT” Justice Minister admitted overcrowding in pre-trial detention centres. The OSCE was refused access. Bezrodnii later complained he had been severely beaten at arrest, with bruises, hematomas, head blows and a swollen leg requiring medical attention. He was convicted in July 2010, but the sentence was quashed and sent for re-examination.

The common factual core concerns alleged inhuman and degrading detention conditions, ill-treatment, denial of family visits and food parcels, obstruction of monitoring, and ineffective complaints to Moldovan, Russian and “MRT” authorities.
001-189092:
**Case summary: Elčić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**

**Elčić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 34524/15 and 5 others) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee. The judgment is dated 17 January 2019 and was adopted after deliberations on 13 December 2018. The applicants were represented by Mr M. Alić, a lawyer practising in Tešanj. The respondent State was Bosnia and Herzegovina. Notice of the applications was given to the Government.

The case originated in six applications lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions. Two applicants, Maida Elčić and Muhamed Hasičić, introduced their applications on 19 June 2015. The remaining four applicants—Fehim Musić, Hasib Duraković, Dževad Smaka and Jozo Jaković—introduced theirs on 4 December 2015. The central alleged violation was that final domestic court decisions in the applicants’ favour had not been enforced, or had been enforced only after substantial delay.

The appended table sets out the relevant domestic decisions and the periods of non-enforcement. Maida Elčić relied on a Tešanj First Instance Court decision of 30 July 2008. The non-enforcement period began on 5 April 2010, and enforcement remained pending for more than 8 years, 7 months and 17 days. Muhamed Hasičić relied on a Tešanj First Instance Court decision of 3 July 2008. The non-enforcement period also began on 5 April 2010 and was pending for the same duration: more than 8 years, 7 months and 17 days.

Fehim Musić relied on two domestic decisions. The first was a Zenica Cantonal Court decision of 5 June 2008. Non-enforcement began on 30 October 2008 and remained pending for more than 10 years and 23 days. The second was a Zenica First Instance Court decision of 31 December 2012. Non-enforcement began on 8 April 2014 and remained pending for more than 4 years, 7 months and 14 days. Hasib Duraković relied on a Zenica First Instance Court decision of 29 September 2006. Non-enforcement began on 30 October 2008 and remained pending for more than 10 years and 23 days. Dževad Smaka relied on a Zenica Cantonal Court decision of 5 June 2008. Non-enforcement began on 30 October 2008 and remained pending for more than 10 years and 23 days. Jozo Jaković relied on a Zenica First Instance Court decision of 29 September 2006. Non-enforcement began on 30 October 2008 and remained pending for more than 10 years and 23 days.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the existence of final domestic decisions, the dates from which enforcement was not carried out, and the prolonged failure of the Bosnian authorities to execute those decisions. In several cases, the non-enforcement lasted for more than a decade. The complaints concerned the State’s failure to enforce binding judicial decisions within a reasonable time. The table indicates that all enforcement proceedings were still pending when the details were compiled. The case thus concerns the alleged breach of Convention rights arising from systemic or prolonged non-enforcement of final court decisions by Bosnia and Herzegovina.
001-194001:
**Case: Hodžić and Sirćo v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**  
**Applications nos. 34526/15 and 34530/15**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section**  
**Judgment delivered 27 June 2019**

The case originated in two applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 18 June 2015. The applicants, Adis Hodžić and Adil Sirćo, were represented by Ms. H. Kapetan, a lawyer practising in Travnik. Notice of the applications was given to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Mourou-Vikström, Ravarani, and Schukking, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 6 June 2019 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment was delivered on 27 June 2019 and is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applicants’ central complaint was the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions. The appended table sets out the relevant facts. Both applicants had obtained domestic decisions from the Sarajevo First Instance Court, both dated 30 August 2013. Despite these decisions, the authorities allegedly failed to enforce them within a reasonable time, and enforcement remained pending.

For Adis Hodžić, born 29 June 1967, the relevant domestic decision was issued by the Sarajevo First Instance Court on 30 August 2013. The start date of the non-enforcement period was 17 December 2013. At the time the case was before the Court, the end date of the non-enforcement period was still pending. The length of the enforcement proceedings therefore exceeded five years, four months and twenty days. This prolonged failure to enforce the domestic decision formed the factual basis of his complaint.

For Adil Sirćo, born 25 June 1962, the relevant domestic decision was also issued by the Sarajevo First Instance Court on 30 August 2013. The non-enforcement period began on 8 April 2014. As with Hodžić, enforcement was still pending, and the length of the enforcement proceedings exceeded five years and twenty-nine days. This delay similarly grounded his complaint.

Both applications were introduced on 18 June 2015. At that point, the domestic decisions had not been enforced for a substantial period: approximately one and a half years for Hodžić and just over one year for Sirćo. However, the enforcement remained unresolved for years afterward, eventually exceeding five years in each case. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the existence of final domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour, the dates on which non-enforcement began, the absence of any completed enforcement, and the extensive duration of the pending enforcement proceedings.

The applicants alleged that the failure to enforce the domestic decisions violated their Convention rights. The Court’s task was to determine whether the State had complied with its positive obligation to enforce final domestic decisions within a reasonable time and whether the applicants had an effective remedy for the delay. The case thus concerned the respondent State’s alleged failure to execute final court decisions, the protracted nature of the enforcement, and the resulting deprivation of the applicants’ rights under those decisions. The Court gave notice of the applications to the Government and considered the complaints on the basis of the facts set out in the appended table.
001-198885:
**Romeva v. North Macedonia** (Application no. 32141/10) concerned the applicant’s complaint that she was deprived of her pension in breach of legal certainty, contrary to Article 6 § 1 ECHR and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant was born in 1947 and lived in Skopje. Under the respondent State’s pension system, employers submitted employment data, while the Pension and Disability Fund kept records.

In May 2000, while unemployed and receiving social benefits, the applicant was instructed by the Employment Bureau to apply for a retirement pension. On 22 May 2000 she applied to the Fund with only basic personal details, attaching no employment documents. On 23 May 2000 the Fund granted her a monthly pension of MKD 6,462, finding she had completed 35 years, 10 months and 24 days of service—the sole qualifying condition then. The decision became final and she received payments.

In 2007, an internal audit found incomplete records for several recipients. In the applicant’s case, her employment booklet was missing. The Fund sought verification from her employer for 1963–1967 but apparently obtained no further evidence. On 18 October 2007, acting proprio motu, the Fund annulled the 2000 decision and refused her pension. It said the information about her 1963–1967 employment was incorrect because she had not in fact worked then, so she lacked the required 35 years. It relied on section 258 of the Administrative Proceedings Act and section 145-A of the Pension and Disability Insurance Act. Payments stopped.

The applicant appealed, arguing that section 145-A entered into force on 14 June 2006 and could not be applied retroactively to a 2000 decision. In April 2008 the Second-Instance Commission dismissed her appeal. In November 2008 the Administrative Court quashed that decision, agreeing that section 145-A had been applied retroactively. In March 2009, however, the Second-Instance Commission issued a fresh dismissal, relying on section 249(2) of the Administrative Proceedings Act: reopening was justified because erroneous documents had been used, allegedly endorsed by the applicant when she applied. In October 2009 the Administrative Court dismissed her action, finding the Fund’s form concerning her 1963–1967 employment illegible and insufficient. On 26 April 2010 the Supreme Court upheld the refusal as lawful.

The applicant argued that domestic law made the Fund responsible for collecting, keeping and processing employment data, while employers supplied it. She had never submitted employment records and could not challenge data controlled by the Fund. Her central complaint was therefore that a final, executed pension decision was retrospectively annulled years later based on records she neither created nor could verify, violating legal certainty and property rights.

Other relevant facts: in 2008 the Fund sued for reimbursement of MKD 645,138 as unjust enrichment; the courts granted it, final in January 2014, and enforcement began. In 2012 the Fund filed a criminal complaint alleging falsified employment information, rejected because the limitation period had expired. After criteria changed, the Fund granted her a new pension in November 2009 under the age criterion, which she continued receiving. The alleged violations thus arose from the annulment of a final pension and recovery of paid sums under Article 6 § 1 and Protocol No. 1.
001-196897:
J.D. and A v. the United Kingdom concerned two British women whose Housing Benefit was reduced under the 2012 Housing Benefit (Amendment) Regulations, often called the “bedroom tax.” They alleged that the reduction discriminated against them contrary to Article 14 ECHR, taken with Article 8 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, on grounds of disability (J.D.) and gender/sex (A).

The scheme, Regulation B13, reduced Housing Benefit for social-sector tenants deemed to have more bedrooms than they needed: by 14% for one extra bedroom and 25% for two or more. Claimants could seek temporary Discretionary Housing Payments (DHPs) to cover shortfalls, but these were discretionary, cash-limited, and uncertain.

First applicant J.D. had lived since 1993 in a three-bedroom social rented house with her adult daughter, who has severe brain damage from oxygen deprivation, profound physical and learning disabilities, is a wheelchair user and registered blind. J.D. cares for her full-time. The house had been specially adapted to meet her daughter’s needs, including wide doors, an internal lift, ramps, ceiling hoists, an accessible bathroom and a changing bed. Because the household comprised two people in a three-bedroom home, J.D.’s Housing Benefit was cut by 14%, leaving a rent shortfall. DHPs were awarded only temporarily; her last award expired in March 2017, and no suitable smaller adapted accommodation was available. Her complaint was that the reduction discriminated on grounds of disability by failing to recognise her daughter’s need for the adapted home and by relying on discretionary payments.

Second applicant A had lived for over 25 years in a three-bedroom social rented house with her son. She had been allocated the larger house because of a shortage of smaller accommodation. A had been raped by a violent former partner, X, who had served a long prison sentence for attempted murder and continued to threaten her; her son was conceived as a result of the rape. Under a Sanctuary Scheme, her home was fortified and adapted with a “panic room,” security monitoring, police flagging and multi-agency support. Her Housing Benefit was also reduced by 14% for under-occupation. A received temporary DHPs, but in 2015 a refusal led to an eviction threat; the Secretary of State intervened and the local authority reversed the decision, accepting it had failed to consider the adaptations. A alleged sex/gender discrimination: the reduction jeopardised her ability to remain in the only safe, specially adapted home, and DHPs were not adequate protection.

In domestic proceedings, courts accepted prima facie discrimination on disability and sex, but the Supreme Court ultimately dismissed both claims. It applied the “manifestly without reasonable foundation” test to welfare policy and held that the Secretary of State could reasonably rely on DHPs for exceptional needs rather than creating exemptions in Regulation B13. The Strasbourg applications therefore asked the European Court to determine whether the benefit reduction violated Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key factual issue was whether the applicants’ disability-related and gender-based safety needs made the under-occupancy deduction unjustifiably discriminatory.
001-196682:
**Case: Tsukur and Others v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 53132/18 and 2 others), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Committee judgment, Strasbourg, 17 October 2019.

The case originated in three applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of their detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. The relevant facts are set out in the appended table.

**Application no. 53132/18**, introduced on 2 November 2018, was brought by Mykola Volodymyrovych Tsukur (born 3 December 1978), represented by Sergiy Mykolayovych Rybiy (Dnipro). He was detained in Kyiv SIZO from 11 March 2016 to 9 August 2018—a duration of 2 years, 4 months and 30 days. The space per inmate was 2.5 m². His specific grievances were overcrowding; lack of fresh air; a mouldy or dirty cell; lack of toiletries; lack of privacy for the toilet; no or restricted access to warm water; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; poor quality of food; no or restricted access to potable water; and no or restricted access to a shower.

**Application no. 53181/18**, introduced on 5 November 2018, was brought by Borys Pavlovych Gulchuk (born 16 February 1993), also represented by Sergiy Mykolayovych Rybiy. He was held in Kyiv SIZO from 21 June 2015 to 18 September 2018—3 years, 2 months and 29 days. The space per inmate was 2.6–3.5 m². He alleged overcrowding; lack of fresh air; infestation of the cell with insects or rodents; a mouldy or dirty cell; lack of privacy for the toilet; no or restricted access to warm water; lack of toiletries; poor quality of potable water; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; poor quality of food; and no or restricted access to a shower.

**Application no. 59802/18**, introduced on 27 November 2018, was brought by Vadym Sergiyovych Koval (born 24 December 1991), represented by Oleksandr Anatoliyovych Ignatov (Dnipro). He was detained in Dnipropetrovsk detention facility No. 4 from 7 November 2014 to 26 November 2018—4 years and 20 days. The space per inmate was 3.1 m². His complaints were lack of fresh air; overcrowding; poor quality of food; no or restricted access to a shower; lack or insufficient quantity of food; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; lack of or insufficient natural light; lack of or insufficient electric light; lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities; and lack of toiletries.

These facts were central to the alleged violations. The complaints about detention conditions engage Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. Relevant factors include the length of detention, cell space, overcrowding, ventilation, hygiene, sanitation, access to showers and potable water, food quality and quantity, bedding, lighting, privacy and infestation. The applicants also alleged that no effective domestic remedy existed, engaging Article 13 of the Convention, because they could not obtain redress in Ukraine for the allegedly inadequate conditions.
