The Court, sitting as a Committee composed of André Potocki, President; Ganna Yudkivska; Yonko Grozev; and Liv Tigerstedt, Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 26 September 2019 and delivered judgment on 17 October 2019. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The provided text does not include the Court’s substantive findings or any award, but the key alleged violations concern prolonged detention in overcrowded and inadequate conditions in Kyiv SIZO and Dnipropetrovsk detention facility No. 4, together with the absence of an effective remedy in domestic law.
001-191369:
In *Sanchyshyn v. Ukraine* (Application no. 81639/17), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 7 March 2019. The case originated in an application against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 24 November 2017. The applicant, Bogdan Ivanovych Sanchyshyn, born on 31 October 1970, was represented by Mr O.V. Mytsyk, a lawyer practising in Lviv. Notice of the application was given to the Ukrainian Government.

The factual details relevant to the application are set out in the appended table. The domestic criminal proceedings concerning the applicant began on 31 August 2009 and ended on 25 May 2017. Their total length was 7 years, 8 months and 26 days. The proceedings were considered at two levels of jurisdiction. The provided excerpt does not describe the specific criminal charge, the procedural steps taken, or the reasons for the delay. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the commencement and conclusion dates, the total duration, and the fact that the case was reviewed at two jurisdictional levels.

The applicant complained primarily of the excessive length of the criminal proceedings. He alleged that the proceedings against him were not concluded within a reasonable time, contrary to Article 6 §1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal. The overall duration of more than seven and a half years formed the basis of this complaint. In assessing such complaints, the Court generally considers factors such as the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant, the conduct of the authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant. Although the excerpt does not set out those factors in detail, the length of the proceedings was central to the applicant’s claim that Ukraine had violated his Article 6 rights.

The applicant also complained of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law in respect of the excessive length of the proceedings. This raised an issue under Article 13 of the Convention, which requires an effective remedy before a national authority for arguable violations of Convention rights. In length-of-proceedings cases, an Article 13 complaint usually concerns whether domestic law provided an effective mechanism either to expedite the proceedings or to compensate the applicant for their excessive duration. The Court commonly examines Article 13 together with Article 6 §1 in such cases.

The applicant further raised other complaints under the Convention, but the provided text does not specify them. Procedurally, the application was introduced on 24 November 2017, after the domestic proceedings had ended on 25 May 2017. Notice was given to the Government, and the case was considered by Judges Síofra O’Leary (President), Mārtiņš Mits and Lado Chanturia, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 14 February 2019 and adopted the judgment on 7 March 2019. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In summary, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that criminal proceedings against the applicant commenced on 31 August 2009 and concluded on 25 May 2017, lasting 7 years, 8 months and 26 days across two levels of jurisdiction. The applicant alleged that this delay violated Article 6 §1 and that no effective domestic remedy existed under Article 13. The case therefore concerns primarily the reasonableness of the length of criminal proceedings in Ukraine and the availability of an effective domestic remedy for that delay.
001-193259:
The applicant, Hugo Johannes Charles van de Kolk, is a Dutch national born in 1990 who lives in Alphen aan den Rijn. On 19 August 2009, when he was nineteen, he was arrested on suspicion of distributing child pornography—three pictures of a sixteen-year-old girl—in April of that year. He was informed of his right to consult a lawyer.

At the police station he was taken into police custody. Before he had consulted his lawyer, who was not immediately available, but with his consent, police began a social interview concerning his personal circumstances and personality, not the suspected offence. He told officers he had cavernous hemangiomas in his brain and spinal cord. He said this did not affect his functioning except possibly his trust in others, and that although he could play football he could not head the ball. When his lawyer became available, the interview was suspended so he could consult by telephone. Afterwards he said his lawyer would visit later that afternoon and that, on the lawyer’s advice, he would answer no further questions. The interview ended, and he met his lawyer later that day.

On 20 August 2009 the applicant was interviewed twice, including about the suspected distribution of child pornography. At the beginning he said he would prefer to have his lawyer present. He was told this was not possible, and the interview began. He answered questions. During questioning, officers noticed a spasm-like movement of his arm and asked if he was having an epileptic fit. He confirmed that he was. The interview was interrupted and a doctor was called. He said the seizure could have been caused by stress and other factors. The interview then resumed. A final interview took place on 21 August 2009. Audio recordings were made of all interviews. He was released from police custody on 21 August 2009.

In the domestic proceedings, on 25 March 2011 the Regional Court of The Hague found him guilty of distribution of child pornography and sentenced him to a suspended two-week prison sentence and eighty hours’ community service. It considered that he should have been able to consult a lawyer before his first police interview. However, it found that the later interviews did not appear to have been conducted without his having been able to consult a lawyer, and that their content did not substantially differ from the interview conducted without legal assistance; it therefore considered a finding of procedural non-compliance sufficient. The applicant appealed.

On 3 July 2013 the Court of Appeal of The Hague quashed the Regional Court’s decision, convicted him of the same offence, and sentenced him to forty hours’ community service. On his complaint about lack of legal assistance during police interviews, counsel argued that the suspect had the mental age of a fifteen- or sixteen-year-old and a brain disorder that might cause epileptic seizures, but submitted no medical data. The Court of Appeal found no indication to the interviewing officers of such mental age or that the disorder could cause a seizure. It considered that, after the spastic movement, the officers had correctly consulted a physician before resuming. It did not agree that they should reasonably have regarded him as vulnerable or underage. Accordingly, as an adult at the time, he was not entitled to have a lawyer present during interview under the Salduz case-law. The conviction relied on, among other evidence, the victim’s complaint and further police statement, the applicant’s 20 August 2009 statement that he had sent photographs and uploaded them, a third party’s statement about receiving two photographs, and a police record showing the photographs were accessible via a profile name on an image-hosting website.

The applicant appealed in cassation to the Supreme Court, complaining about the refusal to allow him legal assistance during police questioning. On 18 November 2014 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal with summary reasoning under section 81 of the Judiciary (Organisation) Act.

Under domestic law at the relevant time, following the earlier Salduz judgment of 27 November 2008, the Supreme Court held on 30 June 2009 that an arrested suspect could derive an entitlement to consult a lawyer before police interview, but not to have a lawyer present during police interviews; underage suspects were additionally entitled to a lawyer or confidant during interviews. On 22 December 2015, after the national proceedings, the Supreme Court accepted a right to legal assistance during police interviews, expected to apply from 1 March 2016. Article 457 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allows revision of final convictions on the basis of a European Court of Human Rights ruling finding a violation in the proceedings leading to conviction, if necessary for legal redress.
001-193083:
The applicant, Barry Doyle, an Irish national born in 1985 and serving a life sentence for murder, lodged an application against Ireland on 12 July 2017. He complained that, after his arrest, he was not entitled to have a solicitor present during police interrogation, representing an alleged failure by the State to vindicate his fair-trial right under Article 6 § 3 (c).

On 9 November 2008, the applicant killed S.G., aged 28, in Limerick. It was a case of mistaken identity: the applicant had set out to kill another man at the behest of a criminal figure during a gang feud. He shot and wounded S.G. in the street, pursued him into a back garden and shot him several times, inflicting five wounds including a fatal head wound.

On 24 February 2009, police searched the applicant’s residence and arrested him at 7.15 a.m.; he was brought to a police station shortly before 8.00 a.m. He was informed of his rights, including access to a solicitor, and requested a particular solicitor, who was notified. At 9.55 a.m. the solicitor spoke to him by telephone for two minutes. The first interview began at 10.12 a.m. and lasted fifty minutes. All interviews were video-recorded and conducted without the solicitor physically present. Neither the applicant nor his solicitor requested the solicitor’s presence; it was later confirmed that, under police practice at the time, such a request would have been denied.

Another solicitor, Mr O’D., arrived at 11.00 a.m. and represented the applicant. Further interviews took place that day, but the applicant made no admissions. On 25 February, three interviews took place, lasting almost five hours in total. The District Court extended his detention by 72 hours, with his solicitor present. In a tenth interview that night, police told him that his former girlfriend, G, the mother of his child, had been arrested in Dublin on suspicion of withholding information and was being detained and interviewed; they gave him details of her replies. He requested no further consultations and made no admissions.

On 26 February, during interviews, police stressed G’s detention and separation from her child and the victim’s innocence. In the thirteenth interview, the applicant asked to consult his solicitor; questioning stopped and a telephone consultation of about two minutes took place. In the fourteenth interview, he again asked to speak to his solicitor, saying the earlier call had been inadequate; later he repeated the request. The interview was briefly suspended, then officers asked background questions until 6.35 p.m. The solicitor arrived at 6.52 p.m. and spoke with him for about ten minutes. A police memo later recorded that the solicitor said, off the record, that the applicant would admit to the murder if G were released. Police replied that they wanted the truth; the solicitor said there would be no admissions before release, and police replied that an induced confession would not be accepted. The solicitor left. In the fifteenth interview, beginning at 7.42 p.m., the applicant first refused questions, then said he had been present at the scene. An officer said the solicitor had telephoned; the interview was suspended for a four-minute consultation. On resuming at 7.51 p.m., the applicant admitted shooting the victim and gave details and a map; the interview ended at 9.05 p.m. G was released at 9.00 p.m. In the sixteenth interview, he refused to answer questions. Further interviews followed on 27 and 28 February. On 28 February at 3.15 p.m., he was charged with murder.

The applicant pleaded not guilty in the Central Criminal Court. The first trial in 2011 was inconclusive. The second trial began on 16 January 2012 and lasted 22 days. He sought to exclude his admissions. The trial judge held a ten-day voir dire, viewed over twenty hours of recordings, heard evidence and submissions on threat, inducement, oppression, fairness and legal access, and ruled on the eleventh day. The judge found the prosecution had to prove admissibility beyond reasonable doubt. On legal access, he noted two consultations before the admissions and the solicitor’s presence in court for the detention extension; he found no breach of the constitutional right to legal advice and held police could continue interview 14 when the applicant complained the short telephone call was inadequate and the solicitor was expected within an hour. On oppression, he found the applicant physically and mentally strong, in control, and the interviews careful, patient, professional and not oppressive. Promptings about the truth, G and the child might objectively amount to inducement, but were not immediately acted on and were dissipated by the solicitor consultation and interaction, breaking any causative link; the admissions in interview 15 were voluntary and not caused by oppression, threat or inducement. He considered fundamental fairness in the round.
001-208280:
**Summary of *Gawlik v. Liechtenstein* (Application no. 23922/19)**

The case concerns the dismissal without notice of Lothar Gawlik, a German national and deputy chief physician at the Liechtenstein National Hospital, the only public hospital in Liechtenstein. He worked under an indefinite contract and was directly subordinate to Dr H., the chief physician. In September 2014, after a colleague indicated an unusual rise in patient deaths, Gawlik examined the hospital’s electronic medical files. He found notes suggesting that four patients had died after morphine administration and concluded that Dr H. had practised active euthanasia.

On 9 September 2014, Gawlik met with the President of the Parliamentary Control Committee and voiced his suspicions. On the President’s advice, he lodged a criminal complaint against Dr H. with the Public Prosecutor’s Office on 11 September 2014. The prosecution opened proceedings concerning suspected killing on request and participation in another person’s suicide. Police seized the patients’ paper files and questioned Dr H. On 19 September 2014, after further electronic research, Gawlik informed the prosecutor that he suspected active euthanasia in six additional patients and was questioned by police. He stated that his aim was to avert harm to hospital patients.

The hospital had an internal anonymous reporting system, the Critical Incident Reporting System, but it is unclear whether a change in its handling was communicated within the hospital. Gawlik did not use it. Hospital-commissioned reports, including one by an external Swiss palliative expert, concluded that no active euthanasia had occurred. The patients were in palliative situations; morphine had been used for pain and breathing difficulty, not to end life. Some prescriptions “without upper limit” might not have been necessary, but such doses had not actually been administered. The reports suggested that if Gawlik had consulted the paper files, he would have realised his suspicions were clearly unfounded.

Gawlik was suspended on 26 September 2014 and dismissed without notice on 17 October 2014. The hospital claimed the trust relationship was irretrievably destroyed because he had failed to verify his allegations and had not raised them internally before going to external bodies. Criminal proceedings against Dr H. were discontinued in December 2014; proceedings against Gawlik for deliberately casting false suspicions were also later discontinued.

Gawlik sued for unlawful dismissal, arguing that his whistleblowing was justified. The Regional Court dismissed his claim, finding an important reason for dismissal under the Civil Code. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding that the dismissal was unjustified and that the disclosure was covered by freedom of expression. The Supreme Court then reinstated the dismissal, finding that Gawlik, a senior employee, had relied only on incomplete electronic files despite having access to full paper files, and had thus seriously breached trust.

The Constitutional Court dismissed Gawlik’s complaint. It accepted that Article 10 of the Convention applied indirectly to the employment relationship and that there was a public interest in proper medical treatment. It also accepted that Gawlik was a whistleblower and did not act from personal motives. However, it found that he had failed to verify his serious allegations in the patients’ paper files and had acted irresponsibly given the gravity of accusing a colleague of euthanasia. Therefore, his dismissal did not violate his right to freedom of expression. The court left open whether he should first have attempted internal reporting. The alleged violation therefore centred on whether the dismissal for external whistleblowing about suspected euthanasia breached Article 10.
001-212150:
Case M.L. v. Slovakia (Application no. 34159/17, ECtHR 14 October 2021) concerned protection of private and family life in defamation proceedings. The applicant, M.L., a Slovak national born in 1948, was the mother of a deceased Roman Catholic priest. Her son had been convicted in 1999 of sexual abuse and threatening the moral education of young people—specifically, attempted non-consensual oral sex with a minor boy—and in 2002 of disorderly conduct for consensual oral sex with an adult man in a public place. Both convictions became spent in 2001 and 2003. He died in 2006.

In 2008, three tabloid newspapers published articles about his sexual-abuse conviction and a possible link to his supposed suicide. The articles claimed he had confessed to abusing minor boys and to bisexuality before his suicide; that his bishop knew of the criminal charges; and that the Church had provided a guarantee enabling him to avoid detention, be released, or not be convicted. One article published photographs of him. The articles named him and disclosed intimate or distant private details in sensational language, including descriptions of “disgusting paedophile orgies.”

The applicant sued the publishers in August 2008 under Articles 11 and 15 of the Slovak Civil Code, seeking post-mortem protection of her son’s personal integrity and protection of her own personal integrity. She argued that her son had confessed only to disorderly conduct, not sexual abuse; that one alleged victim had retracted his accusation; that both convictions were spent; that there was no evidence of any Church guarantee; and that her son had actually died from drug intoxication and medical negligence. She claimed the articles contained false and misleading factual allegations and disproportionate value judgments intended to cause sensation and increase sales. She also said the publication prompted adverse reactions and questions from neighbours and people who knew her son, harmed her mourning, and worsened her health.

In 2012 the District Court ordered each defendant to publish a formal apology for untrue allegations about her son but dismissed her financial claims. It found the criminal convictions were public-interest matters journalists could report, but some allegations—especially the Church guarantee—were untrue, based on an unauthenticated partial record and unverified interviews, for which publishers bore objective responsibility. It rejected her own claim because she had not lived with her son and his personal non-pecuniary rights were not transferable.

The Regional Court later quashed that judgment for insufficient reasoning. In 2014 the District Court dismissed the entire action. It treated the son as a public figure who should tolerate more criticism, found journalists entitled to report facts from the criminal file and publish his photograph, and considered other sources credible in light of the conviction. The Church guarantee was not proven, but the bishop’s office appeared to have tried to help. The Regional Court upheld this in 2015. In 2017 the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, finding no procedural violation.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Articles 6 and 8 that the domestic courts failed to protect her and her late son’s private and family life, failed to distinguish facts from value judgments, apply proportionality, and provide reasoned decisions. The core alleged violation was Slovakia’s failure to grant effective post-mortem and personal protection against the tabloid articles.
001-213901:
In *Gražulevičiūtė v. Lithuania*, the applicant, Edita Gražulevičiūtė, is a Lithuanian rheumatologist and clinical researcher. In 2011 she was involved in clinical trials of the drug tocilizumab. One patient, V.S., died on 14 April 2011. V.S.’s daughters asked the State Medicines Control Agency (SMCA) to investigate whether the applicant had properly performed her duties. Following an unscheduled good clinical practice inspection, the SMCA identified two “critical (dangerous)” violations: failure to accept the patient for an unscheduled appointment and failure to report serious side-effects. Ten significant and six minor violations were also found. The inspectors suggested that the researchers’ actions may have caused damage to V.S.’s health and led to her death.

By orders of 10 and 12 January 2012, the SMCA suspended the applicant from the first and second tocilizumab clinical trials, prohibited her from starting new trials, and published information about the suspension and critical violations on its website. A criminal investigation later obtained an expert report concluding that V.S. died of acute sepsis, not because of the applicant’s actions.

The applicant challenged the suspension decisions. In December 2013 the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court fully allowed her claim. It found that the inspectors’ conclusions were incorrect and based partly on subjective statements by V.S.’s daughters. It held that the applicant had advised V.S. to go to hospital, that another doctor confirmed this, and that the applicant had not failed to report serious side-effects because V.S.’s initial ankle pain was not a serious side-effect of the trial drug. It also found that the applicant’s maternity leave was not decisive, since she was not the only researcher. The court annulled the suspension orders as unjust. That decision became final on 21 December 2013.

The applicant then sought damages from the State for pecuniary and non-pecuniary harm caused by the suspension. In November 2015 the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court partly granted her claim, awarding EUR 6,128 for lost income relating to the first trial and EUR 200 for non-pecuniary damage. It relied on the earlier final judgment and found the SMCA’s suspension unlawful. The SMCA appealed.

In January 2017 the Supreme Administrative Court reversed that decision and rejected the damages claim. It held that the annulment of an administrative decision did not automatically make the State liable under Article 6.271 of the Civil Code. It conducted a broader assessment and found that the SMCA had acted within its competence to protect clinical trial participants and ensure reliable data. Re-examining the facts, it concluded that the applicant had an increased duty of care and had not ensured proper medical care or unscheduled appointments. It therefore found no unlawful State action and no basis for compensation.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the later damages judgment effectively overturned the earlier final decision that had exculpated her, violating res judicata and her right to a fair hearing. She also complained under Article 8 that her suspension and the public disclosure of the critical violations damaged her reputation and private life, and that she received no adequate compensation. Finally, she alleged a lack of an effective domestic remedy. The key facts for these alleged violations are the earlier final finding that she committed no critical violations, the subsequent contrary assessment by the Supreme Administrative Court, the public disclosure of the suspension, and the absence of compensation for the professional and reputational harm caused.
001-213406:
M.F. v. Norway (Application no. 5947/19) concerned an Article 8 complaint by a Norwegian mother about the foster-care placement of her daughter, X (born December 2016), and the restrictions on her contact rights.

The applicant had older children, Y and Z, from a previous relationship. From 2013, child welfare services had concerns about her care of them, including poor hygiene, late school arrival, and school absence. Assistance measures were provided, but concerns continued after she moved municipalities. In 2016 she lived with B, with whom she later had X and a son. Police stopped a car driven by B, suspected of drug driving, and found illegal drugs in their apartment, which police described as chaotic and unhygienic. While pregnant with X, child welfare services raised concerns about the unborn child because of B’s substance abuse and criminal record and the earlier care measures.

After X’s birth in December 2016, a midwife filed a notice of concern citing B’s lack of interest and the applicant’s inadequate hygiene and indifference to the newborn’s needs. Further visits, notifications about B’s drug use, reviews, and assistance measures followed. The relationship ended in spring 2017, and the applicant moved with the children to her mother’s home.

On 29 May 2017, child welfare services applied for a care order for X, envisaging placement until adulthood and possible adoption. They argued contact should be limited so that X could attach securely in foster care. In September 2017 the County Social Welfare Board held a hearing. In December 2017 it found serious shortcomings in the applicant’s care, including failure to see X’s needs. It also noted Y and Z’s school absence as “gross educational neglect.” It found she blamed others, failed to set boundaries, and that her care deficits were not merely situational. Further assistance measures were deemed unlikely to improve her skills. It ordered long-term foster placement and set contact at two hours, three times per year, supervised.

The applicant sought judicial review. In February 2018 the District Court upheld the care order. It applied the best-interests principle and the main rule that children should remain with parents unless the situation is clearly untenable. It examined her capacity to “mentalise” and provide emotional care, finding a damaged ability to form relations affecting her caring skills. It relied on prior proceedings concerning Y and Z, where an expert found she could not read children’s signals, could “mentally disappear,” and had caused serious neglect. As to X, reports noted possible lack of emotional attachment, lack of routines for feeding and sleep, missed diaper changes, and excessive time in chairs. The court-appointed expert found X well-functioning in foster care but inherently vulnerable, with initial instability amounting to neglect; X recognised the applicant but turned away and was more attached to foster parents. The District Court found emotional neglect, held treatment would take years, and concluded X could not wait. It also limited contact because X was in a critical attachment phase and likely to remain in foster care throughout childhood.

The High Court refused leave to appeal in May 2018; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in July 2018. The County Governor later identified shortcomings in child welfare handling. After the Strasbourg application, the care order was lifted in June 2020 and X returned to the applicant in July 2020. The Article 8 complaint concerned the foster placement and contact restrictions.
001-207848:
Efendić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 37130/19) is a European Court of Human Rights case from the Fourth Section. The applicant, Mirsad Efendić, born in 1944, was represented by Mr O. Eterović, a lawyer practising in Sarajevo. The application was lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention on 28 June 2019. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the application. The Court sat as a Committee composed of Armen Harutyunyan (President), Jolien Schukking and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. It deliberated in private on 21 January 2021 and delivered judgment on 11 February 2021. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The case concerns the alleged non-enforcement of a domestic decision. According to the appended table, the relevant domestic decision was given by the Sarajevo Municipal Court on 30 June 2014. The start date of the non-enforcement period was 12 June 2018. At the time of the application and the Court’s examination, the enforcement proceedings remained pending. Their length was recorded as more than two years, five months and twenty days. Those dates and the pending status form the core factual basis of the applicant’s complaint.

The applicant complained specifically of the non-enforcement of the domestic decision. The available text does not describe the substantive content of the Sarajevo Municipal Court decision, the obligations it imposed, or the parties against whom enforcement was sought. Nor does it set out the steps taken by the domestic authorities, any reasons for the delay, or whether the applicant pursued separate remedies. Nevertheless, the central allegation is clear: a domestic court decision existed, enforcement was not completed, and the enforcement proceedings remained unresolved for a significant period. In Convention terms, non-enforcement complaints of this kind ordinarily raise issues under the right to a fair trial, particularly the reasonable-time and execution-of-judgments requirements under Article 6 § 1, and may also engage the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the existence of the Sarajevo Municipal Court decision of 30 June 2014; the beginning of the non-enforcement period on 12 June 2018; the continued pendency of enforcement; and the duration of more than two years, five months and twenty days. The applicant’s essential complaint is that the respondent State failed to secure the effective and timely enforcement of that domestic decision. The excerpt does not indicate the final outcome on the merits beyond the fact that the Court delivered judgment. Any assessment of whether the delay was justified, whether it was attributable to the State, or whether the applicant was afforded adequate redress would depend on fuller reasoning not included in the provided text.
001-213407:
E.H. v. Norway (Application no. 39717/19) concerns an Article 8 complaint by a Norwegian father, E.H., about the replacement of foster care with adoption of his son, X. X was born in June 2015 to B, the applicant’s former partner. The parents were not in a relationship at the time of birth. During pregnancy and after birth, a midwife and social workers raised serious concerns about both parents’ caregiving abilities. On 15 June 2015, when X was only weeks old, he was emergency placed in a foster home; the County Social Welfare Board authorised the placement the next day. The mother contested the emergency order, but the father was not initially a party.

In July 2015, the child welfare services requested a care order. The father had five supervised visits with X before the Board issued a care order on 21 October 2015. The Board found that B had mild mental retardation and an expressive language disorder, lacked fundamental caregiving abilities, and that X would risk serious neglect if left with her. Assistance measures were considered inadequate. The father was granted supervised contact of two hours, four times a year. He supported the care order but sought more contact.

A psychologist’s expert report in March 2016 found X had extraordinary care needs, including epilepsy, severe eczema, and significant far-sightedness. B could not meet his ordinary or special needs. The father had clear cognitive and reflective limitations, weak interaction skills, low stress tolerance, and could become loud and hot-tempered with X, but he was positive and more able to use guidance. The expert recommended that X remain in foster care with limited contact—three two-hour sessions yearly per biological parent. B later withdrew her City Court challenge, making the care order final.

In November 2017, the child welfare services applied to withdraw the parents’ parental responsibilities and authorise X’s adoption by his foster parents. X was then two and a half and had lived with the foster parents since he was three weeks old. The Board granted adoption in January 2018. It found reunification unrealistic, a point both parents accepted, and concluded adoption was in X’s best interests because of his attachment to the foster parents, lack of attachment to his biological parents, vulnerabilities, need for stability, difficult contact sessions, and the risk of future uncertainty or litigation.

The father and mother challenged the decision. They argued the City Court should appoint an expert on adoption but made no formal request. The City Court declined to appoint an expert and relied on general research and knowledge. After a hearing in June 2018, it upheld adoption, finding X exceptionally vulnerable, closely attached to his foster parents, and without attachment to his biological parents. Adoption would provide safety and predictability; otherwise, X would remain in long-term foster care with possible future proceedings. The biological principle had to yield. The foster parents had not consented to post-adoption contact. A dissenting lay judge considered general research insufficient and adoption too drastic.

The High Court refused leave to appeal in November 2018, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in January 2019. Under the Child Welfare Act, parental responsibilities may be withdrawn and adoption authorised if parents are permanently unable to provide proper care or if the child has become so attached to the current environment that removal would cause serious problems. The applicant alleged that the adoption decision violated his right to family life under Article 8, raising issues of proportionality, the child’s best interests, less restrictive alternatives, expert evidence, contact rights, and biological ties.
001-211777:
In *Sanchez v. France* (Application no. 45581/15), the applicant, Julien Sanchez, a French national, local councillor, mayor of Beaucaire, and Front National candidate for the French parliamentary elections, complained under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that his criminal conviction for incitement to hatred or violence violated his freedom of expression. The conviction arose not from comments he personally wrote, but from his failure to promptly delete third-party comments posted on the publicly accessible “wall” of his Facebook account.

On 24 October 2011, the applicant posted a political message criticising F.P., a UMP MEP, deputy mayor of Nîmes, and his political opponent. Third parties then added comments to the wall. S.B. wrote a comment referring to Nîmes being “turned into Algiers,” mentioning kebab shops, mosques, drug dealers, prostitutes, sharia, and ending with “Thanks [F.] and kisses to [L.].” L.R. posted three further comments associating Muslims with crime, insecurity, veiled women, drug trafficking, and halal economic development, including statements such as “Drug trafficking run by the muslims” and “stones get thrown at cars belonging to ‘white people’.”

L.T., the partner of F.P., had a North African-sounding forename. On 25 October 2011, she saw the comments, felt personally insulted, and believed the reference “kisses to [L.]” targeted her. She went to S.B.’s hairdressing salon; S.B., unaware the Facebook page was public, deleted his comment. On 26 October 2011, L.T. lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant, S.B., and L.R. On 27 October 2011, the applicant posted a message asking users to be careful with their comments, but did not delete the existing comments. Investigators later found that L.R.’s comments were still visible on 6 December 2011, while S.B.’s had been removed.

The applicant stated that he had not written the comments, could not monitor the large number of posts from over 1,800 Facebook friends, consulted the wall daily but rarely read comments, and only learned of L.R.’s comments when summoned. He later restricted public access to his wall. He argued the remarks fell within freedom of expression and were not directed personally at L.T.

Domestic courts convicted the applicant as principal under section 93-3 of the Law of 29 July 1982 on audiovisual communication. Under that provision, as interpreted by the Constitutional Council, the producer or administrator of an online public communication service could be liable for third-party messages only if aware of their content before posting or if he failed to act promptly after becoming aware. The courts found no evidence he knew before posting, but held that as an elected Front National member and public figure he had knowingly made his Facebook wall public, authorised friends to post, and should have been especially vigilant. They found he consulted the wall daily, failed to remove the offending comments promptly, and left L.R.’s comments visible until investigators saw them. The comments were held to target Muslims as a group and L.T. as an individual, and were capable of arousing rejection, hostility, or hatred.

The Nîmes Criminal Court convicted him on 28 February 2013 and fined him EUR 4,000; the Nîmes Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 18 October 2013, reducing the fine to EUR 3,000 and ordering EUR 1,000 costs to L.T. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 17 March 2015, holding the offence established and Article 10 not breached. The applicant then applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the criminal conviction for failing to delete third-party comments constituted an unjustified interference with his Article 10 rights.
001-207474:
In *Velichko v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1973, was disabled (group III) and had been diagnosed with HIV in 1996. On 22 October 2010 he was detained on remand at the Izmayil Detention Centre (SIZO) on suspicion of theft and informed the doctor of his HIV status. Between October 2010 and May 2011 he was diagnosed with HIV (clinical stage IV), hepatitis C, and other conditions. Doctors prescribed treatment for several illnesses but he received no antiretroviral therapy (ART).

On 18 May 2011 the head of the Izmayil SIZO wrote to the judge hearing the criminal case that the applicant’s health was deteriorating and that he urgently needed ART at the regional AIDS centre in Odesa, which was not available at the Izmayil SIZO. The judge suspended the proceedings and ordered his transfer to the Odesa SIZO for examination and treatment. He was transferred on 27 May 2011.

According to the Odesa SIZO authorities, on 7 June 2011 the applicant was offered ART and tuberculosis chemotherapy but refused and gave no written explanation. On 10 June 2011 the regional AIDS centre confirmed HIV and diagnosed tuberculosis; outpatient tuberculosis treatment and ART were prescribed on the SIZO premises. A certificate signed by an official and two doctors recorded that he again refused ART. On 24 June 2011 he was offered outpatient treatment and refused again. On 12 August 2011 the Odesa SIZO head reported that the applicant had refused prescribed outpatient ART three times and proposed transferring him back to Izmayil SIZO, while assuring treatment would be provided if he consented.

On 16 August 2011 the Izmayil Court allowed the transfer back, noting that the refusal could be seen as deliberate protraction of the criminal case, and resumed proceedings. On arrival, the applicant stated he would refuse ART at the Izmayil SIZO or any penitentiary institution; this was certified in writing by medical staff and an officer.

On 8 November 2011 the applicant complained to the Ombudsman that, despite his critical condition, authorities refused inpatient ART and treatment for concomitant diseases in a specialised hospital. The outcome is unknown. In December 2011 he and his lawyer sought a change of preventive measure to allow inpatient treatment in an AIDS hospital. On 12 January 2012 the court ordered a forensic examination to establish whether he could remain in detention. On 19 January 2012 he complained to the Odesa Regional Prosecutor’s Office about the lack of ART. On 8 February 2012 his CD4 count was 79 cells/mm3. On 13 March 2012 a blood test detected hepatitis.

On 15 and 22 March 2012 the Odesa SIZO head informed the applicant’s lawyer that he had HIV, tuberculosis, pneumonia, candidosis, hepatitis, splenomegaly, hypertension, venous insufficiency, and multiple organ dysfunction, and that treatment was offered. The authorities again cited his 2011 refusals. On 21 March 2012 the prosecutor dismissed his complaint as unfounded because he had refused outpatient ART in June 2011 and later in any penitentiary institution.

On 16 April 2012 the applicant asked the European Court of Human Rights for an interim measure, saying he lacked necessary medical examination and treatment. On 23 April 2012 the Court indicated under Rule 39 that he should immediately receive appropriate inpatient treatment in a hospital specialising in AIDS and concomitant diseases. A forensic report that day confirmed his diseases but found them not incompatible with detention. He was admitted to the Izmayil District Infectious Hospital on 14 May 2012 and released from detention on 16 May 2012 due to poor health. The interim measure was lifted on 6 July 2012. The case concerned alleged lack of medical treatment in detention and lack of an effective domestic remedy.
001-208764:
**Case: Cauchi v. Malta** (Application no. 14013/19), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 25 March 2021.

The applicant, Catherine Cauchi, a Maltese national born in 1941, owned a property at 19 Dar il-Bebbux Street, Ħal Għaxaq. In 1967 she granted the property under a temporary emphyteusis for seventeen years at MTL 25 per year (approximately EUR 58). The property was later sub-leased. When the emphyteusis expired on 26 February 1984, a couple (“couple A.”) were occupying it as their sole ordinary residence. They had carried out substantial works to make the property habitable, a condition they had accepted to obtain the lease. They relied on the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, as amended by Act XXIII of 1979, to retain the property under a lease at a controlled rent.

The rent remained very low. It was increased in line with inflation but capped, and from 27 February 1999 the legal rent should have been MTL 100 per year (about EUR 116). However, couple A. continued paying MTL 50 because the applicant did not seek an increase. From 2010 they paid EUR 185 per year; from 2013, EUR 197.31; and from 2017, EUR 200 per year. The tenants owned no other property, and Mr A. had a low wage, periods of unemployment, and later a pension of EUR 515 per month.

In 2017 the applicant brought constitutional redress proceedings. She alleged that the Ordinance, as amended by Act XXIII of 1979, imposed a unilateral lease for an indefinite period without enabling her to obtain a fair and adequate rent, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. She sought compensation dating back to 1984 and eviction of the tenants. Expert evidence showed that the property’s 2017 sale value was between EUR 165,000 and EUR 174,000, and its market rental value was around EUR 398.75 per month, or EUR 4,785 per year. One court expert estimated annual rental values rising from EUR 701 in 1984 to EUR 5,775 in 2017. The controlled rent was therefore far below market levels.

On 31 October 2018 the Civil Court (First Hall), in its constitutional competence, found a violation of the applicant’s property rights. It awarded her EUR 20,000 in compensation and declared that the tenants could no longer rely on the relevant law to retain title. The court found that the difference between market rental value and the rent received was “enormous if not shocking,” that the rent was not compatible with current Maltese society, and that the law lacked procedural safeguards. However, it refused to order eviction, considering the interference lawful and pursuing a legitimate social-housing aim, and stating that it was not the appropriate court to order eviction. Instead, it barred the tenants from relying on Article 12(2)(b)(i) of the Ordinance in future eviction proceedings. In fixing compensation, it considered the market discrepancy, the social aim, uncertainty over recovering the property, the thirty-four years of disproportionality, the applicant’s delay in suing until 2017, and the State’s inertia. One third of costs were awarded against her.

The applicant did not appeal, asserting that the Constitutional Court was not an effective remedy because it systematically reduced awards. Even after the judgment, she could not evict the tenants because Act No. XXVII of 2018 provided that, despite a judgment in the owner’s favour, eviction could not be requested without first using the new procedure under that Act. In 2019 she filed a case before the Rent Regulation Board under Article 12B, seeking an increase in rent; those proceedings were still pending in May 2020. Article 12B allows owners to seek rent of up to 2% of the open-market freehold value, subject to means testing and possible gradual increases.

The alleged violation therefore concerned the disproportionate amount of rent received under Malta’s rent-control regime and the effectiveness, particularly after the 2018 amendments, of the remedies and compensation available to the applicant.
001-212829:
**Summary of W.A. v. Switzerland**

The case of *W.A. v. Switzerland* concerns the applicant's challenge to his subsequent preventive detention (*nachträgliche Verwahrung*) following the completion of a twenty-year prison sentence. The applicant, a Swiss national born in 1960, was convicted by the Zurich Jury Court in 1993 of murder and intentional manslaughter and sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. The court found that he had murdered a man in a particularly violent manner in 1983 and, in 1990, had induced his partner to strangle an acquaintance, whose corpse he subsequently dismembered. Psychiatric expert G. diagnosed the applicant with a personality disorder and alcohol intoxication, concluding that his capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of his acts was substantially diminished at the time of both offences.

Importantly, the sentencing court decided *not* to order preventive detention under Article 43 § 1 of the then-applicable Criminal Code. It reasoned that preventive detention in practice rarely lasted more than five years, whereas a long prison term would better serve the aim of protecting society from the applicant, who was considered very dangerous due to his abnormal mental state.

The applicant served his full sentence until 8 October 2010. In 2009, while he was still incarcerated, the Public Prosecution Office applied for his subsequent preventive detention under Article 65 § 2 of the Criminal Code, a provision that had entered into force in 2007. This provision permits courts to order preventive detention after sentencing if new facts or evidence reveal that the requirements for such detention were already met at the time of conviction but were unknown to the court.

In 2012, the Federal Court found that new facts justified reopening the proceedings. A 2009 psychiatric report by expert P., using new analytical methods unavailable in the 1990s, concluded that the applicant had not been alcohol-dependent but suffered from dissocial personality disorder and psychopathy—conditions deemed untreatable and associated with a very high risk of further violent offences. These facts had not been known to the Jury Court in 1993.

Following the reopening, the Zurich District Court ordered the applicant's subsequent preventive detention in 2013, relying on reports from experts P. and R. It found that the requirements for preventive detention had been met both at the time of conviction and currently, citing the applicant's serious mental disorder and the very high risk he posed if released. Appeals to the Zurich Court of Appeal and the Federal Court were dismissed in 2014 and 2015 respectively.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 (right to liberty), Article 7 § 1 (prohibition on retrospective punishment), and Article 4 § 1 of Protocol No. 7 (right not to be punished twice). The Federal Court rejected these claims, finding that preventive detention measures were comparable to penalties and thus subject to the *nulla poena sine lege* principle, but concluded that the retrospective application did not impose a heavier sanction than the law applicable at the time of the offence. It further held that reopening to the convicted person's detriment had been permissible under the old law and that the detention had a sufficient causal connection with the original conviction.
001-209330:
**Poltoratskyy v. Ukraine** (Application no. 11551/13) is a European Court of Human Rights case from the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee. The judgment was delivered on 22 April 2021 and is final, though subject to editorial revision. The applicant, Mr Boryslav Yevgenovych Poltoratskyy, is a Ukrainian national born in 1976 who is serving a life sentence in Vinnytsya Prison no. 1. He lodged his application on 21 August 2012, complaining under Articles 3, 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court gave notice of those complaints to the Ukrainian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Government stated that they were not in a position to provide observations on admissibility or merits, while the applicant submitted observations.

The underlying facts, as submitted by the applicant and not contested by the Government, are central to the alleged violations. On 12 December 1995, the Ivano-Frankivsk Regional Court found the applicant guilty of several counts of aggravated murder and robbery and sentenced him to death. On 22 February 1996, the Supreme Court upheld that verdict. Subsequently, on 2 June 2000, following legislative amendments, the Ivano-Frankivsk Court commuted the applicant’s death sentence to life imprisonment. Since then, the applicant has remained in prison serving that life sentence. His parents have visited him in prison in accordance with the applicable legal rules.

The alleged violations concern three connected issues. First, under Article 3 of the Convention, the applicant complained that his life imprisonment offered no genuine prospect of release. In essence, he alleged that a life sentence without a realistic possibility of release amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment. The relevant legal framework on life imprisonment is set out in *Petukhov v. Ukraine (no. 2)*, which the Court referenced. The key fact relevant to this complaint is the applicant’s 2000 commutation from death penalty to life imprisonment and his continued incarceration under that sentence.

Second, under Article 8, the applicant complained about restrictions on his right to family visits during his sentence. Although the facts state that his parents have been visiting him in accordance with applicable legal rules, the applicant nevertheless alleged that the prison visit regime interfered with his right to respect for family life. The legal provisions governing visiting entitlement in Ukrainian prisons are addressed in cases such as *Trosin v. Ukraine*, *Bigun v. Ukraine*, and *Starishko v. Ukraine*. The key facts are therefore the applicant’s imprisonment, his parents’ visits, and the restrictive legal framework governing family visits for life-sentenced prisoners.

Third, under Article 13, the applicant complained that he had no effective domestic remedy in respect of his Article 3 and Article 8 grievances. This complaint is derivative of the first two: he alleged that Ukrainian law did not provide an effective mechanism to challenge either the lack of a genuine release prospect under his life sentence or the restrictions on family visits.

Procedurally, the applicant was granted legal aid and represented by Mr Gennadiy Tokarev, a lawyer practising in Kharkiv. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna. The Court deliberated in private on 25 March 2021 and adopted the judgment on 22 April 2021. The case therefore focuses on the compatibility of Ukraine’s life-imprisonment regime and prison-visit restrictions with Convention rights, as raised through the applicant’s specific conviction, commutation, and family-visit circumstances.
001-208589:
**Baranin and Vukčević v. Montenegro** (Applications nos. 24655/18 and 24656/18) concerns the alleged ill-treatment of two men by unidentified police officers during opposition protests in Podgorica on 24 October 2015, and the alleged failure of the Montenegrin authorities to conduct an effective investigation and provide an effective remedy, contrary to Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention.

On 24 October 2015, an opposition coalition organised protests in front of Parliament. Police, including the Special Police Unit and the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit (“SAU”), were deployed. At some point protests became violent: some protesters tried to enter Parliament and threw stones and Molotov cocktails. The authorities ordered the gathering terminated, and further incidents occurred in the city that night. In total, 54 people were injured, including 29 police officers and 25 protesters.

At about 10:30 p.m., the applicants were near the protests but did not participate. While avoiding a group of protesters, they approached police in a side street and were allowed to pass. A few metres further on, several masked police officers approached them, ordered them to lie on the ground, verbally insulted them and kicked them. One officer pressed the second applicant’s head to the ground with his foot. An SAU Hummer and other vehicles were present. The incident was filmed from a nearby office window and posted on YouTube.

The applicants sought medical help on 27 and 28 October 2015. The first applicant had painful haematomas on both inner thighs and around his left eyelid; the second had haematomas on his left ribcage and the back of his left knee. They reported the incident to police on 30 October 2015. The State prosecutor’s office (“SPO”) opened a case against unknown SAU officers for ill-treatment. The SAU’s report of 25 October 2015 did not mention the incident.

The investigation encountered serious difficulties. Video footage was of poor quality, and officers had worn masks and helmets, making identification allegedly impossible. The SPO requested GPS data and information about SAU vehicles; the SAU stated that officer Lj.P. had been responsible for nine vehicles, including the Hummer, but had not driven any. A pharmacy and bakery camera yielded no useful footage. Police radio recordings were unavailable because the recording system had not been functioning. A medical expert report in February 2016 confirmed minor bodily injuries caused by blunt force, fists or feet.

On 21 June 2017, the Constitutional Court found violations of both the substantive and procedural aspects of Article 3. It held that the applicants had suffered inhuman and degrading treatment at the hands of unidentified SAU officers; the force had been excessive, disproportionate and unprovoked. It also found that the SPO’s investigation had not been thorough, independent or prompt: the SPO had failed to interview journalists or SAU officers, had repeatedly asked the police—who were in the same chain of command as the alleged perpetrators—to identify the officers, and had not identified anyone in over 19 months. The Police Directorate had likewise failed to conduct an effective internal investigation. The court ordered a thorough, prompt and independent investigation.

After that decision, the SPO interviewed a journalist, TV director, pharmacy owner, SPU commander and 54 SAU officers. The SAU officers were questioned “as citizens” and were not obliged to answer; they claimed that masks and chaos made recognition impossible. In November 2017, the SPO concluded that an offence had undoubtedly been committed but that the perpetrators could not be identified. The investigation remained ongoing. Separately, the SAU commander was convicted of aiding perpetrators by concealing identities and sentenced to five months’ imprisonment. The applicants also obtained civil compensation of €5,000 each. The Strasbourg applications allege the ill-treatment and the lack of an effective investigation and remedy.
001-211138:
The case of **Szőlősi v. Hungary** (Application no. 46382/20) is an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, **László Szőlősi**, born in 1974, was represented by **Dániel András Karsai**, a lawyer practising in Budapest. The Hungarian Government were given notice of the application.

The application was introduced on **12 October 2020**. It was assigned to the First Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of **Erik Wennerström** (President), **Lorraine Schembri Orland**, and **Ioannis Ktistakis**, with **Attila Teplán** as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on **1 July 2021** and delivered its judgment on **22 July 2021**. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The central alleged violation concerns the **excessive length of criminal proceedings** brought against the applicant in Hungary. According to the appended table, the domestic criminal proceedings began on **21 October 2014**. At the time the application was lodged and at the time of the table, the proceedings were still **pending**. The total length was recorded as **more than six years, six months and thirteen days**, involving **two levels of jurisdiction**.

These facts are the key elements relevant to the complaint under the Convention. The applicant complained that the duration of the criminal proceedings exceeded a reasonable time, which in Convention terms most naturally engages **Article 6 § 1**, guaranteeing the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. However, the supplied text does not quote the specific Article or set out the Court’s reasoning on the merits. It also does not identify the nature of the criminal charge, the complexity of the case, the applicant’s conduct, or any delays attributable to the domestic authorities—factors normally considered when assessing whether the length of proceedings was reasonable.

The applicant also raised **other complaints** under the Convention, but the provided extract does not specify what those complaints were or the facts underlying them. The only substantive factual information supplied is the timeline and procedural posture of the criminal case: it commenced in October 2014, remained unresolved, lasted over six and a half years, and involved two levels of jurisdiction. Because the full text excerpt ends after the facts and appended table, it does not include the Court’s final assessment, findings of violation, just satisfaction, or costs. The summary therefore is limited to the procedural history and the core alleged violation of excessive length of criminal proceedings.
001-210304:
The case of *Myasnikov and Ulyanov v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 61919/19 and 32809/20) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered in Strasbourg on 10 June 2021. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The case originated in two applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 16 November 2019 and 14 July 2020. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law; they also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The first applicant, Stanislav Yevgenovych Myasnikov, born in 1981, was represented by Andriy Vitaliyovych Pustyntsev and Oleksandr Anatoliyovych Ignatov, both of Dnipro. He was detained in Dnipro Penitentiary Facility No. 4 from 26 February 2018 and, as reflected in the appended table, remained there pending for more than 3 years, 2 months and 2 days. His personal space was 3–3.5 sq. m per inmate. He alleged lack of or insufficient electric light, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, a mouldy or dirty cell, infestation with insects or rodents, lack of privacy for the toilet, lack or inadequacy of hygienic facilities, poor bedding and bed linen, poor quality food, and no or restricted access to a shower.

The second applicant, Igor Volodymyrovych Ulyanov, born in 1993, was represented by Oleksandr Volodymyrovych Vavrenyuk of Pyatykhatky. He was detained in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 2 May 2018 and, as of the table, had been held pending for more than 2 years, 11 months and 26 days. His personal space was only 1.64–2.78 sq. m per inmate, indicating severe overcrowding. He alleged lack of fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack of or insufficient electric and natural light, poor bedding and bed linen, lack of toiletries, lack or insufficient quantity of food, restricted access to a shower, overcrowding, and poor quality food.

The key alleged violations therefore concern the conditions of the applicants’ detention and the absence of an effective domestic remedy. The facts emphasise prolonged detention, very small living space—especially Ulyanov’s 1.64–2.78 sq. m—and numerous material deficiencies affecting health, hygiene, privacy, light, air, and nutrition. Myasnikov’s space of 3–3.5 sq. m also fell below the 4 sq. m benchmark often used in the Court’s case-law. Since both detentions were still pending, the complained-of conditions were ongoing rather than isolated. The lack of effective remedy allegation means the applicants claimed that no domestic authority could adequately prevent or redress those conditions. The Court deliberated in private on 20 May 2021 and adopted the judgment on 10 June 2021.
001-214012:
In *Budimir v. Croatia*, the applicant, Jovan Budimir, was a Croatian national of Serb ethnicity, born in 1951, living in Beli Manastir. A car mechanic by profession, he worked as a certified motor vehicle inspector for a private company. On 29 May 1997 he was issued a special licence to perform vehicle inspections. On 5 October 1998 he carried out a standard inspection of a tractor and confirmed its roadworthiness. Ten days later, on 15 October 1998, the same tractor collided with a police car. An extraordinary inspection the following day found that the tractor’s braking system had been defective. This event triggered criminal, administrative and employment consequences.

In March 1999 the Ministry of the Interior lodged a criminal complaint alleging that the applicant had falsified the tractor’s inspection record. He was charged in July 1999. On 23 May 2001 the Beli Manastir Municipal Court acquitted him because it could not establish that he had committed the offence. Expert evidence indicated that the tractor’s brakes could have become defective during the ten days between the inspection and the accident.

Meanwhile, on 16 March 1999, the Ministry revoked the applicant’s licence to carry out vehicle inspections under section 277(2) of the Road Safety Act. That decision was deemed final, and his employer immediately dismissed him on 30 March 1999 because loss of the licence made continued employment impossible. The applicant challenged the revocation. On 23 May 2001 the Administrative Court quashed the Ministry’s decision for failure to establish all relevant facts and remitted the case. On 29 August 2001 the Ministry again revoked the licence, relying on an expert opinion from its Centre for Forensics stating that the brakes could not have become defective in the interim. On 4 December 2003 the Administrative Court again quashed that decision, finding that the Ministry had not allowed the applicant to comment on the expert findings and had not resolved contradictions between the expert evidence in the criminal and administrative proceedings. On 10 May 2004 the Ministry returned his licence, taking into account his criminal acquittal. He had therefore been unable to work as a certified inspector for about five years.

The applicant also challenged his dismissal. On 4 July 2005 the Zagreb Municipal Court dismissed his claim, finding the summary dismissal lawful and holding that his employer had not been obliged to offer him another post while proceedings were pending. That judgment was upheld on 2 May 2006.

On 21 September 2006 the applicant brought a civil action against the State under section 13 of the State Administration Act, seeking damages for unlawful or wrongful conduct by administrative authorities. He claimed pecuniary damage because the licence revocation had led to his dismissal and unemployment. The Osijek Municipal Court dismissed the action on 26 February 2009; the Osijek County Court upheld that decision on 5 May 2011; and on 4 September 2013 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law. The Supreme Court held that the Ministry had acted in line with section 277(2) because there had been reasonable doubt, and that a wrong application of law or wrong fact-finding, even if later quashed, did not necessarily amount to unlawful conduct. It accepted damage and causal link but found no liability. The applicant’s constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible on 6 March 2014.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 10 June 2014. The Court gave notice only of the complaint concerning respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention, declaring the remainder inadmissible. The alleged violation concerned the revocation of his professional licence and his consequent inability to work as a certified motor vehicle inspector for some five years, despite his criminal acquittal and the repeated quashing of the administrative revocation decisions.
001-213525:
**Summary of *Borgovan v. Romania* (Application no. 23553/15)**

The case of *Borgovan v. Romania* concerns a Romanian national, Mr. Lucian Borgovan, who lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 6 May 2015. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that civil proceedings regarding his access to the legal profession were unfair and violated the principle of legal certainty due to divergent domestic case-law.

The key facts are as follows: At the relevant time, the applicant worked as a legal counsel. On 28 June 2010, he requested the Suceava Bar Association to register him as a lawyer without having to sit an exam, a procedure permitted under Article 16 § 2 (b) of the Legal Profession Act for legal counsels with at least ten years of experience. This legal provision was repealed on 31 December 2010.

On 17 February 2011, the Suceava Bar Association invited the applicant and other candidates to sit a written multiple-choice test to evaluate their knowledge of the legal profession's laws, statutes, and code of conduct. Following this evaluation, the Bar Association dismissed the applicant's request on 24 February 2011, stating he had not demonstrated sufficient knowledge. This decision was upheld by the National Bar Association on 8 July 2011.

The applicant then challenged these decisions in court. He also raised an objection against the provisions of the Statute of the Legal Profession and Guidelines of the National Bar Association that permitted such evaluations. This objection was initially allowed by the Bucharest Court of Appeal on 13 June 2013, but on appeal, the High Court of Cassation and Justice, in a final decision on 14 November 2013, dismissed the objection, finding the provisions lawful as they did not add criteria to the law.

Subsequently, the applicant's main action to compel the Bar Association to register him was initially allowed by the Bucharest County Court on 20 February 2014. However, this decision was overturned on appeal. In a final decision on 4 September 2014, the Bucharest Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's action. The court held that evaluating a candidate's professional competence was acceptable and did not breach legal provisions, as confirmed by the High Court's prior ruling. The final decision was served on the applicant on 5 January 2015.

The applicant's complaint centered on the alleged unfairness and lack of legal certainty in these proceedings. The government submitted nine High Court decisions (2012-2014) supporting the view that local bar associations could verify candidates' knowledge without it constituting an exam. Conversely, the applicant submitted twenty-eight High Court decisions (2003-2015) where the court had ruled in favor of legal counsels whose admission was denied after being asked to undergo similar evaluations. In seventeen of these decisions, the High Court found that bar associations, including Suceava's, had improperly exercised their discretionary powers. Thirteen of these decisions were rendered after the Court's judgment in *Ştefan and Ştef v. Romania* and the adoption of the relevant Guidelines. Some decisions also noted that bar associations failed to provide reasons for denying admission, hindering judicial review.

The case thus centers on the applicant's inability to be admitted to the bar without an exam following a written evaluation, and the conflicting domestic jurisprudence on the legality and propriety of such evaluations by local bar associations in the context of admission without examination.
001-210413:
**Case: Rîbac and Rodina-Agro S.A. v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia**  
*(Application no. 28857/14, European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 15 June 2021)*

The case concerns an alleged breach of the applicants’ right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights in the Transdniestrian region of Moldova. The applicants are Mr Pavel Rîbac, a Moldovan national born in 1951 and living in Erjovo, and Rodina-Agro S.A., a company incorporated in the Transdniestrian region of Moldova. They lodged their application on 31 March 2014.

The background to the case lies in the Transdniestrian armed conflict of 1991–1992 and subsequent events, as previously set out in cases such as *Ilaşcu and Others v. Moldova and Russia* and *Catan and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*. The second applicant was created on 6 November 2012 by former members of the kolkhoz Rodina from the villages of Erjovo and Sarateia. Its purpose was to defend their interests against plans by the authorities of the so-called “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”) to transfer land owned by the former kolkhoz to other persons.

On 21 September 2013, the first applicant organised a public meeting for former members of the kolkhoz Rodina. The meeting was intended to discuss the land issue. Sixty-five persons participated in the gathering. On 23 September 2013, the Rîbniţa District Court imposed a fine of 145 MRT roubles on the first applicant for breaching the rules governing public manifestations. The court found that the first applicant had not obtained prior authorisation for holding the manifestation. The first applicant challenged that decision before the MRT Supreme Court. On 31 October 2013, the MRT Supreme Court dismissed his appeal and upheld the fine imposed by the Rîbniţa District Court.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore that the first applicant organised a peaceful public meeting concerning land rights, that 65 people attended, and that he was subsequently punished by the de facto Transdniestrian authorities for failing to obtain prior authorisation. The applicants complained that this sanction interfered with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly guaranteed by Article 11 of the Convention. The case was brought against both the Republic of Moldova and Russia, with the Court examining the application in the context of the Transdniestrian region.

Procedurally, the application was communicated to the Moldovan Government. The Russian Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee of the Court, but that objection was rejected. The parties submitted observations. The Court deliberated in private on 18 May 2021 and delivered its judgment on 15 June 2021. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The relevant domestic law, practice of the Republic of Moldova, and reports by inter-governmental and non-governmental organisations were summarised in *Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*. The key alleged violation remains the punishment of the first applicant for organising a peaceful assembly without prior authorisation, contrary to Article 11 of the Convention.
001-213203:
**Summary of *Mikeladze and Others v. Georgia* (Application no. 54217/16)**

The case concerns four Georgian nationals of the Muslim minority who complained that police physically and verbally assaulted them during arrest and detention, using discriminatory insults, and that the ensuing criminal investigation was ineffective, in breach of Articles 3 and 14 of the Convention.

The events arose from a dispute over an old building in the village of Mokhe, claimed by the local Muslim community as an ancient mosque, which municipal authorities decided to reconstruct as a public library. On 22 October 2014, between sixty and one hundred police officers and municipal representatives gathered as reconstruction began. Fifty to one hundred local Muslim residents, including the applicants, protested. The police formed a cordon separating protesters from officials. The first applicant was a village trustee; his father, the second applicant, accompanied him; the third applicant joined from a neighbouring village; and the fourth applicant, a school librarian, became involved after leaving work.

Accounts of the events differ. The applicants alleged that police used excessive force during arrests and shouted insults, calling them "Tatars"—a term they considered an insult implying their Muslim faith was incompatible with being Georgian. They claimed violence continued at the police station. The Government maintained that the applicants resorted to physical and verbal violence and attempted to break the police cordon; arrests were for resisting lawful orders and breaching public order, with no excessive force or derogatory remarks used.

Fourteen individuals were arrested. The first three applicants faced criminal charges of resisting police; the remaining eleven, including the fourth applicant, faced administrative charges of minor hooliganism and disobeying police. All were released on 23 October 2014.

The first applicant's arrest report recorded redness around his left eye, an excoriation on a wrist, and a bump on his head; he stated injuries occurred during arrest and refused medical assistance. He later complained of headache and disorientation, and medical examination noted a haematoma around the left eye. The second applicant complained of breathing difficulties the following morning. The third and fourth applicants' reports recorded no injuries or complaints.

On 5 November 2014, the first three applicants and seven others complained to the Chief Prosecutor's Office about derogatory language (including "Tatar") and excessive force during arrest and at the police station. They requested that the prosecutor's office, rather than the implicated police, conduct the investigation. The first applicant alleged he was beaten and assaulted at the station; the third applicant claimed seven officers beat him for approximately ten minutes.

A criminal investigation was split in December 2014: one strand concerning the applicants' alleged offences against police, another concerning alleged police exceeding of official powers. Investigative steps in 2014–2015 produced conflicting witness accounts—some confirmed hearing "Tatar" insults and witnessing beatings; others denied any ill-treatment. In April 2021, prosecutors granted the first applicant victim status, finding that officers G.P. and B.A. had punched and kicked him at the police station, and charged both (by then no longer serving) under Article 333 § 3(b) of the Criminal Code. Proceedings against them remain ongoing, and no progress was made regarding the other three applicants' complaints.
