001-207806:
**Zohlandt v. the Netherlands** (Application no. 69491/16) concerned the applicant’s pre-trial detention and his complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, a Dutch national born in 1961, alleged that the assumed risk of recidivism used to justify his extended detention on remand was not based on facts from the case file or the circumstances of the case. He further alleged that the Court of Appeal’s decision of 18 August 2016 lacked adequate justification or, alternatively, sufficient reasons.

The facts arose from an incident on 16 May 2016, when police were notified that a man, Mr U., had been beaten by two men who drove away. Police found U. bruised and bloodstains in his home. The next day, U. lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant, accusing him of attempted murder/homicide, aggravated assault and destruction of property. On 13 June 2016 the applicant was arrested and placed in police custody on suspicion of attempted premeditated aggravated assault and illegal possession of a firearm, ammunition and a knuckleduster found in his home.

On 16 June 2016 an investigating judge ordered the applicant’s initial detention on remand for fourteen days. The order cited serious public-safety reasons, specifically a serious risk that the applicant would reoffend. It relied on factors including that the suspected act had ended only after police intervention, that the applicant’s circumstances and the circumstances of the offence remained unchanged, and that he had previously had contact with police and criminal justice authorities for similar acts.

On 29 June 2016 the Regional Court extended the applicant’s detention on remand for ninety days and dismissed his request to suspend it. The prosecution expected the investigation to finish within weeks and a trial to follow. The applicant argued that he had acted in self-defence, that the investigation had finished, and that the detention was harmful to his family. He did not appeal those decisions. On 29 July 2016 he applied for release or suspension. A trial hearing was scheduled for 23 September 2016. He argued that the detention order rested only on an unlikely risk of recidivism: his prior violent offences dated from 2000–2004, the current acts were arguably self-defence, and detention could exceed any eventual sentence. He also cited family financial and security concerns.

On 3 August 2016 the Regional Court dismissed the applications, finding that the reasons for the extended detention remained pertinent and that the interests of criminal justice outweighed the applicant’s personal interests. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal. He added that police had not stopped the altercation or caught him in the act; he had been arrested a month later at home. He explained that the conflict with U. concerned financial compensation, that U. had invited him and stabbed him in the face, and that in the following month he had not contacted U. and had decided to drop the matter. He also noted he had not committed violent crimes for twelve years, although he had other offences such as menace and drink-driving.

On 18 August 2016 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that serious objections and grounds, as found by the Regional Court, could be derived from the case file and fully justified continued pre-trial detention. It agreed with the impugned decision and its grounds and found no reason to suspend detention after weighing the interests. No further appeal lay. The trial began on 23 September 2016; the Regional Court suspended pre-trial detention subject to a restraining order. On 3 March 2017 the applicant was convicted of attempted premeditated aggravated assault and weapons offences and sentenced to ten months’ imprisonment less pre-trial detention.
001-208534:
In *Fikret Karahan v. Turkey*, the applicant was a Turkish national with previous convictions for PKK-related offences. The case concerned his fair-trial complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention: his inability to examine the key witness against him, the authorities’ failure to serve the reasoned first-instance judgment on him or his lawyer, and the lack of an oral hearing before the Court of Cassation.

In 2000, the applicant’s brother, G.K., was questioned by anti-terrorist police without a lawyer and implicated the applicant, claiming that after his release from prison he had left Turkey and used the code name “Baran” in Romania. Charges against G.K. were later discontinued. In 2003, E.A., a former PKK member, surrendered under the Reintegration of Offenders into Society Act. While questioned without a lawyer, E.A. provided information on about thirty alleged PKK members, including a person with the code name “Mahir,” said to have been active at a PKK camp in Iran. E.A. gave no specific acts attributed to “Mahir.” On 10 September 2003, after being shown a small black-and-white mugshot of the applicant, E.A. identified him as “Mahir” and stated he was certain. The identification record was signed by E.A. and two police officers.

The applicant was later arrested while trying to cross illegally from Ukraine to Poland on a forged passport and handed over to Turkey. In February 2005, he was questioned in the presence of a lawyer. He denied being a PKK member after his release, denied knowing E.A., and denied ever using the name “Baran” or being in Romania or the Iranian camp. He confirmed that the mugshot shown to E.A. was his own 1996 police photograph. His lawyer challenged the reliability of the photo-identification procedure. The indictment relied on the statements of G.K. and E.A.

At trial, G.K. testified in June 2005 and recanted, saying his earlier police statement had been made under pressure and that the applicant had lived in Istanbul and had no terrorist affiliation at the time. The defence repeatedly requested that E.A. be summoned. E.A. did not attend the October 2005 hearing but attended the December 2005 hearing. The applicant was not brought from prison, although his lawyer was present. E.A. testified that he did not know “Fikret Karahan” by name, did not know “Mahir’s” real name, did not remember whether he had identified anyone, and was not certain that the applicant was “Mahir.” He said there had been ten to fifteen people with the same code name and that he had witnessed no specific acts by “Mahir.”

On 18 October 2006, the Istanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant of PKK/KONGRA-GEL membership and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment. The judgment relied on E.A.’s police statement and photo identification, treating the police statement as more credible than E.A.’s later uncertain court testimony. It did not rely on G.K.’s testimony.

The applicant appealed and requested a hearing. His lawyer argued that the reasoned judgment had never been served on the defence, preventing specific appeal grounds. He further argued that the sole witness against the applicant had been heard in the applicant’s absence, had retracted his statement, and that there was no corroborating evidence. On 5 June 2007, the Court of Cassation denied the request for a hearing and upheld the conviction. The applicant alleged that neither he nor his lawyer was notified of that decision. The relevant domestic law required that where evidence consisted only of witness statements, the witness must be heard in court, and a prior written statement could not substitute for that hearing.
001-207849:
In *Duraković and Kreštalica v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Applications nos. 61555/19 and 61795/19), the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 11 February 2021. The Committee was composed of Armen Harutyunyan (President), Jolien Schukking and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was adopted on 21 January 2021. It is final but subject to editorial revision.

The case originated in two applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention on 22 November 2019. The applicants were represented by Mr O. Eterović, a lawyer practising in Sarajevo. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the applications.

The central complaint in both applications was the non-enforcement of domestic decisions. The appended table set out the applicant details, the relevant domestic decisions, the start dates of the non-enforcement periods, and the length of the pending enforcement proceedings.

In the first application, no. 61555/19, the sole applicant was Fehim Duraković, born on 25 February 1953. The relevant domestic decision was issued by the Sarajevo Municipal Court on 4 January 2012. According to the table, the non-enforcement period began on 29 January 2016. The enforcement proceedings remained pending for more than four years, ten months and eleven days. The applicant therefore complained that the domestic authorities had failed to enforce a binding decision in his favour.

In the second application, no. 61795/19, there were three applicants, described as the Kreštalica household: Safija Kreštalica, born on 15 September 1968; Faris Kreštalica, born on 28 May 2010; and Mela Kreštalica, born on 2 February 2000. The relevant domestic decision was issued by the Sarajevo Municipal Court on 18 October 2013. The non-enforcement period began on 16 August 2016. The enforcement proceedings remained pending for more than four years, three months and twenty-four days. These applicants likewise complained of the failure to enforce the domestic decision.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the existence of domestic court decisions, the dates from which enforcement was not carried out, and the lengthy periods during which enforcement remained pending. In both cases, the applicants alleged that the respondent State had failed to secure the execution of final domestic decisions. The table records the enforcement proceedings as “pending” and gives substantial durations of non-enforcement: over four years and ten months in Duraković’s case and over four years and three months in the Kreštalica applicants’ case. Those periods were continuing at the time reflected in the table.

The essence of the alleged violation was the domestic authorities’ failure to enforce binding judicial decisions within a reasonable time. In Convention terms, such complaints typically concern the right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 and the right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, because final judgments may create enforceable entitlements. The Court’s assessment would focus on whether the State complied with its positive obligation to enforce domestic decisions and whether the applicants had effective remedies for the delay. The provided text mainly records the procedure and facts; it does not include the Court’s eventual merits findings or any award of just satisfaction.
001-207366:
This case concerns an alleged breach of the right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, arising from Spanish foreclosure proceedings in which the applicant and his wife were not personally served. The applicant, Hans Johannes Klopstra, is a Dutch national born in 1947 and living in Aachen.

In 1998, Klopstra and his wife bought a plot in Javea, Alicante, and later built a house there. In 2003, they signed a mortgage loan agreement with Barclays Bank for €350,000, secured by the Javea house, then valued at €517,200. The agreement listed their German home address but designated the plot’s parcel address in Javea for service in Spain. In 2006, the Municipality of Javea issued a housing permit that, for the first time, identified the property by its house number and noted that it corresponded to the former parcel address.

In February 2012, the bank sent certified faxes to the couple at the Javea address, stating that they had defaulted since August 2011 on instalments amounting to €17,627.21. The bank terminated the contract and demanded the full outstanding amount of €190,461. Postal delivery was attempted, but only a collection notice was left; there was no evidence that the couple collected it.

On 30 March 2012, the bank started civil foreclosure proceedings before the Denia Court of First Instance, claiming €190,461 plus €57,138.30 in costs. The court asked the Javea Peace Court to summon the applicant and his wife at the parcel address designated by the bank. On 7 June 2012, the postal service reported that service had failed because of “insufficient address details.” Instead of trying other reasonable means of personal notification, the first-instance court on 19 July 2012 ordered service by public announcement on the court-house bulletin board. The couple did not appear or oppose the bank’s claim, so proceedings continued without their defence.

On 18 October 2012, the court announced a public auction, again by public announcement. The auction took place on 24 January 2013. An external company made the highest bid of €219,400. The applicant and his wife were given ten days to submit a higher bid, but they did not. On 27 February 2013, the house was awarded to the external bidder, who sold it on 29 April 2013. In April 2013, the couple learned of the proceedings and went to the court on 2 May 2013, where the 24 January 2013 order was served on them.

On 3 May 2013, they applied to annul the proceedings, arguing that neither the initial summons nor the auction announcement had been personally served, and that they had been unable to oppose the claim or submit a higher bid. The first-instance court dismissed the application on 27 May 2013. Their amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court, relying on Article 24 of the Spanish Constitution (fair trial), was declared inadmissible on 2 February 2015 for lack of special constitutional significance. A public prosecutor’s súplica was dismissed on 12 May 2016, the Constitutional Court reiterating that the issue had been addressed in prior case-law.

The relevant Spanish legislation, section 686.3 LEC, permitted public announcement after unsuccessful service at the address recorded at the Registry. However, the Constitutional Court later held that courts must exhaust all reasonable means of personal communication before resorting to public announcement. The core alleged violation is therefore that the Spanish courts failed to ensure effective personal notification before proceeding, preventing the applicant from accessing court and defending his rights.
001-211017:
In *Cilei and Rosip v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 48145/10 and 8387/15), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints arising from arrests and detention in Transdniestria, the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The applicants, Moldovan nationals Alexandr Cilei and Ivan Rosip, alleged unlawful detention; Rosip also alleged inhuman detention conditions, unlawful seizure of property, and lack of effective remedies.

Cilei was arrested by MRT authorities on 30 January 2008 on attempted murder charges. On 5 June 2009, MRT courts convicted him and sentenced him to eleven years’ imprisonment. He sought annulment before Moldova’s Supreme Court of Justice, but on 10 May 2010 that court returned his extraordinary appeal without examination, stating it lacked competence to review MRT court judgments. He was released on 1 August 2012 after an MRT presidential pardon. His complaint concerned unlawful detention.

Rosip was founder and director of an MRT company. On 20 December 2012, MRT authorities arrested him for allegedly misappropriating funds; detention was repeatedly extended. On 24 December 2012, his personal property—two cars, gold rings, a gold watch, 159 MRT roubles, a company share, and two mobile phones—and company property were seized. On 16 June 2014, the Bender City Court convicted him of abuse of position of trust, sentenced him to one year and eight months and a fine, upheld a civil claim for 1,899,050 MRT roubles, ordered execution against his personal property, and lifted restrictions on company property. On 5 August 2014, the MRT Supreme Court increased the civil award to 2,553,000 MRT roubles (about EUR 212,750), dispensed him from serving the sentence due to limitation expiry, and released him. Enforcement against his property followed; an expert later valued it at 106,002 MRT roubles (about EUR 8,832).

As to detention conditions, Rosip was held in several facilities. In IVS Tiraspol (20 December 2012–14 January 2013), he alleged high humidity, overcrowding, no ventilation, no natural light, smoking, wooden bunks, no bed linen, unsanitary conditions, scarce/inedible food, and parasites. In Hlinaia prison no. 1 (14–22 January 2013), cells were overcrowded and unheated; relatives supplied food and medication. Mainly in Tiraspol prison no. 3 (22 January 2013–5 August 2014), he alleged overcrowding, no bed linen, bad tap water, small windows admitting damp/cold air, very short daily walks, a 20 kg monthly package limit, and hunger. Transfers were in an unheated metal truck with no toilet, sometimes for nine hours in freezing temperatures. He also complained of inadequate medical staff and reliance on relatives’ medication.

After an extraordinary appeal, on 7 April 2015 Moldova’s Supreme Court quashed the MRT judgments against Rosip, finding MRT courts unconstitutional. Rosip complained to Moldovan and Russian prosecutors about unlawful deprivation of liberty and property execution. Russia answered that the complaint did not concern Russian territory. Moldova opened but suspended a criminal investigation for lack of identified perpetrators; no property protection measures were granted because Moldovan law did not provide for them.
001-210257:
The case of *Dimov and Others v. Bulgaria* (Applications nos. 45660/17 and 13 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 8 June 2021. It concerned complaints brought by nineteen Bulgarian nationals under Article 34 of the Convention. The central alleged violation was that the applicants had been unable to vote while effectively serving prison sentences, contrary to Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, which guarantees the right to free elections.

The first application was lodged on 13 June 2017 by six applicants: Dimcho Yordanov Dimov, Asen Todorov Sabev, Ivan Gospodinov Ivanov, Kosta Rumenov Kirov, Todor Petrov Stamenov, and Ivaylo Rumenov Zhivkov. The remaining thirteen applications were lodged between September 2017 and September 2019 by individual applicants: Yuliyan Lyubomirov Zashev, Borislav Dimitrov Ivanov, Svetlomir Nikolov Neshkov, Nazam Nazmi Aziz, Daniel Dimitrov Dimitrov, Miroslav Sabev Sabev, Vladimir Veselinov Nikolov, Dragomir Tanev Manolov, Prokopiy Iliev Prokopiev, Georgi Valev Valev, Kyazim Asanov Veysyalov, Halil Adem Hasan, and Krum Yordanov Kulinski. The applicants were born between 1958 and 1990. The applicants in the first and fourteenth applications were represented by Mr K. Kanev, head of the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee; the remaining applicants were represented by Ms S. Ivanova. The Government were represented by Ms R. Nikolova from the Ministry of Justice.

The key facts concerned two election dates. On 26 March 2017, Bulgarian parliamentary elections were held. The applicants in the first through tenth applications were at that time effectively serving different prison sentences. Because the relevant Bulgarian legislation excluded persons serving prison sentences from voting, they were unable to vote in those elections. On 26 May 2019, elections for Members of the European Parliament were held. The applicants in the first application—except Mr T.P. Stamenov—and the applicants in the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth applications were then effectively serving prison sentences. As a result, under the same legislation, they could not vote in those elections. As regards Mr Stamenov, the Government pointed out, and his representative accepted, that he had not been serving a prison sentence at the time of the May 2019 European Parliament elections.

The Court noted that the relevant legal provisions concerning prisoners’ voting rights had already been set out in *Kulinski and Sabev v. Bulgaria* (no. 63849/09, §§ 10 and 15–22, 21 July 2016). It gave notice to the Bulgarian Government of the complaint concerning the applicants’ inability to vote while serving prison sentences and declared inadmissible the remainder of the second through tenth applications. The case therefore focused on whether the applicants’ exclusion from voting, solely because they were serving prison sentences, breached Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. The judgment was final but remained subject to editorial revision.

001-209373:
**E.G. v. the Republic of Moldova** (Application no. 37882/13), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 13 April 2021 (final 13 July 2021). The applicant, E.G., is a dual Moldovan and Romanian national born in 1977, living in Chișinău. The case concerns the non-enforcement of a prison sentence imposed on one of the perpetrators of a sexual assault against her, raising issues under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention.

On the night of 9–10 February 2008, the applicant was sexually assaulted by three individuals: P.G., R.G., and V.B. Criminal proceedings were opened. The three defendants were initially placed in pre-trial detention but later released pending trial; V.B. was released on 12 March 2008 against a security deposit.

On 17 June 2009, the Centru District Court in Chișinău convicted all three of gang sexual assault under Article 172 § 2(c) of the Criminal Code and imposed suspended sentences. The applicant appealed. On 2 December 2009, the Chișinău Court of Appeal affirmed the convictions and additionally convicted P.G. and R.G. of gang rape under Article 171 § 2(c), sentencing them to six and five and a half years’ imprisonment respectively. It also imposed a five-year prison sentence on V.B. That judgment was immediately enforceable. P.G. and R.G. were taken into custody from the courtroom, but V.B., who was not present, was not detained. On 7 December 2010, the Supreme Court of Justice affirmed the Court of Appeal’s judgment with final effect.

V.B. remained at large. A wanted notice was issued on 14 May 2010. In April 2011, V.B. applied through his lawyer for amnesty under the 2008 Amnesty Act. A similar application by R.G. was rejected in October 2011 because his conviction post-dated the Act and section 5 was inapplicable. On 20 December 2011, the District Court rejected V.B.’s amnesty claim for the same reason. On appeal, however, the prosecution supported V.B., and on 22 May 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal granted him amnesty, reasoning that the offence pre-dated the Act. Subsequent proceedings repeatedly reopened and reversed this decision. On 29 June 2012, the Court of Appeal set aside the amnesty and restored the refusal, but the Supreme Court later annulled that decision for lack of jurisdiction and remitted the case. On 7 March 2013, the Court of Appeal refused to entertain a further reconsideration request.

Meanwhile, on 22 October 2012, the authorities arrested V.B. but released him the same day based on the 22 May 2012 amnesty decision. In September 2013, the District Court reopened the amnesty proceedings and set aside the amnesty; the Court of Appeal affirmed on 18 November 2013, noting that the earlier court had been unaware that V.B. had breached the conditions of his release against security.

Afterwards, the applicant asked whether V.B. was serving his sentence. On 10 January 2014, the police informed her lawyer that no wanted notice had been issued and no search steps taken because neither the prosecution nor the Court of Appeal had directed a search. On 28 January 2014, the prosecution asked the police to enforce the decision setting aside the amnesty. On 31 January 2014, police found that V.B. had left Moldova for Ukraine on 16 November 2013. The prosecution later stated that the courts had failed to forward the final decision of 18 November 2013 to the police within the ten-day period required by Article 468 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. A CIS wanted notice was issued on 20 February 2014, and an international notice on 29 April 2015. According to the Government’s submissions in March 2020, V.B. had still not been found.

The applicant’s complaints under Articles 3 and 8 concerned the State’s failure to enforce the final prison sentence imposed on V.B., including delayed and contradictory amnesty proceedings, failure to search for him, and failures to transmit enforceable decisions to the police. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-210078:
The applicant, Centrum för rättvisa, is a Swedish foundation established in 2002 and based in Stockholm. It represents clients in proceedings concerning Convention rights, undertakes education and research, and participates in public debate on individual rights. It communicates daily by email, telephone and fax with individuals, organisations and companies in Sweden and abroad. It asserts that much of this communication is privacy-sensitive and that, because it scrutinises State actors, there is a risk that its communications have been or will be intercepted and examined through signals intelligence. On 14 July 2008 it lodged an application against Sweden, alleging that Swedish legislation and practice in the field of signals intelligence violated its rights under Article 8 and that it lacked an effective remedy contrary to Article 13. It did not bring any domestic proceedings, contending that no effective remedy existed for its complaints.

Domestically, foreign intelligence is regulated by the Foreign Intelligence Act (2000:130) and signals intelligence by the Signals Intelligence Act (2008:717), which entered into force on 1 January 2009 and was amended in 2009, 2013, 2015 and 2016. The National Defence Radio Establishment (FRA) is authorised to conduct signals intelligence. Signals intelligence involves intercepting, processing, analysing and reporting intelligence from electronic signals, including content and communications data, over airways and cables. Most relevant traffic is cable-based. Cable-based cross-border communications are transferred to collection points, from which limited data traffic is transferred to the FRA. Communications between a sender and receiver both within Sweden may not be intercepted; if they cannot be separated, recordings or notes must be destroyed once their domestic nature becomes clear.

The FRA may conduct signals intelligence only under detailed tasking directives issued by certain authorities, and it may not solely target a specific natural person. Permitted purposes include external military threats, international peacekeeping threats, strategic international terrorism or serious cross-border crime, weapons of mass destruction, threats to societal infrastructure, foreign conflicts, foreign intelligence operations against Swedish interests, and certain actions of foreign powers. The FRA also conducts “development activities”. Interception of cable-based signals is automated and uses selectors; selectors directly relating to a specific natural person may be used only if exceptionally important. Permits are issued by the Foreign Intelligence Court, subject to conditions, for maximum six months, renewable. In urgent cases the FRA may grant a permit itself, subject to immediate court review. The court may sit behind closed doors, with a privacy protection representative present.

Intercepted data must be destroyed in certain cases, including data concerning a specific person lacking importance, protected anonymous authorship or media sources, attorney-client privilege, or religious confession. The FRA Personal Data Processing Act and related ordinances regulate personal data, sensitive data, storage, destruction and communication to other authorities or foreign States. Supervision is carried out by the Foreign Intelligence Inspectorate, which conducted 102 inspections from 2009 to 2017, issuing 15 opinions to the FRA and one to the Government; no inspection led to a decision to cease collection or destroy results. Other oversight includes the Privacy Protection Council, data protection officers, the Data Protection Authority, Parliamentary Ombudsmen and the Chancellor of Justice.

Notification of secret surveillance is required if selectors directly related to a specific person were used, but may be delayed for secrecy and need not be given after one year or where measures concern a foreign power. Individuals may ask the Inspectorate to investigate whether their communications were intercepted; 132 requests were handled from 2010 to 2017, with no unlawfulness established. Other remedies include requests to the FRA for information or correction, appeals to the Administrative Court, and damages claims via the Chancellor of Justice. A 2010 Data Protection Authority report was overall positive but noted that notification had never been used due to secrecy considerations.
001-207136:
In *Khan v. Denmark* (Application no. 26957/19), the applicant, Shuaib Khan, a Pakistani national born in Denmark in 1986, complained that a Danish expulsion order and six-year re-entry ban imposed on him violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects private and family life.

Khan was born and raised in Denmark. His parents and four siblings lived in Denmark; two other siblings lived in the United Kingdom. He had no spouse or children. He stated that he had only broken Punjabi and could not read it, had visited Pakistan two or three times, most recently in 2007, and had no family or friends there. The Danish Immigration Service calculated that, after deducting about ten years of imprisonment, he had been lawfully resident in Denmark for approximately 20 years and 10 months. It also noted that his family owned property in Pakistan and that a Pakistani ID card later listed a permanent address there. His residence permit had been renewed in 2017 until 2021, though he had earlier been charged with staying in Denmark without the required permit after failing to renew it from 2010 to 2015.

Khan had a long criminal record since 2003, including thirteen convictions. These included weapons offences, violence, drugs, driving offences, and unlawful mobile phone possession in prison. Most significantly, in 2008 he received eight years’ imprisonment for aggravated violence, including fatal violence; in 2013 he received three years and six months for aggravated violence and theft; and in 2015 he received six months for aggravated violence. In 2015 he was also given a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period. He was released in March 2017. He was the leader of the gang Loyal to Familia (LTF), which was later dissolved by a City Court in 2020 for having an unlawful purpose and operating through violence.

The offence underlying the expulsion arose on 31 July 2017. Amid an armed conflict between gangs, police established stop-and-frisk zones, including at Blaagaard Square in Copenhagen. During a frisk there, Khan, as LTF leader, allegedly threatened a police inspector on duty. According to the courts, he said something about the inspector having an attitude problem, then told other LTF affiliates “Remember his face” and told the inspector “Watch out,” “Watch out carefully,” and “Watch your back,” while at least one affiliate photographed the inspector. The courts found his tone and attitude threatening and the atmosphere tense. He was charged under Article 119(1) of the Penal Code for threatening a public official, and also for staying without the requisite permit.

In October 2017 the Copenhagen City Court convicted him, sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment and a fine, but issued only a suspended expulsion order, finding that immediate expulsion of someone born and raised in Denmark with limited ties to Pakistan would be disproportionate. In March 2018 the High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the prison sentence to 60 days, again finding expulsion disproportionate. In November 2018 the Supreme Court increased the sentence to three months and imposed unconditional expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. The majority emphasized his serious prior violence, roughly ten years’ imprisonment, LTF leadership, commission of the offence during the suspended-expulsion probation period, and risk of reoffending. One judge dissented, finding the latest offence too minor—spontaneous and short-sentenced—to justify expelling a person with strong Danish ties and weak Pakistani ties. Khan then brought his Article 8 complaint to the European Court of Human Rights.
001-210046:
**Asanović v. Montenegro** (App. No. 52415/18, judgment 20 May 2021) concerns the applicant’s alleged unlawful deprivation of liberty and the lack of an effective domestic remedy, contrary to Articles 5 § 1 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Nebojša Asanović, is a Montenegrin lawyer and longtime representative of an opposition media outlet. In December 2016 the Tax Administration reported to the police that there were indications he had committed tax evasion in relation to his professional activities. The police forwarded the matter to the State Prosecution Office (SPO) in January 2017. On 12 September 2017 a state prosecutor allegedly orally ordered police officer G.M. to gather information from the applicant “as a citizen” regarding the suspected offence. The next morning, G.M. informed the prosecutor that the applicant had not been found at his address and that his phone was switched off. The prosecutor, apparently believing the applicant was hiding, ordered police to find him and “deprive him of liberty.”

At about 9:30 a.m. on 13 September 2017, G.M. and three other officers approached the applicant outside the Court of First Instance in Podgorica and served him with a summons requiring him to come to the police “at once” to provide information as a citizen. The summons warned that non-compliance could lead to him being brought in by force. The applicant claimed he was put into a vehicle and taken to the police station; the Government claimed he was offered a ride without force. After giving a statement, an official report stated that he had been deprived of liberty at 10:40 a.m. on the prosecutor’s order under Article 264 § 1 of the Criminal Code, in conjunction with Article 49, and that he would be brought before the prosecutor. His fingerprints were taken, he was photographed, his belongings—including his glasses—were removed, and he was placed in a windowless cell. At 12:10 p.m. he was handcuffed and taken to the prosecutor, questioned from 12:30 to 13:54 p.m., and then released. He denied the offence and explained that he had been visiting a client in prison, where phone use was prohibited and there was no signal.

The applicant filed a constitutional appeal on 15 September 2017. The Bar Association protested. On 1 November 2017 the Council for Civic Control of Police found the police had acted unlawfully because, as a lawyer, the applicant could not be deprived of liberty without a court decision. On 11 July 2018 the Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal, finding the police and SPO acted lawfully; it said he had not complied with the summons and had been deprived of liberty at 10:40 a.m. following the prosecutor’s order. It did not address other effective remedies.

On 2 October 2018 the Ombudsperson found breaches of Article 29 of the Constitution and Article 5 § 1 (c) of the Convention. It concluded that the applicant had not first been allowed to comply voluntarily with the summons, but was told to go “at once” with police, contrary to Article 259 § 1 of the Criminal Procedure Code. It found he was de facto deprived of liberty from 9:30 a.m., under police control, without legal grounds, since no Article 175 detention reason was indicated.

On 12 October 2018 the applicant brought civil proceedings against the State, seeking compensation and publication for unlawful deprivation of liberty. Those proceedings were later stayed pending criminal proceedings. An indictment for tax and social contributions evasion was issued in April 2019, and the criminal case remained ongoing. The case therefore centers on whether the police and prosecutor’s actions from 9:30 a.m. until release amounted to unlawful deprivation of liberty and whether domestic remedies were effective.
001-213529:
**Jallow v. Norway** (Application no. 36516/19) concerns complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Ebrima Pa Jallow, a Gambian national, sought parental responsibilities for G., his biological son born in Norway in 2011 to K.J. The applicant had been married to K.J., but they divorced around 2003. K.J. later moved to Norway; G. was conceived during her 2010 visit to Gambia and was born in Norway. The applicant never went to Norway, never had custody or parental responsibilities for G., and did not formally recognise paternity, so G. was registered with an unknown father.

G. lived in Norway with his mother and half-brother. The applicant met G. in Gambia in 2015, but the parties disputed the extent of contact and telephone communication; the Government noted G. did not speak English at the relevant time. G.’s mother died on 25 June 2017. G. then stayed with a family friend, later with a maternal uncle, and eventually in a foster home.

Because no one had parental responsibilities after the mother’s death, the City Court had to decide applications under the Children Act. In 2017, a family friend applied then withdrew; G.’s maternal aunt, A.J., applied; and the applicant also applied from Gambia. In January 2018, the City Court dismissed both A.J.’s and the applicant’s applications. It found the applicant had never been to Norway, wanted G. to move to Gambia, knew little of G., had probably met him only once, and had shown limited interest after the mother’s death. It concluded there was a significant danger of inadequate care if he were granted parental responsibilities. A.J. appealed; the applicant was initially not treated as a party due to communication problems, but later joined the High Court proceedings.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the applicant’s inability to attend the High Court hearing. He applied for a Schengen visa in November 2017; it was refused, and his appeal rejected in April 2018. He applied again in June 2018; that application was refused in July 2018, and the Immigration Appeals Board dismissed his appeal on 7 January 2019. The Board found the risk that he would not return outweighed welfare reasons, but noted he could follow proceedings by Skype and that his lawyer could protect his interests.

The High Court had itself written in November 2018 that the applicant’s presence was important for the case and for equality of arms, including to question A.J. and witnesses, and that Skype was not optimal. Nevertheless, after the visa refusal, the High Court refused the applicant’s request to reschedule the January 2019 hearing. It considered the visa decision probably not flawed, found Skype acceptable, emphasised G.’s need for stability, noted the applicant had counsel, and distinguished *Cılız v. the Netherlands* because the applicant had never lived with G. and had met him only twice.

At the hearing on 10–11 January 2019, technical problems meant the applicant was not initially on Skype; his counsel consented to proceed, and he joined later. The High Court dismissed the appeals in February 2019, finding that granting the applicant parental responsibilities was not in G.’s best interests. It noted the applicant did not seek daily care, that parental responsibilities would have no immediate practical effect, and that he lacked sufficient knowledge to participate in decisions. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in April 2019.

In later judicial-review proceedings, the City Court in June 2020 found no “family life” under Article 8 between the applicant and G., but invalidated the visa decision for procedural error because the Board had assessed incorrect facts about the applicant’s ties to Gambia. The applicant lodged his ECtHR application in July 2019, alleging violations of Articles 6 and 8.
001-213853:
**Mucha v. Slovakia** (Application no. 63703/19, ECtHR First Section, judgment 25 November 2021) concerned alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (impartial tribunal) and Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Pavel Mucha, a Slovak national born in 1979 and serving imprisonment, complained that the same tribunal that had previously approved his co-perpetrators’ plea bargains later convicted him, and that those earlier decisions had effectively treated him as guilty before his own trial.

The facts concerned an organised criminal gang operating in Bratislava and other Slovak regions. In 2012, the applicant and nine others were charged with setting up, conceiving and maintaining a criminal enterprise, along with multiple violent offences. Prosecution was initially joint, but eight co-perpetrators were later prosecuted separately after entering plea-bargaining agreements with the Public Prosecution Service. Those agreements required confessions and contained precise factual descriptions of the offences, legal classifications, and penalties. The Specialised Criminal Court (SCC), sitting in the same three-judge chamber of career judges, approved the agreements in judgments dated 19 December 2012 and 7 March 2013. The judgments found the eight co-perpetrators guilty and sentenced them.

Crucially for the applicant’s complaints, the operative parts of those judgments included factual definitions of the criminal acts that referred to the applicant by initials, and sometimes by alias. They described him as a mid-ranking member of the gang who gave instructions, received percentages from extortion, imposed and enforced financial penalties on members, ordered forcible debt collection, arranged the setting of operations, and received and distributed proceeds. The judgments contained little reasoning beyond reciting procedural history and finding the plea bargains lawful and the penalties adequate. They became final on delivery.

The applicant was then tried separately by an SCC chamber with identical composition. On 7 August 2013, he was found guilty as charged and sentenced to twenty-three years’ imprisonment. The factual definitions of four sets of criminal actions attributed to him were identical to those previously summarised in the co-perpetrators’ plea-bargain judgments. The trial court relied on complex evidence, including testimony from co-perpetrators, some of whom were cooperating “penitents.” In its reasoning, it noted that the co-perpetrators’ convictions were a “factual and homogenous part” of the case and were contained in the file.

The applicant appealed, lodged an appeal on points of law, and filed a constitutional complaint. He argued that the prior plea-bargain judgments, delivered by the same judges who later decided his case, had prejudiced the assessment of his guilt and violated his right to an impartial tribunal and to be presumed innocent. His appeals were dismissed, ultimately by the Constitutional Court on 25 June 2019. The Constitutional Court relied on a 2017 unifying decision of the Supreme Court, which held that approving a plea bargain involves no evidence-taking, binds only the convicted person, and does not disqualify the judge from later proceedings against another accused. It also stated that mentioning another person in an earlier conviction does not violate the presumption of innocence, and that such persons should preferably be identified by initials. The Constitutional Court distinguished cases such as *Ferrantelli and Santangelo v. Italy* because the applicant had not argued that the trial court cited extensive extracts from the earlier judgments.

Domestic law and EU law were also relevant: Article 4(1) of Directive 2016/343 and CJEU case-law (*AH and Others*, *UL and VM*) permit references to other accused persons in plea agreements only where necessary for legal categorisation and where it is made clear that their guilt has not been legally established and will be determined separately. The case therefore centred on whether the same tribunal’s earlier plea-bargain findings improperly prejudged the applicant’s guilt or created an appearance of bias.
001-209438:
In *Alimpiev v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*, the applicant, Alexandru Alimpiev, a Russian national born in 1950 and living in Tiraspol, was president of the Tiraspol People’s Court in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). On 31 August 2006 the “MRT” prosecutor’s office began a corruption investigation into him. He was arrested on 17 May 2007 and formally charged with corruption. He remained in detention pending trial until 25 December 2008, when the “MRT” Supreme Court convicted him and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. That judgment was upheld on 18 March 2009. On 24 July 2009, in extraordinary proceedings, the sentence was reduced to five years and he was released under an amnesty.

The case concerned the applicant’s alleged detention in inhuman conditions, failure to observe his rights during detention pending trial, and censorship of his correspondence in prison. On 2 November 2017 the respondent Governments were given notice of complaints under Article 3, Article 5 §§ 3 and 4, Article 6 § 1, Article 8, and Article 13 of the Convention; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Russian Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

As to detention pending trial, the prosecutor periodically sought extensions of the applicant’s detention, and each time a judge granted the request. The applicant was unable to obtain copies of the decisions extending his detention. On 21 July 2008 his lawyer sent a telegram to the president of the “MRT” Supreme Court asking for a copy of a decision of 18 July 2008 extending detention, and asked that the applicant’s Article 34 rights not be hindered by refusal. By reply of 23 July 2008, the president stated that “MRT” law did not provide for defence representatives to obtain copies of decisions issued in response to applications before the courts. On 15 August 2008 the lawyer asked to make copies of selected parts of the criminal file; the request was refused the same day by handwritten note, again on the basis that “MRT” law did not provide such a right. On 18 August 2008 the lawyer asked for copies of all detention-extension decisions, stressing that he had not been involved at the pre-trial stage and needed them for an effective defence, and relying on Article 34.

In applications to replace detention with an alternative measure, the lawyer relied on Articles 3, 5, 6, 8 and 13, arguing that the “MRT” courts had extended detention by merely citing abstract risks—absconding, reoffending or interfering with the investigation—without evidence specific to the applicant. He also described the applicant’s detention conditions and worsening health. On 11 November 2008 the lawyer issued a press release about the case.

Regarding conditions of detention, the applicant described the temporary detention facility in Tiraspol and prison UIN-3 as follows: the cell had no separate toilet or shower; he received no hygiene products or bed linen; the cell was infested with parasites; tap water was bad; the window was very small and allowed damp and cold air; daily walks were very short. Relatives could send only 30 kg of items per month, including bottled water, and the facility food was inedible; combined, he alleged torture through hunger. During trial he was held in a metal cage. On 6 August 2008 his lawyer asked that he sit next to counsel rather than in a cage and that cages in courtrooms be declared unlawful; it is unclear whether a reply was received. A medical certificate showed that on 23 June 2008 an emergency team attended him, diagnosed respiratory problems and moderate persistent asthma, and prescribed medication. He alleged heavy smoking by cellmates exposed him to passive smoke.

Finally, the applicant alleged that all his correspondence was censored during detention. He submitted a copy of a letter sent to him personally by his lawyer; the envelope bore a stamp reading “Verified. Censor (signature), 8/09/2008.”
001-207695:
Lacatus v. Switzerland (Application no. 14065/15) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by Violeta-Sibianca Lacatus, a Romanian national of Roma origin, against Switzerland. She alleged violations of Articles 8, 10 and 14 of the Convention arising from her prosecution and punishment for begging in Geneva under section 11A of the Geneva Criminal Law Act, which makes begging on public highways an offence punishable by a fine.

From 2011, the applicant lived intermittently in Geneva. Unable to find work, she resorted to begging. On 22 July 2011 she was fined CHF 100 under section 11A. On the same occasion, police confiscated CHF 16.75 from her after a body search; no seizure order was issued. Between February 2012 and January 2013, she received eight further summary penalty notices, each imposing a CHF 100 fine for begging on public highways using a cup. On 21 February and 4 March 2012 she was also taken into police custody for three hours each time. Each fine could be replaced by one day of imprisonment if unpaid.

On 14 January 2014 the Police Court of Geneva found her guilty of begging. It imposed a CHF 500 fine, convertible into five days’ imprisonment if unpaid, and upheld the confiscation of CHF 16.75.

She appealed, alleging infringement of her freedom of communication under Article 16 of the Swiss Constitution and Article 10 ECHR; indirect discrimination under Article 14 ECHR and Article 8 § 2 of the Swiss Constitution, read with section 11A; infringement of personal liberty under Articles 7, 10 and 36 of the Swiss Constitution and Article 8 ECHR; and arbitrary interpretation of section 11A because begging was not legally defined. She also requested return of the confiscated CHF 16.75 with interest.

On 4 April 2014 the Criminal Appeals Division dismissed her complaints. It held that the ban did not infringe freedom of expression because it did not prevent her from making her social situation known by other means. It found no indirect discrimination because the law did not target only Roma people and poverty was not a protected ground.

On 10 September 2014 the Federal Supreme Court also dismissed her appeal. It held that the ban breached neither Article 8 nor Article 14 ECHR. On Article 10, it found that her begging was non-verbal conduct. She had not reported any spoken message or political dimension. The message was confined to her private impoverishment or need for help, not addressed to the public as a whole but to individual passers-by to elicit pity and generosity. The communicative aspect was therefore substantially reduced, and Article 10 did not protect her conduct. The Federal Supreme Court further found that confiscation of the CHF 16.75 was not arbitrary, since she had not explained its provenance and it could be viewed as proceeds of begging.

From 24 to 28 March 2015, the applicant was detained in Champ-Dollon short-term prison for failure to pay the fine.

Relevant domestic law provided that section 11A punishes begging with a fine; if begging is arranged or the person is accompanied by minors or dependants, the minimum fine is CHF 2,000. Federal criminal law allows an alternative custodial sentence of one day to three months for negligent non-payment. The Federal Supreme Court had previously upheld Geneva’s blanket ban as a proportionate restriction of personal liberty, justified by public order, safety, tranquillity, and prevention of exploitation and harassment, noting that social assistance was available. It had also rejected indirect discrimination claims absent concrete evidence.

The key alleged violations thus concerned whether criminalising and punishing begging interfered with private life/personal liberty (Article 8), freedom of expression (Article 10), and amounted to indirect discrimination against Roma (Article 14).
001-213706:
In the European Court of Human Rights case *Golub v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 48020/12, judgment of 30 November 2021), the applicant was Nikolay Golub, a Russian national born in 1993. He complained about compulsory military service in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). He alleged that his service amounted to forced labour, that he was unlawfully detained, and that no effective remedies existed. The Court gave notice to Moldova and Russia of complaints under Articles 4, 5 and 13 of the Convention and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The key facts are as follows. In September 2011 the applicant was called up for compulsory military service in the “MRT”. Although he was the sole caretaker of his disabled mother and entitled under “MRT” law to deferral, he and his mother opted for his enrolment in a military education institution under the “MRT” Ministry of Defence. This counted as military service and allowed him to obtain an education diploma. As a cadet, his passport was taken away, he was issued a recruit card, and he was not allowed to leave the premises without the commander’s authorisation.

In November 2011 he left the premises several times to seek medical treatment after alleged ill-treatment or to care for his mother. Upon his return, from 17 to 24 November 2011, he was disciplined for absence without leave and placed in isolation in the Tiraspol Military Command. There he was held in a cell with eight other persons and could leave only once per day to use the toilet.

On 2 December 2011 the “MRT” authorities opened a criminal investigation against him for absence without leave. It was discontinued on 27 January 2012 on non-rehabilitation grounds. On 20 December 2011 he was excluded from the military institute for lack of discipline and unwillingness to continue his military education. He was sent to “MRT military unit no. 40896” in Dubăsari to complete compulsory military service.

On 25 December 2011 the applicant left the military unit on authorised leave but returned several hours late. According to him, as an informal sanction he was ordered to dig a trench. When he refused, he was disciplined and placed in isolation from 26 December 2011 to 9 January 2012 in the military unit’s prison (“гауптвахта”). On 25 February 2012 the “MRT” Minister of Defence granted his request for early dismissal as sole caretaker of his disabled mother and placed him in the reserve. On 27 February 2012 he was informed of this order and left the military unit.

As regards remedies, on 17 May 2012 the applicant complained to the Moldovan and Russian Prosecutor General’s Offices about his unlawful deprivation of liberty. On 9 and 22 June 2012 the Russian Military prosecutor informed him that his complaint had been redirected to the Moldovan and “MRT” authorities. On 19 June 2012 the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office told him that a criminal investigation into his unlawful detention had been initiated that day. On 17 August 2012 the investigation was suspended until the perpetrators could be identified. The relevant materials were summarised in *Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the conscription and enrolment in an “MRT” military institution, the confiscation of the applicant’s passport, restrictions on leaving the premises, disciplinary isolations in the Tiraspol Military Command and military-unit prison, the criminal charge for absence without leave, the alleged forced trench-digging, and the failure, redirection, and suspension of investigations by the Moldovan and Russian authorities. These facts underpin the complaints of forced labour, unlawful detention, restrictions on movement, and lack of effective remedies.
001-210689:

Hriplivîi, a lawyer practising in Chișinău. The respondents are the Republic of Moldova and the Russian Federation. The Moldovan Government were represented by their Agent, Mr O. Rotari. 001-212897:
In *Shabelnik v. Ukraine (No. 3)* (Application no. 54806/18), the European Court of Human Rights considered the applicant’s complaint under Article 7 that a judicial review of his previous conviction resulted in a new punishment imposed after the statutory limitation period had expired.

The underlying events occurred in 2001. In October 2001, an elderly woman, K., was murdered in her flat. In December 2001, a minor, S., was abducted and murdered. The applicant was arrested on 10 December 2001 and charged in connection with S.’s abduction and murder. In February 2002, while questioned as a witness and without a lawyer present, he confessed to K.’s murder and took part in an on-site reconstruction. Criminal proceedings concerning K. were later joined with those concerning S.

On 11 July 2002, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal convicted the applicant of crimes against both victims. For the murders, he was sentenced to life imprisonment under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), (9) and (13) of the Criminal Code, with lesser sentences for abduction, hostage-taking, robbery and extortion absorbed into the life sentence. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 10 October 2002.

In the applicant’s first case before the ECtHR, he alleged that his conviction for K.’s murder had been based on self-incriminating evidence obtained without a lawyer, in violation of Article 6. On 19 February 2009, the Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3. After that judgment became final, the Supreme Court reviewed the case. On 9 September 2010, it excluded the applicant’s confessions but upheld his conviction for K.’s murder on the basis of other evidence.

In his second ECtHR case, the applicant complained about that review. On 1 June 2017, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that only a full retrial could adequately examine the impact of excluding the confessions on the remaining evidence concerning K. That judgment became final on 1 September 2017.

Following the second judgment, the applicant’s lawyer sought review of the 2002 and 2010 decisions. On 16 May 2018, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court partly allowed the request. It quashed the 2002 sentence and the 2010 decision insofar as they concerned the robbery and murder of K., remitting that part for fresh examination. However, it resentenced the applicant on the remaining charges concerning S. under Articles 146 § 3, 147 § 2, 189 § 4 and 115 § 2 (2), (3) and (6), imposing terms of imprisonment and, ultimately, a merged life sentence with confiscation of property under Article 70. Three judges dissented, arguing that the partial severance and resentencing was erroneous and effectively maintained a life sentence despite the reduction in charges.

The Article 7 complaint arises from this 2018 judicial review. The crimes concerning S. were committed in 2001, and the original conviction was in 2002. Under Article 49 of the Criminal Code, a fifteen-year limitation period applied to especially grave offences. Where such an offence was punishable by life imprisonment, the court had to decide whether limitation applied; if it ruled out limitation, life imprisonment could not be imposed and had to be commuted to a determinate term. The applicant alleged that the Supreme Court’s 2018 decision imposed a new life sentence for the S.-related offences outside the statutory time-limit. The key issue is therefore whether the judicial review and fresh sentencing violated Article 7’s prohibition on unlawful or retroactive punishment.
001-211795:
**Summary of *Abdi v. Denmark* (Application no. 41643/19)**

The case concerns the expulsion of a settled migrant from Denmark and a permanent re-entry ban imposed in criminal proceedings, raising issues under the applicant’s right to respect for private and family life.

The applicant, Mohamed Hassan Abdi, is a Somali national born in 1993. He entered Denmark in 1997 at age four with his mother and was granted asylum in December 1997. His father and sister came in 2000, and a younger brother was born in Denmark. By the time of the proceedings, he had lawfully resided in Denmark for about twenty years and two months. His parents and siblings lived in Denmark; he lived with his sister and brother. He had no family in Somalia, had not returned there since leaving as a child, spoke Danish, and had only basic Somali. He had attended primary school and completed a basic commercial programme, and while in custody was enrolled in vocational upper secondary education. He was unmarried, had no children, and no girlfriend in Denmark.

The applicant had a criminal history. As a minor, he was convicted of robbery at age 15 and burglary at age 17, receiving suspended or partly suspended sentences. As an adult, he was convicted and fined seven times, mainly for controlled-substance offences and driving under the influence of psychedelic substances, most recently in December 2016.

In May 2018, the District Court convicted him of illegal possession of a fully loaded 9 mm firearm with ammunition in a public place, committed around midnight on 5 November 2017 jointly with three others, and of two controlled-substance violations: possession of 1.2 grams of cannabis for personal use and 7.4 grams intended for handover to a prison inmate. The firearm had been brought in a car parked 200 metres from the clubhouse of a motorcycle gang, S. The applicant and co-accused were affiliated with or meeting members of another gang, R. Although no ongoing conflict between S and R was proved, police testified that S had been on high alert. The District Court found joint possession in particularly aggravating circumstances under Article 192a of the Penal Code and sentenced him to two years and nine months’ imprisonment.

The immigration authorities gathered personal-circumstances information. The District Court, by a majority, decided on conditional expulsion with a two-year probation period. It found expulsion disproportionate given his long residence, lack of ties to Somalia, and the absence of any prior expulsion order, despite the seriousness of the offence. The dissenting judge favoured unconditional expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban.

On appeal, the Western Denmark High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years and six months. By a majority of five to one, it ordered expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban. The majority found very compelling reasons due to the serious firearm offence and prior convictions. It accepted that expulsion would burden him because of his ties to Denmark, but noted he lacked spouse, children, completed education, or regular labour-market ties. It also considered that he spoke basic Somali and likely knew Somali customs and culture through his family, so he was not entirely without ties or qualifications for return. It concluded that expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban was proportionate to prevent disorder and crime. The dissenting judge would have made expulsion conditional. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in January 2019.

Under the Aliens Act at the time, a permanent re-entry ban automatically followed a prison sentence exceeding two years. A 2018 amendment, not applicable to this crime, lowered that threshold to one year and six months but allowed courts to reduce bans if necessary to comply with international obligations. The key proportionality facts were therefore the applicant’s long lawful residence from childhood, family ties in Denmark, absence of ties to Somalia, limited Somali language, education and employment limitations, serious gang-related firearm offence, prior criminal record, and the permanent re-entry ban.
001-208547:
The case of *Gilligan v. Ireland* concerned four Irish nationals—John, Geraldine, Treacy and Darren Gilligan, members of the same family—who complained that proceedings brought against them under the Proceeds of Crime Act 1996 (“the Act”) exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In November 1996, the Criminal Assets Bureau (“CAB”) applied to the High Court to freeze properties belonging to the applicants, including houses, land and cars, alleging that they represented proceeds of crime. An interim order was made on 21 November 1996. A temporary order under section 3 of the Act followed on 5 December 1996. The first applicant was then in custody in Belmarsh prison, London; he was later extradited to Ireland, convicted of drug offences in 2001 and sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment, ultimately released in 2013. Further section 3 orders were made in December 1996 and on 16 July 1997. The July 1997 order was later held by the Supreme Court, in April 2005, to be the final and operative freezing order.

A key feature of the Act was that a section 3 “interlocutory order,” despite its name, was in substance a final measure: it froze property until, after seven years, the State could seek a disposal order under section 4. A person affected could, however, apply at any time under section 3(3) to vary or discharge the order if the property was not proceeds of crime or if the order caused injustice.

The applicants made numerous attempts to challenge the freezing order. The first applicant brought a constitutional challenge, dismissed in 1997 and upheld on appeal in 2001. In 1998 and 2000, efforts were made to have the order discharged or proceedings struck out on procedural grounds. In December 2004, CAB applied under section 4 for a disposal order, but that application did not progress until the applicants’ other challenges were resolved. In 2008, the Supreme Court rejected the argument that the freezing order could be challenged for alleged procedural unfairness; it held that the proper remedy was an appeal or a section 3(3) application, and that the applicants’ advisers should have understood this since 1997.

The applicants eventually brought section 3(3) applications in 2009. After hearings in 2010, the High Court ruled in January 2011 against them. It found that the first applicant’s evidence about the source of funds was untruthful and implausible, and that most properties were probably acquired through drug trafficking proceeds. It also held that delay was attributable to the applicants, who could have invoked section 3(3) much earlier. The applicants appealed in June 2012. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals on 1 February 2017, stating that the applicants had “slept on their rights” and failed to challenge the orders promptly. The properties were confiscated in June 2017.

The applicants lodged their Convention application on 31 July 2017. The only admissible complaint concerned the length of the proceedings. The key facts for that alleged violation were therefore the nearly 21-year period from the 1996 freezing orders to the 2017 final appeal and confiscation, the unusual final nature of the section 3 order, the availability of the section 3(3) remedy, the applicants’ delayed use of that remedy, their multiple and repetitive challenges, and the domestic courts’ findings that much of the delay was caused by the applicants themselves rather than the State.
001-213730:
**Summary of Case: Csikós and Others v. Hungary**

The case of *Csikós and Others v. Hungary* (Applications nos. 44001/20 and 13 others) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) against Hungary. The judgment, delivered on 2 December 2021, concerns complaints lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The central grievance for all fourteen applicants is the excessive length of their pre-trial detention, a violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial. Some applicants also raised additional complaints under other Convention provisions.

The applications were introduced on various dates between September 2020 and April 2021. The applicants, all Hungarian nationals born between 1963 and 1998, were represented by a small group of lawyers based in Budapest.

The factual circumstances of each applicant are detailed in an appended table submitted to the Court. A review of these facts reveals the core of the alleged violation: in each instance, the applicant was held in pre-trial detention for a significant period, which they argue was unjustifiably long.

**Individual Detention Periods:**

- **Gábor Csikós (b. 1986):** Detained since 26 August 2018 (over 3 years, 1 month at the time of application).
- **Livia Sterpu (b. 1963):** Detained from 14 May 2019 to 6 November 2020 (1 year, 5 months, 24 days).
- **Csaba Galyas (b. 1983):** Detained from 11 December 2018 to 26 January 2021 (2 years, 1 month, 16 days).
- **Tibor Ónodi (b. 1981):** Detained from 6 September 2017 to 9 April 2021 (3 years, 7 months, 4 days).
- **Géza Mészáros (b. 1987):** Detained from 7 February 2018 to 4 December 2020 (2 years, 9 months, 28 days).
- **Alfréd Oláh (b. 1971):** Detained since 20 September 2016 (over 5 years at the time of application).
- **Szabolcs Németh (b. 1980):** Detained since 12 September 2018 (over 3 years, 1 month at the time of application).
- **Péter Kis (b. 1974):** Detained from 13 June 2018 to 26 January 2021 (2 years, 7 months, 14 days).
- **Barbara Sárközi (b. 1998):** Detained since 27 September 2019 (over 2 years at the time of application).
- **Róbert Máté (b. 1976):** Detained from 12 April 2018 to 6 October 2020 (2 years, 5 months, 25 days).
- **Zsolt Lakatos (b. 1970):** Detained since 22 April 2019 (over 2 years, 5 months at the time of application).
- **Károly Pataki (b. 1981):** Detained from 11 May 2019 to 19 March 2021 (1 year, 10 months, 9 days).
- **Attila Filipovics (b. 1982):** Detained since 30 June 2018 (over 3 years, 3 months at the time of application).
- **László Dudás (b. 1988):** Detained since 25 September 2019 (over 2 years at the time of application).

In summary, the case aggregates fourteen separate applications, all alleging that the Hungarian authorities failed to meet the requirement under Article 5 § 3 to justify the continued detention of the applicants or to bring them to trial within a reasonable timeframe. The documented detention periods range from approximately 1.5 to over 5 years, and for several applicants, the detention was still ongoing at the time they brought their case to the Strasbourg Court.
001-207667:
The applicants are Tomas Strøbye (born 1966, living in Frederiksberg) and Martin Rosenlind (born 1987, living in Greve), both Danish nationals. In earlier domestic proceedings, the first applicant was declared legally incompetent to manage his financial and personal affairs by the Copenhagen City Court on 20 March 1984. The second applicant was placed under financial guardianship and deprived of his legal capacity by the District Court of Roskilde on 23 March 2009; that court found he could not manage his financial affairs because of mental disability and needed protection from further debt.

Under section 29 of the Danish Constitution and section 1 of the Parliamentary Elections Act, persons who were legally incompetent did not have the right to vote in general elections. Consequently, both applicants were not entitled to vote in the parliamentary elections held on 18 June 2015. By Act no. 391 of 27 April 2016, persons who were legally incompetent were later given the right to vote in European Parliament elections and in local and regional elections, but not in national parliamentary elections.

The applicants, joined by two other persons, brought proceedings before the Danish courts against the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Interior. They claimed they had been wrongfully denied the right to vote in the 18 June 2015 parliamentary elections and relied, among other things, on Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Ministry contested the claims.

Before the High Court of Eastern Denmark, a written statement by the first applicant was read out. It stated that he had suffered brain damage after being immunised during his first year of life and lived at Egmont folk high school. For many years he had had to share a single vote with his mother, who was his guardian, and he found it humiliating not to cast his own vote. The second applicant stated that he lived in his own flat in a group home, had a mentor who helped him, worked at the Glad Foundation reception desk, felt sad and excluded when not allowed to vote in June 2015, read newspapers and watched news, and was interested in politics. He said he had requested a guardian himself because it was difficult for him to manage his financial affairs.

On 29 June 2017, the High Court dismissed the claim. It considered that the Constitution had continuously been construed as excluding persons deprived of legal capacity under section 6 of the Guardianship Act from voting in general elections, and that Denmark’s international obligations did not imply an absolute right to vote for that limited group. The applicants appealed. On 18 January 2018, the Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s decision. It found that persons deprived of legal capacity under section 6 were legally incompetent and disenfranchised, and that, notwithstanding Denmark’s international obligations, section 1 of the Parliamentary Elections Act applied and no compensation was due.

After the Supreme Court judgment, political focus led to a private members’ bill and a Ministry of Justice analysis. On 3 October 2018, the Ministry concluded that section 29 of the Constitution did not bar changes allowing some persons deprived of legal capacity to manage their assets. An amendment was passed on 20 December 2018 and entered into force on 1 January 2019. It introduced the possibility of partial deprivation of legal capacity; only persons fully deprived remained disenfranchised, while partially deprived persons remained legally competent and retained the right to vote in general elections.

Following the amendment, the first applicant applied to change his guardianship status. On 20 May 2019, his legal incapacitation order was quashed entirely, and he gained the right to vote. The second applicant also applied; by a district court order of 9 November 2019, he was only partially deprived of legal capacity under section 6(2)(2) of the Guardianship Act and consequently was granted the right to vote in general elections. The applicants complained before the European Court of Human Rights of a breach of their right to vote under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, taken alone or read in conjunction with Article 14.
001-245708:
**Case: Ivković and Others v. Serbia**  
*European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, Committee Judgment, 22 July 2021*  
*Application no. 62554/19 and four others*

The case originated in five applications against Serbia lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained of the excessive length of civil and administrative proceedings. The Serbian Government was given notice of the applications. The Court’s judgment was adopted by a Committee composed of Judges Koskelo, Lubarda, and Bošnjak.

The appended table sets out the key facts for each applicant. All applicants alleged that domestic proceedings had lasted unreasonably long. In each case, the table also records a prior domestic decision concerning the length complaint, and in each instance the domestic authority found no violation.

**Ranko Ivković**, born in 1979 and represented by Goran Stamenić of Čačak, lodged application no. 62554/19 on 21 November 2019. The domestic proceedings began on 31 December 2010 and ended on 15 May 2019. They lasted 8 years, 4 months, and 16 days across two levels of jurisdiction. The Smederevo Court of First Instance, in decision R4R.br.27/2017 of 22 September 2017, found no violation.

**Zoran Đorđević**, born in 1966 and represented by the same lawyer, lodged application no. 4559/20 on 10 January 2020. The proceedings began on 6 January 2011 and ended on 30 November 2018, lasting 7 years, 10 months, and 25 days across two levels. The Smederevo Court of First Instance, in decision R4R.br.25/2017 of 28 September 2017, found no violation.

**Jovica Marković**, born in 1966 and represented by the same lawyer, lodged application no. 22108/20 on 23 April 2020. The proceedings began on 14 July 2011 and ended on 20 September 2019, lasting 8 years, 2 months, and 7 days across two levels. The Smederevo Court of First Instance, in decision R4R.br.31/17 of 22 September 2017, found no violation.

**Dušan Janošević**, born in 1930 and without a listed representative, lodged application no. 32920/20 on 20 July 2020. The proceedings began on 19 January 2011 and ended on 8 March 2017, lasting 6 years, 1 month, and 18 days at one level of jurisdiction. The Constitutional Court, in decision Už-3645/2017 of 24 December 2019, found no violation.

**Slavoljub Aksić**, born in 1971 and represented by the same lawyer, lodged application no. 44445/20 on 11 September 2020. The proceedings began on 14 July 2011 and ended on 8 November 2018, lasting 7 years, 3 months, and 26 days across two levels. The Smederevo Court of First Instance, in decision R4R.br.7/2017 of 17 July 2017, found no violation.

The central alleged violation is therefore the excessive length of domestic civil or administrative proceedings, contrary to the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The durations at issue range from just over six years to more than eight years and four months. Most applicants pursued two levels of jurisdiction, while one pursued one level. Although each applicant had previously raised the length issue domestically, the domestic authorities concluded that no violation had occurred. The applicants then brought the matter to Strasbourg. The excerpt provided covers the procedure and facts; it does not include the Court’s subsequent reasoning or final conclusions on the merits or just satisfaction.
001-211892:
Application no. 33567/15 was lodged by Mr Petru Jestcov, a Moldovan national born in 1950 who lives in Chișinău, against the Republic of Moldova and Russia. He was represented by A. Tighinean, a lawyer practising in Chișinău. The Governments were represented by their Agents. The applicant complained under Article 2 of the Convention that Moldova and Russia were responsible for the impunity of the perpetrator of his wife’s murder, whom he alleged was hiding in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (MRT). The case concerned the failure to enforce a custodial sentence after the perpetrator fled.

On 9 November 2010 the applicant’s wife was robbed and murdered in Chișinău, Moldova. An investigation was initiated against several suspected perpetrators, including N.C., a Russian national. N.C. was held in pre-trial detention during the proceedings.
