On 2 December 2011 the Botanica District Court convicted N.C. of being an accomplice in armed robbery and murder and sentenced her to 13 years’ imprisonment. On 11 April 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld N.C.’s appeal, reheard the case, acquitted her of all charges, and released her from detention in the courtroom. On 29 January 2013, in N.C.’s absence, the Supreme Court of Justice finally quashed the appellate judgment and upheld the first-instance judgment against N.C.

On 20 March 2013 the Botanica District Court sent all materials of the criminal file to the Dubăsari Police to enforce the sentence in respect of N.C. On 2 July 2013 the General Police Inspectorate informed the applicant that N.C. had not yet been declared wanted. Following a request from the Dubăsari Police, on 6 May 2015 the Dubăsari District Court declared N.C. wanted.

Following a search notice issued by Moldovan authorities, on 11 September 2015 the Russian authorities traced N.C. to Surgut, Russia, and interviewed her about the circumstances of the case. She claimed to be unaware of her conviction in Moldova, saying that she had moved back to Russia after her acquittal by the appellate court in 2012. On 17 September 2015 the Russian authorities informed the Moldovan authorities of N.C.’s location. On 19 October 2015 they confirmed that she was a Russian national and therefore could not be extradited pursuant to Article 57 of the 1993 Minsk Convention on mutual legal assistance in civil, family and criminal matters.

After communication of the case, on 15 October 2019 the Chișinău District Court requested transfer of the enforcement of N.C.’s custodial sentence to the Russian Federation, relying on Article 2 of the 1997 Additional Protocol to the Convention on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons. On 25 October 2019 the Moldovan Minister of Justice forwarded the request to the Russian Ministry of Justice. On 4 February 2020 the Russian Ministry of Justice directed the Moldovan transfer request to the Surgut City Court. On 10 April 2020 the Surgut City Court granted recognition and enforcement on the territory of the Russian Federation of the custodial sentence in respect of N.C. and ordered her arrest.

The Additional Protocol to the Council of Europe Convention on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons was ratified by Moldova in 2004 and by Russia in 2007. Article 2 of that Protocol concerns persons who have fled from the sentencing State. It provides that where a national of a Party who is the subject of a sentence imposed in another Party seeks to avoid execution or further execution of the sentence by fleeing to the former Party before having served it, the sentencing State may request the other Party to take over execution. At the request of the sentencing State, the administering State may arrest the sentenced person or take other measures pending a decision on the request. The consent of the sentenced person is not required for the transfer.
001-210322:
**Summary of *Bliznyuk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 20789/14)**

The case of *Bliznyuk v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms. Galina Fedorovna Bliznyuk against Ukraine on 5 March 2014. The applicant complained under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life) about the death of her son in suspicious circumstances allegedly involving State agents and the subsequent ineffective investigation.

The key facts begin on 11 August 2001. The applicant's thirty-four-year-old son was stopped twice by separate traffic police patrols for traffic violations. On both occasions, he exhibited signs of severe alcohol intoxication and was taken to a medical centre for testing. The narcologist recorded high alcohol levels in his urine (2.66‰ and 3.7‰) and found him heavily intoxicated. According to police and the narcologist, he behaved adequately, refused medical assistance, and was released after each test. Some witnesses, however, testified that during the second stop, police officers forcibly pulled him from his car, handcuffed him, and beat him with rubber truncheons. These accounts were denied by police, and a later forensic opinion suggested the minor injuries found on his body were unlikely to have been caused by such truncheons.

The next day, 12 August 2001, the applicant's son was found dead in his abandoned car. The initial autopsy concluded he died from acute ischaemic heart disease, complicated by circulatory disturbance, with internal bleeding and minor scratches on his leg unrelated to death. Two experts partly dissented, attributing death to acute heart failure of toxic origin.

An investigation was initiated, but between 2001 and 2012, over twenty decisions refusing to institute criminal proceedings were made and subsequently set aside by higher prosecutors and courts. These authorities repeatedly identified critical shortcomings: contradictory expert evidence on the cause of death; failure to check the applicant's claims that her son had no heart condition; disregard of witness testimonies alleging police beating; failure to investigate the danger posed by the rising alcohol level and its cause; unclear origin of the internal bleeding; and procedural irregularities, such as different police patrols using the same attesting witnesses for offence reports. The applicant consistently alleged that police had beaten her son and forced him to consume alcohol.

In 2013, criminal proceedings were finally instituted against police officers for abuse of power and separately against the narcologist for failure to provide medical assistance. Forensic examinations conducted in 2013 reaffirmed the heart disease as the cause of death, found no causal link between the lack of medical aid and death, and suggested the son likely continued drinking after leaving the medical centre. Consequently, the proceedings against the police officers were terminated in April 2013 for lack of evidence, and this decision was upheld by domestic courts. The proceedings against the narcologist were also terminated multiple times, but those decisions were repeatedly set aside, and the investigation remained ongoing.

The applicant's key allegations before the Court were that her son died at the hands of State agents (police officers) who ill-treated him and forced alcohol consumption, and that the State failed to conduct an effective investigation into these events, thereby violating its positive obligation to protect the right to life.
001-212970:
**Summary of Špadijer v. Montenegro (Application no. 31549/18)**

The case of *Špadijer v. Montenegro* concerns allegations of workplace bullying (mobbing) affecting the applicant’s psychological integrity and the failure of domestic authorities to protect her, in violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Ms. Daliborka Špadijer, a Montenegrin national born in 1978, worked as a prison guard at the Institute for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions (IECS) in Podgorica since 1998. At the relevant time, she held the position of head of shift in the women’s prison.

The events began in January 2013 when the applicant reported five colleagues for indecent behaviour on New Year’s Eve, during which male guards entered the women’s prison and one had physical contact with inmates. Following this report, the applicant faced retaliation. On 12 January 2013, a colleague, N.R., warned her by phone that she should not have reported the others, that many colleagues were against her, and that she should "be prepared for anything." The next night, the windscreen of her car was smashed outside her home. She filed a police complaint, but the State prosecutor found no criminal offence.

Further incidents followed. In March 2013, a prison driver refused to take her home, citing her "sharp tongue." The colleagues she had reported were later fined in disciplinary proceedings. In June 2013, one of them, A.V., insulted her publicly, calling her a "stinking bitch" and spitting near her. When she reported this, the governor confronted her with A.V., who denied it; her request to review video footage was dismissed with the false claim that cameras were not working. She also alleged that between January and August 2013, she was forbidden to organise duty shifts, ignored by colleagues, ordered to make coffee for a prisoner, and that her reports were disregarded.

On 16 August 2013, the applicant formally requested her employer to initiate protection proceedings against bullying. A mediator dismissed her request as unfounded, reasoning that the conduct was not continuous and that some incidents occurred outside the workplace. She then instituted civil proceedings. An expert found she suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder and an adjustment disorder, with a 20% permanent reduction in functioning capacity.

On 19 February 2015, the Court of First Instance ruled against her, finding that the incidents lacked the frequency required for bullying—at least once a week for six months. The High Court and Supreme Court upheld this, adding that the assault did not relate to the employer. On 10 February 2015, just before the civil ruling, the applicant was physically assaulted in a car park by an unknown attacker who warned her to "be careful." Police efforts to identify the perpetrator failed.

The applicant’s constitutional appeal was dismissed in November 2017. She retired in May 2016 due to complete loss of working capacity, with her psychological problems traced to workplace stress in 2013. The case highlights the domestic courts’ narrow definition of bullying, requiring high frequency, and their failure to address the cumulative effect of the incidents or the criminal complaints she filed.
001-208592:
**Moroşanu and Others v. Romania** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, Committee, 16 March 2021; Applications nos. 84271/17 and 4 others) concerned the prolonged criminal investigations into injuries and deaths arising from the Romanian Revolution of December 1989. The five applicants were Romanian nationals who either were shot and injured during demonstrations or were close relatives of persons killed by gunshot. They complained mainly under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the domestic authorities had failed to carry out an effective investigation within a reasonable time.

The underlying events occurred in Bucharest and Reșița during December 1989, when demonstrations led to the fall of the communist regime. Applicant Cristian Florinel Moroşanu was shot on 23 December 1989 in Bucharest; his injuries required medical care for one year and three months and left him with a permanent infirmity. Aurel Iordan was also shot in Bucharest on 23 December 1989 and needed between twenty-three and twenty-five days of medical care. Floarea Portasă and Nicoleta Cîrjă were, respectively, the wife and daughter of a victim killed by gunshot in Bucharest on 23/24 December 1989. Maria Ruvineanțu was the mother of a victim killed by gunshot in Reșița on 25 December 1989.

In 1990, the military prosecutor’s office attached to the High Court of Cassation and Justice opened investigations of its own motion into illegal detention, ill-treatment, and injury suffered by the applicants and other participants in the December 1989 events. The main investigation was registered under file no. 97/P/1990, later no. 11/P/2014. Between 1991 and 2006, in separate proceedings concerning the applicants or their deceased relatives, prosecutors either declined to open investigations or discontinued proceedings. Those cases were nevertheless examined within the main criminal investigation, and the applicants pursued civil claims.

The procedural history of the main investigation resembled that in other Romanian revolution cases, including *Association “21 December 1989” and Others v. Romania* and *Sidea and Others v. Romania*. On 14 October 2015, the military prosecutor’s office closed the main investigation. It found that some complaints were statute-barred, some were covered by amnesty, some were ill-founded, some facts could not be classified as offences, and some were res judicata. That closure was subsequently annulled by the Prosecutor General on 5 April 2016, a decision confirmed by the High Court of Cassation and Justice on 13 June 2016. On 1 November 2016, the military prosecutor ordered a criminal investigation in rem for crimes against humanity concerning the same factual circumstances.

On 5 April 2019, the military prosecutor’s office sent to trial several individuals—including a former Romanian president, a former prime minister, and a former commander of the Romanian air force—for crimes against humanity. At the same time, it discontinued the investigation as to other individuals because some charges were res judicata, some suspects had died, or some facts could not be classified as criminal offences. Those proceedings remained pending before the Preliminary Chamber of the High Court of Cassation and Justice.

The key alleged violation was therefore procedural: that the Romanian authorities had not conducted an effective, prompt, and thorough investigation into the December 1989 events in which the applicants were injured or their relatives killed. The investigation spanned decades, involved repeated decisions to close or discontinue proceedings, and had not reached a final resolution. The Court gave notice only of the complaints concerning the lack of an effective investigation within a reasonable time; the remainder of the applications were declared inadmissible. The case thus centered on whether Romania complied with its Article 2 obligation to investigate deaths and serious injuries caused by state action during the Revolution.
001-209035:
The applicant, Christoph-Herwig Liebscher, born in 1957 and living in Vienna, is an Austrian national. On 21 May 2013 he and his wife divorced by mutual consent and concluded a divorce settlement under section 55a(2) of the Marriage Act before the Döbling District Court, acting as family court. The settlement regulated division of matrimonial assets, custody and residence of their two minor children, alimony, and included an overview of the applicant’s assets and income.

On 13 December 2015 the applicant asked the same court, acting as land register court, to enter into the land register the transfer of his share of the couple’s joint property to his former wife. He submitted a partial engrossment of the divorce settlement issued by the family court on 1 December 2015. It was designated an “excerpt from the … divorce settlement” and reproduced only the chapter concerning real estate. It also contained a family court note that it “contained … all agreements pertaining to the real estate property”. Under section 7(1) of the Land Register Act, the land register is public and can be consulted by anyone without restriction.

By decision of 25 February 2016, the land register court rejected the application. It found that submitting a partial engrossment rather than the “original” did not satisfy section 87 of the Land Register Act. A partial engrossment could not be an original; the complete document was required so the court could examine whether the settlement contained conditions or legally relevant facts affecting registration, as required by section 94(1).

The applicant appealed. He argued that refusal to transfer his property share infringed his right to dispose freely of his property. He maintained that the partial engrossment complied with section 87 because it had been issued by the same judge and stated that it reproduced the relevant part. He also complained that requiring the full divorce settlement breached data protection rules, because highly personal and sensitive data—such as names and places of abode of minor children and his former spouse, alimony amounts, and custody agreements—would become publicly accessible in the document archive. He relied on Article 8, section 1(2) of the Data Protection Act 2000, and Article 52 of the EU Charter, arguing that no legitimate aim or public interest outweighed his privacy.

On 25 April 2016 the Vienna Regional Civil Court rejected the appeal (47 R 108/16d). It confirmed that a partial engrossment was not an “original” under section 87(1) and that even the family court’s statement could not bind the land register court; the original full settlement was needed. It cited an earlier Supreme Court decision, no. 5 Ob 250/15y of 25 January 2016, requiring a complete document. It found a legal basis for the interference regarding Article 8 and the Data Protection Act.

On 24 June 2016 the applicant filed an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court, repeating that the lower courts’ interpretation was incompatible with Article 8 and other laws. He requested a preliminary ruling from the CJEU and a constitutional review. On 11 July 2016 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal (5 Ob 125/16t). It relied on its earlier decision no. 5 Ob 250/15y that a partial engrossment was insufficient under section 87(1); the excerpt’s confirmation could not change that. Under section 94(1), the land register court had to examine the application and documents comprehensively, approving registration only if justified by their content and in the required form. The family court could not bind it on completeness. On Article 8, the Supreme Court found the data protection concerns unpersuasive: examination of the entire document was mandatory under sections 87(1) and 94(1) and served protection of registered property. It stated that inclusion of documents in the document archive was not the subject of the decision and saw no reason to initiate a preliminary ruling or constitutional review.

The applicant alleged violations concerning his personal data and the lack of an effective remedy, and that the refusal infringed his property rights.
001-209358:
The applicant, Olav Omdahl, a Norwegian national born in 1951, lives in Oslo. His grandfather, O.A. Knutsen, died on 24 April 1993. The estate included extensive property, shares, securities and moveable property worth approximately NOK 100 million, with debts of about NOK 10 million. The heirs were three children and two grandchildren; two children, including the applicant’s mother, died before final distribution.

On 5 May 1993 public administration of the estate began before the Probate Court, later the District Court, and an advocate was appointed administrator. Early on, some small properties were sold, but litigation over heirs’ rights to receive assets in kind under the will and a codicil tied up proceeds until the turn of 2005/06. Probate Court decisions to convert further assets were quashed or amended on appeal by the High Court, so no assets could be distributed.

A trust established by the deceased in the Bahamas and managed by a London bank emerged after the applicant’s mother died in 2002. In December 2005 each of the deceased’s children and grandchildren received NOK 5.5 million from it. The trust led to disputes over whether funds belonged to the estate and to tax questions, clarified with the tax authorities from 2006 and finally during winter 2010.

An interim distribution on 1 July 2010 gave each branch of the lineal descendants NOK 10 million. The heirs appealed; the High Court dismissed the appeal on 7 June 2011 and the Supreme Court refused leave on 1 November 2011. Disputes over the sale of shares led to a District Court decision on 11 June 2010, finally settled on 25 March 2011. Other disputes, a recusal motion, and disputes over the sale of shares in a property company and a fish oil factory ended during 2012. Share sales were mostly completed in the first half of 2013, and remaining limited liability companies were wound up in December 2013.

The Probate Court decided final distribution on 1 August 2014. The High Court dismissed an appeal on 27 November 2014, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 7 April 2015. Final distribution was disbursed on 16 April 2015, each branch receiving about NOK 18.9 million. A further distribution decided on 10 August 2015 entailed no payments and became final in September 2015. The administration thus lasted twenty-two years and four months.

In domestic proceedings, on 9 March 2016 the applicant sued the Norwegian Government before Oslo City Court, seeking a declaratory judgment that Article 6 § 1 had been violated because the administration exceeded a reasonable time, and claiming compensation. In its judgment of 15 September 2016, the City Court found that the length alone indicated a violation but considered the estate complex, the applicant not particularly litigious, and many actions brought by other heirs; it found no proven inactivity and no violation, and no compensation. The applicant appealed. After a hearing on 6–7 March 2018, the High Court on 22 March 2018 found no inactivity and considered the administration extraordinary, citing the large number of disputes, codicil-related blockage, sale difficulties, the 2008 financial crisis, and trust and tax complications. It noted that the applicant had argued a High Court ruling of 23 October 1997 was erroneous and blocked progress, but that ruling had become binding and was not appealed. The High Court concluded that there had been sufficient progress and no violation, and no liability. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 21 June 2018. The applicant lodged application no. 46371/18 on 21 September 2018.
001-209992:
In *Valdís Fjölnisdóttir and Others v. Iceland* (Application no. 71552/17), Third Section, judgment of 18 May 2021, the applicants were two Icelandic women, Valdís and Eydís, and a child, Mr X. The first two applicants were a married couple who used a US surrogacy agency and travelled to California, where the third applicant was born in February 2013 through gestational surrogacy. The child was conceived with donor gametes and had no biological link to either intended parent. A California birth certificate named the first two applicants as parents, and the surrogate waived legal parenthood.

Three weeks after birth, the applicants travelled to Iceland. The intended parents applied to Registers Iceland to register the child as an Icelandic national born abroad, relying on the US birth certificate. After being asked further questions, they disclosed that the child had been born via surrogacy. On 18 June 2013, Registers Iceland refused registration. Under Icelandic law, the woman who gives birth is regarded as the mother. The child therefore did not automatically acquire Icelandic citizenship through the applicants and was treated as a foreign national. The Ministry of the Interior confirmed that decision on 27 March 2014.

Because the child was considered a foreign unaccompanied minor, the local child protection committee took legal custody and appointed a guardian, Ms M. The child was initially placed with the first two applicants under a foster-care arrangement. The applicants sought judicial review, asking that the Ministry’s decision be annulled and that Registers Iceland be required to register the first two applicants as the child’s parents based on the US birth certificate.

While the domestic proceedings were pending, the child was granted Icelandic citizenship by Act No. 128/2015 and entered in the national register as a citizen. However, the first two applicants were still not registered as his parents. The first two applicants divorced in May 2015, which invalidated the permanent foster-care agreement and affected their earlier adoption application. The adoption process had already been stalled because the District Commissioner considered the surrogate mother and her husband to be the legal parents/guardians whose consent was needed, and because adoption rules prohibit payment linked to consent. The applicants withdrew the adoption application after divorcing.

In March 2016, the District Court rejected the claims. It held that Icelandic family law treats the birth mother as the legal mother and that recognising foreign surrogacy parentage would conflict with fundamental Icelandic principles and the domestic ban on surrogacy. It accepted that family life existed and that the refusal interfered with it, but found the interference justified to uphold the surrogacy ban and protect others, noting counterbalancing measures such as foster care, residence, and later citizenship. The Supreme Court upheld the rejection in March 2017, but found that no protected family life existed at the time of the registration decision, since the ties had not been lawfully established under Icelandic law until the foster-care approval.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8, concerning the right to respect for private and family life, and Article 14, concerning the prohibition of discrimination. The key alleged violation was the State’s non-recognition of the parent-child relationship between the first two applicants and the child, and the resulting refusal to register them as his parents, despite the US birth certificate, the child’s residence with them, and the foster-care arrangements.
001-209154:
**Sławiński v. Poland** (ECtHR, First Section, App. No. 61039/16, 15 April 2021)

The applicant, Mariusz Grzegorz Sławiński, a Polish national born in 1958 and living in Gniewkowo, complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the criminal proceedings against him were unreasonably long and that there was no effective domestic remedy for that delay. The application was lodged on 11 October 2016, and the Court gave notice to the Polish Government of the complaints concerning the length of the criminal proceedings and the right to an effective remedy.

The underlying criminal case began in 2001, when the Toruń District Prosecutor opened an investigation into alleged fraudulent activity by the applicant’s company, which dealt with debt vindication. The applicant and his business partner were suspected of failing to transmit to a bank several hundred monthly instalment payments collected from individuals who had taken out consumer loans. On 26 February 2002 the applicant was charged with fraud, and the prosecutor placed him under police supervision. On 24 June 2002 he and a co-accused were indicted before the Toruń District Court.

The first hearing was not held until 4 December 2003, almost eighteen months after the indictment. The trial court then held hearings at regular intervals, approximately 100 in total. By 7 March 2006, it had heard over 300 witnesses listed in the bill of indictment. After that point, however, the proceedings progressed very slowly. The first-instance court eventually convicted the applicant of defrauding payments received from over 300 persons, sentencing him to one year and eight months’ imprisonment, suspended on probation, plus a fine. The applicant appealed.

On 23 October 2014 the Toruń Regional Court quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. Between 9 April and 16 June 2015 the trial court held four hearings. On 22 June 2015 the Toruń District Court acquitted the applicant of some charges and convicted him of fraud in a more limited scope, imposing one year’s imprisonment, suspended, and a fine. The applicant again appealed.

On 17 March 2016 the Toruń Regional Court quashed the conviction and discontinued the proceedings because the offences had become time-barred. The judgment was given at a hearing attended by the applicant and his lawyer. The court gave oral reasons, informed the parties that written reasons would be prepared within fourteen days, and explained that the judgment was final and that a cassation appeal was possible. The applicant was served with the written grounds on 12 April 2016.

Separately, on 6 July 2015 the applicant lodged a complaint under the Polish 2004 Act concerning undue delay. On 20 August 2015 the Toruń Regional Court partly allowed the complaint and found that the proceedings had been excessively long. It awarded the applicant 2,000 Polish zlotys (approximately 475 euros). The court noted that the first hearing had been scheduled almost eighteen months after the indictment; that after all meaningful evidence had been gathered by 7 March 2006, the next seven and a half years produced only four more witnesses and a bank evidence request, amounting to a flagrant lack of procedural efficiency; and that the trial court had also taken too long to prepare written reasons for the first-instance judgment. It further observed that the trial court should have been more active in securing the attendance of the applicant and his lawyer, who had contributed to some delays. After the case was remitted, the Regional Court found no further delays attributable to the courts.

The relevant domestic law included the 2004 Act remedy for excessive length and Article 457 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, under which written reasons are prepared automatically when a second-instance court quashes a judgment and discontinues the case, but a party must apply to be served with them. The key alleged violations therefore concerned the unreasonable length of the criminal proceedings and the lack of an effective remedy for that delay.
001-208447:
**Feilazoo v. Malta** concerns a Nigerian national who, after serving a drug-related prison sentence in Malta, was placed in immigration detention and later alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 6 and 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In 2010, the applicant was convicted of drug offences and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment and a €50,000 fine, later converted into a further term of imprisonment in default. Shortly before his release in April 2018, he was questioned about his plans. He wished to return to Spain, where he had previously held a residence permit, but the Spanish authorities allegedly refused to accept him. On 10 April 2018, instead of being taken to an emergency shelter as he expected, he was escorted to the Immigration Office. Inspector D.B. informed him that he could not return to Spain and would be removed to Nigeria, while being detained in the meantime. A Return Decision and Removal Order was issued that day under Article 5(2)(d) of the Immigration Act because he had been convicted of an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment. The Government claimed he requested voluntary departure, which was refused because he was considered a risk of absconding and a threat to public policy or security; the applicant claimed he was not informed of any right to appeal.

When the applicant objected to detention, a violent scuffle occurred. The officers alleged that he became aggressive, resisted handcuffing and bit one officer, leading them to use pepper spray and restraints. The applicant alleged that officers grabbed him by the neck, twisted him to the floor, kicked him in the private parts, knelt on his face and neck, and pepper-sprayed him; he said he could not breathe and passed out. Medical reports documented a fractured left radial head, bruising and abrasions on his face, ears, neck, shoulder and wrists, a swollen thumb, a haematoma on the mastoid process, and severe lower back pain. An expert found blunt-trauma injuries and handcuff abrasions, describing the elbow fracture as grievous.

Criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant for assaulting and resisting correctional officers, causing slight injuries, disobeying lawful orders and disturbing public order. He was placed in pre-trial detention on 12 April 2018. He complained that he was questioned without a lawyer and without being informed of the charges, and that he refused to sign an incomplete statement. In February 2019 he was convicted and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment and a €5,000 fine; on appeal in May 2019 his guilt was confirmed but the sentence was reduced to two years suspended for three years and a €4,000 fine, with immediate deportation ordered after payment. Because he could not pay the fine, it was converted into six months’ imprisonment. He was then moved between prison and immigration detention, including the Safi Detention Centre.

The alleged violations concerned: Article 3, in relation to the alleged ill-treatment on 10 April 2018 and the conditions of his immigration detention; Article 5, concerning the lawfulness of his immigration detention and removal order, including the alleged lack of information about appeal or voluntary departure and his continued detention without a realistic prospect of removal; Article 6, regarding the fairness of the criminal proceedings, particularly the absence of a lawyer and inadequate information about charges; and Article 34, concerning interference with his correspondence and ineffective domestic legal aid representation, including alleged obstruction of access to medical documents and the legal aid lawyer’s failure to contact or represent him. The Court ultimately removed the domestic legal aid representative and granted legal aid for the Strasbourg proceedings.
001-210089:
The case *Caamaño Valle v. Spain* (Application no. 43564/17) concerns the right to vote of the applicant’s daughter, M., a young woman with intellectual disability. The applicant, Maria del Mar Caamaño Valle, is a Spanish national living in Santiago de Compostela. M. was born in A Coruña in 1996. In December 2013, as M. approached adulthood, the applicant asked a First-Instance Judge in Santiago de Compostela to declare M. legally incapacitated and extend her guardianship, but expressly requested that M. should not lose her right to vote.

On 2 September 2014, the First-Instance Judge placed M. under the extended partial guardianship of her mother and revoked M.’s right to vote. The judge reasoned that disenfranchisement was not automatic, but the evidence showed M. lacked capacity to exercise suffrage. The judge found she was highly influenceable, unaware of the consequences of voting, and had deficiencies in political and electoral matters. The decision relied on expert evidence and the judge’s own examination. Under sections 3(1)(b) and 2 of the Spanish Electoral Law (LOREG), a court could withdraw voting rights where it expressly declared the person incapable of exercising suffrage.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the CRPD, especially Articles 12 and 29, required Spain to support her daughter’s exercise of the right to vote rather than remove it. On 11 March 2015, the Regional Court of A Coruña dismissed the appeal. It held that disenfranchisement was lawful and compatible with the CRPD if based on an individualized judicial review. It noted that M.’s intellectual ability was equivalent to that of a child aged six to eight. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal on 17 March 2016.

The applicant then lodged an *amparo* appeal, alleging violation of Article 23 of the Spanish Constitution. The Constitutional Court dismissed it on 28 November 2016 (notified 22 December 2016). It reasoned that universal suffrage under the Constitution was not absolute and that LOREG allowed courts to restrict voting rights individually after incapacity proceedings. It distinguished the broad CRPD concept of disability from the Spanish civil-law concept of incapacity. The court said the restriction did not target disabled persons as a group but applied only to those who, after due process, lacked the minimum understanding and will necessary to vote freely. It found the judgments sufficiently reasoned and not arbitrary.

On 9 June 2017, the applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34. She alleged a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections), alone or in conjunction with Article 14 (non-discrimination) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12. In substance, she complained that her daughter’s judicial disenfranchisement violated her right to vote and discriminated against her on grounds of intellectual disability. She relied on the CRPD and international standards requiring support for persons with disabilities in exercising political rights and prohibiting denial of voting rights based on disability or decision-making ability.

The case therefore raised whether the Spanish courts’ individualized withdrawal of M.’s voting rights breached the Convention. The relevant domestic framework included Article 23 of the Spanish Constitution and LOREG section 3. Later, Institutional Law 2/2018 amended LOREG to eliminate the possibility of depriving disabled persons of the vote and restored voting rights to those affected. International materials, including CRPD Articles 12 and 29, General Comment No. 1, and Venice Commission standards, emphasized non-discrimination and supported political participation.
001-213796:
Apap Bologna v. Malta (App. no. 47505/19), judgment of 9 December 2021, concerned a Maltese national, Mr Louis Apap Bologna, and a unilaterally imposed commercial lease under Chapter 69 of the Laws of Malta. The applicant alleged that the statutory rent regime forced him to receive an insufficient, controlled rent for his Valletta shop, imposing a disproportionate burden on his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. He also questioned the effectiveness of domestic remedies.

The applicant originally owned one-half undivided share of premises at 295 and 296 Republic Street, Valletta, inherited in 1980. The property had been leased in 1922 for four years at GBP 100 per year. Although originally contractual, 1933 Act XXI—now Chapter 69—introduced perpetual protection for tenants, renewing the lease indefinitely and preventing eviction. In 1964 the owners negotiated rent of GBP 150. In 1980, after partition with the co-owner, the applicant became full owner of the interconnected shop at no. 296. Around the same time, the tenancy passed through successions and transfers to three tenants, K., I., and V., who were not recognised by the landlords; attempts to evict them also failed.

Rent remained very low. From 18 April 2001, the landlords refused rent and deposits were made in court: the first was MTL 2,828.84, covering rent from 1982 to 2001; later deposits were MTL 150 (about EUR 395) per annum until 2009. Act X of 2009 raised rent by 15% annually for 2010–2013: EUR 401.82, EUR 462.09, EUR 531.41, and EUR 611.11. From 2014, because the Index of Commercial Value of Property was never published, rent rose by 5% yearly: EUR 641.67, EUR 673.75, EUR 707.44, EUR 742.81, EUR 779.95, and EUR 818.95 for 2014–2019.

In 2017 the applicant filed constitutional redress proceedings, claiming a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. A court-appointed architect valued the entire property at EUR 1.5 million and its annual market rent at EUR 86,540. The legal rent due in 2017 was about EUR 743 annually. The total market rent since 1986 was estimated at EUR 1,603,499. On 4 June 2018 the Civil Court, in its constitutional competence, found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but not of the Constitution, and awarded EUR 100,000 compensation with costs split equally.

Both parties appealed. On 29 March 2019 the Constitutional Court confirmed the violation but reduced compensation to EUR 55,000—EUR 50,000 for pecuniary damage and EUR 5,000 for non-pecuniary damage. It refused to order eviction, considering it lacked jurisdiction, but declared Chapter 69 provisions without effect between the applicant and the tenants, so the tenants could no longer rely on them to justify occupation. Costs were apportioned: first-instance costs remained as before; appeal costs were divided equally between the Attorney General and the applicant; the tenants bore their own cross-appeal costs. The Constitutional Court noted that the architect’s valuation covered the entire shop, whereas the applicant’s interest was limited to his divided part.

After the judgment, the applicant negotiated a new lease at EUR 140 daily—EUR 51,100 yearly—effective 1 October 2019, exceeding the expert’s estimate, plus a lump sum to make up fair rent from the Constitutional Court judgment. Later, due to COVID-19, he agreed to EUR 50 daily. The core alleged violation was the disproportionate burden arising from the perpetual statutory lease and inadequate rent, and whether domestic remedies sufficiently redressed that breach under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-214048:
In *Sandu and Others v. Romania* (Application no. 27855/17 and 19 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined 20 applications against Romania. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of detention in various Romanian police facilities and prisons. One applicant, Ion-Daniel Tudor, died in 2021; his children informed the Court that they wished to continue the application. The Romanian Government was given notice of the applications.

The applicants were detained between 2012 and 2017 at numerous facilities, including Bucharest Police no. 6, Rahova, Jilava, Galați County Police and Prison, Bihor County Police, Oradea, Satu Mare, Arad, Baia Mare, Deva, Gherla, Colibași, Târgu-Jiu, Ploiești, Timișoara, Bistrița, and Târșorul Nou. Detention periods ranged from about five months to nearly five years.

The central alleged violation was overcrowding. The appended table provides square metres per inmate for most applicants, often showing very low personal space. For example, Jan Marian Sandu had 1.52–2.44 m² over three years, two months and thirty days. Costică Caranfil had 1.5–1.8 m² for six months and twenty-one days. Serafim-Dorinel Șipoș had 1.31–2.77 m² for three years, seven months and seven days. Levente-Lorand Pal had 1.45–2.77 m² for almost two years. Emil-Gheorghe Florian had 1.33–2.77 m² for three years, seven months and twenty-three days. Daniel-Tomas Cozma had 1.30–2.94 m² for four years and six months. Mihai-Levente Băla had 1.30–2.29 m² for four years and eleven days. Adrian-Felician Sava had 1.43–2.79 m² for four years, two months and twenty days. Sorin-Andi Pandele had 1.12–2.44 m² for three years and twenty-one days. Zoltan Lingurar had 1.16–2.89 m² for one year, nine months and three days. Other applicants, such as Radu-Lucian Silaghi, Ioan Petran, and Mariana Iordăchescu, had slightly more space but still alleged overcrowding or related defects. In several cases, overcrowding was not continuous; the table notes specific periods when it was absent.

Beyond overcrowding, applicants alleged many specific conditions: bunk beds, lack of fresh air, insufficient natural or electric light, constant electric light, insect or rodent infestation, mouldy or dirty cells, inadequate furniture, poor bedding and bed linen, insufficient outdoor physical exercise, no or restricted access to warm water, no or restricted access to running water, restricted or no shower, poor food quality or quantity, poor potable water, inadequate temperature, lack of toiletries, no or restricted toilet access, lack of privacy for toilet, and lack of leisure or educational activities. These grievances were often cumulative and accompanied the overcrowding allegations.

The case therefore concerned whether these material conditions of detention—especially severe overcrowding, poor hygiene, sanitation, ventilation, lighting, food, and exercise—amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under the Convention. The Court had to assess the facts in the appended table to determine whether Romania violated the applicants’ rights.
001-209520:
**Case: K.I. v. France (Application no. 5560/19), European Court of Human Rights, 15 April 2021**

The applicant, K.I., is a Russian national of Chechen origin born in 1994. He alleged that his deportation from France to Russia would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, exposing him to a real risk of death or inhuman and degrading treatment.

K.I. claimed that in Russia his father had been a Chechen guerrilla fighter. In November 2010, he was allegedly arrested, held in custody, and beaten with an iron bar by Russian law-enforcement officers, who pressured him to infiltrate rebel groups. After he refused, he was arrested again in May 2011, interrogated, insulted, and beaten. Shortly before fleeing Russia, he was arrested a third time, assaulted, and threatened with death. He fled in 2011, transited through Poland, and left his Russian external passport there before reaching France.

In France, K.I. applied for asylum in March 2012 and was granted refugee status in January 2013. The French authorities accepted that he had family ties to Chechen separatists and had refused to cooperate with the Russian authorities. However, in November 2013, about nine months after obtaining refugee status, he was arrested in France on suspicion of involvement in a terrorist conspiracy. In April 2015, the Paris Criminal Court convicted him of participating in a criminal conspiracy to commit acts of terrorism. The court found that he had travelled to Syria in August 2013, via Germany, Poland, Ukraine, and Turkey, to undergo military training and fight with a jihadist group composed of Chechen, Dagestani, and Ingush fighters. He was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment.

Following his conviction, the French Office for the Protection of Refugees and Stateless Persons revoked his refugee status in June 2016 under Article L. 711-6 of the Immigration and Asylum Code, on the grounds that he had been finally convicted of a terrorism offence and that his presence in France constituted a serious threat to society. The National Asylum Court confirmed that decision in January 2019, and the Conseil d’État dismissed his further appeal in July 2020.

A deportation order had been issued in November 2015, and in February 2019 the prefect set Russia as the destination country. K.I. argued that he would still be at risk in Russia because of his family ties to Chechen fighters, his refusal to collaborate, and his membership in a Chechen “teip” allegedly opposed to the regime. He relied on statements that Russian or Chechen authorities had repeatedly questioned his relatives, that FSB agents had told family members he would be imprisoned upon return, and that a friend with refugee status in Germany had been arrested after returning to Russia. He also claimed that Russian officials had contacted him by telephone and Skype after he arrived in France.

The French Government disputed the reliability of this evidence, noting that some witness statements were undated or unauthenticated. Domestic courts found that K.I. had not demonstrated a real and personal risk of ill-treatment if returned. They observed that he had used his Russian external passport to travel to Syria and that there was no evidence he was wanted or charged in Russia. They also referred to reports indicating that returnees from Syria were monitored but that Chechen authorities had reception programmes for some returnees.

Before the European Court, K.I. requested an interim measure under Rule 39 to prevent his deportation. The Court initially granted temporary protection, discontinued it when no enforceable removal decision existed, and then extended it while the application was examined. The central issue was whether enforcing the deportation order would expose K.I. to treatment contrary to Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.
001-211814:
Levon Barseghyan, an Armenian journalist and political activist who chaired a journalists’ club in Gyumri, complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 11 of the Convention about being prevented from holding and participating in a rally and being fined for disobeying police orders.

The case arose after Armenia’s 19 February 2008 presidential election. Opposition supporters, led by candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan, began daily protests in Yerevan, centring on Freedom Square. On 1 March 2008, police cleared the square; later that day, protests escalated into clashes, resulting in ten deaths, injuries and property damage. The President declared a state of emergency in Yerevan for twenty days, banning meetings, rallies, demonstrations, marches and other mass events. Although the decree was formally limited to Yerevan, reports by Armenia’s Ombudsman, PACE and the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights indicated that restrictions on rallies were also applied in other major cities, including Gyumri.

On 2 March 2008 at about 12:30 p.m., Barseghyan went to Theatre Square in Gyumri and tried to enter the square to hold a protest. Police officers stationed there to prevent demonstrations refused him entry. According to the authorities, he called on people present to gather and hold a demonstration. Police ordered him to leave and stop inciting others to assemble. He did not comply and was taken to a police station.

An administrative case was opened under Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences for disobeying lawful police orders. The police then sought an administrative penalty, claiming that no notification or authorisation had been given to hold a demonstration at Theatre Square. Barseghyan counterclaimed that the factual basis was unsubstantiated: he had not intended to organise a rally, no rally was taking place, “calling on people” was not a punishable act, and there was no evidence that 100 or more people had gathered. Under the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, only “mass public events” of 100 or more participants required prior written notification; non-mass events of fewer than 100 participants did not. He therefore argued that the police orders were not lawful.

The police responded that well-known facts did not need proof, including the tense post-1 March situation, a previous unauthorised rally at Theatre Square, and an announcement that Barseghyan would speak at the next rally. They contended that his appearance was not accidental and that the administrative case was justified.

On 10 June 2008, the Administrative Court granted the police claim and fined Barseghyan 50,000 Armenian drams (about €110). It found that police were at the square to prohibit an unnotified demonstration and that there had been no legal basis for holding one. Although the state of emergency was formally in force only in Yerevan, the court reasoned that a mass public event in Gyumri, Armenia’s second-largest city, could have endangered public order and public health, especially without notification. It concluded that the police orders he disobeyed were lawful.

Barseghyan appealed, arguing that the fine violated his Article 11 rights and that the judgment failed to explain the restriction on his right to hold and participate in a rally. On 2 October 2008, the Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible for lack of merit.

He lodged his application with the European Court on 1 April 2009. The complaint concerned the prohibition on holding and participating in a rally and the administrative penalty for disobeying police orders, raising issues under Article 11 regarding freedom of peaceful assembly. The key dispute was whether the interference was lawful and justified, particularly given that the state of emergency was formally limited to Yerevan, that restrictions were nonetheless applied in Gyumri, and that domestic law allegedly did not require notification for gatherings of fewer than 100 people.
001-211020:
**Case Summary: Aslanian v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 74433/11)**

The case of *Aslanian v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* is a judgment delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, sitting as a Committee) on 13 July 2021. The applicant, Rostom Aslanian, is a Russian national born in 1989 who lives in Vărăncău, Moldova. He lodged his application against the Republic of Moldova and Russia on 28 November 2011, complaining under Articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The case concerns the applicant’s conviction for refusing military service on religious grounds in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The applicant is a member of the religious community of Jehovah’s Witnesses in the “MRT.” When he became eligible for the draft, he requested the “MRT” authorities to assign him to civilian service instead of compulsory military service, relying on his religious conscience and beliefs.

In December 2010, the “MRT” authorities denied his request and initiated a criminal investigation against him on charges of draft evasion. On 29 March 2011, the “Rîbnița City and Region Court” convicted the applicant of draft evasion and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment. He was taken into custody in the courtroom. On 7 June 2012, the “MRT” Supreme Court upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant had already been released from detention on 29 March 2012, after having fully served his sentence.

These facts are central to the alleged violations. The applicant’s complaint under Article 9 concerns freedom of thought, conscience, and religion. The essence of the allegation is that he was criminally punished for refusing compulsory military service because of his religious beliefs, and that the authorities failed to provide an alternative civilian service as required by his conscientious objection. The complaint under Article 14 concerns discrimination, apparently alleging that he was treated differently because of his religion or religious community.

The broader context of the “MRT” is also relevant. The Court has previously addressed the situation in Transdniestria in cases such as *Ilaşcu and Others v. Moldova and Russia*, *Catan and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*, and *Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*. The judgment notes that relevant materials concerning the “MRT” are summarised in *Mozer*. This context matters for questions of jurisdiction and the responsibility of the respondent States, although the extract provided focuses primarily on the applicant’s individual facts.

Procedurally, the Court gave notice of the application to both Governments, and the parties submitted observations. The Russian Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The Committee was composed of Judges Carlo Ranzoni, Egidijus Kūris, and Pauliine Koskelo, with Hasan Bakırcı as Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was adopted on 22 June 2021 and delivered on 13 July 2021. It is final, though subject to possible editorial revision.

In sum, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant was a Jehovah’s Witness in the “MRT”; he sought civilian service instead of military service on religious grounds; his request was denied; he was criminally prosecuted and convicted of draft evasion; he was sentenced to one year’s imprisonment; the conviction was upheld on appeal; and he fully served his sentence. Those facts form the basis of his claims under Articles 9 and 14. The provided text does not include the Court’s final merits reasoning or conclusion.
001-207850:
In *Ibrišimović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 11 February 2021; applications nos. 15634/20 and 3 others), four applicants complained of the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 11 March 2020. The applicants were represented by Mr O. Eterović, a lawyer practising in Sarajevo. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was given notice. A Fourth Section Committee composed of Judges Armen Harutyunyan (President), Jolien Schukking and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 21 January 2021 and adopted the judgment on 11 February 2021.

The factual core appears in the appended table. Each applicant obtained a decision from the Sarajevo Municipal Court, but the domestic authorities did not enforce it. The applicants alleged that this non-enforcement violated their Convention rights. The key facts are as follows.

Fikret Ibrišimović, born 1969, application no. 15634/20, had two relevant Sarajevo Municipal Court decisions, dated 12 January 2015 and 6 May 2016. The non-enforcement periods began on 15 April 2016 and 3 November 2016, respectively. At the time of the application, enforcement proceedings were still pending: more than 4 years, 7 months and 25 days for the first decision, and more than 4 years, 1 month and 7 days for the second.

Tarik Ćosić, born 1972, application no. 15641/20, relied on a Sarajevo Municipal Court decision of 21 August 2014. The non-enforcement period began on 10 February 2016. Enforcement remained pending for more than 4 years and 10 months.

Ivica Franjić, born 1975, application no. 15644/20, relied on a Sarajevo Municipal Court decision of 21 October 2014. The non-enforcement period began on 25 March 2016. Enforcement remained pending for more than 4 years, 8 months and 15 days.

Senad Ćubara, born 1967, application no. 15651/20, relied on a Sarajevo Municipal Court decision of 5 February 2016. The non-enforcement period began on 28 April 2016. Enforcement remained pending for more than 4 years, 7 months and 12 days.

All four applications were introduced on the same date, 11 March 2020. The common factual pattern is that each applicant had a final domestic court decision in his favour, but Bosnia and Herzegovina failed to enforce it. The enforcement proceedings were still pending in each case, with delays exceeding four years from the start of the non-enforcement period to the introduction of the applications. The alleged violation therefore concerns the State’s prolonged failure to execute final and enforceable domestic decisions. The most relevant facts for that complaint are the dates and identity of the domestic decisions, the start dates of the non-enforcement periods, the absence of completed enforcement, and the length of the delays. The excerpt does not set out the Court’s legal assessment or final conclusions, but the factual basis is clearly the continued non-enforcement of domestic judgments.
001-211596:
In *Milošević v. Croatia* (Application no. 12022/16), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Croatian authorities punished the applicant twice for the same conduct, contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (the *ne bis in idem* principle). The applicant, a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina living in Bosanski Brod, owned a truck inspected on 29 June 2012 by the Vukovar Customs Office with police assistance. The inspection found that the truck was using red-tinted, state-supported heating oil, which could not lawfully be used as motor-vehicle fuel.

On the same day, the Customs Office found the applicant guilty of a minor offence under the Excise Duties Act for using the heating oil contrary to section 74(2). He was fined HRK 4,800 (about EUR 640) under section 80(3). The penalty notice stated that, as owner, he was responsible; it also warned that an unpaid fine could be enforced and, if enforcement failed, converted into imprisonment. The applicant did not appeal, the decision became final, and he paid the fine.

Also on 29 June 2012, the Customs Office sent inspection and sampling records to its administrative department to calculate tax surcharges. On 2 July 2012, the Osijek Customs Office ordered the applicant to pay HRK 123,000 (about EUR 16,700) in excise duties. This sum consisted of excise duties for the quantity of heating oil involved, increased one hundred times because of its illegal use, under section 76(2) of the Excise Duties Act.

The applicant challenged that decision. On 31 October 2013, the Ministry of Finance quashed it because the quantity of oil subject to excise duty had not been properly determined. On 15 January 2014, the Osijek Customs Office issued a fresh decision ordering payment of HRK 83,025 (about EUR 11,300), again applying the one-hundred-times increase for the illegal use on 29 June 2012. This decision was upheld on appeal. The applicant then brought an administrative action, but the Osijek Administrative Court dismissed it on 20 January 2015, and the High Administrative Court upheld that judgment.

The applicant subsequently lodged a constitutional complaint, arguing, among other things, that he had been punished twice for the same act, contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. On 20 January 2016, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, without addressing his *ne bis in idem* complaint. He applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 22 February 2016.

The relevant law included the Excise Duties Act: section 73 required heating gas oils to be labelled; section 74(2) prohibited using such oils to power motor vehicles or for purposes other than heating; section 76(2) required the owner of a vehicle found using such oil illegally to pay excise duties equal to the fuel-tank volume multiplied by one hundred; and section 80 made such use a minor offence punishable by a fine of HRK 2,000 to HRK 10,000 for natural persons. In 2015, the Act was amended to remove the one-hundred-times increase, with the final proposal stating that the increase had been contrary to the *ne bis in idem* principle and EU jurisprudence and practice. The minor offence for illegal use remained.

The alleged violation therefore arose from two consequences based on the same facts: a final minor-offence fine for using prohibited heating oil, and a later administrative excise-duty charge for the same illegal use, increased one hundred times. The key question was whether these amounted to two criminal punishments for the same offence contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7.
001-210680:
Monir Lotfy v. Cyprus (Application no. 37139/13, ECtHR Third Section, 29 June 2021) concerned an Egyptian national with a long immigration history in Cyprus. He first arrived in 1991, was deported twice, and although granted Cypriot citizenship, it was later revoked. After a second deportation in June 2012, he unlawfully re-entered Cyprus. On 10 February 2013 police arrested him during a random identity check. On 11 February 2013, deportation and detention orders were issued under the Aliens and Immigration Law because he was a prohibited immigrant. He remained in immigration detention until 8 July 2014, when he was deported to Egypt, moving between Nicosia Central Prisons Block 10, Menoyia detention centre, and various police stations.

The main Article 5 §1 complaint was that this detention pending deportation was unlawful. After more than five months, he lodged a first habeas corpus application. On 30 July 2013 the Supreme Court granted it, ordered his immediate release, and found the Government had not shown his continued detention was justified: it had failed to explain steps taken to deport him or whether the Minister had reviewed detention as required. The same day, while still at court, he was rearrested. New deportation and detention orders were issued on the same grounds. A second habeas corpus application was rejected on 28 January 2014; the Supreme Court viewed the detention as continuous since February 2013 and lawful because extensions were based on the lack of Egyptian travel documents, partly due to the applicant’s refusal to cooperate. His judicial-review challenge to the new orders also failed; a provisional suspension was initially ordered subject to a €10,000 guarantee, but he could not provide a guarantor. The main recourse was later dismissed as moot after deportation. His asylum claim, lodged in January 2014, was rejected and his appeal dismissed in 2015 after deportation.

Under Article 5 §4, he alleged there was no effective remedy for challenging his detention, given the rearrest after the habeas corpus release, the rejection of the second habeas corpus, and the ineffective recourse proceedings.

Under Article 3, he alleged poor detention conditions, denial of medical treatment, and ill-treatment. He complained of overcrowding and inadequate facilities, including at Menoyia, where an 18.36 sq m cell held up to eight detainees (he shared with four to seven), and smaller police cells. He alleged refusal of medication and delays in hospital access. He claimed that on 17 July 2013 he was handcuffed to a chair for six hours and assaulted; the Government denied this. On 9 October 2013 he alleged officers beat him at Menoyia; the Government said he assaulted two officers, who were injured. Criminal proceedings against him were discontinued after deportation. On 19 October 2013 he alleged beating when requesting hospital; the Government recorded that he had drunk shampoo and had abrasions but no fracture. On 29 October 2013 he alleged forced showering and humiliation. He was also held in solitary confinement in April and May 2014 for misconduct; the Ombudsman did not investigate after his deportation. Medical records showed he was examined or hospitalised many times.
001-210332:
This case concerns an Article 11 complaint brought by the Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (LO) and the Norwegian Transport Workers’ Union (NTF) against Norway. The applicants alleged that the Norwegian Supreme Court’s decision declaring their announced boycott unlawful violated their right to freedom of association, including collective action.

NTF had a long-standing collective framework agreement with Norway’s largest employer organisation and the logistics association, covering dockworkers in major ports. The Framework Agreement, originally from the 1970s and renewed biannually, secured permanent employment, pay, hours, and a priority-of-engagement clause. Clause 2(1) provided that for vessels of 50 deadweight tonnes or more sailing between Norwegian and foreign ports, loading and unloading should be carried out by dockworkers, except at a company’s own facilities using its own employees. In Drammen, the Administration Office for Dock Work managed dockworkers and ensured permanent employment. Holship Norge AS, a Norwegian subsidiary of a Danish freight group, was not a member of the employer organisations and was not bound by the Framework Agreement. Until 2013 it used the Administration Office. In 2013 it employed four persons who, among other tasks, performed loading and unloading for Holship.

In April 2013 NTF demanded that Holship enter a collective agreement and accept the Framework Agreement. After mediation, NTF issued a boycott notice on 11 June 2013. The stated purpose was to secure a collective agreement enshrining clause 2(1)’s priority of engagement for Holship’s dock work in Drammen. The boycott would block ships involving Holship. NTF also offered to negotiate to minimise negative effects on Holship’s employees.

NTF asked the Drammen City Court for a declaration that the boycott was lawful. In 2014 the City Court and the Borgarting High Court both found it lawful. They held that the purpose was not unlawful, that protecting dockworkers through the Framework Agreement served public interests and reflected ILO Convention No. 137, and that possible redundancies among Holship’s employees did not make the boycott unlawful. They also found no breach of negative freedom of association and noted NTF’s willingness to negotiate.

Holship appealed. The Supreme Court limited the appeal to issues including EEA freedom of establishment and ILO Convention No. 137. The EFTA Court advised that the priority system restricted freedom of establishment, protected only a limited group of workers to the detriment of others, and could affect Holship’s and its employees’ negative freedom of association. In December 2016 the Norwegian Supreme Court, by ten votes to seven, ruled the boycott unlawful. The majority accepted that protecting workers could justify restrictions on freedom of establishment, but found that the priority-of-engagement demand mainly shielded the Administration Office from competition and limited Holship’s market access. It was therefore disproportionate. Even assuming Article 11 protected a right to boycott, that right had to be balanced against EEA freedom of establishment. The majority also held that ILO Convention No. 137 had to yield to EEA law. The minority dissented, finding the boycott justified.

The applicants complained under Article 11 that declaring the boycott unlawful breached their freedom of association and collective action. The key facts for the alleged violation are that the boycott was peaceful collective action by a trade union seeking a collective agreement; the Supreme Court nevertheless declared it unlawful primarily because it restricted EEA freedom of establishment; and it gave that market freedom precedence over Article 11. After the judgment, the Framework Agreement was replaced by a new port and terminal agreement without the priority system. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice only of the Article 11 complaint.
001-213788:
In *Rovshan Hajiyev v. Azerbaijan* (Applications nos. 19925/12 and 47532/13, judgment of 9 December 2021), the applicant was an Azerbaijani journalist and editor of the newspaper *Azadlıq*. The case concerned requests for information about the Gabala Radar Station, a Soviet-era military early warning radar located in Azerbaijan and operated by Russia under a lease until 2012. The applicant alleged that the station caused serious environmental and public-health problems in Gabala and nearby districts. Presidential orders in 2001 and 2003 created Azerbaijani-Russian commissions, chaired by the Minister of Healthcare, to assess the station’s environmental and public-health impact. The applicant sought related reports and information from State authorities under Azerbaijan’s Law on Access to Information, but claimed he was denied access. He also alleged that the domestic proceedings concerning his requests lacked fairness. The applications were lodged under Articles 6 and 10 of the Convention.

In application no. 19925/12, on 27 July 2010 the applicant wrote to the Ministry of Healthcare as editor of *Azadlıq*, invoking the Law on Access to Information. He asked whether the State commission assessing the Gabala Radar Station’s environmental and public-health impact was still active and requested copies of reports prepared by relevant State commissions. On 6 August 2010, the Ministry replied that a report prepared under the presidential order of 26 February 2001 had been transmitted to the Cabinet of Ministers. The applicant considered this response inadequate and sued, seeking an order requiring the Ministry to provide a copy of the report. The Ministry argued that it no longer possessed the report and had given a comprehensive reply. On 3 February 2011, the Nasimi District Court dismissed the claim, finding that the Ministry had complied because it no longer held the report and had informed the applicant. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 2 May 2011, adding that the Ministry had assisted by identifying the Cabinet of Ministers as the holder. The Supreme Court upheld the lower judgments on 5 September 2011.

In application no. 47532/13, on 6 December 2010 the applicant wrote to the Cabinet of Ministers requesting a copy of the same report. The Cabinet received the request but did not respond. In February 2011, the applicant sued in Baku Administrative Economic Court No. 1, arguing that the failure to respond breached the Law on Access to Information and Article 10 of the Convention. The Cabinet of Ministers did not send representatives or submit written pleadings during the proceedings. The applicant reapplied in April 2011 but again received no response. On 23 December 2011, the first-instance court dismissed the claim, reasoning that Article 29.1 of the Law on Access to Information did not obligate information owners to disclose reports of commissions created for a specific purpose. The applicant appealed, arguing that Article 29.1 merely listed types of information to be proactively disclosed and did not limit obligations to provide non-restricted information upon request. He contended that the report was not restricted and was of public interest, needed for his professional work as a journalist. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment on 15 March 2012, and the Supreme Court upheld it on 11 July 2012.

Under the relevant law, State bodies were “information owners” required to ensure access to information, respond to requests, assist in locating information if not possessed, and forward requests to the proper owner within five working days. Refusals had to be written and substantiated. Article 29.1 listed information subject to proactive disclosure, while Article 29.2 generally prohibited requesting those listed types individually, subject to exceptions. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6 and 10 arising from the denial of access to requested information and the alleged unfairness of the domestic proceedings.
001-213522:
**Avci v. Denmark** (Application no. 40240/19), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 30 November 2021, concerned the expulsion of a settled migrant imposed in criminal proceedings. The applicant, Cihan Avci, was a Turkish national born in Denmark in 1993. He later lived in Turkey. The case raised issues under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 14(1) of the Association Agreement between the EU and Turkey, particularly whether his expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban was a disproportionate interference with his private and family life.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were as follows. In 2013, the applicant was convicted of attempting to free a detainee in August 2012 and, in February 2013, participating in a crowd that caused public insecurity. He received a 20-day suspended prison sentence. In September 2018, the District Court convicted him of serious drug offences under section 191(2), read with section 191(1), of the Danish Penal Code, committed between January and April 2017. As part of an organised network, he had received, possessed, and transferred one kilogram of cocaine through extensive sales and deliveries to identified and unidentified buyers. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and given a warning about expulsion.

The Immigration Service gathered information on his personal circumstances. He was born in Denmark, lived with his parents and three siblings, was unmarried, and had no children. He had not completed the ninth grade or any further education. After lower secondary school, he had worked in various jobs, including in a supermarket and as a waiter, and was receiving unemployment benefits when arrested. His maternal aunt and grandfather lived in Turkey. He reportedly spoke Turkish/Kurdish, though not as well as Danish, and had visited Turkey several times on holiday.

On appeal, the applicant disputed parts of this information. He stated that his father’s sister in Turkey had died, that he had no maternal aunt there, and that his maternal grandfather suffered from dementia and he had no relationship with him. He spoke only a little Kurdish, mainly with his father, and mostly Danish with his parents. He did not speak Turkish beyond a few words. He had only visited Turkey as a tourist. He said he had committed the offences because of a gambling debt.

In January 2019, the High Court unanimously confirmed the conviction and sentence but overturned the District Court’s refusal to expel him. It ordered his expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban. The High Court found that the drug offences were very serious, organised, committed with others over several months, and that his personal behaviour represented a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to society. It also found a risk of future offending if he were not expelled, and rejected his gambling debt explanation as mitigating. Although it acknowledged that he was born and raised in Denmark, had family there, and would suffer a particular burden from expulsion, it found he had certain ties to Turkey through his grandfather, Kurdish language, and previous holidays. It concluded that he could establish a life in Turkey and maintain contact with family by phone or internet. The circumstances favouring expulsion were sufficiently compelling to outweigh those against it, and expulsion was not disproportionate under Article 14(1) of the Association Agreement or Article 8 ECHR.

The Appeals Permission Board refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court on 8 March 2019, and the deportation order was enforced on 24 January 2020. Under the Aliens Act at the time of the offence, a permanent re-entry ban was imposed if the sentence exceeded two years. A later 2018 amendment, not applicable to this case, allowed courts to reduce such bans if they would breach Denmark’s international obligations.
001-210537:
In *Toțchi and Others v. the Republic of Moldova, Russia and Ukraine* (Application no. 8833/10), the applicants were two Russian nationals, Mr Iurie Toțchi and Mrs Tatiana Toțcaia, and one Ukrainian national, Mr Marc Fașcevschii. They lived in Bender. Their complaint concerned the death of Ms Iana Faşcevscaia, the first two applicants’ daughter and the third applicant’s wife, after she consumed poisonous mushrooms bought from a public market in Tiraspol, a city controlled by the self-proclaimed Moldovan Republic of Transnistria (“MRT”). The applicants alleged that the authorities failed to protect the victim’s right to life and to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances of her death.

On 6 July 2001, two persons, K.S. and K.V., collected mushrooms in the woods and sold them at a market in Tiraspol. On 8 July 2001, two people who had eaten mushrooms from these sellers were admitted to the intensive care unit of the Republican Clinical Hospital in Tiraspol. More poisoned consumers followed. On 9 July 2001 at 10:35 a.m., hospital staff urgently called the Republican Centre for Hygiene and Epidemiology, reporting the incident and identifying the marketplace where the mushrooms had been bought.

Later that same day, at around 5 p.m., Ms Iana Faşcevscaia bought mushrooms from K.S. and K.V. They showed her a certificate from the market’s veterinary and sanitary laboratory confirming the mushrooms were suitable for consumption. She prepared dinner for her family. At about 4:10 a.m. on 10 July 2001, she felt stomach discomfort and was admitted to the hospital at 6 a.m. Her condition worsened, and on 13 July she was transferred to a hospital in Chișinău, where she died on 15 July 2001.

On 19 July 2001, the Tiraspol Prosecutor’s Office opened criminal investigations against the sellers and the market laboratory expert. On 31 May 2002, both investigations were discontinued. It was found that the sellers could not have known that some mushrooms were poisonous, especially since they had a certificate. The laboratory expert had used a rudimentary method—visual inspection and boiling mushrooms with an onion to observe colour changes—and no market laboratory in the MRT had equipment for biochemical mushroom testing. She was also covered by an amnesty law. The investigation against the sellers was later reopened and discontinued several times; ultimately, they were relieved of criminal responsibility because the limitation period had expired.

The investigation was extended to three officials from the Centre, accused of negligence for failing to react promptly to the hospital’s urgent call on the morning of 9 July 2001 and for not preventing further sale of the dangerous mushrooms despite having time to do so. On 14 May 2009, the Tiraspol city court convicted two officials of negligence.
