It found that had they properly discharged their duties, further sale would have been prohibited and the victim’s death avoided. They were sentenced to three years’ imprisonment but released due to the limitation period. The court also noted serious systemic shortcomings: old regulations for veterinary and sanitary laboratories no longer applied, no new regulations had been adopted, the laboratories lacked testing equipment, and prosecutorial delays allowed responsible persons to avoid liability. The MRT Supreme Court upheld the judgment on 30 July 2009. The Supreme Court of Moldova refused to examine the applicants’ appeal, stating that the judgments had been issued by unconstitutional courts and inviting them to pursue constitutional procedures; it appears they did not do so.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations: the authorities’ failure to protect life after knowing of the poisoning risk, and the failure to conduct a prompt and effective investigation, with delays and limitation periods preventing accountability.
001-210282:
**Case summary: Ancient Baltic Religious Association “Romuva” v. Lithuania (App. no. 48329/19)**

The applicant is the Ancient Baltic religious association “Romuva,” a registered Lithuanian religious association whose communities follow the old Baltic pagan faith. One affiliated community was registered in 1992, and Romuva itself was registered in 2002. Under Lithuanian law, religious associations may be merely registered, traditionally recognised, or granted State recognition. State-recognised status carries additional privileges: religious education in public schools, religious marriages with civil effect, national broadcaster airtime, State pensions for clergy, and land-tax exemptions. Non-traditional associations may obtain State recognition if they have support in society and their teaching and practices do not contravene law or public morals; they may apply 25 years after initial registration, with the Seimas deciding after the Ministry of Justice’s conclusion.

In 2017 Romuva sought State recognition. The Ministry of Justice concluded that it met the legal criteria: it had operated long enough, its teachings did not violate law or public morals, and it had sufficient public support. The Ministry noted that more than 5,000 people identified with the “Baltic faith” in the 2011 census, that the movement had grown, that it was the sixth largest religious movement in Lithuania, and that surveys viewed it positively. Seimas committees, the Government, and the Seimas Law Department supported the draft resolution.

Debates took place on 25 and 27 June 2019. Supporters stressed Romuva’s links to Lithuanian history, freedom of religion, and pluralism. Opponents questioned whether Romuva was truly a religion rather than an ethno-cultural heritage group; argued that the ancient Baltic faith had never been uniform; disputed the comprehensiveness of its beliefs; claimed public support was too small (about 0.17% in 2011); and warned that recognising it would “hollow out” the concept of religion. Some framed paganism as opposed to Christianity. One MP alleged Soviet/KGB/Kremlin links. On 26 June, the Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference sent a letter to members of the parliamentary group “For the Family,” arguing that the notion of an ancient Baltic religion lacked scientific basis, that its beliefs were incomplete, and that public support required wider study. The letter was forwarded among group members.

On 27 June 2019, the Seimas voted: 40 in favour, 31 against, 15 abstentions. The draft resolution failed. Romuva complained to the Seimas Ethics Commission about the KGB allegation. The Commission found that the MP had knowingly spread false and defamatory claims, noting that old Baltic believers had been persecuted by Soviet authorities. A court upheld those findings but held there was no legal basis to order an MP to retract statements made in parliamentary debate; that case remained pending on appeal.

Romuva alleged violations of Articles 9 (freedom of religion), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention. Key facts relevant to those complaints include that other non-traditional Christian associations—Evangelical Baptist, Seventh-day Adventist, Pentecostal, and New Apostolic Churches—had been granted State recognition between 2001 and 2017, often with little debate, while Romuva was refused despite the Ministry’s positive conclusion. Domestically, administrative courts generally cannot review Seimas acts of State governance, and an individual constitutional complaint requires a prior decision based on the challenged legal instrument violating rights and exhaustion of remedies. The case thus concerns whether the refusal, amid hostile parliamentary statements and the Bishops’ Conference letter, amounted to unjustified interference with religious freedom, discriminatory treatment, and a lack of effective domestic remedy.
001-141943:
The case of *Lambertné Bársony v. Hungary* (Application no. 48689/10) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning a Hungarian national’s complaint about domestic civil proceedings. The applicant, Ms Klára Lambertné Bársony, was born in 1955 and lives in Miskolc. She lodged her application against the Republic of Hungary on 18 August 2010 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Hungarian Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi, Agent at the Ministry of Public Administration and Justice. On 6 March 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. A Second Section Committee composed of Judges Helen Keller (President), András Sajó and Egidijus Kūris, with Stanley Naismith as Section Registrar, adopted the judgment on 25 March 2014.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation stem from a civil dispute initiated by the applicant on 20 April 1998. On that date, she brought an action seeking division of the property of her common-law partnership with a person identified as Mr F. The case was heard at first instance by the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Court. It then proceeded on appeal to the Debrecen Court of Appeal. The final judgment in the domestic proceedings was delivered by the Supreme Court on 2 March 2010.

The central fact for the alleged violation is the duration of those domestic proceedings. From 20 April 1998, when the applicant commenced her action, until 2 March 2010, when the Supreme Court gave final judgment, the civil case lasted approximately eleven years and ten months. This period included proceedings at three judicial levels: a county court, a court of appeal, and the Supreme Court. The applicant lodged her Convention application on 18 August 2010, about five and a half months after the final domestic decision. That timing is relevant because applications to the European Court generally must be submitted within six months of the final domestic decision, and her application therefore appears timely in that respect.

Although the provided excerpt does not expressly set out the applicant’s specific complaints in the Court’s own words, the factual chronology indicates that the principal alleged violation concerned the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The key facts relevant to that complaint are the total elapsed time, the successive stages of domestic review, and the subject matter of the dispute, namely division of property from a common-law partnership. The nature of the dispute could affect the assessment of complexity and what was at stake for the applicant. The provided materials do not describe the reasons for the delay, the conduct of the parties, or any periods of inactivity, which would ordinarily be relevant to the Court’s reasonableness assessment. They also do not indicate whether the applicant raised a separate complaint, such as an alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy for the length of proceedings under Article 13 of the Convention. The available text ends after recording the Supreme Court’s final judgment and does not include the Court’s legal reasoning or conclusion.
001-141629:
The case *Kiisa v. Estonia* (Applications nos. 16587/10 and 34304/11, judgment of 13 March 2014) concerned two Estonian nationals, formerly married from 1989 to 2006, and protracted civil proceedings over child maintenance. The first applicant, Karin Kiisa, gave birth to child K. in September 2002; the second applicant, Aare Kiisa, was recorded as the father. In October 2003 the first applicant filed for divorce and division of marital property.

In October 2004 the first applicant sued the second applicant in Harju County Court for child alimony. After preliminary hearings and evidence requests, the second applicant in April 2005 filed a separate action to establish that he was not the child’s father and to contest the civil status record. In June 2005 he requested suspension of the alimony case pending the filiation proceedings. In October 2005 the County Court suspended the alimony proceedings until judgment in the filiation case.

In the meantime, in May 2005 the County Court in the filiation case ordered DNA analyses of the child and the second applicant and obliged the first applicant to take the child for sampling. She appealed unsuccessfully; the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in January 2007. However, the first applicant did not take the child for DNA testing. The filiation action was eventually dismissed by the Harju County Court on 10 May 2012.

In June 2007 the first applicant asked for the alimony proceedings to be resumed, relying on Supreme Court practice that contesting the civil status record did not remove the obligation to provide child support. The County Court resumed proceedings on 20 June 2007 and scheduled a hearing, which was postponed at the second applicant’s request. In July 2007 the second applicant made a compromise proposal; time-limits were extended. Between September and November 2007 the parties exchanged evidence and submissions, and the second applicant requested further adjournments. In October 2007 the court requested evidence from banks and the Tax and Customs Board and ordered the second applicant to submit documents. A hearing was held on 30 November 2007.

On 11 January 2008 the County Court partly granted the first applicant’s action, ordering monthly alimony of EEK 3,000 (about €192). Both parties appealed. On 9 May 2008 the Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. Both applicants appealed to the Supreme Court. On 19 November 2008 the Supreme Court quashed the Court of Appeal judgment and remitted the case for renewed examination. On 21 May 2009 the Court of Appeal quashed the County Court judgment and remitted the case to the first-instance court. The first applicant’s further appeal was refused by the Supreme Court on 7 September 2009.

In January 2010 the first applicant amended her claim, submitted voluminous new evidence and sought interim measures. On 17 February 2010 the County Court ordered interim monthly alimony of EEK 2,175 (about €139). In April 2010 the second applicant sought postponement because his representative was ill. The first applicant submitted further evidence in April and May 2010. A hearing took place on 3 June 2010. On 5 July 2010 the County Court ordered monthly alimony of EEK 5,000 (about €320). Both parties appealed. On 6 October 2010 the Tallinn Court of Appeal reduced the monthly amount to EEK 3,550 (about €227). Both applicants sought leave to appeal, but the Supreme Court refused on 26 January 2011.

The proceedings therefore lasted from October 2004 to January 2011, over six years, including a suspension of about one year and eight months, repeated adjournments, appeals and remittals. Domestic law included constitutional provisions on effective remedies and compensation, the State Liability Act, and Supreme Court decisions indicating that compensation for excessive length of proceedings should be sought before an administrative court. The alleged violations concerned primarily the excessive length of the civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the lack of an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.
001-141668:
The case of **S.J. v. Belgium** (Application no. 70055/10; Chamber judgment of 27 February 2014, later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 19 March 2015) concerned a Nigerian national who alleged that her expulsion to Nigeria would violate **Article 3** (risk of inhuman or degrading treatment), **Article 8** (right to private and family life), and **Article 13** (lack of an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

S.J. arrived in Belgium in summer 2007, when she was eight months pregnant, and applied for asylum on 30 July 2007. She claimed she had fled Nigeria after the family of M.A., the father of her child and the man in whose home she had lived since age eleven, pressured her to have an abortion. EURODAC records showed she had already applied for asylum in Malta on 29 June 2007. Belgium requested Malta to take charge under the Dublin II Regulation, and Malta accepted in September 2007. S.J. nevertheless remained in Belgium while proceedings continued.

In August 2007, during antenatal care, she was diagnosed HIV-positive with a serious immune deficiency requiring antiretroviral treatment. From October 2007 she received ARV therapy at St Pierre University Hospital. She gave birth to her first child in September 2007, a second child in April 2009, and a third in November 2012; M.A. was the father of all three. Medical certificates documented fluctuating CD4 counts and viral loads, changes in treatment, and periods of uncontrolled infection. By 2012–2013, doctors described her situation as worrying for both her and her children, requiring multidisciplinary HIV care, regular blood tests, and medication. She also received psychosocial support from the association Lhiving. M.A. spent occasional periods in Belgium without a residence permit.

Her asylum claim was rejected in May 2010 because of inconsistencies, and the Aliens Appeals Board upheld that rejection in October 2010. Separately, in November 2007, S.J. sought leave to remain on medical grounds under section 9ter of the Aliens Act. The Aliens Office initially considered treatment available in Malta; later, after deciding to examine her asylum claim, it considered treatment and monitoring available in Nigeria. In September/October 2010 the Aliens Office refused her medical regularization, finding HIV medication available in Nigeria, subsidized or free in public hospitals, and that she likely had family support there. On 22 November 2010 she was ordered to leave Belgium by 20 December 2010.

S.J. lodged an extremely urgent request for a stay of execution and an application to set aside the decisions, alleging violations of Articles 3, 8 and 13. The Aliens Appeals Board rejected the stay on 27 November 2010, finding extreme urgency not established because she was not detained and no removal date had been set. The Conseil d’État declared her appeal inadmissible in January 2011, noting that ordinary stay and interim measures were available. Her set-aside application remained pending. She applied to the European Court, which indicated under Rule 39 on 17 December 2010 that Belgium should not expel her and her children pending the proceedings.

The key facts underlying the alleged violations were her severe HIV status and dependence on ARV treatment, the disputed availability and accessibility of equivalent treatment in Nigeria, her three minor children and family ties in Belgium, the risk of irreversible health deterioration if expelled, and the alleged inadequacy of domestic remedies because appeals did not automatically suspend removal. The Chamber declared the application admissible on 18 December 2012.
001-141933:
In *Memishaj v. Albania*, the applicant, Enver Memishaj, an Albanian national born in 1944, worked as an accountant for Tirana City Hall. On 10 December 2001 he was dismissed, effective 11 January 2002. He challenged the dismissal. On 6 February 2002 the Civil Service Commission (“CSC”) quashed the dismissal and ordered his reinstatement. By final decision of 8 May 2003, the Supreme Court upheld the CSC decision. On 15 May 2003 the Tirana District Court supplemented the CSC decision by ordering Tirana City Hall to pay the applicant’s salary for the period between 10 December 2001 and the date of reinstatement. The employer’s request for revision was dismissed on 10 October 2003. An enforcement writ was issued on 4 June 2003.

Despite those final decisions, reinstatement was delayed. On 31 March 2006 the Constitutional Court, acting on the applicant’s constitutional complaint, acknowledged a breach of his right of access to court because the Supreme Court’s decision had not been enforced, but it made no award. Meanwhile, on 1 March 2006 the applicant took up employment with the Ministry of Tourism, Culture, Youth and Sports. On 10 March 2006 Tirana City Hall appointed him to a position in a maintenance company responsible to the City Hall. The applicant challenged that appointment, and on 15 May 2006 the CSC quashed the appointment decision. That decision became final because no party appealed.

Separate proceedings concerned payment of accrued interest. In 2004 and 2006 the applicant successfully sought interest arising from delay in payment of his salary. On 9 April 2008, following a third action, the Tirana District Court found in his favour and ordered Tirana City Hall to pay ALL 774,076 in salary arrears and ALL 105,258 in accrued interest. The court reasoned that, because the applicant had begun employment with the Ministry on 1 March 2006, Tirana City Hall was obliged to pay salary arrears only for the period from 11 January 2002 to 28 February 2006; that obligation ceased *ipso lege* as of 1 March 2006. Relying on an expert report, the court found that salary arrears for that period amounted to ALL 1,720,261, of which ALL 946,185 had already been paid. Accrued interest for the corresponding period was ALL 105,258. An enforcement writ was issued on 11 November 2009. The decision became final around 12 February 2010 after the Supreme Court dismissed the defendant’s appeal. On 31 March 2010 Tirana City Hall paid the salary arrears. The case file did not indicate whether the accrued interest was paid.

In 2010 the applicant lodged a fourth civil action seeking accrued interest for the period between 9 April 2008 and 31 March 2010, and payment of social security contributions by Tirana City Hall. On 30 June 2010 the Tirana District Court found in his favour, ordering Tirana City Hall to pay accrued interest resulting from delayed payment of salary arrears from 9 April 2008 to 31 March 2010 and social security contributions based on his indexed salary. No quantification of the amount was made. On 8 July 2011 and 23 December 2011, respectively, the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld that decision.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 July 2008; it was communicated to the Government on 11 July 2011. The facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore concern the prolonged non-enforcement and delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions awarding reinstatement, salary arrears, accrued interest, and social security contributions. The Constitutional Court had already found a breach of access to court due to non-enforcement of the Supreme Court’s decision, but awarded no compensation, and later enforcement remained protracted. The case thus raises issues under the Convention, particularly access to court, fair trial, and protection of property, based on Albania’s alleged failure to secure timely execution of final judgments in the applicant’s favour.
001-148268:
**Summary of *Taraneks v. Latvia* (Application no. 3082/06)**

The case of *Taraneks v. Latvia* concerns an application lodged by Mr Aivars Taraneks, a Latvian bailiff, who alleged that his criminal trial for corruption was unfair due to police incitement and the use of improperly obtained evidence, violating Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. He also claimed a violation of his right to respect for private life under Article 8 concerning the recording of his conversations and the search of his office.

The events began in November 2001 amid a commercial dispute between companies R.L. and M. A court ordered M.’s property, primarily fur coats, to be seized. The applicant, the senior bailiff in his office, was involved in a dispute over storage costs. He requested an advance payment of LVL 500 from R.L. for purported storage expenses. The seizure order was later quashed, but R.L. lodged an ancillary complaint, which suspended the property’s return.

On 14 December 2001, O.V., the director of R.L., complained to the police, alleging that the applicant and another bailiff were soliciting a bribe to prevent the return of the seized property. Subsequently, the police conducted undercover operations. They recorded telephone conversations between O.V., R.L.’s lawyer S.Ž., and the applicant. On 18 December 2001, a prosecutor approved an "investigative test." O.V., equipped with marked banknotes and a recording device, visited the applicant's office. During their conversation, which was secretly recorded, O.V. offered the applicant LVL 500. The applicant instructed O.V. to divide the money and left to stamp a document. After O.V. departed, the police detained the applicant. Marked banknotes were found hidden under books on his desk, and traces of a luminescent substance were detected on his hands.

The applicant was charged and convicted of demanding a bribe, receiving a five-year prison sentence. Throughout the proceedings, he argued that he had been incited by the police and that the evidence, particularly the audio recordings and the search of his office, was illegally obtained and inadmissible. He contended that the recordings made before the formal approval of the investigative test were unlawful and that the search was conducted without proper judicial authorization.

The Supreme Court of Latvia upheld his conviction, rejecting the incitement claim as speculation. It ruled that the recordings made by private individuals (O.V. and S.Ž.), even with police-supplied equipment, did not constitute a state "operational activity" requiring legal authorization. It also found the search lawful, as it was authorized by a prosecutor in an urgent case with a judge notified within the required timeframe. The applicant's subsequent complaints to prosecutors about the legality of these actions were largely dismissed, with some information classified as a state secret.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations center on the police's use of undercover tactics, including the active involvement of O.V. in offering the bribe, the timing and legal basis for recording private conversations, and the procedures followed for the office search. The applicant's core argument was that these state actions amounted to entrapment and a violation of his fair trial rights, as the courts failed to adequately scrutinize the legality of the evidence obtained through what he described as incitement.
001-145349:
**Summary of *Milinković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 21175/13)**

The case of *Milinković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 February 2013 by Mr. Dragan Milinković, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1977 and residing in Banja Luka. The application was directed against Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the applicant represented by Ms. R. Plavšić and the Government represented by its Agent, Ms. M. Mijić. The crux of the case concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a final and enforceable domestic judgment against the Republika Srpska, one of the two Entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a matter similar to the earlier case of *Momić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows. On 23 February 2009, the Banja Luka Court of First Instance issued a judgment ordering the Republika Srpska to pay the applicant, within 15 days, 34,000 convertible marks (BAM) in respect of non-pecuniary damage, along with default interest at the statutory rate. The judgment also awarded the applicant BAM 4,667 for legal costs, again with default interest. This judgment became final and enforceable on 11 May 2009. To initiate the enforcement process, the Banja Luka Court of First Instance issued a writ of execution (rješenje o izvršenju) on 29 June 2009. Despite these legal steps, the Republika Srpska failed to comply with the judgment.

Consequently, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the non-enforcement. On 16 January 2013, the Constitutional Court delivered a decision in the applicant's favour, finding a breach of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property). This finding by the highest domestic court acknowledged that the applicant's rights had been violated due to the authorities' failure to enforce a final judgment. However, the critical fact is that despite this domestic finding of a violation, the final judgment of 23 February 2009, awarding the applicant compensation and costs, remains unenforced to this day.

The relevant domestic law and practice in this case were previously outlined by the European Court in the *Momić and Others* judgment. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina objected to the examination of the application by a Committee of the Court, but after consideration, the Court rejected this objection. The application was communicated to the Government on 7 May 2013.

In summary, the central factual circumstances relevant to the alleged violations are the issuance of a final and enforceable domestic judgment in favour of the applicant against the Republika Srpska in 2009, the subsequent issuance of a writ of execution, the domestic Constitutional Court's confirmation in 2013 of a breach of the applicant's rights under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to non-enforcement, and the continued, indefinite failure of the respondent State to enforce that judgment, leaving the applicant without the awarded compensation and costs. This situation forms the basis for the applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights.
001-145068:
José Antonio Fernández Martínez, a Spanish national born in 1937 and living in Cieza, was ordained a Catholic priest in 1961. In 1984 he asked the Vatican for dispensation from celibacy; receiving no immediate answer, he married civilly in 1985 and later had five children. From October 1991 he worked as a teacher of Catholic religion and ethics at a State-run secondary school in Murcia under renewable one-year contracts. Under a 1979 Spain–Holy See Agreement and a 1982 Ministerial Order, such teachers were appointed annually by the education authority from candidates proposed by the diocesan Ordinary; appointments renewed automatically unless the Ordinary objected or the authority annulled them for serious academic or disciplinary reasons.

In November 1996, the Murcian newspaper La Verdad published an article about the Movement for Optional Celibacy of priests (MOCEOP). It named the applicant among married priests who had gathered at La Luz to advocate optional celibacy and a more democratic Church. By a rescript of 20 August 1997, the Pope granted the applicant dispensation from celibacy. He lost clerical status and was barred from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the local bishop decided otherwise for lower-level schools, provided there was no scandal. He was notified on 15 September 1997. On 29 September 1997 the Diocese of Cartagena informed the Ministry of Education that his service should end. On 9 October 1997 the Ministry informed him that his employment had terminated with effect from 29 September 1997. In a memorandum of 11 November 1997, the Diocese said his situation had become public and the bishop could no longer sign the authorisation; it also cited avoiding scandal, parents’ sensitivity, and his entitlement to unemployment benefit. The school’s board expressed support for him.

In domestic proceedings, his administrative complaint was unsuccessful, and an administrative court dismissed his appeal on 30 June 2000, finding that termination was the only course once the Diocese had not proposed him. He then brought an unfair-dismissal claim before Murcia Employment Tribunal no. 3. By judgment of 28 September 2000, the tribunal found he had been discriminated against because of his marital status and MOCEOP membership, declared the dismissal null and void, and ordered reinstatement and salary. On appeal, the Murcia High Court of Justice, by judgment of 26 February 2001, allowed the appeal. It considered the teacher-bishop relationship one based on trust, found no violation of the Spanish Constitution’s provisions on equality, freedom of thought and religion, private and family life, or freedom of expression, and held that the contract was temporary and had expired rather than being a dismissal.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal, alleging violations of Articles 14, 18 and 20 of the Spanish Constitution. He argued that non-renewal because he had publicised his MOCEOP membership and dissenting views on priestly celibacy unjustifiably interfered with his private life and religious freedom. The public prosecutor supported the amparo, noting that his public appearance predated the rescript and that his MOCEOP membership had been known. By judgment of 4 June 2007, served on 18 June 2007, the Constitutional Court dismissed the amparo. It found no discrimination on marital-status grounds; no private-life violation because he had voluntarily made his situation public; and, balancing the Catholic Church’s religious freedom and parents’ rights, it regarded the reasons as religious and the measure as not disproportionate. Two judges dissented. A later nullity request, alleging two judges’ Catholic affinities, was rejected on 23 July 2007. On 11 December 2007 the applicant lodged application no. 56030/07 with the European Court of Human Rights, relying on Article 8 alone and with Article 14, and alleging that publicity about his family and personal situation as a married priest caused the non-renewal, incompatibly with Articles 9 and 10.
001-142082:
In *Beganović v. Slovenia* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, Application no. 6625/10, judgment of 3 April 2014), the applicant was Nenad Beganović, a Slovenian national born in 1986. He alleged that the conditions of his detention in Ljubljana prison violated Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

The applicant served his prison sentence in Ljubljana prison from 1 July 2009 to 4 November 2009. He was then transferred to Celje prison until 9 December 2009, when he was transferred back to Ljubljana prison, Section Novo mesto. His complaints did not concern his detention in Celje prison.

From 1 July to 23 September 2009, he was held in the closed section of Ljubljana prison. He occupied three different cells: cell 7 measured 16.8 square metres, while cells 4 and 3 each measured 18 square metres, including a separate sanitary facility of 1.72 square metres. Each cell had furniture and five sleeping places—two bunk beds and one single bed. The applicant claimed that five prisoners occupied each cell; the Government said the number varied between four and five. Each cell had a 107 x 110 cm double casement window that prisoners could open and close. General material, sanitary and health-care conditions were referenced to the Court’s earlier judgment in *Štrucl and Others v. Slovenia*. As to out-of-cell time in the closed section, sentenced prisoners were locked in their cells and could leave only if they applied for activities, most of which took place in a recreation room. There was only one 50-square-metre recreation room per floor, intended for no more than ten inmates.

From 23 September to 4 November 2009, the applicant was held in the semi-open section, in cell 3, measuring 18 square metres including a sanitary facility. According to the Government, cell doors in that section were unlocked except from 9:45 p.m. until 6:00 a.m., and on weekends or holidays until 8:30 a.m. Prisoners could then move freely in a 35.7-square-metre corridor, in co-prisoners’ living quarters, and in indoor or outdoor exercise areas under prison rules. However, the applicant had been transferred to the semi-open section only because of overcrowding, and while there he was not granted outside visits or unsupervised leave.

From 9 December 2009 to 1 April 2010, he was held in the closed section of Section Novo mesto. Unit 5 measured 58.83 square metres and contained four separate rooms: an ante-chamber of 9.98 square metres, a sanitary facility of 1.4 square metres, a smaller room of 18.61 square metres with three beds, and a larger room of 28.84 square metres with five, occasionally six beds. The applicant was mostly held in the larger room with three other prisoners. The unit held seven prisoners in total. Inner doors were unlocked, allowing free movement within the unit 24 hours per day. From 3:30 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., prisoners could also move in the shared corridor and recreation areas. The applicant spent six hours daily outside the unit: two hours outdoors in a 300-square-metre area and four hours in a shared corridor of 108.64 square metres or shared living quarters of 59.04 square metres. He also had access to an outdoor recreation yard for two hours daily.

During imprisonment, he had three consultations with a general practitioner and one psychiatric treatment. He never requested a psychologist or dentist. Temperature data showed that in the second half of July and August 2009, the average late-afternoon cell temperature was about 28°C, exceeding 30°C on seven days. Relevant domestic law, practice and international documents were set out in *Štrucl and Others*. The Court gave notice to the Government and decided to rule on admissibility and merits together, granting the case priority.
001-146410:
The case of *Vajnai v. Hungary (No. 4)* (Application no. 6061/10) concerned an application against Hungary lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention by Mr Attila Vajnai, a Hungarian national born in 1963 and living in Budapest. The applicant was represented by Mr G. Magyar, while the Hungarian Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi. The applicant complained under Article 10 of the Convention that a police measure taken against him for wearing a red star violated his right to freedom of expression. The application was lodged on 23 January 2010 and communicated to the Government on 17 October 2013. The Government objected to the application being examined by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The key facts concerned events on 18 May 2009. On that date, the applicant, a left-wing politician, participated in a peaceful demonstration. He wore a five-pointed red star on his jacket. A police patrol present at the demonstration called on the applicant to remove the star. He did not, or at least the star was then confiscated by the police. This police measure formed the basis of his later complaint that his expression had been unlawfully restricted.

The applicant first complained to the Head of the National Police, but without success. He then challenged the police measure in court. On 29 June 2010, the Budapest Regional Court dismissed his action. The Regional Court held that the display of the red star contravened section 269/B of the Hungarian Criminal Code. Consequently, it found that the confiscation of the star was justified under sections 115(1) and 151(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The applicant sought review. On 8 June 2011, the Supreme Court upheld the Regional Court’s decision. It held that the police measure had been lawful. Importantly, the Supreme Court acknowledged the earlier judgment of the European Court of Human Rights in *Vajnai v. Hungary* (no. 33629/06, ECHR 2008), but reasoned that applying that judgment was not a task of the police officers present at the demonstration. The applicant incurred legal costs of approximately EUR 1,115.

The facts relevant to the alleged Article 10 violation were therefore that the applicant wore a five-pointed red star as part of political expression during a peaceful demonstration; that police officers intervened, demanded its removal and confiscated it; and that the domestic courts upheld that interference by relying on the Criminal Code prohibition on displaying the red star. The domestic courts also declined to give effect to the earlier Strasbourg judgment in the applicant’s favour when reviewing the police action. The applicant’s central complaint was that this measure constituted an unjustified interference with his freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.
001-147443:
The case of *Sociedade de Construções Martins & Vieira, Lda and Others v. Portugal* involves five applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights against the Portuguese Republic by a construction company and its two managing partners. The core of the case concerns the excessive length of domestic criminal proceedings for tax fraud, which were suspended for years pending the outcome of related administrative tax litigation.

The events began in September 1999 when Portuguese authorities launched an investigation into the applicant company’s fiscal activities between 1994 and 1997. This led to two separate sets of criminal proceedings.

The first set was instituted in the Porto Criminal Court in November 2003, with charges brought against the applicant company and the third applicant. After several delays, the trial began in September 2005. However, a key development occurred in November 2006 when the applicants informed the court that they had sought a judicial review of a tax adjustment in the Porto Administrative and Fiscal Court. In accordance with Article 50 § 1 of the Legal Framework for Non-Customs Tax Offences (RJIFNA), the criminal proceedings were suspended on 29 November 2006 until the administrative court issued a final, unappealable decision.

Similarly, a second set of proceedings was brought before the Barcelos Criminal Court in April 2003 against all three applicants for tax offences related to an earlier period. This case was also suspended in November 2003 under the same legal provision, pending the outcome of the same administrative judicial review. The Barcelos court repeatedly sought updates, but the fiscal proceedings remained pending. In April 2007, it formally extended its suspension.

In December 2008, the applicants attempted to expedite both sets of criminal proceedings by applying to the High Council of Magistrates. These applications were dismissed in May 2009 and January 2009, respectively. The Council reasoned that the delays were attributable to the Administrative and Fiscal Court, not the criminal courts, and advised the applicants to direct their requests to the High Council of the Administrative and Fiscal Courts.

Consequently, the criminal proceedings in both Porto and Barcelos remained suspended for years, awaiting the conclusion of the administrative tax case. The applicants also instituted separate tort proceedings against the State in 2006, claiming damages for the excessive length of the criminal proceedings, but these too were still pending as of early 2014.

The central factual issue relevant to the alleged violation is that the suspension of the criminal proceedings, mandated by domestic law, had no statutory time limit when the relevant provision was Article 50 § 1 of the RJIFNA. This contrasted with the general Code of Criminal Procedure, which imposes a one-year maximum for such suspensions. This legal feature effectively resulted in criminal proceedings being stalled for an indefinite period, dependent entirely on a separate administrative process. The applicants argued that this lengthy suspension violated their right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
001-148659:
The applicant, Petru Buzadji, a Moldovan national born in 1947 and living in Comrat, was director of State company B-G. In March 2006 he acknowledged in court that B-G owed a private company USD 594,067 plus penalties (total USD 842,404). He was dismissed on 26 May 2006. From July 2006 he was summoned over alleged defrauding of B-G and appeared whenever summoned. Thirteen criminal investigations were opened against him and his two sons, most on 5 April 2007, and joined on 25 May 2007; his sons were questioned as suspects in May 2007 but not arrested. On 26 October 2006 bankruptcy proceedings were initiated against B-G. On 21 December 2006 the Supreme Court quashed lower judgments, finding the debt fictitious; retrial remained pending.

On 2 May 2007 the applicant was arrested. On 5 May 2007 he was charged with defrauding B-G. The same day the Buiucani District Court ordered 15 days’ pre-trial detention, citing the exceptionally serious charge, complexity, and reasonable grounds to believe he could collude with his sons, not yet interviewed; other prosecution fears were unsubstantiated. The applicant appealed, relying on pending civil debt proceedings, confirmation of the debt by a court-appointed administrator, absence of material showing risk of absconding or interference, his age and health problems needing unavailable in-patient care, family, residence and job, compliance with summonses from July 2006 to May 2007, and the fact that the detention court lacked the investigation file. On 8 May 2007 the Chişinău Court of Appeal upheld the detention, repeating the lower court’s reasons.

On 16 May 2007 the district court extended detention by 20 days, finding grounds valid, most investigative actions done, further measures requiring his participation necessary, and house arrest premature given seriousness, complexity and public interest. On 22 May 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld this, adding a continuing risk of evidence destruction because not all financial documents had been seized. On 5 June 2007 detention was extended another 20 days for the same reasons; on 11 June 2007 the Court of Appeal upheld it, citing the serious offence, alleged damage of almost MDL 9 million (about EUR 553,000), possible 10–25 year sentence, thirteen charges, ongoing investigation, and risks of absconding or influencing B-G staff witnesses.

On 26 June 2007 the district court rejected further extension and placed him under house arrest for 30 days. It noted 55 days’ detention, his participation in investigative actions, weakening grounds over time, the prosecutor’s burden to prove risk, and that severity alone did not justify detention; it found it improbable he would abscond, influence witnesses, or destroy evidence. Conditions barred leaving home, phone calls and discussing the case. On 29 June 2007 the Court of Appeal quashed this and ordered 20 days’ detention, citing complexity, seriousness, possible communication with his unarrested sons, flight to Transdniestria, influencing former staff witnesses, and available prison medical care.

On 16 July 2007 the district court extended detention 20 days, referring to the prosecutor’s position that the investigation was finalised and the file ready to be presented. On 20 July 2007 the Court of Appeal quashed that and changed the measure to house arrest, finding no evidence of continued need, no additional materials on witness influence, his promise to appear, and no specific risk of absconding. House arrest was maintained on 14 September and 14 December 2007. On 12 March 2008 he was released on bail after over ten months of detention/house arrest without breaching restrictions.

The applicant alleged unlawful arrest and that the courts had not given relevant and sufficient reasons for his detention pending trial.
001-144672:
**CASE OF L.M. v. SLOVENIA** (Application no. 32863/05), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 12 June 2014.

The applicant, L.M., a Slovenian woman born in 1971 with a long history of psychotic disorder, complained under Article 5 and Article 8 of the Convention about two consecutive psychiatric confinements between July 2005 and January 2006.

**First confinement – Idrija Psychiatric Hospital.** On 10 July 2005 the police informed L.M.’s family physician that she had broken into an unoccupied house, was difficult to communicate with, and was behaving psychotically. She was referred to the Idrija Psychiatric Hospital and admitted the same day to its closed ward. She signed a consent form for confinement and treatment, but told staff she was “possessed by energetic and physical people” sent through cameras operated by President Bush. She was diagnosed with schizophrenia and given antipsychotic and sedative medication. On 11 July she asked how long she would have to stay and said she would resist. The hospital notified the local court. The court appointed a lawyer and held a hearing on 15 July, at which L.M. said she would rather be at home and did not understand why she had been hospitalised. Medical records suggested she continued to agree to therapy, but on 30 July she gave power of attorney to a lawyer, D.P., saying she was receiving treatment against her will but feared refusing it because medication might be forced on her. On 2 August D.P. informed the hospital that L.M. did not consent to treatment and asked for information about side effects; on 6 August D.P. asked the hospital to stop forcibly administering medication. On 8 August L.M. was transferred to the open ward, and the court terminated the confinement proceedings. She was discharged on 12 August at her own request.

**Second confinement – Ljubljana Psychiatric Hospital.** On 15 August 2005 police took L.M. to emergency services, where she said she was being “raped by the police, the emergency medical technicians, everybody.” She was referred to the Ljubljana Psychiatric Hospital. Her admission record noted dissociated speech, paranoia and megalomaniac delusions; the psychiatrist indicated that she accepted hospitalisation owing to the staff’s presence and that no compulsory measures were necessary. On 17 August she was placed in the closed ward. She received Haldol, Akineton, Lorsilan, later Moditen and Leponex. On 21 August she notified the local court of her confinement and sought an interlocutory order to stop treatment and release her, and lodged a constitutional complaint. On 23 August the court appointed a lawyer, held a brief hearing, and, based on an expert opinion, ordered her confinement in the closed ward until 23 September. Her interlocutory request was dismissed on 24 August. On 3 or 4 September she was transferred to the open ward. The Higher Court allowed her appeals on 9 September and 10 November, finding the lower court’s reasoning inadequate and holding that interlocutory relief was legally possible and that her request to stop medication required separate consideration. Nevertheless, on 12 December the local court terminated the confinement proceedings because she was in the open ward. On 5 January 2006 the Higher Court dismissed her appeal, holding that non-contentious confinement rules no longer applied and referring her to civil injunctive relief. She was released on 19 January 2006 with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia.

**Relevant legal context.** Domestic law permitted involuntary admission where mental illness posed danger or grave harm, with notification to a court within 48 hours. Only closed-ward confinement was subject to judicial review; transfer to an open ward could end proceedings. The Constitutional Court had already found the confinement procedure unconstitutional, requiring counsel, reasoned notification, shorter time-limits, effective judicial review, and regulation of treatment. Ombudsman reports noted that involuntary patients in open wards were not supervised and forced treatment was unregulated.

L.M. alleged under Article 5 that her closed-ward confinements were unnecessary and unlawful, that her open-ward stays were not voluntary, that she was not informed of the reasons, and that she had no effective legal protection or compensation. Under Article 8 she alleged that forced medication and therapeutic procedures interfered with her physical and mental integrity, and that no remedy existed to challenge that forced treatment.
001-145466:
In **S.A.S. v. France** (Application no. 43835/11, Grand Chamber, 1 July 2014), the applicant was an anonymous French national born in 1990. She described herself as a devout Muslim who wore the burqa and niqab in accordance with her religious faith, culture and personal convictions. She emphasised that neither her husband nor any family member pressured her to dress this way. She wore the niqab in public and private but not systematically; she wished to be able to wear it when she chose, particularly during periods of spiritual significance such as Ramadan. She accepted showing her face for necessary identity or security checks, including at banks and airports. Her complaint arose from Law no. 2010-1192 of 11 October 2010, which entered into force throughout France on 11 April 2011.

The Law prohibited anyone from concealing their face in public places. Section 1 provided that “no one may, in public places, wear clothing that is designed to conceal the face.” Section 2 defined “public places” broadly to include the public highway, places open to the public, and places assigned to a public service. It contained limited exceptions for clothing prescribed or authorised by law, justified for health or occupational reasons, or worn in the context of sports, festivities or artistic or traditional events. Section 3 made breach punishable by a fine of up to 150 euros and/or an obligation to follow a citizenship course. Section 4 separately criminalised forcing another person to conceal their face. The Constitutional Council upheld the Law but reserved that the ban could not restrict religious freedom in places of worship open to the public.

The applicant alleged that the ban deprived her of the possibility of wearing the full-face veil in public, even when she chose to do so for religious, cultural and personal reasons. She complained of violations of Articles 3, 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, taken separately and in conjunction with Article 14. The central alleged interference was with her private life and freedom to manifest her religion, and she argued that the blanket public ban was discriminatory and disproportionate.

The legislative background was significant to the alleged violation. A parliamentary commission report found that the full-face veil was a recent and marginal phenomenon in France, affecting around 1,900 women, and concluded that it was not a religious precept but a radical identity affirmation contrary to Republican values of liberty, equality, fraternity, gender equality and human dignity. The National Advisory Commission on Human Rights opposed a general and absolute ban, warning of stigmatisation and exclusion. The Conseil d’État doubted the legal viability of banning the full-face veil alone and suggested narrower measures based on public order or identity checks. The National Assembly adopted a resolution condemning radical practices, and the Bill’s explanatory memorandum stated that concealment of the face was incompatible with “living together,” minimum civility, dignity and public safety.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: the applicant’s voluntary religious dress practice; the general and absolute nature of the ban in all public places, with only limited exceptions; its criminal sanction and citizenship course; France’s justifications based on public order, dignity, gender equality and social cohesion; and the applicant’s willingness to uncover her face for identity checks, which weakened the public-safety rationale as applied to her. The case ultimately required the Court to assess whether France’s blanket public prohibition was justified as necessary in a democratic society.
001-142398:
**Summary of the Case of Radu v. the Republic of Moldova**

The case of *Radu v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 50073/07) concerns an alleged violation of the right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Ms. Liliana Radu, a Moldovan national born in 1969, was a lecturer at the Police Academy in Chişinău.

At the time of the events, the relationship between the applicant and her superiors at the Police Academy was tense, with prior employment-related civil proceedings between them. In 2003, the applicant underwent artificial insemination and became pregnant with twins. On 3 August 2003, due to an increased risk of miscarriage, she was hospitalized and subsequently placed under close medical supervision. Her absence from work was certified by a sick note citing pregnancy and risk of miscarriage as reasons.

On 5 November 2003, the President of the Police Academy requested detailed information from the No. 7 Centre for Family Doctors (CFD), a state-owned hospital, regarding the applicant’s medical leave. Specifically, he asked who had ordered her hospitalization, the dates, the initial and final diagnoses, and the treatment received. In a letter dated 7 November 2003, the CFD disclosed extensive confidential medical information to the applicant’s employer without her consent. The letter revealed that the applicant had been hospitalized due to an increased risk of miscarriage, that it was her first pregnancy, that she was carrying twins, that the pregnancy resulted from artificial insemination, and that she had hepatitis B and a negative blood type. A detailed copy of her medical file was also annexed.

Following this disclosure, the applicant suffered a miscarriage. According to a medical report, stress was a contributing factor. The applicant alleged that the information was not kept confidential and was disseminated throughout the Police Academy, causing her severe stress and anxiety. Her husband, also an employee there, was forced to resign.

In January 2004, the applicant initiated civil proceedings against the CFD and the Police Academy, claiming compensation for the breach of her private life. She argued that her employer had sufficient information about her medical leave and was not entitled to seek further private details, and that the disclosed information was not kept confidential.

On 6 July 2004, the Centru District Court dismissed her action, finding the disclosure lawful due to the employer’s ongoing investigation. The applicant appealed. On 2 November 2006, the Chişinău Court of Appeal quashed the judgment, found her action well-founded, and ordered the CFD and the Police Academy to pay her compensation. The court held that the CFD had disclosed more information than requested. However, on 10 May 2007, the Supreme Court of Justice upheld an appeal by the CFD, dismissing the claims against it. The Supreme Court ruled that the CFD had acted lawfully in providing the medical information, as it was obliged to do so in the context of the employment relationship between the Police Academy and the applicant, and considered the laws on patient rights and reproductive health not pertinent to the case.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the State had failed to fulfil its obligation to secure respect for her private life, as a state-owned hospital disclosed her medical condition without her consent.
001-141644:
**Avotiņš v. Latvia** (Application no. 17502/07) concerned a Latvian applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that Latvia violated his right to a fair hearing by recognising and enforcing a Cypriot default judgment obtained against him without proper service and without allowing him to exercise his defence rights.

In 1999, the applicant signed a deed of acknowledgement of debt with F.H. Ltd., a Cypriot company, declaring that he owed USD 100,000, with interest, to be repaid by 30 June 1999. The deed was governed by Cypriot law and gave Cypriot courts non-exclusive jurisdiction. In 2003, F.H. Ltd. sued the applicant in the Limassol District Court in Cyprus. Because the applicant did not reside in Cyprus, the company applied ex parte for permission to serve him abroad. Its lawyer stated by affidavit that the applicant habitually resided at an address in G. Street, Riga. The Cypriot court ordered service at that address, requiring the applicant to appear within thirty days.

The summons was allegedly sent by recorded delivery on 16 November 2003 to G. Street, and a postal slip indicated receipt on 18 November 2003—a Latvian national holiday and non-working day. The applicant denied receiving it. He claimed G. Street was merely the address where he had signed the loan documents in 1999, not his home or business premises. He did not appear, and on 24 May 2004 the Limassol District Court entered a default judgment ordering him to pay USD 100,000 plus 10% annual interest and costs. The judgment was finalised on 3 June 2004 but did not state whether it was final or what remedies were available.

In February 2005, F.H. Ltd. sought recognition and enforcement in Latvia. Its request gave the applicant’s address as Č. Street, Riga, different from G. Street. The Latvian District Court noticed this discrepancy. The company later explained that Č. Street was the applicant’s officially declared residence, while G. Street had been assumed to be his actual residence. On 27 February 2006, the Riga City Latgale District Court, sitting without the parties, allowed the request in full, recognised the Cypriot judgment, and entered a charge on the applicant’s property in Garkalne.

The applicant only learned of the Cypriot judgment and the Latvian enforcement order on 16 June 2006. He appealed the enforcement order. The Latgale District Court extended the time-limit, finding that he had not received the 27 February 2006 order and no longer lived at his declared address. On 2 October 2006, the Riga Regional Court allowed his appeal and refused recognition, relying on Article 34(2) of the Brussels I Regulation and Latvian law: a default judgment could not be recognised if the defendant was not served in sufficient time to arrange his defence. The Regional Court also found defects concerning proof that the Cypriot judgment was enforceable.

F.H. Ltd. appealed to the Senate of the Supreme Court. At the hearing on 31 January 2007, it submitted a certificate dated 18 January 2007 stating that the applicant had been served on 27 November 2003; the section identifying the person against whom the judgment was enforceable was left blank. The Senate quashed the Regional Court’s judgment and allowed enforcement. It reasoned that the applicant had not appealed against the Cypriot judgment, so his complaints about notification were irrelevant, and that the foreign judgment could not be reviewed on the merits under Article 36 of the Regulation. A writ of execution followed on 14 February 2007, and the applicant paid approximately LVL 90,244.62 (around EUR 129,000).

The applicant alleged that Latvia breached Article 6 § 1 by enforcing the Cypriot default judgment without ensuring that he had been properly served and able to defend himself. The application initially also concerned Cyprus, but that part was declared inadmissible for failure to comply with the six-month time-limit. The key issue was whether the Latvian courts properly examined the service and defence-rights concerns before recognising and enforcing the foreign default judgment.
001-139897:
In *Lakatoš and Others v. Serbia* (App. no. 3363/08, judgment of 7 January 2014), five Serbian nationals complained of violations of Articles 3, 5, 6 § 2 and 8 of the Convention in the context of criminal proceedings.

The case arose from an investigation into numerous robberies committed in northern Serbia during 2006–2007, mainly targeting elderly people, some of whom suffered grievous bodily harm. On 5 November 2007, after a robbery in Kucura, police stopped a suspicious vehicle and arrested one person, PN; the first, second and third applicants allegedly escaped. The next morning, the fourth and fifth applicants allegedly went to give them a lift back to Subotica. Police stopped the vehicle before the town and arrested all five applicants, taking them to Novi Sad Police Station.

On 6 November 2007, the investigating judge ordered DNA samples to be taken. The fifth applicant was later released. On 7 November, police reports stated that the applicants had resisted arrest or tried to escape, so force had been used. Injuries were noted: the first and third applicants had excoriations on their foreheads; the second had redness around his forehead and right eye; the fourth had an excoriation on the left side of his head. The first and third were not given medical assistance because they did not ask for it.

On 8 November 2007, the first to fourth applicants were brought before the investigating judge and complained, in the presence of the public prosecutor, of being beaten by police during arrest and at the police station. The judge recorded injuries to the second and fourth applicants, including neck excoriations and bruises to the shoulder and face. Their lawyer photographed the injuries. The fourth applicant was released; the first, second and third were remanded in custody on suspicion of numerous robberies, based on the severity of the potential sentence and the nature of the alleged crimes. On the same day, police held a press conference. Senior officers allegedly described the applicants as members of a criminal group responsible for the robberies, released their photographs to the press, and said local residents had begun forming “village guard units.” These facts are relevant to the Article 6 § 2 presumption-of-innocence and Article 8 complaints.

On 13 November 2007, court-ordered medical examinations found multiple bruises and haematomas on the first, second and third applicants, including on their heads, ears, necks, arms, legs, shoulders, backs and feet. The fourth applicant did not attend, but earlier photographs showed bruises and excoriations on his shoulder, back and abdomen. The fifth applicant later stated she had been slapped by police on arrest. A later expert report concluded that the injuries had been caused by repeated mechanical force, ruled out a fall, and estimated they were inflicted roughly three, seven and three days before the examination. However, it also noted no clear temporal stages and some discrepancies with the photographs.

On 29 February 2008, the public prosecutor indicted the first, second and third applicants, plus PN, for numerous robberies and attempted robberies; the second was also charged with causing grievous bodily harm to a police officer with intent to resist arrest. The fourth and fifth applicants were not prosecuted. In 2009, the first, second and third applicants were convicted and sentenced to long prison terms. In 2011, the Appeals Court quashed the convictions and ordered a retrial, but they were again convicted in November 2011 and the judgment was upheld in June 2012. A constitutional appeal remained pending, and they were released in December 2012 under an amnesty.

Their pre-trial detention was repeatedly extended from December 2007 to June 2009 on the same grounds: the severity of the potential sentence and the nature of the alleged crimes. The Constitutional Court rejected challenges, finding the detention grounds compatible with the equivalent constitutional right. Additionally, the fourth and fifth applicants’ DNA samples remained stored, with no specific legislation governing their destruction absent a court decision. This formed part of the Article 8 complaint.

001-142403:
In **Grespik v. Hungary** (Application no. 47018/10), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application lodged by Mr László Grespik, a Hungarian national born in 1964 and living in Budapest. The underlying facts concerned his removal from a senior public office and the ensuing protracted domestic litigation.

In February 2002, the applicant was head of the Budapest Public Administration Authority. On 22 February 2002 he was dismissed from the civil service as a disciplinary measure. In the resulting labour dispute, the parties reached a friendly settlement on 22 March 2002: the applicant was reinstated and received damages. However, on the same day, the Prime Minister revoked his mandate to preside over the Authority. Consequently, the applicant left the Authority. This dispute gave rise to four sets of proceedings.

On 2 May 2002 the applicant brought a labour action claiming that the revocation of his mandate had been unlawful. In parallel, the Authority brought a civil action against him seeking invalidity of the friendly settlement and reimbursement of the compensation he had received. The applicant also brought labour proceedings claiming that the disciplinary measure of 22 February 2002 was unlawful, together with a claim for salary arrears.

The domestic proceedings were lengthy and fragmented. The friendly settlement was annulled by a final judgment of the Baranya County Regional Court, acting as a second-instance court, on 3 November 2005. On 2 February 2010, the same court adopted a final judgment establishing that the revocation of the applicant’s mandate on 22 March 2002 had been unlawful. In the labour action concerning the disciplinary sanction, the Zalaegerszeg Labour Court found for the applicant in an interim judgment on 3 April 2007 and established the unlawfulness of the sanction. By contrast, the applicant’s claim for salary arrears and the Authority’s action for repayment of compensation remained pending before the Kúria and the Budapest Surroundings High Court, respectively.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 August 2010. The application was communicated to the Hungarian Government on 5 April 2013. The Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi, Agent, Ministry of Public Administration and Justice. The case was considered by the Second Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Helen Keller, András Sajó and Egidijus Kūris, with Stanley Naismith as Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 25 March 2014 and delivered judgment on 22 April 2014.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were the multiple, interconnected civil and labour proceedings arising from the applicant’s 2002 dismissal and the revocation of his mandate. The litigation began in 2002; some branches were resolved only in 2005, 2007 and 2010, while others were still pending before domestic courts by the time the Strasbourg proceedings were under way. This prolonged duration, the parallel nature of the proceedings, and the repeated delays formed the factual core of the applicant’s complaint that the domestic proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time and failed to satisfy fair-trial guarantees, principally under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
001-147037:
Zalevskiy v. Ukraine (no. 3466/09) concerns a Ukrainian national’s complaint that police ill-treated him during his arrest and that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant lived in Vinnytsya in a flat provided in 1995. He married S. in 1995, and they had a son in 1997. They divorced in 2001 but continued living in the same flat, where conflicts repeatedly occurred. In December 2005 a court fined the applicant for domestic violence against S. and his son.

On the night of 14 February 2006, after S. or a neighbour called the police, three officers arrived at about 11 p.m. The call reported that the applicant was shouting and threatening S., allegedly with a knife. The applicant refused to open the door, saying the police had not identified themselves, it was late, and the corridor light was off. At about 2 a.m. on 15 February, S.’s two brothers arrived and asked him to open. Seeing only the brothers through the peephole, he opened the door. According to the applicant, the brothers and three police officers then burst in and beat him; he did not resist. Police twisted his arms while handcuffing him and broke his right arm. He was allegedly further ill-treated on the way to and at the police station. The Government’s account differed: when the applicant opened the door and saw police, he tried to close it; the officers and brothers pushed in; he fell onto a chair and floor. Because he resisted arrest, officers used force to handcuff him, unintentionally breaking his arm.

At the police station, the applicant complained of pain. An ambulance took him to hospital. He was diagnosed with a displaced fracture of the right humerus, radial nerve neuritis, crushed soft tissue, and bruises on both wrists and jaw. He had surgery on 16 February and remained in hospital until 1 March 2006.

On 21 February 2006 the applicant complained to the prosecutor about ill-treatment by police and S.’s brothers. Domestic authorities repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings, on 14 March, 6 May, 26 September 2006 and 12 February 2007. Higher prosecutors and courts quashed several refusals as incomplete, ordering further inquiry into the medical evidence, the roles of police and S.’s brothers, the applicant’s personality, and the family situation. A key expert report of 18 August 2006 concluded that the arm fracture resulted from a rotary force—the arm being turned about its axis—consistent with the applicant’s account that his arms were twisted behind his back; it could not have been caused by a direct fall. Another expert accepted that wrist bruises could have come from handcuffs, while some other bruises might have resulted from a fall.

The final refusal of 12 February 2007 accepted the authorities’ version: police and the brothers acted lawfully to arrest the applicant and stop dangerous conduct; force was necessary; the fracture occurred while he resisted arm-twisting, wrist bruises came from handcuffs, and other bruises from the fall. This decision was upheld by courts in March 2007 and on appeal to the Vinnytsya Region Court of Appeal and Supreme Court in 2007–2008. The applicant alleged that these facts disclosed ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation.
001-144367:
In *Margaretić v. Croatia* (Application no. 16115/13, judgment of 5 June 2014), the applicant, Bruno Margaretić, was a Croatian police officer in the Osijek-Baranja Police Department. On 23 March 2012 he was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy and abuse of power and authority. The next day, an investigating judge of the Zagreb County Court ordered his pre-trial detention for two months under Article 123 § 1(2) and (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing risk of collusion and reoffending, or alternatively bail of HRK 700,000. The judge found that further evidence was needed, that the second suspect was still at large, and that the applicant might suborn witnesses or reoffend given his police employment. The State Attorney’s Office appealed the bail decision; on 4 April 2012 a three-judge panel reversed it, holding detention necessary to prevent collusion and reoffending. On 6 April 2012 the applicant’s appeal was dismissed, with the panel relying on the risk that he might coordinate his defence with the second suspect, interfere with evidence, and suborn nine police witnesses.

The applicant’s detention was extended repeatedly. On 23 April 2012 the investigating judge extended it for two months on the ground of risk of collusion only, dropping the reoffending risk because the applicant had been suspended from duty. Further extensions followed, largely justified by the need to question the nine witnesses. The applicant repeatedly argued that the witnesses could have been questioned earlier and that his detention was no longer justified. On 9 October 2012 the investigating judge ordered the State Attorney’s Office to question the nine witnesses within fourteen days, noting that the applicant had been detained for over six months and that the prosecution had repeatedly relied on the need to question those very witnesses. The State Attorney’s Office questioned eight witnesses on 20 October 2012 and the last on 24 October 2012. On the same day, it sought an extension on a new ground: the risk that the applicant might coordinate his defence with the second suspect, who was still at large. Detention was extended on that basis despite the applicant’s objections and requests for less restrictive measures. He was finally released on 21 May 2013, after almost fifteen months, subject to a ban on contacting the second accused and seizure of his travel documents. The criminal proceedings remained pending.

In parallel, on 24 March 2012 the applicant was suspended from duty pending the criminal proceedings. His appeal to the Ministry of the Interior was dismissed on 17 April 2012. He brought an administrative action, but on 18 September 2012 the Osijek Administrative Court held a hearing in the absence of the applicant and his representative, refused an adjournment request, and dismissed his action as ill-founded, considering the adjournment request a delaying tactic.

The case thus concerned alleged violations of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention (length of pre-trial detention and whether the grounds remained relevant and sufficient), Article 5 § 4 (judicial review of detention), and Article 6 § 1 (fairness of the administrative proceedings concerning his suspension). The key facts were the repeated extensions based on risk of collusion, the delay in questioning witnesses, the belated shift to the second-suspect ground, the failure to consider alternative measures, and the administrative court’s refusal to adjourn the hearing.
001-146047:
Husayn (Abu Zubaydah), a stateless Palestinian born in 1971 and detained at the US Guantánamo Bay facility, lodged application no. 7511/13 against Poland on 28 January 2013. He alleged that Poland had enabled the CIA to detain him secretly on Polish territory, allowing torture, incommunicado detention, mental and physical abuse, and deprivation of contact with family or the outside world. He further alleged that Poland enabled his transfer from its territory, exposing him to further torture, ill-treatment, secret and arbitrary detention, and denial of justice by the US authorities. He also complained that Poland failed to conduct an effective investigation into these allegations. A related case, Al Nashiri v. Poland, was examined simultaneously.

After 11 September 2001 the US Government began a special interrogation and detention programme. On 17 September 2001 President Bush signed a classified Presidential Finding granting the CIA extended covert-action powers, including authority to detain terrorist suspects and establish secret detention facilities outside the United States in cooperation with host governments. The CIA later established the High-Value Detainees Programme. Abu Zubaydah was the first High-Value Detainee in CIA custody. According to the 2004 CIA Inspector General report, he was captured in Faisalabad, Pakistan, in late March 2002 and transported to a secret CIA “black site,” where he was treated for gunshot wounds.

In August 2002 the US Department of Justice provided an opinion that ten specific Enhanced Interrogation Techniques would not violate the prohibition of torture. These included attention grasp, walling, facial hold, insult slap, cramped confinement, use of harmless insects, wall standing, stress positions, sleep deprivation not exceeding 11 days, and waterboarding. CIA psychologists later proposed twelve such techniques for Abu Zubaydah. From November 2002 the techniques were applied to other suspects in CIA custody, including Al Nashiri. A 2004 CIA background paper described routine capture, rendition, and reception: the detainee was flown to a black site, shackled and deprived of sight and sound, with no interaction except medical assessments; on arrival he was medically assessed and placed under complete American control through “precise, quiet, and almost clinical” procedures.

An investigation had been opened in Poland on 11 March 2008. In the related case, the Chamber sought materials showing the grounds for injured-person status in that investigation and whether detention in Poland had been established. In the present case, the Polish Government stated that a criminal investigation was pending and that they could not address the Court’s questions in detail or produce requested documentary evidence. They offered classified or ex parte access to a document prepared by the Appellate Prosecutor’s Office in Kraków and to case files Ap. V Ds. 12/12/S. The Court requested a comprehensive extract from the non-confidential part of those files by 30 October 2013. The Government did not submit it by that deadline. At the 2 December 2013 fact-finding hearing, they brought a classified document but proposed that it be reviewed in situ only by judges, interpreters, and Polish representatives. After the Chamber directed production of a redacted version, the Government did not produce it.

The Court held a fact-finding and in camera hearing on 2 December 2013 and a public hearing on 3 December 2013. It heard evidence from Giovanni Claudio Fava, Senator Dick Marty, J.G.S., and Senator Józef Pinior. Senator Marty and J.G.S. presented flight-data material concerning Poland and the cases of Al Nashiri and Abu Zubaydah. Documentary evidence came mainly from the applicant, partly supplemented by the Government, and from public-domain material.
001-145580:
The case of *Osakovskiy v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged by Mr Sergey Valeryevich Osakovskiy, a Ukrainian national, against Ukraine. He alleged ill-treatment in custody, unreasonable detention, a lack of access to a procedure to challenge his detention's lawfulness, and excessively lengthy criminal proceedings.

The case involves two sets of criminal proceedings.

**First Set of Proceedings:** In August 2003, a cashier, F., was found fatally injured at his workplace. On 8 June 2004, the applicant was arrested and confessed to the crime. He later claimed this confession was false and extracted through ill-treatment, specifically alleging police applied electric current, suffocated him with a gas mask, and used other torture techniques.

After his arrest, the applicant was assigned a legal-aid lawyer. He participated in a crime scene reconstruction and was indicted on 10 June 2004, when a court remanded him in custody. On 11 June 2004, a pre-trial detention facility (SIZO) medical examination found no bodily injuries on him.

In July 2004, a private lawyer replaced his legal-aid counsel. On 31 July 2004, the applicant, represented by his new lawyer, retracted his confessions, stating they were given under duress, and pleaded innocent.
