According to the guard, the search was conducted privately: detainees entered the stairwell one by one, one guard searched jackets while the other searched detainees, and if a detainee was suspected, the door was closed to create a private space. Only the detainee and two guards were present. The applicant then complained to the Tartu Administrative Court, repeating his allegations and submitting written statements from two of the named detainees. By judgment of 21 September 2011, the Administrative Court rejected the claim, finding the guard’s account reliable and the applicant’s privacy respected.

On appeal, the applicant submitted that the stairwell door windows measured 1 metre by 30 centimetres and that some days after his complaint they had been covered with metal sheets. By judgment of 16 March 2012, the Tartu Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It found the search lasted at most a few minutes, that the applicant had not been certain whether other detainees were present, and that he could not explain exactly where the named detainees had seen the search. It concluded that his privacy had not been violated. It further held that, to manage a large number of detainees, the prison had to be able to carry out a body search when necessary in a location other than a designated private room. A suspicion that a detainee re-entering after a walk had hidden prohibited cigarettes in his underwear was sufficient.

By judgment of 17 October 2012, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, upholding the findings that his privacy and dignity had not been infringed. One judge dissented, reasoning that it was not decisive whether third persons had actually seen the search. A person being searched cannot simultaneously establish what others saw. If a body search occurs where it is not guaranteed that third persons will not see the person’s nudity, the person is bound to feel that his privacy has not been respected and that others might have seen the procedure. Such a situation damages dignity and can cause insecurity, anguish, and degradation.

Relevant domestic law included the Constitution’s protection of private life; the Imprisonment Act, allowing searches for prohibited items by same-sex officers; and ministerial regulations requiring full searches to be conducted where privacy is secured. Prison rules banned keeping tobacco except in designated smoking areas, with cigarettes distributed at the beginning of walks and unused cigarettes deposited afterwards. The Government also noted that the applicant had prior reprimands, including for unauthorised possession of a cigarette, and later received numerous disciplinary punishments mainly involving cigarettes.
001-141910:
In *Beraru v. Romania* (Application no. 40107/04), the applicant, an Israeli national, complained that his Romanian criminal trial for bribery was unfair. He alleged that the domestic courts failed to conduct adversarial proceedings, infringed the rules for taking evidence, did not disclose all evidence, and denied his lawyers proper access to the case file to prepare his defence.

In 2001, Romanian prosecutors began investigating the applicant in connection with the acquisition of CICO, a Romanian company sold at a state auction. He was accused of serious financial crimes, and an international arrest warrant was issued in May 2001. The bribery case arose after prosecutor H.G. reported that she had been offered USD 1.5 million to revoke the warrant. A sting operation was authorised. On 14 June 2002, police officers B.R. and U.I. were caught handing USD 99,700 to H.G.’s husband, H.D. The applicant, S.H., and three police officers were indicted. The prosecution alleged that the applicant had asked S.H. to resolve his legal problems, that S.H. contacted police intermediaries, and that negotiations in Bucharest and Tel Aviv led to an agreement to pay USD 1.5 million, with part of the money sent via Antwerp.

The applicant denied the prosecution’s account. He claimed his relationship with S.H. was hostile because of earlier criminal complaints and eviction proceedings. According to him, S.H. offered to fix his Romanian case for money and other benefits, but he refused. He said he never offered money to H.G.; instead, police officers asked him in Tel Aviv for USD 1.5 million to annul the warrant. He refused and asked his lawyer, A.M., to inform the Romanian authorities. He also claimed the confiscated money was not his and may have come from S.H.’s flat.

At trial, the defence’s access to the file was seriously restricted. Before the Bucharest Military Tribunal, the applicant’s lawyers were initially refused photocopying, then allowed only thirty pages of a roughly four-hundred-page file, with limited hours and only days before hearings. Later, before the Bucharest Court of Appeal, they again faced difficulties and were denied copies of certain documents, including transcripts of intercepted calls. The applicant was tried in absentia but was represented by lawyers of his choice.

The recordings and transcripts were central to the case. A court interpreter noted discrepancies between the Hebrew recordings and the Romanian transcripts and recommended a technical expert report. The court ordered an INEC report, paid for by the applicant, and allowed his expert to participate. Delays followed. The panel composition changed mid-trial from one judge to two; most evidence had already been heard by the single judge and was not reheard. The court later revoked the expert-report order, citing impossibility. INEC eventually reported that the tapes were not original and could be copies, mixes, or fabricated; voice identification required originals and equipment not provided. The court dismissed defence requests for additional evidence about the money’s origin and a deposition from A.M. Defence lawyers sought to withdraw in January 2004, saying they could not properly defend him because of the file-access and evidence problems.

On 26 January 2004, the Court of Appeal convicted the applicant of bribery and sentenced him to seven years, relying heavily on the phone transcripts. On appeal, he also alleged he had not been duly summoned, that the panel composition changed, that the judgment was not publicly pronounced, and that evidence rules were breached. The High Court of Cassation and Justice dismissed his appeal on 14 May 2004, confirming the conviction without ruling on the lawfulness or admissibility of the tapes and transcripts.
001-142305:
In *Luli and Others v. Albania* (ECtHR, 1 April 2014), six applications by Albanian nationals alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (length of proceedings) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property), mainly due to prolonged property restitution and compensation proceedings. The applicants had claims to land confiscated or expropriated under the communist regime.

*Luli and Others* (nos. 31355/09, 64480/09, 64482/09) concerned inherited Durrës property. In 1996 the Durrës Commission issued two conflicting decisions bearing the same number: one recognized rights to 174,000 sq m (restoring 4,200 sq m, first refusal 5,800, compensation for 158,200), while the other recognized only 17,400 sq m (restoring 4,200, first refusal 5,800, no further award). In 2005 the Durrës District Court recognized rights to 400,000 sq m, divided into Plot A (260,000) and Plot B (140,000). For Plot B, the Regional Agency in 2007 restored 53,200 sq m, ordered compensation for 22,960, and left 63,840 undecided. The Central Agency quashed and remitted. In 2008 the Regional Agency recognized only 76,160 sq m, leaving 63,840 undecided. In 2011 the Central Agency quashed that decision; the case was pending before the Tirana District Court. It also declined jurisdiction over the 63,840 sq m because a third party’s rights had been recognized in 2003. For Plot A, 2007 and 2008 decisions were repeatedly quashed and remitted; in 2008 the Central Agency director quashed the decision ex officio. After regional agencies were abolished in 2009, the Central Agency took over but made no final decision. The delays lasted many years.

*Pistulli* (no. 12874/10): in 1995 the Lezhë Commission recognized the applicant’s father’s rights to 25,850 sq m, restored 11,500 sq m, ordered compensation for 5,000 sq m, and gave first refusal for the remainder. In 2000 the applicant registered 5,830 sq m, but the Shëngjin Port Authority occupied it. Her 2006 action to vacate succeeded in 2007, but the Court of Appeal quashed and remitted for procedural irregularities. Her 2007 Supreme Court appeal remained pending until 2010. On rehearing in 2011, the District Court discontinued the case due to her non-appearance.

*Dushallari* (no. 56935/10): in 2007 the Gjirokastra Regional Agency recognized inherited rights. The State Advocate appealed in 2008. In 2011 the Central Agency stayed proceedings pending a Constitutional Court decision on the Property Act; in 2012 it declared itself without jurisdiction. The case remained pending before the Tirana District Court after a March 2012 State Advocate appeal.

*Kekenezi* (no. 3129/12): the applicant bought land and a house in 1992; the property had been confiscated from D. in 1948 and allocated in 1993 to D.’s heir under rehabilitation legislation. After H. sued, the Court of Cassation in 1998 ordered vacation and nullified the applicant’s sale contract. In 2006 the applicant sought annulment of related acts, but in 2007 the Court of Appeal found he lacked locus standi; the Supreme Court upheld in 2011, and the Constitutional Court rejected his appeal in July 2011.

These facts—repeated remittals, jurisdictional conflicts, suspensions, and unresolved property claims—formed the basis of the alleged excessive-length and property-rights violations.
001-146399:
In the case of *Karin Andersson and Others v. Sweden*, eighteen Swedish nationals lodged an application against Sweden on 4 June 2009. The applicants owned property near Umeå, in the vicinity of a Natura 2000 area, and most lived there permanently or part-time. They alleged that they were denied effective access to court regarding decisions on a railway construction project, violating their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The case concerned the planning and construction of a 10 km section of the Botniabanan railway. The National Rail Administration (NRA) applied to the Government in 1999 for permission to construct the railway within a specified “corridor,” recommending an “alternative east” route. The proposed construction affected Natura 2000 areas. Six applicants owned property within this corridor; the other twelve owned property outside it, with distances ranging from 300 to 2500 metres for houses, though some land was closer.

On 12 June 2003, the Government granted the NRA’s application, allowing construction within the corridor under conditions, including adopting a railway plan and environmental compensation measures. The Government stated that the activity could be permitted despite harm to Natura 2000 areas if no alternative solutions existed and the railway was for public interest.

Several property owners, including three applicants, petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court for judicial review of the Government’s decision, arguing it contradicted Swedish and EU law. On 1 December 2004, the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions because it could not determine who was an interested party at that stage; the exact route would not be established until the railway plan was drawn up. The court stated that affected parties could later obtain judicial review of the railway plan decision.

Subsequent proceedings involved permits for construction in Natura 2000 areas and bridges. The Environmental Court, considering itself bound by the Government’s permissibility decision, granted permits. The Environmental Court of Appeal quashed and remanded this in 2006, finding the Government’s decision lacked detailed examination of environmental compensation. In 2007, the Environmental Court again granted permits, limited to examining compensation measures. The Environmental Court of Appeal affirmed this in December 2007, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in May 2008.

In 2005, the NRA adopted a railway plan. Twelve applicants appealed to the Government, complaining about the specific stretch, nuisance like noise, and vibrations. The Government rejected the appeals in June 2007, referring to its permissibility decision. The applicants then petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court for judicial review, claiming their civil rights were affected without court determination, violating the Convention. On 10 December 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the petition, finding the railway plan was in line with the Government’s permissibility decision, which was binding. It stated that if private interests were affected, judicial review could be obtained against the permissibility decision, and its earlier locus standi decision did not compel it to include permissibility issues in the current review.

A dissenting judge considered that the railway plan adoption directly affected individuals and should have prompted full judicial review of all objections.
001-146409:
**Summary of O.G. v. Latvia (Application no. 66095/09)**

The case of *O.G. v. Latvia* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by a Latvian national, Mr O.G., who alleged that his confinement to a psychiatric hospital was illegal. The key facts revolve around two sets of criminal proceedings and the subsequent imposition of compulsory psychiatric measures.

In March 2004, criminal proceedings for internet fraud were initiated against the applicant. During this first set of proceedings, he underwent two inpatient psychiatric examinations and was found to have full mental capacity. In October 2006, he was convicted and given a suspended sentence. However, during the appeal hearings in early 2007, the Riga Regional Court noted the applicant's aggressive and illogical behaviour and ordered an outpatient psychiatric assessment. In April 2007, a psychiatrist diagnosed him with chronic paranoid schizophrenia and recommended outpatient treatment. Consequently, in June 2007, a judge initiated proceedings to apply a compulsory medical measure. A crucial decision was made to examine the case in the applicant's absence, appointing his mother as his legal representative. When she could not attend a subsequent hearing, the court, with the consent of the applicant's counsel, appointed D.A., a psychiatrist involved in his treatment, as his legal representative.

A further inpatient assessment in November 2007 concluded that the applicant was unable to control his actions at the time of the offence and recommended relieving him of criminal liability. On 18 February 2008, the Riga Regional Court imposed a compulsory measure of outpatient psychiatric treatment. This decision was not appealed and became final.

A second set of criminal proceedings for fraud was initiated in March 2007. Based on a new forensic psychiatric assessment in October 2007, which again found him unable to participate in proceedings, the prosecutor decided to pursue a compulsory medical measure. In February 2008, D.A. was again appointed as his legal representative.

On 19 August 2008, the Riga Regional Court held a hearing in the applicant's absence to decide on the compulsory measure. He was represented by a lawyer, A.Ā., and D.A. was also present. The court heard testimony from D.A. and an expert psychiatrist, both of whom recommended involuntary inpatient treatment, a view concurred with by the defence counsel and prosecutor. The following day, the court ordered the applicant's inpatient treatment in a psychiatric hospital. This decision was not appealed in time by his representatives and became final on 2 September 2008.

The applicant only learned of this decision later and attempted to appeal, but was informed by the court that he lacked the standing to do so as his representatives had not appealed. He was taken to a psychiatric hospital by police on 22 October 2009. He was released on 7 June 2010.

**Key Facts Relevant to the Alleged Violation:**

The central issue is the lawfulness of the applicant's involuntary confinement. The key facts are:
- The final decision ordering his inpatient treatment (20 August 2008) was made in his absence.
- He was represented by a court-appointed psychiatrist (D.A.) who was also his treating doctor and recommended inpatient treatment.
- The applicant himself was not present at the hearing and was not represented by a lawyer of his own choosing.
- After the decision became final, he was not permitted to appeal against it because he had not been present at the hearing, a procedure explicitly permitted by domestic law.
- The decision was not enforced until over a year later, after he had been complying with a previous, separate outpatient treatment order.
- He was not informed of the final decision for a significant period.
001-147286:
In *Y v. Latvia* (Application no. 61183/08, judgment of 21 October 2014), the applicant, Ms Y, a Latvian national born in 1959, lived in Liepāja. On 1 November 2007, while she was in the courtyard of her apartment building, two municipal police officers, J.M. and J.L., arrived in a car in connection with an alleged administrative violation—washing a car in a public courtyard. After a conversation, the officers twisted the applicant’s arms behind her back and forced her towards their car. She was eventually released, apparently after neighbours intervened. Soon afterwards she felt ill and called an ambulance; she received an injection. The next day a general practitioner issued sick leave until 12 November 2007 and prescribed painkillers and sedatives. She claimed ongoing health effects more than a year later.

On 2 November 2007 the applicant asked the prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings. She alleged that one officer grabbed and twisted her right arm, shouted that he would teach her a lesson about resisting police, and that the second officer twisted her left arm. She said the officers tried to push her into their car and that she later had haematomas on her upper arms. On 4 November she also complained to the municipal police, seeking an investigation and compensation for mental anguish and material and psychological harm.

A forensic medical expert found two haematomas on each upper arm. The expert concluded they could have arisen in the circumstances described by the applicant but classified them as minor injuries not causing adverse health effects for more than six days. The applicant’s longer medical treatment was considered irrelevant. Three eyewitnesses said the applicant ignored police requests and resisted; the officers twisted her arms behind her back and released her once she stopped resisting. An internal police inquiry disciplined J.M. and J.L. only for failing to properly document the administrative infraction, not for using force.

On 21 January 2008 an inspector terminated the criminal proceedings. He found that the applicant had intentionally disobeyed a lawful police order and that the officers had grounds to detain her. However, they violated section 13 *in fine* of the Law on Police, which prohibited the use of special restraint techniques against women except in exceptional circumstances, such as danger to life or health or armed resistance. The applicant had sustained minor injuries under section 130 of the Criminal Law. Nevertheless, the inspector found no exceeding of official authority under section 317 because there was no substantial harm to state authority, administrative order, or individual rights, given the applicant’s disobedience and resistance. The proceedings were terminated for absence of *corpus delicti*. The applicant was informed she could pursue a private prosecution under section 130.

She did not appeal the termination but lodged a private prosecution complaint with the Liepāja Court, dated 29 April 2008 and received on 30 April, claiming damages under sections 130 and 156. On 7 May 2008 a judge refused to initiate proceedings, holding that the six-month limitation period had expired and that the complaint had been received on 6 May; she also failed to specify the relevant paragraph of section 130. On appeal, the Kurzeme Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 2 June 2008. It held that the last day to bring charges was 1 May 2008 and that, although the complaint was lodged on 30 April, it was physically impossible to complete the necessary procedural steps by 1 May. It also noted she could bring a civil claim. That decision was final.

The applicant alleged that she had been subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment and that she had no possibility of obtaining compensation for the damage sustained. The key facts relevant to those alleged violations are the use of special restraint techniques against a woman contrary to domestic law, the documented minor injuries, the termination of criminal proceedings, the classification of the offence as privately prosecuted, the restrictive six-month limitation period, and the resulting inability to obtain compensation through criminal or private prosecution.
001-148673:
The application was brought by four British nationals—Michael Horncastle, David Blackmore, Abijah Marquis and Joseph Graham—against the United Kingdom. They alleged that admitting witness statements at their trials made the proceedings unfair.

Horncastle and Blackmore were charged, with D., with causing P.R. grievous bodily harm with intent. On 7 May 2005 P.R., a registered alcoholic, was attacked in his flat, suffered extensive injuries and was hospitalised for a month. On 3 June 2005 he made a police statement naming “Horncastle” and describing two other attackers, but said his memory was vague and he had drunk heavily. He died on 23 July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness. The prosecution alleged that B. and M. had burgled another flat, stored stolen goods in P.R.’s flat, and that Horncastle and Blackmore went with D. to recover the property. The defence accepted they went to help recover D.’s property but denied attacking P.R.; they argued M. was responsible. Because P.R. was dead, the prosecution applied under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 to read his statement. The applicants opposed this under section 78 PACE, arguing it was the only admissible evidence against them, could not be cross-examined and was unreliable due to P.R.’s alcoholism, vague memory and description of Blackmore. On 24 January 2007 the judge admitted it as not unfair. After earlier juries were discharged, Horncastle and Blackmore were convicted in November 2007. The judge told the jury the prosecution depended on P.R.’s evidence and gave directions about the lack of cross-examination. On appeal, the applicants argued the statement was sole or decisive evidence. On 22 May 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals. It found substantial independent evidence but accepted the statement was decisive; it relied on statutory safeguards, no section 125 application, full directions and material to attack credibility. On 9 December 2009 the Supreme Court dismissed their further appeal.

Marquis and Graham were charged with kidnapping H.M. On 1 November 2007 six men entered her home, stole property, threatened her with a knife, kidnapped her and took her partner G.P.’s BMW. H.M. gave a statement but identified no one; G.P. described ransom demands. Graham was arrested on 2 November 2007 in G.P.’s car, where a knife was found; H.M. later confirmed it was the knife used. On 4 November 2007 a police officer told H.M. and G.P. the suspects were dangerous and cited relocated witnesses being murdered. On 22 November 2007 they retracted their statements, saying they feared for their families. H.M. later failed to attend court, was arrested, bailed and warned; she then made video statements saying her retraction was due to fear. G.P. said he was not scared but did not want reprisals. Neither attended the May 2008 trial. The prosecution applied to read their statements under section 116(2)(e) on grounds of fear. The applicants argued the fear was not caused by them but by police advice. On 13 May 2008 the judge admitted H.M.’s statement as a witness in fear, finding no police bad faith and no unfairness, but refused G.P.’s statement because fear was not established; a later defence application to admit part of it was refused. Marquis and Graham were convicted on 12 May 2008. They appealed, arguing H.M.’s statement should not have been admitted because the fear was not caused by them and because her evidence was decisive. On 22 May 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals, finding the convictions not decisively based on H.M.’s statement. The Supreme Court dismissed their further appeal on 9 December 2009.
001-144113:
**Pirttimäki v. Finland** (Application no. 35232/11) concerned a Finnish applicant who complained before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (double jeopardy / *ne bis in idem*) and Article 6 § 1 (excessive length of proceedings). The applicant, Mr Pirttimäki, owned shares in a limited liability company. In 2001–2002, a tax inspection was conducted for tax years 1996–2001. The tax authorities concluded that the company was not owned by four English companies, as claimed, but in reality by the applicant and three other Finnish persons in equal shares.

As a result, administrative tax proceedings were brought. In February 2003, additional taxes and tax surcharges were imposed on the company for tax years 1997–1999 and 2001. Separately, additional taxes and tax surcharges were imposed on the applicant personally for disguised dividends. He was ordered to pay tax surcharges of FIM 8,500 for 1997 (EUR 1,429.60), FIM 5,000 for 1998 (EUR 1,021.43), FIM 6,000 for 1999 (EUR 1,211.64), and FIM 10,000 for 2001 (EUR 1,904.50). The applicant challenged these decisions. The Tax Rectification Committees rejected his applications in 2005. The Administrative Courts rejected his appeals in 2007 and 2008, finding that the company was in reality owned equally by four Finnish persons. On 10 August 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal, making the tax surcharge decisions final.

In parallel, criminal proceedings were initiated. On 7 March 2002, based on the tax inspection, the tax authorities asked the police to investigate. The applicant was arrested on 4 June 2002, his office was searched the same day, and he was questioned on 5 June 2002 before being released. The pre-trial investigation concluded on 29 December 2006. On 11 July 2008, the public prosecutor charged the applicant with an accounting offence for incorrect and misleading bookkeeping between 1997 and 2001, and with aggravated tax fraud for giving incorrect information to the tax authorities between 1998 and 2002. The alleged tax evasion amounted to EUR 59,335.69.

On 30 September 2009, the Kotka District Court convicted the applicant as charged and imposed a one-year suspended sentence. The District Court noted that the proceedings had already lasted 7 years and 4 months, that the delay was unusually long and not attributable to the applicant, and that although the proper sentence would have been one year’s imprisonment, the excessive length warranted a suspended sentence. The applicant appealed, arguing that the charges should be dropped because he had already been punished through tax surcharges and because those administrative decisions had become final. On 2 July 2010, the Kouvola Appeal Court upheld the conviction. On the *ne bis in idem* issue, it found that the tax surcharge decisions had become final on 10 August 2009, but because the criminal charges had been brought earlier, on 11 July 2008, there was no procedural impediment to examining the criminal case.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 June 2011. He alleged that the combination of final tax surcharge proceedings and subsequent criminal proceedings for aggravated tax fraud violated the prohibition on double jeopardy under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. He also complained under Article 6 § 1 that the criminal proceedings had been excessively long. The application was communicated to the Finnish Government on 15 March 2013, and the Court delivered judgment on 20 May 2014.
001-145341:
M.E., a stateless Palestinian born in Syria in 1982, entered Denmark in 1990 at age seven and was granted asylum in 1993. He grew up in Denmark but had limited integration, never completing lower secondary school or participating in the labor market. He had an extensive criminal record, including convictions for assault, threats, weapons possession, theft, and human trafficking.

The critical facts relevant to the alleged violations concern his 2006 conviction for twenty-six counts of serious drug offenses involving 2.68 kg of heroin and cocaine committed throughout 2004. The High Court of Eastern Denmark found he played a leading role and sentenced him to seven years' imprisonment plus permanent expulsion from Denmark with a lifetime re-entry ban.

In ordering expulsion, Danish authorities considered M.E.'s ties to Denmark and Syria. He had two children from two marriages in Denmark—a son born in 2001 and a daughter born in 2004—and later married a third woman by Islamic ceremony. His mother, two half-siblings, and paternal uncles lived in Syria. He had visited Syria multiple times, including a six-month stay in 1997 when he worked as a painter.

M.E. opposed expulsion, claiming he feared return to Syria due to: unresolved compulsory military service; potential punishment for his Danish drug conviction; his father's political past; and a personal dispute with a Syrian family. Danish authorities obtained expert legal opinions indicating that under Syrian law, a person convicted and having served sentence abroad could not be retried in Syria for the same offense, and that military draft evasion typically resulted in brief additional service rather than imprisonment.

The Danish Immigration Service found his claims not credible and determined he could be expelled to Syria or Lebanon. The Refugee Appeals Board confirmed expulsion to Syria specifically. Subsequent court proceedings in 2009-2010 rejected his claims that changed circumstances—including his new wife's pregnancy—warranted revocation of the expulsion order. The High Court emphasized that his relationship began after the 2006 Supreme Court judgment, so the parties could not have justified expectations of residing together in Denmark.

M.E. was deported to Syria on November 3, 2010, accompanied by Danish police who provided documentation confirming he had served his sentence. He alleged that upon arrival in Damascus he was detained, interrogated about his Danish conviction, and tortured. He was allegedly released to commence thirty months' military service but exempted after one month due to heart problems. He also faced court summons regarding his Danish conviction, though that case was reportedly discontinued.

M.E. fled Syria in 2011, eventually reaching Sweden where he was granted asylum in 2013. His application to the European Court of Human Rights alleged that his expulsion to Syria violated Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention.
001-140782:
**Case of Vasilyev and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 29266/08 and 248 others) is a European Court of Human Rights case against Ukraine, decided by the Fifth Section Committee on 13 February 2014. The judgment is final, though subject to editorial revision. The case originated in 249 applications lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by Ukrainian nationals whose details appear in appended tables. The applicants complained chiefly about Ukraine’s failure to enforce final domestic decisions in their favour.

According to the facts, on dates listed in the appended tables, Ukrainian domestic courts and labour disputes commissions issued decisions entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions to be taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable under domestic law. However, the applicants were unable to obtain their enforcement in due time. This non-enforcement formed the central factual basis for the alleged violations.

The appended table shows the scale and variety of the claims. For example, application no. 29266/08, brought by Aleksandr Nikolayevich Vasilyev, concerned a final decision of the Suvorivskyy District Court of Kherson of 27 September 2005. Other applicants relied on decisions from local, regional, administrative and appellate courts, as well as labour disputes commissions, issued between 1997 and 2011. Many of these decisions concerned unpaid wages, social benefits, pensions or similar employment-related entitlements. The applicants applied to the Strasbourg Court between 2008 and 2012, often several years after the domestic decisions had become final, reflecting prolonged enforcement problems.

Some procedural developments affected the applications. Several applicants—Mr Bulavko, Mr Ponomaryov, Mr Zavarzin and Mr Bondar—died during the proceedings. Their next of kin expressed a wish to maintain the applications. In other applications, domestic court decisions had been delivered in favour of the applicants’ deceased relatives, and the applicants claimed to be lawful successors in title. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues.

The Court communicated the applications to the Ukrainian Government on 24 June 2013. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy.

The alleged violations arose from the State’s failure to secure timely execution of final and binding domestic judgments. In Convention terms, such non-enforcement typically engages Article 6 § 1, which guarantees the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants essentially alleged that the prolonged inability to enforce decisions in their favour rendered their judicial victories ineffective and imposed a disproportionate burden on them. The case therefore formed part of a broader line of applications against Ukraine concerning systemic non-enforcement of domestic court decisions. The Court was asked to determine whether these delays and failures amounted to violations of the applicants’ Convention rights.
001-142519:
**Case: Li v. Russia (Application no. 38388/07), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Judgment of 24 April 2014**

The applicant, Roman Mikhaylovich Li, is a Russian national born in 1966 who lives in Magadan. He lodged his application against the Russian Federation on 20 July 2007 under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The application was communicated to the Russian Government on 14 January 2013. The Government were represented by Mr G. Matyushkin.

The facts concern the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment awarding the applicant compensation. On 28 January 2003, the Magadan City Court awarded him 30,000 Russian roubles as compensation for unlawful conviction. That judgment became final on 16 February 2003. On 5 March 2003, the applicant obtained the corresponding writ of execution.

According to the applicant, in 2004 the writ of execution was stolen from his office. In September 2007, he therefore asked the domestic courts to issue a duplicate of the writ. On 13 September 2007, a national court refused to issue the duplicate. The decisive reason was that the time-limit for submitting the writ for execution had expired under Article 14 of the Russian Federal Law on Enforcement Proceedings. That provision, in force at the material time, allowed writs of execution to be submitted for execution within three years from the date on which the underlying court decision entered into force. Since the judgment became final on 16 February 2003, the three-year period had expired in February 2006, before the applicant sought the duplicate in 2007.

On 27 September 2007, the applicant also asked the Ministry of Finance of the Russian Federation to execute the 2003 judgment. The Ministry replied that execution was not possible without submission of the writ of execution.

The relevant domestic law reinforced this position. Article 242.1 § 1 of the Budget Code of the Russian Federation provided that enforcement of judicial decisions recovering funds from the budgetary system had to be carried out on the basis of enforcement documents, such as a writ of execution or court order, and in accordance with domestic requirements and time-limits for submission. Article 14 of the Federal Law on Enforcement Proceedings required that such writs be submitted within three years from the entry into force of the court decision on which they were based.

The applicant’s alleged Convention violations therefore centred on the failure of the Russian authorities to enforce a final and binding domestic judgment in his favour. The key facts relevant to those allegations are: the existence of a final judgment awarding him compensation for unlawful conviction; the issuance of a writ of execution in March 2003; the alleged loss or theft of that writ in 2004; the applicant’s attempts in 2007 to obtain a duplicate and to have the judgment enforced; the domestic court’s refusal to issue a duplicate because the three-year enforcement period had expired; and the Ministry of Finance’s refusal to execute the judgment without the writ.

Those facts raised issues under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the right to a fair hearing and the effective enforcement of final judicial decisions, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning the applicant’s right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions, since the compensation award could be regarded as an asset or legitimate expectation. The central question was whether the Russian authorities’ reliance on formal enforcement requirements and the expired time-limit effectively deprived the applicant of the benefit of a final judgment that had never been executed.
001-148642:
In *N.A. v. Norway*, the applicant, a Norwegian national, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that, despite being acquitted of criminal charges, a Norwegian court ordered her to pay compensation to the victims, thereby undermining her presumption of innocence. She also alleged that the compensation decision was not sufficiently reasoned, in breach of her fair-hearing rights.

In September 2009 N.A. and her former husband, U.A., were indicted in Norway. They were charged with causing, or aiding and abetting, aggravated bodily harm to their daughter A, including skull fractures, brain bleeding, retinal bleeding, an elbow dislocation, and permanent brain injury, and with seriously and repeatedly ill-treating their son B, including an arm fracture and other injuries. The alleged acts occurred between August 2005 and January 2008, while the children were in the parents’ care.

In January 2010 the Oslo City Court convicted N.A. and U.A. It found that the children had suffered gross ill-treatment by adults while in the family’s small flat. Although evidence from the defendants and witnesses was contradictory and it could not identify exactly who inflicted each act, the City Court found that each parent had aided and abetted the violence by failing to intervene or prevent it. N.A. received a prison sentence and was ordered to pay compensation.

On appeal, the Borgarting High Court held a jury trial in August–September 2010. The jury answered all questions negatively, and the professional judges accepted the acquittal. In the same judgment, however, the professional judges—sitting without the jury—examined the children’s civil claims for non-pecuniary damages under the Damage Compensation Act. They noted that acquittal did not prevent compensation because the civil evidentiary standard was less stringent than the criminal standard, though Article 6 § 2 set limits. Applying a “clearly probable” standard, the High Court found it clearly probable that N.A. and U.A. had ill-treated the children or aided and abetted such ill-treatment over a long period, and had inflicted or aided in inflicting serious injuries. It relied on medical evidence that the injuries were not accidental, signs of strong violence, B’s post-traumatic stress syndrome, and neighbours’ accounts of children’s screams. It awarded NOK 300,000 to A and NOK 100,000 to B. The High Court stated that this civil decision, based on a lower evidentiary threshold, did not contradict the acquittal.

N.A. appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court’s evidence assessment and reasoning violated Article 6 § 2 and that the compensation award was insufficiently reasoned under Article 6 § 1. In November 2010 the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave to appeal. N.A. then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 3 May 2011.

The key alleged violation was that, despite her formal acquittal, the national court’s compensation judgment effectively found her responsible for the same criminal acts, undermining the presumption of innocence. She also alleged a fair-hearing violation because the judgment allegedly failed to explain why the civil findings did not conflict with the acquittal. The case therefore raised the tension between a criminal acquittal and civil liability based on a lower standard of proof.
001-145653:
In *Tanda-Muzinga v. France*, the applicant, a Congolese national born in 1970, complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that obstacles encountered in obtaining visas for his wife and children under France’s family reunification procedure for refugees violated his right to respect for family life.

The applicant was granted refugee status by UNHCR in Cameroon in 2000, together with his wife and two daughters, Vanessa and Michelle. A third child, Benjamin, was born in Cameroon in 2004 after the applicant had left for France to seek asylum. Although OFPRA initially rejected his asylum claim in 2004, the Refugee Appeals Board granted him refugee status in February 2007. He then received a ten-year residence permit, and OFPRA issued civil-status documents, including a marriage certificate and a family record book.

In June 2007, relying on the family reunification procedure for recognised refugees, he applied for long-stay visas for his wife and three children. The Ministry contacted OFPRA to verify family ties, and the consulate in Yaoundé summoned his wife for an interview in February 2008. She was asked to provide UNHCR/Cameroon travel documents. She submitted such a document in March 2008, but no acknowledgement of the visa application was issued. In June 2008, OFPRA confirmed that it had certified the applicant’s family situation in July 2007, listing his wife and all three children.

After the consular authorities implicitly refused the visas, the applicant appealed. The French Government contended that the birth certificates for Michelle and Benjamin were fraudulent. Checks allegedly showed that certificate no. 1271, presented for Michelle, actually concerned a boy, and certificate no. 78/2004, presented for Benjamin, actually concerned a girl. The Minister argued that the fraudulent documents justified refusing visas for the whole family. The applicant disputed this, arguing that any anomalies arose from dysfunction in Cameroonian civil-status administration. He relied on hospital birth declarations, UNHCR documents, travel documents, photographs, bank transfer records, and later a UNHCR certificate of parenthood.

In September 2008, the Conseil d’État refused an urgent stay of execution, and in July 2009 it dismissed his appeal. It held that the fraudulent nature of at least one submitted document justified refusing all the requested visas. A psychologist later reported that the applicant’s mental health had deteriorated because of the prolonged separation from his family.

Following that decision, UNHCR/Paris indicated that the consulate was willing to issue visas to his wife, Vanessa and Benjamin, but that Michelle required a supplementary civil-status judgment in Cameroon. The applicant’s wife began proceedings there. In April 2010, the consular authorities again refused long-stay visas, maintaining that Michelle’s birth certificate remained doubtful, although Benjamin’s was later authenticated. In June 2010, the Yaoundé tribunal de grande instance reconstituted Michelle’s birth certificate, finding that the original document was a forgery obtained by a third party and that her actual birth declaration was genuine.

In October 2010, the Nantes Administrative Court ordered a stay of execution and directed the Minister to re-examine the application, noting the length of separation and the uncertainty concerning only one child. In December 2010, the French consular authorities finally issued long-stay visas to the applicant’s wife and children. The Government stated that the June 2010 judgment had been provided during re-examination. The case therefore concerned alleged excessive obstacles, delays and refusals in the refugee family reunification process, and their impact on the applicant’s family life under Article 8.
001-148636:
Anthony Aquilina v. Malta (Application no. 3851/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The applicant, a Maltese national living in Canada, owns a 105-square-metre maisonette in Gozo inherited from his parents. In 1960 the property was registered as a “decontrolled dwelling house” under Malta’s Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance. In 1970 his mother leased it to a Maltese couple, C., for 35 Maltese liri every six months—approximately EUR 81.50—later reduced to about EUR 75.70. At that time, the landlord could increase rent, refuse renewal, or change lease terms.

In 1979 Malta amended the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance. Where the tenant was a Maltese citizen occupying the property as an ordinary residence, rent-control rules applied. The landlord could no longer refuse to renew the lease, raise the rent, or impose new conditions except as allowed by law. The applicant alleged that this amendment destroyed contractual freedom and imposed an indefinite lease, preventing him from charging a fair rent or recovering possession, even though the tenants allegedly owned substantial immovable property. In 1998 the Rent Regulation Board reduced the rent to EUR 65.22 per year. Reforms in 1995 for new leases did not apply. In 2009 and 2010 further amendments aimed to gradually eliminate restrictive pre-1995 lease regimes. From September 2010 the rent became EUR 185 per year. The applicant refused rent from 2007, and the tenants deposited it in court. A 2005 court architect valued the rental at EUR 2,912 per year; a 2013 government report valued the rental market at EUR 2,900 per year and the sale value at EUR 58,000. The tenants still reside there.

In 2005 the applicant brought constitutional redress proceedings, alleging that the 1979 amendments—especially Article 5(2) and (3) of the HD Ordinance—breached his property rights. The Civil Court (First Hall) rejected the complaint on 4 June 2008. It found that he remained owner, could evict for tenant breach, that low rent was offset by statutory 15-year increases, and that the interference was proportionate because his mother had voluntarily leased the property. He appealed on 25 June 2008, but the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal as out of time on 3 November 2008. In 2009 the European Court declared a related application inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies.

In 2010 the applicant began a second set of constitutional redress proceedings. He argued that the 2009 amendments did not remedy the violation, that it was unclear whether Article 1531C of the Civil Code applied, and that EUR 185 per year remained unfair. He claimed continuing victim status because he still could not refuse renewal and the rent was inadequate, relying on Amato Gauci v. Malta. On 15 October 2011 the Civil Court (First Hall) rejected the complaint as res judicata: the same parties, object, and cause of action had already been determined; the first judgment had found a fair balance; the amendments had not worsened his position; and new arguments should have been raised earlier. The Constitutional Court upheld that decision on 24 June 2011, calling the appeal frivolous and vexatious.

The relevant law includes Article 5 of the HD Ordinance, which restricted possession and rent increases, and the 2009 Civil Code amendments, including Article 1531C setting minimum rent for pre-1995 leases. The alleged violation is that Malta’s 1979 legislative amendments subjected the applicant to an indefinite compulsory lease at a disproportionately low rent, without a fair balance between public housing needs and his property rights.
001-145018:
In *M.E. v. Sweden*, the applicant was a Libyan national, born in 1982, who arrived in Sweden in July 2010 and applied for asylum. He initially claimed that he had been a soldier and guard at a military base in Tripoli and had transported illegal weapons for powerful clans. In November 2009 he was stopped, detained for about three weeks, interrogated and tortured, then transferred to a military prison. He escaped from a civil hospital with the help of a guard. He feared that if returned to Libya he would face at least ten years’ imprisonment for criminal offences and possible revenge from the clans whose names he had revealed under torture. He later stated that the clans were less interested in him after the 2011 changes in Libya.

In February 2011, the applicant added a new ground for asylum: he was homosexual and had a relationship with N., a transsexual person with a Swedish residence permit. They had met in Sweden, moved in together in December 2010, and married in September 2011. The applicant said his sexual orientation was unknown in Libya and that he had never had a homosexual relationship there. He claimed that if he were returned to Libya to apply for family reunion from there, his marriage to a man would become known, exposing him to persecution and ill-treatment. He later alleged that a Libyan in Sweden had told his brother about the marriage, that his uncle had threatened to kill him for shaming the family, and that homosexuals in Libya had been killed.

The Swedish Migration Board rejected the asylum application in December 2011. It accepted that the applicant was probably Libyan but found his account lacking credibility. It noted contradictions about his passport, inconsistent details about when he met N., a discrepancy in the name on the marriage certificate, and the late disclosure of his relationship. It also found that he had not substantiated a risk from the criminal accusations or the clans. As to family reunion, the Board applied the main rule that a residence permit on family-tie grounds must normally be applied for before entering Sweden. It found no reason to exempt him, concluding it was not unreasonable to require him to apply from Libya.

The Migration Court rejected his appeal in September 2012. It found the general situation in Libya serious but not enough for asylum without individual risk. The documents and scars did not prove future ill-treatment, and the court found the applicant not credible. It did not question that he was homosexual, but found no substantiated risk: his orientation was not known in Libya, it was unlikely that Libyans in Sweden would spread the information merely because he returned, and embassy staff were bound by confidentiality. One lay judge dissented, considering that a leak from an embassy could not be ruled out. The Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in October 2012.

A request for reconsideration was rejected in December 2012; the Migration Board found the alleged family threats did not constitute a permanent impediment to enforcement.

The applicant alleged that expulsion to Libya—or being required to apply for family reunion there—would violate Article 3 (risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment as a homosexual and/or due to his past) and Article 8 (right to private and family life with his spouse in Sweden). The Court applied Rule 39 to prevent deportation during proceedings. Relevant country evidence showed that same-sex acts were criminalised in Libya, homosexuality was socially taboo, and militias had abused gay men. Sweden’s only consulate in Libya, in Benghazi, was closed, although embassies in Algiers and Cairo and a consulate in Tunis handled residence-permit applications. These facts framed the alleged violations.
001-140235:
**Case: O’Keeffe v. Ireland (Application no. 35810/09), European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber, 28 January 2014**

The applicant, Louise O’Keeffe, an Irish national born in 1964, attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned by trustees of the Catholic Bishop of Cork and Ross, the recognised patron, and was managed locally by a parish priest acting for the bishop. The school had two teachers, one of whom, L.H., was principal.

In 1971, a parent complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. This complaint was not reported to the police, the Department of Education, or any other State authority, and the manager did not act on it. During the first six months of 1973, the applicant was subjected to approximately twenty sexual assaults by L.H. during music lessons in his classroom. She and her parents were unaware of the 1971 complaint at that time.

In September 1973, other parents brought similar allegations about L.H. to the attention of the applicant’s parents. After a parents’ meeting chaired by the manager, L.H. went on sick leave and resigned. Again, the allegations were not reported to the police or State authorities. The manager later notified the Department only that L.H. had resigned and named his replacement. L.H. subsequently taught at another national school until his retirement in 1995. Between 1969 and 1973, a State inspector visited Dunderrow National School six times—an above-average number—met L.H., and considered his teaching satisfactory. No complaint about L.H. was made to the inspector.

The applicant suppressed the abuse and suffered significant psychological difficulties without initially connecting them to the abuse. In 1996, police investigating a 1995 complaint by another former pupil contacted her. She made a statement in 1997. L.H. was charged with 386 sexual offences involving about twenty-one former pupils; in 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was imprisoned. His teaching licence was later withdrawn.

The applicant received an ex gratia award from the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal. She also brought a civil action against L.H., the Minister for Education, Ireland, and the Attorney General. Against the State defendants, she claimed negligence in the recognition, examination and supervision of the school; failure to put in place measures to prevent and stop L.H.’s abuse; vicarious liability for L.H.; and breach of constitutional rights. The High Court non-suited the negligence claim and later found no vicarious liability, holding that national schools were privately and clerically managed. The Supreme Court, by majority, dismissed her appeal, finding that the State funded and inspected schools but did not directly control them; L.H. was employed by the manager, not the State, and the State was not liable for the manager’s failure to report the 1971 complaint. One judge dissented, viewing primary education as a joint Church-State enterprise creating sufficient connection for State liability.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant principally complained under Article 3 that Ireland’s primary education system failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973, and under Article 13 that she lacked an effective domestic remedy. She also relied on Article 8 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, alone and with Article 14. Complaints about the length of civil proceedings were settled. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the prior 1971 complaint, the failure to report abuse to State authorities, the State’s regulatory and inspection role, the managerial/denominational structure of national schools, and the unsuccessful domestic civil remedies.
001-148263:
The case of *Borovská and Forrai v. Slovakia* (Application no. 48554/10) originated from an application lodged against the Slovak Republic with the European Court of Human Rights on 16 August 2010. The applicants, Mária Borovská, Mária Buzová, and Štefan Forrai, were Slovak nationals and successors in title to a plot of land (no. 10610) in Košice-Sever. This land, along with other plots, had been expropriated in the 1980s by the socialist State to build a public sports centre, a decision the applicants later argued was legally invalid due to procedural flaws.

In 1994, the applicants filed a civil action seeking the removal of the constructions on their land, or alternatively, a judicial ruling to establish an easement for the sports centre's owner in return for financial compensation. In its 2008 judgment, the Košice I District Court agreed that the 1984 expropriation was legally ineffective and confirmed the applicants as the rightful owners. It also found the constructions were built without valid title. However, the court dismissed the claim for an easement. It reasoned that under the Civil Code, the sports facilities did not qualify as "buildings" (*stavba*) in the strict legal sense, and an easement could only be established for a building's owner. Since the applicants' claim was legally classified as seeking an easement, it had to be dismissed.

On appeal, the applicants argued that the District Court had failed to consider that other, generically similar claims concerning the same sports complex had been successful, with easements granted. They specifically cited a prior case (no. 15C 251/94) where an easement was established on comparable plots. The Košice Regional Court, however, dismissed the appeal on different grounds. While it agreed the expropriation was invalid, it ruled that the State had appropriated the land without legal title, a situation governed by the special Land Ownership Act (Law no. 229/1991 Coll.). This law required restitution claims to be filed by 31 December 1992, a deadline the applicants had missed. The Regional Court concluded that seeking redress under the general Civil Code was therefore impermissible. The applicants’ crucial argument regarding the inconsistent judicial practice went unanswered.

The applicants then lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court, alleging arbitrary dismissal and violations of their rights to a fair trial and property protection. They reiterated that their case fell outside the restitution laws and that the courts had ignored the divergent case-law. On 3 June 2010, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, again without addressing the applicants' argument about the conflicting judicial practice.

The applicants' core complaint to the European Court was that their rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) were violated. They alleged that the domestic courts had arbitrarily dismissed their property claim and, critically, had failed to respond to their key argument: that a number of similarly situated claims concerning the same sports complex had been granted, creating a situation of legal uncertainty and unfairness. The case thus centered on whether the domestic courts' refusal to engage with this argument regarding inconsistent case-law constituted a violation of the right to a reasoned and fair judicial decision.
001-147272:
**Erla Hlynsdóttir v. Iceland (No. 2)** concerns an Icelandic journalist’s complaint under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights that her liability in domestic defamation proceedings violated her right to freedom of expression.

The applicant, Erla Hlynsdóttir, was a journalist for the newspaper *DV*. In its issue of 31 August–2 September 2007, *DV* published an article entitled “Satan’s attacks” about a high-profile criminal investigation involving Mr Y, the founder and director of a Christian rehabilitation centre called Byrgið, and his wife, Mrs X. In December 2006, a television programme had accused Mr Y of sexually abusing female patients and embezzling public funds. Three women subsequently filed police complaints against him. Both Mr Y and Mrs X were suspects in the criminal investigation.

The *DV* article contained interviews and comments from Ms A, one of the women who had complained to the police, and Mr B, the financial manager at Byrgið and a close friend of the couple. Ms A alleged that Mrs X had participated in sexual activities with her and Mr Y, had helped seduce female patients as part of their supposed “healing process,” and had sought sexual encounters with women herself. Ms A also criticised Mrs X’s work as a teaching assistant, stating that it was inappropriate that “the one who hunts for him works in a primary school.” Mr B similarly said that both Mr Y and Mrs X had sexually abused patients and that he found it strange that Mrs X was allowed to work with children. The article also included comments from the couple’s lawyer denying the accusations and from a police officer confirming that Mrs X had suspect status.

In February 2008, Mrs X brought defamation proceedings against Ms A, Mr B and the applicant under Articles 234, 235 and 236 of the Icelandic Penal Code. She sought annulment of the statements, criminal punishment and compensation. She argued that the applicant, as author of the article, was liable for its content.

The applicant relied on Article 73 of the Icelandic Constitution and section 15 of the Printing Act, arguing that responsibility lay with the named interviewees whose statements had been quoted directly. She also claimed the statements were true and accurate, noting that Mrs X had been a suspect in a sexual-offence investigation. The District Court, on 4 December 2008, found one statement attributed to Ms A defamatory but not proved to have originated from her. Only the applicant was ordered to pay Mrs X ISK 100,000 in non-pecuniary damages; the statement was annulled, and other claims were rejected.

Both parties appealed. On 18 February 2010, the Icelandic Supreme Court upheld most of the lower court’s findings. It held that some statements were substantiated or amounted to value judgments. However, it found the latter part of the statement that it was “not appropriate that the one who hunts for him works in a primary school” defamatory. According to the Supreme Court, those words implied that Mrs X was guilty of criminal conduct, which had not been proven. Because the applicant had been identified as the author, she was liable under section 15 of the Printing Act. She was ordered to pay ISK 300,000 in non-pecuniary damages, ISK 100,000 for publication costs, plus interest.

The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 17 August 2010. She complained that the Supreme Court’s judgment interfered with her Article 10 right to freedom of expression and was not “necessary in a democratic society.” The application was communicated to the Icelandic Government on 6 September 2012. The key issue was whether holding a journalist liable for publishing a named interviewee’s statement during public debate about a criminal investigation was justified under Article 10.
001-142521:
The case concerns three Macedonian nationals—Dimitar Miladinov, Dimitrija Golaboski and Georgi Miladinov—private entrepreneurs from Struga and Ohrid. Their applications were lodged in August and September 2009.

On 23 December 2008 an investigating judge of the Skopje Court of First Instance opened an investigation against fifteen people, including bankruptcy trustees, judges, lawyers, notaries and civil servants, concerning bankruptcy proceedings involving company I. The applicants were charged with money laundering; the first applicant also faced charges of abuse of position, fraud and forgery, and the third applicant faced fraud charges. In a single decision, the investigating judge ordered pre-trial detention for thirty days for nine accused, including all three applicants, under section 184(1)(1-3) of the Criminal Proceedings Act. The grounds were risk of absconding, reoffending and interfering with the investigation, based on the gravity of the charges, potential sentence and possible influence on witnesses.

The first and second applicants appealed, arguing that the judge had not given concrete, individualised reasons and pointing to their permanent residence and family ties; the second applicant also cited poor health. The panel dismissed the first applicant’s appeal and replaced the second applicant’s detention with house arrest. The panel then extended the applicants’ detention or house arrest by thirty-day periods on 21 January, 19 February and 20 March 2009. All extension hearings were held in private. The first two extensions relied on all three statutory grounds; after the indictment was lodged on 20 March 2009, interference with the investigation was removed as a ground. The reasons were largely identical and collective: risk of flight due to the gravity of charges, possible sentence and previous or pending criminal proceedings; risk of reoffending due to the nature of the offences and the alleged use of position, special powers and companies.

From 16 April to 16 September 2009 the panel extended detention on its own motion six times, again in private and with identical reasoning, adding that detention or house arrest was the most efficient way to secure attendance at trial. Further extensions followed between October 2009 and January 2010 for the first and third applicants.

The applicants appealed to the Skopje Court of Appeal. They complained that the reasons were insufficient, that their family situation and the second applicant’s health were ignored, that the first applicant’s previous conviction concerned only a traffic offence, and that the wording of the decisions violated the presumption of innocence. The first and third applicants also requested notification of and a public session. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals in private, referring to written submissions by the public prosecutor. It found the reasons sufficient, considered family and residence irrelevant, relied on the nature and gravity of the offences, company ownership or connections, prior records and pending proceedings, and repeated that detention was the most efficient measure to secure attendance. It refused public sessions, finding the relevant provision inapplicable. In January 2010 the applicants were convicted and sentenced, but in September 2010 the Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and released the first and third applicants, finding no grounds for detention.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 5 §§3 and 4 and Article 6 §2. The key facts are the repeated thirty-day extensions based on generic, collective reasons; the private review proceedings without public hearing despite requests; and language in the detention decisions allegedly implying guilt before final conviction.
001-225807:
**Summary of the Case of Emin Huseynov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2)**

The case of *Emin Huseynov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2)* concerns the termination of the applicant’s Azerbaijani citizenship, which rendered him stateless. The applicant, Mr. Emin Huseynov, is a stateless person of Azerbaijani origin, an independent journalist, and the chairman of the Institute for Reporters’ Freedom and Safety (IRFS), a non-governmental organization focused on protecting journalists’ rights.

The events leading to the case began in April 2014, when the Prosecutor General’s Office of Azerbaijan opened a criminal case concerning alleged financial irregularities within several NGOs. As part of this investigation, the bank accounts of numerous NGOs and civil society activists, including the applicant and the IRFS, were frozen. Various human rights defenders were also arrested. In July 2014, the applicant learned that tax authorities had launched an investigation into the IRFS. On 5 August 2014, he was prevented from leaving Azerbaijan at Baku Airport. Fearing imminent arrest after being summoned for questioning, he went into hiding. On 18 August 2014, he clandestinely entered the Swiss embassy in Baku, where he found refuge. The following day, Azerbaijani authorities charged him with illegal entrepreneurship, large-scale tax evasion, and abuse of power, and a court ordered his arrest.

While at the Swiss embassy, on 10 February 2015 and again on 4 June 2015, the applicant submitted requests to the President of Azerbaijan to renounce his Azerbaijani citizenship. On 9 June 2015, the Swiss authorities paid USD 236,281 to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Finance to cover the applicant’s tax debt. Consequently, the Nasimi District Court revoked the order for his arrest and quashed the decision declaring him a wanted person. On 12 June 2015, the applicant left Azerbaijan for Switzerland.

On 27 June 2015, the State Migration Service informed the applicant that his Azerbaijani citizenship had been terminated by a presidential order dated 10 June 2015. The applicant was never provided with a copy of this order, nor was its text made public. On 19 October 2015, he was granted asylum in Switzerland.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that he had been forced to renounce his citizenship, in violation of Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 10 (freedom of expression), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He also alleged under Article 18 that his Convention rights had been restricted for purposes other than those prescribed in the Convention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant, a journalist and human rights defender, was facing criminal prosecution and was effectively trapped in the Swiss embassy when he applied to renounce his citizenship. His tax debt was paid by the Swiss authorities, after which his arrest order was lifted and he was allowed to leave. Shortly thereafter, his citizenship was terminated by a presidential order, leaving him stateless, as he possessed no other nationality. The applicant argued that this sequence of events demonstrated that his renunciation was not voluntary but was forced upon him under pressure from the Azerbaijani authorities. The respondent Government did not provide the Court with a copy of the presidential order terminating his citizenship or the earlier court decisions regarding his arrest. The case raises significant issues under international law, particularly the United Nations Conventions on Statelessness, which prohibit states from depriving individuals of nationality if it would render them stateless.
001-224963:
**Case: Mesić v. Croatia (No. 2) (Application no. 45066/17)**

The case concerns civil defamation proceedings brought by Stjepan Mesić, former President of Croatia (2000–2010), over an online article linking him to the Patria armoured-vehicle bribery scandal. Mesić complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8 of the Convention that Croatian courts had failed to protect his reputation and private life by dismissing his compensation claim.

In 2013, Finnish prosecutors indicted three employees of the Finnish company Patria for aggravated bribery concerning the sale of Patria AMV armoured vehicles to Croatia in 2007. A Finnish Prosecutor General’s press release stated that the defendants were suspected of promising or giving bribes through intermediaries in exchange for actions by the President of Croatia and a director of a Croatian State-owned company. On 16 February 2015, the Kanta-Häme District Court convicted two Patria employees of promising and giving a bribe to the Croatian company director and dismissed charges against the third. Regarding Mesić, the court found that the mere fact he was considered an important lobbying target did not prove he was promised or given a bribe; the identity of three VIPs allegedly promised 1% of the purchase price was not established; and the alleged bribe to Mesić was not supported by sufficient evidence. On appeal, the Turku Court of Appeal acquitted the accused in February 2016, finding no proof of the bribes; Mesić was not mentioned.

On 17 February 2015, the Croatian internet news portal *Dnevno.hr* published an article about the Patria case. It asserted that the Finnish Prosecutor General had confirmed that documents had been sent to Croatia’s USKOK; that Mesić had received a €630,000 bribe from persons just convicted of giving bribes; that two Patria managers directly charged with giving bribes to Mesić and the Croatian company director had been sentenced; and that the joint investigation had “undoubtedly established” that Mesić and the director participated in criminal activities. It called for Croatian authorities to prosecute Mesić. The article also quoted alleged statements by the Finnish Prosecutor General and referred to an indictment mentioning Mesić’s name. Mesić asked the portal to publish a correction, but it refused.

In May 2015, Mesić sued the portal operator in the Zagreb Municipal Civil Court, claiming that three statements in the article were false and injured his honour and reputation. He sought HRK 40,000 in non-pecuniary damages. He submitted that the Finnish court had not convicted anyone of bribing him, that he had no role in the procurement, and that no one had contacted him before publication.

In December 2015, the Municipal Civil Court dismissed the claim. It held that the journalist had relied on the Finnish press release, the indictment, and an alleged telephone interview with the Finnish Prosecutor General; that the information was sufficiently verified and in the public interest; and that Mesić was a public figure. It declined to examine the truth of the allegations and found that the Finnish judgment was not decisive because Mesić had not been charged in Finland. The Zagreb County Court upheld that judgment in April 2016, and the Constitutional Court dismissed Mesić’s constitutional complaint in December 2016, finding sufficient reasoning and no breach of the presumption of innocence.

Before the European Court, Mesić alleged that the domestic courts’ dismissal of his civil action failed to protect his reputation in violation of Article 8. The key facts relevant to that alleged violation are the Finnish court’s finding of insufficient evidence against Mesić, the Croatian article’s unequivocal accusations that he received a bribe and participated in criminal activity, and the domestic courts’ refusal to assess the truth of those allegations while accepting the journalist’s reliance on the indictment and alleged sources as good-faith verification.
001-222915:
Katona and Závarský v. Slovakia (Applications nos. 43932/19 and 43995/19; ECtHR First Section, 9 February 2023) concerns the exclusion of the applicants’ promissory-note claims from satisfaction in insolvency or other proceedings against an individual debtor. The applicants alleged violations of Article 6 (access to court), Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In 2005 the first applicant, László Katona, transferred part of his shares in a business entity to another individual (“the debtor”), who agreed to pay him in instalments. The debtor issued promissory notes in favour of the first applicant as promise of payment. The first applicant later transferred one note to the second applicant, Tomáš Závarský. It was uncontested that the first applicant also had independent parallel claims under the share-transfer agreement, that he could claim under either or both titles, that he did not pursue the share-transfer claims, and that those claims became time-barred.

After non-payment, the applicants sued the debtor over nine promissory notes, with principal totalling EUR 74,000. The Bratislava V District Court issued four payment orders in 2011, 2012 and 2014 ordering payment. After the debtor’s appeals were dismissed, those orders became final, binding and enforceable between 2016 and 2017. A further 2014 payment order was challenged and the proceedings were terminated in 2019 without a merits decision because of the later insolvency.

Between 2016 and 2018 the applicants sought enforcement of the four final orders, and enforcement was authorised. For the second applicant’s EUR 20,000 claim, EUR 1,399 was seized from the debtor’s monthly income; EUR 1,092.93 was paid to him and the rest retained for enforcement costs. Otherwise no proceeds were obtained because no significant assets were found.

Under the Bankruptcy and Restructuring Code, a bankruptcy order stays proceedings concerning the debtor’s estate and terminates enforcement. For individuals, a “debt discharge” was possible. Before March 2017, it followed after bankruptcy and involved a three-year probation period; if fulfilled, outstanding debts became incapable of legal pursuit. From 1 March 2017, Law no. 377/2016 Coll. made debt discharge part of bankruptcy proceedings and provided that claims based on promissory notes issued before a defined date became incapable of being legally pursued.

On 24 January 2019 the Bratislava I District Court issued a bankruptcy order against the debtor, appointed a trustee, and, at the debtor’s request, discharged him of his debts. The decision was not subject to appeal. It automatically terminated the applicants’ enforcement proceedings, and the first applicant’s pending claim was also terminated by analogy. The applicants were not parties to the debt discharge proceedings. In August 2021 the trustee reported that, apart from a small State claim, only the applicants sought to register claims. The District Court confirmed that their adjudicated promissory-note claims were incapable of pursuit under Article 166b § 1(c) of the BR Code and could not be registered or considered in the bankruptcy; no decision on them was needed.

The relevant framework also provided that courts must take such non-pursuability into account even if the debtor did not invoke it. A creditor could seek cancellation of a debt discharge within six years if the debtor lacked an honest aim, and enforcement could not be commenced or continued against estate assets.

The key alleged violation was therefore that final, enforceable judgments in the applicants’ favour were rendered unenforceable by operation of law following the debtor’s debt discharge, in proceedings to which they were not parties and through a decision with no appeal, leaving them without satisfaction or effective remedy.
001-224505:
**Case: Strassenmeyer v. Germany (Application no. 57818/18)**

The case concerned the applicant, Marco Straßenmeyer, a German national convicted of murder in 2016. The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention, namely whether his trial was fair and whether he had been able to examine witnesses against him.
