The central alleged violation was that his conviction was based largely on pre-trial statements made by co-accused who later refused to testify at trial. In addition, before police questioning, the accused persons were not informed of their right to court-appointed counsel.

The underlying offence dated back to 1994, when G. was killed in the Czech Republic. His body was found but not initially identified. In 2012, N. contacted the German police and said that F., who had died in 1994, had confessed involvement in killing a co-worker in the Czech Republic. In 2014, K., a former co-worker, was arrested. Before questioning, he was informed of his rights to remain silent and to consult a lawyer, but, because police used an outdated form, he was not told of his right to court-appointed counsel under Article 136 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. K. implicated the applicant as the killer.

The applicant was arrested the following day and received the same defective rights warning. He denied knowing the victim or going to the Czech Republic. Other accused persons, S. and V., were later questioned. V. gave a detailed statement describing the plan to drug G., drive him to the Czech Republic, and beat him. According to V., the applicant struck G. with a truncheon, later threw a rock at his head, and the body was burned. V. admitted assisting in moving the body. All accused were informed of their rights in the same manner, without the court-appointed counsel warning. After being brought before the investigating judge, they were assigned lawyers and made no further statements.

At trial before the Erfurt Regional Court, the applicant made only a statement about drug abuse; the co-accused exercised their right to remain silent. The Regional Court therefore heard police officers about the pre-trial interviews, over defence objections. It also heard witnesses N., L. and B., Czech police officers, and forensic experts. Experts contradicted parts of V.’s account, including his claim that G. had moved after being set on fire, and noted discrepancies about the distance from the cars. The defence requested a psychological expert opinion on V.’s veracity, but this was refused.

In June 2016, the Regional Court convicted the applicant and K. of murder and deprivation of liberty resulting in death; V. was convicted of murder, and S. was acquitted. The applicant received life imprisonment. The court relied heavily on V.’s pre-trial statement, finding it corroborated by K.’s statements and witness testimony. It admitted the statements despite the failure to inform the accused of their right to court-appointed counsel, citing the seriousness of the offence, the State’s strong prosecution interest, and the unintentional nature of the error. The court also noted that the accused had remained silent at trial and that no recordings of the police interviews existed.

The applicant appealed, arguing that his conviction rested primarily on untested pre-trial statements by co-accused whom he could not examine, and that the rights warning defect rendered the statements inadmissible. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal in 2018, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint. The alleged violations therefore arose from the use of untested co-accused statements as decisive evidence and the failure to inform the accused of the right to court-appointed counsel before police questioning.
001-224776:
In *Irodotou v. Cyprus* (Application no. 16783/20), the applicant, Mr Marios Irodotou, a Cypriot national born in 1964 and living in Paphos, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of private criminal proceedings brought against him, and under Article 13 about the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy. The Court gave notice only of those complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations began with a civil judgment of 18 June 2013, in which the District Court of Paphos ordered the applicant to pay EUR 300 monthly to the Cooperative Credit Company of Geroskipou and East Paphos until a debt plus interest was paid off. On 2 March 2015, Paphos Cooperative Savings Bank Ltd brought a private prosecution against him (case no. 1312/15) for failing to pay instalments due between 1 September 2013 and 1 January 2015.

On 3 April 2015 the applicant was notified of the case for the first time. He pleaded not guilty, and the hearing was set for 5 November 2015. From 5 November 2015 to 22 March 2017, the hearing was adjourned four times, mainly because the District Court lacked time to hear the case. On 28 September 2017, the prosecution notified a change of name after the bank transferred its assets and liabilities to Cooperative Central Bank Ltd, later renamed Cyprus Cooperative Bank Ltd. On 6 November 2017, the court again adjourned for lack of time. On 29 March 2018, the case was postponed at the applicant’s request for health reasons.

On 14 September 2018, the prosecution filed a second change of name, from Cyprus Cooperative Bank Ltd to Cooperative Asset Management Company Ltd. On 24 September 2018, a hearing was postponed because a prosecution witness was absent. On 15 November 2018, the applicant challenged whether the company could prosecute as a legal entity capable of operating as a credit institution, arguing that no counsel could appear for it and the criminal proceedings could not continue. The prosecution sought an adjournment, which was granted, and the case was rescheduled for 15 January 2019. Further adjournments followed on 15 January 2019, 26 March 2019, and 24 May 2019, largely by agreement or for procedural exchanges.

By letter of 5 September 2019, the prosecution applied to the Attorney General to discontinue the case. It explained that mergers had created an issue whether a non-existent prosecutor could initiate a prosecution, that a related Supreme Court decision was pending, that a similar case had ended in a prima facie acquittal at the pre-trial stage, and that continuation no longer served a purpose. It also feared that a dismissal could harm the merged credit institution’s rights in a future prosecution for unpaid instalments. On 23 September 2019, the Attorney General ordered discontinuance by granting a nolle prosequi. On 2 October 2019, the District Court informed the parties that the case was discontinued and the applicant discharged.

The applicant attempted to challenge the discontinuance, arguing that he had not been consulted by the Attorney General, that he had raised the capacity issue on 15 November 2018 but it remained unresolved because of repeated adjournments, that he could not claim losses or expenses, and that he had been treated unfairly after appearing in court for four and a half years. The court replied that discontinuance was an exclusive constitutional power of the Attorney General, not subject to judicial review, and that no discretion could be exercised as to substance, procedure, or costs. The case was closed without an order for costs against the applicant.
001-228167:
In *A.S. v. Italy* (Application no. 20860/20), judgment of 19 October 2023, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) examined an application lodged on 15 May 2020 by Mr A.S., a Tunisian national residing in Agrigento. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Brambilla, and the Italian Government was represented by Mr L. D’Ascia. The case concerned the applicant’s detention in the Italian hotspot at Contrada Imbriacola, on the island of Lampedusa, and the poor conditions of his stay there. The Lampedusa Early Reception and Aid Centre (CSPA) is one of Italy’s designated hotspots under section 17 of Decree-Law no. 13 of 17 February 2017.

The key facts are as follows. On 7 October 2019 the applicant reached the Italian coast aboard a makeshift vessel. On the following day, 8 October 2019, he was transferred to the hotspot at Lampedusa. He remained there until 25 October 2019. On 19 October 2019, while still in the hotspot, he expressed his wish to file an asylum request. On 25 October 2019 he was transferred to a reception centre in Agrigento and formally lodged his asylum request on the same date.

By decision of 29 October 2019, the Agrigento section of the Palermo Territorial Commission rejected the applicant’s asylum request as manifestly ill-founded. The decision was served on him on 2 November 2019. On that same date, he was served with an expulsion order issued by the Prefect of Agrigento, together with an order by the Agrigento police commissioner for his detention at the Caltanissetta Repatriation Detention Centre (CPR) for the time necessary to effect his repatriation.

On 5 November 2019, the Caltanissetta Justice of the Peace declined to approve the detention order for want of jurisdiction and referred the case to the Caltanissetta ordinary court. As a result, the applicant left the CPR. On 21 November 2019 he challenged the expulsion order before the Agrigento Justice of the Peace. By decision of 6 December 2019, the Agrigento Justice of the Peace revoked the expulsion order on procedural grounds.

The alleged violations before the Court centred primarily on the applicant’s stay in the Lampedusa hotspot from 8 to 25 October 2019. He complained that this amounted to a deprivation of liberty without a sufficient legal basis or adequate judicial review, contrary to Article 5 of the Convention. He also alleged that the material conditions in the hotspot were poor and amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The case therefore raised issues concerning Italy’s hotspot system, the de facto detention of migrants, and the reception conditions for persons arriving by sea before they can formally apply for international protection. The subsequent asylum rejection, expulsion order, and brief CPR detention provide context, but the core of the application concerns the lawfulness of the hotspot detention and the conditions there.
001-228673:
The case of *Kapitonov and Others v. Russia* concerns 26 applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights against Russia. The applications were introduced on various dates, primarily between 2017 and 2018. The core of the applicants' complaints revolves around what they allege were disproportionate measures taken against them by Russian authorities in response to their participation in or organization of public assemblies.

The facts, as detailed in the appended table, reveal a consistent pattern across the applications. The applicants were involved in a series of public events, predominantly in Moscow, St Petersburg, and Voronezh. These events were mostly political in nature, including manifestations against corruption (often linked to investigations concerning A. Navalnyy and D. Medvedev), in support of political prisoners and Ukraine, against the re-election of Mr Putin as President, and in support of free elections.

For their participation in these assemblies, the applicants faced administrative charges under the Russian Code of Administrative Offences (CAO). The most frequently cited charges were under Article 20.2, which penalizes violations of the established procedure for organizing or holding a public event. Specifically, they were charged under various parts of this article, including § 5 (failure to comply with the procedure), § 6.1, and § 8. Additionally, many applicants were charged under Article 19.3 § 1 of the CAO, which relates to disobedience of a lawful order by a police officer.

The penalties imposed on the applicants were varied and included both fines and administrative detention. The fines ranged significantly, from a low of RUB 500 to a high of RUB 250,000. Several applicants were also subjected to administrative detention, with sentences ranging from 2 to 17 days. For instance, in one of the larger applications (no. 71203/17), which grouped 11 applicants involved in an anti-corruption manifestation in Moscow on 26 March 2017, penalties included fines up to RUB 20,000 and up to 10 days of administrative detention for three of the applicants. Another applicant, Mr. Zheksimbayev (application no. 21998/18), received two separate sentences of 15 and 17 days of administrative detention for his role in a manifestation in St Petersburg.

These administrative sanctions were challenged in domestic courts, but the final decisions in each case were rendered by various regional city and regional courts, including the Moscow City Court, St Petersburg City Court, and Moscow and Voronezh Regional Courts, upholding the lower courts' rulings between 2016 and 2021. The applicants brought their case to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that these measures violated their rights under the Convention, specifically regarding the disproportionate interference with their freedom of assembly and expression.
001-222790:
The case of *Janáček v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 9634/17), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 2 February 2023, concerns an alleged breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention arising from the Czech Constitutional Court’s failure to communicate to the applicant written observations submitted by the general courts involved in his case.

The applicant, Ladislav Janáček, a Czech national born in 1957, was involved in proceedings concerning the division of matrimonial property with his former wife. On 17 December 2013, the Zlín District Court ruled on the division and ordered the applicant to pay substantial sums to his former wife. The case turned heavily on expert valuation evidence. The District Court relied on an expert, S., after other experts were unavailable or delayed. The applicant later submitted an expert opinion by expert M. The presiding judge then emailed expert S. directly for comments on that opinion, and S. responded the next day. The court preferred S.’s report.

On appeal, the Brno Regional Court partially altered the judgment on 24 March 2015, increasing the total amount the applicant was ordered to pay. It relied on expert S.’s opinion, heard S. and other experts, and rejected the applicant’s objections. The applicant’s subsequent appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 12 January 2016 as manifestly ill-founded. Execution proceedings followed, and the bailiff eventually ordered the sale of the applicant’s immovable property.

On 14 April 2016, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. He argued, inter alia, that the lower courts had relied solely on expert S. without sufficient justification, that the Regional Court had refused an alternative expert report, and that the courts’ formalistic approach had led to an incorrect division of property to his detriment. He invoked Article 11 and Article 36 § 1 of the Czech Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms, Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Constitutional Court invited the District Court, Regional Court, and Supreme Court to submit comments. In May 2016, those courts provided written observations. The Supreme Court explained why the appeal on points of law had been rejected as inadmissible. The District Court judge addressed, among other things, his direct email contact with expert S., explaining that he had approached S. only to speed up the proceedings and that he had not previously known him. A Regional Court judge also commented on expert S.’s appointment and valuation.

These written observations were not sent to the applicant. On 19 July 2016, after a written procedure and without an oral hearing, the Constitutional Court dismissed the constitutional complaint as manifestly ill-founded. The applicant’s representative only learned of the observations after inspecting the file following the decision. When the applicant asked why he had not been given an opportunity to respond, the Constitutional Court replied that, since the observations had not been sent to him, the judge rapporteur had probably considered that they contained no new information or legal arguments.

The alleged violation under Article 6 § 1 therefore concerns the lack of adversarial proceedings: the applicant was unable to familiarise himself with the general courts’ written observations or to comment on them before the Constitutional Court decided his complaint. Relevant domestic law, including the Constitutional Court Act, grants parties and joined parties the right to submit views and inspect the file, while evolving Constitutional Court practice following *Milatová* recommended communicating observations containing potentially new facts, allegations, or arguments.
001-222312:
Axel Springer SE, a Berlin-based publishing house, publishes the daily newspaper *Die Welt*. On 4 October 2013, *Die Welt* published an article headlined “The Stasi woman by Gregor Gysi’s side.” It concerned Ms K., executive director of the political party Die Linke, then chaired by Gregor Gysi. The article alleged that K. had been an agent for the former GDR Ministry of State Security (the Stasi) and discussed the post-1989 disappearance of billions in assets belonging to the SED, East Germany’s former Communist Party. It stated that K.’s name stood for a “particularly unsavoury chapter” in the party’s handling of SED assets; that at the end of 1989 the SED still possessed extensive holdings and 6.2 billion East German marks in cash; that secret bank accounts might exist; that there was no evidence K. was involved in possible criminal activities; but that, according to documents, she remained directly or indirectly involved with companies whose assets derived from the SED’s heritage. It named companies FEVAC and Vulkan, said K. held shares in them as a private individual, and noted that in 1995 the Berlin Higher Administrative Court found that two companies in which she held stakes managed PDS assets on a fiduciary basis. The article also linked K. to the “Association of Friends of the ND,” which allegedly promised large sums to save the party newspaper *Neues Deutschland*, and named her honorary chairwoman.

Two days before publication, Axel Springer sent K. questions, including about her membership in the Association of Friends of the ND. K. refused to answer. After publication, on 11 October 2013, K.’s lawyer demanded a rectification. K. asserted she had nothing to do with the disappearance of SED assets; that FEVAC and Vulkan were founded in 1992 with PDS money on the recommendation and with approval of the Treuhandanstalt; that she became a FEVAC shareholder only in 1998; and that she had joined the Association around 2000 and chaired it since 2002. She also said she had not been a member of the party’s Federal Arbitration Commission since 1 January 2013.

Axel Springer refused to publish the rectification. K. sought an injunction. The Berlin Regional Court initially dismissed her application, finding that the article did not make the alleged connection. K. appealed. On 18 November 2013, the Court of Appeal ordered Axel Springer to publish a rectification under section 10 of the Berlin Press Act. In the main proceedings, the Regional Court again dismissed K.’s application, but on 16 January 2014 the Court of Appeal again ordered publication, on page 8, while rejecting a front-page placement. It reasoned that although the article did not explicitly allege K. concealed SED assets, the average reader would infer such involvement; the statement that there was no evidence of criminal activity did not offset that implication. It found the rectification’s length and content were limited to what was necessary and that K.’s refusal to answer pre-publication questions did not remove her legitimate interest. The date on the rectification was not manifestly incorrect because the first request dated from 11 October 2013, even if later revised.

On 3 February 2014, Axel Springer published the rectification, adding an editor’s note that the information was correct and that the newspaper had no knowledge connecting K. to the disappearance of SED assets. On 14 August 2017, the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider Axel Springer’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons. Axel Springer applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 14 February 2018, alleging that the German courts’ order requiring publication of K.’s rectification violated its right to freedom of expression and press under Article 10 of the Convention. The key alleged violation is therefore the compulsory right-of-reply publication imposed on the newspaper.
001-224366:
This case concerns an Azerbaijani national, Shahla Abbasaliyeva, born in 1959, who complained under Article 8 of the European Convention that the domestic courts failed to protect her reputation and private life from newspaper articles. In August 2011 she was appointed head physician of the outpatient clinic of the Gazakh District Central Hospital. Her brother, Elchin Amiraslanov, had been head of the Gazakh regional OMON and was convicted in connection with the March 1995 attempted coup d’état. He was initially sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment.

Between 23 August and 10 September 2011, the newspaper Gündəlik Bakı published several articles about the applicant’s appointment. The articles identified her by her maiden name, Amiraslanova, and repeatedly linked her to her brother. Headlines and subtitles included “Relatives of the government’s enemies appointed to posts,” “The sister of an OMON member has become Gazakh’s head physician,” and “Shahla Amiraslanova is the sister of Elchin Amiraslanov, who participated in the coup d’état.” The articles stated that she had protested against and “maligned” the State authorities when her brother was detained, questioned how she had been appointed when there were eight candidates, and suggested that her appointment undermined State interests and reflected a perfunctory attitude towards protecting those interests. They also referred to the Health Minister and the head of the Gazakh District Executive Authority.

After the publications, on 12 September 2011, the head of the Gazakh District Executive Authority allegedly asked the applicant to resign. She refused. On the same day, she was dismissed from the head physician post and returned to her previous post as a physician. She brought proceedings against her employer seeking reinstatement and compensation. On 18 November 2011 the Gazakh District Court dismissed her claims, finding that labour legislation had been breached when she was appointed: no written contract had been concluded and the head physician post did not exist in the hospital’s staff schedule. The Ganja Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court dismissed her appeals in February and July 2012.

The applicant also asked the newspaper’s editor-in-chief to retract the articles, but he refused. In October 2011 she sued the editor and authors, seeking a retraction, an apology, and compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. She noted that she had used the surname Abbasaliyeva for twenty-six years after marriage. On 8 February 2012 the Yasamal District Court dismissed her claims. On 25 May 2012 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that judgment. It found as facts that the applicant’s maiden name was Amiraslanova, that her brother Elchin had been convicted, and that she had been appointed and later dismissed. It held that the opinions in the articles about her, her brother, and her appointment were value judgments with a sufficient factual basis, protected by the defendants’ freedom of expression and the right to criticise public officials, including doctors. It added that public officials, including doctors, should tolerate more criticism. It did not specify which opinions it considered value judgments. On 2 October 2012 the Supreme Court dismissed her cassation appeal, reiterating that reasoning.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that the domestic courts had failed to consider that the defendants abused their freedom of expression, violating her right to respect for private life. She claimed the articles exaggerated her appointment and portrayed it as treason by State officials because of her brother’s conviction, and that she was dismissed after publication. The application was lodged on 14 January 2013. The main alleged violation was therefore the State’s failure, under Article 8, to protect her reputation and private life in the civil defamation proceedings, while balancing the newspaper’s freedom of expression.
001-228151:
In *Luca v. the Republic of Moldova* (ECtHR, 17 October 2023), the applicant, Lilia Luca, alleged that Moldova failed to protect her from domestic violence and to support her contact with her children, relying on Articles 3, 8 and 14 of the Convention. She lived with A.I. as an unmarried couple in Italy, where their two children were born in 2006. A.I. returned with the children to Moldova in 2012; the applicant stayed in Italy to work and support the family, joining them in 2015.

According to the applicant, A.I. began psychologically and physically abusing her in October 2015. She reported physical violence on 13 July and 4 November 2016, plus verbal abuse, harassment, emotional abuse, attempts to turn the children against her, and utility disconnections. On 1 August 2016 she sought a protection order for herself and the children. On 2 August 2016 the Ialoveni District Court granted a 90-day order requiring A.I. to leave the common residence, avoid contact, and stay at least 50 metres away; this was upheld on appeal.

The applicant repeatedly complained to police and child protection services that A.I. violated the order. She said he moved into his sister’s part of the same house, that the children moved in with him on 22 August 2016, that he continued making negative statements about her, removed her belongings, and cut off water. She alleged authorities failed to monitor compliance. On 24 October 2016 police said her facts were unconfirmed; a prosecutor had refused criminal proceedings on 7 October 2016, treating the conflict as essentially civil/family.

She sought extension of the protection order. On 2 November 2016 the District Court refused, finding no evidence of non-compliance and describing the conflict as a family dispute without violence; the children lived with their father. Her appeal was dismissed on 24 January 2017. On 4 November 2016 A.I. physically assaulted her, causing bruises to her forehead, arms and buttocks and a concussion; she was hospitalised for eight days. Further protection requests in November 2016 and February 2017 were rejected. Courts found insufficient evidence, no imminent danger, doubted her credibility, and said she was using domestic-violence proceedings for divorce/custody or revenge; they also relied on the children’s wish to live with their father.

Criminal proceedings were opened in November 2016 for breach of the protection order and domestic violence. An earlier administrative fine against A.I. for the 13 July incident was quashed. In November 2019 A.I. was convicted on both counts, given a suspended sentence of two years and three months, and ordered to pay damages; this became final in 2021.

As to contact rights, while the protection order was in force, the children moved in with A.I. and stopped answering the applicant’s calls. On 15 September 2016 the child protection authority declined to set a contact schedule, based on the children’s statements that they preferred their father and refused their mother. A court ordered a schedule on 11 November 2016, and on 26 January 2017 a schedule was set for every second week. The applicant complained A.I. refused compliance; police replied that the children voluntarily refused. In May 2017, at a school visit, the children refused to speak to her or accept gifts. A working group was reportedly created in September 2017, but no records were provided. Divorce proceedings initiated by A.I. in July 2016 ended in 2018 with the children living with their father; the decision became final in 2022. A criminal complaint concerning psychological abuse of the children was discontinued in 2018 after expert reports found no trauma.

The alleged violations therefore concern Moldova’s failure to protect the applicant from domestic violence, enforce protection orders, investigate abuse effectively, and support her parental contact despite A.I.’s alleged interference and the children’s alienation.
001-225318:
In *Zajmi v. Albania* (Application no. 83907/17, judgment of 20 June 2023), the applicant, Ms Çetina Zajmi, an Albanian national born in 1957, had been convicted in criminal proceedings. On 13 March 2013 the Tirana District Court found her guilty of aggravated fraud and sentenced her to fourteen years’ imprisonment. Her appeal was dismissed by the Tirana Appeal Court on 8 November 2013, and the Supreme Court dismissed her further appeal on 25 May 2015. The criminal conviction therefore became final at the latest at that point.

The alleged violation arose from the subsequent constitutional-complaint procedure. On 8 November 2016, Law no. 99/2016 was published in the Official Journal. It shortened the time-limit for lodging a constitutional complaint from two years to four months “of obtaining knowledge of the interference [with a constitutional right or freedom]”. The new time-limit was to enter into force on 1 March 2017. This statutory change was central to the case.

On 27 February 2017—shortly before the new law entered into force—the applicant sent a constitutional complaint through a post office. On the envelope, she wrote the address as “Gj – K.SH, Tirané”. This was incomplete. The postal service did not deliver the mail because the recipient could not be identified. On an unspecified date, the applicant checked with the post office and learned that her complaint had not reached the Constitutional Court. She then re-sent the constitutional complaint on 22 May 2017 to the proper address of the Constitutional Court.

On 16 June 2017 the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s complaint inadmissible as being lodged outside the new four-month time-limit. The same day, the Constitutional Court adopted two separate decisions in the cases of *Pajova* (decision no. 157) and *Ibrahimi* (decision no. 152). In those decisions, it applied the newly introduced four-month time-limit to Supreme Court decisions adopted respectively on 7 May 2015 and 25 June 2015, counting the time-limit from the date of the Supreme Court’s adoption of those decisions. Those parallel decisions are relevant because they demonstrate how the Constitutional Court applied the shortened deadline to earlier final decisions, including decisions issued well before the new law entered into force.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the applicant’s final criminal conviction; the legislative reduction of the constitutional-complaint deadline from two years to four months; her attempt to lodge a constitutional complaint before the new law entered into force; the postal non-delivery caused by an incomplete address; her later re-submission on 22 May 2017; and the Constitutional Court’s refusal to examine the complaint as out of time on 16 June 2017. The applicant’s complaint before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the resulting restriction on her access to the Constitutional Court and/or her right to a fair hearing in the criminal case, in so far as the domestic court refused to consider her constitutional complaint on the merits. The case thus focuses on whether the application of the shortened time-limit, combined with the postal delivery problem, disproportionately and unforeseeably barred her from obtaining constitutional review.
001-224365:
In *Ohanjanyan v Armenia*, the applicant, Suren Ohanjanyan, complained under Article 2 of the Convention about the death of his son, T. Ohanjanyan, during compulsory military service and the alleged failure of the authorities to conduct an effective investigation.

T. Ohanjanyan was drafted in November 2006 and transferred in May 2007 to military unit no. 28418 in Gegharkunik. According to the official account, on 30 August 2007, after the evening roll-call, he left the armoury towards a backup checkpoint and accidentally touched the guy-wires of the antenna mast of an R-419 radio relay station belonging to nearby military unit no. 28233. He was allegedly electrocuted and died instantly. Junior Sergeant A.G. found him lying under the wires; A.G. also received an electric shock when he touched a wire. The body was taken to hospital and then to Yerevan for autopsy.

Military police recorded a 180-volt current in the guy-wire when the radio relay station was switched on. Criminal proceedings were opened for negligence in military duties. The autopsy concluded that death resulted from electrocution, citing electrical wounds on the neck, left wrist, fingers and right toe, plus other abrasions. The applicant disputed this account. He submitted photographs taken before autopsy allegedly showing injuries not recorded by the expert, including missing teeth, head, ear and jaw injuries, and burn marks. A serviceman, D.H., stated that the former unit commander had slapped T. Ohanjanyan; the commander denied it and was not prosecuted.

The investigation had significant problems relevant to Article 2. The scene was not properly inspected at night; the radio relay station was dismantled despite a prosecutor’s order to preserve it; the key guy-wire was examined 38 days later and showed no skin or blood traces; clothing was examined 56 days later. The initial electrical expert concluded in November 2007 that damaged insulation and lack of earthing had connected the mast and guy-wires to mains current, causing electrocution, and that the station had been operated in breach of technical requirements. However, the Ministry of Defence earlier said no electric current was possible there.

Two servicemen, R.A. and K.T., were charged. At trial, a court-ordered combined expert report in 2009 found that the station subframe operated at 27 volts and could not produce 180 volts. It could neither confirm nor reject electrocution. In January 2010 the Regional Court acquitted R.A. and K.T., citing conflicting electrical and medical evidence, procedural defects, failure to establish the exact time and circumstances, and the inconsistency that the same current killed T. Ohanjanyan but only lightly injured A.G. The acquittal was upheld on appeal and by the Court of Cassation.

Further investigation followed. Additional reports upheld the autopsy and confirmed that the station malfunction could not have supplied mains current. In 2016 a domestic court upheld the applicant’s complaint that the post-acquittal investigation was not effective, prompt or diligent, and had failed to address his photographs and alleged injuries. In 2018 the Criminal Court of Appeal found the suspension of proceedings deficient because the specific radio relay station had not been found or examined and other possible causes of death had not been adequately investigated. It concluded that the investigation was not effective within the meaning of Article 2. Nevertheless, by 2022 the investigation remained incomplete, repeatedly suspended and resumed. The applicant died in 2017, and his widow continued the application.
001-228357:
In *A.M.A. v. the Netherlands*, the applicant, a Bahraini national and Shiite Muslim, applied for asylum in the Netherlands in August 2017. He claimed membership in the opposition group “Barbar Revolutionary Youth,” wrote critical articles about the Bahraini regime, and feared persecution because his brother was a political activist who had fled to Germany. He alleged that after a group member was arrested and allegedly tortured, he fled Bahrain for Iran and later the Netherlands. His first asylum application was rejected as implausible and incoherent: the authorities found no evidence of his online activity, noted inconsistencies, considered it unlikely he was wanted given he left Bahrain legally with a valid passport, and found his fear based on his brother unsubstantiated. Judicial review was initially dismissed for late electronic filing; the Council of State quashed that decision, but the Regional Court again declared the review inadmissible in September 2018. The applicant did not further appeal.

In October 2018, removal preparations began. The applicant refused return to Bahrain, claiming he would be arrested immediately and was on a terrorism wanted list; he was willing to go to Iran or Georgia, but those options proved impossible. A detention order was issued. On 18 October, during a final return interview, he was told he could submit a new asylum application but that this would not automatically cancel his flight. He tried but failed to reach his lawyer.

On 19 October, his lawyer emailed him documents from his brother: copies in Arabic bearing the Bahraini Public Prosecutor’s letterhead. He submitted a subsequent asylum application that afternoon. On 20 October, he was transferred to Schiphol Airport and interviewed without a lawyer. He said he had just received the documents, that his name appeared and he was charged with participating in a terrorist organisation, and that the documents were a record of the questioning of someone who had named him. He could not explain how his brother had obtained the originals. At the end of the interview, an officer orally rejected the application, stating the documents were not original and were in Arabic, that there was no time, and refusing a one-week extension. A written decision the same day declared the subsequent application inadmissible because no new elements had been presented. It found the documents had no probative value as they were untranslated, not original, and of unexplained provenance, and concluded the application was merely intended to delay removal. The applicant was ordered to leave immediately. The decision and interview report were faxed to his previous lawyer, and objection and interim-relief remedies were available, but the applicant did not use them. He was expelled to Bahrain later that day.

After removal, he was immediately arrested and detained. His lawyer asked the Dutch authorities to set aside the removal and return him, citing a likely risk of torture; this was refused. His subsequent asylum application was formally rejected in February 2019. On 28 February 2019, he was convicted in Bahrain of possessing weapons and ammunition and participating in terrorist activities, sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine, and initially lost his nationality. He alleged he had been tortured to extract a confession, had an unfair trial, and faced poor detention conditions, restricted family and lawyer contact, and later participated in a hunger strike.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Articles 3 and 13 that the Dutch authorities had failed to sufficiently assess the risk of ill-treatment before expulsion, despite the late evidence, and that this risk materialised. He also alleged that he had no effective remedy to challenge the final risk assessment or the last-minute rejection before removal.
001-223361:
**Summary of *Mamasakhlisi and Others v. Georgia and Russia* (Applications nos. 29999/04 and 41424/04)**

This case before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerns applications lodged by Georgian nationals against Georgia and Russia, stemming from events in the disputed territory of Abkhazia. The applications allege multiple violations of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The first and third applicants, Mr. Levan Mamasakhlisi and Mr. Grigol Nanava, were arrested and tried by the de facto Abkhaz authorities. The second applicant, Ms. Dinara Mamasakhlisi, was the first applicant’s grandmother, complaining of a breach of family life.

**Key Facts:**

On 7 August 2001, an explosive device accidentally detonated in the first applicant's hands in Pitsunda, Abkhazia, causing severe injuries, including the loss of his right hand. He was subsequently detained by the de facto Abkhaz security forces. He alleges that during his detention and questioning, he was subjected to ill-treatment, including beatings, mock executions, and psychological torture, to coerce a confession. He was held incommunicado in a small, dark, unheated cell, denied adequate food and water, and provided with no medical care for his festering wounds for months. Despite his condition, he was convicted of high treason and sabotage by the Abkhaz Military Court on 15 February 2002, after a two-hour trial. The court-appointed lawyer remained silent, and he was ultimately sentenced to twelve years' imprisonment. He was released on humanitarian grounds on 14 February 2007. Subsequent medical examinations diagnosed him with post-traumatic stress disorder and major depression, consistent with his account of torture.

Similarly, the third applicant, Mr. Nanava, was arrested in June 2003 for illegally crossing the border into Abkhazia. He was accused of terrorism, allegedly beaten, and threatened with death to extract a confession. He was convicted and sentenced to six years’ imprisonment in September 2003, again without access to a lawyer of his choosing. He was denied medical care despite his advanced age and ill health. He was released in May 2005.

The applications, lodged in 2004, raised complaints under Articles 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman/degrading treatment), 5 (right to liberty and security), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for family life), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention, as well as Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 (right of appeal in criminal matters).

The applicants primarily blamed Russia for its role as the de facto controlling power in Abkhazia and Georgia for its failure to protect its citizens and investigate the crimes. A significant development was the Russian Federation's cessation of Council of Europe membership in March 2022, which led the Court to appoint an *ad hoc* judge to continue proceedings against it.
001-228992:
**Summary of A.T. and Others v. Italy (Application no. 47287/17)**

The case of *A.T. and Others v. Italy* concerns the detention and accommodation conditions of thirteen applicants in an Italian reception facility, or "hotspot," and raises issues under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and 5 (right to liberty and security) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The judgment was delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 23 November 2023.

The key facts are as follows: On 22 May 2017, the thirteen applicants, all young men claiming to be minors at the time, arrived on the Italian coast aboard a makeshift vessel. Their nationalities include Gambian, Guinean, Senegalese, Malian, Ivoirian, Bangladeshi, and Ghanian. Upon arrival, they alleged that they declared themselves to be minors. Despite these claims, they were transferred to the Taranto Early Reception and Aid Centre (CSPA), which had been designated as an Italian hotspot under Decree-Law no. 13 of 17 February 2017. While at the hotspot, their photographs and fingerprints were taken. The following day, on 23 May 2017, they formally requested international protection.

The core of the applicants' complaint centres on their confinement within this hotspot facility. They alleged that they were effectively detained there and that the conditions of their accommodation were poor and inadequate. They remained in this facility for a significant period. The situation changed only after they submitted a request to the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39 (interim measures). In response to this request, on 13 July 2017, applicants Mr I.C., Mr M.J., and Mr K.I.S. were transferred to facilities specifically for unaccompanied minors. Another applicant, Mr A.T., was transferred to a facility for minors on 15 July 2017.

Subsequent legal developments were inconsistent. According to information provided by the Italian Government, the Taranto Juvenile Court decided on 28 July 2017 that three of the applicants (I.C., M.J., and K.I.S.) should be taken into the care of social services and have a legal guardian appointed. However, no such information was provided regarding Mr A.T. It appears that the public prosecutor did not submit a request on his behalf because he had been transferred to a region outside the Taranto Juvenile Court's jurisdiction.

The applicants were represented by Mr D. Belluccio, and the Italian Government by Mr L. D’Ascia. The Court also received third-party interventions from several organizations, including Defence for Children International, the International Commission of Jurists (ICJ), the AIRE Centre, the European Council on Refugees and Exiles (ECRE), and the Dutch Council for Refugees.

The central factual allegation is that these individuals, who claimed to be minors and were therefore entitled to special protection, were held in a hotspot facility under conditions that amounted to a deprivation of liberty and constituted ill-treatment, before eventually being moved to more appropriate facilities for minors following the Court's intervention.
001-229134:
The case of *Tepljakov v. Estonia* (Application no. 10753/21) concerns an Estonian national, Mr Jevgeni Tepljakov, born in 1976. In a judgment delivered by the Third Section of the European Court of Human Rights on 28 November 2023, the Court considered complaints under Articles 3, 8 and 10 of the Convention. The Court gave notice of these complaints to the Estonian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The applicant was held in pre-trial detention in Pärnu Arrest House in several separate periods between August 2016 and December 2018. These periods ranged from 6 days to 100 days at a time, amounting to 345 days in total. The remainder of his pre-trial detention was spent in Tallinn Prison.

Regarding the alleged violation of Article 3, the applicant complained about the physical conditions of detention in Pärnu Arrest House. The domestic courts found several shortcomings: ventilation and access to natural light were insufficient; the toilet was not adequately separated from the rest of the cell, which he sometimes shared with other detainees; and he had no possibility to spend time outdoors because the arrest house had no outside yard. These factors were relevant to whether the detention conditions reached the severity threshold under Article 3.

As to Article 8, the applicant complained about restrictions on meetings with family members. The domestic courts found that, without any fault on the applicant’s part, the authorities had limited his family meetings to approximately ten minutes at a time. This was relevant to his complaint that the detention regime unjustifiably interfered with his family life.

Under Article 10, the applicant complained about lack of access to an online legal database. The first-instance court initiated constitutional review proceedings. By judgment no. 5-19-41 of 18 December 2019, the Supreme Court of Estonia declared unconstitutional part of section 31(3) of Regulation no. 21 of the Minister of the Interior on the Internal Rules of the Arrest House. That provision allowed detainees to access an online database containing legal acts and court judgments “in so far as the arrest house had technical conditions for it.” The Supreme Court found that this restriction interfered with the constitutional right to freely obtain information disseminated for public use. It noted that the clause left it entirely to each arrest house to decide whether to provide access to the legal database. However, section 311 of the Imprisonment Act, as in force at the relevant time, provided that remand prisoners had the right to access that database. The Supreme Court held that the Imprisonment Act did not authorise the minister to impose further restrictions on such access. The impugned restriction was therefore not based on law and was unconstitutional.

When assessing all the shortcomings in conjunction, the domestic courts awarded the applicant EUR 1,500 in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The applicant had claimed EUR 3,450 before the Tallinn Court of Appeal. Before the European Court, the applicant invoked complaints about the physical conditions of detention in Pärnu Arrest House, the restrictions on meetings with family members, and the lack of access to the online legal database.
001-224554:
In *Cetinja v. Croatia* (Application no. 6959/17), a judgment of 9 May 2023, the European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, examined a Croatian applicant’s complaint that he had been convicted and fined for a minor offence after it had become time-barred. The applicant, Aleksandar Cetinja, a Croatian national born in 1988 and living in Rijeka, lodged the application on 17 January 2017.

The underlying facts concerned an incident on 28 August 2011. After a physical altercation with another person, the applicant, who was under the influence of alcohol, was taken to a local police station at 4 a.m. to sober up. He remained in police custody until 9 a.m., when he was released. By judgment of 12 October 2011, the Delnice Minor Offences Court found him guilty of a minor offence of breach of public peace. It imposed a fine of 728 Croatian kunas (HRK), approximately 97 euros (EUR). The five hours spent in police custody were credited as one day of imprisonment, corresponding to HRK 300, which was deducted from the fine. The applicant was therefore ordered to pay HRK 428 (about EUR 57), plus HRK 150 (about EUR 20) for costs. He later paid these amounts on 11 January 2017, together with HRK 75 charged by the domestic payment agency FINA for compulsory execution, totaling HRK 645.63.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations arose from the subsequent proceedings and the statutory limitation issue. The applicant appealed on 31 October 2011. The High Minor Offences Court dismissed his appeal on 27 May 2015, more than three and a half years later. Its judgment was served on him on 8 March 2016, more than nine months after it was adopted and more than four and a half years after the offence.

The applicant argued that the Minor Offences Act applicable at the time provided for a two-year relative prescription period and a four-year absolute prescription period, both running from the commission of the offence. The relative period could be interrupted only by an action of the relevant authority in relation to the minor offence. If interrupted, it began to run anew. He contended that the High Minor Offences Court’s failure to take any action for three and a half years meant the minor offence had become time-barred under the relative prescription rule. He relied on Supreme Court case-law and a Constitutional Court decision. He also argued that the inordinate delay in serving the High Court’s judgment suggested the judgment had been backdated to comply with the four-year absolute prescription period.

On 13 July 2016, the Constitutional Court declared his constitutional complaint inadmissible, without addressing his arguments, holding that the case did not raise a constitutional issue. That decision was served on his representative on 18 July 2016.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that he had been convicted of a minor offence and ordered to pay a fine even though the offence had become time-barred. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning property, fairness of the proceedings, and the principle of *nullum crimen sine lege*; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The central alleged violation was therefore that the domestic authorities penalized him despite the expiry of the statutory limitation period, and that the delayed proceedings and service undermined the fairness and legality of that conviction and the resulting fine.
001-222920:
In *Lobchuk and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 36871/20 and six others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 9 February 2023. Seven applicants complained under Article 34 ECHR about inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. Applicant Lobchuk also raised other Convention complaints. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications.

The appended table sets out the key facts relevant to the alleged violations. Gennadiy Lobchuk (b. 1975) was held at Dnipro Penitentiary Facility No. 89 from 23 June 2014 to 28 December 2021—7 years, 6 months and 6 days—with only 1–2 m² per inmate. He alleged poor food quality due to his gallstone disease, lack of fresh air, insufficient natural light, inadequate hygienic facilities, restricted showers, insufficient outdoor exercise, no toilet privacy, inadequate temperature, insufficient electric light, and overcrowding.

Oleksandr Kanivets (b. 1988) was held at Dnipro Penitentiary Facility No. 4 from 24 June 2019 and remained there at filing—over 3 years, 5 months and 20 days—with 2.5–4 m² per inmate. He complained of lack of fresh air, insufficient electric light, poor bedding and linen, lack of toiletries, insufficient food, restricted potable water and showers, poor food quality, and overcrowding.

Oleksandr Millyer (b. 1978) was in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 17 October 2019 to 28 October 2021 (2 years and 12 days), with 1.91 m² per inmate. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient natural light, and poor or insufficient food.

Yevgeniy Svyntsov (b. 1983) was in the same Cherkasy facility from 25 January 2019 to 30 August 2021 (2 years, 7 months and 6 days), with under 3.3 m² per inmate. He complained of overcrowding, lack of fresh air, and insufficient or poor food.

Mark Chaus (b. 1974) was held at Poltava Penitentiary Facility from 8 August 2019 to 12 February 2021 (1 year, 6 months and 5 days), with 2.42 m² per inmate. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, no toilet privacy, lack of toiletries, and restricted showers.

Maksym Glyebov (b. 1981) was in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 15 October 2018 to 17 March 2021 (2 years, 5 months and 3 days), with 2.9–7.9 m² per inmate. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient electric and natural light, insufficient outdoor exercise, poor bedding, no toilet privacy, lack of toiletries, insufficient or poor food, a mouldy or dirty cell, restricted potable water, and restricted showers.

Vyacheslav Podvarchan (b. 1972) was held at Romny Detention Facility No. 56 from 17 November 2004 to 3 February 2021—16 years, 2 months and 18 days—with 3.9 m² per inmate. He raised similar complaints: overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient electric and natural light, insufficient outdoor exercise, poor bedding, no toilet privacy, lack of toiletries, insufficient or poor food, a mouldy or dirty cell, restricted potable water, and restricted showers.

The applications were introduced between 20 July 2020 and 2 August 2021. The common allegations concern prolonged detention in overcrowded or materially inadequate facilities, with insufficient space, ventilation, lighting, hygiene, food, water, and exercise, and no effective remedy in domestic law. The excerpt records the procedure and facts but not the Court’s final findings.
001-228118:
**Summary of *Dimaksyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 29906/14)**

The case concerns the death of the applicant’s 18-year-old son, M. Dimaksyan, during compulsory military service in the Armenian army, and the subsequent investigation. The applicant, Mr Aleksandr Dimaksyan, lodged the application against Armenia under Articles 2 (right to life) and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

**Key Facts:**

In November 2010, M. Dimaksyan was drafted and assigned to a military unit of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces. On 5 February 2012, while on watch duty at a base near Hadrut, he was shot and killed by a fellow serviceman, G.A. The incident allegedly occurred when G.A.’s assault rifle discharged unintentionally. A criminal investigation was immediately initiated.

The investigation established that on the evening of the incident, G.A. and M. Dimaksyan responded to a noise. G.A. loaded his rifle out of fear. Later, while repositioning, G.A. failed to close the rifle’s trigger guard despite M. Dimaksyan reminding him it was loaded. As G.A. moved, his finger touched the trigger, causing an accidental discharge that fatally wounded M. Dimaksyan. The forensic report confirmed death from a gunshot wound but also noted non-fatal blunt-force injuries on the body (e.g., bruising to the head), which the investigation did not explain.

Critically, an internal military investigation found significant shortcomings: forged safety-training signatures for G.A., poor supervision by commanding officers, and technical failure of the military medical vehicle during the emergency transport of the wounded soldier. The report concluded the death resulted from poor supervision by battalion administration. Disciplinary penalties were reportedly imposed on six officers, though no documents were submitted.

G.A. was charged with breaching weapon-handling rules causing death by negligence. He pleaded guilty. In April 2013, the Regional Court convicted him and sentenced him to four years and six months’ imprisonment. The court’s judgment focused only on G.A.’s actions and did not address the responsibility of the military command for the systemic failures identified, nor did it investigate the unexplained injuries, the delay in medical evacuation, or whether the broken-down vehicle contributed to the death.

The applicant, as the victim’s legal successor, appealed, arguing he could not fully participate (trial held in Stepanakert), and that the courts failed to examine the command’s responsibility and other critical circumstances. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, stating the first-instance court had fully assessed the arguments. The Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible in September 2013.

**Alleged Violations:**

The applicant complained that the State failed to protect his son’s life (Article 2), that the investigation into the death was inadequate (Article 2), and that he had no possibility to claim compensation for non-pecuniary damage from the State (Article 13). The case raises issues regarding the State’s positive obligation to safeguard the lives of conscripts, the effectiveness of investigations into deaths in military service, and the availability of effective remedies for such violations.
001-223259:
In *Halet v. Luxembourg*, Raphaël Halet, a French national born in 1976, worked for PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) in Luxembourg. PwC provided auditing, tax advice, and consultancy services, including preparing tax returns and obtaining Advance Tax Agreements (ATAs), also called tax rulings, from Luxembourg tax authorities. Halet coordinated a five-person team, although the Government disputed this description and characterized his role as administrative.

Between 2012 and 2014, several hundred ATAs and tax returns prepared by PwC were published, revealing advantageous tax agreements between PwC, multinational clients, and Luxembourg tax authorities. An earlier leak came from auditor A.D., who copied 45,000 pages of documents in October 2010 and gave them to journalist E.P. in 2011. These documents were used in a May 2012 *Cash Investigation* programme.

After that first programme, Halet contacted E.P. in May 2012 and offered further documents. Between October and December 2012, he transferred sixteen documents: fourteen tax returns and two covering letters. Some were used in a second *Cash Investigation* programme in June 2013. In November 2014, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists posted the sixteen documents online as part of “LuxLeaks.” PwC’s internal investigation identified Halet. PwC and Halet entered a settlement in December 2014, under which PwC limited its claim to one euro and registered a €10 million mortgage on his assets. Halet was dismissed.

Following PwC’s complaint, Halet, A.D., and E.P. were prosecuted. In June 2016, the Luxembourg District Court convicted Halet of theft from his employer, fraudulent access to a data-processing system, breach of commercial secrecy, breach of professional secrecy, and laundering/possession. He received a nine-month suspended prison sentence and a €1,000 fine. On appeal in March 2017, the Court of Appeal upheld convictions for theft, fraudulent access/retention, breach of professional secrecy, and laundering, but set aside commercial secrecy. It accepted that the LuxLeaks disclosures concerned a public-interest debate on multinational taxation, tax transparency, and ATAs, and that the documents were authentic.

However, the Court of Appeal refused Halet full whistle-blower protection under Article 10 of the Convention. It found his sixteen documents were of limited relevance: they did not provide essential new information, did not significantly contribute to the already ongoing public debate, and caused reputational and client-confidence damage to PwC. It also noted that the ATA practice had already been exposed through A.D.’s earlier disclosures. Nevertheless, it recognized mitigating circumstances—honourable motive, disinterested action, and no prior criminal record—and imposed only a fine, dispensing with prison.

In January 2018, the Court of Cassation dismissed Halet’s appeal, holding that the whistle-blower assessment fell to the lower courts and was sufficiently reasoned. Halet applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 7 May 2018. He alleged that his criminal conviction for disclosing sixteen documents covered by professional secrecy to a journalist amounted to a disproportionate interference with his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The Grand Chamber granted referral and held a hearing in February 2022. The central issue was whether Luxembourg’s criminal conviction and refusal to grant whistle-blower protection struck a fair balance between professional secrecy and PwC’s interests, on one hand, and Halet’s right to impart information in the public interest, on the other.
001-225329:
**X and Others v. Ireland** (Applications nos. 23851/20 and 24360/20) concerns two challenges to Ireland’s child benefit rules. The applicants alleged that the domestic requirement that a parent be “habitually resident”—which, under section 246(5) of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, excludes anyone without a right to reside in Ireland—discriminates against claimants who are lawfully present in the State but have not yet been granted, or recognised as having, a right to reside. They relied on Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, read with Article 14.

In the first application, X, a Nigerian national, arrived in Ireland in November 2013 and applied for asylum. Her daughter E was born in December 2014 and is an Irish citizen through her father. X and E lived in Ireland’s “direct provision” system for asylum seekers. In September 2015, X applied for residence as the mother of an Irish citizen child. In October 2015, while that application was pending, she applied for child benefit for E. The application was refused in November 2015 because she did not satisfy the habitual residence condition, as she had no right to reside. X was granted a right to reside in January 2016 and thereafter received child benefit. Her domestic claim was limited to the period from E’s birth to the grant of residence, just over twelve months. She argued that E’s Irish citizenship, under the Zambrano case-law of the CJEU, entitled her to benefit from E’s birth.

In the second application, Y, an Afghan national, arrived in Ireland in May 2008 with her husband and first child and applied for asylum, living in direct provision. Her son M was born in April 2013. The family initially used false Pakistani identity documents; their asylum claim was rejected and removal orders were issued in 2012. After establishing their true nationality, they applied again. M was granted asylum in December 2014, communicated in January 2015. The other family members applied for family reunification. While that was pending, Y applied in February 2015 for child benefit for her four children. It was refused in April 2015 because she did not meet the habitual residence condition. Family reunification was granted in September 2015, and child benefit was then paid from that date. Her claim was limited to the eight-month period between M’s asylum grant and the family reunification decision. Y argued that recognition of refugee status declared an already existing status, so entitlement should begin when M was granted asylum, relying on Article 28 of the EU Qualification Directive.

The High Court rejected both claims, holding that child benefit vested in the “qualified person” parent rather than the child, and that the habitual residence rule was generally applied and justified. The Court of Appeal allowed X and E’s appeal, finding that excluding a resident Irish citizen child from a universal child benefit because of her mother’s immigration status breached constitutional equality, but rejected Y and M’s claim. The Supreme Court reversed, holding that child benefit is payable to the qualified person, not the child; the habitual residence requirement applied neutrally to claimants; any indirect effect on the children was justified by the State’s interest in regulating migration and residence; and no discrimination or breach of Article 28 of the Qualification Directive arose. The ECtHR case accordingly concerns whether that regime, as applied to these applicants, violated Article 14 read with Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-229726:
The applicants are four German nationals—Karin Humpert, Kerstin Wienrank, Eberhard Grabs and Monika Dahl—who were State school teachers with civil servant status employed by different German Länder. They were members of the Trade Union for Education and Science and participated, during working hours, in strikes and a demonstration organised by that union to protest worsening working conditions for teachers. They were subsequently reprimanded or fined in disciplinary proceedings for breaching their duties as civil servants. On 10 December 2018 they lodged applications against Germany, complaining in particular about those disciplinary measures and about the prohibition on strikes by civil servants, which they considered incompatible with their right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention.

The individual measures were as follows. Ms Humpert, a primary school teacher, was reprimanded by the Schleswig-Holstein Ministry for Education and Culture on 5 July 2011 for participating in a strike on 3 June 2010 and not teaching one lesson; it was later found she had missed two classes. Ms Wienrank, a vocational school teacher, and Mr Grabs, a secondary school teacher, were each fined EUR 100 by the Lower Saxony School Authority on 10 and 11 January 2011 respectively for unauthorised absence during a strike on 25 February 2009, when they did not give about five lessons each. The strike aimed, among other things, at securing a collective agreement for contractual State employees in the public educational sector and transferring its results to civil servants. Ms Dahl, a secondary school teacher, was fined EUR 1,500 by the Cologne District Government on 10 May 2010 for unauthorised absence during 12 lessons because of her participation in strikes on 28 January and 5 and 10 February 2009; those strikes had the same aims.

The applicants’ actions in the administrative courts were unsuccessful. The administrative courts found that they had breached their professional duties by participating in strikes. They considered that the traditional principles of the career civil service under Article 33 § 5 of the Basic Law restricted civil servants’ freedom of association under Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law through a prohibition on strike action. At first instance, the Schleswig-Holstein, Stade and Osnabrück Administrative Courts upheld the decisions against the first, second and third applicants by judgments of 8 August 2012, 6 December 2012 and 19 August 2011 respectively. The Düsseldorf Administrative Court, by judgment of 15 December 2010, initially considered that the employing State entity had to avoid a breach of Article 11 by discontinuing proceedings against the fourth applicant. On appeal, the Lower Saxony Administrative Court of Appeal, in a judgment of 12 June 2012 in the third applicant’s case, found the prohibition on strikes by civil servants part of the essence of Article 33 §§ 4 and 5 of the Basic Law and not alterable by interpretation in line with Article 11. On 16 May 2013 it rejected the second applicant’s request for leave to appeal by reference to that judgment. In the fourth applicant’s case, the North Rhine-Westphalia Court of Appeal overturned the first-instance judgment on 7 March 2012. On 27 February 2014 the Federal Administrative Court found the disciplinary decision against her lawful, though the fine should have been EUR 300; it considered that Article 33 § 5 could not be interpreted in a Convention-compliant manner and that the legislature had to resolve the conflict. The Schleswig-Holstein Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the first applicant’s appeal on 29 September 2014, and on 26 February 2015 the Federal Administrative Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicants lodged separate constitutional complaints, arguing that the decisions breached Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and that the administrative courts had failed to interpret national law in line with public international law, because the prohibition on strikes by teachers with civil servant status who did not exercise core public authority violated Article 11. On 12 June 2018 the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the complaints (file nos. 2 BvR 1738/12 and others). It found no violation of Article 9 § 3 of the Basic Law and considered the prohibition on strikes by civil servants compatible with Article 11, based on the traditional principles of the career civil service under Article 33 § 5, and serving a functioning public administration and the State’s educational mandate.
001-227718:
**Case: Efgan Çetin and Others v. Türkiye (Application no. 14684/18)**

The case concerned five Turkish nationals—Efgan Çetin, Şermin Çetin, Ayşe Çetin, Hasanali Çetin, and Şerife Yıldız—who lived near planned geothermal energy plants in Aydın. The first applicant owned an olive grove; the remaining applicants lived in the vicinity. Their complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention arose from their inability to obtain judicial review of an administrative decision that no environmental impact assessment (“EIA”) was required for a geothermal plant near their property and homes.

In 2012, the Aydın Governorship issued an EIA non-requirement decision dated 10 January 2012 for a private geothermal plant. A group of claimants, including the applicants, challenged that decision before the Aydın Administrative Court. During an on-site inspection on 27 March 2015 relating to that first plant, the parties noticed a second geothermal plant under construction nearby. The applicants and Government later accepted that this date could be treated as the point when the applicants learned of the second plant.

On 6 May 2015, some other claimants—not the applicants—submitted a freedom-of-information request asking whether the second plant had undergone an EIA procedure. On 18 May 2015, the Governor’s Office replied that on 24 July 2014 it had issued an EIA non-requirement decision for that second plant as well. On 19 June 2015, the applicants brought an administrative action challenging the 24 July 2014 decision. They argued that geothermal energy, although renewable, was not exempt from EIA requirements because such projects could cause chemical pollution, water-quality deterioration, and harm to health and the environment.

The Administrative Court ordered an on-site inspection and expert examination. The expert report of 18 December 2015 found that the project file complied procedurally but lacked scientific, technical, and legislative detail. Experts stated that energy generation could adversely affect flora, fauna, and air quality; gas emissions could pollute the environment and affect human and animal health; olive groves had already suffered irreversible damage; no alternative-site survey had been conducted; and construction had begun without required permits and before the EIA non-requirement decision. By the inspection date, construction was virtually complete.

Nevertheless, on 26 February 2016 the Aydın Administrative Court dismissed the claim as out of time. It held that the thirty-day fast-track period began on 27 March 2015, when the applicants became aware of the second plant during the earlier inspection. It noted there was no proof the EIA decision had been notified, but found that construction was nearly complete by March 2015 and that the applicants’ claim of learning only later was improbable. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the dismissal on 17 November 2016, observing that the administration had not shown the EIA decision was publicly announced as required, but agreeing that the applicants knew by 27 March 2015 and that their June 2015 claim was late.

The applicants complained to the Turkish Constitutional Court that the domestic courts’ formalistic time-limit interpretation breached their right of access to a court. They also relied on the expert report to complain about risks to life, health, home, and their right to a healthy environment, and about not being informed of the plant decisions. On 1 November 2017, the Constitutional Court declared the applications inadmissible: the access-to-court complaint was manifestly ill-founded; the healthy-environment complaint was incompatible ratione materiae; and the private/family-life and home complaints were inadmissible for failure to exhaust remedies.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key alleged violations were therefore the inability to access a court to challenge the EIA non-requirement decision and the failure to protect the applicants’ private lives, homes, and environmental surroundings. The central disputed fact was when the applicants should be deemed to have learned of the second EIA non-requirement decision, and whether the strict thirty-day deadline improperly barred their challenge.
001-222775:
**Summary of Karantalis v. Greece (Application no. 67398/14)**

In *Karantalis v. Greece*, a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered on 31 January 2023, the applicant was Mr Panagiotis Karantalis, a Greek national born in 1973. He was represented by Mr I. Papanastasopoulos. The application was lodged against the Hellenic Republic on 9 October 2014 under Article 34 of the Convention. The case concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically the right of access to a court.

The facts arose from criminal proceedings initiated by the applicant against a lawyer, Mr P.P. The applicant accused the lawyer of infringing Law no. 2472/1997 on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data. The applicant joined the proceedings as a civil party before the Patras Court of Appeal for Misdemeanours, which acted as a first-instance court. By judgment no. 678a-837 of 29 April 2013, the court acquitted Mr P.P.

No ordinary appeal was lodged against the acquittal. The judgment became final and was registered on 22 July 2013 in a special book kept at the Registry of the court. On 30 July 2013, the applicant asked the prosecutor at the Court of Cassation to lodge an appeal on points of law against the acquittal under Article 505 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He argued that the first-instance court had wrongly interpreted or applied Law no. 2472/1997. The prosecutor subsequently lodged an appeal on points of law before the Court of Cassation on 3 September 2013, relying on the same grounds of incorrect interpretation and application of the relevant provisions of that law.

The Court of Cassation heard the case on 11 March 2014. By judgment no. 528 of 11 April 2014, it declared the appeal on points of law inadmissible as having been lodged out of time. The Court of Cassation held that, under Article 473 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, because the impugned judgment was subject to an ordinary appeal, the thirty-day time-limit for lodging an appeal on points of law ran from the date of delivery of the judgment—29 April 2013—and not from the date of its registration in the special book at the Registry, which occurred on 22 July 2013. It reasoned that registration had no legal effect in the present case because the first-instance judgment was subject to an ordinary appeal. By contrast, if the impugned judgment had not been subject to an appeal, or if it had been given on appeal, the thirty-day time-limit would have run from the date of registration.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the Court of Cassation’s dismissal of the appeal on points of law lodged at his request as out of time violated his right of access to a court. The central issue was whether the domestic court’s calculation of the procedural time-limit—running from delivery rather than registration—improperly restricted his ability to have the merits of his appeal reviewed. The applicant had participated in the criminal proceedings only as a civil party, and his request to the prosecutor was made shortly after the judgment was registered. Nevertheless, the Court of Cassation treated the subsequent appeal as time-barred based on the earlier delivery date. The case therefore focused on the compatibility of that procedural interpretation with the applicant’s Article 6 § 1 right of access to a court.
001-223435:
**Summary of *Georgiou v. Greece* (Application no. 57378/18)**

The case of *Georgiou v. Greece* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) by Mr. Andreas Georgiou, a Greek national and former president of the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT). The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically arising from the Greek Court of Cassation's failure to provide reasoning for its tacit refusal to seek a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) during criminal proceedings against him.

The applicant served as ELSTAT president from August 2010 to August 2015. On 10 November 2010, he transmitted revised data on Greece's 2009 fiscal deficit to Eurostat without first presenting it for approval to ELSTAT's seven-member administrative board. He claimed this action complied with the principle of professional independence under the European Statistics Code of Practice, particularly Principle 1.4, which grants the head of a national statistical authority "sole responsibility" for decisions on statistical releases.

Criminal proceedings were subsequently initiated against the applicant for breach of duty.
