On 6 December 2016, the Athens Criminal Court acquitted him of all three charges: (i) breach of the duty of full and exclusive employment with ELSTAT due to his concurrent position at the International Monetary Fund; (ii) breach of the duty to convene ELSTAT's board from November 2010 to September 2011; and (iii) breach of duty for releasing the 2009 fiscal deficit data without communicating it to or obtaining consent from ELSTAT's administrative board.

The prosecutor appealed. On 1 August 2017, the Athens Court of Appeal overturned the acquittal in part, finding the applicant guilty of the third charge—breach of duty—and sentenced him to two years' imprisonment, suspended. The appellate court determined that he had transmitted the data to Eurostat without ELSTAT's consent, in violation of Article 10 § 2 A of Law no. 3832/2010. It found he acted intentionally to gain an illegal moral benefit by strengthening his power as president and effectively usurping the board's powers.

The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. In a memorandum dated 21 March 2018, he explicitly requested that the Court of Cassation seek a preliminary ruling from the CJEU under Article 267 TFEU regarding the correct interpretation of Principle 1.4 of the European Statistics Code of Practice. He argued that without such a reference, his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 would be violated. On 7 June 2018, the Court of Cassation rejected his appeal (judgment no. 977/2018) without any reference to or reasoning regarding his preliminary ruling request.

The ECtHR noted that the relevant domestic and EU legal framework is described in prior judgments, including *Gorou v. Greece (no. 2)*, *Baydar v. the Netherlands*, and *Ilias Papageorgiou v. Greece*. Principle 1.4 of the European Statistics Code of Practice states that heads of national statistical institutes have "sole responsibility" for deciding on statistical methods and the content and timing of statistical releases.

The key issue before the ECtHR was whether the Court of Cassation's tacit refusal of the applicant's request for a preliminary ruling, without any reasoning, violated his right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court declared the remainder of the application inadmissible and gave notice to the Greek Government solely on this complaint.
001-224732:
**Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V. v. the Netherlands (Application no. 2799/16)** concerns a Dutch waste-collection company operating in the Rotterdam port region. In late 2006, the VROM-IOD, a special investigative service acting under the public prosecutor’s authority, began a criminal investigation codenamed “Toto” into another ship-waste collector, I. company, suspected of illegally disposing of polluted waste. An investigating judge authorised telephone interceptions. Some intercepted calls were between an I. company employee and an employee of the applicant company; they contained indications of price-fixing.

In April 2008, a VROM-IOD official recorded those indications in an official report and annexed summary transcripts. In October 2008, the public prosecutor authorised transmission of the report and annexes to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG), simply adding “transmission to NMA approved” by hand. The transmission occurred in June 2009. Further transcripts and audio files were transmitted in 2009 and 2010, after contacts between VROM-IOD and NMA officials about which data might be relevant to a price-fixing investigation. In June 2010, NMA inspectors visited the applicant’s premises, questioned management under caution, and played an intercepted telephone recording.

The NMA concluded that between August 2005 and July 2007 several companies, including the applicant, had coordinated behaviour to allocate contracts and limit price competition in ship-generated waste collection, contrary to section 6 of the Competition Act. In November 2011, the NMA fined the applicant EUR 834,000. The applicant objected, arguing that the intercepted conversations were not “criminal data” transferable under the WJSG because they were irrelevant to the criminal investigation, and that there had been no prior judicial control over the transmission.

The Rotterdam Regional Court held in 2013 that the data did qualify as criminal data but that the public prosecutor had failed to record a reviewable weighing of interests; the handwritten and pre-printed permissions contained no reasoning. It therefore excluded the transcripts as evidence and quashed the NMA decisions, since the NMA had relied mainly on that evidence. The ACM, successor to the NMA, appealed. In 2015, the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed that judgment. It held that the intercepted data fell within the broad definition of criminal data, including potential “by-catch” stored and processed digitally. The transmission could serve a “compelling general interest,” namely the economic well-being of the country. Written reasoning at the time of transmission was not required, and safeguards existed through later civil review of the transmission and administrative review of the fine. It found no violation of Article 8 ECHR: the interceptions had been judicially authorised, the transfer was statutorily grounded, and it was necessary and proportionate. The fact that the ACM itself could not intercept calls did not make use of the data unlawful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention that the transmission of the data to, and their use by, the Competition Authority had not been foreseeable and that procedural safeguards were insufficient. The key alleged violations therefore concern privacy and effective remedy: whether transferring lawfully intercepted criminal-investigation data to a competition authority for administrative fining was sufficiently foreseeable, whether adequate prior judicial control or reasoning existed, and whether domestic remedies provided effective protection. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 April 2025.
001-229125:
**Beltsios v. Greece (Application no. 57333/14)** concerns two alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights: the presumption of innocence under **Article 6 § 2** and the right to a “speedy” review of pre-trial detention under **Article 5 § 4**. The applicant, Ioannis Beltsios, a Greek national born in 1951, lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 29 July 2014.

The case arose from large-scale submarine procurement and repair contracts. In 2000, Hellenic Shipyards signed a contract with German consortium H.-F. for submarines worth over EUR 1.3 billion; in 2002, another contract for submarine repairs exceeded EUR 820 million. After German authorities investigated corruption, Greek criminal proceedings were opened on 30 October 2010 against 41 persons, including the applicant. In 2011, following a preliminary investigation, proceedings were instituted against Beltsios and others. He was accused of unlawfully assisting the German company to obtain the submarine contracts by promising and transferring money to former Defence Minister A.T. and top managers of Hellenic Shipyards. He was also accused of concealing the origin of over EUR 52 million and CHF 2.9 million, and of receiving and transferring those sums as proceeds of corruption.

On 29 September 2011 the criminal file was transferred to an Investigating Judge. The applicant was placed in preliminary detention on 13 January 2014, confirmed on 18 January 2014. On 23 January 2014 he lodged a recourse against the pre-trial detention, seeking replacement by other preventive measures. The prosecutor submitted a proposal to dismiss the recourse on 7 April 2014. The Indictment Division of the Athens Criminal Court of First Instance met on 27 May 2014 and, by order no. 1821/2014 published on 6 June 2014, rejected his recourse. On 10 July 2014, by order no. 2369/2014, his detention was extended for six months, until 13 January 2015. He remained detained until 27 March 2015, when his detention was replaced by preventive measures in connection with his referral to trial. These facts formed the basis of his Article 5 § 4 complaint that the authorities failed to decide “speedily” on his release application.

The Article 6 § 2 complaint concerned separate criminal proceedings against former Minister A.T. and eighteen co-accused, in which the applicant was not a defendant. On 7 October 2013, the three-member Athens Criminal Court convicted A.T. as charged. In its judgment, the court referred to the applicant as a member of a team used by German company F., a close associate and friend of A.T., and a former General Secretary at the Ministry of Interior. It stated that he had received bribe payments on behalf of A.T., had entered consulting contracts with company F. that concealed illegal transactions, and had received other bribes for A.T. The applicant later argued that these findings violated his presumption of innocence because they accepted his guilt before his own trial.

On 23 January 2019, the Athens Criminal Court convicted the applicant of aiding and abetting passive bribery of A.T. involving EUR 1,000,000, sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment, and rejected his objection of nullity based on the alleged breach of the presumption of innocence. He was acquitted of active bribery and money laundering. In 2021, the five-member Athens Court of Appeal allowed his appeal and held that the limitation period had expired, meaning he could no longer be prosecuted. The ECtHR examined whether the statements in the A.T. judgment and the delay in reviewing his detention violated Article 6 § 2 and Article 5 § 4 respectively.
001-223027:
**Y v. France (Application no. 76888/17), European Court of Human Rights, 31 January 2023**

The applicant, a French national born in 1951, is an intersex individual whose birth certificate records him as “male.” Medically, his intersex status was established shortly after birth: he has ambiguous external genitalia, no gonads, neither testicles nor ovaries, and his body has never produced sex hormones. He did not develop male or female secondary sex characteristics or go through puberty. Although he has a male XY karyotype, medical certificates describe “intersex formation” and “clear intersexuality” of the external genitalia. At age 21 he was perceived socially as female; at around 40 he was prescribed testosterone as part of a male administrative assignment, which caused a beard and voice change. He describes this forced alteration as a violation of bodily integrity and a trauma.

The applicant also says he is psychologically and socially intersex. His psychotherapist stated that he had long been forced to “pretend to be a man” and lacked a legal identity reflecting who he is. He is married and has an adopted child.

In January 2015, the applicant asked the Tours tribunal de grande instance to replace the “male” marker on his birth certificate with “neutral” or, failing that, “intersex.” In August 2015, the tribunal granted his request. It found that his sex could not be defined from a genital, hormonal, or psychological standpoint; that the male marker was fictitious; and that replacing it with “neutral” would respect his private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It considered this a rectification of incorrect civil status, not recognition of a third sex.

In March 2016, the Orléans Court of Appeal reversed. It accepted that the applicant was sexually ambiguous and that a fair balance under Article 8 might permit exceptions to civil-status rules. However, it found that his physical appearance and social behaviour were male, noting his marriage and adoption of a child. It also held that French law did not allow any permanent sex marker other than “male” or “female.” Granting the request would effectively recognise another sex category, a matter for the legislature, not the courts.

In May 2017, the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It held that French law does not permit a sex marker other than male or female on civil-status documents. While gender identity falls within Article 8, the binary nature of sex markers pursued a legitimate aim and was necessary for the social and legal system. Recognising a “neutral” sex would have far-reaching consequences and require multiple legislative changes. The Court of Cassation concluded that the interference with the applicant’s private life was not disproportionate.

The applicant complained before the European Court of Human Rights that the refusal to allow “neutral” or “intersex” on his birth certificate violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: his medically documented intersex status and ambiguous sex characteristics; his lifelong assigned male status despite this; his intersex gender identity and social recognition; the domestic courts’ refusal based on the French binary civil-status system; and the claimed impact on his identity, bodily integrity, and private life.
001-228857:
In *Grima and Others v. Malta* (Application no. 18057/20), eight Maltese nationals from the Grima and Parnis England families complained about the effects of Maltese rent-control legislation on their co-owned property at No. 35 Dingli Street, Sliema.

The property was occupied by a tenant under a lease governed by Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta (the Ordinance). Article 12(7) of the Ordinance allowed the tenant to maintain occupation. The rent paid was approximately EUR 466 per year in March 1979, increasing to EUR 685 in 1994, EUR 741 in 2009, EUR 803 in 2013, and EUR 819 in 2016. A court-appointed expert assessed the annual market rental value as EUR 1,398 in 1977, EUR 1,677 in 1982, EUR 2,516 in 1987, EUR 3,075 in 1992, EUR 4,193 in 1997, EUR 5,590 in 2002, EUR 6,150 in 2007, EUR 6,709 in 2012, and EUR 7,268 in 2017. The applicants therefore alleged that the controlled rent was far below market levels.

As to ownership, the Grima family’s predecessor in title acquired a half undivided share in 1982, aware that the property had been occupied under a temporary emphyteusis since 1960 for seventeen years, renewable once. That share belonged to him and applicant Georgina Grima. His share was inherited *ab intestato* in 2015 by applicants Doreen, Georgina, and Joseph Grima in different shares. Today Georgina Grima owns three-eighths of the undivided share of the entire property, while the siblings jointly own one-eighth. The bare ownership of the other half undivided share was vested in the Parnis England siblings (Nicholas, Robin, Stephen, and Johanna Petreski) as of 2004, as universal heirs of their father. Their mother, Margaret Parnis England, held the usufruct over the property after her husband’s death in 2004.

In 2019, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings, complaining of a breach of their property rights and seeking compensation for the period from 1977 to 2017. By judgment of 21 October 2019, the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention and awarded EUR 20,000 in compensation. However, contrary to domestic case law (*Ian Peter Ellis v. Maggur Cassar Reynaud*, Constitutional Court, 27 January 2017), the court held that the applicants’ ancestors had never complained about the situation and that the applicants should not financially benefit from their predecessors’ passivity. It therefore limited compensation to the period after the applicants inherited the property: 2015 for the Grima family and 2004 for the Parnis England family.

The applicants then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 22 April 2020. They complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13 of the Convention that they remained victims of the violation found domestically because the compensation awarded was too low and because the tenants had not been evicted. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning the effects of Act XXIII of 1979 to the Maltese Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.
001-226474:
Case Zammit and Busuttil v. Malta (Application no. 55102/20) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) in a judgment dated 12 September 2023. The applicants were Joseph Zammit and Anna Busuttil, two Maltese nationals born in 1944 and 1956 respectively, both living in Paola. Their case concerned a property in Paola that was subject to a unilaterally imposed lease under Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta (“the Ordinance”). The lease affected the applicants’ property as of 17 December 2007. At that time, the annual rent payable was EUR 291. In 2013, it increased to EUR 335 and would increase every three years thereafter.

A court-appointed expert later assessed the property’s annual market rental value as EUR 2,100 for the years 2007–2012 and EUR 5,800 for 2013–2018. Those figures were substantially higher than the controlled rent actually paid under the statutory lease.

On 27 September 2019, the applicants lodged constitutional redress proceedings. They complained that the application of Article 12(2) of the Ordinance breached their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. They limited their claims to the period ending 31 December 2018, without prejudice to any future action challenging the 2018 amendments that introduced the new Article 12B. By judgment of 17 June 2020, the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 resulting from the application of the law until 2018. It awarded the applicants EUR 15,000 in compensation. The court noted that the applicants had limited their claims to December 2018 and considered that they had a new remedy to pursue in light of the 2018 amendments for the future. No costs were imposed on the applicants. Neither party appealed.

In the meantime, on 3 July 2019, the parties reached an agreement whereby the tenants would pay EUR 2,400 annually in light of the 2018 amendments. That agreement would come to an end when the tenants died.

The applicants subsequently applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 11 December 2020. They complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13 of the Convention. Their central allegation was that, despite the domestic court’s finding of a violation, they remained victims because the compensation awarded was too low. In particular, the domestic award of EUR 15,000 did not adequately reflect the difference between the controlled rent actually received and the property’s much higher market rental value for the period up to 31 December 2018. They also invoked Article 13, arguing that the available domestic remedies had not provided adequate redress for the past violation of their property rights.

The Court gave notice of those complaints to the Maltese Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the long-standing statutory lease, the very low controlled rent compared with market value, the domestic finding of a violation but limited compensation, the 2018 amendments and the 2019 rental agreement, and the applicants’ claim that they remained victims due to inadequate compensation and the lack of an effective remedy.
001-228840:
In *Bellotto and Others v. Italy*, five Italian nationals lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applications were all introduced on 13 January 2021 and were registered as nos. 5170/21, 5172/21, 5174/21, 6223/21, and 7265/21. The applicants were Paolo Bellotto (born 1954), Gianna Cimitan (born 1966), Erminia Bellese (born 1948), Milena Urso (born 1947), and Dorina Sartor (born 1953). They were represented before the Court by Mr N. Zampieri, a lawyer practising in Schio, Italy. The Italian Government was given notice of the applications.

The central factual allegation common to all five applications concerned the retrospective application of section 1(218) of Law no. 266/2005 of 23 December 2005 to proceedings that were already pending. In other words, the applicants complained that a legislative provision enacted in 2005 was applied to their ongoing domestic cases, altering the legal framework governing those cases after they had begun. This retrospective operation of the law formed the basis of their alleged Convention violation. The applicants did not merely challenge the content of the provision in the abstract; they challenged its temporal application to pending judicial proceedings.

The appended table supplies the basic details of each application. Each applicant’s year of birth is listed, and each application was introduced on the same date. The case names follow the first applicant in each application: *Bellotto v. Italy*, *Cimitan v. Italy*, *Bellese v. Italy*, *Urso v. Italy*, and *Sartor v. Italy*. However, the extract does not disclose the precise nature of the underlying domestic disputes, the domestic courts involved, the exact effect of section 1(218) on each applicant’s case, or the specific Convention Articles relied upon. Nor does it set out the Court’s reasoning on the merits or its eventual conclusion. The extract is primarily procedural and factual in nature.

Procedurally, the case was heard by the First Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee. The Committee was composed of Krzysztof Wojtyczek (President), Lətif Hüseynov, and Ivana Jelić, judges, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 12 October 2023 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 16 November 2023. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: (1) the applicants were individuals whose domestic proceedings were pending when Law no. 266/2005 came into force; (2) section 1(218) of that law was applied retrospectively to those pending proceedings; and (3) the applicants contended that this retrospective application violated their Convention rights. The common legal issue was whether Italy’s retroactive legislative intervention in ongoing judicial proceedings was compatible with the Convention. Because the provided extract does not include the Court’s findings or the full appended table, a complete assessment of the merits, including any finding of a violation and the specific Convention provisions breached, cannot be made from this text alone. The extract principally establishes the identity of the applicants, the procedural history before the Strasbourg Court, and the shared factual complaint concerning the retrospective application of section 1(218) of Law no. 266/2005.
001-225900:

Ukraine* (Applications nos. 7501/22 and two others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of Carlo Ranzoni (President), Lado Chanturia, and María Elósegui, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, delivered a judgment on 20 July 2023. The case originated in three applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on the dates shown in the appended table. 001-224581:
**Summary of *Pavlov and Others v. Ukraine* (Application nos. 30722/21 and 2 others)**

The case of *Pavlov and Others v. Ukraine* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) against Ukraine. The applicants lodged their applications under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The case concerns allegations of inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of effective domestic remedies, primarily raising issues under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applications were filed by three Ukrainian nationals: Dmytro Yuriyovych Pavlov (born 1985), Mykhaylo Oleksandrovych Malyshko (born 1988), and Yevgen Igorovych Kondratenko (born 1992).

**Applicant 1: Dmytro Yuriyovych Pavlov (Application no. 30722/21)**

Pavlov was detained at Dnipro Detention Facility No. 4 from 24 February 2020 to 25 February 2021 (1 year and 2 days), and again from 11 March 2021 to 7 April 2021 (28 days). During his detention, he had approximately 2.6 square metres of personal space. He alleged numerous specific grievances, including severe overcrowding, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, infestation of his cell with insects and rodents, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of privacy for the toilet, restricted access to warm water, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack of toiletries, poor-quality bedding and bed linen, poor-quality food, restricted access to showers, and insufficient natural light.

**Applicant 2: Mykhaylo Oleksandrovych Malyshko (Application no. 38250/21)**

Malyshko was held at Zaporizhzhya Pre-Trial Detention Facility across four separate periods: 12–22 January 2021 (11 days), 23 February–2 June 2021 (3 months and 11 days), 9 September–4 November 2021 (1 month and 27 days), and 26 November–7 December 2021 (12 days). Throughout these periods, he had approximately 2.7 square metres of personal space. His complaints included overcrowding, insufficient physical exercise in fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, and lack of toiletries—conditions that persisted across all four detention periods.

**Applicant 3: Yevgen Igorovych Kondratenko (Application no. 3587/22)**

Kondratenko was detained at Kharkiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 11 April 2013 to 10 May 2021—a period of 8 years and 1 month. His personal space ranged from 2.5 to 4.4 square metres. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient electric and natural light, poor-quality bedding and bed linen, poor-quality food, restricted access to showers and potable water, passive smoking, a mouldy or dirty cell, insect and rodent infestation, lack of privacy for the toilet, and lack of toiletries.

**Key Legal Issues**

The applicants collectively complained that the conditions of their detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of Article 3 of the Convention, primarily due to severe overcrowding (with personal space consistently below international standards) and inadequate sanitary and living conditions. They further alleged that no effective domestic remedy existed in Ukrainian law to address these conditions, in violation of Article 13. The Court examined these complaints based on the factual details provided in the appended table.
001-223379:
In *Pleshkov and Pleshkova v. Ukraine* (Application no. 5783/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered a judgment on 9 March 2023. The applicants are two Ukrainian nationals: Mr Dmytro Gennadiyovych Pleshkov, born 1974, and his daughter Ms Alisa Dmytrivna Pleshkova, born 2011. They live separately, in Kyiv and Irpin respectively, and were represented by Ms M. Korniyenko. They lodged their application on 13 January 2020.

The case concerns the alleged failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce a domestic judgment establishing contact arrangements between father and daughter. On 24 October 2016, the Dniprovskyi District Court of Kyiv issued a judgment, later amended by the Kyiv Court of Appeal on 21 February 2017, setting out arrangements for contact between the first and second applicants, who were living separately. The second applicant lived with her mother, L. The mother failed to comply with those arrangements.

Enforcement proceedings began in September 2018 and were still ongoing at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings. According to the facts, the bailiffs imposed two fines on L for non-compliance, but she did not pay them. They also ordered a temporary suspension of her driving licence. Because L repeatedly failed to respond to their summons, the bailiffs unsuccessfully sought the initiation of criminal proceedings against her and a temporary ban on her leaving the country.

On 10 November 2018, the bailiffs organised the only meeting between the applicants. It took place in the presence of L. During that meeting, the second applicant refused to communicate with the first applicant because she was afraid of him. Subsequently, on 26 June 2019, a psychological examination of the second applicant was ordered by the bailiffs. The psychologist concluded that the child’s negative attitude towards her father was linked to the conflict between the first applicant and L. The psychologist indicated that improving the relationship between the first applicant and L. was a precondition for re-establishing “psychological contact” between the applicants.

The Government submitted that a representative of the local child welfare services had been involved in the enforcement proceedings, but they did not provide any further details about that involvement.

The applicants complained under Article 8 of the Convention about the non-enforcement of the contact arrangements. The Court decided to give notice to the Ukrainian Government of the complaint under Article 8 concerning the non-enforcement of the judgment on contact arrangements between the applicants, and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The application was given priority under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. The key issue before the Court was therefore whether the Ukrainian authorities had taken adequate and effective steps to enforce the father’s contact rights and to protect the family life of both applicants, or whether the prolonged failure to secure compliance with the domestic judgment violated Article 8. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.
001-226093:
**Case: Camara v. Belgium (Application no. 49255/22), Judgment of 18 July 2023**

The case concerns Mr Abdoulaye Camara, a Guinean national who applied for international protection in Belgium. He arrived on 12 July 2022 and filed his asylum application on 15 July 2022. When he went to Fedasil, the agency responsible for reception, he was told that the reception network had reached saturation point and that no accommodation could be provided. He had no private network or means of support in Belgium.

From 15 July to 4 November 2022—112 days—the applicant lived on the street. He slept at Brussels Nord and Midi railway stations, in parks, and on makeshift mattresses or cardboard. His bag, containing Guinean documents relevant to his asylum claim, was stolen. He could shower about once a week through the Hub Humanitaire, had only sporadic access to toilets, and relied on associations for food, which was not provided daily; he sometimes ate from dustbins and remained hungry. In October, he suffered from rain and cold as temperatures often fell below 10°C at night.

On 19 July 2022, his lawyer wrote to Fedasil, arguing that the refusal to accommodate him breached the Reception Act of 12 January 2007 and Belgium’s international obligations. On 20 July, the applicant made an ex parte urgent application to the Brussels French-Language Employment Tribunal. On 22 July, the Tribunal ordered Fedasil to secure accommodation—in a reception centre, hotel, or other appropriate establishment—and to provide material support under the Reception Act. It imposed a €1,000 fine for each night he was left outside the reception network, declared the decision immediately enforceable, and granted legal aid for service and enforcement.

Fedasil was notified on 29 July 2022 but did not lodge a third-party appeal. The decision became final on 29 August 2022. It was not enforced. On 12 October, the applicant served an order to comply and a final notice to pay. On 20 October, he requested an interim measure from the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39. The Court granted the measure on 31 October 2022, requiring Belgium to provide accommodation and support. On 3 November, Fedasil invited him to the initial processing centre, and on 4 November he was assigned to the Evere Red Cross centre, later transferred to the Koekelberg Samusocial centre. His asylum application remained pending.

Before the Court, the applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman and degrading treatment due to months of homelessness and destitution despite a legal entitlement), Article 6 § 1 (non-enforcement of the Employment Tribunal’s final decision), and Article 8 read with Article 13 (interference with private life and lack of an effective remedy). The Court communicated those complaints.

The broader context was systemic: Belgium’s reception network had been saturated since September 2021. Fedasil prioritised vulnerable groups and later maintained waiting lists, often accommodating applicants only after they obtained a domestic court order or an ECtHR interim measure. Thousands of similar ex parte applications succeeded, and by 1 March 2023 Fedasil had been ordered more than 7,000 times to accommodate applicants. The Government cited migratory pressure, floods, staffing shortages, local authority restrictions, and processing delays, but domestic courts found Fedasil’s failure to comply with the Reception Act manifest and unjustified.

The key issue is that, despite a final enforceable domestic order recognising the applicant’s right to material support, he remained homeless and without basic assistance for months, requiring ECtHR interim relief before compliance.
001-222917:
The case *Derkach v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 23537/20 and 23615/20) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee and delivered in Strasbourg on 9 February 2023. The Committee was composed of Mārtiņš Mits (President), Mattias Guyomar and Mykola Gnatovskyy (judges), with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention. Both were introduced on 12 May 2020. The applicant, Kostyantyn Yuriyovych Derkach, born in 1982, was represented by Mr A.V. Pustyntsev, a lawyer practising in Dnipro, Ukraine. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The Court deliberated in private on 19 January 2023.

The applicant complained principally of the inadequate conditions of his detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. He also raised other complaints under the Convention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are set out in the appended table and are identical for both applications.

According to the table, the applicant was detained at the Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 13 April 2018 to 14 August 2020. The duration of that detention was 2 years, 4 months and 2 days. The amount of living space per inmate was between 1.7 and 2.6 square metres. This level of personal space indicates significant overcrowding.

The applicant also listed specific grievances about the material conditions of his detention. He alleged infestation of the cell with insects and rodents, lack of fresh air, lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen, lack of privacy for the toilet, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack or insufficient quantity of food, no or restricted access to a shower, overcrowding, and passive smoking. These conditions, cumulatively and over a prolonged period, formed the factual basis of his complaint under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The applicant argued that the combination of overcrowding, poor hygiene, inadequate ventilation, lack of toilet privacy, restricted shower access, insufficient food and exposure to passive smoking made his detention intolerable. The length of detention—more than two years—was also relevant to the severity of the alleged treatment.

In addition, the applicant complained that there was no effective remedy in domestic law by which he could challenge those conditions or obtain redress. That complaint corresponds to Article 13 of the Convention, which guarantees an effective remedy for arguable violations of Convention rights. The Court was therefore required to examine whether the conditions of detention met the standards of Article 3 and whether the Ukrainian authorities provided an effective domestic remedy as required by Article 13.

Both applications concern the same applicant, the same detention facility, the same period and the same factual allegations. They were introduced on the same date, 12 May 2020. The case therefore centres on the cumulative effect of the alleged detention conditions and the absence of an effective remedy in Ukraine.
001-224576:
In *Sharashkin and Others v. Russia*, the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 11 May 2023, adopted on 13 April 2023. The case comprised Application no. 57223/19 and 21 other applications. The applicants lodged their applications under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, and the Russian Government was given notice of them. The case concerned administrative sanctions imposed on individuals who organised or participated in public assemblies in Russia, mainly in Moscow.

The appended table identifies the applicants and the events at issue. These included an anticorruption manifestation in Moscow on 26 March 2017; a manifestation in support of I. Golunov on 12 June 2019; manifestations for fair elections to Mosgorduma (the Moscow City Duma) on 27 July 2019 and 3 August 2019; a manifestation against political repressions on 31 August 2019; and a manifestation in support of A. Navalnyy on 2 February 2021. The majority of the applications concerned the 27 July 2019 Moscow City Duma protest, which was the central event in the case.

The applicants were charged under Article 20.2 of the Russian Code of Administrative Offences, in various paragraphs: § 5, § 6.1, § 2, and § 8. These provisions concern violations of the procedure for organising or holding public events, participation in unauthorised public events, organising unauthorised events, and repeated violations. The penalties imposed included administrative fines and administrative arrest or detention. Fines typically ranged from RUB 10,000 to RUB 20,000, although some were higher or lower. For example, Sharashkin received 7 days’ administrative arrest under § 6.1. Solovyev received an 8-day administrative detention under § 2 for the 27 July 2019 event and a 20-day administrative detention under § 8 for the 31 August 2019 event. Other applicants received fines such as RUB 20,000, 18,000, 15,000, 12,000, or 10,000. Some applicants were sanctioned for more than one event, including Burkhanov, Golovenko, Kravchenko, Pospelov, and Tamkovich. Final domestic decisions were issued by the Moscow City Court on various dates between 2017 and 2021.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained of disproportionate measures taken against them as organisers and participants of public assemblies. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The key alleged violation concerned interference with the right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 11 of the Convention, through administrative charges, fines, and short-term detention. The facts indicate that the penalties were imposed in connection with peaceful protests, many of which concerned electoral or political issues, and that the domestic courts upheld those sanctions. The applicants argued that the measures were not necessary in a democratic society and were disproportionate. The full text provided does not set out the Court’s legal reasoning or final conclusions on the merits, but it identifies the factual basis relevant to the alleged violations. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.
001-228683:
In *Lang v. Ukraine* (Application no. 49134/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) considered whether Ukraine’s decision to extradite the applicant, Craig Austin Lang, to the United States would violate Article 3 of the Convention. The applicant, a US national and former US Army serviceman, had travelled to Ukraine several times between 2015 and 2019 and served in Ukrainian armed formations fighting in eastern Ukraine. He was arrested on 21 August 2019 while re-entering Ukraine from Moldova and was later released on his own recognisance.

On 25 September 2019, the United States requested his extradition under the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. In February 2020, the US expanded the request and added further charges. The amended request listed federal charges in Florida, Arizona, and North Carolina. In the US District Court for the Middle District of Florida, the applicant faced charges including conspiracy to interfere with commerce by violence; interference with commerce by violence; conspiracy to carry and use a firearm during a crime of violence; use and discharge of a firearm during a crime of violence resulting in murder; conspiracy to kill, kidnap, maim or injure persons in Venezuela; and violation of the Neutrality Act. The potential penalties included life imprisonment for the firearm-murder charge and for conspiracy to murder or kidnap, as well as the death penalty for the firearm-murder charge. The Florida charges alleged that the applicant and a co-conspirator had proposed to sell firearms to lure a victim to a meeting with cash, then shot and killed the victim and another person, took the money, and planned to use the funds to travel to Venezuela to fight the regime there.

The applicant also faced charges in Arizona for misuse of a passport, and in North Carolina for passport fraud, aggravated identity theft, visa fraud and misuse, and false representation of a Social Security number.

On 15 October 2019, the US Embassy in Kyiv assured the General Prosecutor’s Office of Ukraine (“GPO”) that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed on the applicant and that he would not be prosecuted for offences committed before extradition other than those for which extradition was granted. On 17 October and 4 November 2019, the applicant asked the GPO to request assurances that he would not be sentenced to death and that he would have an opportunity to seek reduction of any life sentence imposed. He relied on *Trabelsi v. Belgium*, where the Court held that the power of presidential pardon in the US did not satisfy Article 3 requirements. The GPO replied that death penalty assurances had been requested. On 4 August 2020, the US Department of Justice reiterated the death penalty assurances.

On 28 August 2020, the GPO granted the extradition request, finding legal grounds and noting the death penalty assurances. The applicant appealed, arguing that no adequate assurances had been provided concerning the reducibility of any life sentence. On 15 March 2021, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld the extradition decision, finding that the charges were extraditable, not time-barred, and that his asylum applications had been rejected.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that extradition would violate Article 3 because, if convicted, he risked receiving an irreducible life sentence. The Court gave notice of the Article 3 complaint, declared the remainder inadmissible, and indicated an interim measure under Rule 39. The central alleged violation was therefore that Ukraine sought to extradite him despite the risk of irreducible life imprisonment and without sufficient assurances that any life sentence would be reducible.
001-227719:
El-Asmar v. Denmark (Application no. 27753/19) concerns a Danish national detained on remand in March 2017. The applicant had a criminal history including robbery, violence and threats. On admission he was described as “possibly dangerous” and “possibly prone to escape,” with “particular problematic behaviour.” After transfer to Enner Mark Prison on 30 March 2017, he was repeatedly placed in observation or security cells because of aggressive and threatening conduct. Records describe threats to kill guards, smearing toothpaste, attempting to attack a guard with a pencil on 3 April, and later kicking at officers. This context framed the alleged Article 3 complaint about the use of pepper spray.

The central incident occurred on 4 April 2017, while the applicant was in an observation cell. The parties disputed what happened. According to the prison journal, the applicant destroyed his mattress, threw food at the window, urinated under the door, kicked the door and shouted that he would kill staff. At about 4:25 p.m., guards opened the cell door. The guards alleged that the applicant rushed at guard D1 and tried to punch him in the head. D1 pushed him back and, together with guard M1, used pepper spray. The applicant claimed he was passive and had surrendered, but was sprayed in the face and back, momentarily fainted, and was then dragged to a security cell. The guards denied he fainted, saying he continued to resist and shout insults, and that pepper spray made the floor slippery, so two more guards helped carry him to the security cell. They said he was offered medical care and water, which he refused, stating he would “take it like a real man.”

The prison doctor was contacted shortly after the spraying. He reportedly said that if the inmate had only been exposed to pepper spray, there was no need to attend, but asked for a follow-up report. Later that day the doctor was told the applicant appeared unharmed though agitated. The applicant refused examination by a prison doctor because he considered prison doctors biased; he wanted an independent doctor.

On 6 April 2017 the applicant reported guards D1 and M1 to the police for aggravated violence. The police interviewed him in November 2017 and the guards in January 2018. There was no video surveillance in the observation cell, security cell or corridor. In January 2018 the police discontinued criminal proceedings, citing contradictory accounts, the applicant’s refusal of a prison medical examination, lack of video or other witnesses, and the unlikelihood of conviction. Appeals to the Regional Prosecutor were rejected.

Separately, the applicant complained to the prison authorities and the Department of Prisons and Probation. Those bodies found the pepper spray justified under section 62 of the Sentence Enforcement Act, to avert imminent violence. They accepted that no warning was given because the attack was too intense, and that pepper spray was considered gentler than manual force. A later procedural complaint about the police investigation led the police Management Secretariat to find a seven-month investigative delay excessive and regrettable, but it did not find the investigation ineffective; the Regional Prosecutor upheld that decision.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under the substantive and procedural limbs of Article 3 about exposure to pepper spray. His complaint about subsequent confinement to a restraint bed was declared inadmissible. Relevant legal materials included Danish rules permitting pepper spray where necessary, requiring warning if possible and medical relief afterwards. CPT and UNCAT materials expressed concern about pepper spray in confined spaces and its use on persons already controlled or with mental disabilities.
001-226011:
Mokgadi Caster Semenya is a South African international middle-distance athlete and Olympic/world champion. She was born female, raised as a woman, legally recognised as female, and has always identified as a woman. She has a 46 XY difference of sex development (DSD) and naturally elevated testosterone. In 2018, World Athletics (then IAAF) introduced the “Eligibility Regulations for the Female Classification (Athletes with Differences of Sex Development)” (DSD Regulations). These required “Relevant Athletes”—46 XY DSD athletes with testosterone above 5 nmol/L—to take hormone treatment to lower their natural testosterone if they wished to compete in restricted female events, including the 800m, 1500m and mile. Semenya refused, saying the treatment was medically unnecessary, had serious and poorly understood side effects, and forced her to alter her natural body to compete. As a result, she could no longer take part in international competitions.

The background facts relevant to her alleged Convention violations include earlier sex testing after her 2009 World Championships victory, when she was reportedly tested to determine whether she was “biologically male” and told to reduce her testosterone. She underwent hormone treatment despite side effects, then won the 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympic gold. After the 2015 Dutee Chand CAS interim award suspended the previous hyperandrogenism rules, she stopped treatment and won 2016 Olympic gold. The 2018 DSD Regulations applied only to 46 XY DSD athletes, not to XX women with elevated testosterone. Semenya did not dispute that she was a Relevant Athlete but challenged the regulations’ validity.

She lost before the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in an award of 30 April 2019. The CAS majority accepted that the DSD Regulations were discriminatory but found them necessary, reasonable and proportionate to ensure fair competition in female athletics. It accepted evidence that 46 XY DSD athletes had a significant testosterone-related performance advantage in restricted events and that oral contraceptives could lower testosterone without disproportionate side effects. It nevertheless expressed grave concerns about practical compliance, testosterone fluctuations above 5 nmol/L, confidentiality risks, and sparse evidence for the 1500m and mile events. It did not invalidate the regulations. On 25 August 2020, the Swiss Federal Supreme Court dismissed Semenya’s appeal, holding the rules appropriate, necessary and proportionate. It treated the CAS’s seat in Lausanne as the only link with Switzerland and reviewed the award under Swiss arbitration law.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Semenya relied on Articles 3, 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The key alleged violations were: (1) discrimination on grounds of sex and/or DSD status, because only 46 XY DSD women were required to lower natural testosterone; (2) breach of private life, bodily integrity and dignity through compulsory hormone treatment, sex testing/virilisation assessments, and risks of disclosure; (3) inhuman or degrading treatment due to medically unnecessary treatment and side effects; (4) lack of an effective remedy and fair trial, because the CAS arbitration and Swiss Federal Supreme Court review allegedly failed to provide adequate judicial protection. Switzerland’s responsibility arose from the CAS having its seat in Lausanne and the Swiss courts’ refusal to set aside the CAS award.
001-224091:
E.K. v. Latvia (Application no. 25942/20) concerns an Article 8 complaint by a Latvian father that the authorities failed to enforce a final court judgment granting him contact with his daughter, D.K. The applicant married I.B.; their daughter was born in 2013. In October 2016, I.B. left the family home and moved more than 200 km away, taking D.K. Divorce and contact proceedings followed. Interim orders granted the applicant contact, but I.B. obstructed it, including by removing D.K. from preschool and homeschooling her. In 2018, the courts dissolved the marriage and set detailed contact rights: initially every other Saturday, later overnight weekend contact, holiday contact, summer contact, and weekly telephone/video calls. The judgment, final in November 2018, warned that non-compliance could lead to fines, suspension of parental authority, or criminal liability.

After the judgment, contact was almost never exercised. I.B. frequently claimed D.K. was ill. On other occasions, D.K. was brought to the meeting place but immediately driven away or refused to go with the applicant. Sometimes no one appeared. Telephone contact was also restricted. A bailiff issued enforcement reports, but the regional court annulled them, reasoning that the bailiff could only verify presence, not assess why the child refused; a child could not be forced, and the issue had to be addressed through review of contact arrangements. The State Inspectorate for the Protection of Children’s Rights agreed that the bailiff or court could not resolve the child’s refusal; the guardianship institution could assess malicious exercise of parental authority or use a contact person.

The applicant repeatedly asked courts to review contact arrangements and asked the Guardianship Institution to suspend I.B.’s parental authority. Domestic courts acknowledged that the judgment was not being enforced. They modified the order: the mother was to hand over the child, third parties were excluded, video calls were required, and later sessions were to begin at the Guardianship Institution with a neutral contact person. Between June 2020 and January 2021, at least 23 such sessions produced no actual contact. Guardianship assessments found that the parental conflict harmed D.K.; I.B. did not prepare the child for meetings, spoke negatively about the father, took the child to numerous specialists, and did not cooperate. It found I.B. used parental authority maliciously by not complying with the judgment, but it refused to suspend her authority because separating D.K. from her mother would cause greater harm.

The Administrative District Court initially ordered suspension of I.B.’s parental authority, finding she had consciously created fear and obstructed contact. The appellate court reversed, holding that forced contact would traumatise the child and that both parents were partly at fault. The Supreme Court upheld that reversal. Psychological assessments noted D.K.’s hostility toward her father, possible maternal influence, acute stress, and dissociation. Criminal proceedings against I.B. for malicious non-compliance began in 2019, with charges brought in 2021. The mother’s civil claim to change contact was dismissed, and her restraining-order requests against the applicant failed.

The alleged violation is that, despite the final contact judgment and domestic recognition that the mother obstructed contact and influenced the child, Latvian institutions failed to secure practical enforcement of the applicant’s family life. The key issue is whether the State’s positive obligations required more effective measures—bailiff enforcement, guardianship action, parental-authority suspension, or contact-person arrangements—to ensure contact while protecting the child’s best interests.
001-224580:
Zaghini v. San Marino (no. 3405/21) concerns San Marino’s confiscation of EUR 1,892,700 connected to Gianluca Zaghini, an Italian national, after money-laundering proceedings against other persons, not him. He alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining he could not recover the money despite an Italian judgment ordering restitution.

In 2003 Italy investigated Zaghini for tax evasion and unjust profits of about EUR 15 million. Through international letters rogatory, San Marino authorities searched assets linked to Zaghini’s father, G.A. and P.A. They found a bank account in Zaghini’s name and a safe deposit box in G.A.’s name containing EUR 1,892,700. Zaghini’s father had withdrawn EUR 939,500 and EUR 1,006,700 in cash from Zaghini’s account in December 2003. Evidence showed the father gave EUR 1,903,700 to P.A., who asked G.A. to open the safe deposit box; G.A. deposited EUR 1,892,700, while the father and P.A. kept EUR 12,000 and EUR 11,000. In January 2004 San Marino began money-laundering proceedings against the father, G.A. and P.A., not Zaghini. Zaghini’s Italian pre-trial statements admitted depositing about EUR 1.8 million in San Marino from illegal activity.

In 2005 the three co-accused were convicted of money laundering; confiscation of the seized sum was ordered. In 2008 the appeal confirmed the father’s and P.A.’s guilt and confiscation, while G.A.’s case became time-barred. The San Marino courts found the money came from crimes with which Zaghini was charged in Italy; a final Italian judgment was unnecessary, and Zaghini had asked the accused to hide the money while under house arrest. A 2008 execution order confiscated EUR 1,892,700 plus interest under Article 147(3) of the Criminal Code, which made confiscation mandatory for money laundering.

In Italy, Zaghini was convicted at first instance in 2012, but in 2016 the Court of Appeal of Bologna declared the proceedings time-barred and ordered restitution of money preventively seized. From 2017, Zaghini unsuccessfully asked San Marino’s judge for international cooperation to release the funds. The judge rejected the requests because the sums had already been confiscated in the San Marino criminal case and Zaghini was not an extraneous third party: he was the predicate offender and was only spared money-laundering charges because domestic law then barred prosecuting him for laundering. Appeals failed.

In 2018 Zaghini asked the Enforcement Judge to annul the confiscation based on the Italian judgment. This was rejected: the illicit origin of the funds had been established by San Marino courts independently of any Italian conviction, and the Italian time-bar did not mean innocence. The judge relied on Zaghini’s own statements and found he had instigated the movement of money and had not shown a licit origin. The second-instance judge in 2019 upheld the decision, finding the Enforcement Judge competent and that Zaghini had had an adversarial hearing but could not overturn final criminal findings. The third-instance judge rejected further appeals in 2020, confirming the confiscation could not be revoked.

The key alleged violation was therefore that confiscation of Zaghini’s funds in proceedings to which he was not a party left him without an effective remedy to recover his property, despite the Italian restitution order. The Court gave notice only of the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint.
001-225772:
In *Golovin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 47052/18, judgment 13 July 2023), the European Court of Human Rights examined the dismissal of a judge of Ukraine’s Constitutional Court, which the applicant alleged violated Articles 6, 8 and 18 of the Convention. The applicant, Anatoliy Sergiyovych Golovin, a Ukrainian national born in 1952 and living in Kyiv, lodged his application on 23 September 2018.

In August 2006, Parliament appointed Golovin as a judge of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine for a non-renewable nine-year term. On 24 February 2014, Parliament dismissed him “for breach of his judicial oath.” The dismissal was connected to his participation in the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010. The same parliamentary resolution also concerned the applicants in *Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine*. After his dismissal, on 27 February 2014, Golovin challenged the resolution before the Higher Administrative Court (HAC), relying on the Code of Administrative Justice. On 3 March 2014, he also submitted a statement of resignation to Parliament.

On 11 December 2017, the HAC declared the parliamentary resolution unlawful with respect to Golovin’s dismissal. It relied on international and domestic principles of judicial independence and found that Parliament had not respected them. In particular, it cited the Constitutional Court Act provision that judges could not be held liable for the results of their votes. It further found that Parliament had failed to follow the procedure for dismissing a Constitutional Court judge and that no individual liability of Golovin had been established.

Parliament appealed. On 14 March 2018, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court quashed the HAC’s judgment and dismissed Golovin’s claim as unfounded; the full text was issued on 23 March 2018. The Supreme Court held that in its 2010 judgment the Constitutional Court had acted beyond its powers by invalidating binding provisions of the Constitution. It found that the Constitutional Court had failed to ensure the supremacy of the Constitution, had changed the Constitution and constitutional system, had violated fundamental principles of democracy and separation of powers, and had undermined the legitimacy of State authorities. It concluded that Golovin’s participation in that judgment and its consequences were manifestly inconsistent with his judicial oath. It also found that his dismissal procedure had complied with the Constitution and Parliament’s rules.

Crucially for the alleged violations, the Supreme Court distinguished *Oleksandr Volkov v. Ukraine*. It observed that the Constitutional Court is formed through a political process, acts as a “negative legislator” when declaring legislation unconstitutional and as a “positive legislator” when interpreting the Constitution, and is therefore more political than judicial. Relying on *Fischer v. Austria* and *Zumtobel v. Austria*, it considered the Constitutional Court not to be a “court” within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. It concluded that the body that appointed a Constitutional Court judge may apply political accountability where the judge’s conduct does not meet the high standards expected by society.

These facts are central to Golovin’s complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 18. They concern whether he had access to a fair judicial process for contesting his dismissal, whether the dismissal based on his judicial activity unjustifiably interfered with his rights, and whether the measure pursued an improper purpose rather than a legitimate one.
001-227753:
**Case Summary: Nezdymovskyy v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 56163/21 and 879/22)**

The case of *Nezdymovskyy v. Ukraine* concerns two applications lodged against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Pavlo Leonidovych Nezdymovskyy, born in 1983, was represented by Mr V.V. Kushnir, a lawyer practising in Dnipro, Ukraine. The applications were introduced on 6 November 2021 and 18 December 2021. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the applicant’s detention at the Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility. According to the appended table, the applicant had been held in that facility since 20 February 2015, and his detention was still pending at the time of the proceedings. The duration of detention in that facility was therefore more than eight years, four months and twenty-three days. The two applications relate to the same detention facility and the same ongoing period of detention, although they were lodged on separate dates.

The applicant complained of inadequate conditions of detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. The specific grievances recorded in the appended table include overcrowding, with the space available per inmate ranging between only 2.5 and 2.9 square metres. The applicant further alleged a lack of fresh air, a lack of privacy for using the toilet, and the lack or poor quality of bedding and bed linen. He also complained of passive smoking, a lack of toiletries, and a lack or inadequacy of hygienic facilities. In addition, he described a mouldy or dirty cell, no or restricted access to warm water, and no or restricted access to shower facilities.

These factual allegations form the basis of the complaint that the conditions of detention were inadequate, and that no effective domestic remedy existed to address or prevent those conditions. The case therefore raises issues under the Convention concerning the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment and the right to an effective remedy, although the provided excerpt refers generally to the applicant’s complaints under the Convention and notes that he also raised other complaints.

Procedurally, the case was heard by the Fifth Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee composed of Carlo Ranzoni (President), Lado Chanturia, and María Elósegui, judges, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 14 September 2023 and delivered its judgment on 5 October 2023 in Strasbourg. The judgment was adopted on that date, is final, but may be subject to editorial revision.

In summary, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the applicant’s prolonged detention at the Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 20 February 2015 onwards, lasting more than eight years and four months at the time of the applications, combined with severe overcrowding and multiple material deficiencies in detention conditions. The applicant alleged that these conditions breached the Convention and that Ukrainian domestic law provided no effective remedy for his complaints.
001-225678:
**Lagoshenko and Others v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 47045/21 and 5 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered in Strasbourg on 6 July 2023. The judgment was adopted after private deliberation on 15 June 2023 and is final. The case originated in six applications filed against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants’ central complaints were that criminal proceedings against them were excessively long and that Ukrainian law provided no effective remedy for that delay.

The relevant facts are set out in the appended table. Oleksandr Volodymyrovych Lagoshenko (born 1983), application no. 47045/21, introduced his application on 13 September 2021. His criminal proceedings began on 25 March 2015 and were still pending at the relevant time. They had lasted more than eight years, two months and two days, and had been considered at only one level of jurisdiction.

Yuriy Vasylyovych Andriychuk (born 1974), application no. 56240/21, applied on 10 November 2021. His proceedings started on 27 April 2011 and remained pending. Their total duration exceeded twelve years and one month, across three levels of jurisdiction. This was the longest period among the applications.

Rostyslav Romanovych Didukh (born 1965), application no. 58210/21, applied on 19 November 2021. He was represented by Oleg Volodymyrovych Mytsyk of Lviv. His proceedings began on 12 August 2014 and were still pending. They had lasted more than eight years, nine months and fifteen days, at two levels of jurisdiction.

Kostyantyn Sergiyovych Zheludchenko (born 1972), application no. 1398/22, applied on 20 December 2021. Unlike most of the other cases, his proceedings ended on 22 December 2021. They had begun on 26 January 2017 and lasted four years, ten months and twenty-seven days, involving two levels of jurisdiction.

Volodymyr Volodymyrovych Chyrkov (born 1975), application no. 8393/22, applied on 31 January 2022. His proceedings started on 29 August 2017 and were still pending. They had lasted more than five years, eight months and twenty-eight days, at one level of jurisdiction.

Dmytro Valeriyovych Nemazanyy (born 1986), application no. 48029/22, applied on 22 September 2022. He was represented by Anatoliy Volodymyrovych Mulko of Solone. His proceedings began on 10 May 2018 and were still pending. They had lasted more than five years and seventeen days, involving two levels of jurisdiction.

Thus, in five of the six applications, the criminal proceedings were still pending when the applications were introduced. The proceedings lasted from approximately four years and eleven months to more than twelve years. Some applicants’ cases had passed through one, two, or three levels of jurisdiction. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ allegations that the length of the criminal proceedings was excessive and that no effective domestic remedy existed to address or prevent the delay. The Court, sitting as a Committee, considered these complaints in the light of the facts summarized in the appended table.
001-229325:
In *V v. the Czech Republic*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of the applicant’s brother, P.Z., a 30-year-old man suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, after police used a taser at a psychiatric clinic and a nurse administered tranquillisers. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention concerning both the death and the ensuing criminal investigation.

On the evening of 5 November 2015, P.Z.’s family called an emergency line after he became aggressive and threatened relatives. He was taken by ambulance, accompanied by police, to the Psychiatric Clinic of Olomouc University Hospital and admitted to acute care. After examination, he calmed down, agreed to antipsychotic medication (Haloperidol and Apaurin), and was placed in an ordinary room.

Early on 6 November, at about 4 a.m., P.Z. became restless. Staff began preparing an intensive/seclusion room. Following a verbal altercation, he damaged fixtures and doors. When an orderly tried to stop him taking a fire hose, P.Z. knocked him down and severely beat him; staff said he tried to strangle the orderly with the hose. He later ripped ceiling tiles, pulled out electrical wires, and sprayed water on them. Two unarmed security guards failed to subdue him. A nurse called the police at 4:53 a.m.; four officers arrived around 5 a.m.

The applicant, relying on the Public Defender of Rights’ report, disputed the official account. She claimed P.Z.’s behaviour was largely defensive and triggered by realisation that a seclusion room was being prepared. She alleged police acted hastily, only briefly consulted a nurse who had not witnessed the attack, made no attempt to communicate with P.Z., and did not shut off water or electricity. The police claimed immediate intervention was necessary because P.Z. was spraying water onto live electrical wires, threatening everyone present. In a narrow 2.25-metre corridor, officers used a mattress as a shield and forced P.Z. to the ground, but could not restrain him. Officer T. warned P.Z., then fired a taser at his lower back from about 1.5 metres. Because P.Z. continued resisting, the taser was fired repeatedly at another officer’s request. The taser record showed three discharges lasting eight, eleven, and ten seconds. A nurse then administered Apaurin and Tisercin injections at 5:05 a.m. P.Z. became cyanotic, had no palpable pulse, and resuscitation failed. He was pronounced dead at 6:08 a.m., likely from cardiac arrest.

A medical expert report found the immediate cause of death was cardiac arrhythmia. It could not establish unequivocally whether or to what extent natural causes were responsible. Possible contributory factors included stress from the psychotic episode, medication, and the repeated taser use, though the darts were not aimed at the chest or heart. An autopsy revealed a coronary artery anomaly of unclear relevance. Experts were not asked about any interaction between the medication and the taser.

The General Inspectorate of the Security Forces investigated suspected negligent homicide. On 6 April 2016, it set aside the case, finding the police intervention lawful. It concluded that P.Z. posed a direct threat, no other means were available, and the repeated tasering was justified by continuing resistance and aimed away from vital organs. Prosecutors rejected the family’s complaints, and the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional appeal. The Public Defender of Rights later criticised the legal classification and training regarding tasers, inadequate police oversight, and the general disproportionality of tasering a person already on the ground restrained by officers, unless exceptional circumstances existed, such as a risk of electric shock. She also questioned whether the danger remained imminent and noted that positional asphyxia had not been examined. The applicant’s Article 2 and 3 complaints concerning the death and investigation were communicated to the Government.
001-222898:
**Case: Ugulava v. Georgia (Application no. 5432/15)**

The case concerns Giorgi Ugulava, a Georgian national, former Tbilisi mayor and a leader of the opposition United National Movement. He complained under Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention that his pre-trial detention was unlawful and arbitrary, and under Article 18 read with Article 5 § 1 that it was politically motivated.

After the Georgian Dream coalition came to power in 2012, several criminal proceedings were opened against Ugulava. In earlier cases, he was charged with embezzlement, money laundering and related offences. Courts initially refused bail or imposed lesser measures, but the cases formed a backdrop to later detention decisions.

The key detention arose from a fourth set of proceedings. On 5 June 2014 an investigation began into an alleged violent incident at the Marneuli district electoral commission. Separately, a money-laundering investigation was opened after two individuals alleged that Ugulava had invited them into an offshore scheme. On the evening of 2 July 2014, an investigator summoned Ugulava for questioning at 10 a.m. on 4 July. Ugulava stated that he had a pre-planned business trip to Kyiv on 3 July but would shorten it and return early on 4 July. Later that night, a key witness, G.K., alleged that Ugulava had threatened him.

On 3 July 2014 at 5:57 a.m., Ugulava was arrested at Tbilisi International Airport. The arrest report cited aggravated money laundering and relied on the risk of absconding under Article 171 § 2(e) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, without a prior judicial warrant. His lawyers were allegedly denied immediate access to him for four to five hours and denied access to the case file. On 4 July 2014, the money-laundering case was merged with the Marneuli case, and he was charged with money laundering, forgery, coercion and organising activity disrupting public order.

The prosecution sought pre-trial detention, arguing flight risk based on his foreign contacts, frequent travel and attempt to leave despite the summons; risk of influencing witnesses, relying on G.K.’s statement; and risk of reoffending because he had allegedly committed offences while on bail. The defence argued that the arrest was unlawful, lacked factual basis, and that Ugulava had cooperated and informed authorities of his travel. On 4 July 2014, the Tbilisi City Court remanded him in custody, citing reasonable suspicion, gravity of charges, flight risk, obstruction and witness influence. The Court of Appeal upheld this on 8 July 2014.

In February 2015, Ugulava unsuccessfully sought release on bail. The court found the original grounds still valid and said the witness-tampering risk had increased after the prosecution witness list was confirmed. Meanwhile, a fifth set of proceedings was opened concerning the Imedi television company and Lynx Ltd. In March 2015, new charges were brought. The prosecution requested a fresh pre-trial detention order even though the original nine-month detention period was due to expire on 2 April 2015. The defence objected that this was unconstitutional, that the investigation was complete, and that the charges duplicated earlier proceedings. On 15 March 2015, the Tbilisi City Court granted a new detention order without addressing the time-limit objection. The appellate court held that the nine-month period could be calculated separately for different criminal cases.

Ugulava lodged a constitutional complaint. On 15 September 2015, the Constitutional Court ruled that Article 205 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was unconstitutional insofar as it allowed detention where the accused had already spent nine months in pre-trial detention in any other pending case at the time of the new indictment. On 17 September 2015, after fifteen months in detention, Ugulava was released. He alleged that his detention had been arbitrary, inadequately reviewed and politically motivated.
001-225652:
The case B.F. and Others v. Switzerland (ECtHR, Third Section, 4 July 2023) concerns four applications brought by Eritrean and Chinese nationals whose requests for family reunification in Switzerland were refused. The applicants had all been recognised as refugees under the 1951 Refugee Convention, but they were not granted asylum. Instead, they received provisional admission because the Swiss authorities found that the grounds for their refugee status arose only after their departure from their countries of origin and as a result of their own actions (“subjective post-flight grounds”). Under Swiss law, this distinction mattered greatly: refugees granted asylum could bring their nuclear family to Switzerland under section 51 of the Asylum Act without a waiting period or other conditions, whereas provisionally admitted refugees had only a discretionary entitlement under section 85(7) of the Aliens Act, subject to cumulative requirements, including a three-year waiting period and non-reliance on social assistance.

The applicants sought reunification with minor children or a spouse and children. In each case, the Swiss authorities rejected the requests primarily because the applicant remained reliant on social assistance. In some cases, the three-year waiting period or a time-limit for children over 12 was also not met. The Federal Administrative Court accepted that the applicants had de facto settled status and that Article 8 of the Convention was engaged, but it found that the refusals did not breach Article 8. It emphasised that their asylum claims of pre-departure persecution had been rejected as not credible, that their separation from family members had been voluntary or foreseeable, that they could maintain contact and visit relatives abroad, and that the public interest in avoiding social assistance outweighed their private interests.

The specific facts varied. B.F., an Eritrean national provisionally admitted in 2014, sought reunification with her daughter D.E., who was living in precarious conditions in Sudan. B.F. was fully reliant on social assistance, had health problems, and was later found 100% unfit for work; her request was rejected for failure to meet both the waiting period and the non-reliance condition. She alleged violations of Article 8 and Article 14 read with Article 8, arguing discrimination compared with refugees granted asylum. Another applicant, a Chinese national of Tibetan origin provisionally admitted in 2010, sought reunification with his wife and two children in India. He worked full-time as a nursing assistant but earned too little to support the family; his wife had epilepsy. His request was rejected for reliance on social assistance. A third applicant, an Eritrean woman provisionally admitted in 2010, sought reunification with her eldest daughter in Sudan. She worked part-time while caring for three minor children alone and remained largely dependent on social assistance; her request was rejected for the time-limit and lack of financial independence. The fourth applicant, an Eritrean woman provisionally admitted in 2014, sought reunification with her two daughters living in an Ethiopian refugee camp.
