She had health issues and had never found work, though she was not deemed completely unfit; her request was rejected for reliance on social assistance.

The alleged violations centred on Article 8, because the refusals allegedly amounted to a disproportionate interference with family life and, given the applicants’ inability to meet the social-assistance condition, a de facto permanent separation. Some applicants also alleged Article 14 discrimination, arguing that provisionally admitted refugees were treated less favourably than refugees granted asylum without objective justification.
001-228155:
In *Locascia and Others v. Italy*, nineteen Italian nationals living in Caserta and San Nicola La Strada (Campania) complained under Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention that Italy’s poor management of municipal waste collection, treatment and disposal, and its failure to protect them from pollution from the “Lo Uttaro” landfill, violated their rights to life and to private/family life and health/environment.

Campania was under a waste emergency from 1994 to 2009, managed largely by deputy commissioners. By 2007–2008, mayors in Caserta and San Nicola La Strada issued orders describing huge accumulations of uncollected waste, fires releasing dioxin, unbearable smells, traffic obstruction and a public health emergency. Schools and markets were closed or suspended. WHO studies found elevated cancer mortality and congenital malformations in the Naples/Caserta area, especially where illegal hazardous waste disposal and uncontrolled burning occurred, though other factors were also noted.

The “Lo Uttaro” site had previously hosted a landfill operated by Ecologica Meridionale in the late 1980s–early 1990s. In 2001, a technical report declared the area absolutely unsuitable for a new waste plant, citing extremely serious pollution and a predictable environmental disaster. In 2005, a regional remediation plan included permanent safety measures for the site. Nevertheless, in 2006 authorities agreed to open a new waste disposal plant there, and in 2007 the deputy commissioner authorised the ACSA CE 3 consortium to operate it.

Residents brought an urgent civil action. In July 2007, the Naples District Court ordered the plant to cease operating, finding no proper environmental impact assessment, existing pollution, and failure to protect public health. On appeal, the plant was allowed to operate pending an expert report. In October 2007, the expert found groundwater already contaminated and concluded that adding more waste would worsen risks and complicate remediation. The mayor temporarily closed the plant in November 2007.

In November 2007, a criminal judge seized the landfill. The GIP found hazardous waste had been disposed of contrary to authorisation, certifications were forged, groundwater was contaminated, safety measures were absent, the site was unsuitable, and waste exceeded authorised volumes by 4.5 times. In 2016, the ACSA CE 3 managing director and a deputy commissioner were convicted of illegal waste trade; the manager was also convicted of environmental disaster. In 2017, the Court of Appeal acquitted them because the limitation period had expired but upheld civil damages and remediation orders; the Court of Cassation later quashed that judgment for inadequate reasoning.

Environmental characterisation in 2013–2016 confirmed groundwater contamination by arsenic, nickel, antimony, iron, manganese, mercury and fluorides. ARPAC recommended urgent safety measures, a ban on groundwater use, and removal of asbestos-containing hazardous waste. Mayors prohibited groundwater use and cultivation. Remediation was repeatedly delayed, and wells were seized in 2019. The applicants alleged no remediation had occurred by March 2020, while the Government claimed securing work and tenders were underway.

EU Court of Justice judgments also found Italy failed to clean illegal landfills and ensure an adequate waste disposal network in Campania; millions of tonnes of “ecobales” remained. A parliamentary commission found hazardous waste had been disposed of at Lo Uttaro and that authorities failed to monitor and even certified false information. The applicants therefore alleged that the prolonged waste crisis and the reopening/operation of Lo Uttaro, despite known contamination and unsuitability, exposed them to serious environmental and health risks, engaging Italy’s positive obligations under Articles 2 and 8.
001-223278:
**Case of Lyapchev and Others v. Bulgaria** (Applications Nos. 75478/13 and 30713/15) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered on 2 March 2023. The case concerns complaints by Bulgarian applicants that domestic authorities ordered the forfeiture of alleged proceeds of crime.

**First application (No. 75478/13)** was introduced on 28 November 2013 by Spas Dimitrov Lyapchev (born 1972) and Miroslava Dimitrova Lyapcheva (born 1982). The predicate offence was a judgment of the Sandanski District Court of 4 June 2008, final on 1 June 2009, convicting the first applicant of procuring. The offence was committed between January and April 2005 in the applicants’ hotel.

The authorities examined the applicants’ income and expenses over an unusually long period, from 29 March 1990 to 12 February 2007. The forfeited assets included a building bought in 2001 and converted into a hotel between 2002 and 2004; three plots of land bought in 2001–2003; and two cars. According to the Commission for Uncovering Proceeds of Crime, the hotel was worth BGN 918,460 (EUR 470,000), while the remaining properties were worth BGN 41,225 (EUR 21,000).

The domestic courts accepted that forfeiture could be ordered even if the assets had been acquired before the first applicant committed the predicate offence. They found a significant discrepancy between the applicants’ lawful income and their expenditure during the period examined, equivalent to 3,278 minimum monthly salaries. They also noted that other investigations had been opened against the first applicant in 1993 but had not been concluded. On that basis, the courts considered it a reasonable assumption that the assets were proceeds of crime. The final forfeiture decision was given by the Supreme Court of Cassation on 29 May 2013.

**Second application (No. 30713/15)** was introduced on 17 June 2015 by Petyo Kirilov Chupetlovski (born 1973). He had been convicted by a final Supreme Court of Cassation judgment of 16 November 2009 of taking a bribe of BGN 120 (EUR 61) on one occasion in 2007. As a lab technician, he had accepted the money to ensure a false sick leave certificate. When sentencing him to suspended imprisonment, the court described the offence as an “isolated accident” in his life.

The authorities checked his income and expenses from 17 June 1991 to 1 March 2010. The forfeited assets were a flat in the sea resort of Slanchev Bryag, bought in 2005 and valued in 2010 at BGN 62,579 (EUR 32,000), and BGN 88,825 (EUR 45,430) held in bank accounts.

The domestic courts found that during the period examined the applicant had received remuneration under a labour contract totalling 336 minimum monthly salaries, while his daily expenses, calculated using statistical data, amounted to the equivalent of 379 minimum monthly salaries. He had acquired several immovable properties, but for most he proved a lawful source, namely money from his family and from the sale of other property. No lawful source was established for the Slanchev Bryag flat or the bank deposits. The courts considered that the nature of his “criminal activity” could lead to the conclusion that such activity was the source of those assets. The final forfeiture decision was given by the Supreme Court of Cassation on 22 December 2014.

Both applications therefore concerned domestic forfeiture orders based largely on statistical income-and-expenditure comparisons and assumptions linking assets to criminal conduct, including assets acquired before or unrelated in time to the predicate offences. The applicants complained to the European Court about these forfeitures as alleged proceeds of crime.
001-229601:
The European Court of Human Rights case *O.J. and J.O. v. Georgia and Russia* (Applications nos. 42126/15 and 42127/15) concerned two Georgian nationals arrested on 15 March 2012 in Tagiloni, Gali Region, Abkhazia, by a special-forces team of the de facto Abkhaz Security Services. A search of the second applicant’s house allegedly found two hand grenades and a hunting knife. The applicants complained that they were ill-treated during arrest and subsequent detention, held unlawfully, and denied a fair hearing before the de facto Supreme Court of Abkhazia, which convicted them of espionage and sentenced them to imprisonment for endangering the constitutional order of Abkhazia.

The prosecution alleged that in early 2011 the applicants, acting on instructions from Georgia’s Department of Military Intelligence, recruited D.K.—a soldier in the Russian border-guard unit at Tagiloni—as an informant and acted as intermediaries transmitting information to Georgian authorities. Both applicants were charged with espionage on 23 March 2012; the second applicant was also charged with unlawful possession of ammunition and a cold weapon.

The applicants alleged that they were beaten while handcuffed to chairs and subjected to waterboarding during questioning about their ties to Georgian intelligence and the Russian informant. The first applicant alleged that his teeth were loosened with extraction forceps and that he was threatened with rape and internet publication of footage. The second applicant alleged that a rope was tied around his neck to simulate strangulation. Lawyers assigned on 19 March 2012 allegedly advised them to confess to stop the beatings. Both then admitted ties to Georgian military intelligence, though they later claimed the confessions were extracted under torture. They said ill-treatment continued, though less frequently, during twice-weekly questioning by de facto security services and Russian Federal Security Service staff.

The applicants were held for six months at de facto security premises in Sukhumi, then three months at temporary detention facilities of the de facto Abkhaz Ministry of Interior, and later at Dranda Prison. On 16 April 2013, the de facto Supreme Court of Abkhazia convicted them and relied partly on their confessions, despite their claims that the statements were obtained through torture. The first applicant received eleven years and six months’ imprisonment; the second received thirteen years. Although an appeal was theoretically possible within ten days, the applicants considered it futile and did not appeal. They were released on 10 March 2016 after negotiations and interventions by Georgian authorities.

The case also raised issues of State responsibility. The applicants submitted that Russia had exercised effective control over Abkhazia through military forces since 1993. Georgia argued that the de facto Abkhaz authorities survived only through Russian military, economic, financial and political support, and that Abkhazia had been absorbed into Russian military, security and administrative structures. Russia denied involvement, stating that its peacekeepers had withdrawn by 2008, that the events occurred in 2012, and that the applicants were arrested and detained by Abkhaz security services not subordinate to Russia. Russia did not contest the applicants’ factual account but denied evidence of Russian agents’ involvement. Georgia stated it could not obtain information on the facts and did not challenge the applicants’ assertions. The applicants’ complaints thus concerned alleged ill-treatment, unlawful detention, unfair trial and lack of effective remedy, with key factual disputes centering on the circumstances of their arrest, interrogation, confession, trial and detention in Abkhazia.
001-224734:
In *Burando Holding B.V. and Port Invest B.V. v. the Netherlands*, the applicants were two Dutch limited liability companies connected to the I. company, which collected waste liquids from ships in Rotterdam. In late 2006, VROM-IOD, a special investigative service, began criminal investigation “Toto” into I. company on suspicion of unlawful disposal of polluted waste. With an investigating judge’s authorization, it intercepted telephone calls of I. company employees, including calls with an employee of Ships Waste Oil Collector B.V.

Some intercepted conversations indicated price-fixing. In April 2008, VROM-IOD recorded those indications and annexed summary transcripts. In October 2008, the public prosecutor approved transmission of the record and annexes to the Netherlands Competition Authority (NMA) under the Judicial and Criminal Data Act (WJSG) by handwritten note. Transmission occurred in June 2009. In 2009–2010, the prosecutor approved further transmissions of selected transcripts and audio files. Before these transfers, VROM-IOD and NMA officials had contacts about which data were relevant to the price-fixing investigation. The last transmission was approved in August 2010 and took place in September 2010.

The criminal case against I. company was settled in March 2010. On 5 July 2010, the Regional Court, finding a settlement had been reached, declared the public prosecutor inadmissible in the prosecution. The NMA nevertheless used the transmitted data to investigate cartel conduct in ship-generated waste collection. In November 2011, it fined I. company EUR 1,861,000 for coordinating behavior and limiting price competition. The fine was jointly attributed to Port Invest B.V. and Burando Holding B.V. because the NMA considered they had exercised decisive influence over I. company.

The applicants objected, complaining that the prosecutor had not conducted a knowable and reviewable balancing of interests and that there had been no prior judicial control over the transmission. The Regional Court in 2013 accepted that the intercepted telephone data were “criminal data” under the WJSG. It found no reviewable weighing of interests had been recorded: the prosecutor had merely handwritten approval or used pre-printed forms without reasoning. It therefore excluded the transcripts as evidence and quashed the NMA decisions.

The ACM, successor to the NMA, appealed. In 2015, the Supreme Administrative Court for Trade and Industry quashed the Regional Court’s judgment. It held that the data were criminal data, that transmission served a compelling general interest—the economic well-being of the country—and complied with the WJSG. It found no legal requirement for written reasoning at the time of transmission; compliance could be reviewed later. It also found sufficient judicial safeguards, and that the ACM could not reasonably have obtained the price-fixing information less intrusively because such agreements are rarely written. It held the criminal case ended only when the July 2010 ruling became final, so the transmissions fell within the applicable destruction period.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant companies alleged violations of Articles 8 and 13. They argued that transmission of data lawfully obtained in a criminal investigation to another law enforcement authority, and its use by the Competition Authority, were not foreseeable. They also complained that procedural safeguards were insufficient, especially because the transmission was a factual act not subject to administrative appeal, leaving only ex post civil tort review. The ECtHR communicated the complaints under Articles 8 and 13. The Third Section delivered judgment on 16 May 2023; the case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 April 2025.
001-229141:
The case of *Sholomytskyy and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 12260/15 and two others) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, in a judgment delivered on 30 November 2023. The judgment is final but subject to editorial revision. The Committee was composed of Mārtiņš Mits (President), Kateřina Šimáčková and Mykola Gnatovskyy, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The applicants lodged applications against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Ukrainian Government were given notice. The applicants primarily complained of unlawful detention and also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The key facts are set out in the appended table. There are three applicants: Leonid Valentynovych Sholomytskyy (born 1957), Vasyl Vasylyovych Muzyka (born 1988), and Oleksiy Garriyovych Tamrazov (born 1975). Each was represented by a lawyer in Kyiv.

First, Leonid Valentynovych Sholomytskyy filed application no. 12260/15, introduced on 3 March 2015. His representative was Dmytro Oleksandrovych Morgun, Kyiv. The period of alleged unlawful detention was from 16 July 2014 to 17 July 2014. The relevant domestic decision identified is an arrest report of 16 July 2014. His detention therefore lasted approximately one day, beginning with an arrest recorded on 16 July 2014.

Second, Vasyl Vasylyovych Muzyka filed application no. 60551/17, introduced on 3 August 2017. His representative was Olena Olegivna Chernova, Kyiv. The period of alleged unlawful detention was from 00:10 a.m. to 2:35 p.m. on 1 February 2017. The relevant domestic decision is an arrest report of 1 February 2017. His detention therefore lasted about fourteen and a half hours, from shortly after midnight until mid-afternoon.

Third, Oleksiy Garriyovych Tamrazov filed application no. 3999/19, introduced on 24 December 2018. His representative was Dmytro Igorovych Chashchevyy, Kyiv. The period of alleged unlawful detention was from 21 August 2018 to 23 August 2018. No relevant domestic decision is listed in the appended table extract. His alleged unlawful detention therefore lasted approximately two days.

The core alleged violation is unlawful detention. The key facts relevant to that complaint are the precise periods during which each applicant was held, the dates the applications were introduced, and the existence or absence of a relevant domestic arrest report. For Sholomytskyy and Muzyka, the table identifies arrest reports of 16 July 2014 and 1 February 2017 respectively as the relevant domestic decisions. For Tamrazov, no corresponding domestic decision is listed. These facts are central to assessing whether the detentions were lawful and effected in accordance with a procedure prescribed by domestic law, ordinarily engaging Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. The short durations of the detentions do not by themselves establish a violation; rather, the alleged lack of a proper legal basis or procedural safeguards is the essence of the complaints. The applicants also raised other Convention complaints, but the facts supplied in the extract focus primarily on the unlawful-detention allegations. The available text does not include the Court’s full reasoning or final findings on the merits.
001-223716:
**Case: J.A. and Others v. Italy** (App. no. 21329/18), ECtHR First Section, judgment of 30 March 2023. The applicants are four Tunisian nationals. They left Tunisia on 15 October 2017 on makeshift vessels, were rescued by an Italian ship after an emergency at sea, and arrived in Lampedusa on 16 October. They were placed in the Contrada Imbriacola hotspot, an Early Reception and Aid Centre designated as an Italian hotspot under Decree-Law no. 13/2017.

They stayed for ten days. They alleged that they could not interact with authorities and could not lawfully leave the centre; they occasionally left through an opening in the surrounding fence. They described conditions as inhuman and degrading. National reports described the Lampedusa hotspot as a former identification and expulsion centre with bars, gates and metal fences; overcrowded dormitories with up to 36 beds, insufficient bedding, no common rooms, no canteen, and stays averaging about fifteen days. The National Guarantor found that migrants were not allowed to leave even after photographs and fingerprints were taken, amounting to de facto detention without a clear legal basis or judicial scrutiny. The applicants received some information flyers about asylum procedures but said they could not fully understand them, and they underwent identification procedures.

On 26 October 2017, early in the morning, the applicants and about forty others were woken, told to undress, searched, and bused to Lampedusa Airport. There they were asked to sign documents whose content they did not understand and were not given copies. These were later identified as refusal-of-entry orders issued by the Agrigento police headquarters. Only the first two applicants later obtained copies; requests for the third and fourth went unanswered. The Government maintained that the orders were duly served, that the applicants signed receipts, received copies, and were informed of the right to challenge the orders before the Agrigento District Court within thirty days. The applicants were then searched again, their wrists secured with Velcro straps, their phones taken, and they were flown to Palermo. The straps were removed during the flight and reapplied at Palermo Airport. There they met a Tunisian consular official, and on the same day, 26 October 2017, they were forcibly removed to Tunisia.

Domestic law: Article 13 of the Italian Constitution protects personal liberty; police measures affecting liberty must be validated by a judge within 48 hours plus a further 48 hours. Legislative Decree no. 286/1998 governs refusal of entry, hotspot identification, and detention/validation. Constitutional Court judgments 105/2001 and 275/2017 held that retention in reception centres and deferred refusals of entry executed by force affect personal liberty and require judicial review and legislative regulation. EU law also requires written reasons and speedy judicial review for detention.

Alleged violations: Article 3 (inhuman or degrading conditions in the hotspot and treatment during removal), Article 5 §§1, 2 and 4 (unlawful de facto detention, failure to inform promptly of reasons, and lack of speedy judicial review), Article 13 (no effective remedy), Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement), and Article 4 of Protocol No. 4 (collective expulsion). The case therefore concerns whether Italy’s hotspot regime and the applicants’ forced removal breached Convention safeguards against arbitrary detention, poor treatment, lack of remedies, and collective expulsion.
001-223284:
**International Research and Exchange Board v. Azerbaijan** (Application no. 7668/15) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the First Section Committee on 2 March 2023. The applicant is the Baku representative office of the International Research and Exchanges Board (IREX), an international humanitarian organisation registered in Azerbaijan in 1998. The application was lodged on 30 December 2014 and concerned an order to search and seize the applicant’s property and an order freezing its bank accounts in the context of criminal proceedings against various local NGOs and representative offices of international organisations.

On 22 April 2014 the Prosecutor General’s Office opened criminal case no. 142006023 under Articles 308.1 (abuse of power) and 313 (forgery by an official) of the Criminal Code, alleging irregularities in the financial activities of several NGOs. The applicant organisation was mentioned in the decision opening the case but never had “suspect” status.

Regarding the bank accounts, on 26 July 2014 the Nasimi District Court issued an attachment order over all the applicant’s bank accounts pending the investigation. The court cited the need for a complete, comprehensive and objective investigation. The order was said to be appealable within three days. The applicant claimed that the hearing occurred without its representative because it was not notified, and that no copy of the order was sent to it. Because 27 July was a Sunday and 28–29 July were public holidays for Ramadan, the bank only informed the applicant of the freeze on 30 July. On 31 July the applicant obtained a copy of the order and appealed the next day, also requesting restoration of the time-limit. On 7 August the Nasimi District Court refused to restore the time-limit, finding no valid reasons for the delay, and on 18 August the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that refusal. The attachment was lifted only on 10 July 2020.

Regarding the search, on 4 September 2014 the Yasamal District Court authorised investigators to search the applicant’s office and seize legal, financial, accounting and bank documents relating to its activities and its receipt of grants and other financial aid, including documents stored on electronic devices. The court again relied on the need to ensure a complete, comprehensive and objective investigation. The search was carried out on 5 September 2014. Authorities seized twelve laptops, six computer system units, eight video cameras, two photo cameras, one mobile phone, forty-one CDs and DVDs, one hard drive, fifteen flash drives, one audio cassette and thirty-five boxes of documents. On 24 September 2014 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the search warrant. After expert examinations, the seized items were returned on 13 November 2015, but the applicant alleged that the computers were not returned in working condition.

The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the freezing of its bank accounts. It complained under Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the search and seizure at its office. It also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the retention of its computers for about a year and their allegedly unusable return. Finally, it complained under Article 18 that the restrictions were imposed for a purpose other than those permitted by the relevant provisions. The Court gave notice of the complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 18 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the search, seizure and freeze, and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.
001-223380:
In **Z.A. v. Ireland** (Application no. 19632/20, judgment of 9 March 2023), the applicant is a Nigerian national born in 1994. He arrived in Ireland in 2001 aged seven to join his mother and siblings after his father’s death. His mother had come to Ireland in 1999, initially sought asylum, later obtained leave as the parent of an Irish citizen, and became an Irish citizen; all six of the applicant’s siblings are also Irish citizens. Until age 16, Z.A. had permission to remain as his mother’s dependant. He then received permission in his own right, first for one year and later for three years from March 2011, subject to conditions including obeying Irish law and not engaging in criminal activity. In June 2014 he sought renewal and had a pending naturalisation application, but his permission was not renewed.

The key criminal facts concern charges brought in March 2010: one offence of sexual assault and two offences of attempted defilement of a child under 17. The incidents occurred in February and March 2010, when the applicant was 16 and the victim was a 14-year-old girl known to him and other teenage boys. The trial took place in 2014, when he was 20. He pleaded guilty. In October 2014, the Circuit Court imposed a two-year sentence, suspended for three years, plus 12 months’ Probation Service supervision. The judge described the offences as serious, noted the victim’s distress, and referred to a probation report assessing the applicant’s risk of reoffending as moderate. Separately, in July 2014 he drove on a motorway without a full licence and without insurance; in February 2015 he was convicted and fined €300.

In February 2015, the Minister for Justice proposed deportation under section 3 of the Immigration Act 1999. An initial deportation order in April 2016 was challenged and revoked in November 2016. In November 2016 the Minister reconsidered deportation, and the applicant made fresh representations in December 2016. An April 2017 INIS analysis accepted that deportation would interfere with his Article 8 private and family life, given his long residence, education, football career, social ties, and family in Ireland. However, it found deportation proportionate to preventing disorder and crime. It considered his Nigerian cultural ties and relatives, his ability to pursue football in Nigeria, and the possibility of family relocation or visits. It weighed the serious sexual offences, lack of formal rehabilitative therapy, traffic offences, moderate reoffending risk, and public policy/common good. The Minister issued a deportation order on 21 April 2017, requiring him to leave by 4 June 2017.

The applicant sought judicial review, arguing that deportation disproportionately interfered with his Article 8 rights and seeking a declaration that the Immigration Act 1999 was incompatible with the Convention because it lacked an independent review/appeal mechanism before deportation. The High Court rejected the challenge on 30 May 2019, applying domestic *Meadows*/*ISOF* principles: the court would not rebalance the case but would ask whether the Minister’s balancing was flawed or irrational. It upheld the Minister’s treatment of the offences, risk, lack of rehabilitation, and traffic offences, distinguished *A.A. v. the United Kingdom*, and held that judicial review provided an effective Article 13 remedy. Leave to appeal was refused in July 2019, and the Supreme Court refused leave in November 2019. Before the European Court, Z.A. alleged violations of Article 8 (private and family life) and Article 13 (effective remedy), centring on the proportionality of deportation and the adequacy of domestic review.
001-222134:
**Case of Nikolaev and Others v. Bulgaria** (Applications nos. 48806/11 and 11138/12) is a European Court of Human Rights Third Section Committee judgment dated 12 January 2023. The applicants complained about the forfeiture of alleged proceeds of crime in Bulgarian proceedings under the 2005 Act. The case concerned two separate applications.

In the first application (no. 48806/11), introduced on 22 July 2011, the applicants were Zlati Aleksiev Nikolaev (b. 1961) and his son Atanas Zlatev Aleksiev (b. 1987). The predicate offence was fraud committed in 2000 by the first applicant and an unknown person, causing damage of BGN 3,476 (approximately EUR 1,778); the money was later returned to the victim. On 12 March 2001, the Dimitrovgrad District Court approved a plea agreement and sentenced the first applicant to three months’ imprisonment, suspended. In the forfeiture proceedings, authorities examined the applicants’ income and expenses from 1 January 1990 to 22 May 2007. They forfeited two plots of land with houses in Gorna Oriahovitsa. One was bought by the first applicant in 1990; the other was bought in 1994 by the first applicant and his partner for the second applicant. Both properties were substantially renovated and improved after purchase. Court-appointed experts valued them in 2007 at BGN 176,300 (about EUR 90,000). After the domestic proceedings ended, the State sold both properties to third parties.

The domestic courts found that during the relevant period the applicants had no declared revenues. It was not proven that the first applicant had worked; declarations from other people did not validly establish employment or remuneration. No taxes had been paid. A claimed loan was not proven, and the assertion that family friends had renovated the houses for free was rejected as implausible given the substantial works. Under section 4 of the 2005 Act, assets of substantial value could be presumed to be proceeds of crime if no lawful provenance was established. The applicants failed to rebut that presumption. The courts held that no causal link between the predicate offence and the forfeited assets was necessary; the predicate offence merely triggered the forfeiture proceedings. The final decision was given by the Supreme Court of Cassation on 1 March 2011.

In the second application (no. 11138/12), introduced on 9 February 2012, the applicant was Petar Ivanov Glavchev (b. 1999). His father had been convicted by the Plovdiv Regional Court on 5 November 2003, final on 24 January 2007, for pimping committed between 1999 and 2003. The forfeiture authorities checked the father’s income and expenses for 1993–2007. They forfeited a house with a plot of land and outbuildings, acquired in 2005 in exchange for a flat bought for the applicant by his mother in 2001. The Commission for Uncovering Proceeds of Crime valued the property at BGN 57,135 (approximately EUR 29,200). Further assets were also forfeited from the father but were not part of the application. The applicant claimed that the 2001 flat had been bought with money gifted by his maternal grandparents, but the gift was not sufficiently proven. He pointed to no other lawful origin, and his father had not established sufficient lawful income. Again, the courts stated that no causal link between the criminal activity and the assets was required. It was enough that the applicant or his father had not rebutted the presumption under section 4 of the 2005 Act, meaning the assets were deemed proceeds of crime. The final decision was given by the Supreme Court of Cassation on 10 August 2011.

The applicants’ core complaint was that these forfeiture orders, based on statutory presumptions and without proof of a causal link to the predicate offences, amounted to an unjustified interference with their Convention rights.
001-226195:
In *Al-Masudi v. Denmark* (Application no. 35740/21), the European Court of Human Rights examined an Article 8 complaint concerning Denmark’s expulsion of a settled migrant. The applicant, Mr Mohamad Mustafa Hamid Al-Masudi, is an Iraqi national born in 1994. He entered Denmark in 1998 at age three through family reunion and was granted a permanent residence permit in February 2002. He therefore had long lawful residence and strong ties to Denmark. He lived in Nyborg, grew up with his parents and four siblings, had no close family in Iraq, had visited Iraq only once around age ten, spoke broken Arabic, had no education or vocational training, no permanent labour-market attachment, and received cash benefits and parental financial support. He was unmarried but had a Danish fiancée; their child was born in December 2020.

The applicant had a criminal record beginning in 2010. As a juvenile, he was convicted of theft and a weapons offence, robbery, and a Controlled Substances Act violation. As an adult, he was convicted of violence and drug offences in 2013, aggravated violence in 2017, and violence and drug offences in 2018. He also received eight fines between 2013 and 2020 for drug-related violations. In 2017 he received a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period, and in 2018 he was cautioned about the risk of expulsion.

In March 2020, the District Court convicted him of possessing 57.1 grams of MDMA and 12.1 grams of amphetamine for distribution, contrary to Article 191 of the Penal Code, and of keeping a sawn-off shotgun and spare cartridges in an unlocked cabinet at home, contrary to Article 192a, with particularly aggravating circumstances. He was sentenced to two years and nine months’ imprisonment and expelled from Denmark with a lifelong re-entry ban.

In ordering expulsion, the District Court applied section 22 of the Aliens Act and section 26(2), under which expulsion is required unless it would “for certain” be contrary to Denmark’s international obligations, including Article 8. Applying the *Maslov v. Austria* criteria, it considered the seriousness of the offences, his criminal history, length of stay, ties to Denmark and Iraq, and societal need for expulsion. It noted his long residence from age three and weak ties to Iraq, but also his repeated convictions, including robbery, violence and drug offences, prior suspended expulsion and caution, lack of education or stable employment, and dependency on benefits. It concluded that expulsion would not certainly violate Denmark’s international obligations.

On appeal, the High Court upheld the judgment in September 2020, finding that expulsion and the permanent re-entry ban were not disproportionate under Article 8. It stated that his engagement during detention and his fiancée’s pregnancy did not change the outcome. In November 2021, the Appeals Permission Board refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court. The applicant was deported to Iraq in July 2022.

The alleged violation concerns whether the expulsion order and lifelong re-entry ban violated his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8, particularly given his long residence in Denmark, limited ties to Iraq, and family life with his Danish fiancée and child, weighed against his serious and repeated criminal offending.
001-222138:
In *Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine* (Apps. nos. 27276/15 and 33692/15; judgment 12 January 2023), two Ukrainian nationals, both judges of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine, complained about their dismissal by Parliament for alleged “breach of oath,” relying on Articles 6, 8 and 18 ECHR.

The applicants were appointed to the Constitutional Court by Parliament in August 2006. In September 2010, the Constitutional Court declared the 2004 constitutional amendments unconstitutional because of procedural irregularities, thereby restoring the 1996 Constitution. This ruling later became politically contentious. After the 2013–14 Euromaidan protests and the change of power in Ukraine, Parliament on 21 February 2014 reverted to the 2004 Constitution. On 24 February 2014, Parliament adopted a resolution dismissing the Constitutional Court judges appointed under its quota, including the applicants, for “breach of oath.” Parliament reasoned that the 30 September 2010 judgment had unconstitutionally amended the Constitution, usurped parliamentary powers, violated democracy and separation of powers, and changed the constitutional order. It also cited two other Constitutional Court judgments, on social payments and elections, and asked prosecutors to investigate the 2010 judgment. The applicants submitted resignations in March 2014 but also challenged their dismissal.

The first applicant challenged the dismissal in the Higher Administrative Court (HAC). On 18 June 2014, the HAC declared the parliamentary resolution unlawful as regards him. It found that Parliament had disregarded the Constitutional Court’s internal Rules requiring preliminary consideration by the Constitutional Court, and had used a simplified procedure unsuitable for dismissing Constitutional Court judges. It also relied on section 28 of the Constitutional Court Act, which protects judges from liability for their votes. On 2 December 2014, the Supreme Court quashed that judgment. It held that the 2010 judgment had contradicted the constitutional amendment procedure, that the Constitutional Court had no power to invalidate a constitutional norm, and that the applicant’s participation amounted to a breach of oath. It rejected the other two judgments as grounds, finding they fell within judicial discretion. It accepted Parliament’s procedure because the Constitutional Court’s Rules were internal and did not bind Parliament. The second applicant’s similar claim was dismissed on 26 January 2015, relying on the first applicant’s case, and upheld by the Supreme Court on 28 April 2015.

Relevant domestic law allowed dismissal of Constitutional Court judges for breach of oath but also protected them from liability for votes. International materials emphasized judicial independence, security of tenure, and dismissal only for serious misconduct under fair procedures with independent review.

The key alleged violations therefore arose from the legislature’s removal of judges for a judicial decision, the alleged absence of required ethics review, reliance on simplified parliamentary procedure, the Supreme Court’s reversal of the HAC, and the political context, which the applicants said showed interference with judicial independence and improper purposes under Articles 6, 8 and 18.
001-228861:
**J&C Properties Limited v. Malta (Application no. 16680/21)**

This case concerns an application lodged against Malta with the European Court of Human Rights by J&C Properties Limited, a company registered in Ħamrun, Malta. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, stemming from a unilaterally imposed lease on its property.

The key facts are as follows: The applicant company owns a property at 18 St. Joseph High Street, Ħamrun. As of June 2007, this property was subject to a lease imposed under Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta (the Ordinance). The tenant held title under this old, protected lease regime. At the outset, the annual rent payable to the applicant was €390. This amount was subject to periodic increases, rising to €450 in 2013 and €459 in 2016, with further increases linked to the cost-of-living index planned for every three years.

The applicant company initiated constitutional redress proceedings in Malta, arguing that the application of Article 12 of the Ordinance, which governed this lease, breached its property rights. Crucially, the applicant limited its claim to the period ending in December 2017.

Central to the case is the stark disparity between the contractual rent and the actual market rental value of the property. A court-appointed expert estimated the annual market rental value at €4,590 in 2007, €6,300 in 2012, and €9,800 in 2017, for a property with an estimated sale value of €320,000. Over the relevant period, the estimated total market rent was approximately €87,000. In contrast, the applicant’s own expert provided estimates that were half these figures. Even so, the discrepancy between the rent actually received, which was fixed at a few hundred euros annually, and any of the market valuations was substantial.

In a judgment dated 9 July 2019, the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It awarded the applicant €15,000 in compensation and ruled that the tenant could no longer rely on the impugned law to maintain title to the property. In its reasoning, the court acknowledged the significant difference between the two expert valuations and determined that the true value was likely a mean between them. This judgment was subsequently confirmed by the Constitutional Court on 6 October 2020, following an appeal by the State.

Subsequently, proceedings were held before the Rent Regulation Board, where the rent was increased in accordance with 2018 amendments to the Ordinance. Following this rent increase, the tenants vacated the property.

Despite winning the constitutional case and receiving compensation, the applicant company remained dissatisfied. It brought the present application to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that it was still a victim of the violation of its Convention rights. The core of its complaint was that the €15,000 compensation awarded by the domestic courts was too low, given the extensive period during which its property was leased at a rent far below its market value. It argued that this inadequate compensation, coupled with the imposition of the lease itself, continued to constitute a disproportionate interference with its property rights and that it lacked an effective remedy to address this ongoing grievance.
001-222894:
In *Gallo v. Italy* (Application no. 11061/05), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) delivered judgment on 9 February 2023. The applicant, Mr Michele Gallo, an Italian national born in 1939 and living in Fasano, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that he had been unlawfully deprived of his land through indirect or “constructive” expropriation and had received no compensation.

The applicant was co-owner, together with F.L., of a plot of land in Mottola. On 25 July 1974 F.L. sued the Mottola municipality in the Taranto District Court, alleging that the municipality had occupied part of the land without permission and built a road on it. He sought compensation for the dispossession and for depreciation of the remaining land. That first action was struck out on 5 March 1980 because both parties failed to appear at two consecutive hearings. On 6 April 1984 F.L. brought the same damages action again. The District Court ordered an independent expert valuation. On 3 April 1986 the applicant joined the proceedings, claiming that he was co-owner of part of the occupied land and seeking compensation for its dispossession.

By judgment of 29 March 1989, the Taranto District Court declared the occupation unlawful and held that ownership of the land had been transferred to the municipality under the constructive-expropriation rule. The expert assessed the 1974 market value of the applicant’s share at ITL 10,946,450. The court ordered the municipality to pay F.L. ITL 143,139,473 and the applicant ITL 58,891,901 (EUR 30,415), corresponding to the 1974 market value adjusted for inflation.

The municipality appealed. On 14 March 1994 the Lecce Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. The municipality then appealed to the Court of Cassation, arguing, among other things, that the applicant’s compensation claim was time-barred. By judgment of 3 March 1997, the Court of Cassation partly upheld the appeal and remitted the case to the Bari Court of Appeal. On 12 July 2000, the Bari Court of Appeal declared the applicant’s right to compensation time-barred because he had lodged his claim more than five years after the road’s construction was completed on 20 November 1974. It relied on the Court of Cassation’s case-law that, in constructive expropriation, ownership transferred to the administration upon completion of the public works. The applicant appealed to the Court of Cassation, which dismissed his appeal on 23 September 2004.

Later, in judgment no. 735/2015 of 19 January 2015, the Court of Cassation sitting as a full court held that the constructive-expropriation rule was incompatible with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It ruled that individuals were entitled to seek restitution unless they chose to claim damages, and that the five-year limitation period for damages should run from the date the claim was lodged with the court.

Before the European Court, the applicant relied on Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining that he had been unlawfully deprived of his land by constructive expropriation and had obtained no compensation for that deprivation.
001-228530:
**Summary of Key Facts: Bild GmbH & Co. KG v. Germany**

The case of *Bild GmbH & Co. KG v. Germany* (Application no. 9602/18) concerns a complaint under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding freedom of expression. The applicant, Bild GmbH & Co. KG, operates the German news website bild.de. The alleged violation stems from a German court injunction ordering the company to cease publishing unblurred CCTV footage of a police arrest.

The facts originate from an incident on 23 June 2013 at a nightclub in Bremen. Police were called after a customer, identified as D., behaved aggressively towards staff. On 10 July 2013, Bild published an article titled “Here the police beat up D. (28)” along with CCTV footage obtained from the club owner. The video showed several police officers forcing D. to the ground. One officer was visibly seen hitting D. with a baton and kicking him while he was immobilised. A voice-over commentary described the footage as showing police brutality against a defenceless man. A second article and additional footage, showing D.’s aggressive actions prior to police arrival, were published on 12 July 2013.

Officer P. was one of the police officers involved in the arrest. The published CCTV footage clearly showed his face for several seconds as he assisted in restraining D., though it did not depict him using excessive force. On 18 July 2013, P.’s lawyer requested that Bild cease publication of the footage without blurring his face. Bild refused, leading P. to seek an injunction from the Oldenburg Regional Court. P. also sought reimbursement for damages, stating he had been confronted with critical comments from the public and his children.

On 14 May 2014, the Regional Court ordered Bild to stop publishing the unblurred footage. The court acknowledged the footage portrayed an aspect of contemporary society and that the publications concerned the state’s monopoly on force, a matter of public interest. However, it found the publications violated P.’s personality rights. Key factors included P.’s lack of prior public profile, the recording being made without his consent during his professional duties, and the negative consequences he suffered. The court highlighted the editorial presentation, noting the voice-over portrayed P. as a “violent thug.” It also emphasised that Bild had deliberately omitted footage of D.’s prior actions, which had precipitated the police intervention, thereby presenting a biased interpretation.

Bild’s appeal was dismissed by the Oldenburg Court of Appeal on 21 July 2015. The appellate court upheld the finding that publishing the unedited footage without P.’s consent violated his rights. It stressed that the presumption of innocence required cautious or balanced coverage and reiterated the importance of the omitted context. The court stated that pixelation was necessary regardless of whether future reporting portrayed P. negatively or positively, as the footage could then only be seen as portraying a routine police intervention, not a matter of contemporary society. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept Bild’s constitutional complaint on 3 August 2017 without providing reasons.

Bild subsequently lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that the German court rulings violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.
001-249964:
**Metalla v. Albania (Application no. 19646/20)** concerns an Albanian judge’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights about his dismissal from judicial office through Albania’s vetting process. The communicated complaint concerned the applicant’s right to respect for private life. The key facts relate to the decisions of the Independent Qualification Commission (“IQC”) and the Special Appeal Chamber (“SAC”) under the Vetting Act (“VA”).

The applicant, Ervin Metalla, served as a judge at Durrës District Court from 2001, as its President from 2005, and at Tirana Court of Appeal from 2013. He also chaired the Union of Judges from 2011. Vetting institutions found no concerns regarding links to organised crime, professional skills, or general ethical compliance. The IQC refused his request to investigate those remaining criteria.

On 23 July 2018, the IQC dismissed him under section 61(3) VA because of irregularities concerning his brother E.M.’s assets and the applicant’s asset declarations. It found his conduct unethical, stating that judges must act with integrity in extrajudicial activities and that he had engaged in fictitious transactions.

The applicant appealed and again requested assessment of the remaining criteria, arguing that his teaching, legal manuals, and union work showed his contribution to justice. On 30 October 2019, the SAC upheld the dismissal by a 3–2 majority and added a ground under section 61(5) VA: that an overall assessment showed he had undermined public trust in the justice system.

The SAC’s key findings were as follows. The applicant lived in a rented Tirana flat while commuting to Durrës. In 2007 he signed a preliminary sale contract and commercial loan for that flat; ownership would pass after legalisation and registration, which occurred in 2013. From 2008, Council of Ministers’ Decision no. 600/2007 allowed judges a soft loan with State-covered interest above 4% if they or close relatives did not own a dwelling in their judicial district, limited to housing there. In 2011, annexes replaced the applicant with E.M. as buyer and loan debtor. The applicant admitted this was to make him eligible for the soft loan. The SAC held this created the appearance he no longer owned the flat, though he continued living there; the annex was neither notarised nor declared in his 2011 asset declaration.

The applicant also signed a compliance declaration, a Durrës flat purchase contract, and a 5,000,000 Albanian lek soft-loan agreement, with E.M. as guarantor. E.M. mortgaged a 2008 flat as collateral. Through transactions, the loan was transferred to his father N.M.’s account as “debt repayment.” The funds remained available to the applicant but were not declared as disposable liquidity in 2011. In 2012, debt-exchange agreements directed the funds toward a new Tirana flat; N.M. stated the funds belonged to the applicant. The applicant withdrew from the Durrës contract, allegedly due to delays, but the SAC found the sole purpose was to meet soft-loan conditions. He signed a preliminary contract for the new flat but did not declare it in 2012. In 2013, the applicant, E.M., and a real-estate company agreed that the new flat would go to E.M. and the 2007 flat would remain with the applicant.

The SAC concluded that the applicant hid or misrepresented his use of the 2007 flat while benefiting from the soft loan and allowed inaccuracies about his liquidity in his declarations. It found he obtained the loan in breach of legal criteria and appeared to use it for the Tirana flat, not Durrës. It considered the fictitious transactions for personal gain unethical and damaging to public trust. It also treated E.M. as an “other related person” under VA sections 3(14) and 32(4), shifting the burden to the applicant to prove E.M.’s lawful income. E.M. had replaced him as debtor/buyer, guaranteed the loan, paid 1,000,000 lek in 2011, and had prior financial dealings; evidence showed his foreign income was modest. Two SAC judges dissented, disputing the ethics findings, the legal interpretation concerning E.M., and the finding that the transactions were fictitious.
001-248957:
In *Vashchenko and Tretyak v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights examined two applications concerning the Ukrainian Supreme Court’s reversal of final and binding judgments based on later case-law. Both applicants complained under Article 6 §1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that this retrospective review violated legal certainty and their property rights.

The first applicant, Mr Vashchenko, was a judge at the Khmelnytskyi Regional Court of Appeal. In November 2008 he brought an administrative claim against that court, the Ministry of Finance, the State Treasury, and the State Judicial Administration, seeking salary arrears accumulated in 2005–06 and compensation for underpaid income. He relied on special legislation on judges’ salaries, arguing that a judge’s salary should be calculated as a percentage of the Supreme Court President’s salary, which had increased. On 11 June 2015 the Higher Administrative Court upheld lower decisions granting him UAH 70,247.73 (about EUR 6,540) in salary arrears and rejecting his compensation claim. Those decisions became final and were enforced on 2 September 2015. On 19 January 2016, the State Judicial Administration asked the Supreme Court to review the case, relying on a different application of substantive law in another case decided on 20 October 2015. On 30 March 2016 the Supreme Court allowed the review, set aside the lower decisions, and dismissed Vashchenko’s claim in full. It reasoned that although the special law established the amount of a judge’s salary, payment depended on the general law and the State budget, which did not provide for additional payments at the material time. It also referred to its similar position in a resolution of 4 November 2015. There was no indication that Vashchenko had repaid the awarded sum or remained liable to reimburse it; he argued that domestic law precluded reversal of enforcement.

The second applicant, Mr Tretyak, worked since May 2013 at a State-owned energy company in Crimea. After Russia asserted jurisdiction over Crimea, he was dismissed on 19 March 2014 by the new pro-Russian management. In April 2014 he sued the company’s headquarters in Kyiv, seeking reinstatement, unpaid wages, compensation for forced absence, and non-pecuniary damages. On 28 October 2015 the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court upheld lower decisions in his favour. The courts found that the Crimean management had not been empowered under Ukrainian law to dismiss him and awarded unpaid salary arrears of UAH 10,897.83 (about EUR 432) and compensation of UAH 394,128.91 (about EUR 14,500). The decisions became final and enforceable. On 13 May 2016 the company’s Kyiv headquarters requested Supreme Court review, citing divergent application of substantive law in later cases, notably decisions of 16 March 2016 and 23 March 2016. On 12 April 2017 the Supreme Court allowed the review, set aside the decisions on reinstatement and compensation, but left the salary arrears award unchanged. It held that under special legislation on temporarily occupied territories, the dismissal had no legal consequences, so Tretyak should still be considered an employee. As for compensation, it relied on a certificate issued on 3 December 2014 by the Ukrainian Chamber of Commerce and Industry confirming force majeure for the company’s commercial activities in Crimea, and on Article 617 of the Civil Code, which exempts liability in cases of force majeure. It therefore found no grounds to hold the employer liable.

The domestic legal framework, as amended by the 2015 Ensuring the Right to a Fair Trial Act, allowed Supreme Court review where courts of cassation had divergently applied the same substantive law or where a cassation decision conflicted with a Supreme Court resolution. The applicants alleged that this mechanism was used to reopen and reverse final, binding, and already enforced judgments on the basis of case-law post-dating those judgments, thereby breaching legal certainty.
001-249345:
The case of *Hakobyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 21350/19) concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention on 15 April 2019. The applicant, Hrayr Hakobyan, born in 1959, was represented by Diana Shakhramanyan, a lawyer practising in Yerevan. The Armenian Government were notified of the application. The applicant complained of an unfair criminal trial, specifically that he had not been given an opportunity to put questions in court to the witness whose testimony played a significant role in securing his conviction. The final domestic decision was a Court of Cassation judgment of 16 October 2018.

The applicant had been convicted of misappropriation of State funds—described as swindling in particularly large amounts—and forgery of official documents. The central issue in the application concerns the evidence of a witness identified only as H.Z. According to the appended factual details, H.Z.’s statement was the only direct evidence directly implicating the applicant in the alleged swindling of State funds and played the decisive role in his conviction on that count. There was no other direct evidence linking the applicant to the crimes with which he had been charged.

The circumstances of H.Z.’s evidence were disputed. H.Z. was interviewed twice during the pre-trial investigation. Only during the second interview did she make incriminating statements against the applicant. Later, in court, she retracted those statements. She claimed that the investigator had inaccurately recorded them and had tried to confuse her. This retraction made the defence’s ability to question her about the reliability and consistency of her evidence particularly important.

At trial, however, the presiding judge did not allow H.Z. to respond to defence questions related to the charges against the applicant and to her relevant incriminating statement. The judge’s reasons were described as formalistic. In particular, the judge refused to allow the applicant’s representative to question H.Z. about discrepancies between her statements, including about having passed money to the applicant and the circumstances surrounding it. The judge justified this restriction on the ground that H.Z. had been summoned for an additional examination only with regard to the criminal case against herself, and she could not therefore be questioned about other matters.

In substance, the applicant’s complaint was that the domestic courts deprived him of an opportunity to challenge the decisive witness evidence against him. Because H.Z.’s testimony was the sole direct evidence on the swindling count, and because she had changed her account and later retracted it, the refusal to permit defence questioning about the inconsistencies and circumstances of her statements allegedly undermined the fairness of the proceedings. The application therefore raised issues under Article 6 of the Convention, particularly the right to a fair trial and the right to examine witnesses against the accused. The Court, sitting as a Committee of the Fifth Section, communicated the case to the Government and delivered judgment on 2 April 2026.
001-248960:
Petryk v. Ukraine (no. 11103/18) is an ECtHR Fifth Section case concerning the death of the applicant’s son, P.S., during military service and Ukraine’s response under Article 2 of the Convention.

In March 2014 P.S., then 26, married with two minor children, was mobilised. He repaired vehicles. On 18 February 2015 he had brief home leave, said his service would end in about two weeks, and allegedly showed no signs of depression. The applicant claimed he overheard P.S. being threatened by a superior, K.S., but gave no further details. On the evening of 22 February 2015, after returning from active fighting, P.S. told his father by phone that he was very tired and would call later; he never did.

P.S. died that evening from a gunshot wound in the cabin of his assigned lorry. Witnesses, including superiors V.K. and K.S. and soldiers S.K. and S.S., said he had played dominoes, left the dugout, and minutes later a shot was heard. He was found in the locked cabin, face bleeding, a rifle between his legs, with a perforating head wound. The cabin was broken into; he was unconscious but alive, bandaged and taken to hospital with V.K. and K.S., but died en route. The applicant alleged he was taken 64 km away although a hospital was only 14 km away. Most witnesses noticed nothing unusual, though some said P.S. had been upset or irritated after a mobile call; S.K. recalled P.S. saying, “You will not drive the lorry after me,” and appearing sad.

Two parallel investigations began on 23 February 2015: Kuybysheve police case no. 0111 into possible breach of firearm-handling rules, and Volnovakha police case no. 0223 into murder by unidentified persons. They did not coordinate. Case no. 0111 was discontinued on 16 April 2015 for lack of criminal offence. Case no. 0223 was discontinued three times (19 May and 27 June 2015, and 19 July 2016), but those rulings were set aside as unlawful and unfounded; the investigation remained pending.

The case file revealed serious investigative defects. A bone fragment and bullet shell found at the scene were lost without documented seizure. Blood and histological material from the initial forensic examination were destroyed before the parallel investigation requested them. Hand swabs were retrieved only in 2019/2020; gunpowder tests were negative. The lorry and gun were returned to the military unit without thorough forensic examination; further examinations occurred only in 2019 and 2021. P.S.’s mobile phone was stored unsealed and first inspected in May 2016. Although no sent SMS were then recorded, in June 2020 the mobile operator reported that on the day of death P.S. had sent seven SMS to one number. The investigator waited until February 2024 to seek restoration; the operator refused because there was no judicial authorisation and the data had been destroyed. The woman linked to that number was questioned only in March 2024; she admitted speaking to P.S. and owning the number but remembered no details and denied debts. Forensic experts repeatedly could not determine whether self-infliction was technically possible given the wound location and direction, shot distance, body and gun position, witness statements, and other evidence. A posthumous psychiatric examination in November 2024 treated suicide as established and found no mental disorder.

Separately, the family’s State allowance was initially refused but granted in 2019 after courts found the internal report unlawful; they later received non-pecuniary damages. These facts underpin the Article 2 complaint that P.S.’s death and the investigation were not adequately handled.
001-248396:
**Petkanych and Others v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 55046/16, 32999/17, 19581/18 and 15510/19) is a Fifth Section case, judgment dated 12 February 2026, concerning allegedly ineffective domestic investigations into medical negligence that resulted in the deaths of the applicants’ next of kin. The applicants are relatives of the deceased patients. The central alleged violation is that Ukraine failed to conduct effective investigations, contrary to the procedural obligation under Article 2 of the Convention.

**Application no. 55046/16 (Petkanych and Others).** P. was admitted on 19 July 2005 to an infectious diseases hospital with acute respiratory viral infection and intoxication syndrome. She was diagnosed with pleurisy and pneumonia and treated accordingly. After ineffective treatment, she was transferred on 26 July 2005 to Uzhhorod City Hospital, where doctors suspected meningitis and adjusted treatment. On 10 August 2005 she developed severe haemorrhagic meningoencephalitis, fell into a coma and died. The applicants lodged a criminal complaint on 15 August 2005; an investigation opened on 19 September 2005. In February 2006 forensic experts found serious shortcomings in her medical assessment and treatment, but an additional opinion in August 2007 stated that multiple doctors had been involved and no single doctor could be identified. In April 2008 only the coordinating doctor, T., was charged. Later expert reports were contradictory: one in September 2009 found no negligence or causal link. T. died in March 2010. Two acquittals were quashed on appeal. A further forensic examination was ordered in June 2015, results received in December 2017, but as of May 2019 the case was still pending before the first-instance court. Civil claims were also lodged.

**Application no. 32999/17 (Gorbata).** In August 2010, the applicants’ daughter, O., was examined by an ambulance doctor and taken to hospital, but the duty doctor refused admission because she lived outside the hospital’s area. She was taken to City Hospital no. 3 and died shortly after arrival from acute myocardial infarction. An internal inquiry reprimanded emergency doctors for poor admission organisation but found no treatment defects. Criminal proceedings were initiated in September 2010. A forensic report concluded that death could have been prevented by earlier adequate treatment and was not caused by the treatment administered. Proceedings were terminated for lack of evidence in 2011 and 2012; both decisions were quashed. In 2013 the Court of Appeal noted diagnostic errors, criticised repeated terminations and ignored instructions. Medical records were reportedly lost in 2014, preventing further forensic assessment. No investigative actions were recorded between 2015 and 2019. Proceedings were again terminated in April 2020 and then quashed in June 2020.

**Application no. 19581/18 (Kravets).** The applicant’s husband, M., died on 9 October 2013 from acute gastrointestinal bleeding caused by an advanced chronic duodenal ulcer that had not been diagnosed until late August 2013. Internal inquiries in 2014 found multiple shortcomings, including failure to conduct ulcer diagnostics, and concluded that death could have been prevented. Criminal investigations were merged in March 2014. The investigation was acknowledged as not thorough in November 2014. Forensic examinations were delayed and often inconclusive. A March 2019 report found serious protocol breaches and held doctor K. and another official responsible. K. was charged in August 2019 and convicted in May 2021, but released because the case was time-barred. The investigation remains pending.

**Application no. 15510/19 (Andriyenko).** The applicant’s wife died on 2 September 2016 in Kremenchuk municipal hospital during treatment for a cerebrovascular accident. An investigation into failure to provide medical aid was launched on 14 September 2016. A forensic examination ordered in December 2016 was returned as incomplete in March 2017. The applicant repeatedly complained of inaction. An internal inquiry in 2017 found no breaches. Proceedings against the police investigator for dereliction of duty were later discontinued. A January 2018 forensic report found no treatment breaches and attributed death to an advanced blood disease. A further examination ordered in May 2018 was scheduled for 2020 due to workload. As of December 2020, both the examination and criminal investigation were still pending.

The common facts relevant to the alleged violation are prolonged investigations, repeated terminations and quashed decisions, conflicting or delayed expert reports, lost evidence, failure to comply with instructions, and significant periods of inactivity.
001-248128:
**Makaruk and Others v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 35052/19 and four others) is a European Court of Human Rights case against Ukraine, decided by the Fifth Section on 22 January 2026. The applications concern criminal proceedings arising from traffic accidents and violent assaults, with facts relevant to complaints about procedural delays, repeated remittals, suspensions, ineffective investigations, and unresolved civil claims.

In **Makaruk (nos. 35052/19 and 35871/19)**, on 18 July 2009 the first applicant, Vitaliy Makaruk, was driving when he had a traffic accident with a bus. He and his son, Dmytro, then eight years old, sustained moderate bodily injuries. Criminal proceedings began on 27 July 2009. In October 2009 the first applicant was indicted for breach of traffic rules. The Lutsk District Court repeatedly returned the indictment to the prosecutor because of deficiencies, including lack of thoroughness, missing expert examinations, and inconsistencies between forensic input data and witness testimony. On 30 January 2015, after further investigation, both the first applicant and the bus driver were indicted; the first applicant also became a victim. On 24 February 2015 he lodged a civil claim within the criminal proceedings against the bus driver’s employer and insurer. On 14 August 2018 the District Court acquitted the first applicant, convicted the bus driver but released him due to mental illness, and partly allowed the civil claim. On 5 December 2018 the appellate court upheld the acquittal but remitted the case for fresh examination concerning the bus driver and civil claims. On 14 March 2019 the District Court suspended the proceedings until the bus driver recovered, as he had been paralysed after a heart attack. That suspension was upheld up to the Supreme Court’s final decision of 6 June 2019, and the proceedings remain pending but suspended.

In **Vyazova (no. 23170/24)**, the applicant’s father was hit by a car on 23 July 2014; criminal proceedings began the same day, and he died on 28 July 2014. The applicant lodged a civil claim within the criminal proceedings on 19 December 2014. On 2 April 2015 the local court convicted the driver, but on 4 June 2015 the appellate court returned the case for fresh examination. The case was repeatedly returned because the trial was incomplete and further investigative steps were needed; an investigative experiment occurred on 16 May 2018, and a new forensic examination was ordered on 27 June 2018. After the driver died on 21 January 2024, the Industrialnyy Circuit Court of Dnipro terminated the proceedings on 5 April 2024 due to the suspect’s death.

In **Bondar (no. 31921/24)**, the applicant’s son died on 12 July 2020 from injuries sustained in an assault. Murder proceedings opened the next day, and five individuals were notified of suspicion on 17 July 2020. Forensic examinations concluded that death was caused by acute coronary heart disease, exacerbated by asthma and alcohol intoxication, with stress from bodily harm not decisive. On 10 December 2020 the proceedings were terminated for lack of evidence of a crime. Nevertheless, on 18 January 2021 an indictment under Article 296 § 4 was submitted. On 21 January 2022 the first-instance court terminated proceedings as time-barred, but that was overturned on 2 February 2023. In parallel, proceedings under Articles 121 and 127 began on 26 January 2022. A forensic examination on 16 September 2022 established a direct link between the beatings and the son’s death, leading to cancellation of the earlier termination. Five individuals were notified of suspicion in October 2023, an indictment was submitted on 22 February 2024, and the proceedings were merged on 7 May 2024. The case remains before the first-instance court.

In **Didur (no. 35883/24)**, the applicant alleged that on 19 December 2013 his fellow villager, U., shot him twice in the head with a rubber-bullet handgun at a bus stop. He suffered injuries to his chin, ear, and back of his head. A forensic examination classified the injuries as minor. U. was charged with aggravated hooliganism under Article 296 § 4 and committed for trial on 2 April 2014. The applicant lodged a civil claim on 22 April 2014. Although U. was convicted twice, both verdicts were quashed by the Vinnytsya Court of Appeal because the first-instance court had departed from the indictment and altered an aggravating circumstance on its own motion. On 15 April 2024 the Nemyriv Local Court discontinued the proceedings due to expiry of the statutory limitation period and exempted U. from liability; the civil claim was left unexamined. The appellate court upheld that decision on 6 June 2024, and the Supreme Court rejected cassation on 22 July 2024.
001-250111:
The case *Sobczyńska and Others v. Poland* (Applications nos. 62765/14 and 2 others) concerns the refusal by the President of the Republic of Poland to appoint three Polish applicants to vacant judicial posts despite their successful participation in the competitive selection procedure conducted by the National Council of the Judiciary (NCJ), and the absence of any judicial review of that refusal. The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

At the material time in 2006, the applicants were junior judges (*asesorzy sądowi*) in district courts. Under the law then in force, a junior judge generally had to serve at least three years before appointment to a full judicial office. In 2006 the applicants applied for vacant district court judge posts in Słubice, Jelenia Góra and Gliwice. Their candidacies were approved by the relevant general assemblies of judges and by the NCJ. Between October 2006 and February 2007, the NCJ forwarded their applications to the President of the Republic with motions that they be appointed.

In August 2007, the NCJ informed the applicants that the President did not intend to appoint them. After they requested the President to remedy the alleged breach of law in November 2007, the President issued a decision on 3 January 2008 refusing to appoint nine candidates, including the applicants. The decision was published in *Monitor Polski* on 16 January 2008 and contained no reasons. This was reportedly the first time a President had declined to appoint candidates indicated in an NCJ motion.

The applicants sought review before administrative courts. In January 2008 they complained of inaction by the President. Between February and March 2008, the Warsaw Regional Administrative Court declared the complaints inadmissible. It held that the President’s competence to appoint judges was not subject to review by administrative courts; the President was not a public administrative authority for this purpose; and the act of appointment, although affecting an individual, did not fall within the administrative function. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed their cassation appeals in October 2012.

After the President’s decision was published, the applicants also sought annulment before the Regional Administrative Court. In 2011 that court declared their appeals inadmissible on similar grounds. The Supreme Administrative Court again dismissed their cassation appeals in October 2012.

The first two applicants lodged a constitutional complaint in April 2008, arguing that section 55(1) of the 2001 Act on the Organisation of Ordinary Courts allowed the President to refuse appointment without reasons despite the NCJ’s approval, contrary to constitutional guarantees of equality, access to a court and access to public service. On 19 June 2012 the Constitutional Court discontinued the proceedings as inadmissible, reasoning that it reviews the constitutionality of laws, not the application of the Constitution, and that Article 179 covered all matters relating to presidential appointment of judges. Three judges dissented. In 2013 all three applicants filed essentially similar complaints. In June 2013 the Constitutional Court refused to entertain them, finding that the administrative courts had applied the 2002 Act rather than section 55(1), and that the complaint about lack of reasoning was time-barred. Appeals were dismissed in March 2014.

Relevant law included Article 179 of the Constitution, under which judges are appointed by the President upon an NCJ motion, and section 55(1) of the 2001 Act, which mirrored that wording. The NCJ procedure involved vacancy notices, court board and general assembly review, the Minister of Justice’s opinion, NCJ assessment, and a resolution and motion to the President. NCJ resolutions on candidates were not appealable. The alleged violations therefore arose from the unreasoned presidential refusal and the lack of any judicial remedy to challenge it, despite the applicants’ prior successful selection by the NCJ.
001-249583:
The applications were lodged against Ukraine by Anatoliy Leonidovych Sinko (born 1959), Oleg Petrovych Karpenko (born 1974), and Yuriy Yakovych Pushkar (born 1950) on 18 December 2020, 12 March 2021, and 27 August 2021 respectively.

In Sinko’s case, his mother was admitted to hospital on 26 August 2011 for planned examination and treatment of knee osteoarthrosis. After examination by doctor S., further health problems were found, and she agreed to surgery to remove an abdominal hernia, performed on 6 September 2011. Her condition deteriorated the next day, and she died on 9 September 2011 from exacerbation of cardiovascular disease. Internal and regional health examinations found significant shortcomings in the preoperative examination, surgery, and postoperative care leading to death.
