Criminal proceedings began on 25 December 2011. Forensic examination no. 171 identified shortcomings by doctor S. On 5 July 2012 Sinko was granted victim status; on 3 August 2012 doctor S. was charged with medical negligence causing death. The prosecutor returned the case for additional investigation due to procedural defects and violation of doctor S.’s defence rights, ordering another forensic examination. The second examination, by the same experts, confirmed the first. An indictment was drawn up on 29 April 2013. On 11 December 2013 doctor S. was convicted; the appellate court changed the sanction. On 20 November 2014 the Higher Specialised Court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. On 31 March 2015 the appellate court ordered forensic examination no. 81/к, which found no specific contraindications for surgery and no direct causal link between doctor S.’s actions and the death, despite shortcomings. On 24 September 2015 the case was returned to the trial court. The indictment was returned twice, and the case was remitted several times. On 10 January 2019 the trial court acquitted doctor S., relying mainly on examination no. 81/к and dismissing earlier expert examinations as inadmissible. On 17 June 2020 the Supreme Court, in Sinko’s absence, upheld the acquittal. The courts noted that the 2012 and 2013 examinations involved surgeon B., who was also a member of internal medical commissions; the additional examination used the same experts, so both examinations and the questioning of those experts were inadmissible. No direct causal link was established because other doctors involved in postoperative treatment had not been assessed.

In Karpenko’s case, his 79-year-old father had chronic kidney and urinary diseases. On 28 March 2015 he felt unwell; on 2 April 2015 he was taken by ambulance to a district hospital in Sumy. On 7 April 2015 he was transported to a regional hospital with a urinary department and underwent urgent surgery. Two hours later he was transported back to the district hospital; on arrival his condition worsened and he died that day. Karpenko refused a post-mortem, alleging death due to inappropriate treatment and transportation. Criminal proceedings began on 21 December 2015. A forensic examination on 14 June 2016 found no signs of negligence, could not establish the exact cause without a post-mortem, and found no contraindications to transportation. Further examinations on 15 February 2018 and 10 February 2021 reached the same conclusions. On 6 April 2021 proceedings were discontinued for lack of evidence. On 19 January 2023 the investigating judge quashed that decision for failure to carry out necessary investigative actions, assess evidence, and substantiate termination; the investigation resumed.

In Pushkar’s case, his 27-year-old son was admitted on 29 September 2009 with acute pancreatitis and died on 13 October 2009 of severe complications. Pushkar alleged the death resulted from an unconsented blood purification procedure, failure to test tolerance to medications, and errors in diagnosis and treatment. In December 2009 an investigator began pre-investigative inquiries but repeatedly refused to open criminal proceedings. A post-mortem began on 14 October 2009 and ended on 14 January 2010. Pushkar alleged medical staff forged documentation, changed records, and forged his son’s signature; investigators never examined those allegations. Experts concluded death resulted from intoxication and pancreatitis complications. On 21 March 2011 a Ministry of Health commission found several errors that had aggravated his son’s condition but generally adequate treatment. On 16 December 2012 criminal proceedings were instituted under Article 140 § 1 of the Criminal Code (medical negligence). On 30 January 2013 the investigator terminated proceedings for lack of evidence; that decision was later quashed. Pushkar repeatedly complained of inactivity, and another investigator was appointed. A supervising police department and a prosecutor confirmed the inactivity of both investigators. The investigator did not reply to requests, and no medical personnel were questioned. On 20 June 2018 a forensic examination confirmed adequate treatment. Pushkar disagreed and requested an additional examination. On 25 June 2020 a new examination was ordered but never performed. On 27 January 2025 the investigation was closed for lack of evidence.

001-249236:
In *Shabratskyy and Shabratska v. Ukraine* (no. 19234/18), the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of the applicants’ son, D.Sh., in the Ukrainian army and the domestic investigation. The applicants alleged violations of Article 2 of the Convention, concerning both the circumstances of his death and the State’s alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation. The first applicant died in 2024; the second applicant continued the case.

D.Sh. was commander of a reconnaissance and sabotage squad in the Aidar military unit based in Lysychansk, fighting in eastern Ukraine under the Ministry of Defence. He allegedly accused his superiors, company commander I.R. and platoon commander A.Y., of unlawful activities and reported them to the State Security Service. In early March 2015 he told his parents he might be killed by or on the instruction of I.R. and A.Y. On the evening of 25 March 2015 he telephoned them, mentioned a severe headache, and said he planned a brief visit. The unit doctor heard him speaking “in raised tones” with his girlfriend and asking for sedatives. An acquaintance, V.T., said D.Sh. possessed confidential incriminating information about I.R. and A.Y., had been threatened by them, and that evening said he feared for his life and asked V.T. to take him out of Lysychansk.

On 26 March 2015 at about 10:50 a.m., D.Sh. died on military premises. Fellow soldiers K.M. and D.S. said he woke them by firing shots into the wall, told them to stand against the wall and pointed a gun at them; when K.M. asked what was happening, D.Sh. hit him with his left hand, holding a grenade. They left the room. Later, gunshots and a grenade explosion were heard. Witness accounts conflicted about the number of shots, their order relative to the explosion, and timing. D.Sh. was found dead with a perforating gunshot wound to the head and multiple grenade injuries, including a torn-off left hand.

A criminal investigation began that day. The register referred to murder but also noted possible suicide. Police inspected the scene and seized the gun, magazine, bullets, shells and grenade fragments. A May 2015 forensic report said D.Sh. died from combined gunshot and blast injuries and could not exclude self-infliction; no struggle or defence injuries were found. June 2015 experiments suggested it was technically possible for him to pull the grenade pin and shoot himself. The applicants were questioned and described his conflicts with I.R. and his report about unlawful activities. D.Sh.’s girlfriend, A.S., said he had distrusted K.M. and D.S. and had sounded distressed shortly before death; she was never questioned due to difficulties locating her. In March 2016 the investigation was discontinued for lack of evidence, concluding suicide. A court overturned that in June 2016 and ordered resumption.

Later evidence undermined the suicide conclusion. In January 2019, swabs from D.Sh.’s right hand showed no gunshot or explosion residue. Another forensic report found it impossible for him to have shot himself after the grenade exploded, because the wound was inflicted by the left hand, which had been torn off. A July 2021 experiment indicated the grenade exploded while held in his left hand, with him standing, and that a left-handed person might have shot him after the explosion. A November 2021 explosives report ruled out two seated scenarios and found the standing scenario plausible. Meanwhile, authorities repeatedly criticised the investigation as stagnant, incomplete and ineffective, noting failure to question witnesses, ignored prosecutor instructions and delayed measures requested by the applicants in 2016. By 2024, some witnesses could not be located; the investigation remained pending.

001-249380:
**Case Summary: Epidavr S.R.L. v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 29895/16)**

Epidavr S.R.L. is a Moldovan company, registered in Chișinău, specialising in the sale of consumer goods. The case concerns searches of its commercial premises, seizure of its possessions, and the alleged resulting restriction of its business operations. The applicant relied on Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

On 22 September 2015, Moldovan authorities initiated a criminal investigation against the company for tax evasion by a criminal group. An investigator’s internal report later stated that Epidavr might be involved in the criminal activity under investigation.

On 3 November 2015, the prosecutor issued four search orders for the applicant’s headquarters, sales points, and warehouses at four locations. The orders were submitted for authorisation by an investigating judge. Except for the location, their text was identical. They referred to an organised criminal group that allegedly created or acquired “ghost” companies to facilitate tax evasion, money laundering, cash withdrawal, and legalisation of smuggled goods. The orders stated that Epidavr might have been involved and had carried out suspicious transactions with ghost companies between 2010 and 2015. The searches were aimed at identifying and seizing broad categories of accounting records, audit reports, invoices, VAT declarations, contracts, cash-flow records, employee salary information, digital devices, stamps and seals of offshore companies, financial resources, and other documents and objects reflecting the company’s economic activity.

On 5 November 2015, the Centru District investigating judge authorised all four searches, using the same broad wording as the prosecutor’s orders. Between 7 and 9 November 2015, police searched the four locations and seized all accounting documentation and all information carriers. On 9 November 2015, the company requested the return of the accounting server, arguing that its seizure had blocked the company’s economic activity.

On 10 November 2015, Epidavr appealed against all four search warrants. It argued that it had had no procedural standing in the criminal proceedings when the searches were ordered; that there was no reasonable suspicion it had committed a crime; that the warrants contained no reasons and were extremely broad, giving investigators unfettered discretion; and that the search and seizure had made the company unable to operate.

On 19 November 2015, the Chișinău Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal concerning the first location, endorsing the prosecutor’s and investigating judge’s reasoning. It found that the prosecutor’s request was not vague or merely formal because it was based on the decision to initiate criminal proceedings and the investigator’s report.

On 24 and 30 November 2015, a differently constituted panel of the Chișinău Court of Appeal allowed the appeals concerning the second and third locations. It quashed the authorisations and rejected the prosecutor’s search requests as unfounded. The court found that the search warrants lacked reasons; the judge relied solely on the investigator’s report; ownership of the premises was not verified; there was no convincing evidence that the locations contained relevant evidence; and no showing that the information could not be obtained by other means, such as document seizure, audit reports, or tax inspections. It also criticised the overly broad and imprecise list of premises and the vague, wide-ranging objects to be seized. The court noted there was no substantiated causal link between Epidavr and the criminal proceedings and that the company had not been mentioned after the investigation was initiated. It suggested that seizure of objects or documents under Article 126 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would have been more appropriate.

On 14 December 2015, the same panel that had upheld the first search allowed the appeal concerning the fourth location, quashing the authorisation and rejecting the search request for the same reasons given on 24 and 30 November.

According to the Government, all seized documents and objects were examined and later returned to Epidavr, though no date was specified. The case file indicated no further proceedings concerning the company after the searches. The applicant complained that the search warrants were unlawful and that the seizure of its assets and the resulting restriction of its operations violated Articles 6 and 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-249134:
The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) case *Villás v. Hungary* (application no. 33134/21) concerns the alleged lack of impartiality of Hungary’s Constitutional Court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant, Szilárd Villás, a Hungarian national born in 1979 and living in Budapest, had served for 22 years as a court bailiff. His service was terminated *ex lege* on 31 January 2020 after he refused substitute employment within the judiciary. The termination stemmed from Act no. LXXXI of 2019, which abolished the status of court bailiffs as of that date.

The background to the reform is central to the complaint. According to public information from the Ministry of Justice, in September 2017 the Government examined the need for a systemic reform of the court bailiff service on the initiative of Ms H., then President of the National Judicial Office, a State agency responsible for the central administration of courts. Having endorsed her recommendations, the Government introduced bills to Parliament. Bill T/7844 became Act no. LXXXI of 2019 on 19 November 2019. It amended aspects of judicial employment and eliminated the court bailiff status.

On 23 July 2020 the applicant filed a constitutional complaint under section 26(2) of the Constitutional Court Act. He challenged the constitutionality of the legal basis for the institutional reform, notably Act no. LXXXI of 2019. In support, he submitted the Ministry of Justice information indicating that the recommendations underlying the reform had been made by Ms H.

On 23 February 2021, a five-judge Constitutional Court panel declared the complaint inadmissible for absence of victim status. Ms H. – by then a member of the Constitutional Court – was both the rapporteur and the president of that panel.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 that the Constitutional Court panel was not impartial because it included Ms H., who had initiated in a previous capacity the very legislative amendments he was challenging. The alleged violation therefore concerns objective impartiality and the appearance of bias: a person who had promoted the challenged reform later adjudicated, and led the panel deciding, the constitutional challenge to it. The case does not concern the merits of the dismissal itself, but the fairness and impartiality of the constitutional complaint proceedings. The ECtHR gave notice of the Article 6 § 1 complaint and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The application was lodged on 18 June 2021. The applicant was represented by P. Szegi, a Budapest lawyer, and the Government by Z. Tallódi of the Ministry of Justice. The judge elected in respect of Hungary withdrew from sitting. The case was assigned to a Committee. The Second Section Committee comprised Judges Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir (President), Gediminas Sagatys and Juha Lavapuro, with Dorothee von Arnim as Deputy Section Registrar. It deliberated on 17 February 2026 and delivered judgment on 17 March 2026. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.
001-249370:
In *Ukrayinskyy and Others v. Ukraine*, 42 Ukrainian nationals detained at Zhovti Vody Correctional Colony No. 26 complained under Articles 3, 8, 13 and 34 of the Convention about inadequate detention conditions, the lack of an effective domestic remedy, and alleged hindrance by prison authorities of their right of individual application to the European Court of Human Rights. The applications were lodged in August 2019; the applicants were represented by lawyers from the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group (KHRPG).

The applicants alleged severe overcrowding, damp and mouldy cells, poor or absent lighting, unsanitary premises, infestations of bedbugs and cockroaches, rodents, leaking pipes and flooding, limited access to drinking water, interruptions in cold and hot water, insufficient showers and laundry facilities, toilets lacking privacy and in disrepair, poor-quality food served in unsanitary conditions, shortages of clothing, footwear and hygiene items, and frequent power cuts. These claims followed KHRPG monitoring visits in March 2019. An 18 March 2019 KHRPG report stated that conditions failed to meet standards and harmed prisoners’ health. Some 84 detainees, including 11 applicants, had earlier submitted complaints to domestic authorities.

The Government disputed the allegations. It claimed the KHRPG monitors photographed sealed, unused premises and presented a misleading picture. It asserted that renovations had been carried out, windows and doors replaced, anti-fungal treatment applied, pest control implemented, and that heating, water and sanitation met standards. It also explained that water was cut off daily from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. and from 11 p.m. to 5.30 a.m., and electricity from 8 or 9 a.m. to 2 or 3 p.m., owing to utility arrears. In July 2020 the Ministry of Justice decided to close Zhovti Vody Prison, and applicants began to be transferred.

As to Article 34, the KHRPG report noted that prison administration openly recorded the names of prisoners who approached the monitors for “further work” and that prisoners feared pressure after the monitors left. After the applications were communicated to the Government in 2020, prison authorities organised interviews with applicants about their complaints. In March and August 2020, some applicants made written or oral statements saying they had no complaints about detention conditions, while many declined to comment. Some statements alleged that KHRPG representatives had given them blank forms to sign. In September and October 2020, five applicants submitted handwritten statements alleging coercion, insistent demands, deception, inducement and pressure to withdraw their applications. After these statements were sent to the Government, the authorities re-interviewed those applicants in December 2020 and January 2021; the Government said some recanted or refused to comment, and one denied pressure. No copies of those later statements were submitted.

Domestic reports partly corroborated the applicants’ account. The Ombudsperson’s 2017 report noted recurrent violations at Zhovti Vody Prison, including insufficient living space, leaks, outdated sanitary equipment, lack of flushing cisterns, poor ventilation and lighting, dirty or rusty dishes, and tensions between staff and prisoners. A July 2020 press release stated that most violations remained unremedied, that water and electricity were cut off owing to arrears, and that food provision was deficient.

Finally, the Court lost contact with many applicants after their representatives ceased cooperating, and because applicants had only provided the prison’s address and had since been released or transferred.
001-248682:
The case of *Vanesyan and Others v. Armenia* concerns three applications lodged against Armenia with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants all complained of the excessive length of their pre-trial detention. In one application, no. 38190/23, the applicant also raised a complaint under Article 5 § 1 (c) of the Convention. The Armenian Government was given notice of the applications. The Fifth Section Committee, composed of Andreas Zünd, Diana Sârcu and Mykola Gnatovskyy, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 5 February 2026 and delivered judgment on 26 February 2026. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The first application, no. 35710/22, was introduced on 12 July 2022 by Samvel Vanesyan, born in 1954, represented by Hayk Alumyan in Yerevan. Vanesyan was detained from 3 June 2020 to 23 January 2023. His detention therefore lasted 2 years, 7 months and 21 days. The detention order and related appeals were examined by the First Instance Court of General Jurisdiction of Yerevan, the Lori Regional Court and the Criminal Court of Appeal. His complaint before the European Court focused on the excessive length of this pre-trial detention.

The second application, no. 8336/23, was introduced on 4 February 2023 by Hovsep Ashkarian, born in 1999, represented by Liparit Simonyan in Yerevan. Ashkarian was detained from 7 October 2020 to 13 October 2023. His total detention lasted 3 years and 7 days. The relevant detention order and appeal review were handled by the First Instance Court of General Jurisdiction of Yerevan and the Criminal Court of Appeal. He likewise complained that the length of his pre-trial detention was excessive.

The third application, no. 38190/23, was introduced on 7 October 2023 by Samvel Grigoryan, born in 2001, also represented by Liparit Simonyan in Yerevan. Grigoryan was detained from 21 August 2021 to 21 August 2025, a total length of 4 years and 1 day. The courts identified in connection with his detention were the Syunik Regional Court, the First Instance Criminal Court of General Jurisdiction of Yerevan and the Criminal Court of Appeal. In addition to the excessive-length complaint, Grigoryan also alleged a violation of Article 5 § 1 (c) of the Convention, concerning the lawfulness of his arrest or detention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the prolonged periods of pre-trial detention imposed on each applicant. The shortest period complained of exceeded two years and seven months, while the longest exceeded four years. Each period was authorised or reviewed by domestic courts at first-instance, regional and appellate levels. The applicants’ central complaint was that these detentions were excessively long. For Grigoryan, the case also raises the additional issue of whether his detention satisfied the requirements of Article 5 § 1 (c). The appended table supplies the core factual details, while the available text does not set out further background such as the specific charges, evidence, or reasons given by the domestic courts for continuing detention.
001-248397:
**Dzyon v. Ukraine (Application no. 44249/17)** concerns an Article 2 complaint by Mr Valentyn Dzyon, a Ukrainian national, that State agents were responsible for his son’s death and that the ensuing investigation was ineffective.

The applicant’s son, a police investigator at the Staromiskyi district police station in Vinnytsya, died on 19 May 2010 from a gunshot wound to the chest in his office. He also had scratches and bruises on his head. The pistol found at the scene belonged to his superior, S. The same day, the police station was inspected.

Forensic examinations concluded that the bullet entered the front of the chest, exited the back, was fired from close range from in front of the deceased, and followed a downward trajectory. Experts ruled out a shot from behind. The son could have been sitting behind his desk. There was no objective evidence that his body had been moved after death. The head injuries could have occurred shortly before death, possibly through contact with blunt objects such as the pistol bolt or surrounding objects during a fall. No other injuries suggesting assault or struggle were found. Experts also noted no signs of increased suggestibility, fantasising, or suicidal ideation.

The applicant testified that his son had had work-related disputes with superiors K. and S. On the day of his death, the son allegedly told his mother that K. and S. were “bitches.” Later, K. telephoned the applicant, saying the son had barricaded himself in his office and that K. “did not want to go to prison.” The applicant later alleged that K. and S. had pressured his son to arrest a suspect, L., in order to take a bribe; when he refused, he was allegedly beaten and shot by superiors and colleagues. His wife and other son corroborated this. L.’s lawyer confirmed an argument about the arrest.

S. claimed he had left his service pistol in a safe, with the key in a drawer. He said that after access to the son’s office was obtained, he heard a gunshot and found the son had shot himself. K. partly confirmed this, describing the son as quiet and introverted but without open conflict. Another investigator, Ts., saw the son slumped over the desk with a pistol in his right hand after the shot. Other colleagues described a generally friendly atmosphere but noted the son was isolated and often stayed late.

The investigation was lengthy and contradictory. Initially opened for official negligence, it led to S. being charged and, in 2013, convicted with a suspended sentence. The court rejected the applicant’s murder allegations. However, the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal quashed that decision due to numerous contradictions and inconsistencies in witness statements and forensic evidence, ordering a fresh investigation. It noted that the authorities had not properly examined the lack of motive for suicide, the murder allegation, or the claim that the son had stolen S.’s pistol.

A new investigation was opened in 2013 into murder, theft of a weapon, abuse of power, and expert misconduct. Numerous further examinations and witness interviews followed. In 2020, proceedings against S. for negligent storage of a weapon and official negligence were terminated because the limitation period had expired, a decision upheld on appeal and by the Supreme Court. In 2022, an additional forensic medical report found that the head bruises could not have resulted from an agonal fall and questioned witness accounts of the son’s position when shot. In 2024, an investigation was opened into alleged torture and murder by colleagues and joined to the main proceedings. The investigation remains ongoing.

The applicant complains under Article 2 that State agents caused his son’s death and that the investigation was ineffective, delayed, and failed to resolve serious contradictions in the evidence.
001-249223:
D.M., an Afghan national of Hazara origin, applied for asylum in Sweden in October 2015. He claimed to be an unaccompanied minor born in 1999 and from Mazar-e Sharif. However, German records showed he had previously been registered under a different name and a 1993 birth date. He declined a medical age assessment, and Swedish authorities treated him as an adult. After an initial Dublin transfer decision to Germany was quashed because the transfer deadline expired, his asylum claim was processed in Sweden.

In his first asylum proceedings, D.M. claimed protection based on a land dispute, participation in a demonstration, conversion to Christianity, and Hazara ethnicity. The Migration Agency held several interviews and in October 2017 rejected his claim, finding that he had not established his identity or age as probable and that his credibility was undermined by inconsistent identity information. It accepted that he was Afghan and later that he was from Mazar-e Sharif. It found that his baptism and church attendance were not sufficient to show genuine Christian conviction; his statements about conversion were vague, inconsistent, and lacked depth. It also rejected his land-dispute and demonstration claims as vague and speculative. Although Hazaras faced difficulties, the Agency found no general need for protection, and the security situation in Mazar-e Sharif, Kabul, and Herat was not so severe that all civilians were at risk. The Migration Court dismissed his appeal in March 2018, and the Migration Court of Appeal denied leave to appeal in May 2018.

Subsequent requests for residence permits or re-examination were refused, although he received a temporary study permit from 2018 to 2019. After that deportation order expired, he applied afresh for asylum in June 2022. He repeated his earlier grounds and added risks arising from the Taliban takeover, his continued Christian activity, social-media threats, his westernisation, and his Hazara ethnicity. In March 2023 the Migration Agency again rejected the application. It maintained that his identity was not probable, found no reason to depart from earlier credibility findings, and held that his baptism, church involvement, and written evidence did not prove genuine conversion. It found no support for social-media threats, no general risk to Hazaras or westernised returnees, and no province in Afghanistan with indiscriminate violence at a level conferring protection. It also found his return route via Kabul to Mazar-e Sharif safe and no exceptionally distressing circumstances.

The Stockholm Migration Court dismissed his appeal in May 2023. It found the investigation sufficient, refused live witness testimony but accepted written statements, and agreed that his conversion was not genuine. It concluded that he would not reliably be perceived as an apostate or Christian convert and faced no personal risk as a Hazara or westernised returnee. The Migration Court of Appeal denied leave to appeal in August 2023. Later impediment applications were also dismissed, but the European Court of Human Rights indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 in November 2023, staying deportation.

Before the Court, D.M. alleges that removal to Afghanistan would breach Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention and that the domestic proceedings failed to meet the required standards under those Articles, alone or in conjunction with Article 13. The key alleged risks concern his claimed conversion/apostasy, Hazara ethnicity, westernisation, Taliban rule, land dispute, demonstration involvement, and the general security situation. Central to the case are the Swedish authorities’ adverse findings on identity, credibility, and the genuineness of his religious conversion.
001-249581:
**Case Summary: Selimyan and Others v. Armenia (Applications nos. 2991/16 and 2 others)**

The case *Selimyan and Others v. Armenia* concerns three applications lodged against Armenia before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The judgment was delivered by the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, on 16 April 2026. The applicants are Davit Selimyan, Arine Sukiasyans Salmasi, and Taron Simonyan. The core complaint is that they were unlawfully deprived of their liberty, contrary to Article 5 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to liberty and security and requires any deprivation of liberty to be lawful and justified under one of the permitted exceptions.

The key factual details are set out in the appended table to the judgment. All three applicants were arrested on the same date: 23 June 2015. Davit Selimyan was born in 1996 and was represented by Ani Chatinyan, located in Vanadzor. Arine Sukiasyans Salmasi was born in 1979 and was represented by Hasmik Harutyunyan and Araks Melkonyan, both located in Yerevan. Taron Simonyan was born in 1988 and was represented by the same two lawyers from Yerevan. Each applicant introduced their application to the European Court of Human Rights on 23 December 2015—exactly six months after the date of arrest. The applications were registered as nos. 2991/16, 5234/16, and 5294/16.

The Armenian Government was given notice of the complaints under Article 5 § 1 concerning the lawfulness of the applicants’ arrest. This indicates that the central issue communicated to the Government was whether the arrest and subsequent deprivation of liberty complied with the requirements of Article 5 § 1. That provision permits deprivation of liberty only in specific circumstances, such as lawful arrest or detention on reasonable suspicion of an offence, and only in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law. The applicants’ common allegation is therefore that their arrest on 23 June 2015 lacked a proper legal basis, was not carried out in accordance with domestic procedural rules, or otherwise fell outside the exhaustive list of permissible grounds for detention under Article 5 § 1.

The provided judgment extract does not contain a detailed narrative of the circumstances surrounding the arrests. It does not state where the arrests occurred, what suspicions or charges, if any, were involved, which authorities carried them out, how long the applicants were detained, or what domestic legal remedies were pursued. Nor does the extract include the Court’s legal reasoning or final conclusions on the merits. Instead, the factual foundation is limited to the information in the appended table: the applicants’ identities, dates of birth, representatives, date of arrest, and date of application.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are thus narrow but significant. First, all three applicants were deprived of their liberty by Armenian authorities on 23 June 2015. Second, each complained to the European Court that this deprivation of liberty was unlawful under Article 5 § 1. Third, the Government was notified of that specific complaint. Fourth, the applications were filed on 23 December 2015, six months after the arrest. Because the full judgment excerpt does not elaborate on the arrest’s legal basis or the Court’s assessment, the summary is necessarily confined to these essential procedural and factual elements. Any finding of a violation would depend on missing details about whether the arrest complied with Armenian law and whether it fell within an Article 5 § 1 exception.
001-249691:
The case **F.B. and Others v. the Netherlands** (Applications nos. 28157/18 and six others) concerns seven applicants—one Azerbaijani, one Moroccan, and five Dutch nationals—who were convicted by Dutch courts of serious crimes, including multiple murders, manslaughter, attempted murder, participation in a criminal organisation, and firearms/document offences. Each was sentenced to life imprisonment. They applied to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34, alleging that Dutch legislation and practice made their life sentences **de jure and de facto irreducible**, contrary to **Article 3** of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court communicated only the Article 3 complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible; one applicant was granted anonymity.

A key domestic development concerned applicant **F.B.** After his conviction and life sentence, the Dutch Supreme Court initially held in **5 July 2016** that imposition of a life sentence was incompatible with Article 3 because Dutch law then lacked a specific review mechanism offering a real possibility of reduction or conditional release. It relied on *Vinter and Others v. the United Kingdom* and *Murray v. the Netherlands*. However, after the entry into force of the **Advisory Board Life-Sentence Prisoners Decree** and related implementing legislation, the Supreme Court reversed course in its final judgment of **19 December 2017**. It held that Dutch law now provided a review system allowing life sentences to be reduced in appropriate cases. Under this system, the first review should occur no later than 25 years after imposition, with an ex officio pardon assessment no later than 27 years from the start of detention, and periodic review thereafter. Life-sentence prisoners may also request a pardon at any time. The criteria include whether continued execution reasonably serves a penological purpose, the prisoner’s behaviour and development, resocialisation prospects, risk of reoffending, and victim impact. The Advisory Board advises on reintegration; the Minister can deviate only with reasons; civil courts can review decisions for Article 3 compliance; and post-sentencing courts can examine detention and reintegration decisions.

Other applicants raised similar complaints. **Remmers, Soerel, and Rasnabe**, convicted in the “Passage” investigation, had their life sentences upheld, and in 2019 the Supreme Court rejected their Article 3 arguments. Rasnabe, a Moroccan national without a residence permit, argued that his status prevented rehabilitation and reintegration, but the Supreme Court found this did not make review impossible. The **Richter brothers** were initially sentenced to 30 years by trial courts reluctant to impose life imprisonment, but appellate courts imposed life after relying on the new review system; their appeals, including complaints about psychiatric disorder and clarity of criteria, were dismissed. **Henriquez**, convicted of murders and fraud, argued that review had to be by an independent judge, but the Court of Appeal held that administrative review by the Minister was acceptable if the criteria were foreseeable and knowable.

The central alleged violation was therefore not the applicants’ guilt or convictions, but the alleged irreducibility of their life sentences. The Dutch authorities maintained that the Pardons Act and Advisory Board Decree created a real prospect of release or reduction, with objective criteria, procedural safeguards, and judicial oversight. The Supreme Court acknowledged that if life sentences were never reduced in practice even under the new system, compatibility with Article 3 could be reassessed, but found no violation at that time. The Azerbaijani Government did not intervene. The ECtHR was thus called on to determine whether the Dutch life-sentence review mechanism satisfies Article 3 both in law and in practice.
001-248392:
In *Selami v. Greece* (Application no. 43274/16), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Kledi Selami, an Albanian national born in 1984, concerning criminal proceedings in Greece. The applicant was charged with intentional homicide and other crimes. By judgment no. 65-78/2011, the Syros Assize Court found him guilty and sentenced him to life imprisonment. He appealed.

The key events relevant to the alleged Convention violations occurred on 22 September 2014, when the Northern Aegean Assize Court of Appeal held the appeal hearing. The applicant appeared in person. Because he did not speak Greek, but only Albanian, the presiding judge appointed an interpreter. The applicant then requested an adjournment. He stated that he had been trying to sell property in his home country to obtain the resources to hire a lawyer of his own choosing. The appellate court refused the adjournment, finding the request vague and ill-founded. Since the applicant had no representative, the court appointed Ms H.H., from the relevant list of lawyers, as his defence counsel under Article 340 § 1 of the Greek Code of Criminal Procedure. The court then suspended the hearing for one hour so that the applicant and the appointed lawyer could prepare his defence.

When the trial resumed, the applicant again requested an adjournment in order to hire a lawyer of his own choosing. The appeal court refused and proceeded with the hearing. By judgment no. 46-55/2014, it found the applicant guilty as charged and confirmed the sentence of life imprisonment.

The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law with the Court of Cassation, represented by a lawyer of his own choosing. He complained, among other things, that the Northern Aegean Assize Court of Appeal had wrongly refused his request for an adjournment to hire a lawyer of his choosing. He further claimed that the one-hour suspension granted by the appeal court had been inadequate for preparing his defence and that the interpreter had not been made available to him and his representative during that time. By judgment no. 1339/2015 of 18 December 2015, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It held that the presiding judge’s obligation was limited to appointing a lawyer for the defendant; that it was the lawyer’s and the defendant’s omission that they had not informed the court that the time granted was inadequate; and that, after the appointment of Ms H.H. from the relevant list of lawyers, no request for an adjournment in order to hire a lawyer could be raised.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b) and (c) of the Convention that he had been deprived of legal assistance of his own choosing and had not been given adequate time and facilities to prepare his defence with the lawyer appointed by the court. The case therefore centred on whether the Greek courts’ refusal to adjourn, the immediate appointment of a defence lawyer, the one-hour preparation period, and the alleged lack of interpreter assistance during that period violated the applicant’s fair-trial rights. The Albanian Government did not intervene in the proceedings.
001-248201:
In Damian v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 32935/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant, Livia Damian, a Moldovan national born in 1977, complained about domestic court decisions annulling the contract by which she had become owner of a non-residential building in Chișinău. The Court gave notice of those complaints and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The property dispute began in 2002, when Chișinău local authorities allowed a private company L. to erect a building. Another private company M. sued the local authorities, alleging that company L.’s building blocked access to its premises, and sought transfer of similar real estate. On 5 July 2005 the Economic District Court ordered the local authorities to transfer a specific non-residential building to company M. No appeal was filed, and the judgment became final. A political party had rented the building from the local authorities since 2002. The local authorities later transferred ownership to company M., which registered it.

On 10 May 2006 company M. sold the building to E.P., whose purchase and property right were notarised and registered. On 25 November 2006 E.P. sold the building to the applicant for MDL 321,000 (about EUR 18,800). The contract was authenticated by a notary, and the applicant registered her property right on 27 November 2006. At the time of sale, the real estate register contained no limitation or condition on E.P.’s title. After buying the building, the applicant discovered that the political party occupied it. Her requests that it vacate were unsuccessful.

Meanwhile, the political party asked the local authorities to sell it the building through privatisation. On 21 December 2006 the Republican Commission of the Privatisation Agency authorised the political party to privatise the building, and it paid the State MDL 500,000 (about EUR 29,000).

On 5 March 2007 the applicant sued the political party, seeking eviction and annulment of the privatisation decision. The political party counterclaimed, seeking annulment of the contracts between company M. and E.P. and between E.P. and the applicant. It also requested reopening of the proceedings between company M. and the local authorities. On 26 August 2008 the Economic Court of Appeal annulled the final judgment of 5 July 2005 because the political party, an affected third party, had not been involved. The political party participated in those proceedings; the applicant was apparently unaware of them. E.P. had died on 2 June 2007.

After several retrials, on 19 April 2011 the first-instance court rejected the applicant’s action and granted the political party’s counterclaim. It reasoned that annulment of the 2005 judgment destroyed company M.’s basis for ownership, so company M. could not validly sell to E.P.; that contract was null and void. The court also annulled the E.P.–applicant contract as fictitious because the applicant had never taken possession of the building. On 13 March 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, repeating the nullity and fictitious-contract findings and noting the applicant’s lack of possession. It also observed that the political party had obtained privatisation approval in 2003 for MDL 204,000 (about EUR 12,800) and, as tenant, had priority. On 8 November 2012 the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the lower courts’ decisions.

The applicant lodged her application on 20 April 2013. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that she acquired and registered what appeared to be clear title, paid the purchase price, and faced retrospective annulment of her ownership because a final judgment underlying her predecessor’s title was reopened and annulled without her involvement. The domestic courts also treated her contract as fictitious due to non-possession, even though the building was occupied by a tenant. These facts underpin her complaints about unfair proceedings under Article 6 § 1 and disproportionate interference with property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-249586:
The case *Shkuropatskyy and Others v. Ukraine* comprises four applications against Ukraine (nos. 9085/24, 6025/25, 11089/25 and 14768/25) lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Fifth Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 16 April 2026, adopted after private deliberations on 26 March 2026. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law.

The appended table provides the key facts relevant to those allegations.

**Anton Yevgenovych Shkuropatskyy** (born 1991), represented by O. O. Pogibko (Odesa), introduced application no. 9085/24 on 29 February 2024. His civil proceedings began on 25 November 2021 and were still pending. The total duration was recorded as more than 4 years, 1 month and 29 days, involving two levels of jurisdiction. Because the proceedings had not ended, the alleged excessive length was ongoing.

**Anatoliy Anatoliyovych Govorukha** (born 1972), represented by R. V. Serdyuk (Prosyana), introduced application no. 6025/25 on 14 February 2025. His civil proceedings began on 16 March 2016 and ended on 16 October 2024. They lasted 8 years, 7 months and 1 day, across three levels of jurisdiction.

**Yevgeniya Valeriyivna Pankina** (born 1986) introduced application no. 11089/25 on 7 April 2025. Her civil proceedings began on 2 April 2018 and ended on 9 December 2024. They lasted 6 years, 8 months and 8 days, across three levels of jurisdiction.

**Volodymyr Anatoliyovych Shylin** (born 1969) introduced application no. 14768/25 on 10 April 2025. His civil proceedings began on 13 January 2022 and ended on 16 April 2025. They lasted 3 years, 3 months and 4 days, at one level of jurisdiction.

The central alleged violation is therefore the unreasonable duration of civil litigation. The longest periods are those of Govorukha, whose case lasted over eight and a half years, and Pankina, whose case lasted almost seven years; both involved three judicial levels. Shkuropatskyy’s case is significant because the proceedings remained pending after more than four years. Shylin’s case is shorter but still exceeded three years at a single level. The applicants also allege that Ukrainian law did not provide an effective domestic remedy by which they could challenge or obtain redress for those delays. These complaints ordinarily engage the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and the right to an effective remedy.

The provided extract sets out the procedural background and factual details from the appended table, but it does not include the Court’s full legal reasoning, findings on admissibility or merits, or the final operative order. The key factual focus for assessing the alleged violations is the total duration of each civil proceeding, the number of jurisdictional levels involved, whether the proceedings were pending or concluded, and the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy.
001-249587:
The case *Kyryk and Gonchar v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 6200/25 and 7881/25) concerns two separate criminal proceedings in Ukraine, lodged with the European Court of Human Rights in February 2025. The Fifth Section Committee delivered judgment on 16 April 2026.

In the first application, Stefaniya Mykhaylivna Kyryk (born 1987) complained about the investigation into her husband’s death. On 12 August 2018, her husband was riding a motorcycle when he collided with a car driven by V. He sustained severe injuries, and a criminal case was opened. He died in hospital on 25 August 2018. Although the applicant repeatedly requested victim status, she was granted it only on 14 November 2018. Investigators questioned witnesses and took other steps. On 26 December 2018, the case was closed for lack of evidence of a criminal offence; expert conclusions stated that V. had no technical possibility to avoid the collision. On 21 January 2019, an investigative judge overturned that closure, doubting the thoroughness and completeness of the investigation. After reopening, a crime scene reconstruction was conducted with the applicant, and forensic metallurgical and engineering examinations of the motorcycle were carried out. On 31 March 2021, the case was closed again for absence of a criminal offence. On 11 May 2021, the investigative judge annulled that decision as premature, noting that investigators had failed to exhaust all means of verifying key circumstances and to address the applicant’s arguments. It is unclear whether further investigative actions occurred, apart from a road traffic technical examination appointed in 2022. On 24 June 2024, an expert report concluded that traffic organisation at the intersection did not comply with regulatory standards. Nevertheless, on 29 August 2024, the investigator closed the case, finding no traffic violations by V. directly linked to the accident. On 14 October 2024, the appellate court upheld the first-instance decision and dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the closure. These facts are relevant to alleged violations concerning the length and effectiveness of the investigation into the death.

In the second application, Mykhaylo Ivanovych Gonchar (born 1950) complained about criminal proceedings arising from a road accident. On 29 July 2019, while riding a scooter, he was cut off by a car driven by P. He fell and sustained injuries classified as moderate by a forensic medical expert. Criminal proceedings were initiated the next day. On 19 March 2020, P. was served with a notice of suspicion, and the two-month pre-trial investigation period began. An indictment was issued on 17 June 2020 and sent to the trial court on 22 June 2020. On 24 June 2020, the applicant lodged a civil claim within the criminal proceedings. On 15 September 2021, the local court convicted P. of traffic rules violations and sentenced him to two years of community service. However, on 20 October 2025, the Sumy Court of Appeal quashed the verdict and terminated the criminal proceedings. The appellate court held that, under mandatory legal provisions, the proceedings had to be terminated because the two-month pre-trial investigation time-limit had expired and had never been extended, while the bill of indictment was submitted to the trial court after that period. These facts are relevant to alleged violations regarding the length of proceedings and the eventual termination of the case on procedural grounds, which prevented a final determination of the criminal charge and the applicant’s civil claim.
001-247827:
In *R.E. and Others v. Iceland* (ECtHR, Second Section, judgment of 13 January 2026, final on 13 April 2026), four Icelandic nationals complain under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, alone and in conjunction with Article 14, that the Icelandic authorities failed to conduct effective investigations into their complaints of sexual violence and discriminated against them on grounds of gender. The applicants are R.E., X, Y and S.O.

R.E. alleged rape by co-worker K in October 2017. She recalled heavy drinking, little of the evening, and waking to K having intercourse with her while she could not move or speak; her tights were torn and her trousers broken. She reported the incident in December 2017. K admitted intercourse but said it was consensual. The police questioned K in October 2018 and six witnesses, but did not question a bartender R.E. identified as having seen her intoxication and K buying her drinks. In January 2019 the Reykjavík Metropolitan Police discontinued the investigation. The State Prosecutor upheld that decision in May 2019, citing conflicting accounts, no direct witnesses, R.E.’s limited recollection, absence of further evidence, and consensual intercourse the following morning.

X, then 17, alleged rape by co-worker F in July 2017. She said she woke to F on top of her, froze, felt pain, and that he pulled her hair and spanked her. The Emergency Reception Unit recorded minor bruises and semen on her underwear. F claimed the sex was consensual. Eight witnesses were questioned. The District Prosecutor discontinued the case in May 2019; the State Prosecutor upheld this in August 2019, finding insufficient evidence and reasonable doubt as to whether F realised consent was absent.

Y, also a minor, alleged sexual assault by T at a campsite in July 2018. She was heavily intoxicated and remembered little. Witnesses said T held her up and took her to a tent; one saw T atop the fully clothed Y, who was not moving or talking. T claimed consensual activity but had bragged about oral sex; a message from him asked whether she remembered or was “too drunk”. Y was later diagnosed with PTSD. The police discontinued the investigation in June 2019; the State Prosecutor upheld this in September 2019, citing no direct witnesses, conflicting accounts of intoxication, and insufficient proof that T realised Y could not resist.

S.O. alleged assaults by R. and A. in a hotel room in June 2012. She initially engaged consensually with A., but when R entered she froze, stopped participating and said her non-consent should have been obvious. She reported in May 2018. Both men claimed a consensual threesome. Witnesses and mental-health records supported her distress. The District Prosecutor discontinued the case in June 2019; the State Prosecutor upheld this in October 2019, describing it as “word against word”, with no witnesses and a six-year delay, and unlikely to lead to conviction.

Domestically, rape was defined in Article 194 of the General Penal Code; a 2007 amendment stressed sexual autonomy, and a 2018 amendment expressly defined consent. Criminal procedure required expeditious investigation, and State Prosecutor instructions prioritised sexual offences. International materials, including CEDAW, the Istanbul Convention and GREVIO, noted concerns about high dismissal rates and low convictions in sexual-violence cases. The core alleged violations are therefore that the police and prosecutors failed to investigate non-consensual sexual acts effectively and that the handling of these cases reflected gender-based discrimination.
001-250112:
In *Leocádio de Lemos v. Portugal* (Application no. 34122/23), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined a complaint by Joel Leocádio de Lemos, a Portuguese national born in 1984, living in Silveira. The application was lodged on 4 September 2023. The case concerned the alleged excessive length of the review of the lawfulness of the applicant’s pre-trial detention. He relied on Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 and Article 13 of the Convention. The Court gave notice to the Portuguese Government only of the complaint concerning the length of that review and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The underlying facts concerned criminal proceedings for drug trafficking. On 10 November 2017 the applicant was questioned by the investigating judge at the Torres Vedras Criminal Court. On the same day, the investigating judge ordered his remand in custody. On 27 November 2017 the applicant requested house arrest with electronic surveillance; that request was dismissed on 28 November 2017. On 4 December 2017 he appealed the remand decision to the Lisbon Court of Appeal. On 5 December 2017 the Torres Vedras Criminal Court declared the appeal admissible. On 5 January 2018 the public prosecutor at the Torres Vedras Criminal Court submitted observations on the appeal. On 23 January 2018 the file was sent to the Lisbon Court of Appeal. On 30 January 2018 the public prosecutor at the Lisbon Court of Appeal issued an opinion under Article 416 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 1 February 2018 the applicant was notified and given ten days to reply under Article 417; he replied on 8 February 2018. On 28 February 2018 the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the investigating judge’s decision of 10 November 2017 to keep him in pre-trial detention. On 1 March 2018 the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal, lodged on 11 December 2017, against the decision rejecting his request for house arrest with electronic surveillance. The applicant was released from pre-trial detention on 28 November 2018.

In 2018 the applicant brought an action against the State in the Lisbon Administrative Court, claiming EUR 3,000 for damage caused by the alleged excessive length of the review of his pre-trial detention. On 25 June 2023 the Lisbon Administrative Court dismissed the action. It observed that the 30-day time limit to decide the appeal in Article 219 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had been complied with. It further noted that, according to a Supreme Court judgment of 16 March 2018, such an appeal neither suspended the proceedings nor barred the investigating judge from suspending the pre-trial detention or replacing it with another measure. It considered that the time taken to decide the review was therefore not incompatible with Article 5 § 4 of the Convention and that, in any event, it was necessary to ensure compliance with procedural rules, notably the adversarial principle and the requirement for a three-judge panel to decide the appeals.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the examination of his appeal against pre-trial detention had been excessively long and that he had lacked an effective domestic remedy in that regard. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the dates of his detention, appeal, and the appellate court’s decision, together with the domestic compensation proceedings. The Court’s notice was limited to the length-of-review complaint under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 and Article 13; the other complaints were declared inadmissible.
001-247913:
The case *A.N. and Others v. Greece* concerns applications brought by Afghan unaccompanied minors who sought international protection in Greece and were accommodated at the Samos Reception and Identification Centre (“Samos RIC”) between February 2019 and May 2020. The applicants alleged that their living conditions and treatment violated the Convention, essentially complaining of inhuman and degrading reception conditions and failure to protect them as vulnerable minors.

The general factual background was severe overcrowding. The Samos RIC had an official capacity of 648 persons but in practice hosted several thousand, including families, single men, and unaccompanied minors. An informal settlement known as “the Jungle” developed on adjacent land, consisting of tents and makeshift shacks without electricity, running water, toilets, or waste disposal. Medical and psychosocial support was extremely limited. The “safe zone” for unaccompanied minors had insufficient capacity, accommodating fewer than one hundred minors while hundreds remained outside. Containers were overcrowded, lacked heating and adequate bedding, and provided little privacy. Temporary guardianship by prosecutors was formalistic and ineffective in practice. Transfers to mainland shelters were delayed for months, even after the European Court of Human Rights indicated interim measures under Rule 39 requiring suitable accommodation.

Individually, D.F. arrived on 4 February 2019 and was registered as an unaccompanied minor. He remained in the Jungle until mid-May 2019, then moved to the minors’ section. A place was found in November 2019 but delayed owing to bedbugs and medical checks. After a Rule 39 measure in December 2019, he was transferred to Thessaloniki in January 2020. A.N. arrived on 6 June 2019 and was placed in the safe zone; after Rule 39, he was transferred to Attica in January 2020 and then to Switzerland. S.N. arrived on 4 February 2019, initially registered as an adult, but was recognised as a minor in April 2019; he stayed in the Jungle until mid-May 2019 and was transferred to Athens in February 2020. A.A. arrived on 13 September 2019, stayed in the Jungle, was registered in November 2019, and was transferred in January 2020 after Rule 39. M.H. arrived on 3 March 2019, initially recorded as born in 2002, corrected to 2004 in November 2019; he stayed in the Jungle until mid-April 2019 and was transferred in January 2020. A.N. (application no. 13892/20) arrived on 24 July 2019, was initially registered as an adult born in 1993, arrested and detained as an adult in October 2019, then recognised as a minor in November 2019. He attempted suicide in February 2020 and was transferred only in May 2020 after further interim measures. A.M. arrived on 13 September 2019 and was registered as an unaccompanied minor; he was transferred to the safe area in June 2020, where a 22 sq. m dormitory housed eleven other minors, and then relocated to Finland.

The applicants alleged they were left for months in overcrowded and unsanitary conditions without adequate supervision, psychological support, or legal guardianship. They slept on the ground or wooden pallets covered with plastic, lacked regular sanitation, and were exposed to violence, theft, and illness. Some suffered skin infections, respiratory problems, and PTSD symptoms; one attempted suicide. They argued that the situation reflected structural deficiencies and that authorities failed to transfer them promptly despite knowing their minor status and vulnerability. The Government acknowledged overcrowding and the informal settlement but maintained that basic services were provided, that transfers were prioritised, and that deficiencies were temporary due to migratory pressure and COVID-19. Third-party interveners supported the applicants’ accounts of inadequate shelter, hygiene, healthcare, and guardianship. The core alleged violations concerned the failure to provide humane, age-appropriate reception conditions and effective protection for unaccompanied minors.
001-248167:
In *Gavrysh and Kosynets v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 62835/19 and 10392/25), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 22 January 2026. The judgment was adopted after private deliberations on 18 December 2025. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The case originated in two applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications.

The applicants are two Ukrainian nationals: Andriy Yuriyovych Gavrysh, born in 1973, and Sergiy Vitaliyovych Kosynets, born in 1972. Kosynets is represented by Mykhaylo Vasylyovych Kozachuk, a lawyer based in Kyiv. The central complaints in both applications concern the excessive length of civil proceedings before the domestic courts and the lack of any effective remedy in Ukrainian law for that delay. Such complaints ordinarily engage the fair-trial guarantee under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

The appended table provides the key factual details relevant to the alleged violations. In application no. 62835/19, Gavrysh introduced his application on 25 November 2019. The underlying civil proceedings commenced on 30 March 2007 and ended on 30 November 2020. The proceedings therefore lasted 13 years, 8 months and 1 day and passed through three levels of jurisdiction. This exceptionally long duration forms the factual basis of his complaint that the domestic courts failed to determine his civil case within a reasonable time. Because the proceedings were still pending when he applied to the European Court, his complaint also raises the question whether he had an effective domestic remedy to challenge or obtain redress for the delay.

In application no. 10392/25, Kosynets introduced his application on 21 March 2025. His civil proceedings began on 21 September 2021 and were still pending at the time the case was before the Court. Their duration was therefore more than 4 years, 2 months and 13 days, and the case had already passed through two levels of jurisdiction. As with Gavrysh, Kosynets complained that the length of the civil proceedings was excessive and that no effective remedy existed in domestic law. Because his proceedings remained pending, the alleged violation is continuing.

The judgment records the procedural history and factual details relevant to those alleged violations, including the dates of introduction, the start and end dates of the domestic civil proceedings, the total duration of each case, and the number of jurisdictional levels involved. The applicants’ core allegation is that the civil proceedings to which they were parties exceeded a reasonable time and that Ukrainian law did not provide them with an effective remedy for that delay. No further substantive details of the underlying civil disputes are set out in the provided extract. The Court’s assessment would therefore turn on the length and complexity of the proceedings, the conduct of the parties and authorities, what was at stake for the applicants, and the availability and effectiveness of domestic remedies for delay.
001-247822:
In *Gahraman v. Azerbaijan* (Apps. 14307/17 and 44088/18), the ECtHR Third Section reviewed an Azerbaijani national’s complaints. Applicant Elgiz Gahraman, born 1986, Baku, was member of Nida civic movement. Context: On 28 July 2016, A.A., senior ruling party official, publicly supported constitutional amendments before Sept 2016 referendum, including removing 35-year minimum age for presidential candidates. He cited Shah Ismail Khatai, 16th-century ruler who ascended at 14 and died at 36. Media speculated amendment aimed to allow President’s son into politics. Same day applicant posted on Facebook: “God willing [his] life will be as short as that of Shah Ismail.” Authorities allegedly saw this as veiled reference to President’s son.

On 12 Aug 2016 applicant was arrested. He claimed five plainclothes officers took him to Organised Crime Unit, where narcotics planted en route were “discovered” during search.
001-249251:
The case *Borzenkov and Others v Russia* concerns three applications against Russia lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained principally of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment, with some also raising other Convention complaints. The key facts concern alleged physical ill-treatment by Russian law-enforcement officers, contemporaneous medical evidence, and largely unsuccessful domestic complaints.

**Application no. 5841/23 – Daniil Konstantinovich Borzenkov (born 2001).** On 24 February 2022 at about 9:15 p.m., Russian Guards officers apprehended Borzenkov while he was on his way to a Moscow demonstration against the war in Ukraine. He alleged that officers hit him with rubber truncheons on the ribs, head and legs. He was taken to the Mezchanskiy police station in Moscow, where an administrative offence record was drawn up. A medical certificate dated 25 February 2022 from Moscow City Polyclinic No. 62 recorded a contusion of the soft tissues of the left thigh. On 4 March 2022 he complained to the Tverskoy District Investigative Department in Moscow; on 28 March 2022 the complaint was transferred to the Internal Security Department of the Moscow Police, and he received no further information. His appeal under Article 125 of the Russian Code of Criminal Procedure against the authorities’ inaction was dismissed on 28 July 2022 for lack of subject-matter, upheld by the Moscow City Court on 4 October 2022. He was fined under Article 20.2(5) of the Administrative Offences Code, final on 9 September 2022.

**Application no. 7877/23 – Natalya Borisovna Krisko (born 1967).** On 1 June 2020 at about 7 p.m. in the Krasnodar region, Krisko alleged that intoxicated police officers grabbed her by the wrists and pushed her down, causing her to hit the back of her head on the steps of a bank. She was allegedly held against the railing of the stairs for 20–30 minutes in front of passers-by. Medical evidence included an ambulance call card of 1 June 2020 and an extract from her medical record of 2 June 2020 from Kurganinskiy Central District Hospital, recording bruises to the chest and upper limbs and bruising; photographs of injuries were also taken. She complained on 3 June 2020 to the Labinskiy Inter-district Investigative Committee. Between 3 July 2020 and 23 October 2021, there were nine refusals to open a criminal case. Her Article 125 appeal against the last refusal was dismissed on 9 August 2022 and upheld by the Krasnodar Regional Court on 20 October 2022. She was not charged with any offence.

**Application no. 11065/23 – Kseniya Vladimirovna Viktorova (born 1977).** On 21 April 2021, while on her way to a rally protesting the arrest of opposition politician A. Navalnyy, Viktorova was forcibly apprehended by police. Officers allegedly used a rubber truncheon and a stun gun against her. She was taken to a police station for preparation of an offence report. The following day she saw a doctor, who documented contusions to the left forearm, right and left hips, and left knee joint. She first complained to the 16th police department in St Petersburg on 15 May 2021. Refusals to open a criminal case were issued on 27 July 2021 and 28 July 2022. Her Article 125 appeal against the refusal of 28 July 2022 was dismissed by the Oktyabrskiy District Court in St Petersburg on 2 November 2022, upheld on appeal on 18 January 2023.

In essence, each applicant alleged physical ill-treatment by police or Guards in the context of protests or public encounters, supported by medical documentation, and each faced refusals, inaction, or unsuccessful domestic court challenges. The case therefore centres on alleged Article 3 ill-treatment and the effectiveness of domestic investigation and remedies.
001-248220:
In *Lukashuk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 9079/24), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Andreas Zünd, Diana Sârcu, and Mykola Gnatovskyy, delivered a judgment on 22 January 2026. The judgment was adopted on 18 December 2025 and is final, though subject to editorial revision. The applicant, Artem Mykhaylovych Lukashuk, born in 2002, lodged the application against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on 13 March 2024. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the application.

The applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that there had been no effective investigation into the ill-treatment to which he had been subjected by private individuals.

The key facts, as set out in the appended table, are as follows. On 1 March 2019, the applicant, who was 16 years old at the time, was punched in the face by a certain Ch., who was 15 years old. As a result, the applicant sustained a fracture of his nasal bones. On 3 March 2019, the applicant’s mother lodged a criminal complaint. On 14 March 2019, an investigation was launched, and on 19 March 2019, a preliminary medical examination was carried out.

Although the investigation began promptly, it was repeatedly terminated by decisions of the investigator. Those terminations occurred on 23 September 2019, 25 December 2019, 27 May 2020, and 27 February 2023. Each of those decisions was subsequently quashed as unsubstantiated—by a prosecutor or an investigating judge—on 5 November 2019, 6 February 2020, 23 November 2020, and 27 April 2023 respectively. In July 2023, the investigator obtained a statement from Ch. Finally, on 26 June 2024, the investigation was closed because of the lack of constituent elements of a crime.

The applicant therefore alleged that the domestic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the ill-treatment inflicted on him by private individuals, contrary to the procedural obligation under Article 3 of the Convention. The central issue in the case is whether Ukraine complied with its duty to investigate adequately and promptly the serious ill-treatment suffered by the applicant, who was a minor at the time, and whether the repeated terminations and eventual closure of the criminal proceedings rendered the investigation ineffective.
001-247833:
In **Z v. Iceland** (Application no. 3538/21), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints that Icelandic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into alleged sexual harassment and discriminated on gender grounds in handling such cases, contrary to Articles 2, 8 and 14 of the Convention. The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 2002, was 16 at the time.

On 14 June 2019 the applicant attended a festival. In the early hours of 15 June she went to a co-worker’s tent. At 6:20 a.m. she sent a friend a video showing she was unwell; the footage captured the back of O.’s head, a 23-year-old man. She alleged that O. was groping her without consent, though this was not visible in the video. She said she passed out from intoxication and woke around 8:00 a.m. with her underwear on but trousers pulled down and jumper lifted to her breasts. She heard a belt being loosened. O. was beside her with his jumper removed and belt undone. She alleged he touched her breasts and genitals over and under her clothing. She pushed him away about three times and told him to stop; he stopped only when she left the tent.

On 15 June she attended the Emergency Reception Unit for Victims of Sexual Abuse. She declined a gynaecological examination but requested STD testing. Child Protection Services were notified because she was a minor. On 19 June she gave a police statement with a child protection worker present and provided the video.

O. was interviewed on 15 July. He denied guilt but admitted acting “a little wrong” before asking. He claimed he found the applicant half-asleep, they cuddled for warmth, and he touched her breast under her jumper with her bra between them. He said he stopped immediately when she appeared uncomfortable and shook her head, lasting about five seconds. He denied touching her genitals or removing clothing, but acknowledged she was a minor. Shown the video, he recognised himself and said it looked “very wrong,” explaining he had been trying to squeeze her.

The case was investigated under Article 199 of the General Penal Code on sexual harassment. Police took ten witness statements; none were direct witnesses. Several witnesses confirmed the applicant described waking to a man groping her with her trousers down and jumper up, and saw her shortly afterwards in shock, traumatised and crying. One described a later panic attack upon seeing O., requiring an ambulance. Three witnesses said they received Snapchat messages from the applicant that night describing unwanted sexual advances and a man not letting her out of the tent, with photos of her crying and a man’s head on her chest. Because Snapchat messages delete automatically, they were not preserved. Police did obtain a screenshot of two witnesses expressing concern that she said she was held against her will.

On 30 March 2020 the District Prosecutor discontinued the case, finding conviction unlikely. It cited her limited recollection, the lack of preserved messages, unclear video evidence, and a medical report containing no information about the alleged violations. Although O. admitted touching her breast, the prosecutor gave him the benefit of the doubt because he said he stopped upon realising lack of consent, leaving uncertainty about intent under Article 199. The State Prosecutor upheld that decision on 7 August 2020, again noting insufficient evidence and uncertainty as to intent.

The applicant complained that the authorities failed to effectively investigate the alleged sexual violence and discriminated against her on gender grounds in handling such cases. The Court gave notice of those complaints under Articles 2, 8 and 14; the remainder was inadmissible. The AIRE Centre intervened.
001-248594:
In *Zubco and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 49508/15 and 2 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 19 February 2026. The case mainly concerns alleged restrictions by the authorities of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”) on the applicants’ rights to freedom of expression and freedom of assembly, in the territory of the Republic of Moldova. Several applicants also alleged unlawful deprivation of liberty and inhuman detention conditions. The applicants relied principally on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention; some also invoked Articles 3, 5 § 1, 6, 8 and 13, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The first applicant, Alexandru Zubco, was born in the “MRT” and was a member of an NGO defending human rights in the region. His family continued to live in the “MRT”. On 15 April 2014, he was denied access to the “MRT” after the “KGB” imposed a ban on him because of his human rights activities. He challenged the ban in the “MRT courts” but was unsuccessful. The “Supreme Court of Justice of the MRT” gave a final decision on 26 February 2015, served on him on 8 April 2015. His main complaint was under Article 10, alleging interference with his freedom of expression.

The second application was brought by Vladimir Yegorov, a Russian journalist and human rights activist, and NP “IPC Apriori”, an “MRT”-based human rights NGO. The NGO invited Yegorov to act as an international observer to monitor and publicly cover the “MRT presidential elections” of 11 December 2016. He was also invited to speak at several public events organised by the NGO. On 8 December 2016, when he attempted to enter the “MRT” from territory under the sovereign control of Moldova, the “KGB” refused him entry. The applicants challenged that refusal in the “MRT courts”. On 11 May 2017, the “Supreme Court of Justice of the MRT” rejected their claims without examining them, on the ground that they had failed to submit valid powers of attorney. The applicants complained under Article 10 (interference with freedom of expression) and Article 11, namely Yegorov’s restriction on participation in a public event and the NGO’s restriction on organising a public event.

The third application, *Jukoveţ and Others*, concerned a peaceful public meeting held in Tiraspol (“MRT”) on 2 June 2018, organised by the “Communist Party”. The “Tiraspol district court” imposed administrative sanctions on the applicants for participating in an unauthorised meeting.
