Maria Jukoveţ received six days’ administrative arrest and was detained from 7 to 13 June 2018 in cells nos. 3 and 6 of the “Tiraspol militia” pre-trial detention centre. Alexandr Samonii received fourteen days’ arrest and was detained from 11 to 25 June 2018 in cell no. 15. Alexander Nevskiy received ten days’ arrest and was detained from 2 to 12 June 2018 in cells nos. 20, 3 and 15. Antonina Samonii, Vera Kaput and Nadezhda Bondarenko were each fined 368 Transnistrian roubles (about €19.50 at the time).

These applicants alleged that they were held for between 6 and 14 days in the same detention centre in inhuman conditions. They claimed overcrowding, with under 4 sq. m of personal space per detainee, and a deplorable state, including insufficient electric lighting, clogged toilets not separated from the cell, inadequate bedding and linen, lack of fresh air, toiletries, adequate food, potable water, showers and medical assistance. Some challenged the district court decisions before the “Supreme Court of Justice of the MRT”, without success. Their complaints concerned Article 11 (punishment for participating in a peaceful public assembly); some also alleged Article 3 (inhuman conditions of detention) and Article 5 § 1 (unlawful deprivation of liberty).
001-248961:
**Case Remez v. Ukraine (Application no. 25395/19)** concerns the alleged ineffectiveness of Ukraine’s investigation into ill-treatment suffered by a minor, Sofiya Andriyivna Remez, during her father’s failed attempt to kidnap her. The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 2014, was represented by her mother, Anastasiya Viktorovna Gaybadulova. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 June 2019. The applicant complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention.

The key facts begin on 8 June 2017, when the applicant—then two years and eight months old—was walking on a suburban street in Kherson with her grandmother. Her father, the former husband of her mother, grabbed her from her grandmother’s hands and pushed her into a nearby car. Bystanders intervened and stopped the attempted kidnapping. The same day, the applicant’s mother complained to the Korabelnyi District Police Department in Kherson, which immediately ordered a forensic medical examination.

On 8 June 2017, a paediatrician diagnosed the applicant with abrasions and haematomas of the upper limbs and torso. On 9 June 2017, a forensic medical doctor examined her and found abrasions and haematomas on both forearms and a bruise on the left abdomen beneath the costal arch. The doctor concluded that the injuries were minor and could not have resulted from a fall from the applicant’s height. That same day, the police opened criminal case no. 12017230020002105 concerning the infliction of minor bodily injuries under Article 125 § 1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.

On 30 June 2017, the police closed the criminal case for lack of evidence. On 10 October 2017, the Kherson City Court quashed that closure, citing lack of reasoning and the police’s failure to take any procedural action other than ordering the forensic examination. On 25 December 2017, the police again closed the case for lack of evidence. On 5 April 2018, the Kherson City Court quashed that decision for procedural irregularities, including the failure to send the closure decision to the applicant, represented by her mother, or to submit it to the court.

The applicant’s mother repeatedly sought procedural action. On 19 December 2017, 17 May, 30 July, and 27 November 2018, she lodged applications with the police asking for specific investigative steps. On 16 January, 6 June, 16 August, and 17 December 2018, she complained to the Kherson City Court about police inactivity, and the court ordered the police to examine her applications.

On 16 November and 28 December 2018, the Kherson Regional Police Department wrote to the applicant’s mother acknowledging the ineffectiveness of the investigation. It informed her that investigator B. had been dismissed for failing to perform his duties and that investigator K. had been assigned to the case. The new investigator was given instructions from the prosecutor’s office dated 23 February 2018 and was ordered to accelerate the investigation.

On 8 January 2019, the mother again asked the police to perform procedural actions, including questioning her as a victim, questioning eyewitnesses, and informing her of the investigation’s results. On 12 February 2019, the Kherson City Court ordered the police to examine that application. On 13 February 2019, the police rejected it on the ground that the applicant was not a party to the criminal proceedings. On 27 March 2019, the Kherson City Court overturned that refusal and found the refusal to perform certain procedural actions unlawful. On 8 September 2021, the police closed the criminal case for lack of evidence.

These facts—prompt medical evidence of injury, repeated closures for lack of evidence, repeated judicial findings of procedural defects, prolonged failure to question the victim and witnesses, refusal to recognise the mother’s procedural role, acknowledged investigative ineffectiveness, and eventual closure years later—form the factual basis for the applicant’s complaints that the investigation was ineffective and that she lacked an effective remedy.
001-250107:
In *K.A. v. Austria*, the applicant, a Kosovo national living in Austria, was convicted of prolonged domestic violence against his wife and four children and ordered confined in a forensic-therapeutic centre (then called an institution for mentally ill offenders). His complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 and Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d)–(e) arise from that confinement and from the examination of the child witnesses.

Family life was marked by frequent violence. In May 2021, after the applicant allegedly beat his children, his daughter B. called the police. His son C. told police that the applicant had struck their mother with a drill and threatened C. with a knife; C. fled. Police issued a restraining order, but the applicant refused to leave and was arrested. C. also alleged that the applicant later telephoned and threatened to kill the family. The applicant was taken into pre-trial detention on 31 May 2021 and denied the allegations.

During the pre-trial investigation, the three younger children were cross-examined as particularly vulnerable victims on 30 June 2021 via audio-video link. The applicant, his defence lawyer and the prosecutor were in a separate room and could see and question them. An Albanian interpreter provided only summary translations during breaks, not continuous interpretation. The children gave detailed accounts of longstanding violence. The applicant and his lawyer asked few or no questions. The wife and eldest daughter refused to testify. At trial in December 2021, the children did not attend; they said further testimony would be too distressing and asked that recordings or transcripts of their cross-examinations be used. Over defence objection, the court played the recordings and read the transcripts. The defence requested that the children be summoned for additional questioning, but the court refused because they had lawfully refused to testify.

Psychiatric expert Dr K. found the applicant had an accentuated personality structure or suspected personality disorder and alcohol abuse. Her examination was practically impossible because he denied everything and blamed his family. Assuming the children were credible, she described him as a classic “family tyrant” — narcissistic, dominance-oriented, lacking empathy, with sadistic tendencies. She considered him criminally responsible but found that, if the children’s statements were credible, the criteria for confinement under Article 21 § 2 were met: a severe mental or emotional abnormality and a high probability of serious violence against testifying family members. The Regional Court convicted him, sentenced him to eight years, and ordered confinement. It relied on the children’s credible statements and Dr K.’s report. Appeals were dismissed. The Supreme Court held that the applicant and counsel had been present at the cross-examinations, could ask questions, and that the summary translation did not violate his rights. The Court of Appeal upheld the confinement, later confirming in 2024 that a “severe and persistent mental disorder” need not match ICD or DSM categories and that the risk persisted.

The alleged violations were therefore twofold. First, under Article 5, the applicant argued that it had not been reliably shown that he was a person of “unsound mind” and that his confinement and subsequent review were unjustified. Second, under Article 6, he complained that he could not effectively challenge or question the prosecution witnesses because the child witnesses had been examined with only summary interpretation and later refused to testify at trial, while their recorded statements were admitted as evidence against him.
001-248395:
In *Martynovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 69358/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined the temporary suspension of the applicant’s licence to practise as an advocate. The applicant, Roman Yuryevich Martynovskiy, a Ukrainian national born in 1965, received his advocate’s licence in 1993 and worked in Sevastopol, Crimea. In October 2012, the Sevastopol Bar elected him to represent it in the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar (“HQDCB”), a governing body of the Ukrainian Bar.

On 7 December 2012, the HQDCB held its first meeting. The applicant did not attend, saying he had not been informed. Lawyer D. complained to the HQDCB that the applicant’s absence violated Article 62 of the Rules of Professional Conduct, adopted on 17 November 2012 and published on 18 January 2013, which required advocates elected to self-government bodies to refrain from actions that could block those bodies’ work. D. claimed that the HQDCB had posted notice of the meeting on its website and asked that the applicant’s licence be suspended.

On 24 January 2013, the head of the HQDCB transferred D.’s complaint to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Regional Bar of Zakarpattya (“QDC of Zakarpattya”), relying on Article 63 § 2 of the Rules, which required complaints against advocates elected to self-government bodies to be examined by a regional Bar outside the region where they were elected. The applicant learned of the complaint in February 2013. On 5 March 2013, he objected that the website notice did not mention him by name or address; that the HQDCB had adopted its Rules at the 7 December meeting, showing its work had not been blocked; that D. wrongly stated he had been elected by the Chernigiv Bar rather than Sevastopol; and that the transfer was unlawful under the Law on the Bar, which required complaints to be examined where the advocate practised. He also questioned how D.’s rights had been violated.

On 17 April 2013, in the applicant’s absence, the Disciplinary Chamber of the QDC of Zakarpattya suspended his licence for six months for failing to attend the meeting and violating Article 62. It asserted, without concrete evidence, that all HQDCB members had been informed via the website. The applicant was informed on 22 April 2013. The decision was upheld on 16 May 2013. His appeal to the HQDCB did not have suspensive effect. He complained that the QDC lacked competence, that the HQDCB head had no power to transfer the complaint, and that his right to equality of arms was violated because he was not informed before the hearing. His suspension also prevented him from attending an HQDCB meeting on 19 April 2013.

The HQDCB’s review stalled. It held hearings in 2013 but reached no decision, and held none in 2014. In July 2014, the Bar Council changed the HQDCB’s Rules so that a draft decision was rejected unless a majority of members voted in favour. In 2016, the rapporteur prepared a draft granting the applicant’s appeal and annulling the disciplinary decisions. On 22 July 2016, 19 of 30 members attended; 11 voted in favour, 6 against, and 2 abstained. Under the amended Rules, the draft was rejected, so the licence suspension remained.

The applicant sought judicial review in October 2016, arguing that the Rules had been applied retroactively, that he had not been informed of the December 2012 meeting, that the transfer was unlawful, and that he learned of the 17 April 2013 hearing only after it occurred. Related proceedings and delays followed. In April 2021, the Kyiv District Administrative Court found the Bar bodies’ decisions lawful; the Supreme Court gave a final decision on 9 December 2021. The applicant claimed he could only access that decision in November 2022.

The ECtHR application, lodged on 19 September 2013, concerned alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention arising from the suspension of the applicant’s advocate’s licence. The key facts relevant to those allegations include the in-absentia disciplinary sanction, allegedly inadequate notice and evidence, the contested transfer of the complaint, retroactive application of rules, lack of suspensive effect and effective judicial review, prolonged proceedings, and the resulting interference with the applicant’s professional and private life.
001-248953:
In *Gatsko and Panov v. Ukraine*, the applicants were two Ukrainian nationals and leaders of political party D. The case concerns their conviction for holding a peaceful demonstration and related proceedings.

In December 2012, the second applicant had been found guilty of violating the procedure for holding public events, but the criminal proceedings were closed as time-barred. That decision was not part of the application.

On 1 April 2013, the first applicant notified the Novi Petrivtsi Village Council that on 10 April 2013 he intended to organise a demonstration outside the President of Ukraine’s residence at 19 Ivana Franka Street, Novi Petrivtsi. The aim was to draw attention to poor road infrastructure. Up to 500 participants were expected. The Village Council asked the Kyiv District Administrative Court to prohibit the demonstration. On 5 April 2013, that court banned the D. party from holding it, citing a local executive committee decision of 31 July 2012 on public events and possible disruption of flood-damage roadworks at the location. Both applicants were present when the decision was announced and did not appeal.

According to the applicants, on 10 April 2013 they went to the President’s residence with journalists to check whether the roadworks mentioned by the court were actually taking place. While leaving, police stopped them, took them to a police station and later to the Vyshgorodskyy District Court. They were accused of breaching Articles 185 and 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The same day, the first applicant was fined UAH 170 (about EUR 16) for participating in a demonstration and refusing to follow a police officer. Although he said he did not appeal, the Government produced a Kyiv Region Court of Appeal decision of 3 June 2013 rejecting his appeal. The second applicant was also fined for disobeying a police officer under Article 185, and the court ordered further investigation into the remaining accusations. He did not appeal that fine.

On 11 April 2013, the second applicant appeared again before the Vyshgorodskyy District Court, which found him guilty of conducting a demonstration on 10 April despite the 5 April ban. The court found that he had organised the demonstration and sentenced him to seven days’ administrative detention under Article 185-1 § 2. It relied on police witness statements and statements by the Head of the Novi Petrivtsi Village Council, who said the second applicant had told him he planned to organise the demonstration. The court also noted the earlier December 2012 decision, whose proceedings had been closed as time-barred. After the hearing, the second applicant was taken to a temporary detention centre, where he met his lawyer. The lawyer appealed the same day, arguing that the second applicant had merely been checking for roadworks and had not been demonstrating. A Court of Appeal hearing was scheduled for 19 April 2013; the lawyer requested witness testimony and video footage, but the court allegedly refused without justification. On 19 April 2013, the Kyiv Region Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.

On 12 April 2013, the first applicant went to Novi Petrivtsi intending to demonstrate for the second applicant’s release. He was detained, brought before the Vyshgorodskyy District Court, met his lawyer and signed a legal representation contract, then was released. On 13 April 2013, the same court sentenced him to five days’ administrative detention under Article 185-1 § 2 for repeatedly violating the procedure for holding demonstrations under 1988 Soviet-era rules, referring also to Article 39 of the Constitution. It found that he had organised the meeting, relying on statements of people who had been with him and on the fact that he had notified the authorities only one hour before the planned demonstration. His appeal was dismissed by the Kyiv Region Court of Appeal on 28 May 2013.

The application was lodged on 9 August 2013. In 2018 the Court informed the applicants that the case file had been lost and invited them to resubmit. A new application form signed on 29 January 2019 was received on 3 April 2019, along with a copy of the original. These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints about interference with peaceful assembly, their prosecution and administrative detention, and procedural fairness in the administrative offence proceedings.
001-248598:
In *Simoncini v. San Marino*, the applicant, Massimiliano Simoncini, a San Marinese national, complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention about domestic proceedings no. 37/2020, which concerned the annulment of his appointment as *Commissario della Legge* (CoL), a first-instance judicial office. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of those complaints to the San Marinese Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The case arose from a dispute over the lawful composition of the Judicial Council in plenary session (*Consiglio Giudiziario Plenario*, “CGP”), the body responsible for judicial appointments. The applicant had served as an *Uditore Commissariale* since 2009 and was confirmed in that office in 2012. Having more than four years’ experience, he was eligible for appointment as CoL. In 2018 the CGP began a recruitment procedure for a CoL post. On 12 February 2019, by eleven votes in favour, the CGP decided to proceed by internal recruitment and appointed the applicant as CoL. Parliament acknowledged the appointment on 15 March 2019, and the applicant took up service on 22 March 2019.

However, two other *Uditori Commissariali*, X and Y, who had also been potential candidates, challenged the appointment in administrative proceedings no. 13/2019. They alleged, among other things, that the CGP had not been lawfully composed because judge C, a Judge of Appeal still serving a probationary period and not yet confirmed on a permanent basis, had participated in the CGP. They also complained of missing reports, lack of criteria, absence of reasons, and failure to notify interested candidates. The applicant did not initially participate in those proceedings and later failed to intervene because his request was out of time.

The legal background involved conflicting interpretations of the rules governing the CGP’s composition. In 2018 the CGP had taken the view that supplementation could include judges in the same category/functions even if not permanently confirmed. Later, Qualified Law no. 1/2020 introduced an authentic interpretation, with retroactive effect, providing that the CGP should be composed primarily of magistrates confirmed on permanent basis. On 28 September 2020, relying on that interpretation and on a *pro veritate* opinion, the CGP of its own motion (*autotutela decisoria spontanea*) annulled both the recruitment decision and the applicant’s appointment, on the ground that the CGP had been defectively composed when it appointed him. The applicant then brought proceedings no. 37/2020 challenging that annulment.

The domestic courts rejected the applicant’s claims. The first-instance judge found that the retroactive legislative interpretation pursued a compelling public interest and was not arbitrary; that the CGP could annul its own administrative act ex officio under domestic law; and that the presence of C had vitiated the appointment. On appeal, the Judge of Appeal for Civil Liability Actions of Magistrates upheld that reasoning on 9 January 2024. It held that the annulment was justified by the defective composition of the CGP, that the legislative intervention was necessary, reasonable, and proportionate, and that the applicant had no subjective right to retain an unlawful appointment. It found no violation of Articles 6, 8, 13, or 14, and considered parts of the appeal abusive or delaying. The applicant was ordered to pay costs.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 9 May 2024. The key alleged violations under Articles 6 and 8 concern whether the annulment of his judicial appointment, following a retroactive legislative change and an ex officio decision by the CGP, breached his right to a fair trial and his private life.
001-249527:
In *Khoman v. Ukraine* (Application no. 12308/19), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1954, complained under Article 2 of the Convention that Ukraine failed to carry out an effective investigation into her son’s death during military service. The application was lodged on 14 February 2019. The Court gave notice only of the complaint about the allegedly ineffective investigation; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The applicant’s son, A.K., was called up in April 2015 under a special military mobilisation. He served in Maryinka, Donetsk region, near a combat zone. On 25 June 2015, he died on premises occupied by his military unit after sustaining head injuries in unclear circumstances. An ambulance crew pronounced him dead immediately. For unknown reasons, the body was taken to a hospital rather than a morgue. That evening, after the hospital telephoned police, a criminal investigation was opened into murder. A police officer inspected the body in the ambulance.

A post-mortem examination was performed from 26 June to 10 July 2015. The expert found death resulted from a blunt-object head injury involving subdural haemorrhage and cerebral oedema. No alcohol odour was noted at autopsy on 26 June 2015. Although blood and stomach samples were extracted for toxicological analysis, they were ultimately disposed of due to a lack of transportation or preservation facilities. No toxicology test was therefore conducted.

On 2 July 2015, an internal inquiry concluded, based on evidence from two soldiers and their superior, that A.K. had been intoxicated, tripped over a balcony doorstep, fell, hit his head, and died. Later, the applicant learned of bullying allegations in the unit. One fellow soldier claimed he had been told A.K. was hit in the head before falling. She asked the investigator to examine those matters.

From 5 July to 27 October 2017, a commission of experts examined the case file. It concluded that the fatal head injuries resulted from at least seven “traumatic impacts” with limited-surface blunt objects. Because the objects could not be identified, and given the nature of the trauma and injury localisation, a fall from standing height could not be ruled out. There was no indication the fall was accelerated or the body dragged. It was impossible to establish whether the blunt objects were fists or feet. The experts also could not determine whether A.K.’s injuries resulted from tripping over the balcony doorstep, and noted that no forensic toxicological analysis for alcohol had been performed. In September 2019, A.K.’s former superior changed his account, saying A.K. had tripped and fallen during mortar shelling.

The investigation was discontinued three times for lack of indication of a criminal offence—on 23 September 2015, 28 February 2018, and 24 December 2019. Each decision was quashed—on 11 March 2016, 12 March 2019, and 8 April 2020—as premature, ungrounded, and unlawful. In April 2020, the Donetsk garrison military prosecutor criticised the investigation as incomplete: it had followed only the “accidental death” version without verifying other witness and applicant accounts, had not carried out measures regarding all involved persons, and had not performed a single investigative measure aimed at solving the crime and establishing the truth. No factual update after 2020 was provided. The alleged violation is thus the State’s failure to conduct an effective investigation under Article 2.
001-247917:
In **Felemez and Others v. Türkiye** (Applications nos. 30027/20 and 3 others), the European Court of Human Rights’ Second Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 22 January 2026. The case concerns four Turkish applicants who were dismissed from their employment and whose requests for reinstatement were examined by domestic courts. Their common complaint before the European Court was that the domestic court decisions lacked reasoning or contained inadequate reasoning. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, and the Turkish Government were given notice.

**Öner Felemez** (born 1986), represented by Mervan Eren Gül of Diyarbakır, introduced application no. 30027/20 on 29 June 2020. He sought reinstatement to his post after being dismissed from a private firm that was a subcontractor of Mardin Municipality under an emergency legislative decree, based on alleged links with the PKK. The Mardin Court of First Instance decided on 27 April 2018, and the Gaziantep Regional Court of Appeals decided on 19 February 2019. The Turkish Constitutional Court decided on 31 December 2019 (no. 2019/11080).

**Zeynep Yorgun** (born 1988), represented by Sabahattin Kaya of Van, introduced application no. 34403/20 on 13 July 2020. She requested reinstatement after dismissal on suspicion of affiliation with the PKK/KCK. The Van 2nd Labour Court decided on 2 May 2018, and the Erzurum Regional Court of Appeals decided on 8 November 2018. The Constitutional Court decided on 9 December 2019 (no. 2018/37791), with notification on 11 December 2019.

**Fırat Gümüş** (born 1971), represented by Hediye Saltan of Diyarbakır, introduced application no. 11548/21 on 21 January 2021. He requested reinstatement following dismissal on grounds of suspicion of affiliation with a terrorist organisation. The Diyarbakır 6th Labour Court decided on 19 June 2018 (2017/1174 E., 2018/842 K.). The Constitutional Court decided on 4 November 2020 (no. 2019/2868).

**İbrahim Ay** (born 1980), represented by Rehşan Bataray Saman of Diyarbakır, introduced application no. 36831/24 on 21 November 2024. He sought reinstatement after dismissal on suspicion of affiliation with a terrorist organisation under legislative decree no. 677. The Diyarbakır Labour Court decided on 7 June 2017; the Gaziantep Regional Civil Court decided on 15 November 2017; and the Court of Cassation decided on 2 July 2018. The Constitutional Court decided on 24 October 2024 (no. 2023/2579), notified on 1 November 2024.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that, in each case, the applicants’ dismissal and reinstatement disputes were reviewed by first-instance courts, appellate bodies, and the Turkish Constitutional Court, but the applicants considered those decisions to be insufficiently reasoned. The applicants therefore complained of a lack of reasoning or inadequate reasoning in court decisions. The ECtHR Committee, composed of Judges Stéphane Pisani, Juha Lavapuro, and Hugh Mercer, deliberated in private on 18 December 2025 and adopted the judgment on that date. The appended table provided the applicant details, representatives, dates, and domestic court decisions. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.
001-249810:
In *Levchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 58785/15), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1961, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention about the seizure of his car in criminal proceedings concerning third parties. The central issue was whether that seizure, and its prolonged retention, unlawfully and disproportionately interfered with his property rights.

On 4 April 2014 the applicant bought a used car. It was later established that the car had been sold to him on the basis of a forged authority form. In December 2014 a criminal investigation was launched into fraudulent property appropriation in that regard.

On 28 May 2015, while the applicant was driving the car, the Uman traffic police stopped him and withheld the vehicle because it was listed as wanted by the police. The car was taken to the local traffic police pound. On 25 June 2015 the investigator applied to the Zhytomyr Bohunskyi District Court for seizure of the car. On 30 June 2015 that court allowed the application at a hearing attended by the prosecutor, but the applicant was not notified of the hearing. The applicant later challenged the ruling on appeal once he discovered it existed.

In his appeal, the applicant relied in particular on Article 171 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provided that if an investigator did not apply for seizure of property within one day of its temporary withholding, the property was to be immediately returned to the person from whom it had been withheld. In the applicant’s case, however, the investigator applied for seizure about one month after the car was withheld. He also argued that the seizure was disproportionate. On 5 August 2015 the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal rejected the appeal as unfounded. It stated in general terms that the Bohunskyi Court had complied with the applicable legal provisions and that the legitimate owner of the car had not yet been established.

On 25 March 2016 the applicant was granted the procedural status of victim in the ongoing criminal proceedings. He applied many times for the seizure to be lifted. On 1 December 2016 the Bohunskyi Court allowed one such application in part. Although it upheld the ban on disposal or encumbrance of the car, it ordered that the car be transferred to the applicant for safekeeping. The court noted that the applicant had victim status, that the car showed no traces of involvement in an offence, and that continued storage in an open outdoor space at the police pound since 28 May 2015 meant it would deteriorate.

On 4 November 2019 the same court lifted the seizure altogether. It noted that no investigative measures had been carried out in the criminal investigation since September 2016 and that no suspicion had been announced. The judge also referred to the fact that the applicant’s bona fide ownership of the car had never been questioned. On 17 June 2020 the criminal investigation was discontinued because it was found impossible to identify any suspects.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were therefore the seizure of the applicant’s car in proceedings against third parties, the delay in applying for seizure contrary to national procedural rules, the lack of notification of the seizure hearing, the prolonged restriction on disposal or encumbrance until November 2019, and the applicant’s unchallenged bona fide ownership and later victim status. These factors formed the basis of his complaint that the interference with his property was unlawful and disproportionate.
001-250034:

001-248592:
In *Stalović v. Serbia* (Application no. 35786/22), the applicants are Marko Stalović, a Serbian national of Roma origin, and Sandra Stalović, an Austrian national, who are married. They complained to the European Court of Human Rights of racially motivated police ill-treatment and the lack of an effective investigation.

On 21 April 2017 the applicants reported a car theft to Mladenovac Police Station, stating their passports had been left in the car. They were then subjected to a polygraph test and “informal” questioning at the Belgrade Police Directorate. No minutes were made of those interviews. The applicants were placed in separate rooms. The first applicant alleged that he was forced to kneel, slapped, kicked in the stomach, struck on the hands with a leather whip, suffocated with a plastic bag, threatened with shooting and electrocution, insulted with the racist phrase “Gypsy mother,” and warned that his children would be placed in care. The second applicant alleged threats of detention, accusations of being “the mask of an organised criminal group,” racist insults such as “white woman with a black man” and “Shqiptar in disguise,” and threats to take her children.

They were later returned to Mladenovac Station, where they gave formal statements. The minutes recorded the interviews as ending at 9.30 p.m. and stated that the applicants had no remarks and that the first applicant had no complaints about police treatment in Mladenovac or Belgrade. At 10.35 p.m., the first applicant was medically examined. The report documented head injuries, red spots near the left kidney region, and a pressure mark on his right knee. A further examination the next day revealed multiple head injuries and muscle pain. On 26 April 2017 he was diagnosed with PTSD attributed to the incident.

On 9 May 2017 the applicants lodged a criminal complaint against eight police officers, alleging ill-treatment because of the first applicant’s Roma origin. The prosecutor instructed the Department for the Control of Lawfulness of the Police to gather information. Five officers were questioned by 31 August 2017, while the applicants were heard on 8 December 2017. The officers denied ill-treatment but admitted informal questioning after the polygraph. Other officers present during parts of the questioning were not interviewed. The first applicant said he had not been informed what he was signing. The second applicant claimed psychological ill-treatment but said she had not given a statement at the Belgrade Police Directorate.

On 17 May 2018 the Prosecutor’s Office rejected the criminal complaint. It relied on the officers’ statements and the signed minutes showing no complaints. It also referred to CCTV footage from Mladenovac Station showing the applicants leaving without visible injuries. The first medical report was disregarded because the first applicant had no identity documents; the second was disregarded as made the day after the alleged ill-treatment; photographs were disregarded as undated. The second applicant’s psychological complaint was not addressed. The second-instance prosecutor upheld that decision on 29 August 2018.

In parallel, the applicants brought a discrimination claim against the State. On 1 June 2020 the Belgrade Court of Second Instance found that police officers had applied unjustified physical and psychological pressure amounting to degrading treatment. It awarded the first applicant EUR 4,700 and the second EUR 1,700 in non-pecuniary damages. It found their claim credible that the conduct was motivated at least partly by the first applicant’s Roma origin and the second applicant’s marriage to him, and that the State had not disproved this. That judgment became final on 17 December 2020.

On 28 October 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional appeal concerning the rejection of their criminal complaint. It found the investigation adequate, thorough, and prompt, and held that discrimination could not be breached unless another constitutional right had first been violated. Before the European Court, notice was given only of the complaints concerning alleged ill-treatment by police; the remainder was declared inadmissible.
001-249525:
**Kis and Levchuk v. Ukraine (App. no. 910/18)** concerns the alleged lack of an effective investigation into an attack on two Ukrainian nationals who participated as a same-sex couple in a 2015 social experiment in Kyiv. The applicants complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention that the authorities failed to investigate treatment they suffered because of their sexual orientation.

In 2015, the online magazine *Bird in Flight* organized an experiment, similar to one in Moscow, to gauge Ukrainian society’s tolerance toward same-sex couples. On 15 July 2015, the applicants walked through central Kyiv holding hands for about an hour, accompanied by bodyguards and filmed. After nothing happened, they escalated their public display of affection. With the organizers’ approval, one applicant sat on the other’s lap on a bench on Khreshchatyk Street, holding a bouquet.

A group of young people approached, asking whether they were patriots and wanted their nation to be best. The applicants replied that patriotism, for them, meant supporting equality. The group reportedly made remarks such as “The guys have [this place] mixed up with America” and “Europe! Europe!” They then pepper-sprayed and kicked the applicants. Bodyguards intervened immediately, so the physical confrontation lasted only three to five seconds. The applicants did not seek medical help or undergo a forensic medical examination.

On 22 July 2015, the experiment video was published online; some attackers’ faces were visible. News websites reported on it. On 29 July 2015, the first applicant filed a criminal complaint for himself and the second applicant, describing the attack and asking police to open a case under Article 161 § 2 of the Criminal Code—violation of equality committed with violence—and to investigate discrimination against them as homosexuals. He did not mention injuries and referred to the online video. The second applicant also complained. When questioned on 4 August 2015, he said he had not sought medical assistance; police stated he refused a forensic medical examination.

On 5 August 2015, police opened proceedings under Article 296 § 2 (group hooliganism), not Article 161. On 12 August 2015, they closed the case for lack of evidence, citing only the victims’ statements, no eyewitnesses, no usable video surveillance, and the second applicant’s refusal of an allegedly obligatory forensic examination. The lawyer was informed on 2 October and received a copy on 25 November 2015. She appealed, arguing police failed to include the magazine’s video, interview the cameraman, or classify the offence under Article 161, and wrongly treated forensic examination as obligatory. Courts and prosecutors repeatedly set aside closure decisions as premature and returned the case for investigation.

In May 2016, the lawyer sought reclassification under Article 161; police refused in June 2016 because no elements were apparent from unidentified persons. Police later collected mobile phone base-station data but reported inability to question the magazine’s editor or journalist or identify perpetrators. In September 2017, the applicants recognized a woman allegedly from the attacking group in a video from an unrelated picket and identified a group, S.; there was no apparent follow-up. By 2021–2023, police still reported difficulties identifying perpetrators; in July 2023 they questioned the editor and sought access to mobile operators’ data. The criminal proceedings remain pending.
001-249234:
**Musina and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 48419/16) concerns four Ukrainian applicants—relatives of A.M.—who complained under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights about A.M.’s death while he was under State control and about the alleged ineffectiveness of the investigation.

A.M., then 40 and medically fit, was called up for military service in April 2014 under a special mobilisation. He was due to be discharged in March 2015. An order for his discharge was dated 25 March 2015, but he remained in the military unit for several days to complete formalities.

At about 11 p.m. on 27 March 2015, a patrol found a heavily drunk soldier, V.S., lying near the gasmask distribution tent, about 20 metres from the central checkpoint. His upper and lower limbs were tied, and he had had a gag in his mouth, which he had removed to call for help. The guards freed him and let him go towards the barracks without obtaining explanations.

At about 6.10 a.m. on 28 March 2015, the patrol found A.M. dead inside the same tent. His wrists had been tied behind his back with two plastic hose clamps, his feet tied with electric cable to a tent pole, and his mouth covered with adhesive tape. A textile gag fell out when the tape was removed.

A criminal investigation was opened into murder/sudden death, but the register entry noted no indication of violent death. The military authorities claimed A.M. was no longer in service and thus outside military command jurisdiction; the investigation was allocated to the Novomoskovsk city police. Separately, the military prosecutor’s office investigated possible security/access omissions by the military unit; that inquiry was discontinued on 30 June 2015 for absence of a criminal offence.

At the scene, A.M.’s wristwatch was found outside the tent. A sniffer dog picked up a scent, went towards the checkpoint, reached the fence, and lost it. Several soldiers, including the patrol, were questioned. They claimed nothing unusual except drunk comrades and the V.S. incident. V.S. said he had been drinking with A.M. and two “unidentified” soldiers; he remembered little and alleged an unidentified soldier had gagged him. Two soldiers said they drank with A.M. and V.S. until about 2 p.m. on 27 March and knew nothing later.

A death certificate of 30 March 2015 attributed death to acute coronary insufficiency. A forensic report of 10 April 2015 concluded coronary insufficiency exacerbated by heavy alcohol intoxication. It noted minor injuries—sores and bruises on A.M.’s mouth and cheeks—before death, but no causal link to death. It also observed dried soil around and inside his nostrils and on his mouth. A later forensic examination in November 2015 again found no causal link between the tying of A.M.’s hands and feet and his death.

The investigation was marked by alleged omissions. On 16 June 2015, the criminal investigation unit reported that military unit management refused to provide information on who had been present on 27–28 March 2015. On 27 June 2015, police discontinued the investigation for absence of a criminal offence, relying on the forensic report. On 6 July 2015, the prosecutor’s office quashed that decision as premature and unlawful, and the first and second applicants were granted victim status. A November 2015 operational meeting noted that prosecution instructions had not been followed and that serious omissions had undermined the investigation.

In January 2016, cytological examination found no DNA; blood on the tape and gag could not be attributed because no blood samples had been provided, and skin cells under A.M.’s fingernails were unsuitable for analysis. The acting commander, R.K., was first questioned only on 18 June 2016. He said A.M. stayed beyond 25 March to hand over his position, denied knowing who tied A.M. or V.S., and stressed the unit was secure with strict access control, ruling out unauthorised persons.

The investigation was discontinued again on 30 November 2016, quashed on 3 March 2017, and terminated again on 30 March 2017 in nearly identical terms. The investigator had been disciplined several times for poor quality. The applicants therefore alleged that A.M. died in State-controlled military custody in suspicious circumstances and that authorities failed to protect him and to conduct an effective investigation.
001-249530:
Case Simoncini v. San Marino (Application no. 3106/24) concerns disciplinary proceedings against Mr Massimiliano Simoncini, a San Marinese national born in 1963 and a member of the San Marino judiciary. The proceedings arose from misconduct he committed in February 2023. On 13 July 2023, the Judicial Council (Consiglio Giudiziario), sitting as a court of first instance, found him disciplinary liable under section 12 of Constitutional Law no. 1/2021 and imposed the sanction of a warning (ammonimento).

On 4 September 2023, Simoncini appealed to the Constitutional Court (Collegio garante della costituzionalità delle norme) under section 16(10) of Constitutional Law no. 1/2021. By decree of 12 September 2023, the President of the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible because Simoncini was not represented by a lawyer. Legal representation was mandatory under section 9(1) of Qualified Law no. 55/2003 and section 12(1) of the Constitutional Court’s Internal Regulations.

On 15 September 2023, a lawyer appointed by Simoncini submitted a brief formally ratifying the appeal, thereby seeking to remedy the initial lack of representation. The lawyer argued that Simoncini had initially filed the appeal without a representative because it was difficult to find a lawyer during the summer holidays, and that he had been entitled to do so under certain provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which also applied to disciplinary proceedings. However, by decree of 22 September 2023, the President of the Constitutional Court again declared the appeal inadmissible. The President reiterated that representation was mandatory and held that the lawyer’s ratifying brief had been submitted after the expiry of the 30-day time-limit for appeal.

Simoncini subsequently filed a plea of nullity (querela nullitatis), seeking annulment of the two decrees, and a constitutional complaint challenging several provisions regulating the disciplinary proceedings. At the time of the European Court’s judgment, no decision appeared to have been delivered on those applications.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Simoncini lodged his application on 20 January 2024. The Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, gave notice to the San Marinese Government of the complaints raised under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention concerning the right to a tribunal established by law and the right to a reasoned decision. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Government was represented by its Agent, Ms S. Bernardi, while Simoncini was represented by Mr A. Masiello, a lawyer practising in Borgo Maggiore.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore centre on the disciplinary finding and warning imposed by the Judicial Council, and particularly on the Constitutional Court’s refusal of Simoncini’s appeal on procedural grounds—first for lack of mandatory legal representation, and then because the later ratification by counsel came after the expiry of the appeal deadline. Those procedural rulings, together with Simoncini’s challenge to the applicable disciplinary-proceedings provisions, form the factual basis for his Article 6 § 1 complaints about the right to a tribunal established by law and the right to a reasoned decision. The Court gave notice only of those Article 6 complaints; the other complaints were rejected as inadmissible. The judgment was adopted on 19 March 2026 and delivered on 9 April 2026, and is final but subject to editorial revision.
001-247909:
In *Vykhor v. Ukraine* (Application no. 36618/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The applicant, Pavlo Oleksandrovych Vykhor, a Ukrainian lawyer born in 1978 and living in Kostyantynivka, lodged the application on 30 April 2014.

The applicant was a defendant in criminal proceedings initiated in May 2013, which remained ongoing at trial stage as of January 2024. He was charged with defrauding V.O., his client, by inciting him to hand over money allegedly demanded by judicial and police authorities to ensure favourable treatment of V.O.’s criminal case.

The alleged violations arose mainly from covert investigative measures used against the applicant. On 23 May 2013, an investigating judge of the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, relying in particular on Articles 246–248 and 263 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, issued two similarly worded orders authorising the tapping of the applicant’s two mobile telephones and audio and video monitoring. The judge stated, without further detail, that there were sufficient grounds to believe that information of fundamental importance for preventing, detecting and ending criminal offences could be obtained. The judge also noted the police’s argument that the information could not be obtained by other means.

On 31 May 2013, a prosecutor from the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office authorised the police to organise a “controlled transaction”, under which V.O. would receive marked bills to hand over to the applicant.

By November 2013, the applicant learned that key evidence in his case had been obtained through those covert measures. The prosecution file included transcripts of his telephone conversations and of a meeting with V.O., recorded by law-enforcement authorities under the 23 May 2013 authorisations. Copies of those authorisations were also included in the file.

On 28 February 2014, the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court declined to consider the applicant’s appeals against the investigating judge’s authorisations, finding that they were not subject to appeal. The applicant subsequently lodged numerous criminal, disciplinary and civil complaints challenging the covert measures. He alleged, in particular, that the 23 May 2013 authorisations had been given unlawfully and without an assessment of whether there was a reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence. He further alleged that the measures constituted an unlawful and disproportionate interference with the confidentiality of his private communications. In March 2017, he applied to the Kostyantynivka City District Court seeking exclusion from his criminal file of evidence obtained through the disputed measures.

According to the parties’ latest submissions, as of January 2024 the criminal proceedings were still at the trial stage, and no decision had yet been taken on his complaints concerning the covert measures.

The ECtHR gave notice of the applicant’s complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 13: that the covert investigative measures were incompatible with his right to respect for private life and correspondence; that he lacked effective remedies for that complaint; and that the criminal proceedings against him were excessively long. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. In its judgment of 22 January 2026, the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, examined those issues.
001-248636:
**Case: Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 5067/23), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, Judgment of 3 February 2026.**

The applicant, Zlatan Begić, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1975 and living in Tuzla, is a high-ranking official of the Democratic Front and a member of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He does not declare affiliation with any of the “constituent peoples”—Bosniacs, Croats, or Serbs—and therefore belongs to the constitutional category of “Others.”

The applicant complained under Articles 14 and 17 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 about his ineligibility to stand for election to the position of Chair/Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives. The Court gave notice of those complaints to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The relevant constitutional framework derives from the 1995 Dayton Agreement. Bosnia and Herzegovina consists of two Entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska, plus the Brčko District. The Constitution distinguishes “constituent peoples” from “Others and citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.” At State level, power-sharing arrangements include a vital interest veto, an Entity veto, a House of Peoples composed of five Bosniacs, five Croats and five Serbs, and a tripartite Presidency with one Bosniac, one Croat and one Serb. Although no ethnic requirement applies to election to the House of Representatives, Article IV § 3(b) of the Constitution requires each chamber to select from its members one Serb, one Bosniac and one Croat to serve as Chair and Deputy Chairs, with the position of Chair rotating among those three persons. Consequently, persons who do not declare affiliation with a constituent people, such as the applicant, are not eligible to serve as Chair or Deputy Chair of that chamber.

On 1 December 2022, two members of the House of Representatives nominated the applicant for the position of Chair/Deputy Chair. According to the minutes of that meeting, his nomination was not put to a vote because it did not comply with the House’s Rules of Procedure. This refusal is central to the alleged violations, as it is said to result from the constitutional requirement that the position be held only by a Serb, a Bosniac or a Croat.

The Constitution provides that the Convention and its Protocols apply directly in Bosnia and Herzegovina and have priority over all other law, and that rights under listed international agreements are secured without discrimination. Article IX § 3 further states that officials appointed to institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be generally representative of its peoples. However, the Constitutional Court has held in decisions nos. U 5/04 and U 13/05 that the Convention does not have priority over the Constitution and that it lacks jurisdiction to review the Constitution’s conformity with the Convention. The relevant constitutional provisions have neither been amended nor declared unconstitutional.

The case therefore concerns whether the applicant’s exclusion, based on his status as an “Other,” from candidacy for Chair/Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives breaches his rights under the Convention and its Protocols, particularly the prohibition of discrimination and the right to free elections.
001-249531:
In *Novák v. the Czech Republic*, the applicant is a Czech father of two daughters, born in 2014 and 2018. In April 2021, after he and the children’s mother separated in Brno, they agreed to share custody. In September 2021, the mother petitioned for divorce and sought sole custody, while the applicant sought shared custody. From January 2022, the mother refused shared custody, though the applicant maintained regular contact, including Tuesday overnight visits and alternate weekends. Attempts at counselling did not produce agreement.

In May 2022, the Brno Municipal Court granted the applicant interim shared custody, but on 14 June 2022 the Brno Regional Court reversed that decision, finding no urgent need for an interim measure because the mother was caring for the children and the applicant had regular contact. On 14 July 2022, the Municipal Court awarded shared custody on a weekly basis, relying on a counselling report and the children’s guardian ad litem, who considered both parents capable and the children’s relationships positive. The mother appealed, and her appeal had suspensive effect.

On 28 August 2022, the mother unilaterally relocated with the children from Brno to Prague and enrolled them in school there. She proposed that the applicant see them every other weekend and during holidays, plus telephone/online contact. The applicant informed the social welfare authority, which declared the children “endangered.” On 7 September 2022, he applied for interim measures seeking custody or, alternatively, the children’s return and re-enrolment in their original schools, arguing that the mother had breached Article 877 of the Civil Code by changing their residence without his consent.

On 12 September 2022, the Municipal Court dismissed the interim shared-custody application, citing the Regional Court’s June decision and finding no urgent need because the applicant retained contact and the mother cared for the children. It dismissed the return application because the required deposit had not been paid on the day of filing. The applicant filed a second return application on 20 September 2022, which was dismissed on 21 September 2022: the court found no sufficient endangerment under the Special Court Proceedings Act and held that residence and schooling should be determined in proceedings on the merits. The appeals were dismissed on 2 December 2022. The Regional Court acknowledged the mother had relocated without agreement but found the applicant had not shown that the children’s care was seriously impaired or endangered; it also considered further change contrary to their best interests. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 5 April 2023 as manifestly ill-founded.

On 20 April 2023, the Regional Court overturned the shared-custody judgment and granted the mother sole custody, with the applicant having contact every second weekend and during holidays. It found both parents capable but held that circumstances had significantly changed: the children had adapted well to Prague over eight months, lived near other family, and the distance of over 200 km made shared custody impractical. It also relied on the children’s wishes to remain with their mother in Prague and visit the applicant in Brno. The mother was ordered to collect the children from Brno and share travel costs. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal on 17 October 2023.

Later enforcement proceedings revealed repeated refusals by the mother to hand over the children, fines imposed on her, and an expert finding no danger from the applicant; in February 2025 she was convicted of obstructing contact. The ECtHR application concerns the appellate court’s refusal to uphold the first-instance shared-custody judgment after the mother’s unilateral relocation and the refusal of interim measures, raising issues under Article 8 of the Convention regarding the applicant’s right to family life.
001-248687:
The case concerns three applications lodged against Ukraine: no. 1129/18 by Vadym Mykolayovych Mogyla, born in 1986 and introduced on 21 December 2017; no. 50410/18 by Petro Ivanovych Stetsenko, born in 1974 and introduced on 9 January 2019; and no. 34853/24 by Firma Svitlana, TOV, a company registered in 1996 and represented by Pleskach Vyacheslav Yuriyovych of Gozhuly, introduced on 8 November 2024. The applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention that their access to a court had been restricted. In application no. 1129/18, the applicant also raised other complaints under the Convention.

Mogyla filed an administrative claim on 24 November 2008 challenging a local council’s refusal to allocate him a plot of land. The claim was reconsidered several times. On 26 January 2011 the Higher Administrative Court confirmed that it should be examined within administrative proceedings. On 30 September 2014, in the second round of consideration, the Higher Administrative Court remitted the case to the first-instance administrative court for a new consideration. On 21 June 2017, however, the Higher Administrative Court ruled that the claim fell to be examined in civil proceedings and terminated the case. Consequently, Mogyla’s claim was not determined on the merits.

Stetsenko’s complaint arose from proceedings concerning his claim about a local court’s refusal to grant him access to a case file relating to his property. On 21 June 2018 the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal ruled on his request for full or partial exemption from, or deferral of, payment of court fees of approximately EUR 34. He relied on an alleged lack of funds and submitted official tax certificates showing his family’s monthly income of approximately EUR 139, which was significantly lower than the applicable minimum family subsistence level. The Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the request, holding that he had “failed to provide relevant evidence to prove his allegedly difficult financial situation,” without further explanation. The Supreme Court upheld that ruling on 17 September 2018.

Firma Svitlana’s complaint concerned commercial proceedings relating to registration of property. On 26 July 2024 the Poltava Regional Commercial Court dismissed the company’s request for exemption from or deferral of a court fee of UAH 27,252 (approximately EUR 650), based on its alleged lack of funds, income or assets. In support, the company provided copies of financial reports and bank statements. The court reasoned that under Article 8 of the Court Fee Act only individuals, not legal entities, could be released from the obligation to pay court fees. On 31 July 2024 the court returned the claim for failure to pay the court fee. On 12 August 2024 the Eastern Commercial Court of Appeal dismissed the company’s request for deferral of the appellate court fee of UAH 2,422 (approximately EUR 60), applying the same reasoning. On 11 September 2024 the appellate court returned the company’s appeal against the 26 July 2024 decision for failure to pay the appellate court fee. On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court refused to open cassation proceedings, essentially upholding the appellate court’s reasoning.
001-249970:
In *Romani and Cancelli v. Italy* (Applications nos. 54213/19 and 61041/19), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) considered two applications against Italy concerning the effectiveness and duration of civil proceedings arising from alleged medical negligence that resulted in the deaths of the applicants’ next of kin.

The first application, *Romani v. Italy* (no. 54213/19), was introduced on 10 October 2019 by Nazzareno Romani and Stefano Romani, born in 1964 and 1967 respectively and residing in Pesaro, represented by Fabrizio Dini. Their mother was hospitalised from 2 to 17 January 2004 and died on 18 January 2004. On 29 April 2005, the applicants brought a civil action against the hospital seeking compensation for damage resulting from their mother’s death, which they alleged had been caused by negligence on the part of the medical staff. The civil proceedings lasted 14 years across three levels of jurisdiction and ended with a judgment of the Court of Cassation on 15 April 2019.

The second application, *Cancelli v. Italy* (no. 61041/19), was introduced on 14 November 2019 by Giovanni Cancelli, born in 1959 and residing in Maglie, represented by Lilia Lucia Petracchi and Federico Di Salvo. His daughter, who had suffered from congenital heart problems since birth, was hospitalised from 12 to 20 December 1999. On 29 December 1999, the hospital decided not to readmit her, and she died the same day. On 18 January 2001, the applicant brought a civil action against the hospital seeking compensation for damage allegedly caused by medical negligence in his daughter’s treatment. The proceedings ended with a judgment of the Court of Appeal on 14 May 2019, after the case had been remitted to that court by the Court of Cassation on 10 January 2017. In total, the civil proceedings lasted 16 years and 7 months over four levels of jurisdiction. In parallel, Cancelli sought and obtained €3,660 in compensation for the excessive length of the proceedings under Law no. 89 of 24 March 2001 (the “Pinto Act”); that compensation was awarded in 2020.

Before the European Court, the applicants relied on Articles 2 and 6 of the Convention. They complained of the ineffectiveness and length of the domestic civil proceedings concerning the alleged medical negligence that had resulted in the deaths of their next of kin. In particular, the core alleged violation concerned the procedural limb of Article 2, namely the State’s obligation to ensure an effective and timely judicial response to deaths allegedly caused by medical negligence. The Court gave notice of the complaint concerning Article 2 in its procedural limb to the Italian Government, represented by Agent Mr L. D’Ascia. The remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible. Thus, the case focused on whether the Italian civil proceedings provided an effective procedural mechanism under Article 2 and whether their duration undermined that effectiveness.
001-250036:

001-249515:
**Case: Ismayilova v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 44031/17 and 41494/20), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 7 April 2026.**

The applicant, Khadija Ismayilova, is an Azerbaijani investigative journalist born in 1976, living in Baku. The case concerns a travel ban imposed on her after her conditional release from prison.

In September 2015, the Baku Court of Serious Crimes convicted her of large-scale misappropriation, illegal entrepreneurship, tax evasion, and abuse of power. She was sentenced to seven years and six months’ imprisonment and barred for three years from holding managerial and financial posts in public and local self-government bodies. Her appeal was dismissed in November 2015. In May 2016, the Supreme Court quashed several convictions, upheld only illegal entrepreneurship and tax evasion, reduced her sentence to three years and six months suspended on probation for five years, and imposed a two-year ban on managerial and financial posts. Her release was conditional on not changing her permanent residence without prior notification to the Binagadi District Enforcement Department.

In June 2016, during her first meeting with a bailiff, the applicant learned that a travel ban had been imposed for the duration of her probation. On 19 June 2016, she challenged the ban before the Binagadi District Court, seeking its removal. She stated that she had received invitations to international conferences from international organisations and NGOs and that attending such events was essential to her work as an investigative journalist. She also sought permission to accompany her mother to Türkiye for heart surgery, submitting medical documentation.

On 28 June 2016, the Binagadi District Court dismissed her application. It found that allowing her to leave Azerbaijan at will would limit the authorities’ ability to monitor her behaviour during probation and might hinder her rehabilitation, thereby frustrating execution of the sentence. It also noted that there were no guarantees she would return to Azerbaijan.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the first-instance court had failed to address her reasoning or assess her personal situation and had relied on irrelevant arguments. She contended that her conduct after the Supreme Court’s May 2016 decision—including regular self-reporting to the Enforcement Department, a clean record, and her professional and social reputation—undermined the court’s claims about lack of return guarantees and inability to monitor her.

On 15 August 2016, the Baku Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal, holding that the restriction was necessary to oversee execution of her conditional sentence during probation. On 8 December 2016, the Supreme Court upheld that decision, served on the applicant on 16 December 2016.

On 7 July 2019, the applicant asked the Binagadi District Court to revoke her suspended sentence, remove her conviction, and lift the travel ban, arguing that more than half of the probationary period had elapsed. On 9 August 2019, the District Court refused, finding insufficient evidence of rehabilitation and no bailiff opinion supporting it. Her appeal was dismissed by the Baku Court of Appeal on 20 September 2019, again for insufficient evidence of rehabilitation. On 6 February 2020, the Supreme Court upheld that decision.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 and Article 13 that the travel ban violated her right to leave the country and that she had no effective domestic remedy. She also complained under Articles 8 and 10, and under Article 18 taken together with Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, that the travel ban violated her private and family life and freedom of expression, and that her Convention rights were restricted for purposes other than those prescribed. Third-party comments were submitted by the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and Article 19 in application no. 44031/17.
001-248854:
In *Gazin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 43898/19), the applicant, Mr Andriy Yuriyovych Gazin, a Ukrainian national born in 1967 and living in Dnipro, complained to the European Court of Human Rights that domestic proceedings concerning alleged medical malpractice were ineffective. The application was lodged on 10 August 2019.

The facts concern medical treatment in 2012. On 3 August 2012, the applicant was admitted to Dnipro Municipal Clinic No. 4 with acute flank pain. He was diagnosed with a ureteral stone and renal colic. In the early hours of 4 August 2012, duty doctor M.P. performed urinary catheterisation. The applicant alleged that his condition later deteriorated: he developed fever, lower abdominal pain, and increased urinary frequency. He was diagnosed with acute pyelonephritis and received treatment. He was discharged on 17 August 2012 in satisfactory condition.

In October 2012, the applicant was readmitted to the same clinic with complaints of increased urinary frequency—up to once every hour—and blood in his urine. Medical tests revealed a urethral stricture, described as a traumatic narrowing of the urethra, and chronic cystitis. On discharge, doctors noted that despite treatment his urinary frequency had not significantly improved.

On 6 June 2013, following a complaint by the applicant against M.P., the police instituted criminal proceedings into medical malpractice. During the investigation, police obtained the applicant’s medical records and questioned both the applicant and M.P. Three forensic examinations were performed. The final forensic report, completed in December 2015, concluded that the applicant’s injuries—including urethral stricture, cystitis, and chronic urinary retention, classified as medium-severity injuries—had resulted from an improperly performed catheterisation.

Within the criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged a civil claim, first against the clinic and then against M.P. He argued that M.P.’s medical intervention had caused him severe pain and suffering. He sought more than UAH 3 million, equivalent to more than EUR 100,000 at the relevant time, in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

On 28 September 2016, M.P. was formally notified of suspicion of medical negligence under Article 140 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 5 December 2016, the criminal case against him and the applicant’s civil claim were referred to the Leninskyi District Court of Dnipro for trial.

During the trial, the court heard the applicant and four witnesses. Both the applicant and M.P. submitted new forensic evidence. M.P. relied on a report stating that his actions had corresponded to medical practice standards and that the applicant’s complications might have been caused by reasons unrelated to the catheterisation. The applicant submitted a report indicating otherwise.

As of October 2025, the trial against M.P. remained pending at first instance, with no decision taken either on the criminal charges or on the applicant’s civil claim. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the serious medical harm allegedly caused by the catheterisation, the forensic finding that it resulted from improper performance, and the prolonged failure of the domestic criminal and civil proceedings to reach any final determination for over a decade. The applicant’s complaint before the Court is that these domestic proceedings were ineffective, depriving him of timely adjudication and an adequate remedy for the alleged medical malpractice.
001-248198:
In **Nikitin v. Estonia** (Application no. 49257/22), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Vladimir Nikitin, an Estonian national born in 1968 and a life prisoner in Viru Prison. He complained under Article 8 of the Convention that prison authorities violated his right to respect for private and family life by refusing to allow him short-term meetings without a glass partition. The alleged violation concerned eight short-term meetings with his wife and her son between 2 June 2018 and 19 December 2019. During those meetings, the applicant was separated from his visitors by a glass partition and could communicate only through an intercom system.

In November 2020, the applicant applied to the Viru Prison authorities for compensation for those meetings. The prison authorities dismissed the application. They stated that the applicant had never asked for meetings to be held without the glass partition, which would have been a more appropriate remedy and was required under the State Liability Act. They also referred to general security considerations for short-term meetings, without linking them to the applicant’s personal situation, and to alternative means of communication. The authorities noted that section 31(21) of the Internal Prison Rules gave prison authorities discretion to allow meetings without a glass partition in certain situations, but they did not indicate that the applicant’s circumstances fell within any of the listed categories. In later submissions before the Tartu Administrative Court and the Tartu Court of Appeal, the prison authorities confirmed that the applicant’s situation did not fit any of the exceptions under section 31(21).

On 31 May 2021, the Tartu Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the prison authorities’ decision. The court referred to alternative means available for maintaining contact and found that the interference with the applicant’s rights had not been sufficiently severe to warrant compensation. It also considered that the requirement in section 31(2) of the Internal Prison Rules that a glass partition be used during short-term meetings was proportionate to the need to ensure prison security, and it noted that section 31(21) provided exceptions. The applicant appealed.

On 28 February 2022, the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment. It considered that alternative means of contact existed and that the applicant had been passive in addressing the issue. The interference was therefore not particularly severe. The court noted that the applicant had never complained about the visit arrangements and had never requested visits in a room without a glass partition. He had thus failed to use a primary remedy—an application to oblige the administrative body to adopt a decision or take measures (*kohustamiskaebus*)—which was a prerequisite for a compensation claim. The court admitted, however, that this remedy might not have been effective in preventing interference with respect to each meeting request. It also stated that it did not consider the use of the glass partition unlawful, referring, among other things, to the applicant’s general dangerousness. Even assuming the use of the partition had been unlawful, the court said monetary compensation would not have been warranted.

On 7 June 2022, the Supreme Court refused to examine the applicant’s appeal on points of law. Before the European Court of Human Rights, the complaint concerning the use of a glass partition during short-term meetings was communicated to the Government, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 on account of the refusal to allow him short-term meetings without a glass partition.
001-156080:
The factual record concerns an application brought by Mr György Gazsó, a Hungarian national born in 1963 who lives in Telki, against Hungary. The applicant, represented by Mr D. Karsai, a Budapest lawyer, lodged application no. 48322/12 under Article 34 of the Convention on 24 July 2012. The Hungarian Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi, Agent at the Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged that litigation in his labour dispute had lasted an unreasonably long time and that there was no effective remedy available to him in that regard. He relied on Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention. On 13 November 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. At the same time, the Court proposed the pilot judgment procedure under Rule 61 of the Rules of Court to the parties, and the parties submitted comments in that respect.

The domestic facts concern a labour dispute between the applicant and his former employer. Between 25 February 2002 and 18 May 2005, litigation was in progress between the applicant and his former employer. That litigation eventually obliged the former employer to re-employ the applicant. The applicant did not accept the position that was offered to him in pursuit of the re-employment order. New litigation therefore started on 5 January 2006.

On 18 November 2008, the Budapest Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s action. On appeal, on 9 July 2010, the Budapest Regional Court reversed that decision and found for the applicant. The respondent then pursued a petition for review before the Kúria. On 29 February 2012, the Kúria reversed the appeal judgment and found for the respondent. These are the domestic decisions and dates identified in the supplied record.

The applicant’s factual allegations are framed around the overall duration of the labour dispute, including the earlier litigation period from 25 February 2002 to 18 May 2005 and the new litigation beginning on 5 January 2006, which continued through the domestic decisions up to 29 February 2012. The alleged lack of an effective remedy relates to that same labour dispute. The record does not set out further details of the domestic proceedings, such as the specific delays attributable to each stage, the reasons for the duration, the exact claims and defences in the labour dispute beyond the re-employment issue, or the content of the parties’ submissions beyond the fact that they commented on the proposed pilot judgment procedure. The application number, lodging date, representation details, communication date, and the domestic decisions listed above are the principal factual elements stated in the record relevant to the alleged violations.
001-157761:
In *Miclea v. Romania* (Application no. 69582/12), the applicant, Alexandru Miclea, complained under Articles 3 and 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights that he had been ill-treated by two police officers at the Arad police station on 8 August 2010 and that the subsequent investigation and proceedings were ineffective and unfair.

According to the applicant, at around 4 a.m. on 8 August 2010 he and friends were involved in a fight outside a bar. Police arrived, the aggressors fled, and the applicant and his friends were taken to the police station to give statements. While waiting, the applicant saw officer D.C.I. behaving roughly with an arrestee and commented that police, as State authority, should not hit people. D.C.I. allegedly became angry and asked another officer, M.C., to “take him to the toilets to teach him how to speak.” When the applicant resisted, the two officers allegedly took him outside and then into a back office, handcuffed him to a radiator, and punched and kicked him. Another officer intervened after hearing screaming. One of the alleged assailants warned the applicant not to report the incident or he would be beaten again. The applicant and his friends were then escorted home.
