The Government disputed this account. It stated that police had been called to stop a street fight and that the applicant and his friends already had torn clothes and injuries when police arrived. They were taken to the station for statements. Witnesses S.L. and D.V. gave statements and initially did not wish to lodge complaints. The applicant and his friends were later escorted home. An investigation was opened but closed on 23 August 2010 after a bar attendant and a shop worker said they had seen or heard nothing.

Medical evidence was central. Later on 8 August, the applicant was diagnosed with maxillofacial trauma and contusions of the lower lip and thorax. A forensic certificate of 9 August documented a sutured cut on the lower lip, bruising on the upper lip and left chest, excoriations on the left back, grazes and bruising on the right elbow, right leg and left knee, and wrist excoriations. The injuries were consistent with impact with or on a hard object on 8 August and required about nine days of medical treatment.

On 15 September 2010 the applicant complained against the two officers for abusive conduct and bodily harm, requesting that S.L., S.N. and K.E. be heard. He was heard on 23 September. The case was transferred because the officers were not military. In February 2011, S.L. and S.N. gave statements saying they had heard the applicant screaming outside the station and later saw his injuries; the applicant told them police had beaten him. Later typed statements added further details.

In March 2011 the prosecutor joined the case with other complaints against the same officers. The prosecutor declined to pursue “abusive investigative conduct” because the applicant had not been under investigation. Police internal affairs took statements from the accused officers, who denied assault, and from three other officers who suggested the injuries came from the street fight. On 12 January 2012 the prosecutor decided not to pursue the charges, finding the applicant’s account contradicted by the officers and not established with certainty. The applicant’s challenge, which again requested witness K.A., was dismissed on 7 February 2012. On 18 April 2012 the Arad District Court finally rejected his complaint and damages claim as manifestly ill-founded. It found it not proven beyond reasonable doubt that the officers had abused him, noting discrepancies—whether he was beaten inside or outside, and whether he was handcuffed behind his back or to a radiator—and that his injuries could have come from the street brawl.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Article 3 substantive and procedural violations, and the Article 6 fair-trial complaint concerning reliance on police statements and failure to hear key witnesses.
001-155102:
**PSMA, spol. s r.o. v. Slovakia** (Application no. 42533/11, judgment 9 June 2015) concerned a Slovak company’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged that a final and binding judgment in its favour had been quashed after the Prosecutor General lodged an extraordinary appeal on points of law, following a petition by the opposing party. The central issue was whether this extraordinary review breached the applicant’s right to a fair trial, particularly the principles of legal certainty and finality of judicial decisions.

In 1995 the applicant company contracted with Slovak Radio, the national public-service broadcaster, to act as exclusive agent for selling advertising broadcasting time. The contract was amended several times and was valid until 31 December 2007. In 2004 the relationship deteriorated over the amount of business generated in 2003. Slovak Radio billed the applicant for the difference between estimated and actual profit. When the applicant did not pay, Slovak Radio terminated the contract for fundamental breach. The notice period expired on 30 September 2005.

In 2006 the applicant sued Slovak Radio for indemnity of approximately €693,000, calculated as average yearly commission over five years and including barter transactions. On 14 May 2007 the Bratislava I District Court granted the claim in full. It proceeded under Article 101 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure because Slovak Radio, despite being represented, filed no observations and failed to attend hearings without valid excuse. The court found the termination valid because it had not been contested and held that barter transactions were properly included in the indemnity calculation.

Slovak Radio appealed. It acknowledged the legal basis for some indemnity but disputed the barter component. On 28 November 2007 the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. It found Slovak Radio’s procedural passivity unjustified and held that the barter-related compensation claim was distinct from the indemnity claim. The judgment became final on 9 January 2008 and enforceable on 12 January 2008.

Slovak Radio then filed a constitutional complaint, which was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 for failure to exhaust an ordinary appeal on points of law. It also petitioned the Prosecutor General. On 23 October 2008 the Prosecutor General lodged an extraordinary appeal against both judgments. He argued that the lower courts had erred by treating the termination as valid merely because it was uncontested, and that they should have examined the validity of the contract and the notice independently. He also challenged the inclusion of barter transactions. The Supreme Court suspended enforceability on 8 December 2008.

The applicant argued that the extraordinary appeal was inadmissible because Slovak Radio could have used an ordinary appeal on points of law; that the Prosecutor General exceeded the petition’s scope; and that the principal had relied on, rather than challenged, the termination notice. It also complained that the Supreme Court ignored its observations and denied access to the case file. On 12 August 2009 the Supreme Court allowed the extraordinary appeal, quashed both lower judgments, and remitted the case for fresh examination, finding failures to examine the contract’s and notice’s validity.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded on 25 November 2010. Before the European Court, the applicant maintained that the quashing of a final judgment in its favour through an extraordinary appeal initiated at the losing party’s request violated Article 6 § 1, undermining legal certainty and res judicata.
001-155374:
**Kovárová v. Slovakia (Application no. 46564/10)**

The applicant, Eva Kovárová, a Slovak national born in 1947 and living in Bratislava, lodged an action on 9 May 2007 with the Bratislava V District Court. She sought a ruling that a meeting of flat owners in her block of flats held on 24 April 2007 was contrary to law and that the decisions adopted at that meeting were void. The defendant was a community of owners of residential and non-residential premises in the building, an entity with legal personality registered with the local District Authority.

On 2 January 2008, a lawyer acting for the defendant informed the District Court that the defendant had ceased legally to exist on 14 December 2007, having been struck out of the relevant register because administration of the building had been transferred to a specialised agency. On 24 January 2008, the applicant requested that the hearing scheduled for 28 January 2008 be postponed sine die, stating that she had just learned of the striking out and needed time to analyse the situation. The hearing was adjourned.

On 3 March 2008, the District Court discontinued the proceedings on the grounds that the defendant had ceased to exist and had no legal successor. It held that neither the individual flat owners nor the newly contracted administration agency could be considered as having succeeded to the defendant's position.

On 20 March 2008, the applicant appealed, arguing first that the administration agency was the successor and proceedings should have continued against it, and second that the court should have stayed the proceedings pending the outcome of separate proceedings challenging a decision taken at another meeting of flat owners on 11 September 2007 to wind up the defendant. If those proceedings ended with a ruling declaring the winding up void, the striking out would lose basis and proceedings could continue.

On 30 May 2008, the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the first-instance decision, noting that the defendant had lost capacity to be a party and that there was no alternative to discontinuance. No reasons were offered for the latter conclusion. On 7 July 2008, the applicant appealed on points of law under Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure, arguing that the Regional Court had provided neither factual nor legal grounds for its conclusion, rendering it unreviewable. On 7 May 2009, the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible, holding that the alleged shortcomings did not fall within Article 237(f) and that staying proceedings was an option, not a duty. It did not examine the merits.

On 17 August 2009, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against all three levels of the ordinary courts, arguing that the discontinuance was unlawful, that the courts had wrongly failed to examine the merits of her claim, and that this breached her rights of access to court and to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 16 December 2009, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. Regarding the Regional Court, it found the complaint out of time. Regarding the Supreme Court, it found that relevant reasons had been given and the decision was not arbitrary. It noted that if the separate proceedings declared the winding up void, the applicant could seek reopening, though the defendant would not automatically come back into existence without an incorporation decision by the District Authority.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 concerning access to court and a fair hearing.
001-156263:
**Summary of K.F. v. Cyprus**

The applicant, K.F., was a Syrian national of Kurdish origin. He entered Cyprus illegally in February 2005 and applied for asylum. He claimed that after participating in the 2004 Qamishli Kurdish demonstrations, he was arrested, detained for fourteen days and ill-treated, then held for two and a half months in Damascus prison. After bribing officials, he was released but later learned that an arrest warrant had been issued against him. He also claimed that the family of a woman with whom he had eloped had killed her and was seeking him, prompting his flight from Syria.

In August 2008, the Asylum Service rejected his application. It found contradictions between his written application and his interview: he had initially said he came to Cyprus “for living,” but later claimed persecution. The Reviewing Authority dismissed his appeal in June 2009, again finding his account inconsistent and not credible. It also doubted an Arabic document he submitted, which allegedly ordered his arrest, because he had not produced the original and because the translation predated his claimed receipt. In January 2012, the Supreme Court dismissed his recourse, upholding the credibility findings and concluding that he had left Syria for personal reasons and had not shown a risk of persecution if returned.

In August 2009, deportation and detention orders were issued against him; he was detained but released in December 2009 after those orders were revoked. In May 2010, he joined a Kurdish protest encampment in Nicosia against the asylum authorities’ policies. On 11 June 2010, police carried out a mass early-morning operation involving about 250 officers. A total of 149 protesters were transferred to police headquarters; 22 were deported the same day. The applicant was among 44 people arrested. Authorities treated them as unlawful residents or “prohibited immigrants.” Some already had deportation orders, while the applicant was charged with unlawful stay. Deportation and detention orders were also issued against 53 detainees, including the applicant, under the Aliens and Immigration Law.

The applicant alleged that he was not informed of the reasons for his arrest and detention. The Government claimed he was informed orally and later served with written notice on 18 June 2010, but refused it; the applicant denied refusing service and said he only learned of the orders from his lawyer after Rule 39 proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights. On 12 June 2010, he and others sought an interim measure; on 14 June 2010, the Court indicated that Cyprus should not deport him to Syria. The measure was maintained in September 2010 for five cases, including his, and lifted in June 2012 after he left Cyprus for Northern Iraq.

He remained detained at Larnaca Police Station. In March 2011, he escaped, was injured, hospitalised, and returned to custody. He was released on 20 April 2011 after the deportation and detention orders were revoked. He filed habeas corpus proceedings in January 2011, arguing that his detention violated EU and Convention standards. The Supreme Court dismissed the application in March 2011, and his appeal was later dismissed as moot because he had been released.

Before the European Court, K.F. complained that deportation to Syria would breach Article 3; that there was no effective remedy under Article 13; that his detention violated Article 5 §§ 1(f), 2 and 4; and that deportation would breach Article 4 of Protocol No. 4, concerning collective expulsion. The key facts relevant to these alleged violations were the rejection of his asylum claim on credibility grounds, the mass arrest and removal operation against Kurdish protesters, the boilerplate deportation and detention orders, the alleged failure to inform him of the reasons for detention, the prolonged immigration detention, and the intended deportation to Syria.
001-154354:
In *Santos Silva v. Portugal* (Application no. 52246/12), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application lodged on 31 July 2012 by José António Oliveira Santos Silva, a Portuguese national, against Portugal. The applicant complained principally about the length of civil proceedings, invoking Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The application was communicated to the Portuguese Government on 4 March 2014. The applicant was represented by a lawyer, and the Government by its Agent.

The domestic proceedings began on 19 December 2005, when the applicant brought an action in the Santa Maria da Feira Court against several defendants concerning a right to use a water channel. He rectified the initial application on 3 January 2006. Procedural complications arose early because some defendants had died. On 15 February 2006, defendant J. informed the court that defendant A.J. had died in 1973 and that his heirs lived in Brazil. On 19 February 2006, defendant I. filed a defence and stated that her husband, defendant A., had died in May 2005.

On 5 May 2006, the Santa Maria da Feira Court stayed the proceedings pending inheritance proceedings concerning the deceased defendants and set a deadline for the applicant to submit death certificates. On 27 November 2006, the applicant applied for leave to continue the proceedings against the heirs through an *incidente de habilitação de herdeiros*. After being notified by the court, he submitted the relevant documents on 9 January 2007. On 2 July 2007, the court admitted the heirs as parties. The main proceedings were later resumed, but the exact date is not specified.

Further delays followed. On 23 April 2008, the applicant was notified that the court had failed to summon defendant A.G. On 27 January 2010, the Santa Maria da Feira Court interrupted the proceedings because of lack of action by the parties. On 26 January 2011, the applicant informed the court of the new address of defendant A.’s heir. The proceedings were subsequently resumed, again on an unspecified date.

On 24 November 2011, the Santa Maria da Feira Court dismissed the applicant’s claim as time-barred. The applicant appealed on 6 December 2011 to the Porto Court of Appeal. On 4 June 2013, the Porto Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance decision and ordered a new trial. The case was still pending at first instance at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are the overall duration and the procedural delays. More than seven years elapsed between the filing of the action in December 2005 and the appeal decision in June 2013, and the case remained unresolved at first instance thereafter. Factors included the need to identify and join heirs of deceased defendants, one of whom had died decades earlier and whose heirs were in Brazil; the stay pending inheritance proceedings; the court’s failure to summon at least one defendant; periods of interruption or inactivity; and the eventual time-bar dismissal, later overturned on appeal. The applicant took various steps, including rectifying the claim, requesting habilitation of heirs, filing documents, and providing updated addresses. The domestic courts’ handling of these matters formed the factual basis for the complaint that the proceedings exceeded a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1.
001-158279:
The applicant, Markus Veikko Pentikäinen, born in 1980 and living in Helsinki, is a photographer and journalist employed by the weekly magazine *Suomen Kuvalehti*. On 9 September 2006 he was sent by his employer to photograph the “Smash ASEM” demonstration in Helsinki, held in protest against the Asia-Europe Meeting. He was to report for the magazine’s print edition and publish online once the demonstration ended.

Before the event, Finnish Security Intelligence assessed the demonstration as hostile and without a clear political message. The police had difficulty contacting the organisers. Two earlier Helsinki demonstrations that year had turned violent. The announced march was to run from the Kiasma Museum to near the ASEM summit venue. Posters invited participants to wear black and referred to bringing “mayhem” to Helsinki’s streets.

The demonstration began at 6 p.m. About 500 bystanders, a core group of demonstrators, and some 50 journalists gathered. Violence soon broke out: bottles, stones, and paint-filled jars were thrown at police and the public. Police cordoned the area, announced that a peaceful demonstration was allowed but not a march, and later declared the event a riot. From 6.30 p.m. to 7.17 p.m. they sealed off the area. Police allowed families and media representatives to pass through, though projectiles were thrown at times. They repeatedly ordered the crowd to disperse. The applicant claimed he first heard the order around 8.30 p.m. and understood it as applying only to demonstrators. He called his employer and decided to stay. Around 9 p.m. a police officer told him personally he had one last chance to leave. The applicant said he was reporting for *Suomen Kuvalehti* and would follow the event to the end; the officer left him alone.

Later, police broke up remaining demonstrators and apprehended protesters. The applicant claimed he heard an officer shout, “Get the photographer!” He was taking photographs when apprehended. He told the officer he was a journalist and presented his press card; the officer later confirmed this. The applicant did not resist. The stated basis for apprehension was contumacy towards police. He was taken to a detention bus and then a police station, where he said he again identified himself as a journalist and wore his press card visibly. He claimed his camera equipment and memory cards were confiscated. The Government maintained that once police learned he was press, his equipment was treated as journalistic material and not confiscated; he retained the photographs. A Deputy Parliamentary Ombudsman report noted that police checked detainees’ mobile phones, though it was unclear whether the applicant’s phone or memory cards were inspected.

The applicant was detained from 9 September at 9.26 p.m. until 10 September at 3.05 p.m., about seventeen and a half hours. He was interrogated on 10 September between 1.32 p.m. and 1.57 p.m. Police apprehended 128 people in total; most were released on 11 September. The applicant was the seventh detainee interrogated and the sixth released after minors.

On 23 May 2007 the public prosecutor charged the applicant with contumacy towards the police under Chapter 16, section 4(1), of the Penal Code. On 17 December 2007 Helsinki District Court found him guilty but waived punishment under Chapter 6, section 12(3), treating the offence as comparable to an excusable act because of conflicting expectations from police and his profession. The court found police orders lawful, clear, and applicable to everyone, and concluded that restricting his freedom of expression was justified. The applicant appealed, arguing his apprehension and conviction violated the Constitution and Article 10. On 30 April 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal without further reasons. On 1 September 2009 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that his Article 10 rights were violated because police ordered him to leave, he could not transmit information during his detention, and he was suspected, charged, and convicted, creating a chilling effect on his work.
001-157967:
The applicant, Andrey Lunev, a Ukrainian national, lodged an application against Ukraine on 17 January 2013. He alleged inadequate medical assistance in detention, ill-treatment intended to discourage him from applying to the European Court, and failure to investigate that ill-treatment.

**Medical assistance.** In January 2012 he was arrested for suspected drug trafficking and on 30 January placed in Starobilsk SIZO. On arrival he was diagnosed with HIV stage 3, chronic bronchitis, toxic encephalopathy/neuropathy from drug use, and tuberculosis residual changes. The Government said he refused a CD4+ count and a blood test in February 2012 and sought no medical help until 8 January 2013, although records show a September 2012 tuberculosis examination and X-ray and November 2012 bronchitis and kidney pain in another facility. On 8 January 2013 he was diagnosed with chronic bronchitis and treated. On 9 January he was found unconscious. The SIZO head asked a court to expedite proceedings or release him for urgent treatment. On 10 January the court kept him in detention but ordered placement in a specialised prison or civilian hospital. He was hospitalised from 9 to 11 January with acute serose meningoencephalitis and was soporose; on 11 January he returned to the SIZO medical unit until 15 February and was also held at least once in Alchevsk ITT. On 17 January he requested hospital placement, citing need for psychiatric examination for ART, correct tuberculosis staging, epilepsy treatment and adequate care. At the end of January his lawyer received a call from an unknown man posing as a prosecutor’s employee, asking whether she represented the applicant and whether he had applied to the European Court; she confirmed. On 4 February the medical unit reported HIV since 2010, chronic bronchitis and toxic encephalopathy; his CD4+ count had been 374 in October 2010 and he had refused treatment. On 19 February a domestic court sentenced him to six and a half years for drug trafficking. On 26 February his CD4+ count was 119. On 7 March the Government said hospitalisation was unnecessary. On 12 March ART was recommended; on 14 March admission to Lugansk Temporary Detention Centre No. 17 Hospital was approved. He was hospitalised from 20 to 25 March and later from 29 March to 5 April and 12 April to 12 May; ART was prescribed on 16 April. On 24 May the Lugansk Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction and remitted the case. On 19 June the Bryankovskyy Town Court released him under house arrest, noting he needed treatment unavailable in detention.

**Ill-treatment and investigation.** On 25 January 2013 he was placed in Alchevsk ITT. On 30 January, after acute liver pain, an ambulance was called and he was taken to hospital, returning about 4 p.m. He alleged that at about 5.25 p.m. two policemen from the regional police office beat him and told him to write that the SIZO provided adequate treatment; one hit his liver six or seven times, the other his kidneys four times, after which he wrote the statement. On 31 January his lawyer complained in court; he was diagnosed with possible blunt abdominal trauma, but a surgeon found no acute surgical pathology. He and his lawyer complained to the prosecutor, alleging pressure to withdraw his medical complaint and confess. On 14 February a forensic expert found no injuries. On 25 February the Alchevsk Town Prosecutor terminated proceedings for lack of evidence. On 26 March the Alchevskyy Town Court quashed that decision, finding the investigation not thorough and cellmates not questioned. On 24 April an ambulance station reported the blunt abdominal trauma diagnosis and beating complaint. On 25 April proceedings were again terminated. Cellmate K. said the applicant was absent 40–60 minutes and returned claiming two unknown policemen beat him to force him to refuse treatment, with a red cheek and swollen liver. Officer So. denied involvement; surveillance was not working from 26 January to 4 February. On 3 June the prosecutor quashed the 25 April decision as premature and unsubstantiated. On 27 June proceedings were terminated again. On 4 November the Alchevskyy Town Court quashed that decision, finding the lawyer’s complaint inadequately investigated and no explanation why a confrontation with officer So. was impossible.
001-156248:
**Andonovski v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia** (App. no. 24312/10) concerned a Macedonian surgeon who alleged police ill-treatment on 17 September 2004 and an ineffective investigation into his allegations, contrary to Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1948 and in poor cardiac health, parked in Kumanovo and received a parking ticket. He followed a police car to discuss it. The parties gave conflicting accounts. The applicant claimed he flashed his lights; the police claimed he sounded his horn, shouted, kicked the car and spat at them. The applicant alleged that when he approached, officers P.J. and M.A. insulted him. P.J., a neighbour with whom he had bad relations, opened the car door hard, striking his legs. Both officers then grabbed him by the shoulders and neck and punched him. P.J. kicked and punched him all over, kneed him in the back causing fractures to two spinal vertebrae, and M.A. kicked his lower back. He was handcuffed and taken to Kumanovo police station, where he said the beating continued until he lost consciousness. An ambulance was called about an hour later. He was hospitalised from 17 to 28 September 2004.

Medical evidence was central. Kumanovo Hospital recorded head contusion, concussion, chest and back bruises, and arm bruises. Skopje City Hospital noted a compressive fracture of two vertebrae, concussion, head trauma, and contusions. Dr Z.T. later certified serious bodily injury with permanent consequences. A Forensic Institute report concluded that multiple blunt impacts caused concussion, vertebral fracture and widespread bruising, amounting to serious bodily injury with a considerable but not permanent negative effect. The applicant’s heart condition was also noted.

The police officers’ own reports admitted some force: twisting his arms, kicking his leg, and P.J. punching his head after the applicant allegedly bit M.A. The Ministry’s internal control department concluded that the applicant had insulted and resisted the officers and bitten M.A., and that the force used—twisting arms and handcuffing—was necessary and justified.

In parallel criminal proceedings, the applicant was convicted of assaulting police officers and sentenced to five months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years. The domestic courts relied mainly on the officers’ and some witnesses’ accounts and largely disregarded the medical evidence of the applicant’s serious injuries. The conviction was upheld on appeal. Witnesses S.H. and V.V. gave mixed accounts: they did not see the alleged bite and described the applicant as shouting and resisting, but generally did not confirm serious police violence.

The applicant filed criminal complaints against P.J. and M.A. for assault, serious bodily harm, abuse of office, false testimony and degrading treatment. The prosecutor initially rejected the complaint, relying on witness statements and the internal police report. The applicant then pursued a subsidiary prosecution. An investigating judge opened an investigation for serious bodily injury, supported by the 2006 Forensic Institute report. However, the public prosecutor repeatedly refused to take over the prosecution. In 2009, the trial court stayed the proceedings after the applicant reportedly withdrew his subsidiary indictment; he objected, saying he had not understood the judge and had wanted the public prosecutor to prosecute ex officio.

These facts formed the basis of his complaints that he had been subjected to police brutality and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into it.
001-155824:
**Summary of A.K. v. Liechtenstein (Application no. 38191/12)**

The case originated in an application against Liechtenstein lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by A.K., a German national, on 14 May 2012. The applicant alleged in particular that the five judges of Liechtenstein’s Constitutional Court had been partial, notably because of the procedure they used to reject his motions for bias, in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. The Court communicated only that impartiality complaint to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying facts concerned a long-running dispute between the applicant and F.H. over property rights in 75% of the bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. In December 2009, the Regional Court granted an interim injunction preventing the Real Property and Commercial Registry from registering certain changes decided at an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting of 23 July 2004. Those changes included F.H.’s removal as a representative and supervisory board member and the applicant’s election as managing director. The injunction confirmed an earlier provisional order.

After the Court of Appeal quashed the first injunction in March 2010 and remitted the case, the Regional Court issued a fresh identical injunction on 30 July 2010. It found that the applicant had not acquired 75% of the bearer shares and had therefore not validly represented that shareholding at the shareholders’ meeting. It held that interim injunctions could secure declaration claims and preserve the status quo, and that such measures were necessary to prevent irreversible damage to F.H. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 23 September 2010.

On 22 October 2010 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against the Court of Appeal’s decision. On 7 November 2011 the Constitutional Court informed him that judges B., Bu., S., V. and W. would deliberate on his complaint in private on 28 November 2011. Shortly before that date, the applicant—then unrepresented—filed motions for bias against all five judges and against the secretary, V.

His bias allegations were extensive. He claimed the Constitutional Court had previously failed to quash decisions of lower courts in related proceedings, had taken over a year to assign judges, and discriminated against German nationals. More specifically, he alleged that judge B. had refused suspensory effect and interim measures in related proceedings and belonged to committees whose members included Supreme Court judges and judge H., F.H.’s brother. Judge Bu. allegedly worked for the Government by preparing expert reports and teaching government seminars and worked regularly with judge H. Judge S. was said to be a member of the supervisory board of a state-owned company. Judge V. had been a professor at Liechtenstein University, had worked for the Government, and was a close friend of judge H. Judge W. was allegedly a partner of a lawyer against whom the applicant had brought inheritance proceedings; another lawyer in his firm had represented EMK Engineering, and W. had previously worked in judge H.’s law firm.

On 28 November 2011 the Constitutional Court dismissed the bias motions. It stated that each challenged judge had not participated in the decision on his own motion, with the four remaining judges deciding. It reasoned that prior adverse decisions, five-year judicial terms, previous government work, and regular contact or friendship with F.H.’s brother did not objectively cast doubt on impartiality. It added that, in a small country such as Liechtenstein, excessively strict standards would disproportionately obstruct justice. The same day, the Constitutional Court allowed the applicant’s complaint only as regards the length of proceedings and dismissed the remainder.

The key alleged violation before the European Court was therefore that the Constitutional Court lacked impartiality under Article 6, especially because the challenged judges themselves effectively took part in the process by which the bias motions against them were rejected.
001-159732:
In **G.S.B. v. Switzerland** (ECtHR, Third Section, 22 December 2015, app. no. 28601/11), the applicant, a Saudi Arabian and American binational living in Miami, complained that Switzerland’s transmission of his banking data to US tax authorities under a Swiss–US mutual assistance arrangement violated Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. The Court communicated those complaints; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The case arose from the UBS tax affair. In 2008, the IRS discovered that thousands of US taxpayers held undeclared UBS accounts or economic rights in such accounts. UBS faced criminal prosecution. In February 2009, UBS entered a deferred prosecution agreement and paid USD 780 million. The IRS then issued a “John Doe summons” seeking identities and account data for some 52,000 US customers. To avoid a Swiss–US legal conflict, Switzerland and the United States concluded Agreement 09 on 19 August 2009. Under it, Switzerland agreed to process the IRS mutual assistance request concerning UBS’s American customers under the 1996 Swiss–US double taxation convention (CDI-US 96), covering approximately 4,450 open or closed accounts. The IRS requested data on US taxpayers who, between 2001 and 2008, had authority to sign or other access rights to UBS accounts in Switzerland. The Swiss Federal Tax Administration (AFC) ordered UBS to provide complete customer files.

UBS transmitted the applicant’s file to the AFC on 19 January 2010. On 7 June 2010, the AFC granted mutual assistance and ordered the documents to be sent to the IRS. The applicant appealed. On 21 September 2010, the Federal Administrative Court set aside the decision because his right to be heard had been breached, and remitted the case. After receiving the applicant’s observations, the AFC again granted mutual assistance on 4 November 2010. The applicant appealed, alleging that the decisions lacked a legal basis and violated the ECHR and other treaties, including the prohibition of retroactivity, respect for private life, the presumption of innocence, equality and non-discrimination, and the right to remain silent.

On 2 March 2011, the Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It held that Protocol 10, which amended Agreement 09 (“Convention 10”), was binding on Swiss authorities and, as later international law, took precedence over earlier treaties such as the ECHR, absent *jus cogens*. It found that even if Article 8 ECHR applied, the interference was justified under Article 8 § 2: Convention 10 provided a sufficient legal basis, and Switzerland’s interest in honouring its international commitments and avoiding serious diplomatic and financial consequences outweighed the applicant’s interest in keeping his financial affairs secret. It rejected the retroactivity complaint, finding that the parties intended retroactive application and that mutual assistance procedural rules could apply retroactively. As to Article 14, the applicant alleged that Convention 10 discriminated by singling out UBS customers rather than customers of other banks. The court said it could not review Convention 10’s conformity with the Constitution or earlier treaties and applied it despite the different treatment.

The Federal Court declared the applicant’s further appeal inadmissible on 11 April 2011. The applicant’s banking data were transmitted to the US tax authorities on 14 December 2012. As of 2014, he stated that the US tax inspection was ongoing and that he had not been criminally charged. The ECtHR’s examination therefore focused on whether the disclosure and transfer of his banking data, and the UBS-specific scheme, breached Articles 8 and 14.
001-155352:
The case arose from an application to the European Court of Human Rights by Pierre and Viviane Lambert, David Philippon and Anne Tuarze—respectively the parents, half-brother and sister of Vincent Lambert. Vincent, born in 1976, sustained severe head injuries in a road-traffic accident on 29 September 2008, leaving him tetraplegic and completely dependent. Since June 2009 he had been cared for at Reims University Hospital and received artificial enteral nutrition and hydration through a gastric tube. A 2011 assessment by Liège University Hospital described him as being in a chronic neuro-vegetative state, “minimally conscious plus.” Later expert evidence in 2014 found a vegetative state with irreversible brain damage, no functional communication, non-conscious reactions, and a poor prognosis.

After carers noticed apparent resistance to care, Dr Kariger initiated the collective procedure under the French Law of 22 April 2005 on patients’ rights and end-of-life issues (“Leonetti Act”). A first decision in 2013 to withdraw nutrition and reduce hydration was implemented in April 2013 but was suspended by the Châlons-en-Champagne Administrative Court on 11 May 2013. The urgent-applications judge found procedural shortcomings: Vincent’s parents had not been properly informed, their views had not been respected, and the decision amounted to a serious and manifestly unlawful breach of the right to life.

A second procedure began in September 2013. Dr Kariger consulted six doctors and held meetings with the family. The family was divided: Vincent’s wife Rachel and six siblings supported withdrawing artificial nutrition and hydration, while the applicants opposed it. On 11 January 2014 Dr Kariger decided to discontinue artificial nutrition and hydration. He reasoned that Vincent had irreversible brain damage, that treatment was futile, disproportionate and had no effect other than to sustain life artificially, and that continuing it amounted to unreasonable obstinacy. He also considered that Vincent would not have wished to live in such a dependent state.

The applicants challenged the decision. On 16 January 2014 the Administrative Court suspended it. It accepted that artificial nutrition and hydration could constitute treatment under the Leonetti Act, but held that Dr Kariger had incorrectly assessed Vincent’s wishes. There were no advance directives and no designated person of trust. Remarks Vincent had allegedly made to his wife and brother were not a formal expression of wishes. His apparent resistance to care and conflict with his parents did not establish a clear wish to refuse treatment. Referring to the 2011 Liège assessment, the court found Vincent was minimally conscious, so treatment was not merely artificial life support and could not be considered futile or disproportionate. It found a serious and manifestly unlawful breach of the right to life.

On appeal, the Conseil d’État ordered an independent expert medical report and received general observations. The experts concluded that Vincent was in a vegetative state, brain damage was irreversible, he could not communicate functionally, his reactions were non-conscious, and the prognosis was poor. On 24 June 2014 the Conseil d’État set aside the Administrative Court’s judgment and dismissed the claims. It held that the French legal framework was compatible with Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention, because withdrawal required strict safeguards: a finding of unreasonable obstinacy, consultation with doctors, the care team, family or person of trust, consideration of the patient’s wishes, and court review. It found the procedure valid and the statutory conditions met. Dr Kariger could rely on Vincent’s prior informal wishes, and the family’s disagreement did not prevent the decision.

The applicants then applied to the ECtHR on 23 June 2014. They alleged that withdrawing Vincent’s artificial nutrition and hydration would breach France’s positive obligations under Article 2 (right to life), amount to ill-treatment or torture under Article 3, and infringe his physical integrity and private life under Article 8. The Chamber applied Rule 39 and granted priority; the case was later referred to the Grand Chamber. The key factual issue was whether the French framework and the specific decision to withdraw life-sustaining treatment from an incapacitated patient in a vegetative state, without advance directives and with a divided family, respected Convention safeguards.
001-155006:
Yegorov v. Slovakia (Application no. 27112/11) is an ECtHR case brought by a Ukrainian national, Volodymyr Yegorov, alleging violations of Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention. The complaints concerned his bringing before Bratislava I District Court on 16 June 2010, his arrest on 27 July 2011, remand orders of 16 July 2010 and 29 July 2011, and the proceedings on his interlocutory appeal against the 29 July 2011 remand.

The applicant was continuously deprived of liberty in Slovakia from 25 June 2002 to 19 September 2013. He was initially remanded on several charges, including what later became a charge of conceiving, setting up and supporting a criminal and terrorist group. That charge was separated in 2005. He was later convicted of attempting to legalise proceeds of crime and released on 13 July 2010. Immediately upon release, he was taken to the Border and Foreigners Police, ordered administratively expelled, banned from re-entry for five years, and detained at Medveďov pending expulsion.

While at Medveďov, on 16 July 2010 he was seized by police and brought to Bratislava I District Court for questioning in a murder case. After a private session, the District Court remanded him in pre-trial detention on the murder charge. He stated on record that he wished to appeal and would give reasons once he received the written decision. On 19 July he submitted written reasons in Russian (received 21 July); the written remand decision was served on 21 July, and the file was sent to the Regional Court the same day. He sent further reasons on 26 July (received 28 July). On 28 July the Regional Court dismissed his appeal as unfounded, stating he had submitted no reasons. The Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible on 7 December 2010. It found no arbitrariness: the submissions had not been available to the Regional Court, remand appeals must be decided swiftly (within five working days), the applicant had been heard at first instance, and his lawyer had taken no effective steps.

On 27 July 2011, after acquittal on the first murder charge, the applicant was released but immediately re-arrested and served with a 2003 charge concerning a criminal and terrorist group. On 28 July the prosecution sought detention on several charges. On 29 July the Specialised Criminal Court remanded him under Article 71(1)(a) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prevent flight and further offending. It cited his non-national status, unstable residence, foreign travel, other pending charges, and prior conviction. The applicant appealed, arguing that his arrest was unlawful because he was not informed of the reasons, contesting the detention grounds, complaining of over nine years’ deprivation of liberty, and alleging a pattern of arbitrary consecutive remands. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 8 August 2011.

On 19 September 2011 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, relying mainly on Article 5 §§ 1 and 3. He repeated that he had not been informed of the reasons for his arrest, that the courts ignored the unlawfulness argument, and that his detention was arbitrary, particularly because he had faced the charges for eight years and been continuously detained. On 18 October 2011 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. It found the arrest report sufficient, considered the Supreme Court to have dealt with the lawfulness argument implicitly, and held that, although total detention exceeded nine years, the contested decision concerned only detention from 27 July 2011 and had not yet become unconstitutional. The Supreme Court later released him on 22 February 2012, expressing doubts that ten years’ detention might be arbitrary and self-serving, that statutory maxima had been exceeded, and that his detention involved one criminal matter including offences for which he had already been detained from 2002 to 2005. Other Constitutional Court judgments found Article 5 violations concerning speediness and the repeated-remand pattern, but no just satisfaction was awarded.
001-154149:
In *Milić and Nikezić v. Montenegro* (Apps. 54999/10 and 10609/11, judgment 28 April 2015), two Montenegrin nationals detained at the Institution for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions (IECS) alleged that prison guards tortured and ill-treated them on 27 October 2009, and that Montenegro failed to conduct an effective official investigation. They shared a cell with five other detainees. On that date, the first applicant was to be transferred to a disciplinary unit and the cell was to be searched.

The applicants alleged that guards entered the cell, grabbed the first applicant, threw him onto the concrete corridor floor, handcuffed him, and beat him with batons and fists while swearing at him. They further alleged that two rows of guards beat him as he was taken away. The second applicant alleged that when he protested, four guards kicked and beat him with fists and batons; after he was taken into the corridor, eight more guards continued beating him, and the beating resumed after he returned to the cell. The Government disputed this, claiming the applicants resisted and obstructed guards, and that the second applicant attacked a guard without reason.

Medical and witness evidence was mixed but significant. The first applicant initially refused examination by the prison doctor, saying he was healthy and not ill-treated. Later, his mother observed bruises on his face and body, and his lawyer saw a bruise under his eye and a large bruise on his calf, describing him as frightened and mentally broken. The second applicant was examined by a prison doctor after the Deputy Ombudsman intervened; the Ombudsman described the resulting reports as barely legible and inconsistent. An external forensic examination on 4 November 2009 found light injuries: a 10-day-old haematoma 8 x 15 cm on his left thigh and haematomas under both eyes, with an undated report also noting bruises around his eyes. Several detainees said they saw the first applicant beaten; three confirmed the second was beaten by guards in the cell and corridor. Some guards admitted using force, including one who said he hit the first applicant once with a baton.

The Ombudsman visited the applicants, noted visible injuries, and in March 2010 found their rights had been violated, concluding they had not resisted and that force was unjustified. Disciplinary proceedings against three guards followed; they were found responsible and fined 20% of their salaries for abuse of position or exceeding authority, having used disproportionate force. However, criminal complaints were rejected. In February 2010 the State prosecutor found that two guards had used force within official powers to overcome resistance, and in October 2010 rejected the complaint regarding other guards. Attempts at subsidiary prosecution failed: the indictment was treated as a criminal complaint, and the request for an investigation was dismissed in March 2011, upheld on appeal, for lack of reasonable suspicion that torture or ill-treatment occurred, the courts finding the force necessary. The Constitutional Court rejected the applicants’ constitutional appeal on procedural grounds.

The applicants also complained that the video recording omitted the corridor beating, that another camera recording was not obtained, and that there was a conflict of interest because a deputy State prosecutor was the prison governor’s daughter and the Deputy Supreme State Prosecutor was his wife. In civil proceedings, the Supreme Court ultimately awarded them EUR 1,500 each, holding the force unjustified and degrading but not amounting to torture or inhuman treatment. The ECtHR case therefore concerned the alleged substantive violation of Article 3 and the alleged failure to investigate effectively.
001-150653:
In *A.V. v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national, was arrested on the evening of 29 December 2006 on a street in Kyiv and taken to the Shevchenkivskyy District Police Department. According to him, police officers struck him down, handcuffed him, took him to their car, allegedly planted small bags of cocaine on him, and continued to beat him, with threats of sexual abuse, until they reached the police station. At the station, he was asked to empty his pockets in the presence of two attesting witnesses and produced bags containing cocaine.

At 10 p.m. the police ordered his administrative detention under Article 263 of the Administrative Offences Code for violating drug-circulation rules under Article 44. He was interviewed and wrote a confession admitting that he had unlawfully bought cocaine for personal use. He later claimed that the confession was forced and dictated by a police officer. He was placed in a police cell and alleged that he received insufficient food and water, was held in poor sanitary conditions, and was locked for one night in a dirty, stinking toilet. He felt unwell and suffered acute lower back pain.

On 2 January 2007, after a specialist report found 1.18 grams of cocaine, criminal proceedings were instituted against him under Article 309 § 2 of the Criminal Code for illegally purchasing and storing narcotic drugs in large quantities. That day the investigator ordered his arrest and detention as a criminal suspect for up to 72 hours. He was questioned again and gave details about purchasing the drugs. His lawyer, hired by his parents, joined only after the interview had gone on for a considerable time. In the lawyer’s presence, the applicant complained of poor health. The Government said a medical examination diagnosed intercostal neuralgia and considered his health satisfactory.

On 5 January 2007 the prosecutor refused to approve pre-trial detention, and the applicant was released on a written undertaking not to abscond. After release, ambulance teams diagnosed acute pyelonephritis and lumbosacral radiculitis. Further examinations followed, and from 9 to 19 January he received inpatient neurological treatment for spinal osteochondrosis, vertebrogenic lumbodynia, and pain/muscular tonic syndrome. A psychiatrist later noted signs of post-traumatic stress disorder.

On 22 January 2007 the District Court found that the investigator’s 2 January decision to arrest and detain the applicant as a criminal suspect had been unlawful because the grounds for such arrest had existed from 29 December 2006. On 9 February 2007 the prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers over the applicant’s allegations, finding no elements of an offence and relying on police explanations and custody records. A linguistic expert later reported that the 29 December confession had been written by the applicant with another person dictating the text. At trial, the applicant sought to exclude his 29 December and 2 January statements as obtained in breach of his rights, but the court refused.

Throughout trial, the applicant denied the charges, claiming the drugs had been planted and that he had been psychologically pressured and physically ill-treated. The officers and investigators denied the allegations. The attesting witnesses stated that when the applicant produced the bags, he told them they contained cocaine and showed no visible injuries. On 8 July 2008 the District Court convicted him and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment, suspended with two years’ probation, finding no indication of ill-treatment or procedural violations at the time of his initial self-incriminating statements. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 7 November 2008, and the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on 22 May 2009, relying in part on the original self-incriminating statements.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged ill-treatment by police contrary to Article 3, lack of access to a lawyer at the initial stage of investigation under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c), and use of evidence obtained through ill-treatment to secure his conviction under Article 6 § 1.
001-150217:
In *Micu v. Romania* (Application no. 41040/11, ECtHR, 13 January 2015), the applicant was a Romanian border guard officer investigated by the National Anticorruption Department (NAD) for bribe-taking. The case concerned his complaints under Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention arising from events on 9–10 March 2010.

On 8 March 2010 a NAD prosecutor authorised a warrant to appear for the applicant. On 9 March 2010, two police officers enforced it at his workplace at 8:40 a.m. and took him to the NAD offices. The warrant stated only that his presence was required for him to be heard as an accused; it gave no further reasons. He was left waiting until noon, when he was informed of the criminal investigation and accepted a publicly appointed lawyer after initially refusing to appoint his own. He told the prosecutor he had diabetes and needed insulin treatment from his workplace, and asked that his wife be notified if he were placed in custody. The record of his statement indicated he was heard from noon until 9:34 p.m.; the Government later claimed this was a clerical error and that questioning actually ended at 12:34 p.m., after which the prosecutor dealt with co-accused and witnesses. At 7:08 p.m. he was charged with bribe-taking; he refused to make a further statement. At 9:15 p.m. the NAD placed him in police custody for 24 hours on suspicion of accepting money from Turkish nationals to allow them to leave Romania. He alleged that from 8:40 a.m. until formal custody he was effectively deprived of liberty at the NAD, beyond the lawful purpose of a warrant to appear, contrary to Article 5.

He also alleged Article 3 violations. He had suffered from type-two diabetes since 1997 and had been on insulin since 2009, requiring two injections daily. He claimed that while under the authorities’ control he was not allowed food, was denied medical examination or treatment, and at the detention centre his syringe, insulin and glucose meter were confiscated. He said he had not eaten all day and was not given food suitable for his condition or utensils, causing physical and psychological suffering. The Government disputed this: it stated that once he informed the prosecutor, his treatment kit was retrieved from his workplace within 30 minutes and he used it without restriction, and that a police officer bought him food. However, on 9 March at 10:30 p.m. the detention nurse recorded that his condition was relatively good but that he required insulin morning and evening and had high blood sugar. A doctor on 10 March confirmed the insulin regimen.

Domestically, the Court of Cassation refused pretrial detention on 10 March 2010, finding the evidence inconsistent and no grounds other than offence seriousness; this was upheld on 8 April 2010. The applicant was convicted in 2011 but acquitted on appeal in 2013. He filed criminal complaints against prosecutors G.B. and L.P. for abuse of office, unlawful arrest, improper investigation and torture. These were dismissed as non-existent offences, with courts saying his complaints concerned investigative acts and should be raised within the pending criminal proceedings, not through separate criminal complaints. He therefore alleged Article 13 because no effective domestic remedy existed for his Article 3 and 5 complaints.
001-155819:
**Summary of M.N. and Others v. San Marino (Application no. 28005/12)**

The case originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by four Italian nationals against San Marino. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention, claiming they were denied access to a court to challenge a decision that affected their private life and correspondence.

The factual background stems from criminal proceedings instituted in Italy in or before 2009 against individuals suspected of conspiracy, money laundering, and other financial crimes. The investigation centered on a network of companies linked to San Marino Investimenti S.A. (S.M.I.), which was suspected of facilitating money laundering for Italian clients through fiduciary operations. As part of this investigation, Italian authorities issued a letter rogatory to San Marino in May 2009, seeking assistance to obtain documentation and conduct searches in San Marino banks and trust companies.

On 27 November 2009, the San Marino first-instance tribunal (Commissario della Legge) accepted the request, ordering a broad investigation into all banks and fiduciary institutes. The purpose was to acquire banking documents, emails, and other records related to S.M.I. and any accounts traceable to it, including those of third parties. Critically, the order warned that documentation could not be used for purposes other than the specified criminal proceedings.

Subsequently, the Commissario ordered that Italian citizens who had entered fiduciary agreements with S.M.I. (1,452 individuals, including the applicants) be notified of the decision. The applicants were served with these notifications between January and June 2011. Although not charged with any crimes, their documents were seized as part of the investigation.

The applicants challenged the seizure decision before the judge of criminal appeals (Giudice delle Appellazioni Penali), arguing they were not persons charged and that the seizure violated principles of the San Marino Declaration on Citizens’ Rights. They contended there was no link between the crimes and their positions. However, the judge declared their complaints inadmissible, ruling they lacked juridical interest because they were not direct victims of the seizure. The court held that only persons involved in the investigation or subjected to coercive measures could challenge an exequatur decision, and any grievances should be raised in Italian jurisdictions.

The applicants appealed to the third-instance criminal judge, reiterating their complaints under the Convention. They argued that the seizure was irrelevant to the crimes and only aimed to identify Italians dealing with S.M.I., and that they were not allowed to present submissions. The third-instance judge confirmed the appeal decision on similar grounds, finding no juridical interest and rejecting constitutional complaints.

The applicants also filed objections with the Commissario to revoke the seizure, but these were discontinued, with the Commissario noting that third parties could be subject to such measures. A further objection to restrict the use of seized documents was rejected, as the original decision already limited their use.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicants, as third parties not charged with any crimes, had their documents seized through an exequatur decision. Their attempts to challenge the seizure in San Marino courts were consistently rejected for lack of standing, effectively denying them access to a court to contest the measure. This formed the basis of their complaint that they were denied access to court, in violation of Articles 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention.
001-150676:
Ms Nada Nikolić, a Croatian national born in 1964 living in Vukovar, lodged application no. 5096/12 against Croatia on 9 December 2011. She alleged that national authorities had not adequately responded to the killing of her husband, Lj.N.

Vukovar was heavily attacked by the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serbian paramilitary forces from August to November 1991 and occupied at the end of November 1991. It was part of the UN Protected Area from 1992 to 1996. In 1996 UNTAES was established; its mandate ceased on 15 January 1998 and transfer to Croatian authorities began.

On 2 October 1991, between 4 and 5 p.m., during a general alert, two unknown uniformed, armed men apprehended Lj.N. in the basement or courtyard of a building in Kudeljarska Street, Vukovar, and drove him away. On 24 November 1991 his body was found in the River Danube at Novi Sad, Serbia. A 25 November 1991 autopsy found death was caused by a hand-gun gunshot wound.

In 2004 the applicant sued the State for damages in the Vukovar Municipal Court. In connection, the Vukovar Municipality State Attorney’s Office asked police for information. The police thereby first learned of the death and opened an enquiry. On 24 January 2005 police interviewed the applicant; she said her husband had been abducted from the basement by two Croatian soldiers. She named B.Š., K.Š., J.T., S.P., M.P. and J.M. as present; K.Š., S.P. and M.P. had died. That day J.T. said two uniformed, armed, masked men had taken Lj.N. On 3 February 2005 B.Š. said he had joined the Croatian Army in August 1991 and was visiting his wife K.Š. and children in the same basement; he denied being present. On 15 February 2005 Vukovar police lodged a criminal complaint with the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office against an unknown perpetrator, classifying the offence as a war crime against the civilian population.

On 5 May 2009 the applicant told the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office that B.Š. had been present. She said that after K.Š. died around 10 November 1991, one abductor came to take J.M.; B.Š. whispered, “This is the man who took Lj.[N.]”. She said B.Š. lived in Zagreb. On 9 July 2009 Zagreb police interviewed B.Š., who denied being present or knowing the abductors. On 21 July 2009 Vukovar police interviewed J.M., who said she was present but did not see the men. On 24 March 2011 a Zagreb County Court investigating judge heard B.Š., who repeated his statement. On 3 May 2011 a Vukovar County Court investigating judge interviewed the applicant, who repeated her statement. On 12 November 2011 Vukovar police told the Vukovar County State Attorney’s Office they had found no new information.

The applicant’s civil claim was dismissed on 18 September 2008. The Vukovar County Court upheld that decision on 21 April 2009 and the Supreme Court on 16 February 2011, finding the claim time-barred. Her constitutional complaint was dismissed on 12 July 2011.
001-158037:
In *Milenković and Veljković v. Serbia* (Apps. nos. 7786/13 and 47972/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined complaints by two Serbian nationals, Ms Dobrica Milenković (born 1957) and Mr Miroslav Veljković (born 1966), both from Vladičin Han. They had been employed by DP “PK Delišes,” a socially-owned company based in Vladičin Han. The case concerned Serbia’s alleged failure to enforce final domestic judgments awarding them salary arrears and social insurance contributions.

The first applicant obtained a judgment from the Vladičin Han Municipal Court on 20 October 2003 ordering the debtor to pay specified salary arrears and social insurance contributions. It became final and enforceable by 31 October 2003. On 31 December 2003, at her request, the same court ordered enforcement and awarded her enforcement costs. The second applicant obtained a similar judgment on 18 February 2004, which became final and enforceable by 11 April 2004. On 4 May 2004, the court ordered enforcement and awarded him enforcement costs.

Despite these final and enforceable judgments, the debtor did not pay. The debtor’s status and subsequent proceedings were central to the non-enforcement. On 18 February 2004, the Privatisation Agency ordered the restructuring of the debtor. Later, on 30 January 2014, the Leskovac Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against it. The applicants duly reported their claims based on the judgments to the insolvency administration. At the time of the Strasbourg judgment, the insolvency proceedings were still ongoing, and the applicants had still not been paid.

The alleged violations therefore concerned the State’s failure to ensure enforcement of final domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour. The key facts were that the applicants held final, enforceable, and undisputed monetary claims against their employer; enforcement orders were issued; the debtor nevertheless failed to comply; and the debtor’s restructuring and insolvency prolonged the non-enforcement for many years. The applicants appeared to bear no fault for the delay. The ECtHR was called upon to assess whether this situation breached Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, guaranteeing access to court and fair trial, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, protecting property. Those provisions require the State to secure effective enforcement of final judgments and to respect possessions.

The domestic-law context involved the status of socially-owned companies and Serbian rules on enforcement and insolvency, as outlined in cases such as *R. Kačapor and Others v. Serbia*, *Jovičić and Others v. Serbia*, *Marinković v. Serbia*, and *Ferizović v. Serbia*. Procedurally, the first application was lodged on 18 December 2012 and the second on 5 July 2013. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The Court deliberated on 29 September 2015 and delivered judgment on 20 October 2015.

In essence, the case turned on whether Serbia could justify the prolonged non-enforcement of final judgments because the debtor was a socially-owned company subject to restructuring and later insolvency, and whether that situation violated the applicants’ rights under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-152597:
In *Prilutskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40429/08), a Fifth Section judgment of 26 February 2015, final on 26 May 2015, the applicant, Mr Igor Prylutskyy, a Ukrainian national born in 1960 and living in Donetsk, alleged that the State had failed to take appropriate preventive measures to protect his son in a life-threatening situation and that the criminal proceedings concerning his son’s death had been ineffective. The application was lodged on 31 July 2008 and communicated to the Government on 3 September 2012.

The events arose on the night of 30 September 2006 during “AutoQuest”, a location-based driving game in Donetsk. Teams moved by car between locations, solved riddles to find the next destination, and competed to reach the final point first. The applicant’s son was a passenger in P.’s car. P. lost control and collided with a pillar. P. was injured, while his three passengers, including the applicant’s son, died.

On 1 October 2006 the Donetsk Region police opened an investigation under Article 286 § 3 of the Criminal Code concerning the fatal accident. The applicant was admitted as a victim on 3 October 2006. On 19 February 2007 the prosecutor’s office told him the case was complicated, required expert examinations, and that the activities of the game’s organisers were being examined. On 23 February 2007, however, the police refused to institute criminal proceedings against the organisers.

Psychiatric examinations became central. On 10 July 2007 experts found that P. had been aware of and able to control his actions at the time of the accident, but had later developed a chronic mental disability, including organic brain impairment and amnesic syndrome, and required mandatory psychiatric treatment. On 24 October 2008 the regional prosecutor’s office rejected the applicant’s complaint about investigative ineffectiveness and found no grounds to replace the investigator. The case was referred to the Kuybashevskyy District Court on 5 February 2009 to decide on compulsory medical measures. On 15 March 2010 the chairman of the Donetsk Region Council of Judges requested prompt consideration, noting repeated adjournments and unreasonable length. A repeat psychiatric report on 28 February 2011 confirmed the earlier conclusions.

On 8 June 2011 the first-instance court found that P. had committed a crime by violating traffic safety rules, exceeding the speed limit and losing control, causing the deaths. Nevertheless, relying on the psychiatric reports, it ordered compulsory outpatient psychiatric assistance because P. had later become unable to control his actions. The applicant appealed, arguing that the medical findings were wrong and that P. should have been brought to the hearings. On 24 January 2012 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal quashed the decision and remitted the case for additional pre-trial investigation, noting witness statements suggesting P. might have made a sharp turn to avoid a pedestrian; it found the facts had not been properly established. After further investigation, the case was again referred to the first-instance court on 31 October 2012. The authorities maintained that P. had exceeded the speed limit, lost control and caused the deaths, but proposed compulsory medical measures because of his post-accident mental disability. As of 26 March 2013 the proceedings remained pending.

Relevant domestic law included Article 286 of the Criminal Code and section 36 of the Automobile Roads Act 2005, which required local authorities, with approval of road-management and traffic-safety bodies, to regulate use of public roads for mass events and required permission for motor sports competitions on public roads. These provisions were relevant to the alleged failure to prevent the dangerous driving game.
001-150668:
**Rinas v. Finland (Application no. 17039/13), ECtHR, Fourth Section, Judgment of 27 January 2015**

The applicant, Pavel Vladimirovic Rinas, a Russian national living in Finland, complained that Finnish authorities violated the *ne bis in idem* principle. His application was lodged on 5 March 2013. The only complaint communicated to the Finnish Government concerned *ne bis in idem*; the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The case arose from parallel tax and criminal proceedings concerning the applicant’s failure to declare income from foreign companies, treated as disguised dividends. In 1998, a tax inspection of the applicant’s Finnish company found no irregularities. However, in 2004–2005, the tax authorities inspected his foreign companies. A preliminary report was issued in December 2005 and a final report in February 2006.

On 22 December 2005, the tax authorities imposed additional taxes and tax surcharges for the 1999 tax year; the surcharges were EUR 6,727. On 26 June 2006, further additional taxes and surcharges were imposed for the 2000, 2002, 2003 and 2004 tax years, with surcharges ranging from EUR 824 to EUR 5,000. The applicant sought rectification, but the Tax Rectification Committee rejected his applications on 4 October 2006. He later appealed to the Helsinki Administrative Court in December 2009, asking for the tax decisions to be quashed and the surcharges withdrawn. The Administrative Court rejected the appeals in April 2011, finding an oral hearing unnecessary because witnesses had already been heard in the criminal proceedings. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal in September 2012.

In parallel, in April 2005 the tax authorities asked the police to investigate aggravated tax fraud for the tax years 1998–2004. In November 2008, the public prosecutor charged the applicant with aggravated tax fraud for 1999–2000 and 2002–2004, alleging failure to declare income from foreign companies, resulting in too little tax. The tax authorities joined a compensation claim of EUR 48,870.

In June 2009, the Vantaa District Court convicted the applicant of aggravated tax fraud, imposing a suspended prison sentence of 1 year and 6 months and ordering compensation of EUR 48,870 plus interest. On appeal, the Helsinki Appeal Court held an oral hearing and in December 2010 dismissed the charges for 1999–2000 without examining the merits. It found that the tax surcharges and the criminal charge concerned the same failure to declare income, and that for 1999–2000 the taxation had become final before charges were brought, so criminal proceedings were barred by *ne bis in idem*. However, it upheld the conviction for 2002–2004 because charges had been brought before the rectification time-limit expired. The sentence was reduced to 10 months suspended, and compensation to EUR 10,718 plus interest.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, which granted leave in September 2011 only for 2002–2004. In May 2012, the Supreme Court upheld the Appeal Court judgment. It reasoned that the tax rectification decisions had not become final before the time-limit for rectification ran out, because the same time-limit applied to further appeals to the administrative courts. Since the applicant still had a right to appeal to the administrative courts when charges were brought, and exercised that right afterwards, the tax decisions for 2002–2004 were not final at the relevant time.

The key alleged violation was therefore whether imposing tax surcharges in administrative tax proceedings and subsequently convicting the applicant of aggravated tax fraud for the same undeclared income amounted to repeated punishment or prosecution contrary to the *ne bis in idem* principle. Domestic law included the Tax Assessment Procedure Act, the Penal Code, Supreme Court precedents KKO 2010:46 and KKO 2013:59, and the 2013 Act on tax surcharges imposed by separate decision, which sought to prevent parallel proceedings but lacked retroactive effect.
001-158504:
The case concerns Qing Xu, a Chinese national born in 1964, living in Parede, Portugal. She worked as a Chinese-Portuguese translator, was married to a Portuguese national, had two young children, and had lived in Portugal for at least 20 years. In December 2010, Portuguese authorities opened criminal proceedings against her, her husband, and others for aiding illegal immigration, money laundering, and forgery.

In April 2011, before her arrest, she wrote to the Attorney General and the Immigration and Borders Service stating that she knew she was under investigation and was willing to be questioned. She even suggested specific dates. On 9 June 2011, a public prosecutor issued an arrest warrant under Articles 254 and 257(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, citing sufficient evidence and risks that she would abscond, obstruct the investigation, or continue criminal activity. She was arrested at home on 14 June 2011 between 5 and 6 a.m., and questioned by an investigating judge on 15–16 June.

She challenged the arrest and sought alternative measures. She argued there was no risk of absconding: she had no criminal record, two young children, a permanent residence in Portugal for at least 20 years, and was willing to surrender her passport. She proposed lesser measures such as prohibiting contact with co-defendants and avoiding places attended by immigrants. On 16 June 2011, the investigating judge rejected her arguments. The judge found an evident risk of absconding because she was a Chinese national and, once confronted with the seriousness of the allegations, could flee to China. The judge also found risks of obstructing the investigation, since many witnesses remained to be examined, and of continuing criminal activity. She was remanded in custody. By contrast, co-defendants B.G., J.G. (her Portuguese husband), and M.M. received non-custodial measures such as passport surrender, contact bans, and weekly police reporting.

She appealed. In July 2011, the prosecutor requested that the case be classified as particularly complex; in August the judge granted this and extended pre-trial detention to 12 months. On 14 September 2011, the Lisbon Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal. It stated that the prosecutor’s reasoning that she would not voluntarily appear “could not eventually be justified,” but the warrant was not unlawful. It accepted there was no high risk of absconding because she had volunteered and had not fled. However, it upheld detention due to a high risk to the investigation—particularly given the nature of the Chinese community in Portugal—and the risk of continuing crime, which it said family circumstances or electronic surveillance could not prevent.

From October 2011 to February 2012, she filed three release requests and two requests to expedite the inquiry. The investigating judge repeatedly rejected release, saying the grounds remained unchanged or strengthened. The Prosecutor General rejected expedition requests as ill-founded given the case’s complexity. Periodic reviews in 2012 upheld detention.

On 29 January 2013, the judge replaced detention with house arrest and electronic surveillance; she was released from pre-trial detention on 30 January 2013. On 20 February 2013, the Lisbon Criminal Court acquitted her of money laundering and forgery but convicted her of aiding illegal immigration, imposing a five-year suspended sentence with an annual EUR 1,500 payment. She was released from house arrest and appealed; proceedings were still pending as of 29 April 2015.

The applicant alleged that her pre-trial detention was arbitrary, unreasonably lengthy, and imposed because of her foreign nationality. Key legal provisions required detention to be necessary, proportionate, and a last resort; arrest without flagrante only if there were well-grounded reasons to believe the suspect would not voluntarily appear; and non-national status alone should not suffice to establish flight risk.
001-154344:
In *Alves v. Portugal* (Application no. 79925/12), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, Committee) gave judgment on 30 April 2015. The applicant, Ms Cretka Ivanic Alves, a Slovenian national born in 1953 who lives in Braga, Portugal, lodged an application under Article 34 of the Convention on 4 December 2012. The application was communicated to the Portuguese Government on 4 March 2014. The Slovenian Government was informed of its right to intervene but did not do so. The applicant was represented by a Braga lawyer, and the Portuguese Government by the Deputy Attorney General.

The domestic case concerned a civil liability action for professional negligence.
