On 22 November 2006, the applicant sued F., a lawyer who had represented her in earlier proceedings, in the Braga Court, claiming damages. F. was notified on 12 December 2006. On 25 January 2007, F. filed his defence and requested that his professional liability insurer be joined to the proceedings. The applicant filed a reply on 8 March 2007. On 11 July 2007, the Braga Court accepted the insurer’s intervention. The insurer was summoned on an unknown date and filed submissions on 14 September 2007; the applicant replied on 11 October 2007.

Between January and April 2008, the parties disputed whether the applicant had legal capacity to be a party. On 28 April 2008, the judge issued a despacho saneador and absolved F. from the proceedings because the applicant allegedly lacked legal capacity. The applicant appealed to the Guimarães Court of Appeal. By decision of 4 December 2008, the Court of Appeal held that she did have legal capacity and ordered the first-instance court to re-examine the case. In February 2009, the proceedings were allocated to the Braga Court. On 29 April 2009, the judge issued directions identifying established and outstanding matters.

From 28 May to 6 November 2009, the parties made three requests, to which the judge responded within less than one month. The case was set for hearing on 10 March 2010, but it was adjourned to 15 June 2010. A second hearing took place on 7 October 2010. On 29 October 2010, the Braga Court partially found in favour of the applicant. Both parties appealed to the Guimarães Court of Appeal, which dismissed the appeals on 20 October 2011. The parties then challenged that decision before the Supreme Court, which dismissed the appeals on 29 May 2012.

Thus, the domestic civil proceedings lasted approximately five years and six months from filing to final decision: about three years and eleven months at first instance, one year on appeal, and seven months before the Supreme Court. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are the overall length of the proceedings and the procedural stages that may explain or contribute to delay, including the insurer’s intervention, the dispute over the applicant’s legal capacity and the ensuing appeal, the remittal of the case, and the adjournment of hearings. Although the excerpt does not set out the legal complaint, the chronology indicates that the case concerned the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings, primarily under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.
001-156073:
In *Temchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 30579/10), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Anatoliy Georgiyevich Temchenko, a Ukrainian national born in 1942 and formerly rector of a State-owned university. He was arrested on 29 September 2009 on suspicion of receiving bribes as rector and detained in Kryvyy Rig’s temporary detention facility and later the SIZO remand centre.

Before arrest, the applicant had type-2 diabetes, and an endocrinologist had advised that insulin treatment be commenced and adjusted in hospital. The domestic courts ordered and extended his detention, citing risks that he might abscond, hinder the investigation, or continue criminal activity, though often without concrete supporting facts. appellate courts upheld detention relying on unspecified evidence and medical documents indicating he was fit for detention.

While in detention, the applicant’s health deteriorated. He was diagnosed with ischemic heart disease, hypertension, chronic pancreatitis, kidney pathology, and diabetes. The SIZO medical unit lacked specialist staff and equipment. Medical staff and outside doctors repeatedly stated that he required in-patient treatment in a specialist endocrinology or cardiology institution; the head of the SIZO medical unit even asked the judge to change the preventive measure because adequate treatment was impossible in the SIZO. The judge did not respond. The applicant received insulin in the SIZO, partially bought by himself or supplied by relatives, and had intermittent hospital treatment. Forensic medical reports of 12 November 2010, 28 January 2011, and 8 June 2011 found his condition grave and unstable, worsened by inadequate treatment, and at risk of fatal complications such as cardiac arrest, brain haemorrhage, or aortic dissection unless he received comprehensive specialist in-patient care. They also considered transportation undesirable or potentially fatal.

The applicant repeatedly requested release in 2010 and 2011, arguing poor health and that he could no longer hinder the investigation because he was no longer rector. The District Court rejected those requests, saying he could influence witnesses and was receiving medical aid, without citing concrete facts or assessing the adequacy of treatment. On 16 March 2011, under Rule 39, the European Court indicated that the Government should ensure he received treatment in the specialised institutions identified in the January 2011 report. He was later hospitalised locally and, in July 2011, taken to Kyiv, where heart surgery was prescribed. In May 2011 he was convicted of bribery and sentenced; in October 2011 the sentence was changed to suspended imprisonment and he was released.

A separate alleged Article 5 issue concerned his detention from 29 January to 9 March 2010, which was not covered by any court decision. The District Court nevertheless found it justified because he had been awaiting committal for trial.

As to conditions, the applicant alleged dampness and poor food in the SIZO, and that the prescribed special diet was not provided there but brought by relatives. He complained of transportation in an ordinary van 26 times and a police car once, with inadequate ventilation and heating, sometimes lasting up to three hours; later he was transported by ambulance with a doctor 19 times. He also alleged that the train carriage to Kyiv was unsuitable and that he was handcuffed to hospital beds, though he did not raise the handcuffing complaint domestically. His complaints to prosecutors were rejected. The key alleged violations therefore concerned Article 3 (inadequate medical care, detention conditions, and transportation) and Article 5 (unlawful or unjustified detention).
001-153910:
In *Vamvakas v. Greece (No. 2)* (Application no. 2870/11), the applicant, Alexandros Vamvakas, a Greek national born in 1953, complained in particular of a violation of Article 6 § 3 (c) of the European Convention on Human Rights, concerning his right to legal assistance in criminal proceedings. The application was lodged on 20 December 2010.

On 16 January 2006, the Athens Criminal Court of Appeal, composed of three judges and acting as a court of first instance, convicted the applicant of fraud and forgery to the detriment of a bank and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. At that time he was detained in Korydallos Prison, appeared in person, and was assisted by a lawyer of his own choosing, N.G.

Later, on 11 February 2009, a hearing took place before the Criminal Court of Appeal, composed of five judges. The applicant had meanwhile been transferred to Grevena Prison. He appeared in person and was assisted by two lawyers of his choosing, N.T. and E.P. The hearing was adjourned and scheduled to resume the next day. On 12 May 2009, the proceedings were again adjourned because of a lawyers’ strike, until 20 May 2009. Before the end of the 12 May hearing, the court informed the applicant that he would not be summoned to appear at the 20 May hearing.

Before the 20 May 2009 hearing, the applicant informed the court in writing that he would not be present but would be represented by his lawyers. However, neither N.T. nor E.P. attended. The court concluded that at the 12 February 2009 hearing the applicant had expressed a wish for a ruling on his appeal. It therefore appointed G.M. as official counsel and adjourned the hearing until 27 May 2009 so that G.M. could familiarise himself with the case file. At the hearing, G.M. argued that the offences were petty rather than serious and invited the court to consider mitigating circumstances. On 27 May 2009, the Court of Appeal reduced the applicant’s sentence to seven years’ imprisonment for the same offences. It rejected the argument that the offences fell under tort law, holding that Act No. 1608/1950 applied, but accepted mitigating circumstances.

On 1 June 2009, the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. He complained of the erroneous application of the relevant legislation, particularly Act No. 1608/1950, and argued that the offences were tortious and had become statute-barred. He also relied on Articles 6 and 7 of the Convention. He prepared the appeal himself, evidently with some legal assistance, and lodged it through the Grevena Prison authorities. On 5 November 2009, while in Grevena Prison, he received a summons to appear at the Court of Cassation hearing on 5 February 2010.

On 30 December 2009, the applicant asked the President of the Court of Cassation to appoint an official lawyer because of his financial hardship. On 2 January 2010, the President appointed F.K. to represent him at the 5 February 2010 hearing and/or at any other hearing in the case.

By judgment of 25 February 2010, finalised on 29 March and authenticated on 28 April 2010, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on points of law as abandoned. It found that the applicant had been duly summoned and had failed to appear. The applicant claimed that after F.K.’s appointment he had contacted him from prison and that F.K. had assured him he would attend. According to the applicant, F.K. did not inform him before or after the hearing why he had been absent; only later, in a telephone conversation, did F.K. say that he had telephoned the Court of Cassation registry to request an adjournment. The applicant stated that he learned of the Court of Cassation’s judgment on 18 October 2010.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 6 § 3 (c) violation are therefore the appointment of State-funded counsel for the cassation hearing, counsel’s alleged failure to attend or secure an adjournment, the lack of effective communication with the imprisoned applicant, and the Court of Cassation’s decision to dismiss the appeal as abandoned without examining its merits.
001-156069:
The case *Metalla and Others v. Albania* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 16 July 2015) involved four applications (nos. 30264/08, 42120/08, 54403/08 and 54411/08) lodged under Article 34 by nine Albanian nationals between 13 June and 8 October 2008. The applicants complained about Albania’s failure to enforce final administrative decisions recognising their inherited property rights and awarding restitution or, where restitution was impossible, compensation under domestic law. The alleged violations therefore centred on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

Application no. 30264/08 (*Metalla*) concerned a Shijak Commission decision of 9 August 1995 recognising the applicants’ inherited title to 1,020 sq. m of land. Of that, 747 sq. m were restored, while the remaining 272 sq. m were occupied and were to be compensated in one of the ways provided by law. The decision remained unenforced.

Application no. 42120/08 (*Bushati*) concerned a Shkodër Commission decision of 8 February 1995 recognising the applicant’s and other heirs’ inherited title to a two-storey building and 500 sq. m of surrounding land. Because the 500 sq. m plot was occupied, compensation was ordered, and the building was to be restored. The applicant claimed he had brought legal actions in 1995 and 1997 against a third party but discontinued them due to pending proceedings elsewhere. It appears the third party later built unauthorised constructions on the land. The Commission decision remained unenforced.

Application no. 54403/08 (*Metalla and Others*) concerned a Shijak Commission decision of 12 May 1994 recognising inherited title to 5,527 sq. m. Some 5,000 sq. m were restored; the remaining 527 sq. m were occupied and were to be compensated. That decision also remained unenforced.

Application no. 54411/08 (*Metalla and Others*) concerned a Durrës Commission decision of 13 August 2007 recognising inherited title to 65,000 sq. m. Of that, 60,000 sq. m were restored. The remaining 5,000 sq. m, described as arable land, roads and channels, were occupied and were to be compensated. This decision likewise remained unenforced.

The common factual core was therefore the existence of final domestic administrative decisions granting property restitution or compensation, and the authorities’ prolonged failure to execute them. The occupied portions could not be physically restored, so domestic law provided for compensation in one of the legally prescribed forms. Yet none of the applicants received the relief ordered.

The Court noted the relevant domestic law and practice set out in *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania* and *Ramadhi v. Albania*. New property valuation maps were approved in 2013 and 2014. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers also examined Albania’s broader failure to enforce final judicial and administrative decisions awarding compensation for unreturned property. Decisions in March and June 2014 and June 2015 recognised a structural problem, urged concrete action, and noted an action plan and draft law for an effective compensation mechanism. Those materials contextualised the alleged violations: the applicants’ final decisions were not enforced, leaving them without restitution or compensation for occupied property.
001-157538:
The applicant, Tadej Korošec, a Slovenian national born in 1980, lives in Ljubljana. He suffers from progressive spinal muscular atrophy and requires twenty-four-hour assistance with daily activities. He alleged under Article 6 of the Convention that court proceedings to which he had been a party were unfair.

In 2006 the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute of the Republic of Slovenia awarded him an assistance and attendance allowance set at 70% of the reference amount. On 28 May 2009 his general practitioner applied for an increase, citing worsening condition, particularly respiratory function, and stating that the applicant needed twenty-four-hour assistance from a family member or lay care assistant, together with permanent professional assistance. At that time the applicant organised care through students and relied significantly on family members.

On 9 July 2009 the Institute’s first-instance disability commission, composed of an internal medicine specialist and an occupational medicine specialist, examined medical documentation from an internal medicine doctor, a pulmonologist and a clinical neurologist, and examined the applicant. It reported that he did not need permanent professional medical assistance. On 20 July 2009 the Ljubljana unit of the Institute dismissed his request based on that opinion. The applicant appealed on 28 July 2009.

On 23 September 2009 the second-instance disability commission, composed of an occupational medicine specialist and a specialist neuropsychiatrist, examined the file and again reported that the applicant did not need permanent professional assistance and could be cared for by a combination of care assistants without specific medical knowledge and by family members. On 24 September 2009 the Institute dismissed the appeal, relying on the second-instance commission and on the 1998 Decision on Assistance and Attendance Allowance for Beneficiaries Suffering from a Severe Disability, under which a higher allowance required twenty-four-hour family assistance and further professional medical assistance.

On 22 October 2009 the applicant brought court proceedings against the Institute before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court and requested an independent expert. On 30 September 2010 the court heard his testimony, reviewed the file, dismissed his claim, and rejected the independent expert request, finding the first- and second-instance commission opinions together with other evidence sufficient to establish that he did not need professional assistance. On 2 November 2010 he appealed, challenging that conclusion and the failure to appoint an independent medical expert, arguing that the court lacked medical expertise to assess his care needs. On 24 January 2011 the Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the first-instance court had relied on commission opinions given by experts and that both commissions had considered the medical records.

On 9 March 2011 the applicant sought leave to appeal on points of law. He argued that the lower courts’ refusal to appoint an independent expert was contrary to Supreme Court case-law, under which the Institute’s Disability Commissions could not be considered independent in proceedings against the Institute and should not be used as evidence. On 17 May 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the challenged decisions had not departed from established case-law. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (the record gives the date as 28 July 2007), and on 11 June 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed it with reference to section 55.b of the Constitutional Court Act.

The record also notes that social courts carry out judicial review of the Institute’s decisions; under the Civil Procedure Act, a court should obtain an expert opinion if it lacks the necessary expertise. A domestic Supreme Court decision of 7 November 2006 (no. VIII Ips 3/2006) held that the opinions of the Institute’s disability commissions could only be expert opinions in pre-judicial proceedings within the Institute, not in judicial proceedings, because they were opinions of representatives of one of the parties.
001-159211:
**Kristiansen v. Norway (Application no. 1176/10)** concerned an applicant, Mr Jørgen Kristiansen, who alleged that his criminal trial was unfair because he was not heard by an impartial tribunal, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The alleged violation arose from the participation of a juror, “J,” in the High Court proceedings that convicted him of attempted rape.

On the night of 9 March 2008, Ms A, then 17, and the applicant, then 23, left a party together to buy mineral water. They used a car borrowed from Ms A’s boyfriend. After talking and listening to music, they tried to return, but the car battery was flat. The applicant called Mr B, a taxi-driving friend, who later collected them. The applicant claimed that he and Ms A had kissed and touched voluntarily. The Sarpsborg City Court rejected that account and, on 18 September 2008, convicted him of attempted rape and other offences. On appeal, the Borgarting High Court, sitting with a jury, convicted him again on 5 February 2009, sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment and ordered him to pay NOK 60,000 in compensation to Ms A.

The High Court found that when Ms A rejected the applicant’s advances, he did not stop but moved over to her seat, held her arms behind the neck support, and physically overpowered her during a struggle. He continued until Mr B’s car lights appeared. Mr B noticed nothing conspicuous about Ms A, but she later cried and was in despair at the party, and her boyfriend understood something was wrong.

The impartiality issue arose during a pause in the High Court trial, after both Ms A and the applicant had testified. Juror J told the presiding judge that she was the foster mother of a child who had been in the same school class as Ms A. She had had contact with Ms A at birthday celebrations and class outings years earlier, and said she had a picture of Ms A as a “quiet and calm” girl. She had no further personal knowledge of her. The judge informed the prosecutor, defence counsel and Ms A’s assistant advocate. Defence counsel moved to disqualify J under section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act and Article 6 § 1 ECHR. Ms A’s advocate supported the motion; the prosecutor expressed understanding but did not take a stance.

The High Court refused to disqualify J. It found that the contacts were sporadic and old, and that J’s image of Ms A as quiet and calm could not influence her assessment of the victim’s explanation or guilt. J therefore took part in the jury deliberations and vote, and later in sentencing and compensation deliberations with professional judges.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. On 26 June 2009, the Supreme Court rejected the appeal by three votes to two. The majority held that prior contacts and J’s general “picture” of Ms A were not enough to show lack of impartiality. It considered “quiet and calm” a neutral observation, not a credibility assessment, especially since the jury had heard Ms A’s evidence. The minority disagreed, finding the accusation serious and stigmatising and the victim’s credibility decisive. It considered that J’s statement, made after the evidence and positively loaded, could easily give the impression that J favoured the victim’s credibility, making the applicant’s fear of partiality objectively justified.

The applicant lodged his application on 23 December 2009. The case was communicated to the Norwegian Government on 17 July 2013, and the Chamber judgment was delivered on 17 December 2015.
001-158472:
In *Myumyun v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 67258/13), the applicant, Mr Nuray Bayramali Myumyun, complained that Bulgaria failed to provide an adequate procedural response under Article 3 of the Convention to his ill-treatment by police officers intended to obtain a confession from him.

On 20 February 2012, officers N.K. and I.K. of the Pavel Banya police summoned the applicant to the police station for inquiries about a reported burglary. No formal criminal investigation had yet been opened. At the station, according to findings later made by the Bulgarian criminal courts, the applicant was taken to a room with three officers. After one officer left, I.K. struck the applicant’s left shoulder with a wooden bat, and after further blows the applicant fell to the ground. N.K. then kicked him and repeatedly hit him with a rubber truncheon. Another officer, T.A., entered with an electroshock prod and administered an electric shock to the applicant’s left leg. The beating continued intermittently, with further electric shocks, hitting and kicking. When the applicant’s head was low, he was kicked on the nose and began bleeding, after which the beating stopped.

The applicant sustained a haematoma on his nose and haematomas and bruises on his upper left back, left side of the torso and left shoulder. The next day, a forensic doctor confirmed numerous haematomas and bruises on his face and upper body, likely caused by hard blunt objects and cylindrical objects. At about 4 p.m., N.K. prepared a written statement on the applicant’s behalf saying he knew nothing about the burglary and presented it for signature. The applicant was released around 5 p.m.

After the applicant complained, criminal proceedings were opened against the three officers. On 1 February 2013, they were charged with causing minor bodily harm while carrying out their duties under Article 131 § 1 (2) read with Article 130 § 2 of the Criminal Code. Because that offence carried a penalty of up to one year’s imprisonment, the prosecutor informed the applicant that the officers’ criminal liability would be waived and replaced with administrative penalties under Article 78a of the Code.

The applicant asked the authorities to consider charges under Article 282 § 1 (abuse of office) and Article 287 (coercing a confession or statements). The prosecutor’s office replied that it had no competence concerning Article 282 and apparently did not reply concerning Article 287. When the applicant later asked the trial court to refer the case back for consideration of Article 287, the court refused. It said the applicant was not a party to the proceedings and that Article 287 did not apply because the ill-treatment had occurred before criminal proceedings were instituted, when the applicant was not yet an accused, witness or expert as required by that provision.

On 12 December 2013, the Kazanlak District Court found that the three officers, acting in concert, had wilfully caused the applicant light bodily harm. It applied Article 78a, waived their criminal liability, and imposed administrative fines of BGN 2,000 each (about EUR 1,023). It did not disqualify them from police work. The court treated their good character and the least serious type of bodily harm as mitigating, while their joint action and infringement of the applicant’s Convention rights were aggravating. The Stara Zagora Regional Court upheld the judgment on 25 April 2014, making it final.

In separate disciplinary proceedings, N.K. and I.K. received three-year bans on promotion competitions for unlawfully detaining the applicant, but the commission found none of the officers had ill-treated him. T.A. received no disciplinary penalty. Later, in a damages action, an administrative court found the police directorate liable and awarded the applicant BGN 4,000 (about EUR 2,045) in non-pecuniary damages, though that judgment was not final.

The alleged Article 3 violation therefore concerned whether the penalties imposed—administrative fines and no dismissal—were sufficient for ill-treatment aimed at extracting a confession.
001-151000:
The applicant, Timo Veikko Kiiveri, is a Finnish national born in 1960 who lives in Tampere. He owns 90% of the shares in a limited liability construction and decoration company and is its managing director and a board member. In 2005 the tax authorities inspected the company and concluded that it had failed to declare and pay considerable taxes, paid salaries off the books, and engaged in other fraudulent activity. On 8 September 2008 the tax authorities imposed additional income tax and tax surcharges on both the company and the applicant for tax years 2002, 2003, 2005 and 2006. He apparently did not appeal, and the bailiff seized the imposed sums. The tax years 2002, 2003 and 2005 became final on 31 December 2008, 31 December 2009 and 31 December 2011 respectively; the appeal period for 2006 elapsed on 31 December 2012.

In June 2007 the police started a criminal investigation into the applicant’s activities. On 6 March 2009 the prosecutor charged him with accounting offence and two counts of aggravated tax fraud. The first count concerned tax years 2000–2006 and his role as managing director and board member: he was accused of deducting fabricated receipts, failing to declare the company’s real income, paying salaries off the books, and causing the company’s tax to be too low. The second count concerned tax years 2000–2003 and 2005–2006: he was accused of failing to declare his own income and causing his personal tax to be too low. The tax authorities joined the charges and sought compensation for approximately the avoided taxes.

On 9 September 2009 Tampere District Court convicted him as charged of two counts of aggravated tax fraud and accounting offence. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, ordered to pay EUR 685,080.66 plus interest compensation, with sums already seized in the administrative proceedings deductible, and banned from business activities for six years.

On 9 October 2009 he appealed to Turku Court of Appeal, seeking to quash the judgment and dismiss the charges, relying also on ne bis in idem and relevant case-law. On 15 September 2010, after an oral hearing, the Court of Appeal largely upheld the judgment, found part of the accounting offence aggravated, and ordered EUR 20,000 more compensation. On ne bis in idem, it reasoned that for tax years 2003, 2005 and 2006 the appeal period had not elapsed when charges were brought in 2009, so no issue arose; for 2002, taxation became final on 31 December 2008 before charges, but because another kind of tax appeal remained available, ne bis in idem did not prevent examination.

On 12 October 2010 he appealed to the Supreme Court, repeating his grounds and seeking a stay. On 27 February 2012 the Supreme Court dismissed without examining the merits the part concerning tax year 2002 because the tax surcharges had become final in 2008, before the March 2009 charges, preventing examination. It otherwise upheld the lower judgment, finding no ne bis in idem issue for the other years because the appeal periods had not elapsed when charges were brought; the sentence was reduced to 2 years 10 months. On 21 August 2012 he lodged an extraordinary appeal seeking reopening based on incorrect application of law and the prohibition on self-incrimination; it was apparently refused in March 2013. On 22 August 2012 he lodged an application with the ECtHR alleging, in particular, a violation of the ne bis in idem principle.
001-153349:
**Summary of Nalbandyan v. Armenia (Applications nos. 9935/06 and 23339/06)**

The case concerned three Armenian nationals—Bagrat Nalbandyan (first applicant), his wife Narine Nalbandyan (second applicant), and their daughter Arevik Nalbandyan (third applicant)—who lived in Vardenis, Gegharkunik Region. On 8 June 2004, criminal proceedings were instituted regarding the murder of a local girl who was the third applicant's classmate. The applicants alleged violations of the Convention arising from ill-treatment in police custody in June and July 2004, the absence of an effective investigation into those allegations, deprivation of effective legal assistance, and the first applicant's unlawful denial of access to the Court of Cassation.

The first applicant alleged that on 8 June 2004 he was taken to Vardenis Police Department and unlawfully detained without formal arrest, where he was continually beaten to coerce a confession to the murder. On 24 June 2004, the Gegharkunik Regional Court convicted him of maliciously disobeying police officers and sentenced him to fifteen days' imprisonment. The first applicant claimed this decision was fabricated to legitimize his continued unlawful detention.

The second and third applicants alleged they were subjected to constant pressure from law enforcement from 8 June 2004, frequently taken to the police department, and coerced to confess or incriminate each other. On 30 June 2004, the second applicant and other residents complained to the General Prosecutor and Chief of Police about the first applicant's unlawful detention and the family's terrorization.

On 8 July 2004, the second applicant was allegedly invited to the police department, ordered to testify against her husband, and upon refusal, beaten by Chief Vi.H., Deputy N.H., officers K.N. and K.M., and Deputy Regional Prosecutor F.B. She was beaten on her feet with a baton, and when she fainted, officers revived her and continued beating. Officers then brought the third applicant, locked her in a dark rat-infested room, and threatened to rape her unless the second applicant confessed. Both first and second applicants subsequently confessed.

The third applicant alleged she was taken to the police department numerous times, humiliated, threatened with rape, and pressured to implicate her mother. She saw both parents with signs of ill-treatment. On 10 July 2004, after being questioned as a witness, she was allegedly beaten by Deputy Prosecutor F.B. and others, leaving her bedridden for days. Medical examinations on 14 and 16 July 2004 documented bruising on the second applicant's feet and concussion and bruising on the third applicant's head, back, and arm.

The applicants alleged they were deprived of effective legal assistance. On 9 July 2004, they refused an investigator-invited lawyer due to mistrust, and their later request to be questioned with state-appointed lawyer K. present was refused. During court proceedings, hearings were allegedly conducted amid constant disorder, threats, and physical abuse by the victim's relatives. Lawyer S. was forced to miss hearings due to safety fears, and her final pleading was submitted by post. On 1 July 2005, the Court of Appeal proceeded without her after the applicants allegedly dispensed with her services. The Court of Cassation later left her appeal unexamined on the ground that she was no longer authorized.

The applicants' complaints of ill-treatment, lodged with the Ombudsman and General Prosecutor, were examined by Senior Assistant Y.I., who on 31 August 2004 refused to institute criminal proceedings based on statements from the alleged perpetrators. The applicants were not informed of this decision.
001-153770:
**Tatar v. Switzerland (Application no. 65692/12)**

The applicant, Mehmet Ali Tatar, is a Turkish national born in 1950. He arrived in Switzerland in June 1988 and claimed he had been detained and tortured by Turkish authorities in 1987–88 because of his membership in a Turkish Communist Party. He and two politically active sons were recognized as refugees and granted asylum in 1994. His wife and other children later joined him. In 1990 he suffered a serious work injury and received an invalidity pension. His children and grandchildren are Swiss nationals, though he retained contacts in Turkey.

In 2001, the applicant killed his wife during a dispute, shooting her three times in the head and once in the stomach. In 2003 he was sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. Psychiatric evidence diagnosed a recurrent depressive disorder with psychotic symptoms, classified as schizophrenic disease syndrome, and he was found to have diminished responsibility. His imprisonment was postponed so he could receive treatment in a closed psychiatric facility. In 2009, the Federal Office for Migration revoked his asylum status because of the serious crime, but did not withdraw his refugee status under the 1951 Refugee Convention.

In April 2010, he was paroled on condition that he remain in psychiatric care for three years. He was later moved to an open residence with continuous psychiatric supervision, but suffered relapses requiring temporary stays in a closed psychiatric hospital. Expert reports indicated he could not live independently, required regular psychotropic medication and therapy, and would relapse into hallucinations and psychotic delusions, potentially harming himself or others, if treatment stopped. Expulsion was expected to worsen his condition, especially to Turkey, where he said he felt persecuted. He was also appointed a legal guardian.

In June 2010, the Zurich Migration Office revoked his residence permit and ordered him to leave Switzerland within three months. His appeals failed. Before the Federal Supreme Court, he argued that he had not been adequately heard, that non-refoulement still applied, that removal would endanger his life because of his deteriorating mental health, that he faced a blood feud with his wife’s relatives, and that he risked torture or inhuman treatment in Turkey. He mentioned Article 8 in a heading but did not substantively claim a violation of private or family life.

On 2 August 2012, the Federal Supreme Court dismissed his appeal. It held that he could be returned to Turkey despite his refugee recognition because he had committed a serious crime. It found it unproven that expulsion would make his mental health life-threatening, noting psychiatric facilities existed in Turkey. As to the blood-feud risk, it found he had not substantiated that Turkish authorities could not protect him and that he could relocate; his wife’s relatives had visited Switzerland and merely avoided him. As to torture for past TCP membership, his political activities were over 20 years old, Turkey’s human rights situation had changed, and family members had visited Turkey without difficulties.

The expulsion order remained in force, though no removal date was set. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2, 3, 6 and 8 of the Convention, claiming his proposed expulsion exposed him to inhuman and degrading treatment, threatened his physical and moral integrity, and that the Federal Supreme Court proceedings were unfair. Rule 39 was not applied because expulsion was not imminent.
001-153960:
**A.T. v. Luxembourg** (Application no. 30460/13) concerned a British national, A.T., who complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the European Convention on Human Rights that his criminal proceedings in Luxembourg were unfair because he lacked a lawyer during police questioning and did not receive effective legal assistance during questioning by the investigating judge.

The charges arose from an investigation ordered on 9 October 2009 into alleged rape and indecent assault of a girl under sixteen, aggravated by the perpetrator’s position of authority over her. On 4 December 2009 A.T. was arrested in the United Kingdom under a European Arrest Warrant. He was surrendered to Luxembourg on 17 December 2009. On arrival at Luxembourg airport at 2.45 p.m., he was served with the warrant. At 3.20 p.m., he was questioned at a police station in the presence of an interpreter. The police report stated that A.T. initially refused to make any statement and, referring repeatedly to British legislation, claimed his right to legal assistance. After receiving explanations about Luxembourg procedure, he agreed to take part in questioning. No lawyer was present. He was informed of the victim’s statements and the suspicions against him, denied all charges, and gave his version of events. At the end of the interrogation, he requested legal assistance for the next day’s interrogation before the investigating judge. He was then transferred to Luxembourg Prison.

On the morning of 18 December 2009, A.T. was questioned by the investigating judge with an interpreter. He was informed of his right to choose a defence lawyer or have one officially appointed. He availed himself of that right and was assigned Mr W. as officially appointed counsel. He was then questioned in the presence of his lawyer and interpreter, made statements on the facts, and confirmed his police statements. He was later released on 10 March 2010 subject to conditions.

At trial, the District Court on 31 March 2011 sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment with a three-year partial probation period. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 7 February 2012. A.T.’s lawyer complained that after extradition he had been heard by police without legal assistance, despite requesting it. The Court of Appeal relied on the police report and concluded that, although A.T. had initially requested a lawyer, after the applicable procedure was explained he agreed to give statements without counsel. On 22 November 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, finding no violation of Article 6 § 3 because he had agreed to make statements absent counsel.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, A.T. alleged unfairness, specifically the lack of effective assistance before the police and the investigating judge. On 4 November 2013, the Court communicated the complaint concerning lack of effective assistance before the police and the investigating judge to the Luxembourg Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The British Government declined to intervene, while Fair Trials International was granted leave to intervene.

Later, in 2013, Luxembourg prosecutors corresponded with UK authorities regarding extradition to serve his sentence. They stated that the police report showed A.T. had neither been assisted by nor offered a lawyer during the 17 December 2009 police hearing. As to the 18 December 2009 interrogation, they said an officially appointed lawyer assisted him and that access to counsel before interrogation had not been restricted.

The key alleged violation therefore centred on the initial police interrogation after surrender, where A.T. had requested legal assistance but was questioned without counsel. The domestic courts treated his eventual agreement to speak as a waiver. The case engaged the Salduz line of authority and Luxembourg’s subsequent circulars and Police Memorandum No. 49/2011, which extended effective lawyer access to police interrogations in preparatory investigations.
001-157286:
The applicant, Daniel Berland, a French national born in 1987 and in the specialised hospital centre of Sevrey, lodged application no. 42875/10 against France on 21 July 2010, alleging a violation of Article 7 §1.

On 12 September 2007, aged 20, he went to the workplace of C.G., his former girlfriend, who after threats and violence had told him she no longer wanted to see him. He inflicted several stab wounds on C.G., who died from a massive haemorrhage from throat and thorax wounds, and wounded two other people. On 14 September 2007 he was placed under judicial investigation for premeditated murder and intentional wounding, remanded in custody, and the Prefect ordered his compulsory admission to Sevrey CHS. Expert psychiatric boards found that at the material time he had a mental disorder impairing his discernment and ability to control his actions under Article 122-1 of the Criminal Code.

On 8 September 2008 the public prosecutor asked the Dijon investigating judge to refer the case to the Investigation Division for a ruling on lack of criminal liability under Article 706-20 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, derived from the 25 February 2008 Act. On 30 September 2008 the judge found sufficient evidence to commit the offences and plausible reasons to apply Article 122-1, and ordered transmission to the Principal Public Prosecutor. On 18 November 2008 the Principal Public Prosecutor called for referral under new Article 706-122. On 25 November the President noted the applicant could not appear for medical reasons. At the 27 November hearing, his representative argued that applying the new procedure breached the non-retroactivity of harsher criminal legislation: it required the Investigation Division to rule on commission of the offences when imposing indefinite compulsory psychiatric treatment, tantamount to conviction and sentence not applicable in 2007.

On 18 February 2009 the Investigation Division found sufficient evidence that he had “intentionally killed C.G.” and lacked criminal liability because of mental disorder impairing discernment and control. It ordered compulsory hospitalisation under Article 706-135, finding his disorder risked the safety of others and required long-term hospital care. It also imposed a 20-year prohibition on contact with the complainants and on possessing or carrying weapons, as preventive measures under new Article 706-136, and sent the case back to Dijon Criminal Court for civil liability and damages. It rejected objections based on immediate application and Article 7, characterising the finding as not a conviction but a factual situation with legal consequences; the hospitalisation as preventive, not a penalty, under medical and administrative authority; and the 25 February 2008 Act and 16 April 2008 Decree as applicable.

The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on Articles 6 §1 and 7, arguing that no punishment without law precluded immediate application of a procedure exposing him to measures not entailed under former legislation. Before the Court of Cassation, the public prosecutor considered it impossible to find sufficient evidence that he acted “intentionally”, since criminal insanity precluded ruling on the mental element, and called for deletion of “intentionally”. On 14 April 2010 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal, holding that Article 112-1 of the Criminal Code did not apply to preventive measures for criminal insanity under Articles 706-135 and 706-136.

On 23 February 2011 the Prefect of Saône-et-Loire denied requests for unescorted leave. Assessments indicated his health allowed possible unescorted leave, but after contacting the Dijon public prosecutor about the 18 February 2009 prohibitions, the Prefect considered it impossible to guarantee he would not contact the complainants, and allowed future leave only if escorted.
001-150234:
**Case Summary: Elberte v. Latvia**

The case of *Elberte v. Latvia* (Application no. 61243/08) concerns the removal of tissue from the applicant’s deceased husband without her knowledge or consent, and the subsequent failure of domestic authorities to provide an effective remedy.

The applicant, Ms Dzintra Elberte, is the widow of Mr Egils Elberts, who died on 19 May 2001 following a car accident. His body was transported to the State Centre for Forensic Medical Examination (the Forensic Centre) in Riga for an autopsy. During the autopsy, a forensic expert, N.S., removed a 10 cm by 10 cm piece of dura mater from the body. The Government claimed this was lawful, as N.S. had checked the deceased’s passport for a stamp indicating an objection to tissue removal and found none. The applicant contested this, stating the passport was at their home at the time. She was not informed of the tissue removal and only discovered it approximately two years later when the security police informed her of a criminal inquiry into illegal organ and tissue removal.

The applicant first saw her husband’s body when it was returned for the funeral on 26 May 2001. She observed that his legs had been tied together, and he was buried in that condition.

The criminal inquiry, initiated in March 2003, investigated an agreement between the Forensic Centre and a German pharmaceutical company for the supply of tissue. Investigators found that experts at the Forensic Centre were paid for removing tissue, which was sent to Germany and transformed into bio-implants. The inquiry established that experts did not contact relatives to obtain consent, instead relying only on checking passports for objection stamps. Testimonies from relatives indicated they would not have consented had they been asked.

A central legal dispute arose over whether Latvian law at the time operated under a system of "presumed consent" (where removal is allowed unless the person objected) or "informed consent" (where removal requires express permission). While prosecutors concluded that the experts had breached the Law on the protection of the body of a deceased person and that the tissue removal was unlawful, the criminal proceedings were repeatedly discontinued. The final decision to discontinue was based on the expiry of the statutory limitation period.

However, this decision was challenged by the experts involved. On 26 June 2008, the Riga City Vidzeme District Court upheld their appeal, quashing the discontinuation decision. The court found that the domestic law did not impose an explicit obligation on experts to inform relatives of their right to object to tissue removal. Consequently, the experts could not be held criminally liable for failing to do so. The court concluded that the experts’ actions did not constitute a crime.

The applicant alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that the removal of her husband’s tissue without her consent or knowledge violated Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the Convention. She further complained that the subsequent criminal proceedings were ineffective, violating her right to an effective remedy under Article 13, and that the treatment of her husband’s body amounted to degrading treatment under Article 3. The case was communicated to the Latvian Government under Articles 3 and 8.
001-156272:
**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy and Satamedia Oy v. Finland* (Application no. 931/13) concerns two Finnish limited liability companies that challenged Finland’s interference with their publication of personal tax data. The first applicant, Satakunnan Markkinapörssi Oy, had published the *Veropörssi* magazine since 1994, which annually disclosed the taxable income and assets of natural persons—information that is public under Finnish law. In 2002, the magazine published data on 1.2 million individuals, roughly one-third of all taxable persons in Finland, organized by geographical area. The second applicant, Satamedia Oy, operated a text-message service from 2003 that allowed users to query taxation information about named individuals, using a database compiled from the magazine’s published data. Both companies were owned by the same persons.

In response, the Data Protection Ombudsman contacted the companies and advised them to cease publishing taxation data in the manner and to the extent carried out in 2002. When the companies refused, the Ombudsman requested the Data Protection Board to forbid the processing of taxation data as done in 2002 and its transfer to the SMS service. The Ombudsman argued that the companies had no right under the Personal Data Act to establish such personal data registers and that the journalism derogation did not apply.

The Data Protection Board initially dismissed the request in January 2004, finding that the journalism exemption applied and that the SMS service fell outside the Act because the data had already been published. The Ombudsman appealed to the Helsinki Administrative Court, which rejected the appeal in September 2005, holding that the magazine had a journalistic purpose and that publishing the data served the public interest.

The Ombudsman further appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, which in February 2007 requested a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) on the interpretation of Directive 95/46/EC. In December 2008, the CJEU ruled that the activities constituted “processing of personal data” under the Directive. While journalism should be interpreted broadly, derogations from data protection must apply only insofar as strictly necessary to reconcile privacy with freedom of expression. Activities involving data from public documents could be classified as journalistic if their object was to disclose information, opinions, or ideas to the public, regardless of the medium or profit motive.

In September 2009, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the earlier decisions and referred the case back to the Data Protection Board. It found that publishing the entire database collected for journalistic purposes could not be regarded as journalistic activity. The public interest did not require such extensive publication of personal data, and the derogation in the Personal Data Act had to be interpreted strictly. The SMS service was likewise not protected. Consequently, the Board in November 2009 forbade both companies from processing taxation data in the manner and extent of 2002 and from forwarding such information to the SMS service.

The SMS service was shut down after the Supreme Administrative Court’s decision was served. The magazine continued publishing taxation data in autumn 2009 with only one-fifth of its previous content, then ceased publication entirely. The companies’ subsequent appeals to the Turku Administrative Court and the Supreme Administrative Court were rejected in October 2010 and June 2012, respectively. The domestic courts held that the case concerned only the Data Protection Board’s decision and that the matter had already been determined by the Supreme Administrative Court; they found no violation of the prohibition of censorship or freedom of expression.

The applicant companies alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 had been violated, that the proceedings were excessively long, and that they had been discriminated against vis-à-vis other newspapers.
001-159375:
**Gasimli and Others v. Azerbaijan** (Applications nos. 25330/11, 25340/11, 25345/11, 25361/11 and 25645/11) concerned five Azerbaijani nationals who stood as candidates in the parliamentary elections of 7 November 2010. Mr Natig Jafarov was self-nominated, while Mr Ali Gasimli, Mr Tazakhan Miralamli, Mr Parviz Hashimov and Mr Eyyub Umudov were nominated by the coalition of the Popular Front and Müsavat parties. They sought registration in various single-mandate constituencies.

Under the Electoral Code, each parliamentary candidate nomination had to be supported by at least 450 voters’ signatures. The applicants submitted signature sheets containing more than 450 signatures to their respective Constituency Electoral Commissions (“ConECs”). Before registration, the sheets and other documents had to be verified by special ConEC working groups. None of the applicants was invited to participate in that examination.

The ConECs refused registration in each case after working groups found many signatures invalid, leaving fewer than 450 valid signatures. Invalidity grounds included: falsified or repeat signatures; incorrect voter information; signatures by voters with expired identity cards; signatures from voters registered outside the constituency; uncertified corrections; signatures allegedly obtained by “deceptive means”; and unspecified “other grounds.” None of the applicants was invited to the ConEC meetings at which refusal decisions were taken. The working group documents—expert opinions, minutes, records, result tables—and the ConEC decisions were generally made available only after the refusal decision. Some documents were never provided or were disclosed only during later judicial proceedings.

Each applicant complained to the Central Electoral Commission (“CEC”). They alleged that the invalidation findings were factually wrong, unsubstantiated and arbitrary; that no handwriting experts were involved; that the ConECs failed to corroborate suspicions by contacting voters; and that easily rectifiable errors were used to invalidate signatures without the required 24-hour notice and opportunity to correct them. They also argued that the procedure violated the Electoral Code because they were not informed in advance of the examination of signature sheets or ConEC meetings and did not receive the examination minutes at least 24 hours beforehand. They further claimed that certain invalidity grounds—such as recently expired identity documents, unspecified “other grounds,” or signatures that merely “appeared” falsified—were unlawful. Some applicants also alleged that local officials and police pressured voters or signature collectors to withdraw signatures. Some submitted voters’ statements confirming their signatures, but the CEC ignored them.

The CEC conducted its own working group examination, again without inviting the applicants. It also found large numbers of invalid signatures, leaving fewer than 450 valid. The numbers and grounds differed significantly from the ConEC findings; some signatures were invalidated because they “appeared” to have been falsified. The CEC rejected the applicants’ complaints. Applicants were not invited to CEC meetings, and relevant documents were again only provided after decisions, sometimes never or only during judicial appeal.

The applicants appealed to the Baku Court of Appeal, repeating their complaints. They relied on domestic law and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, claiming that their right to stand for election had been infringed. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed their appeals, finding the arguments irrelevant or unsubstantiated. The Supreme Court then dismissed cassation appeals as unsubstantiated, without detailed examination, finding no grounds to doubt the electoral commissions or the Baku Court of Appeal. The case therefore concerned alleged arbitrary invalidation of signatures and procedural unfairness in candidate registration, affecting the right to stand for election.
001-158950:
In *Blesa Rodríguez v. Spain* (Application no. 61131/12), the applicant, a Spanish professor at La Laguna University’s Faculty of Pharmacy, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that he had not been tried by an impartial tribunal. The case originated in a criminal complaint filed by La Laguna University on 27 May 2003, accusing him of forgery. The university alleged that he had submitted a falsified curriculum vitae in a public tender for pharmaceutical establishment licences.

On 6 February 2004, investigating judge no. 1 suspended the criminal investigation, finding no objective reasons to believe a crime had been committed. The university appealed. On 19 May 2006, the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Audiencia Provincial allowed the appeal, quashed the suspension, and ordered further investigation. That chamber included Judge A. as president, along with Judges S. and C. On 19 January 2008, the investigating judge confirmed the end of the investigation and the continuation of abbreviated proceedings. The applicant appealed, but on 21 June 2008 an Audiencia Provincial chamber composed of Judges S. (president), Sa., and C. declared the appeal inadmissible.

On 8 June 2010, the Audiencia Provincial ordered that the case be sent for trial and indicated that the trial bench would be composed of Judges A. (president), S., and G. However, at the preliminary hearing on 1 July 2010, the bench was instead composed of Judges A. (president), G., and Sa. as substitute judge. The defence lawyer was informed at the beginning of the hearing that the composition had changed, although the applicant claimed he was not personally given the names of the new judges. The trial hearings on 15 and 20 July 2010 proceeded before the same bench.

On 27 July 2010, that bench convicted the applicant of forgery and sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment, suspension from office for the same period, and a fine of EUR 25 per day for eight months.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court, alleging lack of impartiality by two judges. First, he claimed that Judge A. had previously sat on the appellate bench that had heard the appeal against the suspension of the criminal investigation. Second, he claimed that Judge Sa. had participated as a substitute judge while simultaneously being an associate professor and administrative employee at La Laguna University, the complainant. He argued that this university role was incompatible with Judge Sa.’s judicial role.

On 20 May 2011, the Supreme Court rejected these complaints. Regarding Judge A., it found that the applicant had failed to challenge him despite being informed of the bench composition on 8 June 2010. Under section 223(1) of the Organic Law on the Judiciary, a challenge must be made as soon as the ground is known. The Supreme Court also held that the 2006 decision merely found the investigation incomplete and did not undermine objective impartiality. Regarding Judge Sa., the Supreme Court acknowledged that the late notification of the new bench composition was unjustified, but found that the alleged circumstances did not fall within the statutory grounds for challenge or incompatibility. The applicant had not shown that Judge Sa. had an interest in the outcome or any link between his university role and the criminal proceedings. The Supreme Court did, however, reduce the sentence to one year and six months’ imprisonment and a fine for four months because the proceedings had lasted over seven years.

The applicant then filed an *amparo* appeal before the Constitutional Court, alleging breach of his right to an independent and impartial tribunal under Article 24 of the Spanish Constitution. On 7 March 2012, the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible for non-exhaustion, finding that he had failed to raise his impartiality complaints in the earlier judicial proceedings. The order was served on 13 March 2012. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 September 2012, alleging a violation of Article 6 § 1.
001-150788:
Mr Andrej Furman, a Slovenian national born in 1955, lived with M.P. from 1991 to 1997. Their daughter, P., was born on 14 December 1993. After the couple separated in 1997, the applicant agreed with the Maribor Social Work Centre to pay child maintenance. On 23 February 1998, a further agreement established a provisional contact schedule from 24 February to 13 April 1998. When no permanent agreement could be reached with M.P., the applicant asked the Centre on 24 February 1998 to issue a contact order. He sought regular contact: every Tuesday afternoon, every second Thursday afternoon, every other weekend, one week during the winter holiday and one month during the summer holiday. However, from 13 April 1998, M.P. stopped allowing contact between the applicant and P.

The first hearing was set for 18 June 1998 but was adjourned at M.P.’s request because she was on holiday. On 14 June 1998, M.P. informed the Centre that she would live abroad from 1 July 1998 to 31 August 1999 for doctoral studies and asked for the proceedings to be suspended. The applicant objected. The Centre made three visits to M.P.’s Maribor address but could not find her. On 30 July 1998, it asked her employer, Maribor University, for her foreign address. Meanwhile, on 26 August 1998, the applicant sought an interim contact order.

On 4 September 1998, Maribor University replied that M.P. was studying in Graz, Austria, but that her address was unknown; it offered to serve her with a summons. A hearing scheduled for 22 October 1998 was adjourned because the university could not reach her. On 29 October 1998, the Centre issued an interim order granting the applicant contact once a month and for one week during both the winter and summer holidays. The applicant was to collect and return P. at M.P.’s permanent address in Maribor.

Another hearing on 10 December 1998 was adjourned because M.P. could not be served. On 12 January 1999, Maribor University provided the address of the Austrian university where M.P. was studying. The Centre sent the interim order and a summons for a hearing on 11 February 1999 to that address. On 24 February 1999, M.P. appealed against the interim order, arguing that she and her daughter were temporarily living in Graz and that the schedule could not be implemented. On 1 March 1999, the Centre rejected her appeal as out of time. She then appealed to the Ministry of Labour, Family and Social Affairs.

On 28 April and 18 June 1999, the Centre submitted the applicant’s requests for enforcement of the interim order to the Maribor Administrative Unit. On 24 August 1999, the requests were granted. On 16 September 1999, M.P. appealed, claiming that the decision had not been correctly served on her and objecting to the order’s contents. On 27 September 1999, the Ministry upheld her appeal, quashed the interim order and remitted the provisional contact schedule for fresh examination by the Centre. The Ministry found that service of the interim order and the summons to the 11 February 1999 hearing had not complied with administrative procedure. It noted that if a party was absent or lived abroad, she had to be invited to appoint a representative authorised to receive official mail.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that he had been unable to enjoy family life with his daughter because the Slovenian and Austrian authorities had failed to act with due diligence in regulating and enforcing contact. The application, no. 16608/09, was lodged on 23 March 2009 and communicated to the Governments on 3 July 2012. The key alleged violation was under Article 8, arising from the prolonged inability to secure contact, procedural delays, difficulties serving M.P. in Austria, and the eventual quashing of the interim contact order.
001-155357:
**Summary of the Case of Caraian v. Romania**

The case of *Caraian v. Romania* (Application no. 34456/07) concerns an application lodged by Mr. Vasile Caraian, a Romanian national, against Romania. The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically his right to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence, stemming from how domestic authorities handled criminal proceedings against him after they were discontinued due to the statute of limitations.

The facts of the case span over a decade and involve three distinct rounds of proceedings. In August 1996, the applicant was arrested and remanded in custody on suspicion of intellectual forgery and use of forged documents. He was later indicted in September 1997 for a broader set of offenses, including bribery, influence peddling, complicity in fraud, and forgery. After a trial, the Sibiu County Court acquitted him in June 2000. However, upon the prosecutor’s appeal, the Alba Iulia Court of Appeal overturned the acquittal in December 2000, convicting him and sentencing him to three years’ imprisonment.

This conviction was subsequently quashed by the Court of Cassation in March 2002, which ordered a complete re-investigation due to significant procedural flaws and superficial fact-finding by the prosecution during the initial investigation. This marked the beginning of the second round of proceedings.

In the re-investigation, the National Anticorruption Prosecutor’s Office discontinued proceedings for bribery and influence peddling in June 2003, finding no unlawful act. The case was then forwarded to the Sibiu Prosecutor’s Office, which, on 31 July 2003, discontinued the criminal investigation for complicity in fraud and forgery. Critically, this order stated that while the applicant’s criminal liability was "undeniable," the criminal action was time-barred. The applicant challenged this, requesting that the investigation continue to establish his innocence. The investigation was briefly reopened but was again discontinued on 14 November 2003 on the same grounds: the acts were proven, but the proceedings were time-barred.

The applicant appealed this decision. In July 2004, the Sibiu District Court allowed his appeal, quashing the prosecutor’s order. The court found that the investigation had been conducted improperly by the same prosecutor who had confirmed the indictment and instructed the prosecutor’s office to clearly determine the extent of the applicant’s involvement and other issues. This initiated a third round of proceedings.

On 21 March 2005, the Sibiu Prosecutor’s Office once again discontinued the investigation. Relying on evidence from the entire case file, it concluded that the applicant was guilty of the offenses, but that the proceedings were time-barred. The applicant appealed, arguing that the prosecutor’s order was unlawful, unsupported by evidence, and that the investigating authorities had failed to follow the court's mandatory instructions from July 2004. He requested that the court quash the order, retain the case for examination, and acquit him on the merits.

The Sibiu District Court dismissed his appeal on 2 February 2006, upholding the prosecutor’s decision. It held that the investigating authorities had followed the court's instructions, that the applicant’s guilt was established by the evidence, and that his own statements amounted to an acknowledgment of forging documents. The applicant’s final appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Bacău County Court on 30 March 2007. The final judgment acknowledged the lawfulness of the prosecutor’s order, holding that the evidence proved the applicant had committed the offenses and that the prosecutor had correctly determined the proceedings were time-barred.

Consequently, the applicant’s central complaint before the European Court was that the domestic courts, by dismissing his appeals, had endorsed a prosecutor’s order that declared him guilty without a formal trial or conviction, thereby breaching his right to be presumed innocent. He also complained of the excessive length of the proceedings.
001-155827:
In **Tolmachev v. Estonia** (Application no. 73748/13), the applicant was an Estonian national, Kirill Tolmachev. On 17 September 2012, a police officer fined him EUR 80 in misdemeanour proceedings for breach of public order, namely breaking a glass panel of a bus shelter. The applicant contested the decision before the Viru County Court. He denied the act, challenged the assessment of witness statements, complained that the police had failed to present him to a witness for identification, and alleged that the police decision did not specify the local public-order provisions he had allegedly breached.

The County Court summoned the applicant to a hearing on 21 March 2013 at 12:30 p.m., stating that his participation was mandatory. The summons warned that under Article 126 § 2 of the Code of Misdemeanour Procedure, if a complainant failed to appear despite being notified of the obligation to participate, and the hearing was not adjourned, the court would refuse to examine the complaint. The applicant’s counsel, a police representative and witnesses were also summoned. The summons sent to the applicant’s known address could not be served personally on 4 February 2013 because he was absent; his mother refused to accept it and said he was living abroad. Counsel received the summons on 8 February 2013. On 20 March 2013, the County Court admitted the complaint and scheduled the hearing.

On 21 March 2013, the applicant did not appear. His counsel asked the court to examine the matter without him because he was abroad and his return date was unknown. The applicant’s father, present as a spectator, said the applicant would not return to Estonia within five years. The County Court refused to examine the complaint, issuing reasons on 2 April 2013. It found that the applicant had failed to inform the authorities of his new address, but concluded that because his father knew the hearing time and the applicant’s intention not to return, the applicant must have been aware of the hearing through his parents and counsel.

The court held that the case could not be examined without the applicant. A misdemeanour court had to hear the matter in full and verify the factual and legal basis of the police decision. The applicant had specifically complained that the police failed to present him for identification; interviewing him and presenting him to the witness were therefore important steps impossible in his absence. Adjournment would serve no purpose because he would not return within the one-month maximum adjournment period, and counsel had not requested an adjournment but examination without the applicant. The court relied on Article 126 § 2.

Counsel appealed, relying, inter alia, on Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention—the right to defend oneself through legal assistance of one’s own choosing. The receipt of the summons was not disputed. On 23 May 2013, the Tartu Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the first-instance ruling. It noted that under Article 126 § 1 the court could decide whether the complainant’s participation was necessary and that the County Court had given reasons why it was. It was unclear how the County Court could have remedied the alleged failure to present the applicant for identification without him. No further appeal lay against that ruling.

The applicant alleged that the refusal to examine his complaint because he was absent, even though his counsel was present, violated his right to a fair trial and his right to defend himself through legal assistance of his own choosing.
001-156265:
Case Oliari and Others v Italy (Applications nos. 18766/11 and 36030/11) concerned six Italian nationals in three same-sex couples: Enrico Oliari and Mr A.; Gian Mario Felicetti and Riccardo Zappa; and Riccardo Perelli Cippo and Roberto Zaccheo. They lived in stable, committed relationships and complained that Italian law prevented them from marrying or entering any other type of civil union, leaving their relationships without legal recognition and discriminating against them because of their sexual orientation. They invoked Articles 8, 12 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court communicated the complaints under Article 8 alone and in conjunction with Article 14.

Oliari and Mr A. requested marriage banns in Trent in July 2008; the request was refused. They challenged the refusal before the Trent Tribunal, arguing that Italian law did not expressly prohibit same-sex marriage and that any exclusion was unconstitutional. The Tribunal rejected the claim, holding that the Civil Code required spouses to be of opposite sex, that there was no fundamental right to marry, and that there was no discrimination because the limitation applied generally. On appeal, the Trent Court of Appeal referred the constitutional issue to the Italian Constitutional Court. In judgment no. 138/2010, the Constitutional Court declared the challenge inadmissible. It accepted that homosexual unions, understood as stable cohabitation between two people of the same sex, fell within Article 2 of the Constitution and deserved legal recognition of relevant rights and duties. However, it held that Parliament had discretion to decide the form of recognition and that marriage under Article 29 and the Civil Code referred only to opposite-sex marriage. It found no unreasonable discrimination. The Court of Appeal then rejected the applicants’ claims in September 2010.

Felicetti and Zappa began their relationship in 2003, moved in together, registered their cohabitation, and designated each other as guardians in case of incapacity. In February 2011 they requested marriage banns; their request was refused in April 2011. They did not pursue the Civil Code remedy because, after the Constitutional Court judgment, it was considered ineffective.

Perelli Cippo and Zaccheo had cohabited since 2002, opened a joint bank account, and registered their cohabitation. In November 2009 they requested marriage banns; the request was refused. They challenged the refusal before the Milan Tribunal, which rejected their claim in June 2010, relying on Constitutional Court judgment no. 138/2010. They did not appeal further because the remedy was considered ineffective.

Under Italian law, same-sex couples could not marry, and no alternative civil union or registered partnership existed, either for same-sex or heterosexual couples. “Cohabitation agreements” were not specifically regulated, though later private contracts could govern some financial aspects of living together. Some municipalities established symbolic civil union registers, but these had no legal effect. Italian case law, including Court of Cassation judgments in 2012 and 2015, recognized that same-sex couples had a right to respect for private and family life and that the legislature should act, but held that there was no right to marry or to register a foreign same-sex marriage.

The applicants alleged that Italy’s failure to provide any legal framework allowing same-sex couples to marry or enter a civil union violated their right to respect for private and family life and discriminated against them. They stressed their stable relationships, mutual support, cohabitation, and repeated attempts to obtain official recognition, all of which were refused. The domestic authorities consistently left recognition to Parliament, which had not enacted legislation. Comparative European material showed that many Council of Europe states had introduced same-sex marriage or civil partnership. The case therefore concerned whether Italy’s lack of any legal recognition or alternative to marriage for same-sex couples breached Article 8 and Article 14 of the Convention.
001-151051:
Petr Rohlena, a Czech national born in 1966 living in Brno, lodged application no. 59552/08 against the Czech Republic on 4 December 2008. Relying on Article 7, he alleged that, in convicting him of a continuous criminal offence, the domestic courts had applied criminal law retroactively to his detriment.

On 29 May 2006, the Brno municipal prosecutor indicted him for repeatedly abusing his wife physically and mentally while drunk, at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. He was accused of verbal abuse, hitting her head with his hand and fist, slapping her, holding her by the throat, trying to strangle her, throwing her against furniture or onto the ground, pushing her down stairs, and kicking her. He was also accused of hitting the children, gambling away household money, and smashing crockery. His wife sustained haematomas, bruising, and a fractured nose, and sought medical assistance on 26 June 2000, 18 July 2003, and 8 February 2006, following assaults on 24 June 2000, 17 July 2003, and 8 February 2006. The prosecutor alleged a continuing offence of abusing a person living under the same roof under Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b) of the Criminal Code, because conduct before that offence was introduced on 1 June 2004 amounted to violence against an individual under Article 197a and assault occasioning bodily harm under Article 221.

On 18 April 2007, the Brno Municipal Court found him guilty as charged for conduct at least between 2000 and 8 February 2006. It sentenced him to a suspended term of two and a half years’ imprisonment, five years’ probation, supervision, and alcohol-dependency treatment. Evidence included statements from the applicant, his wife, witnesses, and the couple’s children, who reported ten verbal insults, four incidents of grabbing and strangling, and monthly verbal or physical assaults. The applicant admitted quarrels and physical violence, including slapping and hitting with his fist. The court applied Article 215a as in force since 1 June 2004, extending it to earlier acts because they had been punishable at the time at least under Article 197a. It found a relatively high degree of danger due to the duration, considered the two-to-eight-year range under Article 215a § 2, but imposed a lower suspended sentence due to extenuating circumstances.

On 6 September 2007, the Brno Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal contesting the established facts and evidence. It found no defects and held that the classification conformed to the Criminal Code. On 21 February 2008, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, in which he complained that Article 215a had been applied to conduct before 1 June 2004. The Supreme Court held that a continuation of a criminal offence constituted a single act, classified under the law in force when the last occurrence was completed; earlier acts were punishable at least under Article 197a or Article 221 § 1; and his conduct disclosed the elements of Article 215a §§ 1 and 2(b), since abuse required duration and several years satisfied that element.

On 10 June 2008, the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal alleging unfair proceedings and retroactive detriment. It held that the domestic decisions were logical and coherent and had no prohibited retroactive effect.

Relevant domestic law provided that criminality was assessed under the law in force at the time of the act, with a more favourable later law applied. Article 89 § 3 defined a continuation of an offence as individual acts driven by the same purpose, comprising the same offence, similarly executed, close in time, and pursuing the same object. Article 215a, introduced on 1 June 2004, punished abuse of a relative or cohabitant by up to three years, or two to eight years if continued over a lengthy period. Article 197a punished threats by up to one year or a fine; Article 221 § 1 punished assault with intent to cause bodily harm by up to two years.

Later, because the applicant committed another offence while on probation and did not undergo alcohol treatment, he was required to serve the prison sentence. He began serving it on 3 January 2011. According to the Government, he was conditionally released on 17 May 2012.
001-155082:
In *Lhermitte v. Belgium*, the applicant, Ms Geneviève Lhermitte, was convicted of murdering her five children and sentenced to life imprisonment.
