The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights in January 2013, alleging Austria's failure to enforce the return orders violated his family rights. The Court granted interim measures in December 2012 but lifted them in February 2013.
001-163451:
The applicants are five Sudanese nationals—R.B.A.B., her husband H.S., their daughters X and Y, and son Z—who entered the Netherlands on 28 April 2001. The parents sought asylum separately, and R.B.A.B. also applied for the children. They claimed to be from Dilling, South Kordofan, and said H.S. had attracted Sudanese authorities’ attention through opposition movement M. After interviews in May, August and November 2001, the Deputy Minister intended to reject the claims due to contradictions and lack of knowledge about tribes, topography and movement M. On 17 January 2002 their asylum requests were rejected. Appeals were declared inadmissible for failure to submit grounds; an objection was dismissed on 10 September 2002.

On 12 April 2003 they filed a second asylum request on essentially the same grounds. On 14 April 2003 the Minister rejected it, finding no new facts or altered circumstances; no appeal was lodged.

On 14 June 2005 they filed a third asylum request, alleging that if returned to Sudan their daughters X and Y would be subjected to FGM due to tribal and social pressure. In interviews on 16 June 2005 the parents said they opposed FGM but could not protect the daughters. They submitted a Sudanese Embassy document of 26 April 2005 stating they were Sudanese citizens but lacked documents for a laissez-passer. On 17 June 2005 the Minister intended to reject the request, doubting its sincerity because FGM had not been raised earlier. Citing WBV 2004/36 and a 3 February 2004 Ministry report, she considered that higher-educated women in larger cities could avoid FGM, while rural/low-educated women had little choice. Because identity, origin and asylum statements were not credible, the applicants had not shown they fell outside the educated group. She also noted H.S. had accepted a negotiated penalty for shoplifting. In comments of 20 June 2005 the applicants said R.B.A.B. had only primary education and offered an IQ test. On 20 June 2005 the Minister rejected the request, stating it was for the applicants to prove identity and background.

A domestic provisional-measures judge ruled in the applicants’ favour, quashed the decisions and remitted the case, noting the daughters were uncircumcised, FGM was widespread, legal protection ineffective, and the earlier credibility finding concerned the parents, not the daughters’ protection. The Minister appealed. On 25 August 2005 the Administrative Jurisdiction Division quashed that ruling and rejected the appeal. It held the applicants bore the burden under section 31 of the Aliens Act 2000 and, given the final 17 January 2002 credibility decision, the Minister could reasonably find they had not shown compliance with policy conditions, lack of protection, or absence of an internal relocation alternative.

Later, X gave birth in 2011 and 2013; in 2015 she received a Netherlands residence permit and said she no longer wished to maintain the application insofar as it concerned her. In 2012 Y’s residence request was rejected; her objection was rejected on 29 December 2015, the Minister finding her parents opposed FGM and that she had not substantiated identity or Dilling origin. Z applied in 2013 under the long-term children regulation, seeking family permits; this was rejected and later again on objection. In September 2014 the Deputy Minister declined discretionary admission; related proceedings ended without further information.

Country material described FGM as widespread in Sudan, generally not prosecuted, prevalent in North Sudan, with urban educated families increasingly refusing it and no evidence of internal relocation to avoid it.
001-165250:
The application was lodged on 15 October 2010 by Mr Vladimir Nikolayevich Ruban, a Ukrainian national born in 1972 and serving a life sentence. He alleged in particular that, in sentencing him, the domestic courts had not applied the most lenient criminal provisions, contrary to Article 7 of the Convention.

On 13 August 1996 the Voznesensk local prosecutor’s office began investigating the murder of four persons on 12 August 1996. On 18 October 1999 the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office began investigating the murder of A., and on 10 November 1999 the Slavyansk Police Department began investigating hooliganism concerning R. On 22 November 1999 the three investigations were joined. Several persons, including the applicant, were suspected of committing the crimes as a group. On 14 December 1999 the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office charged the applicant in absentia and placed him on the wanted list; the investigation concerning him was suspended until his apprehension, while proceedings continued against other suspects.

On 23 December 2002 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal convicted and sentenced G., P. and F. for those crimes. On 2 February 2004 the Slavyansk Local Court ordered the applicant’s detention. On 28 June 2007 he was apprehended in the Smolensk region, Russia. On 31 March 2008, after extradition to Ukraine, the investigation was resumed. He was charged with participation in an organised criminal group together with G., P., F. and two deceased persons. He was accused of strangling A., killing four persons with G. in 1996, and inflicting grievous bodily harm on R. in a murder attempt linked to extortion of R.’s brother; all allegedly as a group. On 22 May 2008 the investigation was completed, and on 26 June 2008 the case was transferred to the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal.

On 10 July 2009 that court, as a first-instance court, found the applicant guilty of aggravated murder and banditry and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The applicant and his lawyer appealed, saying guilt had not been proved. On 15 July 2010 the Supreme Court upheld the judgment. The same day his lawyer submitted an additional appeal arguing that the Court of Appeal should have applied the most favourable wording of the Criminal Code, in force between 29 December 1999 and 29 March 2000, when the death penalty had already been abolished but life imprisonment had not yet been introduced. The Supreme Court stated that the sentence had been correct.

Under the 1960 Criminal Code, before 29 December 1999, aggravated murder under Article 93 was punishable by eight to fifteen years’ imprisonment or death. On 29 December 1999 the Constitutional Court declared the death penalty unconstitutional and void from that date. Law no. 1483 of 22 February 2000 replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment; it entered into force on 29 March 2000. The 2001 Criminal Code provided for ten to fifteen years’ imprisonment or life imprisonment for aggravated murder under Article 115 § 2. A 2008 Amendment Act on Humanisation established retroactive application of laws mitigating criminal liability. On 26 January 2011 the Constitutional Court held that after 29 December 1999 the 1960 Code had not become a new law mitigating liability for particularly serious crimes and that the interim period did not mean the sanction provided only a maximum fifteen-year term. It concluded that the amendments introduced by Law no. 1483 replacing the death penalty with life imprisonment should be understood as a new act mitigating liability with retroactive effect.
001-168860:
**Summary of Manucharyan v. Armenia (Application no. 35688/11)**

The case of *Manucharyan v. Armenia* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Spartak Manucharyan, an Armenian national, on 31 May 2011. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention because his conviction was based on untested witness evidence—specifically, his inability to obtain the attendance and examination of a witness against him. This complaint was communicated to the Armenian Government on 11 July 2013, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The facts arise from the murder of K.S., who was shot dead at approximately 1:30 a.m. on 1 July 2009 in Alaverdi. Later that day, the applicant presented himself to the police, surrendered a gun, and confessed to the murder. He was charged with murder and illegal possession of firearms. The same day, police interviewed K.M., K.S.'s girlfriend, who had witnessed the shooting. She stated that the applicant, her neighbour, had yelled and sworn before shooting at K.S.'s car moments after she got out of it. The applicant subsequently denied the charges and refused to testify.

On 14 January 2010, the applicant's brother, V.M., was killed. At an additional questioning on 9 March 2010, the applicant retracted his confession, claiming he had confessed to cover up for V.M., who had a newborn baby and cared for their parents. He stated there was no longer any need to protect V.M. because he was dead. The applicant's alibi was that he had visited V.J., a friend of his father, at around 10:30 p.m. on the night of the murder and stayed until around 2:30 a.m. However, V.J. was interviewed on 12 March 2010 and denied the applicant had stayed that late, stating the applicant arrived around 10 p.m., stayed only about an hour and a half, and left with V.M. at around 11:30 p.m. V.J. reiterated this account during a formal confrontation with the applicant.

The prosecution relied on statements from several witnesses, including K.M., K.S.'s sister S.S., K.M.'s parents S.M. and A.M., and V.J., as well as forensic evidence showing gunshot residue on the applicant's clothes. The case was referred to the Lori Regional Court for trial, with the first hearing scheduled for 21 May 2010. K.M. was summoned but failed to appear. The Regional Court repeatedly ordered her attendance, compelling her appearance through police enforcement, but she remained absent. Certificates indicated she was absent from her residence, and on one occasion her mother stated she was abroad. The Regional Court eventually examined the case in K.M.'s absence and convicted the applicant on 4 November 2010, sentencing him to thirteen years' imprisonment. The court relied heavily on K.M.'s pre-trial statements, which were the only direct evidence incriminating the applicant.

The applicant appealed, complaining that K.M., the sole eyewitness, had not been examined in court. The Criminal Court of Appeal summoned her for a hearing on 11 January 2011, but she again failed to appear. The applicant sought to have her statements declared inadmissible, but the Court of Appeal failed to address this application. On 26 January 2011, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, relying on the same evidence and not addressing K.M.'s non-attendance. The applicant's appeal on points of law was declared inadmissible by the Court of Cassation on 12 April 2011 for lack of merit.

The key alleged violation is that the applicant's conviction was based decisively on the untested pre-trial statement of K.M., the sole eyewitness, whom the applicant never had an opportunity to examine or have examined in court, thus breaching his right to a fair trial under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention.
001-160270:
In *Kalda v. Estonia*, the applicant, Romeo Kalda, an Estonian national born in 1974 who was serving a life sentence, alleged that his right under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights to receive information through the Internet without interference by public authorities had been violated. The case concerned prison refusals to allow him access to certain Internet resources.

At Pärnu Prison, on 21 July 2005, Kalda asked the prison governor for access to the online version of *Riigi Teataja* (the State Gazette), the online decisions of the Supreme Court and administrative courts, and the HUDOC database of European Court of Human Rights judgments. The governor refused. After domestic court proceedings, the Supreme Court of Estonia, on 31 May 2007, held that refusing access to the online *Riigi Teataja* was lawful because a paper version was available. However, it found that refusing access to the administrative court rulings and HUDOC was unlawful. It noted that from 1 January 2007 the primary official version of *Riigi Teataja* was online and only five printed control copies existed. Prisons therefore had to ensure detainees could reasonably search and familiarize themselves with legal acts. The Supreme Court also held that prisoners’ constitutional right to obtain information disseminated for public use under Article 44 § 1 of the Estonian Constitution had to be protected equally, absent statutory restrictions.

Kalda was later transferred to Tartu Prison. On 18 October 2007, he requested access to three websites: www.coe.ee (Council of Europe Information Office in Tallinn), www.oiguskantsler.ee (Chancellor of Justice), and www.riigikogu.ee (Estonian Parliament). He claimed he was involved in legal disputes with prison authorities and needed the sites to defend his rights in court. The Ministry of Justice dismissed his complaint on 23 November 2007. On 17 July 2008, Tartu Administrative Court granted access only to www.coe.ee, ordering supervised access via a specially adapted computer. It reasoned that HUDOC contained ECtHR rulings only in English and French, while Estonian translations were available on www.coe.ee; the burden of translation should not fall on Kalda. It found www.coe.ee similar to the judicial decisions database permitted under section 31-1 of the Imprisonment Act. Access to the other two sites was not foreseen by that provision, and Kalda could request information directly. The Tartu Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 31 October 2008.

On further appeal, the Supreme Court’s plenary session, on 7 December 2009, dismissed Kalda’s appeal and upheld Tartu Prison’s appeal, quashing access to www.coe.ee. The Supreme Court examined section 31-1 of the Imprisonment Act, in force from 1 June 2008, which prohibited prisoners from using the Internet except on specially adapted, supervised prison computers allowing access only to official legislation databases and the judicial decisions database. The three requested sites did not fall within those exceptions. The Supreme Court accepted that the restriction interfered with the right to obtain information under Article 44 § 1 of the Constitution but found it constitutional and justified by the aims of imprisonment: protecting public safety, maintaining legal order, and steering detainees toward law-abiding behaviour. It cited risks of misuse, prohibited communication, security threats, and increased control costs. It noted that detainees could access the ECtHR website, ratified Council of Europe treaties via *riigiteataja.ee*, printed works in prison libraries, and could contact the Parliament and Chancellor of Justice by post or information request. The restriction was considered “low intensity.” Four judges dissented, finding access to all three sites should be allowed because the sites did not generally threaten safety, supervised computers existed, and the information aided court access. Kalda lodged his application on 16 March 2010.
001-168377:
In *El Ghatet v. Switzerland*, the applicants—Saleh El Ghatet, a Swiss and Egyptian national living in Switzerland, and his son Mohamed Saleh El Ghatet, an Egyptian national living in Egypt—complained that Switzerland’s refusal of family reunification breached their right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The father entered Switzerland in 1997 and applied for asylum, which was rejected. His son remained in Egypt with his mother. In 1999 the father married a Swiss national and obtained a residence permit; a daughter was born in 2000. The son visited Switzerland for three months in 2002 on a tourist visa and re-entered in July 2003 for family reunification. In 2004 the father obtained a permanent residence permit and then Swiss nationality. However, after difficulties at school and with his stepmother, the son returned to Egypt in January 2005, where he was cared for by his mother and paternal grandmother. The father separated from his wife in 2006.

On 1 March 2006, when the son was 15½, the father applied for family reunification, relying on his custody under Egyptian law. The Cantonal Migration Office refused the request in February 2007. On appeal, the Cantonal Court in September 2007 granted it. Although the statutory requirements under Article 17 § 2 of the Residence of Foreign Nationals Act were not met, the court held that the applicants’ Article 8 interests prevailed over public interests and ordered a residence permit. The Migration Office then sought the Federal Office of Migration’s consent. In March 2008 the Federal Office refused, finding the requirements unmet and the cantonal decision contrary to Federal Supreme Court case-law.

The applicants appealed to the Federal Administrative Court. In July 2009 they informed authorities that the son’s mother had moved to Kuwait with a new spouse, leaving the son in the exclusive care of his paternal grandmother. In February 2010 the Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It found the statutory requirements unmet and held that Article 8 could not be relied on because the son had reached adulthood and was not dependent on his father.

A further appeal to the Federal Supreme Court was dismissed in July 2010. That court found the relationship between father and son was not “paramount,” despite the father’s custody under Egyptian law. It noted the father had not sought reunification immediately after arriving in Switzerland; the son had been cared for by his mother and grandmother in Egypt until he was 18; he had lived almost all his life in Egypt and had stronger social and personal ties there; and he had returned to Egypt after a prior 1½-year stay with his father. The court also observed that the father had then preferred the son to live with his mother, that integration in Switzerland would now be harder, and that the father had close ties to his daughter in Switzerland and could not be expected to relocate. It distinguished *Tuquabo-Tekle v. the Netherlands* because there the sole surviving parent had sought reunification promptly and the child faced forced marriage. The ECtHR later refused an interim measure under Rule 39.

The applicants alleged that this refusal violated Article 8. The key issues concerned the son’s minority at application but adulthood by decision, dependency, custody, the delay in applying, care arrangements in Egypt, and the strength of family ties versus integration prospects.
001-161809:
