001-160619:
**Case: A.K. v. Liechtenstein (No. 2), App. No. 10722/13 (ECtHR, 18 Feb. 2016)**

The applicant, A.K., a German national born in 1970, was involved since 2004 in civil litigation with F.H. over ownership of 75% of bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. In June 2005, F.H. sued A.K. in the Regional Court, seeking transfer of specified bearer shares and a declaration that A.K. never owned them. The action was served on A.K.’s counsel on 18 June 2005. A.K. unsuccessfully challenged the Liechtenstein courts’ jurisdiction; the Regional Court accepted jurisdiction based on assets in Liechtenstein. His appeal was dismissed in February 2006, and his constitutional complaint on jurisdiction was dismissed in March 2007.

The Regional Court then held hearings on 31 May, 28 June, and 6 September 2007, hearing the parties, counsel, and twelve witnesses. After the final hearing, no judgment was issued for more than two years. A.K. requested a decision in April 2009. On 28 December 2009, the Regional Court upheld F.H.’s action, finding F.H.’s account more credible. It ordered A.K. to hand over the shares and declared he had never owned them. A.K.’s appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 27 May 2010, and his appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 13 January 2011. The domestic civil proceedings thus lasted almost seven years.

On 18 February 2011, A.K. lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging violations of Articles 6, 13, and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. He specifically complained about the excessive length of the proceedings, stressing that the outcome affected his means of subsistence, and claimed there was no effective domestic remedy to speed up the proceedings or complain about delay.

A central issue arose on 8 May 2012, when A.K. challenged all five Constitutional Court judges called to decide his complaint. He alleged bias: President B. had delayed appointments and was a close friend of Vice President H., brother of F.H.; Judge Bu. worked for the Government and with Judge H.; Judge Sn. had published on judicial appointment; Judge S. sat on a state-owned company’s supervisory board; and Judge W. had law-firm connections to opposing parties and Judge H. On 15 May 2012, the Constitutional Court dismissed the bias complaints. The procedure was that each challenged judge did not participate in the decision on the complaint against himself, but the five challenged judges sat on the bench deciding complaints against the others, with the four remaining judges deciding each individual challenge. The court found no objectively justified doubts about impartiality.

On the same day, the Constitutional Court partly upheld A.K.’s complaint. It found a violation of the Article 6 § 1 reasonable-time requirement due solely to the two-year and three-month delay between the last Regional Court hearing and its judgment. It did not find the total duration unreasonable, noting A.K.’s own interlocutory proceedings. Because Liechtenstein law lacked express redress for such delay, the court ordered the State to bear court costs and reimburse fees as compensation. It dismissed the remainder, including property and independence complaints.

A.K. then applied to the ECtHR, alleging that the Constitutional Court judges had been partial, particularly because of the procedure used to examine his bias complaints, in breach of Article 6 § 1. He further complained about the length of the civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 and the lack of an effective remedy for that length under Article 13.
001-164515:
The first applicant, Khalaf M. Al-Dulimi, born in 1941, is an Iraqi national living in Amman, Jordan. According to the UN Security Council, he was head of finance for the Iraqi secret services under Saddam Hussein. The second applicant, Montana Management Inc., is a company incorporated under Panamanian law with its registered office in Panama; the first applicant was its managing director. The applicants alleged that Swiss authorities confiscated their assets pursuant to a UN Security Council resolution without any procedure complying with Article 6 of the Convention.

After Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990, the UN Security Council adopted Resolutions 661 (1990) and 670 (1990), imposing an embargo. On 7 August 1990 the Swiss Federal Council adopted the Iraq Ordinance providing for economic measures against Iraq. The applicants alleged that their Swiss assets had been frozen since that date. Switzerland became a UN member on 10 September 2002.

On 22 May 2003, UN Security Council Resolution 1483 (2003) superseded Resolution 661 (1990), among others. It required states to freeze and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq funds of the former Iraqi Government, Saddam Hussein, senior officials of the former regime, their immediate family members, and entities owned or controlled by them. The Iraq Ordinance was amended, notably on 30 October 2002 and 28 May 2003. On 24 November 2003, a sanctions committee created by Resolution 1518 (2003) was tasked with listing the individuals and entities concerned. On 26 April 2004, that committee added the second applicant and the first applicant to its list. On 12 May 2004, their names were added to the national list under Article 2 of the Iraq Ordinance. On 18 May 2004, the Federal Council adopted the Confiscation Ordinance on confiscation of frozen Iraqi assets and transfer to the Development Fund for Iraq; it was initially valid until 30 June 2010 and later extended to 30 June 2013.

The first applicant sought removal from the 1518 Sanctions Committee’s list. On 25 August 2004 he asked the Federal Department for Economic Affairs to suspend the confiscation procedure. On 5 November 2004 the Swiss government supported his application to the Committee. On 3 December 2004 the Committee Chair said the application was under consideration and requested supporting documents. On 21 January 2005 the first applicant asked to give oral evidence; no action followed. On 1 September 2005 the applicants sought continuation of the Swiss confiscation procedure. On 22 May 2006 the Federal Department sent a draft confiscation decision, which the applicants challenged on 22 June 2006.

On 16 November 2006, the Federal Department for Economic Affairs ordered confiscation of CHF 86,276.85 belonging to the first applicant and CHF 164,731,213 and CHF 104,739,882.57 held in the second applicant’s name at two banks, to be transferred within ninety days to the Development Fund for Iraq. It relied on the Sanctions Committee lists and stated that Switzerland could not delete a name unless the Committee did so. It noted that an administrative-law appeal could be lodged with the Federal Court.

On 19 December 2006, Resolution 1730 (2006) created a delisting procedure. The applicants appealed to the Federal Court against the three confiscation decisions, arguing that the confiscation breached property rights and that the listing procedure violated procedural safeguards under Article 14 ICCPR, Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention, and the Federal Constitution. They argued that Swiss authorities could review the conformity of the listing with those instruments. On 23 January 2008, the Federal Court dismissed the appeals in three almost identical judgments, confining itself to verifying that the applicants’ names appeared on the Sanctions Committee lists and that the assets belonged to them. It granted a brief final period before implementation to allow a new delisting application under Resolution 1730.

After the application was lodged, a delisting application under Resolution 1730 was rejected on 6 January 2009. SECO authorised releases from frozen funds for lawyers’ fees and court costs, amounting to approximately CHF 850,000 and over CHF 200,000 respectively. On 6 March 2009 the Swiss authorities stayed execution of the confiscation decisions pending the European Court proceedings. On 20 December 2013 further confiscation decisions were issued concerning assets in the first applicant’s name in two banks, to be transferred to successor funds if the application was rejected or the 2006 decisions were confirmed on review; the Federal Administrative Court suspended related proceedings on 7 May 2014.
001-165755:
**Summary of Mikhno v. Ukraine (Application no. 32514/12)**

The case of *Mikhno v. Ukraine* concerns the tragic crash of a military aircraft during an air show in Lviv, Ukraine, and the subsequent failures of the Ukrainian authorities to adequately investigate and provide redress. The application was brought by two Ukrainian nationals: Mrs. Nina Mikhno and her granddaughter, Miss Anastasiya Mikhno.

**Key Facts:**

On 27 July 2002, the Ukrainian Air Force organized a military aviation show at the Sknyliv aerodrome in Lviv to commemorate the 60th anniversary of the 14th Air Force Corps. The event, attended by several thousand spectators, included a live aerobatics performance by military pilots. Among the attendees were the second applicant, Anastasiya Mikhno—then five years old—accompanied by her father, Sergiy Mikhno, and her mother, Tetiana Mikhno. Sergiy was the son of the first applicant, Nina Mikhno.

During the aerobatics display, an SU-27 military aircraft piloted by two colonels crashed into the static aircraft display area where numerous spectators were gathered. Both pilots successfully ejected before the aircraft exploded. The crash resulted in the deaths of 77 people and injured over 290 others. Sergiy and Tetiana Mikhno, who were at the epicenter of the accident, died at the scene from multiple fractures and severe cerebral trauma. The second applicant, Anastasiya, witnessed her parents being crushed by the aircraft while she was inside the cabin of an IL-76 airplane on static display. Although she sustained no physical injuries, she subsequently underwent psychological rehabilitation for emotional trauma.

Following the tragedy, multiple concurrent investigations were initiated by various bodies, including a Special Government Commission established by the President of Ukraine. The Commission’s investigation revealed significant organizational and safety failures. Key findings included: the pilots had only one training flight as a team, which was not a proper rehearsal; a planned on-site rehearsal was cancelled due to fuel shortages; the pilots were provided with a different aircraft than the one used in training; they flew without mandatory anti-gravitation suits; and they immediately began the performance upon arrival without familiarizing themselves with the new site. Critically, during the performance, the aircraft exited the designated aerobatics zone, but ground directors failed to warn the pilots or direct them back. The lead pilot then attempted a manoeuvre he had never practised, leading to a loss of control and the fatal crash.

The applicants alleged that the State authorities were responsible for the deaths of their relatives and failed to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances. They further complained that the domestic courts handling their claim for damages lacked independence and impartiality, that the proceedings were inordinately lengthy, and that there were no effective remedies for the length of proceedings complaint.

**Relevance to Alleged Violations:**

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations center on the State’s failure to prevent the tragedy through adequate safety measures and its subsequent failure to provide an effective and timely investigation. The Special Commission’s findings of multiple organizational failures—including inadequate training, cancelled rehearsals, and the absence of proper safety protocols—point directly to State responsibility. Furthermore, the applicants’ complaints regarding the lack of judicial independence, the excessive length of proceedings, and the absence of effective remedies for procedural delays highlight additional violations under the Convention, particularly concerning the right to a fair trial and an effective remedy.
001-162217:
The application (no. 74681/11) was lodged against the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia by Mr Osman Sulejmani, a Macedonian national born in 1958 and living in Tetovo. The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the confiscation of his vehicle in criminal proceedings against a third person.

On 12 April 2006 the applicant concluded a sales contract with Sh.A. to purchase a concrete mixing and transport lorry (“the vehicle”) for the equivalent of EUR 5,000 in Macedonian denars. On 15 May 2007 he lent the vehicle to his company. On 6 October 2008 the Ministry of the Interior temporarily seized the vehicle and its registration certificate from him to examine the chassis; a record of temporarily seized objects was issued.

On 1 February 2010 the Struga Court of First Instance acquitted Sh.A. of forgery of a document concerning the vehicle’s chassis number and rejected an indictment against I.S. It found that it had not been established that Sh.A. had altered the chassis. Under section 102(3) of the Criminal Proceedings Act, it advised the applicant, who had claimed compensation in the criminal proceedings, to pursue that claim in a separate civil action. That judgment became final on 21 July 2010.

On 16 November 2010 the applicant asked the first-instance court to return the vehicle. On 3 December 2010 the court heard him; he said he had bought the vehicle from Sh.A. for EUR 25,000 and could not have known at the time that its chassis number had been forged. On 6 December 2010 the court, relying on Article 100-a(3) of the Criminal Code, found no grounds to confiscate his vehicle: he had not known and could not have known that it had been used to commit a crime. It also ordered return of the registration certificate.

On the public prosecutor’s appeal, on 24 January 2011 the Bitola Court of Appeal quashed that decision. Relying on Article 100-a(2), it found that the chassis had been forged and that the vehicle, in the interest of public safety, could not be declared roadworthy. It referred to Article 100-a(3) and instructed the first-instance court to assess whether continued use of the vehicle would constitute the offence of using a forged document.

On 22 February 2011 the first-instance court dismissed the applicant’s application and ordered confiscation of the vehicle and registration certificate. Referring to Article 100-a(2) and (3), it found the chassis number had been forged and the vehicle could be used to commit an offence; for that reason and for road safety, confiscation was necessary. It referred to section 532(1) of the Criminal Proceedings Act and found that, although there were no proceedings against the applicant and he was not an offender, confiscation was necessary for general safety.

On 11 March 2011 the applicant appealed, arguing wrong application of Article 100-a(2) and (3) and that he had not known the vehicle had been used to commit a crime. On 19 May 2011 the appellate court dismissed the appeal and upheld the confiscation. It stated that it was true the applicant did not know the chassis had been forged, that he had registered the vehicle as last buyer, obtained a driving licence and paid a large amount. However, it considered that under Article 100-a(2) objects used to commit an offence are confiscated regardless of ownership if general safety, public health or ethics require it; the applicant’s lack of knowledge did not satisfy Article 100-a(3). The first-instance court had correctly found that use of the vehicle with forged identification numbers would affect road-user safety and general safety. The decision appears to have been served on the applicant on 2 June 2011.
001-167797:
CASE OF OTGON v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA (Application no. 22743/07) is a European Court of Human Rights case. The applicant, Ms Svetlana Otgon, a Moldovan national born in 1963 and living in Călărași, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that she had received insufficient compensation after domestic courts established a violation of her rights. The application was lodged on 20 April 2007 and communicated to the Moldovan Government, represented by Agent V. Grosu, on 30 November 2009.

The facts arose on 26 October 2005, when the applicant and her twelve-year-old daughter drank tap water in their apartment and soon felt unwell. On 29 October 2005 the daughter was admitted to hospital with a diagnosis of serious acute dysentery. The applicant was admitted with the same diagnosis on 31 October 2005 and discharged on 13 November 2005, one day after her daughter.

The applicant sued the local utilities provider, a State-owned company, seeking 100,000 Moldovan lei (MDL), approximately EUR 6,700 at the time, in compensation for harm to her health and related inconveniences, including subsequent investigations and disinfection.

On 1 March 2006 the Călărași District Court found in her favour. It relied on sanitary, medical and technical reports which showed that near the applicant’s apartment block the sewage pipe was situated above the drinking-water pipe and was leaking. The water pipe had cracked on 26 October 2005, allowing sewage water to infiltrate the drinking-water pipe. The court also found that the pipes had been in use since 1977, although their expected lifespan was fifteen years. Five people who had drunk water from the same pipe were admitted to hospital with the same diagnosis around the same time as the applicant. Taking into account the physical and mental suffering caused to the applicant and her daughter, the District Court awarded MDL 10,000, approximately EUR 648 at the time.

Both parties appealed. On 26 April 2006 the Chişinău Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s appeal and partly accepted the provider’s appeal. It reduced the award to MDL 5,000, approximately EUR 310, on the basis that both the sum claimed by the applicant and the sum awarded to her were exaggerated. The parties appealed further. On 25 October 2006 the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the judgment of 26 April 2006. It found that the lower court had considered the nature and seriousness of the mental suffering caused to the applicant and the degree of guilt of the defendant. That judgment was final.

The applicant then applied to the European Court of Human Rights. Her central complaint was that, despite the domestic courts’ establishment of a violation of her rights, the compensation ultimately awarded was insufficient. The key facts relevant to that alleged violation were therefore the confirmed contamination of the drinking-water supply by sewage; the resulting serious illness of the applicant and her daughter; the finding that the State-owned utilities provider was responsible; and the domestic courts’ decisions on damages, which reduced the initial award from MDL 10,000 to MDL 5,000. The European Court was thus called upon to assess whether that compensation was adequate for the purposes of Article 8 of the Convention.
001-159880:
In **Milojević and Others v. Serbia** (ECtHR, Third Section, 12 January 2016), three Serbian police officers—Ivan Milojević, Miodrag Radosavljević, and Petar Veličković—complained that their dismissal from the Ministry of Interior violated their right to private life and that the domestic judicial decisions upholding those dismissals were arbitrary. The Court communicated those complaints; the remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible.

The first and second applicants were arrested and charged on 26 April 2004 with abuse of power and instigation to abuse of power. Criminal proceedings were instituted, and the Ministry simultaneously began disciplinary proceedings and suspended them. On 7 June 2004, the Ministry dismissed both under Article 45 of the 1991 Ministry of Interior Act, relying on the fact that criminal proceedings were pending. Their appeals were rejected. The disciplinary proceedings were later stopped without a merits decision because their dismissal had made them redundant. Both were acquitted on 29 November 2004, and the acquittals became final on 29 March 2005.

After acquittal, they brought civil proceedings seeking annulment of the dismissals. The Municipal Court accepted their claims and ordered reinstatement, reasoning that Article 45 conferred broad discretionary power on the Ministry, left room for abuse, and that the applicants had been acquitted and dismissed without any disciplinary finding. The District Court upheld those decisions. However, in 2007 the Supreme Court quashed them. It held that the Ministry had lawfully exercised discretionary power under Article 45, that the acquittals and lack of disciplinary decisions were irrelevant, and that the lower courts had exceeded their authority by reviewing the necessity, proportionality, and correctness of the dismissals.

The third applicant was indicted in 1999 for unauthorized possession of weapons and ammunition. He was convicted in December 1999 and sentenced to one year’s imprisonment. In June 2000, the Ministry dismissed him under Article 45; no disciplinary proceedings were instituted. His conviction was confirmed in 2001, but after reopening, he was acquitted in September 2005, and the acquittal became final in February 2006. His civil claim for annulment initially succeeded before the Municipal Court in October 2006, but the District Court quashed that decision in February 2007, and the Supreme Court upheld it in August 2007, using reasoning similar to the first and second applicants’ cases: the dismissal was based solely on the initiation of criminal proceedings, and the later acquittal did not affect its legality.

The relevant legal framework was Article 45 of the 1991 Ministry of Interior Act, which allowed dismissal of police officers if criminal proceedings were pending or if they ceased to meet employment requirements. The Act did not expressly address the consequences of acquittal. Later, the 2005 Police Act repealed this regime and allowed only suspension pending criminal proceedings. The Constitutional Court, in decisions from 2011 and 2012, held that Article 45 gave a possibility, not an obligation, to dismiss, and that civil courts had to assess the lawfulness and proportionality of such dismissals and the purpose of the discretionary power. It found that failure to do so violated fair-trial and work rights.

The applicants alleged that dismissing them because criminal proceedings were pending—and refusing to revisit that dismissal after acquittal—breached their private life and produced arbitrary judicial decisions. The third applicant also noted that a co-defendant charged with the same offence was acquitted and remained employed, while he had received separate compensation for detention and reputational damage.
001-165750:
In Svitlana Atamanyuk and Others v. Ukraine, four Ukrainian applicants (relatives of the Mykhayliv family) complained about the Ukrainian authorities’ response to the 27 July 2002 Sknyliv air-show disaster in Lviv. The Air Force organized a military aviation show to mark the 60th anniversary of the 14th Air Force Corps, attended by several thousand spectators. During an aerobatics display, an SU-27 piloted by Colonels V.T. and Y.Y. crashed into the static aircraft display and spectator area and exploded. Both pilots ejected safely, but 77 people died and nearly 300 were injured. Four members of the Mykhayliv family—the first applicant’s daughter, her husband and their two daughters—died at the scene. The third applicant, who attended the show, suffered post-traumatic stress reaction.

The applicants alleged that the State failed to protect their relatives’ lives and to investigate effectively. The Special Government Commission found serious organisational and safety failures: the pilots had only one joint training flight, not a rehearsal; an additional training flight and on-site rehearsal were cancelled; the pilots were not informed of the aerobatics zone or spectator placement; they flew a different aircraft from the one used in training and without mandatory g-suits; they began immediately without familiarising themselves with the site. During the display the aircraft left the designated aerobatics zone, whose boundary was about 150 metres from spectators. Ground directors did not warn or redirect them. The first pilot then performed an unpractised manoeuvre not in his mission order. He made a technical error, the second pilot did not intervene, and control was lost, causing the crash.

The applicants further alleged inhuman and degrading treatment in the aftermath. They claimed that military authorities immediately cleaned the site, piled bodies, washed away blood and small remains, buried fragments and tried to prevent photography, thereby concealing evidence. Senior officials allegedly fled, obstructing emergency access. The Government denied this, saying law enforcement arrived promptly and bodies were inspected and transported carefully. The first and third applicants said they waited hours in heat at the mortuary and had to search through decomposing bodies and fragments. Forensic experts examined the bodies on 5 August 2002, finding fatal cerebral trauma and other injuries, based on external examination. The applicants complained that autopsies were performed despite objections, that a gold earring and body fragments, including Mrs Mykhayliv’s head extracted from the engine, were not returned. The Government said unidentified fragments were buried in a common grave after identification efforts; a distorted female head could not have been Mrs Mykhayliv’s because experts found her head completely destroyed.

Multiple investigations were opened by a presidential Special Commission, the Ministry of Defence, Lviv City Council, Prosecutor’s Office and an NGO. The applicants alleged that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the deaths; that the courts hearing their damages claim were not independent and impartial; that those proceedings were excessively lengthy; and that they had no effective remedy for the length complaint. These allegations formed the core of their applications to the European Court of Human Rights.
001-168382:
In **Naku v. Lithuania and Sweden** (Application no. 26126/07), the applicant, Ms Sniegė Naku, a Lithuanian national, worked at the Swedish embassy in Vilnius from 2 March 1992 until 2 January 2006. She began as a receptionist and translator and was later promoted to cultural, information and press officer. Her 2001 contract described her as an information officer handling cultural affairs, social secretarial duties, and replacements. A 2005 job description titled her “Cultural, Information and Press Officer,” with duties including coordinating cultural and information events, budgets, press matters, translations, and financial support applications. In 2004, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry issued her an accreditation certificate describing her as part of the embassy’s administrative-technical staff and stating that she had no diplomatic immunities or privileges. Her terms of employment provided that Lithuanian law applied to tax, social security, overtime, leave and dismissal, and that dismissal required objective grounds.

The applicant was also chairperson of the embassy’s locally employed staff trade union, registered in 1999. Between 2004 and 2005, the union complained about working conditions and proposed a collective agreement. The embassy refused, stating it was not bound by the Lithuanian Labour Code because of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

In autumn 2005, a Swedish counsellor became her superior and conflict arose over her duties. On 8 November 2005, the embassy drafted a new job description, which she disputed. The next day, the ambassador gave her a “letter of caution” alleging difficulties in cooperation, lack of performance, and constant questioning of duties, and asked her to resign within two days or face other action. She was asked to hand over her keys and leave the premises. On 11 November 2005, she went on sick leave and was later hospitalized for a neurological condition.

On 23 November 2005, the embassy proposed dismissing her for gross misconduct, citing allegations that she called a colleague “unbalanced,” opened a security-risk window, and held a private meeting at the embassy. She replied that these were pretexts linked to her trade-union activities and that she had received no prior warning. On 30 December 2005, the embassy dismissed her effective 2 January 2006 under Article 136 §3(2) of the Lithuanian Labour Code for gross misconduct. It also claimed she had not provided further sick certificates, although she maintained that certificates were delivered.

She sued the Swedish embassy in the Vilnius Regional Court, seeking a declaration that her dismissal was unlawful, reinstatement, and damages. She argued that dismissal while on sick leave violated Lithuanian law, that the misconduct allegations were false, and that her health and reputation had suffered. Sweden claimed State immunity from Lithuanian jurisdiction.

On 5 June 2006, the Vilnius Regional Court left the merits unexamined because Sweden invoked diplomatic immunity. It accepted limited immunity but found that her position as head of culture and information projects presupposed a public-law civil-service relationship linked to Swedish sovereignty. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling, holding that the job title alone showed her duties contributed to Sweden’s sovereign functions and that she had not proven otherwise. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal, ruling that all administrative and technical staff at a foreign embassy contribute to the represented State’s sovereign functions and are therefore in its civil service. It held that Sweden’s demand for immunity was sufficient to bar the Lithuanian courts. It also refused to refer the case to the European Court of Justice.

The applicant alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that the Lithuanian courts’ upholding of Sweden’s immunity deprived her of access to a court, contrary to Article 6 §1 of the Convention. The key alleged violation was that the Lithuanian courts failed to properly examine the nature and scope of her duties and instead relied on her job title and Sweden’s immunity claim, despite her being a locally employed worker under a private-law labour contract governed by Lithuanian law and without diplomatic immunity. The application was lodged on 18 June 2007 and communicated to the respondent Governments on 7 December 2010.
001-165230:
The case of Adam v. Slovakia concerned allegations of police ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation in Slovakia. The applicant, Jaroslav Adam, was a Slovak national of Romani origin who was sixteen years old at the relevant time. On 18 December 2010, a twelve-year-old boy was mugged and his mobile phone taken. Police searched the area with the boy and his father and, around 8 p.m., spotted the applicant, another minor, and a third person, all of Romani origin. The boy identified them as his assailants, and they were arrested.

The circumstances of the arrest were disputed. The Government maintained that the suspects resisted and tried to flee, so police used “self-defence mechanisms for holding and grabbing” and no injuries were sustained. The applicant denied resisting or being restrained. The three were taken to the county police station. Breathalyser tests indicated they had consumed alcohol, and the applicant was slightly intoxicated. They were held in rooms used as offices, not detention cells.

The applicant alleged that during preliminary questioning police used psychological pressure and physical violence to obtain a confession. He claimed he was slapped and punched in the head, forced to remain standing without sitting, lying down, or resting throughout his detention, and given no food or water. The Government denied ill-treatment, saying the suspects were kept separately, checked every fifteen minutes, and had access to a toilet with drinkable water.

In the early hours of 19 December 2010, the applicant was charged with robbery. A lawyer was appointed, and between noon and 1 p.m. he was interviewed by an investigator in the presence of his mother and lawyer. No ill-treatment was mentioned. Later he was placed in a provisional detention cell; documents stated he reported no violence and had received dinner. He was released at 6:05 p.m. and taken home. His mother later declined to give evidence and made no mention of ill-treatment. An appeal against the charge also did not raise ill-treatment, and the charge was withdrawn on 12 January 2011.

On 5 January 2011, the applicant and his associates filed a written criminal complaint with the Ministry of the Interior against county police officers. They alleged pressure to confess, slapping until confession, forced standing, lack of food and water, and failure to notify guardians. A medical report dated 19 December 2010 recorded an allegation of a slap to the right cheek, a sensitive and slightly swollen cheek, no haematoma, and a slight injury requiring recovery under seven days.

The complaint was examined by the Control and Inspection Section, which dismissed it on 9 March 2011. It reasoned that the applicant had not complained during his interview with his mother and lawyer, that the medical findings did not match later claims of sustained beating, that any injury could have occurred during a resisted arrest, and that the officers were only guarding him and had no reason to pressure a confession. Appeals to the prosecution authorities were dismissed in September 2011. A separate complaint about failure to notify guardians, provide food and water, and hear him promptly was rejected without explanation in June 2011.

The applicant then lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging violations of Article 3 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation), Article 13 (no effective remedy), and Article 14 (discrimination), relying on known police violence against Roma in Slovakia. On 10 April 2012, the Constitutional Court rejected it as manifestly ill-founded, saying he had not raised ill-treatment before the investigator or in his appeal against the charge, and that the availability of those means excluded its jurisdiction.
001-164434:
The case concerns an application by Mr Isteyfo Özçelik, a Netherlands national born in 1959, against the Netherlands. He complained under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention that the lawfulness of his continued detention had not been decided “speedily”. The detention arose from a measure of placement in a Persistent Offenders Institution (ISD).

On 21 May 2010 the Almelo Regional Court convicted the applicant of shoplifting and imposed an ISD measure for two years. The measure aims to protect society and prevent reoffending, and may last a maximum of two years from the date the judgment becomes final. The Regional Court ordered a review six months after the judgment became final on 5 June 2010. On 1 December 2010 the Regional Court declined to terminate the measure because there was still a high risk of reoffending. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed by the Arnhem Court of Appeal on 19 April 2011.

On 19 May 2011 the applicant’s personal case officer reported that his placement at FPA De Cederborg was progressing reasonably, but that if the measure were terminated he would immediately have no income, housing or daily activities, making the risk of reoffending high. Continuation was recommended. On 9 June 2011 the Regional Court prolonged the measure, finding a considerable likelihood of reoffending after release.

The applicant appealed against that prolongation on 15 June 2011. This appeal is central to the alleged violation. On 8 November 2011 his counsel inquired about the progress of the appeal and requested priority. On 18 November 2011 counsel requested an interpreter speaking Aramaic or Assyrian and named a suitable interpreter.

On 12 December 2011 a hearing took place before the Court of Appeal. The applicant could not understand the Assyrian interpreter. With his agreement, the case was adjourned for up to three months to allow written questions to be put to his counsellors and for the case officer to be heard as an expert witness, with an Aramaic interpreter required at the next hearing. After three months, counsel again inquired about progress on 13 March and 2 April 2012. The hearing resumed on 10 May 2012. The case officer testified that the applicant was no longer addicted, that the risk of reoffending was maximally reduced, that treatment possibilities had been exhausted, and that the applicant was in a halfway house awaiting sheltered accommodation. Accommodation became available on 11 May 2012.

On 16 May 2012 the Court of Appeal delivered its decision. It held that the appeal had not been dealt with speedily within the meaning of Article 6 ECHR, as more than ten months had passed since the appeal was lodged, and considered that finding sufficient satisfaction. It nevertheless terminated the measure because execution had not been sufficiently expeditious at all stages, the difficult progress could not be attributed solely to the applicant, the institution could have signalled earlier that no further treatment was possible, and accommodation and reduced risk made continuation unnecessary.

Under domestic law, the ISD measure is governed by Article 38m of the Criminal Code and has a maximum duration of two years. Interim reviews are possible, and if continuation is no longer required the measure must be terminated. Article 509gg of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the Court of Appeal to decide as speedily as possible on appeals involving the ISD measure. The key facts relevant to the Article 5 § 4 complaint are therefore the continued detention measure, the 15 June 2011 appeal against its prolongation, repeated requests for progress, the interpreter-related adjournment, the resumed hearing on 10 May 2012, and the decision of 16 May 2012—approximately eleven months after the appeal was lodged.
001-164682:
**Žekonienė v. Lithuania** concerned a Lithuanian applicant, Janina Žekonienė, who alleged that her provisional arrest in March 2010 was unlawful and arbitrary and that the conditions of her detention were inadequate.

The events arose from a pre-trial investigation into her son, V.Ž. On 17 February 2010 Šakiai police arrested him on suspicion of unlawful possession of narcotic substances with intent to distribute. The same day police searched the apartment the applicant shared with her son and found small plastic bags. The next day they searched her daughter’s apartment; the applicant provided the keys and was present. Police found plastic bags, digital scales, and remnants of herbal substances. The son was later detained.

On 2 March 2010 police discovered that V.Ž. had unlawfully brought a mobile phone into detention. Although most data had been deleted, recovered text messages from his fiancée included statements such as “mother already knows what to do,” “It’s all hidden now,” and “Your mother was questioned today and almost got arrested.” Those messages contributed to suspicion that the applicant had hidden drugs from investigators.

On 3 March 2010, the applicant—then 69 years old—went to Šakiai Police Station to bring her detained son food and clothes. At 4 p.m. an investigator placed her under provisional arrest under Article 140 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The arrest decision stated that she was suspected of drug possession with intent to distribute and that arrest was necessary to prevent her from fleeing, interfering with the investigation, or committing further crimes, because she was suspected of having hidden drugs. The record stated that her rights, including the right to a lawyer, were explained; she refused to sign. She was placed in a cell near her son, and her husband was informed.

On 4 March she was served with an official suspect notice alleging that in February 2010 she had acquired drugs, kept them in her daughter’s apartment for distribution, and distributed them. She was questioned with a lawyer, denied the crimes, and refused further questions. She became weak and suffered headache and chest pain; an ambulance was called and she received first aid. Her lawyer requested release, arguing she had committed no crime and that the arrest was intended to pressure her to testify against her son. At 3:50 p.m. she was released because the necessary investigative actions had been completed and there were no grounds to believe she would interfere. The next day the prosecutor rejected the release request as unfounded. On 30 September 2010 the investigation against her was discontinued for insufficient evidence. Her son was later convicted.

The applicant brought civil proceedings for damages. She argued that the arrest was unfounded and unnecessary: the investigation against her was discontinued; she was almost seventy, ailing, had difficulty walking, no prior convictions, was retired, and lived with her husband. She claimed she had voluntarily come to the police station and that there had been no prior indication that she was suspected or interfering. She alleged the real purpose was to force her to testify against her son. She also claimed pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, including health deterioration and humiliation before her son and villagers. At the domestic hearing she added that police searched her purse and tried to strip-search her, and that her cell was damp, dilapidated, and smelled from the toilet, making her nauseous.

Domestic courts dismissed her claim. They held that discontinuance did not make the arrest unlawful from the outset, finding sufficient grounds based on the plastic bags, drug remnants, and the son’s phone messages. They also noted she had not appealed the prosecutor’s refusal to release her. The courts did not address her detention-condition complaints. Appeals failed, and the Supreme Court refused to examine the case. The ECtHR therefore examined whether the provisional arrest complied with the Convention’s requirements, particularly whether the exceptional conditions for provisional arrest were met, and whether the detention conditions raised a separate violation.
001-166950:
In *Moog v. Germany* (Applications nos. 23280/08 and 2334/10), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Claus Moog, a German national, that German court decisions concerning contact with his son, D., violated his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant lodged the applications in 2008 and 2010, the second also on behalf of his son.

D. was born in July 1998. His parents separated in 1999, and D. lived with his mother, Ms K. From 1999 onward, the parents were in continuous dispute over contact and custody. Initially, the father was granted contact, later fixed at eight hours every Saturday. The mother was repeatedly accused of failing to cooperate, and the Family Court warned and eventually fined her. In 2002, an expert considered that D. enjoyed contact with his father but that the parents instrumentalised the child and could not communicate, so joint custody was impossible. The mother was granted custody, while the father received six hours of contact per week and a contact facilitator was appointed.

In 2003, the Cologne Court of Appeal found that the mother had “intentionally sabotaged” contact and warned that custody might have to be reconsidered. However, later that year the same court quashed a fine against her, relying on a paediatrician’s report that D. showed mental abnormalities after contact with the father, caused by parental conflict; enforcing contact would therefore harm the child. In 2005, the mother applied to suspend contact. D. told the court he no longer wished to see his father. In 2006, the child’s paediatrician stated in an affidavit that D. had been deeply traumatised by forced contact and parental hostility, had aggressive outbursts, and needed psychotherapy. Attempts at supervised contact failed after the mother and child were advised not to speak to the applicant on medical grounds.

In 2007, the kindergarten director recommended continuing contact, finding D. overly controlled by his mother and in need of a counterbalancing authority figure. The Family Court provisionally granted monthly contact, ordered the mother to prepare D. and not influence him against his father, and warned of fines. The first visit failed when D. refused to leave with the applicant. The Youth Office reported that D. wanted peace and did not want to see his father, while his teacher said the father lacked empathy. The Family Court fined the mother EUR 3,000.

In February 2008, the Court of Appeal quashed the fine. It cited a psychologist’s certificate that the mother suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder and doubted her ability to prepare D. for contact. It also noted D.’s stated unwillingness and preferred therapy to forced contact. In December 2008, the Family Court suspended the applicant’s contact until 31 December 2011. It found that the severe parental conflict would create a serious loyalty conflict for D., that the mother’s stress disorder prevented cooperation, that forced contact could retraumatise the child, and that D. needed trauma therapy.

The applicant appealed. In January 2009, a custody expert preliminarily opined that contact would not endanger D.’s welfare. In May 2009, custody remained with the mother, although the court noted her obstructive attitude. In June 2009, the Court of Appeal confirmed the contact suspension, acknowledging that the mother had effectively achieved her aim, but relying on D.’s repeated statements that he did not want to see his father and associated him with court proceedings. It considered a period of respite necessary and stated that the loyalty conflict was not solely the mother’s fault. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s complaint in August 2009. The applicant alleged that these decisions, especially the three-year suspension of contact, violated his Article 8 right to respect for family life.
001-168853:
**Case Summary: Galaida and Coposciu v. the Republic of Moldova**

The case of *Galaida and Coposciu v. the Republic of Moldova* (Applications nos. 29732/07 and 41421/07) was a judgment delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) on 24 November 2016. The case originated from two separate applications lodged against the Republic of Moldova under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants, Nicolae Galaida and Vitalie Coposciu, both complained of inadequate conditions of their detention and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law to address these grievances. The applications were communicated to the Moldovan Government, and the Court deliberated on the facts and merits.

The first applicant, Nicolae Galaida, was detained at Prison no. 17 from 16 June 2007 to 25 March 2008, a total duration of 9 months and 10 days. During his detention, he was afforded approximately 4.48 square meters of personal space. The specific grievances relevant to the alleged violation were a lack of sufficient natural light, a lack of adequate heating, and overcrowding. These conditions formed the basis of his complaint under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment.

The second applicant, Vitalie Coposciu, experienced a significantly longer and more fragmented period of detention across multiple facilities. His detention began on 3 February 2006 and continued with various transfers until 25 June 2015. He was held in Prison no. 13, Prison no. 1, and Prison no. 3 for durations ranging from as little as 6 days to over 3 years. Throughout his extensive detention, the space allocated per inmate was recorded at 1.5 square meters, a figure significantly below acceptable standards. The specific grievances cited across his numerous detentions were consistent and severe, including overcrowding, poor quality of food, lack of adequate heating, and, at times, lack of fresh air. For instance, his detention at Prison no. 1 from 15 March 2006 to 8 August 2006 involved poor food quality, overcrowding, and inadequate heating. His longest continuous period at Prison no. 13 from 15 March 2012 to 25 June 2015 was marked by overcrowding, a lack of adequate heating, and poor food quality.

The core legal issue before the Court was whether these conditions of detention amounted to a violation of Article 3 (prohibition of torture, inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention. The facts presented in the appended table—specifically the extremely low square meterage per inmate, which fell well below the minimum standard of 4 square meters recommended by the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), and the consistent grievances regarding heating, light, and food—were central to the assessment. The applicants argued that the State failed to provide them with humane conditions of detention and offered no domestic mechanism for redress, thereby violating their fundamental rights under the Convention. The case was ultimately decided based on these key factual elements concerning the physical conditions of their imprisonment and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.
001-169957:
In *Sagvolden v. Norway*, the applicant, Torill Sagvolden, was a Norwegian national who acquired an apartment in Housing Cooperative X in March 2004. Before moving in, the cooperative discovered that her son, Mr A, had caused serious problems in Housing Cooperative Y, where the applicant had previously lived and where her son had cohabited with her. The Board therefore asked for a written undertaking that Mr A would not move into the new apartment. In May 2004, the applicant’s lawyer confirmed that she, not her son, would move in and that her household would consist of one person. The Board maintained its approval on that basis.

Mr A later moved into the applicant’s apartment. Between 2005 and 2008, he repeatedly engaged in violent assault, frightening behaviour, and harassment against neighbours in Housing Cooperative X. He was convicted by Oslo City Court on 10 March 2006 and 23 June 2008, receiving prison sentences. The courts described him as aggressive, intrusive, and prone to conspiracy perceptions, and found that his conduct seriously harmed neighbours’ sense of safety in their homes. He was also subjected to several restraining orders prohibiting contact with four neighbours between 2007 and 2009.

In April 2009, the cooperative issued an order requiring the applicant to sell her apartment under the Housing Cooperative Act 2003, relying on serious disturbance and nuisance. When she refused, the cooperative instituted proceedings for compulsory sale. The applicant objected, arguing that the Board’s decision did not validly authorise compulsory sale, that her son’s offences were dated and the situation had improved, that she was eighty years old and increasingly dependent on her son, that she had no realistic alternative housing, and that less intrusive measures should be considered. She also requested an oral hearing under the ordinary procedure, since domestic law required such examination if objections against compulsory sale were not “clearly groundless.”

On 26 April 2010, Oslo City Court rejected her objections as clearly groundless and ordered compulsory sale. It held that the part owner was responsible for household members’ conduct, that Mr A’s behaviour constituted substantial default, and that no prior warning was needed because the conditions for eviction under section 5-23 were met. It further found that the applicant’s age did not outweigh the neighbours’ interests. The High Court rejected her appeal on 5 August 2010, deciding on the written file without an oral hearing and agreeing that the objections were clearly groundless. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 1 October 2010.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 about the absence of an oral hearing before the national courts in the compulsory-sale proceedings, despite the serious consequences for her home. She complained under Article 8 that the compulsory sale was not “necessary” in a democratic society. The key facts relevant to those complaints were the domestic-law requirement of an ordinary procedure with an oral hearing unless objections were clearly groundless; the national courts’ determination that her objections were clearly groundless and could be decided in writing; the long-running serious harassment by her son; the applicant’s confirmation that only she would occupy the flat; her age and dependence on her son; and her claims that the situation had improved and that less intrusive measures were available. Subsequent proceedings validated the sale and led to eviction steps. The applicant died in November 2015.
001-163799:
**Case: Tchankotadze v. Georgia (Application no. 15256/05)**

Zurab Tchankotadze, a Georgian national, chaired the Civil Aviation Agency of Georgia (“CAA”) from March 2002 to March 2004. In January 2003, the Constitutional Court declared unconstitutional the “annual regulation fee for transport activities” imposed on civil aviation companies, effective 1 April 2003. The judgment indicated that the CAA could instead provide services through freely negotiated contracts. After that date, the applicant signed contracts in March and August 2003 with Sakaeronavigatsia, Tbilisi International Airport and Air-BP-Georgia under which the CAA charged a monthly “fee for services rendered in relation to the regulation of activities.” The CAA received about GEL 600,000 between April and September 2003. In November 2003, he issued Order no. 1, applied retrospectively from 1 October 2003, under which the CAA collected further fees from 22 companies, amounting to about GEL 774,376 by March 2004. Prosecutors alleged that these measures disguised the old unconstitutional regulation fee and circumvented the Constitutional Court’s judgment.

In February 2004, criminal proceedings were opened against unnamed CAA and Ministry officials. On 16 March 2004, the applicant was charged with repeated abuse of power under Article 332 §§ 1 and 3(a) of the Criminal Code and arrested. Pre-trial detention was ordered on 19 March for three months and extended on 14 June until 16 September 2004; that extension was final and not appealable. After 16 September 2004, detention was not formally extended, yet the applicant remained in custody. On 1 February 2005, he complained to the trial court that his detention since 16 September 2004 was unlawful. On 16 March 2005, the court committed him for trial and maintained detention based on the “nature of the charges,” without addressing his complaint. These facts underpinned his Article 5 § 1 complaint that his pre-trial detention was unlawful.

The Article 6 § 1 fairness complaint concerned the trial. An accountancy expert concluded that the CAA’s fees were based on valid legal acts, that the companies suffered no financial damage, that the fees were passed on to consumers, and that the applicant received no personal profit beyond salary and travel allowances. Company representatives confirmed they had freely entered contracts or paid under Order no. 1 and suffered no loss. CAA officials testified that the CAA was not state-funded and that contracts were necessary to avoid collapse of civil aviation regulation. Nevertheless, on 8 August 2005, the Tbilisi City Court convicted the applicant for the contracts and Order no. 1, acquitting him on one episode. It found he breached the Constitutional Court judgment but gave little reasoning, rejected his arguments without explanation, and disregarded the expert report. He was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment and banned from public office for two years. The Court of Appeal in December 2005 acquitted him regarding 14 companies but upheld the remaining conviction and reduced the sentence to four years. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in September 2006. He was released in March 2008 after serving the full sentence.

Finally, for Article 18, the applicant relied on a December 2003 speech by presidential candidate Mikheil Saakashvili, who publicly threatened that the applicant should remove a deputy CAA chairperson or “go to jail.” After Saakashvili’s election, the deputy resigned, the applicant was investigated and arrested in March 2004, and the deputy later entered parliament on Saakashvili’s party list. The applicant alleged that the prosecution and detention were politically motivated. He lodged his application on 12 March 2005, complaining of breaches of Articles 5 § 1, 6 § 1 and 18.
001-165758:
**Wenner v. Germany** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, App. No. 62303/13, judgment 1 September 2016) concerned a German prisoner’s complaint that the refusal to provide him with drug substitution treatment during imprisonment—and the refusal to have the medical necessity of such treatment examined by an external addiction expert—violated Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1955, had been addicted to heroin since 1973. He also suffered from hepatitis C since 1975 and had been HIV-positive since 1988. He was considered 100% disabled and received a disability pension. Between 1991 and 2008, his heroin addiction was treated with medically prescribed substitution therapy, mainly Polamidon. From 2005, he reduced the dosage and additionally consumed heroin.

In 2008, he was arrested on drug-trafficking suspicion and detained on remand in Kaisheim Prison. His substitution treatment was interrupted against his will. In June 2009, he was convicted and sentenced to several years’ imprisonment. The court also ordered his placement in a drug detoxification facility. He was transferred to a rehabilitation centre in Günzburg in December 2009, where he received abstinence-based treatment without substitution. In April 2010, the detoxification order was terminated and he was returned to Kaisheim Prison.

While in prison, the applicant suffered chronic pain from polyneuropathy, often spending most of his time in bed. An external doctor, H., suggested that the prison medical service reconsider substitution treatment, and recommended examination by a drug-addiction specialist. The applicant also obtained an opinion from Dr B., an external addiction specialist, who concluded that substitution treatment was medically necessary. Dr B. stated that substitution was internationally recognised as the best therapy for long-standing opioid addicts, that forced abstinence caused serious physical and mental strain, and that substitution could prevent deterioration, reduce infection risks, and make hepatitis C treatment possible.

In June 2011, the applicant requested Diamorphin, Polamidon, or another heroin substitute, or alternatively that an external specialist examine whether substitution was necessary. He relied on the Federal Medical Association’s Guidelines for Substitution Treatment of Opiate Addicts, arguing that substitution was the standard treatment for his condition and should be continued in detention.

The prison authorities refused the request in January 2012. They argued that substitution was neither medically necessary nor suitable for rehabilitation. Relying on the prison doctor, they said the applicant no longer suffered physical withdrawal symptoms after three years in detention, his HIV and hepatitis C were stable, and no treatment requiring substitution was needed. They also claimed he could use prison to wean himself off opioids, that prior substitution had not prevented drug use or crime, and that he had consumed drugs in detention, so substitution could pose risks. The Augsburg Regional Court upheld the refusal and found no need for an external addiction expert. The Munich Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint.

Relevant domestic law under the Bavarian Execution of Sentences Act entitled prisoners to medical treatment if necessary to detect, cure, prevent aggravation of, or alleviate illness. Federal Medical Association Guidelines recognised substitution as a scientifically tested therapy for opiate addiction and required continuity of substitution during imprisonment. Council of Europe standards required equivalence of prison health care with community care. Statistical data showed that opioid substitution programmes were available in prisons in many Council of Europe states.

The applicant alleged that refusing him substitution treatment, and refusing an external expert review, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3, given his severe chronic pain, long-term addiction, and medical conditions.
001-166689:
In *Johansen v. Germany* (Application no. 17914/10), the applicant, a German national, was convicted by a penal order issued by the Frankfurt am Main District Court on 16 October 2008 for withholding and embezzlement of employee salaries. She was fined 100 daily rates of EUR 50. The central issue was whether she had validly received the penal order, because her later objection was rejected as out of time.

According to the record of service, a courier attempted to hand the penal order to the applicant at her home on 7 November 2008 at 2:10 p.m. When personal delivery was not possible, the courier placed the penal order in the mailbox attached to her residence, which constituted substituted service under Article 180 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

On 27 December 2008, the applicant filed an objection and applied for reinstatement of the proceedings. She claimed the penal order had never been served on 7 November. She said she first learned of it on 20 December 2008, when she found a court cashier’s bill in her mailbox demanding payment of the fine. She asserted that on 7 November she had checked her mailbox in the presence of her lawyer and found neither the penal order nor any notice of deposit.

In support, her lawyer, husband, and mother provided affirmations in lieu of an oath. They stated that the lawyer and applicant had returned to her house around 12:15 p.m. after a hearing at the Hanau District Court; her husband and mother were already there. No one rang the doorbell; the applicant’s dogs would have barked if someone had. Around 3:30 p.m., when the group left, the applicant took the mail from her mailbox and checked it. There was no official court letter, which would have been in a conspicuous yellow envelope. The lawyer also submitted that the private postal company J., responsible for delivering court mail, was unreliable and had become insolvent in December 2008.

The District Court rejected the objection as inadmissible and refused reinstatement on 9 April 2009. It relied on the record of service, which under Article 418 of the Code of Civil Procedure has probative value unless counter-evidence shows there was no possibility the certified facts were correct. A police interview of the courier revealed that she said she always rang doorbells and left a notification notice if no one answered; she confirmed her signature but said her husband filled in the date and time. She did not remember the specific delivery. The company reported no known irregularities. The court found the applicant’s account fabricated because the witnesses were close to her, she had initially omitted some of them, and it was unusual to check mail in front of family. Even if the courier failed to ring the doorbell, actual service by placing the order in the mailbox was valid.

The Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 10 June 2009, endorsing the District Court’s reasoning. It found insufficient counter-evidence: the courier and her husband had no motive to embezzle or forge, and the affirmations could not prove the penal order was absent. It said the applicant might have been inattentive and thrown it away or ignored it. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider her complaint on 22 September 2009 without reasons.

The applicant alleged a breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, arguing that the refusal to accept her late objection and reinstate the proceedings denied her a fair trial and effective access to court to challenge the criminal conviction. The key facts therefore concerned the validity of substituted service, the weight of the service record, and the domestic courts’ treatment of her counter-evidence.
001-163331:

001-169654:
**Case summary: Lindstrand Partners Advokatbyrå AB v. Sweden (Application no. 18700/09)**

The applicant was a Swedish law firm, Lindstrand Partners Advokatbyrå AB (formerly Hagenfeldt Advokatbyrå AB). The case arose from tax audits and coercive measures carried out by the Swedish Tax Agency in 2006–2008 concerning three companies, including SNS-LAN Trading AB (“SNS”) and Draupner Universal AB (“Draupner”). The Tax Agency suspected tax evasion through irregular transactions with a Swiss company and considered that Mr Toivo Jurik, who was connected to the Swedish companies, had a decisive role.

In March 2008, the Tax Agency applied to the County Administrative Court for permission to use coercive measures against SNS, including search and seizure of documents. Since SNS had been liquidated and had no premises, the Agency sought to search two locations connected to Mr Jurik: a flat/registered address of Draupner and the offices of the applicant law firm, where Mr Jurik had an office. The Agency requested that SNS not be notified in advance because of the risk that documents might be destroyed. On 10 March 2008, the County Administrative Court granted the application and made it immediately enforceable.

The search took place on 14 March 2008. At the flat, 19 files, an external hard disk drive, and a torn document were seized; a computer hard disk and a USB memory stick were copied. The law firm’s premises were then searched, including the offices of Mr Jurik and Mr Möller, but no relevant material was found there. During the flat search, the Tax Agency decided on-site to audit Draupner and took an interim decision to use coercive measures against it, allowing searches at both the flat and the law firm. That decision was later confirmed by the County Administrative Court.

The applicant requested that the seized and copied material—especially the external hard disk and USB stick—be exempted from the audit, arguing that it was protected by attorney-client privilege because SNS and Draupner were clients and the devices had been used by Mr Jurik in his law practice. The courts dismissed the request, finding that the applicant lacked legal standing because the coercive measures had not been directed against the law firm and the material had been seized from Draupner. The Administrative Court of Appeal held that the applicant was not sufficiently affected to appeal; the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal.

Draupner also sought exemption of documents. The courts generally rejected those requests, holding that material found at Draupner’s premises was presumed to belong to its business and be eligible for audit. They found no attorney-client privilege because the Tax Agency had not ordered the law firm to provide information and the documents had not been seized at the law firm. Some private documents were later exempted.

The applicant also challenged the impartiality of a co-opted judge in the Administrative Court of Appeal who was a Tax Agency civil servant on leave. The objection was rejected by the domestic courts.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key complaints concerned the search and seizure at a law firm, the copying and potential examination of privileged material, the refusal to recognize the applicant’s standing to seek exemption, the alleged lack of effective judicial review, and the alleged lack of impartiality. The audits were eventually discontinued, no tax decisions were issued, and all documents were returned.
001-162424:
**Abdi Mahamud v. Malta** (Application no. 56796/13) concerned a Somali national, Ms Sagal Abdi Mahamud, born in 1992, who entered Malta irregularly by boat on 6 May 2012. On arrival she was registered by immigration police, given an identification number, and served with a Return Decision and a Removal Order under Article 14(2) of the Immigration Act. The Return Decision stated she was a prohibited immigrant because she had no means of subsistence and was liable to become a charge on public funds. The Removal Order, issued after her request for voluntary departure was rejected, provided that she would remain in custody until removal and that an entry ban would be issued. Both documents advised her of a right to appeal to the Immigration Appeals Board within three working days.

On 9 May 2012 the applicant submitted a preliminary questionnaire indicating her wish to apply for asylum. She was interviewed by the Office of the Refugee Commissioner on 21 May 2012. Her asylum application was rejected on 30 June 2012, partly because she allegedly gave insufficient convincing evidence that she came from central or southern Somalia. The Refugee Appeals Board dismissed her appeal on 18 December 2012. By the date she lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights, 19 August 2013, no steps had been taken regarding her removal. In practice, Malta did not effect removals to Somalia or Somaliland.

The applicant’s detention was central to her complaints. She was held at Lyster Barracks Detention Centre in Ħal Far. She alleged that her continued detention was arbitrary and unlawful and that she had no effective remedy to challenge its lawfulness, relying on Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention. She also complained about detention conditions under Article 3.

A significant factual issue concerned her vulnerability. From arrival she suffered from headaches, earaches, fainting, and other medical problems, and was frequently hospitalised. She showed severe anxiety and depression, which worsened after her asylum rejection. In October 2012 the Jesuit Refugee Service referred her to the Agency for the Welfare of Asylum Seekers (AWAS) for release from detention on vulnerability grounds. In December 2012 she was interviewed briefly by AWAS, in English, assisted by another detainee who was not fluent in the language. On 10 August 2013 she was verbally informed she would be released, but she remained detained when she applied to the Court on 19 August 2013. She was eventually released on 12 September 2013. The applicant argued that the AWAS vulnerability assessment procedure had a determining impact on continued detention yet was not adequately regulated by law, gave no written reasons, and offered no appeal.

As to conditions, the applicant described Lyster Barracks as prison-like and basic. Zone C held over eighty women and was so crowded that some slept on metal tables. Zone D was less crowded but lacked privacy and sanitation. She complained of a lack of constructive activities, overcrowding, limited open-air access, communication difficulties, lack of information, and extreme temperatures. She also highlighted the lack of female staff: male soldiers allegedly entered the women’s dormitory each morning while they slept and removed sheets during head counts, forcing her to sleep fully dressed, including her headscarf. She further complained of limited access to medical care and a lack of interpreters for medical communication.

The case therefore focused on whether her prolonged immigration detention, the absence of judicial review, and the conditions at Lyster Barracks violated Articles 3 and 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention.
001-168864:
**Summary of *Svystoruk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 50067/13)**

The case of *Svystoruk v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Viktor Petrovych Svystoruk, a Ukrainian national, on 26 July 2013. The application alleged that the Ukrainian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the murder of his daughter, Inna Puzyr.

The underlying facts are as follows. On 11 August 2007, Inna Puzyr was found stabbed to death by the roadside. The Poltava Regional Police immediately instituted criminal proceedings for suspected murder. Initially, the applicant was summoned only as a witness, and his request to join the proceedings as an aggrieved party was refused. Subsequently, on 18 August 2007, his other daughter, V.K., was admitted as an aggrieved party.

The investigation was marked by a series of arrests and releases. On 25 August 2007, a local resident, O.T., was arrested. He initially confessed but later retracted his statement, alleging police ill-treatment. The proceedings against him were discontinued due to a lack of corroborating evidence. On 7 September 2007, V.K. formally complained to the police about the investigation's ineffectiveness and her inability to meaningfully participate, noting she was denied access to the case file and poorly informed of progress. The police denied any irregularities.

The investigation was suspended on 10 October 2007 due to a lack of leads, but this decision was quickly quashed by the prosecutor's office, which noted the investigation had been "perfunctory." In November 2007, V.K. again complained of ineffectiveness, suspecting her sister's husband, R.P., and pointing to investigative delays that had resulted in the loss of important evidence.

In January 2008, the police acknowledged significant inadequacies in the investigation, reprimanded supervisors, and replaced the lead investigator. A breakthrough appeared to occur on 5 March 2008, when R.P. was arrested and confessed to the murder. However, he later retracted his confession, claiming it was given under duress. Consequently, on 15 August 2008, the proceedings against him were also discontinued due to irreconcilable discrepancies between his retracted confession and other evidence. The case was suspended again.

Over the next several years, the investigation was repeatedly renewed and suspended. In May 2009, the Deputy Minister of Interior ordered a renewal after reviewing the file, noting that leads to at least two potential perpetrators had not been properly followed and that virtually no action had been taken in 2008. Despite this, the pattern of suspension and renewal continued into 2011 due to insufficient investigative measures.

A key development occurred on 15 April 2013, when, under a new Code of Criminal Procedure, the applicant was finally admitted as an aggrieved party and granted access to the case file. After reviewing the file, the applicant complained to the Minister of Interior on 19 August 2013. He argued that the entire investigation had been marred by prohibitive delays and inactivity, with authorities having focused excessively on a single theory (the husband's involvement) rather than conducting a prompt and comprehensive examination of objective evidence. He provided specific suggestions for further investigative steps, including potential witnesses and the type of weapon used.

The authorities responded by stating that while no new leads had been uncovered, his suggestions would be considered. This pattern of acknowledging suggestions but reporting no progress continued in response to further complaints. The applicant's core complaint to the Strasbourg Court was that the investigation into his daughter's murder was ineffective and protracted, violating Ukraine's obligation under Article 2 of the Convention to conduct a thorough and prompt investigation into a death caused by violence.
001-160800:
In *Meier v. Switzerland* (Application no. 10109/14), Third Section, judgment of 9 February 2016, the applicant was Beat Meier, a Swiss national born in 1946, detained in Regensdorf. In 2003 the Zurich Court of Appeal sentenced him to four years and four months’ imprisonment for multiple sexual acts with minors and multiple acts of sexual coercion. In 2010 the execution of that sentence was suspended and replaced by preventive detention designed to prevent reoffending. Because he was subject to a custodial measure, Swiss law—Article 90(3) of the Criminal Code—applied the prison work rules by analogy.

The alleged violations arose from the requirement that Meier continue working after reaching retirement age. In December 2011 he requested exemption from the prison work requirement. On 19 March 2012 the Judicial Enforcements Office of the Canton of Zurich refused. After he refused to work, Pöschwies Prison on 29 May 2012 placed him under a stricter regime, confining him to his cell and confiscating his television and computer for fourteen days. That disciplinary decision was revoked on 31 July 2012, but the refusal of exemption was upheld by the Directorate of Justice and Internal Affairs on 20 June 2012, the Administrative Court of Zurich on 10 January 2013, and the Federal Court on 18 July 2013.

The Federal Court held that compulsory prison work was not in itself contrary to human rights or Article 4 of the Convention. It pursued aims such as developing or maintaining work capacity, structuring daily life, maintaining order, fostering social behaviour, and, for prisoners over 65, avoiding the harmful effects of isolation and mental or physical deterioration. Work had to be tailored to the prisoner’s abilities; lighter or therapeutic activity could be used. Pension rules under the Old-Age and Survivors’ Insurance Act did not apply because prison work was not comparable to competitive employment. Voluntary work was considered insufficient to achieve the aims of compulsory prison work.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Meier complained that requiring him to work after retirement age breached Articles 4 and 14 of the Convention—prohibition of forced or compulsory labour and discrimination. Relevant domestic law included Articles 7 and 10 of the Federal Constitution (human dignity and personal freedom), Articles 74, 75, 81 and 90 of the Criminal Code (dignity, resocialisation, normal life, support, and compulsory work matched to ability), and Article 103 of the Zurich Justice Enforcement Order.

International materials included ILO Convention No. 29, Article 2(2)(c) of which excludes work exacted as a consequence of conviction under public supervision; European Prison Rules 2006 Rule 105.2, stating that sentenced prisoners who have not reached normal retirement age may be required to work subject to fitness; and CPT concerns about older prisoners required to work beyond retirement age. Switzerland replied that the work requirement applied to all inmates but was tailored, medically unfit prisoners were exempt, and special arrangements existed for retired prisoners. A comparative survey showed that 16 Council of Europe States did not require prisoners to work beyond retirement age, while 12 had no explicit rule but often granted practical exemptions. The central alleged violation was that Switzerland’s continued work requirement for a retired preventive-detention prisoner amounted to compulsory labour and age- or status-based discrimination.
001-163909:
**Kleutin v. Ukraine (no. 5911/05)** concerned an application lodged on 7 January 2005 by Mr Denis Vasilyevich Kleutin, a Ukrainian national born in 1979, against Ukraine.
