He alleged that he had been beaten by police during apprehension on 22 January 2004 and that no effective investigation followed. He also complained that his arrest and pre-trial detention were unlawful, that he lacked effective judicial review of his detention, and that conditions in Odesa SIZO were inhuman and degrading.

On 22 January 2004, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant and two others in connection with a robbery committed the previous night. The same day, an investigator arrested him at 1:40 p.m. on suspicion of robbery. The applicant alleged that police officers, including K.—the brother of an alleged accomplice—came to his apartment, threatened him with firearms, struck him on the head and body, and fractured two ribs while trying to force him to confess. He said he was then forced to go to the police station. His sister, who was in another room, testified that she heard raised voices but did not witness the alleged beating. The Government maintained that no force or pressure was used and that the applicant voluntarily agreed to go with officers. A police officer later stated that no physical force was needed because the applicant did not resist. On 4 June 2007, the prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officer, finding no force had been applied. The applicant’s complaints during the criminal trial led the District Court to order the prosecutor’s office to investigate the ill-treatment allegations in March 2005 and again in May 2007, but these orders were not complied with in time. The applicant also alleged that K. forced his sister to give false evidence. Medical records were disputed: authorities said he was healthy on admission to Odesa SIZO and had no complaints, while the applicant alleged an X-ray showed he lacked part of his third left rib.

As to detention, on 24 January 2004 the Prymorsky District Court of Odesa remanded the applicant in custody in the absence of the applicant and without setting a maximum duration, relying on the gravity of the charge, his previous convictions, and risks of absconding or obstructing justice. On 18 March 2004, again in his absence, detention was extended for one month. After the investigation was completed and the case sent to trial, committal hearings on 5 May 2004 made no ruling on further detention. The case was twice remitted for additional investigation, on 18 June 2004 and 18 April 2005, without addressing his continued detention. On 15 September 2005, the District Court maintained detention without reasons or time-limits. The applicant repeatedly requested a non-custodial preventive measure, but the court replied that such petitions had to be lodged and examined at a hearing. On 8 June 2007, he was convicted of group robbery and involving minors in a crime, sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, and released on 22 January 2009 after the Supreme Court rejected his appeal.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant was held in Odesa SIZO from 26 January 2004 to 23 November 2007. He alleged insufficient living space, poor sanitation, prolonged confinement indoors, and no outdoor activity. Government records listed cells mostly measuring about 6.7–7.9 square metres intended for four detainees, with some larger cells. The Government claimed conditions were adequate, with furnishings, partitioned toilets, ventilation, natural light, and running water. The CPT had recommended at least 4 square metres per prisoner. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s Convention complaints.
001-167490:
The applicant, a Swiss hairdresser born in 1954, had compulsory accident insurance. In 1995 she was hit by a motorcycle and suffered head and neck injuries. She was initially certified totally unfit for work. A long dispute followed between her and her accident insurer over whether her continuing health problems were causally linked to the accident and whether she remained incapacitated. Multiple medical reports conflicted: some found a causal link and total incapacity, while others found no causal link or only 10–20% incapacity. In 2002 she was granted a full disability pension by the social security authority, and in 2005 the Social Insurance Court found a causal link and remitted the case to the insurer for a benefits decision.

The insurer then invited her to undergo a functional-capacity evaluation, which she refused. The insurer sent a formal notice under Article 43(3) of the Social Security Act warning her about the consequences of refusing to cooperate, but it did not mention the possibility of covert surveillance. In October 2006, the insurer commissioned private investigators who secretly monitored her on four dates over twenty-three days, for several hours each time. They followed her over long distances and produced a detailed report and video footage. The applicant apparently became aware of the surveillance on the final day. The insurer initially refused her representative access to the report, but later sent her the report and footage and stated that a fresh neurological assessment was necessary. She again refused examination and asked for a decision on her benefits.

In March 2007 the insurer refused benefits based on the surveillance images and her refusal to undergo a neurological examination. Later, using the images, an expert assessed her incapacity at 10%. In April 2008 the insurer refused to destroy the images and granted benefits based on 10% disability. The applicant appealed, seeking compensation, a higher pension, and removal of the surveillance material from her file. She argued that the surveillance was reprehensible, inappropriate, and an attack on her personality.

In 2009 the Social Insurance Court held that the surveillance lacked a legal basis, so the monitoring record was inadmissible; the expert opinion relying on it also had no probative value. It further held that she was entitled to refuse further examinations. The insurer appealed. In 2010 the Federal Court reversed, relying on earlier case law that secret surveillance of insured persons by accident insurers was lawful under Articles 28 and 43 of the Social Security Act, at least where limited to public activities. It found the surveillance file to be valid evidence. It concluded that images of her walking her dog, driving long distances, shopping, carrying groceries, and lifting her arms above her head without obvious restriction contradicted the medical reports. It held that a neurological reassessment was necessary and admissible because she had refused to cooperate. The Federal Court therefore quashed the Social Insurance Court’s decision except as to interest on arrears.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the secret surveillance ordered by her compulsory accident insurer violated her right to respect for private life under Article 8, and that the use of the surveillance material and related proceedings breached her right to a fair trial under Article 6. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that a public-function insurer had secretly monitored her daily activities without a clear prior warning or specific legal basis, then used the footage as evidence to reduce or deny her social-insurance benefits.
001-163356:
In *Geotech Kancev GmbH v. Germany* (Application no. 23646/09, judgment of 2 June 2016), the applicant was a German limited company specialising in soil sampling by drilling for geological examination, including assessing building-site suitability and constructing wells. It complained that its obligation to participate in and contribute to the Social Welfare Fund in the German building industry (“SOKA-BAU”) violated its right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention, particularly the negative aspect of that right, and its right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Fund was jointly set up by employers’ associations in the building industry and the trade union IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt through collective agreements, notably the Collective Agreement on Social Welfare Proceedings in the Building Trade (“VTV”). The VTV regulated contributions and entitlements relating to the Supplementary Pension Scheme for the Construction Industry (“ZVK”) and the Holiday and Wage Equalisation Fund (“ULAK”). The Federal Ministry for Labour and Social Affairs declared the VTV generally binding under the Law on Collective Agreements. As a result, all employers in the building industry, including those not belonging to an employers’ association, were obliged to contribute 19.8% of gross wages to the Fund.

The applicant was not a member of any employers’ association party to the collective agreements. However, the authorities considered its drilling activities to fall within the VTV’s scope; Article 1 § 2(v) no. 6 expressly listed drilling as a covered activity. In 2004 the Fund sent the applicant information about the welfare schemes and contributions. The applicant did not respond. In 2005, after enquiries, the Fund informed the applicant of its duty to contribute and opened an account. The applicant’s lawyer objected in April 2005.

In October 2007 the Wiesbaden Labour Court ordered the applicant to pay EUR 63,625.58 in welfare fund arrears to the ZVK for September 2002 to March 2004, and to submit wage slips for January 2006 to June 2007. The court found that the VTV bound all building employers and covered the applicant’s drilling activities. The applicant appealed, arguing that the generally binding effect violated the negative aspect of its freedom of association because it was forced to contribute to a fund jointly established by employers’ associations and a trade union, despite belonging to neither. It also claimed the obligation prevented it from founding its own association due to lack of funds.

In June 2008 the Hesse Labour Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It held that the generally binding effect did not oblige the applicant to join either an employers’ association or the Fund. Although non-members could not control the Fund through the associations, that disadvantage and any pressure to join were insufficient to breach the negative aspect of freedom of association. The obligation also did not prevent the applicant from founding its own association, and most contributions would be reimbursed if properly declared. The court found the scheme served the public interest by addressing high employee fluctuation and preventing distortion of competition. The Federal Labour Court rejected a further complaint in December 2008, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the applicant’s constitutional complaint in February 2009.

Relevant facts also included that the Fund did not make individual employers or employees members; only the collective agreement parties were members. It administered supplementary welfare schemes financed on a solidarity basis, operated as a non-profit entity, was state-supervised, and published annual reports. Insolvency proceedings over the applicant were opened in March 2010, but the administrator authorised counsel to continue the European Court proceedings.
001-159882:
The case *M.R.A. and Others v. the Netherlands* (ECtHR, 2016) concerned five Afghan nationals—a married couple and their three children—who alleged that their removal from the Netherlands to Afghanistan would breach Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention, and that they lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

The first applicant, born in 1959, entered the Netherlands in April 1999 with his wife and two eldest children and applied for asylum. He claimed he had joined the PDPA in 1978, performed guard duties, and then served for six months as a guard at Pol-e-Charki prison, where political prisoners were held. In 1982 he transferred to KhAD/WAD, the Afghan security service, as a construction engineer until 1992. He built offices and ammunition depots, claimed the rank of major or lieutenant-colonel, was decorated, and had some involvement with party propaganda and political affairs. He denied knowing of serious human rights abuses, aside from one incident he later retracted. After the communist regime fell, he fled to Mazar-e-Sharif and worked as an engineer. In 1998 Taliban fighters raided his home, found his PDPA card and medals, and detained him for about seven months. He was questioned about his KhAD/WAD past and released after a bribe on condition that he leave Afghanistan; he had been believed executed. He fled abroad.

The Dutch authorities rejected his asylum claim under Article 1F of the 1951 Refugee Convention. They found serious reasons to consider that he had knowingly and personally participated in KhAD/WAD human rights violations, relying on his voluntary guard service, transfer to KhAD, rank, decorations, political affairs role, and knowledge of systemic torture. He claimed that removal would expose him to Taliban or mujahideen reprisals because of his communist and KhAD/WAD background, and that a relative had been killed. The authorities found no individual real risk: no one was specifically looking for him, his past detention occurred under different political conditions, and while former communists might face some risk, not all did.

The second applicant, born in 1966, had studied education, taught from 1989 to 1991, and joined the PDPA women’s organisation. She was beaten once for wearing a short burka during the Taliban period while her husband was detained. Her asylum claim was rejected because authorities found no real personal risk; the single burka incident was insufficient, and the Taliban were unlikely to remain interested in her. She was later excluded from categorical protection.

The third applicant, born in 1991, arrived as a child. As an adult, his asylum claim was rejected because he had two criminal convictions for public violence and posed a public-order danger. He argued that as a westernised young man he faced Article 3 risk in Afghanistan. His later asylum and family-life residence applications were also rejected. His Article 8 claim was based on family life with his parents and siblings in the Netherlands, but the authorities issued a return decision. A provisional measure suspended that decision pending objection proceedings.

In 2011, the second, fourth, and fifth applicants were granted temporary asylum residence permits under a new policy for westernised Afghan school-aged girls; the fifth applicant had been born in the Netherlands. The first applicant’s fresh asylum request was again rejected under Article 1F, and an entry-ban intention was issued. The alleged violations therefore centred on the first applicant’s Article 3 risk upon removal despite Article 1F exclusion, the second applicant’s claimed risk as a former PDPA member and spouse, the third applicant’s Article 3 and Article 8 family-life claims, and the alleged lack of an effective Article 13 remedy against removal.
001-169520:
In *Colloredo Mannsfeld v. the Czech Republic* (Apps. nos. 15275/11 and 76058/12, ECtHR First Section, 15 December 2016), the applicant, Jerome Colloredo Mannsfeld, a Czech national, pursued restitution of movable property formerly kept at Opočno Castle. The property had been confiscated from his predecessor in 1942 by the German Secret State Police as an enemy of the Reich. After World War II, the Czechoslovak State confiscated it again in 1945 under the Beneš decrees because the predecessor was considered German. That expropriation was quashed in January 1947 after authorities found him to be of Czechoslovak nationality and loyal to the State. The property’s later fate was disputed.

In 1992 the applicant’s father and his cousin sought restitution. The applicant entered the proceedings as heir after his father died in 1998. One earlier set of proceedings returned 68 paintings and is not part of these applications. The two later sets form the basis of the case.

In the second proceedings (application no. 15275/11), the Pardubice District Court on 27 October 2006 ordered the National Heritage Institute to return certain movable property. It found that the applicant’s predecessor had owned the property on the critical restitution date, 25 February 1948, and that the statutory conditions were met. On 18 October 2007, however, the Hradec Králové Regional Court reversed and dismissed the action, finding that the property had been taken before 25 February 1948 and that restitution legislation therefore did not apply.

The key fair-trial complaint arose from how the Regional Court reached that conclusion. At the hearing on 8 October 2007, the court did not raise new evidence or questions with the parties; it merely heard their comments before adjourning for judgment. Its decision relied on two documents: a letter of 24 June 1947 from the national administrator of Opočno Castle and a decision of the Ministry of Agriculture of 30 April 1947 declaring the castle State cultural property (“the 1947 decision”). The 1947 decision had not been disclosed or raised with the parties, and they had no opportunity to comment on it. The Regional Court noted it was aware of the document through the exercise of its functions.

On 11 February 2009, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law. It noted the appellate court’s reliance on the 1947 decision but did not address the applicant’s argument that he had not seen it and could not comment. On 11 August 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal as manifestly ill-founded, holding that the requirements of Article 121 of the Code of Civil Procedure were met and that facts generally known or known to the court through its functions need not be proved.

In the third proceedings (application no. 76058/12), the District Court dismissed the remainder of the restitution claim on 22 April 2009, referring to the earlier judgments. On 27 January 2011, the Regional Court upheld that decision, relying on a Ministry of Agriculture letter of 27 May 1957 referring to the 1947 decision. Despite repeated requests, the 1947 decision was not produced to the parties. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal on 28 November 2011, and the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal on 19 April 2012 as manifestly ill-founded.

The applicant alleged that he had not had a fair trial and that his property rights had been breached. The central facts relevant to those alleged violations were the domestic courts’ use of the 1947 decision without disclosing it to the parties or allowing them to comment, allegedly violating fair-hearing and equality-of-arms guarantees, and the resulting rejection of his restitution claim, which affected his asserted property rights.
001-162214:
Balajevs v. Latvia (Application no. 8347/07) concerned a Latvian national, Mr Murads Balajevs, who alleged under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights that he had been ill-treated by three detainee escort officers at Riga Regional Court on 8 May 2006 and that Latvia had failed to conduct an effective investigation.

On 8 May 2006 the applicant was transferred from Central Prison to Riga Regional Court and placed in a holding cell. At 11:25 a.m. he asked escort officers to call an ambulance because he had waist pain and nausea. The ambulance arrived at 11:35 a.m.; he was found to have kidney stones and renal colic and was given painkillers. Later, when the pain returned, he again asked for an ambulance, shouting and cursing. The Government claimed that officer M.P. entered the cell to calm him, the applicant tried to hit M.P., and M.P. used physical force and a restraint technique under the Law on Police to prevent the attack. The applicant alleged that around 1:30 p.m. the officers refused to call an ambulance; when he continued asking for medical help, an officer entered the cell and kicked him in the chest, causing him to fall. While he tried to stand, he was kicked several more times. Other officers allegedly came, one forced him to the floor and kicked him in the back. At 1:48 p.m. the officers called an ambulance, which arrived at 2:04 p.m. The applicant told staff he had been hit on his left side and had previously suffered a right kidney rupture. The ambulance log noted no visible injuries. He was taken to Olaine prison hospital, where he was diagnosed with a fracture of the third lumbar vertebra and contusion of the left kidney. He was discharged on 19 May 2006.

Medical evidence was disputed. The Government relied on an extract stating that an X-ray on 6 May 2006, two days before the incident, had already revealed a lumbar vertebra fracture, and that his condition appeared “similar” after an X-ray on 9 May 2006. The prison hospital recorded a transverse process fracture and left kidney contusion but no bruises or scratches. It could not provide information about his care before 8 May 2006.

The applicant’s complaint was received by the Internal Security Office of the State Police on 17 May 2006, and criminal proceedings for exceeding official authority began on 2 June 2006. A forensic expert concluded on 19 September 2006 that the lumbar fracture was moderately severe and could have been caused by a blunt object on 8 May 2006, but a fall against a solid object could not be excluded. The applicant could not identify the officers from photographs; the officers denied excessive force. A witness, S.Š., said he saw two or three officers enter the applicant’s cell and kick “something,” and heard groaning. The first investigation closed in October 2006, accepting the officers’ account. The deputy chief prosecutor quashed that decision in January 2007, finding the investigation superficial and requiring scene inspection, verification of statements, and expert clarification on whether the injury pre-dated 8 May 2006.

A second expert report in March 2007 stated that the applicant could have remained mobile after the fracture and that the injury might have pre-dated 8 May 2006. The investigation closed again, but the chief prosecutor quashed it in June 2007, citing failure to properly verify the officers’ evidence at the scene, failure to consider S.Š.’s evidence, and failure to question other detainees. In the third round, the scene was visited, S.Š. was questioned again, and fourteen detainees were questioned; some had heard noise and shouts. The investigation closed on 24 April 2009, finding discrepancies in the applicant’s accounts, no corroboration of chest or head injuries, and the possibility that the fracture resulted from a fall against a hard object, matching the officers’ version. The prosecutor upheld that decision in May 2009, finding no offence and that force had complied with the Law on Police. The applicant did not appeal further, and the prosecution later said the time-limit had expired.
001-169521:
In *Vaščenkovs v. Latvia* (Application no. 30795/12, ECtHR, 15 December 2016), the applicant, Maksims Vaščenkovs, a Latvian national born in 1986, complained under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that the Latvian courts had failed to provide sufficient reasons for the suspicion that he had committed robbery when extending his pre-trial detention. He died on 3 November 2015, and his grandmother informed the Court that she wished to pursue the proceedings on his behalf. The application was lodged on 16 May 2012. On 10 July 2014, the complaint was communicated to the Government under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4, while the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The relevant facts began in July and August 2011, when the police opened four criminal investigations into three thefts and one robbery; these were joined on 29 August 2011. On 12 August 2011, the police arrested the applicant on suspicion of robbery. He was held on that basis until 14 August 2011, when he was placed under arrest on suspicion of theft. On 15 August 2011, the police applied to the Ludza District Court for his pre-trial detention in relation to the theft investigation.

On 16 August 2011, an investigating judge granted that application. The judge’s reasoning referred only to a suspicion of theft under section 175(3) of the Criminal Law, said to be confirmed by evidence gathered in the criminal case. The applicant appealed, but on 2 September 2011 the Latgale Regional Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the suspicion of theft was confirmed by information in the file. No further appeal lay against that decision.

On 19 September 2011, the public prosecutor charged the applicant with robbery, theft, involving a minor in theft, and petty theft. On 28 September 2011, the case was transferred to the Ludza District Court for adjudication, with the prosecution setting out its case and evidence. On 17 October 2011, the investigating judge decided to keep the applicant in detention, reasoning that the accusations of theft, robbery, petty theft, and involving a minor in theft were confirmed by evidence. No appeal lay against this decision.

On 28 December 2011 and 23 April 2012, the applicant’s detention was extended. The judge stated that detention was based on suspicion of theft, noted that in other criminal proceedings the applicant had been declared a suspect for petty theft and robbery, and said there had been no change in the reasons given in the 16 August 2011 detention order, which had been re-examined in subsequent decisions. In February, June, and August 2012, the applicant complained to the Ludza District Court that it had failed to assess his detention in relation to the alleged robbery.

On 6 August and 2 November 2012, and on 25 January 2013, the judge continued the detention using largely the same wording. She additionally noted that the twenty-four-month maximum period under section 277(7) of the Criminal Procedure Law had been observed because the applicant was also accused of an especially serious offence—robbery—under section 176(2). Those decisions were not subject to appeal.

Under domestic law, section 277(6) allowed a maximum of twelve months’ detention for a serious offence, while section 277(7) allowed up to twenty-four months for an especially serious offence. The alleged violation therefore concerned whether the domestic courts gave sufficient, specific reasons for the suspicion that the applicant had committed robbery, particularly when later extensions and the longer statutory maximum relied on that robbery charge, while the courts’ reasoning largely repeated earlier theft-based justifications and generic references to evidence.
001-162179:
Cunha Martins da Silva Couto v. Portugal (Applications nos. 69053/13, 69374/13, 69377/13, 71135/13 and 8088/14) is a case before the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, brought by Mr José Luís Cunha Martins da Silva Couto, a Portuguese national born in 1961 and residing in Porto. The case originated in five applications lodged against Portugal under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Portuguese Government was represented by Mrs M. F. da Graça Carvalho, Deputy Attorney General. On 21 November 2014, the applications were communicated to the Government.

The applicant complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of an effective remedy in that respect. These allegations engage Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and Article 13, which requires an effective remedy for arguable Convention violations.

The appended table provides the key factual details of each application. In Application no. 69053/13, introduced on 28 October 2013, the domestic proceedings began on 21 April 2009 and ended on 13 February 2014. Their total duration was approximately 4 years, 9 months and 25 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.

In Application no. 69374/13, introduced on 30 October 2013, the proceedings began on 20 February 2009 and, according to the last information received by the Court on 26 May 2015, were still pending. Their length at that point was approximately 6 years, 11 months and 13 days, again across two levels of jurisdiction.

Application no. 69377/13, also introduced on 30 October 2013, concerned proceedings that likewise began on 20 February 2009 and were still pending as of 26 May 2015. The total duration was also approximately 6 years, 11 months and 13 days, with two levels of jurisdiction.

In Application no. 71135/13, introduced on 1 November 2013, the civil proceedings started on 16 May 2009 and ended on 28 November 2014. They lasted approximately 5 years, 6 months and 14 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.

Finally, in Application no. 8088/14, introduced on 30 December 2013, the proceedings began on 13 October 2010 and ended on 27 June 2014. Their total length was approximately 3 years, 8 months and 14 days, also across two levels of jurisdiction.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the prolonged duration of several civil proceedings involving the same applicant, with some cases remaining unresolved for nearly seven years by the time the Court last received information. The applicant alleged not only that the proceedings were excessively long, but also that the Portuguese legal system failed to provide an effective domestic remedy to challenge that length. The Court would need to assess whether the duration of each set of proceedings exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1, taking into account factors such as complexity, the conduct of the applicant and the authorities, and what was at stake. It would also need to determine whether an effective remedy existed under Article 13 for the length complaints.

The judgment is dated 26 April 2016 and is stated to be final, although it may be subject to editorial revision. The excerpt supplied focuses primarily on the procedural and factual background and the applicant’s complaints, rather than setting out the Court’s ultimate reasoning or disposition.
001-161369:
**Morari v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 65311/09, judgment of 8 March 2016)** concerned an allegation of police entrapment and the fairness of criminal proceedings.

In January 2008, the Balti police organised an undercover operation to identify a criminal group producing and circulating forged documents. They placed an advertisement in a local newspaper stating: “Need help with obtaining passport (Romanian-Bulgarian)” and provided a telephone number. The applicant, Oleg Morari, a Moldovan national interested in obtaining a Romanian passport to facilitate work in Romania or the European Union, called the number. He met a person identifying himself as E., who claimed also to be seeking a Romanian passport. They agreed to inform each other if either found an easy way to obtain one.

Later, the applicant’s friend D. recommended a person called Z., who could arrange a Romanian passport quickly. Both D. and Z. later confirmed that D. had made this recommendation in March 2008. Z. asked for EUR 1,500, which the applicant did not have.

About three weeks after first meeting E., E. called the applicant to ask whether he had found a way to obtain a passport. The applicant told him about Z. and proposed putting E. in contact with Z. E. refused direct contact, said he lacked money, but mentioned an acquaintance, T., also interested in a Romanian passport. E. proposed that the applicant act as intermediary between Z. and T., telling T. the price was EUR 2,300; the EUR 800 difference between Z.’s price and T.’s payment would be split between the applicant and E. The prosecution did not contest this account. The applicant agreed.

The applicant then discussed matters with Z., who gave him a list of documents needed for T.’s new Romanian identity card. The applicant claimed he believed the card would not be forged and that Z. would merely represent T. before the Romanian authorities. Z. disputed this, stating he had told the applicant from the outset that the identity card would be false and he should avoid travelling to Romania with it.

On 3 April 2008, the applicant met T., obtained documents and an advance of EUR 750, and gave T. a receipt. He passed the money and documents to Z. The identity card was produced in the United Kingdom and reached Z and then the applicant by mid-April 2008. On 16 April 2008, the applicant met T., gave him the identity card in exchange for the remaining money, and was arrested.

A criminal investigation began on 17 April 2008 for manufacturing and trading forged official documents. Z. concluded a plea agreement, admitted guilt, and received a suspended four-year sentence.

During proceedings, the applicant argued he had been entrapped by E. and T. and asked for them to be heard. The first-instance court refused, citing the law permitting undercover officers to testify only if they consented. On 17 December 2008, the Balti District Court convicted the applicant of participating in producing and selling a false Romanian identity card, fining him about EUR 200. The judgment did not address his entrapment claim.

His appeal complained that the offence resulted from police incitement and that E. and T. had not been heard. The Court of Appeal initially agreed to hear them but later reversed that decision. On 4 March 2009, it dismissed the appeal, rejecting entrapment solely because the applicant had first telephoned the newspaper number. It found no need to hear E. and T. since their statements were not used against him. The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed his appeal on 8 July 2009.

The applicant alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that he had been the victim of entrapment, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The key fair-trial issue was whether the domestic courts adequately examined his incitement claim and his inability to confront the undercover individuals allegedly involved.
001-162114:
**Topallaj v. Albania** (Application no. 32913/03, judgment 21 April 2016) concerned Albanian civil and property proceedings. The applicant, Marketin Topallaj, later a U.S. citizen, became involved in 1996 with land near the Tirana–Durrës road on which fuel tanks and a petrol station stood. Albanian courts had recognised certain landowners’ inherited rights over 24 hectares. In April 1996 the Tirana District Court quashed a property commission’s refusal and allocated the landowners 56,500 sq. m, ordering that the fuel tanks and installations be restored at no cost because their value was less than 20% of the land’s value. That judgment became final in May 1996, and the landowners obtained a property certificate.

Acting on the landowners’ behalf, the applicant concluded agreements in January and February 1996 to finance privatisation of the fuel tanks and installations in exchange for future ownership. In May 1996 he concluded a notarised sales contract for almost all of the fuel tanks and installations for USD 100,000 and registered title in his name. He also concluded two loan agreements with one landowner. He thereafter represented the landowners in proceedings protecting their property rights.

Between 1996 and 2000, State bodies repeatedly challenged the landowners’ rights. After the Supreme Court dismissed one challenge in 1999, the Ministry of Economy and State-owned oil companies obtained supervisory review. In May 2000 the Supreme Court Joint Benches reopened the proceedings. The case was reheard through several remittals until 2009, ultimately in the landowners’ favour. In 2007 the property agency recognised inherited rights over 24 hectares and ordered compensation for 183,500 sq. m, a compensation issue later pursued in separate proceedings.

Separately, in 2002 and again in 2005, the landowners sued the applicant to annul the 1996 agreements and sales contract as absolutely null and void. The applicant alleged that the fresh claim was signed only by the landowners’ lawyer, without proper authority, and was time-barred. He also alleged forgery, sought a stay pending a criminal complaint, and repeatedly challenged the bench. The presiding judge withdrew, but the District Court President set aside that withdrawal. In April 2006 the District Court declared the agreements and contract absolutely null and fictitious. It found that the property was State-administered when concluded, no rights had been transferred to the landowners, no joint company or loans existed, and the sales price matched the alleged loans. It ordered erasure of the applicant’s May 1996 property registration.

The Court of Appeal upheld that decision in May 2007. A dissenting judge found no evidence that the transactions were fictitious, considered the claim time-barred and unauthorised, and stated that the applicant’s procedural requests had been ignored. The Supreme Court declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible in January 2010, and the Constitutional Court rejected his appeal in November 2010, finding no impartiality breach and deferring to the lower courts’ factual assessment.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key facts relevant to those alleged violations were the annulment of his registered contracts and erasure of his property registration, allegedly depriving him of possessions; alleged unfairness, bias, and improper court composition, including military judges in the Court of Appeal; rejection of requests for withdrawal and evidence; lack of reasoned decisions; complaints that the claim was unauthorised and time-barred; the excessive length of proceedings; and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.
001-167806:
In *B.A.C. v. Greece* (Application no. 11981/15), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) examined an application by a Turkish national, born in 1977 and living in Athens, who complained about Greece’s prolonged failure to decide his asylum request. He alleged violations of Article 8 § 1 of the Convention, alone and in conjunction with Article 13, and of Articles 3 and 13 taken together, on account of the Ministry of Public Order’s failure for twelve years to take any decision on his asylum application.

The applicant had been a pro-communist and pro-Kurdish political activist while studying in Turkey between 1994 and 1999. In 1997 he opened a literary café frequented by people sympathetic to those political views. In 2000 the Turkish police arrested him, and he was prosecuted for infringing the State constitutional order under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. He was held in the “white (isolation) cells” at Kandra Prison. He went on hunger strike for 171 days, causing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a condition capable of causing irreversible damage or death. Because his life was at risk, the Turkish authorities released him.

In 2002 the applicant fled to Greece and applied for asylum on 15 January 2002. On 18 February 2002, the General Secretary of the Ministry of Public Order rejected the application at first instance with summary reasons. On 21 March 2002, the applicant appealed. On 29 January 2003, having been summoned before the Advisory Board on Asylum, he submitted documents showing he had suffered torture in Turkey because of his political opinions, including a medical report from the Greek Medical Centre for the Rehabilitation of Torture Victims and an Amnesty International document. That same day, the Advisory Board issued a favourable opinion. Under Article 3 § 5 of Presidential Decree No. 61/1999, the Minister for Public Order should then have decided within twenty-four hours whether to grant international protection. However, by the time the application reached the Court, the Minister had taken no decision and had neither ratified nor rejected the Board’s opinion.

Between 2003 and 2015, the applicant lived in Athens and attended a police station every six months to renew his asylum-seeker’s card. Under domestic law, that card was not a residence permit. It only prevented expulsion and allowed him to remain in Greece with “tolerated status” while his application was pending. Asylum seekers in his position could not work, undertake vocational training, marry, obtain a driving licence, hold a bank account, or apply for family reunion.

In 2003 his wife joined him from Turkey, but her presence became lawful only in 2008 when she obtained a short-term work permit. In 2010 they had a son. In 2011 his wife returned to Istanbul with the child because of health problems, and the couple divorced in 2012.

Separately, on 5 August 2005, the Turkish Interpol Office issued an extradition request based on accusations similar to those already assessed during the asylum proceedings. On 12 March 2013 the applicant was arrested in Patras. On 26 March 2013, the indictment division of the Patras Court of Appeal unanimously rejected extradition, citing the risk of ill-treatment for his political opinions and the vague and abstract description of the alleged offences. The prosecutor appealed, but on 26 April 2013 the Court of Cassation upheld the rejection.

The applicant repeatedly sought a final decision. He wrote to the Ombudsman on 21 March and 25 June 2012, and to the Minister for Public Order on 19 November 2013, 16 June 2014, and 27 February 2015. Correspondence among authorities on 23 February 2007, 16 October 2012, 14 November 2012, and 28 January 2015 confirmed that his asylum application was still pending before the Minister. These facts formed the basis of his complaints about prolonged uncertainty, restrictions on his private and family life, and the absence of an effective remedy.
001-159915:
The case of *Sindely v. Hungary* (Application no. 54602/11) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 23 August 2011 by two Hungarian nationals, Mr András Sindely and Mrs Andrásné Sindely, a married couple living in Piliscsaba. The case concerned a civil damages action brought by the applicants against the first applicant’s employer after the first applicant was deliberately shot by a colleague on 7 December 2001. The shooting caused serious injuries and left him disabled. The central alleged violation was the excessive length of the ensuing civil proceedings, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time.

In 2004, the first applicant and his family, including the second applicant, sued the employer for damages. On 14 June 2005, the president of the Pest County Labour Court ordered that the case receive priority treatment. Despite that order, the proceedings progressed slowly. On 19 January 2006, the Pest County Labour Court delivered an interim judgment establishing the legal basis of the claim—that is, finding the employer’s liability well-founded. That interim judgment was upheld by the Pest County Court on 5 January 2007.

The remaining issue, the exact amount of compensation, was not decided until 9 November 2010, when the Pest County Labour Court issued its judgment. That decision was upheld and partly amended by the Pest County Court in a final judgment on 4 May 2011. Thus, the domestic civil proceedings lasted approximately seven years from their initiation in 2004 to their final resolution in May 2011. A particularly notable delay occurred between the liability ruling, finalised in early 2007, and the quantification of damages in late 2010, a gap of nearly four years.

These facts were the core of the applicants’ complaint before the Strasbourg Court. They argued that the Hungarian authorities had failed to conduct the civil proceedings within a reasonable time, especially given the first applicant’s serious disability and the priority order issued in 2005. The lengthy delay in determining compensation allegedly prejudiced them and rendered the civil remedy ineffective. The application was communicated to the Hungarian Government on 8 January 2015. The Fourth Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Tsotsoria, Wojtyczek, and Kucsko-Stadlmayer, deliberated in private on 15 December 2015 and adopted its judgment on 12 January 2016. The judgment is final but subject to editorial revision. The key factual focus for the alleged Article 6 § 1 violation was therefore the overall duration of the civil case, the ineffectiveness of the priority measure, and the prolonged interval between establishing liability and fixing the compensation amount.
001-164920:
The case *Jovanović v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 21497/13 and 21907/13) originated in two applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 March 2013 by Mr Radoslav Jovanović, a Serbian national born in 1943 and living in Niš. He complained about the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in his favour against socially/State-owned companies, because enforcement proceedings were stayed while the debtors underwent privatisation-related restructuring. The applications were communicated to the Serbian Government on 16 September 2014. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The first set of enforcement proceedings concerned the company “FŽV Želvoz a.d. Smederevo.” On 28 April 2010 the applicant brought an enforcement action before the Smederevo Court of First Instance. On 15 December 2010 that court ordered direct enforcement of an outstanding invoice based on a credible document. On 15 June 2011, however, the Privatisation Agency ordered the debtor’s restructuring as part of the privatisation process. Consequently, on 25 October 2011 the enforcement proceedings were stayed. The applicant appealed on 3 November 2011, but his appeal was rejected on 10 February 2012. On 21 March 2013 he urged the court to continue enforcement. On 7 June 2013 the court informed him that the debtor was still undergoing restructuring and that enforcement could not continue. It appears the applicant did not appeal against that decision.

The second set concerned “Vagonka a.d. Niš.” On 11 January 2010 the applicant brought an enforcement action before the Niš Commercial Court. On 29 January 2010 that court ordered direct enforcement of an outstanding invoice. However, on 4 November 2009 the Privatisation Agency had already ordered the debtor’s restructuring. On 4 February 2010 the enforcement proceedings were stayed because the debtor was undergoing restructuring. The applicant did not appeal, and that decision became final on 17 February 2010. On 20 March 2013 he urged the court to continue enforcement. On 22 March 2013 the court informed him that the debtor was still undergoing restructuring and that enforcement could not continue.

The relevant domestic law referred to cases such as *R. Kačapor and Others v. Serbia*, *Vlahović v. Serbia*, *Crnišanin and Others v. Serbia*, *Adamović v. Serbia*, and *Marinković v. Serbia*, which set out the Serbian framework on enforcement and the restructuring of socially/State-owned companies.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant held final enforcement orders in his favour, but those orders remained unexecuted for years. In both cases, the debtors were socially/State-owned companies undergoing restructuring ordered by the Privatisation Agency. The domestic enforcement courts stayed the proceedings and later refused to continue them solely because restructuring was ongoing. In the first case, the applicant appealed the stay but was unsuccessful; in the second, he did not appeal the stay. The applicant’s repeated requests in 2013 to continue enforcement were also unsuccessful. The case therefore concerns complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the right of access to court and execution of final judgments, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning protection of property, arising from the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions against State/socially-owned debtors in restructuring.
001-163662:
The applicant, Juozas Pugžlys, a Lithuanian national born in 1966, complained to the European Court of Human Rights about his treatment during criminal proceedings in Poland. He was arrested in the Netherlands in April 2003 on suspicion of leading an international organised criminal group and of six counts of kidnapping for ransom. He was detained on remand and transferred to Poland in October 2003. In a separate case, he was convicted of armed robbery in 2005 and served that sentence from January 2006 to July 2010. In the main case, he was indicted in April 2004; after jurisdictional issues, the trial proceeded before the Lublin Regional Court. In January 2010 he was convicted of six kidnappings and leading an organised criminal gang and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment. His appeal was dismissed in December 2010, and the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal in April 2012.

The main alleged violations concerned the “dangerous detainee” regime, courtroom conditions, defence rights, and family contact. On 21 October 2003, the Lublin Remand Centre Penitentiary Commission classified him as a “dangerous detainee” under the Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences. The authorities relied on the suspicion that he had committed offences within an organised criminal group, the violent and ruthless nature of the alleged crimes, his personal situation, his knowledge of boxing and combat techniques, and an alleged “high degree of depravity.” The regime was reviewed and reaffirmed every three months until it was lifted on 25 July 2012—about nine years. The renewal decisions and requests used similar wording, referring to the charges or convictions, his personal circumstances, low moral character, and lack of participation in social rehabilitation. His appeals against these decisions were dismissed by domestic courts, which found the measures lawful and based on thorough assessments.

As to courtroom conditions, the Government acknowledged that during hearings before the Lublin Regional Court the applicant was held in a metal cage separating him from judges and the public, and that while in the cage his hands remained handcuffed. The applicant alleged he was placed in the cage, with hands and legs shackled, during all approximately 104 trial hearings. The Government claimed this occurred only at some hearings. The dimensions of the cage and the position of guards were unclear. This formed part of his Article 3 complaint.

Regarding fair trial and defence rights, the applicant was Lithuanian. Interpreters were generally provided—initially Lithuanian, occasionally Russian if he agreed, and Lithuanian from January 2007. His court-appointed lawyer spoke only Polish. The applicant asked for a different lawyer, saying he could not communicate with him, but the request was refused. He could meet the lawyer during trial recesses, but allegedly in the presence of an interpreter and police officers or court personnel; requests for unsupervised meetings were denied. He had access to the case file with an interpreter, and the trial court agreed to provide translations of documents, though he later argued translations were not actually supplied unless he paid. The appeal court found no breach of defence rights; the Supreme Court held that guards were necessary because he was detained on remand and that translations of essential documents sufficed.

Finally, he complained under Article 8 about restrictions on family contact. He was allowed two ten-minute phone calls per week, sometimes one fifteen-minute call, plus additional calls. Visits by his common-law wife and daughter occurred regularly, between two and four times yearly from 2004 to 2009 and eight times in 2010, lasting thirty minutes to two hours. Correspondence was not restricted. The Court communicated complaints under Articles 3, 6, 6 § 3(b), (c), (e), 8, and 13; other parts were declared inadmissible.
001-165951:
Aleksandr Mihhailov, a stateless person born in 1976 living in Narva, lodged an application with the European Court on 28 October 2010, alleging that police had used unwarranted violence during his arrest and later detention at a police station.

On 29 April 2009, shortly before 6 p.m., Narva police received a call about two men near Kreenholmi and Kerese streets; one was reportedly carrying a knife, while the other was drunk and had difficulty walking. Officers S.B. and E.V. found the applicant and M.Z. at a public playground. The applicant alleged that, although drunk, he was not aggressive or abusive; S.B. punched him in the jaw, he fell and briefly lost consciousness, was handcuffed, and was then punched and kicked until he lost consciousness, waking at the police station. The Government, relying on the criminal investigation, stated that the applicant behaved aggressively, swore, waved his hands, and disobeyed orders. E.V. forced him to the ground; Officers S.J. and N.S. helped handcuff him. He resisted, kicked the police car, and was restrained on the ground. While being placed in the van, he hit his left temple against the door. He remained aggressive during transport.

At the police station, the applicant alleged that S.B. kneed him near the left ear, repeatedly punched and kicked him, at one point put his head under a running tap, and beat him again after E.V. returned; he lost consciousness and later had blood on his face. The Government said he remained aggressive and was restrained; he fell off a chair twice, and officers later left him on the floor. At 7.45 p.m. a report was drafted stating he had been taken to sober up and noting a dirty face and abrasions on his head.

At 1.42 a.m. on 30 April 2009 an ambulance was called. The applicant complained of head and wrist pain, nausea, vomiting, and hearing loss in his left ear. He was found to have haematomas on the left cranium and a swollen right wrist, and was diagnosed with an intracranial injury and a fracture of the right hand/wrist. He was taken to hospital, where he was diagnosed with concussion. A CT scan at 6.26 a.m. showed no haemorrhage or intracranial pathology, and he was released. At 2.15 a.m. police took a statement from him at the hospital, and at 2.40 a.m. drafted a misdemeanour report alleging drunkenness and breach of the peace. On 1 May 2009 an ambulance was again called; he was diagnosed with concussion and had a haematoma around the left ear, oedema around the left eye, and bruises on the neck and upper limbs.

On 30 April 2009 the applicant complained to police of ill-treatment. After initial difficulties, a criminal investigation was opened on 5 May 2009. Investigators took statements from the applicant, M.Z., detainees A.P., M.S., and R.L., police officers, children who witnessed the arrest, and ambulance staff. A.P. and R.L. said they heard or saw the applicant being beaten at the station; M.S. heard shouting but saw no beating. M.Z. said he saw the applicant beaten at the station, but later, during photo identification, said there had been no beating at the playground. The children said officers used force but did not punch or kick the applicant during the arrest. A forensic medical expert concluded on 13 August 2009 that the injuries had been caused by blunt force, likely shortly before the applicant saw a doctor, possibly on 29 April 2009, but the exact cause could not be established.

On 20 January 2010 the police investigator discontinued the criminal investigation, finding no evidence that officers had committed abuse of authority and that the force used had been lawful and not excessive. The prosecutor approved this on 15 February 2010. The applicant appealed on 15 March 2010, but the State Prosecutor’s Office rejected the appeal as out of time on 23 March 2010, and the Tartu Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 30 April 2010.

Separately, on 25 May 2009 the East Police Prefecture fined the applicant for breach of the peace. On 17 November 2010 the Viru County Court acquitted him, finding no evidence of the misdemeanour, setting aside unlawfully obtained hospital statements, finding M.Z. reliable that police had unduly influenced him by letting him hear the applicant being beaten, and concluding that evidence had been collected unlawfully, infringing the applicant’s honour and dignity and endangering his health.
001-169662:
The applicant, Georgie Paposhvili, a Georgian national born in 1958, arrived in Belgium via Italy on 25 November 1998 with his wife and a child. They applied for asylum the next day. Under the Dublin Convention, Germany refused a take-back request and Italy accepted responsibility on 4 June 1999. The asylum application was refused on 11 June 1999, and a further application lodged on 22 September 1999 under a false identity was rejected. Between 1998 and 2005 the applicant was convicted of theft, robbery and related offences; in 2005 the Ghent Court of Appeal sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment for involvement in a criminal organisation. He was held in several prisons and later in the Merksplas closed facility for illegal aliens.

In 2006 he was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (Binet stage B). He received chemotherapy in 2007; an Antwerp University Hospital report of 11 February 2008 described his condition as life-threatening and estimated life expectancy at three to five years. By 2011 his leukaemia had progressed to Binet stage C. He also suffered from tuberculosis, COPD, hepatitis C and, after a 2015 stroke, permanent paralysis of the left arm. From December 2014 he received Ibrutinib. Medical reports in 2015 stated that discontinuing treatment would result in death, that he needed specialised haematology care and a donor stem cell transplant, and that such treatment would not be available in Georgia. Belgian medical advisers considered his condition serious but did not find a direct threat to life or a critical state.

The applicant made several regularisation requests. A first request on exceptional grounds (20 March 2000) was declared devoid of purpose and unfounded on 30 March 2004. A second request (28 April 2004) was declared inadmissible on 5 April 2007; the Aliens Appeals Board rejected his set-aside application on 29 February 2008. A third request on exceptional grounds was refused on 7 July 2010, when the Aliens Office also issued an order to leave the country and a detention order, served on 11 July 2010. His wife and three children were granted indefinite leave to remain on 29 July 2010. A stay/set-aside application concerning the 7 July 2010 decision and order was rejected by the Aliens Appeals Board on 16 March 2015 because the applicant did not attend or appoint representation.

On medical grounds, a first request on 10 September 2007 was refused on 26 September 2007 because he was excluded as having committed serious crimes, following a ministerial deportation order of 16 August 2007. The Aliens Appeals Board dismissed his challenge on 20 August 2008, noting that no removal measure accompanied the decision. A second medical request of 3 April 2008 was refused on 4 June 2008; the Aliens Appeals Board rejected his set-aside application on 21 May 2015, and the Conseil d’État declared his appeal on points of law inadmissible on 9 July 2015.

Removal measures included an order to leave under the Dublin Convention of 10 June 1999, the ministerial deportation order of 16 August 2007 imposing a ten-year re-entry ban, the 7 July 2010 order to leave and detention, and an order to leave with immediate effect of 18 February 2012. The applicant was transferred to Merksplas in July 2010, and a Georgian travel document was issued on 16 July 2010. On 28 July 2010 the European Court of Human Rights requested Belgium not to remove him pending the Aliens Appeals Board proceedings; he was released on 30 July 2010. On 23 July 2010 he had applied to the Court alleging that removal to Georgia would risk his life and physical well-being and violate his family life under Articles 2, 3 and 8. He died on 7 June 2016; on 20 June 2016 his wife and three children expressed the wish to pursue the proceedings. The Georgian Government intervened.
001-161975:
**Armani Da Silva v. the United Kingdom** (Application no. 5878/08), Grand Chamber, 30 March 2016.

The applicant, Patricia Armani Da Silva, is the cousin of Jean Charles de Menezes, a Brazilian national shot dead by London police on 22 July 2005. She alleged that the decision not to prosecute any individual officer for the fatal shooting breached the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the Convention, which requires an effective investigation capable of establishing the facts, determining whether force was justified, and identifying and punishing those responsible.

The relevant facts began with the 7 July 2005 London suicide bombings and the failed bombings of 21 July 2005. Police launched Operation THESEUS 2 to locate suspects, including Hussain Osman, believed to be living at 21 Scotia Road. Commander McDowall’s strategy was to use covert surveillance and then, once safe, stop and arrest suspects away from the premises, supported by specialist firearms officers from SO19. However, SO19 was not deployed to Scotia Road in time. On the morning of 22 July, Jean Charles de Menezes left 17 Scotia Road. Surveillance officers followed him; he was initially described as a “good possible likeness” to Osman, then “not identical.” Conflicting accounts existed as to whether a positive identification was made. He boarded a bus, then another, and entered Stockwell underground station. The DSO ordered SO19 to stop him from entering the tube. CCTV showed him walking calmly, wearing a thin denim jacket and carrying nothing. On the platform, he entered a train and sat down. Two specialist firearms officers (Charlie 2 and Charlie 12) followed, pushed him back into his seat, and shot him multiple times, killing him. They claimed they believed he was a suicide bomber about to detonate a device.

The IPCC investigated. Its Stockwell One Report (January 2006) found serious operational failings: briefings that “stoked” the officers’ fears, the failure to deploy SO19 earlier, unclear command, and an altered surveillance log. It concluded the death resulted from a combination of circumstances but found no evidence of a deliberate cover-up. The CPS considered prosecutions for murder, gross negligence manslaughter, misconduct in public office, forgery, and perverting the course of justice. In July 2006, the CPS decided no individual officer should be prosecuted: the firearms officers genuinely believed they acted in self-defence; commanders’ errors did not meet the high threshold for gross negligence manslaughter; and evidential difficulties (inconsistent accounts, missing CCTV, no proof of log forgery) meant no realistic prospect of conviction. Only the Office of the Commissioner of the Police of the Metropolis was prosecuted under health and safety law.

The applicant complained that the absence of individual prosecutions meant the investigation was not effective for Article 2 purposes, because it did not lead to a determination of whether the force was justified or to punishment of those responsible. The Grand Chamber examined whether the decision not to prosecute breached the United Kingdom’s procedural obligation under Article 2.
001-168380:
Mr Goran Šilović, a Serbian national born in 1952 and living in Belgrade, lodged application no. 32883/08 against the Republic of Serbia with the European Court of Human Rights on 19 March 2008. The Serbian Government were represented by their Agent, initially Ms V. Rodić and later Ms N. Plavšić. On 18 December 2014 the application was communicated to the Government.

In the domestic proceedings, on 10 June 2002 the applicant filed a claim with the former Supreme Military Court in Belgrade for payment of certain benefits. On 10 August 2007 the Supreme Court of Serbia, which had taken over the jurisdiction of the former Supreme Military Court in Belgrade, rejected the applicant’s claim. The applicant received that judgment on 2 October 2007.

The supplied record does not describe the nature of the benefits, the reasons for the domestic rejection, or any specific allegations or arguments made by the parties in the proceedings before the European Court. It therefore contains no further concrete facts relevant to the alleged violation beyond those dates and the domestic claim and judgment.
001-166954:
In *Goryayeva v. Ukraine* (Application no. 58656/10), the European Court of Human Rights considered the death of the applicant’s son, A.G., while in police detention and the subsequent domestic investigation.

The applicant, Ms Zoya Georgiyivna Goryayeva, is a Ukrainian national born in 1938. Her son, A.G., was born in 1966 and suffered from tuberculosis, AIDS, drug addiction, and an infected phlegmon on his right shin. On 4 May 2007, A.G. was arrested on suspicion of drug-related crimes and placed in a temporary detention centre (“ITT”) belonging to the Mykolayiv police. On 7 May 2007, the Tsentralnyy District Court of Mykolayiv ordered his pre-trial detention.

While in the ITT, A.G. was attended by ambulance doctors and received medical treatment. On 19 May 2007, he was transferred to the surgical ward of a local hospital for treatment of his phlegmon. After treatment, doctors considered that he could be held in detention facilities, and he was returned to the ITT.

According to domestic investigations, at about 9:30 p.m. on 23 May 2007, an ITT officer heard moaning from A.G.’s cell. A.G. was alone. The officer checked the cell and saw him with his mouth open, breathing heavily, and saying that he felt bad and needed air. ITT officers removed him from the cell, took him to the entrance area for fresh air, and administered first aid. An ambulance arrived at 9:43 p.m. and confirmed that A.G. was dead.

A post-mortem examination concluded that A.G. died from ischaemic heart disease aggravated by acute heart failure. Linear strangulation bruises were found on his neck, indicating interrupted asphyxiation. The report stated that asphyxiation had been attempted about ten minutes before death and could have aggravated his chronic illnesses.

The domestic investigation was protracted and repeatedly restarted. Between 2007 and 2012, investigators at the local prosecutor’s office refused more than fifteen times to initiate criminal proceedings. Those decisions were quashed as unsubstantiated by supervising prosecutors and courts, and further pre-investigation inquiries were ordered. On 14 December 2012, criminal proceedings were initiated under the 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure. On 27 March 2013, an investigator terminated the proceedings, finding no elements of a crime on the part of the ITT officers. On 24 July 2013, the Zavodskyy District Court of Mykolayiv quashed that decision as unfounded, noting that the investigator had failed to take necessary measures.

On 3 October 2013, the investigator again terminated the proceedings, concluding that there was no evidence that ITT staff had caused A.G.’s death. He admitted that certain evidence could not be obtained: bed linen and a rope fashioned from bed linen found in the cell had been destroyed after the post-mortem examination, so they could not be further examined; reconstruction of events was therefore impossible. A site inspection had been carried out on 24 May 2007, but no video-recordings, sketches, or photographs were made.

Based on the available evidence, the investigator found that A.G. had unsuccessfully attempted suicide shortly before his death by asphyxiating himself with a rope made from bed linen. Medical findings indicated death by interrupted mechanical asphyxiation, with neck injuries suggesting heart failure resulting from the attempted strangulation. As to his detention conditions, medical evidence suggested no acute condition requiring hospital admission during his stay in the ITT; he had been medically supervised. His serious illnesses, including tuberculosis and HIV, meant his physical condition would gradually deteriorate in any event. The investigator concluded that ITT officers could not have envisaged the fatal outcome, and that A.G. had received appropriate nutrition and had not refused food.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the death of a detainee with known serious health conditions and drug addiction, possible self-harm or suicide in custody, the adequacy of medical supervision and emergency response, and the repeated failures, delays, and evidential deficiencies in the domestic investigation. These matters implicate Ukraine’s positive obligations under Article 2 of the Convention to protect the life of a person in detention and to conduct an effective investigation into a death in custody.
001-163911:
In Kulyk v. Ukraine (Application no. 30760/06, judgment 23 June 2016), the applicant, Anatoliy Kulyk, alleged that police officers had ill-treated him, that the investigation into his complaints was ineffective, and that his right of individual application to the European Court of Human Rights had been interfered with.

The relevant events began on 30 December 2002. Kulyk saw three young men on the premises of the nearby Shargorodskiy Food Products Factory. Because of earlier thefts from the factory, he climbed over the fence, entered an abandoned building through an opening in the wall, heard adult voices, and quickly returned home. Five to ten minutes later, police officer L. arrived at his house. Kulyk alleged that L. had a gun, swore at him, grabbed him by the collar, struck him on the head with the gun handle, and kicked him after he fell. His mother-in-law intervened and asked L. to stop. L. then took Kulyk to the police station and accused him of stealing aluminium sheets.

At the police station, Kulyk alleged that L. kicked him in the kidneys in the presence of two officers. Later, L. and another officer, P., allegedly beat him about the head and body for 15–20 minutes, and officer G. joined them, seeking a confession to theft. Kulyk was then placed in a cell. That night he complained of headache and sickness. A man in a white coat gave him Analgin and Dimedrol, but later medical-unit information indicated he received no ambulance assistance. On the morning of 31 December 2002, he was taken to court, fined for disobeying police, returned to the station, and signed a statement that no physical force had been used and that he had no complaints. The same day, authorities decided not to prosecute him for theft, finding he had no intent and had entered the factory out of curiosity.

Kulyk later suffered headaches, nausea and fever. He was hospitalised from 3 January to 11 February 2003. Medical records noted bruises mostly on the left side, scratches, and a large left-thigh bruise. Diagnoses included closed brain injury, brain contusion of medium severity, two broken ribs, post-traumatic pneumonia, and kidney, face and body injuries. A May 2003 forensic report found medium-severity injuries caused by a blunt hard object, possibly on 30 December 2002.

The police version was that factory employees had asked L. to check noises. They saw Kulyk run, fall when climbing through a conveyor opening and over a fence, and later fall at his house. He hid in a coal bunker. Police denied beating him. Kulyk’s mother-in-law testified that she saw L. aim a blow or kick at Kulyk while he lay on the ground. Experts said the injuries could have resulted from falls or beatings.

After Kulyk complained in February 2003, prosecutors repeatedly refused or terminated proceedings for lack of evidence; those decisions were often quashed and reinvestigated. Proceedings for abuse of power began in October 2004, and officers P. and L. were charged in April 2005. However, the case was terminated in October 2008 for absence of evidence, with authorities concluding the injuries likely resulted from falls and no evidence could be found after six years. The investigation was criticised for delays and failures to question witnesses or doctors, obtain medical records, and conduct timely reconstructions.

Separately, in September–October 2010, premises connected to Kulyk’s representative were searched/inspected in unrelated criminal proceedings concerning online pornographic material. Police seized three computers from an office used by the representative/human rights organisation. One allegedly contained confidential correspondence with the Court in this case. Complaints about the seizure led to a refusal to institute criminal proceedings. The representative was reportedly acquitted in August 2013.

The applicant therefore alleged violations of Article 3 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation) and Article 34 (interference with the right of individual petition).
001-160223:
In *Salikhova and Magomedova v. Russia* (Application no. 63689/13, judgment of 26 January 2016), the applicants were the mother and wife of Mr Sakhrab Abakargadzhiyev. They alleged that he had been abducted by State agents in Dagestan, Russia, had subsequently disappeared, and that the authorities had failed to investigate the matter effectively.

At the material time, Mr Abakargadzhiyev lived with the applicants and other relatives in Makhachkala. For about eighteen months before the incident, he had allegedly been suspected of illegal activities and followed by Dagestani law-enforcement agencies, particularly the Centre against Extremism (CPE). On 20 May 2013, at about 6 p.m., he drove his white GAZ Volga-3110 car to visit relatives. At about 6.45 p.m., on Engelsa Street, his car was stopped and he was abducted by eight armed, masked men dressed in civilian clothing. They drove two civilian vehicles: a silver VAZ-21014 with a registration number partly reading “A067” and a black VAZ-21099. A relative called Mr Abakargadzhiyev during the abduction and heard him screaming. Shortly afterwards, the first applicant and a relative went along his route and found his car with police officers from the Sovetskiy district police station. The police said he had been abducted minutes earlier and told them to wait at home; they took his car to the police station.

About twenty days later, CPE officers searched the applicants’ home. Around 20 June 2013, the applicants obtained video footage of the abduction from a local resident. They recognised one abductor’s voice as that of a CPE officer named “Shakir” and informed the authorities. On 1 July 2013, a burnt male corpse was found near Gurbuki village. On 23 December 2013, the authorities identified the body as Mr Abakargadzhiyev through DNA testing. The applicants disputed this, stating that the corpse had several gold teeth while their relative had none.

The applicants complained of the abduction to the Sovetskiy police immediately and again on 24 May 2013. A criminal case was opened on 14 June 2013. Investigators examined the crime scene on 3 June and the car on 6 June, but collected no useful evidence; fingerprints were unfit for identification. They questioned witnesses, including Mr Ma.Ma., who had recorded the abduction on his mobile telephone. The video was seized on 21 June. The first applicant provided DNA samples. In June and July 2013, she received anonymous text messages claiming her son had become a “shahid” and had been set up by a neighbour working for the police. On 5 September 2013, a caller claiming to be an FSB officer said he was holding the victim and demanded a ransom; RUB 50,000 was deposited, after which the number was disconnected. Call logs placed the caller in Volgograd.

The applicants requested voice analysis of the abduction video. It was ordered, but experts found the voice unfit for identification. CPE officer Shakir N. was questioned; he admitted participating in the June search of the applicants’ home but denied any involvement in the abduction. He claimed the victim supported Wahhabism and had aided terrorist groups. An internal inquiry could not verify the allegations due to conflicting statements. The investigation was suspended on 30 December 2013, resumed in January 2014, joined with the case concerning the burnt corpse, and remained pending.

The Government denied State involvement but did not dispute the applicants’ factual account. The applicants alleged that the abduction and disappearance were attributable to State agents and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation.
001-161527:
The applicant, Manuel Luís Sousa Goucha, is a Portuguese national born in 1954 who lives in Fontanelas. He is a well-known television host and publicly declared his homosexuality in 2008. The events at issue concerned a live talk show, *Five Minutes to Midnight* (*5 Para a Meia-Noite*), broadcast on RTP2 between midnight and 1 a.m. on 28 December 2009. The programme was presented by F.C. and featured two well-known media guests. During a quiz, F.C. asked, as the most important question, “Who is the best Portuguese female TV host?” The possible answers included three female television hosts and the applicant; the applicant was the “correct” answer. In the transcript, guest J.M. first chose another guest, referred to as “the pregnant one” (option B, C.V.), and F.C. then revealed that the answer was Manuel Luís Goucha. F.C. described J.M.’s earlier answer as dishonest and contrary to his beliefs, while J.M. said he had known the answer and had been about to say it.

In 2010 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint for defamation and “insult” (*injúria*) with the Lisbon Criminal Department for Investigation and Prosecution. The defendants were the State-owned television company RTP, the production company, the television presenter F.C., and the directors of programming and content. The applicant complained that including his name among the possible answers had damaged his reputation and dignity. On 2 March 2011 a public prosecutor discontinued the proceedings, stating that the defendants had not intended to offend him.

The applicant sought to intervene in the proceedings as an assistant to the public prosecutor (*assistente*) and lodged private prosecution submissions with the Lisbon Criminal Investigation Court against the defendants. The defendants challenged those submissions by requesting that a judicial investigation be opened. On 24 June 2011 the investigating judge dismissed the case (*despacho de não pronúncia*). As regards the individual defendants, the judge found insufficient evidence of defamation or insult, so the case could not proceed to trial. The judge stated that the defendants had not intended to attack the applicant’s honour, nor had they anticipated doing so; the subjective element of the offence was therefore unverified. The judge noted that the applicant was a public figure and must be used to having his characteristics captured by comedians for humour. The judge referred to public knowledge that the applicant’s characteristics reflected behaviour attributed to the female gender, such as his way of expressing himself, his colourful feminine clothes, and the fact that he had always lived in a world of women. The judge also noted that the applicant had recently made his homosexuality public and that the defendants never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. As regards the two defendant companies, the proceedings were discontinued under Article 11 of the Criminal Code, which excludes legal persons from liability for defamation and insult.

The applicant appealed against the decision not to indict the natural defendants before the Lisbon Court of Appeal. He argued in particular that the reason his name had been included in the list of possible answers was his sexual orientation. On 17 April 2012 the appeal was dismissed.
