The Court of Appeal upheld the Criminal Investigation Court’s decision, finding insufficient evidence of defamation. It stated that not everything the complainant considers offensive should be so regarded, but rather what the majority of reasonable people would consider an offence to social and individual values of respect. It cited the context of a comedy show and treated the question as one of the many jokes typical of such shows. It repeated that the applicant was a public figure, that his characteristics reflected behaviour attributed to the female gender, and that the defendants had never intended to criticise his sexual orientation. It considered that the expression, used in a playful and irreverent context and in the show’s normal style, even if in bad taste, did not reach the legal threshold for protection of honour and consideration. The applicant alleged that the unfavourable outcome of his defamation case before the Portuguese courts was discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, citing Article 14 of the Convention.
001-163358:
Dirk Petschulies, a German national born in 1952, lodged application no. 6281/13 against Germany on 22 January 2013. He alleged that his continued preventive detention in a supervised residential facility affiliated to a psychiatric hospital—extended retrospectively beyond the former statutory maximum of ten years—breached Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

His criminal history was central. In 1977, he was convicted of offences committed while drunk, sentenced to one year’s imprisonment, and ordered into a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code, based on diminished responsibility attributed to alleged infantile brain damage and drunkenness. He was detained in psychiatric hospitals from December 1977 to October 1980. In 1981, however, the Göttingen Regional Court quashed that judgment. It reconvicted him, sentenced him to one year and eight months’ imprisonment, and made no psychiatric detention order. Re-examining his condition with new medical techniques, the court found he had never suffered from a pathological mental disorder and had not acted with diminished responsibility. It rejected the earlier findings of infantile brain damage and found that, although he had an abnormal personality, he was neither a psychopath nor an alcoholic.

In December 1984, the Hildesheim Regional Court convicted Petschulies of seven counts of dangerous assault, four counts of assault, coercion, and two counts of attempted coercion, all committed between December 1982 and May 1984. It sentenced him to six years’ imprisonment and ordered preventive detention under Article 66 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The offences were violent: he punched and kicked victims, including schoolchildren, strangers, and homeless people; he also set an Alsatian dog on victims, causing serious bites, and attacked two homeless people with a knife. Psychiatric and psychological experts found him fully criminally responsible for most offences, with only two possibly affected by alcohol. They found no pathological mental disorder, but noted a personality differing from the majority in lacking empathy and seeking dominance, and a propensity to commit serious violent offences.

After serving his prison sentence, he was placed in preventive detention on 7 May 1990. By 7 August 2000, he had spent ten years in preventive detention. Under the law in force at the time of his conviction, initial preventive detention could not exceed ten years. However, a 1998 amendment abolished that maximum with immediate effect, allowing continued detention if there was a danger of serious offences. The Lüneburg Regional Court therefore ordered continuation. In 2001, he was convicted of assaulting his daughter and sentenced to four months’ imprisonment. In 2003, he was transferred to a detoxification department; in 2005, the Göttingen Regional Court ordered further preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital rather than a detoxification facility, considering rehabilitation prospects better there. From March 2011, he was allowed provisional residence in Friedland Castle, a supervised residential facility.

On 19 July 2011, the Göttingen Regional Court again ordered continued preventive detention in a psychiatric hospital under Article 67d § 3, applying the Federal Constitutional Court’s stricter transitional criteria of 4 May 2011. It found that Petschulies suffered from a “mental disorder” under the Therapy Detention Act—a dissocial personality disorder with marked psychopathic elements—and that this caused his previous offences. An expert, relying on case files because Petschulies refused examination, found a high risk of most serious violent crimes if released, especially when drunk, given his lack of empathy and potential for random violence. The court found detention of more than twenty years proportionate because no suitable alternative accommodation existed. His appeal was dismissed in September 2011, and his constitutional complaint was declined without reasons in July 2012.

At the relevant time, he resided in supervised facilities with limited freedoms—shopping twice weekly, escorted outings, and work therapy—but received no specific treatment for his mental condition or alcohol abuse. He was released on 15 September 2014. The alleged violation was that this retrospective extension of preventive detention beyond the former ten-year maximum breached Article 5 § 1.
001-169210:
**Summary of *Guk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 16995/05)**

The case of *Guk v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Viktor Guk, a Ukrainian national, on 21 April 2005. The applicant alleged multiple violations of the Convention, primarily under Articles 3, 8, 13, and 34.

In 2001, the applicant was convicted of murder, attempted murder, and illegal possession of firearms, receiving a life sentence. This was later reduced to fifteen years in 2009. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations pertain to his detention conditions and treatment in various penal institutions.

**Alleged Ill-Treatment (Article 3):** The applicant claimed that upon his arrival at Sokalska Prison on 15 October 2004, he was beaten by several guards, resulting in an eye injury (later diagnosed as traumatic mydriasis) and multiple bruises. He alleged that his complaints to prison officials went unheeded and that he received no medical assistance for these injuries. His attempts to send complaints to a prosecutor were allegedly obstructed by prison authorities. When his complaint was eventually addressed in 2006, the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation, citing a lack of evidence, a decision later upheld by domestic courts.

**Conditions of Detention (Article 3):** The applicant described severe conditions in Sokalska Prison from 2004 to 2007. He was held in a twelve-square-meter cell with three others, spending 23 hours a day inside without physical exercise. He alleged the cells were damp, unventilated, and inadequately heated, and that he was for a time detained with inmates suffering from open tuberculosis. He further complained of humiliating treatment when outside his cell, including being handcuffed, escorted by guards with a dog, and having a felt bag placed over his head. He also alleged inadequate food and water, and that his complaints about these conditions were not examined.

**Medical Assistance (Article 3):** The applicant, who suffered from hypertension, claimed he did not receive adequate medical treatment and was not allowed to keep necessary medication. A prosecutor's inquiry in 2005 found the medical assistance adequate, a finding the applicant unsuccessfully challenged in domestic courts.

**Restrictions on Family Life (Article 8):** During his detention, the applicant's contact with his family was severely restricted. He was entitled to visits only once every six months, for a maximum of four hours. These visits were often shorter due to high demand. He was separated from his family by a glass partition, placed in a cage, and conversations were monitored. He was denied any intimate contact with his wife. Furthermore, he was allegedly not allowed any telephone calls between October 2004 and November 2005, and subsequently only once every three months.

**Hindrance of the Right of Application (Article 34):** The applicant also complained that in 2012, while at Zamkova Prison, his correspondence with the Court was opened and read by the administration, and that he was persecuted for communicating with the Court, including being placed in solitary confinement for several months and having his documents and pen confiscated.

The applicant initially also complained of being obstructed in substantiating a previous application to the Court by being denied access to his criminal case file.
001-168816:
In *Kiril Zlatkov Nikolov v. France*, the applicant was a Bulgarian national convicted in France in connection with an international prostitution ring. He lodged two applications with the European Court of Human Rights in 2011 and 2012. The Court gave notice of the case to the French Government in respect of complaints under Article 5 § 3 (prompt judicial review of detention), Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 6 § 1 (discrimination in fair-trial rights), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). Other complaints were declared inadmissible.

The investigation began in 2009 into an international prostitution ring. Telephone interceptions authorised by the Chambéry liberties and detention judge captured two conversations on 4 September 2009 that appeared to incriminate the applicant. A judicial investigation was opened on 2 October 2009 for living on the earnings of prostitution as part of an organised gang, human trafficking as part of an organised gang, and criminal conspiracy. An arrest warrant was issued on 28 July 2010 and later converted into a European arrest warrant. The applicant was arrested in Germany and handed over to the French authorities at 11:45 a.m. on 16 December 2010. He was brought before the Strasbourg public prosecutor and immediately placed in administrative detention. He first appeared before the investigating judge at 10:56 a.m. on 20 December 2010, when he was placed under formal investigation. At about 5 p.m. that same day, the Lyons liberties and detention judge interviewed him and remanded him in custody. The nearly four-day period between his transfer to France and his first appearance before a judge was central to the Article 5 § 3 complaint.

Although the alleged offences were classified as serious crimes, the interviews and confrontations during the investigation were not video-recorded, relying on an exception in the seventh paragraph of Article 116-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for organised crime. On 17 June 2011 the applicant applied to the Investigation Division of the Lyons Court of Appeal to have various procedural steps declared void, including the detention order, interviews and confrontations, and telephone interceptions. He also submitted preliminary rulings on constitutionality concerning Articles 64-1 and 116-1. On 6 September 2011 the Investigation Division dismissed most of his application and referred the constitutional questions to the Court of Cassation. On 14 September 2011 he appealed on points of law, relying on Articles 5 § 3, 6 § 1 and 14 of the Convention and the constitutional principle of equality.

On 18 January 2012 the Court of Cassation referred the constitutional questions to the Constitutional Council. On 6 April 2012 the Constitutional Council declared the seventh paragraphs of Articles 64-1 and 116-1 unconstitutional because they infringed equality, but the abrogation was prospective only, applying to persons questioned or interviewed after publication of the decision. On 10 May 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It held that the constitutional ruling did not benefit him retroactively; that he had not been questioned in police custody; and that the absence of video recording of his interviews by the investigating judge did not violate his Convention rights because he had legal assistance, could review the transcripts, request corrections, and challenge his statements. It also held that only the person concerned could complain about the lack of video recording of others’ questioning. The Article 13 complaint concerned the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy for these matters. The applicant was convicted and ultimately released in June 2015 after serving his sentence.
001-167110:
Cano Moya v. Spain (Application no. 3142/11) concerned a Spanish prisoner, Vicente Manuel Cano Moya, who complained that prison disciplinary sanctions violated his right to be presumed innocent and his freedom of expression, and that domestic authorities obstructed his right of individual petition to the European Court of Human Rights.

At the time, the applicant was on remand in Foncalent Prison, Alicante. On 20 October 2009, the Alicante Prison disciplinary board found him guilty of three disciplinary offences under the General Prison Rules: threatening prison officers (very serious, Rule 108(b)); disobeying officers’ orders (serious, Rule 109(b)); and damaging prison property (serious, Rule 109(e)). The punishments were four weekends in isolation for the threats, twenty days without group recreational activities for disobedience, and twenty days without group recreational activities for property damage.

The applicant appealed to the post-sentencing judge No. 2 of the Comunidad Valenciana. On 17 November 2009, that judge partly allowed the appeal and revoked the sanction imposed for disobedience. Because the applicant had been transferred to Villena Prison, attempts to serve him personally failed; he was eventually served on 28 January 2010 and signed an acknowledgment. A further reforma appeal was rejected by the same judge on 18 February 2010, and that decision was also served on him.

The applicant then lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court, invoking Articles 20 (freedom of expression) and 24 (presumption of innocence) of the Spanish Constitution. On 22 March 2010, the Constitutional Court requested his case file; the post-sentencing judge sent it on 12 April 2010. On 30 September 2010, the Constitutional Court declared the amparo appeal inadmissible as devoid of special constitutional significance. The decision was served on 7 October 2010.

On 22 December 2010, the applicant requested a copy of his case file from the post-sentencing judge in order to submit it to the European Court of Human Rights, relying on sections 234 and 454 of the Judicature Act. On 4 January 2011, he notified the Court of his intention to apply; the Registry invited him to submit an application form by 11 March 2011. On 26 January 2011, the judge refused his request, saying the case was still pending before the Constitutional Court.

The applicant sent his application form on 2 February 2011, raising complaints under Article 6 § 2 and Article 10 § 1 of the Convention. He enclosed the Constitutional Court’s decision but not the lower post-sentencing decisions, although he referred to them. On 4 February 2011, he informed the judge that the Constitutional Court had already decided and that he needed a certified copy before the Court’s deadline. On 22 February 2011, the judge’s registrar rejected the request, stating that the European Court could request the case file itself. That decision was served on 4 March 2011.

On 3 March 2011, the European Court acknowledged receipt of the application and asked for all relevant domestic decisions by 3 June 2011. The next day, the applicant informed the Court that he could not obtain a copy of his file and complained that the domestic authorities were hindering his defence. He renewed his request on 14 March 2011. On 1 April 2011, the post-sentencing judge again refused, stating that other courts could request case files directly. That decision was served on 6 April 2011, and the applicant informed the Court of the refusal on 7 April 2011.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 2 and Article 10 § 1 concerning the disciplinary sanctions, and complained that the refusal to provide his case file hindered his right of individual petition under Article 34 of the Convention.
001-161738:
**Summary of Seton v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 55287/10)**

The case of *Seton v. the United Kingdom* concerns the applicant, Mr. John Edward Seton, who was convicted of murder in 2008 and alleged a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The conviction stemmed from the shooting death of Mr. Jon Bartlett on March 31, 2006. The prosecution’s case was that Seton, a drug dealer who owed the victim £24,000, shot him and then fled to the Netherlands before being extradited to the UK.

The central issue arose from Seton’s defense. He claimed that the murder was committed by a third party, Mr. Pearman, a man with previous convictions for drug, firearm, and murder offenses who was serving a life sentence at the time. According to Seton, he had been involved in a drug deal with both Bartlett and Pearman, and it was Pearman who had driven off in the silver Vauxhall Vectra used in the shooting.

During the investigation, police interviewed Pearman, who answered "no comment." Subsequently, Pearman made two phone calls from prison—to his son and his wife—in which he denied any involvement in the murder and claimed he had never heard of Seton. As a category A prisoner, Pearman would have known these calls were being recorded. At Seton’s trial, the prosecution sought to admit these recordings as hearsay evidence under section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The defense objected, but the trial judge ruled the recordings admissible.

In his ruling, the judge considered the factors in section 114(2) of the Act. He found the evidence had "extremely strong probative value" as Pearman appeared to be expressing genuine outrage at being implicated. While Pearman refused to testify, the judge noted that police enquiries had found no connection between Pearman and either the victim or the applicant, and no evidence of his involvement. The judge acknowledged the defense’s argument that the statements were self-serving, as Pearman knew he was being recorded, but considered this a matter of weight for the jury, not a ground for exclusion. He also noted the evidence was reliable (taped) and that Pearman’s bad character had already been put before the jury. The recordings were played at trial, and the jury asked to hear them a second time during deliberations.

Seton was convicted by a majority verdict and sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 30 years. His appeal to the Court of Appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge's decision, finding that he had properly considered all relevant matters under section 114(2). It noted that compelling Pearman to attend court would have been a "fruitless exercise" as he would have refused to give evidence, and that the defense could still argue the statements were self-serving.

It was this admission of hearsay evidence—the recorded phone calls of an absent witness whom the defense could not cross-examine—that formed the basis of Seton’s application to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that it rendered his trial unfair.
001-163438:
**Gyuleva v. Bulgaria** (Application no. 38840/08) concerned a Bulgarian national, Ms Valentina Atanasova Gyuleva, born in 1947 and living in Plovdiv. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention because she was not notified of civil proceedings brought against her and could not defend herself.

The case arose from an earlier restitution dispute over a flat occupied by the applicant and her family. Between 1992 and 2000, proceedings ended with the pre-nationalisation owners being recognised as the true owners. That earlier matter led to a prior Strasbourg judgment finding violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1 due to the length of proceedings. In February 2002, those owners sold the flat to Mr and Mrs P. They then brought *rei vindicatio* proceedings against the applicant. The first-instance court allowed their claim in October 2002. Although appeals continued, the applicant vacated the flat on 10 January 2003 and moved to Hrabrino, registering her address there on 4 February 2003.

On 4 May 2005, Mr and Mrs P. brought a new action against the applicant for unjust enrichment, claiming compensation for her occupation of the flat between 1 February 2002 and 10 January 2003. On 16 May 2005, the Plovdiv District Court issued a summons, sent to the mayor of Hrabrino for service. On 16 June 2005, the mayor returned it, stating that “no such person has been registered” in the village. On 8 July 2005, at the claimants’ request, the Plovdiv Regional Directorate of the Interior issued a certificate confirming that the applicant’s last declared address was in Hrabrino. Despite this, the District Court made no further attempts to locate her. On 26 August 2005, it concluded that her address was unknown and published a notification in the State Gazette under Article 50 § 1 of the 1952 Code of Civil Procedure.

The court then appointed an ex officio lawyer to represent the applicant, and all subsequent documents were served on that lawyer. The applicant alleged that the lawyer failed to contact her, failed to appeal, made no evidentiary requests, and did not meaningfully contest the claimants’ arguments, including a possible partial time-bar objection.

On 6 April 2006, the Plovdiv District Court allowed the unjust enrichment claim, ordering the applicant to pay BGN 3,573 plus interest. On appeal by Mr and Mrs P., the Plovdiv Regional Court, in a final judgment of 10 July 2006, ordered her to pay an additional BGN 1,006.21. The applicant only learned of the proceedings and judgments on 22 February 2008, when a bailiff notified her to pay. She ultimately paid BGN 8,767.07, approximately EUR 4,473.

The applicant relied on additional facts suggesting the authorities could have found her. In 2004, she was appointed as a juror at the Plovdiv District Court for 2005–2009 and received hearing notices at her brother’s address in Plovdiv. At that same address, in 2007 and 2008, she received two summonses relating to other proceedings brought by Mr and Mrs P., as well as the February 2008 bailiff notice. She was also a well-known piano teacher at the Academy of Music, Dance and Fine Arts in Plovdiv, whose workplace could have been known to the authorities.

Domestic law required summonses normally to be served by court officials, municipality, village mayor, registered mail, or at the person’s workplace. Service by publication in the State Gazette was a last resort where the address was genuinely unknown, but the court had to satisfy itself through checks that this was so. Reopening civil cases was possible if a party had been deprived of participation or had an ex officio representative appointed despite a known address, subject to strict time limits.

The key alleged violation was therefore that the authorities treated the applicant as of unknown address and served her only by publication, despite available information, then appointed a lawyer who allegedly did not adequately defend her, leaving her unable to participate in the unjust enrichment proceedings until after final judgment and enforcement.
001-161381:
In *Menéndez García and Álvarez González v. Spain* (European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Applications nos. 73818/11 and 19420/12, judgment of 15 March 2016), the applicants were two Spanish nationals: Gerardo Menéndez García, born in 1964 and living in Gargantada, and Sigifredo Álvarez González, born in 1956 and living in Sant Jordi de Cercs. The first applicant was represented by a lawyer; the second was self-represented.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation concern the excessive length of criminal proceedings. In 2000 the applicants acted as intermediaries or purchase agents in the sale of three cars to a company. On 20 November 2000, criminal investigations were opened by the Gijón investigating judge against the applicants and eight other suspects for fraud and forgery of documents. In April 2001 the applicants were detained, charged with document forgery, informed of their rights as detainees, and interrogated by the Guardia Civil in the presence of counsel.

A significant delay followed. On 8 November 2004, the investigating judge issued a decision ordering the opening of oral proceedings and sent the case file to the Asturias Audiencia Provincial. However, the hearings before the Audiencia Provincial did not take place until 6 May 2009—approximately four and a half years after committal and eight and a half years after the investigation began. On 5 June 2009, the Audiencia Provincial convicted the first applicant and sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment, and convicted the second applicant and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment, for fraud and document forgery.

The applicants requested a sentence reduction for undue delay under Article 21 of the Criminal Code. The Audiencia Provincial refused. It acknowledged that the proceedings had been “unusually” long but attributed the duration to the complexity of the case: difficulties gathering evidence in different jurisdictions, the large number of parties, problems notifying some defendants, and the applicants’ lawyers’ lack of celerity in presenting submissions.

The applicants appealed in cassation. On 27 May 2010, the Supreme Court partially ruled in their favour, sentencing both to three years and eight months’ imprisonment for fraud. It rejected their undue-delay claims, accepting that the proceedings might have appeared excessively long but finding that the Audiencia Provincial had provided a sound and detailed justification. Both applicants then filed amparo appeals with the Constitutional Court, complaining, among other things, about the excessive length of proceedings. By decisions of 20 May and 12 September 2011, served on 25 May and 23 September 2011, the Constitutional Court declared the appeals inadmissible for lack of constitutional relevance under Article 50 § 1(b) of the Organic Law on the Constitutional Court.

The applicants lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 November 2011 and 22 March 2012. On 12 September 2013, the complaints concerning the length of proceedings were communicated to the Spanish Government, while the remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible by the President of the Section under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The central alleged violation was therefore that the criminal proceedings lasted excessively long, contrary to the right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The key timeline runs from the investigation in November 2000 to final domestic decisions in 2011, with notable delays between investigation and committal and between committal and hearing.
001-162864:
**Case: Fürst-Pfeifer v. Austria (Applications nos. 33677/10 and 52340/10)**

The case originated in two applications lodged against Austria with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms Gabriele Fürst-Pfeifer, an Austrian psychiatrist born in 1964. Since 2000, she had been registered as a psychological expert for court proceedings, particularly in custody and contact-rights disputes, public-care decisions and child-abuse cases. Her work focused mainly on psychological examinations of children and adolescents in custody and contact disputes.

On 23 December 2008, an article was published online on “meinbezirk.at” and in the free regional weekly print publication *Bezirksblatt*. The article was headlined “Disclosed: Court Expert for custody proceedings a case for therapy” and alleged that the applicant suffered from mood swings, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, hallucinations and paranoid ideas, yet continued to work as a court-appointed expert. It stated that she had examined over 3,000 married couples in custody disputes over the previous 12 years. The article relied on a 1993 psychological expert report by Dr. M., commissioned in civil proceedings concerning an alleged breach of promise of marriage, which reportedly found those impairments and suggested they were hereditary. It added that the applicant had later been introduced to the expert community at the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court and that her integrity had been beyond reproach for a decade. The article also included comments from a Green Party member who had filed a criminal complaint against her, the Youth Advocate at the Lower Austria Regional Government, and the Vice-President of the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court. It noted that she had stopped answering her phone and withdrawn from her cases.

Following publication, the applicant faced questions from colleagues and patients, and proceedings were initiated at the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court to determine whether she remained fit to serve as a court-appointed expert. Her mental status was also to be examined.

The applicant brought separate actions against the online and print publishers under section 8a of the Austrian Media Act, seeking damages and publication of the judgment. She claimed that the article, especially the passages about the 1993 psychological report, violated her intimate personal sphere and compromised her publicly. She did not argue that the expert report itself had been obtained unlawfully.

The St. Pölten Regional Court and the Innsbruck Regional Court initially allowed her actions, awarding €5,000 in damages each and ordering publication. They found that an average reader would link the 1993 opinion to her current work and question her professional quality. The article touched her intimate sphere, was incomplete, exaggerated and manipulative, and was not directly linked to her public life because custody proceedings were not public. They also considered that she appeared able to manage her illness and work without impairment.

However, the Vienna Court of Appeal (30 November 2009) and the Innsbruck Court of Appeal (11 February 2010) set aside those judgments and dismissed her actions. They agreed that the article affected her intimate personal sphere and was capable of compromising her, but found the published information true and sufficiently balanced. They held that her work as a registered court expert belonged to the public sphere, was closely linked to the administration of justice and had considerable influence on judges’ decisions. Given the sensitivity of custody proceedings and the dominant role of experts, any well-founded doubt about an expert’s psychological integrity warranted investigation in the public interest. The courts therefore treated the article as justified reporting on a matter of public concern.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that the Austrian courts had failed to protect her reputation and private life against the defamatory allegations. The key issue was whether the publication of intimate psychiatric details was justified as true information directly related to public life and the public interest in the fitness of court experts.
001-164454:
In *Krahulec v. Slovakia* (Application no. 19294/07), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 5 July 2016; it became final on 5 October 2016. The applicant, Mr Štefan Krahulec, a Slovak national born in 1945 and living in Zvolen, lodged his application on 30 April 2007. He alleged that Slovakia’s rent-control scheme imposed restrictions on his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 7 June 2011.

The property at issue was a house in Piešťany built by the applicant’s grandfather in 1929. The family retained ownership under the communist regime, and ownership was transferred to the applicant from his mother on 21 December 1998. The house contained four flats: two measuring 108 sq. m and two measuring 123 sq. m.

At the time the application was lodged, the flats were occupied by tenants under regulated rents. The tenants or their predecessors had acquired the right to use the flats through municipal decisions taken between 1953 and 1986. After 1 January 1992, that right of use was transformed into tenancies with regulated rent for an indefinite period. Under the applicable legislation, the applicant had to accept that the flats were occupied by those tenants and could charge no more than the maximum rent fixed by the State. He had no possibility of unilaterally terminating the leases.

In 1999, the maximum monthly rent chargeable for the flats was the equivalent of approximately EUR 13 to EUR 33. Following several increases, by 2004 the applicant could charge EUR 115 per month for each smaller flat and EUR 124 per month for each larger flat. The applicant claimed that in practice he received less than the statutory maximum and pursued several property disputes with tenants and the local municipality.

The parties disputed the market rent. The applicant relied on data from the National Association of Real Estate Agencies, claiming that monthly market rent for similar flats reached EUR 600 to EUR 800 between 2004 and 2007. The Government submitted an expert valuation putting the monthly market rent in 2010 at EUR 265.50 and EUR 325 for the applicant’s flats. Rent control ended for the first flat in May 2007, for the second and third flats in August 2007, and for the fourth flat in April 2008.

The relevant domestic law and practice concerning Slovakia’s rent-control scheme were set out in *Bittó and Others v. Slovakia* (no. 30255/09, 28 January 2014). In *Bittó*, the Court found that the rent-control scheme violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Under Article 46, it held that the violation originated in a systemic legislative and practice problem affecting many flat owners, with 13 other applications pending concerning about 170 persons. The Court noted gradual measures, including Law no. 216/2011 allowing annual 20% rent increases from late 2011, and a possible right from 2017 for landlords to claim the difference between market and controlled rent if municipalities had not housed hardship tenants by the end of 2016. However, those measures did not address the prior situation. The Court stated that further measures were needed and that Slovakia should introduce a specific, clearly regulated compensatory remedy. Implementation of *Bittó* remained pending.

The key alleged violation was therefore that the rent-control scheme forced the applicant to keep tenants, capped his rent far below market levels, and prevented him from terminating leases, thereby interfering with his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-163054:
In *Tuchin and Tuchina v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40458/08), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) gave judgment on 26 May 2016. The applicants, Ukrainian nationals Anatoliy Andreyevich Tuchin and Svetlana Aleksandrovna Tuchina, are the parents of a woman who died after a road accident. They lived in Odessa and were represented by V.V. Sudakov. The application was lodged on 29 July 2008 under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants alleged that there had been no effective investigation into their daughter’s death. On 3 June 2013 the application was communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

The central event occurred on 30 April 2002, when the applicants’ daughter was struck by a car driven by P. while crossing the street. She died in hospital as a result. The subsequent criminal investigation was marked by prolonged failure to bring the case to a proper conclusion. Between April 2002 and October 2010, the prosecution authorities issued at least ten decisions refusing to institute or discontinuing criminal proceedings against P. because his actions allegedly lacked *corpus delicti*. All of those decisions were quashed by supervising authorities as unsubstantiated, and further investigations were ordered. This repeated cycle meant that for more than eight years no final determination of criminal responsibility was reached.

On 9 July 2009 the first applicant lodged a civil claim against P. within the criminal proceedings, and on 15 July 2009 he was granted the status of an aggrieved party. Nonetheless, on 26 October 2010 the Odessa Suvorivskyy District Court discontinued the criminal proceedings against P. as time-barred. The Odessa Regional Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 21 December 2010, and the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters upheld it on 20 November 2012.

On the same date, the Higher Specialised Court issued a separate ruling identifying serious shortcomings. It stated that the pre-trial investigation had been perfunctory and lengthy; that since 2002 hardly any investigative measures had been taken; that the numerous refusals to institute criminal proceedings had been unfounded and had eventually been quashed; that guidelines for remedying investigative shortcomings had been ignored; and that the overall duration of the investigation—over ten years—had been unjustified. The Higher Specialised Court concluded that the criminal investigation had not complied with domestic legislation or the Convention and instructed the relevant authorities to prevent similar violations in the future.

For the alleged violation, the key facts are therefore the death of the applicants’ daughter in a road traffic accident, the repeated and ineffective decisions not to prosecute the driver, the eventual discontinuance of proceedings as time-barred, and the domestic court’s own finding that the investigation was perfunctory, protracted and non-compliant. These facts underpinned the complaint that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation into the death, engaging the procedural obligation under Article 2 of the Convention to protect the right to life. The issue was whether the authorities acted with sufficient promptness, diligence and effectiveness to establish the circumstances of the death and any responsibility for it.
001-163822:
In *Soares v. Portugal* (Application no. 79972/12), the applicant, António Alberto Mota Soares, was a Portuguese chief corporal in the National Republican Guard (GNR) stationed at the Góis territorial post. On 7 November 2009, he sent an email to the General Inspectorate of Internal Administration entitled “Suspected misuse of money.” He alleged that Commander M.C. of the Arganil GNR post had misused public funds. According to the email, in December 2008 the Coimbra GNR Territorial Group had distributed money to territorial posts for a Christmas dinner. At Arganil, allegedly only Commander M.C. and Corporal M. attended the dinner, and the full amount allocated to the post’s military was paid to the restaurant manager in exchange for a receipt. Soares stated that it seemed the Commander had since taken his family to that restaurant, with the cost deducted from the unspent dinner money. He said he had learned of the matter through rumours among military personnel at Arganil, who had not reported it for fear of reprisals, and requested secrecy because he was also a GNR member.

The Inspectorate forwarded the email to the GNR General Command and the Lousã public prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor investigated but discontinued proceedings on 28 February 2010, finding no evidence of the alleged offence. The Inspectorate discontinued its own inquiry on 21 June 2010. The GNR opened an internal inquiry on 4 December 2009; after hearing Commander M.C. on 23 December 2009, it was converted into disciplinary proceedings against the Commander on 9 February 2010. Those proceedings were discontinued on 30 July 2010 for insufficient evidence.

On 22 April 2010, Commander M.C. filed a criminal defamation complaint against Soares. On 7 July 2011, the public prosecutor charged Soares with aggravated defamation, alleging that the email had intentionally attacked the Commander’s honesty, honour and professional reputation. The Commander also claimed EUR 5,000 in damages. On 17 January 2012, the Lousã Criminal Court convicted Soares of aggravated defamation and sentenced him to 80 day-fines totalling EUR 720, plus EUR 1,000 in damages. The court found the rumour unproved, concluded that Soares intended to undermine the Commander’s honour, knew the allegation was untrue, and could easily have clarified its authenticity with the restaurant owner. It held that whistle-blowing could not justify unsubstantiated suspicions. The Coimbra Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 19 September 2012.

Separately, on 3 August 2011, the GNR General Command instituted disciplinary proceedings against Soares. On 20 February 2013, the inquiry report concluded that he had breached his duty of loyalty by failing to inform his hierarchical superiors through the proper chain of command. It noted that all investigations into his allegations had been discontinued and that he had been criminally convicted. On 27 March 2013, Soares received a disciplinary sanction of six days’ suspension, suspended for twelve months. He apparently did not appeal that sanction.

Relevant domestic law included Criminal Code Article 180, which criminalises defamation, including accusations framed as suspicion, and Article 184, which aggravates the offence where the victim is an agent of authority. GNR rules required members to refrain from statements affecting the Guard’s cohesion or reputation or breaching hierarchical discipline, and imposed a duty of loyalty requiring faults to be communicated through hierarchical channels.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Soares complained under Article 10 that his criminal conviction for reporting an alleged misuse of public money violated his right to freedom of expression. The key issue was whether the conviction and related sanctions constituted a justified interference with his right to impart information of public interest, particularly in a military context.
001-159906:
In *Bărbulescu v. Romania* (Application no. 61496/08), the applicant, a Romanian national born in 1979, worked from 1 August 2004 to 6 August 2007 for a private company as a sales engineer. At his employer’s request, he created a Yahoo Messenger account to respond to clients’ enquiries. On 13 July 2007, the employer informed him that his Yahoo Messenger communications had been monitored from 5 to 13 July 2007 and that the records showed he had used the Internet for personal purposes, contrary to internal regulations. The applicant replied in writing that he had used Yahoo Messenger only for professional purposes. The employer then presented a 45-page transcript of his communications. It contained all messages exchanged with his fiancée and brother during the monitoring period and concerned personal matters. It also included five short messages exchanged with his fiancée on 12 July 2007 through a personal Yahoo Messenger account; those messages did not disclose intimate information.

On 1 August 2007, the employer terminated the applicant’s employment contract for breach of internal regulations, which strictly prohibited using company computers, photocopiers, telephones, telex and fax machines for personal purposes.

The applicant challenged the dismissal before the Bucharest County Court, arguing that the decision was null and void because the employer had violated his right to correspondence protected by the Romanian Constitution and Criminal Code. On 7 December 2007, the County Court dismissed his complaint. It found that the employer had complied with Labour Code dismissal procedures and that the applicant had been informed of the rules prohibiting personal use. Monitoring his Yahoo Messenger communications during working hours, even if illegal, could not affect the validity of the disciplinary proceedings. Since the applicant claimed he had used Yahoo Messenger only to advise clients, checking the content was the only way to verify that defence. The employer had the right to monitor use of company computers and to check how professional tasks were performed. The court noted that employees had been warned that their activity was under surveillance, including by notice no. 2316 of 3 July 2007, which the applicant had signed, and that another colleague had been dismissed for personal Internet use. The Internet at work was a professional tool, and the employer could monitor personal use to prevent damage to IT systems, illicit activities, or disclosure of commercial secrets.

The applicant appealed, claiming that e-mails were protected by Article 8 of the Convention as “private life” and “correspondence”. He also complained that the County Court had refused to hear witnesses to show the employer suffered no harm. On 17 June 2008, the Bucharest Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the County Court judgment. Relying on EU Directive 95/46/EC, it found the employer’s conduct reasonable and the monitoring of communications the only method of establishing whether there had been a disciplinary breach. The employer had the right and obligation to ensure the company’s functioning and could check how employees completed their tasks. Since the applicant denied personal use after being warned, the employer was entitled to monitor and transcribe his Yahoo Messenger communications. The Court of Appeal concluded that the violation of his correspondence was the only way to achieve a legitimate aim and that a proper balance had been struck between protecting his private life and the employer’s right to supervise its business.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the employer’s decision to terminate his contract had been based on a breach of his right to respect for private life and correspondence and that the Romanian courts had failed to protect that right.
001-164470:
In *Nait-Liman v. Switzerland* (Application no. 51357/07), the applicant, Abdennacer Naït-Liman, was born in Tunisia in 1962, later acquired Swiss nationality, and lived in Versoix, Geneva. He alleged that on 22 April 1992 Italian police arrested him and took him to the Tunisian Consulate in Genoa, after which Tunisian agents transferred him to Tunis. From 24 April to 1 June 1992, he claimed he was arbitrarily detained and tortured at the Tunisian Ministry of the Interior on the orders of A.K., then Minister of the Interior. He described being held in the “roast chicken” position, deprived of sleep and basic physiological needs, beaten on the soles of his feet with a baseball bat, and struck with telephone cords. He submitted that he suffered medically attested physical and psychological injuries, with a plausible causal link to the alleged abuse. He fled Tunisia in 1993, sought asylum in Switzerland, and was granted political asylum in 1995.

In 2001, while A.K. was receiving treatment in a Swiss hospital, the applicant lodged a criminal complaint in Geneva for severe bodily injury, illegal confinement, insults, endangering health, coercion, and abuse of authority, and sought to join as a civil party. The proceedings were discontinued because A.K. had left Switzerland and could not be arrested. In 2003, the applicant allegedly consulted a Tunisian lawyer, who advised that a civil action in Tunisia was impossible or would never succeed. On 8 July 2004, he brought a civil claim before the Geneva Court of First Instance against Tunisia and A.K., seeking CHF 200,000 plus interest for non-pecuniary damage caused by the alleged torture.

On 15 September 2005, the Court of First Instance declared the claim inadmissible for lack of territorial jurisdiction. It found that the Swiss courts had no jurisdiction under the Federal Law on Private International Law (LDIP), because the defendants were not domiciled or habitually resident in Switzerland and no unlawful act or detrimental result occurred there. It also rejected jurisdiction under the “forum of necessity” in section 3 LDIP, finding no sufficient connection with Switzerland: the alleged acts occurred in Tunisia in 1992 by Tunisian State agents, and the applicant’s later asylum and residence in Switzerland did not suffice. The Cantonal Court rejected his appeal on 15 September 2006, noting his difficulty in suing in Tunisia but holding that the defendants enjoyed immunity because the alleged torture was an act *iure imperii*, relying on *Al-Adsani v. the United Kingdom*.

On 22 May 2007, the Federal Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal. It held that section 3 LDIP required cumulative conditions: no Swiss forum otherwise, impossibility or unreasonableness of proceedings abroad, and a sufficient connection with Switzerland. The first condition was met; the second was problematic but left undecided; the third was absent. All specific features of the case pointed to Tunisia, except the applicant’s residence in Italy at the time, and his later move to Switzerland was a subsequent fact not forming part of the case. The Federal Court therefore found that the Swiss courts lacked jurisdiction, without examining immunity.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that the Swiss civil courts’ refusal to examine his compensation claim for non-pecuniary damage caused by alleged torture violated his right of access to a court. The key alleged violation concerned the denial of jurisdiction based on lack of sufficient connection to Switzerland and the forum of necessity, rather than the merits of the torture claim. The Redress Trust and the World Organisation Against Torture intervened. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 15 March 2018.
001-164917:
E.S. v. Romania and Bulgaria (Application no. 60281/11) concerns the alleged disruption of family life under Article 8 of the Convention after the applicant’s daughter was taken from Romania to Bulgaria and retained there by her paternal grandparents. The applicant, a Romanian national, gave birth in Spain in 2004 to a daughter. The father, R.E.N., was Bulgarian. After the couple separated in 2008, the child lived for periods in Spain, Bulgaria and Romania. From June 2008 she stayed in Romania with her maternal grandmother while the applicant worked in Spain. In November 2008 the paternal grandparents visited Romania, took the child out with the maternal aunt’s consent, expelled the aunt from the car, and drove the child to Bulgaria without the applicant’s knowledge or consent. The child remained in Bulgaria with the paternal grandparents.

The applicant alleged that Romania and Bulgaria failed to respond adequately to the abduction and retention, disrupting her family life. In Romania, she began custody proceedings in July 2008. The District Court awarded her custody on 30 January 2009, but the father later appealed out of time, arguing that he had lived in Bulgaria and had not been properly summoned. In December 2009 the County Court quashed the decision and remitted the case because the father had not been legally summoned. After further proceedings, the District Court again granted custody to the applicant on 11 November 2010. On appeal, the County Court reversed in October 2011 and granted custody to the father, finding that the child had lived in Bulgaria for four years, did not speak Romanian, and was integrated there. On 9 January 2012 the Piteşti Court of Appeal quashed that decision and restored custody to the applicant. Her request for interim measures in Romania was refused because the child had already lived in Bulgaria for over three years and removal was considered contrary to her interests.

In Bulgaria, the applicant sought recognition and enforcement of the Romanian custody judgments. In May 2009 the Pazardzhik Regional Court recognised the January 2009 judgment, upheld on appeal in April 2010. Enforcement began in August 2010. Attempts to serve the father failed, and a handover was scheduled for 9 February 2011 with police and social services. The child was not found; the father was fined and another handover was set. A social services report warned that abruptly removing the child from her settled environment would harm her and that she needed assistance to re-establish a relationship with her mother. The Supreme Court of Cassation then suspended enforcement and, in January 2012, quashed the recognition because the father had not been properly summoned. A second recognition of the later Romanian judgment was granted in May 2012, upheld in April 2013, and became final in May 2014. However, in July 2014 the Pazardzhik District Court suspended enforcement at the father’s request because he had started change-of-custody proceedings and because the child was settled in Bulgaria, spoke only Bulgarian, and had a close relationship with her paternal grandparents.

The applicant also tried international mechanisms. The Hague Convention had not entered into force between Romania and Bulgaria at the relevant time, so Bulgaria refused her return request. A request under Brussels II bis was also refused by Bulgaria. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation therefore concern the child’s abduction and retention, the conflicting and delayed custody decisions, the repeated difficulties in obtaining recognition and enforcement in Bulgaria, and the Bulgarian authorities’ eventual suspension of enforcement based on the child’s integration and pending custody proceedings.
001-218132:
**Case: Jurišić v. Croatia (No. 2), app. no. 8000/21, Judgment 7 July 2022**

In this case, Mr Stjepan Jurišić alleged a fresh violation of Article 8 of the Convention because of his prolonged inability to have contact with his son, I.R. (born 2006). A prior judgment, *Jurišić v. Croatia* (no. 29419/17, 16 January 2020), had already found a violation of Article 8 due to non-enforcement of contact decisions; its execution remained pending before the Committee of Ministers. The new application concerned the subsequent period.

A final 2010 contact order granted the applicant contact every other weekend and part of school holidays. In enforcement proceedings, the child’s treating psychiatrist, J.G., warned that further expert evaluation or court questioning would harm the child; he proposed gradual meetings in his office. The applicant refused, claiming bias and manipulation. On 29 January 2020 the Slavonski Brod Municipal Court again terminated enforcement of the 2010 order. Relying on expert reports recommending gradual contact and finding coercive enforcement of the outdated order counterproductive and traumatising, the court held the order impossible to enforce. The Zagreb County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 17 June 2020, and the Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible on 21 October 2020.

In parallel, the mother initiated fresh contact proceedings in 2019. A guardian ad litem reported that I.R. was willing to give his father “one final chance” at Dr J.G.’s office; the applicant refused. The Social Welfare Centre proposed weekly Friday meetings in a neutral place without the mother. On 2 November 2020 the court issued a fresh contact order for supervised weekly contact, later progressing to every other weekend and holidays once contact was continuous and trust established. The court strongly criticised both parents: the mother had obstructed contact, ignored professional help, and delayed proceedings; the applicant denied the child’s medical issues, questioned experts’ competence, insisted on contact on his own terms, involved police during disputes, and refused to cooperate with the treating doctor. The court stressed that contact is the child’s right, not the parent’s, and that both parents’ conduct harmed I.R. The Zagreb County Court upheld this decision on 10 May 2021.

Attempts to enforce the new order also failed. On 2 and 9 January 2021, visits to the child’s home resulted in no contact. On 25 June 2021, the mother brought the child to a meeting, but the parents argued and the child left, saying he was fourteen and did not wish to be there. On 2 July 2021, the parents argued again; the applicant told the child his mother could go to prison, and the child left. On 7 July 2021, the child immediately refused contact, alleging past abuse. On 20 and 27 August 2021, he refused to speak, and on 8 September 2021 the applicant did not attend.

The mother was convicted twice of obstructing contact: for December 2015–August 2016 and April–June 2015, receiving suspended sentences. Three further criminal complaints for later periods remained pending. The key alleged violation was whether Croatia failed, under Article 8, to enforce contact rights and protect the applicant’s family life despite the prior judgment and fresh contact order.
001-221480:
The case of **Naddur v. the Republic of Moldova** (Application no. 22939/19) concerns criminal proceedings in Moldova in which the applicant’s first-instance acquittal was reversed on appeal and replaced with a conviction, without the appellate court rehearing the witnesses or the victim. The applicant, Mr Issam Naddur, is a Ukrainian national born in 1966 and living in Kiev. He was represented before the European Court of Human Rights by Mr I. Cernolev, a lawyer practising in Chișinău. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 12 April 2019. The Moldovan Government was represented by its Agent, Mr O. Rotari. The Ukrainian Government decided not to intervene in the proceedings under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b) of the Rules of Court.

The case was heard by the Second Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Jovan Ilievski, Lorraine Schembri Orland and Diana Sârcu, with Dorothee von Arnim as Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 22 November 2022 and delivered its judgment on 13 December 2022.

Factually, the applicant was charged with fraud. The prosecution alleged that he had been part of a group of persons who had defrauded a foreign businessperson of a large amount of money. The case therefore depended substantially on the evidence of the victim, the applicant and numerous witnesses, as well as other material in the case file. At first instance, the court heard the victim, the applicant and numerous witnesses, and examined all the available evidence. After that full evidentiary examination, the first-instance court acquitted the applicant.

The Chișinău Court of Appeal then reversed that acquittal and found the applicant guilty as charged. The key fact relevant to the alleged violation is that the Court of Appeal did not hear anew any witnesses or the victim. Instead, it merely read out their statements from the case file. Despite the first-instance court’s contrary assessment, the Court of Appeal considered that those statements confirmed the applicant’s guilt. Thus, the applicant was convicted on appeal on the basis of a fresh evaluation of testimony that had originally been given before the first-instance court, without the appellate court directly re-examining the witnesses or the victim.

The applicant challenged the Court of Appeal’s judgment by lodging an appeal on points of law. He argued, among other things, that the Court of Appeal had failed to conduct a fully-fledged hearing by not hearing the witnesses anew, as required by the Code of Criminal Procedure before reversing his acquittal. The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law and upheld the Court of Appeal’s judgment.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the criminal proceedings against him had been unfair. In particular, he alleged that the Court of Appeal had convicted him without hearing the witnesses anew. The case therefore mainly concerns whether an appellate court’s reversal of a first-instance acquittal and entry of a conviction, without rehearing the witnesses or the victim, complied with the fair-trial guarantees of Article 6 § 1, especially where the first-instance court had heard all the evidence and assessed credibility in reaching its acquittal.
001-215177:
This case concerns an application lodged on 19 September 2018 by A.L., a Slovak national; S.M., a Norwegian national; their child X; and J.L., the child’s grandmother, against Norway. The applicants complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights about Norwegian child welfare proceedings and measures concerning X. The Court gave notice of the Article 6 and Article 8 complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

X was born in mid-January 2015. On 26 March 2015, when she was about two months old, she was taken into emergency foster care. The emergency decision stated that the hospital had contacted child welfare services after the parents left with X even though the hospital had indicated that she needed treatment and was not ready to leave. Child welfare services had offered close follow-up because the family needed substantial practical guidance on feeding, nursing, sleep and routines. Concerns included that the parents left X alone on a nursing table or sofa, and that A.L. switched off an alarm that vibrated to alert S.M. that X was crying. A.L. had also “shooed” the child when she cried. X reportedly developed irregularly due to lack of interaction and social stimuli. The parents refused an offered stay at a family centre. The foster home’s address was not disclosed, and the parents initially received supervised contact for one hour every fourteen days.

The emergency placement was confirmed by the County Social Welfare Board on 31 March 2015, upheld by the District Court on 25 June 2015, and became final when the High Court refused leave to appeal on 30 October 2015. A care order application followed. In November 2015, contact was reduced to one hour every sixth week, upheld by the Board in February 2016. The Board rejected the care order in March 2016, after which contact was increased to one hour every third week. In September 2016, the District Court upheld the Board’s decision. In November 2016, the High Court quashed that judgment on procedural grounds because one judge had been biased. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal in January 2017.

The case was retried before a different District Court in October 2017. The first and second applicants were present with legal aid counsel, gave evidence, and twenty witnesses were heard. A court-appointed expert and a privately appointed expert provided reports. The Commission of Child Welfare Experts found no significant issues with the court-appointed expert’s report but identified major shortcomings in the private expert’s report.

In its judgment of 16 November 2017, the District Court noted that X had been in emergency foster care since March 2015. It considered evidence of early developmental concerns, delayed motor skills, elevated care needs, and limited interaction between parents and child. Expert evidence indicated both parents had reduced caring skills: the mother had difficulty understanding X’s needs, possibly linked to her own psychological and traumatic background, while the father was described as intense and invasive. The mother’s hearing disability was not considered decisive. Although contact sessions had improved, X showed adverse reactions, and the parents had not benefited sufficiently from guidance. The court found serious deficiencies in care if X were returned and set contact at three times a year for one hour, supervised. It also authorised non-disclosure of the foster home’s address due to pressure from the parents and X’s need for peace. Contact was to take effect immediately. The High Court refused leave to appeal in March 2018, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Committee dismissed the appeal in June 2018.

Before the ECtHR, the Article 8 complaints concerned interference with family life through emergency placement, the care order, restricted contact, and non-disclosure of the foster home. The Article 6 complaints concerned the fairness of the proceedings, including the retrial, expert evidence, appeal restrictions, and procedural safeguards. The Slovak and Czech Governments and the Ordo Iuris Institute intervened.
001-219220:
Chakvetadze v. Georgia (Application no. 55949/10) concerned a Georgian national, Zurab Chakvetadze. On 25 December 2008 police stopped him in Tbilisi and searched him, allegedly seizing a Subutex tablet and a bullet. A search of his apartment that same day found heroin, another bullet, and USD 230,050 in cash. The cash was seized as evidence and deposited with the National Bank of Georgia. The applicant was charged with unlawful acquisition and possession of narcotic substances and ammunition.

On 23 September 2009 the Tbilisi City Court acquitted him of the heroin charge but convicted him in respect of the Subutex tablet and bullet. He received one year’s imprisonment and a fine of GEL 352,000. Crucially, the trial court found that the seized cash was not linked to the criminal proceedings and ordered its return to the applicant, unless he chose to use it to pay the fine. On 4 December 2009 the Tbilisi Court of Appeal maintained only the criminal fine and ordered his immediate release. The Supreme Court rejected his appeal on points of law on 12 March 2010.

On 14 April 2010 the Court of Appeal issued two writs of enforcement: one for the criminal fine and one requiring the police to return the seized cash. The applicant was informed that the police had been instructed to enforce the return order. On 25 April 2010 the National Bureau of Enforcement invited him to pay the fine voluntarily, together with a 7% enforcement fee of GEL 24,640. The applicant gave a power of attorney to another person to receive the cash, transfer USD 220,000 to individuals he claimed were co-owners, and use USD 10,050 to partly pay the fine. However, the police did not return the money. In May 2010 the applicant repeatedly asked the police to comply with the return order and complained to the prosecutor about the delay, but apparently received no response.

The return order remained unenforced for almost two years. On 30 November 2011 the police retrieved the cash from the National Bank and called the applicant to the police station. After he signed a report confirming return of the cash, a bailiff appeared and seized the entire amount to enforce the criminal fine and the related enforcement fee—before the applicant had physically taken possession of the money. The remaining excess of GEL 4,714 was returned to him on 4 February 2012.

The applicant alleged that the prolonged failure to enforce the final judgment ordering return of his cash violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. He also argued that the formal return on 30 November 2011 was a sham because the money was seized immediately, and that the authorities’ delay had prevented him from paying the fine voluntarily, making the 7% enforcement fee unlawful and unfair. Domestic courts rejected his challenge, holding that the enforcement fee became due in April 2010. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The key alleged violations therefore concern the delayed enforcement of a final judgment in the applicant’s favour and the resulting interference with his possessions.
001-216464:
In *Vool and Toomik v. Estonia* (ECtHR, 2022), two Estonian nationals complained under Article 14 read with Article 8 about Estonia’s statutory rule that remand prisoners may not receive unsupervised long-term family visits, while convicted prisoners generally may. Both applicants were held on remand and denied long-term visits by prisons relying on section 94(5) of the Imprisonment Act, despite prosecutorial restrictions on contacts later being lifted or relaxed.

The first applicant, Mr Vool, was suspected of extortion and membership in a criminal organisation and was remanded in April 2014. Initially, the Prosecutor General imposed complete isolation and restricted visits, correspondence and telephone use. In September 2014, these restrictions were partly lifted to allow short-term visits, letters and calls with his cohabiting partner, mother and brother; in November 2014, all additional restrictions were lifted. However, Tallinn Prison refused his repeated applications from February 2015 for long-term visits with his partner, citing section 94(5). Between September 2014 and November 2016, he had 51 short visits—32 with his partner—along with 351 telephone calls, correspondence and parcels. He was convicted in September 2016 and became eligible for long-term visits after the judgment took effect in November 2016. Domestic administrative courts dismissed his challenge. In 2016, the Supreme Court refused to declare section 94(5) unconstitutional, finding the ban proportionate. It emphasised the risk that unsupervised visits could facilitate witness manipulation or evidence destruction, referring to the criminal organisation’s support networks and use of threats and violence. It also found different treatment of remand and convicted prisoners justified because convicted prisoners could no longer obstruct ongoing proceedings. In 2017, it upheld the refusal.

The second applicant, Mr Toomik, was suspected of handling large quantities of narcotics and was remanded in December 2011. The prosecutor initially prohibited short and long visits, correspondence and telephone use with next of kin. In August 2012, the Court of Appeal allowed correspondence, telephone use and short-term visits; in December 2013, it lifted all restrictions. From September 2012 to June 2014, he had 46 short visits—35 with his partner and 8 with his daughter—plus letters, calls and parcels. He was convicted in May 2013; the conviction became final in June 2014, after which he could seek long-term visits. In April 2014, Tartu Prison refused his request for a long-term visit with his partner under section 94(5). The administrative court awarded €500 compensation, but the appellate court reversed. In October 2017, the Supreme Court upheld the refusal as proportionate, citing the charges, repeated convictions and risk of influencing proceedings; it noted his remand status ended less than a month after the refusal. A dissenting judge argued the ban was disproportionate because all additional restrictions had already been lifted in December 2013.

In 2019, in an unrelated case, the Supreme Court en banc declared section 94(5) unconstitutional *ex nunc*, holding that it did not allow separate proportionality assessment of long-term visit bans from detention justification and disproportionately interfered with family life in practice. It gave limited retroactive effect. Both applicants sought reopening; the Supreme Court refused in 2020. The alleged violations concerned discriminatory and unjustified interference with family life: although the applicants had short visits, calls and letters, they were categorically denied unsupervised long-term family visits solely because they were remand prisoners. Domestic courts initially justified this by risks to criminal proceedings, but the later constitutional decision criticised the absence of individualised balancing.
001-219226:
## Case Summary: Drelon v. France

The case of *Drelon v. France* concerns applications brought by Mr. Laurent Drelon, a French national, alleging violations of Articles 8 (right to respect for private life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The core issues involve the collection and retention of personal data reflecting his presumed sexual orientation and the repeated rejection of his offers to donate blood.

The key facts begin in November 2004, when Mr. Drelon attempted to donate blood at a facility operated by the Établissement français du sang (EFS). During the mandatory pre-donation interview, he was asked if he had ever had sexual intercourse with another man. He refused to answer, and his donation offer was consequently rejected. During this process, the EFS recorded personal data about him in its computer database. This entry included a contraindication code "FR08," which was specifically used at the time for men who had sex with men (MSM). The recorded disqualification was noted as valid until the year 2278.

In 2006, Mr. Drelon attempted to donate again. He was informed he was still listed under code "FR08" and was deferred. He requested and received a copy of his personal data, which confirmed the permanent contraindication registered from his 2004 attempt. A subsequent attempt in 2016, despite presenting negative tests for HIV and hepatitis, was also rejected, with the interviewing doctor noting his prior rejections were due to his presumed homosexual behavior.

Mr. Drelon pursued legal action on two fronts. First, in 2007, he filed a criminal complaint for discrimination, arguing that the EFS's actions and data retention were unlawful. This complaint was ultimately dismissed. The Court of Cassation ruled in 2015 that while the lower court's reasoning was flawed, the data collection was legally permissible. It found the processing fell under a statutory exception for preventive medicine performed by health professionals, which did not require the individual's express consent for recording sensitive data.

Second, from 2009 onwards, Mr. Drelon challenged the ministerial orders that defined blood donation contraindications. He sought the repeal of these orders, which initially imposed a permanent deferral for MSM. In 2017, the Conseil d'État (France's supreme administrative court) dismissed his challenge against the 2016 Order. This order had replaced the permanent ban with a twelve-month temporary deferral for MSM. The Conseil d'État justified this measure based on statistical evidence showing a significantly higher HIV prevalence among MSM and the lack of data to assess the risk of a shorter deferral period. It concluded that the measure was based on sexual behavior rather than orientation and did not constitute illegal discrimination.

The case raises significant questions about the balance between public health safety in blood transfusion and the right to private life and non-discrimination. It highlights the tension between a state's precautionary measures to prevent disease transmission and the potential for such measures to be stigmatizing or overly intrusive into an individual's personal life.
001-221637:
In *Gherardi Martiri v. San Marino* (Application no. 35511/20, judgment of 15 December 2022), the applicant, an Italian national, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1 about San Marino’s alleged failure to protect her property from an organised fraud and about delays in related civil proceedings. The central facts concerned her dealings with Banca Commerciale San Marinese S.p.A. (“the bank”), its employees and third persons.

In 2005 the applicant sold property in Rimini. The buyer required an account at the bank, and €200,000 as an advance, later followed by €1,300,000 sale proceeds, were paid into a current account there. In 2009 she learned that the account balance was zero and that €80,000 of a credit had been used. Bank documents showed that from 2005 M.R., a person she had only recently met, had made investments and transfers using a power of attorney which she denied having knowingly given. She claimed the mandate was undated, unregistered in the bank’s system, bore no bank employee signature or stamp, and contained a contested scribbled signature. On a day in 2005 when she was at the bank, M.R. and bank management allegedly made three high-risk investments totalling €1,100,000. Funds were also transferred to persons she did not know. Criminal investigators later found that the transactions caused her a loss of about €700,000 and that M.R. had acted without a regular mandate; the bank’s information system recorded no such mandate, and bank officials were aware of the irregular operations. Some repayments were made, but the fraud charge was time-barred and neither M.R.’s profit nor wilful intent was fully proven.

In 2011 the applicant reported the matter to San Marino’s banking supervisory authority (“BA”). The BA said it would gather information but lacked power to settle disputes between banks and customers, which fell to the judiciary. In late 2011 the bank was placed under extraordinary administration, and in 2012 it ceded its branch and legal relations to Asset Banca S.p.a. Criminal proceedings began in 2012 on the applicant’s fraud complaint. In 2014 the investigating judge discontinued them as time-barred. The appeals judge reopened the investigation, finding it incomplete, but in 2017 the investigating judge again discontinued the case as time-barred, while confirming that M.R. had acted without a regular mandate, that the bank had not objected to the high-risk transactions, and that serious irregularities had occurred.

In 2015 the applicant brought a civil action against M.R., bank officials, the bank and Asset Banca, seeking compensation. In 2017 Asset Banca was placed in administrative compulsory winding-up. In 2018 the civil judge declared the action inadmissible against Asset Banca and impossible to continue against the other defendants because the applicant had pleaded joint and several liability. She then sought inclusion as a creditor in the winding-up liabilities, but the liquidators refused. Her objection was initially assigned to the wrong judge; in 2019 the judge found a lack of competence and ordered reopening before the competent judge. Those proceedings remained pending. In 2021 the Magistrate confirmed inadmissibility while the winding-up remained registered; although the winding-up was later declared illegal in 2022, the company remained inoperative and reimbursement impossible.

The applicant therefore alleged that San Marino breached its positive obligations under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 by failing to protect her property from organised fraud by the bank and third persons, and that the civil proceedings were excessively delayed under Article 6 § 1. The Court gave notice of these complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.
001-219641:
The applicant, Theo National Construct S.R.L., is a Romanian road-construction company. It alleged a “raider attack”, namely the illegal seizure of its goods with the assistance of presumedly corrupt courts and law-enforcement agencies. In 2007 it agreed with Moldovan businessman and political-party leader Mr Ș. to enter Moldova. Under a 4 April 2007 agreement, the applicant was to become a 50% partner in company Q, contributing 23 pieces of road-construction equipment worth over EUR 1 million. The remaining capital was controlled by company S., controlled by Mr Ș. (49.77%), and another company (0.23%). On 5 April 2007 company Q admitted the applicant as a 50% partner.

On 25 April 2007 the Moldovan Chamber of Commerce (MCC) valued the equipment at EUR 1,031,965, based on documents and pictures. On 3 May 2007 the State Registration Chamber registered charter amendments; company Q’s statutory capital rose from MDL 236,621 to MDL 17,540,179.
