On 8 May 2007 the applicant imported the equipment; at customs’ request, the MCC physically examined it and confirmed the earlier valuation. In October 2007 company Q signed a MDL 393 million road-renovation contract with the State Road Administration. It took bank loans exceeding EUR 1.5 million, pledging the equipment; the applicant’s CEO also pledged his Chișinău house. By 2010 delays were generally caused by delayed State payments. In early 2010 the applicant learned that company Q’s CEO had given interest-free loans of about MDL 4.5 million to company S. without consultation, in breach of the charter. Relations deteriorated; the CEO was changed and recovery proceedings began. By early 2011 company Q had no financial difficulties.

On 25 May 2010 company S. brought administrative proceedings before the Chișinău Court of Appeal against the MCC, seeking annulment of the 25 April 2007 valuation. It did not name the applicant as a defendant. The court later involved the State Registration Chamber, company Q and the applicant. The applicant alleged procedural irregularities. Although a 21 December 2010 request postponed a hearing to 20 January 2011, the file contained minutes of a 22 December 2010 hearing with the plaintiff present and an impossible case number. Those minutes recorded new claims to annul the 8 May 2007 valuation and the 3 May 2007 registration, to reinstate the parties, and to enforce immediately. At the 20 January 2011 hearing—the applicant’s first and last—the applicant said no such supplement was in the file. Minutes stated the next hearing would be 2 February 2011; summons and confirmation forms allegedly showed handwritten corrections from 2 March to 2 February.

On 2 February 2011 the applicant was absent. The Chișinău Court of Appeal annulled the MCC valuation reports and the State Registration Chamber’s decision of 3 May 2007, reinstated the parties as before 3 May 2007, and excluded the applicant from company Q. Transactions after 3 May 2007 were unaffected. Immediate enforcement was ordered without stated reasons. On 3–4 February 2011 the State Registration Chamber enforced the judgment; officer A.B., later found to be the wife of the deputy president of Mr Ș.’s party, signed the decision. Company Q’s capital fell to MDL 236,662. The applicant’s action against the Chamber was dismissed. On 3 March 2011 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court of Justice, complaining of late involvement, manipulated documents, unanswered arguments, wrong administrative jurisdiction and time-bar. On 20 May 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without addressing those arguments.

After 4 February 2011 company Q’s management changed; the recovery actions were withdrawn. The equipment continued to be used by company Q. A bank later sought possession of the pledged equipment. In 2013 the Supreme Court ordered its transfer to the bank; the CEO’s house was also taken, and in 2014 bankruptcy proceedings began against company Q.
001-218022:
The case *Alleleh and Others v. Norway* concerns an Article 8 complaint about Norway’s expulsion of the first applicant, Ms Neima Aden Alleleh, and its effects on her family life with her Norwegian husband and four Norwegian citizen children.

The first applicant arrived in Norway in September 2001 and applied for asylum, falsely claiming to be Somali and giving a detailed but untrue personal history. Her asylum application was rejected in 2002, and her appeal dismissed in January 2003. She remained in Norway unlawfully. In May 2003 she sought revision of the refusal, admitted giving false information before, but then gave a new false story and false identity papers—still claiming Somali origin. The Immigration Appeals Board refused revision in November 2005.

Meanwhile, in 2002 she met the second applicant, a Norwegian citizen. They married in April 2004, while she had no lawful residence in Norway. Less than two weeks later, she applied for residence based on the marriage, repeating the same false information. She was granted temporary residence in September 2005, renewed in November 2006. In 2007 she applied for and was granted Norwegian citizenship by claiming Somali citizenship, signing a declaration that the information was correct and that citizenship could be revoked if she had given false information or concealed relevant facts. The couple’s children were born in 2005, 2009 (twins), and 2013.

In 2014, police suspected she was actually Djiboutian. When questioned in June 2014, she maintained her false account. In November 2014 she was warned of possible citizenship withdrawal and expulsion; in December 2014 she finally gave her correct identity and country of origin. In June 2015 her Norwegian citizenship was withdrawn, and in November 2015 she was expelled with a two-year re-entry ban. The Immigration Appeals Board dismissed her appeal in March 2016. It accepted that expulsion would negatively affect the children but found that the father could adequately care for them in Norway, that the family could move to Djibouti, and that the seriousness of her repeated immigration violations and general deterrence outweighed the children’s best interests.

Before the domestic courts, the Oslo City Court upheld the expulsion in 2017, finding her false information gross, repeated, and intentional over roughly 13 years. The children were denied standing and acted only as interveners. The Borgarting High Court reversed in April 2019, finding the expulsion disproportionate vis-à-vis the children: the mother was the primary caregiver, the children were strongly attached to her, two twins were somewhat vulnerable, the youngest was closely attached, and the father worked long hours, creating a risk of unusually heavy burden. The Supreme Court reversed in December 2019 and upheld the expulsion. It stressed that her residence and citizenship were based on false identity and information, making family life precarious from the outset. It found no exceptional circumstances or unusually great burden on the children: they were generally well-functioning, had not suffered prior separations, would remain with their father and siblings in a familiar environment, the two-year ban was limited and could be lifted, contact was possible, and there was no insurmountable obstacle to family life in Djibouti.

The alleged violation was therefore Article 8 ECHR, requiring a fair balance between immigration control, the seriousness of the first applicant’s prolonged falsehoods, and the children’s best interests and family life.
001-219500:
The application was lodged against Croatia with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 September 2016 (application no. 53563/16). The applicant is Dalibor Hrnčić, born in 1977. He was represented by Ms L. Horvat (Lidija Horvat), a lawyer practising in Zagreb. The Croatian Government were given notice of the application. The applicant complained of the inadequate conditions of his detention. The supplied record does not describe any domestic proceedings, earlier domestic decisions, or domestic remedies.

The appended factual table describes three successive periods of detention in two Croatian prisons. From 20 April 2010 to 22 March 2011, the applicant was held in Varaždin Prison for 11 months and 3 days. The table records 2.43 m² of space per inmate for that period. From 23 March 2011 to 13 April 2011, he was held in Zagreb Prison for 22 days, with 2.79 m² per inmate. From 14 April 2011 to 23 January 2012, he was again held in Varaždin Prison for 9 months and 10 days; for this later Varaždin period, the recorded space per inmate was between 2.21 and 2.62 m². The listed periods run continuously from 20 April 2010 to 23 January 2012, with a transfer to Zagreb Prison between 23 March and 13 April 2011.

The table sets out the specific grievances concerning those conditions. They include overcrowding; lack of fresh air; inadequate temperature; no or restricted access to a shower; lack of or insufficient physical exercise in fresh air; lack or inadequate furniture; insufficient number of sleeping places; no or restricted access to warm water; lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities; lack of privacy for the toilet; and lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen. The list repeats several of these grievances across the periods, including overcrowding, lack of fresh air, inadequate temperature, no or restricted access to a shower, lack of or insufficient physical exercise in fresh air, lack or inadequate furniture, insufficient number of sleeping places, no or restricted access to warm water, and lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities.

In substance, the applicant alleged that the material conditions of his detention were inadequate. He relied on the recorded amount of space per inmate and on the alleged deficiencies in facilities, hygiene, ventilation, heating, bedding, sleeping arrangements, privacy for the toilet, and opportunities for physical exercise in fresh air. The record does not contain any further concrete events, domestic proceedings, or arguments by the parties. It identifies only the applicant, his representative, the respondent Government, the date of introduction, the complaint about detention conditions, and the tabulated detention periods, space per inmate, and specific grievances. No other facts beyond those in the application and appended table are supplied.
001-215350:
**Summary of Vlasenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 17863/13)**

The case of *Vlasenko v. Ukraine* concerns two primary alleged violations of the European Convention on Human Rights: the prosecution authorities’ access to the applicant’s banking documents, in breach of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and a ban on his travelling abroad, contrary to Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement). The applicant, Mr Sergiy Volodymyrovych Vlasenko, was a Ukrainian national and a Member of Parliament (MP) at the material time, enjoying parliamentary immunity from certain measures without prior parliamentary consent.

The events began after the applicant lost a civil dispute to his former spouse, Ms. O., and was ordered by the Kyiv District Pecherskyy Court on 21 February 2012 to pay her 125,000 Ukrainian hryvnias. This judgment became final on 31 October 2012. Subsequently, on 23 November 2012, the Pecherskyy Court, without notifying the applicant, imposed a ban on him travelling abroad at the request of a bailiff. The stated purpose was to ensure enforcement of the judgment and prevent the applicant from evading it by leaving Ukraine.

Relying on this ruling, on 14 December 2012, the State Border Service prevented the applicant from boarding a flight from Kyiv to Strasbourg, despite his invocation of MP immunity. On 18 December 2012, criminal proceedings were instituted against him for deliberate non-compliance with the judgment. On 26 December 2012, the applicant transferred the full amount due plus enforcement fees to the Bailiffs Service.

Despite this payment, on 16 and 23 January 2013, the investigating judge of the Pecherskyy Court granted the investigator’s applications for temporary access to virtually all of the applicant’s banking documents in two banks for the entire period of the accounts’ existence. These rulings were made without summoning the applicant, based on the judge’s finding of a real risk of modification or destruction of the information. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, such access to bank secrecy data could be granted ex parte under specific conditions.

The applicant’s application on 21 January 2013 to review the 16 January ruling, citing his full compliance with the judgment, was apparently disregarded. Consequently, on 24 January 2013, the State Border Service again refused to allow him to leave Ukraine for Strasbourg as part of a parliamentary delegation to the PACE, even though he presented documentary proof of debt payment. On 28 February 2013, the Bailiffs Service transferred the paid money to Ms. O. On 5 March 2013, the criminal proceedings against the applicant were discontinued due to the absence of constituent elements of a crime.

Nevertheless, on 13 March 2013, the State Border Service once more prevented him from boarding a flight to Brussels on the same grounds. The enforcement was declared completed on 5 April 2013, and the travel ban was finally lifted by the Pecherskyy Court on 9 April 2013. The applicant complained about the prosecution authorities’ access to his banking documents and the travel ban that remained in effect despite his compliance with the judgment and his parliamentary status.
001-220890:
In *Ilyin and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 74852/14, judgment of 17 November 2022), nine Ukrainian nationals who were followers of the Unification Church (“UC”), founded by Rev. Sun Myung Moon, complained under Articles 9 and 11 of the Convention about Ukraine’s refusal to register their religious community. They had formed a community named the “Holy Spirit Association for the Unification of World Christianity” Religious Community in the Kyiv Obolonsky District. Its constitution stated that its faith followed Christian theology, the Bible, and Rev. Moon’s work *Divine Principle*.

In 2001, the applicants and others applied to the Kyiv City State Administration (“the Administration”) to have the community registered as a legal entity. The Administration requested a report from the Department of Religious Studies and Analytical Work of the State Committee for Religious Affairs. In a report dated 11 November 2001, the Committee described the UC as “one of the most widespread non-traditional synthetic religions,” aimed at unifying not only Christianity but all world religions. It said Rev. Moon sought to reinterpret the Bible through Taoism. The report emphasised UC teachings on “blood purity,” “true families,” sexual harmony, and blessings by Rev. Moon. It stated that UC doctrine involved creating a material and technical basis for God’s Kingdom on Earth through unpaid labour and donations. It also noted that some international experts denied that Moon’s teachings belonged to Christianity, criticised their allegedly anti-Semitic nature, and warned that UC doctrine could complicate inter-confessional relations in Ukraine. The Committee recommended an in-depth study of the community’s socio-religious activities and worship before registration.

On 26 December 2001, the Administration informed the founders that it would continue examining the community’s social activities and worship practices. A similar communication apparently followed in August 2002. In April 2007, responding to a complaint by Mr Ilyin, the Administration said it had received complaints about a destructive influence on participants in UC seminars in the Kyiv region. It also said it had been prevented from effectively examining the legality of the community’s activities because the community refused to allow an Administration official to observe its seminars.

The file contained three complaints. A mother said her son attended a 21-day UC seminar, had limited contact with her, returned changed, and became overly involved in UC activities. A former participant alleged being forced to study UC doctrines for fourteen hours a day, being isolated from family during seminars, and being prohibited from making telephone calls or reading non-UC material; he said he slept on the floor and was often ill. A father said his son joined a Kyiv “youth centre” later revealed to be associated with the UC, was forced to attend seminars, and subsequently abandoned his studies and began begging for the UC.

In June 2007 the community reapplied for registration. On 30 August 2007, the Department of Religious Affairs and Protection of Freedom of Conscience of the State Committee for Nationalities and Religion reported to the Administration. It repeated background information and described the UC as a new religious trend combining Eastern religions with elements of Christianity, rather than a branch of Christianity. It stressed UC teachings on family and marriage, mandatory blessing by Rev. Moon, collective marriage ceremonies, strict regulation, subordination to leadership, and missionary “leadership seminars.” It referred to international press reports of UC business monopolies in banking, hotels, and energy drinks. It also said UC representatives visiting Ukraine’s regions had considered establishing commercial entities, buying shares in leading companies, and investing in charitable projects to create a UC lobby within NGOs and small political parties.

The refusal to register the community formed the basis of the applicants’ alleged violations under Articles 9 and 11. They argued that the denial of legal-entity status unjustifiably interfered with their right to manifest their religion and to associate for religious purposes. The key factual issues concerned whether the authorities’ concerns about UC doctrine, alleged coercive practices, complaints from relatives and former members, and purported socio-economic or political activities could justify refusing registration.
001-216349:
**Mickovski v. North Macedonia** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, judgment 24 March 2022; final 5 September 2022; applications nos. 39107/18 and 39726/18) concerned the alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The applicant, Vlado Mickovski, a Macedonian citizen born in 1964, lived in Vraneshtica and had operated a registered bailiff practice in Kichevo since registering with the Chamber of Bailiffs in 2006. He applied both as a natural person and on behalf of his bailiff practice as a legal person.

The key facts began on 3 February 2011, when the Gostivar Court of First Instance opened a criminal investigation against the applicant for negligence in the performance of his duties as a bailiff. The allegation concerned the alleged double enforcement of a pecuniary claim. On 11 April 2011, the Chamber of Bailiffs ordered the suspension of his bailiff practice as a compulsory measure under section 60(2) of the Enforcement Act. The Minister of Justice appointed a deputy bailiff, M.D. from Struga, to carry out necessary activities during the suspension. Income from services provided by the deputy bailiff on behalf of the applicant was credited to the applicant’s practice, except for certain fees charged by the deputy.

On 22 June 2011, the Constitutional Court rejected as res judicata the applicant’s request for an abstract constitutionality review of section 60(2). On 21 November 2011, after the criminal investigation was terminated for lack of evidence, the Chamber lifted the suspension. The relevant suspension period was therefore from 11 April to 21 November 2011.

The applicant subsequently sued the State and the Chamber under the Obligations Act, seeking compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage caused by the suspension. He claimed approximately EUR 10,418 for actual damage, including employee salaries and office maintenance costs; approximately EUR 23,845 for loss of income; and approximately EUR 15,450 for harm to reputation.

On 2 March 2016, the Kichevo Court of First Instance granted the claim against the State for EUR 10,418 in actual loss, relying on an expert report, employment-suspension decisions, bank statements, utility bills and a services agreement. It dismissed the non-pecuniary claim, finding that the applicant had neither been convicted nor fined, and found no need to examine the claim against the Chamber. On 10 November 2016, the Gostivar Court of Appeal accepted the established facts but overturned the judgment and dismissed all claims. It held that the State could not be liable in the absence of wrongful conviction or imprisonment under sections 549 and 553 of the Criminal Proceedings Act. On 17 May 2018, the Supreme Court upheld that judgment. The applicant also made several requests between April and December 2011 and on 17 January 2018 to initiate disciplinary proceedings against the public prosecutor and judge involved in the criminal investigation; no such proceedings were initiated.

The relevant legal framework included the Obligations Act’s general compensation provisions, the Criminal Proceedings Act’s compensation rules limited to unjustified deprivation of liberty or conviction, and the Enforcement Act. At the time, section 60(2) allowed suspension of a bailiff’s practice after a criminal investigation was opened relating to official duty. A later 2016 amendment provided that suspension could occur only if an indictment had been confirmed.

The alleged violation was that the temporary suspension of the applicant’s bailiff practice, following a criminal investigation that was eventually terminated for lack of evidence, together with the domestic courts’ refusal to award compensation, interfered with his rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The ECtHR gave notice to the Government only of that complaint and declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible.
001-219068:
**P.H. v. Slovakia** (Application no. 37574/19) concerned a 16-year-old Roma girl who was arrested on 17 January 2017 after being caught committing petty theft at a shopping mall. She was transported by Officers A and B to a county police station. According to the applicant, during the car journey the officers threatened to put her in a cage, insulted her because of her Romani origin, and each slapped her once. The Government denied any physical or verbal abuse, relying on police records stating that no coercive measures were used because she was a minor, cooperative, and not expected to abscond.

At the police station, the applicant admitted further thefts. A prosecutor instructed that she should not be detained and should be released after paperwork. A female officer searched her. Officer A then completed records alone with her. When she asked to use the toilet, he accompanied her. The bathroom area was on the second floor at the end of a corridor with a window measuring 116 by 140 cm, with a sill 90 cm high, opening by tilting. Officer A stated that he showed her the toilet, stood less than a metre away, and turned his back to wait. He then saw her falling out of the open window. She fell 770 cm to the ground, suffering severe injuries, including an endocranial injury, four rib fractures, four other skeletal fractures, a pneumothorax, and lung contusions. She was initially unconscious and reportedly in a coma for over a month. She later said she had no recollection of the fall but believed the mistreatment from the car likely continued at the station. Her brother submitted a statement saying he heard her shouting to be released and heard threats, insults, and racial slurs, before officers ran downstairs saying she had jumped.

The investigation was fragmented. Criminal proceedings were opened, quashed, and reopened against unknown officers for failing to guard the applicant under an internal police decree. The prosecution service found no grounds for criminal prosecution but considered it a disciplinary matter. Officer A was disciplined with a one-off 5% salary reduction for turning his back and failing to ensure proper guarding; mitigating factors included that the applicant was not dangerous and was expected to be released. A separate investigation into the alleged abuse in the police car was terminated in July 2017, finding no suspicion of wrongdoing. It reasoned that coercion was unnecessary, that slapping from the front seats was implausible, and that the applicant’s retrograde amnesia made her selective memory of abuse doubtful.

The applicant’s requests for review were dismissed. The prosecution service stated that the investigation was limited to the police-car ill-treatment, while the circumstances of her fall were outside its scope. The Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, noting no standalone right to criminal prosecution of third parties. The Ombudsperson found no violation.

The applicant alleged that Slovakia failed its positive obligations to protect her life and well-being while in police custody and to conduct an effective, prompt, independent, and adequate investigation into her fall, the alleged ill-treatment, and possible racial motives.
001-219493:
In *Perspektyvnyy v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 6 October 2022 in two applications, nos. 9225/20 and 6773/21. The applicant, Volodymyr Igorovych Perspektyvnyy, a Ukrainian national born in 1993, was represented by Mr S.M. Rybiy, a lawyer practising in Dnipro. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The first application was introduced on 4 February 2020 and the second on 16 January 2021.

The case concerned the applicant’s detention at Dnipro detention facility no. 4 from 13 May 2013 to 11 March 2020—a total of 6 years, 9 months and 28 days. The factual table records that the applicant had between 2.5 and 3.8 square metres of personal space per inmate. This limited space is central to the allegation of overcrowding and to the assessment of whether the detention conditions reached the severity threshold under Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant alleged that the conditions of his detention were inadequate and that there was no effective remedy in domestic law. The specific grievances listed were extensive: infestation of the cell with insects and rodents; lack of fresh air; lack or inadequacy of hygienic facilities; lack of or poor-quality bedding and bed linen; lack of privacy for the toilet; lack of toiletries; lack or insufficient quantity of food; a mouldy or dirty cell; no or restricted access to a shower; overcrowding; passive smoking; poor-quality food; and poor-quality potable water.

In Convention terms, these complaints principally engaged Article 3, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The cumulative effect of the alleged overcrowding, poor sanitation, restricted hygiene, inadequate food and water, exposure to passive smoking, and unhygienic cell conditions formed the core factual basis for the Article 3 complaint. The duration of detention—almost seven years—was also relevant because the Court assesses the severity of detention conditions in light of the length of exposure and any cumulative physical or mental suffering.

The applicant also complained under Article 13 of the Convention that he had no effective domestic remedy for the alleged violation of Article 3. That complaint depended on the same factual circumstances: the absence of a domestic mechanism capable of preventing, stopping, or providing adequate redress for the allegedly inhuman and degrading conditions in Dnipro detention facility no. 4. The Court noted that the applicant raised other complaints under the Convention as well, but those are not detailed in the provided extract.

The two applications concerned the same applicant, the same facility, the same period, and identical grievances, and were therefore dealt with together. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are thus the lengthy detention, severe overcrowding measured by square metres per inmate, and a combination of material and sanitary deficiencies that allegedly amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment, coupled with the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy.
001-216463:
The applicant, Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS), is a Swiss-law association established in 1962 and based in Geneva. Its statutory aim is to defend workers and its member organisations, particularly in trade-union and democratic freedoms; it states that it organises or participates in dozens of gatherings each year in the Canton of Geneva. The respondent is Switzerland.

The case arose during the COVID-19 pandemic. The first cases were reported in Wuhan, China, on 31 December 2019. The new coronavirus was first detected in Switzerland on 25 February 2020, in the Canton of Ticino. On 28 February 2020 the Federal Council declared a “special situation” under section 6(1)(b) of the Epidemics Act and adopted an ordinance prohibiting public or private events involving more than 1,000 persons. On 11 March 2020 the WHO described the situation as a pandemic. On 13 March 2020 the Federal Council replaced that ordinance with Ordinance 2 on measures to tackle coronavirus (O.2 COVID-19), closing schools, universities and training establishments and prohibiting public or private gatherings of more than 100 persons; cantonal authorities could grant exemptions for gatherings exercising political or training rights. On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council announced an “extraordinary situation” under section 7 of the Epidemics Act and amended O.2 COVID-19. From 17 March 2020, all public and private gatherings were prohibited, the exemption for political rights was removed, and Article 10(d)(1) made intentionally organising or conducting a prohibited gathering punishable by up to three years’ custody or a fine. On 20 March 2020 gatherings of more than five persons in public places were prohibited. On 8 April 2020 the measures were extended until 26 April 2020. On 29 April 2020 a relaxation from 11 May 2020 was announced, and on 20 May 2020 religious worship was allowed to resume from 28 May 2020.

CGAS lodged its application with the Court on 26 May 2020. Relying on Article 11 of the Convention, it alleged that, following O.2 COVID-19, it had been obliged to cancel a gathering planned for 1 May 2020 and had withdrawn its authorisation request. More generally, it claimed that it had been deprived of the possibility of organising or participating in public meetings. It submitted that the Federal Council’s ordinances were generally applicable measures and that no appeal lay against them to a domestic court; it said this was why it had not applied to national courts.

On 27 May 2020 the Federal Council announced further reopening: from 30 May 2020 the ban on gatherings was relaxed to a maximum of 30 persons; from 6 June 2020 private and public gatherings of up to 300 persons, including political gatherings, were authorised again; events of more than 1,000 persons remained prohibited until the end of August; and on 20 June 2020 the prohibition on gatherings was lifted, although masks remained compulsory. On 19 June 2020 the Federal Council declared a return to the “special situation” as of 22 June 2020.

Domestically, Federal Council ordinances cannot be challenged by abstract review before the Federal Supreme Court under Article 189(4) of the Constitution and section 82(c) of the Federal Supreme Court Act; implementing acts may be appealed, and the ordinance’s conformity with higher-ranking law may be examined in a preliminary ruling. In Geneva, gatherings on public land require authorisation; decisions can be appealed to cantonal courts and then to the Federal Supreme Court. On 18 August 2020 the Administrative Division of the Geneva Court of Justice examined Article 6 of O.2 COVID-19 in a preliminary ruling and found it had a sufficient legal basis, with public health interests prevailing over the party’s interest in demonstrating. On 12 August 2021 the Federal Supreme Court declared an appeal inadmissible for lack of current purpose because the requested demonstration date had passed and the five-person gathering ban had been lifted on 30 May 2020.
001-216352:
Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (no. 13472/18) concerned Serghei Cosovan, a Moldovan national born in 1971, a businessman and local councillor. On 26 September 2017 he appeared at a prosecutor’s office after being summoned and was arrested on suspicion of abuse of office and fraud. On 29 September 2017 the Chișinău Court ordered his pretrial detention for 30 days. It found a reasonable suspicion and risks that he might abscond, reoffend or obstruct the investigation, citing a particularly serious offence punishable by up to 15 years. The Court of Appeal upheld this on 16 October 2017, adding that he could receive adequate medical treatment in detention and, if necessary, be transferred to a public hospital. Detention was extended repeatedly on essentially the same grounds. His lawyers argued he had known of the investigation since 2014, had never absconded or interfered, and had appeared voluntarily in 2017.

The Article 3 complaint concerned his serious medical condition. Cosovan had hepatitis C and decompensated cirrhosis with severe hypersplenism and oesophageal varices. After arrest, prison doctors and public specialists confirmed the diagnosis. In March 2018 a Medical Council prescribed albumin and plasma transfusions, specialist hepatology review and assessment for a liver transplant. However, treatment was delayed; prison hospital no. 16 lacked a hepatologist, accreditation and a contract with a liver-transplant institution. The Ombudsman found his condition worsening and said urgent hepatologist review was needed. Later recommendations called for transfer to a specialised public hospital. The applicant complained that prescriptions and refusals were not properly documented or explained, and that a family doctor supervised his treatment. In November 2018 an expert found his illness was on the list permitting release from sentence and that his life expectancy was limited. In October 2018 the CPEDAE found discrimination because pretrial detainees with serious illnesses could not be released on health grounds in the same way as convicted detainees.

On 24 April 2018 the investigating judge replaced detention with house arrest. He found no evidence of absconding or witness pressure, noted the terminal nature of the illness, and held that continued detention risked suffering amounting to torture. But as Cosovan left prison no. 16, police re-arrested him in a new prosecution opened on 1 March 2018. On 27 April 2018 another judge ordered 30 days’ detention without mentioning the existing house arrest; the house arrest was annulled in May 2018. The applicant remained in detention and was convicted in July 2018, although the case was later retried. He was eventually released on health grounds on 18 November 2019 and died on 25 March 2021.

The alleged violations were twofold. Under Article 3, the authorities allegedly failed in their positive obligation to provide adequate medical treatment for a person with a serious illness in its terminal phase and failed to consider whether continued detention was compatible with that condition. Under Article 5 § 3, the pretrial detention orders allegedly gave insufficient reasons: courts relied on repetitive, abstract risks and did not adequately address the applicant’s deteriorating health, the length of detention, or his prior compliance with the investigation.
001-219556:
Case De Legé v. the Netherlands (Application no. 58342/15) concerns an alleged breach of the privilege against self-incrimination under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Mr Levinus Adrianus de Legé, is a Dutch national born in 1934, resident in Spain since 2000. In 2005, Dutch tax authorities obtained from Belgian counterparts information about Luxembourg X Bank accounts, including balances from 1994 and 1996. The information had been stolen from the bank and discovered in a Belgian criminal investigation. Luxembourg banking secrecy prevented lawful transmission of such data to foreign tax authorities without the account holder’s cooperation. The applicant was identified as an account holder.

On 7 March 2007, the tax inspector wrote to the applicant, stating that he appeared to hold foreign bank accounts not declared in his income or capital tax returns. He was asked to complete forms declaring past or present foreign bank accounts after 31 December 1994 and to provide copies of all bank statements for 1 January 1995 to 31 December 2000. The inspector relied on section 47(1) of the General State Taxes Act, which obliged taxpayers to provide relevant information and documents. The applicant, through counsel, refused, invoking the privilege against self-incrimination. He argued that such requests were followed by additional tax assessments and fines, making Article 6 applicable under its criminal head, and that the authorities could not obtain the information without his cooperation. His spouse similarly refused.

On 25 July 2007, the inspector warned that estimated additional assessments would be issued. On 22 November 2007, he informed the applicant that he intended to increase taxable income for 1995 and taxable capital for 1996 based on estimates and to impose statutory fines of 100% of the additional assessments without remission. The fines could be reduced to 50% if he complied before assessments, or 75% if he cooperated during objection. The applicant did not respond. On 28 December 2007, additional income and capital tax assessments were issued with 100% fines.

The applicant objected in January and March 2008. While those proceedings were pending, the State brought civil interim proceedings to compel disclosure of foreign accounts and documents. On 27 November 2008, the provisional-measures judge ordered the applicant to declare whether he held foreign bank accounts after 31 December 1995 and to provide information and documents, including bank statements for 1996–2000. Compliance was required within fourteen days on pain of penalty payments of EUR 5,000 per day, up to EUR 50,000. The applicant did not appeal. On 9 December 2008, he submitted forms declaring a joint X Bank Luxembourg account and provided bank statements and portfolio summaries.

In the resumed tax proceedings, the inspector used the actual figures from these documents to recalculate the assessments downward. The fines were reduced to approximately EUR 1,400 and EUR 825, and later further reduced by the courts for length of proceedings, but the fines remained. The applicant challenged the use of the compelled documents to recalculate the tax fines, arguing that this breached his privilege against self-incrimination. Domestic courts rejected the complaint. They classified bank statements and portfolio summaries as “will-independent” material under Saunders v. the United Kingdom, holding that Article 6 did not preclude their use for tax fines. The Supreme Court affirmed, reasoning that forced surrender of existing bank documents does not make them will-dependent and that the inspector could assume their existence after identifying the account holder.

The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 19 November 2015, relying on Article 6 § 1. The central alleged violation is that documents obtained under threat of substantial penalty payments were used to recalculate punitive tax fines, thereby compelling him to provide evidence against himself in proceedings amounting to a criminal charge for Convention purposes.
001-217605:
In *Foutas Aristidou v. Cyprus*, the applicant, Christakis Foutas Aristidou, a Cypriot national born in 1955 and living in Limassol, complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of criminal proceedings and the delay by the authorities in bringing the case against him after the investigation had concluded.

The underlying criminal case concerned an allegation of indecent assault. On 26 January 2010, following a complaint, the applicant visited the place where the alleged offence took place with the police. He was questioned, charged by the police, and pleaded not guilty. On 8 April 2010, the police forwarded the investigation file to the Police Prosecution Service. The file was returned to the police with instructions from the Attorney General to prosecute on 22 March 2011. An indictment was then prepared, and on 6 July 2011 the case was listed with the District Court of Limassol (case no. 9886/11). The applicant appeared in court for the first time on 26 September 2011, when he again pleaded not guilty.

The case was postponed several times, mainly because the court did not have time to hear it. The hearing eventually commenced on 18 September 2013. On 25 June 2014, the District Court of Limassol found the applicant guilty of indecent assault. On 9 July 2014, taking into account the applicant’s personal circumstances, as well as the delay in filing the indictment with the court and the delay in the proceedings, the court sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment. On 3 October 2014, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal (no. 180/14).

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 4 March 2015. The Court gave notice to the Cypriot Government of the complaint concerning the length of the criminal proceedings under Article 6 § 1 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Government was represented by the Attorney General of the Republic of Cyprus.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the chronology and conduct of the domestic proceedings. The applicant was charged in January 2010. The investigation file was sent for prosecution in April 2010, but the case was not listed until July 2011—about fifteen months later—and his first court appearance was in September 2011. After that, the case was repeatedly adjourned because of court scheduling difficulties, and the hearing did not begin until September 2013, nearly two years after the first appearance. The trial court convicted him in June 2014 and sentenced him in July 2014; the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in October 2014. Thus, the applicant’s Article 6 § 1 complaint focused on the overall duration of the criminal process and, specifically, on the delay between the conclusion of the police investigation and the bringing of proceedings before the court. The domestic courts’ own acknowledgment of delay—reflected in the sentencing decision—was also relevant to his complaint. The ECtHR delivered its judgment on 7 June 2022.
001-219293:
In the European Court of Human Rights case *Gerasyutin and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 23698/20 and 3 others), the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 29 September 2022. The case concerned four applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates in 2020 and 2021. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants’ common complaint was that criminal proceedings against them had been excessively long and that Ukrainian law provided no effective domestic remedy for that delay. The relevant facts were set out in an appended table.

The first applicant, Oleg Vladyslavovych Gerasyutin (born 1969), represented by Maksym Igorovych Bezukh, lodged application no. 23698/20 on 25 May 2020. His criminal proceedings began on 25 September 2012 and ended on 26 November 2019. They therefore lasted 7 years, 2 months and 2 days and passed through three levels of jurisdiction.

The second applicant, Sergiy Oleksiyovych Butenko (born 1983), represented by Sergiy Oleksandrovych Kulbach, lodged application no. 53149/20 on 25 November 2020. His proceedings started on 22 November 2016 and ended on 24 May 2021. Their total duration was 4 years, 6 months and 3 days across two levels of jurisdiction.

The third applicant, Igor Mykolayovych Bidun (born 1968), lodged application no. 27783/21 on 21 May 2021. His criminal proceedings began on 21 February 2009 and ended on 18 November 2020. The total length was 11 years, 8 months and 29 days across three levels of jurisdiction. The judgment was rendered in his absence and served on him at a later date, a fact relevant to the procedural history and the overall duration of the case.

The fourth applicant, Viktor Ivanovych Chernyak (born 1947), represented by Andriy Bogdanovych Romanyuk, lodged application no. 30696/21 on 4 June 2021. His criminal proceedings began on 10 February 2009 and were still pending at the time of the application. They had therefore lasted more than 13 years, 6 months and 9 days and had involved three levels of jurisdiction.

These facts are central to the alleged violations. The applicants did not complain about the substantive outcome of the criminal proceedings as such; rather, they alleged that the duration of those proceedings was unreasonable and that no effective remedy existed in domestic law to address the delay. In Convention terms, these complaints engage Article 6 § 1, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy for arguable Convention violations. The durations range from approximately four and a half years to more than thirteen and a half years, with most cases passing through multiple levels of jurisdiction. One case was still pending, and one involved a judgment rendered in absentia. These features form the factual basis for the applicants’ claims of excessive length and lack of effective redress. The provided excerpt records the procedural background and the applicants’ complaints, but it does not include the Court’s full legal reasoning or final disposition.
