001-220887:
This case concerns Mr Zouhair Dahman Bendhiman, a Spanish national born in 1975, married with two children. He and his wife were long-term unemployed; the family lived on social welfare benefits of €662.89 per month until May 2020, when this increased to €876.85. In March 2011 the Madrid Housing Authority (IVIMA) allocated him public housing in Navalcarnero and signed a seven-year subsidised tenancy agreement. Rent was €393.21 per month, plus communal expenses and property tax; non-payment allowed termination. IVIMA later granted rent reductions of 75%, then 90%, reducing his monthly rent to €49.10.

In October 2013 IVIMA sold 32 public-housing blocks, including the applicant’s, to a private company, A.G., later transferred to E.C. E.C. became the applicant’s landlord. It stated that the tenancy terms were maintained, but refused to recognise the 90% reduction, demanded the full rent plus communal expenses, property tax and CPI adjustments. From November 2013 to October 2017, the applicant paid the reduced €49.10 for only eleven months.

In November 2017 E.C. brought summary civil verbal proceedings seeking €14,420.72 in arrears and the applicant’s eviction. The applicant opposed the claim, arguing that E.C. lacked standing because an administrative court had declared the sale of the housing blocks null and void; that the amount claimed was wrong; that summary eviction proceedings were inadequate to address complex ownership and validity issues; and that, if the 90% reduction remained valid, he owed the legitimate owner €8,637.72. The first-instance civil court initially stayed the proceedings pending the administrative decision, but the Madrid Audiencia Provincial overruled the stay in May 2019 and resumed the case.

On 10 July 2019 the first-instance court ordered the applicant to vacate the dwelling and pay €14,420.72, finding that he had not proven payment of the rents due. The applicant appealed. On 7 October 2019 his appeal was declared inadmissible because he had not paid or secured the debt as required by section 449 of the Civil Procedure Act. His further appeal (recurso de queja) was dismissed on 9 January 2020, without examination of the merits. Although the applicant had been granted legal aid, Spanish law and case-law treated the section 449 payment/security requirement as essential and not exempted by legal aid, which covered court fees and appeal deposits but not the overdue rent debt.

In parallel administrative proceedings, the sale by IVIMA was declared null and void on 21 May 2018, upheld on 14 May 2019 and final in 2020, because tenants had not been heard and public-interest and approval requirements were not met. The applicant was not a party. Enforcement remained pending, and the effects of the nullity on individual tenants were left to the civil courts. His eviction was repeatedly postponed and adjourned sine die in July 2021.

The applicant’s amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court alleged breach of access to a court and discrimination based on lack of economic means and social origin. It was declared inadmissible on 8 July 2020 for failure to show special constitutional importance. Before the European Court of Human Rights, he complained under Article 6 § 1 that the summary first-instance proceedings had not duly answered his submissions and that the appeal bar denied him access to a court, and under Article 14 that this was discriminatory because his inability to pay or secure the debt stemmed from his indigence and social origin. The central issue was whether requiring an indigent tenant, despite legal aid, to pay or secure overdue rent before appealing unjustifiably restricted access to court and discriminated against him.
001-219490:
In *Suslov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 46298/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) examined complaints brought by Merabi Otarovich Suslov, born in 1963, against Ukraine. The application was lodged on 10 August 2019, and the applicant was represented by Kharkiv lawyer A.A. Kristenko. The judgment was delivered on 6 October 2022, after deliberations on 24 February 2022, and was rectified on 8 December 2022 under Rule 81. The Committee consisted of Judges Lətif Hüseynov (President), Lado Chanturia, and Arnfinn Bårdsen, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Registrar.

The applicant’s principal medical conditions were hepatitis, diabetes, and mercury poisoning. The central factual allegation was that he did not receive adequate medical care while in detention. He also raised other complaints under the Convention, including under Article 34, arguing that the Ukrainian Government had failed to comply with an interim measure imposed by the Court under Rule 39.

The most significant procedural fact is the interim measure. On 14 November 2019, the Court, acting under Rule 39, indicated to the respondent Government that the applicant should be immediately transferred to a specialist civil hospital in order to complete his medical examinations with respect to Hepatitis C according to the doctor’s recommendations. The Court further required that medical examinations concerning mercury poisoning be conducted in compliance with the doctor’s recommendations, and that the applicant be provided with the necessary medical treatment for both Hepatitis C and mercury poisoning in accordance with the doctor’s recommendations given on the basis of those examinations. On the same day, the case was given priority treatment under Rule 41, and notice of the application was given to the Ukrainian Government.

The Russian Government did not avail itself of the right to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention. The Armenian Government did intervene under Article 36 § 1 and Rule 44 and submitted written comments. The appended table provided only limited additional factual information: the application number and introduction date, the applicant’s name and year of birth, and the principal medical conditions—hepatitis, diabetes, and mercury poisoning. It also repeated that the applicant alleged inadequate medical care in detention and complained that the Government had failed to comply with the Rule 39 interim measure.

Accordingly, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are: (1) the applicant’s serious medical conditions while detained; (2) his claim that Ukrainian detention authorities failed to provide adequate medical care; (3) the Court’s urgent Rule 39 indication requiring his transfer to a specialist civil hospital and specific examinations and treatment for Hepatitis C and mercury poisoning; and (4) his further complaint under Article 34 that Ukraine did not comply with that interim measure. The provided text sets out the procedural and factual background; it does not include the Court’s detailed merits findings or the full appended table. The case therefore concerns both the adequacy of medical care in detention and the respondent State’s alleged non-compliance with a binding interim measure of the European Court of Human Rights.
001-215170:
Case Lukošin v. Lithuania (Application no. 25059/20) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Second Section, sitting as a Committee, with judgment delivered in Strasbourg on 18 January 2022. The applicant, Andrej Lukošin, a Lithuanian national born in 1973, was detained at Pravieniškės Correctional Facility. He lodged his application on 9 June 2020, complaining under Article 3 of the Convention about inadequate conditions of detention and about the domestic courts’ failure to award him compensation. The Court gave notice to the Lithuanian Government only of the complaint concerning conditions of detention and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The case concerns two distinct periods of the applicant’s detention at Pravieniškės Correctional Facility.

The first period ran from 18 June to 18 August 2018. During that time, the applicant was held in dormitory-type rooms. He complained to the domestic administrative courts that he had been kept in overcrowded conditions. The administrative courts found that for 47 days he had only 2.97 square metres of personal space. That level of personal space was below the relevant domestic regulations. The domestic courts therefore accepted that the applicant’s detention conditions had breached national standards concerning personal space.

The second period ran from 5 September to 3 October 2018. During that period, the applicant was held in disciplinary cells. He complained that the cells were dilapidated and not properly lit. The administrative courts upheld those complaints. They found that the relevant domestic regulations had been breached during the entire 29-day period. The domestic courts thus acknowledged that the material conditions in the disciplinary cells fell short of domestic requirements.

In both sets of domestic proceedings, the courts found violations of domestic regulations but did not award the applicant any monetary compensation. Instead, they considered that the mere acknowledgment of a violation constituted sufficient just satisfaction for any non-pecuniary damage the applicant had sustained. The applicant then brought the matter to the European Court of Human Rights.

Before the Court, the applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that he had been detained in inadequate conditions and that he had not been awarded any compensation. The core alleged violations were therefore twofold: first, that the overcrowding during the first period and the dilapidated, poorly lit disciplinary cells during the second period amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment contrary to Article 3; and second, that the domestic authorities’ response—finding violations but awarding no compensation—failed to provide adequate redress for those alleged Article 3 breaches.

The Government submitted observations in the case. The Court deliberated in private on 14 December 2021 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The excerpt provided sets out the subject matter and procedural background, centering on the applicant’s Article 3 complaint about conditions of detention and the lack of compensation. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the two detention periods, the domestic findings that the applicant had insufficient personal space for 47 days and was held in inadequate disciplinary cells for 29 days, and the domestic courts’ decision that acknowledging those violations was sufficient without any monetary award.
001-221503:
Elmazova and Others v. North Macedonia (Apps. 11811/20 and 13550/20) concerns alleged segregation of Roma primary-school pupils in two state-run schools in Bitola and Shtip. Eighty-seven Roma applicants—children and parents—complained under Article 14 ECHR and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 that they suffered discriminatory treatment in education. They were represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and a Skopje lawyer. The ECtHR gave notice only of the Article 14 and Protocol No. 12 complaints.

In Application no. 11811/20, applicants lived in Bair, Bitola. G.S. and T.A. were state primary schools in the same catchment area, with G.S. designated as the compulsory-admission school. Parents could request transfer to another school with the admitting school’s consent. The applicants alleged that Roma children from Bair were enrolled at G.S., while ethnic Macedonian children from the same or neighbouring catchment attended T.A. T.A. allegedly allowed transfers of Macedonian pupils from G.S. but refused Roma pupils. In 2018/19, T.A. had seven Roma pupils and G.S. had five ethnic Macedonian pupils. Over 80% of G.S. pupils were Roma, and it was known as the “Romani or Gypsy school.” The applicants alleged inferior education at G.S.—fewer courses, less-skilled teachers, inadequate resources—and that segregation prevented interethnic contact and Roma integration. The Constitutional Court found 83.5% Roma at G.S. and 95.1% Macedonian at T.A., and stated that Bair children attended two ethnically divided schools. It nevertheless rejected the complaint, finding statistics insufficient; the applicants had not shown concrete transfer requests or refusals, and parents had voluntarily enrolled them at G.S. Three judges dissented, finding sufficient evidence of different treatment. By 2021/22, all 77 first-grade pupils at G.S. were Roma. In 2022, the domestic Commission found indirect discrimination/systemic segregation and recommended stricter catchment enforcement.

In Application no. 13550/20, the child applicants attended G.D. in Shtip. They alleged that in 2017/18 and 2018/19 first grade had three classes—two mixed and one Roma-only, each with 18 pupils—excluding Roma pupils from regular education and equal opportunities. The Constitutional Court found fewer ethnic Macedonian pupils enrolled because many transferred to out-of-catchment schools; Roma made up 64% of first-grade pupils in 2017/18 and 67% in 2018/19. It confirmed a Roma-only class but found no evidence Roma pupils received inferior education or different treatment. It held that ethnic composition alone did not automatically prove discrimination and that the complaint was premature because ordinary civil remedies under the Discrimination Act should be exhausted. In 2021/22, of 78 first-grade pupils, 63 were Roma, 14 Macedonian, and one Turkish; they were divided into four classes, two Roma-only. The Commission again found indirect discrimination and systemic segregation.

Domestic law required schools to admit catchment-area children, while transfers required consent. The Discrimination Act allowed civil discrimination claims, and Ombudsman reports since 2011 had documented Roma segregation and non-compliance with catchment rules in Bitola and Shtip.
001-216184:
**Case: Bjarki H. Diego v. Iceland (Application no. 30965/17), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 15 March 2022.**

The applicant, Bjarki H. Diego, an Icelandic lawyer and former director of the loan division and member of the group credit committee of Kaupþing Bank hf., complained that his indictment and conviction for financial offences after Iceland’s 2008 financial crisis violated his right to a fair trial. The ECtHR communicated two main alleged violations: the lack of an independent and impartial tribunal, and the manner in which he was interviewed during the investigation. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

Kaupþing collapsed on 9 October 2008. A Special Prosecutor was later established. Following a Financial Supervisory Authority complaint of 1 October 2009 concerning alleged market manipulation, several investigations were opened into Kaupþing’s pre-collapse trading. The applicant was among twelve former employees investigated. From 9 March to May 2010, the Vesturland District Court authorised telephone tapping of the applicant’s numbers. The Special Prosecutor’s initial request cited four investigations—Al Thani, Holt, CLN and Desulo—and suspected that the applicant had taken part in decisions concerning allegedly criminal conduct. Later reports referred to him as a “suspect.”

On 19 April 2010, the applicant was questioned in the Al Thani investigation but was not prosecuted in that case. On 14 May 2010, he was questioned in the Holt investigation as a witness, not as a suspect. He was not accompanied by a legal representative and does not appear to have been notified of any right to have one. He was informed of his obligation to testify truthfully and of his right not to incriminate himself. On 12 November 2011, he was questioned again in the Holt investigation, this time as a suspect, with defence counsel present.

On 15 March 2013, the applicant was indicted on seven counts of fraud through abuse of position. Three counts concerned allegedly improper loans to Holt Investment Group Ltd.; four concerned allegedly improper loans to Desulo Trading Ltd. He was accused of participating in decisions to grant loans in disregard of the bank’s rules and without properly protecting its interests. On 26 June 2015, the Reykjavik District Court convicted him on six counts and acquitted him on one Holt count, sentencing him to two and a half years’ imprisonment. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Iceland, by judgment of 6 October 2016, partly overturned the lower judgment, convicted him on all seven counts, and upheld the sentence.

Before the Supreme Court, the applicant argued that the case should be dismissed because he had been questioned as a witness on 14 May 2010 while actually being treated as a suspect. He also sought dismissal based on the telephone tapping and the use of transcripts of calls between him and two lawyers; those requests were rejected because the lawyers were not his defence counsel.

A further impartiality issue arose on 5 December 2016, when media disclosed Supreme Court judges’ financial interests. The applicant learned that Justice V.M.M., who had adjudicated his case, had owned shares in Kaupþing and Landsbanki before their collapse. Justice V.M.M. had owned 36 Kaupþing shares, with a nominal value of ISK 360 but a real value of about EUR 140 in October 2008, and Landsbanki shares acquired for ISK 14,753,256, valued at ISK 8,518,692 (about EUR 62,860) on 3 October 2008, before being lost in the collapse. Justice V.M.M. was appointed to the Supreme Court in September 2010.

Relevant domestic law included Article 70 of the Icelandic Constitution, guaranteeing a fair trial before an independent and impartial court, and section 6 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which disqualifies judges where circumstances may justifiably raise questions about impartiality.
001-216196:
In *Fu Quan, s.r.o. v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 24827/14), the applicant was a Czech limited liability company whose two associates, one also its managing director, were prosecuted for tax evasion in 2005. On 27 April 2005 the Prague Municipal Prosecutor’s Office ordered the seizure of the company’s property under Article 347 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, including clothing merchandise and a leased vehicle, on suspicion that the accused might transfer assets to China. The merchandise, valued at CZK 62,424,027 (about EUR 2.4 million), was seized between May and June 2005 and entrusted to the Office for Government Representation in Property Matters. Complaints against the seizure were dismissed. The associates were eventually acquitted on 27 February 2009; the court found it unproved that the alleged tax evasion had occurred. The seized funds were returned in 2010, and on 22 July 2010 the Municipal Court ordered the merchandise returned to the company. The goods were handed back in September 2010 after roughly five years’ storage.

In January 2011 the company sought compensation from the Ministry of Justice under the State Liability Act, claiming CZK 63,294,609. It primarily alleged that the stored clothing had deteriorated, become unsaleable, and sold for only CZK 536,663. It also claimed for stolen office equipment, enforcement due to unpaid telephone bills, and a leasing penalty. The Ministry dismissed the claims, stating it was not liable for the passage of time and that the alleged depreciation was unsubstantiated. The company then brought court proceedings.

The domestic courts dismissed the action. The District Court found the company lacked locus standi because it had not been a party to the criminal proceedings against its managing director and associate; it could not therefore claim damage arising from those proceedings. The Municipal Court upheld that reasoning, holding that claims under sections 8 and 9 of the State Liability Act for unlawful prosecution or custody belonged to the prosecuted individuals, not the company. It also found no causal link between the custody/indictment and the alleged damage from five-year storage, and noted that the company had not argued irregular official conduct. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on points of law in November 2012, reiterating that only a party to proceedings in which an unlawful decision was issued could claim compensation for that decision. The Constitutional Court dismissed the constitutional complaint in September 2013 as manifestly ill-founded, finding no arbitrariness.

Before the ECtHR, the company alleged violations of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key facts relevant to those allegations are that the company owned the seized merchandise but was not a party to the criminal proceedings; the goods were stored for five years and allegedly deteriorated; the prosecution ended in acquittal; and the domestic courts refused compensation mainly because the company was not a party to the criminal case and had not framed its claim as one for irregular official conduct. The applicant complained that this formalistic and restrictive interpretation of national law deprived it of access to a court and an effective remedy, and that the seizure, storage, return of its property, and refusal of compensation violated its property rights. The ECtHR First Section judgment was delivered on 17 March 2022; the case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 June 2023.
001-215176:
The applicants are E.M., a Czech national born in 1976, and her two sons, B (born 2005) and C (born 2008). E.M. moved to Norway in 2005 to live with A, a Czech national resident in Norway since 1986. Both children were born in Norway. On 20 May 2011 they were placed in emergency care because of concerns about sexual abuse and violence. The parents later lived apart; E.M. initially had weekly contact, later twice-weekly, until contact stopped at the end of August 2011 after further statements and a police investigation. E.M. filed for separation in autumn 2011.

In domestic proceedings, on 8 February 2012 the County Social Welfare Board took B and C into public care and placed them in foster homes. It found serious neglect and physical abuse, did not further assess possible sexual abuse, and considered that returning them to E.M. would likely lead to serious neglect. E.M. was granted supervised contact of two hours four times a year; A was granted none. On 4 July 2012 the District Court upheld the care order but withdrew E.M.’s contact rights. It found serious care deficiencies, physical punishment, probable sexual abuse by A, and E.M.’s awareness/failure to stop it; it did not decide whether she actively participated. Contact was withdrawn due to E.M.’s conduct, the children’s stress reactions and their association of her with violence and abuse. On 4 March 2013 the High Court restored supervised contact of two hours twice a year. It found insufficient grounds to believe E.M. sexually abused the children or knew of A’s abuse, but found she failed to shield them, slapped them, caused significant fear and was jointly responsible for neglect. It relied on expert psychological assessments and noted likely long-term fostering. The Supreme Court Appeals Committee refused leave on 21 May 2013.

On 10 December 2014 E.M. applied to lift the care order. The child welfare services sought continuation, removal of E.M.’s parental responsibilities for both children, refusal of contact for her and A regarding B, and authorisation of C’s adoption. After a hearing on 15–17 September 2015, the Board decided on 24 September 2015 not to lift the care orders, to withdraw E.M.’s parental responsibilities for B and C, to refuse her contact with B, and to authorise C’s adoption. For B, it cited E.M.’s repeated media exposure of the children, including photos and texts about sexual violations, causing strain and risks through future access to information.

E.M. appealed to the District Court. After hearings on 25–27 May 2016 with 18 witnesses, a Czech Republic submission and the children’s representative, the District Court gave judgment on 30 June 2016. It found E.M.’s caring abilities had improved, but B had PTSD from complex continued neglect and needed secure care not provided by those who caused the trauma; C had less extensive needs and strong foster attachment. B did not want to return, citing painful experiences and violence; C said he did not want anything to do with his parents and wanted to stay where nobody was mean. Sensitive material, including B’s health and sexual-abuse information, was found online. The court found E.M. could not provide needed care. It upheld refusal of contact with B for special and compelling reasons: B feared being alone with E.M., showed severe physical anxiety, and on 9 March 2015 staff considered forced contact an immediate health risk. For C, despite partly positive contact reports, he showed adverse reactions including agitation, anxiety, trouble sleeping and defecating in his pants; contact was not in his best interests at that time. The District Court refused C’s adoption because it would sever biological family ties, especially with B.

E.M. appealed; A made an ancillary appeal. The High Court refused leave on 28 November 2016. On 24 January 2017 the Supreme Court Appeals Committee dismissed E.M.’s further appeal as having no prospects. E.M. lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 July 2017 on behalf of herself and the children, complaining under Article 8 about the decisions not to lift the care order, to withdraw parental responsibilities and to refuse contact.
001-221266:
The applicant, Hana Pejřilová, a Czech national born in 1983, lodged application no. 14889/19 against the Czech Republic on 12 March 2019. She married in 2012. Because the couple could not conceive naturally and her husband had a serious disease, they approached an assisted reproduction centre. On 26 June 2014 the husband’s sperm was cryopreserved; he signed a consent form for preservation for infertility treatment. The form stated further written consent was required before each thawing and that, unless clearly determined otherwise, storage would be discontinued on the donor’s death. On 15 December 2014 the applicant and her husband signed informed consent forms for IVF, thawing his sperm and ICSI; they agreed to notify the centre of relationship changes that could cause treatment to end. The husband died on 16 June 2015 before further steps; the record does not show the applicant had begun hormone treatment or had ova collected.

On 7 September 2015 the applicant asked the centre to fertilise her eggs with her late husband’s cryopreserved sperm. The centre refused, saying this was contrary to law, and suggested court proceedings for a settlement. On 26 October 2015 she sued the centre, seeking an order to perform the treatment in accordance with his wishes as shown by the consent forms. At a 4 April 2016 hearing both parties were ready to settle, but the Plzeň-City District Court did not approve the settlement because it contravened section 6 of the SHS Act, which required consent less than six months old.

On 22 July 2016 the Plzeň Regional Court upheld that decision. It said the SHS Act allowed infertility treatment only for a couple, not a single woman without a partner; the aim was to give a child an initial chance to grow up with both parents. The applicant and her husband ceased to be a couple upon his death. His later wishes could not be prejudged or replaced by a court, and his earlier consent was not a binding “previously expressed wish” because it was not in the required form. On 28 November 2016 the district court dismissed her action: she was no longer part of a couple and there was no valid informed consent from her late husband.

On 30 May 2017 the regional court upheld the dismissal. It found the request contrary to sections 6 and 8 of the SHS Act: assisted reproduction could be performed only on the application and written consent of the infertile couple, with consent less than six months old. Even the initial consent did not mean the husband would not have changed his mind, and further consent could not be replaced by a court decision. On 21 February 2018 the Supreme Court dismissed her appeal on points of law. It considered family life required an actual family and a mere wish to found one was not protected; the failure to complete the procedure could interfere with private life. It referred to comparative legislation and the explanatory report. It found it in the child’s best interests to be born to a complete family with both parents at least at conception; after the man’s death the infertile couple no longer existed. The six-month consent rule protected the sperm provider and allowed revocation. It was unclear whether the husband would have wished fatherhood after death, as he had signed a form containing an explicit destruction-on-death provision. The centre was not obliged to perform the procedure. The applicant was not deprived of all opportunities to become a mother; she could conceive naturally or with another partner.

On 8 November 2018 the Constitutional Court dismissed her constitutional appeal. It held the lower courts had adequately examined her arguments and reasoned their findings; the Supreme Court had considered the constitutional dimension and Court case-law; the conclusions were compliant with the Constitution; there was no European consensus. Legislation on assisted reproduction was based on moral, cultural, religious and ethical values, primarily for the legislature. A dissenting judge considered the law should only prevent a child being born against a man’s will; in his view the legislation had been misused and the courts should have determined the husband’s wishes.
001-216535:
The case of **Bartus and Others v. Hungary** is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on **31 March 2022** by the First Section, sitting as a Committee (Judges Poláčková, Sabato and Derenčinović; Attila Teplán, Acting Deputy Section Registrar). It originated in **five applications** lodged against Hungary under Article 34 of the Convention: nos. **10214/21, 21911/21, 26912/21, 31833/21 and 35908/21**. The Hungarian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants’ main complaint was the **excessive length of civil proceedings**, contrary to **Article 6 § 1** of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time. In applications nos. 10214/21 and 35908/21, the applicants also raised other Convention complaints, but the common and central alleged violation was the length of the civil proceedings.

The appended table sets out the key facts relevant to that alleged violation. 

- **Application no. 10214/21** was introduced by **László Bartus** (born 1961), represented by Karsai Dániel András (Budapest). The domestic proceedings began on **6 May 2016** and were still pending at the relevant time. Their total length was **more than 5 years, 8 months and 19 days**, involving **two levels of jurisdiction**. The application was lodged on **26 January 2021**.

- **Application no. 21911/21** was introduced by **Jázmin Anna Vrabecz** (born 1981), represented by Gerencsér Éva (Budapest). The table records proceedings from **13 November 2014 to 6 October 2017**, and further proceedings from **26 June 2019 to 6 October 2020** (service: 31 October 2020). The total length was **4 years, 2 months and 5 days**, at **one level of jurisdiction**. The application was lodged on **26 April 2021**.

- **Application no. 26912/21** was introduced by **László Szűcs** (born 1987), represented by Hatlaczki Gyula (Nagykáta). The proceedings began on **28 August 2014** and ended on **17 December 2020**, lasting **6 years, 3 months and 20 days**, with **two levels of jurisdiction**. The application was lodged on **19 May 2021**.

- **Application no. 31833/21** was introduced by **Katalin Tonté** (born 1972), represented by Visontai Csongor (Budapest). The proceedings began on **15 May 2015** and were still pending. Their total length was **more than 6 years, 8 months and 7 days**, involving **three levels of jurisdiction**. The application was lodged on **11 June 2021**.

- **Application no. 35908/21** was introduced by **Tibor Gyula Pál** (born 1960), represented by Fahidi Gergely (Budapest). The proceedings began on **26 June 2017** and were still pending. Their total length was **more than 4 years, 6 months and 12 days**, with **two levels of jurisdiction**. The application was lodged on **5 July 2021**.

These facts were relevant because the applicants alleged that the Hungarian State had failed to ensure that their civil proceedings were concluded within a reasonable time. The durations ranged from over four years to more than six years, and several cases were still pending at the time of the table. Multiple levels of jurisdiction were also involved. The subject matter of the underlying civil disputes is not detailed in the appended table. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.
001-218131:
**Case: Ferhatović v. Slovenia (Application no. 64725/19)**

The case concerns the seizure of three large bags of copper wire from the applicant, Mr Sebastjan Ferhatović, a defendant in criminal proceedings, and the police’s decision to hand the wire over to Company E., from which the wire had allegedly been stolen. The applicant complained that this handover breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property).

In February 2009, police noticed three men pushing an unlicensed white Mazda van while the applicant drove behind in a car. They later learned that an identical Mazda had been seen near two burglaries at Tobačna Street in Ljubljana on 5 and 6 February 2009, where a large quantity of copper cable was stolen from Company E. Police then saw several people unloading copper products and wire from a Mazda van into the applicant’s garage; the van resembled one captured on surveillance footage from the burglary scene.

On 8 February 2009, acting under an investigating judge’s search order, police searched the applicant’s address and seized eight large canvas bags containing mostly copper wire. A seizure certificate indicated the wire had been seized from the applicant. Police later concluded that the dimensions of wire in three of the bags corresponded to cables stolen from Company E. On 24 April 2009, without a court order, police gave those three bags to Company E. The remaining five bags were returned to the applicant on 11 May 2009.

In April 2010, police filed a criminal complaint accusing the applicant of concealment under Section 217(1) of the Criminal Code—accepting peeled copper cables knowing they came from a crime. Damage to Company E was estimated at about EUR 23,000. Charges were lodged in December 2011, but in November 2012 the prosecutor withdrew them, and the criminal proceedings were discontinued in December 2012.

In January 2013, the applicant asked the Ljubljana District Court to return the three bags, each allegedly weighing around 800 kg. The court replied that they had been handed to Company E in April 2009.

The applicant then sued the State for EUR 13,750, the alleged value of the unreturned wire. He claimed he collected and sold waste metals and had stored the wire for over two years to sell in larger quantities at a higher price. He relied on Section 224 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which requires seized items to be returned to their owner or holder if criminal proceedings are discontinued and no confiscation occurs.

In the civil proceedings, Company E’s representative said the wire had later been sold and the money given to the company director. He could not confirm the wire came from the stolen cables because it had been cleaned and cut and was not examined when collected. A police officer testified that the seized wire certainly originated from the kind of cables stolen from Company E, but such cables were available everywhere. He said police considered the wire belonged to Company E due to the chain of events, but the bags were not weighed and no court order authorized the handover.

Domestic courts ultimately dismissed the applicant’s compensation claim. A local court found he had not proved ownership of the wire with certainty and that, although the wire likely came from the stolen cables, it could not reliably be established that it belonged to Company E. It suggested the conditions for return to Company E under Section 110(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act had therefore not been met. However, it held that the police had acted with due care and reasonable grounds, so their conduct was not unlawful. The Higher Court dismissed the appeal, finding no compensable damage because the applicant had not proved ownership. The Supreme Court dismissed his further appeal, and the Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint.

The key legal issue was whether the police’s handover of the copper wire to Company E without a court order and without conclusive proof of ownership violated the applicant’s property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.
001-220866:
Mindaugas Marcinkevičius, born in 1971, lives in Vilnius and is a founder and shareholder of Vilniaus Prekyba. In 2015 he lodged a complaint with law-enforcement authorities alleging that Vilniaus Prekyba had, through financial deals, avoided taxes, damaged the State and unjustly enriched N.N., another founder and major shareholder. A pre-trial investigation opened in August 2015. On 19 August 2016 the prosecutor discontinued it, finding no grounds that the deals were unlawful; the senior prosecutor upheld that decision on 21 November 2016. On 23 November 2016 the applicant asked to reopen the investigation, citing new facts. On 1 December 2016 he answered written questions from a Delfi journalist for an article about his conflict with N.N. and the proceedings. On 21 December 2016 the prosecutor dismissed the reopening request and forwarded the material to the tax authorities. On 2 January 2017 a pre-trial investigation judge upheld the discontinuation; the same day Delfi published the article quoting the applicant. On 10 January 2017 the applicant sent his allegations to the tax authorities. On 17 February 2017 the Vilnius Regional Court finally upheld the discontinuation. On 1 March 2017 the senior prosecutor dismissed his complaint, and on 9 March 2017 the tax authorities opened an inquiry into N.N.’s tax compliance; it was still pending as of December 2021.

In the article, the applicant said documents showed that companies belonging to Vilniaus Prekyba had allegedly been used to transfer shareholders’ money to N.N.’s personal accounts, avoiding Lithuanian taxes and appropriating other shareholders’ funds; that one company, T., had allegedly laundered more than EUR 20 million and hidden at least EUR 3 million in taxes; and that the main goal had been to appropriate profit without paying taxes in Lithuania. He also said: “It is obvious that not only we [the shareholders] but also the Lithuanian State have sustained huge damage.” N.N. sued, alleging false and defamatory statements of fact. He complained of three statements but not the following sentence about contacting the company, shareholders’ meetings and the prosecutor. He argued the statements were unsupported and formulated as facts, and asked for a public retraction. The applicant argued they were value judgments, based on documents submitted to authorities, not insulting, and that N.N., as a public figure, had to tolerate criticism.

On 22 December 2017 the Vilnius District Court partly allowed N.N.’s claim. It found the first two statements and the first sentence of the third statement were value judgments with sufficient factual basis and not insulting. It found the second sentence of the third statement (“It is obvious…”) a verifiable statement of fact, false and insulting: the applicant knew prosecutors had twice declined to confirm his allegations and had not proved damage. It ordered retraction. The applicant appealed. On 18 February 2019 the Vilnius Regional Court quashed that finding, treating the phrase in context as subjective, abstract and exaggerated opinion; it dismissed N.N.’s appeal. N.N. appealed on points of law. On 2 October 2019 the Supreme Court quashed the Regional Court decision because it had admitted new documents without allowing N.N. time to respond, and remitted the case.

In fresh proceedings, the applicant submitted additional financial reports. On 25 February 2020 the Vilnius Regional Court refused the new evidence and upheld the District Court: the sentence was affirming, lacked concrete facts and denigrated N.N. On 4 March 2020 Delfi published a retraction. The applicant’s appeals on points of law were refused by the Supreme Court on 12 March, 29 April and 27 May 2020 as raising no important legal issues. The applicant complained that the statement was a value judgment and that the retraction order violated his freedom of expression.
001-217039:
Case: **Lings v. Denmark** (Application no. 15136/20) concerns a Danish retired physician, Mr Svend Lings, convicted under Article 240 of the Danish Penal Code for assisted suicide and attempted assisted suicide. He complained that his conviction violated Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, arguing he had merely provided general information about suicide.

Lings, born in 1941, practised as a physician until 2010. Around 2015, he founded “Physicians in Favour of Euthanasia” and prepared an online guide, “Medicines suited for suicide.” It contained a detailed suicide procedure, a list of about 300 common pharmaceuticals, doses, combinations, caveats, and advice on ensuring death, including combining medication with a plastic bag over the head and a rubber band around the neck. Publishing the guide was lawful in Denmark.

In February 2017, in a radio interview, Lings said he had assisted a patient with a terminal pulmonary condition to die by administering Fenemal. The Patient Safety Authority reported him to police for violating section 240 and withdrew his medical licence, meaning he could no longer prescribe medication. He was charged with two counts of assisted suicide and one count of attempted assisted suicide.

Count 1 concerned an attempted assisted suicide on 23 March 2017. A, who had neurological diseases, wanted to commit suicide. Lings spoke and emailed with A and asked a co-defendant to prescribe Fenemal for A, knowing A would use it for suicide; Lings could not prescribe it himself after losing his licence. The attempt failed.

Count 2 concerned B, who was paralysed after a stroke, no longer found life worth living, and wanted to die. Lings visited B and advised him how to commit suicide according to his guide. He also discussed procuring pills with another person. B’s former wife later contacted Lings; a supply was obtained, and B died in May 2017. The Supreme Court found Lings had procured medications for B knowing they were intended for suicide, although Lings denied personally providing them.

Count 3 concerned C, an 85-year-old woman with many infirmities but not seriously ill. She wished to die and had already procured pills herself. Between 17 July and 6 August 2018, she exchanged at least nine emails with Lings. He asked what medication she had, confirmed it was “excellent,” recommended the general guide, helped her find it, and advised combining the medication with a plastic bag over her head, stating: “If you are able to go through with it, you will be 100% certain. Remember in that case that it is necessary to put a rubber band around the neck.” C was found dead on 10 August 2018 with a plastic bag over her head.

The Supreme Court upheld convictions on all three counts and imposed 60 days’ suspended imprisonment. The majority held that Lings’ advice to C was specific and significant assistance, not exempt because it was based on a lawful general guide, and found no Article 10 breach. A minority would have acquitted on count 3, finding that he merely passed on information already publicly available, did not encourage suicide, and that Article 10 protected giving and receiving information. Lings maintained that his conviction violated Article 10.
001-219984:
In *Muhammad v. Spain*, the applicant, Mr Zeshan Muhammad, a Pakistani national who had lived in Spain since 2005 and held a long-term residence permit, alleged that a police identity check was carried out because of his dark skin colour. On 29 May 2013, while walking in a Barcelona street known for pickpocketing, he and his friend K.A. were stopped by two National Police officers. According to the applicant, when he asked whether he was being stopped because of his skin colour, an officer replied: “Yes, because you are black, and that’s all. I am not going to stop a German citizen.” He protested, and the officer allegedly slapped him, arrested him, called him “monkey”, and threatened negative consequences for his residence permit. His friend K.A. was also reportedly asked to show identification and complied. The police disputed this account. They claimed they approached the applicant only after he laughed at them and used disrespectful slang; he then refused to identify himself. He was taken to a police station, where he showed his NIE, was released, and received an administrative notice for refusing to identify himself and showing an insolent attitude. The police report did not mention K.A.

The applicant attempted to file a criminal complaint the same day but claimed two police stations refused to accept complaints against officers. The next day he lodged a handwritten criminal complaint. Criminal proceedings were opened and then discontinued, later briefly revived on appeal, but ultimately dismissed. Those proceedings concerned alleged defamation, bodily harm, unlawful detention, humiliation, intimidation, and forgery—not the allegedly discriminatory identity check. The police maintained that the applicant had refused to show his documents. K.A. could not be summoned, though the applicant submitted his notarised witness statement. No relevant video footage was found. The criminal proceedings were discontinued in 2015 and that decision became final in 2016.

In parallel, on 7 April 2014, the applicant brought an administrative State liability claim, alleging that the identity check was discriminatory and caused humiliation, exclusion, and marginalisation. He sought acknowledgment of unlawfulness, a public apology, EUR 3,000 in non-pecuniary damages, and publication of the judgment. He submitted statistical expert reports, reports from the Spanish Ombudsperson, ECRI, CERD, and NGOs documenting widespread racial profiling by Spanish police. He requested that the officers be heard and that video footage be obtained. The police submitted a report denying racial motive and citing his defiant attitude. The administrative authorities discontinued the claim on 6 November 2014 for lack of evidence and no causal link. Judicial review rejected his proposed evidence—including the friend, officers, and expert—and dismissed the appeal in September 2015, finding contradictory evidence and no causal link. A voidness application and an *amparo* appeal were unsuccessful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, relying on Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, the applicant complained that he had been required to identify himself solely because of his race, amounting to racial discrimination and a violation of his private life, and that the domestic authorities had failed to effectively investigate his allegations of racial profiling. The key alleged violation was therefore discriminatory identity checking and the State’s alleged failure to investigate and remedy racial discrimination.
001-215708:
Fischer v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 24314/13, judgment of 24 February 2022) concerned a German national, Václav Fischer, and his minority shareholding in the Czech joint-stock company Cestovní kancelář FISCHER, a.s. Fischer originally owned 100% of the company. In November 2003 he entered into a consortium agreement with K & K Capital Group a.s., controlled by K.K. The agreement provided that if the company’s share capital were increased, both parties would have the right to participate proportionally. Fischer then transferred 75% of the shares to K & K Capital Group, retaining 25%.

On 3 March 2004, the company’s general meeting, using K & K Capital Group’s votes, adopted a resolution to increase the company’s share capital from CZK 1,000,000 to CZK 11,000,000. The shareholders’ pre-emptive subscription rights were excluded so that the newly issued shares could be offered to Kapitálová společnost K & K a.s., another company controlled by K.K. The stated aim was to reinforce the company’s internal financial resources because of negative equity and insufficient capital. Fischer objected and voted against the resolution. As a result, his shareholding fell from 25% to 2.3%.

Fischer applied to the Prague Municipal Court to have the capital-increase resolution set aside. He argued that the resolution breached Article 204a § 5 of the Commercial Code and the consortium agreement. In his view, pre-emptive rights could be excluded only for a serious reason, and no such reason existed: the new shareholder brought nothing valuable that existing shareholders could not have provided. He alleged the real purpose was for K.K. to seize control of the company.

Before that application was decided, the company’s general meeting on 17 December 2004 approved a merger with three other companies. The merger was recorded in the Commercial Register on 18 March 2005. It substantially increased the merged company’s share capital and diluted Fischer’s holding further, from 2.3% to 0.07%. Fischer also challenged the merger resolution, arguing that he still held 25% and that the merger had not been approved by the required 90% majority.

In the capital-increase proceedings, the Prague Municipal Court dismissed Fischer’s application on 13 April 2005. It found the resolution lawful and noted that, even if unlawful, it could not be set aside under Article 131 § 3(c) of the Commercial Code because the later merger had already been recorded in the Commercial Register. The High Court upheld that decision. The Supreme Court later quashed it, holding that Article 204a § 5 had not been complied with. On remittal, however, the High Court again upheld the dismissal. It accepted that the resolution breached the consortium agreement, was contrary to good morals, and circumvented the law, but held that it could not be set aside under Article 131 § 3(b) because third parties had acquired bona fide rights through the merger. The Supreme Court endorsed that reasoning, observing that Fischer could seek damages and just satisfaction under Article 131 § 4. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint, finding that his access to court was secured by the Supreme Court’s review and that share ownership did not guarantee unchanged influence over the company.

In the merger challenge, the Prague Municipal Court dismissed Fischer’s application on 17 January 2012. It reasoned that, because the capital-increase challenge had failed, he no longer held 25% at the relevant time; the merger had been approved by the required majority; and, in any event, Article 131 § 3(c), and possibly (b), barred setting the resolution aside because the merger was already registered. The High Court upheld that judgment on 17 May 2013.

Fischer complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 of the Convention that the domestic courts refused him access to a court to protect rights breached by the general meeting resolution. He also complained that, as a consequence, his property rights had been violated.
001-216720:
**CASE OF D.S. AND OTHERS v. HUNGARY**  
(Applications nos. 41602/17 and 9 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, First Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 31 March 2022. The applications were lodged against Hungary under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates shown in the appended table. The Hungarian Government were given notice of the applications. The central complaint was the excessive length of the applicants’ pre-trial detention. Some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The appended table lists ten applicants and the relevant detention facts. **D.S.** (born 1992), represented by Karsai Dániel András, Budapest, was detained in three periods: 12 June 2014 to 12 December 2014 (6 months 1 day); 22 December 2014 to 11 August 2015 (7 months 21 days); and 19 August 2015 to 15 October 2015 (1 month 27 days). He was also under house arrest from 12 to 22 December 2014 and from 15 October 2015 to 26 May 2017. His application was introduced on 31 May 2017.

**Zsanett Horváth** (born 1989), represented by Karsai Dániel András, was detained from 6 September 2017 to 9 April 2021, a total of 3 years 7 months 4 days. Her application was introduced on 2 February 2021. **Viola Mező** (born 1990), same representative, was detained from 5 April 2019 and remained in detention at the time of application, exceeding 2 years 10 months 4 days; the application was introduced on 29 January 2021. **János Norbert Bodnár** (born 1991), represented by Kiss Dominika Szilvia, was detained from 31 January 2019 and remained in detention, exceeding 2 years 11 months 25 days; application introduced 11 February 2021. **Máté Mihály Gémes** (born 1988), represented by Karsai Dániel András, was detained from 2 June 2019 and remained in detention, exceeding 2 years 8 months 7 days; application introduced 11 February 2021.

**Anita Király** (born 1978) and **Csaba Király** (born 1970), represented by Kiss Dániel Bálint, were each detained from 25 January 2018 to 5 October 2021, a total of 3 years 8 months 11 days. Their applications were introduced on 26 March 2021. **László Szilárd Bedő** (born 1978), represented by Kiss Dominika Szilvia, was detained from 25 April 2019 to 21 May 2021, a total of 2 years 27 days; application introduced 25 March 2021. **József Horváth** (born 1975), same representative, was detained from 21 June 2019 to 17 June 2021, a total of 1 year 11 months 28 days; application introduced 12 April 2021. **Melinda Kolompár** (born 1988), represented by Karsai Dániel András, was detained from 18 July 2018 and remained in detention, exceeding 3 years 6 months 22 days; application introduced 16 April 2021.

These facts were relevant to the alleged violation of the right to liberty and security, in particular the requirement under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that detained persons be entitled to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. The applicants complained that their pre-trial detention was excessively long. The case therefore concerned lengthy, and in several instances ongoing, pre-trial detention, multiple separate detention periods, and one instance of house arrest. The Court’s judgment addressed those complaints, while some applicants also raised additional Convention issues.
001-215716:
The applicants, A and B, are Georgian nationals living in Georgia. A is C’s mother, and B is C’s son. C was born on 24 November 1994 and killed on 25 July 2014 by her partner D, B’s father and a police officer.

In 2011, when C was 17, D kidnapped her for marriage. Under constant threat, she cohabited with him from December 2011 until June 2012, when she returned to her parents’ home pregnant after physical and psychological harassment. From December 2011, C and her family allegedly suffered regular verbal and physical abuse from D, who threatened to kill C and her parents and referred to his police status and connections. In July 2012 C called police about a threat to kill A; no response followed. On 31 August 2013, after an argument over child support, D beat C at her parents’ house. Three patrol officers, D’s acquaintances and colleagues, interviewed C in D’s presence, dismissed wife-beating as commonplace, allowed D to interfere and prepared a report inaccurately describing a “minor family altercation”. C refused to sign, but D forced her to sign while threatening to kill her, which officers overheard. An officer warned her not to contact police without valid reason. D left with the officers.

The same day C filed a criminal complaint with a local prosecutor against D and the officers. On 4 September 2013 a prosecutor interviewed C, D and one officer; D denied ill-treatment. On 9 September 2013 D gave a written undertaking not to abuse C or her family; the prosecution decided not to open a criminal investigation.

On 5 July 2014 C complained to the General Inspectorate that D had assaulted her in public on 3 and 5 July 2014. Witness statements allegedly confirmed that between April 2011 and July 2014 D used his official position to abuse C: flaunting his service pistol at least seven times, threatening false charges against C’s father and brother, and saying he was part of law enforcement. On 20 July 2014 D was promoted to senior police lieutenant. On 25 July 2014 the General Inspectorate interviewed C about her complaint. She reiterated systematic physical and psychological harassment but asked that D not be treated too harshly because he was the father of her child. Shortly after, D stalked her; eyewitnesses saw a loud argument in a public park. D drew his service pistol and fired five shots at C’s chest and stomach at close range, killing her instantly.

Criminal proceedings against D began that day. He was charged with murder and told investigators the relationship had been strained by jealousy and that C had provoked and humiliated him by saying her private and sex life did not concern him. On 17 April 2015 the Kutaisi City Court convicted D of premeditated murder of a family member, sentencing him to 11 years. His insanity defence was rejected by forensic examination. The conviction became final on 15 February 2016 and did not refer to gender-based discrimination.

On 22 January 2015 A, for herself and B, asked the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office to open a criminal investigation into police and prosecutors’ failure to protect C and respond to domestic-violence reports, arguing negligence may have been influenced by gender-based discrimination. On 19 February 2015 a criminal case was opened into the police officers’ alleged failure; they said they did not think the incident was violent. A was interviewed on 27 February 2015. Between March and August 2015 five witnesses were interviewed; most described the 31 August 2013 incident as particularly violent. A repeatedly enquired about progress; on 20 March 2015 she was told an investigation into police negligence had been launched. She received no response about her complaint against prosecutors. In March 2016 a regional prosecutor said the police-negligence investigation was pending, no charges had been brought and victim status was not then necessary. A again received no response concerning prosecutors.

On 22 January 2015 A also sued the Ministry of the Interior and Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office under Article 1005 of the Civil Code, claiming GEL 120,000 non-pecuniary damage for failure to protect C’s life. On 24 July 2015 the Tbilisi City Court partly allowed the claim, awarding GEL 20,000. It found a causal link between police/prosecutor inactivity and C’s killing; noted police did not interview C or witnesses, did not issue a restraining order and did not restrict D’s service pistol; and found prosecutors failed to investigate adequately. The judgment became final on 29 June 2017 after the Supreme Court terminated proceedings.
001-218941:
In *P.C. v. Ireland* (Application no. 26922/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 1 September 2022, final on 1 December 2022. The applicant, P.C., an Irish national born in 1940, had made Pay Related Social Insurance contributions and qualified for the State Pension (Contributory) (“SPC”) at age 66 in February 2006. He received approximately €230 per week.

In March 2011, the applicant was convicted of sixty counts of sexual assault and fourteen counts of rape. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment, with the final three years suspended, and expected release in March 2020. Under section 249(1)(b) of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, persons undergoing imprisonment or detention in legal custody were disqualified from receiving benefits under Part 2 of the Act, including the SPC. As a result, his pension payments ceased when he was imprisoned.

The applicant alleged that this disqualification left him practically destitute. His only income was a prison gratuity, initially €18.90 per week and later reduced to €11.90 because age-related ailments and a wrist injury prevented him from doing prison work. He claimed he had no money for extra food, personal clothing or small electronic appliances, and that the stoppage would cost him over €100,000. He further noted that prisoners with private pensions or other income could receive funds lodged into their prison accounts, whereas his contributory State pension was stopped.

In 2013, the applicant issued proceedings against the State. He sought a declaration that the impugned provision was unconstitutional and incompatible with the Convention, damages, and an injunction requiring payment of his pension. He invoked Articles 3, 5, 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and sought a declaration under section 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 together with compensation.

Evidence before the High Court showed that the SPC is non-means-tested; about 30–40 prisoners had their SPC payments stopped each year; the average annual cost of maintaining a prisoner was approximately €65,000; and some prisoners in the applicant’s age group worked in prison for €4.50 per week.

The High Court dismissed the case in April 2016. It held that the contributory SPC was not a property right for constitutional or Convention purposes, emphasising the partly tax-funded nature of social welfare and the State’s need for flexibility, with a wide margin of appreciation in economic and social matters. It rejected the discrimination claim, finding the comparison with private pensions not like-for-like and noting that the rule applied to all social welfare benefits. Withholding the SPC was considered objectively rational and proportionate because the benefit was intended for basic living costs, while imprisonment met essential needs. The High Court also rejected the Convention claims under Articles 3, 5, 6 and 8, and found no breach of Article 14.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the statutory disqualification interfered with his rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, discriminated against him contrary to Article 14 read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and denied him an effective remedy under Article 13 because the Supreme Court allegedly did not determine his Convention complaints or award adequate redress. The Court gave notice of those complaints and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.
001-220415:
The case concerns Vegotex International S.A., a Belgian company based in Antwerp, and complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention arising from tax-recovery proceedings. In 1995 the tax authorities rectified Vegotex’s 1993 tax return, disallowing deductions linked to a stock-exchange transaction and investment costs, and imposed a 50% penalty. After its administrative objection was rejected in 2000, Vegotex brought court proceedings in December 2000 seeking to set aside the penalty. Meanwhile, on 24 October 2000, the tax authorities served a “demand for payment interrupting the limitation period,” expressly stating that it was not aimed at enforcing the disputed tax debt but only at interrupting the limitation period.

In 2004 the Court of First Instance largely upheld the assessment and penalty, reducing the penalty to 10% only as regards investment costs. Vegotex appealed, arguing that the State’s right to recover the 1993 tax was time-barred. It relied on Court of Cassation case-law from 2002 holding that a demand for payment in respect of a disputed tax debt did not validly interrupt the limitation period. While the appeal was pending, the Belgian legislature enacted the Miscellaneous Provisions Act of 9 July 2004. Section 49 provided that a demand for payment must be interpreted as interrupting the limitation period under Article 2244 of the Civil Code even where the disputed tax debt was not certain and of a fixed amount. The provision was intended to apply retrospectively to pending proceedings.

In 2007 the Antwerp Court of Appeal found that the 2000 demand did not interrupt the limitation period under Article 2244, and that section 49 was not applicable. However, it held that the limitation period had been suspended under Article 2251 of the Civil Code while the tax debt was contested, so recovery was not time-barred.

Vegotex appealed on points of law. The advocate-general at the Court of Cassation proposed substituting new grounds for those of the Court of Appeal: the limitation period had been interrupted by the demand under section 49, so Vegotex’s ground of appeal was inadmissible for lack of interest. Vegotex received the submissions on 5 March 2009 and filed a memorandum on 9 March 2009. It argued that if the Court of Cassation substituted its own grounds, it would breach Article 6 by depriving Vegotex of any opportunity to challenge the new grounds. It also said that objections remained, including that retroactive application of section 49 violated Article 6, and that these should be debated before lower courts.

On 13 March 2009 the Court of Cassation followed the advocate-general’s approach. It held that section 49 was not interpretative but had to be applied retrospectively in accordance with the legislature’s intention. The demand of 24 October 2000 therefore interrupted the limitation period, and recovery was not time-barred. The contested decision had a proper legal basis in the new ground, so Vegotex’s appeal was inadmissible for lack of interest.

The alleged Article 6 § 1 violations were therefore: (1) legislative intervention during pending judicial proceedings, through retrospective application of section 49, affecting the outcome; (2) breach of the right of access to a court and the adversarial principle because the Court of Cassation substituted its own grounds for those of the Court of Appeal, allegedly preventing Vegotex from effectively challenging the new basis for the decision; and (3) failure to comply with the reasonable-time requirement, given proceedings from the mid-1990s until 2009.
001-219946:
In *Dolenc v. Slovenia* (Application no. 20256/20, judgment of 20 October 2022), the applicant was a Slovenian neurosurgeon who in 1992 performed surgery in Ljubljana on Israeli citizen E.M. E.M. later suffered severe disability. In 1995 E.M. sued the applicant for medical negligence in Israel, serving the claim during the applicant’s visit there. The proceedings continued before the Tel Aviv District Court. The applicant, represented by an Israeli lawyer, submitted a defence, medical expert opinions, his own written statement, and statements from eleven witnesses—mostly doctors and nurses at Ljubljana University Hospital—as well as an expert opinion on Slovenian law.

The key procedural dispute concerned the examination of the applicant and his witnesses. In 1999 the Israeli district court decided they would be examined by video link. The Slovenian Ministry of Justice stated that no bilateral civil legal assistance treaty existed with Israel, but the Hague Evidence Convention applied; however, neither the Convention nor Slovenian law allowed direct video-link examination. The applicant refused video-link examination and repeatedly requested that he and his witnesses be examined before a Slovenian court under the Hague Evidence Convention. Israeli courts rejected those requests, finding video-link examination balanced the parties’ interests and was technically possible. In June 2003, after the applicant maintained his refusal, the Israeli district court excluded his main written statement and ordered that his witnesses be examined in Slovenia under the Hague Evidence Convention.

The Hague request was sent in September 2003. In January 2004 the Ljubljana District Court raised issues concerning translation, interpretation, costs, cross-examination under Slovenian law, and participation of foreign lawyers. The Slovenian Ministry forwarded these concerns to Israel, but delays and unanswered queries followed. E.M. allegedly later sought to discontinue the Hague procedure due to difficulties. In April 2004 the applicant cancelled his Israeli lawyer’s power of attorney. The Israeli court ordered that documents be served at the former representative’s office; the applicant disputed being informed of this and later decisions. After no progress for fifteen months, in September 2004 the Israeli district court cancelled the Slovenian examination and decided to take evidence in Israel. Hearings in late 2004 proceeded without the applicant appearing; additional deadlines for a concluding statement were allegedly not communicated to him.

In June 2005 the Israeli district court excluded the applicant’s witness statements and Slovenian-law expert opinion because the witnesses had not been directly examined, attributing this to the applicant’s conduct. Since foreign law was not proven, the court applied Israeli law and found the applicant fully liable for E.M.’s damage, relying on evidence including alleged failure to perform a CT scan and inadequate postoperative care.

The applicant’s admitted complaint under Article 6 § 1 concerned the Slovenian courts’ recognition of those Israeli judgments. He alleged that recognition violated his fair-trial rights because the Israeli proceedings had not examined his witnesses, had excluded his evidence and submissions, and had served court documents on his former representative rather than on him. The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the video-link/Hague Convention dispute, the exclusion of his evidence, the service on former counsel, and Slovenia’s subsequent recognition of the resulting Israeli judgment.
001-219684:
The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 13 October 2022 in the case of *Khuren-Ool and Others v. Russia*. The case originated in applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants complained principally of permanent video surveillance of detainees in pre-trial or post-conviction detention facilities. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Court deliberated in private on 15 September 2022 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The key facts are set out in the appended table. The case involved six applications. The first applicant, Ivan Alimovich Khuren-Ool, born in 1973, lodged applications nos. 77300/17, introduced on 20 October 2017, and 29430/18, introduced on 5 May 2018. He was detained in IK-23 in the Krasnoyarsk Region from 23 January 2018 to 14 November 2018. The specific circumstance relevant to the surveillance complaint was that the video surveillance was conducted by opposite-sex operators.

The second applicant, Artem Mikhaylovich Lazarev, born in 1986, lodged application no. 33010/18, introduced on 16 August 2017. He was detained in IK-34 in the Krasnoyarsk Region from 13 July 2015 to 11 August 2017. The relevant specific circumstance was again the use of opposite-sex operators for video surveillance.

The third applicant, Roman Vladimirovich Chernoknizhnyy, born in 1979, represented by Nataliya Yevgenyevna Reyzer of Syktyvkar, lodged application no. 41663/18, introduced on 22 July 2018. He was detained in SIZO-1 in the Komi Republic from 17 April 2021, and remained detained at the time of the application. The alleged violation involved opposite-sex operators and detention in different cells with video surveillance.

The fourth applicant, Vladimir Fedorovich Ivanyutenko, born in 1972, represented by Leonid Leonidovich Krikun of St Petersburg, lodged application no. 58934/19, introduced on 12 November 2019. He was detained in SIZO-6 in St Petersburg from 22 February 2019 to 15 February 2020. The specific circumstance was video surveillance by opposite-sex operators.

The fifth applicant, Gulruz Nurilloyevich Azizulloyev, born in 1983, lodged application no. 23017/21, introduced on 13 April 2021. He was detained in IK-25 and IK-31 in the Komi Republic from 9 June 2019 to 21 November 2021. The alleged violation again involved opposite-sex operators and detention in different cells with video surveillance.

Overall, the case concerns allegations that permanent video surveillance of detainees, particularly where monitored by opposite-sex operators and across different cells, violated the applicants’ rights under the Convention. The applicants also raised other complaints, but the principal facts relevant to the alleged violation are the continuous surveillance in the listed detention facilities during the stated periods.
001-220556:
The case originates in six applications against Russia. The applicants complained of a lack of impartiality of the tribunal because the prosecuting party was absent in administrative-offence proceedings. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The applications were introduced between 10 January 2020 and 2 March 2020. The final domestic decisions identified were given between 30 July 2019 and 12 November 2019, all by the Moscow City Court. In every case, the penalty was a fine of RUB 10,000, imposed on each applicant where an application was brought by two applicants. The supplied record does not describe the underlying administrative-offence events, the first-instance decisions, or the domestic courts’ reasoning.

Application no. 5386/20 was introduced on 10 January 2020 by Leonid Abramovich Razgon (born 1960) and Danil Alekseyevich Levenstam (born 1982), represented by Ernest Aleksandrovich Mezak (Nantes). Application no. 6789/20 was introduced on 18 January 2020 by Kirill Vadimovich Chirkin (born 1993) and Renaldo Zaurovich Dzhindzholiya (born 1981), represented by Mr Mezak. Each applicant was fined RUB 10,000. The final domestic decision was given by the Moscow City Court on 26 August 2019.
