001-220712:
The case *Hovhannisyan and Nazaryan v. Armenia* (Applications nos. 2169/12 and 29887/14) concerned the death of A. Nazaryan, a 31-year-old Armenian army officer, on 27 July 2010 at military base no. 12. The first applicant was his mother and the second applicant his sister. They complained under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the State had failed to protect his life and had not conducted an effective investigation into his death.

The official initial report stated that A. Nazaryan had fatally shot himself in the trench with his assigned assault rifle. Criminal proceedings were opened for incitement to suicide. However, the scene examination described his body seated next to a rock, with the rifle barrel in his mouth and the stock between his legs. A fired cartridge, blood-like traces, and a magazine containing twenty-nine bullets were seized. Captain H.M., present at the base, removed A. Nazaryan’s notebook from his pocket and gave it to Major M.N., asking him to keep it secret because he feared his fingerprints might be on it. The notebook contained a note stating that A. Nazaryan was “tired of everything” and that it was no one’s fault but his and his parents’. Forensic document examination attributed the note to A. Nazaryan, but the applicants disputed this.

Evidence gathered during the investigation indicated that A. Nazaryan had been subjected to humiliation, physical violence, and systematic ill-treatment by superiors and conscripts. Captain H.M. admitted hitting him on 19 July 2010 during an argument; Lieutenant V.H. also allegedly beat him. Several conscripts—A.H., M.M., and H.K.—reportedly mocked and abused him. A Minister of Defence order later found that Captain H.M. had abused his position, assaulted A. Nazaryan in front of staff, created an unhealthy moral environment, and that this led to ill-treatment by conscripts and ultimately to A. Nazaryan’s suicide. The order also found that the situation had been concealed from command.

The autopsy concluded that death resulted from a gunshot wound to the mouth. It also found other bruises and abrasions on A. Nazaryan’s body, some inflicted shortly before death, and alcohol intoxication. A later forensic commission concluded that self-infliction was possible, but did not rule out that another person could have inflicted the injury; it found no traces of the body being moved. A posthumous psychological examination linked the suicide to humiliation, debasement, and ill-treatment by officers and conscripts.

Captain H.M., Lieutenant V.H., A.H., M.M., and H.K. were charged and convicted in 2013, receiving prison sentences. Nevertheless, the applicants alleged that the investigation was ineffective. Key procedural concerns included that numerous servicemen were placed in disciplinary isolation after the death and questioned while confined; several later retracted pre-trial statements, alleging duress, beatings, and prolonged interrogation. The trial court refused to exclude those pre-trial statements. The applicants also complained that requests for further forensic examination—including handwriting analysis abroad and testing of blood traces and other injuries—were refused, and that discrepancies existed regarding the scene examination date, cartridge serial numbers, initial reports of death in a trench versus beside a rock, and missing photographs. The Court of Appeal reviewed the case in a cassation-style manner without a full evidentiary hearing, and the Court of Cassation declared the appeals inadmissible. The applicants therefore alleged that Armenia violated its substantive and procedural obligations under Article 2.
001-216686:
The applicant, Marina Gloveli, a Georgian national born in 1958 and living in Tbilisi, is a practising lawyer with over twenty years’ experience. She also served as a judge in the Tbilisi Court of Appeal between 1999 and 2005. She participated in competitions for vacant judicial positions six times, most recently in October 2017. The present case concerns her latest attempt to obtain a judicial appointment.

In earlier domestic proceedings, on 9 February 2016 the applicant and two other unsuccessful candidates lodged a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court. They alleged that sections 36(4), 49(1)(a) and 50(4) of the Act of 13 June 1997 on Courts of Ordinary Jurisdiction did not comply with Articles 29 and 42 of the Constitution, arguing in particular that no court had jurisdiction to examine disputes concerning judicial appointments. On 10 March 2017 amendments to the Courts Act entered into force, making decisions of the High Council of Justice (HCJ) on judicial appointments appealable to the Supreme Court. On 7 April 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected the complaint, concluding that the amendments had created a new judicial remedy through the Qualifications Chamber of the Supreme Court, which had jurisdiction to examine appeals concerning allegedly arbitrary refusals of judicial appointments.

On 18 October 2017 the HCJ announced a new judicial competition. The applicant applied for a vacant position as a judge in a court of appeal and submitted documents confirming her professional and academic achievements. On 25 November 2017 the HCJ announced that she had been admitted to the competition. On 29 December 2017 HCJ members interviewed her and individually assessed her using score sheets. On 20 January 2018 she was notified that her application had been rejected because she did not meet the minimum competency score. She later obtained copies of the score sheets completed by the HCJ members who had interviewed and assessed her.

On 2 February 2018 the applicant lodged an appeal with the Qualifications Chamber seeking invalidation of the HCJ decision under section 354(3)(b) of the Courts Act. She alleged that the decision was arbitrary and discriminatory. In support, she submitted a recording of a televised statement by N.J., a non-judicial member of the HCJ, who claimed that during the competition several HCJ members had had “protégé” candidates and had arbitrarily lowered the assessment scores of other judicial candidates. She also argued that the very low scores assigned to her by several HCJ members indicated bias.

On 6 February 2018 the Qualifications Chamber declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that because she had not achieved the minimum pass score in the competency component, her candidacy had not been put to a vote before the HCJ. Therefore, the precondition in section 35(12) of the Courts Act was not met; the HCJ had not examined her application for appointment and had not issued a decision refusing appointment that could be challenged before the Qualifications Chamber. The Qualifications Chamber further held, referring to earlier European Court cases Beaumartin v. France and Sigma Radio Television Ltd v. Cyprus, that it did not satisfy the requirement of a court or tribunal with “full jurisdiction” to review the facts of the case, and that its decision followed its established practice (case no. სსპ-2-17). The decision stated that it was final and not amenable to appeal.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court on 3 April 2018.
001-216193:
The case *Tetik and Others v. Turkey* (Application no. 25885/19 and 37 others) is a 2022 European Court of Human Rights judgment concerning 38 Turkish applicants. The central complaint was the non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions awarding them compensation against Yüksekova Municipality, despite earlier findings by Turkey’s Compensation Commission that the non-enforcement breached their right to a fair trial.

Between 2008 and 2010, the Yüksekova Civil Court of First Instance ruled in three sets of civil proceedings that the applicants were owed compensation for receivables arising from labour agreements with the Municipality. The judgments became binding. However, the Municipality did not pay the awarded sums, except for the compensation in the first set of proceedings brought by the applicants in application no. 26026/19. This persistent failure to execute the judgments formed the core of the applicants’ complaints.

In 2011, 2012 and 2013, the applicants applied to the ECtHR, alleging non-enforcement of domestic judicial decisions in their favour. In 2013, the Court declared those applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. It held that the applicants should first use the Compensation Commission established under Law no. 6384, which provided a domestic remedy for complaints including non-enforcement of domestic decisions.

In 2014, the Compensation Commission awarded the applicants non-pecuniary damage for the excessive length of the proceedings. It also transmitted its decision to the Municipality and requested that the judicial decisions be executed. Despite this, the underlying compensation awards remained unpaid. The Commission’s decision thus acknowledged a fair-trial breach but did not secure actual enforcement of the judgments. In the same year, the applicants applied to the Constitutional Court, complaining that the Municipality had still failed to enforce the relevant judicial decisions despite the Compensation Commission’s decision.

While those Constitutional Court applications were pending, in July 2018 a provision was added to Law no. 6384. It empowered the Compensation Commission to deal with applications pending before the Constitutional Court concerning, among other things, non-enforcement complaints. Later in 2018, the Constitutional Court found the applicants’ applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, namely the Compensation Commission. This left the applicants in a procedural cycle: the ECtHR had sent them to the Compensation Commission; the Commission found a breach but did not enforce payment; the Constitutional Court then sent them back to the same Commission. On unspecified dates, some minor parts of the receivables were paid to some applicants, but the essential awards remained unexecuted.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: final and binding domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour; prolonged non-payment by a public municipality; a domestic compensation remedy that only awarded non-pecuniary damages and requested execution without success; and subsequent inadmissibility decisions that failed to provide effective redress. The alleged violations concern the continuing non-enforcement of judicial decisions, implicating the right to a fair trial in its execution-of-judgments aspect and, in substance, the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions, because the applicants were deprived of the compensation they had been awarded. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected. The Court deliberated on 22 February 2022 and delivered judgment on 15 March 2022.
001-219194:
In *Anatoliy Yeremenko v. Ukraine*, the applicant was a Ukrainian journalist working for the weekly newspaper *Dzerkalo Tyzhnya*. On 12 March 2005 it published his article “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case,” later posted on the newspaper’s website. The article alleged systemic corruption in the Donetsk commercial courts. It described case no. 27/37, in which a judgment had allegedly been based on a forged copy of a guarantee letter even though the original was in a criminal case file, and said the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal had relied on that copy. It also described an alleged scheme under which clients paid a law firm, cases were assigned to the “right judge,” and a “black triad” ensured the desired outcome. The article quoted Ch., a company director, who claimed an organised group operated in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, citing case no. 8/55 and a letter to a parliamentary sub-committee. No judge was named in the article.

On 7 April 2005 six judges from those courts applied for “preventive measures and securing of evidence.” They claimed the article contained false, negative statements damaging their honour, dignity and professional reputation, including references to an “organised group,” the “pressure of the system,” cases being distributed to the right judge, and the “black triad.” They asked for the article’s removal from the website. On 8 April 2005 the Voroshylovsky District Court ordered the editorial board to remove the article from the newspaper’s website pending defamation proceedings. The decision merely restated the claimants’ request and cited Article 152 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, without real reasoning. On 26 August 2005 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the removal, reasoning that internet information was publicly accessible and difficult to control, so removal was the only protective measure. It acknowledged that the legal basis cited was erroneous because no defamation claim had yet been lodged, but refused to quash the ruling. The Kyiv Court of Appeal later rejected the applicant’s cassation appeal on 15 January 2008. The article was removed by 18 August 2005.

Defamation claims were filed in April and August 2005. The judges sought retraction and damages, arguing that the article undermined judicial authority. On 20 October 2005 the Petrovskyy Local Court partly allowed the claim. It found paragraphs 8 and 9 defamatory and untrue. It held that statements about an “organised group” and a corrupt scheme amounted to accusations of criminal offences, which under the presumption of innocence required proof by a court verdict; no such proof existed, and the security service had found no evidence of an organised group. The court rejected the applicant’s reliance on the Press Act because Ch. was not a State official and his letter was not an official document. It treated the applicant and Ch. as co-authors, but considered the applicant less culpable, though he had failed to verify the information. The court ordered the newspaper to publish a retraction and the applicant to pay UAH 333 in non-pecuniary damages per claimant plus legal and court fees, amounting to about EUR 331 and EUR 430.51; Ch. was ordered to pay UAH 1,000 per claimant. The Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the merits on 27 January 2006, reducing fees, and the Kyiv Court of Appeal rejected the final cassation appeal on 5 November 2007 without detailed reasoning. The applicant complained under Article 10 that the interim removal order and the defamation judgments violated his freedom of expression, particularly in relation to public-interest allegations of judicial corruption.
001-220665:
In *Marina Aucanada Group S.L. v. Spain* (App. no. 7567/19, Third Section, judgment 8 November 2022), the applicant is a Spanish limited liability company. It complained under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that it had not been directly served with a summons in judicial administrative proceedings concerning annulment of a public call for tenders, despite being an identifiable interested party.

On 4 February 2015, the Port Authority of the Balearic Islands published a call for tenders for management of moorings at the old Port of Alcúdia. On 7 April 2015, the Alcúdia City Council brought judicial administrative proceedings before the High Court of the Balearic Islands, seeking annulment of the call because it allegedly infringed a 2004 agreement between the City Council and the Port Authority. The proceedings were admitted on 20 April 2015. The High Court requested the administrative file and ordered that it be provided to “any interested party” within five days, with nine days to appear as interested parties.

Meanwhile, on 5 May 2015, the applicant company submitted a tender. On 18 May 2015, its tender and three others were accepted for consideration. On 7 May 2015, following the High Court’s instructions and relying on section 49 of the Administrative Jurisdiction Law and section 59 of Law 30/1992, the Port Authority published a public notice (*edicto*) in the Official Gazette of the Balearic Islands, dated 27 April 2015, informing interested parties of the proceedings and inviting them to participate. None of the tenderers was directly served with a summons, either then or later. Press articles in 2015 and 2016 reported the proceedings and identified the applicant company as a tenderer; one article dated 8 June 2015 expressly linked the tender procedure to the City Council’s appeal.

The City Council later sought suspension of the tender as a precautionary measure. The Port Authority objected, noting that tenders had been opened and were under consideration, and added the relevant minutes to the file. On 18 May 2016, while proceedings no. 113/2015 remained pending, the Port Authority selected the applicant company’s tender as the most advantageous. On 31 March 2017, the High Court upheld the City Council’s claim and annulled the call for tenders and secondary acts because it violated prior undertakings. The applicant said it learned of the proceedings through the press and applied on 20 April 2017 to intervene and appeal.

The applicant appealed in cassation to the Supreme Court, arguing that identifiable interested parties had to be directly summoned. On 17 April 2018, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that publication of the *edicto* complied with section 49 and that a party acquiring a legitimate interest *ex post facto* could still appear; it did not examine the merits. A plea of nullity was rejected by the High Court on 14 June 2018 on the same basis. The applicant then lodged an *amparo* appeal, complaining that its right to be directly summoned and to a fair hearing had been breached because the authorities and courts knew its identity but failed to inform it of the pending proceedings, even though it had won the tender before judgment. On 18 December 2018, the Constitutional Court declared the *amparo* inadmissible for lack of constitutional relevance.

The alleged violation therefore concerns Article 6 § 1: whether Spain failed to ensure that the applicant company, as a known and identifiable interested party whose successful tender was later annulled, was directly summoned and given a real opportunity to participate in the administrative judicial proceedings. The domestic courts considered the published *edicto* sufficient; the ECtHR gave notice of the Article 6 § 1 complaints.
001-219309:
**Case: Nadtochiy v. Ukraine (Application no. 32899/13)**  
The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined a Ukrainian applicant’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, alleging unlawful and disproportionate deprivation of her property.

The applicant, Ms Zinayida Sergiyivna Nadtochiy, was granted a plot of land by the Sumy Town Council on 4 June 2008, free of charge, for the construction of a house as part of the privatisation process. She planned to begin construction within two years but did not do so, instead using the land primarily for gardening.

In August 2011, the Deputy Prosecutor of the Sumy Region brought civil proceedings against the applicant, seeking to have her title to the land declared void. This became the first set of proceedings. The prosecutor argued that the designated use of the land contradicted the town’s general zoning plan and violated the town’s right to construct apartment buildings on the land. On 9 February 2012, the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal gave a final decision rejecting the prosecutor’s action. The court found that the prosecutor had not challenged the Council’s decision of 4 June 2008 and that the applicant’s use of the land for gardening was not a reason to deprive her of it.

In February 2012, the prosecutor brought a second action, this time against both the Council and the applicant. The second action relied on similar grounds but additionally argued that the Council’s decision of 4 June 2008 had not been based on a detailed zoning plan or specific construction limits. On 25 July 2012, the Kovpakivskyy District Court of Sumy allowed the prosecutor’s second action. That judgment was ultimately upheld by the Higher Specialised Court of Civil and Criminal Matters on 18 January 2013. The courts declared the Council’s decision of 4 June 2008 and the applicant’s title to the land void, and the land was returned to the municipality. The courts held that, when transferring the land to the applicant, the Council had failed to develop a detailed zoning plan and specific construction limits, thereby failing to serve the interests of the community.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that she had been deprived of her land for no legitimate purpose, since no apartment building had been erected on it. She also alleged a violation of the principle of legal certainty, arguing that the second set of proceedings—which led to her deprivation—had re-examined matters already determined with final effect in the first set of proceedings. Finally, she complained that no compensation had been paid to her, even though it had been the fault of the authorities that she was deprived of the land.

The key alleged violation therefore concerned the annulment of her land title and the return of the plot to the municipality. The central factual issues were the original free transfer of land for housing construction, the applicant’s failure to build and use of the land for gardening, the prosecutor’s two successive challenges, the final rejection of the first claim, the later success of the second claim based on deficient zoning and construction planning, and the absence of any compensation. The Court was thus called upon to assess whether the interference with the applicant’s property was lawful, pursued a legitimate aim, was proportionate, and struck a fair balance, including with respect to procedural certainty and compensation.
001-220013:
M.T. and Others v. Sweden (ECtHR, First Section, App. No. 22105/18, 20 October 2022) concerned Sweden’s refusal to grant residence permits to a Syrian mother and her minor son in Syria based on family reunification with another son/brother who had subsidiary protection in Sweden. The applicants alleged that the refusal breached Article 8 (family life) and Article 14 read with Article 8 (discrimination), because the Temporary Act suspended family reunification for subsidiary-protection beneficiaries while refugees retained a more favourable regime.

The first applicant (M.T.) is the mother of the second (A.A.K.) and third (M.A.K.) applicants. The second applicant arrived in Sweden in March 2016 at age 15 and applied for asylum. In November 2016, the Migration Agency granted him a 13-month temporary residence permit as a person eligible for subsidiary protection under the Aliens Act and the Temporary Act, based on the security situation in Syria. It found no individual reasons for refugee status. His permit was extended in October 2017 for two years.

In February 2017, while the second applicant was still a minor, the first and third applicants applied at Sweden’s embassy in Khartoum for residence permits citing family ties to him. The third applicant, also a minor, additionally cited an eye injury requiring medical care, study plans, and reunion with brothers in Sweden. The first applicant’s husband/father lived in Saudi Arabia; several siblings were in Sweden, Germany, or Turkey.

In August 2017, the Migration Agency rejected the applications. It noted that under Chapter 5, section 3(4) of the Aliens Act, a parent of an unmarried child who is a refugee or otherwise in need of protection could normally receive a permit if the child had arrived in Sweden separately from both parents. However, under section 7 of the Temporary Act, that rule did not apply if the person in Sweden had a temporary residence permit as a subsidiary-protection beneficiary and had applied after 24 November 2015. Because the second applicant applied after that date and held subsidiary-protection status, the mother could not receive a permit. The third applicant’s application was rejected on the same basis and because no other grounds existed. The Agency found no breach of Sweden’s international commitments.

The Migration Court upheld the refusal in October 2017, and the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in November 2017. The applicants relied on Article 8 alone and with Article 14. They argued that the Temporary Act had suspended their right to family reunification and that treating subsidiary-protection beneficiaries differently from refugees was discriminatory. The second applicant turned 18 in August 2018, after which he would generally no longer be eligible for reunification with parents or siblings.

The Temporary Act, in force from July 2016 to July 2019, was introduced after Sweden received about 163,000 asylum seekers in 2015. It reduced family reunification to EU minimum standards: refugees were limited essentially to the nuclear family, while reunification for subsidiary-protection beneficiaries was suspended. It contained a safety provision allowing a permit if refusal would breach an international convention. The preparatory works considered the restrictions compatible with Articles 8 and 14, reasoning that refugees generally have longer-lasting protection needs. UNHCR and the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights criticised the distinction and its impact on Syrians, most of whom received subsidiary protection. The case thus concerned whether this blanket temporary suspension and the differential treatment of subsidiary-protection beneficiaries breached the applicants’ family-life and non-discrimination rights.
001-215132:
In *Radmilli v. Malta* (Application no. 28711/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application lodged on 17 May 2019 by Alessandra Radmilli, a Maltese national born in 1948 and living in Sliema. The case concerned a long-standing statutory lease over her property and the adequacy of domestic redress for an alleged breach of property rights.

The property had originally been leased to a third party under temporary emphyteusis by the applicant’s ancestors. Although that contract expired in 1980, the tenant remained in occupation because Act XXIII of 1979 amended Chapter 158 of Malta’s laws. Under that regime, the tenant retained the property under a lease at approximately €420 per year, with only slight increases over time. As a result, the applicant, as owner, could not recover possession or obtain a market-level rent.

In domestic constitutional proceedings, on 15 February 2018 the Civil Court (First Hall) found a violation of the applicant’s property rights. It observed that the original legitimate aim of the rent legislation had diminished, particularly after 1995 when most of the property market was liberalised. Given the growing discrepancy between the controlled rent and market value, especially from 2008, the court awarded €30,000 in pecuniary damages and €1,000 in non-pecuniary damages. It also declared that the tenant could no longer rely on the impugned law to maintain title to the property. The applicant was not ordered to pay costs.

Both the State and the tenant appealed. On 14 December 2018 the Constitutional Court confirmed the finding of a violation but reduced the pecuniary award to €25,000. It reasoned that it should not depart from the limits of compensation usually awarded in similar cases. The applicant was ordered to pay one quarter of the costs of the appeal.

A further complication arose from Act No. XXVII of 2018, which entered into force on 1 August 2018. Article 12B provided that, even where a judgment had been given in the owner’s favour, the owner could not lawfully request the eviction of the occupier without first availing himself of the new procedure established by that law. This provision was relevant to the effectiveness of the domestic judgment and to the applicant’s ability to recover her property.

At some point before 8 May 2020, the applicant regained possession of the vacant property. Nevertheless, she had brought the case to Strasbourg, complaining about interference with her property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were the expiry of the emphyteutic contract in 1980, the statutory continuation of the tenant’s lease at a very low rent, the domestic courts’ recognition that the rent regime had become disproportionate, the compensation eventually awarded, and the 2018 legislative measure that restricted eviction despite a favourable judgment.

The Court was therefore called upon to assess whether the prolonged restriction on the applicant’s property rights, and the redress provided by the Maltese authorities, struck a fair balance between the tenant’s interests and the applicant’s right to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions.
001-214780:
In *Boguta and Tereshchenko v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) examined two Ukrainian applications alleging that domestic authorities failed to conduct effective investigations into the deaths of the applicants’ relatives. Application no. 13094/19 was lodged by Volodymyr Boguta on 28 February 2019; application no. 37726/19 was lodged by Yuliya Tereshchenko on 7 July 2019. The Ukrainian Government was given notice, and the Court adopted its judgment on 13 January 2022.

Boguta’s son, B., was found dead on 13 January 2007 on the ground floor of an unfinished 18-storey building in Truskavets, where he had been on vacation with his wife and friends. A same-day inspection and medical examination concluded that he died from multiple injuries caused by a fall from height, with no signs of violent death. Between January and May 2007, the Truskavets Town Prosecutor’s Office issued three decisions refusing to institute criminal proceedings; these were set aside as premature. A June 2007 medical examination found injuries atypical for a fall from height, repeatedly confirmed in 2009 and 2012. In January 2008, a criminal investigation into possible intentional murder was opened and transferred to Truskavets police. In March 2008, an investigator closed it for lack of evidence, accepting accident; that decision was quashed in April 2008. In October 2009, the case was transferred to Lviv Region police. Between October 2011 and October 2013, the investigator terminated proceedings four times; each decision was set aside by prosecutors and the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv. Those rulings noted failures to resolve discrepancies between witness statements and medical expert conclusions and to perform investigative steps ordered by prosecutors and courts. In March 2015, the case was transferred to Ternopil Region police. In March 2020, the investigator again closed it for lack of evidence; the Ternopil City Court quashed that decision in August 2020 as ill-reasoned. The investigation remained ongoing.

Tereshchenko’s daughter, U., was found dead on 25 June 2016 near a multi-apartment building in Kharkiv where her acquaintance Ye. lived. A criminal investigation for possible intentional murder began the same day. The applicant alleged that Ye., who had several convictions, was involved. A 27 June 2016 medical examination found minor head injuries, bruises and cuts on the left forearm, and an injection mark on the right arm. The expert concluded that death was caused by cardiomyopathy and blood circulation disorder against a background of medium alcohol intoxication. Between June 2016 and March 2017, the investigator issued three decisions closing the investigation for lack of crime, treating the death as natural. These were set aside by the Kominternivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office and District Court, which noted failures to question persons who had seen U. before her death (including Ye), to assess the evidence properly, especially the origin of the injuries, and to follow instructions on investigative steps. In March 2017 and October 2018, the Kominternivskyy District Court ordered police investigators to step out because of unjustified protraction. The investigation was still pending.

In both applications, the applicants complained of ineffective investigation into the death of their relatives, raising the procedural aspect of the right to life under Article 2 of the Convention.
001-217415:
**TB Inžinjering d.o.o. v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 8181/21) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the prolonged non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment obtained by a private company against a public authority. The applicant company, TB Inžinjering d.o.o., was represented by Mustafa Alić, a lawyer practising in Tešanj. The application was lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 10 December 2020. The respondent Government were given notice of the application.

The central factual basis of the alleged violation was that the applicant company had obtained a domestic decision in its favour, but that decision was not enforced. The relevant domestic decision was issued by the Zenica Municipal Court on 4 October 2017. It was issued against the municipality of Maglaj, meaning that the debtor was a local public authority. The applicant therefore held a final and enforceable domestic judgment, but the authorities failed to secure its execution.

According to the appended table, the non-enforcement period began on 2 July 2018. At the time of the proceedings before the European Court, enforcement remained pending. The length of the enforcement proceedings was recorded as more than three years, eight months, and twenty-seven days. This prolonged failure to enforce the domestic decision formed the core of the applicant’s complaint.

The applicant complained specifically of the non-enforcement of the domestic decision issued in its favour against the municipality of Maglaj. In Convention terms, such a complaint typically raises issues under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair hearing, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The essential allegation was not that the domestic court had decided the underlying dispute incorrectly, but that the State had failed to ensure that a final judicial decision in the applicant’s favour was actually executed. Because the debtor was a municipality, the failure to enforce the judgment engaged the responsibility of the respondent State, which is required to organise its legal and administrative systems so that final judgments are executed within a reasonable time.

The case was heard by the Fourth Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Armen Harutyunyan, President, Jolien Schukking, and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, judges, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 5 May 2022 and delivered its judgment on 25 May 2022. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the applicant company obtained a favourable domestic decision from the Zenica Municipal Court on 4 October 2017; the debtor was the municipality of Maglaj; enforcement did not occur; the non-enforcement period started on 2 July 2018; and enforcement remained pending for over three years and eight months. These facts indicate that the applicant was unable to realise the benefit of a final judgment for a substantial period. The case thus concerns the State’s obligation to enforce final domestic decisions, especially where the debtor is a public body, and the alleged breach arising from the prolonged failure to do so. The excerpt provided does not include the Court’s full legal reasoning or final disposition, but it clearly identifies the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment as the factual foundation of the applicant’s complaint.
001-218074:
**Case: Goulandris and Vardinogianni v. Greece (Application no. 1735/13)**

The applicants, Georgios Goulandris and Christianna Vardinogianni, are Greek nationals and a married couple living in London. On 17 September 2003 they purchased a coastal plot in Korakia near Kranidi, Argolida. On 5 October 2004, an urban-planning inspection found that two stone walls had been built on the property without the required building permit: one wall was 119.5 metres long and 1.9 metres high, and the other was 99.4 metres long and 1.8 metres high. The inspection report named the first applicant as owner, declared the constructions unlawful, and imposed an administrative construction fine of EUR 18,102 plus an annual preservation fine of EUR 1,802 for each year the walls remained.

The report was received by an employee of the applicants on 4 November 2004. No complaint was filed against the fines. In March 2005, after a reduction, the first applicant paid EUR 7,414.78, covering the construction fine and stamp duties. In November 2011, the municipality issued notices to recover preservation fines of EUR 5,379.80 from each applicant as co-owners. On 29 November 2011, the first applicant paid the total amount of EUR 10,759.60.

Separately, the inspection report was sent to the public prosecutor in January 2005. In July 2006 a bill of indictment was issued against both applicants. On 17 September 2008, the one-member Nafplio Criminal Court of First Instance convicted them of jointly and intentionally constructing the walls without a permit. The building permit relied on authorised only a 0.6-metre-high fence. The court sentenced them to seven months’ imprisonment, taking into account the offence’s severity and their personal circumstances, and converted the sentence into a fine of EUR 10 per day.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the administrative fines were criminal in nature and had become final when paid, so the later criminal prosecution and conviction breached the ne bis in idem principle under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, as well as domestic res judicata rules. On 16 December 2011, the Nafplio Court of Appeal dismissed that plea. It held that administrative acts do not have res judicata effect for criminal courts; that the construction and preservation fines were not criminal sanctions but administrative measures aimed at ensuring compliance with urban-planning law; and that the fines did not amount to a final criminal conviction. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction and sentence, suspending the sentence for three years.

On 4 June 2012, the applicants appealed on points of law, again complaining of a breach of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. On 11 September 2012, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It reasoned that res judicata under Article 57 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies only to final criminal judgments; that criminal sanctions are imposed by criminal courts for criminal justice purposes, while administrative sanctions exercise an administrative function; and that administrative sanctions cannot be considered criminal punishment under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. Therefore, the cumulative imposition of administrative fines and criminal sanctions for the same unlawful constructions did not violate ne bis in idem.

The applicants later submitted the walls for regularisation under Law no. 4178/2013, completed in October 2017. Before the European Court of Human Rights, they alleged that Greece had violated their right not to be tried and punished twice for the same offence under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, focusing on whether the administrative fines constituted criminal penalties and whether the later criminal conviction duplicated punishment for the same conduct.
001-215166:
In *Atristain Gorosabel v. Spain* (Application no. 15508/15), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention. The applicant, Javier Atristain Gorosabel, a Spanish national, alleged that while held incommunicado he was denied a lawyer of his own choosing and was unable to communicate with his lawyer before and during police questioning, leading him to make self-incriminating statements that supplied evidence used for his conviction.

The case arose from an anti-terrorist investigation by the Audiencia Nacional concerning the Basque terrorist group ETA. On 29 September 2010, the Guardia Civil arrested the applicant. On 30 September 2010, investigating judge no. 2 of the Audiencia Nacional authorised his detention incommunicado to prevent frustration of the ongoing investigation, which primarily sought to locate explosives. The detention was ordered and supervised by a judge. Once authorised, the applicant was assigned State-funded legal aid. He was informed of his rights, including the right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself. However, because of the incommunicado regime, he could neither choose his own lawyer nor meet privately with the assigned legal-aid representative before being interviewed by police.

During the incommunicado detention, the applicant gave two statements to the Guardia Civil, both in the presence of the legal-aid representative. On 1 October 2010, he stated that he had “cooperated” with ETA, describing attempted kidnapping, verifying a businessman for possible assassination, and providing information about police officers so an attack could be planned. He also indicated a storage room where explosives were kept. A subsequent search there revealed explosives, detonators, USB keys, terrorist manuals, ammunition, and other material. On 3 October 2010, after again being informed of his rights, and despite his legal-aid representative’s opposition, he gave a second statement revealing a hidden firearm, cartridges, USB keys, and false licence plates. Those items were later found at his home. His legal-aid representative repeatedly tried to contact him but was told that communication was restricted because of the incommunicado detention.

The applicant was examined daily by a forensic doctor. He reported no mistreatment but claimed that the Guardia Civil had threatened to arrest his girlfriend if he did not cooperate. On 4 October 2010, he was brought before the investigating judge. He stated that his police statements had been obtained during five days of incommunicado detention and were therefore self-incriminatory. His incommunicado detention was then lifted, and he was able to appoint a lawyer of his own choosing.

On 16 April 2013, the Audiencia Nacional convicted him of membership of a terrorist group and possession of explosives, sentencing him to seventeen years’ imprisonment. The conviction was based essentially on seized computer material, explosives found at his home and at locations he had indicated, statements by co-defendants, witness evidence, and his silence at trial. The courts ruled out mistreatment and found that his statements had been given freely and voluntarily. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 18 March 2014. The Constitutional Court declared his *amparo* appeal inadmissible on 7 November 2014 for failure to justify its constitutional relevance.

The ECtHR complaint therefore focused on the impossibility of being represented by a lawyer of his own choosing and communicating with that lawyer before and during incommunicado detention. The applicant argued that this breached his fair-trial rights and tainted the self-incriminatory statements and derivative evidence used against him.
001-219988:
The applicant, Tom Mortier, a Belgian national born in 1976 living in Rotselaar, is the son of G.T., who had chronic depression for about forty years and had been treated by psychiatrist B. The respondent is Belgium. In 2011 G.T. considered euthanasia; her general practitioner Dr W. did not wish to act as main doctor and referred her to Professor D. On 29 September 2011 Prof D saw her and agreed to become her main doctor, referring her to psychiatrist Dr V. On 17 November 2011 Dr V considered the request premature and referred her to Dr V.D. On 12 January 2012 Prof D referred her to psychiatrist Dr T, who met her on 17 January. On 20 January G.T. agreed to be assisted by Dr V.D.; it was suggested she inform her children. On 31 January she emailed the applicant and her daughter about her euthanasia request and suffering; her daughter respected her wishes, while the applicant did not reply. On 7 February Prof D contacted Dr B, who saw no chance of improvement; on 10 February Dr B wrote to Dr T describing serious chronic conditions and a bleak outlook. On 14 February G.T. lodged a handwritten euthanasia request; Prof D formally became main doctor, and Dr T reported G.T. was rational, informed, under no third-party pressure, and could be assisted. On 17 February Dr V.D. examined her and on 20 February reported she could be assisted. Prof D saw her again on 22 February and 8/12 March. On 27 February she drafted a body-donation statement. On 29 February she donated EUR 2,500 to LEIF, run by Prof D, whose members included Dr T and Dr V.D. On 12 March Dr B concluded there was no point contacting her children. On 20 March P.D. became a person of trust. On 3 April a meeting set euthanasia for 19 April. On 10 April Prof D assured her that her wishes would be respected. On 19 April 2012 Prof D performed euthanasia; G.T. died at 11:15 a.m. in a public hospital in the presence of friends. The hospital informed the applicant on 20 April 2012.

On 20 June 2012 the Federal Euthanasia Board received Prof D’s registration document. On 26 June 2012 the Board, co-chaired by Prof D, found the euthanasia complied with the Euthanasia Act. Dr C later examined G.T.’s medical file on 2 August 2013 and noted the euthanasia declaration was not in it. The applicant requested a copy of the registration document from the Board on 23 October 2013 and 4 March 2014; on 19 March 2014 the Board refused, citing legal confidentiality. On 16 February 2014 he complained to the Medical Association; he says the outcome was not communicated because of confidentiality. On 4 April 2014 he lodged a criminal complaint against persons unknown. On 8 May 2017 the Crown Prosecutor discontinued for insufficient evidence. On 2 May 2019 the investigation was reopened. An expert report of 5 May 2020 concluded G.T. had intolerable, incurable mental suffering, requested euthanasia freely and constantly, the statutory waiting period was respected, and two psychiatrists were consulted; it noted the applicant learned of the death unfortunately and the file lacked the Board declaration and assessment. Prof D was interviewed by police on 16 June 2020. The Crown Prosecutor found compliance and sought closure; the applicant declined to have Prof D summoned. On 11 December 2020 the Pre-Trial Division found no grounds for prosecution and closed the investigation; no appeal was lodged. The applicant complained under Articles 2, 8 and 13.
001-220164:
**Case Summary: Bahtić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**  
*(Application no. 4034/22, European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 27 October 2022)*

The case originated in an application lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Anfisa Bahtić, born in 1973, was represented by Kenan Buljubašić, a lawyer practising in Zenica. The respondent Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the application. The application was introduced on 11 January 2022 and was decided by a Committee of the Fourth Section composed of Judges Armen Harutyunyan, Jolien Schukking, and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar.

The central factual basis of the applicant’s complaint was the non-enforcement of a domestic decision issued in her favour. Specifically, on 9 October 2020, the Zenica Municipality Court issued a decision in the applicant’s favour against the City of Zenica. Despite that domestic court decision, the authorities did not enforce it. The relevant period of non-enforcement began on 23 November 2020. By the time the case was examined by the European Court of Human Rights, the enforcement proceedings remained pending. The appended table records the length of the enforcement proceedings as “more than 1 year(s) and 9 month(s) and 23 day(s),” with no end date because enforcement had not been completed.

The applicant therefore complained to the European Court that the domestic decision issued in her favour had not been enforced. This failure to enforce a final or enforceable domestic decision formed the core of her alleged violation. In the Convention context, such a complaint ordinarily concerns the obligation of the State to ensure that judicial decisions are executed and to protect the applicant’s rights under the fair-trial guarantees and the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions. However, the factual summary provided focuses primarily on the prolonged non-enforcement itself: a domestic court decision in the applicant’s favour against a public authority, the City of Zenica, remained unsatisfied for an extended period, and enforcement proceedings were still pending.

Procedurally, the Court, sitting as a Committee, deliberated in private on 6 October 2022 and adopted the judgment on 27 October 2022. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore limited but significant: (1) the applicant obtained a domestic decision in her favour on 9 October 2020; (2) the decision was against the City of Zenica, a public authority; (3) enforcement did not begin effectively or was not completed, with the non-enforcement period starting on 23 November 2020; (4) the enforcement proceedings were still pending at the relevant time; and (5) the applicant turned to the European Court on 11 January 2022, complaining that the domestic decision remained unenforced. The essence of the case is the State’s alleged failure to secure timely enforcement of a domestic court decision in the applicant’s favour.
001-215913:
In Davtyan v. Armenia (Applications nos. 54261/13 and 18361/16; judgment of 1 March 2022), the European Court of Human Rights considered complaints by Samvel Davtyan, an Armenian national born in 1968. The case concerned alleged ill-treatment in police custody, the alleged failure to carry out an effective investigation, and the fairness of his criminal trial because the courts relied on a confession allegedly obtained under duress. The complaints arose under Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention.

On 23 September 2011 at 8:30 a.m., the applicant was taken to the Principal Department for the Fight Against Organised Crime (PDFAOC) of the Armenian Police. He alleged that police officers immediately subjected him to several hours of ill-treatment, hitting him on various parts of his body. At 11:30 a.m., an investigator of the Principal Department for Investigations (PDI) questioned him and placed him under arrest. The alleged ill-treatment reportedly continued. The applicant claimed he was stripped, handcuffed by his hands and feet to a chair, beaten with rubber batons, subjected to electric shocks, and kicked on the soles of his feet, back, ribs, and other areas, while officers demanded that he confess to a crime.

At 11:30 p.m. that day, the applicant was admitted to a police temporary holding facility. Medical records documented injuries including a wound and swelling on the left temple, reddish traces on his back, wounds on both shins, swelling of the right hand, swelling of both feet, and a wound on the right wrist. A notification of these injuries was sent to the PDI. On 24 September 2011, the PDI investigator questioned the applicant, who confessed to the crime. On 1 October 2011, the investigator examined the holding facility’s medical register. On 3 October 2011, the applicant refused to testify about his injuries. On 4 October 2011, a forensic medical expert, ordered by the investigator, confirmed part of the injuries and found they had been inflicted by a blunt hard object.

In October 2011, the applicant appointed a lawyer, who contested the forensic examination results and alleged ill-treatment. On 6 April 2012, the PDI investigator took statements from two PDFAOC officers who had arrested the applicant. Both gave identical one-paragraph statements denying ill-treatment and claiming the applicant resisted arrest, that force was used, and that he fell during the incident, which may have caused his injuries. The investigator asked no questions.

In June and July 2012, the applicant complained in detail to the General Prosecutor and requested an investigation by the Special Investigative Service (SIS). The July complaint was forwarded to the SIS, which questioned the applicant on 15 August 2012. He maintained his complaint but refused to answer questions about his injuries. On 23 August 2012, the SIS refused to institute criminal proceedings, relying on the two officers’ statements and the applicant’s refusal to testify. It concluded that his injuries resulted from the lawful use of force by arresting officers seeking to prevent his flight. The applicant’s appeals against that decision were dismissed by the courts.

Separately, the applicant was convicted and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. In reaching that verdict, the courts relied, among other evidence, on his confession of 24 September 2011 and rejected his requests to exclude it. The applicant therefore alleged that he had been ill-treated in custody, that no effective investigation followed, and that his trial was unfair because the conviction rested on a confession allegedly obtained under duress.
001-220010:
In *Lysak v. Ukraine* (Application no. 52299/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Ms Svitlana Vasylivna Lysak, a Ukrainian national born in 1949 and living in Cherkasy. The applicant was a private entrepreneur. The Court gave notice only of her complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. Her essential allegation was that equipment belonging to her and located on municipal land had been unlawfully dismantled, and that she had been unable to obtain compensation for that interference.

The facts concerned three kiosks—temporary structures for selling goods—that the applicant owned and operated on municipal land in three locations in Cherkasy. The municipal authorities considered that her rights to use the land had expired. The applicant challenged that assessment before the Cherkasy Regional Commercial Court. That court issued preliminary injunctions on 14 August 2008 and 19 May 2009 prohibiting the municipal authorities from dismantling her equipment. In a final decision of 31 March 2010, the commercial court declared the authorities’ assessment unlawful and ruled that the applicant continued to have the right to rent the land in question.

Separately, on 28 April 2009, the city executive committee ordered the municipal working group dealing with unlawful structures to proceed with the removal of the applicant’s equipment. Mr K., a member of that group and director of a municipal company, was directed to provide equipment for the dismantling operation and to arrange storage of the dismantled equipment. On 28 May 2009, despite the commercial court’s interim injunction, the municipal working group dismantled the applicant’s equipment and its contents—kiosks, cash registers and a stock of goods for sale—and placed them in storage. The applicant alleged that the equipment had been damaged during dismantling and had become unusable, and that the stock of goods had been lost.

Subsequent domestic proceedings confirmed elements of unlawfulness. On 21 September 2010, the Cherkasy Sosnivsky District Court, in a final decision, declared the executive committee’s decision of 28 April 2009 unlawful. It specifically noted that the decision had been taken in disregard of the commercial court’s injunctions. The applicant also lodged a criminal complaint accusing city officials of abuse of public office and other crimes. Mr K. was eventually charged with criminal dereliction of duty. Within those criminal proceedings, the applicant brought a civil claim for damages against Mr K. and the State Treasury. On 4 October 2013, Mr K. was found guilty but released from serving his sentence. The civil claim was dismissed, with the court stating that it could be resubmitted in separate civil proceedings. The conviction was later quashed and the case remitted for further investigation, most recently on 16 February 2016; no further developments were reported.

The applicant also sued the city council and the city executive committee in the administrative courts, seeking a declaration that their actions in removing her equipment had been unlawful, as well as damages. On 22 January 2014, the High Administrative Court upheld the lower courts’ decisions rejecting the claim. Those courts reasoned, in particular, that it would be appropriate for the applicant to seek compensation within the framework of the criminal proceedings against Mr K.

Thus, the key facts relevant to the alleged violation under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 are that the applicant’s possessions were dismantled despite court injunctions; a final domestic decision later declared the underlying removal decision unlawful; and the applicant was nevertheless unable to obtain compensation through criminal or administrative proceedings. The ECtHR’s review focused on whether this amounted to an unlawful interference with her property rights and a failure to provide compensation.
001-220885:
In *A and Others v. Iceland*, four Icelandic nationals—parents A and B and their children X (born 2008) and Y (born 2011)—complained about child-protection proceedings that culminated in the parents’ loss of custody. The case concerned alleged violations of the right to respect for private and family life, particularly the authorities’ handling of sexual-abuse allegations after the father was acquitted in criminal proceedings.

In October 2015, X’s school notified the municipal child protection committee that X had described domestic violence and drawn a picture suggesting her father had touched her and her brother on their “private parts.” X reportedly said the drawing showed “the penis which entered my vagina.” The father was arrested, questioned, and held in pre-trial detention for four days. At Children’s House interviews, X initially did not disclose abuse, but later described her father touching her private parts with his penis and finger and applying cream. Y initially denied any touching, but after being placed in foster care in September 2016, his foster mother reported urinary and bowel problems and said Y had disclosed that his father applied cream to his genitals and told him not to tell his mother. In a later interview, Y said his father rubbed his penis, applied cream, and inserted a finger into his rectum.

Child-protection authorities found the family home disordered and the children badly cared for. The mother was receiving treatment for depression and anxiety. The children were temporarily placed outside the home, then returned to their mother after the father moved out. In February 2016, X was placed in temporary foster care. In September 2016, Y was also removed and placed in the same foster home after concerns that he was having extensive contact with the father. A psychologist later concluded that the mother lacked sufficient capacity to have custody, citing neglect, possible violence, emotional problems, and her failure to protect the children, including by allowing contact with the father and pressuring X to change her statement. Reports in 2017 found neither parent fit to care for the children, and the committee sought custody deprivation.

In March 2017, the father was indicted for sexual offences against X and Y. On 22 November 2017, the Reykjanes District Court acquitted him of all charges, finding guilt not established beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution did not appeal.

In the separate custody proceedings, a court-appointed psychologist in May 2018 found the children’s accounts consistent and credible, the parents’ custody capacity lacking, and both children genuinely afraid of their father. The children had bonded with their foster parents and wished to remain there. The Reykjavik District Court granted custody deprivation in June 2019. The Court of Appeal overturned that decision in November 2019, finding the committee had failed to reconsider the case after the acquittal and that less intrusive measures had not been properly explored. On 10 March 2020, the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeal and deprived both parents of custody. It held that the criminal acquittal was not determinative in child-protection proceedings, which must be assessed under the children’s best interests. It found the children had severe fear of the father and that the mother, despite efforts, could not provide adequate protection, partly because she intended to remain married to the father and the children mistrusted her.

The children remained in permanent foster care, with limited contact for the mother and no contact for the father. The applicants’ surviving complaints concerned Article 8, especially whether the custody deprivation and contact restrictions were justified and whether the authorities improperly relied on abuse allegations after the father’s acquittal.
001-220537:
**Summary**

*N.V. and C.C. v. Malta* (Application no. 4952/21) concerned a Maltese mother, N.V., and her British partner, C.C., who complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights about a Family Court order that severely restricted their family life.

N.V. had a son, E., from a prior marriage to J. After separating, N.V. obtained custody of E., while J. had access rights. In 2009 N.V. moved to Malta with E. and began living with C.C.; they later had a child together in 2016.

In 2012 J. brought Family Court proceedings concerning access. Tensions included C.C.’s presence during visits. In July 2015, after an incident, J. alleged that C.C. had come to his house, threatened to kill E., and had psychological problems. N.V. claimed instead that C.C. had been the victim of violence. J. sought custody and the forced removal of E.

On 1 October 2015, relying in part on a sealed Children’s Advocate report that was not disclosed to the parties, the Family Court ordered N.V. not to expose E. to C.C., with immediate effect. It also warned N.V. about hindering J.’s access and ordered monitoring. N.V. asked for variation and for C.C. to be heard and evaluated. On 28 October 2015, without a hearing, the court dismissed her requests, citing only “some of the reasons” in the objection and giving no specific reasoning.

A psychologist’s report of 25 November 2015 later found that E. was fond of C.C., missed him, and that there was nothing dangerous or untoward in their relationship; it recommended continued contact. Despite this, the October decree remained in force. As a result, N.V. and C.C., while expecting their child, could not live together or be together when E. was present; C.C. could not assist N.V. in everyday needs.

In constitutional redress proceedings in 2016, the applicants alleged breaches of Article 8 and Article 6. Under Article 8, they argued that the decree unjustifiably interfered with their de facto family life. Under Article 6, C.C. complained that an order affecting him was made although he was never a party to the Family Court proceedings, never heard, and despite requesting to be heard. Both applicants complained that the Children’s Advocate report was sealed and inaccessible. N.V. complained that decisions affecting her were made without oral hearings and without reasoning, and that she had no effective remedy because challenges had to be brought before the same judge who had issued the decrees. They sought annulment and damages.

In September 2016, as their child’s birth approached, the applicants sought an interim measure allowing them to be together when E. was present. The constitutional court declined but invited a cautious arrangement in the child’s best interests; after the birth, they resumed living as a family.

The First Hall, Civil Court, in 2019 found breaches of Articles 8 and 6 and annulled the 1 October 2015 decree. On appeal, the Constitutional Court in 2020 set aside the Article 8 finding as unnecessary because the decree had been annulled, and dismissed C.C.’s Article 6 claim because he was not a party to the original proceedings. It confirmed Article 6 violations regarding N.V., particularly the lack of oral hearings and unreasoned decisions. The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 January 2021.
001-217436:
**Case: Arnar Helgi Lárusson v. Iceland**  
**ECtHR, Third Section, Application no. 23077/19, judgment 31 May 2022 (final 10 October 2022).**

The applicant, Arnar Helgi Lárusson, is an Icelandic national born in 1976 who lives in Reykjanesbær. After an accident in 2002, he was left permanently paralysed from the chest down and uses a wheelchair for mobility.

In 2015, the applicant and an association of people with spinal injuries brought civil proceedings against the municipality of Reykjanesbær and its holding company, F., which owned one of the buildings. They challenged the lack of wheelchair access in two buildings housing municipal arts and cultural centres. They sought a declaratory judgment requiring accessibility improvements.

The first building, Duushús, was a three-storey arts and cultural centre made up of two adjoining houses built in 1877 and 1954–70, extensively renovated between 2006 and 2014. The applicant requested a wheelchair lift between floors, ramps between ground-floor galleries no steeper than 1:20 as required by building regulations, and changes to the main entrance threshold. The second building, 88 Húsið, was a two-storey former engine house built in 1963 and used as a municipal youth centre since 2004. The applicant requested a wheelchair lift between floors, ramps no steeper than 1:20 from the car park to the building and between rooms, and a designated disabled parking space within 25 metres of the entrance. He also sought ISK 1,000,000 (about EUR 7,300) in non-pecuniary damages.

The plaintiffs argued that the buildings did not comply with applicable building regulations and that the lack of access prevented the applicant and other wheelchair users from enjoying their private life on an equal basis with others, contrary to the Icelandic Constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights, and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

A court-appointed assessor found that Duushús had no lift between floors, a ramp between ground-floor halls with an incline of approximately 1:7 and a width of 96–161 cm, and a 51 mm threshold at the main entrance. At 88 Húsið, there was no lift between floors, no lift or ramp between the different halls, a ramp from the car park to the entrance with an incline of approximately 1:9, and no designated disabled parking space by the entrance.

On 24 November 2016, the Reykjanes District Court ruled in favour of the defendants. It found that access needed improvement but that the buildings did not violate the applicable building regulations because they had been built before those regulations took effect. The municipality was nevertheless under a legal obligation to work towards improving wheelchair access to public buildings and public service institutions. The court noted that the municipality had begun an accessibility initiative and held that municipalities had a margin of appreciation in prioritising such projects; separation of powers prevented courts from ordering specific action where authorities had discretion.

The plaintiffs appealed. Before the Supreme Court, they did not expressly rely on the Convention but referred to their earlier submissions and invoked equality and non-discrimination. On 25 October 2018, the Supreme Court upheld the lower judgment. It noted that the CRPD had been ratified but not incorporated into domestic law, so it could not be directly relied on, although domestic law should be interpreted harmoniously with international obligations where possible. It held that the municipality had complied with its legal duty to devise an accessibility strategy under legislation enacted with regard to international human rights obligations, including the CRPD, and had acted on that strategy. Disability matters had been transferred from the State to municipalities in 2010; municipalities were autonomous in matters entrusted to them by law and in the use of their funds, and had a wide margin of appreciation in prioritising improvements. The Supreme Court did not address the Convention or the equality and non-discrimination arguments.

The ECtHR gave notice to the Government only of the complaints under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention; the remainder of the application was inadmissible. The core alleged violations concerned the lack of wheelchair access to public cultural and social buildings and alleged discrimination in the enjoyment of private life and social participation.
001-216454:
The applicant, Edvin Starkevič, was a Lithuanian police officer. In October 2015, police arrested V.M. on suspicion of burglary. V.M. later told the police internal affairs division that, during his detention, the applicant had asked him to steal goods. V.M. said he subsequently met the applicant and persons linked to him in public places on 25 October and 11 November 2015.

On 12 November 2015, internal affairs opened a pre-trial investigation into suspected abuse of office. Based on V.M.’s statements and security-camera footage, a prosecutor sought court authorisation to intercept the applicant’s electronic communications, conduct secret surveillance, and use a criminal conduct simulation model. The court authorised these measures on 16 November 2015. V.M. was allowed, no more than twice, to agree to the applicant’s demands to obtain stolen goods in exchange for payment, with the actions recorded.

On 8 January 2016, V.M. met the applicant in a public place and gave him a bottle of whiskey. The applicant was arrested in flagrante delicto. A notice of suspicion alleged that, between 25 October 2015 and 8 January 2016, the applicant—acting with his wife, I.S., and another person, J.R.—had asked V.M., a suspect in another case, to illegally obtain handbags, sports shoes, and whiskey. The applicant denied the accusations but refused to testify.

On 29 January 2016, the applicant was notified of a disciplinary investigation based on information that he had possibly committed abuse of office, thereby damaging the police’s prestige and possibly discrediting an officer’s name. He was invited to provide an explanation by 5 February 2016. He instead asked the police to rely on his statements from the pre-trial investigation, where he had refused to testify. The disciplinary proceedings were suspended pending the criminal investigation.

On 9 September 2016, the prosecutor discontinued the pre-trial investigation. He found no corpus delicti because there was no significant pecuniary or non-pecuniary damage to the State or police, no major public reaction, and no disruption of police work. However, he considered that the applicant’s conduct contained elements of a disciplinary violation and forwarded the file to the police for disciplinary assessment. The prosecutor’s decision relied on evidence from the criminal conduct simulation model, V.M.’s testimony, other witnesses, CCTV footage, telephone data, and the whiskey bottle. The applicant did not appeal that decision.

On 26 October 2016, a disciplinary investigation report found that the applicant’s actions were contrary to law and had features of a crime. It stated that he had used his police position for personal gain, encouraged another person to break the law, and breached police ethics and service rules. It concluded that he had discredited an officer’s name. On 27 October 2016, the police dismissed him under the Statute of Internal Service.

The applicant challenged his dismissal in administrative proceedings, arguing that disciplinary and criminal proceedings had different grounds, that he should have had a proper opportunity to explain and submit evidence, that the disciplinary findings lacked concrete evidence, and that evidence obtained through the criminal conduct simulation model should not have been used in disciplinary proceedings. He did not expressly raise the presumption of innocence. The administrative courts dismissed his claims, finding that the misconduct notice was sufficiently clear, that his refusal to explain was his own defence tactic, and that the prosecutor’s decision was admissible proof. They also held that, even excluding the simulation-model evidence, other evidence sufficiently supported the dismissal.

The case before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the applicant’s complaints about the right to a fair hearing, the presumption of innocence, and respect for private life, mainly because information obtained during the criminal investigation—including secret surveillance and simulated criminal conduct—was used in the subsequent disciplinary proceedings that led to his dismissal.

001-215735:
In *Centroprom Holding AD Beograd v. Montenegro* (Application no. 30796/10), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 10 February 2022. The case originated in an application lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by Centroprom Holding AD Beograd, a company, against Montenegro. The application was introduced on 10 May 2010. The applicant company was represented by Ms V. Čejović, a lawyer practising in Bar. The Montenegrin Government were given notice of the application.

The Court sat as a Committee composed of Lətif Hüseynov (President), Lado Chanturia and Arnfinn Bårdsen, judges, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. It deliberated in private on 20 January 2022 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment was final but remained subject to possible editorial revision.

The applicant company’s principal complaint was the excessive length of civil proceedings. It also raised other complaints under the Convention, although the provided extract does not identify those additional complaints or describe them in detail. The key facts relevant to the length complaint are set out in the appended table.

According to that table, the relevant starting point for the length of proceedings, or the date of entry into force of the Convention in respect of Montenegro, was 3 March 2004. The domestic civil proceedings ended on 2 April 2015. The total length of the proceedings was therefore 11 years and 1 month. The proceedings involved three levels of jurisdiction.

The fact that the Convention entered into force in respect of Montenegro on 3 March 2004 is significant for the Court’s temporal jurisdiction. In principle, the Court could examine the length of the civil proceedings only from that date onward, unless earlier periods were relevant as background. The table indicates that the relevant period for the excessive-length complaint was calculated from 3 March 2004 until the final termination of the proceedings on 2 April 2015. This produced a total duration of over eleven years across three judicial levels.

The application was lodged on 10 May 2010, while the domestic civil proceedings were still pending. The domestic proceedings continued for approximately another five years after the application was introduced, ending on 2 April 2015. Thus, the applicant company complained that the domestic courts had failed to decide the civil case within a reasonable time, as required by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. That provision guarantees, among other things, a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.

The provided judgment extract does not set out the underlying subject matter of the civil dispute, the specific procedural steps taken by the domestic courts, or the Court’s ultimate conclusions on the merits and just satisfaction. Rather, it focuses on the procedural history and the duration of the proceedings. The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the application was lodged on 10 May 2010; the relevant Convention period began on 3 March 2004; the civil proceedings ended on 2 April 2015; they lasted 11 years and 1 month; and they passed through three levels of jurisdiction. Those facts formed the basis of the applicant company’s complaint that the length of the civil proceedings was excessive and incompatible with the reasonable-time requirement under the Convention.
001-219944:
The case of **Fabbri and Others v. San Marino** (Applications nos. 345/21, 6319/21, 6321/21 and 9227/21) concerned four applications brought by Mario Foschi, Stellino Fabbri, Andrea Forcellini—all San Marinese nationals—and Angelina Marro, an Italian national. The applicants were injured parties or complainants in separate criminal investigations in San Marino. Their common complaint was under **Article 6** of the Convention: because criminal proceedings against the alleged offenders were discontinued after the charges became time-barred due to the authorities’ inactivity, the applicants could not have their civil claims determined within the criminal proceedings, as San Marino law permitted.

In **Mr Foschi’s case**, in August 2014 he lodged a complaint with the Italian police against MKT, a Bulgarian national, for fraud and misappropriation of EUR 354,370. The Italian investigation found insufficient evidence, considered the matter essentially civil, and concluded that most transfers occurred outside Italian jurisdiction. The file was transferred to San Marino in July 2015, and a criminal investigation was opened. However, the assigned investigating judge took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice invited submissions on the non-observance of investigation time-limits. A new investigating judge was assigned in February 2020. In March 2020, that judge found the offence time-barred because no investigative act had occurred after the file was opened. The Prosecutor agreed to discontinuation without prejudice to any future civil claims. The discontinuation decree was issued in March 2020.

In **Fabbri and Marro’s case**, in April 2016 they complained against N., a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for personal injury. They stated their intention to join the eventual proceedings as civil parties, asked to be informed if proceedings were discontinued, and appointed lawyers. A criminal investigation was opened, but the investigating judge again took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice invited submissions concerning the investigation time-limits. In November 2020 a newly assigned investigating judge declared the charge discontinued because it had become time-barred. He noted that no investigative measures had been undertaken and that N. had not even been notified of the investigation. In any event, absent evidence, no criminal proceedings could ensue. The Prosecutor agreed later that month.

In **Mr Forcellini’s case**, defamation proceedings had been initiated in 2015 by a teacher against his parents.
