In March 2018 the trial judge found the parents guilty and sent the file to the investigating judge to consider investigating third persons. A criminal file was opened against V. and D. for private violence and persecution against the fourth applicant, then a minor. A request to join the proceedings as a civil party was submitted. The assigned investigating judge took no steps. In November 2020 a newly assigned judge archived the case, finding it time-barred and noting that no investigative acts had been undertaken and no evidence collected. The Prosecutor agreed.

The legal framework, notably Law no. 93/2008, required the investigating judge to complete investigations within peremptory time-limits. Once those limits expired, proceedings were considered published and the case could be discontinued. Criminal Code Article 54 imposed a three-year limitation for relevant offences. The Code of Criminal Procedure allowed injured parties to pursue civil actions separately or within criminal proceedings, and time-bar did not bar civil action unless the civil action was also time-barred. Victims could join as civil parties, but had no right to know investigative acts before publication.

The alleged violation arose from the authorities’ failure to conduct timely investigations, causing charges to become time-barred and proceedings to be discontinued. As a result, the applicants allegedly lost the opportunity to have their civil claims determined by the criminal court, contrary to Article 6. The Chamber judgment was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 24 September 2024.
001-215898:
Pukhyr and Others v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 10791/20 and six others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, delivered on 24 February 2022. The case concerned seven Ukrainian nationals who applied to the Court between 2020 and 2021. The Government was given notice. The applicants complained principally of inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. They also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The first applicant, Yuriy Pukhyr (b. 1990), was held in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 28 May 2012 to 14 August 2019—7 years, 2 months, and 18 days. He allegedly had only 1.5–2 m² of personal space and suffered overcrowding, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of fresh air, insufficient natural light, restricted access to potable and warm water, poor water quality, restricted showers, inadequate hygiene facilities, no toiletries, poor bedding and bed linen, inadequate temperature, poor and insufficient food, insufficient outdoor exercise, and no privacy for the toilet.

Valentyn Tunitovskyy (b. 1986) was held in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 31 March 2015 to 22 February 2021—5 years, 10 months, and 23 days—with 2.5–2.7 m². His complaints included lack of fresh air, inadequate hygiene, a mouldy or dirty cell, poor bedding, and insufficient outdoor exercise.

Andriy Zakharchenko (b. 1981) was detained in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 14 April 2017 to 11 March 2021—3 years, 10 months, and 26 days—with 2.04–2.98 m². He alleged overcrowding, insects/rodents, mould or dirt, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, no toilet privacy, restricted warm water, no toiletries, poor bedding, poor and insufficient food, restricted showers, inadequate hygiene, and insufficient electric light.

Yevgeniy Nemchenko (b. 1962) had been held in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility since 2 September 2019—more than 2 years, 4 months, and 13 days at introduction—with 2.5–6.1 m². He complained of lack of fresh air, insufficient electric light, poor bedding, insufficient food, restricted showers, poor food, no toiletries, and overcrowding.

Igor Podushkin (b. 1978) was detained in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 3 December 2018—more than 3 years, 1 month, and 12 days—with 2.27–4.26 m². His grievances included insects/rodents, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygiene, insufficient outdoor exercise, no toiletries, insufficient food, mould or dirt, restricted showers, overcrowding, passive smoking, and no toilet privacy.

Yanush Kondrashov (b. 1990) was held in Dnipro Penitentiary Facility no. 4 since 2 April 2018—more than 3 years, 9 months, and 13 days—with 3.6–3.65 m². He alleged overcrowding, insects/rodents, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygiene, restricted showers, poor potable water, mould or dirt, no toiletries, poor food, insufficient outdoor exercise, and poor bedding.

Sergiy Raulets (b. 1996) had been held in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility since 23 February 2018—more than 3 years, 10 months, and 23 days—with 2.4–2.9 m². He complained of restricted showers, overcrowding, mould or dirt, lack of fresh air, poor potable water, poor bedding, no toiletries, passive smoking, and insufficient outdoor exercise.

The core alleged violations thus concern prolonged detention in overcrowded, unsanitary, poorly ventilated and lit conditions, with inadequate access to water, showers, hygiene, food, bedding, and outdoor exercise, and the absence of effective domestic remedies.
001-187510:
**CASE OF OTEGI MONDRAGON AND OTHERS v. SPAIN** concerned five Spanish nationals—Mr Arnaldo Otegi Mondragón, Mrs Jacinto García, Mr Díez Usabiaga, Mrs Zabaleta Tellería and Mr Rodríguez Torres—who lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights in January 2015. The only complaint communicated to the Spanish Government was an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, namely the right to a fair hearing before an impartial tribunal. The applicants alleged that the panel of the Audiencia Nacional’s Fourth Section that tried them in the so-called “Bateragune” case lacked impartiality because it included a presiding judge who had previously shown bias against the first applicant.

The factual background involved two sets of criminal proceedings. In the first, on 2 March 2010, the first applicant was convicted by the Fourth Section of the Audiencia Nacional of encouragement of terrorism and acquitted of unlawful assembly and association. During the oral hearing, after the applicant had given evidence, the presiding judge asked him whether he condemned ETA’s violence. He refused to answer, and the judge replied that she “already knew that he was not going to give an answer to that question.” On appeal, the Supreme Court ruled on 2 February 2011 that this question and the judge’s reaction objectively revealed a preconceived opinion about the applicant’s guilt. It declared the judgment void and ordered a retrial before a different panel. On 22 July 2011, a new panel acquitted the first applicant.

Meanwhile, in 2009, criminal proceedings were brought against all five applicants in the Bateragune case. They were accused of belonging to, and being linked with, the terrorist organisation ETA, specifically through an alleged attempt to create a political party under ETA’s control. These proceedings were allocated to the same Fourth Section of the Audiencia Nacional, composed of the same judges who had sat in the earlier case against the first applicant, including the same presiding judge, though she was not the judge rapporteur. The first applicant challenged the entire panel, arguing that the presiding judge’s previously established bias created an objectively justified doubt about the impartiality of the whole section. On 26 April 2011, a special chamber of the Audiencia Nacional rejected the challenge, finding that the new proceedings concerned different charges and that no bias was shown.

On 16 September 2011, the Audiencia Nacional convicted the first and third applicants of membership and leadership of a terrorist organisation, sentencing them to ten years’ imprisonment. The second, fourth and fifth applicants were sentenced to eight years for belonging to a terrorist organisation. All were also disqualified from standing in elections for the same periods. On appeal, the Supreme Court, by a 3-to-2 majority on 7 May 2012, reduced the sentences to six years and six months for the first and third applicants and six years for the others, but rejected the impartiality complaint. It held that bias shown in previous, different proceedings did not automatically contaminate the judges in later proceedings. Two dissenting judges disagreed; one found a violation of impartiality, while the other considered the evidence insufficient for conviction.

The applicants then lodged amparo appeals. On 22 July 2014, the Constitutional Court, by 7 votes to 5, rejected the main appeals, finding that the doubts about the presiding judge’s impartiality were not objectively justified because the earlier and later proceedings concerned different offences. Five dissenting judges considered that the applicants’ right to an impartial tribunal had been violated. A separate amparo by the third applicant was also rejected on 22 September 2014. The key issue before the ECtHR was therefore whether the prior finding of bias against the presiding judge, combined with her participation in the later Bateragune trial, created objectively justified doubts about the impartiality of the tribunal for all applicants.
001-187818:
**Summary of *Grabovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 4442/07)**

The case of *Grabovskiy v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Nikolay Aleksandrovich Grabovskiy, a Ukrainian national born in 1969, regarding criminal proceedings against him and the conditions of his detention.

The events stem from an incident on 22 July 2005, when a sales clerk, G., was attacked in a Kharkiv shop, suffering multiple cuts including a penetrating chest wound. She identified the applicant, whom she knew, as her attacker. The domestic courts found that the applicant attacked G. and seized cash belonging to her employer. The applicant, however, maintained throughout proceedings that G. owed him money. He claimed he went to the shop to collect the debt, but G. attacked him with scissors. He stated that while defending himself, he hit her, seized the scissors, and stabbed her. When an alarm sounded, he took the money and fled.

The applicant was arrested late on 22 July 2005. He alleged that his request for a lawyer during police questioning was ignored. However, police records dated 23 July 2005 indicated that his procedural rights, including the right to legal aid, were explained to him, and that he chose to waive his right to legal assistance. On 25 July 2005, a forensic medical examination noted injuries to the applicant's jaw and hand, consistent with his account of a fight.

The applicant was charged with aggravated robbery. During his trial before the Kharkiv Kyivsky District Court, which began on 17 October 2005, the applicant stated he wished to defend himself and waived his right to legal assistance. He later alleged he was forced to do so by police guards in the courtroom. He repeated his version of events and requested certain witnesses be called, but the trial court refused, stating he failed to identify them and deemed his allegations an obfuscation tactic. On 18 October 2005, the applicant was convicted and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment. The court relied on, among other things, the applicant's trial admissions, the victim's testimony denying any debt, and testimony from the applicant's girlfriend and the victim's relatives who also denied knowledge of any debt.

The applicant appealed on 14 November 2005, raising evidentiary matters and requesting a lawyer. He reiterated this request on 6 January 2006. On 2 February 2006, the Court of Appeal's Vice-President asked the regional Bar association to assign a lawyer, but there was no follow-up. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 20 July 2006, with the applicant present but unrepresented. His subsequent request to the trial court for a lawyer to prepare a cassation appeal was denied on 28 August 2006. The Supreme Court rejected his appeal on points of law on 28 February 2007.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant was held in various facilities, including the Kharkiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO) from 17 August 2005. He complained of overcrowding, specifically a cell with 24 sleeping places holding over 50 inmates. The Government provided cell occupancy data showing varying square metres per sleeping place, ranging from 1.34 to 2.09. The applicant was also treated for various medical issues during detention.

Finally, the applicant complained that domestic authorities failed to provide him with copies of certain documents needed for his application to the Court, including witness statements and records, despite having copies that were of poor quality.
001-181882:
The applicant, Robert Tadeusz Danilczuk, a Polish national born in 1965 and currently detained in Czarne Prison, Poland, brought an application against Cyprus concerning conditions at Nicosia Central Prisons.

On 14 September 2010 he was placed in detention on remand at Nicosia Central Prisons pending criminal proceedings before the Limassol District Court (case no. 25536/10). On 11 January 2011 he was convicted of offences including burglary, theft, road traffic offences and unlawful residence. On 24 January 2011 the court imposed four concurrent sentences ranging from six months to two years, running from 5 September 2010. He was released on 18 May 2012 after his sentence was suspended by presidential decree.

The applicant alleged that he had been held in overcrowded cells with only 0.5 to 1.7 sq. m of personal space. He said the cells were cold and lacked adequate light; there were no toilets in the cells; he sometimes waited two to three hours to use a toilet; and when the cells were locked he had to urinate into a bottle and defecate into a waste bag. He did not specify the exact periods.

The Government stated that he had been detained from 14 September 2010 to 18 May 2012 in three parts of the prison. From 14 September 2010 to 24 January 2011 he was in Block 5, which held remand prisoners; after conviction he was transferred to Block 2B, where he remained until 5 October 2011; and from 5 October 2011 until his release he was in Block 2A. Block 5 had up to 68 remand prisoners, 34 double cells of 6.21 sq. m, eight toilets and eight showers; it was almost certain he shared a cell, giving him 3.10 sq. m. Block 2B, then unrenovated, had 26 double cells of 9.98 sq. m, two large cells of 19.55 sq. m accommodating five to seven detainees, and a 90 sq. m dormitory for 20 to 50 inmates; daily occupancy varied from 80 to 124. Depending on placement, his personal space could have been 4.99 sq. m in a double cell, about 2.8–3.9 sq. m in a larger cell, or 1.8–4.5 sq. m in the dormitory; in spring or winter, with 94–110 inmates, it would have been 2.04–3.2 sq. m. Block 2A, renovated, had 41 double cells of 9.80 sq. m for 82 prisoners, giving 4.9 sq. m, and six toilets, six showers and three urinals. General conditions included central heating, corridor air conditioning, cell fans, insulated windows, and movement outside cells from 6 a.m. to 5/6 p.m. and within blocks until 9/10 p.m. Following the CPT’s 2012 report, the prison discontinued switching off cell bells at night; order no. 32/2008 provided for toilet access, though no records were kept of night openings; detainees could leave up to three times between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m.

The CPT’s 2012 report on its 2008 visit found severe overcrowding, prisoners lacking night toilet access, and degrading use of makeshift receptacles. Its 2014 report on a 2013 visit welcomed renovation of Block 2 but found continuing overcrowding and difficulty accessing toilets at night. The Ombudsman’s 6 September 2011 report similarly described crowded, unsuitable detention areas, insufficient hygiene facilities, and complaints that deactivated night cell bells forced detainees to use bottles and waste bags. Domestic law provided for damages for violations of detainees’ rights, and the Ombudsman served as national preventive mechanism under the Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture.
001-188360:
**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Vasilevska and Bartoševič v. Lithuania* (Applications nos. 38206/11 and 18054/12) concerns the annulment of inherited property rights and the subsequent, protracted restitution process, raising issues under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicants, Lithuanian nationals, are the heirs of their grandfather, P.S. In 1991, P.S. applied for the restoration of his property rights to land nationalized by the Soviet regime. In 1994, authorities acknowledged his right to restitution. Consequently, on 28 September 2004, the Vilnius County Administration (VCA) restored his rights by granting him 8.17 hectares of land near Vilnius.

In 2005, P.S. sold two portions of this land: 0.50 hectares to S.M. and 1.27 hectares to Ž.J. The sales were notarized. P.S. passed away in July 2005, and the applicants received their inheritance certificate in December of that year.

Subsequently, the prosecutor of the Vilnius Region initiated three separate legal actions to annul parts of the original restitution. The prosecutor argued that certain plots, totaling 3.52 hectares, were covered by forest of "national importance." Under domestic law, such forests within city limits could only be owned by the State.

The domestic courts ruled in favor of the prosecutor in all three cases. They annulled P.S.'s property rights to 2.50 hectares, 0.15 hectares, and 0.87 hectares. As the applicants were P.S.'s heirs, the courts also annulled the sale agreements for the land sold to S.M. and Ž.J. and ordered the applicants to reimburse the buyers. The applicants were ordered to pay S.M. approximately EUR 14,340 and Ž.J. approximately EUR 54,660 (which they paid in 2013, along with bailiff’s expenses).

Regarding the annulled 2.50 hectares that had not been sold, the applicants were simply deprived of this land. In total, they lost rights to 3.52 hectares of land and incurred significant financial liabilities.

Following these annulments, a subsequent restitution process was initiated by the National Land Service (NLS) to compensate the applicants for the 3.52 hectares. This process proved to be lengthy and complex. The applicants expressed a preference for a residential plot in Vilnius or the return of land in Kryžiokai. They were informed of long waiting lists (over 4,800 candidates) and were offered various alternatives, including land in rural areas or monetary compensation, which they declined.

Over the years, the applicants participated in meetings to select substitute plots. They chose several plots in 2012 and 2016, but the process was fraught with delays. In 2012, chosen plots were not allocated. In 2018, they refused a plot offered in joint ownership. By October 2018, over a decade after the annulment process began, the NLS had only restored their rights to a fraction of the land—0.23 hectares—leaving 3.29 hectares still unresolved.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights. The core of their case is that the annulment of their property rights effectively imposed an excessive and disproportionate individual burden on them. They lost land they had inherited and were forced to pay substantial sums to third parties, while the state's subsequent attempts to provide restitution were plagued by excessive delays and failed to adequately remedy their losses. The key factual issue is whether the Lithuanian authorities, through their actions, struck a fair balance between the public interest (protecting state-owned forests) and the applicants' fundamental right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions.
001-181595:
In **Falzon v. Malta** (Application no. 45791/13), the applicant was Michael Falzon, a Maltese former member of parliament and government minister who later wrote weekly opinion columns. The case concerned his complaint under **Article 10** of the European Convention on Human Rights that Maltese courts had fined him for defamation, thereby violating his freedom of expression.

The dispute arose from a public speech in May 2007 by Dr Michael Falzon (“M.F.”), deputy leader of the Malta Labour Party. M.F. stated that he had received an anonymous email and threatening letters and had complained to the Commissioner of Police (“CoP”). He described contacting the CoP, asking for an investigation, and authorising the police to proceed against whoever was responsible. A journalist, K.S.N., then published an article about the email and an alleged admirer being questioned by police.

On 13 May 2007, the applicant published an opinion piece in *Maltatoday* entitled **“Policing one’s enemies.”** The article opened by referencing the Stasi and questioned how political parties viewed the police. It criticised M.F. for persuading the CoP to investigate what the applicant described as a trivial anonymous email. It suggested the CoP had offered to act discriminatorily depending on who the culprit turned out to be. It further stated that police had traced the email’s sender, impounded his computer, and required him to sign daily at police headquarters even though he was not accused of a crime. The applicant asked whether M.F. had “successfully used the Police Force to control the freedom of an innocent, law-abiding private citizen whom he suspected could be a political enemy.” He also questioned whether the police were interfering in Labour’s internal politics and whether M.F. carried more influence with the CoP than the Deputy Prime Minister. He called for an inquiry by the Minister of the Interior.

M.F. sued the applicant and the newspaper editor for libel under the Press Act. The applicant defended the article as fair comment, value judgment, and substantially true based on M.F.’s own public statements. He argued that M.F., as a public figure, was subject to wider limits of acceptable criticism. The CoP testified that he had not been persuaded or influenced by M.F.; M.F. had requested a normal appointment, shown him a threatening letter, and later provided the email. The CoP passed the matter to the Criminal Investigation Department and said it received no priority.

The Court of Magistrates found the applicant guilty of defamation and ordered him to pay €2,500 in damages; the editor was also liable for €1,000. It accepted that politicians faced wider criticism but found the article damaged M.F.’s reputation. It rejected the defences because it was not proved that M.F. had manipulated the CoP, used the police for personal aims, or acted as a “deus ex machina” pulling strings.

The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. It held that the applicant’s assumptions were not fair comment and exceeded just criticism. M.F. had a right to report the matter to police, and the attack was not supported by factual evidence. Freedom of expression had to respect objective veracity and restraint.

The applicant then brought constitutional redress proceedings, alleging a breach of Article 10. The Civil Court dismissed the claim, finding that the article implied abuse, even if the word “uses” did not exactly mean “manipulate.” The Constitutional Court also dismissed the appeal. It accepted that the interference was prescribed by law but found no Article 10 violation. Politicians had wider criticism limits, but still retained reputation rights. The court found that the article contained factual assertions disguised as questions, such as “Has not M.F. ...”, and that allegations of illegitimate or abusive influence had not been proved. The fine was not considered particularly severe. The applicant’s Article 10 complaint was communicated to the Maltese Government; other complaints were declared inadmissible.
001-187200:
**Bradshaw and Others v. Malta** (Application no. 37121/15) concerns twenty-four Maltese nationals and a Maltese company who jointly owned 274 Republic Street, Valletta—a four-storey, 864-square-metre property known as the King’s Own Band Club (“KOBC”). In 1946, the applicants’ ancestors voluntarily leased the property to KOBC for GBP 500 annually (approximately EUR 1,164.69). In 1955, Maltese law introduced specific rules for leases to band clubs. Under the Civil Code and the Re-letting of Urban Property (Regulation) Ordinance, the applicants were obliged to renew the lease annually and could not demand an increase in rent. The applicants claimed that by 2014 the property’s market rental value was EUR 269,100 per year. Part of the property was used as a band club, while part operated as a restaurant and bar, which the applicants said generated around EUR 150,000 or more annually for the caterer.

The applicants alleged an ongoing violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, arguing that they were denied peaceful enjoyment of their property without adequate compensation. They also alleged discrimination under Article 14, taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They pointed out that 2009 amendments to the Civil Code allowed increases in certain commercial rents and established a cut-off date of 2028 for existing protected commercial leases, but those amendments did not cover properties leased to clubs. As a result, club leases remained subject to annual renewal and frozen rent, unlike commercial leases.

In 2011, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings against the Attorney General, the Prime Minister, and KOBC. In 2013, the Civil Court (First Hall), in its constitutional jurisdiction, found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the interference was disproportionate, noting the disparity between the rent received and the property’s estimated rental value or the income generated from the bar/restaurant. It awarded EUR 300,000 in damages, payable half by the Attorney General and Prime Minister jointly and half by KOBC. The court found no discrimination.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court reversed in 2015. It accepted that the applicants owned the property but held that, because the 1946 lease had been entered into voluntarily with knowledge of its consequences, the applicants could not complain of a violation. Even if inflation had made the rent low, the principle of *pacta sunt servanda* applied. It also found that the 2009 amendments did not affect the applicants’ position. A request for retrial was rejected in 2016.

Meanwhile, in 2014, new regulations increased club rents by 10% annually until 2016, then by 5% until 2023, and thereafter by inflation. From 2015, tenants also had to pay an additional 5% of annual income from economic activity. As a result, the applicants received only EUR 2,876.26 in 2015 and EUR 3,017.20 in 2016.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the long-standing statutory rent control, the applicants’ inability to terminate the lease or increase rent, the voluntary origin of the 1946 lease, the dramatic gap between actual rent and market value, the profitable commercial use of part of the premises, and the differential treatment of club leases compared with commercial leases after the 2009 reforms. These facts formed the basis of the complaints of disproportionate interference with property rights and discriminatory treatment.
001-187455:
Mr Roger Delecolle, a French national born in 1937 and living in Paris, lodged an application against France on 5 June 2013. He alleged a violation of Article 12, complaining that he had been denied the right to marry because his marriage was subject to the authorisation of his supervisor or the guardianship judge.

On 23 June 2009, when he was seventy-two, the guardianship judge of the Paris District Court of the 15th Administrative District placed him under enhanced protective supervision (curatelle renforcée) for five years, following an initial request by his adoptive daughter. The judge relied on medical certificates from Dr M.F. (25 November 2008) and Dr J.-P.B. (14 March 2009), and appointed M.-C.M. as supervisor. The applicant sought lifting of the measure, or ordinary supervision, or reduction to twenty-four months. On 18 December 2009 the Paris Regional Court dismissed those requests. It noted that Dr R. had excluded dementia but found slight cognitive impairment and psychological fragility and vulnerability, and that the applicant lacked capacity to manage or dispose of his property, though he could hold a bank account and cash card.

The applicant asked his supervisor to authorise his marriage to M.S., a friend since 1996 and his partner since 2008. The supervisor interviewed them separately and together and refused on 17 December 2009, stating that she had known the applicant only a few months. On 21 December 2009 the guardianship judge ordered a social inquiry by the UDAF into the applicant’s living conditions, lifestyle, social status and circle of friends. The applicant appealed against that order. That same day the judge also commissioned a medical opinion on his capacity to marry. On 18 January 2010 the psychiatrist reported that the applicant suffered from intellectual disorders; while able to consent to marriage, he was considered incapable of dealing with its property and financial consequences. The psychiatrist also gave personal opinions and described some of the applicant’s arguments as bordering on absurd.

On 1 March 2010 the Paris Court of Appeal declared the appeal against the inquiry order inadmissible. It held that a vulnerable adult’s interests allowed the guardianship judge to order such inquiries, and that a supervisee could marry only with the supervisor’s authorisation or, failing that, the judge’s. On 1 June 2010 the UDAF reported a financial stake at the heart of a major family conflict; the applicant’s daughter and M.S. accused each other of being interested in his fortune, and it was unclear whether he was being influenced. The applicant was deeply affected and appeared to see marriage as ensuring assistance and companionship.

On 24 June 2010 the guardianship judge, after hearing the applicant and his daughter, dismissed the marriage request. The judge found his attachment to M.S. insufficient, noted that both were former alcoholics and that the applicant apparently still drank, and considered that he sought safety against a break-up and loneliness. Financial implications were unclear because he was torn between his daughter and M.S. The applicant appealed.

On 6 September 2011 the Paris Court of Appeal upheld the refusal. It cited serious disorders and the medical certificates, stating that anosognosia prevented him from planning joint life and understanding marriage’s financial and legal implications. It noted unreasonable management since living with M.S., 250,000 euros of work after his wife’s death, questionable storage of furniture, a draft handwritten will of 14 August 2009 in M.S.’s favour, assets of about 6,000,000 euros, and deteriorated relations with his daughter M.D. It concluded that mutual affection existed but that his psychopathological condition and failing grasp of finances prevented informed consent.

The applicant appealed on points of law and raised a QPC on Article 460(1) of the Civil Code. On 29 June 2012 the Constitutional Council declared that provision constitutional. On 5 December 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, holding that the Court of Appeal had lawfully reasoned from the medical certificates and file that he could not give informed consent. The applicant died on 4 February 2016; M.S. later indicated an intention to pursue the application.
001-181859:
**Summary of Aganikyan v. Armenia (Application no. 21791/12)**

The case of *Aganikyan v. Armenia* originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Armenia with the European Court of Human Rights on 2 April 2012 by Mr. Hrayr Aganikyan, an American national residing in Yerevan. The applicant’s sole complaint, which was communicated to the Armenian Government, concerned the excessive length of criminal proceedings brought against him. All other aspects of the application were declared inadmissible. The central facts of the case relate to the protracted nature of these proceedings, which spanned nearly seven years from the initial investigation to the final appeal.

The proceedings began on 30 December 2004, when an investigator instituted a criminal case against the applicant for alleged usury. Over the next year and a half, the investigation expanded to include additional charges. On 20 June 2005, the applicant was formally charged with professional usury. Subsequently, on 15 October 2005, a separate case concerning fraud was initiated and merged with the usury case. By 7 March 2006, the charges against the applicant were significantly amended to include fraud in large amounts, extortion, usury, and forgery of evidence. During this pre-trial phase, the authorities ordered a search of his apartment, confiscated his property, and imposed a written undertaking not to leave his residence. He was later detained for two months following a successful prosecutor's appeal against an initial refusal of detention.

On 14 July 2006, the bill of indictment was approved and the case was sent to the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court. The trial phase, which commenced on 18 August 2006, was characterized by numerous adjournments. Between August 2006 and October 2007, the court held twelve hearings that were postponed, primarily due to the absence of victims and witnesses. The proceedings were further delayed when the presiding judge's powers were suspended in October 2007, leading to a new judge taking over and ordering the examination of the case to start anew in November 2007.

From November 2007 to December 2010, the trial continued with an additional forty hearings. These were adjourned for various reasons, including the absence of the applicant or his lawyer (and applications lodged by them), the absence of victims or witnesses, and applications by the prosecutor or the court’s own motion. Throughout the proceedings, the court heard from forty-seven witnesses and examined extensive documentary and expert evidence. On 31 January 2011, the District Court delivered its judgment, finding the applicant guilty on five counts, including fraud, extortion, and usury, and sentencing him to nine years' imprisonment, property confiscation, and a fine.

The applicant and the prosecutor both appealed. On 3 October 2011, the Criminal Court of Appeal rejected the appeals and upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law. On 21 November 2011, the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible for lack of merit, thus finalizing the domestic proceedings. The applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights focused on the length of this entire process.
001-180296:
**Summary**

*Cuenca Zarzoso v. Spain* (Application no. 23383/12) concerned a Spanish national, Mr Miguel Cuenca Zarzoso, born in 1930 and living in the San José district of Valencia since 1962. He alleged that Spain had breached his right to respect for his home under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights because of excessive night-time noise caused by licensed bars, pubs, and discotheques near his home.

Since 1974, Valencia City Council had allowed licensed entertainment premises to operate in the area. In 1983 the Council resolved not to permit any further such premises, but the resolution was never implemented and new licences continued to be granted. A 1993 university study commissioned by the Council found that night-time weekend noise levels in San José were notably higher than the legal norm. In 1994 the applicant became president of the local neighbourhood association and lodged complaints and requests to withdraw licences. The Council responded that some premises were inactive, others were not especially noisy, and many licences had expired.

In 1996 the Council adopted a municipal ordinance on noise and vibrations. In December 1996, published in January 1997, the area where the applicant lived was designated an “acoustically saturated zone.” In July 2000, at the applicant’s request, the pub in his building’s basement was required to install a noise limiter. Nevertheless, noise levels did not decrease, and the applicant installed double glazing and air conditioning to cope with having his windows closed.

In 1999 the applicant brought a State liability claim before the City Council, relying on constitutional rights to life, physical integrity, privacy, and inviolability of the home. After no response and then a denial by the Council, he complained to the Valencia High Court. The evidence included municipal reports from 1998 and 2000 stating that night noise had exceeded 65 decibels before the saturated-zone declaration and that limits were still exceeded after corrective measures. An expert report measured street noise up to 70 decibels and estimated bedroom noise at 50–60 dBA, compared with a recommended night-time maximum of 30 dBA. Medical evidence linked his anxiety to the noise, and a court-appointed expert found that nocturnal noise necessarily altered his sleep and produced an anxious depressive syndrome. The City Council disputed that noise inside the applicant’s specific flat was proven to exceed limits, noting variations by height and aspect and its enforcement efforts.

In June 2003 the High Court dismissed the claim, finding no causal link because there was no evidence that noise in the applicant’s particular flat exceeded limits. It noted that he had replaced his windows before requesting an interior measurement under the ordinance and that his fourth-floor flat would likely be less noisy. The applicant filed an *amparo* appeal, initially dismissed in October 2004. After the ECtHR’s judgment in *Moreno Gómez v. Spain*, the public prosecutor appealed and the Constitutional Court admitted the case in January 2005. In September 2011 the Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the cases were not identical, that the applicant had not proved excessive noise inside his flat, that the Council had adopted specific measures, and that his health problems were not shown to be directly caused by noise. Three judges dissented, arguing that under *Moreno Gómez* the decisive factor was proof of excessive street noise in an acoustically saturated area, not measurements inside the individual home, and that the expert report confirmed health effects.

The alleged violation therefore centred on whether Spain failed to protect the applicant’s home and private life from severe, prolonged noise pollution, and whether the domestic courts imposed an excessive evidentiary burden by requiring proof of noise levels inside his specific dwelling.
001-183126:
**Gafà v. Malta** (App. no. 54335/14) concerned Kenneth Gafà, a Maltese national arrested on 11 December 2010 on suspicion of murdering his former partner. On 13 December 2010 he was charged with wilful homicide and remanded in custody. From arraignment until August 2012, he filed ten bail requests, all rejected. After he had been held for the maximum statutory period, he became entitled to bail under Article 575(6)(a)(iii) of the Criminal Code, namely after twenty months for a crime punishable by nine years’ imprisonment or more.

On 22 August 2012 the Court of Magistrates granted bail subject to stringent conditions: he had to appear at all hearings; not go abroad or abscond; not contact prosecution witnesses; not commit voluntary crimes; report daily at the District Police Station between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.; observe a curfew from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.; notify address changes; deposit EUR 15,000 in the court registry; and provide a personal guarantee of EUR 25,000. Breach of any condition would forfeit EUR 40,000 to the State.

The Attorney General appealed, arguing the conditions were too lenient, and sought a higher deposit and a ban on the applicant entering locality R, where the victim and her family lived. The applicant objected and requested a reduction, saying he had been detained over twenty months, was unemployed, and could not pay. On 7 September 2012 the Criminal Court rejected the Attorney General’s request to increase the deposit but added the condition that the applicant could not be in the vicinity of locality R. It rejected the applicant’s reduction request.

The applicant made further requests to reduce the deposit in October and December 2012 and January/February 2013. He argued that he remained in detention solely because he could not afford the deposit, despite being legally entitled to bail, and noted that the main witnesses had already been heard. The Attorney General opposed, citing the seriousness of the crime, risk of absconding or tampering, and the victim’s family’s fear. The courts repeatedly refused to reduce the amount, finding it balanced the seriousness of the offence and the need to secure compliance.

On 22 July 2013 the applicant asked the court to accept his mother and relatives as surety instead of the deposit, offering inherited property valued at EUR 95,000. On 2 August 2013 the court accepted his mother as surety by hypothec over the property. On 6 August 2013, after he signed the personal guarantee and his mother effected the hypothec, he was released after thirty-two months of pre-trial detention.

In constitutional redress, his first complaint about detention exceeding fifteen months was rejected in 2012. His second complaint, filed in February 2013, alleged that the “exorbitant” deposit made bail illusory. The First Hall rejected it on 3 July 2013, finding he had not sufficiently documented his finances or shown an objective inability to find a surety. The Constitutional Court rejected his appeal on 31 January 2014, holding that the onus was on him to prove the deposit was excessive; he had only later proposed his mother as surety although the property was available earlier; and EUR 15,000 was justified given the crime’s seriousness, especially since a surety was permitted.

Later, on 7 April 2014, he was found to have breached bail conditions and bail was revoked. On 26 January 2015 an indictment issued, and on 20 July 2015 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to thirty-five years’ imprisonment.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a breach of Article 5 § 3, claiming that the excessive bail conditions—particularly the EUR 15,000 deposit—prevented him from effectively enjoying bail and prolonged his detention. The complaint concerning detention following the grant of bail was communicated to the Government; the remainder was declared inadmissible.
001-187686:
**Case Summary: Bosyy v. Ukraine (Application no. 13124/08)**

The case of *Bosyy v. Ukraine* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Vasyl Ivanovych Bosyy, a Ukrainian national, on 8 February 2008. The applicant was convicted of aggravated robbery in 2006 and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. The Court declared the complaints regarding the fairness of the criminal proceedings inadmissible, focusing instead on the conditions of the applicant's detention, alleged ill-treatment, monitoring of correspondence, and hindrance of his right to individual application.

The facts concern the applicant’s detention in various facilities from 2005 to 2012. He was held in a pre-trial detention centre (SIZO) in Kropyvnytskyi, followed by correctional colonies no. 6 and no. 78. The applicant alleged that the conditions in the correctional colonies were inadequate. Specifically, he claimed severe overcrowding, stating he was held in a dormitory measuring 6 by 8 square meters with twelve double bunk beds. He also complained of regular electricity cuts, inadequate lighting, poor quality food, and unsanitary conditions involving pests such as cockroaches, mice, and rats. The Government disputed these claims, submitting that the dormitory measured over 41 square meters with ten beds and that food and sanitation were compliant with regulations, though they admitted to reducing voltage for energy-saving purposes.

Regarding ill-treatment, the applicant alleged he was beaten by guards upon arrival at the first colony in October 2006, tortured, humiliated, and placed in a disciplinary cell. He further claimed that in March 2007, guards attempted to place him in a psychiatric clinic. The Government denied all allegations of ill-treatment. The applicant lodged numerous complaints with domestic authorities regarding this alleged persecution, though he later withdrew two complaints in 2010, citing heightened emotions.

A significant portion of the case concerned the monitoring of the applicant’s correspondence and his right to communicate with the Court. Under domestic law at the time (Article 113 of the Code on the Enforcement of Sentences), prison authorities automatically monitored prisoner correspondence, except for specific exemptions. While correspondence with the Court and the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights was exempt from monitoring by law, the applicant alleged that prison authorities intercepted, reviewed, blocked, and delayed his mail, including letters to the Court, and intimidated him for applying to the Court. The Government denied these allegations. Records indicated that despite monitoring domestic mail, the applicant corresponded extensively with international and domestic entities.

Finally, the applicant complained of hindrances to his right of individual application. He alleged that authorities denied him access to his criminal case file, preventing him from obtaining necessary documents. The Government countered with evidence showing the applicant had examined his file in late 2011 and early 2012. Additionally, there were procedural issues regarding the applicant's legal representation where he twice revoked and then reinstated the authority of his lawyer, Mr. E. Markov, leading to administrative complications with the Registry.

The Court delivered its judgment on 22 November 2018, assessing these facts against the Convention articles concerning the prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment, the right to respect for correspondence, and the right to individual application.
001-183542:
**T.K. v. Lithuania (Application no. 14000/12)** concerned a Lithuanian national, granted anonymity, who alleged that: (1) the police’s taking of his spectacles after arrest amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment; and (2) his criminal trial was unfair, particularly because he could not examine certain witnesses. The European Court of Human Rights communicated those complaints to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The applicant lived with V.K. and two boys, Ra.K. and Ro.K. In October 2011 he was convicted of causing physical pain to the boys and attempting to influence a witness; he was released after time served. In July 2011 V.K. complained that the applicant had shown pornographic films to the children and sexually abused them in 2009. On 22 August 2011 the boys were questioned by a pre-trial investigation judge and a psychologist. They described sexual abuse. Ro.K., then seven, said his mother had told him to testify and that if he and his brother stayed silent, their father would be released and their mother imprisoned. V.K. was present at the police station but not in the questioning room. Later forensic psychological and psychiatric examinations concluded that the boys could remember the events and had no tendency to fantasise, but noted the two-year delay and influence from both parents; the experts recommended no further questioning because of stress.

The applicant was arrested on 23 November 2011. In 2012 he was charged with sexual assault of a young child and possession of child pornography. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to eleven years’ imprisonment. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in December 2013, and the Supreme Court refused to examine his further appeals in 2014.

As to the fair-trial complaint, the applicant repeatedly asked the prosecutor and courts to confront or cross-examine V.K., arguing that she had coached the children and had motives to fabricate the accusations. The prosecutor refused a confrontation during the pre-trial investigation, and the courts upheld that refusal. At trial, V.K. could not be located; police reported that she was hiding from authorities and had no registered residence. The Court of Appeal initially agreed to summon her, and the prosecutor supported that step, but summonses failed and she never appeared. The appellate court proceeded without her, noting that the trial court had not relied on V.K.’s testimony when convicting the applicant. The applicant also requested examination of experts, teachers, neighbours and doctors, and inclusion of material from an earlier criminal case allegedly showing V.K. had lied or coached the children; those requests were refused as irrelevant or unnecessary. His conviction rested mainly on the boys’ statements to the pre-trial judge and experts, plus testimony from Z.S. and V.F. He alleged a breach of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention.

As to the spectacles complaint, during the applicant’s arrest on 23 November 2011 a body search resulted in his spectacles, telephone and comb being taken. While in pre-trial detention he complained that the spectacles were not returned. In April 2012 the prosecutor ordered the investigator to resolve the matter, and the spectacles were returned on 20 April 2012. The applicant later brought civil proceedings, claiming difficulties in reading, writing and communicating, and worsened eyesight. The first-instance court awarded him EUR 1,000 in non-pecuniary damages, finding the taking unlawful and degrading. The appellate court acknowledged there had been no legal basis for taking the spectacles, but reduced the remedy to an acknowledgment: there was no proof they were prescribed, no medical evidence of worsened eyesight, he had managed to write without them, and he could have requested their return earlier. The Supreme Court refused his appeal. He alleged that the deprivation amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment.
001-187251:
**M.T. v. Estonia (Application no. 75378/13)** concerned the continued coercive psychiatric detention of O.T. and the procedural safeguards surrounding review of that detention.

The applicant, M.T., a stateless person living in Tallinn, was the mother and court-appointed guardian of her son O.T., born in 1984. In May 2010, the Harju County Court found that O.T. had restricted active legal capacity. Relying on a forensic psychiatric opinion of March 2010, it concluded that he suffered from permanent paranoid schizophrenia and could not understand or control his actions. M.T. was appointed his guardian.

In October 2010, O.T. committed acts of a sexual nature against a ten-year-old girl and threatened to kill her. In the resulting criminal proceedings, a forensic psychiatric expert confirmed the earlier diagnosis and found that O.T. posed a danger to society and needed coercive psychiatric treatment. In May 2011, the Harju County Court terminated the criminal proceedings and ordered coercive psychiatric treatment, which began in June 2011.

In December 2012, M.T. applied to the Tartu County Court to discontinue O.T.’s coercive treatment or replace inpatient treatment with outpatient treatment. She relied on a June 2012 opinion by a medical committee composed of O.T.’s attending doctor and Dr E.K., acting head of the hospital’s coercive treatment department. That opinion stated that contact with O.T. was deficient, his answers were sparse, he denied the offence and did not consider himself mentally ill, and he remained dangerous. M.T. argued that the opinion was not impartial and requested an independent expert assessment.

In February 2013, the Tartu County Court dismissed her application. It relied on a December 2012 opinion by another medical committee, composed of O.T.’s attending doctor and Dr S.K., head of the coercive treatment department. That opinion stated that O.T.’s condition was unchanged, that he had deficient contact, sparse and incoherent answers, inappropriate laughter, and faked psychotic experiences, and that continued treatment was necessary. The court found no need for an additional expert opinion, since Article 403 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allowed reliance on the medical committee’s opinion.

M.T. appealed. In March 2013, the Tartu Court of Appeal quashed the decision because the first-instance court had not held oral proceedings. At the rehearing in May 2013, O.T. received State-funded legal aid and a lawyer. The court heard Dr S.K., who said O.T. had not recovered, did not adhere to treatment, accused his mother of poisoning him, and could not be treated as an outpatient. O.T. said he understood nothing and did not wish to make statements. The County Court again dismissed the application.

M.T. appealed, arguing that O.T.’s dangerousness had not been established, that no independent expert assessment had been carried out, and that the hospital committee opinions were superficial and repetitive. She also invoked Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, arguing that O.T. himself should have been able to initiate review proceedings at reasonable intervals. She pointed to Article 402-1 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and its explanatory annex, under which persons subjected to coercive psychiatric treatment had no such right.

In July 2013, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It held that independent expert examination was mandatory only when coercive treatment was initially ordered, not when discontinuation or replacement was sought. The danger posed by O.T. had already been established in 2011. In September 2013, the Supreme Court refused M.T.’s request for legal aid for a further appeal, stating that she had no personal rights to protect in the proceedings and that O.T.’s legal aid lawyer could appeal instead.

The ECtHR application alleged that the review proceedings concerning O.T.’s continued confinement did not meet Article 5 procedural requirements, particularly regarding the use of expert medical evidence and O.T.’s inability to initiate such review himself.
001-187465:
**Summary of *Bakchizhov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 24874/08)**

The case of *Bakchizhov v. Ukraine* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 May 2008 by Mr Aleksandr Viktorovich Bakchizhov, a Ukrainian national born in 1969. The applicant was convicted of inflicting bodily injuries and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, a conviction upheld on appeal. He served his sentence in Boryspil Correctional Colony from 13 April 2007 until his release on probation on 17 June 2011.

The core of the applicant’s complaints concerned the conditions and treatment during his detention. He alleged that he was held in overcrowded, dirty cells with poor ventilation and insufficient winter heating. He claimed that healthy prisoners were housed with inmates suffering from HIV and tuberculosis and that food and water were unsatisfactory. He provided details of four cells where he was held, citing severe overcrowding, such as a 70-square-metre cell accommodating 50 prisoners and a 45-square-metre cell holding 35.

The applicant further alleged ill-treatment by guards, including physical and verbal abuse, threats, and arbitrary solitary confinement. He complained of frequent cell searches during his absence, which left his belongings in disarray, and of nighttime searches, which caused him stress. He also stated that personal documents from his case file went missing.

Regarding medical care, the applicant contended that he received inadequate assistance. He claimed he did not undergo a thorough examination or receive a long-term treatment strategy, only occasional symptomatic care.

Additionally, the applicant alleged that under threat of disciplinary punishment, he was forced to perform overtime labour, often twelve to fourteen hours a day, seven days a week, without adequate remuneration.

He also complained that prison authorities monitored all his correspondence, including letters to and from the Court, selectively failing to send or delaying them. He cited an instance where a letter to the Court was not sent and claimed a letter from the Court was received a month late. Consequently, he resorted to sending some letters via friends.

The Government contested the applicant’s account. They submitted that inmates with tuberculosis were detained separately, food and water were of adequate quality, and heating maintained temperatures between 18°C and 20°C. They provided medical records showing the applicant received treatment for various conditions, including bronchitis, radiculoneuritis, and dermatitis, and claimed his health was generally stable. The Government could not provide information on alleged ill-treatment or searches, as records had been destroyed. They denied forced labour, stating he performed standard prison work with remuneration or unpaid maintenance work for no more than two hours daily. They also denied monitoring all correspondence.

Separately, the applicant complained about hindrance in accessing his criminal case file. While he was provided with some documents upon request, the Brovary Town Court informed him in 2008 that the file did not contain certain cassation appeals or Supreme Court judgments. He was only provided with a copy of the Supreme Court’s judgment in April 2009, after the Court requested it. Full access to his case file was granted only after his release in 2011.
001-188374:
In *Kin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 46990/07), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Vira Maksymivna Kin, a Ukrainian national born in 1956 and principal of a private school in Dubno, Rivne Region. The case concerned criminal proceedings against her and events of 29 May 2000, raising issues under Article 3, Article 5 § 1, and Article 8 of the Convention, as well as the length of criminal proceedings under Article 6 § 1.

On 30 March 2000 criminal proceedings were initiated against the applicant for failure to comply with a court decision ordering the reinstatement of a teacher at the private school. According to the applicant, at about 9:00 a.m. on 29 May 2000, Dubno police officers broke down the front door of her house. Inside, an investigator from the Dubno inter-district prosecutor’s office ordered her to go to his office for questioning. When she refused, the investigator asked police officers to ensure her compulsory appearance. The police allegedly beat her, twisted her arms behind her back, and forced her out of the house barefoot. She was placed in a police car and taken to the investigator’s office. She was released at about 1:00 p.m. The next day, a doctor noted injuries to her shoulders.

On 2 June 2000 the applicant complained to the Rivne regional prosecutor’s office. A medical expert found five bruises to her shoulders and injured left shoulder ligaments, caused by blunt solid objects; the expert stated the injuries could have been sustained in the circumstances she described. On 30 June 2000, after a pre-investigation inquiry, the prosecutor’s office refused to initiate criminal proceedings against the police officers for lack of constituent elements of a criminal offence. On 20 March 2001, following her complaint, the Prosecutor General’s Office reversed that decision as unsubstantiated and ordered an additional inquiry. The applicant was not informed of the decision taken within that inquiry. In 2016 the Office of the Government Agent learned that the file on those inquiries had been destroyed after expiry of the statutory retention period.

Separately, the criminal case against the applicant proceeded slowly. On 9 April 2001 the investigation was discontinued because of the insignificance of the offence. On 2 August 2001 the Dubno Town Court quashed that decision as unfounded and ordered further investigation. On 14 August 2001 the investigation was completed and the case was referred to the Dubno Town Court. On 30 January 2004 and 13 March 2006 the Dubno Town Court issued judgments, which were quashed by the Rivne Regional Court of Appeal. On 30 January 2007 the Dubno Town Court convicted the applicant of failure to comply with a court decision and fined her, but released her from punishment because the statute of limitation had expired. On 17 April 2007 the Rivne Regional Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and upheld the judgment. On 13 November 2007 the Supreme Court refused to examine her cassation appeal because she had not complied with procedural rules.

On 29 May 2003 the applicant lodged a civil claim seeking damages for violation of the inviolability of her home and her unlawful arrest and ill-treatment on 29 May 2000. On 9 July 2007 the Dubno Town Court found that she had been ill-treated and unlawfully taken from her home to the investigator’s office. It found that the authorities had acted unlawfully and violated her rights to inviolability of home, liberty, and respect for human dignity. It awarded her UAH 500 (approximately EUR 73) in non-pecuniary damage. On 26 May 2008 the Lviv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that judgment. The applicant appealed on points of law, contesting the amount. On 8 May 2009 the Higher Administrative Court found the appeal improperly prepared and set a time-limit to rectify shortcomings. On 13 July 2009 it returned the appeal without examining the merits because she had failed to comply with procedural requirements.

The Court gave notice of the complaints under Article 3, Article 5 § 1, and Article 8 concerning the events of 29 May 2000, and under Article 6 § 1 concerning the length of the criminal proceedings. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.
001-187195:
**CASE OF ILIĆ v. SERBIA** (Application no. 26739/16), a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 23 October 2018, concerned a Serbian national, Mr Njegoš Ilić, born in 1960 and living in Kragujevac. The only complaint communicated to the Serbian Government on 5 October 2017 was the length of civil proceedings; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The key facts concern civil proceedings instituted by the applicant on 14 December 2006 against the Kragujevac Clinical Centre, seeking damages. During the first-instance proceedings, eleven hearings were held, while five scheduled hearings were not held. On 20 May 2011, the Kragujevac Court of First Instance rejected the applicant’s claim as unfounded. On 26 December 2011, the Kragujevac Appellate Court quashed that decision and remitted the case for reconsideration.

In the resumed proceedings, the applicant twice sought recusal of the acting judge, but both motions were rejected. On 4 October 2012, after three held hearings, two hearings that were not held, expert examination, and an increase in the applicant’s claim, the case was transferred to the Kragujevac High Court. On 20 March 2013, following two further recusal requests—one of which was granted—the High Court rejected the damages claim as unfounded. The applicant appealed. On 21 August 2014, the Appellate Court rejected his appeal and upheld the High Court’s decision. The applicant then filed an appeal on points of law, which the Supreme Court of Cassation rejected only on 21 December 2016.

In parallel, on 7 February 2013, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court complaining about the length of the still-pending civil proceedings. He sought €3,000 in non-pecuniary damages and publication of the Constitutional Court’s decision. The Constitutional Court transferred the case file to the Appellate Court, which was competent under Article 8a of the Law on the Organization of the Courts to deal with length complaints in pending cases. However, on 23 September 2014, the Appellate Court held that it no longer had jurisdiction because the civil proceedings had ended. The file was returned to the Constitutional Court. On 6 November 2014, the Constitutional Court sent it back to the Appellate Court, which on 28 November 2014 again found it lacked jurisdiction and forwarded the file to the Supreme Court of Cassation. The applicant appealed.

On 22 January 2015, the Supreme Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s appeal and upheld the 28 November 2014 decision. It also partially accepted his complaint concerning the length of proceedings and awarded him €200 for non-pecuniary damage, rejecting the remainder of his claim. On 21 October 2015, the Constitutional Court rejected the applicant’s appeal regarding the length of proceedings. It found that although the impugned proceedings had lasted seven years and eight months, they were very complex, the applicant had largely contributed to their length, and the competent courts had acted efficiently.

The alleged violation therefore concerned the length of civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The central facts are the approximately decade-long civil litigation, repeated remittals, recusal motions, transfers, delayed appellate/final review, and the applicant’s domestic length complaint, which resulted only in a €200 award. The ECtHR’s examination was limited to whether that duration and the domestic response complied with the reasonable-time requirement.
001-186424:
Case No. 41749/12, *Martinović v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, concerned an application lodged on 12 June 2012 by Božana Martinović, a Bosnian national born in 1955 and living in Assemini, Italy. She complained about the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in her favour, raising issues under the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time and the protection of property. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The first set of proceedings began with a decision of 4 December 2006 by the Cantonal Prosecutor of the Hercegovina-Neretva Canton granting the applicant reimbursement of witness costs of BAM 519. Enforcement then stalled. On 29 February 2008 the Mostar Municipal Court rejected enforcement as unenforceable; the Cantonal Court quashed that decision on 18 September 2008. A writ of execution followed on 19 November 2008, but an objection was upheld on 19 June 2009. On 1 April 2010 the Cantonal Court again quashed and remitted the case. On 18 February 2011 the Municipal Court partly accepted the objection, especially concerning interest from 4 January 2007 and interest on enforcement costs; the Cantonal Court upheld this on 2 December 2011. The Supreme Court dismissed revision on 19 September 2013. On 23 December 2013 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found a violation of the applicant’s right to trial within a reasonable time because the 18 February 2011 decision had not been enforced. It ordered the Canton to take enforcement measures but awarded no non-pecuniary damages. On 21 October 2014 the Constitutional Court confirmed that the decision remained unenforced. It was finally enforced on 18 December 2014, when the applicant was paid in cash.

The second set concerned a Municipal Court judgment of 3 April 2009, final on 16 December 2009, ordering a certain P.M. to pay the applicant BAM 1,959 in civil proceedings costs. The applicant requested enforcement on 31 October 2010. She sought acceleration on 14 September 2011, 4 November 2011 and 5 October 2012. Only on 5 December 2012 did the Municipal Court issue a writ of execution. After an objection was dismissed on 13 June 2013, P.M. appealed. On 17 September 2013 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the reasonable-time right due to the duration of the enforcement proceedings before the Municipal Court. It ordered the Cantonal Court to rule urgently on P.M.’s appeal but again awarded no non-pecuniary damages. The Cantonal Court dismissed the appeal on 16 October 2013. On 11 June 2015 the Municipal Court issued another writ of execution, and on 4 August 2016 the judgment was enforced by payment into the applicant’s bank account in Bosnia and Herzegovina; she apparently still lived in Italy.

These facts were relevant to the alleged violations because both final decisions in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced for years. Domestic courts repeatedly delayed or remitted enforcement, and although the Constitutional Court recognised unreasonable delay, it did not compensate the applicant. The case therefore focused on the length and effectiveness of enforcement proceedings and the lack of adequate redress.
001-184496:
The case of **Çeki v. Turkey** (Application no. 50070/10) was a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered on 10 July 2018. The applicant, Mesut Çeki, a Turkish national born in 1977, was detained at Kırıkkale F-type prison when he lodged the application on 25 June 2010. He was represented by lawyer C. Tombul, and the application was communicated to the Turkish Government on 4 September 2012.

The facts concerned the applicant’s arrest and prolonged detention in criminal proceedings for membership of a terrorist organisation. On 1 October 2004, he was taken into police custody on suspicion of being a member of a terrorist organisation. On 5 October 2004, he was brought before a judge at the Ankara Assize Court, who ordered his detention on remand. The judge relied on the nature of the offence, the state of the evidence, and the severity of the potential penalty. On 15 March 2005, the Ankara public prosecutor indicted him before the Ankara Assize Court for membership of a terrorist organisation.

On 31 January 2008, the Ankara Assize Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment. It also ordered that his detention continue. On 6 May 2009, the Court of Cassation quashed that judgment and remitted the case to the Ankara Assize Court for further examination. On 10 November 2009, the 11th Chamber of the Ankara Assize Court held a further hearing; both the applicant and his lawyer were present. At the end of that hearing, the court again ordered the continuation of the applicant’s detention.

On 10 December 2009, the applicant’s lawyer filed an objection against the 10 November 2009 detention decision. On 21 December 2009, the 12th Chamber of the Ankara Assize Court dismissed the objection without holding a hearing. In doing so, it relied on the written opinion of the public prosecutor, which had not been communicated to the applicant or his representative. This non-communication and absence of a hearing formed a central element of the alleged Convention violations, particularly regarding the judicial review of detention under Article 5 §4. The applicant complained that the procedure for challenging his continued remand was not adversarial and did not allow him or his lawyer to respond to the prosecutor’s submissions.

Subsequently, on 28 August 2012, the Ankara Assize Court once more convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment. On 8 July 2013, the Court of Cassation upheld that judgment. The relevant domestic law was described by reference to *Altınok v. Turkey*, *Demir v. Turkey* (dec.), and *A.Ş. v. Turkey*.

In essence, the case concerned the lawfulness and procedural fairness of the applicant’s detention on remand, especially the refusal of his objection to continued detention without a hearing and without disclosure of the public prosecutor’s written opinion. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: the initial remand in 2004; the lengthy criminal proceedings and continued detention; the 2009 quashing of the first conviction; the 10 November 2009 continuation order; and the 21 December 2009 dismissal of the applicant’s objection on the basis of an uncommunicated prosecutor’s opinion. These facts raised issues under the Convention, principally the right to have the lawfulness of detention reviewed by a court in an adversarial procedure.
001-180843:
The case of *Galea and Others v. Malta* (Application no. 68980/13) concerned six Maltese nationals who alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants held the *utile dominium* of a portion of land in Zabbar, Malta, by way of sub-emphyteusis expiring in 2047; the State held the *directum dominium*. Their ancestors had acquired the property through inheritance, and it included a shop rented to third parties as a snack bar.

In 1965, a Governor’s declaration under the Land Acquisition (Public Purposes) Ordinance declared 80 sq. m. of the property, including the approximately 50 sq. m. shop, as needed for a public purpose. The Government took possession, demolished the shop, and planned to build a civic centre and service roads. In 1972, however, the plan changed: the road was repositioned, and a new, larger shop was built at Government expense mostly on the applicants’ land. That shop was leased to the same third party for use as a snack bar. The part of the land taken but not used was returned to the applicants only in 1988. Extra-judicial requests for return of the property used as the snack bar failed. In 2010, the Commissioner of Land extended the third party’s lease until 2020 at a rent of about EUR 2,100 per year. Also in 2010, following Act I of 2006, a President’s declaration offered EUR 13,000 for the 1965 taking, based on a 2005 architect’s valuation.

The applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings in 2010. They complained that their land had not been taken in the public interest and that they had been deprived of their possession without compensation and without access to a court to claim compensation. The first-instance Constitutional Court upheld their claims in 2012. It found that the taking was not in the public interest because the property had been leased to third parties for commercial purposes, and that the applicants had received no compensation for 45 years. It also found that the 2010 offer was inadequate, based on an old valuation and far below the property’s value, and that the applicants had lacked procedural safeguards or access to court. It annulled the declarations, ordered return of the property, and awarded EUR 40,000 in compensation.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court in 2013 partly reversed. It held that the original 1965 taking had been in the public interest and that the later commercial use of the snack bar did not remove that public-interest character. Nevertheless, it found a violation of the applicants’ property rights because they had been deprived of their property for many years without compensation: the unused portion was returned only after 23 years, and the used portion remained uncompensated. The Constitutional Court awarded EUR 10,000 in non-pecuniary damages, stated that any pecuniary claim could be pursued under Article 12(3) of the Ordinance with 5% interest, and annulled the return order.

The applicants refused to collect the award, and in January 2014 the Commissioner deposited it in court. In September 2015, the Government asked the applicants to submit evidence of title. Before the European Court, the applicants alleged that they had been deprived of their possessions without compensation and had no possibility of accessing a court to raise their compensation claims.
001-182213:
In *Leonov v. Russia*, the applicant, Sergey Aleksandrovich Leonov, a Russian national living in Moscow, complained about domestic court decisions concerning his son, A., born in August 2007. The child initially lived with both parents at Leonov’s flat, where he was registered, received paediatric care, and attended nursery school. In November 2009, the mother, Ch., left Leonov, moved to her parents’ home, and took A. with her. A. remained with his mother thereafter.

In March 2010, Leonov applied for a residence order so that A. would live with him. Ch. counterclaimed for residence with her and requested an interim measure pending the proceedings. She alleged that Leonov might abduct A. to Belarus and had already tried to take him from nursery school. On 26 April 2010, the Timiryazevskiy District Court granted the interim measure, forbidding Leonov from contacting A. or collecting him from nursery without Ch.’s prior permission. The court reasoned that the child was then living with his mother and that the measure was proportionate to ensure execution of the future judgment. Leonov learned of the order on 30 April 2010, when nursery staff refused to let him see his son.

Childcare authorities inspected both parents’ flats and found both suitable. In June 2010, one childcare authority said that, because of his young age, A. should live with his mother until five or six. The court ordered a psychological expert examination. In November 2010, the experts found that A. was equally attached to both parents, that both were equally capable of raising him, that contact with both was beneficial, and that the serious parental conflict could harm the child psychologically. In December 2010, another childcare authority nonetheless recommended that A. live with his mother, citing his age, established routine, and nursery attendance.

The proceedings were also affected by conflict between the parents. In June 2010, Ch. physically attacked Leonov when he hugged A. at a public beach. She was later convicted of assault and battery. Leonov also objected to the trial judge, alleging she had said that the Timiryazevskiy District Court always made residence orders in favour of mothers. In February 2011, the Moscow City Court quashed the interim measure as unconnected to the subject matter, disproportionate, and prejudicial; a fresh request was rejected in April 2011.

On 12 April 2011, the District Court granted residence to Ch. and dismissed Leonov’s claim. It found a serious parental conflict, but accepted that both parents were capable and that the child was equally attached to each. It noted Ch.’s criminal conviction was not yet final and held the charges were not decisive. It emphasised that A. was under four, had an established life with his mother and attended nursery there, and that changing residence would harm him. Leonov’s better housing and finances were not decisive, and the childcare authorities favoured the mother. The court called Leonov’s request “premature,” suggesting he could reapply when A. was older. The Moscow City Court upheld that judgment in June 2011. Later, in December 2011, a court set a contact schedule for Leonov and the paternal family after Ch. prevented contact.

Leonov complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the refusal to make a residence order in his favour and the interim measure restricting contact during the proceedings violated his right to respect for family life, the principle of equality of spouses, and amounted to sex discrimination. The key facts concern the alleged reliance on a maternal presumption, the interim contact ban, the expert finding of equal parental attachment and capacity, and the domestic courts’ preference for the mother based on the child’s young age and established residence.
001-186117:
