In *Annen v. Germany (No. 2)*, the applicant, Klaus Günter Annen, a German national born in 1951 and living in Weinheim, was an anti-abortion campaigner who operated the website *babycaust.de*. The site compared abortion with the Holocaust. Its starting page showed graves and the text “then: Holocaust”; clicking led to “Abortion – the new Holocaust?” A link titled “Life or death?” led to “Prayer requests for Germany,” from which users could reach a location-based alphabetical list of doctors who performed abortions, including their names and practice addresses, and requests to pray for them. The site stated: “Perverted doctors murder unborn children at the request of the mothers.” It also urged prayers for doctors “who personally undertake the AGGRAVATED MURDER of abortion killing,” and said counselling centres were enabling “the unpunished aggravated murder of children in their mother’s womb.” These statements formed the basis of the later injunction.

Dr Q., one of the listed doctors, first sought a civil injunction to remove his name and address. On 23 May 2006, the Mannheim Regional Court refused, holding that it was a fact Dr Q. performed abortions and that the rest was covered by freedom of expression; it found no comparable “pillory effect.” Dr Q. appealed and modified his request, seeking an order that Annen desist from labelling abortions, such as those performed by Dr Q., “aggravated murder.” On 28 February 2007, the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal granted the injunction. It found the website could be understood as a personalised accusation that Dr Q. had committed the criminal offence of aggravated murder. Although “aggravated murder” could be a moral judgment, the overall presentation did not exclude a criminal-law reading. The applicant had emphasised the term, compared abortion to the Holocaust, and had not mentioned section 218a of the Criminal Code, which exempted abortions such as Dr Q.’s from criminal liability. The Federal Court of Justice refused legal aid for an appeal, and on 2 July 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit Annen’s constitutional complaint without reasons.

On 15 January 2010, Annen applied to the European Court of Human Rights. He alleged that the domestic order to desist from labelling abortions “aggravated murder” on his webpage violated his freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. On 3 January 2017, the Court communicated the Article 10 complaint to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3.

The relevant German law included Article 5 of the Basic Law, which protects expression but limits it by general laws and personal honour; Criminal Code provisions on aggravated murder (Art. 211), abortion (Art. 218), and the exception to liability (Art. 218a); and Civil Code provisions (Arts. 823 and 1004) allowing injunctions to prevent violations of personality rights. The Federal Constitutional Court’s 1993 judgment regarded abortions performed within twelve weeks after counselling as unlawful but not punishable. The domestic courts therefore treated the applicant’s statements as potentially actionable accusations of criminal conduct against a named doctor, rather than merely abstract moral criticism. The key alleged violation was that the civil injunction disproportionately restricted Annen’s Article 10 right to express his anti-abortion views.
001-180841:
The case originated in an application against Montenegro lodged on 24 May 2011 by ten nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The applicants were represented by Mr I. Darmanović, a lawyer practising in Podgorica. The Montenegrin Government were represented by their Agent, Ms V. Pavličić. The applicants’ complaints concerned the non-enforcement of a final court settlement concluded in their favour.

On 28 February 1996, the applicants and the debtor, JSP “Tara” Cetinje, reached a court-approved settlement before the Cetinje Municipal Court. Under the settlement, the debtor undertook to pay the applicants specified amounts in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The settlement became final on the same date. The debtor ultimately paid only part of the amounts determined in the settlement.

On 26 May 1997, the Podgorica Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. On 19 August 1997, the applicants submitted their respective claims based on the settlement. In the course of the insolvency proceedings, the Podgorica Commercial Court acknowledged the applicants’ claims.

On 23 December 2009, the Podgorica Commercial Court terminated the insolvency proceedings against the debtor, but continued the proceedings against the debtor’s estate. That decision was upheld by the Appellate Court on 9 April 2010. The proceedings are still pending.

On 14 October 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ constitutional appeal on procedural grounds.

The court settlement in question remains partly unenforced to the present day.

As to the debtor’s legal status, it appears from the case file that, at the time the court settlement was concluded and became final, the debtor was a company predominantly comprised of State-controlled capital. The Government neither contested this nor provided any evidence to the contrary.
001-180505:
In *Edina Tóth v. Hungary* (Application no. 51323/14), the European Court of Human Rights considered a Hungarian mother’s complaint that the Hungarian State failed to help her reunite with her abducted son, thereby disrupting her family life. She relied on Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

The applicant married H.B., a Hungarian citizen, in the United States in 2000. Their son was born in the US in 2003 and had dual citizenship. The family returned to Hungary in 2004. On 26 December 2004, after a quarrel, H.B. took the child and left for an unknown destination. He telephoned a few times over the next two weeks, but after January 2005 all contact ceased. The applicant has had no contact with her son since then.

The applicant filed for divorce. In November 2005, the Szentendre District Court issued an interim measure placing the child with the applicant; this became final in January 2006. In February 2007, the District Court pronounced the divorce, granted the applicant sole custody, terminated H.B.’s parental rights, ordered child maintenance and gave H.B. no visiting rights. The judgment became final in April 2007. H.B. did not participate in the proceedings and was represented by a guardian ad litem; the judgment appears to have been served on the guardian but not on H.B.

The applicant repeatedly sought State assistance. In November 2005 she lodged a criminal complaint alleging child abduction. Police carried out identity checks on H.B. in December 2005 and March 2006 in Sopron, where he declared an address. The applicant complained that the authorities failed to interrogate him despite these opportunities. A warrant was issued in May 2006, but the investigation was suspended later that month because H.B.’s residence had become unknown. In May 2007, police again checked H.B.; he gave an incomplete London address, claiming the child was with his grandmother, and was released. The investigation was resumed and then terminated in August 2007 for lack of offence, on the basis that unlawful change of a minor’s residence requires intent and H.B. was allegedly unaware of the custody judgment. A 2008 complaint about failure to pay child maintenance was terminated for the same reason. A 2008 complaint of endangering a minor was terminated in 2009 for lack of evidence. In 2013, after a school-book notice revealed the child was registered in Sopron, the applicant’s father lodged another complaint; the investigation was suspended in October 2013 because H.B.’s address again became unknown and a warrant was issued.

Enforcement efforts were also ineffective. In February 2006 the applicant requested enforcement of the interim custody measure. In March 2006 the bailiff visited H.B.’s registered address but found neither H.B. nor the child there; it appeared they might be in the US. No further measures were apparently taken. In 2012 the applicant was told that the bailiff was not responsible because H.B. and the child were abroad and diplomatic steps were required.

Internationally, the applicant contacted the Ministry of Justice in 2007. In 2009, international and European warrants were issued against H.B. in separate fraud proceedings. H.B. was later detained in Canada, expelled, escaped, and reportedly booked a flight to Vienna under a false name; Austrian cooperation produced no result. In 2012, Hungary made a Hague Convention request to the US, which was transferred to Canada; both were unsuccessful. In 2013 Canada was asked to establish the child’s residence but could not. On 8 May 2014 H.B. was apprehended in Budapest and the child was finally located. Because the applicant was then living abroad, the child was temporarily placed with her father in Csobánka.

The alleged violation thus concerns the State’s repeated failure to enforce custody and reunite the applicant with her son: delayed and suspended investigations, missed opportunities to interrogate or detain H.B., ineffective bailiff action, and unsuccessful international cooperation, leaving the applicant without contact from January 2005 until 2014.
001-181210:
In *Sinkova v. Ukraine* (no. 39496/11), the applicant, a Ukrainian national and member of the St Luke Brotherhood artistic group, complained under Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 5 and Article 10 of the Convention. The case arose from a December 2010 performance at Kyiv’s Eternal Glory Memorial and Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. On 16 December 2010, Sinkova and three others fried eggs in a frying pan over the Eternal Flame; two companions grilled sausages on skewers; another filmed. The participants made no speeches and displayed no posters. To reach the flame, Sinkova stepped over a wreath sculpture and on the inscription “Glory to the Unknown Soldier.” Police approached, said the behaviour was inappropriate, but did not interfere. Sinkova posted the video online with a statement protesting the pointless burning of natural gas at the memorial, estimating monthly taxpayer costs and suggesting Communist Party members keep eternal flames lit manually. The video used a Soviet song and titles such as “Recipe of the day” and “Eternal fried eggs on the eternal flame.”

After public complaints, criminal proceedings were opened. One participant, D., was questioned, admitted participating in a protest against gas waste, expressed regret, and identified Sinkova from passport-office photographs. Investigators questioned Sinkova’s grandmother and mother, who said she did not live at her registered address, was away in western Ukraine, and gave no contact details. On 18 February 2011, the case against Sinkova and two unidentified persons was severed, and she was declared wanted the same day. Her lawyer later claimed no summons had been sent before her arrest and that she learned of the charge only when arrested.

On 17 March 2011, the investigator sought her detention pending trial, citing the serious charge (three to five years’ imprisonment), her having absconded/wanted status, and risks of reoffending or obstructing truth. On 25 March, a court ordered her arrest to bring her before court. She was arrested on 29 March at another person’s flat. On 31 March, with counsel, she confessed and expressed remorse. On 1 April, the Pecherskyy District Court remanded her in custody, relying again on the serious charge, her wanted status, and risk of obstruction; it rejected character evidence and did not discuss personal guarantees from deputies. The Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld this on 11 April. She was indicted on 25 May. On 17 June, her release application was refused based on the charge’s seriousness, nature/circumstances, and wanted status; she was released on 30 June under an undertaking not to leave town.

On 4 October 2012, she was convicted of desecrating the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier by a group following prior conspiracy and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, suspended for two years. The court rejected her claim that the act was only a protest and noted she showed no remorse. On 18 December 2012, the appellate court upheld the conviction, saying desecration could be insulting or disrespectful regardless of motive, and that any Article 10 restriction was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim. Her cassation appeal was rejected on 11 April 2013. The key allegations were thus that her pre-trial detention violated Article 5 and that her prosecution and conviction for the performance violated her Article 10 freedom of expression.
001-187476:
In *Gestur Jónsson and Ragnar Halldór Hall v. Iceland* (Applications nos. 68273/14 and 68271/14), the applicants were Icelandic attorneys appointed as defence counsel for two defendants, Y and Z, in a criminal case involving fraud and market manipulation. During 2012–2013, repeated disputes arose over prosecution evidence, disclosure, deadlines, and trial scheduling. The applicants and other defence counsel sought postponements and access to evidence; the District Court and Supreme Court rejected several requests.

On 8 April 2013, the applicants wrote to the District Court judge stating that they could not, for reasons of conscience, continue as defence counsel. They alleged procedural violations, including late evidence, lack of access to important documents, telephone tapping, and unfair procedure. They asked to be relieved of their duties under the Attorneys’ Act. The judge refused. The applicants replied that they would not attend the trial set for 11 April 2013.

On 11 April, the clients attended with new defence counsel; the applicants were absent and not summoned. The judge relieved them of their duties, appointed replacement counsel, postponed the trial, and the prosecution requested contempt fines. A new trial was held in November 2013 before a different judge. On 12 December 2013, the clients were convicted, and in the same judgment the applicants were each fined ISK 1,000,000 under Section 223(1)(a) and (d) of the Criminal Procedures Act for offending the court and causing unnecessary delay by not attending the trial. The judgment was delivered in the applicants’ absence. They had not been notified that the court was considering fines and had no separate hearing before the District Court on that issue.

The applicants appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing violations of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 70 of the Icelandic Constitution. They claimed they were penalised without notice or an opportunity to defend themselves; that they had valid reasons to resign; that the fines were imposed after they were no longer defence counsel; that their conduct did not occur “during proceedings”; and that the fines were excessive, lacked a statutory maximum, and violated legality and *lex certa* principles. They also relied on Article 7 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 7.

Before the Supreme Court, there was an oral hearing. The applicants were represented by counsel but did not give statements or call witnesses. On 28 May 2014, the Supreme Court majority upheld the fines. It found the applicants’ conduct unlawful and contrary to their clients’ interests. Although the fines were substantial and thus amounted to criminal punishment, the majority held that the lack of a special District Court hearing was cured by the appeal, because the applicants could defend themselves before the Supreme Court. It cited *Weber v. Switzerland* and *T v. Austria*. The minority agreed the conduct was unlawful and the fines criminal, but would have annulled the fines: the District Court should have held an immediate hearing, notified them of the charges, and allowed them to object. Instead, fines were imposed months later without notice, and no legal provision permitted remittal.

The applicants therefore alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that the domestic judgments violated Articles 6 and 7 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 7, principally because a criminal fine was imposed on defence counsel without prior notice or an adequate opportunity to be heard. The Chamber judgment of 30 October 2018 was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 22 December 2020.
001-185031:
In *Bondarenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 27052/09 and 11 others), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 28 June 2018. The case originated in twelve applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government. The central alleged violation was that the applicants’ pre-trial detention had been excessively long. Some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The applicants were held in pre-trial detention in Ukraine during criminal proceedings. According to the appended table, Borys Bondarenko was detained from 23 October 2006 to 20 August 2010, a period of 3 years, 9 months and 29 days. Oleg Galimon was detained twice: from 14 February to 2 November 2007 (8 months and 20 days) and from 4 August 2009 to 25 October 2010 (1 year, 2 months and 22 days). Sergey Kukhtin was detained from 7 November 2010 to 6 December 2011 (1 year and 1 month). Gleb Zelenov was detained from 8 February 2008 to 9 August 2010 (2 years, 6 months and 2 days) and again from 15 February 2011 to 5 June 2012 (1 year, 3 months and 22 days).

Vadim Tokunov was detained from 22 September 2009 to 22 July 2014 (4 years, 10 months and 1 day). Oleg Volokin had three separate periods: 3 July 2008 to 27 July 2009 (1 year and 25 days), 4 November 2009 to 28 March 2012 (2 years, 4 months and 25 days), and 17 September 2012 to 15 November 2013 (1 year, 1 month and 30 days). Tamara Nekrasova was detained from 2 March 2012 to 23 September 2015 (3 years, 6 months and 22 days). Aleksandr Grebeshkov had four periods: 21 September 2009 to 16 December 2010 (1 year, 2 months and 26 days), 26 April 2011 to 13 March 2012 (10 months and 17 days), 10 July to 21 December 2012 (5 months and 12 days), and 11 March to 19 June 2014 (3 months and 9 days).

Gennadiy Chernov was detained from 26 August 2005 to 15 December 2008 (3 years, 3 months and 20 days) and again from 20 May 2010 to 10 June 2014 (4 years and 22 days). Oleksandr Kharkiv was detained from 9 August 2010 to 27 September 2012 (2 years, 1 month and 19 days) and again from 1 March 2013 to 26 June 2015 (2 years, 3 months and 26 days). Aleksandr Tverdokhleb was detained from 1 March 2011 to 25 June 2013 (2 years, 3 months and 25 days). Andriy Yolkin was detained from 24 July 2012 and remained in detention at the time of the application, a period exceeding 5 years and 9 months.

These facts underpinned the applicants’ complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial. The applicants alleged that the Ukrainian authorities had kept them in pre-trial detention for unjustifiably long periods without adequate justification. The case therefore required the Court to assess whether the length of the detention, whether continuous or cumulative across separate periods, exceeded the reasonable-time requirement and whether the domestic authorities had provided sufficient reasons for prolonging detention.
001-187931:
**Case Name:** *R.I. and Others v. Romania* (Application no. 57077/16)

The case concerned a Romanian mother, R.I., and her two children, M.I. and I.I. The mother had been in a stable relationship with R., but after the relationship ended in 2010, the children initially remained with her, while R. was to have unrestricted access and participate in their upbringing. In November 2013, however, R. took the children from the mother’s home without her consent. From then until May 2014, the mother saw them only occasionally and always in the father’s presence; after 6 June 2014, all contact stopped.

The mother began custody proceedings on 25 November 2013 and sought an interim injunction. On 5 May 2014, the Bucharest County Court issued a final interim decision ordering that the children reside with their mother and that the father pay monthly child support. The mother immediately sought enforcement. On 6 June 2014, she went to the children’s school to collect them, but the father appeared, became abusive, and the police had to intervene; she could not take the children home. Subsequent bailiff meetings failed: on 17 July 2014 the father and children did not attend, and on 14 August 2014 the children attended but refused absolutely to return to their mother, alleging that she had shouted at and occasionally beaten them. Enforcement therefore could not proceed.

The child protection authority became involved. Reports in early 2014 found the children well cared for at the father’s home and no signs of abuse, but noted anxiety and distress caused by parental conflict. A psychologist later recommended counselling. A social assistant in February 2015 reported that the children refused to see their mother because of alleged beatings and meanness. A more detailed expert psychological report of 17 November 2015 found no indication of physical abuse by the mother, but found indicators of psychological abuse in the form of parental alienation exercised by the father. It described the father as corresponding to the profile of an “alienator parent” and recommended counselling and ending the children’s involvement in the parental conflict.

Meanwhile, on 24 September 2014, the Bucharest District Court granted the mother physical custody and ordered child support. The father initially appealed but later withdrew. Enforcement was extended to the return of the children. The father moved with the children to Năvodari, contested enforcement, and in September 2017 obtained a stay pending appeal. His appeal was dismissed in May 2018. On 16 July 2018, at a bailiff meeting, the children again refused absolutely to move in with their mother.

In separate custody proceedings, on 20 March 2017 the Bucharest District Court awarded physical custody to the father, relying on the children’s long stay with him, their refusal to move, and their attachment to him. On 24 April 2018, the Bucharest County Court reversed that decision. It found that the mother was not at fault for the non-enforcement of the 5 May 2014 decision, that the Romanian State had a positive obligation to take urgent measures to return the children to her, and that the father’s alienation of the children had been allowed to continue. It warned that family ties risked becoming permanent broken and that future visiting arrangements would be illusory.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore centre on the Romanian authorities’ prolonged failure to enforce final court decisions granting the mother custody or residence and to prevent the father’s alleged parental alienation. Despite repeated requests to bailiffs, police, and child protection authorities, and despite expert findings of alienation, the children remained with the father for years. The application alleged that this failure breached the applicants’ right to respect for family life, and possibly their right of access to court, under the Convention.
001-183395:
**Case summary: O’Sullivan McCarthy Mussel Development Ltd v. Ireland (ECtHR, App. No. 44460/16)**

The applicant, O’Sullivan McCarthy Mussel Development Ltd, is an Irish company that has cultivated mussels in Castlemaine Harbour, County Kerry, since the late 1970s. Its business involves annually fishing immature “mussel seed” in the harbour and re-laying it for cultivation. The activity requires an aquaculture licence, a sea-fishing boat licence, entry of the boat in the Register of Fishing Boats, and an annual mussel-seed fishing authorisation from the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine. Castlemaine Harbour was designated a Special Protection Area (SPA) in 1994 under the Birds Directive and a Special Area of Conservation (SAC) in 2000 under the Habitats Directive, making it part of the Natura 2000 network. In 1993, a public notice had stated that designation was not envisaged to change traditional usage.

Following EU infringement proceedings, the Court of Justice of the European Union held in December 2007 in *Commission v. Ireland* that Ireland had failed to ensure aquaculture programmes likely to affect SPAs were subject to appropriate prior environmental assessment under the Habitats Directive. To comply, the Minister considered commercial activity could not continue until assessments were completed. On 6 June 2008, a statutory instrument prohibited mussel-seed fishing in 24 locations, including Castlemaine Harbour, from 9 June to 1 July 2008. The applicant, which had just purchased a new boat for €1 million, was informed that day and protested. The Department replied that baseline data had to be gathered for the required assessment, that Castlemaine was prioritised, and that interim resumption would be sought from the European Commission.

In August 2008, the applicant received an authorisation beginning 23 August, but the prohibition remained in force. On 3 October 2008, after the Commission accepted an interim assessment, the Minister removed Castlemaine Harbour from the prohibition. Fishing resumed on 5 October 2008. By then, natural predators had decimated the mussel seed. Because mussels need two years to mature, the financial consequences were felt in 2010, when the applicant had no mussels for sale. It estimated lost profits of €289,599. It claimed no viable alternative seed source existed and that, had it known of the restriction, it would not have bought the new boat.

In 2009, the harbour was opened and the applicant obtained the usual seed. In August 2009, a new fisheries Natura permit was required for fishing in SACs/SPAs. In 2010, the applicant could not fish during the first authorised period because it lacked that permit; when it later fished, seed had again been depleted by predators. It estimated a further loss of €119,941. The Government said it had begun compliance work immediately after the CJEU judgment, coordinated with BIM, the Marine Institute and NPWS, negotiated with the Commission, and completed the Castlemaine appropriate assessment in April 2011, which found no anticipated environmental disturbance from mussel fishing.

In February 2009, the applicant and another company sued the State in the High Court for breach of legitimate expectation, operational negligence and breach of the constitutional right to earn a livelihood. In May 2013, the High Court found for the applicant, awarding €275,000 for 2008 and 2010 losses. The State appealed. In February 2016, the Supreme Court overturned the findings: there was no legitimate expectation, and the majority rejected operational negligence and any duty of care. A minority would have upheld negligence for 2008 only.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 8 due to economic loss attributed to the authorities without compensation, violation of Article 13 concerning an effective remedy, and, under Article 6, excessive duration of domestic proceedings.
001-187474:
**S.S. v. Slovenia** concerns a Slovenian mother, S.S., diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, whose parental rights over her fourth child, E., were withdrawn, leading to E.’s adoption by her foster parents. S.S. alleged violations of Articles 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention, complaining that the withdrawal of her parental rights, E.’s adoption, the denial of contact, and the State’s treatment of her mental illness infringed her rights and lacked effective remedies.

S.S. had four children. Her first child was placed in foster care in Slovenia in 2005; her second was placed in foster care in France and later adopted; her third lived with his father in France from December 2010. E. was born on 31 December 2010. Social services quickly noted concerns about S.S.’s ability to care for E., her refusal of psychiatric examination and medication, and her unstable lifestyle. In late January 2011, S.S. travelled to France and left E. with her mother, who was unwilling to care for the child. On 1 February 2011, the Cerknica Social Work Centre removed E., placed her in a crisis centre, and then with foster parents. A final removal and care order followed in March 2011. E. remained with the foster parents.

In March 2011, the Centre applied to divest both parents of parental rights. S.S. received legal aid and was represented. A first-instance decision in November 2012 withdrew her rights, but the Higher Court quashed it in April 2013, requiring clarification whether her conduct resulted from mental illness or voluntary action. On remittal, psychiatrists found S.S. suffered from schizophrenia that was treatable but incurable, with poor prognosis, impaired insight, reduced empathy, and permanent inability to care for E. Another expert found no emotional bond between S.S. and E. and considered contact forced and burdensome for the child. In April 2014, the Ljubljana District Court again withdrew her parental rights under section 116 of the Family Act, prioritising E.’s best interests and permanent stability. The Higher Court dismissed her appeal in October 2014, and the Constitutional Court dismissed her complaint in December 2015 by five votes to three. The majority held that the withdrawal was not based on mental illness as such but on her permanent incapacity to care for E. and the absence of any prospect of reunification. Dissenting judges criticised the severity of the interference, E.’s right to know her parents, and the authorities’ failure to sufficiently support bonding.

Contact between S.S. and E. occurred sporadically from 2011 to 2014, usually supervised. Reports described S.S. as largely passive and distant; E did not initiate contact. The Centre advised S.S. to seek court regulation of contact if dissatisfied. After the Constitutional Court decision, contact stopped. In May 2016, the foster parents adopted E.; S.S. was not a party to the adoption proceedings. When S.S. then sought contact, the Koper District Court dismissed her application in August 2016, relying on an expert opinion that contact would be harmful or traumatic for E. and that no family-type attachment existed. The Higher Court dismissed her appeal in April 2017, and the Supreme Court rejected leave to appeal in August 2017. Her request for legal aid for a constitutional complaint was refused as having no prospects, and she did not lodge a constitutional complaint. Before the European Court, she alleged violations of Articles 6, 8, 13 and 14, focusing on the withdrawal of parental rights, adoption, denial of contact, discrimination linked to mental illness, and lack of effective remedies.
001-181847:
Boldijar and Others v. Romania (Application no. 46831/14 and 15 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 29 March 2018. It originated in 16 applications lodged against Romania under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates between 2014 and 2016. The applications were communicated to the Romanian Government. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of their detention.

The applicants were detained in a range of Romanian police arrest facilities, prisons and a prison hospital. Their detention periods varied from several weeks to several years; some were still pending when the applications were lodged. Facilities included Miercurea-Ciuc, Codlea, Bistrița, Ialomița County Police Arrest, Poarta Albă Prison Hospital, Slobozia, Rahova, Cluj County Police Arrest, Gherla, Colibași, Bucharest General Police Arrest, Craiova, Drobeta Turnu Severin, Târgu-Jiu, Gorj County Police Arrest, Teleorman County Police Arrest, Giurgiu, Jilava, Ploiești and Arad prisons.

The core alleged violation concerned Article 3 ECHR, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The applicants alleged that the material conditions of detention were so poor that they reached the threshold of severity. The appended table shows that overcrowding was a central issue. Many applicants had extremely limited personal space, often ranging from 0.87 to 2.14 sq m, 1.08 to 1.48 sq m, 1.13 to 1.98 sq m, 1.21 to 1.7 sq m, 1.44 to 1.72 sq m, 1.47 to 2.7 sq m, 1.57 to 2.52 sq m, or around 1.88–1.97 sq m. In some facilities the space was greater, for example 3.39–9.2 sq m, but applicants still alleged other serious deficiencies.

The recurring grievances included overcrowding; insufficient sleeping places; lack or inadequacy of hygienic facilities; no or restricted access to showers or warm water; lack of privacy for toilets; poor-quality bedding and bed linen; lack or inadequate furniture; mouldy or dirty cells; infestation with insects or rodents; lack of fresh air; insufficient natural or electric light; inadequate temperature; passive smoking; poor-quality food and potable water; lack or insufficiency of outdoor physical exercise; and lack or restricted access to leisure or educational activities. Some complained of cells being constantly lit or lacking toilets.

Specific examples illustrate the allegations: Remus Boldijar complained of 0.87–2.04 sq m and overcrowding at Miercurea-Ciuc and Codlea; Romeo Gabriel Ardelean and Robert Andreas Bedners alleged similar overcrowding at Miercurea-Ciuc; Vasile Meterez alleged multiple facilities with spaces as low as 1.97–2.2 sq m; Grigore-Alin Gornoavă alleged 1.08–1.48 sq m at Craiova; Costel Păun alleged 1.44–1.72 sq m at Jilava for nearly three years; Claudiu-Florian Isac alleged overcrowding and rodent infestation at Jilava and Ploiești; Florin Șumăndan alleged poor food and infestation at Arad.

The case therefore concerns whether the cumulative effect of overcrowding and poor material conditions amounted to degrading treatment contrary to Article 3. Severity would be assessed by duration, space, sanitation, ventilation, food, exercise and cumulative conditions.
001-183817:
**Summary of *Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria* (Application no. 5734/14)**

The case of *Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria* originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Austria with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 January 2014. The applicant, Aviso Zeta AG, was a bank based in Vienna that purchased and held shares, predominantly in the "IF" company, for third parties. The applicant company and IF were closely related, sharing management personnel and staff. A separate investment advisory firm, the "A. company," acted as a key distribution partner for the applicant.

Following a significant decline in the value of the IF shares beginning in the second half of 2007, numerous legal proceedings were initiated against Aviso Zeta AG. The case at issue concerned a civil action brought in 2009 by two clients, F.M. and H.H., who sought to annul their purchase of IF shares. The Vienna Commercial Court ruled in favour of the clients in April 2012, holding the applicant company liable for inadequate advice provided by the A. company, citing the close professional ties between the two entities.

While the Vienna Court of Appeal overturned this decision in September 2012, the Supreme Court, in a judgment delivered on 17 June 2013 by a five-judge panel, restored the Commercial Court's ruling. The Supreme Court found the applicant company liable, reasoning that its significant interest in selling IF shares meant it was responsible for the inadequate information provided to the clients by the A. company.

The central violation alleged in this case stems from the involvement of Judge N. on the Supreme Court panel that delivered the 17 June 2013 judgment. The applicant company later discovered that Judge N. had a personal conflict of interest. Specifically, Judge N. had personally purchased IF shares whose value had subsequently dropped.

Crucially, Judge N. had previously declared himself biased in other comparable cases involving IF shares and had been permitted by the Supreme Court to withdraw from them. In those prior cases, Judge N. had even considered filing a personal lawsuit for his own financial losses, with the applicant company being a potential defendant. The applicant only learned of Judge N.'s participation in its case upon receiving the Supreme Court's judgment, making a prior challenge impossible.

The applicant company subsequently filed an action for nullity, which was heard by a different section of the Supreme Court. The Court acknowledged Judge N.'s history but rejected the action. It ruled that under Austrian law, judicial bias was not a ground for nullifying a final decision, unlike the legal exclusion of a judge. The Supreme Court found that Judge N.'s situation was not “particularly grave” enough to warrant an exception.

The applicant company alleged that this situation constituted a breach of the principle of impartiality under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. It argued that the participation of a judge with a known personal financial interest in the case, who had previously withdrawn from similar matters, objectively compromised the impartiality of the proceedings before the Supreme Court. The domestic courts, by refusing to nullify the judgment, failed to remedy this fundamental procedural defect.
001-184651:
In *Sandu and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (ECtHR, Second Section, 17 July 2018, final 3 December 2018), eight applications were lodged by 1,646 Moldovan natural persons and three companies. The applicants lived in the villages of Doroțcaia, Pîrîta, Molovata Nouă, Pohrebea and Cocieri, on the left bank of the Dniester in the Dubăsari region, an area under Moldovan control. Their farmland was located near these villages, but across a road linking the northern and southern parts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic” (“MRT”). That road, cutting through Moldovan-controlled zones, was controlled by the “MRT” authorities. The applicants alleged that they were denied access to their land, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, and that they had no effective remedies.

The applicants had obtained title to their plots from Moldova through the “Pamântul” land privatisation programme. Some land was later transferred by gift or inheritance. The three applicant companies rented land from owners during the relevant period. Farming was the applicants’ main source of income. To reach their land, they had to cross the “MRT”-controlled road.

Between 1992 and 1998, the applicants used or rented the land without interference. In 1998, the “MRT” authorities set up checkpoints to monitor agricultural products crossing the road, and the applicants had to pay various taxes and fees to the “MRT”. In August 2004, the “MRT” authorities declared that the land owned or rented by the applicants belonged to the “MRT”. The applicants were told they could continue working it only if they paid rent to the local “MRT” authorities. They refused, because they were already lawful owners or renters under Moldovan law. As a result, all access to the land was blocked, the harvest was lost, and some agricultural machines were seized. No work was done for the following two years, making it difficult to restore the land’s productivity.

The applicants complained repeatedly to the “MRT” authorities, requesting a right of passage, but were refused on the basis that the land was “MRT” property. They also complained to the Moldovan authorities, who replied that they had no means to compel the “MRT” to allow free passage. The applicants asked the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office to open a criminal investigation. Complaints to the Russian embassy and the OSCE were unsuccessful, and protests took place in 2005 asking Russia to intervene.

Specific company applicants documented losses. Agro-Tiras S.R.L. rented 450 hectares across the road; “MRT” customs seized a tractor and wheat for alleged failure to declare importation. Posedo-Agro S.R.L. rented land in Cocieri; “MRT” customs seized barley and apples, imposed fines and temporarily seized trucks and tractors. It complained to the Moldovan Government, OSCE and Dubăsari prosecutor. Agro-S.A.V.V.A. S.R.L. also showed it rented land and could not cultivate it.

The Moldovan Government cited laws compensating villagers for losses, including price differences, pensions, tax breaks, credits, diesel fuel, and direct compensation of almost 39 million Moldovan lei (about EUR 2.3 million) in 2004–2007. In 2006, Moldova negotiated a temporary “MRT” registration mechanism allowing landowners to cultivate the land and be exempt from “MRT” payments; it was renewed annually.

The applications were lodged in 2004–2006 and communicated to the Governments in 2013. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were the “MRT” control over access, the 2004 property declaration and rent demand, the resulting blocked access, lost harvests and seizures, and the alleged absence of effective remedies.
001-186116:
**Summary of Jishkariani v. Georgia**

The case of *Jishkariani v. Georgia* (Application no. 18925/09) concerns a complaint lodged by Ms. Mariam Jishkariani, a Georgian psychiatrist and director of the NGO "Empathy," which provided rehabilitation services to torture victims. The applicant alleged that the domestic courts failed to protect her right to reputation under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights against defamatory statements made by the then Minister of Justice.

The events stem from a professional agreement between the applicant's NGO and the Ministry of Justice in October 2003 to create a psychosocial rehabilitation office in Tbilisi Prison No. 1. The applicant was also a member of the Public Monitoring Commission and the Inmates' Mental Health Research and Monitoring Commission. In September 2005, an inmate with mental health issues, transferred to the prison hospital based on the applicant's medical opinion, physically assaulted hospital staff. This incident, alongside a separate inmate death, fueled media allegations of corruption and mismanagement in the penal system's medical department.

On 16 September 2005, the Minister of Justice, Mr. K.K., spoke live on Rustavi 2 television, explicitly naming the applicant. He accused her of "grossly exceeding her powers," writing illegal medical conclusions, and being involved in corrupt "business" dealings. He claimed her "scribbles" led to the unjustified transfer of inmates and that she would be investigated alongside the Medical Department director. On 20 September 2005, the newspaper *Rezonansi* published an interview where the Minister further alleged the applicant was the "most important figure" in corruption, had "made a nest" in the monitoring council for personal gain, and was an "accomplice" in taking money from inmates.

The applicant filed a civil defamation suit against the Minister. She argued her conclusions were based on verifiable medical documents and that the corruption allegations were false, noting she was never formally accused. However, the domestic courts ruled against her. The Tbilisi City Court applied the Freedom of Expression and Speech Act, classifying the applicant as a "public figure," which required her to prove three cumulative conditions for defamation: the statement's falsity, resulting damage, and the speaker's knowledge of falsity or gross negligence.

While the court found the Minister's accusations "may have contained erroneous facts," it held the applicant failed to prove the other two conditions. It reasoned she did not demonstrate specific harm and that the Minister had taken "measures to verify" information by ordering an internal investigation three days prior to his televised statement, thus negating a finding of gross negligence. The court deemed his statements part of an important public discussion and acceptable criticism. The Court of Appeal upheld this judgment, emphasizing the applicant's obligation as a public figure to tolerate such criticism. The Supreme Court declared her appeal inadmissible in May 2008.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the domestic courts' failure to grant her any redress for the Minister's defamatory statements violated her right to respect for private life, specifically her professional reputation, under Article 8 of the Convention. The core of her alleged violation is that the national legal framework and its application failed to provide adequate protection for her reputation against false, public accusations of criminal and unethical conduct made by a senior government official.
001-183546:
**Summary of *Smirnov and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 74889/16 and 7 others)**

The case of *Smirnov and Others v. Russia* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) by eight Russian nationals. The applications, lodged between November 2016 and October 2017, concerned the inadequate conditions of their detention in various Russian penal colonies (IK). The applicants primarily complained under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment, and some also raised complaints under Article 13 regarding the lack of an effective domestic remedy for their grievances.

The core facts of each application revolve around the specific, severe deficiencies in the detention facilities where the applicants were held. A central and recurring issue was severe overcrowding. In several facilities, the personal space allotted to each inmate was drastically below acceptable standards. For instance, in IK-6 in the Republic of Chuvashiya (applicant Troitskiy), 50 inmates shared a space providing only 1.5 square meters per person. Similarly, in IK-8 in the Bashkortostan Republic (applicant Shiyanov), the space was 1.4 square meters per inmate among 180 prisoners. In IK-11 in the Nizhniy Novgorod Region (applicants Klokov and Tolstykh), the space per inmate was 1.6 and 1.4 square meters, respectively. This lack of space was frequently coupled with an insufficient number of sleeping places, forcing inmates to share beds or sleep in shifts.

Beyond overcrowding, the applicants detailed a range of other degrading conditions. Sanitary and hygiene facilities were widely reported as inadequate or severely restricted. Many applicants complained of a lack of privacy for using the toilet, restricted access to toilets, and insufficient access to showers and warm water. For example, in IK-6, 50 inmates had to share a single toilet. The quality and quantity of food were also a common grievance, described as poor, with some applicants noting a lack of access to potable water.

Environmental factors contributing to the poor conditions included a lack of fresh air and insufficient natural and electric light. Several applicants reported infestations of their cells with insects or rodents and the presence of mould. A significant health concern raised was the practice of sharing cells with inmates infected with contagious diseases, a complaint lodged by applicants Smirnov, Troitskiy, and Klokov.

Furthermore, the applicants faced material deprivations. These included a lack of or inadequate furniture, poor or non-existent hygienic facilities, and a lack of basic toiletries. Access to activities was also limited, with one applicant (Shiyanov) noting a lack of or restricted access to leisure or educational activities. In one case (Troitskiy), the applicant also alleged a lack of requisite medical assistance.

The durations of detention under these conditions varied significantly. Applicant Klokov endured the longest period, over five years in IK-11, from June 2012 to August 2017. Other applicants faced periods ranging from just over one year (Smirnov and Shalyakin) to more than two and a half years (Tolstykh and Poskrebyshev). For some, like Tolstykh, Poskrebyshev, Shalyakin, and Artemenkov, their detention was ongoing at the time of application.

In summary, the applications detailed a systemic failure to provide humane detention conditions, characterized by extreme overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, poor nutrition, and environmental health hazards. These factors collectively formed the basis of the applicants' claims that their treatment violated Article 3 of the Convention, and that they lacked an effective remedy at the national level to address these violations, contrary to Article 13.
001-181850:
In *Prokhorenko and Others v. Russia* (Application no. 12204/15 and 2 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 29 March 2018. The applications were lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants’ principal complaint was the inadequate conditions of their detention. In application no. 12204/15, the applicant also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The facts are set out in the appended table. The first applicant, Artem Aleksandrovich Prokhorenko, born 1 July 1985, introduced application no. 12204/15 on 15 February 2015. He was detained at IZ-47/1 St Petersburg from 21 November 2008 to 26 April 2015, a total of 6 years, 5 months and 6 days. He was held with 4 inmates and had approximately 2 m² of personal space. His specific grievances included overcrowding, lack of privacy for the toilet, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, insufficient natural light, insufficient electric light, no or restricted access to a shower, insufficient physical exercise in fresh air, inadequate temperature, and constant electric light. These conditions formed the factual basis for his alleged violation concerning detention conditions.

The second applicant, Yevgeniy Valeryevich Petrov, born 12 January 1975, introduced application no. 63371/16 on 20 October 2016. He was detained at IZ-1 Nizhniy Novgorod from 5 September 2016 to 3 October 2016, a period of 29 days. The cell held 11 inmates, with approximately 2.6 m² per inmate. His grievances included lack of fresh air, poor quality food, infestation of the cell with insects or rodents, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of privacy for the toilet, lack or poor quality of bedding and bed linen, and lack of requisite medical assistance. These conditions were central to his complaint of inadequate detention.

The third applicant, Denis Sergeyevich Bankin, born 12 April 1977, introduced application no. 77886/16 on 12 December 2016. He was detained at IZ-6 Moscow from 15 August 2015 to 22 July 2016, lasting 11 months and 8 days. The table records 1.2 m² per inmate. His specific grievances were overcrowding, no or restricted access to running water, and no or restricted access to a toilet. These facts pointed to particularly severe overcrowding and lack of basic sanitation.

Overall, the case concerns three applicants held in different Russian pre-trial detention facilities over different periods. Their complaints focus on allegedly inhuman and degrading conditions of detention, including overcrowding, poor sanitation, lack of privacy, insufficient ventilation, light, exercise, shower access, and, in one case, inadequate medical assistance. The Court deliberated in private on 8 March 2018 and adopted the judgment on 29 March 2018. The judgment is final but subject to editorial revision. The appended list provides the detailed factual matrix relevant to the alleged violations.
001-180281:
In *Healy v Ireland* (App. no. 27291/16), the applicant, Mary Healy, an Irish national born in 1946, had been treated for a pituitary brain tumour since 1982. In 1995 she became a patient of Dr B, a consultant endocrinologist. An August 2000 MRI showed no significant change since 1995, though the tumour remained large. After tests, Dr B told her by telephone in September 2000 that the tumour was “very unsatisfactory.” Because she believed the 1982 surgery had removed almost the entire tumour, she understood this to mean rapid growth and grave danger. Dr B prescribed a newly available drug, injected monthly by her GP from September 2000. She developed severe gastrointestinal side effects; the dose was halved. In January 2001 she was hospitalised with vomiting, diarrhoea, exhaustion, headaches, cramps and spasms, and severe hypothyroidism later found to be an unknown side effect of the drug. She received further injections in February and March 2001 and began seeing another endocrinologist.

In May 2004 the applicant commenced High Court civil proceedings against Dr B and the hospital. She alleged negligence in prescribing and monitoring the drug, and claimed her consent was vitiated by insufficient or misleading information about her condition and treatment. The statement of claim was served in October 2004. Dr B defended in February 2005 and sought particulars, supplied in June 2005. The hospital defended in June 2005 and also sought particulars. According to the Government, eleven interim motions were brought between February 2005 and September 2008. In October 2009 the case was included in a “positive callover” and a hearing was set for April 2010. The hearing ran from 13 April to 7 May 2010; judgment was given on 20 May 2010.

The High Court dismissed all claims. It preferred the defence experts and found that Dr B had complied with the drug’s therapeutic indications, adequately monitored the applicant, and fulfilled his duty to explain the treatment. It accepted that the applicant misunderstood the exact state of her tumour, but held this was not caused by Dr B, who had given accurate and appropriate information. It found she gave valid informed consent. Only the gastrointestinal side effects required warning; other potential side effects had not materialised.

The applicant appealed on 1 July 2010. The appeal remained pending before the Supreme Court until transferred to the Court of Appeal on 29 October 2014. It was heard on 30 July 2015 and dismissed on 17 November 2015. The Court of Appeal found no basis to disturb the findings on treatment or consent. It held that Dr B reasonably considered the condition serious and requiring treatment, that surgery was impossible, and that medication was the only alternative; he explained the benefits and unpleasant side effects. A “do nothing” option was “somewhat unreal.” The Supreme Court refused leave on 8 March 2016.

The applicant lodged her ECtHR application on 12 May 2016. The facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the duration of the civil proceedings—from May 2004 to the final refusal of leave in March 2016, nearly twelve years—and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay. The domestic law note refers to *Nash v DPP* (24 October 2016), recognising at least in principle a possible damages claim for breach of the constitutional right to a timely trial, but that judgment post-dated the applicant’s domestic proceedings and application. The ECtHR case concerned complaints under Article 6 §1 (length of proceedings) and Article 13 (lack of an effective remedy).
001-188382:
In *Sergey Smirnov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 36853/09), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Mr Sergey Aleksandrovich Smirnov, a Ukrainian national born in 1965. On 3 April 2008 the applicant shot and seriously injured a person and was arrested at the scene. He remained in detention during criminal proceedings, mainly at the Kharkiv pre-trial detention centre. On 14 April 2009 the Kharkiv Court of Appeal sentenced him to ten years and six months’ imprisonment with confiscation of property; the Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 29 December 2009. He served his sentence in several correctional colonies, including the Slovyanoserbsk Correctional Colony in the Luhansk Region from 11 May 2010 to 7 April 2011. He was transferred to a semi-open institution in May 2015 and released in December 2015.

The Court communicated four main sets of complaints to the Ukrainian Government: conditions of detention at the Slovyanoserbsk Colony, allegedly inadequate medical assistance in detention, alleged interception and monitoring of his correspondence, and the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection without reasons.

As to conditions of detention, the applicant was placed in a single-occupancy cell on 13 May 2010 at his own request because he feared attacks by other inmates. Later prison reports stated that he refused to move to a dormitory, citing fear of violence. He claimed that the isolation cell measured 4.5 sq. m in total, including toilet and washbasin, with only about 1 sq. m of living space. After the case was communicated, he further alleged that average living space in the colony’s dormitories was 2.8 sq. m per inmate, relying on a CPT report of 23 November 2011 which noted overcrowding in most dormitories.

Regarding correspondence, the applicant alleged systematic monitoring of all his mail. He stated that on 22 July and 9 September 2009 the prison administration handed him two letters from the Court, and on 18 December 2010 a letter from the parliamentary secretariat, all of which had been opened. Prison registers showed that between July 2009 and December 2010 he sent at least forty-seven letters to public entities covered by monitoring, including courts, the High Council of Justice, the prison department and Parliament. These entries often contained brief summaries or were marked as applications, petitions or complaints. By contrast, letters to the Court and his lawyer were marked as “sealed letter.” Under domestic law, correspondence with the Court, international institutions and prosecutors was exempt from monitoring; from February 2010, correspondence with lawyers was also exempt.

On medical care, the applicant alleged inadequate treatment for digestive, back and other conditions. He was diagnosed with chronic gastroduodentitis in January 2010 and treated in the Kharkiv SIZO medical unit in April 2010. In February 2011 a colony doctor recommended transfer to Luhansk SIZO hospital for examination and treatment, but no transfer followed. In October 2011 a civilian hospital diagnosed acute pancreatitis, duodenopathy, gastric stasis, oesophagitis and chronic hepatitis and prescribed medication and a diet. The next day a colony doctor recommended hospitalisation at Temnivka prison hospital; the applicant refused, saying he mistrusted prison doctors. He later alleged that medication and dietary recommendations were not provided. He had osteochondrosis since 1998; in 2012 an MRI was performed and a surgeon recommended specialist neurological examination and treatment, which he alleged was not implemented. In 2013 a traumatologist prescribed painkillers, anti-inflammatory medication and a back-support device, also allegedly not implemented. In 2015 he underwent spinal surgery in a civilian institution and was later recognised as a Category 2 disabled person. He also suffered bronchitis, fungal nail infection and heart-related conditions.

The case therefore centred on the applicant’s allegations that his detention conditions, medical care and correspondence while imprisoned violated the Convention, and that no effective domestic remedy existed for those complaints.
001-181394:
In *Patalakh v. Germany* (Application no. 22692/15), the applicant, Ivan Patalakh, a Russian national, complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention that the German courts failed, or significantly delayed, reviewing the lawfulness of his remand detention. He alleged this caused the automatic and arbitrary continuation of his detention, violating his right to liberty and security.

On 30 October 2013, the Frankfurt am Main District Court issued an arrest warrant against the applicant on strong suspicion that he had aided aggravated fraudulent conversion, corruption, corruption in commercial practice and aggravated tax evasion involving several million euros. The warrant was based on a risk of absconding, given the possible heavy sentence, his lack of legal residence or significant ties to Germany, and the fact that his wife was a co-accused. There was also a risk of collusion. He was arrested the same day and placed in remand detention. The warrant was later expanded, and in December 2014 the prosecution charged him with multiple counts of aiding aggravated fraudulent conversion, corruption and tax evasion. The main proceedings opened in May 2015, trial began in June 2015, and in July 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment. The conviction was not final at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings. The arrest warrant was set aside in October 2016.

The detention-review history was central. From January 2014, the applicant unsuccessfully challenged his remand detention. On 28 July 2014, the Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal ordered the prolongation of detention and directed that the file be resubmitted by 28 October 2014 for the next periodic review. It transferred competence for further reviews to the court with general jurisdiction until then. On 24 October 2014, the prosecution submitted the file to the Court of Appeal and requested an extension under Articles 121 et seq. of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant requested release on 7 November 2014 and later lodged complaints of bias against judges and complained about delay. The Court of Appeal encountered difficulties in obtaining the file, making enquiries of the Frankfurt Regional Court and later the Darmstadt Regional Court. The applicant’s lawyer submitted material in March 2015, and the applicant twice asked for a prompt decision. On 21 April 2015, he lodged a constitutional complaint alleging that the absence of a decision violated his right to liberty. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to accept it on 27 April 2015 without reasons. On 15 May 2015, the applicant was served with the Court of Appeal’s decision, taken on 15 April 2015 and issued on 13 May 2015, ordering continued remand detention. The Court of Appeal found a continuing risk of absconding and no undue delay in the criminal proceedings, considering detention proportionate. It did not address the duration of the review proceedings or give reasons for the delay.

Under German law, remand detention may exceed six months only where particular difficulty, unusual extent of investigation or another important reason justifies it. The Court of Appeal reviews such extensions and further reviews at least every three months. There is no fixed time-limit for the Court of Appeal’s decision, and time is suspended if the file is submitted before the deadline. The applicant’s complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 were communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.
001-181393:
In *R.Š. v. Latvia*, the applicant, a Latvian national and licensed pilot undergoing aviation training, was a passenger on a private flight on 16 August 2008 from Riga to Tukums. The flight was organised by KD.C., a company providing private flights and pilot training. D.K. was its sole shareholder and board member. KD.C. did not operate commercial flights and had not been certified as an air operator. The aircraft, a Piper PA-31, was owned by KD.C. It was piloted by G.V., who had begun but not completed differences training for that aircraft type and lacked authorisation from the Civil Aviation Agency to fly it. Shortly after take-off, G.V. lost control in cloudy weather; the aircraft crashed and caught fire. The pilot died. The applicant and other passengers suffered serious injuries. The applicant sustained life-threatening injuries, permanently lost vision in his right eye, and suffered lasting health damage. He could later work only with limitations and could not operate aircraft independently.

The Transport Accident and Incident Investigation Bureau found that the primary cause was human error: G.V.’s insufficient skills and experience to operate a multi-engine Piper PA-31 under instrument flight rules. Contributing factors included poor weather and “unsafe supervision” by the Civil Aviation Agency in ensuring compliance with aviation legislation and visual flight rules. The report also found that KD.C. had failed to follow up on G.V.’s training, check his documents, or properly verify his qualifications before handing him the aircraft. It recommended a mandatory handover procedure to prevent unqualified pilots from flying. Yet the investigation and later testimony indicated that, at the material time, Latvian law did not regulate how general-aviation aircraft should be handed over or who must verify a pilot’s qualifications. Commercial aviation was regulated; general/private aviation was not.

Criminal proceedings were brought against D.K. for negligence and air-traffic safety violations. He was convicted at first instance but acquitted on appeal, and the Supreme Court upheld the acquittal. The courts found that D.K. had not been shown to have committed the required offence, that he was not a transport employee or aviation specialist, and that the duty not to fly without qualifications rested on the pilot. The Senate also noted that no domestic rule at the time required an aircraft owner to verify pilot qualifications; owner liability under the Chicago Convention arose only from 18 November 2010, and a domestic prohibition on handing over aircraft to unqualified pilots was added to the Law on Aviation only in 2013.

The applicant also sued KD.C., D.K., and the insurer for damages. KD.C. was declared bankrupt and later dissolved with no successor. The civil courts dismissed the claims: D.K. was not the aircraft owner; the pilot was not his employee; no unlawful act or causal link was established; and the pilot had acted arbitrarily contrary to the plan to fly with an instructor. The insurer refused coverage because the pilot lacked the right to operate the aircraft. The applicant therefore received no compensation. Before the European Court of Human Rights, he alleged under Articles 2 and 8 that he could not obtain compensation for harm from the accident and that the State should be responsible for shortcomings in the legal regulation of private-flight safety. Those complaints were communicated to the Latvian Government.
001-182853:
**CASE OF VUJOVIĆ v. MONTENEGRO** (Application no. 75139/10) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, Committee), delivered on 15 May 2018. The applicant, Mr Igor Vujović, was a Montenegrin and Norwegian national born in 1973, living in Oslo, Norway. He was represented by Mr Đ. Čepić, a lawyer practising in Belgrade. The Montenegrin Government was represented by its Agent, Ms V. Pavličić.

The case arose from criminal proceedings connected with a traffic accident in which a child died. On 26 April 2000 criminal proceedings were brought against the applicant and one other person. On 25 February 2003 the Court of First Instance in Podgorica convicted the applicant of endangering public traffic and sentenced him and his co-accused to one year and six months’ imprisonment. In 2006 the High Court in Podgorica quashed that judgment and remitted the case back to the Court of First Instance.

On 18 April 2007 the Court of First Instance again convicted the applicant and his co-accused, but reduced the sentence to one year and four months’ imprisonment. On 13 November 2009 the High Court reduced the sentence of the applicant’s co-accused, but upheld the first-instance judgment in respect of the applicant. The applicant’s appeal against that judgment was rejected on 14 June 2010.

The applicant then lodged a further appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 26 October 2010 the Supreme Court rejected it. On 11 December 2010, complaining about the overall length of the criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged an action for fair redress with the Supreme Court. That action was rejected on 31 December 2010. On 19 April 2013 the Constitutional Court rejected his ultimate appeal.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 December 2010 under Article 34 of the Convention. On 3 December 2014 the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings was communicated to the Government. Pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court, the complaint concerning the outcome of the criminal proceedings was declared inadmissible. Therefore, the only alleged violation examined by the Court concerned the excessive length of the criminal proceedings, an issue falling under the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The key facts for the length complaint are the chronology and duration of the proceedings. The criminal case began on 26 April 2000. A first-instance conviction was reached on 25 February 2003. It was quashed in 2006 and remitted. A second conviction followed on 18 April 2007. Appellate proceedings continued until the High Court decision of 13 November 2009 and the rejection of the applicant’s appeal on 14 June 2010. The Supreme Court rejected his further appeal on 26 October 2010. Thus, from the institution of proceedings to the final criminal-law decision, the case lasted approximately ten and a half years. The applicant also pursued domestic remedies specifically directed at the length complaint, but the Supreme Court rejected his fair-redress action on 31 December 2010 and the Constitutional Court rejected his appeal on 19 April 2013.

This procedural history, particularly the repeated remittal and successive appeals, formed the factual basis for the alleged violation of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The Court adopted its judgment on 15 May 2018.
001-180288:
**Ciocodeică v. Romania** (Application no. 27413/09) concerned a Romanian national, Maria Ciocodeică, who alleged under Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the State failed to effectively assist her in enforcing a final judgment awarding salary entitlements and that she had no effective remedy for the non-enforcement.

In 2004 the applicant sued her employer, private company C.G.H.T., seeking annulment of her dismissal and salary entitlements. On 29 September 2004 the Timișoara Court of Appeal gave a final judgment in her favour, ordering the company to revoke its dismissal decision and pay all salary entitlements from 17 October 2003 until the judgment, updated and index-linked, plus costs. The judgment was validated by the Timiș County Court on 15 November 2004.

On 21 January 2005 the applicant began enforcement through bailiff office M.S.R. & S.A.I. The bailiff served a payment notice on the company in January 2005, but the company refused to comply and challenged the enforcement. In February 2005, at the company’s request, the Timișoara District Court suspended enforcement, subject to a deposit of ROL 4,000,000, about EUR 90. The applicant sought urgent lifting of the suspension in May 2005, arguing she needed the salary payments for herself and her infant, but the court dismissed the request for lack of imminent damage.

In June 2005 the District Court allowed the company’s objection and annulled the enforcement because the bailiff had failed to serve the company with a copy of the enforceable judgment. The applicant’s appeal on points of law was dismissed in October 2005, making that annulment final. The company also obtained annulment of a bank-account restriction because it had been issued after the suspension. The bailiff later issued another payment notice in June 2005, posted with the enforceable judgment at the company’s entrance in July 2005. In November 2005 the applicant asked whether the company had complied; the bailiff replied that it had not. After that, no further exchange occurred. In May 2007 the bailiff issued a report declaring the enforcement time-barred under Article 389 of the old Code of Civil Procedure, because six months had passed since the last enforcement act and the creditor had remained passive. It was unclear whether the applicant received that report.

The applicant pursued other remedies. In May 2005 she sought immediate enforcement under Article 5803 of the old Code. In August 2005 the District Court ordered a coercive fine of ROL 500,000 per day, but in December 2005 the County Court allowed the company’s appeal, holding that the fine was not appropriate because the debt could be enforced by a bailiff. She also complained to the Ministry of Justice in July 2005; the complaint was rejected because the underlying judgment was final. In 2005 she filed criminal complaints alleging refusal to execute the judgment. An investigation began in December 2006 against the company administrator, M.D., but in February 2008 the prosecutor discontinued proceedings, finding no offence, and imposed an administrative fine of RON 1,000, about EUR 250. Her challenges were dismissed through January 2009. The company was later liquidated and struck off the register in 2014.

The applicant therefore alleged that the Romanian authorities failed to assist her in enforcing a final judgment against a private debtor and that available remedies—complaints against the bailiff, disciplinary or civil liability, and criminal proceedings—were ineffective.
001-179853:
The case of *Starenkiy and Rudoy v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 44807/10 and 15752/14) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges André Potocki (President), Síofra O’Leary, and Mārtiņš Mits, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 11 January 2018 and adopted after private deliberations on 7 December 2017. Both applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Ukrainian Government was notified of the applications. The applicants principally complained of inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. They also raised other complaints under Convention provisions.

The first applicant, Demyan Ivanovych Starenkyy, born 23 November 1968, introduced application no. 44807/10 on 20 May 2008. He was detained in Sokalska correctional colony no. 47 from 21 June 2006 to 27 March 2012, a total of 5 years, 9 months, and 7 days. During this period, he had approximately 3 square metres of personal space per inmate. His specific grievances were that the shower was available only once a week; there was no isolated toilet; nutrition was bad; the cell lacked ventilation; and in summer the cell became very hot and lacked fresh air. These conditions formed the factual basis for his complaint that detention conditions were inadequate and that no effective domestic remedy existed to address them.

The second applicant, Igor Vasilyevich Rudoy, born 26 May 1969, was represented by Vyacheslav Yuryevich Malyar of Odessa. He introduced application no. 15752/14 on 27 January 2014. He was held in Kyiv SIZO no. 13 from 10 November 2010 to 25 January 2014, a total of 3 years, 2 months, and 16 days. He had approximately 2 square metres per inmate. His specific grievances were severe overcrowding—20 inmates in a cell measuring 30.2 square metres; lack of heating in the cell; lack of hot water; lack of ventilation; other inmates smoking in the cell; lack of drinking water; lack of daylight; high humidity and mould on the cell walls; lights kept on for 24 hours; shower available only once a week; and bad nutrition. These facts underpinned his Convention complaint about inadequate conditions of detention and the absence of an effective remedy.

The Court’s judgment concerned the alleged violations arising from these conditions and the alleged lack of domestic redress. The available text does not set out the Court’s full reasoning or final conclusions on each complaint, but it records that the applications were communicated to the Government and that the Court deliberated and adopted its judgment. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the duration of detention, the amount of space per inmate, and the specific material conditions—especially overcrowding, sanitation, ventilation, heating, humidity, lighting, and nutrition—experienced by each applicant.
001-186770:
Case Dainelienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 23532/14) is a European Court of Human Rights case against Lithuania lodged on 18 March 2014 by Ms Dalia Regina Dainelienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1944. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the independence and impartiality of the Supreme Court. On 13 September 2017 that complaint was communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying criminal case began in April 2009, when the applicant was notified that she was suspected of organising the embezzlement of high-value property. She was charged in May 2009 and denied guilt. In July 2011 the Vilnius Regional Court found the charges incorrectly classified because the total value of the allegedly embezzled property was not high. It reclassified the charges as a less serious offence, held that prosecution had become time-barred, and discontinued the proceedings. The prosecutor appealed. In October 2011 the Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case.

On re-examination, in June 2013 the Vilnius Regional Court convicted the applicant, imposed a fine of LTL 12,000 (about EUR 3,475), and ordered her to pay part of the damages claimed by a company, amounting to LTL 2,800 (about EUR 810). In October 2013 the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and upheld the conviction in full.

In January 2014 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 17 February 2014, a three-judge selection panel refused to examine the appeal, finding that it did not comply with Article 368 § 2 and Article 369 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“CCP”), which set formal and legal requirements for cassation appeals. The chair of that selection panel, Judge V.G., was the father of M.G., the prosecutor who had acted in the applicant’s case before both the first-instance and appellate courts. This relationship is central to the alleged violation.

Domestic law provided that parties could seek removal of judges. Under Article 58 § 1(1) of the CCP, a judge could not participate in proceedings if he or she was a close family member or relative of a prosecutor in those proceedings, and Article 59 required a judge to withdraw on that basis. However, the cassation admissibility procedure was different. Under Article 372 § 2, the President of the Supreme Court or the Chair of the Criminal Division composed a panel of three judges to decide whether to accept an appeal. The appeal was admitted if at least one judge voted in favour, and a judge on that panel was not precluded from later deciding the merits. The decision was final and not appealable, though reasons had to be given.

Crucially, the CCP contained no provisions allowing parties to be informed of the composition of the initial three-judge selection panel or to request removal of those judges. Only after an appeal had been accepted and set for written examination did Article 3741 § 1 require that parties be informed of the chamber’s composition and of their right to request removal of judges.
