The alleged Article 6 § 1 violation was therefore that the Supreme Court’s refusal to admit the applicant’s cassation appeal was decided by a panel chaired by the father of the prosecutor who had prosecuted her, creating an appearance of bias or lack of impartiality. The key facts are the close familial relationship between the selection-panel judge and the prosecutor in the same case; the judge’s participation in a final, unreviewable admissibility decision; the general domestic prohibition on judges related to prosecutors participating; and the absence of any procedure allowing the applicant to learn the panel’s composition or seek recusal at that preliminary stage.
001-181278:
Vella v. Malta (Application no. 73182/12) concerned Josephine Mary Vella, a Maltese national born in 1932, who owned 14 Kirkop Square, Kirkop, a two-storey tenement of about 175 sq.m. She inherited it with her brothers and became sole owner by partition in 1998. The property had been requisitioned in 1955 and allocated to the San Leonard Band Club. The owners never recognised the club as tenant or accepted rent from it; a 1958 judgment held this was permissible because the tenement had not been leased as a dwelling. Rent was paid to the owners by the housing authority at 30 Maltese lira annually—about EUR 70, or less than EUR 6 monthly. The applicant later claimed the 2007 rental value was about EUR 1,747 monthly; the Government disputed this, relying on a valuation of another property, 3 Kirkop Square, at about EUR 1,021 monthly.

The applicant alleged the band club made extensive structural alterations without consent or permits, destroying the historic layout and devaluing the property. The Government argued she had not pursued domestic remedies and that the alterations increased value. She also alleged the club breached the tenancy by manufacturing fireworks and running unauthorised commercial activities, such as a bar and wedding venue; the Government said these were unproved. From 2008 the club began depositing rent in court.

An adjacent property owned by the applicant and her brothers had also been requisitioned and assigned to the band club. In 1993 the Court of Appeal declared that requisition null and void as not in the public interest, and damages for structural alterations were later awarded.

In 2007 the applicant brought constitutional redress concerning the 1955 property. She alleged breaches of Article 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to the requisition and continued occupation, seeking compensation and release. In October 2011 the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional jurisdiction upheld her claims. It found the requisition served a private entity, was not in the public interest, and was disproportionate; the derisory rent imposed an excessive burden, violating Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It also found Article 14 violated because only her property had been requisitioned for the band club. It awarded EUR 60,000 compensation, three quarters payable by the Director of Social Housing and one quarter by the band club, and ordered the club to vacate within three months.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court in May 2012 partly upheld the judgment. It confirmed a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 only because the requisition was disproportionate, but held it was in the public interest for social and cultural purposes. It found no Article 14 violation. It revoked the eviction order, holding that compensation sufficed to redress the unfair balance and the lease’s validity was not at issue. It confirmed the EUR 60,000 award and sharing. It reasoned that disproportionality had not persisted since 1955 but only after the 1980s; the applicant had received rent and only instituted proceedings in 2007, so reduced compensation was legitimate. Since the property was taken in the public interest, compensation need not reflect market values. It retained the award because the property was not vacated, and held that damages for depreciation from structural works fell outside the constitutional complaint. The applicant was ordered to pay costs of the cross-appeal and half the judicial costs.
001-184671:
In *Ruiz Pena and Perez Oberght v. Malta* (Applications nos. 25218/15 and 25251/15), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) delivered judgment on 17 July 2018, final on 17 October 2018. Both applicants were detained at Corradino Correctional Facility in Paola, Malta, and alleged that their conditions of detention violated Article 3 of the Convention.

The first applicant, Mr Ruiz Pena, a Venezuelan national, had been detained since September 2009 and was serving a ten-year sentence imposed on 21 March 2012. Since 10 January 2013 he had been held in Division 3, cell no. 148. He never requested a transfer because this would have meant losing his individual cell and being placed in a dormitory, harming his privacy. He alleged that his cell had one window and one air vent, but the vent was clogged and the window was too high, requiring him to climb onto the sink to open or close it. Ventilation was inadequate, and the cell was extremely hot in summer and cold in winter. He claimed he was not given a heater despite requests and had only one blanket, with additional blankets and clothes coming from NGOs. In summer temperatures reached 35–40°C, and two fans he purchased merely circulated hot air. He had to flush the toilet with a bucket because of low water pressure, sometimes using more than one bucket, which was especially deplorable in summer. The old building’s ceiling released dust allegedly harmful to his lungs. Tap water was rusty and filthy, so he purchased drinking water. His prison job paid only €0.60 per day. The Government stated he received €34.77 every four weeks under “gratuity” and “Work and Pay” schemes since 2015, and that a six-pack of water cost €2.24.

The second applicant, Mr Perez Oberght, a Dominican national, had been detained since 24 November 2009 and was serving a nine-year sentence imposed on 15 October 2012. Since 27 January 2012 he had been in Division 3, cell no. 155, except one day in Division 6 on 3 October 2015. The Government said that after the complaint was communicated, he was asked whether he wanted a transfer and refused. He alleged that his cell window was over two metres high and difficult and dangerous to open; metal bars limited natural light; and although there were two ventilation openings, one was blocked, so ventilation was insufficient. The water was not drinkable, so he bought water. The Government stated he received €41.58 every four weeks from gratuity and Work and Pay schemes. He claimed ceiling dust affected his asthma; the Government said the dust was normal for Maltese stone and that he never requested paint. He also alleged humidity and lack of a heater caused frequent flu; the Government attributed humidity to his blocking the vent with a towel and failing to maintain the cell. He complained of poor light, making reading difficult; the Government cited ceiling and wall lights, a portable lamp, three skylights, and 400W bell lamps. Finally, he alleged the spiral staircase was unsafe for emergencies, as a stretcher could not be carried down and evacuation two at a time was impossible; the Government pointed to a walkway between divisions.

The applications were lodged on 1 July 2015. The complaint was communicated to the Government on 25 February 2016, and the remainder of application no. 25218/15 was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. Relevant domestic law appeared in *Story and Others v. Malta*, and relevant material in *Yanez Pinon and Others v. Malta*.
001-184673:
Case Abdilla v. Malta (Application no. 36199/15) concerned an application against Malta by Jean Pierre Abdilla, a Maltese national born in 1975 and detained at the Corradino Correctional Facility, Paola. He was serving a sixteen-year prison sentence and a EUR 40,000 fine for drug-related offences, imposed on 3 December 2009 and confirmed on appeal on 19 September 2013. He lodged his application on 25 September 2015, alleging a violation of Article 3 of the Convention because of the conditions of his detention and a lack of an effective remedy under Article 13 read together with Article 3. The application was communicated to the Government on 8 February 2017.

The applicant was placed in Division 2, cell no. 88, on 10 December 2009. He remained in various Division 2 cells, except for two brief periods in 2011 in Division 6, a high-security unit, lasting nine and eleven days, the latter ending on 4 December 2011. From 4 December 2011 until 26 December 2014 he was held in cell no. 45, and thereafter in cell no. 70. He alleged that Division 2 was around 200 years old, required extensive maintenance, and lacked light and air. The windows were triple-barred, and three skylights were kept closed even during summer, causing excessive heat. He described the environment as squalid and foul-smelling.

As to cell no. 45, the applicant claimed it was nearly underground, structurally condemned, poorly ventilated, and affected by fumes and excessive heat from a nearby bakery. It was humid and cold in winter, and the triple bars meant he could barely see outside. Cell no. 70 was very small, had little ventilation, and made him feel claustrophobic. He also claimed he hardly ever had access to running water.

The applicant complained that food in Division 2 was poor quality, non-nutritious, and served in too-small portions. Between 1 and 4 September 2015, prisoners allegedly had to be taken to hospital because of food poisoning, and mice were found dead in a dirty kitchen. Toilets had no automated flushing system; inmates had to flush using a bucket. Running water in cells was intermittent, and available water was not potable. Inmates could buy bottled water, but their ability to do so was limited by lack of money. Showers often lacked hot water, were dirty, and were insufficient: mostly only one shower was available for all Division 2 inmates, with two in summer. One shower tray was broken and cracked, creating a risk of injury.

Telephone calls were very expensive and became more costly on 3 December 2014. Complaints to the prison authorities were unsuccessful. The prison allowance was too low, making tuck-shop goods expensive and affecting inmates’ ability to buy water and make calls. The applicant also alleged health issues and being confined to bed; the emergency buzzer in his cell never worked. When he tried to use it, no one came for thirty minutes, and staff then reprimanded him. Petitions and other inmates’ constitutional cases about the conditions produced no change.

The relevant domestic law was set out in Story and Others v. Malta, and relevant material in Yanez Pinon and Others v. Malta. CPT standards cited in the case state that a single-occupancy cell should measure 6m² plus space for a sanitary annexe, usually 1m² to 2m². The case therefore focused on whether the cumulative detention conditions amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3 and whether Malta provided an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.
001-181202:
**Mockutė v. Lithuania** concerned Neringa Mockutė, a Lithuanian lawyer who was involuntarily admitted to Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital on 7 May 2003. She had prior psychiatric treatment in 1992, 1994, 1996, and 2002. In February 2003 she began meditating at the Ojas Meditation Centre, the Lithuanian branch of the Osho movement. On 7 May 2003 she suffered an emotional breakdown at the Ministry of Economy: she became agitated, left work, undressed at home, and screamed from her balcony. Her family called an ambulance, and she was taken by force to Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital. She refused to consent to admission or treatment; her cousin signed the consent form. She was physically restrained and forcibly given neuroleptics. She remained in hospital for 52 days, until 26 June 2003, diagnosed with a transitory psychotic disorder. During her stay, medical records noted that doctors questioned her about the Ojas Centre, sought to form a “critical attitude” toward her non-traditional religious beliefs, and continued psycho-correction directed at her meditation. The applicant alleged that psychiatrists pressured her to renounce meditation, mocked it, said it harmed her mental health, told her to follow Catholicism, and delayed her release when she refused to accept their views.

As to Article 8, on 17 June 2003, while she was still hospitalized, the LNK television programme *Srovės* aired. It featured her mother and sister, identified by their real first names, who claimed the Ojas Centre had a destructive influence. Doctor D.Š., a head of division and psychiatrist at Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital, was interviewed on hospital premises. She disclosed that a young woman (called “Violeta”) had acute psychosis, was being treated at Vilnius Psychiatric Hospital, had studied in the United States for a master’s degree, and had held an important State job. The programme implied Osho followers took part in sex orgies and linked the applicant’s psychosis to meditation. Although her full name was not used, the applicant alleged that these details, together with her mother’s and sister’s participation, made her identifiable. She also alleged that information about her health was disclosed to her mother without consent. She responded with an open letter in August 2003, confirming the broadcast was about her.

As to Article 9, the applicant complained that the psychiatric hospital prevented her from practising her religion by attempting to cure her of meditation and alter her religious convictions. In 2006 she sued the hospital for non-pecuniary damage. The first-instance court found unlawful forced hospitalization, a privacy breach, and a religious-freedom breach, awarding her damages. The Court of Appeal upheld the unlawful-detention finding but reversed the privacy and religion findings, holding that she was not sufficiently identifiable from the broadcast, that disclosure to her mother was not a breach, and that attempts to make her critical of her beliefs did not restrict religious rites. The Supreme Court refused to admit her appeal. She applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 14 December 2009, alleging violations of Article 8 (private life and confidentiality) and Article 9 (freedom of religion).
001-183206:
**Salakhbekov and Abukayev v. Russia** (Applications Nos. 28368/09 and 28636/09) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by two Russian nationals against the Russian Federation under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants had taken part in the clean-up operation at the Chernobyl nuclear disaster site and were entitled to certain social benefits. In 2008 they applied for a recalculation of those benefits. Their claims were granted by domestic courts, which issued judgments in their favour. These judgments therefore became final domestic decisions recognizing the applicants’ entitlement to recalculated social benefits.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Convention violations arose after those favourable final judgments. The applicants complained that the time limits for lodging appeals against the final judgments were extended and that the final judgments in their favour were subsequently quashed. In other words, although domestic courts had already resolved the benefit recalculation claims in the applicants’ favour, the appellate process was later reopened through an extension of appeal time limits, and the final judgments were set aside. The Court communicated to the Government the complaints concerning the extension of the time limits for lodging appeals and the subsequent quashing of the final judgments. The remainder of application no. 28368/09 was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

Procedurally, the applications were lodged with the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant in application no. 28636/09 was represented by Mr Z.S. Salimov, a lawyer practising in Makhachkala. The Russian Government were represented initially by Mr G. Matyushkin, Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights, and later by his successor, Mr M. Galperin. On 24 April 2017, the complaints concerning the extension of appeal time limits and the quashing of the final judgments were communicated to the Government. The Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee, but after considering that objection, the Court rejected it.

The Court also noted that the relevant domestic law and practice governing the restoration of time limits for appeal were summarized in **Magomedov and Others v. Russia** (nos. 33636/09 and 9 others, §§ 35–43, 28 March 2017). That reference frames the central legal issue: the domestic practice permitting appeal time limits to be restored or extended, thereby allowing final judgments to be challenged and quashed. For the applicants, this practice was directly linked to the loss of their final judgments granting recalculation of Chernobyl-related social benefits.

The alleged violations therefore focused not on the initial benefit eligibility dispute, but on the fairness and legal certainty of the domestic proceedings after the applicants had already obtained final judgments in their favour. The case concerned whether the retrospective reopening and quashing of those final judgments, through extended appeal deadlines, infringed the applicants’ Convention rights. The Third Section Committee comprised Branko Lubarda (President), Pere Pastor Vilanova and Georgios A. Serghides, with Stephen Phillips as Section Registrar. The judgment was delivered on 29 May 2018, following private deliberations on 7 May 2018.
001-183373:
In *Novotný v. the Czech Republic* (ECtHR, App. no. 16314/13, judgment of 7 June 2018), the applicant, František Novotný, alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. The case concerned his inability to challenge a final judicial declaration of paternity after DNA evidence proved he was not the biological father.

The applicant was born in 1942. In 1965 he had a sexual relationship with a woman who gave birth to a daughter, Z., on 2 March 1966. The applicant denied paternity. Z.’s legal guardian brought proceedings on her behalf in the Jihlava District Court. After Z.’s birth, but before those proceedings, the mother married another man.

On 23 April 1970 the District Court declared the applicant to be Z.’s father and ordered him to pay maintenance. The court relied on witness evidence, documentary evidence, a “bio-hereditary” blood test, and a finding that the applicant had had intercourse with the mother between 300 and 180 days before Z.’s birth. Under Article 54 of the Family Code, a man who had intercourse with the mother in that period was presumed to be the father unless there were serious grounds to exclude paternity. Another man had also had intercourse with the mother at the relevant time, but the blood test excluded him. The applicant appealed and requested another expert opinion. The Brno Regional Court refused, finding the facts sufficiently proved, and upheld the judgment on 2 June 1970. It became final on 10 June 1970.

In 2011 the applicant asked the Prosecutor General to challenge his paternity in court. By letter of 21 June 2011, he was told that the requirements of Article 62 of the Family Code were not met: Z., by then an adult, did not want to challenge paternity, it was not in her interests, and the applicant had not produced expert evidence credibly disproving paternity.

On 29 February 2012 the applicant and Z. underwent a DNA examination. The report of 19 April 2012 unequivocally confirmed that the applicant was not Z.’s father. On 9 May 2012 the applicant made a new request to the Prosecutor General. On 12 September 2012 the Prosecutor General refused, explaining that paternity had been determined by a judicial declaration under Article 54 of the Family Code, not by a statutory presumption under Articles 51 and 52. Once such a judgment became final, Czech law provided no possibility to challenge it. The Prosecutor General’s competence under Articles 62 and 62a applied only to statutory presumptions of paternity.

Relying on Article 6 § 1, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor General’s decision. He argued that he had proved he was not Z.’s biological father, requested that the Prosecutor General be ordered to initiate proceedings, and claimed that Articles 61 § 1 and 62 § 1 of the Family Code were unconstitutional. On 13 December 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint. It noted that his paternity had been established by a final judicial decision and that the Prosecutor General’s competence could apply only if all legal requirements were fulfilled, which was not the case.

The relevant domestic law allowed a court to declare paternity under Article 54 and allowed the Prosecutor General to challenge paternity under Article 62 where the child’s interests required it and parental time-limits had expired. However, the Prosecutor General treated that power as unavailable where paternity had already been established by a final judgment. Constitutional case-law, including references to *Paulík v. Slovakia*, recognised Article 8 and Article 6 concerns where alleged fathers lacked any procedure to deny paternity, but the Constitutional Court found no such avenue available to the applicant because his paternity had been judicially determined and had become final. The ECtHR application was lodged on 19 February 2013 and communicated to the Government on 19 February 2015.
001-179878:
Mr Charalambos Nicholas, born in 1951 and living in Larnaca, is a Cypriot and British national. After his dismissal from Cyprus Airways Ltd as a trainee pilot, on 26 June 1998 he brought a civil action before the District Court of Nicosia for wrongful dismissal and defamation (no. 7562/98). The defendant company was represented by a law firm. On 29 December 2006 the District Court dismissed the action. On 9 February 2007 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 43/07); a bench of three judges heard the appeal. At the hearing on 11 March 2007, Mr P.G.P., managing partner of the defendant’s law firm, appeared for the defendant company and addressed the Supreme Court. Other lawyers from the same firm had previously appeared before the appeal bench for the defendant. On 21 April 2010 the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal unanimously.

The applicant alleged that after the Supreme Court judgment he discovered that the son of one of the judges on the bench, Judge A.K., and the daughter of Mr P.G.P. were married and both worked at Mr P.G.P.’s law firm. His domestic lawyer had not requested the judge’s exemption because he lacked sufficient knowledge of the relevant facts at the time. The applicant had not instructed him to do so because he found out only after the appeal ended. The applicant complained of a lack of impartiality, under the objective test, concerning Judge A.K.

Under the code of judicial practice adopted on 17 March 1988 and amended on 21 July 1989, 18 September 2003, 30 November 2006 and 4 October 2011, the version applicable when the applicant’s case was heard—after the 30 November 2006 amendment—provided that a judge did not sit alone or on a bench at any level in cases in which lawyers appearing before him or her were close relatives. Close relatives were parents, spouses, children, children’s spouses, siblings, siblings’ children and siblings’ spouses. The practice did not apply to minor matters. The earlier version, as amended on 21 July 1989, had also excluded cases where lawyers appearing were partners or employers of a judge’s close relatives; the 30 November 2006 amendment removed that stipulation. A later amendment of 4 October 2011 added spiritual relationships, father-in-law/son-in-law relationships and relationships between fathers-in-law. Judges precluded from sitting, or who for personal reasons considered it inadvisable to sit, were exempted. The Supreme Court examined the composition of its bench only when a party raised the issue; recusal for personal reasons was at the judge’s exclusive discretion.

Domestic law on finality provided that once a judgment was delivered, signed and filed, the court could not rehear arguments or change or set it aside, except in limited circumstances: under Order 25, Rule 6 for clerical mistakes or accidental slips or omissions; under Order 35, Rule 13 where an appeal dismissed for non-appearance could be reinstated; and under the Supreme Court’s exceptional inherent jurisdiction to correct errors or omissions, set aside an order or judgment on appeal, or reopen an appeal. That inherent power was limited, including to errors or omissions reflecting the court’s manifest intention or to facts arising after judgment was reserved, and did not permit reopening to raise new arguments. In Educational Service Commission v. Zena Poulli (19 November 2001), the full bench set aside an appeal judgment because interested parties had not been notified of the appeal or counter-appeal and ordered a rehearing. In Ioannis Adamou and others (15 October 2015), the Supreme Court reopened a case because it had not examined a preliminary objection and corresponding grounds of appeal.
001-183586:
**Ashayev and Others v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 24329/08 and six others) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 14 June 2018, adopted after private deliberations on 24 May 2018, and is final subject to editorial revision. The applicants lodged their applications against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, and the applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

The common complaints were that civil proceedings in Ukrainian courts had been excessively long and that there was no effective remedy in domestic law for that length. These allegations correspond to complaints commonly examined under the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time and the right to an effective remedy (typically Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention). The appended table sets out the key factual details for each applicant.

**Application no. 24329/08**, introduced on 14 May 2008, was brought by Aleksey Dmitriyevich Ashayev (born 17 December 1948). His civil proceedings ran from 5 November 1997 to 6 July 1999 (1 year, 8 months and 2 days) and from 27 August 2000 to 15 November 2007 (7 years, 2 months and 20 days). Both sets of proceedings went through three levels of jurisdiction.

**Application no. 32126/11**, introduced on 17 May 2011, was brought by Lyudmila Grigoryevna Denisenko (born 10 May 1942).
001-187574:
Pázsi and Others v. Hungary (Application no. 72595/13 and eight others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 15 November 2018 and adopted after private deliberations on 25 October 2018. The case arose from nine applications lodged against Hungary under Article 34 of the Convention between 2013 and 2015. The applicants were János Pázsi, Ferenc Sánta, Beshir Ademi, György Hunvald, Ali Zaki Toohaw, Bertalan Kovács, Mihályné Zsíros, Bettina Zsíros-Vagyóczki, and Leonárd Weinek. Notice of the applications was given to the Hungarian Government.

The applicants’ principal complaint was that the criminal proceedings against them were excessively long, contrary to the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 §1 of the Convention. In application no. 39649/15, brought by Leonárd Weinek, the applicant also complained under Article 13 that he had no effective domestic remedy for the excessive length of the proceedings.

The appended table set out the key facts. Pázsi’s proceedings ran from 8 August 2008 to 3 July 2013, a total of 4 years, 10 months and 26 days at one level of jurisdiction. Sánta’s ran from 10 May 2009 to 17 April 2014, 4 years, 11 months and 8 days at two levels. Ademi’s ran from 27 August 2009 to 2 September 2014, 5 years and 7 days at two levels. Hunvald’s ran from 1 October 2010 to 12 February 2015, 4 years, 4 months and 12 days at two levels. Toohaw’s ran from 31 December 2008 to 27 November 2014, 5 years, 10 months and 28 days at three levels. Kovács’s ran from 22 March 2010 to 1 May 2015, 5 years, 1 month and 10 days at two levels. Mihályné Zsíros’s ran from 15 February 2010 to 6 May 2015, 5 years, 2 months and 22 days at two levels. Zsíros-Vagyóczki’s ran from 16 April 2010 to 6 May 2015, 5 years and 21 days at two levels. Weinek’s ran from 30 November 2010 to 12 February 2015, 4 years, 2 months and 14 days at two levels.

Thus, the alleged delays ranged from about four years and two months to nearly five years and eleven months. Most proceedings involved two levels of jurisdiction, one involved one level, and one involved three. The applications were introduced on various dates between 13 November 2013 and 6 August 2015. The underlying criminal charges are not described in the provided extract; the case focuses on the duration of the proceedings and, for Weinek, the availability of an effective remedy. These facts formed the basis for the complaints that the domestic criminal proceedings failed to satisfy the reasonable-time requirement under Article 6 §1 and, in one application, that Hungarian law lacked an effective remedy under Article 13 for that delay.
001-183558:
Ciobotaru and Others v. Romania (Application no. 23572/14 and 3 others) is a case before the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), judgment delivered on 14 June 2018 by a Committee. The applicants—Vasilică Ciobotaru, Marius Galan, Marian Dragotă and Vasile-Adrian Panaite—lodged applications against Romania under Article 34 of the Convention on the dates shown in the appended table. The applications were communicated to the Romanian Government. The common complaint was that the applicants’ conditions of detention were inadequate, raising issues under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The key facts are set out in the appended table.

Ciobotaru (application 23572/14, introduced 28 April 2014; born 4 June 1980) was detained in Focșani Penitentiary from 15 February 2013 to 5 September 2014, a period of 1 year, 6 months and 22 days. He allegedly had only 1.43 m² of personal space. His specific grievances were overcrowding, lack of toiletries and infestation of the cell with insects or rodents.

Galan (application 73773/14, introduced 13 November 2014; born 18 September 1972; represented by Alina Gherman, Iași) was held in Iași Penitentiary and Botoșani Penitentiary from 28 October 2011 onward. The duration was described as more than 6 years, 5 months and 17 days and was still pending at the relevant time. His space per inmate ranged from 1.26 to 2.2 m². He complained of overcrowding, lack or inadequate hygienic facilities, insect or rodent infestation, no or restricted access to showers, poor quality food, lack of toiletries, lack or poor quality bedding and bed linen, lack or insufficient outdoor physical exercise, and inadequate temperature.

Dragotă (application 22053/15, introduced 25 May 2015; born 18 November 1958) was detained in Rahova Penitentiary from 10 September 2014 to 21 January 2016, i.e. 1 year, 4 months and 12 days. His space was 1.93–2.4 m² per inmate. He alleged overcrowding, lack or inadequate hygienic facilities, no or restricted access to warm water, lack of fresh air, inadequate temperature, lack or inadequate furniture, lack or poor quality bedding and bed linen, and infestation with insects or rodents.

Panaite (application 41700/15, introduced 16 October 2015; born 14 June 1974) was first held in Timișoara Arrest Centre from 17 January 2009 to 15 March 2009, a period of 1 month and 27 days. He was then held in Timișoara, Rahova and Arad Penitentiaries from 15 March 2009 to 14 October 2015, a period of 6 years and 7 months. His space was 2–2.7 m² per inmate. He complained of inadequate sanitary facilities, lack of fresh air, lack or insufficient electric light, lack or poor quality bedding and bed linen, lack or inadequate furniture, lack of toiletries, lack or insufficient outdoor physical exercise, insect or rodent infestation, bunk beds, no or restricted showers and poor food. He also alleged overcrowding, except during two periods in Arad Penitentiary: 5 November 2010–14 May 2012 and 25 May 2012–9 August 2012.

Overall, the case centres on allegations that detention in Romanian facilities, with very small living space and poor material conditions, amounted to inadequate conditions of detention under the Convention.
001-181584:
**Summary of *Tlapak and Others v. Germany* (Applications nos. 11308/16 and 11344/16)**

The case of *Tlapak and Others v. Germany* concerns two applications brought by four parents against Germany under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were members of the Twelve Tribes Church, residing in two communities in Wörnitz and Klosterzimmern, Germany. They challenged decisions by German courts to partially withdraw their parental authority and separate them from their children.

The factual background is critical to the alleged violations. In 2012, media reports emerged regarding the Twelve Tribes Church's endorsement of corporal punishment, specifically caning, as a method of discipline. Subsequently, in August 2013, a television reporter provided video footage to local authorities and a family court. This hidden-camera footage documented ten separate instances of children aged three to twelve being caned by community members, often non-parents.

Based on this footage and testimony from former members, the Ansbach Family Court issued an interim order on 3 September 2013, withdrawing the applicants' rights to decide their children's residence, health, and education. The court found a reasonable likelihood that the children would be subjected to caning and "restraining," a practice involving holding a child's limbs and pressing their head down. On 5 September 2013, the youth office took the community's children into care, aided by police who searched the premises and found a wooden rod. Although medical examinations revealed no physical signs of abuse, the children were placed in foster families. The applicants' son (application no. 11308/16) and two daughters (application no. 11344/16) were separated from their parents; their youngest son was initially placed with his breastfeeding mother.

The main proceedings followed. A court-appointed expert concluded that the applicants held a loving attitude but considered corporal punishment with objects an appropriate and necessary parenting method. The expert opined that there was a likelihood bordering on certainty that they would apply such punishment, causing significant developmental and psychological harm. Less intrusive measures were deemed insufficient because the applicants' religious convictions made them unwilling to abandon these methods or cooperate with authorities.

On 22 October 2014 (Tlapak) and 21 October 2014 (Pingen), the Family Court upheld the withdrawal of parental rights, citing a high, concrete probability of systematic corporal punishment. The courts emphasized that such punishment violated the children's human dignity and right to physical integrity under the German Basic Law and the Civil Code. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants' appeals on 26 May 2015 and 10 June 2015, respectively, confirming the reasoning. It found that the applicants' religious beliefs prevented them from credibly distancing themselves from corporal punishment, and that they might leave Germany to avoid supervision. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit their constitutional complaints.

The applicants complained under Article 8 (right to respect for family life), Article 6 (right to a fair trial), Article 9 (freedom of religion), and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (right to education), alleging disproportionate interference, insufficient factual foundation, and religious discrimination. The case was communicated to the German Government regarding Article 8.
001-183376:
In *Kartvelishvili v. Georgia*, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 3 and Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention. The applicant, Giorgi Kartvelishvili, a Georgian national, was serving sentences for murder and for refusing to obey a prison officer. On 6 January 2006 he was placed in Tbilisi Prison No. 7.

On 8 August 2006 prison officers conducted a surprise search of his cell. The inmates, including the applicant, were ordered into the corridor while the search was filmed. A written report stated that a penknife had been found under the mattress on a bed later identified as the applicant’s. The applicant was never shown or asked to sign that record. On 11 August 2006 he was charged with possessing a prohibited item under Article 378 § 2 of the Criminal Code.

At trial, which began on 12 February 2007, the prosecution relied mainly on the prison officers who had conducted the search. The applicant asked the court to examine the seven inmates who had shared his cell, arguing that they could describe the exact circumstances of the search, including whether the officers abused their powers or whether the knife could have been planted in his bed. He stressed that the charge rested solely on the officers’ statements and that the cellmates had never been interviewed during the pre-trial stage. The prosecutor opposed the request, noting that the cellmates were convicted prisoners. The Tbilisi City Court refused the application as unsubstantiated, finding that the applicant had not sufficiently demonstrated the need for those witnesses and that they were not trustworthy because of their criminal convictions.

The officers later gave inconsistent accounts of where the knife was found: between the mattress and blanket near the footboard; between the mattress and sheet near the headboard or pillow; or falling to the floor when the mattress was lifted. They also said the cell door had been open, so the cellmates could have observed from the corridor. The video recording showed officers examining the mattress about one metre above the floor; a metal object fell and was picked up, but it was unclear whether it had fallen from the mattress. The prosecutor conceded that the video did not establish with certainty where the knife was found. The applicant argued that a cellmate could have planted the knife and repeatedly sought the cellmates’ examination before the trial court, the appellate court, and the Supreme Court. On 1 March 2007 the Tbilisi City Court convicted him and sentenced him to three years. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal rejected his request to examine the cellmates, upheld the conviction, and increased the sentence to four years. On 11 February 2008 the Supreme Court rejected his cassation appeal without an oral hearing. These facts formed the basis of his Article 6 complaint that he could not obtain the attendance and examination of defence witnesses under the same conditions as prosecution witnesses.

As to Article 3, the applicant complained about detention conditions and inadequate medical treatment. On 7 November 2007 he reported fever and a cough and was transferred to the prison hospital. He was diagnosed with advanced pulmonary tuberculosis and early-stage hepatitis C. Doctors planned anti-TB DOTS treatment first, followed later by anti-HCV drugs. He began DOTS on 13 November 2007, received intensive hospital treatment, and continued antibiotics in prison. Tests later showed negative sputum cultures and no recurrence of TB. In 2010 blood tests showed low HCV activity; doctors prescribed anti-HCV drugs, warned of side effects, and the applicant postponed treatment in a written note dated 2 June 2010. The case file contained no further health information.
001-183337:
The case originated in an application lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina with the European Court of Human Rights by the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vrhbosna, a Roman Catholic community based in Sarajevo, on 16 May 2013. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; those complaints were communicated to the Government on 28 March 2017, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The central factual background concerns the authorities’ prolonged failure to enforce a final domestic decision ordering the relocation of public schools from property belonging to the applicant in Travnik.

By a decision of 9 May 2003, which became final on 4 September 2003, the Human Rights Chamber for Bosnia and Herzegovina found that the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina had discriminated against the applicant in its enjoyment of the right to freedom of religion under Article 9 of the Convention. It ordered the Federation to ensure that public schools housed in the Archdiocese High School building in Travnik were relocated and to reinstate the applicant in the premises within one year. The Chamber rejected the applicant’s request for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

Implementation was not completed within the ordered period. By an agreement of 21 May 2004, the Federation undertook to reinstate the applicant by 1 July 2006. The Travnik Municipal Council subsequently adopted implementing decisions, and one public school was moved from the premises. However, full compliance remained outstanding.

Enforcement proceedings then became protracted. On 23 June 2010 the Travnik Municipal Council issued a writ of execution. On 5 October 2011 the Travnik Cantonal Court quashed that decision and remitted the case. On 17 October 2011 the Travnik Municipal Court held that it lacked jurisdiction. On 16 May 2012 the Cantonal Court quashed that decision and remitted the case again. On 3 July 2012 the Municipal Court held that decisions of the Human Rights Chamber were not subject to enforcement proceedings. The applicant appealed on 12 July 2012, but as of 28 August 2017 the Cantonal Court had still not ruled on that appeal.

On 30 October 2012 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina determined that the Federation had not yet fully enforced the 9 May 2003 decision. In February 2017 the applicant initiated civil proceedings against the public school still occupying its premises, seeking relocation and damages for use of the premises between 1 February 2014 and 1 June 2017. On 14 July 2017 the Municipal Court in Travnik ruled in the applicant’s favour, awarding 270,360 convertible marks in pecuniary damages and 6,713 marks for costs and expenses, and ordering the respondent to vacate the premises within 30 days. On 20 December 2017 the Cantonal Court in Novi Travnik upheld that judgment. By 20 February 2018, however, the Central Bosnia Canton had submitted a revision petition to the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the public school had still not been relocated.

These facts were relevant to the alleged violations under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In substance, the applicant complained that the final decision in its favour remained unenforced for years, that enforcement proceedings were repeatedly frustrated by jurisdictional and procedural obstacles, and that it continued to be deprived of the use of its property despite the final ruling. The case therefore concerned whether the domestic authorities’ failure to secure timely compliance with a binding decision violated the applicant’s right of access to a court and its right to the peaceful enjoyment of its possessions.
001-179867:
**Case: Sharxhi and Others v. Albania (Application no. 10613/16), judgment of 11 January 2018.**

The applicants were eighteen Albanian nationals and one Italian national. In 2009 the first two applicants purchased a plot of land in Vlora, in the Uji i Ftohtë–Tuneli coastal area. In 2010 the Vlora Municipal Council for Territorial Planning issued a building permit for a five-storey residential and commercial building, the “Jon Residence.” The remaining applicants bought flats in the planned building. Construction was completed in 2012, the building was registered with the Immovable Property Registration Office, most flats were occupied, and a pool bar/pizzeria opened.

On 3 November 2013, without prior notice, officials of the National and Vlora Construction and Urban Planning Inspectorates (NUCI and MUCI), supported by State Police, surrounded and cordoned off the Jon Residence with yellow police tape marked “Crime scene – no entry.” Residents were prevented from entering their flats or retrieving valuables. The authorities said they were inspecting the legality of the building permit. No formal administrative act was presented. The applicants learned of the situation through the media or security guards. The Ombudsman later wrote that the building had been seized without a formal act and that the cordoning off was unlawful.

The applicants sought urgent judicial protection. On 7 November 2013 the Vlora Administrative District Court issued an interim order under the Code of Civil Procedure and the Administrative Disputes Act. It stayed administrative actions by any public authority that could interfere with the applicants’ peaceful enjoyment of their properties, pending a decision on the merits, provided the applicants brought a merits claim within ten days. The court found that the applicants had legally acquired their flats, were being prevented from accessing them, and faced irreparable harm. It also noted that the authorities had not documented their administrative action. The interim order was executable despite appeal. The applicants’ lawyer informed the NUCI and urged enforcement, but received no reply. The NUCI appealed.

Despite the interim order, the authorities continued. On 27 November 2013 the Council of Ministers ordered the expropriation in the public interest of properties affected by environmental rehabilitation of the Uji i Ftohtë–Tuneli coastline. It awarded compensation of approximately ALL 462,919,230 for the building, with a deadline of 28 December 2013. The decision was published on 3 December; the applicants learned of it through the media. On 2 December the mayor of Vlora requested NUCI assistance with demolition. The Jon Residence was demolished with explosives between 4 and 8 December 2013. On 20 January 2014 the Administrative Court of Appeal terminated the interim-order proceedings because the building had already been demolished and the subject matter had ceased to exist.

On the merits, the District Court on 28 January 2014 declared the authorities’ actions of 3 November 2013 arbitrary and in flagrant breach of Albanian law. The Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 6 May 2016. In separate expropriation proceedings, the District Court on 6 March 2014 found the expropriation unlawful and a “de facto expropriation,” increased compensation, and found serious procedural violations. The Court of Appeal largely upheld this in September 2014, but in January 2015 the Supreme Court stayed execution of the decision, and the case remained pending. No compensation was paid to the applicants. The Immovable Property Registration Office refused to issue ownership certificates because the building no longer existed. Criminal complaints against officials were rejected.

The applicants alleged that the authorities’ disregard of the administrative court injunction violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the cordoning off, expropriation and demolition interfered with their peaceful enjoyment of possessions; under Article 8 that preventing access to their homes interfered with respect for their homes; and under Article 13 that no effective domestic remedy existed for these violations. The core facts are that, despite a binding interim order prohibiting interference pending the merits, the authorities sealed, expropriated and demolished the applicants’ lawfully built and acquired homes and shops, rendering the injunction moot and leaving the applicants without compensation or effective redress.
001-186126:
Case Aliyev v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 68762/14 and 71200/14) concerns Intigam Aliyev, a prominent Azerbaijani human-rights lawyer and chairman of the Legal Education Society (“LES”), an NGO specialising in legal education and human-rights reporting. He alleged violations of Articles 3, 5 §§ 1, 3 and 4, and Articles 8, 11 and 18 of the Convention.

In June 2014 Aliyev spoke at a PACE side event, reporting human-rights abuses in Azerbaijan. Afterwards, pro-government media and officials launched a smear campaign, describing him and other defenders as foreign agents, traitors, or a “fifth column” funded by Western donors. On 13 May 2014 the Prosecutor General’s Office opened criminal proceedings under abuse-of-power and forgery provisions concerning alleged financial irregularities in NGOs, including LES. On 7 July 2014 LES’s and Aliyev’s bank accounts were frozen.

On 8 August 2014 Aliyev was summoned to the Prosecutor General’s Office as a witness. After a thirty-minute interview, he was charged with illegal entrepreneurship, large-scale tax evasion, and aggravated abuse of power. The charges alleged he failed to register grant agreements with NED, Human Rights House Foundation and others; lacked authority to sign them; withdrew funds as salaries and fees; earned illegal profit; and evaded taxes. The Nasimi District Court ordered three months’ pre-trial detention, citing the seriousness of the charges and risks of absconding or influencing witnesses. Appeals and requests for house arrest or bail were rejected, and detention was extended. In December 2014 further charges of high-level embezzlement and forgery were added; tax-evasion charges were reclassified as very large scale, with alleged illegal profit raised to AZN 496,729 and unpaid taxes to AZN 65,636.

On 7 August 2014 the Nasimi District Court authorised a search of LES’s office and “other places of storage.” The next day, investigators searched Aliyev’s home and his brother’s home; on 9 August they searched LES’s office. They seized all documents, computers, USB drives and electronic devices, including case files for over 100 applications pending before the European Court and domestic proceedings. His complaints that the searches lacked a legal basis, were unrecorded, and improperly seized privileged case files were dismissed.

While detained in the Baku pre-trial facility, Aliyev described overcrowded, poorly ventilated, unsanitary conditions, lack of outdoor exercise, inadequate food and water, and constant light. He had pre-existing health problems; his condition deteriorated and he fainted in court on 24 October 2014. Medical examinations revealed osteochondrosis, spinal hernias and disc protrusions, kidney issues and prostate masses, but doctors prescribed outpatient treatment. Requests for forensic or independent medical examinations were refused. He also complained of poor transport and court-cell conditions. His attempts to obtain redress were left unexamined for lack of jurisdiction.

In April 2015 Aliyev was convicted on all charges and sentenced to seven and a half years’ imprisonment; this was upheld on appeal. In March 2016 the Supreme Court Plenum reduced the sentence to five years suspended and he was released. His criminal trial is pending in a separate application. International bodies, including the UN Human Rights Committee and the UN Special Rapporteur on human-rights defenders, reported concerns about politically motivated prosecutions, stigmatisation and criminalisation of NGO activists in Azerbaijan. The ECtHR communicated complaints under Articles 5 §§ 1, 3, 4, 8, 11 and 18, focusing on whether the detention, searches, interferences and restrictions were justified or pursued improper purposes.
001-185308:
**Summary of *Cabral v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 37617/10)**

The case of *Cabral v. the Netherlands* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Euclides Cabral, a Netherlands national, on 25 June 2010. The applicant alleged that his criminal conviction for a street mugging was based solely or to a decisive extent on the statements of a witness, identified as V., whom he had not been able to effectively examine, in violation of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention, which guarantees the right to examine witnesses against the accused.

The factual background involves four charges against the applicant: three supermarket robberies and one street mugging outside a discotheque. The prosecution's case heavily relied on statements made to the police by V., an accomplice in the supermarket robberies who also implicated the applicant in all four crimes. V. initially confessed to police and named the applicant as a co-perpetrator.

The domestic proceedings unfolded across three levels. Before the Regional Court, V. was summoned as a defence witness. Regarding the street mugging, V. was not a suspect, so he was compelled to testify. He provided a statement disculpating the applicant, claiming he had not witnessed the robbery and had only heard from bystanders that the perpetrators did not include the applicant. This exculpatory statement was disbelieved by both the prosecutor and the court, leading to V. being charged with perjury. The Regional Court convicted the applicant on all four counts.

On appeal, V. was again summoned but this time remained silent on all charges, including the street mugging for which he was facing a perjury prosecution. Despite his refusal to be cross-examined, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on all charges. For the fourth charge (the street mugging), the evidence cited in the judgment consisted of the supermarket manager's report, a cashier's statement, and V.'s confession to the police naming the applicant.

The applicant then appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that using V.'s police statements without allowing for cross-examination violated his defence rights. The Advocate General advised that V.'s evidence was "sole and decisive" for the fourth charge. However, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, relying on its existing case-law. It held that the applicant had been given a sufficient opportunity to cross-examine V. The fact that V. refused to answer questions did not, in itself, render his prior police statement inadmissible under Article 6 § 3 (d).

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: (1) The applicant's conviction on at least one charge was based decisively on statements made by V. to the police. (2) V. was summoned by the defence at both the trial and appellate stages. (3) During the appeal, where the conviction was finalised, V. refused to answer any questions, thereby denying the applicant any opportunity for effective cross-examination on his police statements. (4) Despite this refusal, the domestic courts used V.'s untested police statements to ground the conviction, finding that the opportunity to summon him was sufficient. This situation formed the basis of the applicant's complaint to the European Court that his right to examine a decisive witness against him had been violated. The case also notes a subsequent shift in Dutch Supreme Court case-law in 2013, which reversed the position held at the time of the applicant's conviction.
001-181068:
In *Grytsenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 56576/08 and three others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) considered applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The Committee comprised André Potocki (President), Síofra O’Leary and Mārtiņš Mits, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was adopted on 1 February 2018 and delivered in Strasbourg on 22 February 2018. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

The applicants complained primarily of the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. In application no. 56576/08, the applicant also raised other complaints under the Convention, but the appended table does not set out their details.

The key facts concern four applicants and the duration of their civil proceedings:

**Application no. 56576/08** was introduced on 10 November 2008 by Leonid Ivanovych Grytsenko (born 1956). His civil proceedings began on 30 June 1997 and ended on 6 June 2006, lasting 8 years, 11 months and 8 days across three levels of jurisdiction.

**Application no. 21916/09** was introduced on 31 March 2009 by Sergey Gennadiyevich Nefedov (born 1959). It concerned four separate sets of proceedings: 11 May 2005 to 16 November 2006 (1 year, 6 months and 6 days, two levels); 29 March to 23 April 2007 (26 days, two levels); 6 August 2007 to 3 December 2008 (1 year, 3 months and 28 days, two levels); and 5 May 2010 to 7 February 2012 (1 year, 9 months and 3 days, two levels). These formed the basis of his length complaint.

**Application no. 54466/09** was introduced on 1 October 2009 by Georgiy Volodymyrovych Khrykin (born 1945). It involved two civil cases: 24 November 2003 to 20 October 2006 (2 years, 10 months and 27 days, three levels); and 22 February 2007 to 11 June 2010 (3 years, 3 months and 21 days, three levels).

**Application no. 26724/17** was introduced on 31 March 2017 by Volodymyr Fedorovych Kunayev (born 1960). It concerned two sets of proceedings: 25 June 2007 to 8 February 2008 (7 months and 15 days, one level); and 13 May 2011 to 23 November 2016 (5 years, 6 months and 11 days, three levels).

The alleged violations therefore arise from the length of civil proceedings in each applicant’s domestic cases. Under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, civil disputes must be determined within a reasonable time. The applicants argued that delays ranging from several months to almost nine years, and in some cases spanning multiple proceedings and appeal levels, were excessive. They further complained under Article 13 that Ukrainian law did not provide an effective remedy to challenge or obtain redress for those delays. The Grytsenko application additionally raised other Convention complaints, but only the length-and-remedy allegations are detailed in the provided factual table. The Court’s factual focus was thus the duration of each proceeding, the number of jurisdictional levels involved, and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.
001-181877:
In *Voykin and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 47889/08), four Ukrainian applicants—Mr Voykin, his wife, his mother-in-law, and his mother—complained under Articles 3, 5, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The case arose from an alleged assault by a police officer, subsequent criminal proceedings against the first applicant, and police searches of family homes.

The central Article 3 complaint concerned the second applicant. On the night of 18–19 June 2008, she alleged that M., a police officer and colleague of her husband, approached her in the street while heavily drunk and in plain clothes. She claimed he searched her bag, grabbed her by the neck, strangled her, and hit her head with a heavy object. She sought medical help and was diagnosed with neck bruises, concussion, and situational neurosis. She immediately called the police and later complained to the prosecutor’s office.

The investigation was protracted and repeatedly restarted. On 28 June 2008 the Kalyninskyy police refused to open a criminal case. After the second applicant complained, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office quashed that refusal on 25 July 2008, noting that the investigation had wrongly been handled by the police force to which M. belonged. Further refusals followed on 1 and 14 August 2008; each was annulled as premature or incomplete. Forensic examinations in August and October 2008 found a neck bruise and concussion caused by blunt objects, consistent with her account, though no visible head injuries were documented. M. and his witnesses denied ill-treatment, claiming the second applicant was drunk and aggressive and that he had not touched her. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to charge M., relying on conflicting witness statements, the insignificance of injuries, and the fact that M. had not acted in an official capacity. Higher prosecutor complaints were dismissed or forwarded, leaving her without a criminal investigation.

The first applicant, a district police officer, alleged that after his wife’s complaint, the Kalyninskyy police threatened him and his family with dismissal, prosecution, or worse. In September 2008, criminal proceedings were opened against him for abuse of power and forgery relating to a 2008 administrative offence report. He was summoned, but stayed away, citing fear and knee surgery. On 13 September 2008 a court authorised his arrest, and on 19 September he was declared wanted. He was arrested on 29 June 2009 at the home he shared with his wife. On 3 July 2009 the court ordered his pre-trial detention without detailed reasoning. On 21 July 2009 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal quashed that ruling and released him, finding the first-instance court had failed to justify the strictest preventive measure. He was later convicted of abuse of office, forgery, and bribe-taking, with various appeals and reclassifications.

The Article 8 complaints concerned searches of the flats of the third and fourth applicants. In September 2008, police searched the third applicant’s flat, allegedly breaking the door, threatening the occupants, failing to show a warrant, and planting cannabis. The fourth applicant’s flat was searched on 16 September 2008, and again in February 2009, with documents allegedly planted or irrelevant items seized. The third and fourth applicants complained repeatedly, but prosecutors refused to investigate the police actions, and the courts did not provide copies of the search authorisations.

Overall, the facts alleged ill-treatment by police and a failure to investigate it, retaliatory criminal proceedings and unjustified detention, and unlawful home searches without effective remedies.
001-187923:
**Summary of *Yakushev v. Ukraine* (Application no. 15978/09)**

The case of *Yakushev v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Igor Viktorovych Yakushev, a Ukrainian national born in 1971, on 7 March 2009. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, concerning his right to respect for private and family life. The core of the complaint related to the domestic courts' refusal to allow him to challenge his legal paternity of a child, K., despite conclusive genetic evidence that he was not the biological father.

The key facts are as follows: On 17 November 1993, a woman identified as M. gave birth to a daughter, K. At the time, the applicant had been having relations with M., although he was married to another woman and did not cohabit with M. On 2 December 1993, based on his belief that he was the father, the applicant submitted a formal declaration accepting paternity of K., thereby becoming her legal father.

Several years later, in 2005, the applicant began to have doubts about his paternity. In July 2006, shortly after his marriage to M. ended in divorce, he initiated proceedings in the Malyn District Court to challenge his paternity of K. The central issue in the domestic proceedings was the interpretation of Article 56 § 2 of the Ukrainian Marriage and Family Code. This provision stated that a person who had registered as a child's father based on his own declaration did not have the right to challenge that paternity if, at the time of the declaration, he had been aware that he was not the child's father.

On 24 March 2008, the District Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The court's decision was based on a genetic expert's opinion which excluded him as K.'s biological father. Crucially, the court found that the applicant had the right to challenge his paternity because there was no evidence in the case file to suggest he knew he was not the father when he accepted paternity in 1993.

This decision was overturned on appeal. On 29 May 2008, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal quashed the ruling and dismissed the applicant’s claim. The appellate court held that under Article 56 § 2, the applicant did not have the right to challenge his paternity. It reasoned that at the time he accepted paternity, he was aware he was not the biological father. To support this conclusion, the Court of Appeal pointed to circumstantial evidence: the applicant and M. had not been married before K.'s birth, they had not been living together (noting in particular that the applicant lived in another town between February and April 1993), and the applicant had been married to another woman at the time.

The applicant then appealed on a point of law to the Supreme Court of Ukraine, arguing that the Court of Appeal had no evidentiary basis to conclude he had known he was not the father in 1993. He contended that the appellate court had overstepped its authority in drawing such a conclusion. On 9 September 2008, the Supreme Court of Ukraine rejected his appeal as unfounded, effectively finalising the domestic decisions against him.

Consequently, the applicant brought the case to the European Court of Human Rights. He had exhausted all domestic remedies and complained that the dismissal of his claim, which prevented him from legally severing his paternal link to a child who was proven not to be his, constituted a violation of his right to respect for his private life under Article 8 of the Convention. The Court gave notice of this specific complaint to the Ukrainian Government.
001-186048:
Big Brother Watch and Others v. the United Kingdom concerned three joined applications brought against the UK by companies, charities, organisations and individuals. The applicants alleged that UK electronic surveillance programmes, disclosed after Edward Snowden’s revelations, violated their rights under Articles 8, 10 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed their electronic communications were likely to have been intercepted by UK intelligence services, obtained from foreign governments, or acquired from communications service providers.

The case focused on two principal surveillance routes. First, GCHQ allegedly operated a bulk interception programme, referred to as TEMPORA, tapping fibre-optic cables and storing large volumes of data. Under section 8(4) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000, the Secretary of State could authorise warrants for “external communications”. Two processing systems were described: one using simple selectors such as email addresses, and another using processing rules and complex queries to identify material of intelligence value. Section 16 of RIPA prohibited selecting intercepted material for examination by reference to an individual known to be in the British Islands, but this protection did not apply equally to related communications data.

Second, the applicants complained about UK access to material obtained by the US National Security Agency through PRISM and Upstream. PRISM involved targeted requests to internet service providers under US Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act approval. Upstream involved collecting content and communications data from fibre-optic cables and infrastructure. Leaked documents suggested GCHQ had access to PRISM from July 2010 and had acquired information obtained through it.

Domestically, the first applicants sought declarations that relevant legislation was incompatible with the Convention, but were told the Investigatory Powers Tribunal had exclusive jurisdiction over human rights complaints against intelligence services. The second applicants brought no domestic proceedings, believing no effective remedy existed. The third applicants—ten human rights organisations—complained to the IPT that the intelligence services and the Home and Foreign Secretaries had violated Articles 8, 10 and 14 by accessing or receiving intercepted communications and data from the US under PRISM and Upstream, and by intercepting, inspecting and retaining their communications under TEMPORA and section 8(4). They sought disclosure of relevant policies and guidance.

The Government adopted a “neither confirm nor deny” approach. The IPT therefore proceeded on assumed facts: that the NSA had obtained the applicants’ communications and data via PRISM or Upstream and passed them to GCHQ, where they were retained, stored, analysed and shared; and that GCHQ had intercepted their communications under TEMPORA and similarly retained, stored, analysed and shared them. The IPT held public hearings and a closed hearing, assisted by Counsel to the Tribunal, to examine secret internal arrangements.

In its December 2014 judgment, the IPT found that PRISM/Upstream engaged Article 8 but that adequate safeguards, signposting and oversight existed; it also found the section 8(4) bulk interception regime Convention-compliant and rejected discrimination and separate Article 10 claims. In February 2015, however, it declared that, before certain disclosures were made, the PRISM/Upstream regime had contravened Articles 8 and 10, though it now complied. In June 2015, it found that Amnesty International’s emails had been lawfully intercepted under section 8(4) but retained too long, and that Legal Resources Centre communications were lawfully intercepted but an internal selection procedure was not followed. Both amounted to Article 8 breaches, but no compensation was awarded.

The Strasbourg applicants maintained that the scope and magnitude of these surveillance programmes violated the Convention, particularly through bulk interception, foreign intelligence sharing, insufficient legal safeguards and discriminatory distinctions affecting non-UK persons. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 25 May 2021.
001-182605:
In *Yalanskyy and Galunka v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights examined two applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention. The Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, was composed of André Potocki (President), Síofra O’Leary and Mārtiņš Mits, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 3 May 2018, adopted after private deliberations on 12 April 2018, and is final but subject to editorial revision. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

Application no. 15131/17 was introduced on 8 February 2017 by Yaroslav Igorovych Yalanskyy, born 17 January 1975, represented by Olena Viktorivna Shapoval in Kyiv. The key fact for his complaint is that criminal proceedings involving him began on 22 September 2008 and were still pending at the time the application was lodged. By then, the proceedings had lasted more than nine years and five months and had passed through three levels of jurisdiction. The alleged excessive length was therefore continuing, rather than a completed delay.

Application no. 36543/17 was introduced on 12 May 2017 by Nadiya Mykhaylivna Galunka, born 27 October 1959, represented by Mykhaylo Yosypovych Bordyuk in Chervonograd. Her criminal proceedings began on 15 February 2010 and were also still pending. They had lasted more than eight years and one month and had involved one level of jurisdiction. As with Yalanskyy, the central factual basis for her complaint was the prolonged duration of the criminal case against her.

Both applicants complained of the excessive length of criminal proceedings and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. In Convention terms, such complaints normally concern the right to a hearing within a reasonable time and the right to an effective remedy for that delay. The applicants alleged that the Ukrainian authorities had failed to determine their criminal cases within a reasonable period and that no effective domestic mechanism existed to provide redress for the delay. These complaints were the principal matters communicated to the Government.

In addition, in application no. 36543/17, Galunka raised another complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention. The provided text does not set out the factual background of that additional complaint or the Court’s assessment of it. It is therefore not possible to summarize its specific factual basis from the excerpt. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are thus the dates and duration of each applicant’s criminal proceedings, their pending status at the time of application, the number of jurisdictional levels involved, and the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy. The applicants were not, in this excerpt, challenging the merits of the criminal charges as such; their complaints focused on delay and the lack of remedy. The portion of the judgment supplied does not include the Court’s final legal findings or conclusions on the merits.
001-183338:
The applicant, Hani Abdul Khani Kabbara, a Canadian national born in 1984 and living in Canada, lodged an application against Cyprus on 29 March 2012. He alleged ill-treatment by police officers during detention at Limassol central police station and the absence of an effective investigation into his complaint.

On 27 February 2011, police were informed of illegal ATM withdrawals with a fake credit card in Limassol. The applicant alleged that, while in front of the ATM, he was attacked from behind by a police officer, arrested without a warrant, and taken to the police station, where he was detained for six hours with his hands handcuffed behind his back. He said officers tortured him to confess to theft using a forged credit card, repeatedly beat him with a wooden stick and a metal chair, punched and kicked him, broke a tooth, threatened to kill him, refused him asthma medicine and hospital care until his lawyer, C.H., intervened. He was taken to hospital around 3.30 p.m. He alleged that police told the doctor he had fallen, that no painkillers were given until the Canadian Consul visited, and that the doctor gave no proper explanation.

The Government’s account, based on investigation files, was that Special Constable G.S., in uniform, approached the applicant at the ATM, identified himself as police, and asked for identification. The applicant allegedly struck him and fled; during the chase he fell and hit his head. A struggle followed. He was arrested for assaulting a police officer and resisting lawful arrest. He was taken to the police station around 9.30 a.m., searched, and handed to the Economic Crime Investigations Office. An interview took place between 1 p.m. and 1.30 p.m. with an interpreter. At about 1.35 p.m., a body search recorded abrasions on his left forehead and left shoulder blade. His lawyer visited from 3.05 p.m. to 3.30 p.m. and complained that the applicant had been ill-treated. He was taken to Limassol General Hospital around 3.50 p.m. A District Court arrest warrant was issued at 3.30 p.m. He was discharged at 11.20 p.m. On 28 February and 8 March 2011, the District Court ordered and extended his detention on remand; on 16 March 2011, it ordered detention pending trial.

Medical examinations at Limassol General Hospital recorded a cephalohaematoma, abrasions, nasal oedema, a bruised lip, a broken upper incisor, chest bruising, wrist abrasions/oedema, knee abrasions and spinal sensitivity. CT scans showed no fractures. A private practitioner, Dr S.J., examined the applicant on 7 March 2011 and noted restricted movement, cervical tension, a 10 x 5 cm chest bruise and loss of half an upper incisor. G.S. was also examined and diagnosed with lumbar strain, and was given nine days’ sick leave.

On 2 March 2011, police appointed Chief Inspector M.M. to conduct an administrative investigation. M.M.’s report of 26 April 2011 found the ill-treatment allegations unproven and recommended closing the case. In July 2011, the Attorney General referred the complaint to the Independent Authority for the Investigation of Allegations and Complaints against the Police. Investigator A.S. reported on 10 October 2011, singling out four officers as suspects. He found the applicant’s testimony unconvincing and concluded that no criminal or disciplinary charges were justified. The IAIACAP president adopted the findings on 16 November 2011, although he rejected evidence that the applicant had no external injuries. On 13 February 2012, the Attorney General concluded that some force had been used but that it was necessary and proportionate to prevent the applicant from fleeing, and closed the file.

In separate criminal proceedings, the applicant was charged with 439 offences, later reduced to theft, assault occasioning actual bodily harm to G.S., and resisting lawful arrest. On 14 September 2012, the District Court convicted him on all counts; on 19 September 2012, it imposed concurrent sentences. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on 19 February 2013. He was then deported and placed on a stop list.

On 9 April 2013, after gaps and inconsistencies were identified, the Attorney General appointed two new investigators. They treated nine officers as suspects, took statements from forty-nine people, including the Canadian Consul, and gathered CCTV, photographs, police diaries and court records. The Canadian Consul’s statement of 22 April 2013 described the applicant at the hospital as being in a wheelchair and on a drip.
001-183862:
The case *Hülya Ebru Demirel v. Turkey* (Application no. 30733/08, judgment of 19 June 2018) concerned alleged sex discrimination in access to public employment and unfairness in administrative court proceedings. The applicant, a Turkish woman born in 1976, passed a civil-service examination on 17 October 1999. She was informed by the State Personnel Department that she had been appointed as a security officer at the Kilis branch of TEDAŞ, the State-run Turkish Electricity Distribution S.A. TEDAŞ later refused to appoint her because she did not meet the requirements of “being a man” and “having completed military service.”

On 4 September 2000 the applicant challenged that refusal before the Gaziantep Administrative Court. On 9 May 2001 the court stayed execution of the refusal, finding that being male was not a requirement for the post. On 23 July 2001 TEDAŞ offered her a six-month probationary contract, and she began working. On 4 October 2001 the Gaziantep Administrative Court annulled the refusal. It held that the military-service requirement applied only to male candidates and that no rule prevented women from serving as security officers at TEDAŞ; rejecting her solely because of her sex was unlawful.

TEDAŞ appealed. On 12 April 2002 the Twelfth Division of the Supreme Administrative Court stayed execution of the lower judgment. On 11 June 2002 TEDAŞ informed the applicant that her contract had been terminated on 27 May 2002 as a result. On 26 December 2002 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the 4 October 2001 judgment. It reasoned that because the post required completion of military service, it had been reserved for male candidates, so the refusal had been lawful. On 23 October 2003 the Gaziantep Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s case following that reasoning.

The applicant appealed, arguing that this interpretation breached equality and Turkey’s positive obligation of non-discrimination. She relied on the Constitution, CEDAW Article 2(d), ICESCR Article 3, and EU rules prohibiting sex discrimination in access to employment. On 16 November 2007 the Twelfth Division upheld the dismissal without addressing those arguments.

A related development occurred on 6 December 2007. The Supreme Administrative Court’s General Assembly of Administrative Proceedings Divisions decided the case of R.B., another female TEDAŞ candidate rejected for the same reasons. The General Assembly held that the military-service requirement applied only to men and that refusing to appoint R.B. on that ground was unlawful.

The applicant then sought rectification of the 16 November 2007 decision, relying on R.B. and her right to a fair hearing. The judge rapporteur opined that the decision should be rectified in light of R.B. and Turkey’s CEDAW Article 11 obligations regarding equal employment opportunities. On 24 June 2009, however, the Twelfth Division dismissed the rectification request, finding that none of the applicant’s grounds fell within the exhaustive list in section 54(1) of the Administrative Procedure Act.

The applicant alleged violations under Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8 of the Convention, complaining that the refusal to appoint her and her subsequent dismissal were discriminatory on grounds of sex. She also complained under Article 6 that the administrative proceedings were unfair, particularly because the courts failed to address her discrimination arguments and refused rectification despite the inconsistent General Assembly ruling in R.B.’s case. The Court communicated the Article 14/Article 8 and Article 6 complaints; the remainder of the application was inadmissible.
